title: Designing Multi-Agent AI Systems for Collaborative Learning: Strategic Questioning Patterns and Cognitive Development in Large-Scale Online Learning
citation: Xiaojie Niu, Jingjing Zhang (2026). Designing Multi-Agent AI Systems for Collaborative Learning: Strategic Questioning Patterns and Cognitive Development in Large-Scale Online Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Niu, X. & Zhang, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: As large-scale online learning environments increasingly integrate AI technologies to support collaborative learning, understanding how learners strategically interact with different AI agent roles becomes critical for effective system design. Grounded in Bloom’s Taxonomy and Graesser and Person’s question taxonomy, this study examines questioning strategies employed by 411 doctoral students interacting with three distinct AI agents — Teacher, Assistant, and Companion—in a large -scale online course, and compares cognitive development trajectories between AI -mediated and human peer dialogues. Using clustering analysis on 224 AI -directed questions and sequential analysis of cognitive levels coded via Bloom’s Taxonomy, we identified three strategic patt erns: Teacher-Focused Quick-Response Strategy (35.7%), Assistant -Focused In -Depth Strategy (27.7%), and Teacher -Focused In - Depth Strategy (36.6%). AI -involved dialogues showed higher cognitive -level variability (average progress of 0.48) compared to human dialogues (0.02), suggesting AI agents accelerate cognitive transitions while human interactions provide stability. These findings illuminate design principles for multi -agent systems that balance AI efficiency with human collaborative depth.

title: Structural Signals and Role Archetypes: The Emergence of Roles in a Distributed Epistemic Game
citation: Jenna Matthews (2026). Structural Signals and Role Archetypes: The Emergence of Roles in a Distributed Epistemic Game. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Matthews, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Roles in collaborative learning are often scripted or assigned; in distributed epistemic games (DEGs), however, they emerge through interaction over time. This study analyzes the first Polymath Project, a large -scale mathematical collaboration, to show how roles crystallize in practice. Using canonicalized epistemic move sequences, temporal distance metrics, and cross-method clustering, I identify two converging empirical signals. First, participant distance matrices display visible “plaid” structures—evide nce that contributors gravitated into role-like repertoires even before clustering. Second, across five analytic pipelines, three participant groupings (‘consistent companionships’) persisted: Proof Builders, Paired Refiners, and Process Integrators. Their recurrence across methods supports viewing them as durable role archetypes. Conceptually, the findings show that roles in DEGs are emergent and self- organizing; methodologically, they demonstrate how structural and reflexive analysis (via AIRR) can jointly surface roles -in-practice, advancing methods for studying collective intelligence and informing the design of systems that support dynamic role ecologies.

title: Biased Chatbot Interaction as Preparation for Collaborative Learning
citation: Tanmay Sinha, Kumaran Rajaram (2026). Biased Chatbot Interaction as Preparation for Collaborative Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Sinha, T. & Rajaram, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Twenty-five teachers engaged in individual preparation with chatbots deliberately designed to exhibit biased stance s on the learning topic of AI adoption in higher education before engaging in collaboration with their human peers. Through intermediate reflections, we probed into how everyone consolidated their learning from the initial human -AI collaboration, whether and how this affected reasoning during groupwork, a nd how everyone consolidated their learning post human-human collaboration. Results showed that while teachers recognized and critiqued biases of the chatbots, their group discussions deepened understanding of ethical concerns and the complexity of bias ed views, leading to a more nuanced and criteria- driven endorsement of AI for education. Overall, our design fostered reflection and perspective-taking, although some teachers remained resistant to changing their views based on feasibility concerns.

title: How Simulation Design Shapes Academically Productive Talk: An Epistemic Network Analysis of Teacher Discourse in Middle-School Physics
citation: Wei Jia, Kexin Li, Gaowei Chen (2026). How Simulation Design Shapes Academically Productive Talk: An Epistemic Network Analysis of Teacher Discourse in Middle-School Physics. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Jia, W., Li, K., & Chen, G.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
tpack_tk_labels: Immersive VR / AR; Simulations & Scientific Modeling
conceptualisations_list: Accountable Talk & Dialogic Discourse; Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)
abstract: Dialogic teaching, through Academically Productive Talk (APT), enhances student learning. While digital simulations are common in science education, their specific impact on teacher discourse patterns remains underexplored. This study examines how simulation design, Multiple Representations (MR) versus Single Representation (SR), shapes whole -class discourse structure and teachers’ use of APT moves. One teacher and 99 eighth-grade students from two classes in Western China participated. Using Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) and discourse analysis of 147 teacher talk turns, we compared APT patterns between two conditions. ENA revealed distinct strategic repertoires: the MR condition showed an integrated, collaborative network centered on reasoning and building on ideas, involving more students in shorter, focused turns. The SR condition exhibited a linear, teacher- guided pattern dominated by elicitation and challenge, with longer explanations from fewer students. Overall, simulation design relates to teacher facilitation and student participation, suggesting that multiple representational tools may afford more collaborative-dialogic classrooms.

title: Supporting Students’ Shared Epistemic Agency Discourse with GAI via Learning Analytics Augmented Meta-discourse
citation: Yawen Yu, Can Sun, Gaowei Chen (2026). Supporting Students’ Shared Epistemic Agency Discourse with GAI via Learning Analytics Augmented Meta-discourse. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Yu, Y., Sun, C., & Chen, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of a learning analytics -augmented meta- discourse environment in fostering students shared epistemic agency discourse in a Generative AI (GAI) learning context. Two types of learning analytical tools and meta- discourse were utilized to support students ’ epistemic understanding of critical discourse, thus, to support students’ epistemic agency discourse. A total of 48 project management students participated in the 18-week course, engaging in four online discussions and two meta-discourse sessions. Findings show that the intervention significantly improved students' epistemic understanding of critical AI discourse. Furthermore, students demonstrated progress in their shared epistemic agency discourse, moving from inform ation sharing to more projective and regulative activities across the three phases of discussion. Students with high epistem ic understanding showed a stronger tendency to build on, evalua te AI information, and create joint action plans, in contrast to low- understanding students who primarily used AI information for idea negotiation. These results underscore the critical role of pedagogical design in utilizing GAI as an epistemic tool to support collaborative knowledge advancement.

title: Collaboration and Competition in Educational Gameplay: Strategic Student Decision -Making
citation: Tianyu Ma, Jennifer Kahn (2026). Collaboration and Competition in Educational Gameplay: Strategic Student Decision -Making. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Ma, T. & Kahn, J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Design-Based Research (DBR)
abstract: This study examines how middle school students engaged in strategic decision- making when collaboration and competition were tightly intertwined in an educational gameplay setting. Drawing from a design-based research study of an afterschool program, six students played Isles of Ilkmaar, a multiplayer game designed to support data science learning. Using Activity Theory as an analytic lens, we traced how students mobilized tools, interpreted rules, and negotiated roles in the game’s diner competition. Analysis of three gameplay episodes showed students adapting in real time, moving from tool learning to contested claims and finally to rule negotiation. Findings highlight that collaboration and competition were not separate modes of activity but operated together, with conflicts often catalyzing adaptation and role change. This work contributes to CSCL by showing how collaborative learning can be sustained under competitive pressures, offering implications for the design of educational environments that integrate both cooperative and adversarial elements.

title: Exploring Variations in Teacher Modelling and Scaffolding Through Chatbot Interactions in Middle School Classrooms
citation: Henrik Tjønn, Sten Ludvigsen, Anders Mørch (2026). Exploring Variations in Teacher Modelling and Scaffolding Through Chatbot Interactions in Middle School Classrooms. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Tjønn, H., Ludvigsen, S., & Mørch, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this paper, we develop new insights into how teachers can model, scaffold and coach students when using tailored chatbots in a school subject. Our interaction analysis, based on a cognitive apprenticeship framework, shows how t eachers affirm student statements regarding the chatbot's lack of knowledge structures. W e identify a few instances of teacher elaboration on the chatbots' subject -specific knowledge structures during classroom interactions. Teachers mainly provide concrete scaffolding support for the tasks and confirm students' questions and claims about inaccuracies in chatbot outputs. Our analysis also indicates that the balance between modelling and scaffolding depends on how specific sequences in teaching and learning activities are executed.

title: Peer Feedback’s Role in Undergraduates’ Interdisciplinary Collaborative Learning Outcomes and Regulated Learning Patterns
citation: Guo Su, Wenli Chen, Gaoxia Zhu, Yubei Shi, Li Wei, Chencheng Le (2026). Peer Feedback’s Role in Undergraduates’ Interdisciplinary Collaborative Learning Outcomes and Regulated Learning Patterns. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Su, G., Chen, W., Zhu, G., Shi, Y., Wei, L., & Le, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Boundary Crossing & Brokerage; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: Interdisciplinary collaborative learning (ICL) is critical in 21st- century education, yet supporting disciplinary boundary crossing remains challenging. Peer feedback has the potential to help students cross boundaries by identifying the gaps between single-disciplinary and interdisciplinary approaches. However, the impact of peer feedback on ICL outcomes and regulated learning patterns is underexplored, despite the critical role of regulatory processes in students’ engagement in collaborative learning. This study employed a counterbalanced design with 52 undergraduates randomly assigned to two clusters experiencing conditions with and without peer feedback in reverse sequence. Group concept maps and verbal discussions from the 50-minute learning task were collected and analyzed. Results showed that groups performed significantly better with peer feedback in involving diverse perspectives, integrating knowledge, and reflecting on solution impacts and limitations. Additionally, students learning with peer feedback demonstrated an evaluation-engaged regulatory pattern, whereas they showed a planning- engaged regulatory pattern when peer feedback was not given. These findings suggest peer feedback’s potential for supporting ICL.

title: How Do Pre-Service Teachers Integrate Multiple Peer Feedback Messages? Identifying Different Integration Patterns
citation: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar (2026). How Do Pre-Service Teachers Integrate Multiple Peer Feedback Messages? Identifying Different Integration Patterns. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Hornstein, J., Greisel, M., & Kollar, I.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: Computer-supported peer feedback is a valuable approach to enhancing student learning in CSCL environments. Yet, little is known about how learners process multiple peer feedback messages. In an exploratory study with N = 100 pre-service teachers who analyzed classroom cases, provid ed feedback, and integrat ed feedback from two peers, we aimed to identify different feedback integration patterns (RQ1) and investigated how these are predicted by objective feedback features and perceived feedback quality (RQ2). A hierarchical cluster analysis yielded three integration patterns: a confirmation pattern, a conflict pattern, and a selective integration pattern. Multinomial logistic regressions revealed that objective feedback features—specifically accuracy, relevance, and implementability —predicted these i ntegration patterns, whereas perceived feedback quality did not. These findings highlight that integrating multiple peer feedback messages is a complex, feature- dependent process . In addition, t hey offer implications for designing adaptive, computer-supported peer feedback systems in CSCL settings. Aims of the study Peer feedback, conceptualized as a collaborative learning process, has been extensively examined within the area of Computer -Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) and has consistently been demonstrated to facilitate student learning (Özbek et al., 2024; Zong et al., 2021). Although current research provides strong evidence that providing feedback constitutes a powerful mechanism for learning, how learners actually use the feedback they receive from their peers effectively remains rather unclear . This is espec ially the case when learners receive feedback from more than one peer, that is when they need to integrate multiple peer feedback messages (Lundstrom & Baker, 2009; Nicol et al., 2014). Nevertheless, systematic theoretical frameworks and empirical investigations elucidating how learners integrate multiple peer feedback messages remain scarce. Drawing on research concerning learning from multiple documents (List & Alexander, 2019), we posit that the optimal integration of multiple peer feedback messages entails four steps: identification, separate representation, simultaneous relation, and relational designation. After relationships between the multiple peer feedback messages have been identified, students need to connect these multiple peer feedback messages through synthesis and reconciliation (List & Alexander, 2019). Yet, it remains unclear (a) to what extent and in what ways learners engage in these integration processes when integrating multiple peer feedback messages , and (b) how both objective feedback features (relevance, accuracy, implementability, structural quality) and the perceived quality of the received feedback (adequacy, subjective quality) influence this integration process. The present study seeks to provide empirical evidence to address these questions. Peer feedback in the context of CSCL The peer feedback process basically consists of four phases ( Kollar & Fischer , 2010). In the task performance phase, students work on a task and produce an initial task solution (e.g., a written case analysis). These initial task solutions represent the product on which peers then formulate feedback in the feedback provision phase. This is followed by the feedback reception phase, during which students process the feedback they have received and compare it to their initial task solutions . The feedback process ends with the revision phase, in which students revise their initial task solution based on the feedback they have received. In the context of CSCL, peer feedback is regarded as an important instructional method, as learners collaborate and digital technologies can support the peer feedback process (Zong et al., 2021). From a sociocultural perspective (Vygotsky et al., 1978), students in the peer feedback process may provide support to each other’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD), enabling them to operate in their ZPD and thus advance their actual development. This is achieved by helping each other through asking questions and offering suggestions for possible revisions. From a socio -cognitive perspective, the reason for the effectiveness of peer feedback lies in the fact that important cognitive processes take place during both feedback provision and feedback reception (Nicol & McCallum, 2022; van Popta et al., 2017). 80 Compared to analogue forms of peer feedback, computer -supported peer feedback offers several advantages, such as greater flexibility in application (both synchronous and asynchronous) and the ability to randomly, anonymously, and automatically assign feedback pairs (Chen, 2016; Cho & Schunn, 2007; Panadero & Alqassab, 2019). Furthermore, computer -supported peer feedback processes can easily be structured by incorporating instructional support into each phase (e.g., through the provision of assessment criteria, rubrics, or training; Alqassab et al., 2018; Dmoshinskaia et al., 2021) and easily monitored by the teacher (Farahani et al., 2019). Several empirical studies have confirmed these advantages in CSCL contexts, showing that computer - supported peer feedback processes can positively impact student performance ( Özbek et al., 2024; Zong et al., 2021), particularly when supported by instruction (Hornstein, Keller et al., 2025). Integrating multiple peer feedback messages Although the feedback reception phase in the peer feedback process is conceptually complex and has received relatively limited empirical attention, it offers considerable potential for promoting student learning (Nicol et al., 2014). When learners engage with feedback from their peers, they need to compare their initial task solutions with the feedback messages received. This comparison exposes them to alternative perspectives, encourages critical reflection on their prior understanding, and potentially supports the refinement of their initial task solution (Nicol & McCallum, 2022). Such learning benefits may even be larger when students receive feedback messages from multiple peers rather than from a single peer, as integrating multiple peer feedback messages is likely to involve even deeper cognitive processing (Cho & Schunn, 2007). However, despite their importance, the nature of these integration processes remains insufficiently explored. Empirical investigations into how students process and learn from multiple peer feedback messages are still scarce. In one study, Li et al. (2010) provided each participant with feedback from two peers, explicitly noting that feedback quality might vary and that conflicting suggestions could occur. Students were therefore required to compare both feedback messages and decide which comments to incorporate into their revisions. Interestingly, the study found no significant relationship between the quality of the feedback participants received and subsequent revision quality. By contrast, Cho and Schunn (2007) reported that students who received feedback from multiple peers produced essays of higher quality than those who received feedback from only one peer. More recently, van Meenen et al. (2023) examined how students process discrepant peer feedback using eye -tracking data and simulated feedback comments. Their results revealed pronounced individual differences: while some learners recognized inconsistencies but disregarded them, others actively attempted to reconcile these discrepancies. These findings indicate that students do not automatically engage effectively with multiple peer feedback messages; instead, they display diverse integration patterns, ranging from largely ignoring the feedback to actively resolving conflicting information. However, despite these initial findings, it is still unclear exactly how (high-quality) integration of multiple peer feedback messages looks like. To advance our understanding of how learners integrate feedback from multiple peers, we used the Integrated Framework of Multiple Text Use (List & Alexander, 2019). This framework describes how individuals engage with, process, and construct meaning from multiple text s and comprises three stages: preparation, execution, and production. In the preparation stage, learners orient themselves toward the task by considering external task features, personal perceptions, and individual factors such as prior knowledge, which shape their cognitive engagement. During the execution stage, students employ metacognitive monitoring and cognitive strategies—including comprehension and cross -textual linking—to connect and integrate information across texts until they determine whether their cognitive goals are met. Finally, in the production stage, learners translate the cognitive and affective outcomes of text processing into external products, such as written work, which may or may not fully reflect their internal conceptual, emotional, or belief-based changes. Within this model, processing activities—particularly those related to information integration—play a central role. A key process identified by List and Alexander (2019) is cross -textual linking, which involves establishing meaningful connections between multiple texts to ensure mindful integration (Berndt et al., 2018) . This process unfolds in four sequential steps. First, during identification, learners search for potential relationships between texts. Second, they create separate representations of the r elevant information from each text independently. Third, through simultaneous relation, they draw explicit connections between the content of the different texts. Finally, during relational designation, learners classify the identified relationship, determining whether it reflects similarities, additions, or contradictions. After identifying relationships between sources, learners engage in synthesis, defined as the integration of information from multiple texts into a coherent and comprehensive understanding. During synthesis, the information across multiple texts may align, complement , or contradict each other. When discrepancies arise, learners perform reconciliation, a sub -process of synthesis, which may take several forms: they may attempt to resolve conflicts between multiple texts, favor one text over another, or disregard the conflict entirely. Successful 81 synthesis marks the completion of the integration process (List & Alexander, 2019). Therefore, this model implies that learners may exhibit varying approaches to integrat e multiple texts. Applied to the processing of multiple peer feedback messages, this may result in distinct patterns of peer feedback integration. These integration patterns are important for the design of CSCL environments, because without understanding the m, current CSCL tools might inadvertently overload students or encourage superficial processing when assigning multiple peers . The influence of objective feedback features and perceived feedback quality on integration Recently, Hsiao and Rajagopal (2023) applied the Integrated Framework of Multiple Text Use to propose a design framework intended to support students in integrating multiple peer feedback messages within thesis writing circles. Although they did not test their model empirically, their work illustrates that theoretical insights from research on learning with multiple documents can provide a valuable foundation for understanding how students combine feedback from different peers. Building on this premise, the present study aims to empirically examine the processes by which students integrate multiple peer feedback messages and to investigate how the characteristics of received feedback influence this integration. Based on prior research, we posit that the features of feedback messages students receive from peers can shape how they integrate them . Thereby, both objective feedback features and the perceived quality of the feedback are likely to play a role. Objective feedback features include the content and structural quality of the feedback (Nelson & Schunn, 2008; Wu & Schunn, 2020). Content quality refers to the accuracy and relevance of the feedback—that is, whether it correctly addresses the task. Structural quality, in contrast, concerns the presence of specific feedback element s, such as reminders of task requirements (feed up), evaluations of student performance (feed back), or suggestions for improvement (feed forward; Hattie & Timperley, 2007). Effective structural feedback is also expected to be clear, illustrative, and targ eted at the aspects of the task that require attention, and it may include explanations or examples that clarify why certain aspects are correct or incorrect (Gielen & De Wever, 2015). Wu and Schunn (2020) found that explanations in feedback increase the likelihood of its implementation, and that this effect may be even stronger when learners receive multiple peer feedback messages. By contrast, Nelson and Schunn (2008) observed that summaries and concrete solution suggestions were more likely to prompt implementation than explanations. Despite these mixed findings, evidence suggests that objective feedback features play a critical role in guiding how students integrate feedback. In addition to objective feedback features, the recipient’s perception of the quality of the feedback they received may influence the integration process (Strijbos et al., 2021). Perceived feedback quality encompasses both the adequacy of feedback (e.g., fairness, usefulness, and acceptance ; Strijbos et al., 2021 ), and subjective evaluations of specific feedback elements (e.g., feed up, feed back, feed forward; Hattie & Timperley, 2007). Strijbos et al. (2021) demonstrated that students’ perceptions of fairness, usefulness, and acceptance predict their motivation to improve and their affective responses. Conversely, Huisman et al. (2018) found no effect of perceived feedback quality on peer feedback outcomes. Although findings are somewhat inconsistent, perceived feedback quality appears to influence how students engage with feedback. Overall, previous research suggests that both objective feedback features and perceived feedback quality can affect subsequent processes on the part of the feedback recipient. However, most prior studies have focused on feedback implementation, whereas research on how learners integrate multiple peer feedback messages prior to implementation remains limited. We propose that both objective feedback features and perceived feedback quality are likely to influence feedback integration (Richter & Maier, 2017). For example, if one feedback message contains inaccurate information , while another is correct (content quality), the recipient needs to reconcile the conflict during integration, whereas integrating two accurate messages may require less effort. Similarly, if a student perceives one peer feedback message as useful and another as not, the latter may be ignored. Empirical studies testing these assumptions are currently lacking. Research questions The present study investigates how pre-service teachers integrate feedback they received from multiple peers and examines how objective feedback features (accuracy, relevance, implementability, structural feedback quality) and perceived feedback quality (adequacy, subjective quality) shape this integration process. Specifically, the study addresses the following questions: (1) Can different integration patterns be distinguished empirically? (2) Do objective feedback features and perceived peer feedback quality predict integration? 82

title: Student, Hybrid, or AI?: Examining Authorial Roles and Network Structures in GenAI- Supported Collaborative Learning
citation: Shaoming Chai, Zhenhai He, Tongwu Jiang (2026). Student, Hybrid, or AI?: Examining Authorial Roles and Network Structures in GenAI- Supported Collaborative Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Chai, S., He, Z., & Jiang, T.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
tpack_tk_labels: Generative AI & LLMs; Collaborative Platforms & Forums
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) reshapes collaborative learning, understanding how authorial roles interact within evolving network structures is crucial. This exploratory case study explored authorial roles and social network structures in a Knowledge Forum -based computational thinking course. We analyzed 527 discussion notes from 54 undergraduates using Social Network Analysis (SNA) and deep learning classification. Notes were categorized into four roles: pure student (Stu), direct GenAI outputs, Student -GenAI (SG) hybrids, and Student-GenAI-Student (SGS) iterations. Results showed student-only contributions dominated (73.8%), with GenAI-involved notes at 26.2%. Network analysis revealed Stu roles as primary information hubs with high centrality, while hybrid SG/SGS roles were less central than expected. Findings suggest that without explicit guidance, students remain core connectors and AI-facilitated knowledge brokerage is underutilized. Educational practice must intentionally scaffold hybrid roles to foster balanced, integrated knowledge flow in GenAI -supported collaborative learning.

title: Towards Teachers-AI Collaboration for Professional Development in Learning Design
citation: Shatha N. Alkhasawneh, Davinia Hernández-Leo (2026). Towards Teachers-AI Collaboration for Professional Development in Learning Design. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Alkhasawneh, S. N. & Hernández-Leo, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) can enhance learning design (LD) by exploring stakeholders’ preferences for five conceptual GenAI -based conversational agent functions —Authoring Assistant, Inspiration Hub, Design Feedback, Possibility Engine, and Ethics Guardian—adapted from the GenAI Speculative Functions Framework for LD. Proposed for the TRAILS teacher professional development platform, these functions target underexplored early phases of LD. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, 56 participants evaluated these functions, their support needs across design phases, and related opportunities and concerns. Findings reveal a two- pillar demand: creative inspiration, prioritized in the Investigation phase through the Inspiration Hub, and drafting efficiency, prioritized in the Authoring phase through the Authoring Assistant. The analysis revealed role- dependent value: experienced practitioners favored generative and creativity -oriented functions, while prospective teachers emp hasized diagnostic and feedback support. The Ethics Guardian emerged as an essential ambient safeguard. The study offers practical guidance for integrating human- centered GenAI into teacher professional development platforms and human-AI collaboration in LD.

title: Socially Shared Metacognitive Regulation (SSMR): Comparative Analysis of Strategies and Adaptations in Teams with Divergent Outcomes during CPS
citation: Vishwas Badhe, Ramkumar Rajendran (2026). Socially Shared Metacognitive Regulation (SSMR): Comparative Analysis of Strategies and Adaptations in Teams with Divergent Outcomes during CPS. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Badhe, V. & Rajendran, R.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Collaborative problem-solving (CPS) for ill -structured problems is an integral part of various learning settings, where teams apply varied SSMR strategies and perform necessary adaptations. The effective application and adaptation of SSMR strategies contribute to CPS success, making their investigation crucial for understanding SSMR's in CP S. This study undertakes a comparative analysis of SSMR strategy application and adaptation in teams with divergent outcomes during ill -structured CPS. Five engineering teams (N Learners=20) completed four -hour programming- related ill- structured CPS tasks in a closed lab setting. Teams were classified as more and less successful outcome teams (MSOT and LSOT) using an evaluation rubric. Verbal interactions ( of 20 hours) were analyzed using a mixed- methods approach combined with comparative thematic analysis. Considerable differences were found between MSOT and LSOT regarding SSMR strategy application and adaptation. These differences are presented through comparative frequency analysis and thematic representations, revealing distinctions in how MSOT and LSOT strategize and adapt during CPS.

title: Close Encounters: Teacher Proximity and Student-Reported Emotions While Using ST Math
citation: Sotheara Veng, Yiqin Chao, Rosa Mykyta-Chomsky, Teomara Rutherford (2026). Close Encounters: Teacher Proximity and Student-Reported Emotions While Using ST Math. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Veng, S., Chao, Y., Mykyta-Chomsky, R., & Rutherford, T.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Students’ academic emotions are critical to learning (Pekrun et al., 2002; Tan et al., 2021) and are linked to teacher actions (Meyer & Turner, 2007), some of which require close proximity. Prior studies emphasize the importance of proximity in shaping cl assroom environments, student behavior, and math anxiety (Shores et al., 1993; Quinnell, 2022). Yet, research on proximity is limited, especially in technology-mediated classrooms where teachers may not necessarily be in close proximity to students. This study examined the moment -to- moment, bidirectional relationship between student -reported emotions and teacher proximity during ST Math sessions. Using multilevel vector autoregression on experience sampling data from 92 elementary students, we found that frustration was associated with closer subsequent proximity, but it is the opposite for boredom. Conversely, closer proximity predicted lower subsequent boredom. These findings suggest that teacher proximity may play an important role in managing students’ emotions in technology-mediated settings.

title: Farm Harvests and Airplane Engines: Contextualizing Database Exercises in Relatable Contexts with a Learnersourcing Workflow
citation: Yuzhe Zhou, Alejandra J Magana, Tianyi Li (2026). Farm Harvests and Airplane Engines: Contextualizing Database Exercises in Relatable Contexts with a Learnersourcing Workflow. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Zhou, Y., Magana, A. J., & Li, T.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Developing learning materials that are relatable to students with varied backgrounds poses substantial challenges for instructors. This paper introduces a learnersourcing workflow designed to empower students as creators of personalized educational content , specifically through generating and peer -reviewing worked examples (WEs) that connect computing concepts to real -world scenarios. We empirically evaluated this learnersourcing approach within a database programming course and collected 127 student -generated WEs. The WEs contextualized database problems within diverse and novel scenarios, ranging from agricultural management to aircraft maintenance. Although some WEs had incomplete problem statements or incorrect solutions, most were complete, clear, and educational. In addition, student peer assessments of the WEs are aligned with instructor evaluations. We discuss the lessons learned regarding how a structured learnersourcing workflow can help students contextualize computing concepts and support learning.

authors_list: Khanlari, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Knowledge Building is a collaborative approach that treats ideas as improvable knowledge artifacts and engages learners in advancing collective understanding. To support this, educators need analytics that reveal deep discourse patterns. This paper introduces a semantic analysis tool for Knowledge Building that uses natural language processing to illuminate conceptual dynamics in student -generated content. The tool takes a glossary of curriculum terms and student notes, preprocesses text with spaCy, and computes semantic similarities using a transformer model. By analyzing word -to-term relationships, it identifies curriculum coverage, related concepts beyond official terms, and evidence of conceptual growth. We outline the tool’s design, demonstrate its outputs through network visualizations, and discuss implications for formative assessment, curriculum design, and longitudinal tracking, positioning it as a flexible analytic for studying and fostering knowledge -creating discourse.

title: An Item Response Theory Model for Multiple Resubmissions
citation: Xiang Liu, Mo Zhang, Chen Li, Hongwen Guo, Amy Ko, Min Li (2026). An Item Response Theory Model for Multiple Resubmissions. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Liu, X., Zhang, M., Li, C., Guo, H., Ko, A., & Li, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Item response theory models (IRT) are commonly used to model students' responses to test items. Under IRT, the associations among item responses are modeled by a latent variable. However, most IRT models are not suitable for modeling multiple resubmissions which are common in a learning environment. Students may be allowed to revise and resubmit multiple times after each submission. In this paper, we develop an IRT model for multiple resubmissions. The utility of this model is demonstrated through analyzing a real data set from a recently developed novel authentic assessment of programming skills.

title: Estimating Teacher Orchestration Load in Co-located and Online CSCL: Multimodal Data Analysis
citation: Lubna Hakami, Ishari Amarasinghe, Davinia Hernández-Leo (2026). Estimating Teacher Orchestration Load in Co-located and Online CSCL: Multimodal Data Analysis. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Hakami, L., Amarasinghe, I., & Hernández-Leo, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA); Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Classroom Orchestration
abstract: Teacher orchestration load has been an area of interest in the field of Computer - Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) as it reflects the real -time cognitive and emotional burden teachers experience. Orchestrating CSCL activities, especially in differen t learning environments, may impose stress on teachers. This study investigates teacher orchestration load when using a scripting tool, focusing on two learning settings: co- located and online. Multimodal data combined self -reports with physiological measures to capture teacher orchestration load. In this context, electrodermal activity (EDA) was used to capture physiological indicators of teacher orchestration load. EDA peaks corresponded with self - reported stressful moments, serving as an additional indicator for estimating orchestration load. Results revealed higher orchestration load in co-located settings compared to online. Moreover, factors such as the number of students and task type affect teacher orchestration load in both settings. Understanding these factors can support the design of teacher-supporting technologies that may assist in balancing teacher workload.

title: Bridging Group and Individual: Transitional Spaces in Collaboration
citation: Xuesong Cang, Michael Tissenbaum, Sadhana Puntambekar (2026). Bridging Group and Individual: Transitional Spaces in Collaboration. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Cang, X., Tissenbaum, M., & Puntambekar, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates how learning traverses between collective and individual levels in collaborative learning by introducing the concept of Transitional Space, the temporary and interactional zone where collective knowledge constructions outpace or below individual understanding. Using an approach that integrates students’ knowledge complexity levels and participation patterns, we model both group-level dynamics and individual trajectories. Results from two groups reveals that while higher -level engagement often align with increased knowledge at the group level , most individual students within the group deviate significantly from these patterns. These divergence highlights the fragile and contingent nature of transitions, which indicates that students must need a space to reconcile group-generated ideas with their own thinking, the Transitional Space. By identifying occurrence of such divergence, this study makes transitio ns empirically visible. The findings also contribute to theory by challenging assumptions of a spontaneous internalization and providing a methodological bridge between collective discourse and individual learning trajectories.

title: When Peers Outperform AI (and When They Don’t): Interaction Quality Over Modality
citation: Caitlin Morris, Pattie Maes (2026). When Peers Outperform AI (and When They Don’t): Interaction Quality Over Modality. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Morris, C. & Maes, P.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: As AI increasingly enters the classroom, what changes when students collaborate with algorithms instead of peers? We analyzed 36 undergraduate students learning graph theory through peer collaboration (n=24) or AI assistance (n=12), using discourse analysis to identify interaction patterns shaping learning outcomes. Results suggest a collaboration quality divide: high-quality peer interactions generated curiosity and engagement that AI couldn’t match, yet low-quality peer interactions performed worse than AI across dimensions. AI showed a paradoxical pattern, building confidence in knowledge while reducing curiosity and deeper engagement. Interaction quality emerged from dynamic patterns rather than individual traits, with early discourse markers predicting outcomes. Students treated AI as a transactional information source despite its collaborative design, revealing fundamental differences in human versus algorithmic engagement. Our findings suggest AI in education need not replace peer learning but can recognize struggle and support both peer and AI interactions toward productive learning experiences.

title: Frame Alignment and Feedback in CT-ified Science Classrooms
citation: Connor Bain, Uri Wilensky (2026). Frame Alignment and Feedback in CT-ified Science Classrooms. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Bain, C. & Wilensky, U.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
conceptualisations_list: Co-Design & Participatory Design; Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: While computational thinking (CT) is an integral part of modern scientific inquiry, STEM teachers struggle to incorporate these ideas in classrooms. We report on the efforts of a design-based implementation research project in which teachers participate in a constructionist co-design process to design and then implement CT -ified STEM units in their classrooms. Using feedback teachers left on student responses from these unit implementations, we utilize a basic bag-of-words model to show that teachers did specifically attend to student learning at the intersection of CT and STEM. We then further explicate this evidence through a qualitative think-aloud interview with one of the teachers who designed and implemented a curriculum based around computational models in biology. What we find is evidence that STEM teachers in CT -ified classrooms can assess both CT and S TEM skills at the same time though this intersection still needs additional attention in terms of tools and PD for teachers.

title: A Multimodal Study of Emotion Regulation in Student Dyads During Computational Model Building
citation: Ashwin T S, Srigowri Mayasandra Prasanna, Joyce Fonteles, Gautam Biswas (2026). A Multimodal Study of Emotion Regulation in Student Dyads During Computational Model Building. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: S, A. T., Prasanna, S. M., Fonteles, J., & Biswas, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Collaborative problem solving (CPS) requires coordination of cognition and affect in complex, open-ended tasks. This study examines how pairs of high school students regulate learner-centered emotions (engagement, confusion, frustration, boredom, and delight ) while constructing computational models in a STEM+C context. Extending Gross’s (2015) process model to the group level, we analyze temporal dynamics of synchronized and unsynchronized emotional states during CPS. Multimodal data from six dyads (video, audio, system logs) were coded for CPS activities (e.g., information sharing, consensus building) and emotion transitions. Emotional alignment predominated, yet brief misalignments (especially between engagement and confusion) were frequent and often precipitated interpersonal regulation. Temporal analysis identified two dominant pathways: (1) transitions from misalignment to alignment that restore shared engagement, and (2) transitions between aligned states that shift partners from shared confusion to engagement. These pathways primarily occurred during information pooling and integration phases. Quantitative results show that effective regulation predicts higher model - building performance, with sustained engagement emerging as the stable endpoint of productive collaboration. The findings provide a temporal, group- level account of how students collectively manage emotion to sustain effective problem solving.

title: Exploring Cognitive, Social, and Metacognitive Dimensions of Student -Student-LLM Collaboration in Problem Solving
citation: Victoria Delaney, Ibrahim Oluwajoba Adisa (2026). Exploring Cognitive, Social, and Metacognitive Dimensions of Student -Student-LLM Collaboration in Problem Solving. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Delaney, V. & Adisa, I. O.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: If large language models (LLMs) are to be framed as collaborative tools, it is important to understand the nature of LLM collaboration and how it may differ from human collaboration. To this end, we studied problem solving episodes between undergraduate dyads and ChatGPT, observing the extent to which students’ interactions with ChatGPT mediated their cognition, social interactions, and/or metacognition. We found mixed results among dyads (including one that avoided ChatGPT altogether) and elaborate on four cases in -depth, highlighting interactions between students and juxtaposing them with ChatGPT collaboration. Dyads that collaborated with ChatGPT spent more talk turns monitoring its output whereas dyads who collaborated with each other developed more cognitive and metacognitive awareness of the task. Our findings raise implications for tradeoffs that educators should consider when deciding if and when to introduce LLMs into problem solving.

title: Quantifying Knowledge Convergence through Change Point Detection of Word Abstractness in Collaborative Discussions
citation: Hironori Egi (2026). Quantifying Knowledge Convergence through Change Point Detection of Word Abstractness in Collaborative Discussions. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Egi, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The quantification of knowledge convergence often relies on qualitative c oding, limiting insights into how the dispersion of abstractness evolves during collaborative discussion. This study proposes a quantitative method that models each discussion as a time series of abstractness and applies change point detection to identify distributional shifts in its mean and dispersion. Six groups engaged in ten- minute discussions. Nouns in their utterances were extracted and assigned abstractness scores, after which change-point detection was applied to each group’s abstractness sequence with a minimum segment size of 20%, and the number of change points was determined by BIC. Results showed that the mean followed a U -shaped trajectory while the standard deviation showed the inverse in four groups , reflecting a mid - discussion phase in which abstract reasoning was anchored in concrete examples. These results demonstrate that knowledge convergence appears as interpretable s hifts thereby bridging qualitative analysis of knowledge convergence with quantitative segmentation.

title: Small Arguments, Big Ideas: Fostering Children’s Collaborative Reasoning with LLM Agents
citation: Hecong Wang, Meng Wang, Erfan Farhadi, Asad Shahab, Yuanzhu Li, Haozheng Du, Carolyn Rose, Hangfeng He, Zhen Bai (2026). Small Arguments, Big Ideas: Fostering Children’s Collaborative Reasoning with LLM Agents. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Wang, H., Wang, M., Farhadi, E., Shahab, A., Li, Y., Du, H., Rose, C., He, H., & Bai, Z.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Collaborative reasoning is at the core of critical thinking, problem solving, and effective communication, with growing attention being devoted to developing pedagogical and technological supports that enhance it. While many existing conversational agents (CAs) for education emphasize comprehension or factual recall during reading, the use of advanced reasoning behaviors, such as persuasion and inquiry, may further foster children’s engagement in collaborative reasoning. Based on recent advancements in large language models (LLMs), we created CAs that engage children in collaborative reasoning through argumentation during book-reading activities, by operationalizing three dialogue types from Walton’s framework of dialogue and argumentation: information- seeking, persuasion, and inquiry. We conducted a four-day exploratory study with 18 8-year-olds at a literacy-focused summer camp. Our findings revealed that while asking questions can support children’s collaborative reasoning, incorporating even small amounts of persuasion and inquiry elicits significantly more reasoning behaviors, especially explanations, clarifications, and reflections, from the children.

title: A Design Space for Dialogic Assessment in CSCL
citation: Rolf Steier, Magnus Hontvedt, Jacob Davidsen, Charlotte Beal, Morten Oddvik, Marit Solem (2026). A Design Space for Dialogic Assessment in CSCL. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Steier, R., Hontvedt, M., Davidsen, J., Beal, C., Oddvik, M., & Solem, M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Dialogic assessment remains remarkably unexplored as a research and design setting in CSCL. We address this gap by developing a design space to support future partnership-based work in our field. Our design space reflects a 1.5- year investigation of dialogic assessment practices and perspectives conducted through literature review work, focus group interviews with practitioners, formal and informal discussions with colleagues and prototype development work with technology designers. First, we frame the design space concept before arguing for the relevance of dialogic assessment as a potential CSCL activity. Then, we present our design space through a cumulative distillation of four relevant perspectives and seven design dimensions. Finally, we conclude by laying out an agenda reflecting how this design space can inform future work and prompt innovative assessment practices.

title: Flexibility Before Fluency: Exploring How Flexible Strategies Emerge through Collaborative Problem-Solving
citation: Seiyon Lee, Shan Zhang, Hongming Li, Ji-Eun Lee, Avery Closser, Anthony F. Botelho (2026). Flexibility Before Fluency: Exploring How Flexible Strategies Emerge through Collaborative Problem-Solving. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Lee, S., Zhang, S., Li, H., Lee, J., Closser, A., & Botelho, A. F.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: In K-12 math education, it is important not only to foster fluency but also flexibility in the problem- solving process. Prior works have focused on measuring learning in terms of efficiency or productivity by examining the extent to which students can optimize their problem-solving paths to involve the fewest number of steps. Limited work has paid attention to the notion of flexibility, or the ability to understand and navigate different paths to the same problem. In this study, we examine how middle school students’ use a dynamic notation tool to explore flexible solution paths during collaborative problem solving (CPS) activity. Results show that there are differences in patterns of CPS process between students who demonstrated greater flexibility and those who did not. Specifically, they differed in their engagement with higher-level operations. We discuss the implications for supporting students’ flexible problem solving and teachers in orchestrating CPS for similar goals in classrooms.

title: Using Multimodal Analytics-Supported Reflective Assessment to Promote Undergraduates’ Productive Social-emotional Interaction
citation: Yuqin Yang, Xiaoru Li, Daner Sun, Xueqi Feng, Gaoxia Zhu (2026). Using Multimodal Analytics-Supported Reflective Assessment to Promote Undergraduates’ Productive Social-emotional Interaction. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Yang, Y., Li, X., Sun, D., Feng, X., & Zhu, G.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA); Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: This quasi -experimental study investigated the effects of multimodal analytics - supported reflective assessment (MA SRA) on undergraduates' collaborative knowledge advancement and socio -emotional interactions. The experimental group ( n = 48 ), utilizing MASRA with visualized analytics and reflective prompts, was compared to a comparison class (n = 38) using portfolio assessment. Analysis of 4034 discussion notes revealed the MA SRA group significantly outperformed the comparison class across six colla boration dimensions, achieving nearly double the collective knowledge advancement. The experimental class demonstrated more positive and fewer negative socio -emotional interactions, alongside more frequent “negative → positive” transitions. Furthermore, MA SRA strengthened the co- occurrence of metacognitive discourse and positive socio- emotional dynamics, suggesting it enhances students' ability to regulate emotions and maintain group cohesion. These findings indicate that MA SRA is a scalable model that effectively fosters both cognitive -level knowledge innovation and productive socio- emotional dynamics in collaborative learning environments, offering evidence-based strategies for higher education. Knowledge building (KB) is a deep constructivist teaching model emphasizing collective responsibility for idea improvement and community development. Technology -supported KB has shown promise in fostering higher - order skills among university students, incl uding critical thinking, metacognition, and disciplinary literacy (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 2003; Moss & Beatty, 2006; Scardamalia, 2006; Yang, van Aalst, et al., 2020). However, realizing this potential depends heavily on students’ social interactions, particularly socio-emotional interactions, which involve behaviors such as expressing care, developing trust, fostering belonging, and promoting a sense of community ( Bakhtiar et al., 2018; Kreijns et al., 2003 ). Effective socio -emotional interactions are critical in collaborative inquiry, as they support team functioning, motivation, and cognitive engagement (Näykki et al., 2014; Pekrun & Perry, 2013; Pekrun, Vogl, et al., 2017). Positive socio- emotional interactions facilitate conflict resolution, help-seeking, collective planning, and behavioral engagement, whereas negative interactions—arising from cognitive challenges, motivational issues, or interpersonal dynamics —can impede learning and reduce satisfaction (Blumenfeld et al., 1996; Kempler & Linnenbrink, 2013; Lajoie et al., 2015; Näykki et al., 2014). Despite this, research on promoting socio- emotional interactions using technology remains limited, especially in complex, open-ended learning contexts. Reflective assessment involves monitoring, reflecting on, and adjusting one’s learning using evidence from rubrics or analytics, fostering metacognitive awareness and self -regulation (Yang, Zhu, et al. , 2022). Multimodal analytics-supported reflective assessment (MASRA) extends this approach by providing learners with real-time, multimodal data — behavioral and self -report— on their cognitive, metacognitive, and emotional processes (Blikstein & Worsley, 2016; Tao & Zhang, 2021; Yang , Chen, et al., 2020; Yang, Zhu, et al., 2022;). MASRA integrates planning, monitoring, reflecting, and regulating, enabling students to identify challenges, adjust strategies, and transform negative socio- emotional experiences into constructive learning signals, while reinforcing positive affect and self-efficacy (Panadero, 2017; Efklides, 2011). Previous studies confirm MASRA’s effectiveness in enhancing cognitive engagement and agency, particularly for low -achieving students in knowledge-building environments (Yang, 2019). However, its role in fostering socio-emotional interactions and the underlying mechanisms remain underexplored. Socio-emotional interactions play a crucial role in collaborative learning. Positive interactions—such as mutual respect, support, and care—are associated with deeper cognitive engagement, successful problem -solving, and higher motivation (Rogat & Linnenbr ink-Garcia, 2011; Näykki et al., 2014; Lajoie et al., 2015; Mullins, Deiglmayr, & Spada, 2013). They also facilitate monitoring information exchange, inclusive planning, and team behavioral engagement (Rogat & Adams-Wiggins, 2014; Kempler & Linnenbrink, 2013 ). Negative interactions, however, can stem from cognitive, motivational, or interpersonal challenges and may reduce help-giving, impede learning progress, and generate persistent negative emotions (Andriessen et al., 2013; Järvenoja & Järvelä, 2009; 254 Näykki et al., 2014). Recent research has highlighted the importance of multimodal analytics in capturing these complex social-emotional dynamics, offering richer insights than single -source measures (Isohätälä et al., 2020; Huang & Lajoie, 2023). Socio-emotional dynamics are often subtle and difficult for learners to perceive during ongoing inquiry. By integrating multiple data streams, MASRA externalizes these tacit interaction patterns, reducing the cognitive burden of self -diagnosing group climate. Visualizing these dynamics provides concrete evidence that prompts learners to enact repair-oriented transitions, linking metacognitive reflection directly to collaborative regulation. This aligns with recent CSCL insights on how carefully designed analytics-supported dashboards foster reflective assessment (Gutiérrez-Braojos et al., 2025). This approach not only supports individual learning but also cultivates a shared sense of community, collaborative planning, and collective responsibility (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2014). The present study addresses a gap in the literature by exploring how MASRA can support productive socio-emotional interactions in university KB contexts. We designed teaching activities and reflective materials to generate rich multimodal interaction data, which were analyzed using content analysis, lag sequential analysis, and cognitive network visualization. The study investigates (1) the effects of MASRA on socio- emotional interactions among undergraduates, (2) differences in socio- emotional dynamics acr oss students with varying academic performance, and (3) the relationship between socio- emotional interactions and individual learning outcomes in collaborative knowledge construction. By integrating reflective assessment with multimodal analytics, this res earch provides empirical insights into fostering positive social -emotional engagement and enhancing both cognitive and emotional dimensions of learning in higher education. The following research questions were investigated: RQ 1. Do the undergraduates with multimodal analytics -supported reflective assessment design perform better in advancing collective knowledge? RQ 2. Do the undergraduates with multimodal analytics -supported reflective assessment design engaged more in productive socio-emotion and socio-emotional interaction? RQ 3. How do the undergraduates promote positive socio-emotional interactions through the enactment of multimodal analytics-supported reflective assessment?

title: Effects and Mechanisms of Learning Analytic-Supported Reflective Assessment for Promoting Metacognitive Regulation among Undergraduates
citation: Yuqin Yang, Yangbo Zhao, Xueqi Feng, Daner Sun, Jianwen Sun (2026). Effects and Mechanisms of Learning Analytic-Supported Reflective Assessment for Promoting Metacognitive Regulation among Undergraduates. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Yang, Y., Zhao, Y., Feng, X., Sun, D., & Sun, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)
abstract: Metacognitive regulation is critical for effective learning, yet many undergraduates lack the necessary skills to self-regulate. This study conducted an 18- week quasi-experimental investigation with 88 undergraduates in a Knowledge Building (KB) environment to examine how l earning analytics-supported reflective assessment (LAsRA) influences collaborative knowledge creation and metacognitive regulation. Group Communication Analysis (GCA) and Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) were employed to analyze students ’ discourse and regulatory networks. GCA results showed that the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in knowledge creation, exhibiting highly cohesive discourse. ENA revealed that LAsRA facilitated a critical shift toward socially shared and deep -level metacognitive regulation. Rather than merely monitoring outcomes, students successfully constructed a dynamic collaborative cycle of "goal -setting—process monitoring —reflective evaluation — dynamic regulation." Findings suggest that a nalytics-supported reflective assessment provides an effective pathway to foster a community -level, self -improving regulatory environment, fundamentally enhancing students' metacognitive capabilities and collective knowledge advancement.

title: Extending CSCL Affordances for Multilingual Classrooms: Teacher Perspectives on AI -Supported Collaboration
citation: Pragati Maheshwary, Alina Guha, Shamya Karumbaiah (2026). Extending CSCL Affordances for Multilingual Classrooms: Teacher Perspectives on AI -Supported Collaboration. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Maheshwary, P., Guha, A., & Karumbaiah, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Multilingual classrooms add layers of complexity to collaboration: teachers rarely share every student’s home language, peers struggle to build common ground, and AI translation can miss linguistics nuance. We report findings from focus groups conducted with teachers of multilingual students to gauge their view on AI-supported collaboration across three collaboration pathways: student -student, teacher-student, and student-AI. Teachers welcomed real-time subtitling/translation to support comprehension and questioning, and lightweight tools that surface peers’ ideas via transcripts and highlights for clarifications. They were skeptical of in-class 1:1 student-AI partnering, citing risks to social connection, teacher workload, and scope creep. Using Jeong & Hmelo -Silver’s seven affordances as our lens, we identify where affordances blend within pathways, and where they need rethinking for multilingual equity. We translate teacher concerns into CSCL -aligned design adaptations and contribute extended versions of affordances to guide AI-integrated CSCL that is equitable for linguistically diverse classrooms.

title: Integrating Augmented Reality and Product Design in Makerspaces
citation: Dejan Trencevski, Jina Kang, Vishal Sachdev, Aric Rindfleisch (2026). Integrating Augmented Reality and Product Design in Makerspaces. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Trencevski, D., Kang, J., Sachdev, V., & Rindfleisch, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study aims to explore the affordances of augmented reality technologies (AR) to facilitate studentsʼ product design processes in a business course. We analyze the affordances of AR in the context of a product design activity in an undergraduate classroom. The course is held in a Makerspace lab at a university campus, and it requires students to conceptualize, design, prototype, manufacture, and market new products by using 3D computer -aided design (CAD) software and 3D printing. Our study illuminates that although CAD allows students to visualize and manipulate digitally manufactured 3D objects on a 2D computer monitor surface, it does not allow them to visualize and manipulate those 3D objects in 3D space. However, AR does afford visualization and mani pulation of digitally manufactured 3D objects in 3D space which is why we investigated how do interactions with 3D models in AR impact product design processes for students.

title: Unpacking Flexibility in Teacher Professional Learning on WhatsApp Messaging Network Platform
citation: Iris Saban, Linor Hadar (2026). Unpacking Flexibility in Teacher Professional Learning on WhatsApp Messaging Network Platform. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Saban, I. & Hadar, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines how flexibility manifests as a lived practice within a voluntary WhatsApp-based teachers’ professional community. While flexibility is a recognized affordance of online learning, its role in teacher professional networks remains undertheorized. Drawing on 2,307 posts across 349 conversations among 146 teachers, we conceptualized and measured flexibility through three dimensions: temporal, concerning engagement during discretionary time; sequential, involving the recurrence of conversations; and structural, which maps network connections across discussions. The analysis reveals profound temporal flexibility, with nearly two -thirds of posts occurring outside school hours and over a 40% during holidays and summer break. Although recurring conversations constituted 11% of discussions, they generated 25.4% of posts and were longer with statistically significant differences. These recurring discussions formed the network’s core, effectively integrating teachers and sustaining dialogue. These findings demonstrate that flexibility is not a static design feature but a dynamic, socially constructed practice fundamental to professional growth.

title: Teachers’ Evolving Sentiments and Competencies about Generative AI in Social Media Discourse: A Case Study on X
citation: Karina Vázquez, Davinia Hernández-Leo, Shatha N. Alkhasawneh (2026). Teachers’ Evolving Sentiments and Competencies about Generative AI in Social Media Discourse: A Case Study on X. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Vázquez, K., Hernández-Leo, D., & Alkhasawneh, S. N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines teachers’ evolving sentiments and competencies regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) by analyzing teacher-authored posts on X (formerly Twitter) in 2023 and 2025. Combining qualitative content analysis with automated and manual sentiment analysis, the research is guided by the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers (AI CFT) and Zhai’s teacher agency framework. The study contributes to the CSCL discourse by framing X as a space for informal, collaborative learning. Within this environment, educators share experiential insights and articulate evolving visions of GenAI as a collaborator in their pedagogical practice and professional devel opment. Findings indicate a gradual shift toward more positive and practice -oriented engagement, though concerns about agency, accountability, and professional responsibility remain. A significant link between sentiment and competency suggests that emotional stance shapes readiness to adopt GenAI. The study informs professional development strategies aligned with AI CFT curricular goals , promoting ethical and human-centered GenAI integration in education.

title: Advancing Dialogic Leadership through AI-Enabled Training: Insights from a Design-Based Research Project
citation: Xuanning Chen, Imogen Casebourne, Rupert Wegerif, Pedro Salinas (2026). Advancing Dialogic Leadership through AI-Enabled Training: Insights from a Design-Based Research Project. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Chen, X., Casebourne, I., Wegerif, R., & Salinas, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper reports insights from an ongoing design- based research project on developing an AI -enabled programme for dialogic leadership training. To ensure the effectiveness of the programme, one central challenge must be addressed: Can AI be designed to follow dialogic principles and provide trustworthy, supportive guidance that enables leaders to embed these principles into their practices? To address this, three design strategies were implemented: applying principles of dialogic intelligence and conversa tional heuristics to enhance AI’s capacity for generative dialogue; integrating open- source datasets and psychological frameworks to improve AI’s contextual awareness; and refining human- like interaction features to build AI’s credibility. Guided by these strategies, an initial prototype for leadership in performance reviews was developed and tested with 20 participants, yielding positive results. Looking forward, the project will improve scenario realism, introduce scaffolding mechanisms and develop evaluation mechanisms for a better learning experience.

title: Ways of Knowing in Global Informal Learning
citation: Danielle P. Espino, Kristina M. Lux, Seung B. Lee, Eric R. Hamilton (2026). Ways of Knowing in Global Informal Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Espino, D. P., Lux, K. M., Lee, S. B., & Hamilton, E. R.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: T his paper examines how adolescents develop boundary- crossing STEM competencies through participation in an informal, globally networked virtual learning program. Using post -assessment interviews and recorded sessions of participating youth in Brazil, Kenya, Mexico, and the United States, we focus on two key competencies that emerged: Embracing Other Ways of Knowing and Building Community. These two competences reflect students’ growing ability to engage across cultural and geographic differences and to esta blish inclusive, collaborative practices of learning and working together. The findings underscore the promise of boundary-crossing, project-based environments for developing STEM identities and fostering the human-centered skills necessary for globally connected STEM learning and future collaboration.

title: Collaborative Learning with Concept Maps: Experimental Investigation Using Epistemic Network Analysis
citation: Shigen Shimojo, Yugo Hayashi (2026). Collaborative Learning with Concept Maps: Experimental Investigation Using Epistemic Network Analysis. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Shimojo, S. & Hayashi, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)
abstract: With the aging global population, lifelong learning is gaining attention. However, research on older adults’ learning remains limited. This study reanalyzed collaborative learning with concept maps data from a previous study by applying the Interactive–Constructive– Active–Passive (ICAP)-based utterance analysis and network analysis to examine older adults’ knowledge construction. By comparing them with young adults, we investigated the differences in learning processes and their effects on learning performance. Utterances were ICAP - classified and analyzed using epistemic network analysis. Young adults enhanced their learning by claiming their idea and reconstructing their understanding from others’ knowledge (Constructive and Interactive). Conversely, older adults mainly engaged in recalling information (Active) and reflecting on a partner’s concept map (Interactive). These findings clarify the mechanisms of older adults’ learning from a theoretical computer- supported collaborative learning perspective and highlight the need for designs of support systems that compensate for Constructive and Active.

title: From Idea Consumers to Knowledge Co-Creators: A 3-Year Design Study of Sustained Creative Work Through Cross-Community Partnership
citation: Robert Huang (2026). From Idea Consumers to Knowledge Co-Creators: A 3-Year Design Study of Sustained Creative Work Through Cross-Community Partnership. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Huang, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This three-year design-based research (DBR) study investigates how to shift students from being passive consumers of information to active co-creators of knowledge. Conducted in three iterative phases, the study progressed from a local Grade 2 classroom to a cross-national partnership between Grade 2 (Canada) and Grade 9 (Spain). Using a mixed-methods approach, including a novel AI-based analytical tool (StAS), results demonstrate a clear progression from students reproducing authoritative information to engaging in authentic knowledge synthesis and co -design. These findings provide a model for cultivating epistemic agency by progressively expanding the "public" for student ideas and utilizing multimodal tools for collaborative theory building.

title: Reconceptualize Conversational AI as a Learning Medium, From a Holistic Learning Perspective
citation: Yuqi Wang (2026). Reconceptualize Conversational AI as a Learning Medium, From a Holistic Learning Perspective. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Wang, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Current university policies predominantly restrict conversational AI use in coursework, based on assumptions that students engage with AI under transmission orientations. However, these policies overlook transactional pedagogical possibilities. This study reconceptualizes conversational AI as a medium for holistic learning through structured transactional engagement rather than information delivery. Drawing upon Miller's Holistic Learning paradigm and Computer -Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) principles, we conducted semi -structured interviews with 12 educators enrolled in a Holistic Learning postgraduate course to examine: (1) current perceptions and concerns, (2) capacity to distinguish transmission from transactional AI applications, and (3) necess ary implementation conditions. Findings demonstrate most educators readily recognized conversational AI's pedagogical function depends on prompt design rather than technological properties. I propose integrating CSCL script principles with Miller's six con nection types to operationalize transactional AI through multi-level prompt design. This framework moves beyond the ban-or- permit binaries toward nuanced, pedagogically- grounded implementation that honors both academic integrity and innovative learning design.

title: Scoping Review of Knowledge-Creation Practices Supported by AI: Identification of Research Strands of Different Communities
citation: Jun Oshima, Shotaro Naganuma (2026). Scoping Review of Knowledge-Creation Practices Supported by AI: Identification of Research Strands of Different Communities. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Oshima, J. & Naganuma, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)
abstract: This scoping review examines how AI supports collaborative learning as knowledge creation in varied educational contexts. Unlike previous reviews that discuss learning more broadly, this study focuses on the epistemological and methodological foundations of AI - supported collaboration. Using the PRISMA protocol, the authors analyzed 72 empirical studies published between 2020 and 2025, employing bibliographic coupling and ENA to identify research communities and their research strands. Six research communities emerged, each representing different strands —ranging from cognitive and sociocultural to design -based and systemic approaches. These communities reveal diverse perspectives on AI’s role. The findings indicate that much of the current research centers on individual learning and distal outcomes, while studies oriented toward knowledge creation, especially within CSCL and the LS, remain limited but are increasing. The review highlights the importance of future research prioritizing multimodal, group- level AI collaboration designs, grounded in robust theoretical and

title: Self-organizing Interdisciplinary Team in Generative AI-Supported Collaboration Context
citation: Shotaro Naganuma, Tsubasa Minematsu, Jun Oshima (2026). Self-organizing Interdisciplinary Team in Generative AI-Supported Collaboration Context. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Naganuma, S., Minematsu, T., & Oshima, J.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: We report two -year design- based research (2024: N = 14, 2025: N = 19) on interdisciplinary research practice by doctoral students supported by generative AI (GenAI). The purpose was to explore necessary support s for interdisciplinary team formation by investigating how learners self -organized teams in this community. In both years, participants formed five teams to prepare interdisciplinary research proposals. Their video recordings data were analyzed. Findings revealed that AI -enabled exploratory collaboration experiences functioned as a collaboration history to build students’ networks for the final team decision. We further identified three boundary-crossing patterns (e.g., Wide-Range Explorers ). T hrough these diverse interactions, the community-level interdisciplinary distance converged toward a balance between novelty and mutual understandability. A m ore nuanced understanding of interdisciplinary team formation process in GenAI -supported setting , as well as the development of a visualization system displaying interdisciplinary distance , will benefit interdisciplinary team formation process.

title: Exploring Shared Agency in an Intelligent Immersive Learning Environment for Collaborative Writing
