citation: Yun Wen, Zongran Wang, Lang Xu (2026). Exploring Shared Agency in an Intelligent Immersive Learning Environment for Collaborative Writing. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Wen, Y., Wang, Z., & Xu, L.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_tk_labels: Generative AI & LLMs; Immersive VR / AR
abstract: An increasing number of studies on AI -student collaboration highlight the importance of learner agency in the Generative AI ( GenAI)-powered learning environment . However, limited research has examined how student-AI shared agency can be assessed, and it remains unclear whether individual interaction with AI agents or peer collaboration with AI agents is more effective in developing such agency. This study explores second language (L2) students’ shared agency within an intelligent immersive learning environment for writing. Using WriteCube, a self-developed AR- and AI-enabled writing system, 75 Primary 4 students from two classes in Singapore completed picture-based composition tasks under individual-AI and pair-AI collaboration conditions. Findings revealed no significant performance difference between groups, suggesting a trade -off between interactional richness and task efficiency. Regression results indicated that interaction quality, rather than frequency or language proficiency, positively predicted shared agency, particularly in ensuring equity. The study offers implications for assessing and enhancing learner agency in GenAI-supported L2 classrooms.

title: Combining Collaborative and Adaptive Learning: Constructive–Interactive Engagement through Concept Maps, Teachable Agents, and an Adaptive Tutor
citation: Yugo Hayashi, Shigen Shimojo, Kenneth R. Koedinger (2026). Combining Collaborative and Adaptive Learning: Constructive–Interactive Engagement through Concept Maps, Teachable Agents, and an Adaptive Tutor. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Hayashi, Y., Shimojo, S., & Koedinger, K. R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Integrating intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) with computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) may support deeper learning by combining adaptive feedback with collaborative knowledge construction. This study examined whether integrating adaptive and collaborative supports promotes constructive –interactive engagement. Seventy-four university students participated in an experiment comparing three conditions: ITS-only (adaptive), concept map construction with a teachable agent (collaborative), and a hybrid condition combining both supports. Learning was measured using pre - and posttests, and collaborative processes were examined through concept maps and verbal interaction measures. Results showed that the hybrid condition achieved the highest learning gains, while adaptive support alone produced higher comprehension than collaborative support alone. Process measures showed no significant differences across conditions, suggesting that the hybrid condition maintained comparable levels of collaboration despite additional individual tasks. These findings suggest that integrating adaptive and collaborative supports can effectively support deeper learning in CSCL environments.

title: When Ideas Take Turns: Temporal Embodiment of Disciplinary Engagement
citation: Xiaotian Zou, Daeun Hong, Cindy Hmelo-Silver, Chen Feng, Krista Glazewski, Tianshu Wang, James Lester (2026). When Ideas Take Turns: Temporal Embodiment of Disciplinary Engagement. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Zou, X., Hong, D., Hmelo-Silver, C., Feng, C., Glazewski, K., Wang, T., & Lester, J.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Embodied Cognition & Gestures
abstract: Collaborative problem- solving is central to science education, yet engaging disciplinarily in these settings is fluid, shifting across turns of talk in ways that shape group learning. Capturing these dynamics can provide insights for designing supports that foster deeper disciplinary engagement. This study examines how disciplinary engagement unfolds over time in a game- based science learning environment. Drawing on the Productive Disciplinary Engagement framework, we analyzed 2,415 discourse turns from 24 middle school groups using sequential and temporal analyses. Results revealed distinct pathways and temporal patterns across different groups, shedding lights into differences in learning outcomes. Findings demonstrate the value of temporal -sequential methods for informing scaffold design that supports productive collaboration.

title: Participatory Design for AI in Teacher Education: From Top-Down Directives to Teacher Empowerment
citation: Ekta Shokeen, Ane Vielandt Jensen, Ole Sejer Iversen, Christian Dindler, Marianne Graves Petersen (2026). Participatory Design for AI in Teacher Education: From Top-Down Directives to Teacher Empowerment. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Shokeen, E., Jensen, A. V., Iversen, O. S., Dindler, C., & Petersen, M. G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: Empowering teacher educators to lead technology integration is essential for creating context-sensitive educational futures. This study examines how participatory design workshops can support educators in collaboratively developing sustainable capacity for integrating AI into teacher education. Drawing on a series of three participatory design workshops, the analysis focuses on the collaborative learning processes involved and the professional outcomes they produce. Structured around exploration, co- creation, and reflection, these workshops enabled educators to critically engage with the pedagogical, ethical, and institutional dimensions of AI, fostering both ownership and transformative agency. The findings demonstrate how participatory design can function not only as a design methodology but also as a framework for professional learning. A key contribution of this paper is the demonstration that participatory design supports sustainable AI integration by building e ducators’ capacity for change through the design process.

title: DotQuest: Accessible STEM Games to Support Blind and Visually Impaired Learners
citation: Ariel Han, Rajeev Joshi, Daniel Tsivkovski, Dylan Ravel, Maryam Etezadbrojerdi (2026). DotQuest: Accessible STEM Games to Support Blind and Visually Impaired Learners. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Han, A., Joshi, R., Tsivkovski, D., Ravel, D., & Etezadbrojerdi, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Blind and low vision (BLV) students face persistent barriers to full participation in STEM learning, particularly due to the limited availability of accessible tools. This study introduces DotQuest, a technology probe that integrates haptic feedback, and a conversational agent to create narrative- driven, game -based STEM activities. To examine how such tools might support equitable participation, we conducted interviews with seven Teachers of Students with Visual Impairments (TVIs) across U.S. Analysis reve aled that teachers emphasize the importance of simultaneous tactile and auditory access, the need for classroom tools that foster both independence and inclusion, and the value of designing accessibility from the outset rather than as an accommodation. Fin dings show that multimodal game -based environments can enhance STEM engagement while revealing systemic barriers for BLV learners. This work contributes to the learning sciences by deepening understanding of how multimodal and inclusive design can guide the development of equitable STEM learning environments.

title: Pieces of the Puzzle: Examining Multimodal Interactions in Two Jigsaw Tasks to Inform Collaboration Support
citation: Indrani Dey, Collette Heskett, Mon-Lin Monica Ko (2026). Pieces of the Puzzle: Examining Multimodal Interactions in Two Jigsaw Tasks to Inform Collaboration Support. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Dey, I., Heskett, C., & Ko, M. M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examined students’ verbal and nonverbal collaboration across two jigsaw tasks with differing cognitive complexity. Findings show that combining modalities provides a more complete picture of group dynamics and that interaction patterns vary by task complexity. These insights inform the design of AI partners that adapt support to both evolving collaboration and the task’s cognitive demands.

title: Reconceptualizing Activity Theory for Human-AI Teaming in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning
citation: Jaeyoon Choi, Nia Nixon (2026). Reconceptualizing Activity Theory for Human-AI Teaming in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Choi, J. & Nixon, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) are reshaping the role of technology in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL). Once viewed as mediating tools, AI systems can now act as active teammates that co -construct meaning, share responsibility, and influence team cognition. This paper addresses the lack of theoretical grounding in existing human-AI teaming research by reconceptualizing Engeström’s Activity Theory. Specifically, we extend the six components of the activity system (subject, tool, rules, community, division of labor, and object) to account for AI’s dual role as both tool and quasi-subject within collaborative learning activities. Through this theoretical mapping, we highlight emerging questions for fut ure research, including but not limited to issues of learner agency, trust, equity, and epistemic alignment. We conclude with a call for the CSCL community to revisit and expand its theoretical frameworks to better capture the evolving dynamics of human-AI teaming.

title: Designing Digital Enhancements for Social Emotional Skill in a Collaborative Learning Environment
citation: Enruo Guo, Emily Kerzabi, Jessica Andrews-Todd, Jiangang Hao, Patrick Kyllonen, Stephen Elliott (2026). Designing Digital Enhancements for Social Emotional Skill in a Collaborative Learning Environment. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Guo, E., Kerzabi, E., Andrews-Todd, J., Hao, J., Kyllonen, P., & Elliott, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: This study presents the design and implementation of a fifth- grade Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) curriculum within a hybrid digital collaborative environment. Using a user -centered design approach, we engaged teachers and a school administrator as co - designers over a four -month period to iteratively refine the features and tools from a collaborative learning and assessment system (EPCAL). Key design decisions, such as tailoring class analytics to SEL and integrating feedback and rewards systems, were informed by teacher input. A semester-long pilot study involving two teachers and 22 students demonstrated the feasibility of delivering SEL through a hybrid model using EPCAL. Findings highlight strong teacher engagement and meaningful student participation. This research contributes a scalable framework for hybrid SEL delivery, demonstrating how a participatory design approach can be effectively applied to curriculum and technology enhancements - an approach that can be generalized to other hybrid learning contexts.

title: Linking Physiological Data and Self-Reports: Exploring Engagement in Collaborative Learning
citation: Xiaoran Li, Serkan Ucan (2026). Linking Physiological Data and Self-Reports: Exploring Engagement in Collaborative Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Li, X. & Ucan, S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study investigated the relationship between physiological synchrony and engagement in an authentic collaborative learning context. Heart rate data and self -reported engagement surveys were collected from 32 postgraduate students during a semester -long collaborative writing course. D ata were analyzed using Monte Carlo shuffling, Spearman correlation, and Welch's t -test. Spearman correlation revealed no significant associations between heart rate- based physiological synchrony and any dimension of self -reported engagement. However, pairs exhibiting significant physiological synchrony reported notably higher socio-emotional engagement compared to non- synchronous pairs, with this difference approaching statistical significance. These findings suggest that in authentic learning environments characterized by dynamic complexity, a direct linear relationship between physiological synchrony and engagement may not always be evident. Nevertheless, when physiological synchrony reaches a statistically significant threshold, it appears t o serve as a sensitive indicator of the socio-emotional dimensions of collaboration, highlighting its value for uncovering complex dynamics of student engagement in naturalistic educational settings.

title: GenAI Chatbot for Socially Shared Regulation of Learning in CSCL: Impact on University Students' Learning Engagement and Outcome
citation: Dengkang Chen, Yi Zhang, Jianwen Sun, Yijie Lu, Xiaoge Guo, Fucheng Guo (2026). GenAI Chatbot for Socially Shared Regulation of Learning in CSCL: Impact on University Students' Learning Engagement and Outcome. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Chen, D., Zhang, Y., Sun, J., Lu, Y., Guo, X., & Guo, F.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: Supporting socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is crucial for successful collaborative learning but is challenging due to its multidimensional and context -sensitive nature. While generative AI (GenAI) chatbots have shown promise in addressing these challenges, research has largely treated SSRL and GenAI chatbots separately, with limited empirical exploration of their integration. Furthermore, existing studies on GenAI chatbots supporting SSRL are mainly conceptual or design- focused, lack ing empirical evaluation. Addressing these gaps, we developed SSRLBot, a GenAI chatbot designed to identify SSRL challenges and offer contextual strategies. We conducted a six -week experimental study with 55 Chinese university students, dividing them into two classes: one using SSRLBot ( N = 27) and the other without chatbot support ( N = 28). Learning engagement and outcomes were assessed through questionnaires, platform log data and products. Results showed that SSRLBot significantly improved students’ learning engagement and outcomes, extending the application of GenAI chatbots from content tutor to group moderators in CSCL.

title: Regulating Epistemic Emotions in CSCL: Comparing the Higher- and Lower-Performing Groups
citation: Wenli Chen, Lishan Zheng, Xuanyu Chen, Qianru Lyu (2026). Regulating Epistemic Emotions in CSCL: Comparing the Higher- and Lower-Performing Groups. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Chen, W., Zheng, L., Chen, X., & Lyu, Q.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Epistemic emotions (e.g., curiosity, surprise, confusion) are important indicators of learners’ affective engagement in computer -supported collaborative learning (CSCL). While prior work studied learners’ static epistemic emotions, this study examined their dynamic, sequential patterns by comparing higher - and lower-performing groups. 44 university students participated in collaborative learning ideation tasks in dyads, where their verbal interactions were collected and coded for epistemic emotion s through content analysis and sequential mining. The findings show that high- performing groups manage to channel confusion and curiosity into constructive exploration and affective closure, whereas low -performing groups often fail to resolve such tension, leading to anxiety-driven loops. It highlights the importance of evolving epistemic emotional patterns rather than static affective states to understand and optimize collaborative learning processes and outcomes.

title: The Impact of Shared Feedback Visualization on Student Reflection During Simulation Debriefing
citation: Vitaliy Popov, Anouschka van Leeuwen (2026). The Impact of Shared Feedback Visualization on Student Reflection During Simulation Debriefing. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Popov, V. & Leeuwen, A. V.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: This study examined how a cognitive group awareness tool (RADAR) influences medical students ’ reflective behaviors during online post -simulation debriefing. A between - subjects experiment with 117 medical students compared three conditions: traditional observational debriefing (control), completing a shared decision- making questionnaire before debriefing (light RADAR), and completing the questionnaire with visualized results (full RADAR). Both RADAR conditions increased reflection on decision- making and counseling behaviors. Epistemic network analysis identified three distinct reflection patterns: c ontrol students connected performance review with patient history gathering; light RADAR students linked searching for alternative approaches with communication techniques and counseling; full RADAR students connected performance review with patient partnerships and counseling information. Visualization of assessment discrepancies in full RADAR did not increase feed - forward reflection. This study contributes to understanding how cognitive group awareness tools can enhance reflective learning processes in online simulation-based learning.

title: Exploring Unstructured Collaboration While Navigating Misinformation in Computer -Supported Collaborative Argumentation: Implications for Design
citation: Ram Das Rai, Sahana Murthy (2026). Exploring Unstructured Collaboration While Navigating Misinformation in Computer -Supported Collaborative Argumentation: Implications for Design. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Rai, R. D. & Murthy, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Accountable Talk & Dialogic Discourse; Design-Based Research (DBR)
abstract: The proliferation of socio-scientific misinformation is an inherently social challenge. While Computer -Supported Collaborative Argumentation (CSCA) environments offer a promising pedagogical approach for collective knowledge construction, their effectivene ss relies heavily on productive group dynamics. To avoid over -scripting future interventions, this formative Design-Based Research (DBR) study explores the baseline collaborative breakdowns that occur when students navigate misinformation without explicit social guidance. The study analyzed the audio transcripts of two middle school triads collaboratively mapping arguments about a controversial topic, utilizing established interaction analysis frameworks to evaluate peer talk and social modes of co -construction. Findings indicate that , within these groups , students defaulted to two distinct dysfunctional patterns: an epistemic conflict avoidance pattern, characterized by cumulative talk and quick consensus-building, and a social dominance pattern, characterized by disputational, competitive fact -checking. Structural scaffolds alone appeared insufficient to foster the critical exploratory talk required to evaluate deceptive claims, absent social interaction protocols. The study concludes by offering targeted design implications, suggesting that future CSCA environments might benefit from embedded collaboration scripts, such as structured "Devil's Advocate" and "Lead Fact -Checker" roles, to disrupt these natural tendencies and better support apt epistemic performance.

title: Multi-Level Knowledge Building Engagement: Pathways to Collaborative Problem- Solving and Academic Excellence in Higher Education
citation: Chih Hui Seet, Chih-Hsuan Chang, Huang-Yao Hong (2026). Multi-Level Knowledge Building Engagement: Pathways to Collaborative Problem- Solving and Academic Excellence in Higher Education. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Seet, C. H., Chang, C., & Hong, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Collaborative problem-solving (CPS) is increasingly vital for 21st-century learning, yet research on innovative pedagogy for cultivating these competencies in higher education remains limited. This study evaluated knowledge building (KB) as an innovative pedagogy to foster CPS in a university research methods course with 46 students. By analyzing actual online discourse on Knowledge Forum (KF), the study examined five levels of students’ KB engagement—behavioral, cognitive, thematic, methodological, and pro duct-based—in relation to their academic achievement. Results revealed high levels of active participation, with 54.10% of contributions involving higher -order cognitive activities. Furthermore, multi- level analysis of KB engagement significantly predicted 43.6% of the variance in academic achievement. These findings provide empirical evidence that the KB environment on KF facilitates the practice of CPS while enhancing academic excellence, offering a validated framework for university curriculum innovation.

title: Examining Socio-Cognitive and Affective Dynamics of Team Functioning and Leadership in Medical Simulations
citation: Annamarie Brosnihan, Megan Wiedbusch, Cameron Marano, Lindsey Schulz, Anna Pirner, Shiva Kalidindi, Roger Azevedo (2026). Examining Socio-Cognitive and Affective Dynamics of Team Functioning and Leadership in Medical Simulations. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Brosnihan, A., Wiedbusch, M., Marano, C., Schulz, L., Pirner, A., Kalidindi, S., & Azevedo, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA)
abstract: T eamwork and leadership are critical in promoting team success and positive outcomes in high intensity contexts. Given the urgency during pediatric medical emergencies, it is crucial to understand what support s or impede s successful team dynamics, including cognitive, metacognitive, affective, motivational, and social (CAMMS) processes. Thus, this study explores the dynamics of first -, second -, and third -year medical residents’ ( N = 21) CAMMS processes and their influence on individual and team performance in three team-based pediatric emergency simulated scenarios. Results indicate a significant correlation between motivation and cognitive and social processes, as well as a significant influence of team performance on CAMMS dynamics. Our findings support the need to further examine the impact of individual level processes on medical team functionality and performance. Using multimodal data, future studies will continue to ex plore relationships involving CAMMS dynamics and medical team functioning and performance.

title: Leveraging Generative AI for Iteration in Undergraduate Design
citation: Inés Álvarez-Icaza, Claudia Susana López Cruz, Martha Elena Núñez López, Griselda Esthela (2026). Leveraging Generative AI for Iteration in Undergraduate Design. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Álvarez-Icaza, I., Cruz, C. S. L., López, M. E. N., & Esthela, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Training designers requires not only technical skills, but also the ability to think critically, creatively, and strategically. Design applications powered by Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) are emerging every day, hence educators are concerned about the development of students’ creative abilities. The project is a pedagogical experience mediated by a GenAI tool, the ‘DIAgent’. Through a dynamic interaction between initial sketches, guiding questions, and automated feedback provided by the tool, students iterate their proposals, considering key variables such as form, usability, ergonomics, materials, and technology. This study is conducted with a mixed-method approach as an exploratory study to assess the creative abilities of a sample of 103 undergraduate students after the intervention. This paper presents the tool and the application protocol to be applied in six different design classes as the study’s first phase results, leading to a better understanding of how to redefine the students’ desi gn process.

title: From Regulation to Co-Regulation: A Game-Based Simulation for Human and Simulated Learners during Complex Problem Solving
citation: Roger Azevedo, Megan Wiedbusch, Cameron Marano, Annamarie Brosnihan, Milouni Patel (2026). From Regulation to Co-Regulation: A Game-Based Simulation for Human and Simulated Learners during Complex Problem Solving. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Azevedo, R., Wiedbusch, M., Marano, C., Brosnihan, A., & Patel, M.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This paper presents MetaSim , a game- based simulation designed to foster the development and transfer of metacognitive and self- regulated learning (SRL) skills in human learners. Grounded in contemporary theories of SRL and metacognition, MetaSim targets algebra by integrating cognitive, affective, motivational, metacognitive , and social dimensions of learning and complex problem solving. Central to MetaSim’s design, human learners interact with simulated learners (SLs), who serve as adaptive pedagogical agents (PA), embodying their human learner’s SRL profile. While human learners engage in problem solving, the SLs model, explain, and justify SRL strategies, prompting learners to reflect on and refine their own regulatory behaviors. This paper pres ents a high-level overview of the four phases of teaching and testing the simulated learners’ metacognitive capabilities in MetaSim.

title: Knowledge Network for Innovations in Learning and Teaching (KNILT): Teacher Learning Through Knowledge Creation
citation: Ying Kong, Jianwei Zhang, Aya Isaac (2026). Knowledge Network for Innovations in Learning and Teaching (KNILT): Teacher Learning Through Knowledge Creation. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Kong, Y., Zhang, J., & Isaac, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This research engages teachers as knowledge builders who create minicourses on the Knowledge Network for Innovations in Learning and Teaching (KNILT; https://knilt.arcc.albany.edu/) to support peer teacher learning around authentic issues of educational practice. A content analysis of 42 teacher -designed minicourses examined the types of knowledge addressed and the teaching methods employed to support teacher learning. The findings show that the minicourses devote substantial effort to helping teachers deepen their knowledge of teaching, student learning, curriculum content, and technology, with rich co-occurrence among knowledge themes and learning activities. KNILT operationalizes a learning-as-creating model for professional development, positioning teachers as knowledge builders who advance both their own and their peers’ pedagogical expertise through iterative minicourse design and refinement.

title: Learning Across Levels: Conceptualizing Transitional Space
citation: Xuesong Cang, Sadhana Puntambekar (2026). Learning Across Levels: Conceptualizing Transitional Space. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Cang, X. & Puntambekar, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: This paper conceptualizes Transitional Space as a framework for understanding how learning moves between individual and collective levels in CSCL. While prior research has revealed how groups construct shared meaning, how these collective advances become personally meaningful for individual learners is less articulated in a systematic way . Transitional Space reframes this relationship by conceptualizing learning as a relational movement in which collective knowledge construction and individually understanding continuously influence one another. The framework comprises two complementary facets: enacted Transitional Space capturing the interactional moments when group constructed ideas surpasses/below some members’ current understandings and supported Transitional Space highlighting the designable conditions that support these moments through tools, scaffolds, and structured activities. Two facets link the emergent and designed dimension of cross -level learning, emphasizing how Transitional Space makes visible and actionable the dynamic processes through which collective knowledge becomes individual sense -making, and how design supports these movements across levels.

title: From Words to Networks: AI-Powered Knowledge Graphs for Understanding Collaborative Learning
citation: Ahmad Khanlari (2026). From Words to Networks: AI-Powered Knowledge Graphs for Understanding Collaborative Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Khanlari, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
tpack_tk_labels: Generative AI & LLMs; Collaborative Platforms & Forums
abstract: This paper presents an analytics tool that leverages knowledge graphs to make visible the complex, collaborative discourse in Knowledge Forum. The tool extracts relational triplets (subject, predicate, object) from student posts using a hybrid pipeline combining LLM -based, transformer-based (Triplex), and rule -based (spaCy) methods. Extracted triplets are normalized and visualized as interactive graphs, where nodes represent concepts and edges represent relationships. A case study on the salmon life cycle demonstrates how the visualization surfaces central ideas, thematic clusters, and knowledge gaps, aligning with key Knowledge Building principles. By transforming unstructured discourse into an explorable network, the tool supports students and educators in tracing idea development and identifying opportunities for deeper inquiry.

title: How Active User Count Relates to Group Outcomes in Collaborative Programming: An Implicit Scripts Perspective
citation: Zhenyu Cai, Richard Lee Davis, Roland Tormey, Pierre Dillenbourg (2026). How Active User Count Relates to Group Outcomes in Collaborative Programming: An Implicit Scripts Perspective. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Cai, Z., Davis, R. L., Tormey, R., & Dillenbourg, P.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Collaboration scripts structure how learners work together by prescribing roles, tasks, and expected contributions. When scripts are implicit rather than explicit, learners decide how to enact them, which can shift the number of active participants and potentially outcomes. Prior work suggests sequential tasks may not benefit from multiple simultaneous actors due to the misalignment with the implicit script. Building on this, we test how the number of active users relates to time-on-task and group performance. Using panel data from three sequential Jupyter- notebook assignments, we estimate within- group fixed effects models to examine early-stage and aggregated activity signals. We find that a ctive user count is significantly associated with both outcomes, while early signals show a modest correlation with group scores.

title: From Initiative to Impact: Modeling How Collaborative Initiative Shapes Problem -Solving in STEM Simulations
citation: Rodrigo Hidalgo, Jina Kang (2026). From Initiative to Impact: Modeling How Collaborative Initiative Shapes Problem -Solving in STEM Simulations. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Hidalgo, R. & Kang, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)
abstract: This study examines how collaborative learning unfolds in HoloOrbits, a WebGL- based computer -supported collaborative learning (CSCL) environment designed to teach planetary motion. Using Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA), we analyzed how students initiated (collaborative intiative; CI) and responded to one another’s contributions (uptake; UP) during group inquiry. We found m ost initiatives were procedural, focusing on planning, clarification, and task management, while adaptive and idea-generating initiatives occurred less frequently. Groups where students’ contributions were taken up and extended by peers engaged in more sustained , collective reasoning; whereas others showed more confirmatory or fragmented discourse. These findings position collaborative initiative as a relational construct, with value that lies not in the correctness of individual contributions but in how peer responses take up and build on them to support collective sensemaking. The study underscores the importance of designing CSCL environments that scaffold both student agency and responsiveness, enabling individual contributions to become shared understanding.

title: A Transpositional Grammar Cyber-Social Study of Student–AI Relationships
citation: Christopher Hughes, Akash K. Saini (2026). A Transpositional Grammar Cyber-Social Study of Student–AI Relationships. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Hughes, C. & Saini, A. K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: As AI -mediated feedback becomes embedded in higher education, understanding how learners construe relationships with AI and human reviewers becomes increasingly more important. This pilot applies Transpositional Grammar (TG) to student prompts, AI- generated images, and reflections in a cyber-social learning environment. Graduate students (n = 7; P300– P306) at a Midwestern U.S. research university contributed coursework artifacts coded collaboratively by a human researcher and GPT‑5, yielding Cohen’s κ = 0.761. TG analysis identifies five recurrent transpositions —expansion, visualization, reinterpretation, materialization, and affective deepening —and surfaces relational accountability as a new dimension of learner expectations. The full study (n = 35; P300–P334) will add a second human coder to triangulate interrater reliability and inform the design of affect- sensitive human–AI feedback ecosystems in graduate instruction.

title: Who Gets to Know? Children’s Epistemic Agency in Science eBook Reading with AI
citation: Xuechen Liu, Ying Xu, Jon M. Wargo (2026). Who Gets to Know? Children’s Epistemic Agency in Science eBook Reading with AI. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Liu, X., Xu, Y., & Wargo, J. M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Children’s ability to act as epistemic agents not only support their understanding of concepts but also for shaping how they engage with ideas and participate in knowledge construction within their learning environment. The advancement in artificial intelligence (AI) has provided opportunities for interactive science learning, such as serving as a learning companion in dynamic and dialogic reading. While prior research has examined how children enact epistemic agency in human -to-human interaction, it is unc lear about whether, and if so how, children enact epistemic agency when interacting with AI, a non-human entity. This paper draws on video recordings of two individual children, each reading a science eBook with an AI agent. Using an interaction analysis, we examine how, through both language and embodied action, these two children claimed, evaluated, and negotiated knowledge, positioning themselves as epistemic agents in interaction with the AI agent.

title: A Case Study on the Effect of TAs’ Awareness of Pre-class Report Submissions on Scaffolding in Small-group Discussions
citation: Nozomi Fujikawa, Sanii Mizuno, Shintaro Uchiyama (2026). A Case Study on the Effect of TAs’ Awareness of Pre-class Report Submissions on Scaffolding in Small-group Discussions. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Fujikawa, N., Mizuno, S., & Uchiyama, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In recent years, Teaching Assistants (TAs) have been expected to play a key role in facilitating small-group discussions. However, prior studies have shown that TAs often struggle to provide appropriate interventions, frequently offering task- related explanations without first diagnosing students’ understanding. This study examined whether awareness of students’ pre- class report submissions supported TAs’ diagnostic scaffolding during small-group discussions. A 100-minute class session was video -recorded, and all TA utterances were transcribed and analyzed based on the framework of the Model of Contingent Teaching (MCT), focusing on the diagnostic and intervention phases. The results suggest that although both TAs were aware of students’ pre-class report submissions, only one TA engaged in diagnostic questioning to assess students’ understanding before intervening, whereas the other tended to respond with empathic support without diagnosis. This study extends the MCT to TA-supported learning environments by emphasizing the importance of recognizing pre-class reports and highlighting the interpretive processes that mediate between information awareness and adaptive intervention.

title: Reframing Social Annotation as a Text-Embedded Collaboration Analytics Ecology: The Idea Creation Cycle in
citation: Yeonji Jung, Sophia Soomin Lee (2026). Reframing Social Annotation as a Text-Embedded Collaboration Analytics Ecology: The Idea Creation Cycle in. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Jung, Y. & Lee, S. S.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: While the emergence and evolution of ideas are central to collaborative learning, these processes often remain invisible in digital environments. Social annotation (SA) embeds collaboration within shared texts, forming a distinct ecology where reading, ann otation, and discussion occur as a single, integrated workflow within one representational space. This study introduces the Idea Creation Cycle in Social Annotation (ICCSA), a theory- informed and analytics-operationalized framework that models how ideas mo ve and transform through four recursive phases: sensemaking, anchoring, interactive elaboration, and re -anchoring. Using multimodal SA traces, ICCSA captures the temporal trajectories of ideas, examining how cognition, artifacts, and interaction coevolve within one representational space. A proof -of- concept analysis of undergraduate course data reveals distinctive transition patterns and highlights re -anchoring as a key mechanism of knowledge advancement. Together, these findings position ICCSA as a bridge between CSCL theory and actionable learning analytics, advancing the understanding and support of idea development in text-embedded collaboration.

title: Embodied and Non-Embodied Technologies in Mathematics Learning: A Comparative Study
citation: Injila Rasul, Ivon Arroyo (2026). Embodied and Non-Embodied Technologies in Mathematics Learning: A Comparative Study. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Rasul, I. & Arroyo, I.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics
abstract: WearableLearning is a multiplayer, game-based digital learning environment in which students use mobile devices and collaborate while physically engaging with mathematical concepts such as geometry. This study examines how students learn mathematics in embodied games enabled by WearableLearning compared with a traditional seated digital learning environment. We report results from a randomized controlled trial conducted in a U.S. afterschool program, showing that students with lower prior knowledge benefited the most from the technology-supported embodied learning condition.

title: From Solo to Collaborative: Design Affordances in Multi-User Immersive VR Simulations for Transforming Science Learning
citation: Michelle Lui, Sunnie Gong, Chloe Lok (2026). From Solo to Collaborative: Design Affordances in Multi-User Immersive VR Simulations for Transforming Science Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Lui, M., Gong, S., & Lok, C.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
tpack_tk_labels: Immersive VR / AR; Simulations & Scientific Modeling
abstract: Immersive virtual reality (IVR) shows promise for science learning by enabling visualization of microscopic phenomena and dynamic processes. However, research has focused predominantly on individual learning experiences, overlooking the social nature of learning. This study investigates the collaborative affordances of multi -user IVR for science education through participatory design, involving six teams of undergraduate students and educators who co- created IVR learning simulations. Findings revealed seven science learning affordances: microscopic visualization, spatial relationships, scale traversal, representational connections, perspective-taking, temporal phenomena, and procedural skills—which multi-user IVR amplified through embodied communication, role -taking that grounds collaborative discourse, and distributed perspectives that require coordination. Analysis of designs highlights how narrative structures establish group- worthy joint tasks, fostering six collaborative activity types. Variations in structuring collaborative processes emerged from play- level scripts with undifferentiated roles, and scene -level scripts with defined roles enhanc ing interdependence. Results provide design insights for leveraging IVR ’s spatial and embodied features in collaborative science learning.

title: Epistemic Authority and Interface: A Typological Framework of AI’s Roles in Knowledge Building
citation: Lydia Cao, Bodong Chen, Sebastian Simon, Yee Yin Tan, Stefano Cacciamani, Eliane Chaker Metni (2026). Epistemic Authority and Interface: A Typological Framework of AI’s Roles in Knowledge Building. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Cao, L., Chen, B., Simon, S., Tan, Y. Y., Cacciamani, S., & Metni, E. C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Knowledge Building distinguishes itself from other educational approaches by engaging students directly in the means by which knowledge advances in the world. As artificial intelligence (AI) advances, fundamental questions arise about its implications for KB. This study extended a workshop at the 2024 International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS) annual meeting into a four -month dialogue on Knowledge Forum. Using a dialogical knowledge-making framework, 23 contributors from diverse disciplinary backgrounds and career stages collectively examined theoretical, pedagogical, design, ethical implications at the intersection of AI and KB. Diverse AI roles were discussed and organized into a typological framework along interface type and epistemic authority levels , producing six configurations: directive interaction, collaborative interaction, exploratory interaction, diagnostic environment, reflective environment, and experimental environment. Given the configurations of AI, we propose a design principle of making AI's epistemic position visible and enabling learner-driven navigation across AI roles.

title: Modeling and Analyzing Collaborative Dialogue States in Mathematics Problem- Solving through ONA and Hidden Markov Models
citation: Shan Zhang, Andrés Felipe Zambrano, Hongming Li, Seiyon Lee, Ji-Eun Lee, Anthony F. Botelho (2026). Modeling and Analyzing Collaborative Dialogue States in Mathematics Problem- Solving through ONA and Hidden Markov Models. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Zhang, S., Zambrano, A. F., Li, H., Lee, S., Lee, J., & Botelho, A. F.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Prior research has shown that collaborative dialogue reflects students’ cognitive, social, and regulatory processes, which support deeper learning. However, less is known about how these moves unfold sequentially during collaborative problem solving (CPS), especially in math contexts. This study leverages Markov Chains, Hidden Markov Models (HMM), and Ordered Network Analysis (ONA) to capture and analyze recurring patterns and transitions in dialogue that are representative of collaboration dynamics and obs erve how these relate to students’ perceptions of their interactions, collaboration quality, and performance. We conduct our analyses with data from 22 college students (11 dyads) who worked collaboratively to solve algebra problems in a digital learning environment. Results show that dialogue within problems cycled through agreement, clarification, and self -explanation, indicating stable interaction patterns across five HMM latent states. Findings from ONA suggest that while explanatory talk anchors collab oration, task -grounding and co- constructive exchanges may be more directly associated with effective CPS.

title: Designing for Collaboration: An Engineering Notebook to Scaffold Collaborative Problem- Solving in Middle School Robotics
citation: Toni Earle-Randell, Chris Palaguachi, Joanne Barrett, Jennie Lee, Jina Kang, Maya Israel (2026). Designing for Collaboration: An Engineering Notebook to Scaffold Collaborative Problem- Solving in Middle School Robotics. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Earle-Randell, T., Palaguachi, C., Barrett, J., Lee, J., Kang, J., & Israel, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: Engineering notebooks are pervasive in K-12 robotics as a record of work throughout the competitive season. While these team notebooks are designed to document the engineering design process and students’ learning, they have the potential to foster effective collaboration, with students working together rather than in parallel. Capitalizing on this potential, we introduce a new type of robotics (VEX IQ) engineering notebook designed to facilitate collaborative learning for middle schoolers. By integrating pair programming, the Engineering Design Process, and structured prompts for team and code reflection, our notebook serves as an intervention that trans forms documentation practice, scaffolds collaborative problem -solving, and makes collaboration a central tenet of the engineering experience.

title: “It Wasn’t So Outside of the Box, But It Wasn’t Something I Would Have Thought About”: AI as a Creative Collaborator in Student Problem Solving
citation: Ibrahim Oluwajoba Adisa, Victoria Delaney (2026). “It Wasn’t So Outside of the Box, But It Wasn’t Something I Would Have Thought About”: AI as a Creative Collaborator in Student Problem Solving. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Adisa, I. O. & Delaney, V.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study examines how students experience collaboration with generative AI during creative problem -solving. Using post -interview data, we analyze students’ perceptions of creativity and agency across three human –AI writing modes. Findings show that stude nts treated AI as a responsive collaborator that expanded ideas and supported refinement, but was most valued for structuring and improving efficiency. The richest collaborations occurred when students remained active in both generating and refining ideas. These results highlight how generative AI differentially supports divergent and convergent thinking and suggest that balanced, iterative interaction is key to preserving agency in human–AI co-creation.

title: Are We There Yet? The Roles and Development of GenAI-Based Tools Supporting Collaborative Learning: A Scoping Review
citation: Maya Persico, Daeun Hong, Jerika Miller, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Freydis Vogel (2026). Are We There Yet? The Roles and Development of GenAI-Based Tools Supporting Collaborative Learning: A Scoping Review. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Persico, M., Hong, D., Miller, J., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Vogel, F.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: Tools based on generative AI (genAI), i nteracting with learners in a human -like manner, such as conversational agents and ChatGPT, offer potential to develop adaptive support for collaborative learning. Following PRISMA guidelines, after screening results of searching three databases, our scoping review identified 239 relevant records reporting about genAI tools in CSCL including 138 empirical articles this paper focuses on. They were analyzed in depth regarding genAI tool’s maturity level of implementation in collaborative learning, and the role genAI takes within . Results show studies at different levels of maturity in implementation of the genAI tool ranging from designing the tool or investigating its usability to studies focusing on human learning outcomes. GenAI takes multiple roles simultaneously, mostly providing epistemic and metacognitive scaffolding to individuals or groups. Our results indicate substantial development in the growing number of empirical articles , while pointing out gaps in specific support type provision, especially for school learners.

title: Collaboration Quality in Computational Modeling: Implications for Middle -School STEM+C Learning
citation: Shruti Jain, Namrata Srivastava, Srigowri Mayasandra Prasanna, Clayton Cohn, Umesh Timalsina (2026). Collaboration Quality in Computational Modeling: Implications for Middle -School STEM+C Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Jain, S., Srivastava, N., Prasanna, S. M., Cohn, C., & Timalsina, U.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Collaboration is recognized by NGSS as an important 21st -century skill, yet its role in middle -school STEM+C remains underexplored. This study examines how students collaborate while building computational models (CM) of scientific processes and how it relates to learning outcomes. We coded 16 hours of activity from eight dyads across Meier et al.’s nine collaboration dimensions (e.g., mutual understanding, dialogue management, information pooling) and analyzed links between collaboration quality, model performance, and assessment scores. Findings highlight the dynamics of CM collaboration and the need for scaffolds that promote productive interaction and teach collaboration as a transferable skill.

title: Scaffolding Knowledge Building through Ordered-Epistemic Network Analysis-Supported Reflective Assessment and Meta-Discourse
citation: Xiaojie Zhang, Carol K.K. Chan, Shihui Feng, Jianhua Zhao (2026). Scaffolding Knowledge Building through Ordered-Epistemic Network Analysis-Supported Reflective Assessment and Meta-Discourse. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Zhang, X., Chan, C. K., Feng, S., & Zhao, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)
abstract: This study presents a reflective assessment approach supported by ordered-epistemic network analysis (ONA) tools, designed to enhance students’ knowledge building (KB) and discourse within the Knowledge Forum. While prior research has demonstrated that re flective assessments integrated with learning analytics can improve students’ metacognitive skills and self-regulation in knowledge -building contexts, this study uniquely incorporates ONA -based reflection and meta- discourse to elucidate and promot e the dynamics and trajectories of epistemic moves during the knowledge-building process. The participants comprised 40 Year 5 students engaged in a collective inquiry into metabolism using the Knowledge Forum. Quantitative results indicated that, followin g the intervention, students exhibited increased levels of social and community interaction, alongside more sophisticated epistemological beliefs. Qualitative analysis further illustrated how ONA -facilitated reflective assessment enriched students’ collaborative inquiry process. This work advances pedagogy in knowledge building by demonstrating that ONA -enhanced reflective assessment and meta- discourse can effectively support and deepen collaborative knowledge construction.

title: Facilitating High School Students’ Socially Shared Regulation of Learning Through STEM Inquiry into Local Air Quality and Asthma
citation: Ho Sue Kwon, Catherine Roeroe, Susan A. Yoon (2026). Facilitating High School Students’ Socially Shared Regulation of Learning Through STEM Inquiry into Local Air Quality and Asthma. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Kwon, H. S., Roeroe, C., & Yoon, S. A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: This exploratory study examines how collaborative learning environments mediated by mobile technology facilitate socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) in high school STEM education. Ten high school students in three small groups investigated local air quality and asthma using handheld sensors to collect indoor and outdoor data. We analyzed 3.5 hours of video data using interaction and thematic analysis guided by the cognitive dimensions of SSRL. Findings show that SSRL emerged most prominently in moments of uncertainty which catalyzed collective monitoring, hypothesis generation, and goal -directed planning. Three design features supported these processes: (1) structured autonomy that shifted troubleshooting from external support to student-led, (2) authentic inquiry that turned technological breakdowns into regulatory opportunities, and (3) real -world constraints that extended collaboration. The study contributes to understanding SSRL as a naturally occurring phenomenon in authentic high school STEM contexts and offers design principles for leveraging uncertainty for facilitating SSRL.

title: MIRACLE: Multi-Agent Intelligent Regulation to Advance Collaborative Learning Environment
citation: Shuang Li, Haiyang Xin, Yimeng Sun, Qiannan Niu, Lingyun Huang, Gaowei Chen, Yibing Zhang, Ching Sing Chai (2026). MIRACLE: Multi-Agent Intelligent Regulation to Advance Collaborative Learning Environment. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Li, S., Xin, H., Sun, Y., Niu, Q., Huang, L., Chen, G., Zhang, Y., & Chai, C. S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Classroom Orchestration
abstract: Effective collaboration requires Socially Shared Regulation (SSRL), but students often lack these skills. This study introduces the MIRACLE (Multi-Agent Intelligent Regulation to Advance Collaborative Learning Environment ) system, which supports SSRL by orchestrating metacognitive regulation and proactively providing emotional and motivational support. We conducted a quasi -experimental study with 90 fifth- grade students. The experimental group (n=42) used a collaborative platform CocoNote equipped with MIRACLE, while the control group (n=48) used the same platform with a general GPT assistant. Quantitative results show the MIRACLE group achieved significant gains across SSRL phases (Planning, Monitoring, Reflection) and produced higher -quality collaborative artifacts compared to the control group . Qualitative findings indicate students perceived MIRACLE as an effective facilitator for cognitive, regulatory, and emotional support. This study demonstrates that specialized, orchestrated AI systems are more effective than generic AI in enhancing SSRL.

title: Unveiling Role Dynamics in AR-Based Collaborative Inquiry
citation: Xinyue Jiao, Zifeng Liu (2026). Unveiling Role Dynamics in AR-Based Collaborative Inquiry. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Jiao, X. & Liu, Z.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Augmented Reality (AR) has emerged as a transformative tool in education, offering authentic and interactive environments for collaborative inquiry. However, collaborative interaction among group members in AR-based inquiry, particularly how roles are enacted and exchanged, remains underexplored. This study investigates role interaction patterns in AR - supported collaborative inquiry and analyzes how role dynamics between group members influence learning outcomes. Eighty students working in pairs engaged in AR-based scientific inquiry tasks. Video recordings were coded and analyzed. Cluster analysis shows that three distinct patterns emerged: Balanced, Dominant, and Passive. The Balanced pattern featured reciprocal Question–Respond–Experiment–Share behavioral sequences; Dominant dyads exhibited leader–follower dynamics, while Passive dyads demonstrated minimal engagement and weak regulation. Quantitative results showed that active participation, regardless of balance or dominance , was associated with higher learning outcomes. These findings advance understanding of how role dynamics unfold in immersive learning environments, offering insights for promoting effective collaboration.

title: Inquiry Script Modeling: A Formalism for Scripting and Orchestration of Collective Inquiry
citation: Erfane Ghasempour Khoshroodi, James D. Slotta (2026). Inquiry Script Modeling: A Formalism for Scripting and Orchestration of Collective Inquiry. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Khoshroodi, E. G. & Slotta, J. D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper introduces Inquiry Script Modeling (ISM), a formalism designed to represent and operationalize inquiry -oriented learning workflows in classrooms that adopt a learning community approach. Drawing on prior CSCL research, including process modeling and orchestration frameworks, ISM supports interpretability, temporal sequencing, and adaptability. This paper presents ISM using a use case focused on AI and disinformation, to show how such formalisms can help teachers to design, communicate, and dynamically manage complex collaborative learning scripts.

title: Programming Self-Efficacy and Outcomes, and Programming-oriented Prompting: A Comparison of Two Human–AI Collaboration Configurations
citation: Ying-Tien Wu, Yi-Hong Zeng, Ching-Hui Kuan (2026). Programming Self-Efficacy and Outcomes, and Programming-oriented Prompting: A Comparison of Two Human–AI Collaboration Configurations. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Wu, Y., Zeng, Y., & Kuan, C.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study investigates the effects of GenAI -assisted programming learning on fifth graders’ computational thinking, programming self-efficacy and outcomes, and programming - oriented prompting. A total of 99 fifth graders from four classes participated and were randomly assigned to two GenAI -assisted programming instruction groups with different human– AI collaboration configurations: single student -AI collaboration (SSAC), in which each student worked individually with a computer with ChatGPT, and dyad student -AI collaboration (DSAC), in which two students worked in pairs, collaboratively using a shared computer with ChatGPT. The instruction was implemented over 6 weeks (1 class per week). This study revealed no significant difference in computational thinking between the two groups of students after GenAI-assisted programming instruction ( p>0.05). In contrast, the students in the DSAC group showed significantly higher programming self -efficacy and better programming outcomes ( p<0.05). Moreover, significant differences in the distribution of programming- oriented prompting between these two groups of students were also found ( p<0.05).

title: Teacher Perception and Practices of the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS): Insights from a New England Study
citation: Anupam Raj, Michael Wittmann (2026). Teacher Perception and Practices of the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS): Insights from a New England Study. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Raj, A. & Wittmann, M.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: This qualitative study explores how secondary science teachers understand and implement two core dimensions of the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS): Science and Engineering Practices (SEPs) and Crosscutting Concepts (CCCs). Drawing on semi - structured interviews with ten teachers from schools serving economically diverse communities in a New England state, the analysis reveals distinct orientations toward SEPs . These orientations range from identity -based and assessment -aligned approaches to emerging understanding through professional learning. In contrast, CCCs appeared less intentionally addressed, with most teachers using them as implicit outcomes rather than explicit instructional goals. A few teachers, however, used CCCs to promote interdisciplinary connections and support comparative reasoning. These findings highlight variation in teachers’ enactment of NGSS dimensions and the need for ongoing professional learning that supports integration of SEPs and CCCs. The study contributes to efforts to bridge the gap between policy vision and classroom realities in three-dimensional science teaching and assessment.

title: Designing AI Partner-Embedded Learning Environments to Support AI Literacies
citation: Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Marcelo Worsley, Michael Alan Chang, Chelsea Chandler, Sierra Rose (2026). Designing AI Partner-Embedded Learning Environments to Support AI Literacies. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Ko, M. M., Worsley, M., Chang, M. A., Chandler, C., & Rose, S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Boundary Crossing & Brokerage; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: As AI technologies become increasingly integrated into schools, questions arise about what students should learn about AI and how AI-powered tools can support collaborative learning. This symposium reports on the Institute of Student-AI Teaming (iSAT), which designs AI partners and curricular activity systems to promote AI literacy and collaboration. Unlike most classroom AI tools designed for 1:1 interactions, iSAT develops AI partners as social collaborators that both facilitate group learning and serve as objects of inquiry —helping students “look under the hood” of AI systems. Our multi -year co-design process across three U.S. states engages teachers, students, and parents to build integrated systems of curriculum, technology, and professional learning. The symposium’s six posters span AI design, infrastructure, curriculum, and teacher learning, illustrating how AI can be productively embedded within classroom collaboration. Together, they advance understanding of how AI systems can meaningfully support and transform collaborative learning. Objective of the session As AI technologies become increasingly embedded in education (Reich & Dukes, 2024), so do questions about what students should learn about AI systems (AI literacy) and how AI -powered tools may support (or hinder) student learning. While there is growing excitement about AI’s potential to transform education, decades of research highlight repeated failures of earlier innovations to do so. Scholars argue these failures often stem from underappreciating the infrastructural nature of technology and overestimating its power to drive change in classroom practice (Roschelle et al., 2010). First, technology is infrastructural in that its value lies not in its particular content but in its ability to generate new representations of disciplinary ideas and create opportunities for students to engage more deeply in those ideas (Hegedus & Kaput, 2003). Second, like previous technologies, today’s AI tools will not transform education on their own. Their success depends on how curriculum activity systems—teacher professional learning (PL), instructional materials, and technology —work together to reshape learning environments (Vahey et al., 2013). Their success also depends on how teachers and students work together within the system to support learning. This symposium reports on work from the Institute of Student-AI Teaming (iSAT), an institute that aims to design AI -powered tools and curricular activity systems that promote collaborative knowledge building and student learning around AI -literacy specifically (D’Mello et al., 2024, OECD, 2025). Our project intentionally combines both AI -literacy and AI as a tool for collaborative learning in ways that will enable the AI -partner to serve simultaneously as a collaboration support and an object of inquiry as students think critically about how the AI works. That is, our AI partners play a dual role of supporting student collaboration and as a tool for “looking under the hood” at how AI systems work. Supporting collaborative learning is a longstanding goal of both the ISLS and CSCL community, and is crucial because we know that learning is inherently a social process. Yet, the dominant approach to incorporating AI inside K-12 classrooms focuses on 1:1 interactions between students and AI systems. iSAT’s approach is radically different: we aim to develop AI as a social, collaborative partner that works alongside students and teachers to deepen their engagement with one another. This goal has required that our team engage in multi -year co-design processes to better understand the needs and desires of multiple users 556 and stakeholders (e.g. teachers, students, parents) as we work to develop and refine AI partners, curriculum materials, and professional development to support the development of AI literacies. Over the past five years, our work has involved working with stakeholders in districts across three U.S. states to conceptualize, develop, enact, and refine our curricular activity system. This session will focus on the design of iSAT’s curricular activity system to deepen the field’s conversation about the role of AI -systems in supporting collaborative learning. Across the posters, we will describe how our co- design practices, back -end models, classroom pilot studies, professional learning, and curricular routines and designs worked toward our emerging understanding of the utility of these tools for supporting collaborative learning. Overview of the symposium The 6 posters that constitute the symposium represent our collective efforts to take seriously what it means for AI systems to partner within the curricular activity systems of secondary schools. Poster 1 will detail the trajectory of co-design for our first AI partner, the Community Builder (CoBi) and how the ongoing design, implementation and analysis of the co- design space informed the values of our institute. Poster 2 will present on the design, development, and pilot studies of our second Jigsaw Interactive Agent (JIA) in secondary classrooms and how productive uncertainty was leveraged to design the AI partner interventions to suppo rt small group jigsaws. In Poster 3, we will report on the architecture and analytic pipeline that underlies our two existing AI partners, documenting how the pipeline infrastructure, state detection and dialogue policies inform the AI- partner outputs and interventions. Posters 4-6 address how we built both curriculum materials and teachers’ capacities to leverage them so that the AI partners could be meaningfully integrated into everyday classroom activities. In Poster 4, we examine how curricular routines can support students' sensemaking of their own collaborative practices. In Poster 5, we show how our PL design supported teachers’ learning about AI, our AI literacy curriculum and pedagogical approaches that center student sensemaking. Finally, Poster 6 describes the design and refinement of our curriculum materials that focus on AI literacy, a process guided by co- design, adaptation and refinement with teachers in their classrooms. Scholarly significance This session is both timely and essential. First, AI tools are becoming increasingly embedded in schools and in our world. At the same time, few teachers are currently prepared to teach about AI, use AI -enabled tools, and adopt student-centered, collaborative pedagogies—what we call a triple innovation challenge . We also know that external forces (e.g. social and news media) shape students’ understanding of AI, and that schools/educators play a less significant role (OECD, 2025) This session highlights a new approach to supporting AI literacy through the design of curricular activity systems where AI Partners are meaningfully embedded to support AI literacies through collaborative learning. Structure of the session The symposium will be organized as a structured poster session. The chair of the session will first provide a brief overview of the session (4 mins). Each presenter will give a one -minute elevator pitch to introduce their project (6 mins). Presenters will then move to their respective posters; participants can view posters, demos (if applicable) and engage in discussion. We will invite participants to engage in two “rounds” of poster-viewing (30 mins each), so that co-presenters have a chance to view other s’ posters . Our discussant will synthesize the posters and pose questions for the audience to discuss, focusing on the challenges and affordances of AI -powered systems in supporting collaborative learning in schools (20 minutes). CoBi Origins: Co-design narratives as boundary objects to translate Co-design findings into interdisciplinary implementation Michael Alan Chang Objectives Collaborative and participatory design is increasingly used to inform the design and implementation of AI -Ed tools that are responsive to the needs and lived experiences of interest holders (Ravi et al., 2025). An AI -Ed research team hosts a co -design context, completes an analysis of it, and then responds to the co- design efforts through implementation. While this sequential and linear process simplifies the already complex and interdisciplinary process of building AI-Ed tools, it can constrain both the types of analysis that can be conducted within the co-design context and the ways in which stakeholders can engage in the ongoing design of AI-Ed tools 557 (Chang, under review). Here, I share our efforts in iSAT, where there were parallel, longitudinal efforts to (a) develop and analyze a three- year co-design study with high school youth to surface their hopes and concerns around the use of AI in schools and (b) respond to the findings of those co- design studies to develop AI partners and curricular activity systems that surround the use of the technology. Here, I ask: how does the ongoing design, implementation, and analysis of co- design spaces shape the des ign activities of an interdisciplinary research institute? Perspectives Here, I view stories about co-design activities as an evolving boundary object that guides how large-scale AI-Ed implementation teams take on co-design findings (Star & Griesemer, 1989). Boundary objects are conceptualized as “how artifacts can fulfill a specific function in bridging intersecting practices” (pg. 134, Akkerman & Bakker, 2011). As Star (2010) clarifies, a boundary object is characterized by interpretive flexibility across different contexts, allowing each context to tailor the object to its own needs locally. Finally, boundary objects follow particular trajectories within organizational contexts; once created, boundary objects evolve through local tailoring, standardize over time, and, finally, fade away as the standardization practices begin to constrain possible local adaptations. In turn, new boundary objects are then created.

title: Revisiting Wise and Schwarz’s Provocations for CSCL: Partnerships for Transformation and Educational Change
citation: Breneil Malcolm, Marcela Borge, Alyssa Wise, Marcelo Worsley, Sebastian Simon, Tanner Vea (2026). Revisiting Wise and Schwarz’s Provocations for CSCL: Partnerships for Transformation and Educational Change. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Malcolm, B., Borge, M., Wise, A., Worsley, M., Simon, S., & Vea, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In 2017, Wise and Schwarz proposed eight provocations for the field of CSCL following their interactions and analyses with scholars within the field. We broaden the call to the entire LS community to once again pause, reflect, and discuss a vision for the next 10 years of opportunities, challenges, and impacts we seek to make. This collective ambition is not simply to be responsive to technological changes but also to inform their design and use. Towards this end, we invited researchers from the ICLS and CSCL communities to propose new provocations for us to consider and discuss that focus both on the changing technological landscape and the need to ensure that diverse perspectives and viewpoints are brought into the forefront of technology-enhanced collaboration in meaningful ways.

title: Rise Above State-of-the-Art: Designing New Possibilities of GenAI for Knowledge Building
citation: Jiayu Cheng, Vivian Leung, Yue Zhao, Chen Wang, Bodong Chen, Jianwei Zhang, Yanqing Sun, Sudarshan Kammu, Mei-Hwa Chen, Seng Chee Tan, Yee Yin Tan, Chew Lee Teo, Guangji Yuan, Xueqi Feng (2026). Rise Above State-of-the-Art: Designing New Possibilities of GenAI for Knowledge Building. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Cheng, J., Leung, V., Zhao, Y., Wang, C., Chen, B., Zhang, J., Sun, Y., Kammu, S., Chen, M., Tan, S. C., Tan, Y. Y., Teo, C. L., Yuan, G., & Feng, X.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This symposium presents cutting- edge research that explores how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) can be leveraged to enrich human-AI collaboration in CSCL for Knowledge Building (KB). It challenges prevailing educational paradigms of ‘learning from AI’ and instead it foregrounds collaborative creation, emphasizing how GenAI can be harnessed to enrich epistemic agency empowering learners in knowledge building. Building on four decades of KB research, this symposium aims to enrich both the conceptualization and design of human- AI collaboration for knowledge advancement. Seven interrelated contributions demonstrate emergent KB -AI design approaches, including dialogic approaches that engage learners in collaborative dialogue with AI, and integrated approaches that embed AI affordances into knowledge building environments. These designs span diverse contexts from doctoral interdisciplinary research to K -12 classrooms. Grounded in a design-based approach, this symposium positions these contributions as conceptual artifacts for design advancement and envisions new KB-AI synergies that enable emerging forms of CSCL and knowledge creation.

title: Towards a Robust Theory Toolbox for CSCL: Mechanisms, Models, and AI
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Davinia Hernández-Leo, Peter Reimann, Alyssa Wise, Fanjie Li, Hans C. Arnseth (2026). Towards a Robust Theory Toolbox for CSCL: Mechanisms, Models, and AI. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Ludvigsen, S., Hernández-Leo, D., Reimann, P., Wise, A., Li, F., & Arnseth, H. C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
tpack_tk_labels: Generative AI & LLMs; Simulations & Scientific Modeling
abstract: This symposium aims to foster new scientific discussions about how the CSCL (Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning) field can advance towards more robust theories. Such advancements depend on further development and formalization of models, causal mechanisms, and the creative application of different types of generative AI. The problem description is rooted in the increasing gap between theoretical positions and actual data, also emphasizing that data alone cannot explain any phenomenon. The overarching argument is that computational modeling approaches can be employed to formalize models of collaborative scripts, temporal collaborative processes, multi- level collaboration, and multimodal activities and that varied uses of AI can amplify such efforts . These models can be based on causal mechanisms and can be generalized to collaborative learning phenomena rather than just specific populations. We provide a rich view of the CSCL field that includes pathways to theoretical robustness, practical tools and solutions for collborative learning in the age of AI.

title: Partnering Through Ceremony: A Multimodal Design for Collaborative Healing and Learning
