abstract: This poster presents an early -stage ceremonial design for collaborative learning rooted in Indigenous methodologies and relational accountability. Through multimodal documentation and AI assisted poetic co creation, the work explores how ceremony can support healing centered learning across generations and technologies. The poster highlights design commitments, a simplified conjecture map and emerging expressions that invite discussion about how socio-technical systems can participate in relational meaning making.

title: Using Artificial Intelligence as a Critical Thinking Partner: A Conceptual Demonstration
citation: Spenser Clark (2026). Using Artificial Intelligence as a Critical Thinking Partner: A Conceptual Demonstration. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Clark, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are often uncritical, sycophantic, and can lead to offloading critical thinking (CT). This risks the atrophy of CT skills by removing the practice necessary to maintain them. I argue for using GenAI as a CT partner to encourage a user's CT abilities. Here, I present a framework for creating such a partner through system prompting and conceptually demonstrate how this can be done. Designing an AI critical thinking partner Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers academics a problematic choice. On the one hand, general - purpose chatbots are highly adaptable but are plagued by two significant flaws for scholarly use: sycophancy, a tendency toward uncritical agreeableness, and hallucination, the generation of fabricated information (OpenAI, 2025). On the other hand, other products can automate various research activities but may risk cognitive offloading (see Darwin et al., 2024; Gerlich, 2025; Wang & Sun) . The academic is left to choose between an unreliable conversationalist and tools which do the thinking for them . However, it is possible to use computer - assisted technology to increase CT (Cress & Kimmerle, 2023; Tedla & Chen, 2025). Here, I present a framework for the use of GenAI as a critical thinking partner. In this approach, AI encourages the user's own analytical and evaluative abilities. For AI to behave as a CT partner requires a shift in the AI’s role and persona as a helpful general-purpose assistant to a cognitive guide. System instruction prompts are "behind-the-scenes, system-level instructions that set the AI’s behavior, tone, or scope before any user input" (MIT, 2025) and can be used to constrain the AI to embody a domain-specific role (Borge et al., 2024). Below, I describe a system instruction prompt which can be used to create a CT partner . For the purposes of this paper, I take the etymology of critical (Greek κριτικός (kritikos) meaning ‘able to discern’ or ‘the power of discerning’ (Logeion, n.d.)) and build on it within a research context, defining CT as the set of cognitive processes related to evaluating ideas, considering the implications of propositions, investigating the truth of premises, and interrogating the validity of conclusions. An AI CT partner, therefore, is a chatbot that encourages and cooperates in the exercise of these abilities. The full text of the prompt is as below: # Role and Persona You are a critical thinking partner. Your primary purpose is to assist with the intellectual pursuits of the user in a manner that promotes critical thinking. You will help the user strengthen their arguments, ideas, and analyses through rigorous and constructive discussion. # Behavioral Rules

title: Trans-Ecological Disruptions and Pedagogical Interventions in GAI-Supported Collaborative Learning
citation: Yue Han, Wen Qi (2026). Trans-Ecological Disruptions and Pedagogical Interventions in GAI-Supported Collaborative Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Han, Y. & Qi, W.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: In generative AI (GAI) integrated collaborative learning, conflicts are often misattributed to interpersonal dynamics, ignoring the learning environment's critical role. This mixed-methods case study of 41 middle school students applies a micro- ecological framework to investigate how environmental design flaws trigger trans -ecological disruptions. Using qualitative analysis, Lag Sequential Analysis, Social Network Analysis, and Temporal Exponential Random Graph Models, we robustly reveal that coll aborative conflicts propagate from environmental triggers to group interaction networks via individual cognitive pathways.

title: Fostering Cocreativity in Primary Education Through Viacocrea: Effects on Students’ Creative Products
citation: Maria Sitjà Martín, Manoli Pifarré Turmo (2026). Fostering Cocreativity in Primary Education Through Viacocrea: Effects on Students’ Creative Products. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Martín, M. S. & Turmo, M. P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores how the Viacocrea technology platform enhances cocreative processes in primary education. Twenty-five twelve-year-old students participated in a project- based learning intervention, creating digital infographics collaboratively. Students’ creative outcomes were assessed using Guilford’s creativity dimensions (1950): fluency, flexibility, and originality. Findings show that Viacocrea effectively supported idea generation, adaptation, and originality, embedding creative processes throughout the project. This study demonstrates that technology can foster cocreativity within the curriculum, offering practical insights for teaching collaborative and creative skills in primary classrooms.

title: AI as a Collaborative Partner: EMPA’s Role in Supporting Reflective Teamwork Learning
citation: Aparajita Jaiswal, Ashish Ashish (2026). AI as a Collaborative Partner: EMPA’s Role in Supporting Reflective Teamwork Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Jaiswal, A. & Ashish, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Teamwork requires students to reflect on their practices, yet individualized mentoring is often limited. While AI tutoring systems increasingly support learning, most position AI as external evaluator rather than collaborative partner. We present EMPA, an AI - based collaborative partner that scaffolds teamwork learning through case studies, activities, and videos. Grounded in Schön’s reflection -in-action and reflection -on-action, EMPA encourages students to adapt strategies during tasks and analyze experiences afterwards. Students engage with scenarios and activities while EMPA prompts real -time reflection, then receive personalized summaries and complete surveys that consolidate learning. Early deployment with undergraduates shows EMPA’s potential to help learners examine assumptions, recognize cultural dynamics, and develop strategies for improving collaboration. This study operationalizes Schön’s framework via AI-supported mentoring, positioning AI as a reflective partner to scale practice and strengthen teamwork.

title: Boundary Spanning Narratives in a Constructionist Museum Game
citation: Eda Zhang, Matthew Berland, Yunseo Lee (2026). Boundary Spanning Narratives in a Constructionist Museum Game. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Zhang, E., Berland, M., & Lee, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: Museum learning is highly social (Allen, 2004). To support and enable socioculturally mediated learning, previous studies have demonstrated how designing exhibits for collaboration can yield productive learning outcomes and engagement. However, few studies have explored the learning value of naturalistic collaborative play in museums (in which there are no explicit prompts/scaffolds for collaboration). We present a museum game and both computational and qualitative observations of interaction modes. Visito rs showed diverse collaborative and cooperative behaviors, including clarification, seeking help, negotiation, goal- adaptation, and modeling. Our analysis also revealed that boundary spanning narration (or BSN, Tissenbaum et al., 2017) enabled “talk with evidence of learning.” Additionally, we found that social play (in this case, cooperative and competitive play) varied with the types and amount of BSN. Through the mediation of BSN, two- person visitor groups (“dyads”) co- constructed knowledge, coordinated on tasks, and set shared goals for themselves in non- competitive play, while in competitive play, dyads tended to use BSN towards surveillance and dominating play.

title: Neurodiversity in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: A Literature Review
citation: Greta Heathcote, Alison Nelson, Armando Paulino Preciado Babb (2026). Neurodiversity in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: A Literature Review. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Heathcote, G., Nelson, A., & Babb, A. P. P.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: R ecent evidence has shown a significant prevalence of neurodivergence in the general population, suggesting that many learners, including students and research participants, are neurodivergent. This situation entails potential concerns for both research results interpretations and ethical considerations. In this context, we explore d the intersection of neurodiversity and the CSCL through a review of its international journal and handbook, finding a minimal use of neurodiversity- related terminology , despite indirect references to neurodivergent traits. The study identified 58 publications with potential reference to the neurodivergent population by filtering key terms—such as equity, inclusion, and low ability— that align with neurodivergent experiences, though often without explicit acknowledgment. We conclude that there is a significant gap in explicit consideration of neurodivergent learners within CSCL scholarship and argue that the CSCL community may have inadvertently included neurodivergent participants.

title: What Draws Upvotes? Examining Relationships between Interpersonal Skills and Social Annotation Behaviors in Online Settings
citation: Hanxiang Du, Jiyoung Cheong, Gaoxia Zhu, Xiaoshan Huang, Shan Li, Juan Zheng, Jacqueline Tan (2026). What Draws Upvotes? Examining Relationships between Interpersonal Skills and Social Annotation Behaviors in Online Settings. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Du, H., Cheong, J., Zhu, G., Huang, X., Li, S., Zheng, J., & Tan, J.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: In s ocial annotation learning settings, u pvotes serve as feedback and a source of motivation, social connection, and validation, yet factors influencing upvote patterns remain under-explored. This study examined relationships between upvote count and students’ interpersonal skills, performance, and annotation behaviors . We analyzed 7,482 annotations from 93 undergraduate students using Perusall over seven weeks. We observed no strong correlations between the upvote count and students’ interpersonal skills, automated evaluation score, reply count, or posting order. Objectives and significance Social annotation, which refers to a collaborative process in which instructors and students highlight, comment on, and discuss course materials (Novak et al., 2012), has become a transformative pedagogical approach to promote active learning and community -building in online learning. It fosters deeper reading engagement and comprehension by making thinking visible and creating opportunities for intellectual exchange (Zhu et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2024) . Upvoting is a prevalent feature in social annotation platforms, enabling users to express approval and engage with peers’ contributions (Li et al., 2024). Upvotes can serve as a powerful social signal that influences content visibility and shapes discourse. Previous studies indicate that upvotes in social annotation are associated with both content -related and interpersonal cues and can potentially shape students’ learning experience and perceived learning outcomes (Huang et al., 2024). However, the empirical evidence about the factors behind these upvote count in online social annotation settings remains limited. The current study seeks to address this gap. Specifically, we focused on the following question: What are the relationships between upvote count and students’ interpersonal skills and social annotation behaviors? Study design and methods This study was conducted during the Winter semester in an undergraduate learning media course at a North American university with 97 students (47 female; Age Mean = 20.67). Four students withdrew, yielding a final sample of 93. Students were assigned to 16 small groups and engaged in collaborative reading and discussion activities using Perusall, which allows students to asynchronously annotate course readings by highlighting text, posing texts, and replying. The platform also features automatic scoring that evaluates students ’ contributions based on criteria such as relevance, quality, and engagement. Over the seven -week activities , students were required to annotate ten readings. A total of 7,482 annotations were collected, including original annotations, replies, upvotes, timestamps, and system-generated scores. To examine individuals’ interpersonal competencies, we adapted an interpersonal skills survey based on Riggio’s six dimensions (Lee et al., 2015). The survey consists of seven items measuring self-perceived behaviors such as empathy, open-mindedness, communication, conflict resolution, and adaptability, rated on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly Disagree, 7 = Strongly Agree). A total of 84 participants completed the survey. To address the research questions, we examined the relationship among several key variables. Students’ responses to the interpersonal skill surveys were used to measure their interpersonal skills. The content quality of their annotations was measured using Perusall’s automated evaluation score. W e also explored students’ social annotation behaviors in terms of reply count and posting order. Reply count is the total number of replies an annotation received, and posting order refers to the time an annotation was posted. To identify the posting order, 624 we retrieved the posting timestamp for each annotation within each set of reading materials, with the earliest social annotation marked as 1. In other words, if a document contains n annotations, the most recently posted annotation has the posting order n. Results To address the research question, we analyzed several relationships: (1) upvote count and the automated evaluation score provided by Perusall , (2) upvote count and the number of replies each annotation received , (3) upvote count and the posting order of each annotation, and (4) students’ total upvote count and their interpersonal skill scores . Table 1 presents the results using Spearman correlation. Although the first three variables were statistically significant, all variables were weakly correlated with the upvote count. Posting order and interpersonal skills were negatively and weakly correlated with the upvote count. Table 1 The Correlation between the Upvote Count and Automated Evaluation Score, Online Social Annotation Behaviors, and Interpersonal Skills Automated Score Reply Count Posting Order Interpersonal Skills Upvote count .107* .159* -.050* -.027 *: p < 0.05 Discussion and conclusion This study examined factors influencing upvote patterns in social annotation by analyzing 7,482 annotations from 93 undergraduate students. Contrary to expectations based on social presence theory (Arbaugh et al., 2008) , interpersonal skills showed weak negative correlations with upvote counts. Students with higher self -reported interpersonal competencies did not receive more peer recognition through upvotes. This result challenges assumptions about social dynamics in online learning environments (Chen et al., 2024) . Similarly, Perusall’s automated evaluation scores correlated only weakly with upvotes. This disconnect ion between algorithmic assessment and peer recognition suggests that students value different qualities in annotations than those captured by automated systems. Peer preferences appear to diverge from traditional academic quality metrics. The weak relationship between automated scores and upvotes also suggests caution in using peer feedback mechanisms for assessment purposes. Upvotes appear to r eflect student interests rather than content quality, making them unsuitable as primary evaluation tools. There are limitations to this work. Our findings were based on certain topics in that course and the generalization to other disciplines may be limited. Future research should explore the cognitive and emotional factors underlying topic preferences in upvoting behavior. Understanding why certain topics consistently attract more peer acknowledgement could inform more equitable discussion design. Moreover, investigating student motivations for upvoting through interviews or structured feedback would provide valuable insights into peer recognition patterns. Finally, researchers might explore whether instructor intervention can balance attention across different annotation types. References Arbaugh, J. B., Cleveland-Innes, M., Diaz, S. R., Garrison, D. title: Exploring STEM Teachers’ AI Readiness, Attitudes, and Uses of Generative AI across Teaching Subjects

subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study explores the integration of AI among Taiwanese STEM teachers, revealing a shift from utilitarian tool use toward co -creative partnership. While efficiency - driven tasks currently predominate, innovative applications are emerging in interdisciplinary contexts. Disciplinary norms significantly influence adoption: mathematics teachers prioritize precision, while science and interdisciplinary teachers leverage AI for creative integration. The findings suggest that professional development could provide discipline-specific support to empower teachers as collaborative partners in AI-integrated classrooms.

title: The Relationship between Argumentative Discourse Sequences with Generative AI and Students’ Argumentative Writing Structure
citation: Kyungri Kim (2026). The Relationship between Argumentative Discourse Sequences with Generative AI and Students’ Argumentative Writing Structure. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Kim, K.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This poster examines how sixth- grade students' argumentative discourse with generative AI relates to the structure of their subsequent argumentative writing. Using Pragma- dialectical stages for discourse and Toulmin elements for essays, the study found that AI - mediated dialogue was dominated by confrontation -oriented claim and rebuttal sequences, while students' essays showed stronger transfer of data and backing than rebuttal, warrant, or qualifier use. The findings suggest that generative AI can support evidence -based argument writing when classroom prompts explicitly scaffold warrants, qualifiers, and reflection on opposing positions. Key words: Generative AI, argumentative discourse, AI-learner interaction, sequence analysis, writing transfer

title: Belonging Infrastructure: A Designable Construct for Cultivating Teacher Agency in RPPs
citation: Gregory Benedis-Grab, Alexandra Gendreau Chakarov (2026). Belonging Infrastructure: A Designable Construct for Cultivating Teacher Agency in RPPs. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Benedis-Grab, G. & Chakarov, A. G.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs) often rely on boundary infrastructure to explain how collaboration is organized, but this lens overlooks how teacher agency is cultivated. We introduce belonging infrastructure, the designable features of collaboration that legitimize participant contributions and make belonging visible. Evidence from a teacher co -design workshop demonstrates how this construct provides a new lens for intentionally designing partnerships that foster teacher leadership, build district capacity, and expand who feels authorized to teach computer science.

title: Resolving Conceptual Contradictions through Transformative Integration
citation: Weiyi Xiao (2026). Resolving Conceptual Contradictions through Transformative Integration. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Xiao, W.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: This paper proposes transformative integration as a more desirable approach to resolving contradictions in contemporary educational collaboration. It conceptualizes transformative integration as the generation of thirdness and operationalizes thirdness as a Principle of Transformation (PoT) or as an actionable solution derived from it. In doing so, the paper lays the groundwork for systematically identifying and intentionally cultivating thirdness in practice, thereby supporting creativity- oriented collaboratio n and students’ meaningful participation in democratic, innovation-driven societies.

title: Rotating Leadership of Transactive Discourse through Synchrony and Desynchrony of Multimodal Interaction
citation: Jun Lu, Jun Oshima (2026). Rotating Leadership of Transactive Discourse through Synchrony and Desynchrony of Multimodal Interaction. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Lu, J. & Oshima, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Rotating leadership emerges in successful collaboration. This study investigates the extent to which their multimodal interactions are synchronized or not, along with the rotating leadership of transactive discourse (LoT). Nine groups of three members participated in a 45- minute co-located CPS task, and their spatial positions were collected. The results suggest that in addition to the synchronization of the spatial positioning, desynchronization was observed in rotating LoT. The potential use of the kinesthetic modality is discussed.

title: Dialogic Intelligence: Rethinking the pedagogical goal of CSCL in the context of Generative AI
citation: Rupert Wegerif, Xuanning Chen, Bo Yu, Imogen Casebourne, Kevin Martin (2026). Dialogic Intelligence: Rethinking the pedagogical goal of CSCL in the context of Generative AI. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Wegerif, R., Chen, X., Yu, B., Casebourne, I., & Martin, K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: As generative AI surpasses students in knowledge delivery and examination performance, education faces an unprecedented challenge in defining what human intelligence means. This theory paper argues that our response should be to reclaim, revalue, and rethi nk intelligence itself, advancing dialogic intelligence as a central educational aim. The dominant view of intelligence as an individual, measurable trait reflects print literacy's historical affordances, which have obscured intelligence's fundamentally relational nature. AI's emergence as a ubiquitous cognitive technology necessitates recovering an older understanding: intelligence is the capacity to support the emergence of truth and goodness through responsive relationship—whether between people, with nature, or with technology such as generative AI. While the CSCL community has explored teaching thinking, research has typically focused on collaboration as a means to enhance curricular learning. The dialogic responsiveness of generative AI suggests instead that we should design CSCL to promote dialogic intelligence as an end in itself. We illustrate this agenda through two CSCL design examples that prioritize dialogic intelligence over content mastery. Generative AI and educational aims Generative AI has forced education into a moment of reckoning. When systems such as ChatGPT can pass professional examinations, retrieve information instantly, generate plausible arguments, and simulate dialogue, it becomes difficult to defend educational models centred on individual recall, routine problem -solving, and the production of competent prose. Much early response has been defensive: detecting AI use, designing “AI -proof” assessments, or treating AI simply as a support tool. But these responses avoid the deeper question for the Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) community: what should education aim to cultivate in human learners? CSCL should move beyond treating collaboration mainly as a means of helping individuals master curriculum content and instead place dialogic intelligence at the centre of educational design. Dialogic intelligence is not an individual trait measured by speed, accuracy, or test performance. It is the capacity for meaning, insight, and judgement to emerge through responsive relationships: between people, between people and traditions of knowledge, and increasingly between people and AI systems. Historically, dominant ideas of intelligence were shaped by print culture. Earlier traditions linked intelligence to judgement, discernment, and wisdom exercised in context. Socrates, for example, valued the “living word” of dialogue because it could respond, be questioned, and remain open to revision, unlike the fixed and answerless word of writing (Plato, Phaedrus , 275d). Over time, however, writing and later print culture encouraged a more monologic conception of thought: linear, abstract, decontextualiz ed, and increasingly located within the individual mind (Ong, 1982; Olson, 1994; Toulmin, 1990). By the twentieth century, psychometric testing turned this into a scientific orthodoxy. Intelligence became whatever could be standardized, measured, and compared across individuals (Binet & Simon, 1916/1973; Spearman, 1904). Yet this was never a neutral description of human thinking. It reflected the cognitive demands of print - based schooling. Tasks involving vocabulary, abstract classification, analogy, and formal reasoning were elevated as signs of intelligence because they fitted the dominant educational system. Cross-cultural studies and the Flynn effect later showed how contingent this was: what counts as intelligence changes with cultural practices, technologies, and forms of education (Ceci, 1991; Cole & Scribner, 1974). IQ captures something real, but that “something” is not intelligence in the broadest human sense. It is performance within a historically specific literacy regime. Much CSCL research has significantly advanced understanding of how learners work together productively. However, it has largely remained tied to the print paradigm, treating collaboration as valuable because it improves individual outcomes such as knowledge acquisition, problem -solving, or reasoning performance. The deeper possibility is that intelligence does not merely happen inside individuals and then get expressed in groups. Rather, intelligence can emerge in the shared space of dialogue itself. 641 Research on collective intelligence points in this direction. Woolley and colleagues showed that groups can display a form of collective intelligence not reducible to the abilities of individual members (Woolley et al., 2010). Work in the Thinking Together tradition similarly found that when students were taught norms for exploratory talk, both group and individual reasoning improved (Mercer & Littleton, 2007). Close analysis suggested that explicit reasoning moves alone did not explain the most important moments of insight. Often the decisive shift came in shared attention, pause, tension, or a sudden moment of recognition before explanation could even be articulated. The talk moves mattered, but mainly because they helped open what came to be called dialogic space: the relational field in which new meaning becomes possible (Wegerif, 2008). Dialogic intelligence as an educational aim Dialogic intelligence is not best understood as a possession but as an event. It arises when participants hold perspectives in tension, attend responsively to one another, and remain open to something beyond their current assumptions. Bakhtin’s account of double -voicedness helps here: to think dialogically, one must inhabit one’s own perspective while also entering into another’s (Bakhtin, 1981). Mead’s notion of the generalized other adds that reflective thought depends on taking up the standpoint of a wider community (Mead, 1934/1967). But genuine dialogue goes further than simply reproducing communal norms. It also opens toward what Bakhtin called a superaddressee and what might be described more broadly as an Infinite Other: a horizon of truth, goodness, or understanding that is never fully exhausted by current knowledge (Levinas, 1969; Wegerif, 2025). Generative AI does not possess lived subjectivity, but it can function as a remarkably articulate simulated voice. It can represent the accumulated discourse of disciplines, professions, and traditions. In that sense, AI can give learners access to a power ful form of the generalized other. A student in dialogue with AI can encounter what counts as established understanding in mathematics, science, history, or law. T he educational value of this does not lie in receiving better answers more efficiently. It lies in using that encounter as a platform for further questioning. If students simply defer to AI, they risk conformity to cliché. If they engage it dialogically, they can use it to test assumptions, reframe problems, and move beyond what is already establi shed. This distinction can be illustrated by the provisional findings of two design- based research examples which we have conducted at Cambridge. In one study, AI moderators were introduced into small -group collaborative learning. Early versions failed because they addressed students individually and did not support genuinely shared inquiry. After iterative refinement, however, students reported that the AI began to connect viewpoints, bring ideas together, and raise possibilities the group had not considered. It appeared to support depth, breadth, momentum, and inclusion within the discussion. Importantly, these gains did not register on standard critical thinking measures, suggesting that dialogic intelligence may require different forms of assessment from those used for decontextualized reasoning (Michaels & O’Connor, 2015; Hennessy et al., 2016). In a second project, AI was designed as a dialogic partner for leadership training in difficult workplace conversations. Rather than acting as a compliant assistant, the system was configured to challenge, resist, and force participants to reconsider their habitual responses. Participants reported that this kind of difficult AI interlocutor was valuable precisely because it created the tension needed for growth. In both studies, the key issue was not AI capability in itself, but the quality of the relational space created through interaction. These examples also clarify the difference between dialogic intelligence and what is often called hybrid intelligence. Hybrid intelligence usually refers to combining the strengths of humans and AI so that each compensates for the other’s weaknesses. That is useful, but dialogic intelligence points to something deeper. The most important educational moments do not occur because two separate agents contribute separate capacities. They occur when a shared space of inquiry opens in which new understanding emerges that belongs fully to neither the human nor the machine alone. The implication for CSCL is substantial. The task is no longer simply to design collaboration so that learners achieve predefined curricular goals more efficiently. It is to design environments that open, sustain, and deepen dialogic space. That means fram ing AI not mainly as answer -provider or tutor, but as a dialogic partner that can represent established knowledge while also provoking learners to move beyond it. It also means rethinking assessment so that it attends to relational capacities: how learners connect perspectives, sustain uncertainty, reshape questions, and generate insight together. Generative AI exposes the narrowness of the print -based conception of intelligence on which much modern education has relied. What remains distinctly human is not superior information processing, but care: the capacity to care about truth, to remain answerable for judgement, and to sustain inquiry beyond what is immediately given. If CSCL can make dialogic intelligence its central aim, AI becomes not a threat to education but an opportunity to recover and extend intelligence in its deeper sense: as participation in a shared, open-ended dialogue through which we learn, create, and orient ourselves towards what is true and good. 642 References Bakhtin, M. abstract: This study examines expert perspectives on identifying, evaluating, and monitoring ADHD behaviors in children in the classroom. Eleven clinicians and educators participated in semi- structured interviews. Using open coding, three themes emerged: variability of ADHD behaviors, monitoring ADHD behaviors in context, and opportunities and challenges of wearables for teachers. Guided by Bronfenbrenner's Ecological Systems Theory, our findings suggest that wearable tools can act as mediators within the c hild's learning ecosystem, enhancing communication among teachers, clinicians, and caregivers through objective, context-aware data.

abstract: This study explores how 5th grade students playing a scientific inquiry game interact with (and react to) AI -generated feedback presented by in- game agent characters. We explore how AI conversational agents impact student inquiry and emotional engagement as students build socioscientific arguments. Results indicate that while students initially take up agent feedback to improve their argumentation, prolonged cycles of revision lead to frustration and negative reflections as students struggle to utilize AI feedback.

abstract: To effectively support remote maker sessions, tools are needed that allow distributed embodied collaborations to emerge naturally rather than forcing conformity to existing video conferencing. We present an overview of a multi -year iterative design, testing, and evaluation process of REACH (Remote Embodiment for Augmented Collaborative Help), offering insights into developing similar systems to support distributed embodied collaborations.

title: Complementary Roles of Collaborative Reflection and AI-generated Feedback to Support Students' Science Writing
citation: Indrani Dey, ChanMin Kim, Sadhana Puntambekar (2026). Complementary Roles of Collaborative Reflection and AI-generated Feedback to Support Students' Science Writing. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

abstract: Automated assessment can provide timely feedback on students’ writing, but students often struggle to interpret and apply feedback effectively. This study examined the extent to which collaborative reflection activities can support students to interpret, evaluate, and act on automated feedback to improve their scientific explanations.

title: Collaborative Virtual Reality Worlds, Cultural Play: Re-imagining Game Design through Interactional Tool Exploration

authors_list: Xie, X., Ahmadi, H., & Paré, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This case study explores how interactional tools can support the development of design ideas within a collaborative virtual reality (VR) -based studio. Six participants explored multiplayer VR applications to reflect on existing VR designs and co- design an LGBTQ+ cultural mini- golf game, while documenting their experiences in reflective journals. Our findings extend sociocultural constructionist and socio -materialist perspectives, demonstrating how VR pens, viewed as “non- neutral actors,” shape learners’ design idea generation, refinement, and decision-making.

title: At the Intersection of Cognitive Engagement and Critical Thinking in AI -Assisted Learning
citation: Lu Ding, Erika Cheek, Tami May (2026). At the Intersection of Cognitive Engagement and Critical Thinking in AI -Assisted Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Ding, L., Cheek, E., & May, T.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study examined how cognitive engagement levels, defined by the ICAP framework, relate to critical thinking in student -AI interactions. Analyzing 784 student questions submitted to a GPT -4-powered chatbot in an introductory biology course, we coded each question for ICAP level and applied Newman et al. ’s (1995) critical-thinking indicators. ANOVA results revealed significant differences across ICAP categories: Constructive questions yielded the highest critical-thinking ratios, followed by Active and Passive. However, Constructive questions were mostly clarifying or confirmatory, rarely exhibiting evaluative reasoning. These findings suggest that higher ICAP engagement predicts higher critical thinking, but students often remain at explanatory rather than evaluative levels when interacting with LLMs. The findings shed light on the need for instructional scaffolds that promote both cognitive engagement and epistemic vigilance.

title: ClassMosaic: Leveraging Solution Diversity to Teach Computational Problem- Solving
citation: Laila El-Hamamsy, Engin Bumbacher (2026). ClassMosaic: Leveraging Solution Diversity to Teach Computational Problem- Solving. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: El-Hamamsy, L. & Bumbacher, E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Cognitive Load Theory; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Classroom Orchestration
abstract: A key challenge in K-12 Computer Science (CS) education is teaching computational Problem-Solving (PS). PS instruction research emphasizes the importance of structured whole- class discussions to reflect on solution strategies to foster PS competences. How ever, orchestrating whole-class discussions is challenging for teachers. As such, we drew on PS- and dashboard research to design ClassMosaic, a classroom orchestration tool that supports productive PS-teaching practices. ClassMosaic provides real-time insights into student work to facilitate discussions and promote collaborative learning by enabling collective comparison and reflection. We present ClassMosaic’s design principles and the first user study focusing on perceived pedagogical value with 9 CS teachers. Results show that ClassMosaic aligns with existing CPS instruction practices, and fosters new CPS -teaching strategies, including heterogeneous strategy-based grouping and structured post-discussion adaptations. Future work will further automate PS -based code clustering, and adapt ClassMosaic’s UX/UI to reduce teacher cognitive load, before in-class experiments.

title: Multimodal Analysis of Mathematical Statistics Learning in a CSCL Environment
citation: Masataka Kaneko, Hironori Egi, Takuya Kitamoto, Takeo Noda (2026). Multimodal Analysis of Mathematical Statistics Learning in a CSCL Environment. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Kaneko, M., Egi, H., Kitamoto, T., & Noda, T.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study, a multimodal analysis of learning data collected using a video recorder, high-resolution microphone, and dynamic geometry system, focused on pairs of university students engaged in a mathematical statistics task while collaboratively using HTML -based dynamic content. The qualitative analysis of transcribed text data f rom participants’ discourse was based on Sfard’s commognitive perspective. The results were then compared to the coded data of their behavior, the log data of their manipulating the dynamic content, and the audio data of their conversations . Our findings indicate that there is a relation ship between the transition of learners’ behavioral patterns and the emergence of refined discursive routines.

title: Leveraging CSCL for Social Emotional Learning: Early Insights from a Large -Scale Classroom Study
citation: Jiangang Hao, Patrick Kyllonen, Emily Kerzabi, Wenju Cui, Enruo Guo, Jessica Andrews -Todd (2026). Leveraging CSCL for Social Emotional Learning: Early Insights from a Large -Scale Classroom Study. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Hao, J., Kyllonen, P., Kerzabi, E., Cui, W., Guo, E., & -Todd, J. A.

conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) helps students to develop healthy identities, regulate emotions, build relationships, and make responsible decisions. Effective SEL instruction often relies on group- based activities; however, traditional classrooms without technological support make it difficult to capture the fine -grained interactions among students. As a result, teachers struggle to provide timely feedback and interventions . This paper reports on an ongoing project that leverages a computer -supported collaborative learning (CSCL) environment to implement 36 SEL lessons with fifth and sixth-grade students over the course of a semester. We describe the design and implementation of the curriculum and present preliminary findings from a pilot study. Early results indicate positive feedback from both teachers and students, along with a negative correlation between students’ off -topic chat behavior, characterized by nonsensical or “gibberish” messages , and their learning performance.

title: Yang Jiang, Stephen Elliott Collaborative High School Teacher Learning in Bichronous Online STEM Professional Development

abstract: This study examines how a bichronous model supports collaborative teacher learning in a four-week online bioinformatics professional development. Through analysis of nine high school teachers’ 1,363 asynchronous forum posts and 220 minutes of synchronous sessions, we identified complementary pathways: asynchronous forums supported knowledge building through archived threads and peer resource sharing, while synchronous sessions facilitated real- time collective sensemaking and expert scaffolding. Findings offer design principles for online teacher professional development in emerging STEM domains.

citation: Haowei Li, Amanda M. Cottone, Susan A. Yoon, Zheng Bian, Rebecca G. Wells (2026). Enhancing K-12 Teachers’ Confidence and Competence in STEM Integration Using Blended Learning in Professional Development. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

abstract: STEM-integrated learning in K-12 education is essential for students to build career readiness. However, building confidence and competence in STEM teachers to enact new, cross-disciplinary curriculum is difficult, and the best way to design high-quality professional development (PD) programs for teaching STEM integration is unclear. This study introduces a blended learning PD model that added a new online course to a traditional onsite research experience to scaffold teachers’ comprehension of mechanobiology knowledge and practices of pedagogy. Piloting the model with seven K-12 teachers, we examined how this blended format scaffolded in-person and online collaborative learning . Findings show the online course enhanced teachers’ grasp of complex research concepts and competence in teaching STEM- integrated topics. This study highlights the potential of an online course to promote confidence and competence in teachers conducting cutting-edge, interdisciplinary STEM research.

abstract: This study examines how students and experts differ in their engagement with generative AI (GenAI) during knowledge -creating dialogue. Twenty undergraduate students (10 pairs) and one pair of expert educators collaborated with ChatGPT -4o to address a socio- scientific issue. Using the Knowledge Building Discourse Explorer (KBDeX) and “Good Moves” coding, we analyzed temporal degree centrality and discourse networks to capture epistemic and dialogic processes. Results showed that students’ discourse was largely anchored to AI-generated ideas, with limited transformation through dialogue, whereas experts engaged in self -sustained cycles of problem definition, evaluation, and reframing, using GenAI selectively to extend inquiry. These findings suggest that diffe rences lie not in the availability of ideas but in how discourse is organized to support knowledge creation, highlighting the importance of scaffolding epistemic and dialogic practices for effective GenAI use.

abstract: This study introduces and employs a novel mixed- methods design that integrates computer vision, optical character recognition (OCR), and qualitative video -based interaction analysis to examine multimodal participation in Computer -Supported Collaborative Le arning (CSCL), with a focus on typing as a key form of object -based interaction. This approach integrates two computational tools: a neural network–based system for mapping typing activity in group interaction videos and a screen recording analysis system for extracting typed input. Analyzing a collaborative robotics programming session among middle school students, the findings identify who typed, when, and what was typed, as well as dynamic shifts in participation, tool access, and role negotiation. The study contributes to more inclusive, scalable and grounded analyses of CSCL processes by bridging Artificial Intelligence -enhanced automation with human insight, surfacing patterns that warrant deeper qualitative investigation.

title: Human–AI Learning Alignment in Situated Contexts: A Human-Centered Framework
citation: Shi Ding, Brian Magerko (2026). Human–AI Learning Alignment in Situated Contexts: A Human-Centered Framework. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Ding, S. & Magerko, B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) transforms education, many existing approaches to AI in education emphasize task completion while overlooking learner agency and the sociotechnical nature of learning. This gap limits our ability to understand how AI supports learning in situated contexts. In this paper, we define human–AI learning alignment and present TEACH-AI (Trustworthy and Effective AI Classroom Heuristics) as a learner- centered set of analytical dimensions spanning interactional, learning- oriented, and sociotechnical perspectives. Through an illustrative case analysis, we discuss how this perspective can be used to analyze AI -supported learning settings. This work contributes a conceptual foundation for understanding how generative AI supports learning in situated contexts.

abstract: This paper examines how artifacts and environmental features mediate collaborative design in immersive VR. Situated within activity theory, the study contributes process -oriented methods for researching collaborative VR design.

title: Investigating support for collaboration on the AI Frontier: A Qualitative Study of Middle -Grades Computer Science Classrooms Informed by the MOSAIC Protocol

abstract: This study investigates the relationship between middle school student collaborative behaviors and their activities before and after receiving support while collaborating. Regression analysis of data from the MOSAIC protocol was used to conduct maximum variation sampling for a qualitative case studies to explore how student activity immediately before receiving support predicts whether they receive support focused on collaboration and if they receive this collaborative support or not predicts student activity immediately after they receive support . The characteristics of both the collaboration support provided and the nature of the collaborative tasks play crucial roles in shaping these interactions. These findings highlight the complexity of fostering effective student collaboration and underscore the need for tailored support strategies that consider teachers’ pedagogical moves and the specific features of collaborative tasks.

title: Physiological Indicators of Teacher Stress in CSCL Versus Non-Collaborative Learning Sessions
citation: Eduard Arnau Romeu, Batuhan Sayis, Davinia Hernández-Leo (2026). Physiological Indicators of Teacher Stress in CSCL Versus Non-Collaborative Learning Sessions. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

abstract: This exploratory single -subject study examines teacher physiological stress across Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) versus non -CSCL sessions. One teacher was observed across 22 sessions using biosensors (heart rate variability, electrodermal activity) and questionnaires. Multivariate analysis revealed no overall physiological differences. However, exploratory analysis showed significantly elevated post -session electrodermal activity after CSCL. Given the single-subject design, findings provide methodological insights and hints for new knowledge regarding cumulative arousal, rather than broad generalizations.

title: Beyond Teacher-AI Dyads: A Triadic Synergy Model for Transforming Teacher Professional Development
citation: Kexin Li, Gaowei Chen (2026). Beyond Teacher-AI Dyads: A Triadic Synergy Model for Transforming Teacher Professional Development. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

abstract: Traditional expert-led teacher professional development models often struggle with personalization, scalability, and sustainability. While AI offers new possibilities, the prevailing AI-enhanced models often rely on teacher –AI dyads , raising concerns about opacity and reduced teacher agency. Drawing upon Connectivism and Hybrid Intelligence, we propose the Triadic Synergy Model. This framework formalizes a three -way, networked, and synergistic relationship that strategically integrates the teacher’s agency, AI’s analytical power, and the human expert’s contextual wisdom.

title: The Effect of Group-Awareness on Peer Feedback Quality in Pre-Service Teachers’ Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning
citation: Sebastian Tews, Melissa Özsoy, Meral Roeben, Yasemin Erdemgil, Xiao Zhang, Christiane Lütge (2026). The Effect of Group-Awareness on Peer Feedback Quality in Pre-Service Teachers’ Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

abstract: This quasi-experimental study examined the effect of a group awareness tool on peer feedback quality in video- based collaborative diagnostic reasoning. In total, 54 pre-service teachers collaboratively diagnosed a teaching video in dyads and generated peer feedback for the acting teacher regarding the use of digital media in the classroom. Results suggest a rather detrimental effect on feedback quality when supported by the group awareness tool, indicating the need for additional scaffolding to utilize group awareness.

title: Comparing High School Students’ Collaborative Discourse in Idea-Centered and Procedure-Based Technology-Supported Scientific PBL
citation: Ying-Tien Wu, Ti-Cheng Tsai, Li-Jen Wang (2026). Comparing High School Students’ Collaborative Discourse in Idea-Centered and Procedure-Based Technology-Supported Scientific PBL. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Wu, Y., Tsai, T., & Wang, L.

abstract: This quasi -experimental study compared collaborative discourse between idea - centered and procedure-based science PBL among 61 Taiwanese high school students over 12- week. Using a hierarchical coding framework, student contributions were coded into three levels—information sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge building—at individual and group levels. Results showed idea-centered PBL significantly increased knowledge - building discourse (73.6% vs. 34%) and promoted idea diversification and synthesis. These findings suggest that epistemological framing embedded in platform design shapes students' collaborative discourse.

title: EnactingBoard: AI-mediated Dialogue for Developing Empathic Negotiation Skills in Higher Education
citation: Hideo Funaoi, Yoshihiko Kubota, Hiroshi Kato (2026). EnactingBoard: AI-mediated Dialogue for Developing Empathic Negotiation Skills in Higher Education. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

abstract: This study proposed a three -step learning method to cultivate the skill of sustaining dialogue with emotional opponents and implemented it in the form of the EnactingBoard web application. This system integrates generative AI to simulate adversarial dialogue, reflection, empathic understanding, and counterfactual analysis. This study demonstrates how AI - mediated dialogue can provide a novel approach for developing empathic negotiation skills in higher education.

title: Fostering Metacognitive Awareness for Effective Human–AI Collaboration in Learning
citation: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Davinia Hernández-Leo (2026). Fostering Metacognitive Awareness for Effective Human–AI Collaboration in Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Montobbio, P. B. I. & Hernández-Leo, D.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: This exploratory study investigated whether experiential learning is more effective than direct instruction for developing students' metacognitive awareness of AI's effects on learning. Among 126 first-year engineering students, the experimental group completed hands- on exercises demonstrating productive and counterproductive human– AI collaboration, while controls received equivalent lectures. Using bespoke exercises and a novel questionnaire and construct-level analysis, the experiential group showed significant increases in metacognitive awareness and AI engagement, suggesting that direct experience with AI's cognitive impacts is essential for developing reflective human–AI partnerships.

title: Hierarchical Multi-Agent System for Instructional Design in Music Knowledge Building
citation: Menglian Zhang, Mingyang Zhu, Haiyang Xin, Yibing Zhang (2026). Hierarchical Multi-Agent System for Instructional Design in Music Knowledge Building. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Zhang, M., Zhu, M., Xin, H., & Zhang, Y.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: This study presents a hierarchical multi- agent system (MAS) to support music teachers in designing Knowledge Building (KB) -oriented lessons. The system integrates four expert agents ( KB, musician, music pedagogy and music psychology) to generate holistic instructional design that contain embodied and creative music activities . A preliminary qualitative interview with five primary school teachers shows positive feedback of creativity and applicability. Further work will validate the lesson plan quality, compare with single-agent systems, and examine classroom impact through longitudinal studies. Knowledge Building (KB) in music education Constructivist in music education emphasises active participation and bodily engagement through authentic, social, and reflective experiences (Shively, 2015). M usic education also values culture, affective emotions, and embodied experience (Garnett, 2013; Van Der Schyff et al., 2018). Compared to traditional constructivist education, Knowledge Building (KB) focuses on the continuous and dynamic improvement of ideas through collective learning (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2010). KB pedagogy encourages deeper learning through artifact production, such as composition, improvisation, and performance in music (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2010). Collaborative learning, however, has also been applied widely in music teaching and practice (Forbes, 2020), suggesting a potential link between music education and KB pedagogy. Despite th ese alignments, the direct application of KB pedagogy in music education remains limited. This gap indicates the need for pedagogical and technological innovation to conduct KB principles with creative and affective music learning. Current issue and exploration in KB music lessons A primary school in China implementing KB across subjects provide the context for this exploratory study. Five music teachers (4 female, 1 male; 2-20 years of teaching experience; Grades 2, 4, 5 & 6) joined a semi-structured interview addressing theoretical and practical challenges in applying KB and AI tools in music lessons. After thematic analysis, teachers reported difficulty aligning open-ended KB inquiries with curriculum standards (Tan et al., 2021). Some confuse the fixed-group discussion with the collaborative knowledge-sharing groups. Teachers also ask for strategies that connect deeper music understanding and psychological knowledge in pedagogy. Interdisciplinary skills are needed in KB pedagogy, leading to the use of AI to solve the complex problems in teaching. Existing AI agents often generate too advanced activities for the targeted students’ age. For instance, suggested singing tasks exceeded student’s vocal abilities, and some embodied activities were impractical with the large students amount in Chinese schools. Teachers further requested clearer inquiry prompts and adaptable activities that support creativity and collaboration. These challenges and requirements highlight the need for greater control through a more flexible AI system that better integrates music practice with KB pedagogy. Holistic perspective in music teaching and tool use Teachers prefer an AI system that perform as co-creators, generating synthesised ideas rather than giving concepts and decision. As a complex system, MAS offers such potential by emerge new and unreducible feature through the interaction between individual agents beyond their initial attr ibute ( Chen et al., 2024; Waldrop, 1993 ). Compared to Large Language Model (LLM) and single agent, MAS can not only reduce produce less hallucination (Huang et al., 2025) , but also support complex problems, provide collective intelligence, iterative feedback and flexible subtask management (Li et al., 2024). Accordingly, four experts were designed to reflect the complex and interdisciplinary nature in effective teaching (Mishra & Koehler, 2006) , integrating perspectives from music theories, psychology, classroom dynamics, and ethical considerations of AI (Celik, 2023) . In detail, KB expert ensures collaborative knowledge creation, while the music educator focuses on music pedagogy and curriculum alignment. The musician contributes to expertise in music theory, history, culture, and performances. Finally, the music psychologist deals with motivational, emotional, and cognitive developmental issues. The hierarchical Multi-Agent System (MAS) 710 The hierarchical structure of the Multi -Agent System (MAS) enables modular design and iterative refinement across domains (Talebirad & Nadiri, 2023; Tran et al., 2025). This design aims to generate instructional design (ID) that integrate KB principles with practical music pedagogy, addressing both cognitive and affective aspects, and supports the sophisticated knowledge and teacher control . A supervisor agent manages the overall system goal ( 𝒪𝒪𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐), assigns individual goals ( 𝒪𝒪𝑖𝑖) to sub -agents through Standardised Operating Procedures (SOPs). Teachers input teaching objectives or prepared ID through a chat interface . The supervisor agent synthesises a new ID according to the other agents (see Figure 1). Users can then entre requirements to iteratively refine outputs. The knowledge base contains KB lesson templates , which were validated and adapted by KB experts and music teachers, inquiry prompts, and activity examples supported by musical and psychological literature . Curriculum standards and textbooks ensure practical feasibility. Figure 1 The Hierarchical MAS for the Generation of Music KB Lesson Plan Feedback and future plan System performance was evaluated using Multiagentbench (Zhu et al., 2025). Participants included the 5 music teachers from the previous interview. In a group interview, participants were show about how to input and revise ideas. Three instructional design s about singing and music appreciation for grade s 2, 4 and 5 were generated discussed in terms of KB alignment, pedagogical coherence, applicability, developmental appropriateness. The ID contains KB principles such as collective idea improvement, co- developed artifacts and suggest for student wellbeing. Overall, the new MAS was viewed positively. Teachers found the activities “very creative compared to simple singing activities” and applicable for grade 5 students to move, listen and feel the music (Teacher 2, group interview, September 2025). They also valued the integration of psychological perspectives which support student motivation and engagement. Different from simply a full lesson plan provided by another MAS developed by Xin et al. (2025), this hierarchical MAS can more adequately capture the affective dimensions. However, teachers requested clearer output structures: “The content and activities were basically feasible, but can you make the output clearer—follow the template we always use?” (Teachers 3, group interview, September 2025). Specifically, a novice teacher asked, “I want more inquiries in the lesson plan, better to cover every sentence I need to say in class” (Teacher 5, group interview, Septermber 2025). Experienced teachers agreed this value, especially for preparing demonstration lessons (Teachers 2 and 4, group interview, September 2025). The development of this system and verification of teaching effectiveness have not been complete. More lesson plans revised by experts will be added to the knowledge base to improve comprehensiveness . A validated evaluation scale based on the ADDIE model (Branch, 2009) will be created for experts in KB and music psychologist to scoring. The usability, teacher satisfaction, and learning outcomes will be examined through longitudinal studies. Technical improvement will address reaction speed, stream output, and interface design. Conclusion This study presents a preliminary design of a complex hierarchical MAS for KB informed music instructional design. By integrating KB theory, music pedagogy and psychology, the system offers a more interactive and flexible approach which supports creative, collaborative, and student-centred learning. While further validation is required, findings suggest that MAS can enhance ID while teachers are encouraged to adapt AI-generating lesson plans to actual classroom and cultural contexts to maintain subjectivity (Hesse & Helm, 2025; Pikhart & Al - Obaydi, 2025). title: AI Tools in Arts Learning: A Scoping Review
citation: Jaycee Sansom, Safinah Ali (2026). AI Tools in Arts Learning: A Scoping Review. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Sansom, J. & Ali, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: With the proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in art making, AI knowledge and skills have made their way to arts learning. However, an assessment of the current state of AI tools in arts learning is lacking. This study used scoping review methodology to identify current research trends in AI applications in arts learning, and what gaps exist for future research. 58 papers were reviewed revealing four trends and five gaps and opportunities.

title: Principle-Driven Scaffolding: Implementing and Evaluating LLM-Generated Micro-Scripts in an Informal Learning Community
citation: Hideki Kondo (2026). Principle-Driven Scaffolding: Implementing and Evaluating LLM-Generated Micro-Scripts in an Informal Learning Community. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Kondo, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: How can AI scaffold collaboration in voluntary online communities without over - scripting participation? This poster presents Principle -Driven Micro -Script Generation (PDMSG), an LLM -based approach that translates activity objectives, local constraints, learning principles, and recent community activity logs into optional weekly suggestions for each member. In a seven-week deployment of PDMSG in BookClub, text volume per Presence increased without a corresponding rise in post -count density, and participants rated the suggestions as readable and minimally coercive.

title: Equitable Learning Analytics Dashboards: Roles and Mechanisms in Personalized Learning
citation: Wei Yan, Hyejeong Lee, Donna Dancer, Wonjin Yu (2026). Equitable Learning Analytics Dashboards: Roles and Mechanisms in Personalized Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Yan, W., Lee, H., Dancer, D., & Yu, W.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Communities of Practice & Situated Learning; Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition
abstract: This poster presents a rapid scoping review of equitable learning analytics dashboards (LADs) for personalized learning. Grounded in the integration of self-regulated learning (SRL) theory and situated learning theory, the review synthesizes findings from ten journal articles published between 2023 and 2025. The findings outline four roles and eight supporting mechanisms through which personalized LADs promote equity. This preliminary synthesis highlights inclusive design consideration to support equitable LAD development.

title: Adaptive Support for Collaborative Learning: Effects of Design Features Across Task Types
citation: Lixiang Gao, Frank Fischer, Olga Chernikova (2026). Adaptive Support for Collaborative Learning: Effects of Design Features Across Task Types. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Gao, L., Fischer, F., & Chernikova, O.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This meta -analysis examines how adaptive instructional support facilitates collaborative learning across task types and design features, based on 80 studies. Cognitive - model approaches were most effective for factual knowledge learning , whereas data science approaches showed the strongest effects in problem -solving. Human-involved adaptation yielded smaller effects. These findings suggest adaptive instructional support is most effective when its design features align with task demand s, with data science approaches and system control being particularly effective for problem-solving tasks.

title: Agentic Collaboration with GenAI: A Cautionary but Optimistic Tale
citation: Iris Tabak, Gur Arie Livni Alcasid, Ilana Dubovi (2026). Agentic Collaboration with GenAI: A Cautionary but Optimistic Tale. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Tabak, I., Alcasid, G. A. L., & Dubovi, I.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) extends human performance but may diminish users’ sense of ownership. Drawing on research in CSCL and sociocultural theories of agency, we analyzed 559 naturalistic conversations from the LMSYS -Chat1M dataset, and coded for collaboration (e.g., Externalization, Co- construction) and agency (e.g., Critical Vigilance). Deep collaboration and high agency were infrequent but related. This suggests that CSCL research can inform the design of agency-supportive human-GenAI interactions.

title: Sociotechnical Efficacy in Modeling 3D Interactive Environments
citation: Akin Adediji, Jinhee Lee (2026). Sociotechnical Efficacy in Modeling 3D Interactive Environments. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Adediji, A. & Lee, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines sociotechnical efficacy in 3D environment modeling through the Roblox Developers Forum. Ito & Reich’s (2017) equity- centered principles explore how youth learning participation is fostered in creative spaces. Available curriculum, plugins, and developer feedback built around “hanging out”, “messing around”, “geeking out” (HOMAGO) emphasize the “hanging out” dimension (Ito, 2009). Platforms enhanced by modular, adaptive assets foster equitable access and social connectedness, shifting learning between participatory HOMAGO to supporting agency and connectivist models.

title: Designing an AI-Augmented Knowledge Synthesis Tool for Collaborative Learning
citation: Xinran Zhu, Bo Shui, Ishita Asnani, Liam Magee (2026). Designing an AI-Augmented Knowledge Synthesis Tool for Collaborative Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Zhu, X., Shui, B., Asnani, I., & Magee, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: Knowledge synthesis involves the deliberate integration of diverse information to generate new insights and creative solutions. In CSCL, it is both a process —where students advance collaborative knowledge —and a product that facilitates ongoing learning. We introduce a novel technology that scaffolds students’ knowledge synthesis in collaborative learning environments augmented by generative AI. The poster presents its design rationale, technical details, and future directions for iterative development and classroom implementation to support knowledge synthesis in CSCL.

title: Encouraging Deeper Learning with GenAI: A Review of Pedagogical Constraints on GenAI and Their Impact in Higher Education
citation: Shuang Geng, Di Fan, Juhong Eom, Gahyun Callie Sung (2026). Encouraging Deeper Learning with GenAI: A Review of Pedagogical Constraints on GenAI and Their Impact in Higher Education. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Geng, S., Fan, D., Eom, J., & Sung, G. C.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: This paper reviews how generative AI (GenAI) can be pedagogically constrained to promote deeper learning in higher education. A nalyzing 15 intervention studies comparing constrained GenAI use with free or no GenAI use, we found three delivery methods (process, activity, and tool levels), operationalized through five mechanisms. Results show primarily positive impacts on performance, motivation, and higher order thinking, though nearly half rely on self-reports. The findings highlight the role of constraints in GenAI use, and invite further research explicitly linking constraints to outcomes. Setting There has been rapidly growing interest in finding ways to integrate generative AI (GenAI) into higher education classrooms. Meanwhile, there is little clarity on how GenAI use can be moderated to better facilitate learning. Existing reviews have either explored strategies for GenAI use or evaluated the impact of having GenAI in learning as a whole, but have yet to distinguish the specific moderating or constraint mechanisms and their impact on learning (Batista et al., 2024; Almasri, 2024). To bridge this gap, our review goes beyond a binary view (use versus no use) with the following guiding questions: ● What student-facing constraint strategies for GenAI have been tested in higher education? ● What impact has been observed so far, on what types of learning outcomes? The current paper presents preliminary findings from an ongoing systematic review. We screened journal articles from 2022 (i.e., release of ChatGPT) to 2025, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) standard (Page et al., 2021). To be included, studies had to 1) investigate the impact of GenAI in higher education learning; 2) design and clearly describe a constrained or moderated GenAI use condition; 3) employ a (quasi -)experimental design, where academic or cognitive outcomes were compared between a treatment group of constrained use and a control group of free or no use of GenAI. Systematic search across Scopus, Web of Science, and ACM yielded 1,910 articles, among which 30 met the inclusion criteria. The present analysis reports findings based on half (15) of the final dataset, selected alphabetically by the first author's last name (see full list in References). All studies were collaboratively coded by the first author and at least one other author, with discrepancies resolved through discussion for this preliminary analysis. Results Context of Studies: Interventions showed a balanced representation between eight in STEM and seven in non- STEM disciplines. ChatGPT (or its API) was the primary tool in 14 of 15 cases. Constraint Delivery: Our coding process revealed three main GenAI delivery methods. First, process - level guidelines (n=10) explicitized expectations for use, by delineating permissible forms of assistance (e.g., guiding usage with metacognitive support prompts; Xu et al., 2025). On the other hand, activity -level scaffolds (n=10) embedded constraints within the design of a learning activity, specifying the stages, timing, and conditions under which GenAI may be used (e.g., requiring independent initial attempt, followed by interaction and revision with GenAI; Jiang & Nakatani, 2025). Lastly, tool -level constraints (n=11) configured tools for specific interaction modes, such as limiting outputs to hints (Lee et al., 2024). Constraint Mechanisms: Across interventions, five mechanisms emerged across the four stages of problem-solving: understanding, planning, execution, and revision (Polya, 1945). One mechanism constrained GenAI use to the early stage of draft or brainstorming, with the expectation that these ideas would be refined by the learner. The second and third mechanisms applied to GenAI use in the execution stage: solution first required students to create their own solution first, while no answers primed GenAI to not give out whole answers and instead provide Socratic guidance. Lastly, in the revision stage, mechanisms included revision and verification , 734 as well as attributing and reflecting, where learners were either required to revise and verify AI output, or required to reflect on, and potentially report, how they used GenAI to perform the task. A single intervention often had multiple constraint delivery methods and/or mechanisms, reflecting layered approaches rather than reliance on a single lever. Overall, the pattern indicates a shift from merely restricting access to deliberately structuring how GenAI participates in learning, with mechanisms intuitively chosen to externalize cognition, require evidence-seeking, and align tool behavior with instructional intent. Impact on student learning Learning Outcome: On average, 4.4 outcomes were measured per study. The most common outcome category was Performance (e.g., exam grade, skill evaluation score), totaling 28 outcome measures across 13 (86.7%) studies. Other outcome categories included Motivation and Affect (e.g., intrinsic motivation and engagement), Higher Order Thinking (e.g., critical thinking), Quality of Student Artifact, and Metacognitive Skills. Direction of impact: Treatment groups showed largely positive impacts across student learning outcomes compared to control groups: 75% positive on Performance, 75% on Motivation & Affect, 80% on Higher Order Thinking, and the remaining two categories showed more mixed results. Figure 1 shows the breakdown of directions of impact for each outcome category, combined with a second- level breakdown of measurement type. Measurement Type: Nearly half of the 66 outcomes (48.5%) relied on self-reports, which may have led to positive bias. Notably, outcomes related to Higher Order Thinking and Motivation & Affect, while showing predominantly positive results, relied exclusively on self-report (see Figure 1). Figure 1 Outcome Categories by Direction of Impact and Measurement Type Main bars: Count and percentage breakdown of direction of impact for each outcome category (X -axis). Side bars with hatching patterns: Percentage breakdown of measurement type for each main bar segment. Discussion Empirical findings point to a generally positive impact of constrained GenAI use on student performance, with more mixed results for metacognitive skills or quality of work. However, this direction may be influenced by several biases. In addition to common sources of bias such as the observer effect, limitations of self -reports, or the novelty effect, a unique issue was that in some cases, assessments were made on the GenAI-assisted task itself. Students may have shown higher performance because they had assistance, and not because they truly learned more. Another limitation was that most of these results were gained from comparing constrained GenAI use to no GenAI use. There was a surprising dearth of research (20%) that compared free versus constrained use of GenAI (c.f. comparing no and constrained use of GenAI), which could help provide stronger evidence of pedagogical value by isolating the effects of constraint design rather than GenAI presence alone. Our ongoing analysis of the full dataset aims to delineate such emerging design insights with greater granularity. 735 References Studies included in the review are marked with an asterisk (*).
