title: Technological Competency: A Conceptual Model for Understanding the World Around Us
citation: Matthew Duvall, Chen Wang (2026). Technological Competency: A Conceptual Model for Understanding the World Around Us. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Duvall, M. & Wang, C.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This conceptual paper describes a framework for fostering “technological competency” (TC), integrating ideas from multiple disciplines including literacies, computer science, and computer supported collaborative learning as a social practice, data literacy, AI literacy, and justice-centered computer science education. TC is the ability to (1) ask questions about technology that are relevant both personally and collectively; (2) identify, collect, and curate data to answer these questions; (3) use appropriate tools to analyze this data; and (4) report and re-evaluate this data in discussion with relevant communities. Most importantly, this should be collaborative work between learners of all kinds - researchers, practitioners, students, and other stakeholders. We conclude with practical guidelines for designers of learning experiences: stakeholder collaboration, diversity and inclusion, critical approaches, and effective communication.

title: Idea Tracing Analysis (ITA): A Temporal-Structural Methodology for Modeling Collaborative Discourse and Contextualizing Multimodal Interactions
citation: Xiaomeng Huang, Xavier Ochoa, Madhumitha Gopalakrishnan, Shiyu Zhang (2026). Idea Tracing Analysis (ITA): A Temporal-Structural Methodology for Modeling Collaborative Discourse and Contextualizing Multimodal Interactions. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Huang, X., Ochoa, X., Gopalakrishnan, M., & Zhang, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Understanding learners ’behaviors in collaborative problem solving (CPS) is critical yet challenging due to its dynamic, multimodal nature. We introduce Idea Tracing Analysis (ITA), a method that models collaborative discourse as the evolution of interconnected ideas. ITA represents interactions as temporally aligned idea networks, capturing how ideas emerge, transform, and connect across participants. This approach provides a temporal and structural lens on collaboration, enabling analysis of group-level knowledge-building trajectories and the contextualization of multimodal interactions.

title: Do Anti-democratic Bots Dream of Digital Riots? Modeling Anti-democratic Decision-making and Collective Knowledge Construction Using Natural Language Processing
citation: Renato Russo, Carolina Sotério, Fabio Campos, Paulo Blikstein, Gustavo Oliveira (2026). Do Anti-democratic Bots Dream of Digital Riots? Modeling Anti-democratic Decision-making and Collective Knowledge Construction Using Natural Language Processing. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies

abstract: We introduce a tool for visualizing reasoning trajectories in online interactions. We leverage natural language processing to corpora from Brazilian communities involved in anti - democratic speech to compare bots’ and people’s trajectories around “discourse crossroads” where epistemic stances towards democratic norms shift . We hope to inform tools and intervention design that guide epistemic trajectories toward more productive engagement, highlighting the role of civic education and digital literacy in fostering critical dialogue.

title: Exploring Collaborative Teacher-AI Interaction for Rehearsing Responsive Teaching in Elementary Mathematics Education
citation: Shuman Wang, Gordon Yeung, Miroslav Suzara, Jennifer Osuna, Charis Charitsis, John Mitchell (2026). Exploring Collaborative Teacher-AI Interaction for Rehearsing Responsive Teaching in Elementary Mathematics Education. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Wang, S., Yeung, G., Suzara, M., Osuna, J., Charitsis, C., & Mitchell, J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This proposal introduces TeacherCollab, an AI -supported simulated professional learning community designed to cultivate early- career teachers' (ECTs) responsive teaching in elementary mathematics. Rather than simulating students, TeacherCollab positions AI as collaborative teacher colleagues who model diverse pedagogical lenses while reasoning around authentic students ' work. Grounded in approximations of practice and computer -supported collaborative learning (CSCL) theory, TeacherCollab creates a multi -agent dialogue environment where ECTs interact with AI -generated personas that surface students ' relational dynamics, mathematical strategies , and areas of struggle. A pilot study with 16 ECTs showed that TeacherCollab fostered engagement, reflection, and awareness of multiple perspectives on student learning.

title: The Impact of Conversational Agents on Children’s and Parents’ Engagement During Shared Reading
citation: Dorentina Dedushaj, Kathryn Leech, Isabella Ruel, Grace Lin (2026). The Impact of Conversational Agents on Children’s and Parents’ Engagement During Shared Reading. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Dedushaj, D., Leech, K., Ruel, I., & Lin, G.

abstract: Engagement is an important aspect of parent -child shared reading interactions. However, little is known about the nature of engagement patterns while parent -child dyads engage with AI -powered CAs in at -home reading contexts. In this study, we analyze diver se observable patterns of engagement during shared reading. We examine the overall impact of an artificially intelligent conversational agent (CA) that augments parent-child reading interactions by observing and analyzing engagement patterns betw een parents and children as they read together.

title: Novel Figurative Language to Identify Promising Ideas in Knowledge Building Scientific Discourse
citation: Wakana Tsuji, Marlene Scardamalia, Ahmad Khanlari (2026). Novel Figurative Language to Identify Promising Ideas in Knowledge Building Scientific Discourse. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Tsuji, W., Scardamalia, M., & Khanlari, A.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This research explored grade 4 students ’ novel figurative language to identify promising ideas in knowledge building community discourse . A mixed -method approach— semantic analysis using Word2Vec and qualitative coding—was adopted for the analysis. Results showed figurative language use involved conceptual reframing across science and everyday life domains and embodied perspective -taking. Our next step is to incorporate similarity to resource material and investigate how ideas containing figurative language supports the community discourse. Figurative language and creativity in scientific discourse Figurative language, such as metaphors, play a crucial role in understanding and communicating science concepts (Cameron, 2002), through conceptual mapping of a familiar source domain onto a more complex, abstract target domain (Lakoff & Johnson, 1980). C reating associative connections between remote concepts has been characterized as a capacity for creativ e thinking (Mednick, 1962) . C omputational and neuroimaging studies confirmed a strong correlation between semantic distance in associative word pairs and creativity (Beaty & Johnson, 2021; Liu et al., 2020). Further, a recent study reported that semantic distance between mapped concepts aligns with creativity ratings in metaphors (Yang et al., 2025). Existing evidence is largely derived from elicited data; s emantic distance may serve as a quantifiable indicator of creative metaphor and ideation in naturally occurring discourse. Studies report low levels of metaphor production in the writing of elementary school students (Gardner et al., 1975; Thomas et al., 2025), particularly novel metaphors (Pollio & Pollio, 1974). Novelty (e.g., originality, uniqueness) and appropriateness (e.g., usefulness, value) are two qualities of creativity repeatedly discussed in literature (e.g., Runco & Jaeger, 2012). In knowledge building communities, theory development requires drawing on one’s experience to map the familiar with complex, abstract, theoretical, and distant concepts and create new explanations and accounts. From a socio-cognitive perspective, students are dealing with difficult -to-understand concepts in a community context, trying to communicate to peers. In such contexts, students this age and younger have demonstrated the capacity to exceed curriculum expectations, engaging in metadiscourse and demonstrating significant vocabulary development ( Khanlari et al., 2019 ; Resendes et al., 2015 ). These advances require sociocultural creativity (Glăveanu, 2012): novel conceptual and linguistic affordances are created through social judgement and acceptance (Amabile, 1988) of their value and usefulness to the group. This process is inherently cyclical, as new language develops through divergent alternatives and convergence through adaptation to community norms (Piccardo, 2017). Student discourse is captured in Knowledge Forum technology built to support Knowledge Building. Theory-building epistemic markers (e.g., “my theory,” “a better theory,” “new information,” “this theory cannot explain,” “I need to understand,” “putting our knowledge together”) may foster novel figurative language despite its rarity in grade 4. W e conducted the current pilot data analysis to explore the potential of figurative language serving as means to identify promising ideas, asking the following research question : C an novel figurative language serve as means to identify promising ideas with epistemic value to the community in knowledge building community discourse?

title: Augmentation, Enhancement, or Replacement? Classifying Generative AI Use in Workforce Development Practice
citation: Jacob Hale, Tessa Forshaw, Mari Longmire (2026). Augmentation, Enhancement, or Replacement? Classifying Generative AI Use in Workforce Development Practice. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines how frontline workforce development practitioners use GenAI. A survey of 181 practitioners from seven organizations revealed use cases concentrated in learning and instruction (40%), communication and design (39%), and research and analysis (36%). A typology classifying use cases as augmentation (32%), enhancement (26%), replacement (23%), or unspecified (18%) shows that a majority reflect augmentation or enhancement. These results can inform practical guidelines that optimize human -AI collaboration while minimizing replacement of critical thinking.

citation: Carolyn Rose, Olivia Robinson, Melisa Orta-Martinez, Joey Huang, Kylie Peppler (2026). Investigating Collaborative Weaving Design as a Scaffold for AI Literacy. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Rose, C., Robinson, O., Orta-Martinez, M., Huang, J., & Peppler, K.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This poster presents version 1.0 of a curriculum unit designed to expose students to machine learning concepts related to representation and reasoning, an understudied area in AI literacy. Embedded within a textile art course, this three-week pilot explores whether hands-on weaving activities scaffold or distract from AI concept acquisition. Students design weavable potholders while engaging with an AI agent that demonstrates both capabilities and limitations of large language models.

title: Reflective Assessment for Authentic Research among High School Students: Enhancing Epistemic Agency for Knowledge Building
citation: Lei Ding, Jianwei Zhang, Thomas Underwood, Weiting Qi, Dongni Guo, Alae Sherafat, Lana Hower, Jennifer Muirhead, Maryann Dunn (2026). Reflective Assessment for Authentic Research among High School Students: Enhancing Epistemic Agency for Knowledge Building. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Ding, L., Zhang, J., Underwood, T., Qi, W., Guo, D., Sherafat, A., Hower, L., Muirhead, J., & Dunn, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates how high school students engage with reflective assessment during their authentic research experience. An individual interview was conducted to explore students’ reflections on their use of a reflective assessment document. Grounded theory analysis of the interview data and their reflective assessment document revealed key engagement. As a compelling theme, this document guide s students to interpret research evidence and identify progressive questions. The findings inform educational designs to cultivate epistemic agency in a more student-centered, open-ended, collaborative inquiry context.

title: Using Generative AI as an Epistemic Catalyst for Collaborative Lesson Planning
citation: Yuxin Chen, Drew Gossen (2026). Using Generative AI as an Epistemic Catalyst for Collaborative Lesson Planning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

abstract: This study examines the integration of generative AI to cultivate critical AI literacy and epistemic understanding in pre -service teachers. The AI- generated lesson plan is conceptualized as a boundary object, compelling collaborative groups to negotiate and externalize their disciplinary knowledge and reasoning, considering the 5E inquiry model and discourse structure. A multi-modal analysis is utilized to quantify and qualify shifts in epistemic engagement, serving as a robust testbed for necessary design principles in critical collaboration with intelligent systems.

citation: Shan Zhang, Hongming Li, Seiyon Lee, Ji-Eun Lee, Noah L. Schroeder, Anthony F. Botelho (2026). Assessing Student Collaboration with Multimodal Data and Large Language Models. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

abstract: We introduce a multimodal evaluation approach that leverages large language models to assess group collaboration quality in computer -supported collaborative learning environments. Using synchronized log data, dialogue transcripts, and human-coded annotations from undergraduate dyads working in the Graspable Math platform, we develop a theoretically grounded rubric capturing cognitive, social, and regulatory dimensions of collaboration, and examine the extent to which LLM-generated evaluations align with expert human judgments.

title: A Teacher-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Transparent Essay Scoring and Feedback
citation: Ali Keramati, Mark Warschauer (2026). A Teacher-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Transparent Essay Scoring and Feedback. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We present MAESF, a multi-agent essay scoring and feedback, as a teacher-centered AI tool for scoring and feedback. The system distributes evaluation across specialized agents and enables educators to interactively query and refine rubric -aligned assessments. Evaluated on the ASAP dataset, MAESF outperforms single-agent baselines and approaches human inter- rater reliability. By combining transparent scoring with teacher-in-the-loop interaction, MAESF reframes automated assessment as a collaborative process that augments teacher capacity and supports more consistent, timely feedback.

title: Fostering Preservice Teachers’ Design Thinking by Integrating Generative AI and Analytics-Supported Reflective Assessment in a Collaborative Inquiry Environment
citation: Yuqin Yang, Linbaiyu Chen, Daner Sun, Wangda Zhu, Shiyan Pang (2026). Fostering Preservice Teachers’ Design Thinking by Integrating Generative AI and Analytics-Supported Reflective Assessment in a Collaborative Inquiry Environment. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

abstract: This study examined how integrating generative AI (GenAI) and analytics-supported reflective assessment (ASRA) within a Knowledge Building (KB) environment supports preservice teachers’ (PSTs) design thinking (DT). Participants were 110 PSTs in a semester - long instructional design course. We implemented a design that combined collaborative inquiry, delayed GenAI use, and reflective analytics, positioning GenAI as a design partner. Data from a DT scale and instructional design artifacts were analyzed. Results showed gains in problem discovery and definition and a shift toward more iterative design practices. The study offers a learning sciences account of integrating GenAI and ASRA to support DT in teacher education.

title: Shared Epistemic Agency in A Collaborative Game for AI Literacy
citation: Yue Shi, Lingfei Cao, Zhichun Liu (2026). Shared Epistemic Agency in A Collaborative Game for AI Literacy. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

abstract: This study examines how middle school students enacted shared epistemic agency in Occultation, a collaborative Turing -test game for AI literacy. Analyzing 353 chat messages from 28 students, we find that socio-emotional behaviors — trolling, spamming, and banter — directly triggered epistemic reasoning and regulative coordination, extending Damşa et al.'s (2010) framework. Rather than disruptions, these behaviors functioned as inquiry tools in a low- stakes, teacher -free environment. Findings suggest game -based contexts can productively leverage emotional engagement for collaborative AI literacy learning.

abstract: This paper explores ways tangible interfaces can be used as a scaffolding tool for children to better understand 3D geometrical concepts during familiar cube structural activities, and bridge building activities. The study found that through embedded visual and audio feedback, six- to twelve-year-old children were able to identify and address gaps in their own learning, self -correct, and increase their understanding of 3D geometric concepts. Children were also able to successfully apply their understanding to basic engineering concepts in structural building activities. Overall, this study helped to identify principles for designing a framework for tangible interfaces able enhance children’s learning experiences of 3D geometry.

abstract: This study explored a multi-sourced (peer, AI, teacher) feedback model in enhancing student feedback literacy . Participants were 18 postgraduates registered in an L2 business English writing course. Findings revealed the complementary roles of different sources : peer review developed evaluative judgment, AI addressed linguistic accuracy, and teacher feedback targeted content and logic. The model extends beyond single or doubled sourced feedback practice and has pedagogical implications on instructional design for L2 writing classes.

title: Introducing IDEAL: An Intelligent Design Environment for Active Learning
citation: Chenxuan Meng, James D. Slotta (2026). Introducing IDEAL: An Intelligent Design Environment for Active Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Meng, C. & Slotta, J. D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Text-based curriculum tools inadequately represent spatial, temporal, and interactive dimensions of active learning design in active learning classrooms. Although generative AI offers accessible visualization options, existing approaches prioritize aesthetic plausibility over spatial correspondence with real classrooms. This poster presents the AI-assisted storyboarding component of IDEAL (Intelligent Design Environment for Active Learning), developed over three years of iterative design from 2022 to 2025. Our photobook-based approach constrains AI generation using systematic documentation of a specific classroom, including furniture inventory, technology layout, and spatial configurations, producing planning artifacts that help teachers judge the spatial pl ausibility of instructional scenarios before implementation. Exploratory validation with one experienced instructor suggests proof -of-concept feasibility, while also surfacing design tensions around fixation and cognitive load.

abstract: This study contributes to computer -supported collaborative learning research by examining human– artificial intelligence (AI) dialogue patterns across teams with different experience levels with generative AI (GAI) -supported inquiry -based learning. Epistemi c network analysis of dialogues from 26 teams reveals that teams using GAI support for the second time exhibit projective actions toward their goals through active questioning and concept clarification. In contrast, inexperienced teams rely on GA I scaffolding with passive responses. Notably, goal -oriented questions emerge as critical mediators connecting different question types among first-time user teams.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores how learners move between verbal and digital modalities during face-to-face collaborative knowledge building with the Idea Wall, a spatially manipulable digital canvas. Using qualitative multimodal interaction analysis, we examined a te n minute small group session where middle school students jointly discussed pollution. We found that verbal narration often amplifies digital actions, supporting joint attention and shared understanding. Learners frequently moved between verbal and digital communication, however, misalignments occasionally occurred when verbal and digital exchanges failed to synchronize, creating temporary attention gaps. These findings help us understand both the affordances and tensions of multimodal collaboration, and inform our ongoing design- based research on refining the Idea Wall for smoother cross-modality collaboration.

title: One Size Fits All? Learner-Adaptive Peer Feedback and Perceived Feedback Adequacy in Pre-Service Teacher Education
citation: Alina Sheppard-Bujtor, Martin Greisel, Julia Hornstein, Ingo Kollar (2026). One Size Fits All? Learner-Adaptive Peer Feedback and Perceived Feedback Adequacy in Pre-Service Teacher Education. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Sheppard-Bujtor, A., Greisel, M., Hornstein, J., & Kollar, I.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Peer feedback can effectively facilitate pre -service teachers’ evidence -informed reasoning in CSCL environments. Based on the RESOLV-model, we examine if peer feedback providers plan and formulate their peer feedback messages differently depending on the perceived skill level of the peer feedback recipient. T his will be analyzed by assessing the feedback feature constellations of feedback provided by N =297 pre-service teachers during a psychology course. We expect that the more feedback providers adapt their feedback, the more positively this will affect recipients’ acceptance. Aims and theoretical background Online peer feedback is widely used in the computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) context to foster learning outcomes (Tan & Chen, 2022). It has great potential as a pedagogical approach (Double et al., 2020), as it structures peer interaction in a way that ensures transactivity (Vogel et al., 2016): Optimally, students thoroughly process their peers’ contributions, assess them, react to them, and build upon them to extend their peers’, but also their own understanding of subject-matter information (Yu & Schunn, 2023). Yet, feedback recipients do not necessarily benefit from peer feedback (Li et al., 2020). While it is crucial for recipients to understand their peer feedback in order to learn from it (Nelson & Schunn, 2009) , they can get overwhelmed by, for example, very comprehensive and complex feedback which address es multiple interrelated points (Shulgina et al., 2024). This could be especially challenging for recipients with limited prior knowledge of the topic. To mitigate this, feedback providers need to adapt the scope and depth of their feedback message to the recipient’s skill level. If they do so, this should positively affect the recipient’s assessment of the adequacy of the feedback, leading to more likely implementation of th e feedback in the subsequent revision, and ultimately to better learning outcomes (Strijbos et al., 2021). Accordingly, more adaptive peer feedback messages are expected to improve learning outcomes and are therefore relevant within the CSCL context. Surprisingly, prior CSCL research seems to assume that certain feedback features (such as the presence of explanations and solutions) work in a one -size-fits-all fashion (t o be generally beneficial for subsequent learning, i.e., independently from the recipient’s skill level; e.g., Wu & Schunn, 2020). Yet, in line with research on the expertise -reversal effect (Kalyuga et al., 2003), we assume that the relative importance of feedback features—such as explanations and solutions, which are deemed essential to the recipient’s learning outcome (Wu & Schunn, 2020)—depends on the recipient’s skill level, as evidenced by the quality of their initial task solution performance. Specifically, detailed explanations/solutions would be more important for recipients who have not yet mastered the task as successfully as more competent recipients. In turn, these more competent learners likely require only identification of problems in their solutions. Ideally, the feedback provider should be able to recognize these differences in the recipient’s skill levels and tailor their feedback message accordingly. Based on the RESOLV -model, the feedback provider would evaluate the author’s expertise (Rouet et al., 2017). The feedback provider judges the level of competence exhibited via the feedback recipient’s task performance and based on this, recognizes their skill level. Next, the feedback provider would formulate a goal and a plan on how to adjust their message to match the recipient’s skill level. This aligns with Zimmermann’s (2 002) forethought phase, in which the feedback provider sets the goal to adapt their feedback message to the level of competence they assume the recipient to have. Thereby, feedback providers balance their message between completeness and ease of comprehension. We assume that these kinds of cognitive processes determine the proportion of feedback features (in this case: solutions and explanations) in the feedback message (see Fig. 1). Hypotheses We assume that university students are able to adapt their feedback to their peers’ skills levels, at least to a certain extent. We therefore hypothesize that the worse the recipient’s initial performance is, the more explanations and solutions the provider’s feedback contains (H1), as illustrated in Figure 1. title: If One Hack Week is Pedagogically Effective, Why Not Ten?
citation: Jacob Puthipiroj, Thepchai Supnithi, Nongnuch Ketui (2026). If One Hack Week is Pedagogically Effective, Why Not Ten?. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Puthipiroj, J., Supnithi, T., & Ketui, N.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: While hackathons are established pedagogical tools, questions persist about measuring their impact when integrated longitudinally into curricula. We investigate a data science curriculum incorporating eight Kaggle -based hackathons over ten weeks with 137 participants. Using immersive ethnographic methods, we constructed narrative vignettes illuminating how longitudinal hackathon participation fosters identity development, distributed cognition, and community formation. Drawing on Communities of Practice and distributed cognition as both design principles and analytic lenses, we argue that hackathons, when embedded as recurring curricular structures, function as sites for constructing consequential learning identities.

title: Integrating Individualized Education Programs into AI-based Tutoring Systems: An Interview Study with Teachers
citation: C. Naomie Williams, Margaret Ellen Seehorn, Haiyi Zhu (2026). Integrating Individualized Education Programs into AI-based Tutoring Systems: An Interview Study with Teachers. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Williams, C. N., Seehorn, M. E., & Zhu, H.

abstract: US-based special education teachers use Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) to tailor academic resources for students with disabilities. However, prior intervie ws reveal significant challenges integrating key IEP components – individualized learning goals, accommodations, and progress monitoring – into existing AI -based tutoring and assessment technologies. This paper discusses AI-based tutoring systems ’ m isaligned analytics with teachers’ needs, the level of decision -making AI should have in special education classrooms , and a pathway for adapting AI-based tutoring systems to special education’s needs.

title: Computational Modeling of the Process of Scientific Inquiries
citation: Nanae Watanabe, Masahiro Tada, Shin'Ichi Konomi, Masaya Okada (2026). Computational Modeling of the Process of Scientific Inquiries. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

abstract: Scientific inquiry is a process to understand the complex real world. To automatically assess and foster learners ’ scientific inquiries by a computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) system, thinking processes required for scientific inquiries should be modeled in a machine-readable and traceable form. By using a computational modeling approach, the present study extracted patterns of such thinking processes from the data repository of our educational practices and investigated how the processes can be computationally modeled.

title: Orchestrating a Web-Based Classroom Game
citation: Kai Yan, Jasmine Hu, James D. Slotta (2026). Orchestrating a Web-Based Classroom Game. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Yan, K., Hu, J., & Slotta, J. D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Multi group classroom games create a run time orchestration problem: teachers must coordinate pacing, content visibility, and group progress in real time. We examine this problem through a classroom enactment of Fall of Artica, a role-based inquiry game delivered in WISE. Using group centered audio, photographs, authoring screenshots, and planning notes, we analyzed 31 identifiable episodes across 13 step transitions, 14 post reveal intervals, and 4 whole class checkpoints. Findings show tha t lightweight continue gates and in place media enabled the platform to handle within step pacing and visibility, while teacher intervention clustered around logistics recovery, brief procedural alignment, and concept advancing prompts. Whole class convergence remained teacher led, and externally embedded tools increased local recovery work. These findings suggest that, in role-based classroom inquiry, automation is more effective for pre-structured sequencing and visibility than for interpretive, contingent, and convergence work. We argue that platform support redistributed rather than replaced teacher orchestration, and we derive three design implications for the run time enactment of classroom games.

citation: Erfan Farhadi, Kenneth Fei, Yifan Jiang, Zhen Bai (2026). Meet Bip: Understanding Student–Peer Agent Interaction in an Embodied Exploratory Learning Environment. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
authors_list: Farhadi, E., Fei, K., Jiang, Y., & Bai, Z.

abstract: Peer agents have been shown to enhance learning in K–12 settings, yet the design of LLM-powered embodied peer agents for exploratory learning remains underexplored. This study examines how middle -school students interact with Bip, an embodied conversationa l agent in a Minecraft-based AI literacy game. Inspired by the Intelligent Novice paradigm, Bip observes players, provides hints, and scaffolds reflection during an AI literacy activity. Findings from nine students highlight the importance of spatial awareness, responsiveness, and bounded understanding in supporting exploratory learning. We discuss design implications for embodied agents that foster scientific inquiry.

title: Dropout and Success in Online Higher Education: A Comparative Analysis of Students in Brazil
citation: Andréia Maria de Lima Assunção, Paula Daniela Zapata, Lívia Pizauro Sanchez (2026). Dropout and Success in Online Higher Education: A Comparative Analysis of Students in Brazil. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.

abstract: Despite the significant growth of online higher education, challenges persist regarding how to foster engagement and address dropout rates. Therefore, personalized learning has been identified as bridges to success. This paper examines whether the design of reasonable accommodations based on personalized learning affects the success or dropout rates of students in undergraduate courses at an online higher education university in Brazil. By tabulating and analyzing the public database of student enrollment status before and after the design changes, we observed that personalized learning was associated with higher success rates and lower dropout rates, suggesting that Universal Design for Learning (UDL) and Personalized Learning (PL) can mutually benefit a diverse student population.

title: Imagination, Impact, and Epistemic Justice
citation: Marisa Morán Jahn (2026). Imagination, Impact, and Epistemic Justice. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Jahn, M. M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: In this talk, artist and educator Marisa Morán Jahn presents her work, highlighting how a joyful, playful, and imaginative approach serves as a powerful tool to achieving broad- scale social impact — and ask fundamental questions about society. Jahn’s talk draws on two decades of teaching at MIT, Columbia University, and Parsons/The New School as well as K- 12 youth and creating civic media toolkits including audionovelas for domestic workers, pocket- sized comics for migrant farmworkers, illustrated maps for New York City’s 13,000 English Language Learners, and more. In 2008, she collaborated with a community in rural Honduras to create “Bibliobandido” (in English, ‘story eater’), a literacy movement that centers around a bandit who EATS stories and whose fame rivals Santa Claus. As a living legend still active today, Bibliobandido has transformed the lives of 25,000 young believers in Central and North America. For another civic-scale artwork called “CareForce” (2010-ongoing), Jahn collaborated with the National Domestic Workers Alliance (NDWA) to create a social practice artwork featuring two mobile studios (NannyVan, CareForce One) and a PBS- and Sundance-supported film that amplifies care workers’ voices. In 2020, “CareForce” informed the creation of “Carehaus,” the U.S.’s first intergenerational, care-based co-housing building which Jahn has presented to members of the U.S. Congress to help shape housing policy. Across these projects, Jahn explores how collaboration, storytelling, and design operate as powerful sites of learning— revealing how people make meaning, build empathy, and co-create knowledge through participation. Jahn notes, “I’m fascinated by differences in how we learn and how epistemologies form the bedrock of the worlds we create. Creating art and civic media invites me to stay the most attuned to human subtleties and my environment — and connecting with others.” Her practice offers a model of creating with purpose. Bio: Marisa Morán Jahn (she/her) is an artist of Ecuadorian/Chinese descent whose public art, installations, films, and civic media tools explore “civic spaces and the radical art of play” (Chicago Tribune). title: Productive Entanglements: Patterns of Partnership for Learning Technology Innovation
citation: Alyssa Friend Wise (2026). Productive Entanglements: Patterns of Partnership for Learning Technology Innovation. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.

subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science

abstract: Impactful learning technology innovation doesn’t happen in isolation; it grows through relationships, among researchers, educators, students, technologists, designers, and institutional leaders. While some collaborations are carefully structured, others take root more organically, evolving to meet shifting needs and opportunities. In this keynote, Dr. Alyssa Wise explores how purposeful partnerships drive innovation across the technological, social, conceptual, and practical dimensions of learning, tracing three kinds of partnerships that have unfolded over the past decade in her work. Flexible Coupling articulates how institutional partnerships can leverage complementary strengths without becoming over-structured. In a longstanding collaboration with a university learning analytics service unit, in vivo studies of instructors’ analytics use informed both theoretical models of sense-making and applied tool design. Constructive Responsiveness describes how partnerships with educators can evolve around a shared object of inquiry when goals are not yet fully defined. In work with dental educators implementing an online reflection tool, the collaboration advanced from examinations of reflection quality to generate domain-specific insights into failure attribution and professional identity formation. Finally, Generative Pluralism characterizes interdisciplinary partnerships among researchers or co-designers where the goal is not convergence but conceptual creation. These collaborations embraced multiplicity, surfacing productive tensions, methodological bridges, and new vocabularies for imagining learning technologies. Together, these patterns illustrate partnerships as adaptable forms of collaboration, each suited to different problems, people, and purposes. This talk highlights how designing, studying, and sustaining learning with the support of technology can be supported by purposeful partnerships that bridge disciplines, organizations, and stakeholder perspectives. Bio: Dr. Alyssa Wise is Professor of Technology and Education at Vanderbilt University’s Peabody College, with a courtesy appointment in Computer Science in the College of Connected Computing. She also serves as Director of the LIVE Learning Innovation Incubator, Vanderbilt’s interdisciplinary hub for impactful learning technology innovation. Her research productively integrates tools of computational data science, theories of learning sciences and collaborative learning, and practices of human-centered design to build and study analytic and artificial intelligence systems that promote powerful learning for individuals situated in social context. She also conducts mixed-method investigations into how educational practices are being reshaped by new sources of data and the growing availability of new generative artificial intelligence capabilities. Dr. Wise holds a Ph.D. in Learning Sciences and M.S. in Instructional Systems Technology from Indiana University, as well as a B.S. in Chemistry from Yale University, was previously a Professor of Learning Sciences and Educational Technology and Director of the Learning Analytics Research Network (LEARN) at New York University and has worked in industry, with non-profits, and in classrooms across the Americas. https://tinyurl.com/alyssawisescholar https://peabody.vanderbilt.edu/bio/?pid=alyssa-wise https://lab.vanderbilt.edu/live https://www.linkedin.com/in/alyssawise

abstract: In this talk, Dr. Ananda Marin traces her own history with the methodologies of community-based design research and co-design, linking what she has learned to key organizing constructs in this domain — matters of purpose, place, scale, impact, power, and equity. She shares axioms that were surfaced and re-membered while partnering alongside Indigenous families and most recently with improvisational jazz artists to design generative contexts that move toward collective thriving. From here, Dr. Marin reflects on how partnering can extend the field’s conceptualizations of learning in consequential ways. Sociocultural theories in the learning sciences have conceptualized learning as both the acquisition of practices as well as shifts in the use of cultural and cognitive resources for the purposes of meaning making. She suggests that these theories, which have played a pivotal role in her scholarly trajectory, can be expanded when we theorize alongside scholarship in Indigenous Studies and the work of Black and Indigenous learning scientists who have foregrounded the importance of kinship, relationality, respect, responsibility, reciprocity, and reverence. Turning to questions of human maturation, the talk will invite the learning sciences community to consider the field-wide consequences of theorizing from human centrism. Building with the work of scholars who have reminded us that sociality is organized through the interconnectedness of talk and interaction, as well as four years of conversations and art making with creative musicians, Dr. Marin proposes that wondering about and with sound making can expand our understandings of human learning in ways that are necessary for meeting the challenges we face as a society. Bio: Ananda Marin is associate professor in the Department of Education and faculty in American Indian Studies at the University of California, Los Angeles (Tongva territory). As a learning scientist she aims to bring research on the socio-ecological and cultural nature of learning and development alongside efforts to co-design more just teaching/learning environments. Broadly speaking, her research explores the diversity of ways that multigenerational groups of people organize attention and observation to participate in joint activity, collaborate, and improvise in everyday and professional contexts. abstract: Prolepsis ’Till Infinity calls for an education that recognizes imagination as infrastructure. Dr. Kareem Edouard invites us to rethink how we build STEM spaces that honor culture, creativity, and care as the foundation of learning. His research at the ILLEST Lab challenges systems that reward compliance over curiosity, asking what becomes possible when play, storytelling, and design are treated as serious forms of knowledge, particularly for those most marginalized in STEAM, Black boys. Drawing from his design practices across learning, children’s media, and informal STEAM environments, Dr. Edouard examines how learners develop identity, agency, and understanding through participatory, culturally responsive experiences, highlighting key insights from the learning sciences. For example, in co-design projects with educators and youth, students engage in creative problem-solving and media production, positioning them as knowledge-makers whose ideas actively shape the learning environment. These collaborative partnerships demonstrate how purposeful engagement between educators, researchers, and communities fosters equitable and imaginative learning outcomes. Dr. Edouard envisions an educational future where play, imagination, and community are essential for liberation. This keynote invites us to build toward proleptic, possible, and connected futures already in motion, where creativity and meaning-making shape how we learn, teach, and thrive together. By treating play, imagination, and community as foundational, Dr. Edouard shows how learning and partnership are inseparable in designing educational spaces that cultivate curiosity, empowerment, and cultural relevance. Bio: Dr. Kareem Edouard is an Assistant Professor of Learning Technologies at Drexel University’s School of Education and Co-Director of the Informal Learning Linking Engineering, Science and Technology (ILLEST) Lab. His work explores how design, as a cultural, creative, and communal practice, intersects informal STEM education and children’s media to promote meaningful knowledge transfer across learning spaces. He examines how storytelling and co-creation cultivate belonging, purpose, and imagination in environments shaped by inequity. Through initiatives like the Black Male Animation Lab, Dr. Edouard redefines STEM as a space for cultural creation and collective care, empowering Black boys as designers, storytellers, and innovators. He focuses on Black boys because their experiences sharpen the stakes of equity work in STEM: to support those most marginalized by systemic exclusion is to test whether design can truly be liberatory. His liberatory co-design framework examines how collaborative creation transforms educational systems and expands equity and representation. In the Sneaker Lab, design, material science, and cultural expression are explored for their impact on identity and innovation. The GRIND initiative further investigates how sports, data, and technology can foster community-driven STEM engagement. Dr. Edouard integrates his co-liberty design framing vision into children’s STEM media. This approach combines his experience as a former music video and commercial director with his academic research. As Executive Producer of MayNERD’s Wild World of Science (YouTube Kids), Built From Scratch, and Creative Producer of Work It Out Wombats! (PBS KIDS), he uses media as a conduit to share STEM learning and engagement, which remains at the heart of his work with children’s media. https://drexel.edu/soe/faculty-and-staff/faculty/Edouard-Kareem https://www.linkedin.com/in/kareemedouard https://www.olegreensgroup.com/home Special Session

Through an engaging, dialogic format, the panelists will share stories and artifacts from four participatory design projects and explore common themes and challenges. abstract: This interactive tool paper presents the design and development of an AI-powered chatbot that scaffolds college students’ self-regulated learning (SRL). Grounded in Pintrich’s SRL framework and informed by meta-analytic evidence on effective SRL interventions, the chatbot is designed as a reflective learning partner that supports metacognitive monitoring, strategic deployment, and affective regulation. Using a design-based research (DBR) approach, this study explores how SRL theory can guide the development of generative AI–mediated interactions. We describe the theoretical rationale underlying the tool, articulate key design principles, present the prototype’s architecture, and discuss implications for improving evidence-based, equitable AI scaffolds to enhance undergraduate learning outcomes.

title: Creaticode: An AI Playground for Every Middle School Student

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly influences how we communicate, create, and solve problems, making early AI education essential. Middle school is an ideal time for students to build AI literacy, yet teachers face barriers such as limited tools, steep learning curves, and lack of classroom-ready materials. CreatiCode addresses these challenges by extending the familiar Scratch platform with AI tools and AI-enhanced coding blocks that introduce generative and predictive AI concepts in an engaging, visual way. Supporting all four dimensions of AI literacy: understanding, using, evaluating, and creating, CreatiCode helps students move from AI consumers to creators. The platform includes free teacher support such as tutorials, lesson plans, and slide decks to simplify classroom integration. This paper introduces the CreatiCode AI toolset, describes partnerships with teachers to refine usability and curriculum alignment, and showcases examples of CreatiCode in action that highlight its potential as an accessible AI playground for every middle school student.

abstract: Multimodal presentation of science content can support science learning; however, elementary teachers lack the time and support to find age-appropriate, freely accessible, and Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS)-aligned science videos. This interactive demo will showcase our Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered Video Analyzer, a feature of the Leveraging Online Videos for Elementary Science (LOVE Science) platform, which analyzes YouTube videos to determine alignment to NGSS performance expectations, conceptual complexity, vocabulary level, and relevance across NGSS domains. The LOVE Science Video Analyzer helps teachers make more effective use of the open educational resources already available to them—particularly on YouTube—by providing an AI-powered plug-in that streamlines the process of finding, reviewing, and selecting high-quality science videos to enhance instruction.

title: Making Collaborative Creativity Visible: The Viacocrea Dashboard

abstract: Addressing complex global challenges requires learners to engage in cocreative processes and regulate their contributions at both individual and group levels. However, supporting and visualizing such multifaceted collaboration is difficult. Building on our previous work and the Viacocrea platform, which guides students through cocreation, we have developed the Viacocrea Dashboard—an interactive tool that visualizes group cocreation dynamics and computes creativity indicators using Natural Language Processing and learning analytics. Key metrics are developed that include fluency (idea quantity), flexibility (topic diversity), elaboration (idea richness), and originality (novelty). The dashboard helps students reflect on and regulate their work, draw inspiration from peers, and enhance cocreation strategies, while providing teachers with actionable insights for feedback and support. In this demo, we will present the Viacocrea dashboard, invite the audience to engage in interactive demonstrations, and discuss how Viacocrea can advance the orchestration of collaborative creativity in education.

abstract: LexiLearn is an artificial intelligence (AI) enhanced virtual reality (VR) learning ex- perience for literacy education. The system introduces a novel integration of AI with adaptable haptic interfaces, supporting both wearable gloves and handheld VR controllers. The project investigates how multisensory engagement within an adaptive, generative VR environment can support literacy acquisition, including spelling, reading through interactive and playful move- ment, phoneme–grapheme recognition and recall, and visual–sensory associations. Led by a cross-disciplinary research team, this project explores innovative alternatives to immersive learning environments. It examines how multisensory and AI-driven technologies can be mean- ingfully implemented for diverse learners, aiming to inform and transform the educational prac- tice through practice-based design and research methods.

abstract: Interactive media can be effectively enhanced through advancements in artificial intelligence (AI). Through a research–practice partnership with PBS KIDS, we integrated AI into popular PBS KIDS shows to support dialogic interactions that actively engage children in STEM learning. These interactions help ground abstract STEM concepts in socially meaningful experiences. In this work, we present an interactive web app designed to scaffold children’s learning and engagement at home. We discuss design considerations, challenges related to children’s speech recognition, and insights from iterative testing that informed the app’s current stage of development.

title: CoReTra: Supporting Learners in Identifying Personally Meaningful Contrasts among Readers’ Interpretations
citation: Sae Tanaka, Ryohei Ikejiri, Yuhei Yamauchi (2026). CoReTra: Supporting Learners in Identifying Personally Meaningful Contrasts among Readers’ Interpretations. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Tanaka, S., Ikejiri, R., & Yamauchi, Y.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Writing that involves personally reconstructing what one has read is essential for knowledge transformation, although university students often struggle to make meaningful connections between readings and their own ideas. Existing instructional approaches offer procedural guidance but often do not support deep, personally meaningful integration. To address this issue, we developed CoReTra (Collaborative Reflection through conTrast of interpretations), a web-based system designed to support learners in identifying and integrating personally meaningful contrasts. The system includes two views: the Decomposition View, which allows learners to extract content elements from readings and record notes as cards, and the Integration View, which enables learners to compare cards from different perspectives to refine their interpretations. The system uses large language model (LLM)–based semantic mining to adaptively suggest peer-created cards that represent diverse viewpoints. These features support learners in progressively revisiting and reconstructing their interpretations, promoting deeper reflection in CSCL contexts, while keeping contrast identification learner‑driven.

abstract: This demo showcases an AI-supported, evidence-centered assessment design that scaffolds middle school students’ scientific argumentation in the context of ecosystems learning. Grounded in Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), the assessment links constructs of scientific reasoning and argumentation with AI-driven evidence detection and feedback generation. Students investigate ecosystem dynamics through a NetLogo simulation, construct Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) arguments, and receive adaptive feedback from an LLM- based chatbot. Participants will experience the task, explore reasoning analytics, and see how ECD structures both assessment and AI design. The demo highlights how ECD can ensure a valid, interpretable, and instructionally useful AI system that advances students’ reasoning and supports classroom instruction.

title: Learning in the Wild: PAL's New Tools and Methods for Research in Early Childhood Mathematics
citation: Anastasia Betts, Benjamin Ryon, Elida V. Laski, Sunil Gunderia (2026). Learning in the Wild: PAL's New Tools and Methods for Research in Early Childhood Mathematics. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.

subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: PAL (Personal Assistant for Learning) is an adaptive, smart learning system that operationalizes sociocultural theory, Knowledge Space Theory, and learning sciences principles to support and study early mathematics learning in real-world contexts. PAL guides parents and teachers to facilitate hands-on, socially mediated interactions aligned with each child’s Zone of Proximal Development while generating frequent, fine-grained evidence about children’s mathematical learning. The system integrates a research-grounded knowledge model, an explore–exploit adaptive engine, and a digital assessment system to provide personalized guidance and scalable, ecologically valid measurement. Early pilots show substantial gains in children’s learning and strong associations between adult engagement and child learning. Designed as a learning accelerator and a research platform, PAL provides the Learning Sciences community with a tool for examining learning trajectories, scaffolding dynamics, and conceptual and skill development as they naturally unfold across a child’s learning ecosystem— while producing evidence needed to connect research insights to practice at scale.

title: Trend Trackers: Building Data Literacy Through Problem-Based Learning

abstract: In this demo, we discuss the co-design of an interactive, problem-based science supplement called Trend Trackers. Trend Trackers aims to engage middle school students with socioscientific issues that impact cities and communities all over the world. Students take up the role of a data scientist to address public health problems within the fictional city of Springfield. In this demo, we will explore a challenge in which students are asked to design a vaccination plan to reduce the rates of flu in Springfield. Students engage in interactive and immersive activities to collect wastewater samples, measure rates of flu in the community, and generate evidence through a series of wrangling, visualization, and analysis activities. Students then share their findings and collaborate with their team to co-construct a vaccination plan for Springfield.

title: Supporting Classroom Orchestration and Collaborative Programming with Jupyter Analytics
citation: Zhenyu Cai, Richard Lee Davis, Roland Tormey, Pierre Dillenbourg (2026). Supporting Classroom Orchestration and Collaborative Programming with Jupyter Analytics. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Cai, Z., Davis, R. L., Tormey, R., & Dillenbourg, P.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Jupyter notebooks have been widely adopted in STEM courses that have programming or data science integrated. Jupyter Analytics, a learning analytics system, has been built to provide teachers with visibility into student activity. In combination with its existing functions as an awareness and reflection tool, this demo illustrates how the new code- sharing feature can address the real needs of both instructors and learners within Jupyter notebooks. Specifically, we discuss its potential value in two use cases: (1) supporting teachers in orchestrating live-coding lectures, and (2) helping students merge and synchronize work in collaborative programming. This covers two common pedagogical contexts in higher education: teacher-led lectures and student-centered active learning environments with group projects or collaborative sessions.

title: Learning from the Experts: Exploring Human–AI Feedback through Expert-AI
citation: Tomoki Takizawa, Masahiro Ogino, Maki Sakurai (2026). Learning from the Experts: Exploring Human–AI Feedback through Expert-AI. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Takizawa, T., Ogino, M., & Sakurai, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This demo introduces Expert-AI, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to emulate aspects of human experts’ reasoning and feedback. Drawing on experts’ writings, lectures, and interviews, the system provides dialogic, context-sensitive feedback grounded in expert perspectives, allowing experts to review and refine responses over time. We report preliminary findings from a pilot study in a business idea creation course at a private university in Japan, where students used both Expert-AI and general-purpose generative AI systems (e.g., ChatGPT). The findings suggest complementary roles: students used Expert-AI for conceptual framing and strategic evaluation, and general-purpose generative AI for elaboration and implementation planning. These findings suggest learners’ interpretations of AI feedback may vary depending on how it is presented. Accordingly, the demo presents the text version of Expert-AI alongside early multimodal prototypes including voice and android embodiments to examine how interaction modality shapes perceived credibility, empathy, trust, and engagement in expert-like AI feedback.

title: “Where Do I Start?” A Tool for Interactive Literature Discovery in the Learning Sciences
citation: Morgan Vickery, Elena Bai, Kyle Beyersdorf, Jie Sheng, Aman Desai, Srijita Chakraburty (2026). “Where Do I Start?” A Tool for Interactive Literature Discovery in the Learning Sciences. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.

abstract: The rapid expansion of Learning Sciences scholarship makes it challenging for newcomers to navigate diverse theories, methods, and contexts. We present the Interactive Literature Review Database Template, an open-source tool that turns any corpus into a dynamic, filterable database. As demonstrated by Journal of the Learning Sciences articles and student- built instances, the tool enables sustainable, transparent, and easily updated literature exploration while lowering technical barriers for researchers.

title: Resonate: An Interactive VR Tool for Experiencing Inclusive Education Through the Student Perspective
citation: Xiang Ni, Huangyi Xu, Xin Guan, Ruiqi Zhang (2026). Resonate: An Interactive VR Tool for Experiencing Inclusive Education Through the Student Perspective. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.

abstract: Resonate is a virtual reality (VR) design tool developed to enhance educators’ understanding and implementation of inclusive teaching practices. By enabling educators to experience classroom environments from the perspective of students with disabilities, Resonate bridges critical gaps in teacher preparation and professional development. Leveraging immersive VR technology, the tool extends beyond traditional disability awareness training by fostering structured observation and authentic, experience-based empathy. Distinct from generic simulations, Resonate supports contextualized instructional reflection by allowing educators to test their own teaching materials within simulated disability scenarios. Grounded in Kolb’s experiential learning theory and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles, the tool supports customizable parameter configuration, dynamic content integration, and in-situ annotation. This paper describes Resonate’s features, applications, and contributions to learning sciences research, aiming to support educators in moving toward more actionable inclusive practices.

title: The Connected Spaces Dashboard: Fostering Peer-to-peer Collaboration Through Ambient Maker Profiles
citation: David Hopping, Mike Tissenbaum (2026). The Connected Spaces Dashboard: Fostering Peer-to-peer Collaboration Through Ambient Maker Profiles. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.

abstract: The Connected Spaces Dashboard is a tool designed to foster maker identity development, peripheral awareness, and the promotion of student help seeking behaviors. Developed iteratively across several years, prototypes of the Dashboard range from lo-fi solutions to in-house developed applications. Beneath these external embodiments, there are a number of frameworks and scaffolds developed to facilitate student interactions and engagement with the Dashboard as a rich identity resource. In this interactive demo, participants will have a chance to utilize these scaffolds alongside a specially tailored version of the Dashboard to develop peripheral awareness with their peers.

title: From Thought to Action: Designing AI Coaching Support for Time Management with Cognitive Behavioral and Self-Regulated Learning Strategies
citation: Zilu Jiang, Qiujie Li, Di Xu, Zexin Xu (2026). From Thought to Action: Designing AI Coaching Support for Time Management with Cognitive Behavioral and Self-Regulated Learning Strategies. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Jiang, Z., Li, Q., Xu, D., & Xu, Z.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This demonstration introduces TimeWise, a conversational agent that integrates self- regulated learning (SRL) and cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) to provide personalized, context-aware coaching for time management in online learning. The system leverages learning management system data to visualize study patterns and initiate reflective dialogue grounded in students’ actual learning activity. Through guided interaction, TimeWise engages students in examining their thoughts, identifying irrational beliefs, and reconstructing more adaptive perspectives to restore task-oriented behavior. We present the design principles and illustrative interaction cases that demonstrate how the system operationalizes SRL and CBT integration. This work highlights the potential of combining these frameworks to promote sustained academic regulation in online learning contexts.

citation: Megan Humburg, Joshua Danish, Yeo Jin Kim, Morgan Vickery, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Namrata Srivastava, Sarah Burriss, Krista Glazewski, James Lester (2026). SciStory: A Demo of AI-Supported Socioscientific Learning through Visual Novels. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.

abstract: Our tool demo will explore intersections between narrative-centered learning, AI agents as inquiry scaffolds, and the interdisciplinary exploration of socioscientific issues. We will share our current design of SciStory: Pollinators, an interactive visual novel designed to support middle grades students in developing persuasive arguments to solve socioscientific problems in their community. Discussion will explore how we balance ethical issues around generative AI in our agent design, leverage co-design practices to iteratively improve collaborative game features, and draw on principles from problem-based learning to engage learners in developing solutions for complex socioscientific issues.

title: An Interactive Tool for Using Digital Music Note Manipulatives to Compose Rhythms
citation: Mary DiCioccio, Finn Goehrig (2026). An Interactive Tool for Using Digital Music Note Manipulatives to Compose Rhythms. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: DiCioccio, M. & Goehrig, F.
subject: STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Previous research utilized paper music note manipulatives to help jazz students brainstorm rhythms to use during improvisation. However, there were issues that can be mitigated by digitizing these music note manipulatives. Therefore, this interactive demo presents a website with these digital music note manipulatives, called Measure, to show math, music, and STEAM educators how to use them with their students. Problem context In standard music notation, longer notes often take up less space on the staff than groups of shorter ones, and therefore, notation and audiation are not always logically related, causing students’ confusion (Gordon, 2012). Because of this, in previous work, the first author conducted a study at a summer jazz camp which included paper music note manipulatives were designed and students were taught to use them to brainstorm rhythms to use during improvisation (figure 1). While the use of these manipulatives did impact students’ performance (DiCioccio, in review), there were some practical and educational obstacles involved that can be mitigated by digitizing these manipulatives. For instance, cutting the music note manipulatives was a time-consuming task that can be eliminated by putting the manipulatives on the computer. Also, the manipulatives were very small and thus would regularly fall on the floor and get lost, which would not be an issue with digital manipulatives. Educationally, there is concern that disconnect from audiation while teaching notation, students will not learn to read the notation fluently and make auditory meaning of it (Gordon, 2012). In my aforementioned study, I taught the students the meaning behind the notation, connecting the symbols to sound, and when students independently brainstormed rhythms, I encouraged students to clap, hum, or play the rhythms on their instruments. However, the paper manipulatives themselves did not enforce the auditory connections like digitized manipulatives can. Figure 1 Paper Music Note Manipulatives E xisting tools There are computerized fraction manipulative tools that do not make connections to music, such as the Fraction Strips tool on Toy Theater (Gaspard et at., 2018). Also, there are computerized tools for music composition. For instance, there are tools such as Sibelius (AVID, 2019) that allow the composer to input standard music notation, which do not utilize fraction bars to help users visualize note duration. Also, there exists tools such as GarageBand (Apple, 2025), which allow the user to record musical performance, either on the built-in computer instruments or in real life. Garage Band allows users to clip and organize sections of these recordings but does not allow the user to see the duration of or manipulate individual notes, unless the user records each note individually. Furthermore, there are such tools that are designed for the purpose of music learning. For instance, there is a tool called Learning Music that guides students through lessons on music theory and composition using computer music tools. While this tool utilizes rectangles to show note duration like the tool in this demo, it does not connect these to the numerical values of the note length, nor does it allow for note durations that are smaller than the beat or other, more complicated rhythms, such as swung notes, triplets, or dotted notes. In addition, there is a computerized tool for music composition called Impromptu that, while not built intentionally for interdisciplinary math and music composition, has been studied to be used in this way (Bamberger & DiSessa, 2003). Finally, Toy Theater also has an online tool for composing rhythms using fraction bars. However, Toy Theater’s tool does not use standard music symbols for note durations, nor does it provide time signatures or measures to fit the fraction bars into. Also, Toy Theater’s tool only provides options for whole, half, quarter, and straight eighth notes. Thus, the current tool fills a gap by linking fraction bars, a visual representation of the fractional length of notes, with their corresponding standard music symbol and putting this in context of the measure and time signature, as well as expanding the note options to include dotted notes and swung eighth notes. Theoretical framing As referenced in the problem context, this tool draws upon Gordon’s (2012) Music Learning Theory, as this tool aims to make connections between symbols and audiation explicit. Furthermore, this tool draws upon Constructionism (Papert & Harel, 1991), as it encourages “learning-by-making” by guiding students to learn standard music notation by facilitating rhythm composition. Without the tool, students could compose a rhythm by writing various symbols for durations of notes in standard music notation without learning the auditory meaning of the symbols that they wrote. However, the combination of fraction bars, standard music notation, and auditory feedback is designed to help students learn the meaning of the symbols as they compose. Tool overview To use Measure (Goehrig & DiCioccio, 2026), the digital music note manipulative tool, users will first pick a time signature and tempo. To input a rhythm, they will click on the button with their desired note duration and then click on the measure where they would like to place the note. This will display a fraction bar with the fractional length of the measure for the user to visualize the length of the note. It will also have the numerical fraction and standard music notation symbol so that the user can connect the numerical value with the music notation. If a user tries to input a note in a measure where there is no room, the tool will split the note into two tied notes, where the first measure is filled and the second measure completes the note duration, teaching the users which fractional values sum to the time signature. Once users have input their rhythm, they can press a button which will play the rhythm so that they can hear how it sounds. We opted to put this tool on the internet so that it is free and available to the public and able to be used on any operating system. Uses of the tool This tool has several educational uses. First, it can be used by music educators to teach students how to read rhythms by visually connecting the length of the note to its symbol. To do so, music teachers can have students input rhythms into the tool from pieces they are studying in class and have students practice performing the rhythms along with the tool or after watching and listening to the tool. Also, it can be used by music educators as a tool to teach improvisation and composition, as in my previous work (DiCioccio, in review), where I demonstrated how to use the manipulatives and tasked students to use them to compose their own rhythms. Furthermore, it can be used by math educators to provide an auditory representation of fractions to deepen understanding of the meaning of fractions and fraction operations. To do so, math teachers can represent fractions and fraction operations in the app alongside other representations when teaching, and they can encourage students to model problems in the app when working independently. S etup for the interactive session We will first demonstrate the tool and give an overview of its educational purpose. After that, we will ask the attendees if they have any questions. For in-person attendees, we will then have iPads available for conference attendees to test the tool out for themselves. We will also share the link to the tool with attendees on Whova for online participants to use during the session and for all participants to have available for their future use. Furthermore, we will have paper manipulatives available for in-person attendees to test and compare them to the digital tool. We will share a link for all attendees on Whova with a PDF of the paper manipulatives (figure 1) so they can print and use the paper manipulatives in the future, and for the online participants to print and use during the conference to compare to the digital tool. Discussion While the use of digital manipulatives has its advantages, there are also limitations to their use in comparison to paper manipulatives. First, digital manipulatives are not as tangible as paper manipulatives, making the manipulatives more abstract and possibly losing some of their educational value. This has been shown in several studies that compared student achievement from learning fractions through concrete and digital manipulatives, many of which found that student achievement was higher for those that learned fractions with concrete manipulatives compared to digital manipulatives (Al Farra et al., 2014; Vessonen et al., 2021). However, others have found that digital manipulatives are at least as effective as concrete manipulatives, and that they are more time efficient (Mendiburo & Hasselbring, 2014). Another concern is that while technology is increasingly available (Gray et al., 2021), not all schools will have access to the necessary technology to use the digital manipulatives, where paper can be more accessible due to its lower cost. Future research can study the ways in which these differences impact accessibility and learning. References Al Farra, N. K., Belbase, S., Tairab, H., Qablan, A., Peprah Opoku, M., & Safi, S. K.
