title: Early Science Hub: Designing Interactive Simulations to Support Preschool Educators' Understanding of Science Core Ideas and Cross Cutting Concepts
citation: Tiffany Leones, Danae Kamdar, Ximena Dominguez (2026). Early Science Hub: Designing Interactive Simulations to Support Preschool Educators' Understanding of Science Core Ideas and Cross Cutting Concepts. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Leones, T., Kamdar, D., & Dominguez, X.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: To support preschool educators’ integration of science in their classrooms, our project is co-designing the Early Science Hub (Hub), a professional learning resource based on promising components identified in prior work, with partner educators and curriculum/media designers. The Hub and its components are being designed to leverage technology and include educative features to make the resource widely accessible across early learning contexts. This paper details the design and iteration of one specific Hub component, the interactive simulations of science core ideas and cross cutting concepts designed to support preschool educators’ understanding of these. The session will invite participants to explore the interactive simulations and engage in a discussion to gather their insights and feedback, which can inform potential future iterations.

title: CLUE: A Learning-Goal Oriented AI-Enhanced STEM Inquiry System
citation: Leslie Bondaryk, Ido Davidesco, Na’ama Y. Av-Shalom, Alden J. Edson (2026). CLUE: A Learning-Goal Oriented AI-Enhanced STEM Inquiry System. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Bondaryk, L., Davidesco, I., Av-Shalom, N. Y., & Edson, A. J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
tpack_tk_labels: Generative AI & LLMs; Collaborative Platforms & Forums
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Productive Failure & Problem Solving; Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: Integrating AI into STEM classrooms risks shortcutting the productive struggle that makes inquiry-based learning effective. This session introduces CLUE, a collaborative platform that addresses this risk through rubric-centered AI personalization: rather than deploying generative AI as an open-ended chat interface, CLUE uses curriculum-tuned categorization rubrics to make student problem-solving strategies visible to both learners and teachers. In this way, CLUE’s rubric-centered approach operationalizes sensemaking for any particular curriculum. We conjecture that this design supports teacher noticing, promotes metacognitive reflection, and sustains productive struggle by shifting AI feedback away from answer-giving and toward strategy awareness and peer comparison. We will demonstrate several classroom- tested STEM curricula paired with these AI scaffolds, and attendees will participate in a live collaborative experience to see how CLUE's rubric-based approach makes AI-generated enrichment transparent and purposeful. The session will explore the design opportunities and challenges behind this methodology, invite discussion about alternative approaches, and share directions for future empirical evaluation. Attendees will leave with practical strategies for integrating AI into STEM classes and access to CLUE tools for use in their own classrooms.

title: CoDialogue Space: Design of AI-supported Collaborative Learning Platform
citation: Eunhye Flavin, Kunal Mohindra, Jeonghyun (Jonna) Lee (2026). CoDialogue Space: Design of AI-supported Collaborative Learning Platform. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Flavin, E., Mohindra, K., & Lee, J. J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: This paper introduces CoDialogue Space, a generative AI–supported collaborative learning platform that provides real-time facilitation during group dialogue. While computer- supported collaborative learning holds promise, it often depends on ad hoc analysis, scripted prompts, and static scaffolds. CoDialogue Space addresses these limitations through discursive facilitation strategies, multiuser–AI interaction, adaptive facilitation levels, and instructor- configurable prompts without requiring coding. We present its design features, offering a scalable, theoretically grounded environment for advancing AI-mediated collaborative learning.

title: Lowering Barriers for Designing AI-Embodied Robots for Learning
citation: Amy Eguchi, Emile Kroeger (2026). Lowering Barriers for Designing AI-Embodied Robots for Learning. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Eguchi, A. & Kroeger, E.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This paper presents RoboHearts AI, a web-based platform that enables educators, students, and researchers to easily design and deploy large-language-model (LLM)–powered characters on embodied robots such as Pepper, NAO, and LEGO-based extensions. By combining LLM-driven conversational capabilities with robots’ multimodal features, including gesture, animated movement, gaze, and visual display, RoboHearts AI supports naturalistic, adaptive, and contextualized interactions that extend beyond traditional screen-based chatbots. The paper introduces practical applications across educational and non-educational settings, and proposes two pedagogical scenarios: learning with AI, where robots act as tutors or learning companions, and learning about AI, where students gain AI literacy and deepen their understanding of AI by designing and iteratively refining robot characters. This hands-on demonstration guides participants in character creation and multimodal behavior design. This work lowers barriers to embodied AI adoption and highlights new opportunities for research, instructional innovation, and human-centered learning with AI-embodied robots.

title: TeamLearn: A Multimodal, AI-enhanced Dashboard for Reflection During Collaborative Problem-Solving
citation: Rogers Kaliisa, Crina Damşa, Jan Arild Dolonen, Malcolm Langford, Runar Hilleren Lie, Terje Kristian Lian Thoresen, Richard Nesnass, Krishna Siddharth Rajasekaran (2026). TeamLearn: A Multimodal, AI-enhanced Dashboard for Reflection During Collaborative Problem-Solving. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This demo presents TeamLearn, a multimodal collaboration analytics dashboard designed to facilitate reflection and provide feedback on developing group artifacts during long- term collaborative problem-solving projects. By integrating meetings, documents, and collaboration experience analytics, the dashboard offers visualisations that help groups monitor participation, task progress, and collaboration dynamics. Developed through a design-based research process, the TeamLearn dashboard provides structured opportunities for reflective dialogue. The demo will showcase the dashboard’s core features and illustrate how it can be integrated into collaborative project activities.

title: Introducing Scratch-Quantum: A Block-Based Interface for Quantum Computing Education
citation: Haeun Choa, Seoyeon Lee (2026). Introducing Scratch-Quantum: A Block-Based Interface for Quantum Computing Education. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Choa, H. & Lee, S.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Quantum computing is increasingly recognized as a critical technological domain; however, its mathematical formalisms and Python-based programming interfaces pose substantial barriers for K–12 learners. To address these challenges, this study introduces Scratch-Quantum, a block-based environment that integrates quantum computing capabilities into Scratch. Leveraging IBM Qiskit as a backend, Scratch-Quantum enables learners to construct executable quantum circuits using visual blocks, allowing them to explore qubit initialization, gate operations, and measurement without writing code. This paper presents the design principles and system architecture of Scratch-Quantum and illustrates how learners can explore core quantum phenomena—such as superposition and entanglement—by constructing and running circuits within the tool. We propose this tool as an entry point for introducing quantum concepts into elementary and middle school classrooms by lowering syntactic difficulties and broadening access to quantum computing education.

title: Piano Lab Pro: An Exposure Based Mixed Reality Application to Mitigate Music Performance Anxiety
citation: Ziyi Wang, Hedieh Najafi, Amanda Cowell, Ray Majewski, Moeezo Saleem, Kavya Jeganathan (2026). Piano Lab Pro: An Exposure Based Mixed Reality Application to Mitigate Music Performance Anxiety. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Wang, Z., Najafi, H., Cowell, A., Majewski, R., Saleem, M., & Jeganathan, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Piano Lab Pro (PLP) is an immersive experience for the Apple Vision Pro headset, designed to help piano students practice coping mechanisms for dealing with musical performance anxiety. To accomplish this, PLP allows students to perform a musical piece using a real piano, while having the Mixed Reality (MR) headset simulate a large performance space both visually and acoustically. During their performance, they experience dimmer house light, brighter stage light, and simulated audience presenting distracting behavior. PLP is designed in collaboration with faculty members from the school of music and addresses a practical need to help music students identify their anxiety triggers and practice effective coping mechanisms.

title: SEED: A Teachable-Agent System that Supports Elementary Students’ Self-Explanation by Teaching an AI Chatbot
citation: Seoyeon Lee, Haeun Choa (2026). SEED: A Teachable-Agent System that Supports Elementary Students’ Self-Explanation by Teaching an AI Chatbot. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Lee, S. & Choa, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Self-explanation is a powerful strategy for conceptual understanding, yet elementary students struggle to produce coherent explanations without individualized scaffolding. LLM- based teachable agents offer a promising alternative—positioning the learner as teacher and the AI as student, leveraging the protégé effect to deepen understanding—yet most existing work targets undergraduate learners, leaving elementary students largely unaddressed. This demo introduces SEED (Self-Explanation Eliciting Dialogue), a prototype teachable-agent system that positions the child as the teacher and the AI as a novice learner. SEED features a role- reversal prompt engine, three-stage scaffolding flow, growth visualization, and auto-generated learning notebooks—all designed to sustain the protégé effect. This work demonstrates that LLM-based teachable agents, when designed around developmental principles, can meaningfully support self-explanation among elementary learners.

title: Analyzing Embodied Engagement in Co-located Collaboration through Kinesthetic Modality

abstract: This demo introduces key enhancements to MoDa: A free, open-source web based system designed to support students in making sense of complex systems. MoDa is a domain- specific, block-based computational modeling and analysis tool that allows students to build models side-by-side to real-world data. Our latest enhancements include integrating quantitative data in the system using the Common Online Data Analysis Platform and Activity Player to support structured data-rich investigations, allowing students to use a wider variety of real- world data sources to refine their model toward reproducing important features of system behavior both qualitatively, by reproducing important visual and dynamic behaviors, and quantitatively by allowing closer comparison of patterns, relationships, and variability.

title: TopoLA Dashboard: Making Topological Learning Analytics Accessible for Exploring Learner Behavioral Structure
citation: Hitoshi Inoue, Koichi Yasutake (2026). TopoLA Dashboard: Making Topological Learning Analytics Accessible for Exploring Learner Behavioral Structure. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Inoue, H. & Yasutake, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Topological Data Analysis (TDA) offers powerful methods for understanding structural patterns in learner populations, yet its application in learning analytics remains an emerging field with limited interpretive precedent. This interactive demo presents TopoLA Dashboard, a tool designed to make topological learning analytics accessible to educators and researchers without requiring topology expertise. By applying Zigzag Persistent Homology to behavioral data from the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, the dashboard tracks —the number of connected behavioral components—across the course timeline, alongside composite indicators TEWI and TSI. We connect these constructs explicitly to CSCL concepts i𝛽𝛽n 0 cluding social cohesion and co-regulated learning, while foregrounding a critical interpretive distinction: apparent convergence may reflect learner attrition rather than genuine behavioral alignment. Rather than providing definitive interpretations, the dashboard employs a three-layer framework—objectiv𝛽𝛽e 0 metrics, research-grounded pattern descriptions, and reflective prompts—to support educator sensemaking. We illustrate this framework with an authentic OULAD course example, demonstrating how rising and TEWI values in the weeks preceding an assessment deadline can prompt targeted instructional reflection. Participants will explore authentic OULAD data, experiment with topolo𝛽𝛽g 0 ical parameters, and discuss design implications for emerging structural analytics.

title: Visualizing Curricula in Higher Education: A Semantic Similarity Approach
citation: Harufumi Nakazawa, Ariana Ravitch, Sebastien Brown (2026). Visualizing Curricula in Higher Education: A Semantic Similarity Approach. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Nakazawa, H., Ravitch, A., & Brown, S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Cognitive Load Theory
abstract: Many institutions give students some freedom to choose courses across disciplines. Yet, existing course registration technologies often present courses as a textual list by discipline, leading to extraneous cognitive load and a lack of metacognitive awareness of how course decisions relate to the broader curriculum. To support students in making well-informed course choices, we develop a tool to visualize the entire curriculum based solely on course content. We describe its methodology, features, theoretical underpinning from learning sciences research, and ways to mindfully embed the tool into advising sessions. Problem and motivation In many institutions of higher education, particularly liberal arts colleges, students have considerable freedom to select courses from a broad range of fields. This freedom is intended to allow students to shape their own learning goals proactively and choose courses accordingly (e.g., Amherst College, n.d.; Brown University, n.d.). In practice, however, the exercise of this freedom is mediated by administrative technologies for course browsing and registration, which are often used to guide advising sessions. By structuring the information available to students and faculty, and by guiding their conversations in advising sessions, these tools play a sociomaterial role in shaping course selection and learning outcomes. Many institutions rely on commercial, off-the-shelf registration platforms that often organize courses in a long list by discipline. While these technologies streamline administrative processes, they raise two challenges. First, reading through a long list can impose extraneous cognitive load (de Jong, 2009) on users, hindering their ability to make fully informed course selection decisions. Second, disciplinary boundaries and a lack of interactivity limit students’ ability to develop metacognitive awareness (Flavell, 1976) of how their learning relates to the wider curriculum and their overall learning goals. Moreover, these two points are in fact related: the extraneous cognitive load imposed by such course scheduling tools can divert students’ cognitive resources away from big-picture, metacognitive thinking. Together, these constraints can limit the scope and richness of conversations between students and advisors, raising the risk of making uninformed or unsatisfactory choices. Especially in liberal arts programs, such constraints may cause students to inadvertently gravitate toward familiar disciplines, contributing to a mismatch between students’ exercise of freedom in course selection and these institutions’ missions of promoting interdisciplinary learning. Against this backdrop, we created the Visual Open Curriculum, a supplemental web application for course exploration and academic advising that is especially conducive to liberal arts curricula. First, the app lessens students’ cognitive load by replacing lengthy course lists with a visual and interactive curriculum map, a semantic search engine, and a recommender function. Second, it organizes courses based on content rather than disciplinary classifications and includes a reflectional note-taking tool, which together promote conscious selection of courses according to learning goals. Moreover, recognizing that effective use of technology depends on both the users’ mindful engagement and surrounding social contexts (Salomon et al, 1991; Rook et al, 2024), we provide explicit suggestions on how students and faculty can best integrate this tool into the broader sociomaterial environment of their advising sessions. Overall, the app aims to provide students with increased agency in navigating extensive curricular choices, informed by theories of learning.

title: Extending Immersive Learning with Smell: An Olfactory-Enhanced Virtual Reality System
citation: Ruth Wylie, Orion Dobos, Chris Austin, Byron Lahey, Rezwana Islam, Lauryn Mannigel, Robert LiKamWa, Christy Spackman (2026). Extending Immersive Learning with Smell: An Olfactory-Enhanced Virtual Reality System. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.

abstract: We present VR-O, a virtual reality (VR) system that integrates olfaction into immersive learning environments. The project explores how adding scent to VR experiences can deepen engagement, support learning, and make simulations more authentic, particularly in domains where olfactory perception is central to expertise (e.g., water treatment, wine making). During this Interactive Tools and Demos session, participants will experience the olfactory VR setup firsthand and discuss pedagogical and technical implications for multisensory learning environments.

title: STEPS: An AI Tutor for Scaffolded Problem Solving in Introductory STEM Courses
citation: Joshua T. Arens, Alessandra Napoli, Kiana Fathinezhad, Jordyn Smith, Zhangyang Wu, Nick Haber, Jennifer Schwartz Poehlmann, Shima Salehi, Karen D. Wang (2026). STEPS: An AI Tutor for Scaffolded Problem Solving in Introductory STEM Courses. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Arens, J. T., Napoli, A., Fathinezhad, K., Smith, J., Wu, Z., Haber, N., Poehlmann, J. S., Salehi, S., & Wang, K. D.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Introductory STEM courses often reveal a disconnect between taught content and students’ ability to solve complex, multistep problems. We present STEPS—an LLM-based tutor drawing on principles of deliberate practice—that scaffolds planning, step-by-step reasoning, and verification without giving away answers. Through iterative prompt engineering aligned with a validated problem-solving framework, STEPS was embedded into weekly assignments, quizzes, reflections, and lectures in large-enrollment chemistry and physics courses. We examined plan quality, solution correctness, student engagement, perceived helpfulness and confidence, and performance on targeted concepts. Results show high confidence, strong homework performance on STEPS-assisted problems, and increasing perceived helpfulness, with students shifting from answer-seeking to process-oriented inquiry and demonstrating growing AI literacy. This session will provide a brief overview of the framework, hands-on use of STEPS, and a guided workshop to craft authentically complex problems and translate them into STEPS-style prompts across STEM disciplines. We conclude with actionable guidance for pedagogically sound, learning-aligned AI integration in STEM courses.

title: “How Are You Solving That?”: Improving Learning in Virtual Reality With a Reflective AI Agent
citation: Eileen McGivney, Oluwatomilade Olarinde, Erica Kleinman (2026). “How Are You Solving That?”: Improving Learning in Virtual Reality With a Reflective AI Agent. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: McGivney, E., Olarinde, O., & Kleinman, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) environments provide rich contexts for learning, but learners often struggle to process deeper learning while using them. Reflective activities have been effective at increasing learning from VR, but few studies have engaged learners in reflection while in the learning environment. In this demonstration participants will use our bespoke VR escape room environment to demonstrate an AI-powered reflective agent who is modeled on escape room game masters. While solving logic-based puzzles, the reflective agent acts as a character in the escape room that encourages learners to discuss their problem-solving strategies. Participants in this demo will use the VR system and interact with the AI agent.

title: Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst
citation: Madhuri Singh, Gennie Mansi, Mark Owen Riedl (2026). Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Singh, M., Mansi, G., & Riedl, M. O.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: K-12 teachers employ Engineering Design Challenges to help students learn about the Engineering Design Process hands-on. They use techniques like hard scaffolding questions to guide the students as they think through the different stages of the engineering design process. While useful, the creation of these questions adds to the teacher’s preparation time for their classes. Concept Catalyst uses Large Language Models to assist teachers with the rapid creation of scaffold questions for engineering design challenges. Unlike open-ended chat, Concept Catalyst uses LLMs to summarize and decompose an engineering design challenge into the concepts that students will engage with, allow the teacher to visually manipulate and link related concepts, and to propose scaffolding questions for the teacher to modify or accept.

title: Show Your Work: A Gentle Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks for K-12 Educators

abstract: We are developing a suite of free, web-based, asynchronous introductory Jupyter notebooks designed for K-12 educators with little to no prior experience with programming or with computational notebooks. In contrast to typical “intro notebooks” which focus on technical features, the Show Your Work project builds on theory and findings from the learning sciences and science education to introduce computational notebooks as epistemic tools within specific school subject domains, guiding educators to explore the questions: What role can notebooks play in my specific classroom? What does it feel like to conduct an investigation using a Jupyter notebook? What epistemic and communicative practices are foregrounded and backgrounded by computational notebooks? These materials are likely of interest to ISLS members who work in computing education, computing-integrated STEM education, and/or teacher education, as well as to members who wish to learn more about computational narrative as a new area of focus within the learning sciences. Motivation Jupyter notebooks are a form of computational notebook, an artifact that allows multiple blocks of editable, executable code and its output to be interspersed with rich text in a single document in the spirit of Knuth’s “literate programming” (Knuth, 1984). The name, “Jupyter,” evokes three computer languages commonly associated especially with data analysis – Julia, Python, and R (Perez & Granger, 2015). Since its original release about a decade ago, Jupyter notebooks now support a wide variety of computational languages (Granger & Perez, 2021). While it is not the first example of computational notebooks, Jupyter has been widely adopted due to its availability as a free and open source tool, and the Jupyter infrastructure now forms the foundation of a variety of popular interactive computing environments such as Google Colab and Deepnote. Although they were originally developed as a scientific research and communication tool, there is growing interest in using Jupyter notebooks at the K-12 level. Several research projects have studied the integration of Jupyter notebooks into secondary and intro college instructional materials (Fleischer et al., 2022; Son et al., 2021; Van Dusen, 2020). They are also becoming adopted as a curricular infrastructure including as part of Berkeley’s popular Data 8 “Introduction to Data Science” course activities (data6.org; data8.org), UCLA’s CourseKata high school mathematics curriculum (coursekata.org), and ProDaBi, a data/AI curricular package for secondary students (www.prodabi.de/en/). Most recently Jupyter Everywhere, a free, lightweight, simplified Jupyter interpreter interface that makes it easy for teachers and students to launch, edit, and share Jupyter notebooks without installing special software or services (jupytereverywhere.org). Jupyter notebooks, as a popular example of a broader genre of computational notebooks, are likely to be of particular interest to the Learning Sciences community for theoretical reasons. In a recent paper, Odden and Zwickl (2025) described Jupyter notebooks as an example of diSessa’s notion of computational literacy: highlighting their integration of the material dimension of computational literacy through its support for explicit executable code, the cognitive (epistemic) dimension through users’s ability to test, revise, and keep note of the discoveries they make as they examine the output of their code, and the social (communicative) dimension through the ability to share this blend of code with text, images, and other explanatory media with others. However, there is growing evidence that additional support is needed for Jupyter notebooks to be productively leveraged in K-12 classrooms. Most existing work describes a variety of technical and conceptual difficulties that teachers and students encounter when working with computational notebooks (e.g., Hanč et al., 2020; Johnson, 2020). While the potential for deep epistemic engagement through computational exploration and communication is high (Hüsing et al., 2024), without careful design or preparation notebooks are at risk of surface- level engagements in which students simply execute embedded code and read the output as if it were a printed text. T he need for teacher professional development Beyond the need to address the technical challenges for teachers that are already well-documented in the literature, it is also important to offer pedagogical and epistemological support when introducing new epistemic tools in curricular materials. Ample work has demonstrated that introducing even “authentic” tools in secondary classrooms is only valuable to the extent that they are understood by teachers and students to support sensemaking (Stroupe et al., 2019). For example, students who are asked to use agent-based models to explore the particulate nature of matter are only successful insofar as they identify some compatibility between their representation of the phenomenon and the affordances of the tool (Wilkerson et al., 2018). Inspired from Russ’ (2014) distinction between epistemology “of” science versus epistemology “for” science, here we might similarly articulate computing not only as a practice “of,” but also “for” scientific reasoning. Teachers play a critical role in helping students recognize the potential benefits of a given computational tool for advancing their understanding (Wagh et al., 2025). Thus to maintain disciplinary depth and support all students, teachers need to clearly understand the learning goals that a given activity or tool is meant to support, and be able to notice and respond to student thinking in service of those goals (Robertson et al., 2015). A first step to supporting such understandings is to examine how teachers, as learners themselves, might experience computational notebooks as a sensemaking tool. Even if teachers do recognize the ways in which computational notebooks might function as an epistemic tool, there are still possible ambiguities regarding exactly what aspects of the analysis of complex datasets they can support. This is because data investigations are naturally interdisciplinary, and therefore their role within the curriculum can be ambiguous (Finzer, 2013). There are a number of paths an investigation can take. For example, in our own prior work, we found that teachers might emphasize dramatically different aspects of a data visualization, for instance, focusing on scientific, social, or mathematical learning goals (Wilkerson et al., 2025); a practice consistent with broader findings suggesting that teachers significantly shape how materials are enacted in their classroom (Remillard & Heck, 2014). Thus demonstrating how Jupyter notebooks or other computational narrative tools might integrate into a variety of disciplines, with a variety of potential (e.g. computational, statistical, or content-oriented) goals is consistent with what we know about teachers’ data integration practices. Design principles To address the need for epistemologically and pedagogically oriented teacher professional development experiences, we are developing (with a cohort of approximately 30 pre-service and in-service teachers, using a judicious informant design approach; Scaife et al., 1997) a suite of computational notebooks intended to form the basis of an interactive, self-paced introduction to Python notebooks for K-12 classroom educators. Our rationale, building on the preliminary findings from research described above, is that many practicing teachers are being introduced to notebooks through their integration into curriculum, without time to familiarize themselves with not only the technical but also and more importantly with the epistemological and pedagogical dimensions of these tools. In a preliminary analysis of several existing “Introduction to Jupyter” notebooks developed both for practitioners and for educators, we identified an almost exclusive focus on their technical aspects. This included how a notebook can be run, edited, and what are some of its basic and advanced features. Several also included features that support pedagogical goals such as encouraging a tinkering disposition (“It is easy to break the code this way, but that is a normal part of coding!” from the YouCubed Jupyter introduction) or supporting the inquiry cycle (as demonstrated in CourseKata’s Jupyter introductory materials). Some existing introductory notebooks briefly addressed the epistemic role of notebooks in science, typically through appeals to authority. Building on these initial findings, our sequence of notebooks intentionally foreground the pedagogical potential of notebooks as an epistemic tool, as grounded within use cases across a variety of school subjects. Each notebook is designed to explicitly communicate about eight principles we identified as desirable in our review of existing introductory notebooks including the purpose of leveraging a computational notebook for an activity; providing a comparison to other tools that might be used in such an activity; modeling and encouraging documentation both of code and of users’ thinking; describing the planned use of specific or unique features of the notebook to aid in analysis; supporting specific code learning goals; supporting specific data learning goals; supporting specific content learning goals, and encouraging productive dispositions toward notebook use. Guided by these principles, our suite of notebooks provides teachers with repeated experiences in which they are expected to conduct inquiry using specific combinations of code, data, and content, and to encounter useful or unexpected findings in the process (see next section). As we make clear in our materials, our goal is not necessarily to advocate for the wholesale integration of notebooks into teachers’ work. Rather, as we state explicitly in our introductory notebook, we seek to “introduce [teachers] to what notebooks are, explore how they might be useful, and help [teachers] decide if they are right for [their] classroom.” (Intro Notebook). T he “Show York Work” suite of notebooks The “Show Your Work” sequence of activities is under active development, with five notebooks ready for sharing at the time of writing and an anticipated 10 ready by the time of the ISLS conference. When completed, the materials will include notebooks organized into four phases. Phase 1 provides a basic introduction and early data exploration experience using Jupyter notebooks. Phase 2 provides a variety of notebooks designed to introduce key code and data concepts that are most likely to be relevant to integrating Jupyter data explorations into particular school subjects such as chemistry, physics, statistics, and so on. For these first two phases, most materials are already well-developed and we are in the process of testing and refining them in collaboration with approximately 30 pre-service and in-service teachers. Phase 3 will include deeper dives into key computing and data concepts along with student case studies to encourage teacher noticing as mediated by Jupyter notebook interactions (e.g., Walkoe et al., 2017). Phase 4 will include materials to support teachers in adapting and creating their own notebooks for classroom use. This includes scaffolding their use of more traditional Jupyter documentation materials, and offering guidance on judicious use of generative AI tools, particularly those embedded in notebook development tools such as VSCode, whilst attending to the pedagogical and investigative principles introduced throughout the materials. These third and fourth phases are planned, though we anticipate that draft materials will be available for sharing by the time of the conference. Below, we elaborate on materials associated with Phase 1 and Phase 2 activities. Phase I: Introducing notebooks as computational narratives Our introductory notebook introduces teachers to the idea of a computational notebook as an “interactive lab notebook” in which they can keep, experiment with data and code, and communicate findings. The notebook guides teachers through the basic aspects of navigating, executing, and editing computational notebooks; diagnosing common errors and how to address them; and compares them to other epistemic tools used for data analysis in K-12 classrooms. Teachers then complete a data investigation activity using the well-known Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst et al., 2020), in which they encounter an unexpected non-linear relationship between bill depth and bill length in a population of penguins, and use visualization to explore what other factors (e.g. sex, species, mass, age, etc.) may help explain the irregular distribution (Figure 1). Figure 1 Screenshots from The Introductory Notebook Including an introduction to notebooks (left), an inquiry activity (middle), and scatterplot code that users edit and supplement to address the inquiry question (right). Phase II: Targeting key code and data concepts through “Topic Bundles” The following set of notebooks focus on different disciplinary “bundles.” These are combinations of ideas from computing, data, and science that support specific kinds of subject matter explorations (such as GIS mapping to explore geological phenomena; exploring and visualizing basic descriptive statistics about distributions). Figure 2 features a notebook that introduces time series analysis through an exploration of air quality data as one such disciplinary “bundle.” The notebook introduces computational datetime as a specialised data structure, scaffolds users to generate and annotate lineplots, and to interpret time-series line plots with attention to scale, potential causes, and distinguishing between signal and noise. The notebook uses air quality data collected by local and national governmental organizations, and introduced related scientific concepts required to interpret patterns in the data (e.g. the Air Quality Index or AQI as a composite measure of air quality and PM2.5, Ozone, and Carbon Monoxide as specific air pollutants). through two interactive tasks. Figure 2 Screenshots of the Air Quality Notebook. The beginning segment introduces time series data and associated data structures and visualizations (left), and the major activity involves analyzing the different concentration patterns of three pollutants during a major fire event (right). We are developing similar notebooks that connect to core topics in statistics, physics, engineering, nad more (Table 1). For each, we work to identify one major phenomenon of interest for which patterns revealed through data and computing grant powerful insight into scientific mechanisms; 3-5 core code concepts that are required for the type of analysis that is introduced; and 3-5 data concepts related to the analysis. title: TRAIL: A Human–AI Teaming Research Platform
citation: Mohammad Amin Samadi, Aziz Rangwala, Nia Nixon (2026). TRAIL: A Human–AI Teaming Research Platform. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Samadi, M. A., Rangwala, A., & Nixon, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: TRAIL (Team Research and AI Integration Lab) is a research platform for studying human–AI teamwork and collaborative learning in postsecondary contexts. The system enables multi-condition experiments where human participants work together on a collaborative task with or without an AI teammate. AI teammate behaviors are configured through a personality interface grounded in the Big Five framework. TRAIL provides real-time team chat, automated team formation, integrated survey workflows, experiment chaining for longitudinal designs, and multi-level analytics. Its dual-memory architecture maintains coherent AI behavior across extended interactions, while rich datasets capture communication, trust, and team dynamics. This demo showcases how TRAIL functions as both a classroom and research tool, enabling controlled studies of collaboration, persona alignment, and group processes.

title: LumiBuilder: A Chatbot-Building Tool for Hallucination-Aware AI Literacy
citation: Joey Huang, Xiaoyi Tian, Deniz Ozturk, Daksh Singh, Yasitha Rajapaksha, Tiffany Barnes (2026). LumiBuilder: A Chatbot-Building Tool for Hallucination-Aware AI Literacy. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Huang, J., Tian, X., Ozturk, D., Singh, D., Rajapaksha, Y., & Barnes, T.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Hallucinations, or confident but incorrect responses generated by large language models, present a critical challenge for young learners who increasingly turn to AI for schoolwork and everyday tasks. LumiBuilder is a web-based chatbot building tool designed to help children understand these limitations by constructing their own chatbots and testing how design choices influence model behavior. The tool integrates hallucination awareness scaffolds, including confidence displays, fact checking, model comparison, document verification, and repeated questioning, to support inquiry-based exploration of AI reliability. This interactive demonstration introduces LumiBuilder’s core features and the design principles that shaped its development. Participants will explore the tool, observe how hallucinations emerge through varied prompts, and discuss implications for AI literacy, youth and AI interaction, and the design of learning environments that promote verification, reflection, and calibrated trust in AI systems.

title: Designing a Dashboard for Insights into Complex Skills
citation: Emily Kerzabi (2026). Designing a Dashboard for Insights into Complex Skills. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Kerzabi, E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Cognitive Load Theory
abstract: This paper describes the design and implementation of a functional prototype of a researcher-facing dashboard for insights into complex skills from multi-source data, including school records, chat/communication data, and item responses. Features include statistical insight panels and customizable layouts, incorporating visual cues (color coding by demographic variables) and flexible panel splitting for comparative analysis. Socio-Semantic Network Analysis (SSNA) maps student interactions and content mentions, revealing discourse patterns. The dashboard empowers researchers to uncover meaningful associations and generate analytic insights. Working with and visualizing multi-source, complex skill data Modern complex skill research generates rich datasets. Unlike dashboards designed for instructional decision- making or student self-monitoring, researcher-facing tools must support exploratory data analysis, hypothesis generation, and validation of constructs across diverse data types. The handling, cleaning, and linking of multi- source data can be an arduous undertaking, and tools to support researchers in easily viewing, manipulating, and testing their data are lacking. This paper describes a functional prototype to support researchers in their visualization and analysis of complex data. A study involving a collaborative social and emotional learning (SEL) curriculum (Hao et al., in press) provides the motivating context for developing and testing a flexible and user- friendly data dashboard, with the heart of a data explorer. The study collects various data, including conversation (chat) text from small groups of students, time on screen, and individual responses to teacher questions and personal skill reflections (using different item types and collected during SEL lessons). Simultaneously, researchers collect student school records, including pre/post academic outcomes, student self-report ratings on their social and emotional health, and teacher observations of student SEL skills. With these diverse types of collected data, it is both a challenge and an opportunity to think through and plan exploratory data analyses and data visualizations that may elicit insight into the targeted complex skill. Existing dashboards often focus on teacher, school, or student use; however, unlike teachers or students, researchers often work with multi-source datasets that require complex wrangling, integration, and statistical modeling, and should be guided by the educational learning theories that are the foundation of the research investigation (Wise & Shaffer, 2015). This project addresses the gap for an analyst-oriented analytics platform for investigating complex skills. The foundation for the proposed researcher-facing data dashboard is customizability of data visualizations, which can alert an attentive analyst to dig more deeply into the dataset(s) in meaningful ways. Based on data handling strategies proposed by Nicolini (2012), Goodyear (2020, p. 1052) advocates for “zooming in” and “zooming out” of data, to allow the broad patterns observable in high level data to trigger deeper analysis, and vice versa. The author argues that this capability is essential for generating actionable insights. Goodyear’s 2020 paper on co-configuration in hybrid learning spaces (such as this case of the SEL classroom), and suggests that analytic tools should support iterative refinements, adjustments, and even personalization of their data analysis environment. This approach is particularly relevant for dashboards designed to work with complex, multi- source datasets. To handle and link multi-source data, Bakharia et al. (2020) advocate for using star schema architecture (a powerful and versatile data structure commonly used in business analytics and data warehouses; see Microsoft Ignite, 2024) to organize and group data, allowing for aggregate calculations on grouped variables for various timeframes. Using this architecture, comparative analyses can target specific variables across the dataset that are expected to interact with other variables in meaningful ways based on relevant learning theories. The authors’ work highlights the need for dashboards that allow researchers to correlate diverse data types (e.g., process data, survey outcomes, academic measures) to surface statistically significant relationships, outliers, and group differences. Rather than conducting blind omnibus tests of significance across the various data components, this approach avoids the risk of false positives and misinterpretation that can arise from testing everything without context, and it aligns with the dashboard’s designed features, such as statistical insight panels and customizable visualizations. In addition to traditional statistical analyses and representations, student chat and communication data can be visualized using Socio-Semantic Network Analysis (SSNA). De Liddo et al. (2011) describes a discourse network structure consisting of a concept network (chat content) and a social network (human nodes), which are assumed to be strongly connected. The aim of De Liddo et al.’s discourse-centric learning analytics is to logically c onnect students to the content of learning, thereby providing meaningful insight into what students learn, at what point, and with whom. As further proof of concept, Zhu and Chen (2023) prototyped a similar SSNA model in their Joint Attention-Interaction-Creation framework and were able to effectively model how ideas are generated in collaborative discourse. By integrating an SSNA framework into the dashboard design, this project aims to move beyond static representations of simple correlations and statistical tests to offer researchers a dynamic, interactive environment for exploring complex relationships in SEL data. Finally, because the dashboard is inherently visual, best practices in visual data communication should be followed. Franconeri et al. (2021) offer many concrete insights on how to communicate with data effectively so that data insights become clear. The authors recommend thinking first about the goal of the displayed data; for example, use connected lines to show a continuum of connected data (e.g., avoid bars for time series) to encourage users to see trends over time. One goal of good data visualization is to reduce cognitive load for the data user, which ranges from including direct labels (or hover text) rather than relying on legends, to controlling comparisons with grouping or splitting options, such as the flexibility to view the data in side-by-side panels or overlays with color coding schema to distinguish groups. The authors strongly encourage respecting common conventions for spatial and visual channels (e.g., up for more and left to right for the passage of time), as well as avoiding using visual channels like length or area to plot purely categorical data. This also implies that nested data, such as students in classrooms or groups, follow hierarchical top-down structures to illustrate nested mappings. Following the best practices and analytic frameworks put forth by these studies has the potential to offer researchers a powerful, customizable environment for exploring and interpreting complex skill data. While the data to be used as a basis for this design is from a SEL hybrid-learning school environment, the design principles and practices are transferable to other complex sets of educational data to support actionable insights through dynamic visualization and data exploration tools.

title: Declarative Narrative: Interactive Storytelling with Generative AI

abstract: Generative AI provides us with multiple challenges as well as opportunities. While it is disruptive to the field of writing instruction in some ways, it also allows us to innovate new genres of writing. We present three new interfaces for AI-supported writing, allowing an author of an interactive story to delegate detail, plot, and characterization to the AI while still maintaining narrative control of a story. This demo will present examples of interactive stories using these interfaces and allow participants to play through them, as well as write and share their own interactive stories.

abstract: Recent advances in Generative AI (GenAI) have led to increasing attention in how chatbots and agentic tools may support students’ self-regulated learning (SRL). However, existing works primarily focus on short-term interventions on adult learners, offering limited insights into how GenAI can meaningfully foster SRL and learner agency in K-12 education. To address this gap, we introduce GAILA, a writing platform that integrates stage-specific AI agents with real-time learning analytics dashboards (LADs) to support the forethought, performance, and reflection phases of SRL. For students, GAILA offers structured writing workflows, task-aligned AI agents, and real-time analytics to encourage informed self- monitoring and behavioral adjustments. For teachers, GAILA provides fine-grained configurations of writing stages and agent visibility for pedagogical control. Together, these features enable sustained, classroom-integrated use of GenAI tools and open opportunities for research on how GenAI can support SRL among secondary school students.

abstract: As generative AI rapidly transforms how humans interact with computation, it challenges the foundations of many educational technologies designed to teach coding, modeling, and computational thinking. Systems that were once built around writing or arranging code—whether block-based or text-based—now coexist with tools that generate programs through natural language. This workshop invites the learning sciences and design research community to collectively explore how educational technologies that include coding must be re-envisioned in light of these shifts. What will it mean to “code,” “debug,” or “model” when AI becomes a co-author? How might our existing environments—like MoDa, a block-based modeling platform, or text-based NetLogo simulations—need to be rethought for an era where learners reason through prompts, outputs, and model interpretation rather than syntax and structure? Our goal is to identify key design principles, challenges, and opportunities to guide the next generation of AI-powered computational learning environments. Theoretical background and significance Integrating computational thinking (CT) into science education equips students with powerful tools to explore scientific phenomena, foster deeper conceptual understanding, and engage in authentic scientific practices. The interdisciplinary potential of this work empowers students and practitioners to engage meaningfully with emerging local and global challenges (Barr et al., 2011; Weintrop et al., 2016). Existing literature identifies several core CT practices: abstraction, generalization, decomposition, algorithmic thinking, and debugging (Caeli & Yadav, 2020). Computational modeling, including agent-based modeling (ABM), has long been recognized as a valuable tool that can simultaneously support students' science learning and CT (e.g., Wilkerson et al., 2015; Musaeus et al., 2023; Musaeus et al., 2022). Recently, however, developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have introduced new possibilities for how learners and educators may interact with computational models (Chen et al., 2023). In the future, it may no longer be necessary to write code to create scientific computer models, putting learners in the role of collaborators with generative AI. For decades, coding has served as both a tool for learning and a language for thinking (Papert, 1980; diSessa, 2000). Block-based and text-based environments embody constructionist ideals, empowering learners to express, test, and refine ideas through computation. Yet today, this paradigm is shifting. AI’s ability to generate executable code from natural language redefines what it means to “speak computation.” As we transition from programming languages to prompting, foundational concepts—such as loops, conditions, and agents—risk becoming invisible. At the same time, new epistemic practices emerge: prompt engineering, iterative interpretation of AI outputs, and ethical reasoning about algorithmic agency. This timely workshop for the field of learning sciences demands that we rethink not only curricula, but also what fundamental concepts in programming that we still need to teach and how to design the tools themselves; how they mediate learning, distribute agency, and scaffold understanding when code is no longer the learner’s sole artifact of construction. Organizing team Line Have Musaeus leads research at the Center for Computational Thinking & Design, focusing on computing education, computational modeling, and STEM learning. Her work explores how integrating computational thinking into school subjects supports both student learning and teacher development. She co-designed CoTinker and has extensive experience organizing workshops on computing and AI in education. Tamar Fuhrmann leads research at the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab at Teachers College, Columbia University. She is a founding leader of the MoDa project, focusing on computational modeling in science education. Her work integrates STEM, AI, and constructionist approaches, and she regularly leads professional development and international collaborations. Paulo Blikstein is an Associate Professor at Columbia University and director of the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab. His research focuses on using technology to t ransform learning in STEM and AI. He founded the FabLearn program and has received major awards, including the NSF CAREER and AERA Early Career Award. Ole Sejer Iversen is a professor at Aarhus University and director of the Center for Computational Thinking & Design. His research focuses on computational empowerment, helping young people become active creators of technology. He works at the intersection of participatory design, computing education, and policy, leading large-scale international projects. Workshop goals and intended audience This workshop is designed for researchers, designers, and educators in the learning sciences, computing education, and educational technology who are exploring the future of computational learning in the age of AI. It will particularly interest those developing or studying coding-based environments—such as block-based, text-based, or modeling tools—and those investigating how generative AI transforms students’ epistemic, creative, and design practices. Participants with backgrounds in design-based research, computational modeling, or AI in education will find opportunities to share perspectives, contribute to collaborative redesign activities, and help shape a research agenda for rethinking the role of coding and modeling in AI-mediated learning environments. Outline of planned activities and facility requirements The four-hour workshop (plus one hour for lunch and coffee) will begin with an opening and framing session (20 minutes) introducing key tensions in AI-integrated coding environments. This will be followed by case study provocations (40 minutes), during which participants engage with two computational modeling environments: MoDa, a block-based agent-based modeling tool, and CoTinker, a collaborative modeling environment. Participants will explore and design models while considering how these tools might evolve as learners use AI to generate, modify, and explain models. In the collaborative design challenge (60 minutes), small groups will reimagine an educational technology that includes coding, redesigning it to integrate AI while preserving learners’ epistemic and creative engagement. This will lead into a group synthesis and discussion (40 minutes), during which participants share insights, identify emerging principles, and surface tensions, producing a poster as the group outcome. The workshop will conclude with a closing reflection (20 minutes), focusing on articulating open research questions and opportunities for future collaboration. Participation requirements Participation is open to researchers, designers, educators, and graduate students interested in computational modeling, coding education, or AI-supported learning environments. No specific technical expertise or prior experience with educational learning environments is required. We would like to support a dynamic, collaborative environment in which multiple perspectives on the redesign of coding-based educational technologies can emerge. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past Over the past several years, ISLS conferences have hosted numerous workshops and symposia exploring computational modeling, data science education, and AI-supported learning, for example, Kafai et al., 2025; Wagh et al., 2024; Fuhrmann et al., 2022; Fuhrmann et al., 2024; and McElhaney et al., 2020. These events advanced theoretical and design frameworks for integrating computational practices into science and engineering education. However, few have directly addressed the implications of generative AI for redesigning the educational technologies that include coding, particularly how block-based and text-based modeling environments must evolve when learners can construct programs through natural language. This workshop builds on that lineage but reframes the central question: not how to teach coding, but how coding itself—and the tools built around it—should be reimagined for an AI-mediated future. By convening researchers working at the intersection of computational modeling, design-based research, and AI in education, the session extends ongoing ISLS dialogues toward a new design agenda: understanding how AI reshapes the epistemic and pedagogical foundations of computational learning tools. Expected outcome and outputs The workshop will strengthen a community of practice focused on designing tools that preserve human sense- making and agency alongside AI assistance. It will generate open-ended questions that help rethink computational educational technologies in an AI-mediated context, and build a shared vocabulary around emerging hybrid practices where coding, prompting, and modeling intersect. Rather than defining what the future of coding should be, the session aims to open a dialogue on how our tools—and our field—must evolve to meet it. abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly influential in education, attention must extend beyond AI applications to the technical infrastructure on which those applications depend. Datasets, models, benchmarks, and governance mechanisms are already shaping the future of educational AI, yet these foundational resources are often developed without sufficient engagement with the learning sciences. This workshop explores how learning scientists can contribute to the design of such infrastructural public goods in ways that better reflect what is known about learning, while also addressing concerns related to safety, privacy, ethics, and equity. By bringing together researchers working at the intersection of AI and learning, the workshop seeks to identify promising lines of work, articulate key tensions, and stimulate future collaboration on learning-science-informed AI infrastructure. Overview The learning sciences offer strong conceptual foundations for the design of educational AI, drawing on longstanding research on scaffolding, feedback, self-regulation, and collaboration (Quintana et al., 2004; Hattie & Timperley, 2007; Järvelä et al., 2016; Sawyer, 2022). Yet these principles still only lightly shape the datasets, benchmarks, and model documentation on which AI systems depend. Training data rarely reflect what is known about productive learning interactions; benchmarks tend to measure task completion or factual accuracy rather than the quality of scaffolding or the depth of learner understanding; and model documentation seldom describes how a system's design relates to evidence on how people learn. Recent work by major AI developers signals growing interest in grounding educational AI in learning sciences principles (Jurenka et al., 2024; LearnLM Team, Google, 2025), but without more intentional integration into underlying infrastructure, educational AI risks prioritizing efficiency or engagement over meaningful support for learning. As past waves of "personalized learning" have shown, technology that optimizes for engagement without attending to how learning works can reproduce rather than address longstanding inequities in educational opportunity. This challenge is particularly pressing as new efforts seek to build openly shared educational AI resources as public goods. The K–12 AI Infrastructure Initiative, a five-year, $26 million effort led by Digital Promise and a coalition of partners, is funding the development of tutoring interaction corpora, learning-aligned benchmarks, and model documentation frameworks that embed pedagogical principles by design (Digital Promise, 2025; Roschelle et al., 2025). For such resources to genuinely advance learning, learning scientists must be actively involved in their co-design alongside AI engineers, education practitioners, and policymakers — contributing not only domain knowledge but also the critical perspectives needed to navigate questions of safety, privacy, ethics, and equity. This workshop therefore explores how the learning sciences can be systematically integrated into these infrastructural public goods. It brings together learning scientists, AI developers, education practitioners, and funders to examine where and how learning sciences expertise is most needed in the development of technical infrastructure for educational AI. Its goals are to inform participants about emerging infrastructure efforts and the role learning sciences can play in shaping them, create space for participants to share current work and articulate concerns, identify promising directions for future research and investment, and stimulate the formation of cross- sector collaborations. Building on recent ISLS programming on AI and education (International Society of the Learning Sciences, 2022, 2024), the workshop positions the learning sciences not only as a field that evaluates AI applications after they are built, but as one that can help shape the foundations on which educational AI is constructed. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108776462 GoGoData Participatory Sensing: Students, Educators and Researchers Building Collaborative Data Networks Charles Pimentel charlespimentel@ufrj.br Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) Vithoria Cabreira vithoriacabreira@gmail.com Federal Technological University of Paraná (UTFPR) Walter Akio Goya, Paulo Blikstein, Renato Russo aag2197@tc.columbia.edu, paulob@tc.columbia.edu, renrusso@gmail.com Teachers College, Columbia University Arnan Sipitakiat arnan.s@cmu.ac.th Chiang Mai University Abstract: In this half-day workshop, participants will engage with GoGoData, an open learning plugin that connects the GoGo Board microcontroller, sensors, Internet of Things (IoT) communication, and the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) to support participatory sensing and collaborative exploration of real-time data. Intended audience This workshop is intended for graduate students, educators, and researchers interested in exploring participatory sensing, critical data literacy, and learning technology design through hands-on experimentation. It particularly welcomes those studying or developing tools that connect physical computing, IoT, and real-time data exploration to promote collaborative inquiry and learning. More broadly, the session is open to all participants interested in integrating constructionist and learning sciences perspectives into the design of educational technologies. (Note that GoGoData, the GoGo Board, and CODAP are open-source platforms.) Duration of the event Half-day (3-4 hours, flexible depending on conference scheduling demands). Description of the event The GoGo Board was invented in 2001 as a low-cost and learner-friendly robotics and scientific sensing platform. In the years since, the project has undergone several design iterations, each affording new possibilities for students across diverse ages and backgrounds to explore powerful ideas in computing and STEM. In this workshop, participants will also engage with GoGoData (2025), a new open-source plugin that connects the GoGo Board to the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) for real-time data communication and visualization. CODAP, developed by the Concord Consortium, has a long-standing history as an open-source environment for data analysis and modeling that supports inquiry-based learning. Together, GoGoData, the GoGo Board Kit version 7, and CODAP create a participatory sensing ecosystem that enables students to collect, share, and interpret live data while examining the learning sciences principles underlying the design of these tools [1-3]. Workshop Format The workshop will be organized into five main activities. I - Historical framing. Participants will begin with a brief discussion on the evolution of tangible interfaces within the Learning Sciences and basic education contexts. This discussion will be situated alongside the rise of big data practices and participatory or crowd sensing, showing how learner-generated, real-time data from distributed sensors can reshape inquiry, evidence making, and classroom discourse. The framing will surface design lessons on openness, transparency, and agency, linking data practices to issues of provenance, privacy, and ethics, and highlighting how collaborative data networks can support critical engagement and community action. II - Exploring the GoGo Board 7 / GoGoData / CODAP. Participants will explore the core features of the GoGo Board version 7 and the GoGoData plugin, examining how each component emerged from research data and i terative design decisions. Using onboard controls, they will visualize sensor values, directly before connecting to a computer to interact with GoGoData and its integration with the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP). Through this connection, participants will experience how real-time sensor data can be collected, transmitted, analyzed, and explored within CODAP’s interactive environment. Facilitators will highlight how each feature embodies specific design principles that link tangible experimentation with data-driven inquiry. III - Participatory sensing exploration. Participants will collaboratively select a variable to measure, such as temperature, luminosity, pollution, or sound level, using a GoGo Board 7 kit sensor. Working in small groups, they will connect the GoGo Board to CODAP through the GoGoData plugin and deploy sensors in different internet-connected areas across the UCI campus. Each group will collect and share real-time data through the open-source plugin integrated with the data analysis platform, contributing to a collaborative network of distributed measurements. As data accumulate, participants will analyze emerging patterns across locations, drawing inferences about environmental or contextual factors. The activity will conclude with a collective discussion where groups interpret their findings, reflect on methodological decisions, and connect their insights to broader perspectives on participatory sensing, open data collaboration, and critical data literacy in education. IV - Conclusion and gallery walk. Participants will share and discuss the outcomes of their activities, reflecting on the lessons learned and insights gained throughout the workshop. The session will conclude with a collective show-and-tell, allowing groups to present their findings, highlight key observations from the participatory sensing exercise, and connect these experiences to broader questions about learning, design, and data literacy. V - Post-workshop interaction. Optional follow-up opportunities will be provided for participants who wish to continue collaborating after the session. These interactions may include online discussions, exchange of design ideas, and updates on future developments of the GoGoData platform. Participants will be invited to share reflections, resources, and potential research connections that extend the learning and collaboration initiated during the workshop. Throughout the workshop, facilitators will guide discussions connecting the design of GoGoData, the GoGo Board, and CODAP to learning sciences and constructionist frameworks, emphasizing how participatory sensing and data exploration are enhanced by open-source ecosystems. The session will highlight how openness, transparency, and accessibility in these tools empower learners and researchers to collaboratively collect, analyze, and interpret real-time data. Rather than serving as a technical training, the workshop offers a hands-on exploration of how open, theory-informed technologies developed through over twenty years of design-based research can foster agency, collaboration, and critical engagement with data. Participation requirements No requirements. We invite to join all participants interested in tangible interface design, educational robotics, and data science, irrespective of skill or experience levels. title: Modelling Complex Learning Interactions—A Hands-on Workshop on Heterogeneous Interaction Network Analysis (HINA)
citation: Shihui Feng, Kester Yew Chong Wong, Tongguang Li, Dragan Gasevic (2026). Modelling Complex Learning Interactions—A Hands-on Workshop on Heterogeneous Interaction Network Analysis (HINA). Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Feng, S., Wong, K. Y. C., Li, T., & Gasevic, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Learning is inherently a complex, multi-faceted process situated across learners, tools, and environments. This workshop introduces HINA (Heterogeneous Interaction Network Analysis), a methodological framework for modeling and analyzing complex learning interactions through networked relationships across diverse entities such as students, behaviors, and artifacts. By representing learning process data as heterogeneous interaction networks, HINA provides researchers with a means to uncover latent patterns, measure theoretical constructs, and derive actionable insights into learning processes. This half-day workshop features interactive discussions and a hands-on tutorial with the HINA webtool (hina- network.com), enabling participants to analyze their own data, followed by featured case studies and collaborative discussion on future applications in learning sciences. This workshop will contribute to the learning sciences community by disseminating a novel open-source tool for analyzing complex learning interactions, enhancing the methodological capacity for theoretical development.
