abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted as AI tutors, providing scalable, interactive assistance across a range of topics. Yet there remains a lack of a unified, comprehensive framework for evaluating the pedagogical behaviors these models exhibit across multiple tutoring sessions and varying learning scenarios. This workshop addresses this gap by introducing a two-layer evaluation framework that distinguishes between (1) foundational behaviors that LLMs must demonstrate to be considered pedagogically qualified, and (2) stylistic instructional behaviors that shape their effectiveness as tutors. Participants will refine and apply this framework through hands-on interactions with an LLM-powered tutoring system, engaging in a five-session sequence of introductory Python programming modules. Through this workshop, we aim to advance the application of generative AI tools in education settings in a safe and pedagogically effective manner. Organizers’ backgrounds Eugene Park is a software engineer and researcher in the Personal Robots Group at the MIT Media Lab, where he leads research and system development on LLM-powered AI tutoring platforms. His work focuses on large language models and AI safety with applications in education, and his research agenda is centered on building pedagogically effective and reliable AI tutors. Daniel Wendel is a lead software developer and research engineer in MIT’s Scheller Teacher Education Program. Daniel has served as a core developer, curriculum designer, and research manager on projects spanning agent-based modeling, virtual reality, and AI-mediated learning, and his work focuses on designing scalable learning technologies that strengthen STEM understanding through interactive computer-based environments. Dr. Grace C. Lin is a Learning Scientist and Assessment Designer at MIT whose work focuses on building children’s and students’ capacity to learn. As an educational researcher, Grace has led teams on educational intervention projects using innovative technology from cognitive training games to AI-powered conversational agents, and has contributed to building a practitioner-facing measures repository, particularly its rating systems, of early childhood measurements. More recently, her work has been focusing on child-centered AI, AI education for children and adults, the implications of AI technology, and its influences on human relationships. Dr. Sharifa Alghowinem is a leading research scientist in the field of multimodal AI and Human-Robot Interaction (HRI). Currently stationed at MIT's Personal Robots Group, Dr. Alghowinem specializes in developing AI models to enhance human-robot interaction, with a particular focus on mood and behavior recognition using speech, gaze, and body movements to detect conditions such as engagement, depression and deception. Workshop theoretical background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as AI tutors, offering personalized explanations, adaptive feedback, and conversational guidance across a wide range of learning contexts. Their capacity to generate interactive, context-aware instruction positions them as promising tools for expanding access to high- quality tutoring, particularly in domains such as programming, where LLMs have demonstrated considerable competence. However, despite their growing use in classrooms and learning platforms, the learning sciences community lacks a principled understanding of how these models teach and which pedagogical behaviors support or hinder learning. Prior evaluations of AI tutors have typically focused on behavioral metrics that do not clearly distinguish between pedagogically harmful behaviors and those that are pedagogically effective (LearnLM Team et al., 2025; Macina et al., 2025; Maurya et al., 2025). While valuable, these metrics overlook a central insight from contemporary pedagogical theory: not all instructional traits are equally suitable across learning situations, nor do all teaching styles promote learning in the same way. Friesen & Su (2023) argue that pedagogy is not a fixed set of methods or universally “correct” practices, but rather a context-dependent negotiation between competing pedagogical tensions, such as constraint versus freedom, proximity versus distance, and protection versus exposure. Pedagogy, in this view, “is structured not so much by processes, methods, and outcomes, but by i rresolvable oppositions and the tensions between them”. This perspective highlights that effective teaching cannot be reduced to a single optimal style; instead, instructional behaviors must flexibly align with learners’ needs, contexts, and developmental stages. Bringing this lens to AI tutors underscores the need for an evaluation framework that differentiates essential pedagogical requirements from stylistic instructional variations, ensuring models are assessed not only for pedagogically correct behavior but also for their alignment with pedagogically effective behavior. Moreover, due to increasing domain expertise of frontier LLMs, this can create an illusion of overestimation in their pedagogical performance (e.g. strong performance on programming tasks or reasoning benchmarks may not necessarily translate to an LLM’s ability to teach effectively). A lack of a concrete analysis of LLMs’ pedagogical behaviors risks the misuse of LLMs, and prevents researchers and practitioners from meaningfully developing the instructional quality and reliability of AI tutors. To address this gap, we identified pedagogically harmful behaviors in LLM tutors, such as conceptual inconsistencies, topic drift, and failures to detect misconceptions, and formalize these issues as forms of pedagogical misalignment. Ensuring the absence of such behaviors represents a minimal requirement for safe and trustworthy AI tutoring. Building on this foundation, we introduce a two-layer evaluation framework for pedagogical alignment. The first layer, pedagogical qualification, captures whether an LLM satisfies baseline standards of instructional safety. The second layer, pedagogical personality, characterizes stylistic instructional traits, such as scaffolding depth, adaptivity, metacognitive prompting, and instructional tone, that shape the learning experience and likely modulate learning gains. This workshop aims to refine and operationalize this framework, deepen our shared understanding of pedagogical traits in AI tutors, and collaboratively develop metrics for evaluating them. Through hands-on interaction with an LLM-powered tutoring system, participants will explore how pedagogical safety and pedagogical style intersect, and how these dimensions can inform the design of reliable, aligned, and learning- effective AI-based educational tools. Intended audience and logistics This workshop is designed for researchers and practitioners in educational technology, the learning sciences, AI/ML, and NLP who are interested in the reliable and effective use of generative AI for education. It is particularly relevant for scholars studying AI safety, AI in education, human-AI interaction, or instructional design, as well as developers building LLM-powered educational tools. The workshop is planned as a full-day event to allow sufficient time for hands-on interaction with the LLM-based tutoring system across multiple sessions, group analysis and annotations of pedagogical behaviors, and structured discussions aimed at refining the proposed evaluation framework. To support effective collaboration, we request a room equipped with round tables suitable for small- group work. If possible, we also request basic writing materials, such as sticky notes, paper, pens, and colored markers. Participants will be asked to bring their own laptops to interact with the AI tutor. The workshop is designed for a minimum of 8 and a maximum of 30 participants, ensuring meaningful interaction, hands-on guidance, and productive group collaboration. Outline of planned activities The workshop is organized as a full-day, highly interactive session combining hands-on experience with an AI tutoring system, individual analysis, and structured group discussions. Participants will engage in five short introductory Python programming sessions using an LLM-powered tutor, evaluate the tutor’s pedagogical behaviors, and collaboratively refine the proposed two-layer evaluation framework. (100 minutes) 13:00 – 14:00: Lunch Break (60 minutes) 14:00 – 15:30: Small-Group Annotation and Framework Refinement (90 minutes). 15:30 – 15:45: Break (15 minutes). Transition to whole-group synthesis. 15:45 – 17:00: Large-Group Discussion and Synthesis (75 minutes). 1 7:00 – 17:30: Closing Reflections and Next Steps (30 minutes). Expected outcomes and contributions This workshop will equip participants with a refined and practically grounded framework for evaluating the pedagogical behaviors of LLM-powered tutors. Through hands-on interaction with an AI tutoring system, individual and collaborative annotation exercises, and structured group discussions, participants will collaboratively sharpen the distinction between pedagogical qualification, the foundational behaviors required for safe and trustworthy tutoring, and pedagogical personality, the stylistic instructional traits that influence learning effectiveness. The workshop will produce a consolidated set of pedagogical metrics, including clarified definitions, improved categorizations, and a consensus-based ranking of behaviors along a harmful–to–stylistic spectrum. This refined framework and metric set will support future empirical research and systematic tool development practices. Beyond methodological contributions, the workshop will foster a shared vocabulary and conceptual grounding for analyzing how LLM tutors behave across different learning scenarios. Participants will gain insight into the strengths and limitations of current AI tutoring systems, enabling them to better identify problematic behaviors, understand instructional variability, and connect model behaviors to established learning sciences theory. Thus, this workshop also aims to strengthen the research community at the intersection of AI education and AI safety by identifying open challenges and catalyzing collaborations across the learning sciences, AI/ML, and educational technology domains. abstract: This workshop aims at collaboratively developing a shared taxonomy for the Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) community that captures diverse epistemological, methodological and technological perspectives to help build a common ground for CSCL research. Through pre-workshop Delphi input, hands-on application, and iterative refinement, participants co-construct a framework to support clearer communication, cumulative knowledge building, and more transparent dissemination in CSCL proceedings and journals. The resulting taxonomy and follow-up activities aim to strengthen community identity, foster collaboration, and guide future CSCL research and publication practices. Organizers ● Martin Greisel: Assistant professor/postdoc at the University of Augsburg, focusing on regulation in collaborative learning, peer feedback, and teacher training. ● Burcu Şener: Lecturer at Middle East Technical University, PhD candidate at Bogazici University, focusing on collaborative problem solving, collaborative debugging, computational thinking. ● Sebastian Simon: Postdoctoral fellow at the University of Le Mans with a PhD in Computer Science. During his PhD, he focused on enhancing mobile and co-located Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning with Augmented Reality (AR). In his current Postdoc position, he investigates generative AI agents as collaborative entities in co-located CSCL settings. ● Conrad Borchers: PhD candidate at Carnegie Mellon University, researching data science and HCI applications to improve educational processes. ● Elham Tajik: PhD student at the University at Albany, she focuses on the transformative role of generative AI in education and HCI. ● Bahar Shahrokhian: PhD candidate at Arizona State University, researching multimodal learning analytics and collaboration in co-located learning environments. Intended audience and resources This half-day workshop is intended for all researchers and educators interested and engaged in CSCL, as well as its related domains, including but not limited to: educational psychologists, computer scientists and learning scientists. We particularly welcome researchers from all domains to contribute their vision of computer-supported collaborative learning, with a minimum of 8 to a maximum of 40 participants. We can manage up to 30 in-person and 10 online (Zoom) participants. Regarding resources, we only need a large seminar room with WiFi and a projector that enables group work through flexible tables (i.e., no lecture hall with fixed rows). In-person participants will be asked to bring their personal laptops. Description of the event Theme and goals In recent years, the field of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) has continued to expand in scope, methods, and theoretical foundations. While this diversity reflects the richness and vitality of the field, it also creates challenges for integration and cumulative knowledge building. Researchers draw on a wide range of epistemological, methodological, and technological perspectives, and often work in parallel rather than in concert. This fragmentation can make it difficult to identify shared concerns, trace the development of ideas, or recognize complementarities among approaches. At the same time, the multiplicity of perspectives represents an invaluable resource. If systematically understood and connected, this multiplicity can foster deeper insights into learning processes and the design of collaborative technologies. Previous CSCL workshops have identified the need for a common language across the different domains that are present in the CSCL community. Common language p resents the first step to common ground, a concept that is key to the knowledge building in a scientific community, particularly in one that emphasizes the strength of co-existing paradigms, requiring awareness of semiotic and semantic differences (that may otherwise lead to issues like gatekeeping or siloed research, Kuhn, 1962). Particularly, the 2025 CSCL workshop participants have identified the need for community building in the CSCL field and the potential of a collaboratively created CSCL taxonomy as an artefact for building common ground. Consequently, this workshop has two goals: (1) community building and (2) taxonomy development. To build community, the workshop brings together members of the CSCL community to overcome fragmentation and to harness the richness of the field’s diversity. It will help strengthen a community identity by creating an awareness of what constitutes CSCL and foster a feeling of agency through a common activity centered around the community itself (Wise & Schwarz, 2017). The second goal is to develop a taxonomy for classifying future CSCL research, especially contributions to future conference proceedings and ijCSCL articles. This taxonomy aims to offer a shared framework that reflects the community’s pluralistic character while enabling more coherent navigation, communication, comparison, and synthesis of research. As a tangible outcome and lasting artefact, it aims to promote collaboration across paradigmatic differences in the future. In addition, the process of developing such a taxonomy itself constitutes an effort of community building, thereby also serving the first goal of the workshop. In summary, by collaboratively developing and validating such a taxonomy, supported by a broad proportion of the CSCL community, the workshop seeks to lay the foundation for a more connected and integrated future for CSCL research. Theoretical background and relevance to the field and conference CSCL is inherently multidisciplinary, integrating perspectives from at least the learning sciences, educational sciences, psychology, and computer science. This diversity enriches the field but also introduces substantial variation in researchers’ underlying epistemic stances. According to the AIR model (Chinn et al., 2014), such stances encompass differences in 3 ways. First, researchers have different aims—they seek to achieve different things with their work. Second, they hold different ideals—they disagree on what counts as valid knowledge and good evidence and the criteria by which success is evaluated. Third, they use different reliable processes—they favor different methods for how data is created and interpreted, that is, the methods considered most appropriate to reach their aims. While this pluralism fosters innovation and theoretical breadth, it also poses challenges for mutual understanding in our field. Researchers examining similar phenomena may struggle to find, understand, and interpret each other’s research contributions because they pursue different aims, evaluate knowledge by different criteria, and employ different methods. This is reflected, for example, in the co-existence of different major theoretical traditions (e.g., constructivist and sociocultural, cognitive/information‑processing), a focus on different mid-level theories or theory-driven pedagogical frameworks (e.g., knowledge building, cognitive load theory, theory of immersive collaborative learning) or interactional constructs (e.g., transactivity, socio‑cognitive conflict) and competence frameworks (e.g., collaborative problem‑solving skills), and different analytical and design methodologies (e.g., collaborative analytics or design-based research) (Brown, 1992; Dillenbourg, 1999; Graesser et al., 2018; Kirschner et al., 2018; Makransky & Petersen, 2023; Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2014; Vogel et al., 2023; Vygotsky, 1978; Wise et al., 2023). As a result, communication across perspectives can become fragmented, leading to disciplinary silos and limited knowledge integration within the CSCL community (Wise & Schwarz, 2017), thereby hindering the advancement of knowledge. To remedy fragmentation, a workshop at the CSCL 2025 conference aimed at developing a shared paradigm (see also section “Relationship to similar events conducted in the past” below). However, one main outcome, also advocated by a panel of senior CSCL scholars, was that attempting to unify the CSCL community under a single theoretical or methodological framework would weaken the field’s richness in diversity. Its multi- perspectivity is not a weakness to be corrected, but a strength that enables deeper and more comprehensive inquiry. As a result, the goal should be to bridge epistemic diversity to enable constructive dialogue rather than to simply erase different perspectives and epistemologies. A step toward bridging these differences is to establish a shared vocabulary that enables researchers to articulate their approaches in a comparable manner (Wise & Schwarz, 2017). When organized systematically, such a vocabulary can take the form of a taxonomy—a structured set of dimensions and descriptors that capture from which viewpoint researchers approach their investigation, which phenomenon they study, and how they study it. abstract: Assessment in higher education faces unprecedented challenges, as generative AI now enables students to produce polished assignments in seconds. Many institutions have responded by reverting to pen‑and‑paper exams, a solution that mitigates some concerns but introduces other problems narrowing educational aims. This workshop provides a platform for collaborative exploration and dialogue of how CSCL can offer fresh perspectives and pathways for addressing these challenges and creating opportunities. Grounded in CSCL theory, design, and analytics, this workshop examines conceptualizing AI as a dialogic, collaborative partner; designing innovative assessments; assessing processes rather than products; and using collaborative analytics to support learning in AI‑enriched environments. Key issues for inquiry include: purpose of assessment, design and fine‑tuning of AI‑supported assessment, AI- powered multi-modal analytics and feedback, equity and diversity, researcher–teacher collaboration, ethics-privacy, and public discourse. Together, we work towards re‑envisioning assessment, synergizing research and practice, building collective knowledge and strengthening CSCL's impact and significance in the Gen AI era. Organizing team We are a group of CSCL researchers with shared interests in examining how CSCL can offer perspectives and directions for addressing assessment issues in higher education arising from the use of generative AI. Carol Chan conducts research on knowledge building, focusing on socio-cognitive-epistemic dynamics, reflective assessment, analytics, and teacher professional development. Xiao Hu’s research is on learning analytics, automated assessment and feedback, and AI in education. Her research includes collaborative writing facilitated by real-time analytics dashboards, multimodal learning analytics in collaborative maker activity, and analytics- supported writing in AI environments. Baruch Schwarz's research in CSCL focuses on argumentation, dialogue, and reasoning, particularly examining the roles of technology in boosting collaborative argumentation. Stephen Fiore conducts research on Human-AI teaming, focusing on collaborative cognition, including knowledge building when collaborating with AI, and the role of artificial social intelligence in assessing collaborative learning. Jun Oshima examines how knowledge-building discourse among undergraduate /graduate students can be supported by Generative AI, and examines their interactions with AI from a network-science perspective. Wenli Chen conducts research on human-AI collaboration to augment human learning by fine- tuning generative AI informed by learning sciences theories, developing AI-powered multi-modal learning analytics to assess students’ collaborative learning in classrooms. Manoli Pifarré' examines and designs dialogic, technology-enhanced pedagogies that foster co-creation processes focusing on how interactive technologies—empowered by artificial intelligence and multimodal learning analytics—can assess, visualize, and support group-based creative problem-solving. Intended audience ● CSCL researchers/ graduate students interested in collaboration, assessment and generative AI ● Researchers/graduate students from learning sciences working on generative AI related to assessment ● Higher-education instructors/practitioners navigating new assessment challenges in the AI era with interest in research-informed strategies and collaborative approaches. Duration A half-day workshop will be conducted as a HYBRID event, with onsite and remote participants connected by Zoom and online sharing tools. Participants may register to attend as onsite or virtual attendees. W orkshop description and goals We are facing a global assessment crisis in higher education with the widespread use of AI tools: students can generate polished assignments in seconds, fueling surface learning, plagiarism, and metacognitive laziness, and leading to reliance on ChatGPT (Fan et al., 2025). Public discourse highlights the seriousness of this shift—for example, Bloomberg (May 27, 2025) asked, “Does college still have a purpose in the age of ChatGPT?” Many universities have reverted to in‑person, pen‑and‑paper exams, which mitigate some risks but create others, curtailing the valuable educational goals of inquiry, problem-solving, and collaboration. This workshop is premised on the idea that CSCL is well-positioned to offer directions for rethinking assessment in higher education in the AI age (Schwarz et al., in press). We build on decades of CSCL research on assessing collaboration (Cress et al., 2021), extending to CSCL theory, design, and analytics for assessment practice. Traditional assessments emphasize final products (e.g., essays) that AI can replicate easily. Conversely, CSCL foregrounds collaborative processes (e.g., co‑construction, shared regulation) and CSCL designs such as argumentation, dialogic interaction and knowledge building, can offer new ways to scaffold and assess AI‑human collaboration. Beyond polished output, CSCL analytics can make learning‑collaboration processes visible for feedback and actionable improvement (Wise et al., 2021). This workshop provides a venue for sharing CSCL research and practices to address challenges and opportunities, reflecting on what has been accomplished and examining potential for further inquiry and impact. Our goals are to (a) identify and problematize assessment challenges brought by GenAI through a CSCL lens, (b) examine emerging CSCL theories, pedagogies, and analytics for AI‑enriched assessment, and (c) reflect on assessment practice both as higher‑education instructors and CSCL/learning sciences researchers. We seek to synergize efforts from workshop participants to build collective knowledge, create networks, to address these challenges and to strengthen CSCL’s impact. Theoretical background and themes Theoretical perspective. Since its emergence in the 1990s, CSCL has reconceptualized learning from individual knowledge acquisition to co‑construction of knowledge (Ludvigsen & Steier, 2019). Current concerns about students copying AI‑generated work reflect a continued reliance on surface‑level, transmission‑based conceptions of learning and assessment. Using a CSCL lens, Gen AI use in homework need not be prohibited; instead, it should be scaffolded to support agency, co‑construction, and shared regulation (Järvela, et al., 2023). The knowledge- building model posits collaboration as collective work on continually improvable ideas (Chan & van Aalst, 2018; Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2014). Similarly, AI‑human collaboration can be conceptualized as iterative idea improvement rather than task completion. We need to shift from policing to scaffolding students to leverage AI as a dialogic partner, using AI‑generated transcripts as evidence for learning and collaboration. CSCL knowledge‑building perspectives could provide a theoretical foundation for unraveling the nature of AI‑human collaboration while enriching CSCL theories in AI age. Design‑pedagogy‑technology perspective. CSCL offers powerful approaches for aligning assessment, learning, and collaboration. Research in assessment has shown that assessment can be understood as assessment of learning (evaluating completed work), for learning (supporting improvement), and as learning (making thinking visible) (Wiliam, 2017). Beyond assessing completed work, CSCL approaches—argumentation, collaborative problem‑solving, knowledge building, and maker work, etc.—provide rich opportunities for formative assessment that support collaboration and complement traditional exams/papers. Assessing group interaction and quality of talk, increasingly supported by AI (Hu et al., 2022), offers important indicators of learning. Reflective assessment enables the assessment of collaboration while also scaffolding interaction and idea development (Yang et al., 2024; van Aalst & Chan, 2007), and this could now be enriched with AI. In this way, AI becomes part of an assessment ecology that supports collaborative learning rather than merely reproducing assignment products. Analytics perspective. Contemporary CSCL analytics research now makes it feasible to assess processes beyond easily replicable products. AI‑enhanced collaborative analytics can trace participation, interactions, and revisions through log data, revealing whether students are engaging in meaningful knowledge construction or simply copying outputs (Ouyang et al., 2023). These process‑level data can be fed back to teachers and learners through dashboards to support monitoring, reflection, and improvement. CSCL researchers are well-positioned to design AI-enriched analytics that make collaboration processes and idea development—previously invisible— now visible (Ba et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2022). This process‑focused view emphasizes ongoing work tracing student engagement and activity rather than post‑hoc grading through concurrent, embedded, and transformative assessment. Such analytics assess not only what students produce but how they collaborate—with AI and with one another—to co-construct and to build knowledge. Issues for Discussion: This workshop provides a platform for participants to share ideas as we inquire into how CSCL could address challenges of assessment for new opportunities in the AI era. Grounded in theory, design, and analytics and ecological-ethical considerations, several areas of inquiry include: ● Focus of assessment and expanding theories. Assessment needs to shift from evaluating products to processes–examining how people learn and collaborate with AI. Emerging research on human–AI collaboration highlights cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, and socio-emotional processes, yet more work is needed—for example, on how students take agency and engage in dialogue with AI when tackling assessments to advance learning. Questions also arise about what knowledge, skills, domain-specific competencies, and collaboration processes should be assessed in AI-mediated assessment -- How can AI’s roles shift from merely providing content to supporting co-construction, regulation, and reflection? These shifts call for expanding CSCL theoretical perspectives and engaging with related fields on assessment. Continued inquiry is needed to extend CSCL frameworks to better capture the complexities of learning and collaboration in AI-mediated assessment. ● Collaboration and AI-assessment designs. Building on CSCL designs, researchers can work on productive assessment tasks to replace traditional ones easily emulated by AI and designing AI-enriched collaborative environments. Questions include what we are assessing, what the assessment activity involves, and what resources—peers, AI, and technology—are required. Reflective assessment can prompt students to reflect on their work with AI for ongoing improvement. As well, automatic assessment features can provide teachers with timely information to assess student engagement and to make “on-the-fly” decisions about what support is needed. Design experiments conducted on AI-assessment designs while examining the emerging human-AI collaboration process would help advance both research and practice.. ● Examining AI-supported multi-modal data analysis. Collaborative analytics, combined with AI, can play a central role in assessing learning-collaboration processes via multi-modal data analyses. These could include automatic scoring and annotating student texts and conversations, applying expert-designed rubrics for evaluation, and identifying emerging patterns of behaviors. Information shown in dashboards can support teacher assessment and promote students’ reflection on ongoing work. These analyses open the door to assessing human–AI interactions and designing assessment tasks that capture these dynamics. How these tools and analytics can enhance assessment validity, scalable analysis, providing meaningful insights into collaborative learning processes are important questions. ● Equity and diversity issues. The advent of AI in assessment raises important questions about equity and diversity. AI use may widen existing gaps if students have unequal access to technology, differing levels of guidance, or varying digital literacy. AI technology itself can be biased due to an imbalance in data availability. At the same time, well-scaffolded AI use and mindfully-designed AI tools have the potential to narrow disparities by providing feedback and more accessible pathways for demonstrating student understanding. We need to consider how assessment design and practices can ensure fairness, how AI- based tools can be designed to reduce inequities, and what forms of support learners need to participate equitably in AI-mediated assessment environments. ● Research–practice integration. CSCL-AI assessment for impact involves research-practice synergy developing practical tools and strategies that teachers can use. This involves understanding teachers’ needs and communicating complex findings in accessible, actionable forms. Inquiry such as interviews with teachers about their successful experiences with AI-informed collaboration and assessment could enrich the integration. Supporting higher-education teachers in adopting new views of assessment, collaboration, and AI use—and aligning CSCL research with classroom realities—remain to be investigated. ● Privacy, ethics, and limitations. AI‑supported assessment raises concerns about data privacy, ethical use, and system limitations. Collecting process data—such as interaction logs or conversational traces—requires careful attention to consent, transparency, and responsible data use. Ethical challenges include helping students use AI responsibly, preventing misuse of analytics, addressing bias in AI‑generated judgments, and ensuring students are not harmed by algorithmic errors. Ongoing scrutiny of AI limitations is needed to ensure new CSCL-AI assessment practices remain trustworthy, fair, and beneficial. ● Engagement with the public. The rise of generative AI has sparked widespread public debate, offering CSCL researchers opportunities to engage broader audiences. Public engagement involves helping students, parents, policymakers, and other stakeholders understand the challenges and opportunities AI brings to assessment. By clarifying misconceptions, sharing evidence, success stories, and highlighting responsible uses, CSCL researchers can contribute to more informed public discourse. Outline of planned activities (half-day workshop) Before the workshop: Participants will complete a short survey (a) identifying their research interests in CSCL, assessment, and generative AI, (b) sharing examples of how they have used generative AI in classroom- assessment contexts; and c) proposing key questions for workshop discussion. D uring the workshop: The workshop will be structured to maximize sharing, exchange & knowledge building. • Introduction. Organizers introduce aims and expected outcomes, followed with participant introduction. • Invited panel discussion. 3-4 researchers will be invited to give brief presentations that expand on key themes, also informed by participants’ pre-workshop submissions. • Breakouts and group discussion o Connecting and sharing. In rotating dyads, participants share the big idea or challenge they bring to the workshop, as well as what they hope to gain and contribute. Each person speaks and responds before moving to a new partner. o Knowledge sharing and building: In groups of four, participants rotate and discuss an issue or idea related to their work, focusing on opportunities to develop their research, pursue interdisciplinary collaboration, and take action related to key themes. AI tools could be used to stimulate and help summarize the discussion; each group shares one standout idea from their discussion (online participants will be supported with online collaboration tools) • Closing. Synthesis of what we have learned and reflection on potential actions, including proposed activities on publication, projects, media writing, networking, and community building After the workshop: Participants will form a Google group for communication connecting with CSCL committee /junior researchers and panel discussion planned coming year, opening to CSCL and learning sciences researchers. Expected outcomes and contribution The anticipated outcomes include workshop materials, publication of a paper, collaborative plans for projects and papers; and a Google group for communication for participants and interested ISLS members. Participation requirements Participation requires completing the survey on assessment, CSCL, and generative AI. The survey collects participants’ experience with CSCL and assessment to be shared during the workshop to enrich dialogue. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past (e.g., CSCL or ICLS) This workshop is distinctive in addressing the assessment challenges facing higher education with the rise of generative AI. There could be similar events on CSCL multi-modal analytics and generative AI but few synergizing research and practice for broadening CSCL visions for impacts in assessment in Gen AI era. Facilities and equipment required We will use the conference’s communication platform for remote participants (e.g., Zoom), possibly including other tools, such as Miro (https://miro.com/login/) or Padlet (https://padlet.com/) to support online collaboration.. For on-site participants, internet access, projectors, and a room large enough to accommodate breakout spaces for group discussions are required. Minimal and maximum number of participants We aim for 15 and 25 participants, with a balanced mix of in-person and remote participants, along with the organizing team and invited panelists. Draft call for participation About the Workshop: We invite researchers, graduate students, and practitioners to join this workshop to explore the roles of CSCL in advancing AI-supported assessment. With the rapid rise of generative AI, higher education faces urgent assessment challenges. We propose CSCL offers powerful lenses and tools for rethinking assessment challenges and how learning and collaboration can be assessed in AI‑rich environments. This workshop provides a venue for sharing research, practices, and emerging ideas and future trends on AI‑enriched assessment, including the role of AI as a collaborative partner for knowledge building, process‑focused assessment, assessment design, multi-modal analytics, equity-ethics issues, teacher-researcher collaboration, and public engagement. Together, we will identify ways to address current challenges, examine theories and designs for CSCL-AI enriched approaches, build collective knowledge and reflect on implications for our roles as CSCL researchers and educators. Participants will engage in reflective inquiry, interactive discussions, and community building to reconceptualize assessment and to develop future collaborations on CSCL research for impact. title: Seeing in 360°: Practical and Theoretical Insights for Video Recording in Learning Sciences Research
citation: Brette Garner, Elizabeth Metts, Darryl Yong (2026). Seeing in 360°: Practical and Theoretical Insights for Video Recording in Learning Sciences Research. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Garner, B., Metts, E., & Yong, D.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This full-day workshop addresses the theoretical and practical challenges of using 360° video and multi-camera systems in qualitative research. Drawing on a multi-year research– practice partnership in secondary classrooms, we share insights for implementing a range of recording technologies. We will address theoretical issues, including how each configuration shapes what becomes visible, invisible, and analytically possible. We will also address practical challenges researchers encounter when working with complex video data, including: managing massive file sizes, synchronizing multiple videos, and establishing data storage and processing workflows. Through hands-on activities, attendees will collect, process, and analyze their own 360° footage and practice troubleshooting common pitfalls. We invite researchers at all levels to consider how 360° video and multi-camera set-ups can support responsible, rigorous, and theoretically informed inquiry. Workshop overview This full-day workshop is intended for researchers, including graduate students and emerging scholars, who are interested in using 360° video in their research projects. The workshop organizers have engaged in a multi-year research project using a diverse array of video data collection methodologies, including 360° cameras (e.g., GoPro MAX), standard cameras, and synchronized multi-camera setups. This extensive practical experience has yielded valuable methodological insights, which we are eager to share with the learning sciences community. Workshop goals and participants This workshop is designed for learning scientists who collect, analyze, or theorize with video data, including those who are interested in multi-modal analysis, emerging recording technologies, representations of practice, and ethical considerations surrounding visibility and video-based research. No prior experience with 360 video is required, and we welcome participants at any career stage. The goals of our session are twofold: First, participants will consider the theoretical and analytic affordances of various video recording set- ups, including what is rendered visible and invisible with their methodological choices, and how those choices influence their analysis. It is tempting to think that collecting more data or richer data is always better; that is, that multi-camera set-ups are better than single-camera, or that more immersive 360° videos are preferable to wide- angle views. However, we argue that this is not necessarily so: even the best video recording renders some aspects of an event invisible and unrecoverable, and the technical difficulties of wrangling large data corpora may render some analyses impractical. As researchers, it is important to thoughtfully weigh these choices. In this session, we will engage learning sciences colleagues in deeper theorizing around these issues. Second, we will share practical knowledge and insight into how to use complex video recording set-ups. Across two research-practice partnerships — Project SIGMa (Supporting Instructional Growth in Mathematics; Horn & Garner, 2022) and Project TAU (Teaching Amidst Uncertainty) — we have spent extensive time developing and troubleshooting various video recording set-ups. Using multi-camera set-ups, especially with 360° video, presents many nontrivial challenges: synchronizing multiple cameras, managing different files and file types, as well as processing and storing large files. Building on the theoretical conversation, participants will gain practical knowledge and skills to use 360° cameras and mutli-camera set-ups — including knowledge of equipment (cameras, but also accessories such as SD cards and cables), software, data compression, and data storage requirements. We have refined and synthesized our data management processes to use with our large, multi-site research team, and we want to share this hard-won knowledge with others in the field. Organizing team We are a multi-generational research team involved in a multi-year research–practice partnership, through which we have captured rich, multi-perspective video records in teachers’ classrooms. Elizabeth (senior research assistant) and Brette (co-PI) developed and implemented a variety of data collection protocols. Darryl (co-PI) o ffered technical expertise to develop Mathematica programs to synchronize and process videos. Together, we offer rich experience in both the design and implementation of video data collection protocols. Theoretical background We resurrect Hall’s (2000) question around video recording teaching and learning activities: “How should we expect new technical media for recording human action, along with a growing suite of tools for their analysis, to shape the specific cultural practices of cognitive and educational researchers?” (p. 649). As video recording technology has become increasingly sophisticated and complex in the quarter-century since Hall posed this question, it is vital to consider how such technology shapes our work as researchers and learning scientists. Moreover, Hall argues, video recording is not a neutral practice, and our choices for creating video records are theory-laden. In this workshop, we will consider a) how video both captures and (re)organizes activity and b) how video shapes analytic practices. We examine this through our use of 360° video and multi-camera set-ups. How does mutli-camera 360° video (re)organize activity? Video recordings construct a particular version of an event, where decisions — around what to record and from where — frame the activity of interest in a particular way. Each camera has a fixed field of view, inevitably deleting some elements of the activity entirely; multiple cameras can offer more views, but cannot fully capture everything. Even within what is captured, some elements become foregrounded while anything at the periphery will be backgrounded. What remains in the video record then stands in for the “real” activity that can be studied, replayed, analyzed, and shared. The decisions behind what we are able to capture reflect and embed theoretical and anticipatory assumptions into the video record. These orientations then shape what becomes visible, emphasized, and relevant in any subsequent study of the interaction. When we make decisions about what to capture and what to foreground in the recording, we necessarily change what the event is. This is true for any video record, but it’s important to consider how these implications might be different for 360° video. Although 360° cameras expand the field of view, elements of activity will still be deleted, as they fall outside the audio range or line of sight. While background activity is generally visible, 360° cameras privilege what is physically closer to the camera. In other words, foregrounding is no longer a matter for framing, but of how the placement of the camera affords a particular, spatially organized perspective. How does multi-camera 360° video shape viewing and analysis? Video offers a durable record that can be replayed and edited. This allows us to rebuild fine-grained interactional detail of events, often to a level of detail that exceeds what can be captured using fieldnotes or audio recordings. While multi-camera and 360° recordings expand what is captured, they still present particular points of view. Across different cameras — or, by panning and zooming in a single 360 video — viewers follow different viewing paths can create different senses of “what happened,” producing multiple possible versions of the event. Multi- camera and 360° video can restore some dimensions of the recorded event, affording different interpretive trajectories. Yet, these trajectories are still constrained within the original, recorded theoretical frame. With any video record, what we select for analysis is theoretically and culturally structured (Derry et al., 2010). Multi-camera and 360° recordings change what counts as “selectable” because analysts choose spatial vantage points as well as temporal moments. For example, with 360° video, analysts can decide what becomes “in frame” after the fact, reshaping what becomes visible and analyzable. With a more complex record, the ways we navigate it — how we choose where to look or move throughout the record — require greater reflexivity and transparency about how we structure our analyses and the theoretical assumptions underlie those choices. Ethical considerations The use of video warrants explicit attention to ethics. Immersive and panoramic recordings expand what can be seen, potentially capturing learners who did not anticipate being recorded or activity not visible to teachers or researchers in real time. In an increasingly surveillance-oriented world, these expanded capacities raise questions about consent, circulation, data storage, and the right to opacity. Following Derry et al. (2010), we emphasize the need for transparency and care in decisions about what is captured, who views it, and how these records are used. In this workshop, we will explicitly address issues of visibility, vulnerability, and equity, and invite participants to consider how immersive media can support respectful and responsible research practices. Practical issues for video data collection In addition to discussing theoretical issues, we aim to equip participants with practical knowledge and skills to use complex video recording protocols in their research. As with any technology, there is a learning curve to using n ew cameras and data collection protocols. However, we have found that using 360 cameras, especially in a multi- camera set-up, has presented substantial challenges. Our development of these video methods stems from our own research-practice partnership projects (RPPs), in which we collaborate with secondary mathematics teachers to support their reflection and learning. In this work, we use video recordings to document classroom activity, using them as fodder for both teacher reflection and research analysis. These dual purposes have required us to find ways to make the videos usable and legible for multiple audiences. And while our data collection happens in classrooms, we argue that our processes are of interest to the broader learning sciences community — that is, the challenges we encountered and the solutions we have found are common across many learning environments. Limitations of typical video technologies A typical use of video for capturing classroom interaction includes a single video camera, with either a whole- class view or a focus on a particular group of students. In our RPP work, our teachers frequently use groupwork as a key part of their pedagogical practice. We conjectured that a typical single-camera set-up would be insufficient for our project, as we would need to choose between framing a whole class or one specific group. In early iterations of our RPP work (Horn & Garner, 2022), we addressed this concern by using the Swivl platform. The Swivl captures one video stream with up to five separate audio tracks (one teacher and four student groups). This allowed us to select a single framing for the video (i.e., a whole-class, wide-angle view), but with more detailed audio data on student collaboration. However, the Swivl had serious limitations: Students were only recognizable if they spoke out loud. Students with similar voices were difficult to differentiate. And, of course, many aspects of interaction (e.g., gesture) were simply not available in the video record. Affordances and challenges of multi-camera 360° video To address these concerns, we sought more complex data collection methods that would allow for richer video data. However, with each technological innovation, we encountered new challenges. For the next iteration of our RPP work, we looked for platforms that would allow us to capture video recordings of multiple student groups. During our pilot work, we tried a multi-camera version of Swivl. Similar to the single-video, multiple-audio set- up, the multi-camera Swivl would enable us to easily synchronize multiple video streams. However, the platform requires strong and stable wifi; this is not always available in research settings, particularly in schools. We ultimately developed our own data collection protocol, consisting of: one whole-class camera (with audio from the teacher), a point-of-view camera worn by the teacher, and three 360 cameras at student groups. This multi-camera set-up generally captures the rich record of classroom interaction that we were seeking. With 360 video, individual students are visible and audible — we can more readily tell who is speaking and how often. Students’ body language and gestures are clear, allowing us to attend to nonverbal interactions. We can also better see what students have in front of them — their worksheets, whiteboards, and manipulatives. The point-of-view and whole-class cameras capture the teacher’s movement and conversation throughout the lesson. Taken together, this approach creates rich video records that afford robust analyses of learning. title: Listening to the Land and Sea: Community Learning at Crystal Cove Conservancy

abstract: This community engagement workshop explores how environmental learning can be designed, enacted, and studied across interconnected land and sea systems. Centered at Crystal Cove State Park, participants engage in an immersive field-based experience that illustrates how public landscapes support connections among schools, community organizations, and professional science and land-management communities. Drawing on learning sciences perspectives, the workshop integrates guided exploration of inland and coastal ecosystems with structured reflection and collaborative sensemaking. Participants examine how learning designs incorporate scientific practices, local ecological phenomena, and community relevance, and how participation structures influence inquiry, equity, and civic reasoning. The workshop also considers how Crystal Cove’s existing STEM programs provide a meaningful context for examining field-based learning in environmental and climate education. Participants collaboratively generate design principles and research questions to inform future educational efforts and study. Overview and rationale for the community engagement workshop Across the learning sciences, there is growing recognition that consequential learning is not confined to classrooms but emerges through participation in community life and sustained engagement with meaningful problems that matter to people, institutions, and shared environments. Community-based learning frameworks emphasize learning as a process of developing knowledge, identity, and agency through participation in culturally and socially organized practices that are embedded in everyday activity systems (Lave & Wenger, 1991; Rogoff, 2003). This perspective is particularly salient for climate and environmental education, where learning is inseparable from community histories, public decision-making, and collective stewardship of ecological systems that learners can directly observe, measure, and revisit over time (Bang et al., 2012; Fenwick et al., 2015). Despite increased attention to community-based approaches, the field continues to grapple with how to design and study learning environments that meaningfully connect classrooms, communities, and public institutions at scale, while also supporting equity, civic participation, and rigorous disciplinary learning. Learning scientists face persistent questions about how learners move across settings, how participation structures shape belonging and legitimacy, and how public institutions and shared landscapes function as infrastructures for learning that bridge formal and informal education. Initiatives such as the Environmental and Climate Change Literacy Projects (ECCLPs), a multi-institutional partnership linking universities, school districts, informal learning organizations, and community partners, have emerged in response to these challenges by supporting coherence, relationship building, and mutual learning across educational sectors. This community engagement workshop centers Crystal Cove State Park and the education programs of Crystal Cove Conservancy as an exemplary community-based learning ecology situated within this broader ECCLPs context that connects schools, informal learning environments, and professional science and land- management communities. Crystal Cove provides a distinctive opportunity to examine how learners engage in authentic scientific practices across interconnected land and sea systems, how they develop relationships to public natural resources, and how educators design and facilitate learning experiences that integrate disciplinary inquiry, civic reasoning, and cultural responsiveness. As a public landscape where scientific inquiry is deeply intertwined with conservationand coastal change, Crystal Cove offers a compelling site for examining learning at the intersection of science, community participation, and civic life (Ardoin & Heimlich, 2021).; Sezen-Barrie, et al., 2023). Theoretical background: Community-based learning Learning as situated participation Community-based learning builds from the premise that learning is not simply the accumulation of individual knowledge but a process of participation in social practices and the development of competence in activities that are valued within communities (Lave & Wenger, 1991). From this perspective, learning is inseparable from the s ocial relations, cultural norms, tools, and material conditions within which activity unfolds. Context is not a backdrop for learning; rather, it is constitutive of what is learned and who learners become through participation. Complementary sociocultural perspectives emphasize that learning involves the co-construction of meaning through interaction, dialogue, and joint activity within historically developed practices (Rogoff, 2003). These commitments have shaped learning-sciences research on apprenticeship, collaborative inquiry, and learning across settings, and they provide a strong conceptual foundation for understanding community-based learning environments that span schools, informal programs, and public institutions. Environmental and land-based contexts heighten the importance of this framing because ecological systems are material, dynamic, and consequential for communities. Learners encounter tangible evidence of change, such as shoreline shifts, erosion patterns, biodiversity indicators, and species distribution, and these observations are often connected to public concerns and local decision-making. These conditions create opportunities for learning that link scientific practice with lived experience and collective responsibility, enabling learners to interpret evidence in relation to community histories and future possibilities (Bang et al., 2012; Fenwick et al., 2015). Community histories, relations, and learning infrastructures From a community-based learning perspective, public landscapes and institutions are not neutral spaces but are shaped by layered social, political, and ecological histories that are unevenly experienced across communities. These histories matter for learning because they influence whose knowledge is recognized, how participation is organized, and what forms of engagement are legitimized. In learning-sciences research, shared environments can function as epistemic resources that support modeling, explanation, and argumentation, while also foregrounding questions of access, representation, and civic responsibility. Research suggests that when learners engage with environmental issues that are embedded in community contexts they can revisit over time, they are more likely to sustain inquiry, develop systems-level reasoning, and coordinate evidence with explanation (Hmelo-Silver et al., 2007; Zimmerman & Weible, 2017). Repeated engagement across settings supports iterative cycles of data collection, interpretation, and revision, aligning with learning-sciences work on inquiry, modeling, and the development of scientific argumentation. At the same time, extended participation in community contexts can support affective and relational dimensions of learning, fostering motivation, care, and persistence with complex environmental problems. Crystal Cove as a community-based learning ecology Crystal Cove State Park is one of California’s ecologically and culturally significant coastal landscapes. Established in 1979, the park encompasses approximately 3,936 acres along 3.2 miles of Pacific coastline and extends inland through coastal bluffs, chaparral canyons, and undeveloped backcountry within the South Coast Wilderness area (California State Parks, 2010). Located between Newport Beach and Laguna Beach in Orange County, Crystal Cove includes extensive beaches, tide pools, inland canyons, and a large marine conservation area and underwater park, creating continuity between terrestrial and marine ecosystems (California State Parks, 2011). Ecologically, Crystal Cove is a biodiversity-rich environment supporting diverse bird species, reptiles, amphibians, and rare coastal plants and animals found in Southern California (National Audubon Society, 2012; Californian Wildlife Region, 2013). The park supports a wide range of recreational and educational activities, including hiking, tide-pool exploration, and marine studies, which shape who encounters the park and how learning opportunities can be designed to be accessible and inclusive. In partnership with California State Parks, Crystal Cove Conservancy plays a critical role in expanding public learning opportunities through structured STEM programs. The Conservancy brings more than 7,000 low-income students to Crystal Cove each year, many for their first visit to the ocean, and provides programs at no cost to schools to reduce economic barriers. These programs exemplify community-based learning through sustained engagement, collaboration with scientists and resource managers, extended curricular sequences, and opportunities for youth to contribute data and interpretations that matter to real conservation and management questions. More recently, Crystal Cove Conservancy has attracted interest from university-based researchers studying environmental and climate literacy. The Conservancy’s STEM programs offer a valuable educational setting for examining how students engage with ecological phenomena, scientific practices, and conservation questions in field-based contexts. At this stage, engagement is exploratory and focused on understanding how existing programs contribute to student learning and teacher development. Any research activity is conducted in alignment with Crystal Cove’s established educational mission and supports ongoing efforts to enhance public learning experiences within the park. The workshop is intentionally structured as a focused, immersive experience rather than comprehensive professional development. Participants engage in a sequence of field-based and reflective activities that make visible how Crystal Cove functions as a community-based learning ecology. The workshop combines guided exploration of inland and coastal environments with structured opportunities for sensemaking, allowing participants to examine how learning designs integrate scientific practices, local phenomena, and community relevance. Across activities, facilitators foreground learning-sciences perspectives on participation, boundary crossing, systems thinking, and civic reasoning, while inviting participants to surface problems of practice and design questions from their own contexts. The workshop concludes with collaborative synthesis, where participants connect field experiences to broader implications for research, design, and partnership work in community-based learning. Learning goals and outcomes By the end of the workshop, participants will: • Recognize Crystal Cove as a community-based learning ecology that supports learning across settings, institutions, and communities • Identify design principles that support disciplinary learning, equity, and civic reasoning • Generate research questions and methodological considerations relevant to studying learning across contexts and public landscapes • Build connections with other participants interested in community-based learning, research–practice partnerships, and environmental education Call for participation We invite learning scientists, educators, and community partners to join this half-day community engagement workshop focused on community-based environmental learning at Crystal Cove State Park. This session is designed for participants interested in learning across settings, research–practice partnerships, equity-oriented design, and the role of public institutions as learning infrastructures (Akkerman & Bakker, 2011). Participants are encouraged to bring a question, problem of practice, or research interest related to community-based learning, environmental education, or learning across contexts. The workshop engages participants as co-learners through shared field experiences, structured reflection, and collaborative sensemaking, offering opportunities to connect theory with practice in a public landscape. Grounded in learning-sciences theory and situated within a living learning ecology, the Crystal Cove workshop offers participants an opportunity to examine how community-based learning is designed, experienced, and theorized, while building relationships that support future collaboration and inquiry within the ISLS community.
