abstract: Playful Learning Landscapes (PLL) transforms everyday community spaces like parks, bus-stops, and grocery stores into conduits for caregiver-child interactions and early learning. During this workshop, attendees will visit a series of PLL installations in Santa Ana, CA, which were co-designed by researchers from UC Irvine and Temple University, and families from the Santa Ana Early Learning Initiative, a local grassroots non-profit community organization. Attendees will engage with the PLL installations and learn about the design process and impact of the installations on community members and caregiver child interactions at PLL sites. The session will also demonstrate how this project was conducted in partnership with the City of Santa Ana’s Parks and Recreation and Public Works departments who own and maintain the installations and have begun to replicate them using public funds in other community spaces. Challenges, lessons learned, plans for sustainability, and practical and theoretical insights will be discussed. Playful learning in the community: An interactive tour of community based early learning installations Informal learning environments like children’s museums, zoos, and maker spaces are powerful contexts for supporting young children’s science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) learning and identity. Unfortunately, children from low-income families have less access to these spaces due to a variety of barriers like admission prices, transportation challenges, or even an awareness of their existence. In addition to these barriers, linguistically and ethnically minoritized families can feel alienated in these spaces which rarely center their languages, cultural values, and practices. Playful Learning Landscapes is an international initiative that brings informal learning installations to everyday spaces like parks, bus-stops, grocery stores, laundry mats, medical clinic waiting rooms, sidewalks, and walls (Hassinger-Das, 2018; Bustamante et al., 2019). Playful Learning Landscapes promote the caregiver-child conversations and interactions that decades of developmental and learning sciences research suggest lead to learning, such as conversational turns, STEM language, and hands-on engagement (Bustamante et al., 2020; Hassinger-Das et al., 2021; Pesch et al., 2025). In addition to designing PLLs based on the latest research in developmental and learning sciences, they are also designed in partnership with local families, so the installations build from families’ values, routines, and cultural practices (Bermudez et al., 2023). Understanding learning as a cultural process situates family’s participation in learning environments and design as dictated by values, routines, and cultural practices (Bang & Medin, 2010; Rogoff et al, 2007). Leveraging cultural assets, practices, and values can therefore increase relevance and significance for families, in turn increasing inclusivity, sustainability, and engagement. Partners The PLL work in Santa Ana, CA, is conducted in the context of a long-term research practice partnership between the Santa Ana Early Learning Initiative (SAELI), the University of California Irvine, and the City of Santa Ana. SAELI is a grassroots non-profit community organization bringing together local families, non-profit organizations, and leadership from the Santa Ana Unified School district to support families with children between 0-9 years of age. SAELI is led by director Wendy Gomez and uses a multigenerational approach through which promotoras (e.g., Chen et al., 2023) promote wellness through initiatives on child development, connecting families with resources, and local advocacy projects. On the university side, these projects are led by UC Irvine S chool of Education Professors Andres Bustamante and June Ahn and Temple University Psychology Professor Kathy Hirsh-Pasek. This research team brings expertise in child development, early education, participatory design, and research practice partnerships. The City of Santa Ana supported the project through their Parks and Recreation Department and Public Works Department, with support from the City Manager’s Office, Mayor's Office, and City Council. Other organizations and businesses included in this work were Northgate Gonzalez Market grocery chain, the Santa Ana Unified School District, First Five Orange County, and Orange County Health Care Agency. In this RPP, we endeavored to center families’ voices in all phases of the process from designing the installations, to deciding their locations, to the evaluation research, and dissemination of the findings. Importantly, trust and relationship-building with families were central to the design sessions. Personal stories and family values were shared through informal conversations over meals. These informal opportunities to connect allowed trust to be built over time, which uniquely positioned researchers and families as equals. We believe this allowed families to share openly and addressed traditional power dynamics between researchers and families. Decisions were taken jointly through parallel conversations with partners and interested parties, requiring transparency, trust-building, multiple channels of communication, rapid problem-solving, adaptation, and other forms of invisible relational labor. However, tensions emerged throughout the process particularly when navigating the intersection of large bureaucracies including federal funding, university systems, and city government. The project faced multiple challenges, including changing project timelines and material constraints, changes in organizational leadership, physical limitations of the public spaces designated for installations, and the complex social and political contexts of the community. Given existing power differentials between governmental partners and community stakeholders, our university team played a critical intermediary role, advocating on behalf of the community in certain cases. Whereas in other cases, our community partners stepped up and advocated for the project using their influence as voting constituents and activists in their community. Ultimately, the political capital of all stake- holders was necessary to bring this project to fruition. Research design in the community The Santa Ana PLLs were supported by an Advancing Informal STEM Learning (AISL) award from the National Science Foundation. The project began in 2020, and due to the pandemic, all design sessions in the first year of the project were held on Zoom. We held seven 90-minute co-design sessions where we learned about families histories and experiences with their community spaces, and used participatory design activities such as bags-of- stuff, photo-elicitation, story boarding, and storytelling to encourage families to share their goals and routines in their community spaces (for a detailed description of design process see Bermudez et al., 2023; Garcia et al., 2022; Chew et al., 2022). Through an inductive thematic analysis of these co-design sessions, we surfaced community values, practices, and aspirations such as promoting intergenerational learning, and increasing family time. As part of these themes, we also surfaced ways in which families' own routines and practices already involved STEM concepts and practices. We iteratively combined these themes and existing practices with the science practices and crosscutting concepts from the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) and principles from developmental science for creating high-quality early learning environments that are active, engaging, iterative, social, meaningful, and joyful (Hirsh-Pasek et al., 2015). While a single design could not meet all the criteria, we sought balance across community values, developmental principles, and science learning goals (see Bermudez et al., 2023 for more detail). Further, we were intentional to align these practices with SAELI’s three step design model that included engaging parents in discovery & dreaming, designing, and creating a sustainability plan. Using these design goals and guiding frameworks, we conducted prototype ideation sessions with SAELI families and then subsequent sessions where we created low-fidelity mock-ups of the prototypes for play testing and iteration during the second and third years of the project. Children and parents were interviewed to hear their feedback on the designs and learn about their experiences playing with the physical prototypes. These sessions were key to evaluate factors from usability to how and if families’ interactions aligned with their values and practices. These sessions were held in person at their local Community Center, started with a shared meal, followed by a design activity, reflections and share outs. Through these sessions we iterated and refined the prototypes until they were ready to be shared with our fabrication partners. Fabrication and launch For fabrication, we contracted a Los Angeles based museum installation design shop. We worked closely with their engineers to adapt the co-designed prototypes for durability, usability, safety, cost efficiency, and regulation compliance. All designs were reviewed by City of Santa Ana Parks and Recreation or Public Works departments and UC Irvine’s Facilities Management department. We worked collaboratively with the City of Santa Ana and S AELI to decide where the installations would go, taking advantage of existing city renovation efforts to save costs and create efficiencies when possible. We also worked with legal representation from UCI and the City of Santa Ana to execute a Memorandum of Understanding that the PLL installations were being donated to the city by UCI and the City of Santa Ana would own and maintain them. This process took approximately two years from the beginning of the fabrication process to installation in public spaces. The installations were implemented between Fall 2024 and Spring 2025 with a grand opening ribbon cutting ceremony held on May 10th, 2025, as part of the NSF’s 75th anniversary celebration and Mother’s Day in many Latin American countries. The ceremony was hosted at Madison Park in Santa Ana and attended by the Mayor, Director of Parks and Recreation, several city council members, and the Dean of the UCI School of Education. Data collection Our data collection protocol included baseline observations of STEM language and caregiver child interactions at each of the five installation sites pre-installation as well as a matched comparison site (e.g., for a bus-stop installation we observed a comparison bus stop in the same neighborhood). We also trained SAELI parents to collect surveys at all PLL and control sites of caregiver’s self-efficacy in teaching STEM to their children, perceptions of safety and learning opportunities in their community spaces, and attitudes around the connection between play and learning. We then performed the observational and survey data collection protocol post- installation to examine the impacts of the PLL’s on caregiver child interactions and experiences in community spaces. While post-installation data collection is on-going we expect to present findings from these analyses at the ISLS workshop in June 2026. For a more detailed description of our analytical plans please refer to our project pre-registration on the Open Science Framework. Workshop details The tour will be hosted by UCI Associate Professor and project PI Andres Bustamante, UCI Professor and project Co-PI June Ahn, SAELI Director Wendy Gomez, and several SAELI parents who participated in the design and data collection processes. The hosts will offer insights into the project’s co-design approach, the partnership with the city (challenges and opportunities), parents’ roles as designers, data collectors, and project advocates, impact results, and future plans for policy agenda towards sustainability and scaling. The timetable of activities and sites to be visited are shown below (Table 1). We will also discuss several cross-site design considerations, including Playful Learning Principles, culturally responsive design, the use of public spaces as learning environments, multigenerational engagement, attention to accessibility, and low-burden participation that aligns with families’ everyday routines. Table 1 Timetable of Activities Hour Activity 8:00 am Meet at the conference hotel at 8am PST on June 15th, 2026. We will depart on a charter bus to tour the five PLL sites in Santa Ana. 8:30 am Arrive at Santa Ana, touring the 5 different sites (see text below). 11:30 am End of the tour. The charter bus will be taking people back to the conference hotel. Site 1: Madison Park. Madison Park features the largest of the Santa Ana PLL installation, Parkopolis, the life-sized board game for math and science learning. Parkopolis is a giant board game where children spin life sized dice and advance around the board completing math and science games like playing patterns on musical pipes, and measuring how far you can jump on a giant ruler. Through the co-design process, we learned about games like Basta, a category game that many SAELI families play, and integrated them into Parkopolis games. During the co-design sessions, many families expressed concerns about visiting their neighborhood parks and cited the bathroom facility in the back of Madison Park as a hotspot for illicit activities like drug use and prostitution. In response, the city demolished those bathrooms replacing them with new bathroom facilities in another part of the park, and we constructed Parkopolis where the old bathrooms were transforming a hot spot for criminal activity into a hub for early learning, a powerful example of community voice leading to impact in public infrastructure. Site 2: Abacus bus stop. T he giant abacus at the bus stop on the corner of Main Street and McFadden Avenue in Santa Ana invites families to engage in conversations around numeracy and arithmetic. Many families in our design session reference using an abacus to learn math when they were children in Mexico and other countries in Latin America and wondered why their children’s schools didn’t use an abacus. This installation is a powerful symbol of scalability because it was not funded by our NSF grant. The city of Santa Ana was renovating bus stops in this area and due to the awareness of our projects, leveraged existing funds to execute the design. Site 3: Northgate Gonzalez market. Northgate is a family owned local grocery chain that many of the SAELI families shop at. During our co-design sessions, we used families stories about grocery shopping with their parents growing up or with their children now to develop signage that promote math and science interactions. Examples include a conversion chart between pounds and kilos at the deli and using your senses to pick out the best fruits and vegetables in the produce section. This installation is unique because it demonstrates how local business and the private sector can engage and support this work. Site 4: Angels Park. Angels Park features two PLL installations, La Lotería which is a giant version of the bingo style game that is very popular with local families, and How Tall Am I? which is a statue where children can measure their height in comparison to California animals. Both of these installations are a great example of intuitive design and leveraging existing knowledge to create engaging STEM learning experiences. How Tall Am I? invites immediate engagement through its visual design and integrated measurement markers, requiring only minimal instruction in the form of a single guiding question. Similarly, Lotería is among the most popular family games in this community, lengthy instructions are not necessary. Instead, we simply embed short STEM activities into the playing cards for families to integrate into the game play. In addition to supporting informal STEM learning, both of these installations were co-designed with the intention of supporting intergenerational learning which is a core value of Latine families. Site 5: Washington elementary school. The last stop on the tour will visit the Yo Veo (I See) Mural, an interactive art exhibit where children look for hidden objects that reflect local cultural and community activities. This is another example of a local institution adopting a project design. This mural was funded by the Santa Ana Unified School District, who were renovating this school and directed funds for murals. This school also features a different project, Fraction Ball, a redesigned basketball court for math learning. Future directions During the May 10th ribbon cutting event, the City of Santa Ana made an official proclamation that May will be Early Childhood Education month in the city in recognition of this innovative work. Building on this momentum, we are working with city officials on a resolution to integrate PLLs into the city’s on-going process for new public amenities leveraging existing budget from local institutions. We plan to position SAELI as drivers of future PLL efforts where they engage local community members in a design process of new public amenities that center early learning and build from local families’ funds of knowledge. This work represents a scalable and community centered vision for designing public infrastructure to promote child development and civic engagement. Invitation to ICLS participants This session examines the evolution of a project and partnership from initial creation through implementation, using this project as a live case study to surface challenges, lessons learned, and future directions from different points of view. In doing so, we demonstrate how partnering with purpose can generate meaningful community impact and offer useful insights for other scholars and initiatives seeking to engage in collaborative, community- centered work. abstract: My research investigates how Visible Thinking and dialogic teaching can be integrated to foster interaction, thinking, and a culture of dialogue in EFL higher education. Using design-based research, I have iteratively designed and refined thinking-routine- embedded instruction and am now extending this work along three strands: analyzing thinking and dialogic moves in student discourse, exploring the cultural and affective dimensions that sustain a thinking culture, and refining design principles through curricular-design alignment between conjecture mapping and the curricular spider web. This ongoing program aims to build a theoretically and contextually grounded framework explaining how language, interaction, and design co-mediate learning in East Asian EFL classrooms.

abstract: My research examines how cultural practices (e.g., barbering, cosmetology, fashion design) and epistemologies (i.e., ways of knowing) can be learned and sustained while acquiring computer science (CS) skills. I draw on ethnocomputing and leverage heritage algorithms— hybrids of computing and culture—to create simulations of cultural practices using algorithms. These simulations can be used to teach cultural ways of knowing and making as well as CS skills. Overall, my research focuses on sustaining cultural making practices and cultivating the creative aspects of CS education through community-based participatory design research. In this statement, I share my previous work in CS education and ethnocomputing and situate future strands of my work in STEAM and the learning sciences.

abstract: This paper outlines a research program situated at the intersection of the Learning Sciences, Literacy Studies, and Black Studies. The work investigates how racialized histories of literacy shape contemporary learning environments and how Black learners and communities design countercurricula that affirm joy, resistance, and self-determination. Drawing from archival, ethnographic, and design-based methods, this research advances a theoretical framework of bound literacy—a concept describing how literacy has historically been constrained by antiblackness—and explores what learning might look like when literacy is “unbound.” The program contributes to the Learning Sciences by positioning Black literacies as sites of innovation, imagination, and design, offering frameworks and methodologies for understanding learning as a collective, historical, and liberatory act. Overview My research bridges the Learning Sciences, Literacy Studies, and Black Studies to examine how racialized histories of literacy shape learning and how Black communities design liberatory literacies in response. This paper outlines my research program on “bound” and “unbound” literacies and its contributions to theorizing learning as a site of freedom-making. Theoretical framework: Learning as a liberatory and historical practice My research begins from the premise that learning is not only cognitive or social but also historical and political. Building on sociocultural theories of learning (e.g., Vygotsky, 1978) and critical traditions within the Learning Sciences (e.g., Nasir et al., 2006), I conceptualize literacy as a designed social practice shaped by structures of race, power, and history. To theorize this relationship, I introduced the framework of bound literacy (Massengale, 2024), which traces how literacy in the U.S. popular imagination has been historically “bound” to chattel slavery and its afterlives. This reframes literacy not as a neutral skill set but as a cultural construct used to delimit who counts as a learner. By examining how literacy has been racialized—particularly through associations with Black deficiency—this framework exposes how antiblackness has shaped the epistemological foundations of schooling, assessment, and learning theory. At the same time, I view literacy as a site of resistance and design. Across historical and contemporary contexts, Black people have cultivated literacies that imagine freedom beyond dominant educational systems. Aligning with Learning Sciences scholarship that centers imagination, equity, and design (e.g., Gutiérrez & Jurow, 2018), I argue that Black literacies are world-building practices that create new ways of being, knowing, and learning.

abstract: My research examines learning in complex, rapidly evolving technological domains, particularly quantum information science. Bridging multiple theoretical perspectives, I am currently pursuing two directions: designing learning environments that make ultra-complex STEM accessible to K-12 learners; and theorizing quantum computational thinking to identify concepts, practices, and perspectives that distinguish quantum from classical reasoning. Research agenda and theoretical framing In my research, I am committed to understanding how emerging technologies shape and support learning. I pursue this understanding both via conceptual inquiry and via the design of learning environments that help learners navigate complex, rapidly evolving domains. While some of my previous (e.g., Coelho & McCollum, 2025) and ongoing work involves empirical investigations using AI and NLP technologies to support teaching and learning across K-12 and post-secondary contexts (e.g., Coelho et al., 2025a), this submission focuses on my research in K-12 quantum information science (QIS). My scholarship is primarily grounded in learning sciences traditions that view learning as situated and mediated by material and social interactions (e.g., Cole, 1998; Moll et al., 2006; Pea, 1985, 1993a, 1993b; Rogoff, 2003). I adopt an integrationist stance (Danish & Gresalfi, 2018), deliberately examining learning across one or more interrelated planes (Rogoff, 2008), while critically attending to the analytic affordances and limitations of this approach and maintaining a commitment to understanding the dynamic interplay among learners, social interactions, and context. I also draw on complementary perspectives that have traditionally emphasized the individual – such as constructivism (Kafai, 2012; Papert & Harel, 1991; Wilensky, 2020) – and cognitive sciences (e.g., Bandura, 2010) as generative for understanding and supporting meaning-making, agency, and motivation. I utilize these complementary perspectives to inform my conceptual and empirical contributions to K-12 quantum information science education as described in the subsequent sections. Thereafter, I discuss future directions centered on studying and designing for quantum computational thinking. Current work When I began reviewing the literature on K-12 quantum information science education (Coelho et al., 2025b), I was surprised to find that learning sciences researchers, who have spent decades studying how students understand complex scientific concepts, were almost entirely absent from the conversations. This absence seemed particularly striking given that learning quantum information science requires learners to grapple with ideas that defy classical intuition and mathematical formalisms that create barriers to accessibility even at the college level, let alone in K- 12 settings. These are precisely the kinds of challenges that learning sciences researchers have developed expertise in addressing: making complex, abstract concepts accessible through appropriate representational tools, scaffolding, and cultural practices that support new ways of thinking. And just as this expertise is most needed, national initiatives are pushing for quantum education to begin in middle and high school (NSF, 2020). While computer science and physics education researchers (e.g., Franklin et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2022) have begun important work in this space, the conversations have yet to substantially engage with learning sciences frameworks and methods that could complement and extend these disciplinary efforts. Our review also showed that both theoretical grounding and design conjectures in K-12 QIS education research remain limited. Many initiatives simply ask, “Does it work?” in a Thomas Edison exploratory framework (Stokes, 2011), without interrogating why or under what conditions learning occurs, risking innovations that engage learners but do not reliably support deep understanding. My position paper (Coelho et al., 2025d) argues for a bidirectional opportunity that neither field has fully recognized. QIS education could leverage learning sciences expertise in design-based research to iteratively develop quantum learning environments. This includes principled approaches for creating new representational infrastructures (Wilensky, 2020) that make quantum phenomena accessible while preserving mathematical integrity, as well as participation structures that allow learners to collectively make sense of quantum phenomena, negotiate meaning through shared representations, and transform their participation in disciplinary practices (Lemke, 2001; Pea, 1992; Rogoff et al., 1995). But equally important, and perhaps more provocative, is what q uantum information science offers the learning sciences: a domain that pushes us to reconsider our theories of conceptual change, representation, and learning at the boundaries of human intuition. To put these conceptual arguments into practice, my recent empirical work (Coelho et al., 2025c) investigates how collaborative game making (Fields & Kafai, 2018) leveraging distributed expertise (Pea, 1993) can support students in developing initial mental models of quantum information science concepts and practice while cultivating curiosity, confidence, and identity – early pathways toward a “competent outsider” stance (Sandoval et al., 2025). We found that designing quantum-themed board games created accessible entry points supporting participation without requiring advanced formalism, though supplementary social and material support will also be incorporated in future iterations of the work. Throughout this process, groups mobilized diverse expertise and resources to materialize quantum ideas, illustrating how even quantum-adjacent activities can drive motivation, sensemaking, and participation in ultra-complex STEM domains. Future work Building on my prior work in K-12 quantum information science education, I have begun to articulate a tentative framework for quantum computational thinking (QCT), extending classical computational thinking to the distinct concepts, practices, and perspectives of quantum information science, while attending to the ethical, societal, and justice-related dimensions of access to quantum technologies (Coelho et al., 2025e). This exploration identifies key concepts (e.g., randomness, interference, superposition), practices (e.g., designing probabilistic algorithms, leveraging amplitude amplification), and perspectives (e.g., understanding computation as materially grounded, designing under indeterminacy) that distinguish QCT from classical computational reasoning, while also emphasizing equitable participation and the social and ethical stakes of access to quantum technologies. Conceptually, this work considers how engagement with QCT might prompt learners to develop non-classical intuitions, reason under uncertainty, and approach computation, abstraction, and scientific problem-solving in fundamentally new ways. Looking forward, my K-12 research agenda focuses on two interrelated directions. First, inspired by the STEM novice/expert research literature (Bransford et al., 2000; Erickson et al., 2006) and Science-Technology- Studies investigations of laboratory life (e.g., Latour, 2005; Latour & Woolgar, 1986), I aim to ground a QCT framework in empirical studies of how quantum information scientists think and work, examining the concepts they use, the practices they enact, and the perspectives they bring to reasoning with quantum phenomena and technologies. Second, I plan to build on these insights by designing and iteratively refining K-12 learning environments that scaffold engagement with QCT, leveraging new representational infrastructures and collaborative practices that invite students into developmentally appropriate, quantum-adjacent forms of authentic inquiry. Such activities may include designing games, music, or visualizations that incorporate principles like amplitude amplification or probabilistic reasoning, enabling learners to make abstract quantum ideas tangible, expressive, and personally meaningful. While practical quantum computers remain on the horizon, progress toward them is uncertain and uneven (Eisert & Preskill, 2025). They are not expected to replace classical systems; instead, future systems will likely integrate both paradigms (Preskill, 2018). The field is already shaped by substantial financial investment to address the enormous hardware challenges. Yet an even greater obstacle lies in identifying problems for which quantum approaches provide decisive advantages, beyond those canonical examples discovered decades ago. How we approach quantum reasoning and learning today will influence not only who gets to participate in shaping this emerging field, but also what kinds of problems we even recognize as solvable. The learning sciences contribution, then, is not auxiliary to quantum computing’s development; rather, it is central to its realization. References Bandura, A. (2010). abstract: Youth bring diverse ways of knowing, communicating, and creating meaning to school, yet classrooms often privilege a narrow slice of these practices—treating difference as deficit and leaving many disabled, neurodivergent, queer, or trauma-impacted youth at the margins of participation. These exclusions affect belonging and access to civic, community, and disciplinary life. My research investigates how to design asset-oriented, participatory, and body- inclusive learning environments for young adolescents, where questions of identity and belonging are especially acute. Drawing on sociocultural and critical learning theories, participatory design-based research, and social models of ability and the body, I examine how multimodal repertoires can be recognized and leveraged as learning resources. This agenda advances three strands focused on designing multimodal learning environments that prioritize learner and educator dignity: (1) expanding conceptions of adolescent participation and literacy, (2) designing inclusive multimodal technologies, and (3) positioning youth as co-designers and co-theorists of their learning. Strand 1: Expanding conceptions of youth participation This strand is grounded in my experiences and those of current adolescents regarding secondary schools’ narrow conceptions of participation. Secondary schooling has privileged print and verbal literacies while devaluing embodied, affective, and multimodal avenues for meaning-making. These framings disproportionately exclude multiply-marginalized adolescents and reinforce deficit orientations and hegemonic norms. In my previous work, I employ a social model of disability to explore how schools ‘disable’ and ‘enable’ certain bodies, calling for researchers to shift responsibility for student performance away from the individual and onto the design of the system in which they operate (Vickery, 2023). In my dissertation, I introduce a five- dimensional inter-theoretical framework that conceptualizes the body as simultaneously thinking, feeling, observed, politicized, and autonomous. I also provide methodological guidance for conducting humanizing, dignity-affirming research with youth living in non-normative bodies (Vickery, 2025a) and employ critical resistance narrative analysis to examine how adolescents navigate and resist normative embodied expectations in schools (Vickery, 2025b). Moving forward, I expand normative notions of participation in youth civic education. I extend this work into civic and technical domains—motivated by the current sociopolitical climate. Such work demands multidisciplinary and multimodal competencies that cannot be siloed within individual subject areas. To these ends, I hope to support adolescents’ learning of media, data, digital, and scientific literacies through engagement with culturally relevant issues. Building from epistemic practices in science and engineering education (e.g., evidence evaluation, systems reasoning, modeling), I see opportunities to extend these into literacy/language education (rhetorical device usage, media & data literacy, interpretation of misinformation), social studies/history (complex sociopolitical systems, causal mechanisms), and computing education (engineering ethics, data privacy, transparency, ethical AI adoption). As political systems increasingly disenfranchise multiply-marginalized youth, these literacies become not abstract skills but conceptual and tangible tools for civic and social change. A society of care must acknowledge and design against these barriers. Strand 2: Designing inclusive multimodal technologies This strand is rooted in my experience as a UX designer and researcher, where access and inclusion were often addressed retroactively rather than prioritized from the start. In educational technologies, this reinforces deficit- oriented assumptions about learners whose practices do not align with normative expectations. This work centers on learners’ histories, needs, and desires in the edtech design process, ensuring technologies are proactive, responsive, and adaptive to learners’ needs. In my recent work (Vickery & Danish, 2025), I share my rapid design and iterative refinement of a mixed-reality embodied learning environment for a reverse-inclusion summer camp for youth with moderate-to- severe disabilities, aimed at identifying and addressing barriers to expression and participation. In my 2024 work o n the GEM-STEP project (Vickery et al., 2024; NSF Grants #1908632 & #1908791), I led my team in integrating trauma-informed pedagogies into the facilitation and evaluation of mixed-reality embodied activities (where students use motion-tracking technologies to collaboratively model complex scientific phenomena), demonstrating how centering comfort, choice, and agency can amplify students’ capacities for participation. In Zhou et al. (2025), we investigate how elementary learners' group-divergent embodied practices afford opportunities to learn about complex scientific phenomena. As a Visiting Research Scientist funded by the Engage AI Institute, I design and develop narrative-based, AI-scaffolded, gamified experiences for middle school students that are context-relevant and engage learners in critical thinking about food and environmental justice (Humburg et al., 2025). I build on my dual background in software engineering and UX design to critically engage with how ‘cutting-edge’ technologies such as AI, XR, and asynchronous learning tools are implemented at scale. My prior work has often relied on retrofitting inclusion into technologies – moving forward, I hope to (1) establish trusting partnerships with schools and communities, (2) conduct on-the-ground needs assessments, (3) co-design contextually grounded solutions with these needs prioritized at the onset, and (4) iteratively evaluate implementation. Access and inclusion are not endpoints but baselines; innovation must be defined by—and accountable to—those most impacted. Strand 3: Positioning youth as co-designers and co-theorists of their learning This strand addresses a tension across education and research alike – that too often, youth are positioned as passive users of and participants in designs they had no role in shaping. Thus, these designs (which here include pedagogies, activities, tools, communities, and theories) fail to provide the necessary scaffolding for youth to thrive and learn within them. My work takes an asset-oriented stance, treating adolescents’ perspectives and repertoires of practice as valuable resources for designing more sensitive, equitable, and emancipatory experiences for youth who would otherwise be forced to (at best) change themselves for the sake of compliance. In prior work, I’ve offered autoethnographic accounts of how my traditional notions of research-practice partnerships were challenged and remade in a collaboration with local paraprofessionals, special educators, and youth with disabilities (Vickery & Peabody, Under Review). In my dissertation Article 2 (Vickery, 2025c), I drew on Vygotskian notions of mediation and affect to understand what affective, sensory, and lived experiences are activated for youth with non-normative embodied experiences in the presence of various instructional design elements (i.e. various activity/task framings, technologies, proximity of embodiment, sensory demands, forms of movement, & participation structures). Further, Article 3 positions youth as co-theorists of a framework for dignity-affirming, body-inclusive embodied learning environments (Vickery, 2025d). This strand responds to a recurring theme across my projects—that “grown-ups just don’t get it.” This perceived ignorance strains opportunities for authentic educator–youth relationships and deepens youth distrust of educational systems. To address this, I aim to develop organized, protected “designer spaces”—digital and physical—for youth to co-design community-facing projects and professional development for educators and youth-service providers. Theoretically, this strand validates youth knowledge as legitimate civic and pedagogical insight; methodologically, it redefines youth’s role in research beyond that of participants to that of educators and researchers with the means to help adults “do better.” References Humburg, M., Danish, J., Kim, Y., Hmelo-Silver, C., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., Ryan, Z., Glazewski, K., & Lester, J. abstract: This research agenda examines how Black youth and teachers resist anti-Blackness through critical literacy, STEM learning, and counternarrative practices in urban schools. Grounded in Critical Race Theory and BlackCrit, the work positions race and anti-Blackness as central forces shaping educational experiences while centering Black joy, agency, and knowledge production. Using social design experiment, this research implements justice- oriented dual-credit courses and documents the pedagogical practices of Black teachers. Across iterative cycles of design and analysis, the studies aim to generate new theories of learning rooted in Black cultural wealth while materially improving educational opportunities, well- being, and academic pathways for Black youth.

abstract: My research has focused on supporting the development of computational and data visualization literacies through the design of constructionist tools and the analysis of students’ programming trajectories. During my PhD, I developed PlayData, a block-based programming environment that enables learners to construct data visualizations. To investigate how they engage with the tool, I created methods for capturing and analyzing process data from the environment, including a machine-learning approach for modeling programming trajectories and the use of Epistemic Network Analysis to characterize the connections among students’ Data Visualization Programming moves over time. These approaches reveal how learners navigate open-ended programming tasks and how computational and data-related practices can mutually reinforce one another. Building on this foundation, my research agenda seeks to advance our understanding of how learners develop data and computational literacies and to inform the design of learning environments that foster meaningful engagement with computing. Research background Throughout my research trajectory, I have worked on two inter-related topics: (1) the development of computational tools rooted in constructionist learning perspectives, and (2) unveiling students’ learning trajectories in open-ended tasks focused on programming and data visualization. My research is grounded in prior work on data visualization and computational literacies, both central to understanding and participating in the world today. Data visualization literacy refers to the ability to understand and create visual representations of data. It encompasses being able to read charts, but also to critique, modify, and design new representational forms for data - also referred to as meta-representational competencies (Azevedo, 2000; diSessa et al., 1991; diSessa & Sherin, 2000). Computational literacies (diSessa, 2001) refer to the idea of computing as a way of learning and participating in the world, related to “a set of practices situated in a sociocultural context which utilize external computational media to support cognition and communication” (Kafai & Proctor, 2022 p. 148). In my research, I am interested in understanding how these literacies can mutually support and enhance each other. Regarding the design of tools, I have developed PlayData, a block-based programming environment for constructing data visualizations, informed by a framework that draws upon taxonomies from the Information Visualization field (Fernandez, Freitas, et al., 2024). abstract: My research explores how to support K-12 science teachers’ professional development toward equitable and justice-centered teaching. Positioning teachers and students as those who decide what matters to them in their local contexts, I leverage design-based research to co-design, test, and co-refine pedagogical tools with practitioners. Through this process, I study teacher learning by drawing upon a professional identity development lens. In my most recent work, I study how to support middle school science teachers in customizing high-quality instructional materials and investigate how curriculum customization catalyzes teacher teaching. Looking forward, I hope to explore how community-based curriculum design and customization help science teachers create equitable learning experiences for their students.

citation: Victoria Delaney (2026). Teaching and Learning Mathematics with Artificial Intelligence. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.

abstract: Novel technologies influence the curriculum, pedagogy, and learning in schools. My research explores the impacts of AI-based tools in mathematics education, attending to how these tools influence teaching practice and how students learn to think mathematically. My scholarly goal is to support mathematics and stochastics teachers in developing innovative and robust pedagogies that uphold cognitive demand in learning even as tools that automate humanistic thinking become endemic to schooling. Overview My research centers curriculum, pedagogy, cognition, and AI/LLM automation in mathematics. I am interested in how AI-based tools mediate students’ mathematical thinking and teachers’ development of expert teaching practices to support student thinking. My interests stem from my experience as a high school math teacher of seven years, where I learned that mathematics tools and curricular resources played a major role in lesson orchestration and what my students ultimately learned (Brown, 2011). I conceptualize teachers and learners as agentic, creative, and curious drivers of learning rather than recipients of societal changes influenced by developments in AI automation. I further envision teachers as lesson designers and orchestrators who, when faced with the latest technological disruptions, can design effective instruction based in part on multi-faceted forms of teacher knowledge, including knowledge of how students’ interactions with tools impact their learning. To support teacher learning with insights about AI-tools’ impacts on students’ mathematical thinking, I have recently begun to research students’ AI-mediated problem solving processes (Delaney et al., 2025b). This work is in its second year and involves both well-defined and ill-defined mathematics tasks. I conduct video- recorded task-based interviews and observe the problem solving processes that surround students’ decisions, evaluations, AI trust, and epistemic judgments of mathematics output produced by chatbots. I have initiated this work in both clinical and classroom settings with algebra, calculus, statistics, data science, and numerical reasoning tasks. The findings from these studies inform my own teaching practice and AI adaptations, and with this knowledge, I continuously work to help other teachers develop design skills for an AI-integrated future. Establishing this program requires proficiency with the latest technologies. Under some conditions, technologies can create dynamic, inquiry-driven learning experiences that raise the cognitive demand required to solve nonroutine tasks, such as appraising the quality of a dataset or designing a facial recognition classifier (Delaney & Lee, 2024; Delaney & Selbach-Allen, 2025). In other circumstances, technology can derail students (or teachers) from their learning goals. My research program explores how teachers and students use novel technologies, the affordances and challenges that arise from their technology use, transformations on student and teacher thinking that are mediated by technology, and implications for learning. Theoretical frameworks I draw from theoretical frameworks that foreground the complexity of teaching and learning. I have several lines of research that build from different lineages of theory. When I conceptualize relationships between math curriculum and teaching, I draw from Brown’s illustration of teaching as adaptative, improvisational design work, akin to orchestrating a jazz concert (Brown, 2011). His pedagogical design capacity framework formed the basis of my dissertation, where I studied how statistics teachers adapted and enacted a machine learning curriculum (Delaney, 2025). When I conceptualize teachers’ mathematical professional learning with AI, I draw from teacher knowledge (Shulman, 1986) and teacher noticing (van Es & Sherin, 2008). What teachers attend to, interpret, and how they respond to students is directly related to their knowledge. Yet while teachers are still in the early stages of developing their knowledge, they may not yet have the multimodal forms of expertise to evaluate LLMs’ output and/or claims about students’ mathematical thinking. I am therefore developing theories about when and how mathematics teachers may prompt LLMs as cognitive supports, and what additional (human) supports they need to grow their pedagogical content knowledge and noticing abilities. From the student perspective, I have recently explored knowledge building with AI-based tools (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2020) and building expertise in mathematics with LLMs (Chi & Glaser 1985; Hiebert & Carpenter, 1992). Today’s LLMs can imitate humanistic mathematical reasoning, and can complete most of K- 12 mathematics tasks with minimal prompting specifications. It is therefore necessary for students and teachers to discern how to use LLMs to build knowledge and foster their own expertise rather than bypass the cognitive work involved in mathematics problem solving altogether. Recent work has begun to explore what human learning a nd epistemic agency may look like when LLMs are involved in mathematics tasks, proposing that students’ uses of LLMs are indicative of how much problem solving agency they retain versus offload to intelligent agents (Wu et al., 2025). I intend to extend this work and study how students’ LLM uses mediate their moment-by-moment thinking and what agency they preserve as they develop problem solving skills.

abstract: My research program examines how multimodal interactions with AI shape learning, teaching, and research. I investigate how learners build and express knowledge across verbal, embodied, and digital modalities, and how AI can meaningfully participate in these processes. My work spans three interconnected strands. First, I design AI-based systems that personalize learning by assessing cognitive processes through multimodal data triangulation. Second, I develop human–AI hybrid intelligence approaches for modeling complex, temporally layered learning processes, leveraging methods such as the interleaving approach, epistemic network analysis, and computer vision. Third, I design immersive XR learning environments in which AI agents scaffold embodied STEM learning through interactive multimodal guidance. Across these strands, my goal is to advance theoretically grounded and methodologically rigorous frameworks for understanding and designing human–AI partnerships that enhance multimodal sense-making and meaning-making in learning sciences and CSCL contexts.

title: Learning With and About AI: Building Capacity for Equitable Participation in an AI-Shaped Future
citation: Ibrahim Oluwajoba Adisa (2026). Learning With and About AI: Building Capacity for Equitable Participation in an AI-Shaped Future. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Adisa, I. O.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Design-Based Research (DBR); Co-Design & Participatory Design; Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: My research investigates how learners and educators understand, design with, and collaborate with AI systems, and how these sociotechnical interactions shape equity and participation. Using design-based research, participatory design, and qualitative and computational methods, I study AI education and disciplinary integration of AI in K–12 contexts. My work aims to design equitable learning environments, develop theoretical models of learner engagement with AI, and build cross-disciplinary approaches to teaching with and about AI. Theoretical and methodological foundations that inform my work My research sits at the intersection of the learning sciences, data science and artificial intelligence (AI) education. I am particularly interested in how educators and learners understand, design with, and collaborate with AI systems, and how these sociotechnical interactions shape equity and participation in society. In my work, I frame learning as a socially and materially mediated practice, drawing on sociocultural perspectives that conceptualize knowing as participation in activity systems rather than simply the acquisition of decontextualized concepts (Vygotsky, 1987; Wertsch, 1991). Within this view, AI tools and data infrastructures function as cultural tools (Cole, 1996; Saxe, 1991) that shape what becomes visible, what is considered authoritative, and whose perspectives are deemed valid as knowledge. I also draw on constructionist (Holbert et al., 2020; Kafai & Resnick, 1996; Papert & Harel, 1991) and design-oriented traditions that treat building computational artifacts as a powerful avenue for learning. When students build or critique AI applications and data stories, they are engaging in epistemic work that reveals their assumptions about what counts as evidence, how models relate to the world, and whose experiences are encoded in data (Vakil et al., 2022). I am particularly attentive to how young learners develop both conceptual and sociotechnical understandings of the affordances and limits of AI technologies, and how educators can support these competencies in ways that foster agency, critique, and creativity.

title: What Makes Actions Matter in Virtual Reality? Examining the Effects of Conceptual Congruence and Sensorimotor Engagement on Geometric Reasoning
citation: Doy Kim, Mitchell J. Nathan (2026). What Makes Actions Matter in Virtual Reality? Examining the Effects of Conceptual Congruence and Sensorimotor Engagement on Geometric Reasoning. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Kim, D. & Nathan, M. J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
conceptualisations_list: Cognitive Load Theory; Embodied Cognition & Gestures; Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA)
abstract: This dissertation examines how physical actions in virtual reality influence geometric reasoning through two complementary studies. Study 1 synthesizes nine experiments (N=774) using integrative data analysis to establish baseline mechanisms of embodied geometric reasoning. Study 2 employs a 2×2 experimental design (Target N=200), manipulating conceptual congruence and sensorimotor engagement of physical actions in VR environments to test how these action characteristics affect geometric reasoning. Participants engage with virtual geometric shapes via hand tracking, with multimodal data capturing verbal reasoning, gestures, and VR interactions. This work advances theoretical understanding of embodied learning and evidence-based design principles for immersive learning environments. Motivation and research questions Extended reality (XR) technologies hold promises for engaging and intuitive mathematics learning, yet significant research gaps remain. Current studies often lack a solid theoretical foundation, focus more on whether XR is effective rather than why, under-explore the unique potential of body movement, and devote less attention to mathematics learning than other STEM fields. This dissertation, guided by embodied learning theories, aims to understand how body movement influences mathematics learning in XR. It specifically investigates the effects of physical actions on geometric reasoning through two research questions: (RQ1) How do physical actions and gestures impact geometric reasoning in non-VR settings? and (RQ2) How do interactions with geometric shapes, with different levels of conceptual congruence and sensorimotor engagement, influence geometric reasoning in a VR environment? Theoretical background The intersection of embodied learning theory and XR technology motivates this investigation, with geometry providing an ideal context where physical actions naturally support mathematical reasoning. The Grounded and Embodied Mathematical Cognition (GEMC) framework (Nathan & Walkington, 2017) demonstrates that task- relevant actions that are designed to highlight key mathematical properties facilitate geometric reasoning. In an experiment, Walkington et al. (2022) found that the cognitive relevance of actions matters more than movement itself: task-relevant actions significantly improved reasoning, particularly when accompanied by explanatory gestures, while irrelevant actions showed no benefit despite similar motor engagement. Virtual reality presents unique opportunities and challenges for embodied mathematics learning. Johnson-Glenberg's (2018) embodied learning framework for VR identifies two critical dimensions that this dissertation directly examines: conceptual congruence, which is the alignment between body movement and learning content, and level of sensorimotor engagement, the degree of body involvement. This framework hypothesizes that higher congruency and greater body involvement lead to better learning outcomes. Skulmowski and Rey's (2018) taxonomy of immersive learning further suggests that physical manipulations that are more aligned and integrated with the task create stronger memory traces through the generation of motor codes, though they caution that excessive interactivity without conceptual relevance may increase extraneous cognitive load. These theoretical perspectives converge on key predictions for VR geometry learning: (1) The conceptual congruence of virtual manipulations should matter more than general interactivity, and (2) active manipulation should outperform passive observation, but only when actions align with mathematical content.

title: Co-designing and Implementing Reflective Tools and Routines with Children in Cooperative Inquiry
citation: Elana Blinder (2026). Co-designing and Implementing Reflective Tools and Routines with Children in Cooperative Inquiry. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Blinder, E.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Conceptual Change & Mental Models; Design-Based Research (DBR); Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: Reflection is a valuable component of learning and design processes, yet motivating children to reflect in informal learning contexts can be challenging. My dissertation examines this issue in a university-based Cooperative Inquiry co-design team where children and adults collaborate as equal design partners. Leveraging a DBR approach, I conduct two studies. The first investigates how children co-design reflection tools and processes that align with their values and mental models. The second explores how they use these systems over time and how this shapes their developing self-concept as designers. Through this research, I will contribute an adaptable infrastructure for authentically integrating reflection into child co-design, insights into how DBR can meaningfully include children as co-design stakeholders, and a deeper understanding of how children think, learn, and develop their identities through co-design. Motivation and background The learning sciences have long documented the importance of reflection for a range of learning processes (Dewey, 1986; Moon, 2004; Schön, 2017), with classrooms traditionally serving as important spaces for developing children’s reflective learning. Though less structured and systematic, informal learning contexts can also offer rich environments for reflection and identity development, but it can be challenging to motivate children to pause and reflect in the absence of standard classroom norms and enforcing structures (Gardner et al., 2006). As a doctoral student at the University of Maryland with an interest in how children learn and develop their identities through co-design, I have experienced some of these challenges firsthand through my participation in UMD KidsTeam—an intergenerational co-design team where university faculty and students collaborate with children between the ages of 7 and 12 to design new child-facing technologies. Guided by the Cooperative Inquiry (CI) co-design framework (Druin, 1999; Guha et al., 2013), which aims to involve children as equal collaborators with adults across the entire design cycle, our team employs a variety of established CI ‘design techniques’ aimed at making co-design accessible, engaging, equitable, and empowering for children. One such technique that has been mentioned in the literature, but which has received considerably less attention, is ‘journaling’, which has been described as a tool for “design partners to reflect on their experiences by writing or drawing” (Guha et al., 2013). Despite this directive, CI scholars and practitioners have observed child design partners’ lack of intrinsic motivation to engage in reflective journaling and have reported challenges in communicating the goals and value of this technique in a manner that resonates with children’s personal interests and values (Blinder et al., 2025). Issues with implementing reflective journaling in CI are further complicated by logistical challenges (e.g., time constraints, the need for adult writing support), ideological challenges (e.g., adult discomfort with the solitary school-like nature of written reflection) and adult and child design partners’ conflicting conceptualizations of journaling (with children prioritizing documenting and remembering design ideas and adults prioritizing process- and identity-oriented reflection) (Blinder et al., 2025). These challenges indicate an opportunity to explore additional approaches toward fostering purposeful sustained reflection within CI and other child co-design contexts. In my dissertation, I capitalize on this opportunity by engaging UMD KidsTeam children in contemplating the role reflection can play in their lives and identities as designers through co-designing new developmentally accessible and personally meaningful reflection tools and routines to be used in our co-design context. I then examine how children’s engagement with these reflection approaches and their self-perceptions as designers evolve over time.

title: Science at Work: Science and Learning among Coffee Roasters
citation: Bradley Davey (2026). Science at Work: Science and Learning among Coffee Roasters. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Davey, B.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: For more than a century science education has been guided by a promise that schools will prepare students to use science in everyday life. Yet little research has examined how science is actually used in everyday life. My dissertation takes this gap seriously by studying science and learning as they occur outside of school. Drawing from extended ethnographic fieldwork, I analyze how professionals in the coffee industry use, teach, and learn science in their daily work. Goals of the research My dissertation has three goals: First, to document how science is used outside of laboratories, which have long defined what counts as science. Second, to analyze how learning unfolds through the embodied, material, and social practices that constitute such work. Lastly, to translate those findings into principles for designing science learning environments. Taken together, these goals address a long-standing gap in science education and learning sciences research: the disconnect between the things learned in schools and those used in everyday life. My dissertation argues that reimagining science education-and education more generally-requires renewed attention to the diverse settings in which science and learning occur.

abstract: While AI literacy has gained increasing attention in education, existing frameworks often privilege technical competencies and workforce preparation, overlooking the developmental, relational, and ethical concerns central to early childhood education. Grounded in socio-constructionist theories and an ethics-of-care lens, my dissertation reimagines AI literacy as a care-centered, co-constructed practice within family ecologies. This three-paper dissertation includes: (1) a care-centered critical review of AI literacy frameworks that advances a new conceptualization of early AI literacies in ECE; (2) a techno-ethnographic study investigating parents’ beliefs, practices, and contexts shaping children’s AI learning at home; and (3) participatory co-design with parent–child dyads to iteratively develop a Family AI Literacy Starter Kit. These studies bridge conceptual, perceptual, and design perspectives by identifying gaps in current frameworks, mapping parental engagement, and co-creating developmentally appropriate resources toward justice-oriented early AI literacies in families.

title: Machine Epistemology as a Lens to AI Ethics Education: Forging Early Adolescents’ Epistemic Insights through Constructionist Learning in Upper Primary and Junior Schools
citation: Ziyan Lin, Yun Dai (2026). Machine Epistemology as a Lens to AI Ethics Education: Forging Early Adolescents’ Epistemic Insights through Constructionist Learning in Upper Primary and Junior Schools. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
authors_list: Lin, Z. & Dai, Y.

abstract: K-12 AI ethics education often focuses on topics including bias or privacy but rarely addresses how AI systems generate decisions in ways that create ethical challenges. This gap limits students’ ability to grasp the underlying sources of these ethical issues. Drawing on machine epistemology, which conceptualizes AI as an epistemic agent with distinctive ways of knowing and reasoning, this design-based research investigates how constructionist learning can foster students’ epistemic and ethical insights about AI. The study was implemented during a two-week summer program with thirty-four upper primary and junior secondary students in Hong Kong, integrating hands-on AI activities with guided reflection. Data from classroom interactions, interviews, and student artifacts were analyzed using inductive thematic coding and a deductive framework based on levels of epistemic insight. Preliminary findings show a developmental progression from surface-level descriptions of AI behavior toward emerging conceptual and critical reasoning, alongside persistent misconceptions about AI’s reasoning processes. Goals of the research This dissertation aims to design and investigate a constructionist learning environment that supports early adolescents’ epistemic insights about AI. Specifically, it seeks to: • Develop and refine a constructionist pedagogical framework that integrates hands-on AI activities with guided reflection to support students’ epistemic and ethical explorations of AI. • Examine how students’ epistemic insights develop as they engage with an AI ethics curriculum. • Identify recurring misconceptions and reasoning challenges that arise during the learning process.

title: Learning with the Seasons: Lands and Waters-Based Temporality in Learning and Mobility

abstract: The natural world is an active learning environment and provides a discursive context in which humans make meaning with one another. One way to experience collective meaning making in this learning environment is through group forest walks by walking, storying, and mapping lands and waters which Marin et al. (2020) refer to as ‘learning on-the-move.’ Water specifically creates a visual and sonic landscape where humans shift their attention and movement in response to it. This micro-ethnographic study uses video-based interaction analysis to understand the moment-to-moment unfolding of learning by paying attention to the semiotic layering of talk and movement while on forest walks during monsoon, winter, and summer seasons. The objective of this study is to explore how water shapes learning processes and learning environments as participants attend to relations with water through shifts in their movements, bodies, and conversation in relation to water while on forest walks. Broader implications of this study include using Indigenous ways of knowing to resist erasure and respond to increasing privatization of traditional lands and waters in the Global South. Project background Water mediates and organizes human relationships to the natural world, teaching us to attune to the sights, sounds, and seasonal rhythms of nature. It is also an active subject in organizing human attention and mobility, creating opportunities for humans to follow its sound in search for it, developing sensorimotor skills to swim, float, or traverse it. Knowing about water, however, is different from water-based ways of knowing. Indigenous communities have long relied on water-based ways of knowing about the world, developing kinship with waters and water life, and adapting to change as relationships to water change through the seasons. Alongside these longstanding practices are also issues of climate-change, environmental (in)justice, and increasing privatization of the lands and waters that Indigenous peoples call their home. I do not imagine the natural world to be a pristine, uncontested concept, but recognize that it is saturated with ongoing political struggle, colonial pasts and presents, and are sites where Indigenous futures are made. This dissertation examines how water-based ways of knowing organize human attention, coordination, and mobility, and contribute to resilient Indigenous communities, helping communities adapt to the seasonal rhythms of nature, especially in the context of ongoing dispossession of traditional lands and privatization of forests for industrialization. Participants of this ethnographic study are multigenerational members of the Siddi and Halakki communities, two Indigenous communities that share space in the Uttara Kannada region of southern India where public forests are becoming increasingly privatized and local paper and cardboard processing mills are polluting rivers and waterways. Amidst this violence to their environment, this study asks how learning with water can be a liberatory pedagogical tool, helping communities re-member relationships with lands and waters that are attempted to be dismembered by neoliberal development. Goals of the research Mapping, storying, and walking with land and water are longstanding Indigenous activities, shaping understandings of water through sensory experience and the production of land- and water-based artifacts. Forest walks are a focal activity in this study during which Siddi and Halakki members walk through land, interact with the sights and sounds of water, and build meaning by conversing with one another, centering land in their re- storying. These forest walks bring together multigenerational participation in cultural and linguistic practices, connecting the often-separated worlds of adults and children (Rogoff, 2003). title: Designing for Radical Imagination

abstract: This dissertation examines how learning environments for K–12 teachers can be designed to foster radical imagination through speculative activities. Data were collected across four mathematics teacher education courses at a large U.S. university, and a core group of participants joined a collective inquiry group to explore how to create elements of their imagined futures in their present classrooms. Anticipated findings include design principles that promote radical imagination among teachers, the forms of collectivity that emerged within the inquiry group, and the focal points of teachers’ radical reimaginings of mathematics teaching and schooling. Goals and background The aim of the present study is to design and analyze various learning environments where K-12 mathematics teachers engage with radical imagination and collective futuring. Radical imagination is the act of crafting new possibilities for the future that are not constrained by systemic structures or the status-quo of the “possible.” Neoliberal logics typically locate the source and the solution of (educational) problems in the individual, and thus leave unexamined the structures and collective action needed to challenge systemic forces (Barker & Scheele, 2016). Radical imagination by collectives of teachers, and fostering that imagination through teacher education, intentionally endeavors to rewrite the dominant power structures that maintain the status quo of capitalist, white supremacist, and settler-colonial systems in education. This is of particular importance in mathematics teacher education, as the discipline of mathematics is viewed as politically neutral (Harouni, 2015), which ultimately serves to maintain hierarchies of power and underscores patriarchal ways of knowing (Hesse-Biber et al., 2004). Specifically, this research explores: (1) How can learning environments in mathematics education be designed to contribute to the development of teacher radical imagination, and (2) How can collectives of teachers act on their imagined future in the present? Study design and methods This qualitative dissertation comprises of three studies with data collected in the mathematics teacher education department of a large U.S. university. Across the studies, 40 participants consented to include their data for analysis, and I collected over 170 speculative writing artifacts. title: Epistemic Engagement with Epistemically Elastic Content
citation: Renato Russo (2026). Epistemic Engagement with Epistemically Elastic Content. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.

abstract: This dissertation aims to investigate how non-experts engage with content that presents itself as apparently sound and structurally logical, but dismisses larger contextual factors that make it problematic. I describe how I take a mixed-methods approach to propose a study to be implemented with youth and young adults in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Additionally, I present preliminary findings that result from the first phase of this research project. Project motivation and research goals Imagine someone holds a controversial stance such as “raiding an official building is legitimate as long as this is done to rescue a country from collapse.” Although that may sound contradictory, to many people that is the result of a well-structured reasoning chain. In fact, research has sustained that a sort of public pedagogy is in place to “educate” people so that holding such views actually feels part of becoming a literate citizen (Greenhalgh et al., 2021). In my dissertation, I am interested in studying the intricacies of the processes through which people construct knowledge in ways that seem agentic but result in controversial stances. I am especially intrigued by how processes of agentic knowledge construction find support in ostensibly reasonable argumentation. As Duncan and Chinn (2025) put it, those epistemically fragile arguments are “structurally sound”—that is, they pass many criteria of formal analysis of argumentation, such as relevance, (superficial) sufficiency of evidence, and nature of justification—but are built on weak epistemic processes and on suboptimal evaluative criteria. From that motivation, I arrive at the core guiding inquiry for this dissertation: non-experts construct meaning from content that is epistemically elastic but enveloped in structurally sound arguments; how does that construction of meaning take place in highly social settings that are information-heavy, emotionally-charged, and technology-infused? Examples of those settings are instant messaging apps and social media, spaces that enable a distorted form of learning—that is, learning that is effective but used as a springboard to advance harmful political agendas (Russo et al., 2024). My motivation stated above drives the two components that I intend to address in the Doctoral Consortium: my Methods and Findings. I operationalize that motivation as one main research question and two subquestions that lay the groundwork to answer it: ● (RQ) How do non-experts engage epistemically with epistemically elastic content, that is, content that presents itself as apparently sound and structurally logical, but dismisses larger context that makes it problematic? ○ (RQ 1.1) What epistemic criteria and processes do non-experts rely on as they construct meaning from that type of content? ○ (RQ 1.2) How do pieces of intuitive knowledge and naturalized axioms (Philip, 2011) support those non-experts’ understanding of that content, scaffolding further knowledge construction? In formulating these questions, I refer mainly to literature on epistemic cognition (Sandoval, 2017), particularly the AIR framework proposed by Chinn et al., (Chinn et al., 2020); supplementarily, I refer to literature related to Knowledge-in-pieces (KiP) by diSessa and colleagues (diSessa et al., 2015; Philip, 2011) to investigate how epistemic processes operate on intuitive knowledge and assumptions about the social world.

Co-created by students and faculties, it gathers drawings, collages, photographs, craft, and mixed-media reflections from twenty-eight students. We conceptualize that the works collected here are not meant as representations or products of learning, but as living artifacts of inquiry. The pieces trace climate emotions, interdependence, inequities, and the historical systems shaping climate vulnerability. Each page is a part of a larger conversation: How can we stay with climate grief and still imagine otherwise? How might making art help us think with the world rather than about it? We see this zine as an archive of art that can mediate learning about climate justice, and how learning becomes a practice of attention, relation, and responsibility. abstract: T he Look Again Quilt For millennia, humans used pictures to tell stories. Narrative quilts are a traditional form of pictorial storytelling, dating back centuries. The Look Again quilt is a modern example of a narrative quilt used for science communication and engagement. Since blankets are familiar and often evoke positive feelings, quilting as a science communication media may help avoid top-down cognitive processing that results in public disengagement with science. The Look Again quilt features two realistic eyes, one open and the other closed at the top of the quilt, above an array of blocks, each representing different aspect of biology. For example, including blocks with wavy stitching and layered fabrics that represent the ecosystem at a beach.
