abstract: Impactful learning technology innovation doesn’t happen in isolation; it grows through relationships, among researchers, educators, students, technologists, designers, and institutional leaders. While some collaborations are carefully structured, others take root more organically, evolving to meet shifting needs and opportunities. In this keynote, Dr. Alyssa Wise explores how purposeful partnerships drive innovation across the technological, social, conceptual, and practical dimensions of learning, tracing three kinds of partnerships that have unfolded over the past decade in her work. Flexible Coupling articulates how institutional partnerships can leverage complementary strengths without becoming over-structured. In a longstanding collaboration with a university learning analytics service unit, in vivo studies of instructors’ analytics use informed both theoretical models of sense-making and applied tool design. Constructive Responsiveness describes how partnerships with educators can evolve around a shared object of inquiry when goals are not yet fully defined. In work with dental educators implementing an online reflection tool, the collaboration advanced from examinations of reflection quality to generate domain-specific insights into failure attribution and professional identity formation. Finally, Generative Pluralism characterizes interdisciplinary partnerships among researchers or co-designers where the goal is not convergence but conceptual creation. These collaborations embraced multiplicity, surfacing productive tensions, methodological bridges, and new vocabularies for imagining learning technologies. Together, these patterns illustrate partnerships as adaptable forms of collaboration, each suited to different problems, people, and purposes. This talk highlights how designing, studying, and sustaining learning with the support of technology can be supported by purposeful partnerships that bridge disciplines, organizations, and stakeholder perspectives. Bio: Dr. Alyssa Wise is Professor of Technology and Education at Vanderbilt University’s Peabody College, with a courtesy appointment in Computer Science in the College of Connected Computing. She also serves as Director of the LIVE Learning Innovation Incubator, Vanderbilt’s interdisciplinary hub for impactful learning technology innovation. Her research productively integrates tools of computational data science, theories of learning sciences and collaborative learning, and practices of human-centered design to build and study analytic and artificial intelligence systems that promote powerful learning for individuals situated in social context. She also conducts mixed-method investigations into how educational practices are being reshaped by new sources of data and the growing availability of new generative artificial intelligence capabilities. title: Designing AI to Scaffold Learners’ Cognitive Engagement in Generative Learning
citation: Zhenyao Cai, Shiyao Wei, Shayan Doroudi (2026). Designing AI to Scaffold Learners’ Cognitive Engagement in Generative Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Cai, Z., Wei, S., & Doroudi, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Recent advances in AI have raised concerns about students’ overreliance on automated systems that may complete learning tasks without requiring meaningful cognitive effort and engagement. This paper explores how AI can be designed to scaffold and sustain cognitive engagement in generative learning activities. Drawing on generative learning theory and scaffolding, we present a conceptual account of how AI can guide learners through generative processes such as selecting, organizing, and integrating information, while gradually fading support as competence develops. We illustrate this through the design of an AI -assisted system that helps children (aged 8–13) create educational science videos --- a task that embodies generative learning but poses cognitive challenges for young learners. Our work sheds light on how to integrate scaffolding to foster but not replace meaningful engagement with AI in generative learning.

abstract: Introductory statistics courses are challenging in part because core concepts such as statistical models are highly abstract. Prior work shows that visual representations and embodied pedagogies can each support abstract learning, yet little is known about how they interact. In this study, 112 undergraduates were randomly assigned to pre -instruction with or without visualizations, followed by an embodied intervention (gesture or drawing). Students who received visual pre-instruction outperformed those without visual support on an immediate posttest (Posttest 1). However, pre -instruction type did not directly predict later performance (Posttest 2), nor did it moderate the effectiveness of gesture versus drawing. Exploratory analyses revealed a moderated mediation: the relationship between Posttest 1 and Posttest 2 performance varied by pre -instruction type and students’ reported use of visual information from the embodied intervention. These findings underscore the importance of representational coherency across learning phases, offering new insights for designing instructional sequences in statistics education .

abstract: As AI enters computer science (CS) education, novices need early opportunities to strengthen code understanding. This work responds to this need by investigating pairing mixed- up code puzzles (Parsons puzzles) with self -explanation (SE) prompts. Drawing on learning sciences work, we designed two SE prompts: Select, where students engage in SE by choosing correct options, and Fill, where they engage in SE by typing answers. In an in- depth within- subjects study (N=10), all novices valued SE prompts for understanding code after solving puzzles. Select was strongly preferred to Fill for its efficiency and scaffolding. Fill was removed due to frustration from likely non-learning mental effort. A between-subjects study (N=110) in an intro-level CS classroom compared practice with puzzles -only to puzzles plus Select SEs. The group solving puzzles with Select showed significantly greater pre -to-posttest learning gains with similar perceived in-practice mental effort.

abstract: Rosebery et al. (2016) conceptualized interpretive power as (a) teachers’ attunement to students’ sensemaking as generative for science learning and (b) teachers’ pedagogical practices that build on students’ ideas and experiences. In our professional development (PD) work, we have found that ideologies of whiteness constrain interpretive power. Here, we unpack the role of whiteness in PD discussions with in- service elementary science teachers. We use interaction analysis (IA) to trace the influence of whiteness on discourse, focusing on teachers’ construction of science and students. Following Gholson and Ma (under review), we question the IA premise that ideologies must be named by participants to be considered relevant. To make these ideologies visible, we consider not only the ways that participants carry substrate forward, but also the ways that they omit substrate in subsequent turns. Objectives and purpose Rosebery et al. (2016) conceptualized interpretive power as (a) teachers’ attunement to students’ sensemaking repertoires as generative for science learning and (b) teachers’ pedagogical practices that build on students’ ideas and experiences. Rosebery et al. argued that developing interpretive power supports teachers to see contributions from students of color as equally generative as those of their white peers. In the past decade, researchers have worked to develop teachers’ interpretive power in service of equitable STEM learning (e.g., Kayumova & Dou, 2022; Louie et al., 2025; Miller et al., 2018; Warren et al., 2020). However, in our professional development (PD) work with in-service elementary science teachers (Daniel et al. , 2023; Pierson et al., 2024), we have found that ideologies of whiteness, when not explicitly addressed in PD, constrain interpretive power. Whiteness is a socially constructed ideology that produces privilege and dominance for those racialized by society as white (i.e., White privilege), while producing oppression and marginalization for those society has marked as the racialized “Other” (Battey & Leyv a, 2016; Kolluri & Tichavakunda, 2023). Whiteness shapes teachers’ constructions of science (Mensah & Jackson, 2018) and students (Ma et al., 2025). Specifically, Western Modern Science as a discipline is historically based in “Eurocentric, positivist teachings of science that reify a White, male ownership of science” (Mensah & Jackson, p. 9). Following from this perspective, certain kinds of students are seen as “smart” vs. “disruptive” based on their alignment with white norms (e.g., Gholson & M a, under review). These ideological lenses can constrain teachers’ development of interpretive power by preventing them from recognizing and valuing the contributions of racialized students and their communities. We thus conjecture that explicit attention to whiteness is necessary for teachers’ development of interpretive power. We explore this conjecture using data from a PD session with in- service elementary science teachers, facilitated by Pierson . We use interaction analysis (IA) to trace the influence of whiteness on participants’ discourse. Following Gholson and Ma (under review), we question the IA premise that ideologies must be named by participants to be considered relevant. To make these ideologies of whiteness visible, we consider how participants carry substrate forward and how they omit substrate in subsequent turns. Our analysis reveals how ideas needed for interpretive power (e.g., valuing heterogeneity in science) were omitted and transformed by teachers, reinscribing ideologies of whiteness. Literature review An excerpt from Warren et al. (2020) was foundational to the interaction we analyze. The excerpt describes a science classroom interaction that occurred between Jonathan (an African American boy), his teacher (Ms. V), and his classmates categorizing the su n as living or nonliving. Jonathan wondered aloud how a nonliving sun could produce a living flower. Ms. V perceived this as incorrect and characterized Jonathan’s contribution as “problematic.” Later, she began to recognize the ecological way that Jonathan saw the sun as a life- giving force and the ways that students might encounter words like “living” in relation to the sun (e.g., having a “life cycle” like other stars). We use this example to unpack “science as white property”: an ideology central to our analysis. Science as white property At the core of Jonathan’s experience was the interaction of “structures of race, culture, and language based in whiteness as privilege” (Warren & Rosebery, 2011, p. 98). Whiteness as an ideology maintains racial dominance 23 through structural mechanisms of property and ownership. Legal scholar Cheryl Harris (1993) first articulated this reality by naming whiteness as a form of property. The relationship between whiteness and property was embedded in U.S. society, as humans who were racialized as Black were purchased, sold, and abused as literal property, and Indigenous communities were violently removed from land claimed as the property of white settlers (Kendi, 2016). Whiteness as property has been reified through legal action throughout the nation’s history (Harris, 1993). Harris conceptualized property broadly, encompassing material (e.g., land, financial capital) and immaterial (e.g., social capital, knowledge, cultural) resources. Those who possess whiteness as property ar e afforded rights to use, enjoy, dispose of, and exclude others from these resources. Mensah and Jackson (2018) built on Harris’ (1993) work, identifying science as a specific form of white property historically based in Eurocentric, positivist teachings. Many scholars have identified how science as a discipline is framed as objective, antiseptic, and fixed; an image that emerged in service of settler -colonial and empire-building projects (e.g., Kimmerer, 2013; Mignolo, 2011). Scientific knowledge from non-white, non-male communities is generally rejected as unscientific (e.g., Bang et al., 2012; Rae, 2025; Sengupta-Irving et al., 2021). Because science as white property dictates “what science looks like, who engages in science, and what science is for” (Mensah & Jackson, 2018, p. 9), scientific culture privileges those who hold dominant identities. Individuals’ rights to access and enjoy science decrease as they belong to multiple marginalized communities. Thus, white women have more right s to enjoy science than young Black girls. Young people are generally not considered capable of science (Daniel et al., 2023), and students from marginalized communities with non-dominant cultural knowledge and practices are most often excluded. Interpretive power and whiteness Disrupting whiteness in science is critically important in teacher professional learning. A number of teacher educators have worked toward this end (e.g., Le & Matias, 2019; Shah & Coles, 2020; Sleeter, 2016; Yoon, 2012). For instance, Le and Matias (2019) demonstrated how ideologies of whiteness create seemingly benign, normative practices in science education. When teachers fail to interrogate these norms, they may contribute to exclusionary experiences for marginalized students. By contrast, Shah and Col es (2020) offered a framework of “racial noticing” to support preservice teachers to recognize and respond to race during instruction. In our PD, we hoped that foregrounding interpretive power (Rosebery et al., 2016) would implicitly challenge ideologies of whiteness such as science as white property. The tenets of interpretive power (all students bring generative resources for science learning), stand in contrast to a Eurocentric image of science as authoritative, fixed, and objective. Yet our own attempts to value ontoepistemic heterogeneity did not adequately disrupt racialized norms ( Daniel et al., 2023; Pierson et al., 2024). These challenges serve as the foundation for our research question: What role do ideologies of whiteness play in constructions of science and science learning? Through our analysis, we aim to develop analytic methods that allow us to trace the way whiteness works in interaction to constrain the development of interpretive power, so that we and other teacher educators can design and evaluate approaches to more explicitly and effectively challenge pernicious ideologies of whiteness.

title: Elementary Students’ Developing Understanding of Fractions: Insights from Students’ Gestures
citation: Shereen Oca Beilstein, Tiffany Reyes-Denis, Michelle Perry (2026). Elementary Students’ Developing Understanding of Fractions: Insights from Students’ Gestures. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Beilstein, S. O., Reyes-Denis, T., & Perry, M.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Despite being a foundational topic in elementary school mathematics, fractions persistently challenge students. The purpose of this study was to examine how elementary school students’ gestures convey the varied ways they conceive of fractions, beyond what could be interpreted from their speech alone. Interviews with 21 3 rd- to 5th-grade students indicated that most students described fractions as the division of a whole object into equal parts (i.e., the area model), in both their speech and gestures. But, in many cases, students’ gestures provided additional, necessary context from which to interpret their spoken explanations —providing insight into the grounding metaphors that framed their abstract thinking about fr actions. Also, although students expressed understanding of fraction notation, this was done either in isolation or in relation to the area model. Findings point to enriching instruction that helps students bridge fraction notation to different and multiple models.

title: When Dialogic and Thinking Moves Intersect: An Exploratory Study of Thinking- Routine-Guided Discussions in an EFL Classroom
citation: Jou-Yin Chen (2026). When Dialogic and Thinking Moves Intersect: An Exploratory Study of Thinking- Routine-Guided Discussions in an EFL Classroom. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Chen, J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study reports on an English movie discussion course, where Visible Thinking routines were used to guide students’ analysis of films. Thinking routines were aligned with specific thinking moves to scaffold thinking. As a qualitative exploratory study, it investigates how these routines mediated student interaction and contributed to a thinking culture. Data included two focal groups’ discussions and student reflections, analyzed through dialogic and thinking move coding and thematic analysis. Findings show that routines improved dialogic interaction and strengthened the move of considering viewpoints, but deeper analysis occurred only when moves such as expressing and reasoning co-occurred with explaining/interpreting and supporting with evidence. Thematic analysis identified four elements of a thinking culture: teacher guidance, peer support, structured tasks, and confidence in expression. These findings provide fine-grained evidence of how dialogic and thinking moves intersect and how a thinking culture can benefit learning in EFL classrooms.

title: A three-prong framework for designing theory-based math games
citation: Robin Sharma, Adam K. Dubé (2026). A three-prong framework for designing theory-based math games. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: A common critique of ineffective learning games is their lack of theory-based design and integration of instructional features. While a few game-design frameworks have been proposed, they tend to take a limited approach. Some do not consider emotional aspects of games; others do not consider links between gameplay and learning. An approach that brings together the multiple aspects of educational game design is needed . This is important to build domain-specific thinking, build connections between gameplay and learning, and tap into the emotional and motivational aspects of games. This article describes an iterative approach to math game design by bringing together decades of previous research. It outlines how this approach is applied to create a game for secondary mathematics, specifically geometry. Progression of puzzles based on mathematical complexity, connections between learning objectives and gameplay, and inclusion of emotional elements are described. The challenges, opportunities, and outcomes of the approach are discussed. Gaps in math game design Interactive digital experiences like games can be useful tools for mathematics education as they can transform abstract mathematical concepts into concrete experiences (Potega vel Żabik et al., 2024). For example, games can simulate the abstract nature of mathematical concepts and provide low -stake and real -time interactive environments for mathematical problem solving (Hui & Mahmud, 2023; Klopfer & Thompson, 2020; Sharma et al., 2022). However, it is difficult to design games that incorporate such elements in a meaningful way to create an enjoyable and effective learning experience for adolescents (Vandercruysse et al., 2016). Despite their potential as engaging learning tools, research has shown that math games and interactive experiences have lacked theoretical foundations (Sharma & Dubé, 2024). More generally, researchers have regularly identified the need for theory -based development of educational games to make them more effective in achieving their intended learning goals (Dubé & Dubé, 2021; Vandercruysse et al., 2016). However, the challenge is to integrate learning into games while not taking away the “fun” (Garris et al. , 2002). From the learning perspective, ineffective educational games are criticized for lack of guiding theories and instructional features (Plass et al., 2015). From the fun perspective, ineffective games are criticized for their bad, unintuitive design, and a mismatch between learning goals and gameplay (Plass et al., 2015). It is important to bridge these gaps by grounding the design of math games in discipline and gameplay related theoretical frameworks. In their systematic review, Ke (2016) found that game-based learning (GBL) research has predominantly focused on evaluating the effectiveness of digital games. However, researchers should also elaborate and provide descriptions of theoretical foundations, design decisions, and rationales for their choice of game -interactions (Kiili & Lainema, 2008). In this article, we describe three dimensions to educational game design based on relevant theoretical frameworks. We present a three-prong approach to math game design. It builds on previous frameworks and suggests an iterative process of math game design that considers 1) mathematics instruction and thinking, 2) gameplay interactions tied with learning, and 3) the emotional aspects of games tied with learning. We describe this approach with an illustrative example of our process of creating GeometryBOX, a geometry game for adolescents. Three aspects of educational game design Discipline-specific theory Many researchers have called for educational games to be informed by learning theories guiding their designs (Plass et al., 2020). This can refer to a discipline-agnostic theory of learning (e.g., Constructivism). While such a theory can inform the game type and mode of learning, it does not address disciplinary needs. I t does not inform how the progression and order of in -game tasks align with the development of mathematical thinking. This requires a discipline-specific theory. A discipline -specific theory should be chosen to serve two purposes. First, it guides the in-game instruction and progression based on the requirements and the “ways of thinking” associated with the discipline (Honey & Hilton, 2011; Turkay et al., 2014). This can ensure that the game enables thinking processes in the player that are aligned with the requirements of the discipline (Mayer, 2020). Second, it informs all the subject matter -related aspects of the game, like operationalizing learning objectives for the in- game 61 problems. A discipline -specific theory informs how the in- game problems and gameplay intend to achieve the target learning outcomes (Plass et al., 2020). Gameplay-specific theory As opposed to the discipline specific theory that focusses on progression of in- game problems in line with the thinking process of the discipline, a gameplay specific theory informs the overall design of the game environment and specific player actions tied with the learning objectives. In their systematic review, Ke (2016) identified five themes and ways for integrating learning and playing in digital games. These provide a starting point for how learning goals could be mapped to the interactions offered by the game environment. The five themes are listed in Table 3 later in this article. However, it must be noted that these themes are not mutually exclusive, and one game can integrate learning opportunities in more than one way. The themes identified by Ke (2016) inform broad areas and approaches for integrating learning in games. In addition, it is also important to identify how learning content can be intrinsically embedded into the gameplay and mapped to player’s actions. This is needed to inform how all types of in-game player actions are associated with learning processes and to avoid unnecessary gameplay that can cause distractions and enhance extraneous load which can be detrimental to learning (Mayer & Moreno, 2003). Here, the Learning Mechanic – Game Mechanic (LM-GM) Framework (Arnab et al., 2015) can be a useful tool. It can be used to build a map of learning elements in a serious game with its mechanical/gameplay elements. Here, learning mechanics refers to the objectives, activities, and thinking processes focused on the context of learning. Game mechanics refers to the type of gameplay, game elements, and objects available to the player. This framework provides a starting point for designers to consider these mechanics and identify how gameplay and pedagogy are interrelated in their game. Educational game designers should carefully consider how each interaction a player makes in the game (game mechanic) is associated with the intended learning objective and processes (learning mechanic). This is useful to describe how the actions taken by the players in the games activate the thinking processes required for learning. Emotional design principles Games have the capability to induce achievement emotions that can support learning. Loderer and colleagues (2020) identified five emotional design principles to promote experiences and emotions that aid learning. Carefully considering emotional design principles to inform educational game design can help balance the “fun” and learning in games. Additionally, they can induce emotions conducive to learning like enjoyment and alleviation of boredom. Finally, emotional design principles in games can alleviate t he association of negative emotions, negative math attitudes, and math anxiety in children (Wen & Dubé, 2022; Young et al., 2012). The five principles are visual aesthetic design, musical score, game mechanics, narrative, and incentive system. Visual aesthetic design refers to the in -game visual elements that create engaging and immersive experiences. Musical scores in educational games refer to background tunes, sound effects, and audio feedback to enhance players’ experiences and learning. Game mechanics refer to the interactions and rules that drive the gameplay. Narrative refers to storylines and contextual problem solving that enhance engagement. Finally, the incentive system refers to the rewards and penalties to induce motivation during gameplay. Educational game designers should consider these five aspects at all stages of game development. When thoughtfully applied to its design, emotional design principles can make the game “fun” and “appealing” to the players while keeping intact the intended learning objectives (Mayer & Estrella, 2014). We propose an approach based on the three theoretical aspects of educational game design . Critically, all three should consistently inform design decisions across all aspects of the game (Figure 1). They are applied iteratively and inform the design process at all stages, which can include level design, characters, and in-game problems. Figure 1 Three-Prong Approach to Theory-Based Educational Game Design 62 GeometryBOX – a theory-based game for geometry “GeometryBOX” is designed for students in secondary grades, the game targets the topic of quadrilaterals. It specifically focusses on the following general learning outcomes: (a) to understand the relationships between properties of special quadrilaterals, and (b) to classify special quadrilaterals based on their properties. The game begins with the players assuming the role of a robot that is tasked to control a spacecraft while navigating outer space to collect as many stars as possible. The number of stars collected represents the overall game- score of the players. As they fly, they run out of resources which takes them to the internals of the ship. Here, they solve geometrical puzzles of increasing complexity to rebuild resources and return to the navigation gameplay. Players switch between these two primary types of gameplays as they increase their score (stars). The game finishes after they solve all geometrical puzzles. Discipline-specific theory in GeometryBOX As described previously, we aimed to identify a discipline -specific theoretical framework aligned with the intended learning objectives (geometry learning) and the target audience (adolescents). Additionally, it should inform the progression of in -game pro blems and enable the thinking processes needed to achieve learning objectives. To address these aspects, we used the Van Hiele Model (VHM) of geometric thinking (Hiele, 1999) as the guiding discipline specific theory for our game. It is a hierarchical framework establishing the existence of five different levels of geometric thinking of increasing complexity (Arnal -Bailera & Manero, 2024) . The increasing complexity of levels informed the increasing complexity of puzzles and specifically informed the “level design” of the game. Second, Hiele (1999) outlined the focus of the VHM on visual and non- verbal thinking and exploration which make it appropriate to inform the design of play- and game-based instruction. Finally, VHM is a topic-agnostic theoretical model. GeometryBOX targeted “classification of quadrilaterals”, a sub-topic in plane- geometry, generally included in middle and secondary geometry curriculum (Vízek et al., 2025) . The five levels of VHM are (a) visualization – referring to visual perception and recognition of mathematical objects; (b) analysis – referring to the ability to recognize and name properties of geometrical figures, (c) abstraction – referring to identification of properties and relationships between geometrical figures, (d) formal ded uction – referring to deduction of geometric proofs and understanding hierarchical nature of mathematical properties, and (e) rigor – referring to identification, comparison, and interrelation of different geometrical systems. VHM has previously been used to inform the design of several curricular and instructional materials for geometry (Senk et al., 2022). Table 2 shows how the definition of the VHM levels were operationalized for this topic (Crowley, 1987). Such operationalization is necessary to map how a theoretical model is applied to define the context of gameplay in association with the intended learn ing objectives. It breaks down the overarching aspects of the theoretical framework (VHM levels in this case) in relation to the target topic within the discipline. Table 2 VHM Levels Operationalized in GeometryBOX Van Hiele Level Key learning outcomes (Crowley, 1987) Learning outcomes operationalized for “classification of quadrilaterals” New game mechanics (1) Visualization Recognize and compare geometrical shapes. Compare, classify, and name geometrical shapes. Drag and drop geometrical shapes into respective bins. (20 puzzles) (2) Analysis Discern properties of geometrical figures. Progressively discover key differences between quadrilaterals of different types based on their properties. Drag and drop special quadrilaterals into respective bins. (27 puzzles) (3) Abstraction Establish interrelationship of properties between geometrical figures. Interrelate properties and relationships among different quadrilaterals. Target labels: see the label of the target bin (e.g., rectangles) to drag and drop shapes into. (20 puzzles) (4) Formal Deduction Deduce relationships and new properties based on axioms. Deduce properties of different quadrilaterals based on their diagonals. Slicing: “slice” a quadrilateral along one of its diagonals to get two triangles. (20 puzzles) 63 (5) Rigor Compare and operate within different geometrical systems. Make new shapes based on given conditions. Slicing: “slice” a quadrilateral along its altitudes to get two triangles and a rectangle; Combining shapes: certain triangles can be combined to obtain quadrilaterals. (20 puzzles) Gameplay specific theory in GeometryBOX Themes identified by Ke (2016) provide educational game designers with a tool to define how learning is integrated in the different aspects of the game. The example of GeometryBOX demonstrates integration of learning via all five themes in the context of mathematics. Table 3 describes how learning was integrated into the game based on Ke’s (2016) framework. Framing the in- game learning experiences in association with the five themes provides a clearer picture of how disciplinary learning objectives are integrated within the gameplay (See Figure 2 later in this article). Educational game designers should clearly identify how learning is integrated within their games. The themes identified here also inform the LM-GM map of the game. Table 3 Integrating Learning in GeometryBOX based on Ke (2016) Theme Description Integration in GeometryBOX game Learning as knowledge activation and acquisition Games with problem solving instances as contexts for retrieving previous knowledge and acquiring new knowledge. The game builds players’ knowledge of quadrilaterals, their properties, types, and relationship among properties through puzzles of increasing complexity. Each set of puzzles requires the players to retrieve knowledge acquired from the previous set. Learning via representation, simulation, or contextualization Game objects and rules embody the focus concepts and learning objectives. The game objects are tied to the narrative theme. The puzzles are contextualized in an overall narrative theme. The game objects (e.g., jewels) represent the mathematical objects (e.g., quadrilaterals) targeting the intended learning objectives. Learning via game mechanics and game world Game interactions and mechanics intrinsically represent the learning content. The game mechanics and interactions are centrally associated with the intended learning objectives. In- game puzzles require the players to sort and categorize geometrical shapes, this primary game mechanic mapped to the central learning objective: “classification of quadrilaterals”. Reflective and iterative learning moments in gameplay Learning happens via strategizing and reflective use of knowledge. Specific learning moments are repeated in gameplay. At least 20 puzzles are mapped to each learning outcome mapped to a Van Hiele Level (Table 2) providing iterative learning moments. Higher levels require strategizing, more complex thinking, and use of previous knowledge to solve puzzles. In-game learning supports Game provides cues, feedback, clear instructions, and in-game prompts. The game provides audio and textual feedback based on the players’ moves. It provides explicit hints and definitions associated with the learning objectives. An LM-GM map based on the framework by Arnab and colleagues (2015) is one of the most important parts of the educational game design process. It informs and presents a clear map of player interactions (game mechanics) and how they translate to learning rel ated actions (learning mechanics). All educational games should aim to create and describe the LM- GM map of their games. Table 4 shows the LM -GM map for GeometryBOX (also see Figure 2 later in this article). An LM-GM map lists the corresponding learning and game mechanics, the ways in which they are integrated, and “how” they are integrated. This framework provides a summary to educators and administrators and helps them make decisions about the suitability of the game for their use. When building the LM-GM map of the game, implementation and usage of learning mechanics and game mechanics is described in the context of game features. The exercise of creating an LM -GM map of the game is essential to reflect how different interactions and gameplay are linked to learning. Additionally, it is important to clearly communicate to users and other researchers the reasoning for their design decisions. 64 Table 4 LM-GM Map of GeometryBOX Game mechanic Learning mechanic Implementation via Usage Cut-scenes Story Motivation Feedback Narrative Game environment Levels 1) The overall guiding context and story of the game refer to the narrative theme. 2) The game has additional, story-related gameplay levels and cut- scenes beyond the geometrical puzzles that refer to the narrative theme. 3) Game scores (stars), health bars (shield and energy), and other visual elements (backdrop of game puzzles) also refer to the narrative theme. 4) The game provides textual and audio feedback based on the player actions associated with math learning and the narrative theme. Strategy/Planning Resource management Explore Discover Identify Hypothesize Plan Feedback In-game health bars Puzzles Levels 1) Puzzle solving encourages exploration and discovery by not giving any learning-outcome related instruction. 2) Exploration and discovery are encouraged by not penalizing initial incorrect moves. 3) Players hypothesize an approach to puzzle solving and plan their next move based on game feedback. 4) Complexity of puzzles and learning outcomes follows a hierarchical system where new knowledge is built on the previous. 5) In-game health bars represent the two types of resources available to the players. 6) Players need to identify the best strategy that optimizes resource usage when solving in-game puzzles. Rewards/Penalties Game turns Incentive Repetition In-game health bars Drag and drop action 1) Game turns refer to the action of dragging and dropping geometrical shapes into correct bins and locations. 2) Gameplay provides an incentive for taking the minimum number of turns when players solve a puzzle. 3) Incorrect moves beyond a threshold are penalized, correct moves are rewarded, and successful puzzle solving is rewarded. This is reflected by changes in available resources represented as health-bars. Feedback Motivation Feedback Game task Textual and visual prompts 1) Encouraging and motivational textual feedback prompts based on players’ in-game action (e.g., after a correct/incorrect move). 2) Learning outcome related textual feedback after successful completion of the game-task, i.e. solving a puzzle. Levels Analyze Simulation Repetition Reflection Puzzles Drag and drop action 1) Puzzles with game objects that simulate properties of geometrical objects. Shapes can be dragged-and-dropped on interactive elements to simulate their geometrical properties. 2) Correctly solving a puzzle requires analysis of shapes and application of knowledge. 3) Subsequent puzzles build on learning outcomes of previous puzzles. 4) Similar types of puzzles, referring to similar learning outcomes associated with VHM levels, are repeated several times. 5) Players can retry until the correct solution is found. However, too many incorrect moves deplete health and reduce progress encouraging reflection. Emotional design principles in GeometryBOX 65 Visual aesthetic design We used bright, warm, and contrasting colors in the visual design of the game. All the geometrical figures, that were the primary objects of gameplay, were bright purple in color to create a visually appealing interface (Wen & Dubé, 2023). The overall theme of “outer space” was consistently depicted through all the game objects. For example, the cursor was styled as a “crosshair”. Players solved geometrical puzzles to fix batteries and repair their ship. On the “progress map” screen of the game, the batteries were represented as “lightbulbs” that changed color from orange to green after successful completion of a puzzle. This aimed to create a sense of curiosity and break- down the overall game into smaller goals inducing a sense of achievement (Garg & Baroody, 2024). Musical score Audible feedback from a learning environment has the potential to enhance the perceived pleasantness of gameplay by extending the sensory experience (Nacke et al., 2010). A consistent, low, buzzing sound was used to convey the sound as their ship navigated outer space. Different types of audio feedback were used when players made correct/incorrect moves in the game, successfully completed a level, depleted their energy or shields, collected stars while navigating, an d shot enemy objects. Dynamic sounds along with encouraging phrases like “You’re good” (with a bright audio cue) after a correct move and “Try again” (with a dull audio cue) after an incorrect move were used to keep the players motivated during gameplay (Cayari, 2022). This way, the audio was also aligned with the game situation to induce immersion and emotional engagement (Andersen et al., 2021). Such acoustic characteristics were used in the game to draw attention to important content associated with learning (Collins, 2009; Plass et al., 2020). Game mechanics The central puzzle solving mechanic of the game was to “drag and drop” geometrical shapes into the correct bins to fix the batteries (Figure 2a, 2b). This built energy for the players’ ship to navigate and collect as many stars as possible. Sorting geometrical objects can engage students to build new knowledge based on their existing conceptions (Kobiela et al., 2018). It can help them identify and un derstand the properties of geometrical objects by noticing similarities and differences (Kobiela et al., 2018; Roth & Thom, 2009). Hence, sorting via “dragging and dropping” geometrical shapes into bins was built as the central game mechanic. Other game mechanics in the puzzles were primarily informed by the learning objectives at each level. New mechanics are introduced as players progress to puzzles at higher levels of the Van Hiele Model. They aim to sustain curiosity and enjoyment while preventing boredom and predictive gameplay (Loderer et al., 2020). They also create a sense of excitement as players progress in the game. For example, at puzzles from VHM level four, players are introduced to the “slicing” mechanic. They can break quadrilaterals into smaller diagonals by “slicing” them along a diagonal of their choice. Table 2 shows new mechanics introduced in puzzles at each new VHM level. In addition to inducing positive emotions that aid learning, the game mechanics are introduced in a structured order that is informed by the discipline-specific theory, the VHM model. This avoids a mismatch between progression of gameplay and learning which can enhance self -efficacy and reduce negative emotions such as frustration (Plass et al., 2012). This is associated with the recommendations of (Masek et al., 2017) where “fun” and “excitement” in the game are fundamentally grounded in the problem solving associated with learning. Narrative Narrative in educational games can provide a framework for structural representation of problems (Dickey, 2011). There can be many ways of including narrative in learning games. This is based on the genre of game and core game-mechanics (Ke, 2016) . Our game had a focus on mathematical learning outcomes. The core mechanic involved was “logic and thought during puzzle solving”. Additionally, it was categorized as a “casual puzzle” game as players solve geometrical puzzles to progress. In GeometryBOX, narrative was embedded via environmental storytelling and backdrop missions. Elements of the game environment focused on conveying the narrative theme of the game. Nomenclature for points, rewards, and penalties referred to the narrative theme. Additional gameplay puzzles for the game incentive system were created and were also situated in the overall narrative theme of the game (Figure 2c, 2d). In our game, narrative was integrated as a broadly defined goal with a background plot and adventure missions (Jenkins, 2002). An overarching narrative can create expectations about upcoming events and build suspense that sustains attention for learning (McNamara et al., 2010) . The narrative in GeometryBOX of “fixing batteries” to “repair the ship” and “navigate the outer space” was designed to contextualize learning and provide an overarching story connecting in- game progression, gameplay loop, rules, events, rewards, and penalties (Loderer et al., 2020) . Through all these aspects, narrative was tightly and meaningfully associated with gameplay and learning. It was not included as an afterthought where the story and narrative are only depicted through one aspect (e.g., cut scene and videos) and not tied to gameplay (Naul & Liu, 66 2020). On the contrary, the primary narrative related objective of “fixing batteries” was tied to the central learning objective of solving geometrical puzzles. Figure 2 Examples level screenshots from GeometryBOX Incentive system Rewards and penalties at the center of GBL can help keep the players motivated (Loderer et al., 2020). The incentive system in GeometryBOX is applied in three layers. First, every “game turn” of “dragging and dropping” an object costs a certain number of resources. In this way, players are nudged towards solving the puzzles in minimum possible moves to pres erve the available resources. Hence, they are incentivized for adopting mathematical strategies and discourage “trial and error” based strategy. Second, when players deplete all their resources by making too many incorrect moves, they need to replenish it by completing another game level where they “shoot the debris to clear the boosters” (Figure 2d). This resets their available resources to 100%. This incentive system of managing resources and performance-based progress is dependent on individual learning and gameplay strategy. It aims to increase perceived autonomy and learner control and induce positive achievement emotions (McNamara et al., 2010). The third layer of incentive system is based on collecting “stars” to increase overall points. This layer in tends to enhance the value of learning through “internal compensation”, i.e. achievements in the game (Loderer et al., 2020). After players solve enough puzzles to bring their available resources above a certain threshold, new gameplay is unlocked in which the player controls their spaceship and steers it through an “asteroid field in outer space”. This three -layered, cyclic incentive system in GeometryBOX is intended to create positive achievement emotion of anticipation through feedback, novelty, and repe tition (Pekrun et al., 2014). It also aims to promote optimized gameplay linked with learning as thoughtful, strategized, and mathematical gameplay is rewarded. In sum, GeometryBOX is designed for adolescents to understand the properties and relationships between special quadrilaterals. It is tightly aligned with the learning objectives associated with this topic. This aspect was primarily informed by the VHM, the discipline-specific theory guiding its design. The gameplay and learning were integrated based on the five themes identified by Ke (2016) and are described via its LM-GM map. Emotional design principles were applied to all five features of the game to create a positive and enjoyable learning experience for the players. Discussion This article suggests a three -prong approach to educational game design with an elaborate example of a math game. Educational game designers should follow an iterative process of applying this approach to their design. They should bring these three theoretical approaches together by going beyond previous approaches to educational 67 game design that only consider these aspects independently. In their review of existing educational game design frameworks, Sasupilli and colleagues (2019) identified six prevalent game design models. However, none of them focused on domain specific, play specific, and emotion specific theoretical foundations simultaneously. They were limited to either one or only two of these aspects. For example, the experiential gaming model (Kiili, 2005) does not consider blending learning through game mechanics. In the context of mathematics education, the application of a theoretical framework of math instruction is critical to promote students’ domain -specific mental models for learning (Pirnay -Dummer et al., 2012). This factor becomes much more critical in the context of math as it relies on students’ development of mental models of mathematical objects, their properties, and their relationships (G arg et al., 2025 ; Prayekti et al., 2020). Additionally, the use of Ke’s (2016) framework is needed to address the “what, how, where, and when learning is embedded” in games. This framework helps game designers answer broader questions about leaning in games. It informs design decisions like choice of game genre (simulation versus puzzle), absence or presence of narrative, narrative design (environmental backdrop versus roleplay), representation of learning content (content as game objects versus simulation of concepts), frequency of learning moments in games (exploration and discovery versus immediate feedback), and presence or absence of in-game learning supports. Further, at a finer level, the LM-GM framework (Arnab et al., 2015) helps designers address how all game features (game mechanics) are linked to learning mechanics. Creating an LM-GM map of the game during its design process is crucial to establish granular relationships between pedagogy and gameplay. Finally, to leverage the potential of games to induce emotional experiences for learning, the application of emotional design principles is essential. This can ensure a balance between fun and learning by fostering positive emotions (Byun & Joung, 2018). Specifically for mathematics, enhancing the overall learning experience can be transformative to address concerns with the negative perception of math as being too challenging and uninspiring (Wen & Dubé, 2023). Careful integration of emotional design principles that meaningfully and systematically induce enjoyment, anticipation, and excitement (Putwain et al., 2018) can counter negative impressions of math like fear and anxiety (Budhathoki et al., 2022). Navigating challenges While there are theoretical benefits of applying the three- prong framework to educational games, it also comes with its own challenges and opportunities. It is possible that there is overlap, friction, and conflict when certain game elements are informed by two approaches. The design process for GeometryBOX serves as an example to illustrate how such challenges can be overcome. This is mainly exhibited by two elements: game mechanics and narrative. We describe how all game mechanics were linked to learning via the LM-GM map of the game. The LM-GM map describes the way in which mechanics were implemented and their link with learning processes. In addition, a range of game mechanics were built to create anticipation and excitement as an outcome of the emotional design principles. Further, the addition of new mechanics to create anticipation and excitement was based on the increasing complexity of the discipline -specific VHM model. This way, the design of game mechanics was grounded in all three frameworks that each supported learning through different dimensions. Similarly, learning was integrated through an implicit narrative in the game via environmental storytelling, backdrop, textual and visual references to narrative theme. This was based on Ke’s (2016) framework. Narrative can be beneficial for math learning by providing learners with a framework for representation of problems (Irmayanti et al., 2024; Junkin, 2019). Here, narrative was not included as explicit framing but, rather, the action of solving geometry puzzles to achieve learning outcomes was implicitly linked to the game narrative (solving puzzles = fixing “batteries” = repairing “ship”). Moreover, narrative served as a tool to create an immersive and enjoyable learning experience based on the emotional design principles. This demonstrates how the inclusion of narrative was also informed by two distinct frameworks. Yet, it aimed to avoid contradictory and conflicting experiences. In this case, grounding the narrative in multiple theoretical argument s is likely to strengthen its effects on learning rather than weakening it. Conclusion The GeometryBOX game described in this article is an example of applying distinct but relevant theoretical frameworks of educational game design to create a geometry game. It bridges the gaps between cognitive and domain-specific, gameplay-specific, and emotional foundations of game-based learning. Thoughtful and implicit design of game features tightly tied to learning objectives have the potential to result in positive learning outcomes and make learning an enjoyable experience. We aim to conduct evidence -based, experimental studies on the effectiveness of GeometryBOX on geometrical understanding of adolescents . Game designers should consider this approach to create educational games that are not only grounded in theories of learning and instruction but also harness the power of play in a holistic way. 68 References Andersen, F., Danny, King, C. title: Mediating Mentoring: Examining Digital Accountability within new Teacher Mentoring Dialogue

abstract: In this paper, we examine how digital tools of accountability shape the content of conversations and interactional patterns between mentors and novices. To do so, we analyze a case study of a new teacher and mentor dyad in an equity -oriented mentoring prog ram. We investigate how teachers’ interactions are mediated by digital tools that report out data on their mentoring interactions, with attention to how this digital mediation shapes the depth with which teachers engage in critical inquiry of student thinking. Our findings illustrate that the dyad’s deeper engagement with student thinking occurred when they were not interacting with digital tools of accountability. This paper contributes to an understanding of the ways digital datafication processes can man ifest in embodied teacher learning interactions, shaping the extent to which equity-oriented approaches to mentoring new teachers are realized in practice.
