title: Manga as Counterspaces for Queer Youth Identities
citation: Lisa Lundgren, Khanh Q. Tran, Mario I. Suárez, Colby Tofel-Grehl (2026). Manga as Counterspaces for Queer Youth Identities. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Lundgren, L., Tran, K. Q., Suárez, M. I., & Tofel-Grehl, C.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Social & Civic Studies
conceptualisations_list: Communities of Practice & Situated Learning; Embodied Cognition & Gestures; Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: When tasked with learning, queer youth often encounter limited opportunities to see themselves in ways that recognize their identities, cultures, and epistemologies as sources of knowledge and creativity to learn. Using identity- in-practice, visual storyte lling, and queer rightful presence, we sought to see how queer identities were dignified during a summer camp. Eleven youth participated in a two- week manga- based maker camp where they made animations, comics, and other artistic representations. Through a data analysis process called crystallization, we identified two themes related to queer youth identity: escapism and embodiments of defiance. We argue that counterspaces such as the maker camp offer room for queer youth to play with their identit ies. We offer ways for others to use counterspaces like maker camps as ways to be responsive to youth and their needs by connecting to things they are already interested in and letting them explore identities within those spaces. Purpose Although public acceptance of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and other diverse gender and sexuality- identifying (LGBTQ+) individuals has grown in recent years (GLAAD, 2025), the current sociopolitical landscape is marked by legislative and cul tural attacks on queer and trans (QT) communities at the local, state, and federal levels (Quinan, 2025). These measures uphold the conservative Eurocentric ideals, situated in a white supremacist, settler colonial, and cisheteropatriarchal ideology that s eeks to erase deviant experiences (Leyva et al., 2022). Educational institutions participate in these logics through book bans, surveillance of teachers, and conditions of learning that suppress joy, love, and affirmation, further reifying these ideologica l values (Tran & Pierre, 2025). Within these environments, QT youth often encounter limited opportunities to see themselves in valuable ways, recognizing that their identities, cultures, and epistemologies are meaningful sources of knowledge and creativity to learning. In recent years, scholars have turned towards makerspaces and other creative learning environments as generative contexts for young people to explore their identity in relation to self and community as a sociocultural, historical, and political means (Cala brese Barton & Tan, 2020; Vossoughi et al., 2016). Makerspaces blend art, design, STEM, and storytelling to create conditions for young people to engage in making as a relational, imaginative, and epistemic process related to their learning, historicities, and personal trajectories (Lindberg et al., 2020). These environments can affirm marginalized identities and cultivate a sense of belonging through collaboration, material engagement, and shared authorship (Peppler & Thompson, 2024). Research particularl y focusing on queer and trans youth in makerspace education illuminates that making invites multiple epistemologies and affective-expressive ways that often exceed traditional disciplinary boundaries (e.g., Floegel, 2019; Kitzie & Moorefield -Lang, 2018; Suárez et al., 2023; Tofel -Grehl et al., 2024). Within this research landscape, we argue that these spaces hold additional significance, given how they offer room for QT youth to play with their identity in ways that are often contentious, messy, or otherwise contradictory to dominant social norms that would affirm their self -definition and collective world -making as queer and trans individuals (Leyva et al., 2022; Suárez et al., 2022). Situated within the broader fields of learning sciences, design education, and queer and trans studies in education, this study considers how our creative and insubordinate pedagogies cultivated a queer rightful presence (Tofel-Grehl et al., 2024) by examining how QT youths’ identity is expressed, negotiated, and affirmed within queer-focused makerspace learning environments. We focus on a summer camp program that centers on arts - based, design-oriented learning, where QT youth engage in visual storytelling through manga to explore self and community within a semi-rural, highly conservative community located in the Intermountain West. In particular, this work explores how makerspaces can dignify queer and trans ways of knowing and being, creating in contexts where such ways are often marginalized (and otherwise). Guided by this framing, we investigate the conditions under which visual storytelling can affirm QT identities in rural informal learning contexts. Specifically, we ask: How might an informal summer camp dignify queer and trans identities among youth in rural communities? 446 Theoretical framework We draw on a multitude of theoretical perspectives to situate this work – identity-in-practice, visual storytelling, and queer rightful presence (Holland et al., 1998; Sedawi et al., 2025; Sandoval et al., 2000; Calabrese Barton & Tan, 2020). Identity is posited as an ongoing process of doing, being, and becoming within a sociocultural and material relation of power of the learning context (Gee, 2000). In makerspace education, identity reflects how one’s competence, recognition, and performance are continually negotiated and enacted through participation in disciplinary practices (Andrews & Boklage, 2024; Avraamidou, 2019; Carlone & Johnson, 2007). Within this framing, identity-in-practice refers to the ways learners construct who they are through participati on in patterned activities (Pattinson et al., 2020; Gee, 2000; Wenger, 1998); these interactions create conditions in which learners engage with a community of practice and material conditions, shaping their sense of self and their roles within a collective. While traditional views of identity -in-practice frameworks emphasize participation in authentic settings and activities as central to identity development (Carlone, 2017), for queer and trans youth, such involvement in makerspaces often entails navigating normative boundaries of gender, sexuality, and embodiment that structure epistemological legitimacy ( Suárez et al., 2022; Tofel -Grehl et al., 2024). A queer reframing of identity-in-practice foregrounds how identity works in both relational and resistant ways — that is, how queer and trans youth perform, disrupt, and reconfigure participation through affect, aesthetics, and marginalization. In a sense, QT youth are drawing on their identities in practice as building blocks that shape their every day acts of performance and being within a learning context that affirms their lived realities and their place in STEM worlds (Muñoz, 1999; Tan et al., 2013). In other words, these acts are situated in the material and emotional landscapes of their learning environments and are informed by their interactions (e.g., with themselves, their surroundings, and epistemic tools). From this lens, identity-in-practice is an engagement of identity work, a practice of presence, and a process of self-definition for QT youth. Positioning queer identity-in-practice within a practice-based framework foregrounds the significance of tools, media, and representational forms that mediate participation in makerspace education. Visual storytelling, for instance, functions as both a representational and epistemic practice within design education (Sandoval et al., 2000), which enables youth to externalize ideas, test concepts, and communicate solutions in ways that integrate technical reasoning with personal and cultural narratives and epistemologies (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Tran , 2026). Moreover, multimodal and visual practices support identity development by supporting youth as producers of knowledge rather than passive recipients (Vossoughi et al., 2016); thus, sensemaking through visual storytelling affirms youth’s lived experiences as valid foundations for learning and identity building. For this particular work, we situate manga — a Japanese style of comic book and graphic novels — as a form of visual storytelling, which we argue encapsulates both representational and epistemic practices that embolden youth to make meaning of their knowledge production through makerspaces. Indeed, manga offers youth a medium through which they can engage in design thinking while incorporating identity work in ways that are personally meaningful, socially situated, and congruent with their personhood and well-being. In our previous work, we articulated that manga served as an accessible and identity- affirming medium for QT youth, where engaging in makerspace practices and education supports the reimagining through character development, setting, and narrative lines that reflect the lived experiences, aspirations, and complex emotions of QT youth ( Tofel-Grehl et al., 2024; Suárez et al. , 2022). Building upon this notion of cultivating an identity- affirming makerspace education, this work draws on queer rightful presence (Tofel-Grehl et al., 2024) as the conceptual anchor. Queer rightful presence posits that QT youth should not only have access to learning spaces (e.g., representation in makerspaces, inclusion as absolution, etc.), but also be able to engage and participate as their whole selves without identity negotiation, assimilation, or erasure. This situated view challenges the cisheteronormative norms and assumptions that often define makerspace culture (Andrews & Boklage, 2024), thereby legitimizing QT epistemologies in technical disciplines. Taken together, these theoretical perspectives inform our understanding of makerspace and design education, where QT youth can engage in identity-affirming practices. The development of their queer and trans identities is intrinsically tied to the conditions under which they are recognized, valued, and able to participate without compromising their gendered, sexual, and cultural selves.

title: Examining Youth Authority in Community Member Interviews during the Co- Design of an Environmental Engineering Curriculum
citation: Yuxi Huang, Symone Gyles, Aakriti Bisht, Rossella Santagata, Hosun Kang, Sara Ludovise (2026). Examining Youth Authority in Community Member Interviews during the Co- Design of an Environmental Engineering Curriculum. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Huang, Y., Gyles, S., Bisht, A., Santagata, R., Kang, H., & Ludovise, S.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: This study examines youth authority in interviews with community members during a series of environmental engineering curriculum co -design sessions. Seven high school students, together with teachers, university researchers and informal environmental educators, participated in this multi- session task. The study aimed to understand how youth articulate, realize, and negotiate authority throughout the process. The qualitative analysis of audio recordings from co -design group discussions, formal interviews, reflections, and end- of-year interviews yielded three themes. First, youth authority drew from different sources across different activities. Second, facilitated activities scaffolded youth to realize epistemic and deontic authority. Third, youth authority emerged through adapting and challenging tasks. These findings extend the previous macro-level analyses of power dynamics and suggest that a balance between scaffolding and autonomy is critical to allow youth to exercise authority. This work also contributes to broader literature on power, authority, and equitable youth engagement in curriculum design.

title: Modeling Discourse Shifts in Critical Machine Learning: How Black Girls Reimagine Surveillance through Design
citation: Atefeh Behboudi, Golnaz Arastoopour Irgens, Omer Zahid (2026). Modeling Discourse Shifts in Critical Machine Learning: How Black Girls Reimagine Surveillance through Design. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Behboudi, A., Irgens, G. A., & Zahid, O.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study examines how the discourse of surveillance shifted among middle school Black girls through their participation in a Critical Machine Learning (CML) project grounded in sociocultural learning theories and Critical Race Technology Theory. Using a Quantitative Ethnography research design, this study collected data through students' interaction in their groups over two consecutive sessions within a twelve -session program implementation. Ordered network analysis (ONA) reveals that students initially positioned surveillance in a binary category, either for care or control, with a weak connection between the two. Eventually, students began to position care as a primary purpose of surveillance and justified why care was important. These findings underscore the importance of integrating critical STEM education in schools, providing students with opportunities to engage and question the technologies they design.

title: Developing K-12 Teachers’ Ethical Competencies through Cognitive Dissonance of Gameplay
citation: Ming Ma, Zhichun Liu, Gary K.W. Wong (2026). Developing K-12 Teachers’ Ethical Competencies through Cognitive Dissonance of Gameplay. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Ma, M., Liu, Z., & Wong, G. K.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA); Critical Digital Literacy & AI Ethics
abstract: As AI literacy becomes increasingly integrated into K–12 education, teachers require robust ethical competencies to effectively teach AI ethics in classroom instruction. To address this need, we developed Responsible AI CAB, a scenario- based tabletop role -playing game designed to immerse teachers in real -world ethical dilemmas and foster collective ethical reasoning. Eight technology teachers participated in the gameplay. We employed bipartite epistemic network analysis (ENA) methods to examine teachers’ discourse. Results highlighted that gameplay -induced cognitive dissonance facilitated the development of teachers ’ ethical competencies. This was evidenced by their adoption of multiple stakeholder perspectives under role pressures, their comprehension and application of responsible AI principles in group ethical reasoning through peer challenges or arguments, and their critical evaluation of new information to challenge existing beliefs. These findings inform the design of professional development programs seeking to cultivate the ethical competencies essential for K–12 AI literacy education.

title: Shifting from Cooperation to Collaboration: A Case Study of Medical Students' Collaborative Learning Experiences
citation: Tsung-Liang Tsai, Tieh-Huai Chang (2026). Shifting from Cooperation to Collaboration: A Case Study of Medical Students' Collaborative Learning Experiences. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Tsai, T. & Chang, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates barriers to collaborative learning among medical students in a medical humanities course. Data were collected from 74 second -year medical students in Taiwan, with 23 having received collaboration training. Using grounded theory, we analyzed online discussions, learning portfolios, and interviews. Findings reveal distinct patterns in discussion timing, interaction dynamics, and outcomes between trained and untrained groups. Students' prior success with division- of-labor approaches emerges as an inhibitor to collaborative learning adoption. Notably, consistent implementation of assessment criteria becomes the critical catalyst for shifting students from cooperation to collaboration. This research deepens understanding: learning outcomes alone cannot reveal learning processes; learners' agency must be reconceptualized; curriculum, activities, materials, and assessment require structurally transparent integration.

title: Knowledge Building Design: Bridging Theory and Practice in Teacher Professional Development Through Design Thinking
citation: Chih-Hsuan Chang, Fang-Ying Wu, Mei-Ju Chen, Chih Hui Seet, Bodong Chen, Huang-Yao Hong (2026). Knowledge Building Design: Bridging Theory and Practice in Teacher Professional Development Through Design Thinking. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Chang, C., Wu, F., Chen, M., Seet, C. H., Chen, B., & Hong, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In the AI era, Knowledge Building (KB) pedagogy becomes increasingly vital, yet traditional professional development inadequately prepares teachers to facilitate knowledge - creating learning environments. This study examined how teachers engaged in an online professional development course using the Knowledge Building Design (KBD) model, which integrates design thinking processes with KB principles. Teachers demonstrated high collaborative engagement and clear progression through design cycles, shifting from problem definition to lesson prototyping. Qualitative analysis revealed recursive design patterns, with teachers strategically returning to ideation when facing prototyping challenges. Lesson design quality improved significantly across all KB components, with particularly dramatic gains in actions design. The KBD model effectively operationalizes principle- based pedagogy through structured artifacts, addressing the persistent challenge of translating KB's robust theoretical foundation into practical classroom enactment. Findings demonstrate that collaborative, process-oriented professional development enabled by KBD can transform teachers' pedagogical capabilities for the AI era.

title: Stories of Practice as a Means to promote Teachers' Professional Learning: The Role of AI -Based Chatbots
citation: Osnat Atias, Hava Ben-Horin, Keren Aridor, Ornit Sagy, Yael Kali (2026). Stories of Practice as a Means to promote Teachers' Professional Learning: The Role of AI -Based Chatbots. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Atias, O., Ben-Horin, H., Aridor, K., Sagy, O., & Kali, Y.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study investigates how AI conversational chatbots can support teachers’ professional learning through writing reflective stories of practice within networks of research– practice partnerships (RPPs). We developed “Tell Me Your Story”—a chatbot designed to guide teachers in recounting meaningful classroom experiences and generate structured narratives. Grounded in a framework that conceptualizes identities as story-based, and learning as identity development, the study examined how such interactions help teachers articulate identity stories and promote their professional learning. Ten teachers who integrated citizen science initiatives in their teaching engaged in chatbot -assisted storytelling followed by a meta -reflective interview. The resulting narratives met the criteria of identity stories, with most participants developing new or reinforced insights interpreted as professional identity development. These findings suggest that chatbot -supported storytelling can generate knowledge artifacts that may facilitate collective learning across networks of RPPs.

title: Cultural Contexts as Catalysts for Learning: Integrating Students’ Lived Experiences into Physics Assessments
citation: Clausell Mathis, Colette Periard, Hassaan Azam, John Kelly, Hiba Assi, Maruf Ikram (2026). Cultural Contexts as Catalysts for Learning: Integrating Students’ Lived Experiences into Physics Assessments. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Mathis, C., Periard, C., Azam, H., Kelly, J., Assi, H., & Ikram, M.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study investigates how leveraging students’ cultural resources can support conceptual understanding in a university- level physics course. Drawing on culturally relevant pedagogy (Ladson- Billings, 1995), the resources framework (diSessa, 1993; Hammer e t al., 2005), and the cultural resource enactment framework (Mathis, 2025), the research examines how contextualizing motion-graph tasks within students’ lived campus experiences influences reasoning about kinematics. Forty-eight students completed four tasks, each situated in familiar campus settings, that required interpreting, comparing, and generating position- , velocity-, and acceleration-time graphs. Analysis using a four-dimensional rubric revealed that most students demonstrated scientific reasoning when tasks were culturally and spatially grounded, particularly in single -graph interpretation and comparative reasoning. Student reflections indicated that familiar contexts increased engagement and relevance. Findings provide empirical evidence that sit uating disciplinary ideas in culturally meaningful contexts can enhance both engagement and representational fluency, offering a practical model for culturally grounded assessment design in university physics instruction.

title: An Activity-Theoretical Approach to Teacher Professional Development in Pedagogical AI Agent Design
citation: Haiyang Xin, Qiannan Niu, Shuang Li, Yimeng Sun, Ching Sing Chai, Lingyun Huang, Gaowei Chen (2026). An Activity-Theoretical Approach to Teacher Professional Development in Pedagogical AI Agent Design. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Xin, H., Niu, Q., Li, S., Sun, Y., Chai, C. S., Huang, L., & Chen, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This two-cycle formative intervention study examined why teachers disengage from AI agent creation after professional development —a low engagement paradox—and tested whether systemic redesign could address it. Cycle 1 ( N=218) revealed that despite completing comprehensive TPD, 87% of teachers ceased creating within three weeks, with behavioral tracking and interview analysis identifying systemic contradictions as the source of psychological need frustration rather than ca pacity deficits. Cycle 2 ( N=26) implemented Cultural-Historical Activity Theory and Self -Determination Theory -driven redesign directly targeting diagnosed contradictions, achieving synchronized enhancement of both capacity and willingness. The findings reframe implementation failure as a rational response to need - thwarting systems and offer a replicable CHAT- SDT diagnostic framework for transformative professional development.

title: Preservice Teachers’ Dialogic Talk Moves and Beliefs About Control in a AI-Driven Virtual Reality Classroom Simulation
citation: Yizhen Huang, Nico Klausner-Thimm, Eric Richter, Katharina Scheiter, Dirk Richter (2026). Preservice Teachers’ Dialogic Talk Moves and Beliefs About Control in a AI-Driven Virtual Reality Classroom Simulation. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Huang, Y., Klausner-Thimm, N., Richter, E., Scheiter, K., & Richter, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
tpack_tk_labels: Generative AI & LLMs; Immersive VR / AR; Simulations & Scientific Modeling
abstract: This paper presents two studies investigating preservice teachers’ dialogic teaching practices using an immersive, large language model (LLM) –enhanced virtual reality (VR) classroom simulation environment . Study 1 examined 23 preservice teachers’ perceptions of authenticity, situational interest, and self -efficacy during VR -based classroom debates and analyzed the talk move pattern using hidden Markov model. Participants perceived the simulation as authentic and engaging but relied predominantly on superficial probing questions rather than dialogic moves that deepen students’ thinking. Study 2 explored whether repeated simulation experiences combined with peer feedback influenced beliefs about classroom ownership of ideas and activities among 22 preservice teachers. Mixed -effects modeling indicated significant belief shifts toward student ownership of ideas, moderated by engagement with the simulation. Collectively, the findings suggest that AI -driven VR simulations provide authentic, scalable environments for developing dialogic competence and reshaping teacher beliefs toward more student-centered instructional practices.

title: Multi-Layered Brokering for Family Engagement in Out-of-School STEM: A Case Study of a Statewide Learning Network
citation: Maggie Dahn, Kylie Peppler, Kari Denissen, Keem Anderson (2026). Multi-Layered Brokering for Family Engagement in Out-of-School STEM: A Case Study of a Statewide Learning Network. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Dahn, M., Peppler, K., Denissen, K., & Anderson, K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Boundary Crossing & Brokerage; Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies
abstract: Out-of-school time (OST) programs play a critical role in broadening participation in STEM by offering young people opportunities to explore interests and develop skills beyond formal schooling. Yet, the potential of these programs is constrained by limited and uneven strategies for engaging families —key partners in sustaining youth interest and identity in STEM. This study applies a multi- layered brokering framework to examine how Ignite Afterschool, Minnesota’s statewide OST intermediary, advanced family engagement in STEM programming. Using a qualitative case study approach, we analyze how Ignite brokered resources, knowledge, and opportunities that positioned families as active participants rather than peripheral supporters in their children’s OST STEM learning. Findings show how coordinated brokering across interpersonal and organizational levels can foster more inclusive, culturally responsive, and sustainable forms of family engagement. This work contributes a theoretically grounded model for understanding how network- level intermediaries can strengthen family learning and build connected, equitable OST ecosystems.

title: Students’ Mental Models of AI Chatbots in Inquiry Learning: a Friend, an Instructor, a Browser, and a Partner
citation: Tamar Fuhrmann, Carolina Sotério, Paulo Blikstein (2026). Students’ Mental Models of AI Chatbots in Inquiry Learning: a Friend, an Instructor, a Browser, and a Partner. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Fuhrmann, T., Sotério, C., & Blikstein, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates how high school students perceive and interact with an AI chatbot during a science lab experiment. Analysis of chatbot transcripts revealed four enacted roles in student-AI interaction (Instructor, Browser, Human, and Reflective Partner) that reflect students’ underlying mental models and how they conceptualize the chatbot’s capabilities and relationship. Students’ conversations shifted across these roles, with Browser and Instructor predominating. In contrast, post-activity surveys offered retrospective perspectives that largely framed the chatbot as an Instructor and, less frequently, as a Browser, overlooking the reflective and human-like engagements evident in transcripts. By confronting students’ talk about AI with their live interactions during inquiry, this study highlights mental models as dynamic, enacted in practice, and locally and culturally constructed in conversation, suggesting directions for designing educational AI systems that can accommodate dynamic roles.

title: Making Sense of Systemic Racism in a High School Biology Classroom: The “Just Genetics” Unit
citation: Dalia Hassan, Ravit Golan Duncan, Rishi Krishnamoorthy, Na'ama Av-Shalom, Mariam Hassan (2026). Making Sense of Systemic Racism in a High School Biology Classroom: The “Just Genetics” Unit. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Hassan, D., Duncan, R. G., Krishnamoorthy, R., Av-Shalom, N., & Hassan, M.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Drawing on frameworks for Justice -Centered Pedagogy and Rightful Presence, we designed a genetics unit that engages students with reasoning about racial health disparities in the context of diabetes. The unit focuses on the relationship between past and ongoing structural racial inequities, the resulting non -neutrality o f physical and social environments, and their outcomes for the health of marginalized communities. We provide a design story tracing our design conjecture, how we embodied it in learning activities and artifacts, and the ways in which these were taken up b y high school students in terms of their understanding of the structural aspect of racism. Our findings suggest that while students recognized that racialized groups endure harmful environments, they did not fully grasp how historical and ongoing racism created and reproduces these environments.

title: How Laypeople Resolve Expert Disagreement: The Role of Epistemic Aims and Ideals
citation: Qiuyu Lin, Qianqian Gao, Clark A. Chinn (2026). How Laypeople Resolve Expert Disagreement: The Role of Epistemic Aims and Ideals. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Lin, Q., Gao, Q., & Chinn, C. A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Expert disagreement frequently arises in everyday decision- making, yet little is known about how people’s epistemic thinking shapes their disagreement evaluation and resolution. This study applied the AIR framework of epistemic thinking to examine how laypeople’s personal and epistemic aims and ideals shape their disagreement resolution strategies. Four triads of undergraduate students assessed conflicting dietary recommendations using a web- based collaborative learning environment, synthesizing the multiple documents into their shared visual graphic organizer to analyze the disagreement s. The result showed that students evoked epistemic ideals across three main categories: ideals for authors, for study design, and for documents. The verbal protocol analysis of the students’ conversation revealed that the groups followed different paths to deal with the disagreements; depending on their different aims and ideals, each triad came to different conclusions. Our analyses reveal that laypeople’s epistemic and personal aims and criteria shape their strategies in resolving disagreement among conflicting documents.

title: Examining the Efficacy of AI-based Scaffolds for Multilingual Learners’ Science Inquiry
citation: Jeremy Lee, Janice D. Gobert (2026). Examining the Efficacy of AI-based Scaffolds for Multilingual Learners’ Science Inquiry. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Lee, J. & Gobert, J. D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Traditional STEM instruction for multilingual learners (MLs) often reflects a deficit- oriented approach that focuses on the rote memorization of vocabulary and decontextualized facts, which restricts MLs from meaningful engagement in authentic STEM tasks . Consequently, research has found persistent disparities between MLs and non -MLs’ STEM achievement. This study investigated the efficacy of AI -based scaffolds designed to lower barriers for MLs’ participation in NGSS-aligned science inquiry practices . Using fine-grained log data from an Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS), we analyzed how scaffolds supported MLs’ development of science inquiry com petencies. Results indicated that the automated scaffolds supported MLs’ development in forming a testable hypothesis, testing their articulated hypothesis, and drawing correct inferences about their data, even on a different topic and at a later time when scaffolds were no t available. These findings suggest that AI -based scaffolds can promote equitable access to authentic STEM learning for MLs while supporting their conceptual and language development.

title: Exploring the Influence of Affective Factors on Cognitive Factors in Primary School Students' Scientific Literacy
citation: Cuixin Li, Yang Yang, Yafeng Zheng (2026). Exploring the Influence of Affective Factors on Cognitive Factors in Primary School Students' Scientific Literacy. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Li, C., Yang, Y., & Zheng, Y.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study examined the relationships among affective and cognitive factors of scientific literacy using data from 5,957 4th and 6th graders in China. The SEM results revealed that: (1) a significant internal chain exists within the affective dimension, progressing from curiosity to scientific interest and then to science identity; (2) cognitive factors follow a sequential path from content knowledge to scientific reasoning, and further to inquiry; (3) the direct effects of affective factors on cognitive outcomes are limited, with a more prominent role played by a complete mediation pathway: "curiosity to interest to identity to content knowledge to reasoning/inquiry". Multi- group path analysis further indicated that the overall model structure differs significantly between 4th and 6th graders, with sixth graders showing higher efficiency in transforming curiosity into interest and converting knowledge into reasoning and inquiry. The study provides an integrated model and evidence for stage -specific instructional strategies in K12 science education.

title: Exploring Spatiotemporal Data Through a Space-Time Cube Interface: Affordances and Struggles
citation: Katherine M. Miller, Christopher Lore, Chad Dorsey, Lauren Pagano, David H. Uttal, Robert A. Kolvoord (2026). Exploring Spatiotemporal Data Through a Space-Time Cube Interface: Affordances and Struggles. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Miller, K. M., Lore, C., Dorsey, C., Pagano, L., Uttal, D. H., & Kolvoord, R. A.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Spatiotemporal (ST) data, data that vary across space and time, are at the heart of pressing, socially relevant issues, such as climate change, disease spread, and population trends. Adolescents regularly encounter such data in both school and everyday lif e, and they must develop the data acumen and habits of mind to successfully interpret them. However, ST data are inherently complex and challenging, even for experts, and research on how to best design ST visualizations to foster interpretation is limited. In this study, w e explore how the affordances of two data exploration tools, the CODAP interface and a space- time cube (STC), both benefit and hinder students’ exploration of ST data. We found that students identified the value of being able to view ST data in the STC, pointing out how the STC contained more information, allowed for easier exploration of ST data, and allowed them to see time trends more clearly.

title: From Implementation to Innovation: Re-imagining the role of Practice in Research
citation: Linette Victor (2026). From Implementation to Innovation: Re-imagining the role of Practice in Research. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Victor, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Reverse Translation (RT) is a conceptual framework repositioning educational practice as a generative source of knowledge. Drawing from Design-Based Research (DBIR), Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs), and Improvement Science (IS), RT challenges the conventional theory-to-practice pipeline by beginning with practitioner-identified tensions and insights. It offers a structured process for elevating practitioner insights into theoretical discourse, fostering reciprocal learning, and context-specific innovation. This model is especially relevant for knowledge mobilizers, such as instructional coaches and teacher leaders, who often support others ’growth without sustained opportunities to develop their own practice. RT contributes to the learning sciences by expanding methodologies for practice-initiated inquiry, deepening commitments to equity, and strengthening the relevance and adaptability of contextually grounded interventions. Using vignettes and applied examples, this paper identifies how RT can inform professional development and research design, bridging the research- practice divide in more effective ways.

title: Learning to Look Through the Lens: How Youth Practice Perspective-Shifting Through Filmmaking
citation: Jill Beale, Cass Scheirer, Adam Sherlock, Kayla Desportes (2026). Learning to Look Through the Lens: How Youth Practice Perspective-Shifting Through Filmmaking. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Beale, J., Scheirer, C., Sherlock, A., & Desportes, K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Perspective-taking is essential to critical thinking and empathy development. Perspective-taking involves looking at a situation from a viewpoint that differs from one’s usual viewpoint, and understanding another person’s thoughts, feelings, and how they experience the world. Filmmaking is a medium that affords many opportunities for perspective-taking; yet little is known about how youth practice perspective -taking in filmmaking programs. In this paper, we use qualitative data analysis to examine interview s with three young artists in a summer youth filmmaking program. Our analysis reveals specific instances of perspective-shifting, such as considering the audience’s point of view, which we use to create a codebook highlighting occurrences of perspective-shifting in the filmmaking process. We then examine these sections of dialogue and identify linguistic markers of perspective -shifting in the youth filmmakers’ language. The aim of this research is to inform learning design that supports a young person’s capacity to shift perspectives through creative media production.

title: Optional Self-Explanation Tasks in Practice: Participation Rate, Explanation Quality, and Performance
citation: Steven Moore, Sreecharan Sankaranarayanan, Huy Nguyen (2026). Optional Self-Explanation Tasks in Practice: Participation Rate, Explanation Quality, and Performance. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Moore, S., Sankaranarayanan, S., & Nguyen, H.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: The benefits of self-explanation for learning have been well researched, yet we know little about whether students engage in self-explanation when the tasks are optional. This study investigates participation rates, explanation quality, and their correlation with student performance in an introductory online chemistry course with 129 students. We found that 53% of students voluntarily participated in an optional self-explanation activity and 66.18% of their self-explanations were judged as high- quality by experts. Self-explanation quality was positively correlated with s tudent performance in the course, as measured by formative and summative assessments. These resul ts suggest that while optional self -explanation tasks effectively attract students overall, the intervention may primarily be supporting already high- performing students. Nevertheless, the high quality of generated self-explanations indicates that keeping the activities optional while focusing on increasing the rate of participation could lead to better outcomes at scale when compared requiring mandatory participation.

title: Exploring the Mediating Role of Motivation in the Relationship Between Sense of Belonging and Intention to Leave STEM Majors
citation: Frank E. Melendez-Anzures, Christian Samhir Grijalva Quiñonez, Angeles Dominguez, Genaro Zavala (2026). Exploring the Mediating Role of Motivation in the Relationship Between Sense of Belonging and Intention to Leave STEM Majors. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Melendez-Anzures, F. E., Quiñonez, C. S. G., Dominguez, A., & Zavala, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Intention to leave STEM majors remains a challenge, particularly in Latin America, where psychosocial predictors of persistence are underexplored. Grounded in Self- determination Theory, this study examined whether motivation mediates the relationship between sense of belonging and inte ntion to leave a STEM major. Participants were 945 undergraduates from a private Mexican university who provided self -reports on sense of belonging (SB), intrinsic motivation (IM), extrinsic motivation (EM), and intention to leave STEM (ITL). Structural Equation Modeling indicated that SB was positively associated with IM and negatively associated with ITL, while showing no significant association with EM. IM was negatively associated with ITL and partially mediated the relationship between SB and ITL. EM showed no significant associations with ITL. Overall, the model explained 9% of the variance in ITL. Findings highlight the importance of socially supportive learning environments for fostering intrinsic motivation and persistence-related intentions in STEM majors.

title: Building Models and Relationships: Distribution of Authority in an Elementary Science Classroom
citation: Annabel Stoler (2026). Building Models and Relationships: Distribution of Authority in an Elementary Science Classroom. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Stoler, A.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This paper describes a design-based research study exploring how interactions during modeling activities in a fifth-grade science classroom position students with authority. I explore how authority is inequitably distributed through students’ access to the conversational floor and interactional space, as well as through evaluations of intellectual and social merit. Qualitative coding is used to analyze students’ participation bids during whole -class activities and pedagogical actions that disrupt or perpetuate the inequitable distribution of authority among students in this class. Findings suggest that while authority can be inequitably distributed in a classroom community, teachers can enact moves that disrupt this inequity in moment -to- moment interactions. This has implications for supporting learning environments that foster equitable engagement with science practice and collaborative knowledge construction.

title: “Both Are Useful”: Student Epistemic Navigation in a Co-Designed Science Unit about Traditional Chinese Medicine
citation: Weiying Li (2026). “Both Are Useful”: Student Epistemic Navigation in a Co-Designed Science Unit about Traditional Chinese Medicine. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Li, W.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Design-Based Research (DBR); Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies
abstract: Science education in rural China often privileges Western epistemology, creating disconnects with students ’ community knowledge systems like Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM). This design-based research study addresses this gap through a co-designed three-lesson unit in a rural middle school in central China. The unit on Shanghuo ( 上火, internal heat) positioned TCM and Western science as complementary systems with distinct goals, reasoning processes, and evidence criteria. Using a Knowledge Integration framework, analysis of 40 eighth-graders' responses reveals how students navigated between correspondence -based and reductionist causal reasoning without devaluing community knowledge. Students shifted from binary epistemological stances ( “TCM is superstitious” ) to purposeful differentiation, recognizing when each system serves specific purposes. Three instructional routines supported this work: organizing family knowledge as analyzable data, using parallel comparison structures, and scaffolding dual justification. Findings demonstrate that rural students possess rich epistemological resources that Western -dominant curricula render invisible, offering design guidelines for culturally relevant science pedagogy.

title: Supporting High Schoolers’ Epistemic Vigilance in Everyday Science
citation: Claire LeBovidge, Susan A. Yoon, Clark Chinn, Noora F. Noushad, Huma Hussain- Abidi (2026). Supporting High Schoolers’ Epistemic Vigilance in Everyday Science. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: LeBovidge, C., Yoon, S. A., Chinn, C., Noushad, N. F., & Abidi, H. H.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: The rise of misinformation places new demands on science education to prepare students to critically evaluate information in their daily lives. One approach is to foster epistemic vigilance (i.e., critical awareness of potentially false information). Instr uction that explicitly prompts students to critique information and emphasizes the different components of epistemic vigilance may improve student ability to discern misinformation. This exploratory study examines students’ epistemic vigilance during a task in which they evaluated four everyday sources of scientific information. Students demonstrated situational vigilance toward sources they perceived as untrustworthy. Their evaluative strategies and values shifted depending on the task prompts and source characteristics. These findings suggest that students’ reasoning is context -dependent, with their evaluative strategies and values used to judge credibility varying across situations. Building students’ metacognitive understanding of how these evaluative activities and values interact may support more reliable awareness and reasoning about scientific information in everyday contexts.

title: Dialogues with Objects: Learning through Relational Attunement in Making
citation: Xinxin Feng (2026). Dialogues with Objects: Learning through Relational Attunement in Making. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Feng, X.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: By engaging participants in an expansive example of open- source sharing practice, this study explores how dialogical encounters with others’ designs can inform more just and contextually grounded pedagogies in making. Building on a long- term design-based research partnership among a museum, schools, and community members, the study invited learners to engage with artifacts that carried the histories, relationships, and aspirations of youth makers. Analysis of dialogical sequences—moments of response and counter -response between people and artifacts—identified three forms of dialogical responsiveness: attending to contextual detail, negotiating conflicting representations, and sustaining dialogue through uncertainty. Findings suggest that engaging with materially and historically rich artifacts cultivates empathy, critical interpretation, and ethical imagination, reframing making as a practice of listening and responding to the social worlds that materials embody.

title: Organism-Level Ideas as Productive Resources in a Student’s Evolutionary Reasoning
citation: Julia Svoboda, Sugat Dabholkar, Scott Benjamin, Yiru Wang (2026). Organism-Level Ideas as Productive Resources in a Student’s Evolutionary Reasoning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We present a microgenetic analysis of an interview with a student, Charlie, whose thinking shifts between population-level and organism-level explanations for natural selection. Population-level explanations are typically considered correct, while organism -level explanations have been characterized as containing misconceptions. We argue that this case illustrates how organism -level ideas contributed to productive conceptual dynamics that ultimately supported Charlie in developing a more elaborated and integrated explanation for evolutionary change. Using a combination of knowledge analysis and interaction analysis, we propose that the interview dynamics —which established a shared framing of the conversation as focused on sensemaking— allowed Charlie to activate, examine, and ultimately integrate organism-level ideas into a more coherent explanation for natural selection.

title: Semi-Parametric Non-Linear Modeling of Student-Centered Learning Challenges
citation: Minzhi Liu, Daniel Sewell, Matthew Lira (2026). Semi-Parametric Non-Linear Modeling of Student-Centered Learning Challenges. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Liu, M., Sewell, D., & Lira, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Student-centered learning (SCL) emphasizes learners’ autonomy, engagement, and responsibility for constructing knowledge. Yet when external supports such as scaffolding, guidance, and authentic audiences are limited, learners may encounter heightened unce rtainty and strain. This study uses Electrodermal Activity (EDA) as a real -time indicator of physiological arousal associated with task engagement in unsupported SCL -like tasks and applies semi -parametric spline modeling to characterize temporal dynamics i n the signal. Results indicate recurring arousal patterns that, in relation to task context and theory, are interpreted as possible episodes of heightened challenge, brief recovery, and later stabilization. By relating these patterns to the OLSit (Own it, Learn it, Share it) design framework, the paper highlights the importance of balancing autonomy with timely support. The study contributes both a methodological approach for modeling EDA time series and design hypotheses for supporting productive affective engagement.

title: Opening Black Boxes: Unpacking Blocks to Balance Usability and Expressiveness in Computational Modeling
citation: Adelmo Eloy, Aditi Wagh, Tamar Fuhrmann, Roseli de Deus Lopes, Paulo Blikstein (2026). Opening Black Boxes: Unpacking Blocks to Balance Usability and Expressiveness in Computational Modeling. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: Computational modeling is a key practice in STEM classrooms. Block -based, domain-specific programming environments have made this practice more accessible but may constrain what students can design compared to general -purpose languages. This paper introduces “block unpacking” —allowing high -level primitives to be opened, inspected, and modified—in a domain- specific modeling environment. We implemented this feature in a four- day lesson on eutrophication, in which high school students programmed computational models to represent interactions between algae, bacteria, fish, nutrients, and oxygen. We analyzed 36 interactions with six unpackable blocks across three modeling challenges, examining the computational complexity and scientific relevance of students’ modifications. We found that unpacking enabled students to modify high- level primitives, via parameter and code structure changes, to optimize models and articulate scientific reasoning. We discuss implications for the design of programming environments and instructional materials that aim to balance usability and expressiveness in computational modeling.

citation: Tugce Aldemir, Vivek Sabanwar, Ali Bicer, Donggil Song (2026). Planners and Tinkerers: A Comparative Case Study of K-12 Students’ Engagement with Data Practices in an Ag-STEM. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: In an increasingly data-saturated society, fostering K-12 students' data literacy is an important issue. This qualitative comparative case study addresses this need by examining how eighth-grade students develop data literacy within a 16-week, AI-supported data-driven scientific inquiry leveraging low -cost sensor devices in an Ag -STEM context. Drawing on the frameworks of conceptual and critical data literacy, the study analyzes the distinct pathways of two four -student and three -student groups. D ata sources included project journals, data logs, AI interaction logs, and focus group interviews, which were analyzed through a multi -stage thematic and cross -case analysis. Findings reveal two archetypes, Pragmatic Planners and Messy Tinkerers, who followed distinct yet equally meaningful paths. Each group’s engagement was shaped by different forms of resistance, informational or physical, that transformed confusion into insight. The study suggests that educational designs that embrace productive struggle could support diverse students in developing a deeper understanding of the entire data-driven inquiry.

title: A Mixed-Method Analysis of Facilitator Sensemaking around Social-Emotional Learning in a Refugee Summer Program
citation: Hiba Khatib, Sarah Priscilla Lee (2026). A Mixed-Method Analysis of Facilitator Sensemaking around Social-Emotional Learning in a Refugee Summer Program. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: This study utilizes a mixed -methods approach to analyze facilitator sensemaking around social-emotional learning (SEL). Using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (topic modeling) and grounded theory coding, we analyze two corpora of SEL literature to identify key topics that comprise dominant and critical SEL frameworks. Our findings reveal that while dominant SEL frameworks emphasize institutional language, critical SEL frameworks better reflect the complex cultural negotiations that facilitators navigate in their practice. Qualitative analysis of facilitator interviews validates these computational findings, illustrating how facilitators draw on their own cultural backgrounds as underscored in critical approaches to SEL. This study supports the need for SEL frameworks that can accommodate multiple ways of understanding social and emotional development in culturally diverse contexts.

title: “It’s aligned with my personal beliefs, i can do this”: How Science Educators Navigate Tensions Between Official and Counter Scripts of Science and Learning
citation: Shaghig Chaparian, Olivia Ortiz, Maia Yoshida, Kam Waugh, Jasmine Ma, Ronni Hayden, Latasha Wright (2026). “It’s aligned with my personal beliefs, i can do this”: How Science Educators Navigate Tensions Between Official and Counter Scripts of Science and Learning. authors_list: Chaparian, S., Ortiz, O., Yoshida, M., Waugh, K., Ma, J., Hayden, R., & Wright, L.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: This study examines how informal science educators transform their lived experiences of migration, activism, and encounters with marginalization into pedagogical commitments focused on social justice. Drawing on Holland and Lave’s history-in-person and Gutiérrez’s third-space concepts, we explore how educators’ histories serve as mediational resources that shape teaching philosophies and reconfigure who belongs in science. Using semi- structured interviews with community scientists from Daphnia , an after -school science organization serving marginalized youth, the analysis traces how educators navigated and re - authored official and unofficial scripts about legitimate science and participation. Findings reveal that educators mobilize personal histories to create hybrid pedagogical spaces emphasizing freedom, flexibility, and epistemic justice. These third-space negotiations obscure boundaries between scientific and community knowledge, transforming science into a relational, participatory practice rooted in care and belonging. By conceptualizing informal educators as historical actors, this study highlights their critical role in social transformation.

title: (Re)constructing What Counts: The Politics and Possibilities of Teacher Noticing
citation: Karen Underwood, Ilana Horn (2026). (Re)constructing What Counts: The Politics and Possibilities of Teacher Noticing. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Underwood, K. & Horn, I.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Teacher noticing, defined as teachers’ ability to attend to and interpret classroom events, constitutes a dominant construct supporting teacher preparation programs and professional development. This conceptual paper argues that noticing frameworks do not simply describe professional knowledge, but actively shape what counts as knowledge in teaching. Dominant cognitive and sociocultural approaches privilege analytical, observable, and individually located forms of knowing while overlooking the tacit, embodied, and r elational dimensions that teachers draw on within their practice, carrying political consequences for how teachers are supported. Building on emerging ecological and relational approaches, we argue that reimagining the construct opens possibilities for recognizing the full range of knowledge teachers draw on in their practice. Through an illustrative example with an experienced secondary mathematics teacher, Clark, we explore what becomes possible when research begins from teachers’ lived experience.

title: Negotiating Tensions as Sites of Learning: Teacher-Child Interactions During Mathematical Play
citation: Jingyi Chen, Melissa Gresalfi (2026). Negotiating Tensions as Sites of Learning: Teacher-Child Interactions During Mathematical Play. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Chen, J. & Gresalfi, M.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Play offers rich opportunities for young children to engage with mathematics, yet its classroom enactment often involves negotiating tensions between children’s autonomy and curricular expectations. Drawing on cultural -historical activity theory, this stud y proposes a framework for identifying teacher –child negotiations around rules, representational tools, and agendas and examines how such negotiation shapes opportunities for shared sense -making during math play. Our analysis identified three relational configurations that capture how these negotiations unfold: teacher -dominant coordination, parallel coordination, and joint improvisation. The framework provides methodological and pedagogical tools for examining and intervening playful math learning environments that center children’s agency and shared epistemic authorship.

title: The Power of Scaling Slowly: Negotiation of Science Teaching in a Long Term Research- Practice Partnership
citation: Scott McDonald, Jonathan McCausland (2026). The Power of Scaling Slowly: Negotiation of Science Teaching in a Long Term Research- Practice Partnership. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: McDonald, S. & McCausland, J.

abstract: Moving innovations in education from small initial efforts to broader impacts has been a central challenge of supporting change in schools. This study is a part of a larger design- based research project where we worked in partnership to redesign the secondary science program at The Pennsylvania State University. We used the context as a test-bed for innovations and design-based research to develop “humble” theory and contest theory in teacher education. This study views teacher learning as the sociocultural practice of negotiation of professional vision within a community in broad temporal and physical scales . Professional vision is theorized not as a small scale, local negotiat ion of individual acts of practice , but as the on- going and dynamic collaborative negotiation of a learning community in response to the overlapping political economies of social organizations that occurs across different sites, places, or contexts, spanning decades. Subject/Problem Changing educational systems , and particularly the embedded cultural practices of teaching, requires in -depth, rich, extended engagement focused on building and sustaining trusting relationships. Characterizing this kind of change lies at the intersection of systems of community and individual learning, which are naturally intertwined. To address this complexity and support system change requires the cultivations of a learning environment for multiple role actors (e.g, preservice and in -service teachers, students, university faculty) and as a result involves bridging multiple cultural communities. While teacher learning occurs both in (and outside of) institutions of higher education and K -12 schools, the relationships between these two institutional contexts are often complicated. The culture and practices of K -12 institutional contexts often operate in tension with those of institutions of higher education, described as the two- worlds problem (Braaten, 2018). This tension complicates efforts at systemic change as do the multiple layers of practice involved in the culture of schools (Windschitl & Stroupe, 2017) - students engaged in science practices (as articulated by documents like the National Research Council’s Framework for K-12 Science Education or the Next Generation Science Standards); teachers engaged in designing and enacting learning environments to support students science practices (as articulated by documents/frameworks like Ambitious Science Teaching); and teacher educators engaged in designing and enacting learning environments for teachers (both in- service and preservice) to develop teachers’ practices (by extension, Ambitious Science Teacher Education). This multi -layer complex of interwoven practices contributes to the massive challenge facing attempts to change the culture of schooling, and of particular concern to us, science teaching as a cultural practice. Approaches to supporting these complex cultural shifts frequently involve attempts to “scale -up” changes, most often via curricular interventions in combination with distributed professional learning (e.g., Edelson, et al., 2021). While there has been success with change at scale, at least at the level of school districts attempts at large- scale change are mixed (e.g. Spillane, et al., 2018), generally have been shown to impact only smaller groups of “maverick” teachers more directly engaged with funded projects, or produce superficial changes in practice leaving the instructional core relatively stable (Cuban, 2013). Repeated efforts to change practice over time can also lead to a kind of change exhaustion, where teachers see all change efforts as transitory and choose to wait them out (Del Schalock, 2006). This manuscript describes an approach to school change that conceptualizes scaling in a long- term and organic way. The context is a 15+ year research-practice partnership built around a core community of secondary in-service science teachers, science teacher educators, preservice secondary science teachers, and middle school students. P articipants are in multiple overlapping professional learning experiences, but given our roles our narrative focuses on one activity of the community - an embedded, practice -based science teacher preparation program. The beginning of the partnership is retroactively marked by the meeting of members in 2006 and more officially and externally recognized with a more intentional and structured community of teacher learning that began to form five years later. Regardless, the consistent focus of the community has been on the negotiation and transformation of the cultural practices of science teaching and the intimately related transformation of the identities of the individuals of the community and their institutional contexts – their university, their schools, and more distal impacts on other schools, the state, and the field of science education. 774 Organizational structures are fundamentally dynamic, cultural, and porous. They are constantly being created and recreated by the interactions of the participants that make them up. As participants move between contexts they carry with them and create anew their identities as members of their multiple communities. They are constantly negotiating the work of those communities and how the present set of participants are constructing the meaning of that work. There is historicity to this process, which constrains and affords the possible work of participants and frames their on -going negotiation of meaning. To understand the nature of the organizational interactions (and change) that occur via more localized negotiations of meaning, there is a need to attend to interactions across scales. To see how small moments of interaction and negotiation construct patterns over time and (re)create the constituent communities. Much of the research on organizational change attends to macro scale, change is typically addressed via policies (including curricula and assessments) or other formalized components of organizations (e.g. Spillane, et al., 2018). Other approaches attempt to study change by focusing on micro-scale negotiation of meaning occurring between participants in classrooms or in professional learning contexts (e.g. Gomoll, Hmelo-Silver, & Šabanović, 2022). There is also a meso-scale, the stories and negotiated meanings that are created at the micro -scale and bridge to the creation and reification of macro -scale formalisms. As participants move through various contexts their pathways intertwine and separate creating a temporal fabric as imagined by Kurt Vonnegut’s Tralfamadorians, who see human lives as a kind of temporal skein of yarn. This fabric is woven of stories told between participants about themselves and each other across the contexts that make up their lives and their community participation. To successfully cultivate change in these tapestries of human interaction, we need to attend not just to the individual interactions, or the structure of the entire fabric; we need to think about the creation of learning environments as the creation of space to allow others to become new people, to create new selves that reflect new meanings they have negotiated with each other. To conceptualize this process we draw upon professional vision (Goodwin, 1994) to help us understand these social negotiations and how they continually recreate professional communities and their practices. Professional vision is not the particular lens an individual uses to view social interactions, it is a description of the stabilities and instabilities created by participants through the negotiation of meaning in a communities’ social practices over time. Conceptual/Theoretical framework “Knowing is inherent in the growth and transformation of identities and it is located in relations among practitioners, their practice, the artifacts of that practice, and the social organization and political economy of communities of practice” (Lave & Wenger, 1989, p. 122). Theoretical understandings of and research on teacher learning is often limited by its contextual focus (e.g., universities, schools, professional learning activities) or the conceptualization of teacher learning as individual/cognitive (e.g., knowledge framed as Pedagogical Content Knowledge, beliefs, or dispositions), which often carries with it a deficit framing ( Gray, McDonald, & Stroupe, 2022). In contrast, this study views teacher learning as a sociocultural practice of negotiation of professional vision (Goodwin, 1994) within a teacher community of practice at broad temporal and physical scales. We focus not only on a group of teachers in a single context negotiating a current set of dilemmas regarding changing practice (e.g., McCausland et al., 2023), but as a defining characteristic of an on-going, historical, and dynamic learning community that occurs across different sites, places, or contexts, as well as spanning years of collaborative negotiation, all of which is in response to the overlapping political economies of relevant social organizations. Communities of Practice (Lave & Wenger, 1991) is a well-established framing of how people learn focused on social practice as not just the mechanism of learning, but the definition of the outcome of learning. Learning is viewed as a change in practice, both of the individuals in the community, but also, in interaction with the changes in the norms and practices of the community. Similarly, individuals’ learning can be thought of as changes in identity within the community that are negotiated and manifest through practice with other participants in the community. One of the core pieces of this process identified by Wenger, is the negotiation of meaning. The term negotiation tends to evoke a discourse or even an argument, in the argumentation sense of that concept, between members of a community about the meaning of their practice; however, negotiation is more subtle and implicit in communities of practice. It entails subtle shifts in what is acceptable practice and talk that happen as groups of individuals determine what it is that defines the collective work of their profession. In short, it is a negotiation of professional vision. Over the past ten or more years, Goodwin’s (1994) original notion has often been taken up as a more individually cognitive focused notion (e.g., vanEs & Sherin, 2021), characterizing professional vision as a sort of 775 individual lens for viewing teaching and guiding individual’s decision making. We take a broader and more practice focused conception directly grounded in Goodwin’s original notion: “Discursive practices are used by members of a profession to shape events in the domains subject to their professional scrutiny. The shaping process creates the objects of knowledge that become the insignia of a profession's craft: the theories, artifacts, and bodies of expertise that distinguish it from other professions. Analysis of the methods used by members of a community to build and contest the events that structure their lifeworld contributes to the development of a practice-based theory of knowledge and action." (italics added, 1994, p. 606) It is this building and contesting that we consider to be a characterization of the negotiation of meaning that occurs in communities of practice. This kind of social negotiation is not only seen in the minute -to-minute discourse between members of a professional community ( McCausland et al., 2023), but also in how those members draw on other external communities they participate in, for example, to play with policies cutting across organizational levels of a system (Bateman & McDonald , 2023). Professional vision’s social negotiation focuses on how community norms and understandings shift over longer periods of time and are reflected in the reified and tacit activities of those communities. This can be seen in how teachers change the focus of their own profe ssional learning, the problems of practice they identify, and ideally how those problems without ceilings (Thompson, 2015) are continually renegotiated as the community deepens their understanding of their own goals and practices. Our work uses this more community negotiation focused framing of professional vision as a key construct of analysis to determine the dynamically negotiated objects of knowledge that form the core of a learning community. For the research community to move beyond less productive and deficit framings of professional learning that proliferate in the field such as short term (e.g. one week) sessions or narrowly focused session (e.g. targeting particular curriculum or content topics), we need to have ways of investigating teacher learning at different grain-sizes and scales which conceptualize teacher learning as the complex and embedded social practice that it is. This manuscript is an attempt to tell a richer story of the organic origin, development, and eventu al design-based evolution of a community of teacher learning thorough the negotiation of meaning done to establish the objects of knowledge that make up professional vision. Specifically, we address the research questions: 1) What are the patterns of growt h and development of the objects of knowledge for a teacher learning community that intentionally interweaves university and school contexts? 2) What attributes seem to support the long- term engagement, growth, and learning of such a teacher learning community? Design/Procedure The research-practice partnership in this study developed over the course of 15+ years. In that time, numerous funded and unfunded research projects took place, hundreds of pre -service science teachers were educated, thousands of K-12 science students were impacted, and generations of science education researchers were a part of participating in and investigating teacher learning within the partnership. We say this to indicate the context we are describing is complex both temporally and socially. To attempt to capture this complexity, to describe how the partnership negotiated science teaching and learning over time (Goodwin, 1994), we recognized that traditional qualitative coding of interactions would not suffice, so we turned to narrative methods. By using narrative methods, we can navigate temporal, social, and contextual boundaries to communicate and transmit complex knowledge (Huber et al., 2016) about a dynamic social system of learning. Narrative methods allow us to show how educational contexts might be transformed and render visible “things heretofore unnoticed” (Lewis, 2011, p 504) by telling “real stories” (Gallagher, 2011) that can help shift practices and pedagogies. In fact, narrative methods make it possible to capture the people, places, and events that occur over time in relation to learning. By telling stories it is possible to weave together learning and the context in which learning happens because as Clandinin and Connelly (2000) state, “People are individuals and need to be understood as such, but they cannot be understood only as individuals. They are always in relation, always in a social context” (p. 2). So, while narrative methods are used to delve into an individual’s experience, they can also be used as “an exploration of the social, cultural and institutional narratives within which individual’s experiences are constituted, shaped, expressed and enacted - but in a way that begins and ends that inquiry in the storied lives of the people involved” (Clandinin & Rosiek, 2007, p 42). To gather the narratives, we generated stories based on our memory and we contacted preservice teachers, mentor teachers, and others involved in the community over time to describe “your experience and what you feel are key takeaways about how students learn science and how teachers learn to teach.” Part of this process included revisiting data, that included video, audio, and documents, from previous funded and unfunded projects 776 and articles written that focused on actors in the partnership to help create a timeline of events, confirm particular stories, and support our narration of how the partnership grew over time. Once we gathered the data, we constructed narratives through a process of mutual storytelling to explain the learning in context rather than produce a cause -and-effect relationship (Connelly & Clandinin, 1990). Our process took the form of writing and rewriting narratives based on moments in the larger data corpus that stood out as important (Maclure, 2013). The stories demonstrated the tensions, successes, and serendipitous moments involved in the development of the partnership to help demonstrate the negotiations (i.e. learning) that occurred within it (Rodriguez & Morrison, 2019). Finally, we took the narrative(s) and embedded theory to help us make “connections” between learning and the “individual lives” of the participants and discern the “order and pattern” (Maclure, 2013, p. 229) necessary to produce “humble” theory (Cobb et al., 2003) that goes beyond a report of “what happened.” Below is an abridged narrative intended to provide insight into the data, findings, and analysis. Scott began teaching science methods courses that focused on enactment of inquiry science teaching, specifically the nature of authenticity in science teaching ( McDonald & Songer, 2008).
