title: Designing for Affective Equity in Partnerships
citation: Blanca Gamez-Djokic (2026). Designing for Affective Equity in Partnerships. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Gamez-Djokic, B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Research-practice partnerships (RPPs) have become central to the learning sciences as infrastructures for addressing educational challenges. While much scholarship emphasizes their design principles and effectiveness, less attention has been paid to the affective life of partnerships. This paper advances a conceptual argument that RPPs function as pedagogical sites of affectivity. They not only rely on dispositions such as trust, humility, or perseverance but also cultivate, normalize, and organize which affective orientations become legitimate forms of participation. I call this the ontological goodness of RPPs – the assumption that collaboration is inherently moral and transformative which imbues partnerships with affective demands that shape who can participate fully and on what terms. Reframing purpose as an affective terrain highlights a hidden curriculum of partnership and raises new learning and design questions: what would it mean to design RPPs for affective equity where multiple orientations are legible and recognized as legitimate forms of participation?

title: Embracing the Complexity of a Learning Ecology Design for an Online Asynchronous Undergraduate Science Course
citation: Heather K. Patterson, Dori Do, Jonan Phillip Donaldson (2026). Embracing the Complexity of a Learning Ecology Design for an Online Asynchronous Undergraduate Science Course. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Patterson, H. K., Do, D., & Donaldson, J. P.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Online asynchronous courses present a fundamental challenge in that uniform designs encounter wonderfully diverse learners, creating heterogeneous experiences that traditional analytics fail to capture. This study adopts a complex systems perspective drawi ng on principles from cognitive constructivist, social constructivist, constructionist, and transformative learning theories to understand learning ecologies in an undergraduate marine science course. Using learning experience network analysis (LENA), we analyzed 38 student reflection papers, identifying patterns among struggles, aspects that worked well, and theoretical alignments. Three distinct learning ecologies emerged. Foundational Learner experiences engaged primarily with cognitive constructivist pr ocesses. Collaborator experiences thrived in social meaning-making frameworks. Transformer experiences navigated transformative learning through critical reflection. Rather than universalized designs, we developed ecology- specific design moves that embraced the complexity and messiness of learning. This approach suggested that powerful online learning design requires environments capable of supporting multiple simultaneous learning ecologies rather than flattening student diversity into averaged experiences.

title: Teacher Engagement in Online Micro-Credential Professional Development
citation: Ester Shtaingart, Laila Sliman, Linor Hadar, Tsafrir Goldberg, Arnon Hershkovitz (2026). Teacher Engagement in Online Micro-Credential Professional Development. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Shtaingart, E., Sliman, L., Hadar, L., Goldberg, T., & Hershkovitz, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Micro-credentials promise flexible, competency -based teacher professional development, yet understanding teacher engagement within these platforms remains a challenge. This study explores teacher engagement by analyzing large -scale digital trace data (N=5,271) from eight courses on Israel’s national micro-credential platform. It investigates how engagement can be empirically conceptualized, what are its underlying dimensions, how they predict learning outcomes, and what distinct engagement profiles emerge. Factor analysis revealed three engagement dimensions: forum activity, quiz performance, and learning effort. Regression analysis showed that forum activity was the strongest predictor of course and task completion. Cluster analysis identified three teacher profiles, revealing a misalignment between effort and achievement. These findings provide a data‑driven conceptualization of engagement and inform the design of online professional learning environments.

title: Epistemological Beliefs: A Missing Link in Funds of Knowledge/Identity Scholarship
citation: Evana Nusrat Dooty, Reagan Curtis (2026). Epistemological Beliefs: A Missing Link in Funds of Knowledge/Identity Scholarship. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Dooty, E. N. & Curtis, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Funds of Knowledge & Cultural Wealth; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies
abstract: This paper explores the intersection between Schommer’s Epistemological Belief Model and the Funds of Knowledge/Identity (FoK/I) framework to better understand how teachers’ beliefs about knowledge influence FoK/I approach. Drawing on qualitative data from teacher interviews, the study highlights how naïve epistemological beliefs, such as viewing knowledge as fixed, certain, or exclusively derived from authority, may limit the recognition of FoK/I, while more sophisticated beliefs support the integration of students’ cultural, experiential, and practical knowledge into classroom learning. Findings demonstrate that teachers with constructivist and growth-oriented beliefs are more likely to scaffold learning through students’ FoK/I. Despite the richness of FoK /I scholarship, limited research has examined the role of epistemological beliefs in shaping how teachers utilize students’ FoK/I. This study addresses that gap by offering a conceptual framework that links epistemological beliefs with FoK/I, contributing to broader discussions on equity- oriented pedagogy and culturally responsive teaching.

title: Towards Dignity for Multilingual Learners in Science: A Framework to Examine Dignity- Conferring Classroom Interactions
citation: Caitlin G. McC. Fine, Samuel Lee, Melissa Braaten (2026). Towards Dignity for Multilingual Learners in Science: A Framework to Examine Dignity- Conferring Classroom Interactions. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Fine, C. G. M., Lee, S., & Braaten, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Resisting dignity-denying practices in education is urgent. This paper is guided by Poza’s (2021) call to center racialized multilingual students as rights- bearing individuals through a dignity frame grounded in meaningful participation, social agency, and social equality. Using secondary qualitative analysis of our own prior studies in science classrooms, we reexamine classroom moments to identify how dignity is conferred. Two cases illustrate this frame: bilingual students’ poetic talk during formative assessment, and a teacher’s curriculum design that leveraged multimodality as poetic “talk” and inclusive sensemaking. Findings highlight how discourse moves, translanguaging, and multimodality can confer dignity by affirming students’ humanity and agency. The dignity frame provides educators and researchers with an analytic and pedagogical tool to identify, enact, and design dignity-conferring classroom interactions.

title: Worlding With Bees: iPad Readings and AR Explorations as Multispecies Pedagogies
citation: Kristiina Kumpulainen (2026). Worlding With Bees: iPad Readings and AR Explorations as Multispecies Pedagogies. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Kumpulainen, K.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study examines how children’s encounters with bees, mediated through different digital assemblages, opened distinct possibilities for inquiry, affect, and ethical orientation. Fifty -two Grade 5 –7 students from various schools in urban British Columbia, Canada, either read informational texts and graphics about bees on iPads or used an augmented reality (AR) Bee Explorer app featuring 3D Bee models triggered by flower recognition, with both activities taking place in community garden parks as situated child– bee–technology encounters. Afterward, students responded individually in writing about their feelings toward bees and questions they still wanted to pursue. A diffractive reading of these students’ responses, informed by posthumanist concepts of learning-with and becoming-with, traced how different child–bee–technology encounters enacted divergent pedagogical openings. Responses in the iPad engagement centered on factual knowledge, exemplifying a “learning about” orientation that positioned bees as objects of study. By contrast, the AR engagement prompted ethical and ecological questions alongside affective expressions of care, joy, and responsibility. These differences point to how AR, by staging more immersive and interactive encounters, can amplify affective and ethical orientations that remain less visible in text-based engagements. The study contributes to multispecies pedagogies by illustrating how digital technologies can invite children to think, feel, and inquire with more-than-human life.

title: Creating Artifacts for Expansive Science Teaching through Art-Based Collaboration
citation: Deborah Dutta, Miwa A. Takeuchi (2026). Creating Artifacts for Expansive Science Teaching through Art-Based Collaboration. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Dutta, D. & Takeuchi, M. A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The need for newer ways to enact human- nature relationships calls for educational practices to expand their boundaries of learning. Several educational initiatives have engaged in integrating arts -based practices with science learning to broaden the scope and aims of learning. However, the creation of artifacts that mediate the processes by which science educators can expand their pedagogical repertoire to engage with the emergent possibilities of arts-based practices has received less attention. This study describes collaborative processes between an artist and a pre-service teacher, Becca, which inspired her attempts to reimagine her teaching aims and practices, as part of a summer camp research –design partnership on a community urban farm. The study highlights how the evolution of pedagogical artifacts through collaborations made space for emergent learning anchored in embodied experiences.

title: Bridging Theory and Practice: A Design-Based Research Approach to Strengthening Evaluation in Science Museums
citation: Kari Ross Nelson, Lisa Lundgren (2026). Bridging Theory and Practice: A Design-Based Research Approach to Strengthening Evaluation in Science Museums. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Nelson, K. R. & Lundgren, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This design -based research study examines the relationship between evaluation theory and practice in science museums. Through interviews with six museum evaluators and a broader survey, researchers found that museum evaluators have minimal engagement with formal evaluation theory, relying instead on on- the-job training, templates, and practical tools. This tenuous practice -theory relationship stems from limited formal evaluation training, with most evaluators entering the field through adjacent roles rather than intentional career planning. While evaluators do reference some pragmatic frameworks, they more commonly draw from concrete resources and theories from adjacent fields such as education and psychology. This work-in-progress outlines the first phase of a multi-phase DBR project aimed at co-designing a professional learning tool that strengthens evaluation theory use among science museum evaluators. This research demonstrates how learning sciences methodologies can advance understanding of learning in informal contexts while simultaneously contributing to practice - based theory development in evaluation.

title: Conceptions of Learning With (and Without) Technology in Undergraduate Mathematics Courses
citation: Oleksii Voronkin, Peter J. Woods (2026). Conceptions of Learning With (and Without) Technology in Undergraduate Mathematics Courses. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Voronkin, O. & Woods, P. J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Employing the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework, t his paper investigates undergraduate students’ per ceptions of digital technologies in mathematics education. While technologies are often promoted as catalysts for transforming mathematical learning, little is known about how students themselves conceptualize their value. Based on the qualitative strand of an ongoing mixed- methods study in the UK, we present an emergent analysis of three in -depth student interviews. Thematic analysis yielded three categories: learning without technology, technology as access to learning, and learning through engaging technology. Students frequently regarded technologies as barrier s when they replaced core mathematical activity but valued them as efficient tools for accessing resources or as environments for independent exploration. These findings suggest that students adopt a bounded and strategic stance: resisting substitution, embracing access, and leveraging exploration. Implications are discussed for designing digital environments that support curiosity, experimentation, and differentiated pathways in undergraduate mathematics.

title: Teacher-Developed Design Principles for Assessing Critical Thinking
citation: Kimberly Erickson, Kyle Dunbar, Kelly Mills (2026). Teacher-Developed Design Principles for Assessing Critical Thinking. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Erickson, K., Dunbar, K., & Mills, K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: We describe how nine classroom teachers designed and reflected on assessment practices for measuring critical thinking as part of a larger district Portrait of a Graduate program. Instead of developing a single assessment approach, teachers created a set of design principles that could be used flexibly by other classroom teachers seeking to assess students’ critical thinking. Our findings indicate the importance of grounding assessment of complex, transferable skills in classroom practices and student artifacts.

title: Evaluating the Impact of MathByExample on Student Mathematics Achievement
citation: Anna N. Bartel, Jacklyn Powers, Vivian Hsu, Drew Barrett, Kirk Walters, Jodi L. Davenport, WestEd, Alexandra Huyghe, Julie Booth (2026). Evaluating the Impact of MathByExample on Student Mathematics Achievement. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Bartel, A. N., Powers, J., Hsu, V., Barrett, D., Walters, K., Davenport, J. L., WestEd, Huyghe, A., & Booth, J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study evaluates the impact of MathByExample , an elementary mathematics intervention incorporating worked examples and self -explanation prompts, on fifth -grade student math achievement. Grounded in the worked example effect and self -explanation strategies, MathByExample aims to reduce common misconceptions and improve conceptual understanding in mathematics. We assessed the intervention’s impact using a three -level cluster-randomized control trial involving 1,143 students across 50 schools in Maine. Though the average treatment effect of MathByExample on student math outcomes were not statistically significant, a dosage analysis revealed that the number of attempted MathByExample items significantly predicted mathematics achievement. These findings suggest that consistent engagement with worked examples and self-explanation prompts improved learning outcomes. The results support the value of scalable, low-cost instructional tools rooted in cognitive science and highlight the importance of dosage when implementing such interventions in real -world educational settings.

title: Redesigning a Graduate Program from Instructional Design to Learning Design and Learning Sciences
citation: Jonan Phillip Donaldson (2026). Redesigning a Graduate Program from Instructional Design to Learning Design and Learning Sciences. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Donaldson, J. P.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This design contribution describes the redesign of a graduate program from instructional design to learning design. The objective was to align program structures with the learning sciences while responding to student experiences. Using l earning experience network analysis, I analyzed 118 student reflections across three semesters to identify potential design changes. The redesigned program implements empirically -informed and theory- grounded changes including portfolio-based assessment replacing comprehensive exams, design thinking coursework providing collaboration scaffolding, expanded research practicum for authentic professional work, and flexible specializations. This transformation demonstrates how design- based research methods can inform curricular reform that honors both empirical evidence and theoretical coherence. The process offers a model for graduate programs navigating paradigmatic shifts from knowledge transmission to learning as becoming.

title: Higher-Order Interactions in Learning: Extending Cognitive Load and Self-Regulated Theories through a Network Approach
citation: Koichi Yasutake, Sayaka Tohyama, Hitoshi Inoue (2026). Higher-Order Interactions in Learning: Extending Cognitive Load and Self-Regulated Theories through a Network Approach. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Yasutake, K., Tohyama, S., & Inoue, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: While learning network research focuses on pairwise relationships, we applied higher-order network analysis to three -body interactions among 39 variables (PISA 2015, n=2,189). Our approach, combining network estimation with hierarchical screening and Stability Selection, revealed emergent phenomena: interaction thresholds where two- body effects saturate, competition among multiple regulation processes, and context -dependent motivational reversals. These discoveries extend Cognitive Load and Self -Regulated Learning theories, demonstrating how higher-order analysis can refine learning theories.

title: Teacher Autonomy in Organized Informal Learning
citation: Racheli Davies, Nadav Ehrenfeld (2026). Teacher Autonomy in Organized Informal Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Davies, R. & Ehrenfeld, N.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Researchers often refer to teacher autonomy in either how they learn in professional development or how they make choices about what and how to teach. These two areas of teacher autonomy are usually studied separately, which we argue is problematic, and thus bring them together. We focus on a 4- day summer workshop where teachers were given unusually high levels of freedom to set their own goals and learning. By looking at the choices teachers made we explore what it means for teachers to exercise different kinds of professional judgment. We draw on Boote’s (2006) idea of professional discretion, illustrating how some relied on existing materials and organized them for their classrooms, while others developed new materials that addressed local student needs. By examining these choices, we highlight potential opportunities for how teacher autonomy can be supported to foster more innovative professional practice. Objective Research on teacher autonomy is fragmented across two main bodies of research. The first stems from teacher education and professional development literature and deals with different forms of teacher autonomy or its absence in their learning (e.g., Horn & Garner, 2022; Kennedy, 2019; Lefstein et al., 2020), and the second stems from policy and curriculum investigations and deals with teachers’ freedom to make choices about what they teach and how (e.g., Hong & Youngs, 2016; Pearson & Moomaw, 2005). The gap between these two bodies of knowledge is problematic because autonomy cannot be “provided” without proper support to realize it (Hargreaves, 2016; Marco et al., 2025). For these reasons, we position this paper and investigation at this intersection, in line with scholars who bridge that gap (e.g., Boote, 2006; Severance et al., 2016). From this stance, we argue that teacher curricular autonomy is both necessary and requires support for teachers to exercise it. Our overarching goal, in both practice and research, echoes Boote’s (2006) argument that “developing innovative professional discretion should be the long- term goal of teacher development and curriculum policy” (p. 468). Towards this goal, in this exploratory paper we first define teacher curricular autonomy as teachers’ capacity to make curricular choices and to implement them (Hong & Youngs, 2016; Pearson & Moomaw, 2005). Then, we present Boote’s conceptualization of three levels of teacher professional discretion marked by increased competence: procedural, substantive, and innovative professional discretion. Finally, we illustrate teacher choices in a professional development setting we call organized informal learning, distinguished from more typical PD activities by the high level of autonomy teachers are provided with. Within the context of this 4-day-long summer workshop, we ask, What type of choices did participants make about the structure and content of the curricular materials they developed? What choices did participants make about their own activity within the PD? We explore these questions with an eye towards providing fertile ground for future research and professional development designed to develop teachers’ ability to exercise innovative professional discretion. Prior literature: Connecting two notions of teacher autonomy Teachers’ autonomy in PD activities The last quarter century of research on teacher professional development (PD) is rife with critiques of traditional top-down PD, sometimes referred to as “pull -out” (Cobb et al., 2018) or “commercially available” (Kazemi & Hubbard, 2008). Within such top-down PD activities, teachers are seen as passive consumers of knowledge, with little to no influence o ver what they will learn and how (Lefstein et al., 2020). In contrast, current notions of quality teacher PD emphasize collaborative reflection on problems of teaching raised by teachers and situated in their everyday practice (e.g., Darling-Hammond et al., 2017; Ehrenfeld, 2025). A prominent example of such PD designs are Professional Learning Communities (PLCs; Brodie, 2014; Grossman et al., 2001; Popp & Goldman, 2016; Vescio et al., 2008). However, empirical results of such designs often report challenges in realizing their potential (Horn & Kane, 2015; Kennedy, 2016). In response, researchers advocate for a variety of scaffolding

title: Autonomy, Agency, and Belonging: Adults using Mobile Augmented Reality for Language Learning in the Real-World
citation: Cinamon Sunrise Bailey, Quinn Burke, Tolulope Famaye (2026). Autonomy, Agency, and Belonging: Adults using Mobile Augmented Reality for Language Learning in the Real-World. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Bailey, C. S., Burke, Q., & Famaye, T.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This qualitative multi–case study examines how six adult English language learners appropriated mobile augmented reality (MAR) through Google Lens to support language learning beyond the classroom. Guided by andragogy, mobile learning, and consequential learning frameworks, the study explores how participants used MAR to exercise choice, respond to real-world language needs, and expand their identities as capable actors in English- dominant spaces. Data from MAR activities, interviews, and artifacts show that learners self - directed vocabulary development, mobilized home languages to support understanding, and engaged in just -in-time learning in everyday contexts such as museums, markets, and public transportation. MAR enabled participants to integrate English practice into daily life, enhancing access to information and opportunities for belonging while strengthening confidence to communicate across settings. Findings highlight the potential of MAR to foster autonomy and consequential learning in adult second language education and call for further research on equitable, technology-supported language learning environments.

title: Do Students Recognize Personalization? Comparing Personalized vs. Common- Solution Parsons Code Puzzles as Problem-Solving Scaffolding
citation: Xinying Hou, Zihan Wu, Xu Wang, Barbara J. Ericson (2026). Do Students Recognize Personalization? Comparing Personalized vs. Common- Solution Parsons Code Puzzles as Problem-Solving Scaffolding. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Hou, X., Wu, Z., Wang, X., & Ericson, B. J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Parsons code puzzles, which require students to arrange mixed -up code blocks into a correct program, can scaffold students who struggle while programming. Large language models can generate personalized Parsons puzzles based on students' existing incorrect code. However, the effects of such personalization remain underexplored, especially compared to the standard use of common- solution puzzles. We examined it with 85 students through a programming classroom study: students had access to personalized (PP) or only common- solution (CP) Parsons puzzles as scaffolding. We found that students who received a personalized puzzle rated the solution’s alignment with their own approach as 16% higher than with a common -solution puzzle. We also found preliminary evidence of a mediated pathway through which personalized puzzles improved scaffolding puzzle solution understanding via higher perceived solution alignment. This work offers insights for approachable AI -powered personalization during problem-solving.

title: Design and Development of a Japanese Lesson Study Project through a Research- Practice Partnershipthrough research-practice partnership
citation: Shinya Iikubo, Hajime Shirouzu, Moegi Saito (2026). Design and Development of a Japanese Lesson Study Project through a Research- Practice Partnershipthrough research-practice partnership. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Iikubo, S., Shirouzu, H., & Saito, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: To expand the knowledge base on Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs), this study examines an empirical case of a hybrid RPP model operating within a sociocultural context outside North America. We analyze the 16-year development of a Japanese lesson study project employing the Knowledge Constructive Jigsaw method. The project is examined as an evolving activity system, reorganizing findings from previous research to highlight the contradictions, conflicts, and challenges that emerged, as well as the design strategies implemented to address them, drawing on Cultural-Historical Activity Theory. Our findings demonstrate how RPPs can function as collaborative platforms for practitioners and researchers that can be sustained and developed iteratively by aligning with the principles of Networked Improvement Communities.

title: Evaluating for Ideas: A Method for Scoring Fine-Grained Analyses in Chemistry Assessment
citation: Joel P. Beier, Laura Salman, Michael I. Swart, Samuel Pazicni, Mitchell J. Nathan (2026). Evaluating for Ideas: A Method for Scoring Fine-Grained Analyses in Chemistry Assessment. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Beier, J. P., Salman, L., Swart, M. I., Pazicni, S., & Nathan, M. J.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Understanding how students organize their ideas is a central concern in chemistry education research. Chemistry students coordinate abstract ideas from multiple levels of behavior to explain how a complex system of particles results in observable behavior. While fine-grained constructivist perspectives offer an analytic framework for identifying organizing knowledge structures, researchers sometimes abandon this perspective and adopt more deficit - oriented frameworks when interested in comparing the quality of student responses. The current work presents a method for assigning a composite quality score based on numbers of unique, scientifically valid ideas expressed and the connections drawn between them. This approach uses a syntax -based method to unitize distinct ideas as well as identify and quantify links between them. Preliminary analyses demonstrate that this approach captured the richness, organization, and scoring of students’ reasoning. These findings have implications for how researchers and practitioners assess conceptual understanding and track the reorganization of ideas over time.

title: Building Groupwork Moment by Moment: A Preliminary Typology of Social Bids in Secondary Mathematics Classrooms
citation: Katherine C. Chapman, Elizabeth Metts, Maria Maria Castillo (2026). Building Groupwork Moment by Moment: A Preliminary Typology of Social Bids in Secondary Mathematics Classrooms. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Chapman, K. C., Metts, E., & Castillo, M. M.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Groupwork is often touted as a tool to support mathematics students to build on their own thinking rather than learning concepts by rote, yet supporting robust cooperative sensemaking is a difficult problem of practice. As part of a study on how teachers l earn to facilitate groupwork, we explored how students build a foundation for successful collaboration. Using the sensitizing concept of bids for connection, we analyze how cooperation is established and maintained by students in secondary mathem atics classrooms. We see this as adjacent to work on belonging and rightful presence, while bringing notions of sociomathematical norms into conversations about trust and social cohesion. Importantly, however, we focus on the interaction order rather than on social structures to see what we might add to anal yses of status and authority at an alternate scale. Preliminary findings include an initial typology of bids, and possible implications for facilitating groupwork in mathematics classrooms.

title: Connecting Teacher Sensemaking to Instructional Practice
citation: Christina Kimmerling, Patricia Fuentes Acevedo, Rossella Santagata (2026). Connecting Teacher Sensemaking to Instructional Practice. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Kimmerling, C., Acevedo, P. F., & Santagata, R.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: A large body of research has identified core features of effective professional development (PD). Recently, scholars called for moving beyond core features to understand the mechanisms that support teacher learning. This study contributes to this aim by tracing teachers’ sensemaking of PD to their classroom implementation. In the context of a two-year PD initiative in mathematics, this study investigates the relationship between seven teachers’ perceptions of the PD and their instructional practice. Emergin g findings suggest three profiles of teachers’ conceptualizations of the PD approach to teaching and learning. How teachers conceptualized the PD was tightly aligned with what was observed in their practice. These findings have implications for theories of action to support teacher learning during PD. Objectives A substantial body of research has identified core features of effective professional development (PD) (e.g., Desimone, 2009; Darling- Hammond et al., 2017), recognizing the need for high -quality teacher learning experiences that change teachers’ practices and, in turn, improve student outcomes. Recently, this scholarship has been critiqued for overlooking the theories of action and mechanisms that support teacher learning and the highly contextualized nature of PD programs (Asterhan & Lefstein, 2024). Yet, h ow teachers take up PD learning is informed by their individual and collective sensemaking processes, and situational factors they face (Warner et al., 2022). Moreover, impactful professional learning often requires building teachers’ situation-specific decision- making skills, which is more complex than asking teachers to implement a set of procedures with fidelity (Kennedy, 2019). This suggests that the field needs more fine -grained analyses of how teachers make sense of PD focused on developing their decision-making skills and how that sensemaking is reflected in their instructional practices. This paper aims to serve that purpose. In our context, elementary school teachers participated in PD around Cognitively Guided Instruction (CGI; Carpenter et al., 2015), which aims to increase teacher knowledge of research on children’s mathematical thinking to inform their instructional decision- making. In this study, we ask: How do teachers conceptualize the PD’s approach to teaching and learning? How are teachers’ conceptualizations connected to their instructional practice? Implications from our findings can contribute to refining theorizations of how teachers learn and inform future PD designs that move beyond core features . Theoretical framework We draw on sensemaking theory (Weick et al., 2005), which recognizes sensemaking as an individual cognitive process and as socially situated. Teachers make sense of PD through an iterative, interpretive process of both talk and action; they begin to conceptualize PD learning within their existing understandings and practice, enact these new understandings in their teaching, which then leads to new conceptualizations of PD learning. At the same time, their sensemaking is influenced by the broader context in which they work, including their interactions with colleagues (Spillane et al., 2018) and the guidance they receive from school leaders (Coburn, 2005). Recent research on teacher sensemaking has highlighted its culturally situated (Liang et al., 2025) and socially constructed (Daniel et al., 2023) nature, suggesting that teachers make sense of PD through mental frameworks shaped by not only their district infrastructure but also broader cultural narratives surrounding mathematics teaching and learning. In this paper, participating teachers engaged in PD aimed at improving their knowledge-based reasoning and situation -specific decision -making skills. This type of PD recognizes that teachers must learn to enact particular practices contingent upon what their students understand and aims to develop teachers’ strategies and insights (Kennedy, 2019). In this study, we extend limited research that has investigated the link between teachers’ sensemaking of PD and their classroom decisions (Knapp & Peterson, 1995; Rimbey & Kucan, 2018; Warner et al., 2022), particularly around responsive mathematics teaching that builds on students’ emerging understandings.

title: Maximize Learning and Fun: How to Integrate In-game Learning Supports into Digital Learning Games
citation: Seyedahmad Rahimi, Mahboobeh Mehrvarz, Samaneh Abdoli, Salah Esmaeiligoujar, Bruce McLaren (2026). Maximize Learning and Fun: How to Integrate In-game Learning Supports into Digital Learning Games. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Rahimi, S., Mehrvarz, M., Abdoli, S., Esmaeiligoujar, S., & McLaren, B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Digital learning games have significant potential to enhance student learning by combining engaging gameplay with academic content. While previous reviews have explored learning supports in games, none have specifically focused on in-game, content-related supports in pre -K-12 settings. This systematic review, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, addresses this gap by analyzing 58 studies to examine the design, delivery, and impact of these supports. Findings reveal diverse outcomes, ranging from cognitive to mixed cognitive and non- cognitive goals. Serious games were the most studied genre, followed by puzzle games. A strong link emerged between the integration level of supports —intrinsic inte gration—and positive learning outcomes. The delivery method (system -controlled, user-controlled, or mixed) also influenced effectiveness. Most studies (n = 30) used system-controlled delivery, followed by user-controlled (n = 21) and mixed ( n = 7). These f indings offer guidance for designing learning games that balance engagement and learning.

title: Causal Reasoning Through Drawing: Explore How Students Organise Their Thoughts in Space
citation: Vanessa de Andrade, Michal Haskel-Ittah, Yael Shwartz (2026). Causal Reasoning Through Drawing: Explore How Students Organise Their Thoughts in Space. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Andrade, V. D., Haskel-Ittah, M., & Shwartz, Y.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study aims to explore how drawing supports students' causal reasoning when the conceptual complexity of distant attentional frames is present. Five pairs of students (ages 11-13) participated in 90-minute drawing sessions, where they attempted to link causes and effects across different attentional frames, specifically reasoning about how local food waste may be linked to the decline of polar bears in a remote region. We identified four linking strategies students came up with: gap narrowing, finding p ossible channels, identifying mediating steps, and identifying underlying players. In addition, through a multimodal analysis of video recordings, we explored students' actions and interactions with their drawings in specific episodes when they came up with these strategies to propose causal links across spatial gaps. These findings suggest that drawing serves important interactional functions extending beyond its representational one, which in these cases supported sophisticated causal thinking that resembles scientific reasoning strategies.

title: Small vs. Large Language Models: Comparing Language Models in Generating Productive Failure Math Problems
citation: Seyedahmad Rahimi, Salah Esmaeiligoujar, Deniz Ercan, Maryam Babaee, Ran Gao (2026). Small vs. Large Language Models: Comparing Language Models in Generating Productive Failure Math Problems. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Rahimi, S., Esmaeiligoujar, S., Ercan, D., Babaee, M., & Gao, R.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT -4o can generate high -quality math problems but are resource -intensive and difficult to fine -tune. Small language models (SLMs) like Phi-3 may provide a more practical alternative, as they can run locally and be adapted for specific tasks. In this study, we generated 60 Productive Failure (PF) math problems, with half produced by GPT-4o and half by Phi-3. To ensure comparability, we controlled for grade level, Common Core standard, theme, interest, and prior knowledge. Trained raters evaluated the problems across five PF dimensions. Results showed that GPT -4o ( M = 13.38; SD = 1.88) outperformed Phi-3 (M = 10.67; SD = 2.73), with a large effect size ( d = 1.16). These findings indicate that although GPT -4o currently generates more effective PF problems, Phi -3 shows promising potential. With further fine-tuning and task-specific adaptation, SLMs like Phi-3 may offer a sustainable, cost-effective solution for educational problem generation.

title: “They Have to be More Specific, or AI isn't Gonna Get What You Are Saying”: Exploring AI with Children in an Online AI Literacy Workshop
citation: Tolulope Famaye, Oluwadara Abimbade, Ibrahim Oluwajoba Adisa (2026). “They Have to be More Specific, or AI isn't Gonna Get What You Are Saying”: Exploring AI with Children in an Online AI Literacy Workshop. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Famaye, T., Abimbade, O., & Adisa, I. O.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Children’s growing interactions with AI often occur without an understanding of its underlying mechanisms and potential biases in decision- making. Adopting a socio- constructivist approach, we explore the AI competencies that children (ages 7 –12) developed as they engaged in a five -day virtual workshop. Activities included training AI models with Teachable Machine, producing media with generative AI tools such as Canva, and participating in guided discussions about the societal implications of AI. Findings show that children developed competencies in identifying AI technologies, understanding how AI operates through data, and evaluating AI outputs. These findings suggest that providing opportunities for early hands-on engagement and guided discussion can empower children to reason thoughtfully about how AI works, engage with it in both critical and creative ways, and reflect on its broader societal implications.

title: Infrastructuring for Climate Justice in STEM-Rich Making
citation: Wisam Sedawi, Edna Tan (2026). Infrastructuring for Climate Justice in STEM-Rich Making. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Sedawi, W. & Tan, E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
conceptualisations_list: Co-Design & Participatory Design; Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: This study employs critical participatory design- based research to investigate how integrating infrastructuring practices into a community- based STEM-rich maker program supports youth in responding to urgent, felt challenges of climate change through their making, while also promoting sustainable communities. Grounded in the experiences of middle school youth participating in a year -long, community -centered program, our findings highlight how infrastructural resources (material, relational, social /emotional, and intellectual) enabled youth to engage in meaningful, climate-focused making. These resources became a site for incubating ways of knowing and being, as they emerged as connective tissue linking people, practices, and contexts through acts of making for change. They fostered solidarity and shared responsibility by positioning youth as active agents in generating educative, solution- oriented artifacts for climate justice and reorganizing physical spaces using maker materials. We argue that int egrating infrastructural resources into community-based STEM-rich making supports youth-led responses to climate change and advances justice-oriented outcomes.

title: “He probably did something really, really badder than anything”: Leveraging Black Children’s Sociopolitical Sensemaking as Resources in Co-Learning with Educators
citation: Natalie R. Davis (2026). “He probably did something really, really badder than anything”: Leveraging Black Children’s Sociopolitical Sensemaking as Resources in Co-Learning with Educators. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Davis, N. R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigated how educators interpreted and responded to a case of a Black child’s sociopolitical sensemaking. As part of a larger social design experiment and interviews conducted with 12 justice-oriented teachers, I presented participants with an extended example of a child (“Chase”) describing circumstances surrounding the highly- publicized murder of Freddie Gray. The purpose of this paper is to (1) report on select findings related to educators’ analysis of the Chase example and (2) discuss the relationship between their sensemaking and subsequent pedagogical design thinking. Findings show how many defaulted to developmental lenses that emphasized naivete, empathizing while overlooking the complex reasoning embedded in Chase’s ideas. This shaped the pedagogical possibilities they imagined in response. This work highlights the need for conceptual and methodological tools that attune educators to the sociopolitical and intellectual lives of Black children and, that position children as epistemic contributors and partners in justice-oriented educational design.

title: Simulations to Facilitate AI Literacy for Teachers and School Leaders
citation: Tanmay Sinha, Sayhao Lim, Peter Seow, David Hung (2026). Simulations to Facilitate AI Literacy for Teachers and School Leaders. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Sinha, T., Lim, S., Seow, P., & Hung, D.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: We developed a novel web -based simulation targeting the concept of feed -forward neural networks for an adult educator audience comprising two distinct cohorts of teacher s (N = 24) and school leaders ( N = 23). Both cohorts showed gains in their conceptual knowledge from pretest to posttest, with the school leaders cohort improving relatively more (Cohen’s d = 0.40). Comparative analyses suggested that using our simulation led to lower perceptions of usability and learning effectiveness in school leaders relative to teachers , but higher actual a s well as normalized learning gains on the administered performance assessments. These results highlight a perception-performance discrepancy when learners grapple with less-than-perfectly- intuitive interfaces, which despite resulting in low fluency, lead to better learning.

title: Designing Comic Cons for Scientific Literacy and Sustained Engagement
citation: Eric Kirk, Lisa Lundgren, Gabriel-Philip Santos (2026). Designing Comic Cons for Scientific Literacy and Sustained Engagement. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Kirk, E., Lundgren, L., & Santos, G.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Embodied Cognition & Gestures; Design-Based Research (DBR)
abstract: Preparing scientifically literate individuals who can use science in their day -to-day lives is an important mission for science educators. Research and interventions in service of this often emphasize practical applications in formal settings. However, we argue that informal, adult-focused science events at comic cons offer potential as a venue for cultivating scientific literacy. Promoting scientific literacy in these contexts requires balancing the need for designs that support focused learning goals without detracting from attendees’ personal enjoyment, impeding science identity development, or snuffing out emerging interest in science. Here we present a design conjecture aimed at balancing these competing concerns. Cultivating scientific literacy at adult science entertainment events Public trust in scientists is declining, and many individuals perceive science as something distant, inaccessible, or “not for them” (Kennedy & Tyson, 2023). Cultivating competent outsiders — scientifically literate individuals who can “recognize the moments when science has some bearing on their needs and interests and to interact with sources of scientific expertise in ways that help them achieve their own goals”, is a critical mission for science educators (Feinstein, 2011, p.180). Traditionally, research concerning competent outsiders has been framed with a focus on practical use, such as decision -making surrounding socioscientific issues (e.g., Feinstein & Baram - Tsabari, 2024). Although valuable, we argue that helping learners recognize science as a part of recreational, fantasy, or leisure contexts offers a valuable opportunity for enacting the vision of a competent outsider in science literacy. We present a design conjecture (e.g. Sandoval, 2014) for resources which support comic con attendees in seeking out and evaluating scientific knowledge after they leave comic cons. Specifically, this conjecture targets three outcomes derived from Feinstein’s competent outsider vision: identifying ways that scientific knowledge can enrich one’s life; pursuing scientific knowledge with intention; and aptly vetting new sources and claims. Scientific literacy and adult science entertainment events Informal science learning opportunities which target adult learners in social or recreational contexts are known as adult science entertainment events (i.e., ASEEs; West & Feinstein, 2025). A growing body of researchers have begun to focus on bringing science to everyday spaces and/or bringing everyday spaces to science (e.g., Rosin et al., 2023; Stofer et al., 2019). A specific component of these everyday spaces are those where adults can explore interests and enjoy science, such as science cafes (Childers et al., 2022), collaborations between scientists and breweries (Barrett et al., 2024), or science at art festivals (Rosin et al., 2023). ASEEs offer adults rich, fun social experiences that center science, prioritizing identity and interest development wi th developing scientific knowledge, vocabulary, or practice being obtained incidentally. This framing stands in contrast with other adult - focused informal science learning events such as citizen science bioblitzes or science policy forums which prioritize providing learners with opportunities to engage with science as scientists (West & Feinstein, 2025). Rather than nudging learners towards becoming “marginal insiders” (Feinstein, 2011) by having them engage with science in ways that replicate professional practice (e.g., citizen science), ASEEs offer a venue for participants to engage with science in ways that are directly aligned with their own interest for no reason other than to enrich their own experience (West & Feinstein, 2025). As a result, we see AS EEs as aligning with the spirit of the competent outsider vision of scientific literacy articulated by Feinstein (2011) which centers itself around recognizing instances where scientific ideas can add value to one’s life. Comic convention events as a genre of ASEEs Comic conventions (i.e., cons) are large, multiday leisure events in which fans gather to celebrate popular media, including comics, movies, video and board games, fantasy, sci -fi, and anime. During the event, fans can attend expert or celebrity -led panel discussions about their favorite media, buy merchandise or visit booths on the convention floor, cosplay (i.e., dress up in costume), and attend meet -and-greet events with celebrities (Woo et al., 2020). Fandoms, communities composed of fans of specific media, franchises, or games, are integral to comic 1247 cons. Fans focus on specific objects (e.g. Marvel comics and collectables, Magic the Gathering cards) and are united by “love, devotion, and appreciation” of those objects (Bird, 2002, p. 33). Popular culture fan identity is centered on enthusiasm, appreciation, and social interaction (Vinney et al., 2019). In the learning sciences, fandom has been explored in relation to online discussions of historical fiction (Matthews, 2016). Despite some work on popular culture in the learning sciences, relatively little is known about the intersections between popular culture, fandom identity, and science learning. In recent years, comic cons have begun to feature events which draw on fan ide ntities to cultivate interest in science (Childers et al., 2023). For example, Lundgren and colleagues (2024) found that comic con visitors’ interest and curiosity about science topics were piqued when science topics were paired with scientists dressing up in costume and roleplaying characters from popular culture (“cosplayed”). As an ASEE, the primary focus of this event was cultivating science interest by contextualizing science in an intrinsically meaningful space, however, participants may also learn s cientific ideas and vocabulary through the event. Exploring what science learning occurs during these interest and identity -focused ASEE events and how that learning can be supported presents an opportunity for future learning sciences research. ASEE/Competent outsider tensions and design constraints In their recently advanced research agenda for the ASEE field, West and Feinstein (West & Feinstein, 2025; West, 2022) identify a need for a more concrete articulation of program goals, and design-based research studying how design and implementation decisions shape the impact of these events. Accordingly, we advance a design conjecture for leveraging these events to cultivate competent outsiders (Figure 1). Despite ASEEs’ axiological alignment with the competent outsider vision, two sources of tension aris e. One of these tensions is the fleeting nature of participants’ engagement with science through these events. Previous research into cultivating competent outsiders has focused on environments where sustained engagement is possible (Osborne & Allchin, 2024). Because ASEEs occur infrequently (i.e. once a year) and for a brief time (i.e. a few days), cultivating the skills and dispositions of a competent outsider at ASEEs presents a challenge. A second tension is the need to preserve the recreational experience while helping learners develop concrete, evidence -based strategies for evaluating unfamiliar information. ASEEs’ power lies in their ability to blend science and recreation; compromising this through overly structured experiences which approximate classroom learning run counter to the design features which make them so successful. Leveraging ASEEs as a context for developing competent outsiders means finding ways to extend the learning experience, encouraging sustained engagement with scientific ideas and offering tools for interested learners once they leave the initial event. This must occur without compromising the design features which make these events enjoyable to participants. Design section Figure 1 Conjecture Map for Science Literacy Focused Adult Science Entertainment Event Design 1248 We start with the theoretical conjecture that adult science education events can be used to develop the skills and dispositions of competent outsiders. Lundgren and colleagues (2024, 2025) showed that comic cons can support individuals in seeing ways that science is personally meaningful - an important characteristic of a competent outsider. The activity structure of these events create spaces for participant interactions where fans and cosplaying scientists interact with one another. These interactions cen ter around overlaps between scientific knowledge and fan knowledge, layering ideas from both knowledge funds into an understanding of a science concept (e.g., evolution) which bleeds into both the natural and fictional worlds. Throughout these interactions , scientists and fans also come to recognize one another as members of a shared community which blends norms and values from both scientific and fan cultures. This knowledge layering and mutual recognition help position science as a personally meaningful body of knowledge for fans, and help fans see themselves as science people (Lundgren et al., 2025; Gutwill, 2018). Discursive practices, including comic con norms and values, such as embodying a character through costume and acting, and applying knowledge of a fandom have been studied to understand the mutual recognition that can occur at comic cons (Lundgren et al., 2024). In previous work, Lundgren et al. (2024) found that cosplaying scientists used narrative structure and effective framing to encourage comic con visitors’ interactions with science topics inherent to their particular fandom. For instance, when cosplaying as a Jedi knight from the Star Wars franchise, cosplaying scientists used planets from Star Wars, like Tatooine, to describe geologic processes that occur on Earth and Mars, showing comic con visitors samples of rock with fossilized ripple marks. By telling a story that incorporated the fandom (i.e., knowledge of Tatooine as a desert planet with large dust storms) and science (i.e., scientists can extrapolate ancient environmental conditions from fossilized ripple marks), the scientist and the comic con visitor’s knowledge of science and fandom were combined and celebrated, showcasing the ways science resonates with the fans’ personal interests and values. Although we see this outcome as a valuable end in itself, recognizing the value of science is not sufficient for operating as a competent outsider alone. Competent outsiders must also continually pursue scientific knowledge, and skillfully appraise the quality of new information (Feinstein, 2011). To date, these two features of a competent outsider have not yet been designed for in comic con contexts. Accordingly, we advance design recommendations to support “Scientific Collecting”: a mediating process which draws on the discursive practices endemic to these events and specially designed tools to support these two outcomes (see red highlights in Figure 1). We now turn toward delineating specific elements that comprise the embodiment (i.e. tools) and the mediating process (scientific collecting) of our design conjecture. Supporting scientific collecting as a mediating process Collecting is a central practice for many fandoms and is featured prominently at comic cons through specialized events and vendor exhibitions. Fandoms often collect real -world artifacts (e.g. comics, figurines, playing cards, autographs; Geraghty, 2014). H owever, in some cases, collecting is a central part of the fictional world. For example, in Pokemon, the activity of both real -world players and fictional characters is centered around the goal of catching and training as many species of Pokemon as they can. We argue that framing the sustained pursuit of science ideas as “Scientific Collecting” aligns science learning goals with comic con norms and values. We believe in doing so, this will promote sustained engagement with science ideas beyond the ASEE. To support this mediating process, we propose two tools which ASEE participants can take with them beyond the event: Snowball Materials and Appraisal Materials. Snowball materials Snowball Materials are materials designed to support participants extending their engagement with scientific ideas that were foregrounded in the ASEE event. These materials allow participants to “snowball” interest outwards from the fandom world and into their daily lives, incorporating “proximal” examples embedded in the fantasy world as well as “distal” examples which are concrete examples in the natural world. For example, a comic con booth crewed by cosplaying scientists might focus on ecological princi ples reflected in Pokemon. First, at the proximal end, participants will chat with cosplaying scientists who are cosplaying as Pokemon professors. During the interaction, cosplaying scientists and/or participants might describe interesting aspects about Pokemon and elements of the game, allowing connections between scientists and participants. For instance, a cosplaying scientist might pretend/share that they are a Pokemon trainer who mostly catches Combee. Combee, a bug -type Pokemon, collects Honey, an item in the world of Pokemon, for the queen of their hive. The scientist or participant might then share that this is similar to the real world (the distal example), except that bees need to first collect pollen to make honey. After the interaction, a scienti st will give a “natural history collectors’ card” modeled off Pokemon collectors’ card with information about a real -life bee species common to the area of the comic con. The card also contains resources that highlight other pollinator species, ways to attract pollinators to your home, or pollinator -safe pest management strategies. As interest snowballs it expands, collecting and integrating 1249 increasingly distal examples along the way. We provide examples in an online appendix. These materials are brief, but offer “learn more” extensions which take participants to vetted sites which contain additional information intended for the general public (e.g., the CDC, WWF). These resources may also be leveraged as research tools, tracking post -comicon engagement through clicks. These materials are designed in ways that are congruent with the participating fandom (e.g., modeling materials after a “Pokedex” - a digital reference guide within the Pokemon universe; modeling materials as collectibles themselves). Drawing from fans’ propensity to collect, obtaining all snowball materials could be gamified with a collection element, encouraging collecting of materials with a unique pin or badge that coincide with the event. Snowball materials and collecting them are thus designed to scaffold engagement and offer “just in time” information from reputable sources. Appraisal materials Collectables can be highly valuable, and counterfeits are often produced as a result. Keen collectors often must attend to subtle differences in features to discern an authentic collectable from a counterfeit (e.g., printer identification codes; see Howar d, 2025). Similarly, counterfeit scientific knowledge (e.g., misinformation and disinformation) are often found in contexts where knowledge is valuable. Because it is unlikely for a non- expert to possess the depth of knowledge to evaluate the value of a claim by examining the supporting methods and data, discerning high-quality from misleading information as a competent outsider often involves attending to subtle, surface-level indicators of its authenticity and trustworthiness (e.g., author credentials; Fe instein, 2011). We propose framing information literacy scaffolds in this lens, drawing parallels between fandom collecting practices and epistemic vigilance practices (e.g., vetting author trustworthiness; Sperber, 2010). As part of these appraisal materials, we propose the M aker, Intent, Network, Traceability (MINT) test (see https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1B-6FFOPhmhmqi6BQL5BOMX3_jPM05BjN?usp=sharing), a resource which takes common information literacy practices like corroborating claims across experts, and reframes them in the context of collecting (e.g., “If a claim sounds surprising, shocking, unbelievable, or important, treat it like a collectible. Before you add it to your knowledge collection, make sure it is MINT”). The focus on spotting counterfeits aligns the competent outsider vision with fandom norms and values; these are reliable strategies aimed at evaluating surface -level indicators of trustworthiness, rather than attempting to evaluate the quality of an argument itself with limited expertise. Conclusion: Partnering with a purpose ASEEs are informal science events designed to support adult engagement and identification with the scientific community. We argue that by building a design conjecture with cosplaying scientists to help encourage the development of competent outsiders at comic cons, our research aligns with the 2026 conference theme of partnering with purpose. This design conjecture stands to inform the design of innovative ASEE events which meet the goals of partner scientists, science educators, and fans alike. Although ty pically focused on interest and identity development rather than specific learning goals, we argue that with deliberate design choices ASEEs can also be platforms for promoting sustained pursuit of scientific knowledge and the apt evaluation of new information, thus fostering a competent outsider vision of scientific literacy. For comic cons, this involves providing resources which when combined with community norms and values, foster scientific collecting beyond the event. This conjecture also offers conceptual advances for exploring how and why learning can occur within these environments. In Sandoval's (2014) introduction to conjecture mapping, mediating processes are produced when participants interact with specific tools and tasks. Previous research has explored two mediating processes specific to ASEEs: mutual recognition (James, 2020) and knowledge layering (Authors, 2025). In this paper, we introduced and explored the potential for the mediating process of Scientific Collecting, as supported by existi ng discursive practices and innovative tools. We see this mediating process as a critical process which can build on the success of ASEEs, extending their impact by better positioning learners to pursue reliable, trustworthy scientific knowledge. title: Generative AI for Creative Learning in K-12 Education: Insights from a Systematic Scoping Review
citation: Seyedahmad Rahimi, Maryam Babaee, Salah Esmaeiligoujar, Chris Dede (2026). Generative AI for Creative Learning in K-12 Education: Insights from a Systematic Scoping Review. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Rahimi, S., Babaee, M., Esmaeiligoujar, S., & Dede, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The rapid rise of generative AI (GenAI) presents both opportunities and challenges for fostering creativity in K –12 education. This systematic scoping review synthesized 45 studies (2017– 2025) to examine how GenAI has been applied in creative learning. Fou r categories emerged: (1) creativity assessment, (2) human –AI co-creativity, (3) stakeholders’ perceptions, and (4) creativity enhancement. Findings show strong potential for GenAI to support idea generation, multimodal expression, and assessment of creati ve outputs, but highlight concerns about equity, authorship, and theoretical grounding. While most applications focus on text -based creativity, multimodal and culturally inclusive approaches remain underexplored. This review provides a foundation for responsible and equitable integration of GenAI into K –12 classrooms and captures a field in transition, where new forms of creative expression are emerging and educators are rethinking assessment, authorship, and pedagogy. This review provides a foundation for ethically grounded, developmentally appropriate and theory-driven GenAI designs that enhance, rather than automate, human creativity.

title: Patterns of Student-AI Collaboration in Problem-Solving: An Ordered Network Analysis
citation: Guang Yang, Jinhee Kim, Rita Detrick, Liangjie Fan, Wing Sha Chen, Na Li (2026). Patterns of Student-AI Collaboration in Problem-Solving: An Ordered Network Analysis. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Yang, G., Kim, J., Detrick, R., Fan, L., Chen, W. S., & Li, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This research investigates interaction dynamics between graduate students and AI agents during collaborative problem -solving activities within a curriculum design context. Analyzing 1,569 conversational exchanges, we applied ordered network analysis to ma p behavioral sequences and identify emergent patterns across problem -solving phases. Three dominant interaction pathways emerged: students soliciting AI perspectives, followed by resource provision; students seeking clarification with AI, which responds to refine their understanding; and students prompting elaboration that triggers extended cognitive exchanges. These patterns reveal AI functioning beyond a passive information source, instead operating as an active collaborator that reciprocally shapes problem-solving discourse. Findings indicate the formation of hybrid intelligence environments where human- AI partnerships distribute cognitive work. This research contributes theoretical insights into human -AI collaboration, demonstrates ordered network analysis as a methodology for examining conversational patterns, and offers practical implications for designing educationally productive AI -mediated learning experiences.

title: Designing Teacher Curricular Customization Tools to Enhance Elementary Students’ Language Use for Scientific Sensemaking
citation: Katherine L. McNeill, María González-Howard (2026). Designing Teacher Curricular Customization Tools to Enhance Elementary Students’ Language Use for Scientific Sensemaking. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: McNeill, K. L. & González-Howard, M.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy

abstract: Elementary classrooms are a critical space for engaging students in expansive science instruction. High quality instructional materials can support teachers in shifting and transforming how science is taught at the elementary grades. However, teachers need to customize the curriculum for their specific contexts. By curricular customizations, we mean adaptations or changes teachers make to personalize or localize the materials. Specifically, we are interested in supporting teachers in making principled customizations to support their multilingual learners (MLs). For this project, we ground our design work in a language for science perspective in which we center the diverse and wide- ranging language resources MLs bring to the classroom. In this paper, we share the designs of two curricular customization tools aimed at increasing multimodality during discussions, and an example 4th grade customization that illustrates MLs’ expansive language use for scientific sensemaking. Problem and importance The elementary grades are critical learning spaces for supporting students’ early experiences with science, which includes developing their expansive understandings around what science is, what the discipline entails, who does (and can) do science, and for fostering students’ science identities (NASEM, 2022). Despite the importance of elementary science, relatively little instructional time is devoted to this subject in US schools; on average 17 minutes per day in K-2 and 23 minutes per day in 3-5 (Plumley, 2019). Compounding this issue is the lack of high quality curricular materials (Davis et al., 2016; NASEM, 2022 ) and the limited professional learning provided around elementary science instruction (Plumley, 2019), all of which influence the extent to which elementary teachers feel prepared and able to teach science. However, the growing number of open -source reform-oriented curricular materials, many of which are educative in nature (i.e., include features aimed to support teacher learning), offers a potential solution to this pressing area of concern. Yet, research shows that teachers make sense of and take up educative, reform -oriented science curriculum in varied ways (Davis et al., 2017). This variation is influenced by teachers’ instructional contexts, which includes time allotted for science, availability of materials for science instruction and professional learning around how to implement these materials, and the students that teachers serve (Bennion et al., 2024). Furthermore, when considering minoritized student groups, teachers’ curricular decisions can be impacted by ideas they hold around students’ resources and perceived needs (Katsh -Singer et al., 2016). For multilingual learners (MLs) in particular, teachers’ curricular decisions are often influenced by intertwined beliefs around these students' language-related abilities and needs, and how language is used in science to make meaning and communicate science ideas (González‐Howard & Suárez, 2021). Critically, these beliefs can result in curricular customizations that either expand or narrow MLs’ science learning, particularly in relation to the extent students might use their full language repertoire (i.e., linguistic and multimodal resources; Pierson & Grapin 2021) for sensemaking. Combining curriculum with high quality professional learning can support more expansive customizations (McNeill et al, 2026). Thus, what is urgently needed is curriculum -based professional learning materials and resources that can be implemented in ways that correspond to elementary teachers’ varied contexts, and that target teachers’ understandings and abilities to customize science curriculum to enhance, not minimize, MLs’ sensemaking experiences. Design - theoretical basis of customization tools By curricular customization we mean the adaptations or changes that teachers design to personalize and localize the materials for particular students and settings ( McNeill et al., 2026; Gerard et al., 2022). Specifically, we are interested in the principled customizations teachers make to expand and support how MLs in their class use language to engage in rich sensemaking about phenomena (McNeill et al., 2026). Grounding professional learning in practice based tools is critical, because “Teaching occurs i n particulars – particular students interacting with particular teachers over particular ideas in particular circumstances” (Ball & Cohen, 1999, p. 10). Partaking in this customization work requires practice based tools and collaborative professional learning to reimagine and incorporate language inclusive and expansive practices to support MLs in science. 1262 In addition to grounding the tools in the classroom practice of enacting curriculum, we also draw on translanguaging research (e.g., Otheguy et al., 2015) to support MLs in science. Specifically, this project is grounded in a language for science perspective (González- Howard et al, 2024) in that we center the diverse and wide-ranging language-related resources that students already have, might adopt and could draw upon to engage in knowledge construction work (Warren et al., 2001). For MLs, this includes the linguistic (e.g., written and spoken named languages) and multimodal (e.g., gestures, drawings, graphing) resources students might mobili ze to sensemake (Pierson & Grapin, 2021). Recent research has shown that not only does such a view provide a fuller picture of how students’ figure out scientific phenomena, but it also has the potential to transform MLs’ science learning in more equitable ways (Suárez & Otero, 2023). As such, our design of customization tools for MLs aims to support teachers in fostering opportunities for students to translanguage, enhancing sensemaking moments so that students use all their linguistic and multimodal resources. Design - examples of customization tools for elementary MLs We present two elementary curricular customization tools for illustration. First, the Evaluating Existing Language Opportunities Tool (Figure 1) supports teachers in examining a science lesson plan to identify and unpack which language resources the lesson currently encourages students to use for sensemaking. This tool helps teachers evaluate these existing opportunities in relation to the lesson level learning goals, and then to consider the extent to which the lesson may privilege certain language resources over others. Figure 1 includes a sample completed tool using a lesson from the OpenSciEd Elementary fourth grade unit 4.4 Structure & Function (OpenSciEd, 2024) in which students figure out the overarching question - How do the structure and function of traits of living things benefit them? Although we use the OpenSciEd curriculum as an example here, the tools can be used across different science curricula. Specifically, in this case the tool illustrates that while the lesson has many opportunities for students to share their observations of the focal phenomena, most of those opportunities take the form of students communicating via talk and writing, and presumably in English. Figure 1: The Evaluating Existing Language Opportunities Tool The second curricular customization tool is the Enhancing Sensemaking Discussions Tool (see Figure 2). This tool supports teachers in enhancing the multimodality of sensemaking discussions through strategies such as adding drawings, inviting and using multiple named languages (e.g., Spanish, English), using gestures and incorporating sensemaking displays; strategies that open up the classroom space to broaden what students can figure out and how they can express their evolving scientific ideas (González‐Howard & Suárez, 2021). Figure 2 includes a sample completed tool used in the context of the previously described lesson. The mock- up of the 1263 completed customization tool shows potential customizations to this lesson for multilingual learners. Specifically, this includes translating the Notice & Wonder handout to add Spanish and encouraging students to use the named language of their choice to capture their ideas and questions around the focal phenomena (Poza, 2018). In addition, the plan includes a focus on using gestures to communicate and engage in sensemaking (Suárez, 2020) as well as utilizing lesson materials such as squirrel images and information cards. Figure 2: The Enhancing Sensemaking Discussions Tool Example customization in 4th grade classroom Next, we share an example of the enacted customized lesson in a 4th grade classroom. This elementary school is in an urban setting where the school population is 84% Hispanic or Latinx, 9% White, 5% Black or African American, and 2% Multi-Racial. In terms of languages, 84% of students identify as having a first language other than English and 67% of students have been identified as English Language Learners (ELLs) by the school. Spanish is the most common first language in the school. The transcript comes from the beginning of the initial consensus model discussion as the class is trying to explain how the traits of a tree squirrel and a flying squirrel help the squirrels live in the forest (Figure 3). The classroom discussion starts a t line 1 where Ms. A asks the class what to add to their initial consensus model. In this enactment, we see the teacher, Ms. A, utilizing a number of strategies with a particular focus on encouraging student sensemaking in both Spanish and English as well as the use of gestures both for collaboration and for scientific sensemaking. In the figure, the use of Spanish is in purple text while the use of gestures and physical movement is in blue. For example, in lines 11 -14 Ms. A asks her class about why tree squirrels need claws alternating between English and Spanish in her communication with the class. Furthermore, in terms of gestures we see in line 18 the class spontaneously uses two different hand gestures to indicate agreement with and wanting to build onto Esteban’s idea. While in line 4 with Samuel’s use of his fingers and in line 36 with Ms. A’s use of her arms, the class also uses gestures to illustrate science ideas about different animal traits in relation to structure and function. The curricular customizations Ms. A uses in the lesson enhance her students’ opportunities to engage in rich sensemaking about why the traits of the squirrel are important for survival (e.g. get food faster, climb, glide). Discussion MLs are underrepresented in science and the fastest growing student population in the US (Haas et al., 2021). Further, due to pervasive teacher beliefs around language and how students use language to sensemake and communicate science ideas (Pérez, et al, 2025), MLs often experience limited high quality science instruction (e.g., focus on memorization of science vocabulary; Grapin & Llosa, 2024) . By designing customization tools and professional learning resources, we aim to support elementary teachers to e xpand opportunities for MLs to engage in equitable sensemaking (Lee & Grapin, 2025).
