title: “Crafting” an Engineering Identity: Intersections between Engineering Undergraduates’ Identities as Crafters and Engineers
citation: G. R. Marvez, Sarah Kaczynski (2026). “Crafting” an Engineering Identity: Intersections between Engineering Undergraduates’ Identities as Crafters and Engineers. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Marvez, G. R. & Kaczynski, S.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Crafting and engineering, and the practices they entail, have an interwoven and gendered history. Engineering undergraduate students with prior experience in crafting can bring these practices into their engineering education, but those resources and facet s of their identities are not always recognized by both themselves and members of their communities. In this work, we interviewed ten engineering undergraduates about their experiences with crafting and engineering and how it informed their identities as engineers. Our findings suggest that students see their crafting and engineering work as connected and that they inform one another. Furthermore, their insights point to factors that can influence the formation of their identities as engineers, artists, and/or crafters. This work carries implications for the intentional inclusion of crafting in engineering education to foster creativity and attract and retain more students to the discipline.

title: Youth Climate Storytelling as Transformative Learning: A Scoping Review of Designs, Contexts, and Digital Practices
citation: Asli Sezen-Barrie, Yuxi Huang (2026). Youth Climate Storytelling as Transformative Learning: A Scoping Review of Designs, Contexts, and Digital Practices. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Sezen-Barrie, A. & Huang, Y.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: This scoping review synthesizes 30 peer -reviewed studies (2014– 2024) on youth storytelling in climate change education, illuminating how storytelling approaches foster transformative climate change learning. Findings reveal that storytelling functions as relational infrastructure while relating climate complexity into lived experience, cultivating eco - emotional awareness and agency, and sustaining Indigenous and community knowledge. Across formal and informal settings, educators and youth partnered to co- create stories that merged data, emotion, and cultural meaning. Digital tools such as participatory video, multimedia, and augmented reality expanded access and impact but also raised questions of equity and authorship. By mapping designs, scaffolds, and digital practices, the review offers design implications for research -practice partnerships that nurture belonging, imagination, and civic participation through climate storytelling. The need and the goal As the climate crisis intensifies, educators face an urgent challenge: how to cultivate young people’s capacity to understand, feel, and act in relation to a rapidly changing world. Traditional climate change education often privileges scientific facts, da ta, and predictive models but rarely engages the emotional, cultural, and ethical dimensions necessary for sustained transformation (Walsh, 2022 ). Transformative climate change education reframes learning as an ethical, relational, and action -oriented process that centers justice, hope, and collective capacity (Leite, 2024; Sezen -Barrie et al., 2025). Within this reframing, storytelling emerges as a powerful pedagogical and epistemological approach that binds scientific sense-making with identity, emotion, culture, and community (Gottschall, 2012). Storytelling makes climate data meaningful, futures imaginable, and collective agency possible (Bentz & O’Brien, 2019; Bloomfield, 2024). It allows youth to relate abstract climate concepts into local experiences and shared narratives of resilience, repositioning them as authors of change rather than passive recipients of information. Yet, despite growing interest, the field lacks a compr ehensive synthesis of how storytelling is designed, scaffolded, and studied across learning contexts. Moreover, as digita l media and participatory technologies proliferate from personal storytelling platforms to augmented reality, the need for design frameworks that ensure equity, authenticity, and purpose becomes more pressing. This review addresses a central gap in the learning sciences: the absence of an integrated understanding of how storytelling, across diverse designs, pedagogical functions, and digital practices, shapes transformative climate learning. While storytelling is increasingly recognized as a catalyst for connection, agency, and inclusion, its implementation remains fragmented across specific areas of social science research. Drawing on 30 peer - reviewed studies (2014– 2024), this scoping review was guided by the following research questions: (1) What research designs and learning contexts characterize studies on youth storytelling in climate change education? (2) How do storytelling function and are scaffolded to support climate change education? (3) In what ways do digital tools and frameworks support engaging in storytelling related to climate change? Conceptual framework: Storytelling in climate change education “We are the authors of our lives. We compose our self -narratives and we are composed by them” (Gottschall, 2012, p. 147). In The Storytelling Animal: How Stories Make Us Human, Gottschall (2012) argues that stories are not only how we communicate experiences but also how we construct meaning, identity, and belonging. Storytelling, the structuring and sharing of lived or imagined experiences through narrative form, is thus foundational to human cognition, culture, and communication (Gottschall, 2012). Within education, storytelling functions as both an epistemological and pedagogical approach : a way of knowing the world and of teaching it. In climate change education, it extends beyond communication to become a transformative learning practice , weaving scientific understanding with emotional relations, ethical inquiry, and socio-cultural meaning. Mainstream climate change education often privileges technocratic and positivist paradigms, emphasizing data, models, and prediction (Krasny & Schneider, 2021). While such approaches are essential for understanding biophysical mechanisms, they rarely foste r the emotional, ethical, or civic engagement necessary 1877 for meaningful transformation. Storytelling intervenes by humanizing climate knowledge while translating complex systems into situated experiences and relationships. By embedding abstract concepts in personal or community narratives, it deepens comprehension and fosters empathy (Bloomfield , 2024). In this sense, stories “relocalize” climate learning, situating it within histories of place, culture, and justice rather than abstract global metrics. Storytelling aligns with transformative climate change education frameworks (Sezen-Barrie et al., 2025; Leite, 2024), which highlights attention to learning across epistemologies and improving emotional well -being. Climate stories , especially those from marginalized or Indigenous communities , which operates as counter- hegemonic discourses that challenge dominant narratives of progress and environmental relationships (Leite, 2024; Tuck, McKenzie, & McCoy, 2014). These narratives open epistemic space for lear ners to question assumptions about development, responsibility, and belonging in the Anthropocene. Through engagement with such stories, learners cultivate more pluralistic and justice -oriented understandings of socio- ecological systems. Indigenous storytelling traditions exemplify this transformative potential. In many Indigenous epistemologies, story is both method and ethic: a means of transmitting knowledge and sustaining reciprocal relationships among humans, nonhumans, and the land (Whyte, 2017). Integrating Indigenous storytelling into climate curricula enacts decolonial praxis, repositioning learners as participants in relational webs of care rather than as detached observers of climate data (Tuck et al., 2014). Empirical research reinforces the pedagogical value of storytelling. Pahl et al. (2019) found that climate messages conveyed through stories were significantly more effective at fostering emotional engagement and pro- environmental intentions than statistical presentations. Educational research further shows that storytelling supports identity work: when students create or analyze stories about climate change through oral narratives, filmmaking, or digital media, they articulate their roles, values, and hopes within broader ecological systems (Leite, 2024). In sum, storytelling is far more than a communication tool; it is a transformative framework for learning. It bridges the cognitive, affective, and ethical domains —helping learners think, feel, and act with relational awareness. By integrating storytelling into climate change education, educators can nurture imagination, agency, and care, cultivating learners who are not only informed about the planetary crisis but also empowered to participate in r eimagining its futures. Storytelling, in this sense, becomes both pedagogy and praxis —a way of composing more just and livable worlds.

title: Walking Urban Green Spaces: Secondary Students’ Descriptions of Returning to Embodied Relations with Nature
citation: Jennifer A. Vadeboncoeur, Natacha Monestel Mora, Auralia Brooke, Kristiina Kumpulainen (2026). Walking Urban Green Spaces: Secondary Students’ Descriptions of Returning to Embodied Relations with Nature. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Vadeboncoeur, J. A., Mora, N. M., Brooke, A., & Kumpulainen, K.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: While interactions in nature and urban green spaces have been studied for their benefits to developing, wellbeing, and quality of life, this paper draws on research with secondary students engaged in a walking curriculum to examine how they describe what they are learning through walking, as well as their relations with nature. We utilized central concepts from cultural-historical approaches to the learning sciences —including learning on the move and learning as movement—along with literature from critical geographies to focus our analysis on surfacing embodied relations with nature. We address three themes in this paper: walking as a return to the senses, walking as a return to the body, and walking as a return to relationality. Walking led to learning that was embodied, organic, and emotional, linking curriculum, students’ lived experiences and their values, with real and imagined embodied and emplaced social futures.

title: Syncretic Designs for Young People’s Social and Ecological Imagination across Virtual–Natural Worlds
citation: Edward Rivero, Anu Kajamaa, Kristiina Kumpulainen (2026). Syncretic Designs for Young People’s Social and Ecological Imagination across Virtual–Natural Worlds. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Rivero, E., Kajamaa, A., & Kumpulainen, K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study explores how syncretic designs for game-based learning that interweave digital and physical modalities, human and more -than-human actors, and imaginative and embodied forms of knowing can nurture young people’s social and ecological imagination. While such approaches have been examined in literacy contexts, their potential to cultivate socio-ecological imagination across virtual and natural worlds remains underexplored. Drawing on a Social Design- Based Experiment (SDBE) conducted in an out-of-school program, twelve youth engaged in sustainability design challenges in Minecraft alongside outdoor ecological explorations. The study investigates: (1) how syncretic designs for learning can support youth’s ecological and social imagination across digital and real -world nature contexts; and (2) what pedagogical possibilities emerge when virtual world-making intertwines with embodied experiences in natural environments. Findings show that youth envisioned sustainable futures grounded in their cultural repertoires, designing virtual neighborhoods that reimagined the ecological and social possibilities of their communities.

title: Understanding Teachers’ Feedback Strategies in Classrooms with Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Survey Study with Storyboards
citation: Shintaro Sato, Tomohiro Nagashima (2026). Understanding Teachers’ Feedback Strategies in Classrooms with Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Survey Study with Storyboards. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Sato, S. & Nagashima, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: An increasing number of schools across the world have adopted (and are adopting) adaptive learning technologies. However, how school teachers give feedback in the classroom when students are working with adaptive learning software is underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted an online survey with illustrative storyboards to investigate what kinds of feedback teachers would give to students using intelligent tutors depending on the task difficulty and students’ performance. Our findings showed that teachers prioritize feedback that promotes students’ deep thinking, while feedback that prioritizes accuracy and efficiency (commonly used in intelligent tutors) was the least common among teachers. This study contributes an understanding of teachers’ feedback strategies in classroom environments and how these strategies and adaptive learning technology can mutually complement each other to provide more effective and engaging feedback to students.

title: Exploring the Affordances and Challenges of Participatory Co-Analysis of Clinical Interviews
citation: Hedi Jaza, Marta Kobiela, Amna Fleeh (2026). Exploring the Affordances and Challenges of Participatory Co-Analysis of Clinical Interviews. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Jaza, H., Kobiela, M., & Fleeh, A.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Clinical interviews have long served as a method to learn about individual’s thinking and reasoning in mathematics and science education. Yet, analysis of interviews has often relied solely on researcher interpretations. In this methodological paper, we s hare an alternate approach in which we engaged in co -analysis with research participants. We focus on co- analysis sessions conducted with one preservice teacher (the third author) following her engagement in a task -based clinical interview about s patial rotation. We examine how the co- analysis provided additional insights into the participant’s spatial reasoning and the challenges that arose for both the researchers and participant. Our findings suggest the potential of co- analysis for providing greater understanding of participants’ use of gesture and language.

title: Co-design as a Catalyst for Becoming: Identity, Practice, and Learning Trajectories in Undergraduate Science
citation: Sunnie Gong, Michelle Lui, Aidyn Intykbekov (2026). Co-design as a Catalyst for Becoming: Identity, Practice, and Learning Trajectories in Undergraduate Science. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Gong, S., Lui, M., & Intykbekov, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
tpack_tk_labels: Immersive VR / AR; Simulations & Scientific Modeling
conceptualisations_list: Communities of Practice & Situated Learning; Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: Co-design is a collaborative methodology for creating educational innovations involving researchers, educators, and developers. While research -practice partnerships in the Learning Sciences have historically co-designed with teachers, recent developments have begun involving students. However, research on students’ experiences of co- design remains limited. This study explores what students learn from engaging in co-design through a situated learning framework linking learning to identity formation. Using a multiple case study methodology, the relationships between the identities, learning, and participation of six undergraduate science students were examined in a co -design project for creating educational virtual reality simulations. Findings reveal that identity, practice, and learning exist in dynamic and reciprocal relationships within co -design contexts. Students’ existing identities informed their co- design engagement. Through practice, students developed collaboration skills and learned about themselves which led to diverse identity development trajectories. These findings suggest engaging students as co-design partners creates unique opportunities for integrated learning and identity development.

title: Painting Identities: Artmaking as Identity Work with Youth
citation: Kristina Stamatis, Joseph L. Polman, Marisa Mendoza-Maurer, Andrea Garcia-Vasquez (2026). Painting Identities: Artmaking as Identity Work with Youth. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Stamatis, K., Polman, J. L., Mendoza-Maurer, M., & Garcia-Vasquez, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Co-Design & Participatory Design; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: Recent scholarship has called for the examination of young people’s identifications in relation to histories of marginalization and oppression, and as part of learning trajectories that are simultaneously social, cultural, and historical. The Rehacer el mundo project is a participatory design project with youth, museum educators, artists, and researchers to engage Latine and other historically marginalized youth and families in developing a youth- professional collaborative art exhibit. The project, located in an urban Latine arts museum, was designed to create opportunities for communities of historically marginalized youth to engage in reimagining public discourse. In this paper, we draw upon notions of artmaking to describe the ways youth from historically marginalized communities engage in identity building as historical actors. Our findings illustrate these metaphors have potential to expand understandings of learning and identity development as an inherently cultural process.

title: Reconceptualizing Imagination as Social Practice in Science Education
citation: Hannah H. Ziegler (2026). Reconceptualizing Imagination as Social Practice in Science Education. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Ziegler, H. H.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Social & Civic Studies
conceptualisations_list: Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: In science education, imagination has largely been framed as a cognitive process, with comparatively less attention to its social, political, and ecological dimensions. This conceptual paper reconceptualizes imagination as a social practice that reshapes how we imagine and design possible futures. At the micro- level, I reframe imagination as a subjective and situated practice, shaped by individual histories and sociopolitical contexts. At the meso- level, it is explored as a relational act, co -produced through intergenerational collaboration, care, and the navigation of structural constraints. At the macro-level, an ecological imagination extends this practice to include socioecological relations with more -than-human partners, drawing on Indigenous and pluriversal ontologies. By analyzing imagination across these interacting levels, this paper offers a pathway for designing more just and thriving futures. Purpose: Why imagination matters in science education We often give the most attention to children's imaginative engagement in early childhood or elementary classrooms, usually linked to children's play. However, imagination as a pedagogical practice tends to lose legitimacy as kids grow older, especially in science education contexts. Building on existing cognitive and sociocultural scholarship, I propose theorizing imagination as a social practice that foregrounds its relational and sociopolitical dimensions. Recent work in the learning sciences has advanced speculative approaches to justice- oriented futures (e.g., Arada et al., 2023; Garcia & Mirra, 2023). My argument complements this work by focusing more specifically on imagination as the social and relational practice that undergirds such efforts. My work presents imaginative engagement not as naive dreaming, but as a powerful tool for re -worlding that involves complex ideological struggles against frameworks like neoliberalism. Here, I define imagination as a sociohistorically situated practice of world -making through which certain futures become thinkable, legitimate, and actionable. This practice is best pursued in community, including youth and more -than-human partners. Drawing inspiration from marginalized worldviews, imagination as social practice dis rupts tradition by asking new questions: What are the sources of our imagination, what values does it reflect, and whose imaginations are legitimized? Revisiting existing frames of imagination While important work has examined imagination from cognitive and sociocultural perspectives, imagination in science education remains underdeveloped from an explicitly socioecological and political perspective. Early sociocultural traditions help us understand that imagination is not created from nothing, but uses real -world experiences as building blocks. However, theorizing imagination solely within cognitivist or sociocultural traditions leaves certain political and structural dimensions underexplored. F irst, imagination is not a neutral cognitive skill but is situated in our historical, cultural, and political contexts. Second, these renderings fail to recognize the consequential potential of imagination in both micro- and macro -level systems. Theorizing imagination solely at the level of the individual risks overlooking the relational and structural dimensions that shape what becomes imaginable. In defining imagination as a social practice, I draw from Holland & Lave’s (2019) theory of social practice, which considers how participation shapes a person’s daily lives in relation to power and politics. Imagination as social practice does not seek to understand people’s actions as isolated individual acts, but always in relation to other people, practices, and systems. The remainder of this paper is organized into three sections in which I illustrate how imagination -as-social-practice can open up new o nto-epistemologies at the micro - (intrapersonal), meso- (relational), and macro- (ecological) levels. These analytic levels are not mutually exclusive but offer a framing to discuss key facets of imagination as we contend with political systems, cultural histories, and ideological frameworks. Micro level: The individual imagination From cognition to situated subjectivity 1917 The most prevalent theories around imagination largely establish it as a cognitive function contained within an individual’s mind, with some recognition of cultural contexts. Experiential perspectives acknowledge how children blend existing experiences to create new ways of thinking: Vygotsky (2004) discusses imagination as a cultural activity of dissociating and recombining elements of reality in creative ways. This individualistic framing is evident in Egan’s (2005) articulation of imagination as a set of cognitive toolkits divided by developmental stages. This cognitivist tradition has shaped how imagination is researched and implemented in education—in terms of an individual’s cognitive performance. Numerous psychological studies have since examined how imagination mediates learning, viewing it as a mental technique to enhance comprehension and retention. Nonetheless, these studies bypass explanations around how the individual imagination is shaped by our own histories, cultures, emotions, and relations. Cognitive views have also dominated how the field has conceived of disciplinary practices in science education. Kuhn’s (1977) concept of thought experiments, for instance, describes a decontextualized view of the individual imagination in scientific thinking. While both Kuhn and Vygotsky (2004) imply that the individual imagination consists of subjective renderings of a person’s experiences, a chief focus on the tangible, sensory, and cognitive elements could conceal the value -laden subjectivities that driv e our scientific sensemaking. Thus, an inquiry into the role of aesthetics and wonder in science education enables us to see both the personal and deeply social dimensions of our imagination. While aesthetic experiences are seemingly experienced in private and subjective ways (Wickman et al., 2022), science education is seldom theorized as a subjective experience, despite being full of such moments. What we find interesting, wonderful, or strange depends on the observer, whose experiences are deeply situated. After all, Egan (2005) reckons anything has the potential to be seen as wonderful if “seen in the right light” (p. 92). Then, I argue that changing the so- called “light,” or the subjective lens with which we view the world, can alter what we perceive as wonderful, beautiful, or worth imagining. Science as socially constructed Framing the individual imagination as a social practice also makes visible the sociopolitical conditions which have driven our collective inquiry. Disciplinary knowledge is produced through socially organized processes, rather than existing outside historical and cultural contexts. Latour (1987) frames scientific facts as a set of ideas that are socially constructed, contested, and settled through a community of scientists. In other words, what counts as science is socially and interactionally constructed a mong members of the science community. Thus, disciplinary knowledge consists of a fluid, socially-constructed body of knowledge rather than a permanent, rigid set of concepts. Similarly, Medin & Bang (2014) argue that scientific ideas are often “settled” t hrough a social process. They also speak to how science education reflects the values of its adherents, most often dominated by Western scientists. Establishing the disciplinary canon involves a collective process dominated by those who yield social power. Similarly, I view imagination as a dynamic process subject to power relations; whose imaginations get taken up and pursued are deeply shaped by our subjective judgments and the social positions of those making them. Recognizing the subjectivities of the individual imagination offers an entry point to examine how our politically-shaped values permeate our “scientific” imagination. Imagination is constituted through people’s histories, values, identities, emotions, and relations to place. Afrofuturist practices exemplify how individual imaginations can contest social norms to create new forms of culture. As a form of political worlding, afrofuturism demonstrates how the individual imagination can simultaneously engage in cultural critique, resistance, and counter-stories. Speculative storytelling can also prompt resistance by blurring boundaries of present -future and real-imagined (Tomin & Collis, 2024). An exploration of the subjectivities of our imagination at the intrapersonal level mandates that we challenge dominant onto- epistemologies that shape “current and possible meaning, meaning-making, positioning, and relations in cultural ecologies” (Bang et al., 2016, p. 29). Then, it becomes necessary to critically question how our imagination can marginalize perspectives we often need the most. While this section foregrounds subjectivity, imagination does not remain within individuals; it becomes consequential in relation with others and broader systems. Meso level: The relational imagination Relationality as ethical matters I now examine imagination as a social practice that is not only subjective, but relational. By “relational imagination,” I mean more than collaboration; it references to the co -production of worlds mediated by social norms and roles. I stress the importance of questioning how social hierarchies and dominant narratives shape how we imagine at the interpersonal level. Relational imagination is driven by care, agency, and affect. With whom we imagine is just as important as what we imagine. In line with social practice theory (Holland & Lave, 2019), 1918 social hierarchies are central to imagination. Bang and colleagues (2016) suggest that normative relations in learning environments can reproduce power and inequity. They employ the term “withness designing” to underscore a relational approach, proposing intergenerational engagement with elders and youth to constitute community-based change. The relational imagination emphasizes learning across generations and requires role remediation through re-negotiations of power. Therefore, with whom we work, design, and imagine becomes an ethical matter. Reframing children as co-visionaries Children have been historically positioned as naive and questionable sources of knowledge. Silin (2014) emphasizes the need not only to listen to children but also to dissolve the boundaries between adult-child relations. If we were to view people’s experiences and emotions from a collective perspective regardless of age, then science education should focus on empowering and healing young people. This ideological liberation of age segregation is best pursued through collaboration where adults and children inspire and fuel each other’s imaginations. While both adults’ and children’s ideas may reflect and reproduce problematic social norms, I argue that we are more likely to create radical visions in community. In this sense, relational imagination explicitly centers the co - production of ideas —how people imagine with and for one another. Chang & Philip (2025) illustrate such orientation as they cultivated a co -design space that disrupted normative roles in adult -youth partnerships. They critique co -design work that centers adult stakeholders’ needs; instead, they argue the valued outcome is the negotiation of existing social relationships as newly figured worlds. These relational shifts surface how affect, agency, and imagination are jointly situated in practice. Relational imagination amid institutional constraints These relational practices contend with institutional logics that privatize youths’ emotions. Formal schooling is seldom sufficient in meeting youths’ emotional needs (Vamvalis, 2023). Hence, youths’ abilities to navigate the present and shape their futures are constrained by social structures. This is unsurprising given that American schools were primarily established for socializing students to reward passivity and compliance. As such, schools enculturate students into neoliberal systems rather than prepare them to critique and resist the status quo of science education. Hence, this raises a central tension: How can we design science teaching and learning to help us overcome structural limitations and foster imagination as a path to collective wellbeing? Macro level: The ecological imagination Ecologizing multiple worldviews Macro-level ecological imagination asks not only who imagines what, but with whom and to what ends. The macro level pushes us beyond our human partnerships, toward living well with the natural world, recognizing agency as distributed across human and more-than-human communities. However, these orientations must be accompanied by ontological shifts at the macro level, where multiple worldviews co -shape science education alongside more - than-human partners. I argue that diversity and heterogeneity alone cannot dismantle systems of power and privilege. Thus, the ecological imagination draws from Escobar’s (2018) pluriversal design calls for designing new ways of being in the world—ontologies —centered on culture and community. In particular, pluriversality challenges us to abandon Western assumptions of viewing the world that have jeopardized the fundamental human experience, such as frameworks of modernity (Escobar, 2018; Latour, 2013). Specifically, Latour (2013) calls for ecologization in place of modernization. Such aims necessitate that we interrogate the Western “scientific worldview” that is responsible for establishing subject-object relations. In fact, Latour (2013) contends that nature plays the role of the active subject, sharing agency with other subjec ts. This critique sets the stage for rethinking settled expectations in sciece as part of our ecological imagination. Extending agency to more-than-humans The relational imagination discussed ways to achieve more equitable relations between youth and science. Here, I shift to the absence of ecological onto- epistemologies in science education. Historically, the natural world has been objectified by and differentiated from human culture. This objectification captures the dominant narrative of humans’ exploitation of nature, rooted in science’s dominance over more -than-human beings. It has promoted inequitable extraction of Earth’s resources, and this cost is shared disproportionately among Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC) groups (Monarrez et al., 2022). The troubling history of science has also made its way into classrooms—where the valuing of Western scientific practices denies Indigenous ways of understanding and caring for the natural world (Bang & Medin, 2010). In engineering education, technocratic discourses emphasize the design of anthropocentric solutions at the cost of natural resources (Gunckel & Tolbert, 2018). To 1919 explore the roots of our domineering relations with the natural world, I turn to Latour (2013), who challenges the myth of a nature -culture binary, or “bifurcation.” He calls us naive for deanimating natural entities, which calls for a re-distribution of agency across human and more -than-human actors. This work calls for a reconsideration of dominant Western ontological assumptions about nature and culture to take up relational and Indigenous perspectives on inhabiting an animate world. The work of Lees & Bang (2022) embodies such orientations by centering the Indigenous framing of humans as “a part of,” rather than “apart from,” the natural world. In their STEM summer program, youth explored biodiversity in tide pools while learning about their “beach relat ives.” By referring to the starfish as “he” rather than “it,” more-than-humans were imbued with a sense of personhood. Through this experience, children developed socioecological reasoning while acknowledging the agency of these creatures. In Warren & Rose bery’s (2011) study, Jonathan, a Black boy, challenges the Western classification system for living and non- living things. Jonathan constitutes the sun as a living organism based on its essential role in the ecosystem. His challenge of the canon’s binary classification allowed the teacher to reframe Jonathan as a competent science learner, illustrating the potential for the ecological imagination to disrupt dominant onto - epistemologies that pervade science education. Conclusion: Designing for pluriversality Across the micro, meso, and macro levels, we have reframed imagination as subjective, relational, and socioecological world-making processes. I use these levels as analytic lenses, informed by social practice theory, to trace how imagination operates across subjectivity, relational interaction, and broader socioecological systems. Imagination emerges through our lived histories and social relations, shaping how we interpret and imagine possible futures. Imagination- as-social-practice refutes individualistic notions of thriving, foregrounding collectivity instead.

title: How Students' Mental Models of AI Shape Their Epistemic Cognition of AI -Generated Results: Source and Justification
citation: Toni Rogat (2026). How Students' Mental Models of AI Shape Their Epistemic Cognition of AI -Generated Results: Source and Justification. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Rogat, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The introduction of generative artificial intelligence ( AI) has changed students ’ learning environments . Such rapid changes have the potential to exacerbate the post -truth challenges we face today. Despite the rapid increase in the use of AI in education, there remains a lack of research on how students reason about AI-generated results. Aligned with models of epistemic cognition, this study investigate d students’ mental models about AI and how such models influence their epistemic cognition about AI, particularly regarding source and justification. Results revealed that students’ epistemic reasoning varies depending on their mental models of AI. Students with a web-scraping model indicated that AI-generated results could be unreliable and superficially justified due to the source of information (i.e., the Internet). Students with a training -dataset model emphasized human intention in selecting training data and highlighted critical flaws in AI justification processes based on their understanding of how AI systems function.

title: A Latent Profile Analysis of Math Self-Efficacy and Anxiety in Game-Based Learning
citation: Alireza (Sina) Zandi, Leyla Karami Isheqlou, Jody Clarke-Midura (2026). A Latent Profile Analysis of Math Self-Efficacy and Anxiety in Game-Based Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Zandi, A. S., Isheqlou, L. K., & Clarke-Midura, J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study investigated how math anxiety and self- efficacy shape students’ algebra learning in From Here to There! (FH2T), a digital game for algebraic reasoning. Data from 607 seventh graders were analyzed using Latent Profile Analysis, identifying five p rofiles representing unique combinations of math performance, worry, and emotional reaction. Grounded in Self -Efficacy Theory, the findings show how belief in ability shapes students’ emotional and cognitive experiences in digital learning.

title: Modeling AI-TPACK in Practice: Insights from Teachers’ Multi-Agent Workflow Design
citation: Yimeng Sun, Haiyang Xin, Shuang Li, Qiannan Niu, Ching Sing Chai, Lingyun Huang, Gaowei Chen (2026). Modeling AI-TPACK in Practice: Insights from Teachers’ Multi-Agent Workflow Design. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Sun, Y., Xin, H., Li, S., Niu, Q., Chai, C. S., Huang, L., & Chen, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates teachers’ design behaviors and cognitive underpinnings when designing multi-agent instructional workflows. Analyzing behavioral logs (N=61), cluster and Markov analyses identified three archetypes: Systematic Optimizers iteratively refining complex architectures; Prolific Creators rapidly prototyping pragmatic tools via scaffolding; and Passive Observers exhibiting polarized expert -novice profiles. Subsequent artifact (n=15) and interview (n=12) analyses reveal AI-TPACK integration emerges from a dynamic interplay of systems thinking, pedagogical beliefs, and self- efficacy, not merely from the possession of discrete knowledge. These findings call for differentiated scaffolding responsive to teachers ’ cognitive-behavioral diversity.

title: Concepts, Approaches, and Outcomes in Computational Thinking and Mathematics Integration in K -12: An Umbrella Review
citation: Lingna Xu, Chungsoo Na, Jody Clarke-Midura (2026). Concepts, Approaches, and Outcomes in Computational Thinking and Mathematics Integration in K -12: An Umbrella Review. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Xu, L., Na, C., & Clarke-Midura, J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Despite growing interest in integrating Computational Thinking (CT) into K -12 mathematics, the research remains fragmented. To create a cohesive overview, this umbrella review synthesizes 18 literature reviews, meta- analyses, and scoping reviews published between 2006 and 2025. Our analysis focuses on the what (concepts), how (approaches), and why (outcomes) of CT-Mathematics integration. Our findings reveal a consensus on the benefits of CT -Mathematics integration but a lack of specificity. While common concepts (e.g. , abstraction, geometry) and tools (e.g., Scratch) are identified, the synergistic links between them and the pedagogical strategies for implementation are underexplored. Furthermore, learning outcomes are often studied in broader STEM contexts, obscuring the CT-Mathematics link. We conclude that future research must move beyond demonstrating if integration is effective to explaining how, when, and under what conditions CT -Mathematics integration fosters deep, synergistic learning.

title: Mapping Mathematical Intent: Investigating Conceptual Conflicts in Integrated Math and Computational Thinking Lessons
citation: Asmaa Yazidi Alaoui, Jessi Lajos, Jody Clarke-Midura, Jessica Shumway, Deborah Silvis (2026). Mapping Mathematical Intent: Investigating Conceptual Conflicts in Integrated Math and Computational Thinking Lessons. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Alaoui, A. Y., Lajos, J., Clarke-Midura, J., Shumway, J., & Silvis, D.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: This study investigates how second- grade students build connections between abstract mathematical concepts and concrete actions through the use of robot coding toys to support multiplicative reasoning. Drawing on the Onto-Semiotic Approach, we analyzed video data from three integrated mathematics and computational thinking lessons to identify semiotic conflicts, with a focus on conceptual conflicts. Our findings reveal that these conflicts emerged from four distinct variations: chunking, two loops in a row, usefulness of the last loop, and not locked in loop. These results underscore the critical role of the design of coding toys and offer practical implications for educators. Specifically, the study provides insights into how teachers can anticipate and mitigate these conflicts by being aware of their nature. This awareness can help facilitate students’ ability to connect abstract mathematical ideas, computational code, and concrete actions more effectively.

title: An Exploration of Spatial Typologies for Active Learning
citation: Chenxuan Meng, James D. Slotta (2026). An Exploration of Spatial Typologies for Active Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Meng, C. & Slotta, J. D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Active learning classrooms are continuing to gain popularity worldwide, requiring educators to make effective use of these spatial environments. However, limited systematic frameworks exist to guide the alignment between instructional strategies and spatial configurations, leaving educators uncertain about how to configure and use space for pedagogical goals. This study introduces a typological approach based on Space Coupling Levels (SCL) combined with pattern visualization. Drawing on active learning strategies documented in educational practice, we assessed 50 strategies using the Space Coupling Levels approach, identifying 10 high-dependency cases. We selected five representative strategies for detailed pattern visualization, extracting and visualizing their characteristic spatial geometries and associated interaction patterns through conceptual pattern diagrams. This work establishes an alignment matrix of "activity types × spatial prerequisites" as a comparative baseline, offering researchers a replicable analytical tool while providing educators and space designers with visual design resources.

title: Touch to Think: Supporting Curriculum Design with Tangible Models of the Classroom
citation: Chenxuan Meng, James D. Slotta (2026). Touch to Think: Supporting Curriculum Design with Tangible Models of the Classroom. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Meng, C. & Slotta, J. D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Physical models are routine in architecture but rarely used in curriculum design. This study examines how tangible classroom models support teachers in designing inquiry- oriented lessons. This study compares four representation modalities (2D digital, 2D paper, 3D digital, 3D physical) in a curriculum design task, finding that groups using physical models demonstrated the highest engagements. To understand underlying mechanisms, we conducted in-depth design sessions with two experienced teachers. Analysis revealed that physical models serve as "thinking tools" that help teachers visualize and test pedagogical scenarios. Teachers used models to identify spatial constraints, test activity flows, and rapidly prototype different design alternatives. Through tangible manipulation, teachers were able to link pedagogical goals to concrete spatial implementations, making previously implicit decisions explicit and actionable. This study suggests that physical models can transform curriculum design from abstract text-based planning to embodied spatial-pedagogical reasoning.

title: Designing at the Speed of Trust: Unearthing Implicit Values and Vibes
citation: Ananda Marin (2026). Designing at the Speed of Trust: Unearthing Implicit Values and Vibes. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Marin, A.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Design Based Research (DBR) is a slow, tedious, and overwhelming process. Over the years of their existence, DBR research teams develop into tiny publics where new ways of being and doing develop. While tools such as conjecture maps were developed to support documenting the relationship between theoretical and design-based conjectures, we have found that the conceptual level of these conjectures do not quite capture our idiosyncratic axiologies, or the values, flavor, and vibes that became implicit or taken for granted. In this paper we share reflections from the Choreographing Science project, describing how the choice to end the project by designing something new helped us (1) reveal taken for granted design values and principles that we developed during our 4 years of collaboration, (2) work at a faster, more confident pace, and (3) create something shareable with stakeholders we care about. Shifting design practices to capture cultivated values and vibes As a hallmark of the Learning Sciences, Design Based Research (DBR) (Brown, 1992; Collins, 1992) allows us to advance theories of learning and design together through an iterative, collaborative process of conjecturing, enacting, and analyzing. DBR is a slow, tedious, and often overwhelming process requiring years of engagement. During this time research teams develop into tiny publics (Fine, 2012), where new ways of being and doing can emerge. Bang and colleagues expanded DBR to include attention to relational processes and products as consequential to design (Bang et al., 2016; Bang & Vossoughi, 2016). While tools such as conjecture maps (Sandoval, 2014) were developed to support documenting links between theoretical and design conjectures across iterative cycles, tools for unearthing axiological commitments have remained less clear. In this paper we share a DBR case in which shifting from researcher -led design practices to artistic -led (endogenous) design practices helped us unearth sticky, implicit axiologies we had developed yet taken for granted over our four- year collaboration. As an interdisciplinary team of Learning scientists, Artists, & Scientists, we worked on the Choreographing Science project with a clear sense of our shared values. We set out to disrupt knowledge hierarchies by uplifting embodied, choreographic ways of knowing in order to desettle established ways of doing science that historically dismissed youth perspectives (Vogelstein et al., 2022). We leveraged improvisational choreographic tools for science modeling in the design of summer camps that brought middle schoolers, scientists, & choreographers together. Our traditional social sciences analytic work produced academic papers that highlighted how participants leveraged choreographic tools to make sense of scientific phenomena by doing things like comparing how humans and computational agents interpret and enact movement rules (Wagh, Vogelstein, & Champion, 2024), developing movement rules for scientific entities (Vogelstein, Wagh, & Champion, 2025), and reflecting on the experience of responding to others’ move ment ideas (Vogelstein et al., 2024). While these analytic insights were generative, papers felt limited as our only products. Papers don’t spur movement or make collective choreography. We realized we needed a product that would promote inquiry through movement, and to do so, we switched our mode of design. We let choreographic design methods lead us as we designed a deck of movement cards to support facilitators in getting groups of people thinking by moving together. This process enlivened & aligned our tiny public once more, putting our axiological commitments to practice in the learning spaces we valued most. In this paper we describe how the choice to end our project by switching design methods to design something new helped us (1) reveal consequential, taken for granted design values and principles that we developed during our four-year collaboration, (2) work at a faster, more confident pace, and (3) create something shareable with stakeholders we care about. Our values are reflected in a product that centers uncertainty and begets new questions. Our MOVE about it cards engage our stakeholders as collaborators, replicating our design-based, pedagogical value of engaging our Choreographing Science participants as collaborators and thinking partners. What we made: MOVE about it The Choreographing Science project was a four -year (2021- 2025) DBR project run by Learning Scientists, Dancer-Choreographers, & Scientists who believed that bringing choreographic modeling and agent -based modeling together could help create inroads for middle schoolers to contribute to scientists’ inquiry and support 1957 scientists in learning from both embodied and youth perspectives. Over four years, we iteratively designed and implemented three 1-2 week-long, free summer camps in which middle schoolers, scientists, and choreographers engaged in scientific inquiry together using choreographic and agent -based modeling tools. The structure of the camps foregrounded the use of choreographic practices and tools to raise and explore questions about the scientists’ research topics. Our formal analytic work thus far has resulted in six ISLS papers (not including this), and multiple in-process journal articles. In the Winter of 2025, as we began to plan for the ending of the project, we found ourselves in the midst of a federal funding crisis in the US. This crisis left us uncertain whether or not we would be able to finish our project as planned, and left our team with an urgency to create something useful. Our scientist partners had expressed impassioned interest in bringing the activities and tools from our camps into their labs and classrooms, and our friends and colleagues in a multitude of educational spaces were just as excited to get their communities moving alongside these ideas. It was in this action -oriented, communal context that we refocused our efforts toward creating a tangible product with these communities at the forefront. In the end, we printed 200 copies of a deck of movement prompt cards which we named MOVE about it: prompts to get groups thinking together through movement. The MOVE about it deck included 90 cards in total and was composed of 6 instruction cards, 19 ways in cards, 22 ways through cards, 22 ways together cards, & 21 ways out cards. Through a process of choreographic design which included brainstorming, enacting, and grouping, we developed four main categories of cards (like parent codes) and five kinds of each category (like child codes, see Column 1 Table 1). Ways in cards were simple and meant to get people up and moving in approachable ways, ways through were more complicated, ways together explicitly focused on moving in relation to others, and ways out focused on grounded endings (Table 1). The instruction cards gave descriptions for the four categories of movement prompts in the deck (Column 2 Table 1) as well as three activity proposals (multi -card sequencing, body segmenting, & leaders and mirrors). Additionally, we added a new, vital member to our team: dancer, visual artist, and assistant professor of dance, MK Ford. MK created custom illustrations for all 20 sub- categories of cards. In the rest of this paper, we describe the implicit values displayed in our cards, reflections on the process of designing them, and the new audiences and communities these cards allow us to be in conversation with. We conclude by making the argument that this process enabled us to surface implicit axiologies in our design work and create a functional tool for a multitude of formal and informal learning spaces that will live on far beyond the end date of our work together. Table 1 Descriptions & Examples of the Four Kinds of Cards in our MOVE about it Deck Type of Card Description Example from Deck ways in ways to walk make circles orientation breathe speed Ways in cards build on familiar actions like walking, breathing, and changing direction to offer approachable ways to get a group in motion. Getting people to move together can be challenging: we often sit still to think and forget we have creative, expressive bodies. We hope ways in cards feel doable and spark curiosity. ways through shake coordinate vivid imagery quality balance Ways through cards build on the foundation of ways in, expanding on movement variety, quality, and complexity. Ways through cards invite new coordination patterns and vivid imagery. While ways in help movers trust their instincts, ways through stretch those instincts into uncharted territories and open space to feel surprised. ways together imagination contact if, then spatial relations music & rhythm Ways together cards explicitly focus on moving in relation to others. Ways together cards foster movement “conversations,” where choices are shaped by the group. Through movement conversations, individuals can become a connected whole, shifting from feeling like a group of “I’s” to one “We.” In this space, ideas emerge that can only be understood together. ways out grounding self agency together stillness space Ways out cards provide intentional transitions that honor how movement changes us. Ways out cards ground participants, restore simplicity, and guide toward an ending. Rather than an abrupt stop, ways out cards provide a thoughtful conclusion, respecting the shared experience and preparing integrated, curious bodies for whatever comes next. 1958 Revealing taken for granted values: Reaching for novelty, variety, and surprise Anyone can dance. Any movement (or stillness) can be dance. Dance is not just for trained, lean, not-yet-disabled bodies to perform challenging feats. Interesting and compelling choreography can be danced by any-body and can be sourced from a wide range of movement choices. We take these principles from a lineage of postmodern dance artists that began in the downtown New York City dance scene in the 1960’s (Banes, 1987). Two of their radical commitments remain in our work: choreography can e merge from dancers’ myriad interpretations of movement prompts, and starting with pedestrian movements can be generative. Through our traditional analytic work, we documented our use of movement prompts (or rules) for generating choreography because of their similarity to code that agents follow in ABM. However, we had taken for granted some of the underlying principles and values embedded in our use of movement prompts, which became explicit as we created our cards. Movement prompts for structuring creativity and switching things up Our dance values come from traditions that assert that “good” improvisational dance (Henley, 2025) relies on structure and boundness in order to support expansive embodied explorations. To this end, restrictions are helpful and generative. Asking people to just “dance” will not generate “good” choreography. And by good we mean that the movements are novel in some way or unexpected and surprise us as movers and observers. We value variety and surprise. Prompts should be structured to inspire, switch up, and allow participants the choice of leaving their comfortable movement homeostases (if only for a few seconds at a time). Some of our ways in cards highlight this value. For example, “walk sideways” restricts movements to walking, an everyday way of moving for many people, and instead of enacting it forward, which is very common, the direction is switched to sideways. How one enacts “walk sideways” is still open-ended. You could walk sideways with a mobility aid, at a slow or fast pace, leading with your head or hip, to your right or left, crossing your feet over each other or shuffling. Prompts such as, “circle your elbow,” bring your attention to a body part not often foregrounded in everyday movement, activating creative, unique movement possibilities. The prompts “change your speed,” or, “find a new place in the room,” ask dancers to alter their first impulses, making small changes that open up new possibilities without naming or assuming the presence of body parts. In addition, we also value reminding mover s that silliness and play can generate expansive thinking. Sometimes you just need to “shake to the sky” & see what happens next! Movement prompts for leveraging imagery to try the “impossible” Novelty and surprise were baked into our movement pedagogy. Dance improvisation tools such as imagery and “impossible” tasks were utilized to enact these values. We found that responding to imaginative prompts such as “move like a blade of grass” were more physically challenging than concrete and direct tasks like “walk sideways.” This differentiation led us to create distinct ways in and ways through cards. Some of the more abstract or imaginative movement prompts leveraged movement qualities derived from imagery such as “allow your body to float through the space,” or “travel through the space like a bolt of lightning.” Floating or lightning images were meant to inspire expansive movement qualities and interpretations. Words, however, were not always the best or only way of sparking one’s movement imagination, which brought us to collaborate with MK on adding a visual element. MK’s art, like the grounding image (Table 1, Row 5, Column 3), shows what might be invisible to the eye, but felt in the body. Additionally, their art displays a diverse array of bodies engaging with the movement ideas. The surrealist nature of these provocations (both prompts and images) undergirds the idea of offering “impossible” tasks. You cannot move as fast as a bolt of lightning, nor can you “reach far away through the walls of the room,” or “keep a forcefield between you and someone else.” But we can enact the physical effort and imaginative, communal space of doing so. Not only can we enact these ideas, but it is generative to do so. Stretching our imagination can stretch our movement explorations and choreographic possibilities. Movement prompts for attending to felt sensations as intentional ways to start and end While it became clear that an implicit goal in our work was to get people exploring new ways to move, it also became apparent that beginning and ending these explorations required careful attention. It’s really hard to get a group of people up and moving! We often do not make explicit the vulnerability and bravery it takes to move and dance with others. Even amongst ourselves, a collective of researchers committed to the power of movement for learning, it took a great deal of effort for us to get up from seated, sedentary positions and move. Once we got groups moving, sometimes it was hard to stop. Endings functioned as transitions from a shared movement experience to (most often) a sedentary, verbal discussion. Bringing movers’ attention inward to how their bodies felt while moving acted as a way to ground both the start and end of movement explorations. Some of the ways in cards focused on moving in synchrony with your breath, amplifying movements already happening in your 1959 body: “get bigger as you inhale and smaller as you exhale.” Some of the ways out cards focused on attending to comfort in your body such as, “find a movement that feels like home.” Movements that arise from attending to how your body feels and what it wants to do are good ways to activate movement -based explorations and bring them to a thoughtful close to prepare for whatever comes next. Sometimes choosing what feels “good” or “right” is more important than reaching for novelty and variability in a mover’s interpretations and choice making. Working at the speed of confidence and trust: “This was of me” It took us about six months to design and print our MOVE about it decks. Six months is much shorter than the time it takes to write and revise a journal manuscript (which in the top Learning Sciences journals often takes a few years), but a little longer than the amount of time it takes to write a conference paper like t his one (about a month or two). Our timeline felt fast because of how we moved through the process. We gave ourselves freedom to create without exhaustively describing or defending our rationale or pointing to an empirical moment in our large data corpus to justify each decision we made. Our fast pace was not always easy. It actually made Lauren uncomfortable. She even tried to slow down the group by going back to the data to pinpoint similarities between movement prompts used during our camps and in our developing deck. While the group humored her, they also pushed back against traditional methodological moves that stifled our creative design process. Our collaborator, Curtis Thomas, reminded us that we knew what we were doing and encouraged us to work from a place of confidence and trust: “Who are we trying to convince right now? Because I just believe it. You know, like I have the experience. And to me, I’m like, I don’t necessarily need to go back [to the data] and look because I’m like, oh yeah this was of me.” (Curtis Thomas 5/27/25). For Curtis, returning to the data was a move used to convince others, not ourselves, of the validity of our choices. This shift in design practices felt radical to Lauren who loves and has been trained in the painstakingly slow and labored work of grounding design decisions in empirical evidence. Eventually, we all moved forward with more confidence that our decisions were grounded in what we knew from our designs and implementations, as well as our bodies and experiences as movers. Moving confidently and quickly freed us to consider new questions related to marketing and scope, including purpose & audience, that we previously did not have space for when focused on justifying our decisions to research audiences. Broadening audience Shifting the pace of our design work from the minutia of traditional academic analyses to the more confident, quicker decision-making pace of choreographic design opened us to new kinds of work. We engage d with ideas related to marketing, such as purpose, scope, and audience, that we had not wrestled with before. We worked hard to develop clear and succinct pitches for the usefulness of our deck, articulating our problem space (“When we’re thinking, we often have to stay still and only move to take a break or get the wiggles out of our system. But we are made to move! What if movement could be part of our thinking?”) and affordances (“When we MOVE about it together, we can: (1) see ourselves build on each other’ s ideas, (2) pose questions, explore relationships, and express ideas as a group, and (2) try out many ideas at the same time”). As we focused our pitch, we also worked to specify our audience. This was challenging because we saw the benefits of moving together relevant everywhere, since most human activity entails working in groups and generating a variety of ideas. We focused on our partner scientists who expressed interest in a deck like this, burnt-out educators who are often too exhausted to disrupt business as usual in their classrooms, dance makers and educators, and after-school space educators, all of whom support learning across “classrooms, workshops, laboratories, and community spaces.” Exposing taken for granted axiological commitments Our MOVE about it cards represent the values we cultivated over four -years together: uplifting communities of movers, expansive creativity, rigorous empathy, and openness for change. We made this deck because we wanted to be useful to communities we care about. Our decision to leverage endogenous choreographic design methods to design something new but related to our DBR project initially felt like a move away from DBR. However, we now see this move as serving key DBR goals by acting as a magnifying glass to expose taken for granted axiologies so fundamental and shared that we did not think to make them explicit. Changing the mode of design changed the kinds of axiologies we were able to see embedded in our work. We see this building on calls in DBR to consider designing for spread and not scale (Taylor et al., 2019), in response to learner ingenuity (Brady & Vogelstein, 2022), and towards axiological innovations (Bang et al., 2016). Shifting our leading epistemological logics felt satisfying in the end. We are excited about gifting educators decks, sharing them with our friends and family, creating art with them (Vogelstein et al., 2026), and researching new adaptations. We designed these cards with the hope that they will live a generative like far beyond the end date of our project. title: Gestures Can Speak: Supporting Heritage Language Literacy Through Movement
citation: Sourabh Garg, Shafagh Hadinezhad, Sepideh Shahi, Sharifa Sultana (2026). Gestures Can Speak: Supporting Heritage Language Literacy Through Movement. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Garg, S., Hadinezhad, S., Shahi, S., & Sultana, S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Learning a heritage language in English- dominant contexts poses challenges for children with limited exposure to formal instruction. This study explores how gesture- based supports embedded in a mobile Persian- learning app enhanced letter recall among seco nd- generation Iranian-American children. Each letter in the app was introduced with a hand gesture reinforced through mini -games. During interviews, children were shown letter visuals and prompted with these gestures. Results showed that gesture p rompting increased correct recognition from 48% to 80%. Qualitative responses revealed that gestures served as memory hooks and cross-linguistic bridges, linking Persian letters to familiar English symbols. Findings contribute to embodied learning research, suggesting that gesture -integrated digital tools can support heritage language literacy in bilingual contexts.

abstract: As the impacts of climate change intensify, it is critical to support high school students in developing Critical Science Agency (CSA) and Systems Thinking (ST) to leverage science learning to address environmental concerns in their local communities and beyond. This study is part of a project involving a collaboration between university researchers, informal science educators, and high school students and teachers to codesign a place - and community- based environmental engineering curriculum. We explore pedagogical implications surfaced through the analysis of teacher and student codesign experiences and reflections that focus on community- embedded and relational environmental learning. Findings highlight the importance of physical presence to support critical and informed socio-ecological understanding of place.

title: Teachers as Co-navigators: Scaffolding Student Uncertainty Navigation in Science Learning
citation: Yu Ye, Michelle Jordan, Ying-Chih Chen, Jongchan Park (2026). Teachers as Co-navigators: Scaffolding Student Uncertainty Navigation in Science Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Ye, Y., Jordan, M., Chen, Y., & Park, J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Accountable Talk & Dialogic Discourse
abstract: Uncertainty is inherent in scientific inquiry and can function as either a barrier or a resource for learning. This study examines middle school teachers’ perceptions of students’ responses to uncertainty and the ways teachers scaffold uncertainty navigation in science classrooms. Grounded in frameworks of uncertainty navigation and learning regulation, we conceptualize uncertainty navigation as a multidimensional process across cognitive, affective, and behavioral domains, involving phases of recognition, acknowledgment, and management. Twelve teachers participating in a week -long professional development program engaged in a structured discussion on students’ uncertainty responses and teachers’ facilitation strategies. Qualitative interpretive discourse analysis showed that, without scaffolding, students’ responses to uncertainty were often negatively oriented. Teachers described two complementary co- navigation routes —direct and indirect scaffolding—enacted through strategies across dimensions and phases. The findings provide preliminary support for the conjecture that teachers’ co-navigation scaffolds students’ self -navigation of uncertainty, helping transform uncertainty into a resource for sustained scientific inquiry.

title: Linguistic Cues in Instructor and AI Feedback: Linking Language to Student Motivation
citation: Jingwen He, Zilu Jiang, Zhiru Sun (2026). Linguistic Cues in Instructor and AI Feedback: Linking Language to Student Motivation. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: He, J., Jiang, Z., & Sun, Z.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examined how linguistic cues in instructor feedback relate to students’ motivation and how these patterns differ between human and AI-facilitated feedback. Feedback from 123 undergraduates in an introductory educational psychology course was analyzed using the General Inquirer and Lasswell dictionaries. Correlations between linguistic features and students’ perceived attainment, interest, and utility values revealed that cogn itively rich and action-oriented language (e.g., problem -solving, active verbs) enhanced motivation, while doctrinal and ideological language reduced it. Relational cues expressing affiliation fostered interest value, whereas loss -focused phrasing undermined attainment value. Comparisons showed that AI feedback used more cognitive and affective expressions but also more abstract ideological framing. These findings highlight the motivational importance of feedback tone: effective feedback should be confident yet collaborative and specific yet empathetic. Designing AI systems that balance analytical precision with relational authenticity may better sustain student motivation in feedback-rich environments.

title: Exploring Connections between Teachers’ “Co-Learning” Interactions and their Opportunities to Learn Equity-Oriented Mathematics Instruction
citation: Heather Fink, Melinda Knapp, Taylor Stafford (2026). Exploring Connections between Teachers’ “Co-Learning” Interactions and their Opportunities to Learn Equity-Oriented Mathematics Instruction. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Fink, H., Knapp, M., & Stafford, T.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: There is a pressing need to support pre - and in-service teachers in learning about equity-oriented instruction in mathematics classrooms. In response, our project team designed tools to support mentor teachers (MTs) and teacher candidates (TCs) in “co -learning” (i.e., learning from and with each other) about asset -focused noticing in clinical settings. In this paper, we use conceptions of “togetherness” and “independence” to characterize interactional differences we noted while observing elementary teachers’ co-learning tool use. This study adds nuance to the field’s understanding of teachers’ collaborative learning experiences by pushing beyond the assumption that collaborative learning needs to be harmonious. We offer an illustration of how two teachers, operating in mostly independent and sometimes contentious ways, learned about equity- oriented mathematics instruction. We juxtapose these interactions with another dyad that fits the quintessential mold of an “ideal” partnership, who exuded consistent balance and unity as they, too, co-learned about equity.

title: Multimodal Analysis of Productive Confusion During Virtual Reality Collaboration: An Exploratory Study
citation: Xinyue Jiao, Basel Hussein, Xavier Ochoa (2026). Multimodal Analysis of Productive Confusion During Virtual Reality Collaboration: An Exploratory Study. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Jiao, X., Hussein, B., & Ochoa, X.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Confusion is a common yet complex emotion in learning, which can become productive confusion that promotes deeper understanding and reflection. However, little is known about how such confusion unfolds in collaborative virtual reality (VR) environments. This exploratory study investigates how learners express and regulate productive confusion during a VR collaborative problem -solving (CPS) task. Eight undergraduate students participated in the collaborative VR game. Multimodal data , including in- game recordings, videos, and audio, were coded for verbal and gestural behaviors. Sequential pattern mining and temporal mapping were conducted to reveal multimodal patterns. Results show that confusion was jointly expressed through verbal –gestural coordination, particularly questioning paired with pointing and manipulation. Successful dyads transformed confusion in to resolution through iterative cycles of planning, execution, and reflection. Gestures played a crucial role in establishing shared confusion. This study contributes to understanding how productive confusion operates as an embodied, socially shared process in VR environments.

title: Examining High School Teachers’ Frames in Science Teaching
citation: S Sushil (2026). Examining High School Teachers’ Frames in Science Teaching. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: Using interviews analyzed through comparative case study methods, the study examined themes in two high school science teachers thinking about the topics they’re teaching and synthesized their frames of the topics from these themes. Results revealed distinct frames: one anthropocentric, emphasizing human success, and the other ecocentric, centering planetary interconnectedness and success. The collective nature of these frames and the role of culture in their shaping for the teachers is discussed.

abstract: This study advances the Mirror Agents Framework from conceptual design to empirical usability validation in authentic K -12 programming classrooms. Thirty middle -school students engaged in two iterative learning rounds while the framework implementation captured multimodal beha vioral and metacognitive data. Pre-/post-tests (MAI, JOL) and mixed -methods analyses revealed significant gains in metacognitive monitoring accuracy and self -regulation behaviors, supported by qualitative evidence of reduced agent dependence and enhanced strategy transfer. Findings demonstrate the framework embedded system’s usability as a dynamic metacognitive scaffolding tool and highlight the value of integrating multi -agent feedback loops and teachable -agent calibration for fostering autonomous metacognitive development.
