title: Teachers’ Co-Evolving Insights on E-Learning Design and Design-Aware Learning Analytics
citation: Pakon Ko, Linyuan Wang, Nancy Law (2026). Teachers’ Co-Evolving Insights on E-Learning Design and Design-Aware Learning Analytics. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Ko, P., Wang, L., & Law, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Learning analytics (LA) can provide teachers with timely insights into student learning, helping them adjust learning design (LD) and optimizing educational outcomes. However, the concept of LA is relatively new, and the use of LA integrated with e- learning platforms remains uncommon, particularly among K –12 teachers. This paper reports on a Research Practice Partnership ( RPP) project involving primary and secondary schools to develop a system and workflow that supports the integration of LA into teachers’ everyday professional practice, beginning at the LD stage. A qualitative case study of a teacher team over two years reveals how their professional learning evolved, from identifying meaningful learning analytics questions (LAQs) relevant to their LD context to recognizing the importance of selecting appropriate e- learning tools as a prerequisite for meaningful LA, and finally to incorporating targeted LAQs into their LD decision making process , thereby consciously closing the LD-LA loop in their professional practice.

title: When Understanding Breaks: Interaction Analysis of Knowledge Construction in Multilingual Science
citation: Shubhangi Sonawane, Rafikh Shaikh (2026). When Understanding Breaks: Interaction Analysis of Knowledge Construction in Multilingual Science. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Sonawane, S. & Shaikh, R.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Across India's multilingual classrooms, science is frequently taught in a language that differs from learners' home languages, producing friction at the concept-language interface that depresses participation and understanding. Studying how breakdowns are detected and repaired in real -time is essential for equitable access to disciplinary explanations. This paper argues that microgenetic "repair" sequences constitute the observable unit of progress in multilingual science discourse. Anchored in a Grade 9 se mi-English biology lesson and complemented by student focus group discussions, the analysis identifies triggers for breakdown and traces time- stamped episodes in which understanding is restored through one - word student anchoring, peer-mediated refinement, and teacher-led reframing, alongside partial and no- repair cases. The resulting five- part typology specifies how repair unfolds in whole - class interaction and where it fails from learners' perspectives, yielding designable principles for lesson pacing, visual scaffolding, and question reframing that are feasible under time pressure and redistribute participation authority.

title: Designing AI to Scaffold Learners’ Cognitive Engagement in Generative Learning
citation: Zhenyao Cai, Shiyao Wei, Shayan Doroudi (2026). Designing AI to Scaffold Learners’ Cognitive Engagement in Generative Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Cai, Z., Wei, S., & Doroudi, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Recent advances in AI have raised concerns about students’ overreliance on automated systems that may complete learning tasks without requiring meaningful cognitive effort and engagement. This paper explores how AI can be designed to scaffold and sustain cognitive engagement in generative learning activities. Drawing on generative learning theory and scaffolding, we present a conceptual account of how AI can guide learners through generative processes such as selecting, organizing, and integrating information, while gradually fading support as competence develops. We illustrate this through the design of an AI -assisted system that helps children (aged 8–13) create educational science videos --- a task that embodies generative learning but poses cognitive challenges for young learners. Our work sheds light on how to integrate scaffolding to foster but not replace meaningful engagement with AI in generative learning.

title: Performing sustainability in construction through 3D printing with clay
citation: Anna Keune, Živa Simšič (2026). Performing sustainability in construction through 3D printing with clay. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Keune, A. & Simšič, I.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: The construction industry produces around 21% of global greenhouse gas emissions and faces major decarbonization challenges. Digital fabrication methods such as robotic clay extrusion offer opportunities to support sustainable construction and learning. However, little is known about how young people engage with sustainability through such technologies. This qualitative video -based study, grounded in constructionist and socio- material perspectives, examined how youth aged 11–17 explored sustainability in construction using clay and 3D pen extrusion during an after-school course. Findings show that clay enabled learners to engage with multiple aspects of sustainability, supported by its material properties, particularly the smooth clay-water mixtures central to digital design and extrusion. In contrast, 3D pen extrusion mainly fostered rapid prototyping and early planning. The performative, material qualities of clay encouraged deep physical exploration, suggesting that introducing digital clay extrusion can cultivate a material-driven understanding of sustainability in construction from an early age. The need for learning about sustainable construction The construction industry, which accounts for approximately 21% of global greenhouse gas emissions, faces a significant challenge in meeting the 2030 decarbonization targets. This highlights a critical disparity between current emission rates and the neces sary reductions required to mitigate climate change (United Nations Environment Programme, 2024). Encouragingly, emerging digital construction technologies, such as robotic 3D printing with innovative earth and clay materials and optimized architectural design, offer promise for enhancing sustainability within the sector. These advancements offer solutions to reduce environmental footprints and can reshape climate impacts (Dörfler et al., 2024; Agnusdei & Del Prete, 2022). However, technology innovation alone is not sufficient. To lead the sustainability charge, there is a need to prepare children and young people to tackle the pressing challenges of climate change (UN DESA, 2024) and to provide young people with early experiences to build with the innovative technologies and techniques that promise to advance sustainability in construction (Construction Blueprint, 2023). However, there is a substantial knowledge gap about how young people can learn about how new construction technologies (e.g., digitally controlled robotic extrusion with clay and earth materials) advance sustainable building processes, effective digital designs, and efficient material mixtures. Thus, we asked: What sustainability in construction concepts do young people perform through robotic 3D printing, and how? To address this research question, we adopted a constructionist approach to learning (Papert, 1993) and posthumanist perspectives (Keune, 2022) and were guided by architectural theory (Bredella, 2022) and 3D printing construction approaches (Dörfler et al., 2024). Building on these perspectives, we designed and facilitated a 9-week course for young people to observe and control a robotic clay print and create digital 3D models that they could then physically extrude using plastic (PLA) materials with 3D pens and clay through hand-coiling clay. We analyzed video-recorded interactions among youth regarding sustainability in construction concepts directly driven by 3D printing (e.g., geometry optimization, planning labor use, planning construction sequences, on- site fabrication, and material use optimization). The findings show that different materials shape how young learners perform sustainability in construction. Clay, with its adaptable and reusable properties, enabled engagement with all sustainability in c onstruction concepts. In contrast, PLA filament used in 3D pens primarily supported rapid prototyping and early- stage planning. These differences highlight how clay fosters deeper material exploration and understanding of sustainability in construction compared to PLA -based fabrication. These findings have implications both for the design of educational activities in sustainable construction and for understanding how learning processes can be structured to foster conceptual understanding in architecture and construction. Theoretical background Innovative technologies in construction, such as robotic clay printing, depend on closely linked material and technical processes, often requiring custom-developed material mixtures to achieve consistent extrusion (Dörfler et al., 2024). 3D printing construction technologies are expected to impact the construction lifecycle and promote 2031 sustainability through approaches like on- site printing and optimized labor planning (Agnusdei & Del Prete, 2022). Facilitating aspects of a sustainable construction future, made possible through digital and robotic printing, in educational settings, has implications for equipping young people with core knowledge to tackle global crises. Empirical research on 3D printing in construction informed the design of learning opportunities introducing youth to its processes and implications using age-appropriate, safe materials (i.e., clay instead of cement extrusion). Socio-material approaches to learning about sustainability in construction Our approach to learning is grounded in constructionist theories (Papert, 1993) and socio -material perspectives (Keune & Peppler, 2019). Constructionism asserts that learners internalize complex concepts through the active manipulation of digital and tangible materials toward sharable designs (Papert, 1993). This perspective led us to focus on how conceptual knowledge related to sustainable construction is performed through design with construction materials. Sustainability is enacted as learners organize, plan, and adapt their design decisions. We also built on socio-material approaches to learning, foregrounding how knowledge emerges from entanglements among people, tools, materials, and environments (Keune & Peppler, 2019; Kumpulainen & Kajamaa, 2019; Peppler & Thompson, 2024; Seitamaa-Hakkarainen et al., 2010). These perspectives highlight that learning is co- produced through the properties of the materials. Their weight, resistance, and unpredictability play an active role in learning. Guided by material syntonicity (Keune, 2022), which suggests that attuning to the different properties of materials directs what can be learned, we attend to the particular properties of two construction materials, clay as a promising sustainable resource and PLA as prolifically available throughout educational settings, wondering whether some materials highlight different aspects of performing sustainability over others. Following this trajectory, we were also inspired by socio-material perspectives in architecture and design (Bredella, 2022; Dörfler et al., 2024), which highlight that digital and physical processes are inseparable and produce new material processes that, together, can advance sustainable construction. This perspective directed us to consider construction sites, whether physical, digital, or hybrid, as spaces where learners engage directly with materials, robotic processes, and design tools, experiencing how material properties, temporal rhythms, and collaborative interactions co -produce knowledge about susta inable construction practices. This outlook sees material engagement as the means through which sustainability concepts emerge in 3D printing.

title: Declarative Narrative: New Interfaces for AI-Supported Writing
citation: Chris Proctor, Varun Bhatt (2026). Declarative Narrative: New Interfaces for AI-Supported Writing. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Proctor, C. & Bhatt, V.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is disrupting the cultural practice of writing while supporting the emergence of new writing practices. However, emergent writing practices, and the identities and relationships they support, are dependent on the affordances of commercial GAI infrastructure, leading to a concentration of power over how we read and write. In support of critical literacy pedagogy, we present three new interfaces for GAI - supported writing we have embedded into an existing web application for interactive storytelling. We report on how these interfaces were taken up in a ten -week high school writing club, and compare GAI -supported stories with a corpus of non- GAI stories. We identify several ways in which authors use GAI affordances for rhetorical effect, and find that GAI stories are similar in structure to non -GAI stories. The writing process of GAI stories differs from non-GAI stories, suggesting that GAI may compete with attention to code.

title: Classroom Observations for Children's Reactions to Ambient Identity Cues in a STEM Video
citation: JungEun Ha, Emre Dinç, José Sandoval Llanos, Anna Yinqi Zhang, Brian R. Belland, ChanMin Kim (2026). Classroom Observations for Children's Reactions to Ambient Identity Cues in a STEM Video. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study explore d how children react ed to ambient identity cues in e lementary STEM classrooms. This study was part of a larger project whose goal was to create an equitable and inclusive environment for children to sense belonging in the classroom and STEM disciplines. Data included student survey responses and classroom observation notes about materials used and interactions between the teacher and students as well as among students. For this study, f our participants were selected based on data richness. Thematic analysis was conducted using NVivo 14 with a coding scheme developed based on the conceptual framework. The findings suggest that how ambient identity cues are presented and interpreted are critical to the extent to which minoritized students feel belonging in STEM.

title: Self-Regulated Learning with Generative AI: Student Strategies, Performance-Based Profiles, and Instructional Implications
citation: Daihan Xu, Matheus de Andrade, Diana Martin (2026). Self-Regulated Learning with Generative AI: Student Strategies, Performance-Based Profiles, and Instructional Implications. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Xu, D., Andrade, M. D., & Martin, D.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: This mixed -methods study examines how students enact self -regulated learning (SRL) with GenAI in an authentic undergraduate chemical engineering course. Using an activity-centric SRL lens, we triangulated interviews with students (n = 12) and instructors ( n = 3), a post -course survey (n = 40), course -tool interaction logs, and AI -supported student artifacts. Findings show that GenAI supported SRL across forethought, performance, and reflection by helping students initiate tasks, refine ideas through dialogue, verify outputs, and review their work. Across performance groups, three recurrent profiles emerged: Prudent Architects, Struggling Explorers, and Anxious GenAI functioned primarily as a learning- intention amplifier in SRL, strengthening deeper regulation when mastery goals were strong and reinforcing shortcut -oriented strategies when performance goals dominated. We discuss targeted instructional scaffolds for fostering critical and ethical AI-supported learning.

title: Students’ Journeys with Boundary Tools: Comparing Home and Classroom Encounters with a Lab Experiment
citation: Carolina Sotério, Paulo Blikstein (2026). Students’ Journeys with Boundary Tools: Comparing Home and Classroom Encounters with a Lab Experiment. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Sotério, C. & Blikstein, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Science learning is often confined to culturally scripted spaces such as classrooms, laboratories, and museums, each carrying expectations for how inquiry should unfold. This paper examines what happens when a science tool is intentionally designed to move across those spaces as a boundary tool. “Lab- on-a-Book” is a low-cost, portable kit embedded in a journal format for conducting chemical experiments. We analyze two enactments of the same cyanotype activity (one by an individual student at home and another in a secondary classroom) to explore how learners orient toward experimentation (how they question, hesitate, proceed, or seek validation). Findings show how the tool’s material and cultural design enable distinct forms of inquiry and reflection across contexts, positioning portability as a design strategy for expanding where and how science learning can occur.

title: Analyzing Pre-Service Teachers’ TPACK Development Trajectories through SRL-Supportive Artifacts Production Using SSNA
citation: Keita Kato, Jun Oshima (2026). Analyzing Pre-Service Teachers’ TPACK Development Trajectories through SRL-Supportive Artifacts Production Using SSNA. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Kato, K. & Oshima, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines how the relationships among the knowledge domains of Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) change over time by comparing those who produce higher- and lower-quality self-regulated learning (SRL)-supportive artifacts using Social Semantic Network Analysis . We analyzed the artifacts and reflection journals of 46 pre-service teachers. The results indicated that artifact quality was primarily associated with the SRL support scores. Although not statistically significant, the improvement group tended to show a higher total degree centrality and stronger connections between technological (TK) and pedagogical knowledge (PK) . This paper presents an approach for capturing the temporal development of linking knowledge domains within the TPACK development process.

title: Exploring Learner Engagement in an LLM-Supported Simulation Environment for Complex Systems Understanding
citation: Amit Nair, Man Su, Tomohiro Nagashima (2026). Exploring Learner Engagement in an LLM-Supported Simulation Environment for Complex Systems Understanding. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Nair, A., Su, M., & Nagashima, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
tpack_tk_labels: Generative AI & LLMs; Simulations & Scientific Modeling
abstract: Understanding complex systems is challenging, as learners often rely on linear reasoning and struggle to recognize decentralized and emergent processes. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to support inquiry in simulation- based learning, yet how learners engage with these tools and how such engagement relates to learning outcomes remains underexplored. In this study, we investigate learner engagement within a theory- informed, LLM -supported simulation environment, based on an exper iment with 69 postsecondary students that varied parameter control and questioning agency. Focusing on questioning agency, we examine how interactions with an LLM -based tutor and engagement with exploratory instructional regions relate to posttest performa nce. Results show that greater engagement with the tutor, particularly through content-focused interactions, is associated with higher learning gains. Time spent in exploratory regions also significantly predicts performance. These findings highlight the i mportance of fostering meaningful engagement with both conversational tutors and interactive features in LLM-supported environments.

title: Students’ Traversing between the Real and Mathematical World through Diagrams
citation: Kritika Chitkara, DurgaPrasad Karnam, Sahana Murthy (2026). Students’ Traversing between the Real and Mathematical World through Diagrams. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Chitkara, K., Karnam, D., & Murthy, S.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Diagrams’ role in mathematical reasoning is well -studied. However, their role as cognitive artifacts in the process of triggering the modeling is yet to be fully characterised. The modeling process involves multiple nonlinear steps that connect the real a nd mathematical worlds, ranging from understanding, simplifying, mathematising, working mathematically, interpreting, validating and exposing. We investigate the role of cognitive artifacts in enabling this process in learners. We observe groups of school students in grades - 4th to 7th while they make a scaled map of their surroundings, a task that requires them to model actively. We analyse the role of diagrams they make, as cognitive artifacts in shaping their modeling process, by specifically highlighting how diagrams trigger or enable specific modeling steps. The findings can help in the purposive usage of diagrams as pedagogical tools in bringing real-world contexts into mathematics classrooms in a systematic way.

title: Scaffolding Students’ use of GenAI: A Pilot Examining Higher Education Instructors’ Attitudes and Reported Practice
citation: Ilana Ram, Emad Eid, Olga Chuntonov, Lisa Bosman (2026). Scaffolding Students’ use of GenAI: A Pilot Examining Higher Education Instructors’ Attitudes and Reported Practice. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Ram, I., Eid, E., Chuntonov, O., & Bosman, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: While higher education institutions establish policies for Generative AI (GenAI) use, less attention is given to instructional scaffold s for students’ use of it. To address this gap, we used two surveys (n₁=242, n₂=46; pre -registered before analysis) to evaluate instructors' perceptions toward student GenAI use (RQ1) and SRL-aligned scaffolding practices in teaching (RQ2). We further evaluate alignment between reported practices and SRL theory (RQ3) . Results reveal a paradox: instructors recognize GenAI's benefits for reducing workload and improving understanding, yet worry about impacts on critical thinking and independent learning. Mapping scaffolding practices onto the SRL framework revealed instructors emphasize during -task support while neglecting planning and reflection. Surprisingly, scaffolding practices formed a single construct rather than distinct SRL phases, suggesting lack of differentiated strategies for supporting GenAI-enhanced learning. Findings suggest a possible gap between SRL theory and practice in the GenAI era, pointing to urgent needs for evidence - based professional development moving toward pedagogically-grounded support.

title: Cross-disciplinary mentorship: A First Step Toward Innovative Action Research
citation: Seoyeon Lee, Shelli Rambo (2026). Cross-disciplinary mentorship: A First Step Toward Innovative Action Research. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This qualitative study employs an autoethnographic approach to examine the years - long process of transforming a mentor –mentee relationship into a collaborative partnership centered on shared goals for students within a school community. The reflection draw s on the first author’s enduring professional friendship with a current high school principal, who originally served as her mentor assigned by a school district. The study highlights how teachers can cultivate a supportive professional community, encourage one another in pursuing personal and professional goals, and leverage their collective knowledge and experience to support the youth within their school community better. This study focuses on the author’s reflective dialogue drawn from several years of conversations with a colleague and friend, exploring how their shared vision led to an action research project aimed at improving students’ math learning experience in a school characterized by low socioeconomic status.

citation: Go Shoji, Shigeto Ozawa (2026). Assessing Interdisciplinary Learning in STEAM Education: A Critical Narrative Review. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Shoji, G. & Ozawa, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Interdisciplinary STEAM education increasingly emphasizes integration across disciplines, yet learning assessment has been focused on measuring discrete knowledge outcomes rather than integration processes. This theoretical paper examines assessment approaches in interdisciplinary STEAM and higher education, revealing gaps between educational goals and assessment methods. Through a critical narrative review, we identify three major approaches (objective tests, questionnaires, and performance -based assessments) and analyze their limitations for capturing integration dynamics. Drawing on Actor -Network Theory (ANT), we provide a theoretical perspective for understanding interdisciplinary learning as emergent phenomena arising from human and non -human actor interactions. ANT's translation concept offers a lens for making visible the mechanisms through which learners negotiate meanings and construct new understandings across disciplinary boundaries, contributing toward more equitable and theoretically grounded assessment practices.

title: How Curriculum Mediates Teacher Noticing of Student Work in a Geometry Simulation
citation: Soobin Jeon (2026). How Curriculum Mediates Teacher Noticing of Student Work in a Geometry Simulation. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Jeon, S.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study investigates how secondary mathematics teachers learn to interpret and respond to student work when their noticing is supported by curriculum materials. Curriculum is conceptualized as a mediational resource that shapes how teachers perceive, reason about, and act on students’ mathematical ideas. Using simulation -based interviews, twelve experienced geometry teachers engaged with student work under two conditions: one providing only student-facing materials and another including teacher -facing materials. Teacher noticing was examined as a process of interpretive sense-making, focusing on how teachers made sense of student ideas through the linguistic and representational features of the curriculum. A combined framework of professional noticing and systemic functional linguistics revealed that access to teacher- facing text supported teachers in contextualizing student reasoning within curricular goals and offering feedback that advanced conceptual understanding. The study highlights how teachers’ interpretive activity is shaped by the interaction of tools, language, and representations within a designed simulation environment.

title: Mapping Instructors’ Attitudes Towards Cheating with AI: An Exploratory Analysis Using Forum Analysis
citation: Iman Mohammadi, Ali Keramati, Sina Rismanchian (2026). Mapping Instructors’ Attitudes Towards Cheating with AI: An Exploratory Analysis Using Forum Analysis. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Mohammadi, I., Keramati, A., & Rismanchian, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General

abstract: In teaching and learning environments, cheating and the violation of academic integrity have always been one of the challenges, involving different levels of concerns such as administrative, personal knowledge, learning, and equity. The introduction of lar ge language models has brought cheating in dialogue to the forefront, given the apparent capabilities of these models to complete students’ academic assignments. This study aims to leverage recent dialogues among university professors about cheating with G enerative AI to better understand their beliefs about academic honesty. In doing so, we analyze a corpus of 2.01 million posts (threads and comments) in the r/Professors subreddit discussing cheating after the release of ChatGPT, providing a better understanding of teachers’ motivations to discourage cheating and the strategies they use to do so. We synthesize the why and how of addressing cheating to identify caveats about the future of AI and academic integration. Objectives and significance After the introduction of large language models (LLMs) and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots, the idea of students using these tools extensively to bypass the effort required to complete academic assignments, under the guise of cheating, academic dishonesty, etc., has made headlines (Yusuf, 2024). Cheating and preaching academic integrity are not new phenomena in higher education and K-12 settings (Reddy-Lund, 2025); however, with the broad adoption of these tools, cheating has resurfaced (von Garrel, 2023). Several research projects have been started to identify the level of cheating among students (Sozon, 2024; Rismanchian et al., 2026). On the other hand, many professors have reported taking the initiative to fight cheating with GenAI (Kazley, 2024). Although there is an ongoing effort to better understand how widespread cheating with AI is among students, professors' reaction to the perceived broad usage can change the way they design their instructional policies, their course assignments, and more broadly, the dynamic of teaching and learning might enter into a new era (Sun, 2025; Sumakul, 2022). From the lens of the learning sciences, it is important to understand how these transitions to an era in which GenAI is accessible to all students might or might not align with the learning sciences' epistemology, theories, and praxis (Balabdaoui et al., 2024). This research aims to provide a clearer picture of teachers’ motivations and strategies for addressing students’ cheating and irresponsible use of AI, and to offer a few considerations from a learning sciences perspective that might help better understand how the dynamics of teaching and learning in higher education are evolving. University faculty are currently engaging in sense -making in the open about these shifts, especially in public-practitioner venues. These venues offer a naturally occurring record of how instructors narrate the why (motivations and values) and the how (design and enforcement moves) of academic honesty in the era of GenAI. Mapping these narratives matters for the learning sciences because they reveal the design logics educators are settling on, whether toward surveillance and control, toward redesign for learning, or some hybrid, and the equity/ethics trade-offs implied by each. Building on recent concerns about AI-enabled cheating and the ongoing sense-making among instructors, this study addresses the following research questions: ● RQ1: How do instructors describe their motivations and values in responding to AI-mediated cheating? ● RQ2: What strategies do instructors report using to address or prevent AI-mediated cheating in their courses? This paper contributes: 1) Thematic account of instructors’ motivations for combating AI -mediated cheating (the "why"); 2) A synthesis of methods they report using (the "how"), spanning pedagogical redesign, technological controls, and communication strate gies; and 3) Implications that align (or clash) with learning - sciences commitments to authenticity, equity, participation. 2091 This study is informed by learning sciences perspectives that conceptualize learning as participation in meaningful disciplinary activity rather than the production of decontextualized outputs (Lave & Wenger, 1991; Wenger, 1998). From this perspective, concerns about AI -mediated cheating can be understood not only as violations of academic rules but as disruptions to how learning becomes visible through student engagement in disciplinary practices (Shepard, 2000). This framing guides how we interpret instructors’ motivations and strategies in responding to AI use in their classrooms.

title: Exploring Reflection Quality: Divergent Self-Efficacy Outcomes in Makerspaces
citation: Hyejoo Yun, Shibani Rana, Bertrand Schneider (2026). Exploring Reflection Quality: Divergent Self-Efficacy Outcomes in Makerspaces. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Yun, H., Rana, S., & Schneider, B.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA); Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: Makerspaces are often promoted as environments that build student self -efficacy (Morado et al., 2021), yet not all learners experience gains. This exploratory mixed- methods study examines the relationship between reflection quality and changes in self- efficacy within a semester-long makerspace course. Thirteen graduate students were categorized into gain (n = 7) and loss (n = 6) groups based on pre/post survey scores. Two early reflections per student were coded using ten categories and analyzed for length, breadth, depth, and structure using epistemic network analysis (ENA). Qualitative examples illustrated how these patterns manifested in reflective writing. While both groups produced reflections of similar length and breadth, they diverged in depth and structure. The gain group developed integrative structures linking challenges to evaluation, learning, and future planning, while the loss group provided descriptive accounts of challenges and problem- solving. Findings suggest that reflection quality, not quantity, distinguishes self -efficacy trajectories and that deliberately scaffolding evaluative, forward -looking reflection could potentially support self -efficacy growth in makerspaces.

title: ‘I Spend All My Energy Preparing’: Balancing AI Automation and Agency for Self-Regulated Learning in SmartFlash
citation: Hongming Li, Salah Esmaeiligoujar, Nazanin Adham, Hai Li, Rui Huang (2026). ‘I Spend All My Energy Preparing’: Balancing AI Automation and Agency for Self-Regulated Learning in SmartFlash. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Li, H., Esmaeiligoujar, S., Adham, N., Li, H., & Huang, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: Effective study strategies fail when preparatory tasks consume learning time. While AI educational tools demonstrate efficacy, understanding how they align with self -regulation needs in learners' own study contexts remains limited. We conducted formative design research using an AI flashcard prototype, employing large language models to generate design hypotheses validated through researcher walkthroughs and student sessions. Six students across disciplines completed sessions combining interviews and think-aloud tasks with their materials. Analysis revealed students value automation for addressing overwhelming preparation burden yet require transparent, editable AI outputs to maintain cognitive ownership essential for self - regulation. They conceptualized AI as collaborative partner demanding verifiable reasoning rather than autonomous agent. Metacognitive scaffolding was endorsed when clarifying study direction without constraining choice. Motivational features produced divergent responses. We derive design principles prioritizing editability and transparency, scaffolding metacognition without prescription, and accommodating motivational diversity. Findings identify conditions under which automation supports versus undermines metacognitive development in self- regulated learning.

title: Exploration as Relationship: An Axiological Shift For Native Youths’ Relationships With Digital Storytelling Technologies
citation: Chasity Mayo, Breanne K. Litts, Dallas Haws, Christina Morgan, Tifiny Mills, Eileen Quintana, Analysa Allison, Natalie Billie, Shoshana Begay, Nebo Title VI American Indian Education Program (2026). Exploration as Relationship: An Axiological Shift For Native Youths’ Relationships With Digital Storytelling Technologies. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Mayo, C., Litts, B. K., Haws, D., Morgan, C., Mills, T., Quintana, E., Allison, A., Billie, N., Begay, S., & Program, N. T. V. A. I. E.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Across sociotechnical learning environments, such as with digital storytelling, Native youth often navigate histories of harm in their relationship with technologies, especially as they begin to develop a personal relationship with these tools. In this paper, we look at Native youths’ explorations with digital technologies as a core tenet of relationship building. We view exploration as a space between, specifically in regard to how Native youth self -determine and (re)shape their relational configurations with using digital storytelling technologies to represent their ideas and their community. We examined 17 Native youths’ initial engagements with digital technologies to understand how they begin to develop relationships with digital technologies through exploration. Findings provide evidence that Native youth explore digital technologies across technical and contextual configurations. Insights from this study expand our understanding of how Native youth explore the space between configurations of their ideas and their community as they develop digital storytelling projects. Objectives Indigenous communities in the United States have a complex relationship with digital technologies, often because these technologies dismiss their cultural, technological, and rhetorical sovereignties (Morgan et al., 2025; Winter & Boudreau, 2018). This is done through gatekeeping and blackboxing knowledge, withholding and limiting decision-making power, and developing and distributing both software and hardware that unreciprocates what it takes from the land (Morgan et al., 2025, Litts et al., 2021). Digita l technologies are designed artifacts, meaning that they are imbued with the values of the dominant culture in which they are designed (Benjamin, 2019) and oftentimes ascribe to Western views of time and relationship. Thus, technologies are both a process and a product of culture (Bang et al., 2013) and have both produced and reinforced harmful stereotypes of Native Americans. These harms extend into data misrepresentation and abuse, access -related issues, and exclusion (Dalton, 2002; Drabiak-Syed, 2010). In community research with Indigenous youth, it is important to be aware of these harms and consider the ways in which Native youth relate to and interact with digital technologies, particularly in the context of learning. One way that scholars have examined and considered Native youths’ relationship to digital technologies is through the practice of storytelling. Both Indigenous and non- Indigenous scholars working with Indigenous communities advocate for the integration of Indigenous practices and knowledges, such as storytelling, into educational contexts. The practices of storytelling are vital for cultural sustainment and revitalization, as stories both shape and are shaped by Native youth (McCarty & Lee, 2014). Storytelling is a sacred and intimate practice and the stories shared carry values and histories (Archibald, 2008). Within digital storytelling, there is a desire to support Native youth’s self- determination in terms of who, how, and what stories are told (Litts et al., 2025). Storytelling is also an enactment of sovereignty, self-determination, and self-education (Brayboy, 2005) and is an abundant source of healing that promotes the well -being and self -determination of Native youth, especially as they (re)story historical and ancestral narratives about their communities (Litts et al., 2025). Guided by the significance of stories, we examined how youth explore in relation to digital storytelling and digital technologies. We conceptualize exploration as a relational configuration of the space between ideas and space between people (Tuck, 2009). From this frame, Native youth explore the space between creating and sharing stories with digital technology as a relational configuration with their ideas and with their community. In this study, we are guided by the research question: How does exploration support Native youths’ relationship with digital storytelling technologies? Specifically, we look at two dimensions of exploration — technical explorations and contextual explorations. Technical explorations constitute the ways that Native youth explore the specific 2111 affordances of digital storytelling technologies. We devise technical explorations into three categories — time, sound, and visuals — and examine how these serve as the foundation for establishing a wholistically connected relationship. Contextual explorations refer to where the explorations took place and how the context, such as what cultural activity youth were participating in or the land on which the workshop took place, was directly connected to the stories that Native youth explored. Contextual explorations also showcase how Native youth made their care for their community, their culture, and the land visible through storytelling. The contribution of this work is to invite an axiological shift toward viewing exploration as a tenet of building relationships, particularly those that Native youth build with digital technologies and simultaneously with their community, their culture, and the land. Theoretical framework The space between Our theoretical framework looks at exploration as the space between ideas and the space between people (Tuck, 2009). This space between ideas and people (Tuck, 2009) guides our understanding of exploration as a relational configuration. In our study, we operationalize this configuration as how Native youth explore and self -determine their relationship with using digital storytelling technologies to represent their ideas and their community. This framing helps us follow the two configurations (ideas and people) that Tuck (2009) identifies as core to understanding Indigenous frames of relationship. To extend these conceptualizations of the space between, we draw on two established theoretical threads to frame the importance of exploration for relationship: liminal space (Hogue, 2019) and third space (Bang, 2010; Gutierrez et al. , 1995; Gutierrez et al., 1997). Hogue (2019) applies the concept of liminal spaces to STEM education for Indigenous youth by sharing that liminal spaces are places where “we can communicate about and accept different ways of knowing, learning, and being” (Hogue, 2019, p. 2). Instead of using liminality to refer to a physical learning environment, we draw on liminal spaces to capture the essence of being in transformation. Liminality reflects the transitional elements of exploration, where you are transitioning through different phases of an idea as you refine and craft a vision. The third space is a similar concept, discussed by Bang (2010) and Gutierrez and colleagues (1996; 1997). In the learning sciences literature, the third space acts as a place where “alternative and comp eting discourse and positionings transform conflict and difference into rich zones of collaboration and learning” (Bang, 2010, p. 7). Here we pull at the theoretical threads of the third space to reflect how the tensions that exist because of the complex history underlying digital technologies can be transformed into opportunity for Native youth. To summarize, the space between people and ideas acts as both a liminal space and a third space, as they shift us epistemologically toward regeneration and change. In this sense, the spaces between people and ideas are not viewed as gaps or deficits, but instead are spaces where new relationships and ways of being are possible (Tuck, 2009).

title: Reflecting on the Process of School Change through Leadership and Teacher Narratives: A study of a first-generation school in Southern India

title: Reimagining Learning as a 3-Dimensional Vector: Integrating Behaviorism, Cognitivism, and Social Constructivism

abstract: This conceptual paper proposes the Three -Dimensional Learning Theory (3DLT) model as a new way of integrating three major perspectives on learning. While behaviorism, cognitivism, and social constructivism are often treated as separate paradigms in research , classroom practices reveal that learning naturally unfolds across all three. Drawing inspiration from physics and ongoing work in learning sciences, 3DLT conceptualizes learning as a vector whose behavioral, cognitive, and sociocultural components interact dynamically. The paper first revisits the historical fragmentation among learning theories, then introduces 3DLT as an integrative model, and finally demonstrates its presence in four common teaching methods: lecture-based, technology- based, group- based, and problem -solving learning. Through this analysis, the paper argues that effective teaching involves movement through interconnected dimensions r ather than adherence to a single theoretical stance. Implications are offered for teaching, teacher education, and research design, positioning 3DLT as a framework for a more balanced and multidimensional understanding of how learning occurs. The starting point: Beyond the silos of learning theories Learning theories have long guided educational research and practice, yet they often operate in isolation. In most education programs, behaviorism, cognitive constructivism, and sociocultural theory are taught as distinct paradigms rather than interacting lenses on the single phenomenon: learning. This separation limits how we understand learning and how we design classrooms that reflect its complexity. Behaviorism emphasizes the observable (Pavlov, 1927; Skinner, 1953; Thorndike, 1932), cognitive construct ivism stresses mental processes (Atkinson & Shiffrin, 1968; Chi & Wylie, 2014; Piaget, 1970), and sociocultural theory conceptualizes learning in participation and belonging (Lave & Wenger, 1991; Nasir & Hand, 2006; Vygotsky, 1978). Each contributes powerfully, but when viewed separately they often reduce learning to one dimension. Sfard (1998) warned of the dangers of choosing just one metaphor for learning, a caution that continues to be ignored. In today’s complex classrooms, where students use technology, collaborate, and solve real -world problems, these theories inevitably intertwine. Within any single degree, course, or classroom session, learners are expected to demonstrate competence through the intertwined logics of these theories. From a behaviorist perspective, students are evaluated through observable and measurable performances such as assignments and exams that reinforce desired outcomes (Ertmer & Newby, 1993; Skinner, 1953). From a cognitive view, learning involves encountering new information, experiencing cognitive dissonance, and reorganizing mental schemas through processes of assimilation and accommodation (Chi & Wylie, 2014; Piaget, 1970). Simultaneously, a sociocultural lens reminds us that as learners collaborate, engage in discourse, and participate in community practices, they develop new identities and a sense of belonging (Lave & Wenger, 1991; Vygotsky, 1978). Thus, the lived experience of learn ers already operates as a composite process —behavioral, cognitive, and social — woven together in their educational encounters. In this conceptual paper, I argue that it is time to move beyond linear or siloed understandings, drawing inspiration from physics and other recent work happening in the field ( NASEM, 2018; Nasir et al., 2020) . I advocate for conceptualizing learning as a three- dimensional vector. The Three -Dimensional Learning Theory (3DLT) sees behavior, cognition, and social construction as orthogonal but interdependent axes of growth. Learning is not an isolated shift on one specific dimension but a dynamic movement through a multidimensional space where action, understanding, and participation interact. This idea draws inspiration from integrative thinkers who recognized the mutual shaping of body, mind, and environment (Cobb, 1994; Sfard, 1998). In proposing 3DLT, my goal is to provide a framework that captures the full richness of how students learn in contemporary classrooms and how educators and researchers can better operationalize trajectories of learning and growth. In what follows, I briefly revisit the roots of behaviorism, cognitivism, and social constructivism to show how each offers a partial but important view of the complex phenomenon of learning. Although many other perspectives inform educational theory, this paper focuses on these three for simplicity. I then propose the 3DLT and use examples from classroom practices to illustrate how different teaching methods already blend these perspectives. I conclude by discussing how this framework can enrich teaching and research. 2125 The problem: Theoretical fragmentation The persistence of fragmentation among learning theories is both historical and epistemological. Early educational psychology was dominated by behaviorism, which defined learning as a measurable change in behavior (Bandura, 1977; Pavlov, 1927; Skinner, 1953; Thorndike, 1932). Pavlov’s classical conditioning, Thorndike’s “law of effect,” Skinner’s operant conditioning, and Bandura’s observational learning grounded an entire generation of teaching practices such as drill, reinforcement, and programmed instruction (Ertmer & Newby, 1993). Yet as Lagemann (2000) noted, this scientific pursuit of control often neglected mental life. The cognitive revolution re-centered the learner’s mind, shifting attention toward how information is processed, organized, and transformed (Miller, 1956; Piaget, 1970). Researchers such as Chi and Wylie (2014) extended this view through the Interactive –Constructive–Active–Passive (ICAP) framework, which describes how deeper levels of engagement correspond to more meaningful learning. Despite this progress, cognitive constructivism was still criticized for portraying learners as isolated thinkers, detached from the social and cultural contexts that shape understanding and belonging. Sociocultural theorists responded by embedding the cognitivist learning model within human relationships. Vygotsky’s (1978) Zone of Proximal Development framed cognition as emerging first between people (interpsychological) and then within the individual (intrapsychological). Lave and Wenger (1991) extended this to communities of practice, while Cobb (1994) argued that learning is both social and individual, not either-or. Sfard’s (1998) critique of metaphoric dualism—the acquisition metaphor versus the participation metaphor—captures the root problem. When researchers align exclusively with one lens, they risk flattening learning into one plane of reality. Behaviorism examines the external plane of performance, cognitive constructivism the internal plane of reasoning, and sociocultural theory the interpersonal plane of participation. Each observes a projection of the learning phenomenon rather than its totality. Although each theory has its affordances and constraints, when one is preferred in isolation, the result is one-dimensional thinking in instructional design, teaching, or research. To transcend this, we may treat learning theories not as rival explanations but as an integrated coordinate system. Just as the motion of an object in three-dimensional space cannot be fully described by a single axis, the complex phenomenon of learning cannot be captured through a preferred axis of behavior, cognition, or social interaction alone. The fragmented landscape of theories reflects our analytic convenience, not the learner’s lived experiences. Recognizing this limitation sets the stage for a n integrated model—one that allows educators and researchers to navigate and examine, rather than choose between, the multiple aspects that characterize learning. The proposal: Learning as a three-dimensional vector The Three-Dimensional Learning Theory (3DLT) conceptualizes learning as a vector with three perpendicular yet interdependent axes: behavioral, cognitive, and sociocultural (see Figure 1). Figure 1 The Three-Dimensional Learning Vector 2126 The behavioral axis represents observable actions shaped through reinforcement, feedback, and habit (Ertmer & Newby, 1993; Skinner, 1953; Thorndike, 1932). It captures fluency, accuracy, and skill automatization—processes still vital for foundational mastery (Goldman & Pellegrino, 2015). The cognitive axis reflects internal organization of knowledge, the construction of mental models, and metacognitive control (Chi & Wylie, 2014; Piaget, 1970; Schoenfeld, 1985). It denotes depth of understanding and the learner’s ability to integrate new information with prior schemas . The sociocultural axis embodies interaction, participation, and identity formation within communities of practice (Cobb, 1994; Lave & Wenger, 1991; Vygotsky, 1978). In this model, a learner’s state of learning can be represented by a position vector L (x, y, z), where x, y, and z correspond to behavioral performance, cognitive development, and social participation . The magnitude of L reflects the overall strength of learning, while its direction reflects how learning is distributed across these three components. Teaching moves learners through this space by differentially activating the axes: reinforcement may build fluency, reflection may deepen understanding, and collaboration may strengthen participation, recognition, and belonging. Learning growth, then, is not the triumph of one theory over another but their combined resultant. The 3DLT model can be useful for both teaching and research. Consider a teacher designing a lesson on linear equations. One goal may be procedural fluency in solving equations, another a deeper grasp of what slope and intercept represent, and a third the creation of opportunities for students to explain, collaborate, and begin to see themselves as “math people.” Researchers, likewise, can use the 3DLT model to trace trajectories of learning across contexts by examining evidence of growth along the three dim ensions. However, how each dimension is operationalized will depend on the research question and context. The evidence: Teaching methods as three-dimensional interplay To ground this theoretical proposal in classroom reality, I turn to four common teaching practices that reveal how learning naturally unfolds across behavioral, cognitive, and social dimensions. These four approaches—lecture - based, technology-based, group-based, and problem-solving—illustrate that the 3DLT is not a distant abstraction but already present in everyday instruction. By re -examining each method through this three -dimensional lens, I show how teachers, often implicitly, navigate multiple theories at once and how these blended practices exemplify learning as movement through an integrated space rather than along isolated lines. Before turning to the analysis, it is useful to clarify what these four teaching/learning methods entail. Lecture-based learning refers to direct instruction where teachers primarily present information to students, sometimes supplemented by brief interactions or demonstrations (Bligh, 2000). Technology-based learning (TBL) encompasses the use of digital tools such as simulations, online platforms, or multimedia resources to enhance access and engagement ( Chinn & Iordanou, 2023; Koller et al., 2006). Group- based learning involves students working collaboratively toward shared goals, emphasizing dialogue, accountability, and peer explanation (Johnson & Johnson, 1999; Webb, 2009). Problem -solving centers on engaging learners with complex, often open-ended tasks that promote reasoning, strategy use, and creativity (Jonassen, 2000; Schoenfeld, 1985). In what follows, I re-examine each of these methods through the lens of the Three-Dimensional Learning Theory (3DLT) to show how behaviorism, cognitivism, and social constructivism operate together in everyday classroom practice. Lecture-based learning Lecture-based learning, while often labeled behaviorist, also draws on cognitive and social dimensions. A teacher modeling equations and giving recall quizzes clearly uses reinforcement and feedback (Ertmer & Newby, 1993; Skinner, 1953). Yet when that teacher employs analogies, visual organizers, or prediction questions, they activate cognitive schemas (Piaget, 1970). Adding think-pair-share discussions transforms the lecture into a social activity aligned with Vygotsky’s (1978) Zone of Proximal Development and Cobb’s (1994) participation view. Deslauriers, Schelew, and Wieman (2011) empirically showed that active, socially engaging lectures outperform traditional ones—evidence that integrating all three dimensions enhances learning. Technology-based learning Likewise, technology-based learning (TBL) operates in this 3D space. Behaviorist design appears in drill -and- practice software offering immediate feedback and rewards (Ertmer & Newby, 1993; Koller et al., 2006; Skinner, 1953). Cognitivists emphasize multimedia principles and mental load management (Mayer, 2004), while sociocultural theorists highlight online collaboration and shared knowledge construction (Sfard, 1998; Vygotsky, 1978). Clark (1983) argued that media are merely delivery tools, yet contemporary evidence (Chinn & Iordanou, 2023) shows that technology’s value lies in how it shapes interaction and reasoning. Thus, effective TBL situates learners along all three axes—practice, cognition, and participation. 2127 Group-based learning Group-based learning foregrounds the sociocultural axis but remains multidimensional. Cooperative learning succeeds when interdependence is reinforced behaviorally ( Ertmer & Newby, 1993; Johnson & Johnson, 1999), when peers elaborate ideas cognitively ( Chi & Wylie, 2014 ; Piaget, 1970), and when communities of practice form socially ( Bielaczyc & Collins, 1999; Vygotsky, 1978). Research confirms that explanation and argumentation drive conceptual change during collaborative work (Webb, 2009) . 3DLT interprets these not as parallel benefits but as interactive components of one learning vector. Problem solving Finally, problem-solving epitomizes three -dimensional learning. Behavioral elements appear in guided practice and reinforcement of correct strategies. Cognitive processes dominate through metacognition, productive failure, and transfer ( Kapur, 2016; Schoenfeld, 1985). Sociocultural elements emerge in collaborative inquiry and authentic contexts (Cobb, 1994; Sfard, 1998; Vygotsky, 1978). In science or math classrooms, students negotiating a shared experiment embodies all three dimensions: they apply procedures, reason conceptually, and engage socially. The strength of learning arises from the combined magnitude of these vector components, not from allegiance to a single theory. Table 1 below summarizes how each teaching method draws on behaviorism, cognitivism, and social constructivism, showing that effective instruction rarely aligns with a single theory. Table 1 Teaching Methods and their Connection to Learning Theories. Behaviorism Cognitivism Social Constructivism Lecture-based learning Reinforcement Organization/Schema Dialogue Tech-based learning Feedback Modeling/Visual Virtual Collaboration Group-based learning Accountability Explanation/Elaboration Community Problem-solving Practice Metacognition/Strategy Negotiation The implications: Towards an integrated idea of learning Viewing learning as a three-dimensional vector carries theoretical, methodological, and pedagogical implications. Theoretically, it transforms educational discourse from comparative to compositional. Rather than debating whether behaviorism or constructivi sm is correct, 3DLT suggests that each capture an important aspect of the same phenomenon. This mirrors Goldman and Pellegrino’s (2015) call for integrative perspectives linking curriculum, instruction, and assessment. Methodologically, 3DLT invites mixed analyses that track behavioral data (performance), cognitive indicators (reasoning patterns), and sociocultural evidence (interaction and discourse). Such triangulation echoes the blended approaches in contemporary learning sciences (Chinn & Iordanou, 2023). Pedagogically, 3DLT empowers teachers to design for balance. A math teacher emphasizing drill (x - axis) can intentionally add reflection prompts (y -axis) and peer discussion (z -axis) to move students diagonally through the learning space. A science educator using group inquiry might incorporate structured reflection and reinforcement to stabilize all axes. The new shifts do not abandon any of the three theor ies but orchestrate their interdependence. As Bligh (2000) and Deslauriers et al. (2011) showed, even traditional formats become transformative when re-engineered through multidimensional engagement. In research, scholars could model trajectories of learning vectors across time, mapping how interventions alter the direction and magnitude of L ( x, y, z). This may connect micro -level behavior with macro- level participation, aligning with Vygotsky’s (1978) developmental vision and Lave and Wenger’s (1991) situated learning. Ultimately, 3DLT turns siloed learning theories into a unified spatial theory of transformation. In conclusion, the 3DLT model recognizes what educators intuitively enact: learning is simultaneously behavioral, cognitive, and social. While the learning sciences have increasingly called for integration, this framework provides a formalized, geometric language to map these ideas. Rather than forcing a choice between paradigms, the field’s task is to chart the full vector of human growth. As a brief conceptual paper, this work leaves several aspects of the model for further development. Most notably, learning is ultimately an n-dimensional phenomenon; future iterations of this coordinate system could expand to include other important axes to capture the full richness of a learner’s development. Ultimately, I hope 3DLT proves useful as a learning heuristic for researchers, a design heuristic for instructors, and a communicative bridge for teacher educators seeking to operationalize the multidimensional reality of meaningful education. 2128 References Atkinson, R. title: Sowing Futures: Developing Curriculum Materials for Urban Agriculture within a Community- Based Partnership
citation: Jessica Bautista, Candi Fentress, Mark Fentress, Leslie R. Herrenkohl (2026). Sowing Futures: Developing Curriculum Materials for Urban Agriculture within a Community- Based Partnership. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Bautista, J., Fentress, C., Fentress, M., & Herrenkohl, L. R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this practice -oriented paper, we underscore ICLS’s 2026 theme of “Partnering with Purpose” by describing the process and outcomes of a collaborative project between community members and a large public university. By attending to values of reciprocity, relationships, community expertise, and the power of place, we developed a set of curriculum materials that draw on the expertise of two Black urban farmers in their work to transform educational and agricultural experiences for youth. We outline our collaborative process, project outcomes, and next steps for supporting this and other innovative community partnerships.

title: Brief Community-Building Interventions in an Undergraduate Synchronous Online Course

abstract: A team of six teaching faculty members implemented a community -building intervention in a synchronous online social -sciences course required for all first -year students at a small North American university serving a diverse, international student body. Results from surveys and online platform data suggest that these brief, regular interventions, taking only about five minutes per ninety- minute class period, may facilitate student belonging, psychological safety, and equitable participation. We discuss the nature of the intervention and initial findings, which may be of interest to other instructors, in any discipline, who wish to cultivate community in their classes. Pedagogical objectives While higher-education faculty tend to focus on the content that we teach, fundamentally, we are teaching people. Increasingly, scholars and faculty are recognizing the importance of student belonging in the university classroom (Brady & Gopalan, 2026; Freeman et al., 2007; Healey & Stroman, 2021) , which may be defined as “the extent to which students feel personally accepted, respected, included, and supported by others” (Goodenow, 1993; Jeng et al., 2023) . While building an inclusive classroom community with belonging helps all students, it especially supports the success of students from under-represented groups (Easterbrook & Hadden, 2021; Elliott et al., 2016; Pedler et al., 2022; Walton & Cohen, 2011). In online classes, in particular, a sense of social presence, belonging, and community may be more challenging to cultivate (Gulati, 2022; Rovai, 2002) . We discuss a simple, brief, regular intervention in a first- year course at Minerva University designed to help build community and a sense of belonging. As community emerges from the instructor and students getting to know each other, the intervention aimed to increase the sense of community through spending about five minutes of every class on activities to help the class get to know each other. The goal was to help our diverse students feel more comfortable bringing their authentic selves to class, to feel that they knew each other’s authentic selves, to feel supported and accepted by each other, and to improve the equity of students’ participation and listening. The intervention’s design was based on Odera’s practical experience of integrating community-building time in his classes over the previous five years, including how devoting a small amount of time in every single class meeting helped students to build a habit of checking in on each other. The first three authors are teaching faculty at Minerva University. Morgan and Odera both teach the target course and participated in designing and implementing the intervention, and Sealfon is a collaborator who taught two other first-year courses, Empirical Analyses (EA) and Formal Analyses (FA), that did not implement the intervention. Karmazin is a student who participated in the intervention and helped analyze the data afterwards as a research assistant. Course description and context At Minerva University, all first- year undergraduates take the same four required courses. All courses are facilitated online via a proprietary video- conferencing software. The software is designed to facilitate student engagement via video, chat, and the use of emojis that appear as an overlay over the student’s video feed. The classes are taught live and the video feed of the instructor and students a ppear on screen for the entire class. All classes at Minerva University utilize a flipped -classroom model a nd the classes focus on discussion of topics rather than transmitting information from the instructor to students. The result is a culture of active participation by students in all classes. Each first- year cohort is about 100- 200 students, and class sizes are capped at around 20 students, so there are multiple sections of each course. Different sections of the same course are taught by different faculty members using the same curriculum, assignments, and lesson plans. The required first-year social sciences course, Complex Systems (CX), introduces the social sciences through a complexity science lens, including basic psychology, levels of analysis, emergent properties, power dynamics, and complex causality. The 195 students in the fall 2023 cohort represented 55 countries across all continents, with about 50% from Asia, 23% from Europe, and 14% from Africa. Most students were of typical undergraduate age with a median age of 19. Gender demographics were 55% female, 44% male, and 1% other. 2137 Intervention The community- building intervention was implemented in the fall of 2023 in the CX course and spanned the entire fall semester (14 weeks total, 25 classes of 90 minutes each). The other three first -year courses, in natural sciences, computational sciences, and multimodal communication, taken by the same cohort of students and meeting for the same length of time, did not receive the intervention. The intervention consisted of setting aside time to deliberately build connections among students and between students and the instructor in every class. In all but six classes (19/25 classes), five minutes at the start of class was dedicated to conversations intended to help students get to know each other better and build a sense of community. In the six class periods without five minutes of dedicated community -building time at the start of class, community discussions had already been integrated into the lesson plans to complement course content. The specific format of discussion was left up to the instructor's discretion. Instructors were given a few suggested community-building activities at the start of the semester, but were encouraged to experiment with how they used the community-building time. Suggested discussion prompts included questions such as: “What color best describes how you are feeling today?” “Share a word or two about how you feel about your residence hall.” “What is your breakfast food?” “What is one thing you have learned about yourself since the start of the semester?” “On a scale of 1 to 5, how are you doing today? (Choose ‘No response’ if you do not want to answer the question)” with descriptions of what 1-5 mean, and an invitation for students to share more. Other examples included asking two students in each class to bring an item that is important to them to briefly present to the class, called a “me library” or “me museum”, or sending all students into breakout rooms for three minutes to tell each other a joke. The six CX instructors, including Morgan and Odera, would meet after every week of classes and share tips on how to best facilitate community -building activities in ways that would feel authentic to each instructor. However, instructors did not receive any formal training on how to facilitate the community-building interventions. Data sources Data were collected from two sources for this preliminary analysis. In the fall of 2023, students were surveyed during the 4th week of the semester and after the semester finished right before the start of the spring semester. Data were also collected from Minerva’s online teaching platform. Online platform data from the fall of 2021, 2022, and 2023 were included in the analysis. Survey data The two survey waves collected data on students’ subjective experiences. Students were asked six subjective questions related to their feelings about belonging, psychological safety, and inclusion in each of their four first - year classes. Morgan and Odera designed the survey questions based on relevance to the Minerva University context. Responses were recorded on a 1-5 Likert scale and included a free response option for short explanations or elaborations. Students were not asked anything specifically about the intervention in CX to avoid biasing results. Additional data were collected on objective outcomes that attempted to measure the connectivity of students outside of the classroom. Both waves of the survey included identical questions. Students were not required to fill out the survey, so the researchers offered incentives to encourage participation. Students were entered into a raffle to win clothing with our university’s logo if they completed one wave of the survey and a gift card to a popular doughnut restaurant if they completed both waves. In total, 66 students participated in the first wave and 69 students participated in the second wave. 49 students completed both waves out of a cohort of 195 students, so the response rate of students who completed both waves of the survey was around 25%. We based our analysis on the 49 students who completed both survey waves. Online platform data Data were downloaded from the online platform from fall semesters in 2021, 2022, and 2023. The variables used in this analysis were the talk time (measured in seconds) of each student, the number of emojis used, and chat usage for each student in each class across all first-year courses. The data were cleaned to remove data from students who did not complete the semester or who transferred between sections due to difficulty tracking the student data between both sections. The top 5th 2138 percentile of observations for all variables were also dropped due to bugs on the online platform leading to unrealistic observations in the data. Figure 1 Survey Responses for All First-Year Courses from 2023 For the above Likert-scale questions, a score of 1 represents “not at all” and a score of 5 represents the most positive response (e.g., “fully” or “very well”). Analysis and preliminary results Figure 1 presents the results from both waves for the six subjective assessments included in the survey. Results for all four required first -year courses, taken by the same students, are presented. The course names are abbreviated as follows: Complex Syste ms (CX), Empirical Analyses (EA), Formal Analyses (FA), and Multimodal Communications (MC). This analysis of the survey data focuses on the changes in subjective assessments between the first and second waves. The community- building intervention spanned the entire semester so the prominent effects of the intervention should be reflected in trends across the semester. Furthermore, the four first-year courses vary significantly in terms of content and thus the types of discussion in class. Analyzing the changes between waves controls for these fixed differences between the four courses. In all six subjective questions, the difference in average response between waves in CX compared favorably or as well as changes in average responses in EA and FA. The questions for which CX compared favorably to EA and FA assessed students' feelings of being comfortable being their authentic selves, feeling that they were supported by their classmates, feeling comfortable participating in class discussions, and feelings that they know their classmates' authentic selves. Similar trends were observed in the questions that focused on feeling accepted by classmates and feeling that their classmates listened to their contributions in class. The changes observed between waves in CX and MC were far more similar than different. MC is a course that teaches students tools of self -expression and communication so it is expected that class discussion could facilitate the same feeling of belonging, ps ychological safety, and inclusion that the CX community -building intervention aimed to foster. Indeed, although students felt that their classmates were not listening to their comments as much in the second wave in CX, the opposite was observed in MC. Students provided positive free -response comments regarding the intervention, expressing appreciation for the chance to get to know their classmates better in CX, even though students were not prompted to comment specifically on the community-building intervention. For example, one student shared that, in CX, “we discussed personal values and experiences which gave me a deeper insight into my peers.” Another noted that, across the first-year courses, “In class, most conversation revolves around the subject topics and there was little time for 2139 getting to know each other personally. I highly appreciated the me library to get to know each other in CX.” One student explicitly made the connection between the intervention in CX and their sense of belonging: “Since my prof would have a debrief and ask about our day and what we were feeling that day, it becomes easier to discuss and be myself during classes.” Overall, it appears that classroom dynamics in CX and MC either promoted or protected feelings of belonging, psychological safety, and inclusion compared to the EA and FA courses. But, in the case of CX, it is not clear if this is due to discussions that w ould occur naturally without the community- building intervention or if the intervention contributed to the trends observed in the survey data. A comparison with CX courses before the intervention was implemented can help determine if the intervention actually changed classroom dynamics in CX. Minerva’s online platform records the talk time for each individual student and for the instructor, through recording the amount of time that they are speaking during each class. Figure 2 shows the standard deviation in individual students’ talk time for each class session over the entire semester for 2021, 2022, and 2023. A trend line is fitted to the raw da ta to illustrate the trends across the semester. In the two years without a community- building intervention in CX (2021 and 2022), there is a similar increasing trend in the standard deviation of talk time over the semester. This indicates a growing inequa lity of class participation over time. However, in 2023 with the intervention, there is no clear trend in the standard deviation of talk time over the semester. This suggests that the intervention may have helped foster more equitable student participation in class, which may serve as an indication of classroom equity (Tanner, 2013). Figure 2 Standard Deviation of Talk Time in CX, 2021-2023 Conclusions and relevance Taking the survey and online platform data analysis together, we conclude that there is suggestive evidence that such community-building interventions do affect classroom dynamics and may either promote or protect feelings of belonging, psychological safety, and inclusion in the course. Such brief, regular interventions may affect overall classroom culture through helping all students feel valued and validated, which may also improve equitable participation. Future work will further analyze the online platform data in conjunction with the survey data to investigate potential proxy indicators of community and belonging in individual class sections in the automatically-collected online platform data, such as through building on work in belonging analytics (Lim et al., 2023) and equity analytics (Reinholz & Shah, 2018). As this intervention uses minimal class time as well as no extra time for instructor preparation or training, it may offer an effective and versatile approach to improve community in a wide variety of online and potentially in-person classes. At Minerva Un iversity, professors of the other first -year courses, especially EA and FA, have expressed interest in integrating this community-building intervention into their courses. In Morgan’s experience, some instructors were initially resistant to taking class time away from course content to invest in community building, but all instructors became enthusiastic supporters of the intervention after experiencing its effect on their students and their classes. While this intervention was implemented in small classes of 20 students or less, future work may explore similar interventions in larger online classes, such as via the use of breakout rooms. 2140 References Brady, S.
