abstract: We present the design of a partnership among science education practitioners, molecular biologists , and high school biology teachers. Using Lave and Wenger’s (1991) construct of legitimate peripheral participation, we demonstrate how the partnership created conditions for meaningful engagement in the specialized epistemic and cultural practices of structural molecular biology. The SHAPE MATTERS project facilitated an iterative professional learning program in which 24 teachers and their students engaged in increasingly sophisticated approximations of modeling practices ––from using physical and computational molecular models to presenting molecular stories. The team also developed a continuum of molecular modeling for high school biology. The structural biologists ensured disciplinary authenticity; science educators provided pedagogical knowledge. Our case presents a proof-of- concept for a practical approach that moves beyond generalized enactments of scientific practice by grounding teaching and learning in specific research contexts, supporting teachers and their students to develop experience in nuanced enactments of scientific modeling.

abstract: This paper is led by a dual language kindergarten teacher and presents insights on a multi-year participatory research study on wordless books. We discuss how wordless books can support emergent dual language learners by fostering literacy through storyte lling and creative expression. The paper highlights a case study on how wordless books can empower children to see themselves as competent readers. We argue for a broader definition of literacy that values and includes students’ linguistic and cultural resources, and position wordless books as a tool for equitable access to reading for all children. Objectives of our practice-oriented paper Over the past three years, Arlen and Christine , a dual language kindergarten teacher and a university researcher, have collaborated on a participatory design -based research study (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) examining the potential of wordless books for young dual language learners. Our paper examines how wordless books can serve as a powerful tool for dual language literacy, empowering young learners to take agency in their oral storytelling and reading. When we think of literacy instruction in primary grade levels, it tends to focus solely on phonics, accuracy, and decoding words. This experience can provide a narrow view of literacy, and it views children as passive recipients rather than active meaning makers (Freire & Slover, 1983). It also doesn’t leave ro om for student-driven creative expression, like storytelling. For emergent dual language learners, the act of learning to read in a new language can present an extra level of pressure, setting expectations that they have to somehow quickly master both languages. Wordless picture books offer a different kind of entry point into literacy. It can remove the pressure to perform and instead invite children to build their own narratives using a variety of resources like language, tone, gestures, and imagination. Our paper shows wordless books as a resource to support children’s identities as lifelong readers and empower them by giving children agency in their storytelling. We argue that we need to move away from deficit thinking by highlighting the immense skills children already bring to the world of reading. This means that we must ultimately expand the definition of literacy by exploring ways of being a lifelong literate human being, and help children form a relationship with literature that extends beyond merely decoding words. In this paper, we present a case study that shares how a student with limited Spanish, in a dual language classroom, can communicate powerfully to tell stories when given the tools and space to do so. We follow a kindergarten student (5 year old) who used wordless books to tell stories in both English and Spanish over time. Her storytelling showed how young children can express meaning in complex and personal ways, even when their vocabulary in a second language is limited and still dev eloping. Therefore, we wonder, how can wordless picture books support student autonomy in storytelling for emergent dual language learners? Wordless books Wordless books are picture books with little to no written text. Thus, readers rely on the illustrations and images to read and tell stories. These visual stories invite readers to interpret meaning and construct narratives using their own imagination, lived experiences, and cultural knowledge (Lee, et al., 2025; Razfar & Gutierrez, 2003; Vygotsky, 1978). Our case study draws on literature that positions literacy as a meaning- making social activity. Freire and Slover (1983) argue that literacy is not a mechanical skill to be mastered, but a process of consciousness formation where learners first “read the world” before they “read the word.” His conception of reading was that it was a critical, experiential, and transformative act (Crawford & Hade, 2000). Therefore, reading is inherently social, reflective, and tied to identity, power, and context (Vygotsky, 1978). We argue wordless books can support storytelling, language development, and creative expression, and offer young learners the opportunity to reflec t on their own experiences and prior knowledge (Arif & Hashim, 2008). Wordless books open up storytelling for all children, regardless of their reading level or language proficiency. They invite students to navigate meaning using gesture, tone, facial expression, and oral language across multiple languages (Alvermann, 2002; Dehghani et al., 2013). In doing so, wordless books position students as active participants in the meaning- making process (Freire & Slover, 1983), rather than passive recipients of a fixed and scripted narrative. Wordless books also offer space for children still developing language to engage with complex ideas and express personal insights through their own narrative decisions (Arif & Hashim, 2008; Goriot et al., 2024) . For emergent dual language learners, wordless picture books offer inclusive, flexible, and linguistically accessible 2147 entry points into literacy. Children may even feel freer to communicate authentically by lifting the pressure of correctness and allowing for fluid, spontaneous storytelling. Because the narrative is not fixed by written words, students are free to interpr et and reframe the story in ways that reflect their multilingual and multicultural experiences (Crawford & Hade, 2000). This makes wordless books especially powerful in culturally and linguistically diverse classrooms, where children can exercise autonomy and agency in meaning-making, without being confined by rigid, traditional models of literacy instruction that often feel limited at a young age. Each child, regardless of language or fluency, is encouraged by the pictures in wordless books to construct their own meaning of the story, offering beneficial possibilities for use in all-inclusive learning settings. Designing wordless books into literacy curriculum The design and implementation of wordless books into our literacy curriculum came from a multi -year collaboration between Arlen and Christine. We began the work by searching for and reading research on wordless books in early literacy. We then introduced wordless books to our kindergarten (5- 6 years) classroom, and immediately realized the potential these books had for emergent readers, especial ly as a way to equitably engage and provide access to literacy regardless of the child’s background. Our initial observation of students exploring wordless books was that these books can be a powerful tool for voice and agency. This is important for dual language classrooms and multi-lingual learners because many children in a dual language classroom can often be positioned as “being academically behind” in their literacy or language skills. We took these preliminary observations and focused on designing a learning experience for children with wordless books where they can see themselves as creative meaning-makers, where they can author their own stories, and come to form a solid identity as a reader early on. In Table 1, we outline how we designed our literacy curriculum to incorporate wordless books over the academic school year. Table 1 Outline of Wordless Books in our Literacy Curriculum. Timeline Goals Description of Goals September Exposure and exploration of wordless books Children freely explored wordless books. October-November Sequence of events and details from illustrations Students did picture walks and were encouraged to pay close attention to the details in the illustrations. Based on their observations, students made conjectures about what the story was about and where they thought the story was going. December-January Perspectives in storytelling Students explored how narration and dialogue shape a story. Tried on and played with different voices for different characters. Discussed and practiced how stories can be told in first, second, or third person. February-June Wordless books as part of regular reading practices Wordless books became a regular reading activity that sparked creative and playful conversation. Students regularly chose to read wordless books during their reading time. Case study Arlen teaches in the dual language program, and Christine is a university researcher. Our research was conducted in an elementary school in Southern California, and the case we present in this paper is from Arlen’s dual language (10% English instruction and 90% Spanish instruction) kindergarten classroom. Our focal student, Camila (pseudonym), was a five year old emergent bilingual learner who primarily spoke English at home and was newly acquiring Spanish through the school's dual language program. To explore Camila's storytelling across languages, 2148 we video-recorded her storytelling with wordless books. In November 2024, Camila narrated the wordless picture book Good Dog, Carl (Day, 1985) in English, and in March 2025, she narrated The Girl and the Bicycle (Pett, 2014) in Spanish. When we look at Camila’s number of words spoken across the two video recordings (Table 2), it is no surprise that the total words spoken in English while reading Good Dog, Carl is much higher than when she read The Girl and the Bicycle in Spanish. Table 2 Total Words Spoken when Reading in English and Spanish English (Good Dog, Carl) in November 2024 Spanish (The Girl and the Bicycle) in March 2025 Total Words Spoken 261 111 Average Words Spoken per Page 8 words per page 3 words per page In both recordings, Camila is reading the wordless books to two of her classmates who were attentively listening to the story by her side. We transcribed both video- recorded reading sessions and organized the transcripts by page to arrange her narration with the visual content of the book. Together, we analyzed the two transcripts and found two emerging themes that we present in this paper (Braun & Clarke, 2022). Theme 1: Emotional expression as a storytelling strategy Across our transcripts, Camila demonstrated that emotional expression can be a powerful tool for storytelling. Throughout the Spanish storytelling transcript, Camila relied on her vocal tone, pauses, facial gestures, and nonverbal sounds (like dramatic sighs) to convey a character's or narrator's feelings. The transcript of her Spanish reading of the wordless book was rich with these emotional expressions and was a crucial part of her storytelling. Camila expressed deep understanding of the story even when her Spanish vocabulary was limited, showing how emotional gestures, prosody, and tone can support meaning- making when verbal language is still developing. In her English narration of Good Dog, Carl , Camila primarily used sentences with consistent pacing and a neutral tone. For example, she said, “Carl looks out the window. The baby sneaks out, and the dog comes by”. While this sentence is descriptively accurate of the story, her delivery and oral t elling of it resembled the cadence of classroom read-alouds, where students are taught to prioritize clarity and linear sequencing rather than emotional interpretation and creative storytelling. In contrast, her Spanish narration of The Girl and the Bicycle had nonverbal elements like tone, gesture, and diverse pacing to convey emotional depth. Earlier in the story, she asked, “¿En dónde está mi dinero? ¿Aquí? ¿Aquí?” with a rising intonation while using her whole body to mimic the action of searching for something. Her rising intonation and repetition of “¿Aquí?” created a sense of urgency and concern, as she embodied the character's anxious search for money to buy a bicycle. Later, Camila captured the character’s disappointment by using a different tone to interpret and communicate the emotional arc of the story. She paused and sighed dramatically before saying “Poquito triste,” meaning “a little sad” as she embodied the character’s emotions when she found out the bicycle was gone. Camila effectively communicated the sadness of the moment through her tone shift, softly stating “Poquito triste”, dramatic pause, and pacing. These emotional expressions added depth to the statement, expressing a feeling that extended beyond the image itself and making listeners understand the heavy moment in the story. Therefore, Camila’s use of semiotic resources effectively communicated the feelings and emotional depth of the story despite speaking fewer words – illustrating the true power of embodiment and emotional connections in rich storytelling. Theme 2: Narrative perspectives Camila's storytelling across the two transcripts also revealed a shift in narrative perspectives. When she read Good Dog, Carl in English, her point of view was in the third person, and when she read The Girl and the Bicycle in Spanish, it was in both the third person and first person perspectives. For example, in Good Dog, Carl, she said, “They open the door, and went to the Mommy and Daddy's room, and they played with makeup”. Camila stayed in the third person, narrative perspective throughout her entire reading of the story as she orally described the events of the story. 2149 In contrast, Camila's narration in Spanish showed more fluidity. Rather than sticking to a single point of view, she moved between third person and first person to tell the story. For example, on page 8 of The Girl and the Bicycle, Camila said “No tiene más money, no tiene más monedas,” meaning “She doesn’t have any more money, she doesn’t have any more coins,”. But later, on page 13, she exclaimed, “Ven con yo! No! ¡No quiero, no gracias!” meaning “Come with me! No! I don’t want to, no thank you!”, steppi ng into the character’s voice and embodying what the character would excitedly say in the story. Camila exercised narrative autonomy, shaping the story in deeper ways that felt meaningful to her in the moment. Her inventive dialogue and expressive stance reflect how learners construct meaning by using their voice and lived experience. Instead of simply retelling the events, Camila authored a story that reflected her understanding, feelings, and agency. Concluding remarks One of the most powerful lessons learned from observing students engage with wordless books is how quickly they are able to see themselves as competent readers. Even at a young age, children can step into stories with confidence and agency before they’ve mastered decoding text. They also don’t need to rely on others to access these books. This accessibility gives them the opportunity to take ownership of their reading. As a dual language teacher, this was powerful for students because it encouraged them to take risks and play with language. It was wonderful to see young children feel empowered with their reading, as if they could grab a book and tell a story all on their own. As a result of this work, a parent thanked Arlen for our work with wordless books because her son had a hard time feeling confident while decoding text. However, she mentioned that with wordless books, he was never discouraged and always saw himself as a storyteller and reader. Recently, Arlen saw this parent on campus again, and she shared that her son now reads books and loves being a reader. She attributed his journey and growth as a reader to wordless books because they made him feel like a competent reader as he learned to decode text. As a dual language teacher, A rlen also learned that wordless books encourage emerging dual language students to take risks. While there is clearly a story to tell, wordless books have no script; thus, there is no strict expectation of what students must say. Instead, students are able to freely use the words they already know or play with new and unfamiliar words in their storytelling. Through their experimentation with storytelling, they are able to stretch themselves in a low -stakes and playful way. This feeling of agency and creative freedom is what creates space for incredible growth. We also realized that wordless books served as a tool for equity because the stories welcome every child, no matter their background knowledge. Regardless of the child’s dominant or target language, wordless books provide everyone an opportunity for conversation, making literacy accessible across all learners. The books create a space of inclusivity and allow students to connect, share, and learn from each other. Thus, every child’s unique voice is honored through expression filled with emotion, because although children are reading the author’s art and images, they are ultimately telling their own stories. When children are able to bring aspects of themselves into the classroom, such as their home language or family stories, they naturally create a space f or cultural representation through wordless books. This affirms their identities as competent and agentic storytellers and makes them visible within the classroom setting. Wordless books become a universal resource for students. Institutionalized education often lacks opportunities for every child to be heard and valued. Wordless books remove these barriers, allowing every child to be seen. Throughout our research partnership, we came to realize how intertwined research, teaching, and learning are. Before becoming a teacher, Arlen studied with Fred Erickson, whose work with teachers showed Arlen the power in positioning educators as co-constructors of knowledge. In our work, we made decisions about how wordless books would be integrated into the curriculum and how to collect and analyze our data together. We respected and made space for our intellectual insights and curiosities in this work. Not only has this made our research stronger, but it has also given Arlen the confidence to speak to other educators to reform literacy programs, especially for elementary dual language classrooms. The collaborative participation in research gave Arlen the data and the tools to communicate and share the importance of wordless books in this paper, which invites other teachers to engage in this work as a way to transform and grow our teaching practices. abstract: What happens when teachers and researchers partner to co- design a tangible, embodied game to foster computational thinking? Byte Beads is a game in which children compose and perform sequences of beads associated with actions to represent computational patterns. Initially conceived within computing education, the game evolved as teachers helped shape a design supporting pattern- based reasoning, collaborative embodied sequencing, and executive functioning skills, including attention and cognitive flexibility . Drawing on constructionist and embodied learning traditions, we examine how researcher -practitioner partnerships shaped the evolution of the game and the pedagogical practices surrounding it. Tracing these interactions across relational collaborations, p rofessional development, and classroom enactment, the paper illustrates how partnership itself becomes a site of learning where design, pedagogy and play co-develop. This work contributes to the ISLS 2026 theme of Partnerships with Purpose by conceptualizing partnership as an ongoing process of co-designing and sustaining environments supporting playful embodied learning.

abstract: Given the manner in which climate change is intertwined with histories of racial- capitalism and colonialism and both historical and ongoing stories of community resistance, integrating the sociopolitical aspects of climate change with climate science is cr itical to learning about the subject as a whole. While a substantial body of literature is focused on how to engage students who are on the frontlines of climate injustice, here we ask how to meaningfully engage students of relative economic privilege in meaningful learning around climate and environmental justice. In this paper, we describe the design of a yearlong trajectory within a high school science class, meant to engage students in identifying and questioning dominant narratives within the culture o f a particular school, paying specific attention to dominant narratives that assume the beneficence of STEM and industry (Morales-Doyle, 2025).

abstract: This design paper describes the University of Virginia Innovation Hub, a laboratory school that is based upon a research -practice partnership (RPP) between the University of Virginia and Charlottesville City Schools. The Innovation Hub is committed to providing computationally-rich, community-driven, and project-based instruction to every middle school student in the school division. Instead of pulling students out of existing schools to form a separate laboratory school, the Innovation Hub uses a push-in model to provide experiences for all students across grade levels in a school district. Using principles of effective design- based implementation research as guiding principles, this paper describes the history of the RPP, the iterative refinement of the Innovation Hub, as well as current and future directions of the effort.

abstract: Many education technology(edTech) product rollouts underperform because tools are designed for schools instead of with them. In this practice paper we describe a three -month pilot where an edTech product manager, developer, and designer worked from the school, sat in classrooms, and co- created a Portfolio Analyzer with the Principal, teachers, and students. We adapted Design -Based Implementation Research (DBIR) within a Research –Practice Partnership (RPP) to run short improvement cycles: observe in class , try a change, check it in class, write it into school policy with a scope to review and iterate. The pilot saw strong use in Grades 5, 7, and 9 (~60 students, 10 teachers) with clear improvements to day- to-day usability and review flow, leading to a whole -school rollout decision. We shar e a simple, repeatable pattern for other K-12 schools and edtech teams.

abstract: This practice -oriented paper describes the design of a partnership between StreetCode Academy and the Stanford Institute for Diversity in the Arts, created to connect community learners in a technology education program with university students and resources through a co llaborative learning model. In this endeavor, social capital was emphasized as a lever for engagement to create opportunities for relationship- building across community and institutional networks. These relationships functioned as pathways for reciprocal learning and network expansion, which supported students’ and instructors’ engagement with technical skills and their development as innovators. Preliminary findings indicate increased student interest in continued participation in technology education. Instructors and mentors also reported an increase in confidence, skill development, and sense of purpose. This paper presents design considerations for operationalizing social capital and it shows how community- university partnerships can serve as a two -way bridge for reciprocal learning and network-building to expand pathways into technology education. Objectives and theoretical grounding Despite the growth of opportunities in the innovation economy, participation in computing and technology education continues to be marked by inequity, particularly for students from communities historically excluded from access to institutional networks. While several factors influence engagement and persistence in this area, including inequitable access to digital resources and high -quality STEM learning experiences, another critical factor is how learning environments are designed to recognize and extend existing relationships and forms of support that enable participants to navigate and persist in technology pathways. S ocial capital refers to the relational supports people access and share through family, friends, teachers, and communities (Bourdieu, 1980; Coleman, 1988), and as a potential factor contributing to ongoing marginalization, should be examined more thoughtfully. In STEM research, social capital is often used as an explainer of disparities in tech participation. In this paper, however, social capital is discussed as an existing asset that can be leveraged and designed to activate new, mutually beneficial relationships across institutional networks that expand access and support participation in technology pathways. This paper presents an ongoing partnership between StreetCode Academy, a community- based technology education nonprofit, and Stanford University, a world-renowned institution of higher learning known for its culture of innovation. Founded in 2014, StreetCode Academy is committed to bridging the technology education gap by offering free coding, entrepreneurship, and design classes to youth and their families in communities with longstanding histories of creativity and technological ingenuity, where access to technology learning opportunities is not always equitably available . The Stanford Institute for Diversity in the Arts is a “student-facing and serving organization" committed to offering opportunities to practice leadership, creative expression, and social responsibility through the arts. This partnership extended StreetCode ’s community-based learning model for communities historically underrepresented in formal technology institutions onto Stanford’s campus, a university with a strong institutional emphasis on technology and innovation, intentionally repositioning who participates in and belongs within these spaces. This created opportunities for students and their families to build new connections and engage with university spaces that are not often available or accessible to the public. For many participants, this included taking classes on a university campus for the first time, which positively influenced their sense of belonging and possibility within technology and higher education pathways. It also created meaningful opportunities for 2171 university students pursuing fields adjacent to technology, education, design, and the arts to contribute as mentors and instructors while developing their own perspectives and skills. Through this initiative, they were able to apply their disciplinary knowledge in authentic, culturally grounded contexts, which helped them experience affirmation and support that reinforced their sense of belonging in fields where they may have otherwise experienced marginalization (McGee, 2020). Positioning the role of social capital in tech education is significant because it can serve as an existing and malleable design resource within educational systems. Students bring with them unique social and cultural resources that serve as valuable assets in supporting their learning trajectories (Yosso, 2005). V aluing and leveraging students' existing networks and intentionally curating expanded connections, educators can engage relational dimensions that can be critical to fostering greater participation in technology-related learning pathways and academic settings, particularly among historically underrepresented groups. These relations can positively impact learners’ feelings of inclusion and their self -esteem as they navigate technology-related fields , which positively influence learning and identity development. In this context, social capital was treated as a catalyst as well as an outcome, cultivated to foster social and academic growth among the students and educators participating in the program. In this process, relationships were mutually constituted through ongoing interaction, as participants both drew on and contributed to shared relational networks. These dynamics created opportunities for co -development, where learners and instructors built confidence and capacity through shared engagement. This has the potential to extend existing research on social networks and opportunity (Chetty et al., 2024) , demonstrating how social capital can be intentionally designed within learning environments to encourage reciprocal relationships that help shape participants’ engagement and aspirational trajectories. These theoretical perspectives informed the program’s design, guiding its intention to respect and position all participants as active contributors to the learning culture, and structure community engagement in a way that centered reciprocal identity development, where students, mentors, and instructors developed in distinct but interconnected ways through their engagement in teaching, learning, and collaboration. Design The StreetCode Academy and Stanford University Institute for Diversity in the Arts (IDA) partnership shared three intersecting goals: the first was to increase accessibility to top -tier learning opportunities. StreetCode Academy is committed to providing learning experiences that help participants gain foundational skills in a variety of coding, design, and media platforms. Stanford University is a global research institution of higher education, known for its contributions to the innovation economy. The Institute for Diversity in the Arts, founded 25 years ago, was established to educate, activate, and transform students at Stanford and extend that mission to the local community. The second goal was to advance the conversation around culture, arts, and technology, exploring how these intersect to inspire creativity, expression, and innovation. The third was to bridge perceived and actual divides across communities by fostering belonging and community across institutional boundaries between the university and the local community. Designing for access, belonging, and shared participation To support these goals, the partnership was designed for both entities to contribute in complementary ways. Regarding accessibility, the Institute for Diversity in the Arts provided financial resources so StreetCode could coordinate free transportation, provide free laptop rentals and usage for students, and even offer free meals for participants, removing many of the logistical barriers that can often prevent engagement. Framing access as a design principle helped to promote more equitable participation and expand participants’ connections to social networks through the structural organization of the learning environment. The program design prioritized a family- centered learning environment. This partnership offered intergenerational learning spaces where youth, elders, children, and parents could learn together. This is atypical for many K12 or university classrooms, which are traditionally designed for a specific age range. One participant, a 76-year-old Spanish-speaking StreetCode student, spoke at the final-quarter Demo Day, sharing that it had been her dream to take a course at Stanford, and that, through this program, it was finally achieved. This example illustrates how designing for intergenerational participation supported a spirit of lifelong learning and expanded who could belong in the space while also creating opportunities for individuals across generations to l earn alongside one another and reimagine themselves as technology innovators. 2172 Building on these design choices, this program aimed to operationalize social capital so that learners and instructors could interact as mutual recipients and co-producers of value. This was an intentional move away from traditional one-directional service-oriented models of technology education, toward a more connected and empowering model of shared learning. Grounded in the principle of “learning through participation,” the project centered an epistemology of development that recognized access to diverse people, experiences, and environments as integral to how participants form affirming mindsets and identities as technologists and innovators. Across the program, three design considerations for operationalizing social capital were prioritized: reducing barriers to participation, centering shared participation and belonging, and expanding opportunities for purposeful network- building to support sustained engagement. Implementation A fourteen-week program was developed, encompassing a variety of courses. Courses were thematically designed around the topic of “culture and tech” and introduced participants to cutting-edge and emerging technology. Each course included opportunities to engage in practical, technical use of technology and in theoretical and philosophical discussions about how each person could use these tools to preserve and positively advance their cultural traditions and personal goals. This approach reaffirmed education as a force of personal liberation and advancement for each student as well as their local and global communities. Courses were offered in two seven -week rotations, with sessions held once a week for 2.5 hours each. Offerings included courses like “Storytelling & Tech,” “Music & Tech,” “Design & Tech,” “Jr. Design & Tech,” “Intro to Code,” and “STEMLabs Mechanical Engi neering.” Classes were hosted on Stanford’s campus at the IDA “house” and the Black Community Services Center, where the community room and lobby became classrooms that “felt like home” for students, filled with art, music, and warmth that reflected the students’ community aesthetics and values. Enacting bonding through shared rituals Classes began with a 30-minute ritual called “Huddle-up,” intended to inspire students for the upcoming courses and connect them with one another over food, engaging activities, and presentations by featured students or special guests. Huddle -ups began wit h a shared dinner, during which announcements highlighted past student accomplishments and upcoming events. Activities were designed to have students interact with one another so they could learn about each other. Discussing a topic around a table or acting out a scenario would bring people together. Huddle-ups also featured guest speakers or showcased the work and talents of community members, which often led students to follow up with each other or with a guest speaker about an opportunity they might not otherwise have known about. Following Huddle-Up, students would break into their courses, which were facilitated by several lead instructors and taught by StreetCode alumni, industry experts, and Stanford students. Each class had one or two lead instructors and was supported by three to four mentors. While 66% of classes were taught by Stanford students, every course had a lead teacher or mentor who represented the geographical or cultural background of the StreetCode students. StreetCode community members, industry representatives, a nd the Stanford affiliates were all treated as co -designers who collaborated on curriculum design, logistics, and pedagogy throughout the quarters. Enacting network expansion across community, university, and industry To deepen the connection to industry, each quarter had a day committed to exploring the field. Experiences included a trip to the Stanford innovation program, hosted by the director of publications and co- director of the K-12 Lab, and a visit to OpenAI, where a workshop was led by a former StreetCode instructor and Stanford alumnus and colleague. These trips were designed to strengthen the relationship between these organizations and the StreetCode community, empowering the social capital participants could access through more formal network development. Quarterly courses ended with a Demo Day, a community- wide public celebration that invited members of the broader community to experience a showcase of what students had learned and accomplished. Nearly 20 employees from Amazon and 15 members of Links, a professional organization of African American women, attended one of the Demo Days, along with numerous Stanford students, StreetCode community members, family, and friends. Students presented their work and exchanged information with visiting guests. One student who 2173 created a movie using an AI platform even raised $250 from attendees who wanted to support his continued subscription to the platform beyond the course. Through outside speaking engagements, field trips, and Demo Days, these relationships were nurtured beyond what was gained in the classroom, with enrolled participants expanding their personal and professional networks of opportunities and support. The implementation of each activity and the program overall was thoughtfully curated to expand the realization and potential of social capital across residential, academic, and industry communities, connecting StreetCode students with professors and students at S tanford University; also connecting Stanford University and industry partners and affiliates with genuine opportunities to engage with local community members around relevant and resonant partnerships. In doing so, the program strengthened individual trajectories and cultivated an ecosystem of shared learning and mutual investment. Practice-based learnings There are many context -specific factors that may have affected the efficacy of these efforts. However, early findings are encouraging. Participant feedback collected through post-class surveys indicated that 94% of students expressed a desire to continue learning about technology; and 70% reported an increase in their sense of identity as innovators. These data suggest positive implications for this approach, providing a generative introduction to technology for community participants. In addition, instructor feedback indicated that assuming the role of mentor or teacher supported the development of confidence and skills as they, too, navigated exploratory conversations and reflected on their growth as emerging professionals in computing and education. They also gained valuable first -hand experience designing learning environments aligned with principles they apply in their STEM courses (e.g., design thinking, Universal Design for Learning, Understanding by Design), reinforcing their technical skill development. Teachers also discussed how this experience acted as a space for personal mindset renewal. It provided opportunities to reflect on their relationships with technology and to reconnect with their motivating hopes and aims, empowering their journeys as developing professionals and technologists. In this way, teaching became a creative means of sustaining motivation and recharging their sense of purpose. Meaning- making is recognized as a dimension of well-being (Seligman, 2011). Connecting their academic work to an authentic teaching experience, student - teachers were able to deepen the connection between their learning and real -world practice. This contributed to their positive identity development and overall personal wellness. Outcomes experienced by all participants, students and instructors, point to a reinforcing developmental experience which was supported by shared participation, strengthened relationships, and expanded network connections. Instructors’ growing confidence in their skills and renewed sense of purpose were nurtured by their experiences teaching and supporting students, who affirmed their developing expert ise. Similarly, students’ increased confidence and emerging innovator identities developed through their engagement with near-peer instructors, whose mentorship and presence as accessible role models helped shape their identities as technologists. Relevance Preliminary learnings from this project implicate the need for more research to better understand the degree to which social capital, and in what forms, influences levels of student engagement and sustained participation in computing pathways. Future research might also inquire how a model like this could help to address gaps between student needs and available school offerings, particularly in expanding opportunities to develop technical skills and strengthen psychological supports. Implications for future practice-based initiatives include identifying community assets and opportunities to triangulate practice, bringing together resources that connect community organizations and academic institutions, with opportunities to connect to industry to spur individual and communal development through designed pathways across locally situated learning ecologies. This partnership’s preliminary outcomes suggest the potential for more strategic programming to expand equitable participation , positioning social capital as a designable mechanism for reciprocal learning and network-building across community and university contexts. title: Learning through Partnership: Integrating Disciplinary and Experiential Knowledge in Teacher Education
citation: Richa Sharma, Gomathi Jatin, Subhankar Rana, Rafikh Shaikh (2026). Learning through Partnership: Integrating Disciplinary and Experiential Knowledge in Teacher Education. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Sharma, R., Jatin, G., Rana, S., & Shaikh, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This practice -oriented paper presents a Research -Practice Partnership between (organisation 1), a formal pre -service teacher -education institute (TEI), and (organisation 2), an experiential learning organisation. While the core design of the collaboration was informed by Kolb’s Experiential Learning Theory, this paper demonstrates how the integration of Gandhi’s principles of 3H (Head, Hand and Heart) facilitates non -linear, transformational reflections within a structured design. By analysing a 5- day-long urban expedition in Mumbai, we gained valuable insights about structuring immersive experiences, balancing guidance with autonomy, supporting diverse learners, and maintaining authentic engagement. Based on which we argue that the ‘Heart’ (affective immersion) acts as a catalyst that integrates the ‘Head’ (disciplinary knowledge - Knowledge that) with the ‘Hand’ (procedural knowledge-knowledge how ). The paper also offers design principles for RPPs enabling transition of a "Legitimate Peripheral Participant " (LPP) from ‘periphery’ to the ‘core’ of the learning processes.

title: Playing With Probability: How Brownie Scouts Earned Their Gaming Badge Through Board Game Design
citation: Sonia Tiwari (2026). Playing With Probability: How Brownie Scouts Earned Their Gaming Badge Through Board Game Design. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Tiwari, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This practice-oriented paper presents a design workshop developed in partnership with a Brownie Scouts troop in the San Francisco Bay Area. The two- part workshop engaged seven- to nine-year-old girls (N= 9) in earning their Game Design Badge through board game design using simple, low -cost materials. Learnings from the workshop included children’s partial but functional understanding of probability, improved design confidence after analyzing other games , sense of pride and ownership about self -designed games, peer -to-peer learning opportunities through playtesting, and remixing basic game templates based on personal interests. The project demonstrates how complex topics can be made approachable through characters and storylines. The workshop flow, moving from guided play to independent design, can be adapted in classrooms, libraries, or after-school programs to make complex mathematical concepts more approachable through play and creativity.

title: Beyond Knowing: An Empirical Study of a KBCP-Based Intervention to Promote Metacognitive Awareness and Learning Strategy Use
citation: Tong Pei, Changchen Li, Yan Liang (2026). Beyond Knowing: An Empirical Study of a KBCP-Based Intervention to Promote Metacognitive Awareness and Learning Strategy Use. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: This pilot study addresses the persistent "knowing-doing" gap, where students fail to apply effective learning strategies. We investigated the efficacy of a five- day summer institute curriculum grounded in the Knowledge -Belief-Commitment-Plan (KBCP) framew ork for 34 primary and lower-secondary students. Our findings reveal that this brief intervention yielded statistically significant gains in metacognitive self -report scores and markedly increased the articulation of strategy use in students' learning plans. We attribute this success to the KBCP framework itself, which functions as a metacognitive scaffold to systematically guide learners through self -regulatory processes. These results provide a strong rationale for educators to integrate the full KBCP fra mework, prioritizing metacognitive and resource management strategy instruction.

title: Queer and Trans Theories as Praxis: Analyzing Power and Designing for Learning Toward Justice
citation: Dylan Paré, Miwa A. Takeuchi, Judit Moschkovich, Cindy Cruz, Luis Leyva, Suraj Uttamchandani (2026). Queer and Trans Theories as Praxis: Analyzing Power and Designing for Learning Toward Justice. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: This structured poster symposium, co- chaired by an intergenerational group of scholars, brings together scholars whose work engages queer and trans theories as praxis. Amid intensifying political attacks, we foreground the historical persistence of queer and trans knowledge-making and centering futures in which learning is reimagined toward justice and livability. The contributions examine diverse contexts —including early childhood classrooms, community design spaces, nationalist and parental rights discourses, arts- based learning, and computational simulations —to show how queer and trans perspectives unsettle dominant definitions of learning, reveal the operations of ideology, and foreground desire, embodiment, and affect as vital dimensions of liberatory and justice -oriented learning. Collectively, the six papers demonstrate how queer and trans theories refuse normative closure and open possibilities for more expansive ways of knowing. By attending to the conditions that restrict educational dignity and the practices that envision otherwise, we underscore how learning might be oriented toward dignity, creativity, and collective flourishing.

abstract: Historically, the learning sciences have emphasized how computing construction activities can support learners in building relationships between old and new knowledge in interactions with others while creating artifacts of social relevance. With the ubiquity of socia l media and AI/ML, researchers have turned their attention to the social and ethical implications of computing, proposing that deconstruction—the process of critically examining and understanding how meaning and intentionality are encoded into computing systems and practices that impact people’s lives and the environment —is equally important. In this symposium we bring together researchers investigating how to design deconstruction learning activities in which young people critically evaluate AI/ML systems of social relevance. We present different perspectives on how to design activities and scaffold learners to examine the socio-ethical implications of AI/ML systems. We discuss the role of deconstruction in computing education and its relation to construction activities. Symposium overview The learning sciences have been concerned with how involving learners in the construction of socially relevant computing applications for and with other people can support knowledge construction (Kafai, 2006; Holbert et al., 2021). This interest in construction can be traced back to Papert’s work on constructionism (see Papert, 1991), which argued that knowledge structures are built through the creation of personal and socially relevant artifacts, centering on the connected nature of knowledge with its personal and social dimensions. Today, many tools and educational efforts have embraced constructionism, positioning young people as designers of applications, from commercial products such as Nintendo’s Game Builder Garage and Roblox to educational tools and curricula that have made designing applications a mainstay in most K-12 computing education initiatives (Kafai & Burke, 2014; Oleson et al., 2020; Waite & Sentance, 2021). 2203 Yet, with the ubiquity of social media and AI/ML and their ethical, environmental, and societal implications (Ko et al., 2020), coupled with the political or critical turn in the learning sciences (Politics of Learning Writing Collective, 2017), researchers have turned their attention to the equally important process of deconstruction. Iversen and colleagues (2018) define deconstruction as the process of “critically examining and understanding how meaning and intentionality are encoded into digital artifac ts and practices that impact upon our everyday lives.” Deconstruction involves describing, evaluating and reflecting on the values and intentions embedded in sociotechnical systems used in everyday life while considering their possible implications (Dindle r et al., 2020; Schaper et al., 2023). We argue that such practices can contribute to learners' development of both ethical and functional understandings of AI/ML systems. This involves assessing the properties of a system in terms of its inputs, outputs and materials (e.g., data); inquiring about the intended use and actual use of a system; foregrounding the values, worldviews, and assumptions embedded in the system; and investigating how the system impacts individuals, communities and the environment (Dindler et al., 2023). In this symposium, we bring together researchers taking different approaches to deconstruction to address the following research questions: How can we design activities that scaffold learners to deconstruct AI/ML systems? How does deconstruction support learners in developing their functional and ethical understanding of AI/ML systems? Contributions include presentations about tools and activities that foster deconstruction, participatory approaches that involve teachers in the design of deconstruction acti vities, and insights into learners' thinking processes when investigating socio- ethical issues. Furthermore, we discuss how deconstruction relates to construction and their role in computing education. This session is organized in three sections: (1) the chairs will introduce the topic and participants (~10 min); (2) participants will have seven minutes to share their work; (3) our discussants Jean Ryoo, a learning scientist and computing education researcher that has advocated for equity and inquiry-oriented computing, and Ole Sejer Iversen, a child-computer interaction and activity theory researcher that proposed the term deconstruction, will synthesize and reflect on findings (10 min), followed by a Q&A with the audience and presenters (~15 min). title: Hybridity, Equity, and Conference Design

abstract: This hybrid symposium serves as a conversation and data gathering effort in ongoing iterative design of accommodations through hybrid conferencing in the International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS). We examine recent ISLS conferencing history borrowing the concept of “curb cuts” from disability studies to describe the diffusion of accommodation options. ISLS stakeholder communities (disabled scholars, caregivers, scholars from Majority World, conference organizers), rooted in relevant theory and research, will share perspectives and experiences of accommodation processes and/or the impact of multiple modalities for conference access. We will then engage attendees in discussion breakout groups, facilitated by volunteers across in -person and virtual modalities using Padlet , to generate knowledge and recommendations. We conclude the symposium with a discussion synthesis. The results of this discussion, artifact-generation, and synthesis will inform ongoing iterations of ISLS hybrid designs and conceptualizations of anticipatory design in academic conference spaces, within and beyond ISLS Annual Meetings.

title: Investigating, Understanding, and Generating Concreteness in STEM Education

abstract: What role concreteness plays in education is a key question, especially in STEM where topics can be considered rather abstract. In this symposium, we wish to highlight several issues and opportunities related to concreteness. First, we offer a critical per spective on the value of concrete representations and the learners who use them. Second, we detail a data-driven taxonomy that aims at fully describing concreteness and abstraction, allowing for a fine-grained understanding of these topics. Third, we illus trate how these lines of research can support practice by presenting an automatic approach to the generation of concrete representations. Finally, we open the conversation to other domains of STEM by attempting to connect discourse in mathematics education to other disciplines. We believe that by aggregating empirical evidence, theoretical contributions, and practical implications, this symposium offers a complete overview of the questions around concreteness in STEM education and supports interdisciplinary and impactful conversations at ISLS. Framing our dialogue Designing and investigating concrete or abstract representations for learning has a long tradition in the learning sciences. Scholars have investigated single representations (Kaminski et al., 2008; Trninic et al., 2020), multiple representations (Rau, 2017), as well as sequences of representations, typically progressing from abstract to concrete (concreteness fading, Fyfe et al., 201 5). However, there remains a set of open questions, going beyond representations themselves. First, for which learner is a certain concrete representation helpful and how is this representation - and this learner’s use of it - valued? Second, what key characteristics make a representation concrete, and how can practitioners design and create concrete representations? Finally, it is not clear how these results translate across STEM domains (Kokkonen & Schalk, 2021). This symposium aims to contribute to this debate by highlighting and elaborating on existing issues as well as offering a taxonomy to situate past and future research on concreteness. Specifically, the first contribution discusses how concreteness and abstraction are valued differently during the learning process. The authors offer an analysis of a student who mostly uses a tangible (and thereby concrete) representation and show how the student’s knowledge is valuable in and of itself. They suggest that this reframing of concrete knowledge as valuable warrants a better understanding of what the learning sciences community means by concrete. The second contribution aims to achieve this goal by offering a taxonomy of meanings currently assigned to concreteness in mathematics education. The authors have found eleven axes between concrete and abstract: five that describe how learners may perceive a certain representation as concrete and six that describe how certain attributes of a concept may be mapped to a certain representation. The third contribution moves from theory to practice, describing how generative AI can help producing scalable concrete representations that are both mathematically accurate and relatable. Indeed, although teachers and practitioners may want to leverage concrete representations in their practice, they might not always have the necessary time and skills, and automated approaches could offer an interesting solution. Finally, as the first three contributions are situated in mathematics education, the fourth contribution opens the discussion up to other STEM domains. Specifically, the authors situate the framework for concreteness 2227 fading in chemistry by Beier and colleagues (2024) in the aforementioned semantic taxonomy of concreteness and abstraction. Overall, this symposium offers various perspectives on concreteness in STEM education: learners, representations, practical implications, and variations across disciplines. We thereby touch on systemic issues (who is considered knowledgeable and what representations are valued), offer a way to structure the discourse about concreteness by being more explicit about its meaning, show how this may be applied in practice by generating concrete representations with AI, and open the curtain for other disciplines to join the conversation. We believe that such interdisciplinary and wide conversations are necessary to fully understand the role of concreteness in education and to learn from each other, and we hope this symposium will foster interesting and impactful conversations at ISLS 2026. Who gets to be “concrete?” problematizing concreteness Rosanne Luu, Sofia Tancredi The way abstraction is conceptualized has considerable implications in what actions and representations are taken up and taught within standard academic instruction. In recent decades, learning scientists have questioned implicit conceptualizations of concreteness and abstraction in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education. Constructionists have argued for valuing concreteness as a valid mode of thinking alongside abstraction as a move towards embracing epistemological pluralism (Turkle & Papert, 1992 ). Embodiment scholars have taken up concreteness, conceived of as engaging learners in sensorimotor activity, as the grounding of mathematical concepts (i.e., Abrahamson & Lindgren, 2022; Lakoff & Nuñez, 2000). Educational psychologists have found familia r, physical, and/or sensorial “concrete” representations to be effective tools for scaffolding mathematics instruction (Fyfe et al., 2015). Across these distinct yet related fields of literature, concreteness has been identified as valuable for supporting student learning. Yet, even as several decades of scholarship move to value concreteness, current practices and perspectives position concreteness in ways that often marginalize learners who embrace it. In mathematics education, concrete representations can be viewed as lesser representational forms compared to abstraction, with concreteness conceptualized as a stage to progress away from, rather than as a valuable resource for learning (Luu, 2025). Because of this lesser valuation, students can also be discouraged, in impli cit and explicit ways, from drawing upon concrete, embodied forms of knowledge that would otherwise aid students in their mathematics learning (Takeuchi, 2018). Approaches that value concreteness as critical to development can still treat it as a stage to be overcome. For example, Piaget’s work on the stages of development (Piaget, 1936) has been applied in many domains of research and practice to presume this same kind of progression away from the concrete, where children’s maturation means progression bey ond the kinds of exploration that characterizes the sensorimotor stage. We propose that what is considered concrete or abstract also has implications for who is positioned as knowledgeable (or not) in the classroom. To unpack this claim, we present an illustrative case from a classroom study of mathematics learning. Figure 1. Concrete Egg Carton Representation (Left); Area Diagram Worksheet (Right) Illustrative case analysis We present a case from classroom observational data to problematize existing conceptualizations of representations as concrete or abstract, and how this distinction bears on the positionality of learners who choose to use them. We analyze micro-interactional data to interrogate existing conceptualizations of concreteness within observable evidence of mathematics learning in ecological settings, holding the theory accountable to the practice (Jordan & Henderson, 1995). The data is from a larger project colle cted in the Midwestern United States 2228 examining the use of multiple representations in mathematics. The lesson, titled “Dozens of Eggs,” was intended to help third grade students practice their understanding of equivalent fractions. In the activity, students add together fractions of differing denominators to make a whole, working within denominators that are factors of 12 (e.g., ⅙, ½, ¾). Each student had optional access to a concrete representation, in the form of an egg carton, string, and colored tiles. The string is used to segment the egg carton to change the denominator (initially 12) to represent fractions with denominators of 2, 3, 4, or 6. The teacher instructed students to start with the concrete representation if needed, then to color in their fractions on area diagrams on their worksheets. Figure 1 illustrates the concrete egg carton representation on the left, and an unfilled area diagram worksheet on the right. Our analysis focuses on a three-minute video episode where our focal student, “Ali,” uses the egg carton model as she works through a fraction problem with her partner, “Bea.” The two students are trying to determine whether they could add the fraction 4/6 to 2/12 to equal one whole or less. Ali uses her drawn worksheet to model 2/12, then switches to using her egg carton to find the equivalent of 4/6 in twelfths. Bea has chosen to engage only in the area diagram worksheet. As Ali tries to translate her egg carton model to the drawn worksheet, she argues, “We have to start a new one,” indicating to Bea she doesn’t think adding 4/6 to 2/12 equals less than a whole. Ali gestures to the egg carton model’s four empty spots, saying, “There’s four of them remaining.” Bea and Ali consult Bea’s drawn worksheet, and Bea corrects her that there would be 2/12 as a remainder: “There’s two remaining.” Ali returns to the egg carton model, “adding” in 2/12 with her fingers, and has an “Aha!” moment as she recognizes Bea’s statement as true. Problematizing “concrete” representations First, we problematize the implicit conceptualizations of concreteness and abstraction operating within teaching materials presented to Ali and Bea. The optional precursor egg carton is positioned as “concrete” due to its sensory richness, in contrast to the “abstract” area diagram. The egg carton model does foreground certain qualities compared to the area diagram. The carton offers greater tactile and enactive richness, inviting distinct motor actions with different objects that evoke distinct tactile sensations for the acts of segmenting versus filling in segments. However, the egg carton model does not simplify and is no more context -specific and no more inaccurate than the diagram. The egg carton model is not situated within some highly situated context, such as counting eggs for a cake. We propose the egg carton model is no less symbolic than the area diagram, since the learner coordinates both of these representations with numerical fraction symbols. Thus, when defining abstraction as both the capability to use canonical symbolic represe ntations and the ability to engage with the underlying shared mathematical structure of different problems, these representations are equally abstract. Instead, what positions the egg carton representation as “concrete” in common practice is that it affords the use of certain sensory modalities to engage with the model, modalities that are often deemed invalid and omitted for learning in mathematics education (Tancredi et al., 2022). Given the history of mathematics which privileges visual models as valid and acceptably abstract representational forms (Abrahamson et al., 2019), tactile, haptic, proprioceptive, or vestibular experiences are treated as stepping stones towards later visual abstraction or omitted altogether. In this sense, conceptualizations of abstraction and concreteness reinscribe a modality hierarchy. The ocular is privileged over the sensorimotor, rather than specifying that visual and tactile representations are always encountered through bodily perception–action processes. We argue there is no inherent reason to value the visual model’s affordances over the tactile one for supporting the learning of mathematical concepts. Problematizing “concrete” learners In turn, conceptualizations of concreteness and abstraction in instructional media implicitly position their users differently within classroom practice. We interrogate whether conceptualizing concreteness and abstraction as hierarchical adequately characterizes students’ mathematical strengths. In our illustrative case, the two representations each afforded Ali and Bea the ability to equally engage in mathematical discourse during their fractions problem -solving, regardless of their representational preferences. Ali favored touching and placing strings and physical squares to segment a whole, whereas her peer favored the less stimulating act of coloring in boxes. This does not tell us anything about their relative sophistication in reasoning about fractions. In fact, what it may tell us is simply our learners’ sensory, or personal, preferences. An interpretation of Ali as a more “concrete” learner and therefore less knowledgeable than Bea overlooks Ali’s engagement in mathematical sensemaking during the episode. Ali uses her egg model to conceptualize 4/6 as having a remainder of 4 when the fraction is converted to 12ths, works to connect her carton model with what is represented in her partner’s drawn area diagram, and engages in argumentation with her part ner about the correct answer. The learners in this case do not engage in concreteness as a bridge to abstraction, but rather in a continual dialogue between symbolic and differently-sensorially-situated models. Ali and Bea’s knowledgeability and contributions to their shared 2229 mathematical sensemaking are not limited by binary choices between concreteness and abstraction. Rather, Ali’s use of the “concrete” representation, an action positioned as wholly optional by the lesson, enriches the interaction between her and her partner. Conclusion We problematize the ongoing hierarchization of concreteness and abstraction that positions concreteness as less valuable than or preliminary to abstraction, despite the identified value of concreteness for learning. Conceptualizing concreteness and abstraction as hierarchical fails to adequately characterize the learning- critical affordances of instructional media and the richness of learners’ mathematical activity using these media. We further propose that conceptualizing representations as concrete or abstract can be problematically conflated with how concreteness and abstraction reflect upon the learners participating in the learning activity. Notably, learners with disabilities of ten favor other sensory channels for exploration, such as neurodivergent people’s stimming and blind people’s tactile exploration (Tancredi et al., 2022). When we position sensorimotor action as less valuable, we are rendering learning spaces less accessible to their neurology (Tancredi & Abrahamson, 2024). We must disrupt these notions of sensory periodization (Nolan & McBride, 2015) within individuals’ ontogenetic and microgenetic development if we are to truly liberate concreteness to unfold its full mathematical potential. Disrupting hierarchical conceptualizations of knowing helps challenge deficit discourse s that narrowly define what and who can be successful in mathematics and STEM spaces (Adiredja & Louie, 2020). Conceptualizations of mathematics learning as a sequential endeavor reinforces categories of hierarchy that position students as either ahead or behind, restricting students to narrow pathways of success (Parks, 2010). This manifests in educators’ co -optation of the language of hierarchy to categorize students into “high” and “low” learner profiles, with these labels being leveraged to justify why certain students should be held back in grade level (Myers et al., 2015). As a field, we would benefit from discussions about concreteness and abstraction that have more nuance than current conceptualizations afford, which often position the two concepts as binary and hierarchical. Interrogating concreteness and abstraction will allow us to move as a field towards more expansive ways of knowing and being that, in turn, offer all students richer opportunities to learn. What is concreteness? Organizing concreteness and abstraction Julia Chatain, Charlotte H. Müller, Keny Chatain The words concrete and abstract are central to mathematics education: both when discussing the nature of the discipline or how to teach mathematics. However, we suggest that these terms are used with various meanings, for example, concrete as relatable, specific, tangible, or useful, and abstract as meaningless, universal, virtual, or irrelevant. Past work argued for a finer-grained and multi-dimensional framework of concreteness and abstraction (Chatain et al., 2023; Trninic et al., 2020), as different aspects of concreteness activate different learning mechanisms (Chatain et al., 2023), and result in different learning outcomes (Kaminski et al., 2008; Trninic et al., 2020). For example, Kaminski and co- workers (2008) showed that concrete (as in real -world) examples impair learners' transfer performance when learning about mathematical groups of third order. However, a follow up study showed that making these examples familiar, another interpretation of concrete, erased this difference (Trninic et al., 2020). Generally, we suggest there is a terminological inconsistency or a verbal dispute in the field of mathematics education, that is a disagreement in the semantics of the terms concrete and abstract (Chalmers, 2011). Addressing verbal disputes is often productive, both as output and process. Generally, offering a more precise and finer -grained way of talking about concreteness can enable a better understanding of the effects of concreteness, but also account for the diversity of experiences and effects tied to concreteness, especially for different learners. In this work, we present a data -driven qualitative analysis of 368 papers to map the semantic landscape of concreteness and abstraction through a proposed taxonomy. Specifically, we do not aim to offer one definition of concreteness. Rather, we are asking what meanings of concrete and abstract are frequently found in mathematics education research articles and how they can be organized to facilitate situating research and designing external representations.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this symposium, we consider the diversity of ways that learners conceptualize and engage with places. Building on growing work in the Learning Sciences on learning in/with places, we bring together contributions that highlight the gap between learning with a place and learning about a place by examining cases in which learners complicate ideas of places as good or bad. The contributions show a wide variety of ways this can happen, from students’ changing concepts of a “developed” place, to how prior knowledge of a city can shape one’s perception of neighborhoods as safe or unsafe, to how children might reclaim or resist visions of their school as policed, to how community members resist simplified representation of their places. Together this work suggests increasingly nuanced ways of treating place that can in turn support designs of just learning in places.

title: Artifacts to Support Teacher Learning? Rethinking and Forging New Design Principles
citation: Yasemin Copur-Gencturk, Sebnem Tekin, Marta Kobiela, Zhikun Zhang, Enista Chiniah, Xinyue Chen, Cimpian, Michelle Perry, Elizabeth van Es, Ethan Rubin, Ilana Horn, Rossella Santagata (2026). abstract: Understanding and developing teacher expertise has long been a challenge, especially in the teaching of mathematics. Expertise in teaching requires developing multiple forms of knowledge, instructional practices and commitments, and dispositions and practices to learn in and from teaching. Challenges to accomplishing these different goals have led to new visions for incorporating and leveraging artifacts of classroom instruction—including analog, technologically advanced, and conceptual models—as levers to understand and support teacher learning. Research often privileges asking if artifact-rich learning environments accomplish the desired outcomes, with less attention to how they support teacher learning. In this symposium, we examine different approaches for situating artifacts in pre- and in-service teacher learning contexts. By examining the situated use of artifacts across settings, we gain a nuanced understanding about, and offer design principles for, the productive use of artifacts to improve mathematics teacher learning.

abstract: This interactive poster symposium brings together approaches to working with and studying AI that are not often explicitly connected (and are often placed in opposition to one another), those concerned with the human purposes of creativity and control. The contexts of our studies vary widely: formal education, afterschool or summer programs, community workshops, and professional performing arts. Learners, users, and scholars grapple with the ethics and challenges, as well as the potentials, of AI in their lives and in society. Putting these research projects in dialogue with one another will result in a session that fosters balance and creates a cautious yet hopeful conversation.
