abstract: This symposium brings together a set of posters that focus on science and mathematics teachers’ learning to notice. Teacher noticing is a core construct of teaching, and refers to teachers’ attention, interpretation, and decision-making amidst the “blooming, buzzing confusion” of classr oom interactions. The goal of the session is to examine different ways “learning to notice” is conceptualized and unpack mechanisms that drive teachers’ learning to notice. Symposium overview: Goal, structure, and highlights Teacher noticing, a core construct of teaching (König et al., 2022; Weston & Amador, 2023), broadly refers to teachers’ attention, interpretation, and decision-making of classroom interactions (Jacobs et al., 2010; Sherin et al., 2011). With the growing recognition of noticing as a core practice of teaching, there is an expanding line of research that seeks to understand how to support teachers’ learning to notice (Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; Santagata et al., 2021). Prior research shows that well -designed professional learning opportunities can foster teachers’ learning to notice students’ thinking and teaching in interaction with student learning (e.g., Tekkumru-Kisa et al., 2018; Warshauer et al., 2023). As this knowledge has grown, it has prompted scholars to investigate what constitutes learning of noticing. In this symposium, we pause and ask: How do we think about what constitutes learning to notice? While efforts to support teachers’ learning to notice is evolving, less is understood about the mechanisms of teacher learning to notice (Walkoe & Luna, 2020). Some research investigates how video tagging tools focus teachers’ attention on particular features for further analysis (e.g., Walkoe et al., 2020). Others have considered how different kinds of video clips are selected and situated in professional learning and how collaborative analysis of particular types of clips can shape teachers’ learning (e.g ., Sherin & Dyer, 2017). Recent work has pointed to the role of discourse as a mechanism of teachers’ learning to notice (van Es et al., 2024). However, there is more to be understood about how teachers come to notice complexities of teaching and learning, and designs to better 2318 support that. Going beyond the descriptive account of noticing, in this symposium, our work collectively explores: What drives teachers’ learning to notice? All in all, the goal of our session is to examine different ways “learning to notice” has been conceptualized, and unpack the "mechanisms" that drive teachers’ learning to notice. Using multiple methods such as participatory design research approach and typological analysis of artifacts of teaching , these studies document shifts in teachers’ learning to notice, factors that contribute to teachers’ learning of noticing, and the design choices in facilitating teachers’ learning this complex practice. T he studies identify mechanisms of teachers’ learning to notice such as coding schemes that serve as epistemic mechanisms and collective sensemaking of the complexity of teaching through analysis of classroom videos in professional learning contexts. While some papers zoom in on noticing subprocesses that different video processes afford, others seek to understand teachers’ learning to notice when teachers worked on making links to socio-ecological issues relevant to their lives. Together, these papers advance theory on teachers’ learning to notice, while also considering the situated and relational features of teacher learning. At the same time, they offer methodological tools and frameworks to advance research on learning to notice across math and science. This 90-minute structured poster session will consist of a brief introduction to the session by the session co-chairs (5 min), followed by the interactive discussion of 10 posters (60 min), 10-minutes of commentary from a discussant, Adam Lefstein from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, who brings expertise on teachers’ learning in professional development. We will conclude with 15-minutes of questions and discussion. The discussant will consider commonalities and differences across these studies, surfacing the considerations and tensions for supporting teachers’ learning to notice and mechanisms that drive learning of noticing among math and science teachers across the trajectory of teaching careers. Poster 1: Grounding prospective mathematics teacher noticing in socio- ecological issues: learning to notice in turbulent times Alf Coles, Sigal-Hava Rotem This study addresses the gap between current turbulent times and the seeming ‘objectivity’ of mathematics. We explore what constitutes prospective teachers (PTs) of mathematics learning to notice, during a time of war, the links they make to socio- ecological (Coles et al., 2024) issues of relevance to their lives, and the role of the mathematics teacher educator. Following van Es and Sherin (2002), we conceptualize teacher noticing as attending to and interpreting students' mathematical thinking. Following Mason (2002), we emphasize attention to event details for in -depth interpretation. We focus on “critical events” - moments when teachers notice students' mathematical thinking has potential for deepening. We also bring a notion of “authenticity”, which relates to teachers’ task design choices, and the extent to which tasks include social or ecological issues of relevance to their lives and the extent to which the mathematics includes opportunities for generalization. The study was conducted during wartime, heightening turbulence and data significance. We employed a case study methodology, to research a year- long problem-solving course in a B.Ed. mathematics program. The course focused on a reform in mathematics educati on emphasizing "mathematics in everyday life" and incorporated two design-teach-reflect cycles where participants: 1) photographed and discussed socio- ecological concerns (photovoice method); 2) designed mathematical tasks; and 3) taught and reflected on critical events they identified. Among 23 participants, we focus on Nadin (Bedouin community member) as an illustrative case. Our analysis examines shifts in her articulation of event details, interpretations, the social- ecological issue's authenticity and the role of the teacher educator. The analysis revealed three key findings. First, Nadin was able to bring a highly relevant socio-ecological issue to her classroom, surfacing deeply held beliefs and engaging with students about their beliefs. Secondly, Nadin wrote in great detail and we observed subtle and shifting relationships between detail and interpretation in her accounts, which is of significance to how noticing might be supported. Thirdly, in examining the role of the teacher educator, we uncover the significance of the way space w as offered on the course for PTs to discuss and work on socio-ecological issues of relevance to their lives. Through examining the particulars of one case, our findings offer an example of how teacher preparation, during a time of war, can still support the noticing of prospective teachers, in connecting mathematics to relevant socio-ecological issues. We tentati vely point to a role for prospective teachers’ sharing stories from their lives, and to the power of engaging in design-teach-reflect cycles, in supporting their noticing. 2319 Poster 2: Learning to notice students’ strengths: Coding schemes as epistemic mechanisms in design-based teacher education Thorsten Scheiner This investigation addresses a critical challenge in teacher education: developing teachers’ capacity to recognize and build upon students’ strengths rather than defaulting to deficit -based orientations. While research demonstrates that strength -based noticing practices foster more equitable learning environments (Louie et al., 2021), significant gaps remain in understanding the mechanisms through which teachers develop these sophisticated ways of seeing. This study examines how structured coding schemes function as epistemic tools that bridge cognitive and socio- cultural dimensions of professional learning, offering insights into design -based approaches for transforming teacher noticing practices. The study advances an integrated framework synthesizing professional noticing theory, transformative learning mechanisms, and frame analysis. Professional noticing encompasses attending to critical aspects of student reasoning, interpreting student thinking, and deciding how to respond instructionally (Jacobs et al., 2010). Frame analysis illuminates how interpretive schemas shape what teachers notice and value in student work (Sherin & Russ, 2014). Transformative learning theory provides mechanisms for frame shifting through critical reflection and conscious reorientation of perspective (Mezirow, 2000). The framework positions coding schemes as mediating artifacts that operationalize frame orientations while scaffolding transformative professional development through the dynamic interplay of cognitive restructuring and socio-cultural meaning-making. This exploratory study used a participatory design research approach within an intensive professional learning context. Prospective teachers engaged in three iterative cycles of analysis using a structured coding scheme distinguishing deficit-based, strength-based, and uncommitted orientations across noticing practices. Each iteration incorporated fine -grained examination of transformative mechanisms through structured reflective prompts targeting frame awareness, conscious reframing, and progressive integr ation. Data collection utilized standardized noticing tasks, complemented by reflective journals documenting participants’ evolving interpretive frameworks. Analysis combined quantitative tracking of orientation patterns with qualitative mapping of transformative processes. Analysis revealed three primary mechanisms driving teachers’ learning to notice strengths. First, epistemic visibility emerged through the coding scheme’s dual function as analytical tool and pedagogical scaffold, rendering implicit interpretive frames explicit and actionable. Participants demonstrated systematic shifts from deficit- based toward strength- based noticing practices. Second, collaborative meaning -making facilitated frame shifting through structured protocols that created social spaces for negot iating alternative interpretations of student thinking. Third, reflective reframing supported progressive integration of strength-based orientations through systematic comparisons of deficit-based and asset-oriented perspectives. The iterative design revealed how these mechanisms operated synergistically, with cognitive restructuring mediated by socio-cultural practices of professional discourse and collective analysis. The findings illuminate coding schemes as powerful epistemic mechanisms that render interpretive frames both visible and actionable in teacher education. By functioning simultaneously as analytical tools and pedagogical scaffolds, structured coding schemes support the cognitive work of frame identification while creating social spaces for collaborative meaning -making. This dual functionality bridges individual cognitive transformation and collective professional development, revealing how participatory desi gn research can systematically develop teachers’ capacity for strength- based noticing. The study contributes methodological insights for designing equity- oriented professional learning experiences that leverage the sophisticated interplay between cognitive and socio-cultural dimensions of transformative practice. Poster 3: From noticing to navigating: Pre-service teachers' expansive sensemaking in science instruction Heather Johnson, Tara Barnhart Teacher noticing—especially of student thinking—has become central in teacher education research (Weston & Amador, 2023). Noticing can be cultivated during teacher education (van Es, 2011), but connecting it to student - centered instruction requires space to reflect on the interplay between interpretations, decisions, and institutional contexts (Schwartz et al., 2021). In this study, we explore what pre -service teachers apply from their noticing of expansive sensemaking in videos of accomplished teachers to video analysis tasks in which PSTs design and enact student-centered science experiences. We ground this study in previous work that theorizes that noticing is a learnable skill (van Es, 2011) and that learning to notice is a social activity that takes place when individuals who 2320 share a common interest collaboratively engage with tools and tasks intrinsic to their professional context (Barnhart, 2021). We ground this study in previous work that theorizes that noticing is a learnable skill (van Es, 2011) and that learning to notice is a social activity that takes place when individuals who share a common interest collaboratively engage with tools and tasks intrinsic to their professional context (Barnhart, 2021). We conducted a typological analysis (Miles et al., 2014) of written coursework and fieldwork from PSTs enrolled in a secondary methods course prior to student teaching. Data included their planning documents, video analysis templates, and written reflections for four video tasks: one around an accomplished teacher’s classroom and three around their own teaching. Analysis of what teachers noticed in their own and others’ videos was guided by the Expansive Sensemaking framework (Bautista & Davis, 2024). By applying this framework, the study illuminates how PSTs bridge noticing of student thinking with enacting responsive science teaching. Accomplished teacher video When analyzing videos of accomplished teachers, PSTs attended to how classroom culture shaped student participation. They noticed who was given access to share ideas publicly, how ideas were taken up by the teacher and peers, and how norms and structure supported collaborative learning. PST Videos In their own lesson planning, PSTs designed inclusive tasks that positioned students as epistemic agents and included multimodal participation strategies. They also aimed to expand what "counts" as science and promote diverse ways of knowing. However, enac ting these plans surfaced asset -oriented, equity- oriented, and participation-oriented challenges. Though each PST intended to empower students, their enactments did not always lead to the anticipated engagement. These realizations revealed a gap between in tention and impact, especially in balancing student agency with institutional constraints such as pacing guides and test preparation. Equity-related challenges emerged as PSTs attempted to make lessons culturally relevant. Some PSTs reflected on how their examples did not resonate as expected. PSTs also identified challenges in fostering student-to-student interactions. They reflected on classroom dynamics, noting the need for psychological safety and clearer norms. Importantly, they attributed participation issues to instructional design, not student deficits—demonstrating asset - oriented thinking. Prior work on noticing student thinking has presumed that teachers will apply what they learn to notice in coursework to their own practice. These results support this hypothesis while also highlighting the challenges of responsive instruction and affirming the importance of reflection and collaboration in preparing teachers to sustain asset-based noticing through opportunities to analyze their own artifacts of practice and contribute to the research base for preparing teachers to teach responsively in diverse, authentic contexts. Poster 4: Noticing in college mathematics: Development of noticing discourse in a video-based professional development Patricia Fuentes Acevedo, Christina Kimmerling, Rossella Santagata, Alessandra Pantano, Roberto Pelayo College mathematics classrooms can be marginalizing spaces, particularly for women and students of color (Riegle-Crumb & King, 2010). Persistent inequalities motivate the call for more responsive and equity- oriented college teaching. Teacher noticing is at the core of responsive teaching, with substantial research primarily conducted in K-12 settings (Santagata et al., 2021). Building on K-12 evidence, we developed and tested a video- based curriculum for instructors and graduate and undergraduate teaching a ssistants that fostered expansive noticing of students' mathematical thinking and participation (Santagata et al., 2025). Recent work has emerged suggesting that evidence of learning to notice includes uptaking a particular form of discourse (van Es et al. , 2024). We seek to unpack the relationship between participants' discourse during PD sessions and observed changes in the groups' noticing. We ask: What are the features of participants’ discourse around video- based noticing tasks? Except for a few characterizations of exemplary cases (e.g., Louie et al., 2021), little is known about how educators can learn to notice for equity. We adopt a situative perspective on teacher learning (Borko et al., 2000) and draw on van Es et al.’s (2024) work on learning to notice by engaging in discourse-rich spaces where educators collectively make sense of instruction. Their model characterizes discourse practices that enable participants to learn how to attend to and interpret student thinking. We extend this to student participation. The authors define features of generative noticing for the different purposes that the discourse practices serve. 2321 Participants include three college instructors, five graduate and four undergraduate assistants. They engaged in whole and small group discussions around video clips during four PD sessions. For this study, we selected all segments where small groups discussed noticing prompts after watching a video clip (20 in total) and subsequent whole-group discussions. We portioned the transcribed data into conversational turns and idea units and created analytical memos. Finally, two of us deductively coded the data using van Es et al.'s (2024) features of noticing discourse (Table 1), allowing for emergent codes as well. Table 1 Features of Noticing Discourse Feature of a Noticing Discourse Definition of Feature Negotiating noteworthy phenomena A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending activity, defining what is and is not worthy of attention, and supports learning to decide what to call out and what to ignore. Problematizing and puzzling over objects of teaching and learning A collection of discursive practices that intend to support interpreting and sense-making activity, which is adopting an inquiry stance toward objects of focus, such as offering conflicting viewpoints of what is observed or grappling over intent and meaning. Creating moments for further inquiry of objects of attention A collection of discursive practices that intend to support shaping interactions to gather more information for further attending and interpreting. Being accountable to evidence A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending and interpreting activity by supporting one’s claims with concrete observations, using artifacts of teaching and learning to advance an idea, and elaborating one’s ideas with more specific and precise explanations. Positioning students’ ideas and actions as resources in learning A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending, interpreting, and shaping activity by requiring an openness to seeing what might appear as mundane, or correct/incorrect, as something important and meaningful that can be figured out and used toward understanding. Connecting to their experiences of teaching and learning (emergent A collection of discursive practices that intend to extend the discussion from what was observed in the video to their own past experiences when teaching and/or learning, or with potential future teaching scenarios. Participants discussed aspects related to student thinking and participation, primarily focusing on problematizing objects of teaching observed in the clips, and less frequently engaging in negotiation of noteworthy phenomena. An emergent and predominant feature of their noticing discourse was making connections to their own experiences, which included extending the observed episode to past or potential future teaching scenarios. Additionally, although there is little evidence of positioning students' ideas as resources, participants maintained an asset-based perspective as required by the facilitators. The identified features in our data provide evidence that PD video prompts supported productive noticing discourse among participants and shed light on the processes through which their collective sensemaking contributed to their learning to notice. Our findings reflect the PD emphasis on noticing as multidimensional and are encouraging as they suggest tangible implications for participants' future instruction. This work contributes to the limited literature on how mechanisms for learning to notice take place at the college level. Poster 5: Attending, interpreting, and shaping: How varied ways of working with video connect with subprocesses of teacher noticing Jennifer Richards, Miriam Sherin, Sarah Larison 2322 Research has documented how video- based environments can provide rich opportunities for teachers’ learning, including learning to notice student thinking (e.g., Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; Santagata et al., 2021). Further, advancements in video-related technology have expanded how teachers can engage with video — moving beyond watching and discussing videos to filming and editing their own clips. In this poster, we extend a prior exploration of how teachers noticed student thinking as they engaged in multiple video processes (Richards & Sherin, 2025) by specifying ways in which these video processes map onto posited subprocesses of teacher noticing, contributing to understandings of potential drivers for noticing. The framework we animate specifies several interrelated subprocesses of teacher noticing — attending, interpreting, and shaping (van Es & Sherin, 2021). “Attending” refers to what teachers focus on in classrooms, acknowledging that humans cannot pay attention to everything. “Interpreting” refers to how teachers reason about classroom events. “Shaping” refers to what teachers do in order to support their noticing during or after instruction. While these subprocesses dynamically interact with and influence one another, we think they also reflect important opportunities for learning in their own right. Data come from three iterations of an online, video- based course for early elementary teachers in the United States on mathematical argumentation (Lomax et al., 2017). Twenty -nine in-service teachers participated in the course, in which they engaged in four sequential video processes — recording video in their own classrooms, watching and reflecting on the video, editing clips to share in the course, and interacting with others around their clips. Data sources included interviews and think- alouds with teachers about these video processes and video annotations on clips. Our prior analysis explored the affordances and constraints of each video process for teachers’ noticing of student thinking (Richards & Sherin, 2025). Here, we build on this prior analysis to characterize the noticing subprocesses that different video processes seemed to afford. When teachers recorded video in their classrooms, all three noticing subprocesses seemed to be in play as teachers iteratively focused on student ideas that required attention, sought to make sense of them in real time, and shaped interactions to test working interpretations and gather more information. Watching and reflecting on the video tended to afford continued “interpreting” and “shaping,” as teachers primarily used the video as a tool to make sense of and gain more evidence about student ideas that had intrigued them. Editing clips , in contrast, afforded “attending” with some further “interpreting” as teachers selectively identified moments of student thinking to make visible to colleagues. Finally, when interacting with others around clips , all three subprocesses were again in play as teachers highlighted specific student ideas to consider, discussed varied interpretations, and at times reviewed the video to seek more information. These findings suggest potential implications for targeted video-based designs to facilitate specific noticing subprocesses (e.g., cultivating teachers’ attending by providing multiple opportunities to edit clips). Further research could deepen understandings of how engaging with varied sequences of video processes drives teachers’ learning to notice over time. Poster 6: Developing professional vision through negotiating understanding of videorecorded whole-class talks in mathematics Håvard Johnsrud Evang, Inga Staal Jenset Supporting teacher candidates’ development of ambitious and equitable mathematics teaching is a key challenge in teacher education (Louie, 2018) and requires that teachers adapt their instruction in response to students’ content-specific ideas and ways of participating in the talk (Jacobs & Empson, 2016). Prior research has studied this situation -specific competence through concepts such as ‘noticing of students strengths’ (Jilk, 2016) and ‘equitable noticing’ (Louie, 2018) demonstrating how video- anchored activities may support candidates developing this capacity (Jenset et al., 2024). Building on a recent socio- cultural turn in noticing research (Scheiner et al., 2026), the present study extends this work by investigating how teacher candidates’ professional vision develops as they engage in discussions of video-recorded mathematical classroom talk in Grade 8 settings. This study draws on Goodwin’s (1994) concept of professional vision, defined as the ability to construct relevant knowledge through socio-historically developed practices of highlighting and coding. This framework is used to examine how teacher candidates interpret students’ utterances and actions within recorded episodes of classroom discourse. Adopting a socio- cultural perspective, the study assumes that cultural frames —that is, culturally and historically shaped interpretive lenses regarding school mathe matics, mathematical teaching, and learning (Goffman, 1974; Scheiner, 2021) —function as mediational means that shape these practices. Consequently, the negotiation and adaptation of cultural frames to make sense of students’ mathematical contributions are understood as mechanisms that drive the development of teachers’ professional vision. The study investigates how video- anchored discussions contribute to the development of mathematics teacher candidates’ professional vision. Data consists of approximately 30 hours of video recordings from five 2323 seminars integrated into an existing mathematics-didactics course across one academic year (24 candidates). The seminars were structured to progressively broaden candidates’ highlighting and coding practices, with the goal of fostering increased attention to students’ diverse mathematical reasoning and forms of participation. Candidates’ discussions were scaffolded through an observation rubric and prompts encouraging them to focus on the qualities of students’ contributions, rather than on perceived defici encies or errors. Through reflective thematic and discourse analysis, the study examines how these practices evolved over time and how cultural frames informed candidates’ interpretations of students’ mathematical work. The study yielded three insights into candidates’ professional vision development: (i) a shift from “glossy” to complex understanding of students’ participation, (ii) an expanded understanding of students’ multiple mathematical competencies, and (iii) pers istent privileging of an authoritative view on valuable mathematical outcomes. Video-anchored discussions supported candidates develop richer framing of students as valuable resources in building mathematical knowledge. However, persistent cultural frames constrained candidates’ appreciation of student’s mathematical thinking (Louie, 2018) highlighting the need for teacher education to explicitly challenge these frames to support the development of professional vision for ambitious and equitable teaching. Poster 7: Teacher-designed cases as a tool to support pre-service teacher noticing Tracy E. Dobie, Liza Escobar Aquino, Bailey N. Ondricek, Raven Burton, Angela Warnock Extensive research illustrates the value of supporting teachers’ noticing of student thinking (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010). We respond to the call for more research that investigates learning to notice from an equity frame (van Es et al., 2017) by examining cases (Shulman, 1992) as a tool to support pre-service teachers’ noticing for equity. Teacher noticing is commonly described as having three components – attending, interpreting, and responding (Jacobs et al., 2010). Research on noticing for equity explores various facets of this construct including noticing of individual student histories, anti-deficit discourses, and status and positioning (Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2017). Challenges include supporting pre -service teachers (PSTs) to attend to individual students’ participation (Wager, 2014) and notice more critical dimensions of equity (Graham & Roth McDuffie, 2023). Cases are written narratives describing authentic and complex teaching situations (Shulman, 1992) that can be intentionally designed to investigate certain themes (Dobie et al., 2024). We use cases to help PSTs grapple with the challenges of enacting equitable mathematics and science instruction —or leveraging students’ multiple strengths, honoring students’ diverse lived experiences, dismantling classroom power and status hierarchies, and challenging dominant perspectives (e.g., Aguirre et al., 2013). We partnered with local U.S. teachers, who designed cases exploring themes such as assumptions about multilingual students, inequitable group dynamics, and school structures that disadvantage minoritized students (Dobie et al., 2024). Data include PSTs’ written responses (N=1,036; 224 PSTs) to prompts for six cases that were implemented 2 -4 times each in an elementary math or science methods course. Our team deductively and inductively developed a coding scheme (Miles et al., 2014) capturing a) case details (what PSTs attended to), b) equity-oriented interpretations (PSTs’ reasoning), and c) solutions (ideas about how to respond). Two coders coded every response, and discrepancies were resolved. We highlight three findings: 1) Cases support PSTs to attend to details about students and their actions, 2) Cases and prompts can be designed to support PSTs to make wide-ranging equity-oriented interpretations, and 3) Case prompts elicit solutions that include in-the-moment actions, changes for future instruction, and advocacy- based actions including gathering data and research. We offer frequency counts across the dataset, PST quotes, and case comparisons. As an example, we explore how a subtle difference in prompts influenced PSTs’ breadth of interpretations in two similar cases focused on group dynamics: In one case, 83% of responses offering equity- oriented interpretations focused on a general imbalance in group dynamics; in the other, PSTs reasoned about a general imbalance in group dynamics (39%), as well as the roles of friendship (46%), language (43%), prior school experiences (24%), and gender (15%). Cases have significant potential for supporting PSTs’ noticing for equity including details of specific students’ participation (Wager, 2014) and more critical dimensions of equity (Graham & Roth McDuffie, 2023). Questions remain about trajectories of noticing over time and the impact of noticing in cases on noticing in classrooms. 2324 Poster 8: Accounting for teacher learning in a video club: Learning a noticing discourse Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Elizabeth van Es, Melissa Luna Video-based professional development has been shown to support mathematics and science teachers’ learning to notice for responsive and equitable instruction (Santagata et al., 2021). This vision of teaching calls on teachers to attend to the substantive contributions students make toward the learning goals and adopt an inquiry stance to validate and interpret student thinking to position students’ ideas as resources for their own and others’ learning. What is less understood is how and why these settings support teacher learning. Thus, we ask what might be mechanisms of teacher learning to notice in the context of video- based professional development centered on noticing student thinking? We conceptualize video-based professional development as complex activity systems in which the video clips, the norms for participation, and the cultural and historical practices of professional development all coordinate to influence teachers’ opportunities to learn in these settings (Barnhart, 2021). Our research is informed by an often overlooked feature of complex activity systems of professional development that may be supporting teachers’ learning to notice: the nature of talk that takes place in video- based professional learning contexts. Professional discourse plays a central role in teacher learning (Lefstein et al., 2020), yet less is known about the character of talk that results in teachers’ learning to notice. Data include video recordings and transcripts from two video clubs to support teachers to learn to notice the complexity of teacher -student learning interactions. Video club facilitators prompted teachers to explore the details of student thinking, potential interpretations of their ideas, in relation to teaching. One video club included nine 4th and 5th grade mathematics teachers that met ten times for about one hour over the academic year, approximately once a month. The second video club focused on supporting six middle school science teachers’ learning to notice student thinking and teaching in seven hour -long sessions throughout an academic year. We analyzed an early and late video club meeting for both groups to identify features of a noticing discourse that were present in each meeting (van Es et al., 2024; Table 1). To account for teachers’ learning a noticing discourse, we coded the video club data and wrote analytic memos for evidence and disconfirming evidence of the noticing discourse features, also noting who enacted the talk moves that represented the noticing discourse features. Findings show that both groups shifted in their enactment of a noticing discourse over time. Both groups shifting their talk to highlight more ideas represented in the clips as worthwhile for noticing (i.e., negotiating noteworthy phenomena), pursue these ideas as objects of inquiry for the group to analyze (i.e., creating moments for further inquiry), anchor their analyses of student thinking in classroom evidence (i.e., being accountable to evidence), and demonstrate an openness to explore students’ ideas as resources for learning. Moreover, teachers demonstrated an accountability to the learning community by enacting talk that balanced respecting and honoring teachers' practice represented in the video, while also pressing on what was going on to further understand student thinking and teaching. This finding offers additional insights into features of talk that are enacted to support teachers’ learning to notice, which we argue represents the importance of collective sensemaking as a critical component of noticing discourse in professional learning. Looking across both video-clubs, this study provides evidence for a noticing discourse as key to teachers’ learning to notice, and has implications for design features, such as creating moments for further inquiry, to make video club discourse generative for teacher learning. Poster 9: Science teachers’ learning to notice expansively Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Jennifer Richards There is growing agreement in the field that teacher noticing is critical in ambitious forms of teaching that center students (König et al., 2022; Weston & Amador, 2023). Joining other scholars in exploring the complexities of noticing (e.g., van Es et al., 2022), our ongoing work considers the multidimensionality of teachers' noticing for facilitating students’ sensemaking in science classrooms (Tekkumru- Kisa & Richards, 2025). However, there is much to learn about what supports teachers to develop multidimensional noticing practices. In this study, we explored whether a group of science teachers shifted their noticing through engaging in a specific video- based professional learning (PL) design. Briefly, with multidimensional noticing, we bring together key threads from prior work on noticing, such as the importance of noticing student thinking (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010) as well as pedagogy connected to student thinking (e.g., Tekkumru-Kisa & Stein, 2015), and working toward anti -deficit ways of noticing disciplines and 2325 students (e.g., Louie et al., 2021). Taking a situative perspective on teacher learning (Borko et al., 2000), which emphasizes learning through interaction in activity systems, we sought to embody these noticing practices in PL tools and routines (Greeno, 2006; Sandoval, 2014). This study was conducted within the context of an NSF -funded project, Implementing Practices of Ambitious Teaching for Complex Assessment Tasks (IMPACT). IMPACT PL is centered around the implementation of science performance assessments, providing a laboratory for teachers to work with students’ ideas. Five 8th -grade science teachers from different schools in a large urban district in the United States participated. Teachers engaged in collaborative analysis of performance assessment video clips intentional ly selected to highlight relations between student thinking and ambitious teaching principles (Windschitl et al., 2018) and were consistently asked to focus first on student thinking, then aspects of teaching that seemed to support student thinking. To explore changes in teachers’ noticing, we analyzed teachers’ baseline and exit interviews during which they were asked to share what they noticed and how they might respond to events in a ~7- minute video clip. We separated teachers’ interview transcripts into idea units and coded each idea unit with respect to teachers’ noticing, using the multidimensional noticing framework as an analytical lens (Tekkumru- Kisa & Richards, 2025). At the end of the IMPACT PL, there was growing attention to student thinking among all five teachers. When they noticed student thinking, they began to see what students were saying or appeared to be thinking as valuable, taking an asset-based frame. Moreover, in the exit interviews, teachers focused more on ways to work with students' ideas as opposed to only correcting those ideas. In short, the video- based PL tools and routines seemed to hold promise for supporting shifts in multiple dimensions of teache rs’ noticing in concert with each other. Future research can elaborate on the dynamics of teachers’ noticing practices throughout the PL, particularly how teachers iterated among noticing student thinking and pedagogy. Poster 10: A learning to notice for equity framework Jose Mendez, Elizabeth A. van Es Descriptive accounts of teachers’ noticing for equity contribute to theorizing the complexity of teachers’ in the moment attention and sensemaking to advance responsive and equitable instruction (e.g. Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2022). What is less understood is how teachers learn to notice for equity. Teacher noticing for equity is characterized by teachers ’ attention to multiple dimensions of the classroom environment including linguistic resources, power dynamics, relational interactions, social i dentities, and sociopolitical narratives (van Es et al., 2022). We theorize that learning to attend to equity involves the ability to name these classroom dynamics and see them as interconnected (e.g., Rubin & van Es, 2025). The second dimension involves the development of an interpretive practice , which entails continuously engaging with evidence to better understand and support students’ needs (Sherin & Russ, 2017). The third dimension involves embodied engagement , drawing on recent noticing-as-embodied c onceptualizations that highlight the nuanced and multi -sensory aspects of noticing (Mason, 2002; Scheiner, 2021). Embodied engagement of one’s noticing includes both actions, such as shaping, to position oneself to notice more expansively, and choosing to ignore particular aspects of classroom interactions that are less generative for student learning (Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2022). Embodied engagement that disrupts inequities is a reflection of developing one’s noticing for equity (Scheiner, 2021). We qualitatively analyzed data from a research practice partnership that explored whether and how co - designing and analyzing practical measurement data could provoke a mathematics teacher’s learning to notice for equity (Mendez & van Es, 2025). We adopt sociopolitical perspectives to theorize teachers’ learning to notice as tied to their personal histories and the power -laden environments they teach in (Louie et al., 2021). We also theorize learning as a progression that can support teachers and teacher educators formatively documenting changes in teachers’ noticing over time (e.g., van Es, 2011). Data included transcripts of co- design meetings to develop a survey as a form of practical measurement data and data discussions of iterative cycles of survey implementation. This poster will present a framework for learning to notice for equity that consists of four levels. Each level is characterized by shifts in noticing along the dimensions of attending to equity, interpretive practice, and embodied engagement. As the case study teacher shifted in his noticing for equity, he came to see noticing as multidimensional and integrated, shifting frames to interpret events from an asset- and evidence-based stance. He also made connections to his practice and considered how to disrupt persistent inequities to create a responsive classroom through shaping noticing interactions focused on students’ ideas and patterns of participation. This framework moves from descriptive accounts of teacher noticing for equity to characterize the prog ression of learning to noticing from an equity lens over time. In doing so, this tool offers a framework to study teachers’ 2326 learning to notice for equity, while also providing guidance for designing experiences to support teachers’ expansive noticing. abstract: From Mapuche palikantun rhythms in Chile to Uruguayan rural futures, from WhatsApp organizing at the Mexico-US border to Brazilian constructionist reinterpretations— this symposium weaves together studies reimagining the Learning Sciences through Latin American epistemologies. We gather not to import theories from distant academies, but to honor knowledge systems flowering in our territories: mathematical wisdom in Mapuche weaving, learning that unfolds at the Tijuana -San Diego border, resistance enacted through digital practices. Our work traces how communities transform constraints into creativity, how intergenerational memory becomes a pedagogical method, how the periphery generates its own centers of gravity. Through empirical studies spanning Colombia, Ecuador, and beyond, we demonstrate the generative potential of putting Learning Sciences theories in dialogue with Latin American frameworks —where constructionism converses with conscientização, ethnomathematics meets epistemic footprints, and speculation becomes decolonial praxis. Together, we offer distinctive interpretative lenses that expand the field by centering community knowledge and lived experiences situated in Latin America.

abstract: This hybrid symposium brings together learning sciences research exploring intergenerational identity development in relation to the arts and making as a means of deepening partnership. We look across continents through projects that center art and making as identity work, particularly for people navigating historic oppression, to better understand the ways these creative acts can provide pathways of resistance and reimagination. We follow the conference theme to reimagine the ways that learning scientists interpret “impactful learning experiences” (Fishman et al., 2013) in partnerships that emphasize notions of joy and creation as meaningful forms of reimagining learning in our present global context. Each paper reimagines how intergenerational participants inscribe themselves into the world, positioning acts of identity building as a deeply rooted engagement in possibility. Through this session, we strive to build conversations across these nine projects and in collaboration with attendees toward more nuanced, critical, and culturally grounded notions of partnership. Overview This proposed hybrid symposium brings into conversation learning sciences research exploring how people develop identities across lifespans in relation to the arts —broadly conceived as making and tinkering, creating, writing, composing, and creatively engaging with others toward more transformative futures. Drawing from traditions of design- based research (e.g., Brown, 1992), participatory design research (e.g., Bang & Vossoughi, 2016), testimonio and pláticas (e.g., Delgado -Bernal, 2012), and decolonizing and indigenous methodologies (e.g., Bang, 2020; Patel, 2016), we examine the ways that partnerships resonate and grow alongside the identities of participants when grounded in notions of joy, play, creativity, and belonging (Mirra & Garcia, 2024). In this symposium, we collectively define learning as ontological, a process of becoming someone new (e.g., Lee, 2016), 2340 and view learning and associated identities as expansive, developing along pathways in relation to our histories, communities, partnerships, and collective ecologies (e.g., Bang, 2020; Gutiérrez et al., 2019; Nasir et al., 2020). We see identity as an ever -changing part of human experience, both related to and disruptive of structures of power that have continuously led to oppression and genocide based on race, ethnicity, culture, religion, language, gender, socioeconomic status, ability, and the growing number of traits deemed “illegal” by those in power in the U.S. and other nations. We follow theorists whose work has pushed boundaries of what it means to embody artistry, particularly for historically marginalized peoples whose collective efforts have alwa ys been the catalyst for movements toward more equitable futures (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016). Our aim with this collective conversation is to look across our projects, all of which center art and making as part of learning trajectories through which people build identities (Nasir et al., 2020), particularly for people navigating historic oppression, to better understand the ways creative acts can provide pathways of resistance, reimagination, and transformation in relationship with and to one another, our environments, and the more -than-human beings whose ecologies we share. This session will center on the questions: 1) How can projects focused on identity-building within creative contexts help to reimagine the ways partnerships operate toward more joyful, just, and transformative ends? 2) How can conversations across projects move the learning sciences to more deeply attend to the creativity essential for reinvention of systems and structures? In this symposium, we discuss papers in three 18- minute rounds, ending with collaborative discussion with Dr. McKinney de Royston, audience, and participants, to push back against restrictive notions of identification, instead taking up dialogical approaches to identity (e.g., Akkerman & Meijer, 2011). Across these papers, scholars examine the ways that making and the arts can extend toward more transformative notions of what it means to be and become a certain kind of person (Enyedy et al., 2014). We bring into conversation projects drawing from narrative (e.g., Delgado- Bernal, 2012), proleptic (Lee, 2016), and liberatory notions of identity development across generations (Nasir et al., 2020), and engage in conversations to push these silos toward more holistic and transformative ends. Framing identity building as an artistic process, rather than a solely scientific one, we reimagine how young people and their elders inscribe themselves into the world. We position every act of identification as a potential artistic act of defiance, imagination, and creation toward more transformative futures. In considering the call for this year’s conference, we use these pieces to speak together about the ways that partnership and design can act as levers to engage in joyful resistance and creative reimagining of structures of power (Hayes & Kaba, 2023). The scholars in this symposium draw from sociocultural, sociocritical, and constructionist theories of learning, as well as notions of criticality, embodiment, temporality, and design to reconsider the ways that our work can build knowledge and community collectively. Although the papers feature a variety of methods, all share perspectives that data can and should be representative of the multiple and complex ways learners navigate the world (Bridges, 2020). This complexity is part of our session structure, where we offer both traditional and creative opportunities for participants across modalities to engage and build knowledge collaboratively and in partnership. Despite differences in epistemology and analysis, each project suggests new ways of understanding identity development as a deeply cultural and artistic process of reimagining both oneself and the world. Paper abstracts are listed below alphabetically by first author and referred to here by number. While all papers engage in examining arts and identity development through design, partnership, and collaboration, the projects differ in stages of development and are situated across varying contexts, nations, and continents with an array of participants. Papers 1, 3, 5, and 6 examine the ways university students engage across settings to build identities artistically alongside diverse communities of learners. P apers 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, and 8 take up notions of intergenerational identification and learning to examine the ways that making and the arts can support attunement to new conceptions of self as activist and part of a “political-ethical becoming” (Vossoughi et al., 2021). Paper 9 acts as an overarching commentary across the papers, examining making and tinkering and proposing new ways of framing acts of artistry as supportive of learners’ critical consciousness (Freire, 1970). Each of the papers focuses on a diverse community of learners, where participants with historically marginalized identifications as well as other actors draw upon powerful identity resources (Nasir and Cooks, 2009) to support the reimagining of self and the world as a joyful and creative act, deeply rooted in cultural pathways of learning (Nasir et al., 2020). Together, these papers offer rich groundwork for conversations in the learning sciences, pushing on notions of partnership and learning as identity-making, while interrogating disparate yet deeply interconnected sociopolitical contexts. Paper 1: Identity work in a community and art based engaged university program Sanne Akkerman, Jeroen Vermeulen 2341 This paper reports on identity work taking place in a transdisciplinary community -engaged master’s track at Utrecht University. In this year-long program, students are invited into the everyday life of an urban public park, where they meet, talk with, and collaborate alongside local citizens representing a wide range of interest -based communities, including skaters, graffiti artists, rappers, youth care workers, and caretakers of trees, grass, and water. Through the track, students are asked to move beyond predefined disciplinary orientations and questions. They are challenged to explore the stories and practices of these communities, while inviting and bringing diverse community members and groups together to exchange perspectives and potentially build new relations around central communal themes. In this paper, we examine what it means for students to engage in what in this track is intended as a form of ontological synchronization with what happens and matters to local communities at a specific site and what it means for community members to become involved in prescenery science (Akkerman, Bakker, & Penuel, 2021). Our focus is on identity work that emerges in the process of synchronization and community engagement. Following Akkerman and Meijer (2011), we understand identity work from a dialogical perspective, where people come to explore and dynamically understand themselves through relations and collaborations with others. In the context of this track, we analyze how students and community members from various subcultures develop new understandings by relating to others with less familiar backgrounds and perspectives. We consider motivation letters, reports of interest, week ly meetings during the year and the communal creation of a light -art story and public event over time. Findings show the ways in which students and community members of the park take outside and inside perspectives of others but also develop new shared perspectives in the art works being produced functioning as an effective boundary object (Star, 1989) to materialize and structure the open, and at times discomfortable, educational process of mutual engagement. Paper 2: Joyful immigrant family storytelling during politically perilous times Antero G. Garcia, Alix Dick, Christián Thaniari This paper shares findings from a yearlong community- engaged storytelling project with immigrant parents and their children. In the final weeks before the 2025 U.S. presidential inauguration, immigrant families prepared for the worst, based on President -elect Trump’s ongoing vows to implement “the largest domestic deportation operation in American history” (Colvin, 2023). As the future for immigrant families remained uncertain even in “sanctuary” states like California, the narratives around immigrant life focused on hopeless narratives of struggle (Dick & Garcia, 2024). And yet, despite these dire contexts, immigrant families thrive. Amidst a climate of fear, immigrant families sustain joy not in spite of dire policy consequences but as ongoing, embodied pr actice. This paper shares how immigrant families manifested joyful identities through storytelling in perilous times. This paper builds on sociocultural literacies scholarship that centers immigrant and transnational identities (Bernal, 2001; Delgado- Gaitan, 2005; Villenas, 2005). Further, the emphasis on immigrant family artmaking practices also guides this work (e.g. Flores 2018; 2022). Finally, recognizing family storytelling as occurring with a community of practice (Lave & Wenger, 1991), this project extends understanding of identity and expertise within transnational informal learning environments. This qualitative case study (Dyson & Genishi, 2005; Yin, 2013) was conducted entirely online. Monthly, the community of families would convene online to share and reflect on the multimodal artifacts they created. These meetings concluded with a design prompt to take up for the following month. Methodologically, this project is situated within Chicana feminist plática methodology (e.g. Fierros & Delgado Bernal, 2016; Hannegan- Martinez, 2023). This approach centers participants’ lived experiences as forms of expertise. The ongoing conversation—plática —of each meeting guides how joy is named, measured, and shared in this group. In addition to recordings of community meetings, data for this project included the multimodal artifacts parents and children made together as well as individual interviews conducted with each family twice throughout the yearlong project. All data was inductively coded alongside a cadre of youth and parent community members. These community- created testimonies of hope ( testimonios de esperanza) acted as opportunities to explore political and structural contexts of joy. Participants’ artifacts centered communal expertise and joy tied to familial pride, cultural identity, and expressed hope for future generations. Notably, families centered “struggle” as a kind of superpower. This work, as demonstrated in poems, photo- based family trees, and family -created collages revealed ongoing narratives of solidarity that emerged through c ommunity-based artmaking. Participants’ proleptic vision of cultural identity interweaves multimodal storytelling of joy across varied timescales. In contrast to dominant, deficit narratives of immigrant experiences, findings from this study illuminate an alternative, speculative narrative of immigrant ingenuity. These findings illustrate sustained community joy through collected, family-made artifacts. The field of education does not yet utilize specific forms 2342 of joyful creation by marginalized families; the possibilities for leveraging these as assets for pedagogical application in various settings pose clear guidance for future research and design. Paper 3: Identity work in a community and art based engaged university program Teyona James-Harris, Shirin Vossoughi, Lulu Madise This paper examines educator learning and mutual becoming in a longstanding STEAM and storytelling program serving Black, Latinx/e and Asian/South Asian middle schoolers. We ask: What conditions support learning across an intergenerational collective of ed ucators of color? How do educators describe the identity shifts and forms of mutual becoming they experience over time? Here mutual becoming refers to moments when student and educator learning are dynamically interrelated and mutually generative. Research has identified key conditions that support teachers’ professional learning and efficacy (e.g., communities of practice, guidance around equitable pedagogies, instructional materials designed for teacher learning [Patton & Parker, 2017; Wei, et. al ., 2010]). Yet there is a need to better understand the paradigmatic identity shifts and forms of political- ethical becoming that can emerge for educators in settings that reimagine disciplinary domains and social relations, and practice expansive forms of arts and political education. Here we draw on Vossoughi et al.’s (2021) definition of political-ethical becoming as “not only reorganizing our thoughts but reshaping our relations,” and Rogoff’s (2023) fractals as attuning to mutually constituting processes at smaller and larger scales over time. Utilizing interpretive ethnography (Erickson, 1985) and participatory design research (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) we report on a data set documenting student and educator learning within a 6- week summer STEAM/Storytelling program over eight years through audio -video recordings, field notes, student and educator interviews, and documentation of co- design processes. We share findings developed through qualitative coding and memoing of pre - and post-program educator interviews, analysis of one focal educators’ t rajectory across years, and field notes that capture mutual becoming through educators’ reflections on key interactions with students. Our analytic approach involves working closely with an intergenerational group of educators of color (ages 13-62) who blend the role of teachers, artists, and researchers. Our findings show how participants describe both structural and relational conditions of educator learning as consequential to the identity shifts they experience. Structural conditions include intergenerational apprenticeship, daily debriefs and educator reflections, opportunities to witness and try out others’ pedagogical moves, and fieldnote writing. Relational conditions include intentional community building and care among educators, encouragement to show up as their full selves, and a culture of playful communion that aligned with the forms of artistic creation supported among students. Patterns across field notes and educators’ pre- and post-interviews reveal the ways educator learning and political-ethical becoming involved embodying the artistic ways of being supported with students (e.g., taking our imaginations seriously, embracing the process of creation and learning, engaging in various forms of language work and conceptual revision) in ways that connected with educators’ own complex histories with schooling, learning, and life. One educator, for example, discussed the ways she was taught to avoid mistakes within a rigid schooling context, and how she needed to learn to soften this tendency within herself as she supported our middle school students to embrace process. Another example of language revision shows how the kinds of thinki ng we were supporting our students to engage around rethinking inherited terms was taken up by novice educators. One undergraduate educator referred to Red Winged Black Birds during an outdoor walk as “territorial” and then later revised his language to “protective,” sharing with students the “why” of his revision. Our paper also includes a deeper look at one teacher’s trajectory over time and the ways she took up storywork. Pedagogical storytelling was a routine practice within this setting and involved careful decision making on the part of educators around language and nourishing forms of political education and storytelling for middle school students. This teacher's journey reveals how guided feedback and revision of her story through intergenerational apprenticeship played a key role in expanding not only what she offered youth story listeners, but how she thought about and walked with her own story over time. We also found educators practiced these ways of being in relationships and contexts outside the learning environment, with family and friends. This included discussing the ways they noticed their language changing in conversations with others, and how they are enacting new forms of careful noticing and attunement to others and the world outside the educational settings. We found that all educator interviews narrated this type of “rippling out” of learning as a key indicator of the identity shifts supported by transformative projects. Such findings can support intentional design of the conditions that cultivate transformative educator learning, and ways of conceptualizing educator learning as a deep process of identity work and political -ethical 2343 becoming. Further, mutual becoming both troubles student -teacher binaries common within oppressive educational structures (Freire, 1970) and helps theorize identity shifts in ways that carefully attune to the centrality of relationality and creativity in human learning. Paper 4: “We are all becoming”: Exploring the design of improvisational activity within researcher-artist collaborations and zine making Lindsay Lindberg, Ananda Marin, Shivani Davé, Brenda Lopez, Trinity Collins Artistic identities develop across time, through conversation, and within creative practices. Throughout a co- design project with five improvisational jazz artists, including co -design conversations and performances, artists drew on identity-relevant experiences to reflect on their distinct and developing roles as individuals and ensemble members. We focus on how storywork (Archibald, 2008) shapes artists’ and researchers’ participation in improvised modes of creative activity including art making, music making, and analytic processes. We understand identity as one’s sense of self and the roles they embody in relation to others. From this perspective identities are always in a process of becoming, as individuals participate in and explore the roles that are available to them within communities of practice ( Nasir & Cooks, 2009) . Learning alongside collaborators, we also understand identity as connected to the creation of an expressive multi -modal language that is rooted in experiences and places. title: Insights from International Partnerships on Infrastructuring for Maker Education
citation: Yuval Segev, Yotam Hod, Shiri Kashi, Akshay Nagarajan, Alekh Velayudhan, Ann Berger Valente, Anna Santo (2026). Insights from International Partnerships on Infrastructuring for Maker Education. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Segev, Y., Hod, Y., Kashi, S., Nagarajan, A., Velayudhan, A., Valente, A. B., & Santo, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Maker education is a disruptive innovation spreading globally, fundamentally challenging schooling by shifting focus from abstract ideas to creating and sharing tangible artifacts. Often driven by grassroots enthusiasm rather than top- down mandates, this diffusion lacks corresponding supportive infrastructure from established systems, posing a timely question: What can be learned about the infrastructures and infrastructuring processes required to support the integration of maker learning? Maker education offers an opportunity to employ infrastructuring as a conceptual lens and strategy to analyze the inherent tensions between this movement and formal schooling. This structured poster symposia embodies the Annual Meeting's theme, Partnering with Purpose . It convenes international research groups who actively collaborate with local stakeholders to share diverse insights from their efforts to integrate maker learning into school systems. By illuminating these infrastructuring processes, we aim to inform a more robust theory of sustainable, systemic change within the Learning Sciences.

abstract: This symposium explores how participatory design (PD) can disrupt the "one -size- fits-all" approach by fostering equitable, responsive, and contextually relevant practices in the learning sciences. Leveraging PD to address systemic inequities, the symposium showcases studies that empower immigrant teens as co -designers and learners in crafting experiences for informed civic participation, employ micro-genetic analyses to examine equitable partnerships among diverse stakeholders, explore curriculum co -design in resource-constrained settings to enhance teacher agency, utilise cooperative inquiry for designing inclusive schools for LGBTQIA+ students, and use of participatory design to advance inclusiveness in an international network of informal STEM clubs. This symposium illustrates how PD can change educational spaces and advance the Learning Sciences' commitment to social justice, ethical collaboration, and inclusive practices through case studies, methodological insights, and interactive discussions. Overview and significance Participatory design (PD) is increasingly recognised for its potential to advance equity and inclusion in education. Rooted in collaboration, PD engages learners, educators, researchers, and community members in co -designing learning environments, tools, a nd systems that address diverse experiences and needs. The Learning Sciences community has long emphasised the creation of ethical, inclusive practices that disrupt systemic inequities and foster equitable learning opportunities (e.g., Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Gomez et al., 2021). However, despite the continued focus on inclusion within the learning sciences, empirical evidence and case studies that highlight how marginalised and underrepresented voices are included remain limited. This symposium aligns with the learning sciences’ commitment to social justice by showcasing how PD can challenge the "one -size-fits-all" approach to education. PD provides a pathway to address systemic challenges such as language barriers, identity affirmation, and power dynamics, creating equitable and contextually relevant educational practices (DiSalvo & DiSalvo, 2014; Hoadley, 2017; Vossoughi, 2020). PD fosters inclusive practices that support all stakeholders, particularly in diverse, resource-constrained settings, by including marginalised voices. The symposium presents five contributions that cover a wide range of educational contexts, including empowering immigrant teens as co-designers and learners in crafting civic engagement experiences, using micro- genetic analysis to explore teacher- stakeholder collaborations in curriculum co- design, designing inclusive schools for LGBTQIA+ youth through Cooperative Inquiry, and how participatory design can advance inclusiveness in an international network of informal STEM clubs. These cases illustrate how PD can adapt to real-world constraints, enhance agency, and create educational spaces aligning with the learning sciences' commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion. Through interactive presentations, participants will engage with empirical, methodological, and theoretical insights, fostering discussions that bridge research and practice. This symposium not only advances the understanding of PD as a tool for social justice but also invites the learning 2365 sciences community to reimagine educational research and design for a more equitable future, echoing calls for ethical and inclusive practices (Gomez et al., 2021; Uttamchandani et al., 2020). Paper 1: Participatory design to promote teen civic engagement Nitzan Koren Abstract: This paper discusses the benefits of Participatory Design for empowering and engaging teens from immigrant backgrounds in informed politics. Two roles assumed by teens: co-designers, brainstorming and ideating learning activities for non- citizens to engage in informed politics, and learners, testing and participating in design activities to practice informed politics and improve political skills, knowledge, and self -efficacy. Techniques that led to meaningful civic learning and led to meaningful design recommendations are discussed.

title: From Enrichment to Essential: The Value of the Arts in Education and Learning
citation: Harper Staples, Anna Keune, Sinyoung Kim, Kristiina Kumpulainen, Naomi Thompson, Mary DiCioccio (2026). From Enrichment to Essential: The Value of the Arts in Education and Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: This symposium positions the arts as central to learning. Arts -based education has been shown to cultivate creativity, empathy, and cultural awareness, while supporting academic achievement and well -being. Despite this , the arts remain marginalized in curricula, with funding cuts and narrow evaluation frameworks obscuring their value. Responding to calls to advance knowledge on learning in and through the arts, this symposium seeks to demonstrate approaches to valuing the arts through six contributions that show methodological and theoretical innovations, alongside purposeful partnerships, that capture the value of arts-based education. The symposium will include roundtable presentations within a participatory fishbowl and co-creation of a tangible emotional cartography of insights, advancing future directions for evidencing the value of arts-based education through research, policy, and practice. Symposium overview The arts are central to how we understand learning and knowing and are therefore crucial to the learning sciences (Halverson & Sawyer, 2022). The arts have long been recognized as powerful contexts for cultivating empathy, creativity, and cultural awareness (Eisner, 200 2; Venkatesh et al., 2023) . The arts have also supported academic achievement and positively impacted mental health and wellness (Peppler et al., 2014; Fancourt & Finn, 2019). Unlike other domains, arts -based education engages learners in per sonally meaningful experiences that link identity, community, and imagination (Halverson et al., 2023; Peppler et al., 2023). Importantly, these experiences are also democratic: arts -based education can nurture the pluralism and inclusivity that underpin participatory societies. This value has been affirmed globally; UNESCO, for example, through its 2022 MONDIACULT declaration, emphasizes that culture and the arts are integral to human development, well -being, and creativity, forming the foundation for respect and openness to otherness , which are all skills essential for 21st- century life (UNESCO, 2024). Despite its crucial role, arts -based education often remains marginal in curricula, positioned as “auxiliary” rather than central (Halverson, Saplan & Martin, 2024, p. 300). One challenge lies in evaluating the impact of arts-based education. As Jindal-Snape et al. (2018, p.60) note, attempts to measure “a range of aesthetic and emotive experiences which themselves defy categorization” risk reducing the richness of artistic engagement and obscuring its intrinsic value, namely, its distinctive capacity to “i lluminate our inner lives and enrich our emotional world” (Mowlah et al., 2014, p.4). Compounding this issue, even amid increasing global attention, there remains uncertainty about how the arts are and should be connected to education and assessment (Fleming, Bresler & O’Toole, 2015, p. 1). To address these gaps, more robust and responsive ways of articulating arts -based education, its role, and its purposes are essential. Building on this prior work crystallizes an important opportunity: To articulate the value of arts- based education through approaches that can capture both the distinctive ‘ ways of knowing ’ (Wright, 2012) and the “examples of success that are possible” in arts -based educat ion (Halverson et al., 2024, p. 310), while also 2375 foregrounding the broader social outcomes it enables . Making sense of artistic and cultural experiences requires situated, learner-centered, and embodied perspectives in which “senses, cognition, and emotions are developed together” (Chemi & Du, 2022, pp. 6- 7). This socio -cultural and situative approach to learning through the arts strongly resonates with the learning sciences (Halverson & Peppler, 2018). As such, t he learning sciences are uniquely positioned to advance richer understandings of both how the arts -based approaches shape what can be learned through the arts and how this learning can be made visible and valued. This symposium responds to calls to further investigate how we can show the value of arts -based education in powerful ways. It brings together researchers and practitioners to share and examine diverse ways of valuing arts-based education, whether through methodological and theoretical innovations or through purposeful partnerships with community stakeholders across contexts. title: Telling the Spiders’ Stories: Relationship Building as Essential Infrastructuring for Climate Justice Learning
citation: Helen L. Fitzmaurice, Emily V. Reigh, Chris Jadallah, Michelle Hernandez Romero, Lauren Daus (2026). Telling the Spiders’ Stories: Relationship Building as Essential Infrastructuring for Climate Justice Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
