abstract: There is growing attention to the need to design climate and environmental learning opportunities that support collective action towards more just futures. In this symposium, we explore the many kinds of connections required for collective work: connecting diverse knowledge traditions and cultural paradigms, connecting histories to futures, and connecting youth and teachers with community-based actors who are advancing environmental justice. We use the metaphor of spiderwebs to describe the networks of knowledges, worldviews, and stakeholders that foster visions of more just futures. Moreover, we draw attention to the work of spiders, referring to the human actors who build and sustain these webs. Our studies explore the complexity of maintaining spiderwebs across disciplinary and institutional boundaries and underscore the relational work needed to address the associated power differentials. We argue that this web-weaving constitutes critical infrastructuring for climate justice teaching, learning, and action, and advocate for recognition and support of this indispensable form of labor. Symposium theme and overview Although climate change has typically been treated as a technical problem in science (e.g., Clark, 2024), there is growing recognition that it is a sociopolitical issue that has been driven by capitalism (Oreskes & Conway, 2010), colonialism ( Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2022), and other forms of environmental racism (Bullard, 1993). As a result, climate change exacerbates inequities that already exist for marginalized communities around the world, who face substantial barriers to protection and recovery. Young people today understand the severity of this issue; more than 85% of young people in the US experience climate anxiety (e.g. , Lewandowski et al., 2024). While there is a need to address climate change and the attendant inequities, teaching that is focused solely on histories of oppression can be disheartening and deepen students’ sense of despair about the future. Recent studies have pointed to the power of collective action to help youth develop a sense of critical hope for the future (Schwartz et al., 2023), an approach to “partnering with purpose” that warrants increased attention in science learning spaces. Through engaging in collective action, students develop their own identities as knowers, visionaries, organizers, and builders who can affect social and environmental change. Rather than framing climate action narrowly in terms of mitigation and adaptation, we echo the stance of Isha Clarke, a youth activist from Oakland who explained, “Climate justice is about completely reimagining the way that we live on the planet ... It is about collective liberation and dismantling systems of oppression in every way that they exist” (Milagro Henriquez, 2021). For models of this kind of work, we look to the “lifeworlds 2387 of Black, Indigenous, and Third World peoples” who have repeatedly survived world -ending events and bring long histories of collective struggle against injustice to “[build] the world anew” (Jadallah et al., 2025, pp. 9–11). By learning from and acting in solidarity with these communities who are again on the frontlines of injustice, we can work together to imagine new social systems. We aim to create opportunities for climate learning that are consequential (Hall & Jurow, 2015; Jurow et al., 2016), meaning that they move beyond the acquisition of knowledge and skills by considering the implications for students' lives. Climate and environmental learning are made consequential through spiderwebs, or constellations of people, institutions , and geographies. These spiderwebs bridge sites of formal learning and spaces of community -based action, fostering collaboration across different worldviews, knowledge -building practices, and timescales in ways that promote social transformation. We also shine a light on the importance of spiders, or the individuals who build and sustain relationships across learning ecologies to foster collective action. Sometimes the spiders are the youth themselves. Other times, the spiders are community organizers, parents, teachers, or school district administrators. Spiders do the complex work of navigating institutional norms, constraints, and power dynamics within and across learning environments, working both within and outside of existing institutional structures. The webs that they construct are dynamic and precarious; they are constantly torn, reattached, mended, and reformed , requiring substantial time, skill, and emotional labor to maintain. We position the spiderwebs describe d across our work as critical infrastructure for climate justice teaching, learning, and research. “Infrastructuring” reflects the activity required to “redesign components, relations, and routines of schools” in order to sustain learning innovations (Penuel, 2019, p. 1). Much of the current work on infrastructuring focuses on aspects of the schooling system, such as national standards, district policies, and instructional practices, as well as the people who enact them, such as teachers and administrators. In contrast, we build on the work of scholars who have suggested that infrastructuring for justice -focused innovation in schools requires the inclusion of a wider range of stakeholders, including those whose voices are not typically heard in formal schooling spaces (e.g., Calabrese Barton & Tan, 2022). Similarly, our papers argue that infrastructuring for climate justice requires designing for the inclusion of the experiences and worldviews of communities on the frontlines of climate change. In this symposium, we explore how climate justice learning can be made consequential by creating spiderwebs that bring diverse stakeholders together to work towards social change. Each paper offers a perspective on building these relational webs. Across papers, we present theoretical tools (paper 2), design principles (paper 3), instructional activities and practices (papers 1 and 4), and relational practices (paper 5). We demonstrate how these approaches support learners in building connections across timescales (papers 1 and 2), knowledge systems (papers 1, 2, 3), and school- and community-based learning sites (papers 3, 4, and 5). In this symposium, we position infrastructuring for climate and environmental justice as an essential aspect of “partnering with purpose.” Collectively, we will consider the extent to which the learning sciences community—as individuals, within institutions, and as a field —contributes to the work of web- building and how we can and should deepen that work. The presentation portion of the symposium will be arranged in three sections: (1) The chairs (Drs. Fitzmaurice and Reigh) will introduce the theme of the symposium, provide an overview of the sessions, and ask audience members to briefly reflect on their own involvement in web building [~7 min]. (2) Each presenter will present their work [~10 min each, 50 min total]. (3) Our discussant Heather Clark, a former high school scie nce teacher and expert in justice- focused climate change education who collaborates deeply with teachers, will synthesize and reflect on findings [10 min]. The remainder of the symposium will be devoted to discussion. Audience members will first discuss a series of questions in small groups and share their responses [~18 min]. Questions include: How should teacher educators and researchers engage in building or supporting networks of relationships across institutions, geographies, and positionalities through their work in the context of climate change or environmental justice? What barriers or supports exist within our own institutions for this work? What p ractices have we developed in our individual work contexts that build just and equitable partnerships? How do we negotiate the tensions related to time scales (the urgency of climate change and the long timescales of justice-focused learning surfaced in our studies) or length scales (the global nature of climate change and the importance of engaging learners in critical pedagogies of place and forming local connections)? Finally, the session chairs will facilitate audience questions for the presenters [~10 min]. 2388 Paper 1: Weaving relational webs across generations and geographies Chris Jadallah, Michelle Hernandez Romero, Lauren Daus Theoretical framework Building climate justice necessitates “looking back to look forward” (Winn & Tottenham, 2025, p. 70), where we weave relational webs that connect past, present, and future and that bring together human beings and the rest of the natural world in ways that recognize our mutually connected destinies (Simpson, 2017). Looking back provides an opportunity to re-member the ancestral knowledge and practices from which we have been dis - membered via colonial histories (wa Thiong’o, 2009), which provide a compass for living in better relation with lands and waters (Takeuchi et al., 2024). We theorize learning as a process of re -membering and weaving relational webs (Jurow et al., 2025; Meixi, 2022). In doing so, we draw on conceptualizations of learning as movement across home, school, and other community settings through which learners weave across these spaces, and across time, to “become conscious historical actors who begin to understand their present and future selves in relation to broader historical forces and spatial architectures” (Gutiérrez, 2020, p. 2). These perspectives support our work to design and study new forms of participation, learning, and relational becoming (Meixi, 2022) that are culturally sustaining and revitalizing (McCarty & Lee, 2014).

abstract: The International Learning Sciences Student Association (ILSSA) is the official committee of the International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS) for student and recent graduate scholars within the l earning sciences community. W e explore the importance of partnership and building community as ILSSA’s intergenerational leadership works toward a more just and equitable communal infrastructure. We write together to explore two questions: what does community mean to IL SSA, and how do we support that in ways that are equitable and just? We draw on our positionalities, definitions of community, and duoethnographic discussions of our past, present, and future initiatives using Uttamchandani’s (2020) educational intimacy as our theoretical lens. We position this work as our strategy toward creating more partnerships within the ILSSA board; connections with the communities we represent; embracing the political as inherent to learning processes; and establishing relational scholarly continuity for ILSSA. Our mission: Intergenerational partnerships for community As the official student, postdoc, and recent graduate committee of the International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS), the International Learning Sciences Student Association (ILSSA) is dedicated to supporting the intellectual, social, and professional development of those it serves in ISLS and across the field. ILSSA consists of a board of elected representatives of (primarily) students across the globe with varied areas of expertise. ILSSA functions to advocate for the interests of junior scholars at the society level, liaise between society leadership and general membership, and scaffold the professional, social, and intellectual development of learning scientists -in- training. In a recent board meeting, questions were raised around the association's current infrastructure for in- association communication –particularly whether our current (asynchronous, broadcast -style) communication platforms were accessible, relevant, and approp riate for the diverse lived experiences and needs of our learning sciences scholars-in-training. In short, we realized that ILSSA needed to question whether the means of our labor were congruent with the “ How,” “For What,” “For Whom,” “With Whom,” and “To what ends” (Philip et al., 2018) of ILSSA’s collective vision for early-scholars in the association. ILSSA’s mission statement operationalizes commitment through our charge and six consequent goals, of which one is to promote community, interdisciplinarity, and intellectual exchange among graduate students and postdoctoral scholars within the community . We extend on this goal, exploring how five generations of the ILSSA Board have defined and operationalized our commitment to community building and beyond as a method of establishing intergenerational partnerships. In this work, we investigate these ques tions of intergenerational discourses across five generations of ILSSA board leadership. We situate this symposium as both nuancedly 2424 connected to our conference’s theme, “Partnering with Purpose,” and timely, given the current US and global sociopolitical climate. If ever we were not convinced of the interconnectedness and centrality of politics within the work that we do as learning scientists and educational scholars (Phillip & Gupta, 2020; The Politics of Learning Writing Collective, 2017; Tivaringe & Kirshner, 2021; Uttamchandani et al., 2020; Learning Towards Justice Team, 2025; Vea, 2020), this work is being conducted in the midst of increased violence and erasure of minoritized bodies perpetuating a rhetoric of privilege, whiteness, patriarchy, and division. Many of our authors – the majority of whom reside in the United States – are experiencing the juxtaposition of this violence with a collective call for solidarity and community by those we represent. These juxtapositions prompt us to collectively investigate two critical questions: (1) What does community mean to ILSSA? —understanding the subjective connotations of community — and (2) How do we support community -building in ways that are equitable and just? Expansive literature demonstrates the subjectivity through which community is defined, as mediated by its intersections, including race, class, gender, geopolitics, and other critical lived experiences (Daniel et al., 2023; Dixon & Martin, 2017; Harris et al., 2019; Herrenkohl et al., 2019; Jadallah et al., 2024; Van Wart et al., 2019). We locate this subjectivity through Uttamchandani's notion of educational intimacy, as presented in the Journal of the Learning Sciences (2020). Framework: Embodying Uttamchandani’s educational intimacy Through research findings with Chroma, an LGBTQ+ interest and educational group, and the mediation of feminist and queer politics, Uttamchandani (2020) describes educational intimacy as “relationships that allow for inclusive and productive engagement in advocacy and learning while also mirroring desired future social configurations” (p. 52). He further notes the utility of this framework’s suitability, particularly toward the development and establishment of group- level goals for social transformation. Uttamchandani posits that educational intimacy’s presence within groups is operationalized when two criteria are met: when the group’s framework allows for respectful exchange amongst each other and disagreements are embraced toward transforming the group’s goals; and when relationships within the group demonstrate how group members would want to be treated within the context and community in which they are hoping to advocate . As we embrace this organizational dynamic within ILSSA’s context, we demonstrate educational intimacy through these two criteria and the three core tenets of how educational intimacy is evidenced within learning processes and discourses. Three core features denote the operationalization of educational intimacy within learning processes: prefigurations, feminist and queer politics, and relational activity; the politics and related discourses serve as the connection between these prefigurati ons and their consequent relational activity (Uttamchandani, personal communication, October 3, 2025). Uttamchandani locates prefigurations within the construct of prolepsis – capturing how anticipated desired futures drive present activity – distinguishing an emphasis on social movements within his definition of prefigurations. Here, prefigurations are organizational -level current activities toward achieving desired futures (Curnow, 2022; Uttamchandani, 2020). Relationality within this prefigurative context draws on the development and reorganization of relationships that support the desired futures for organizational forms of advocacy and change. While developed within the niche context of queer prefigurative and relational discourses among Chroma, Uttamchandani (2020) concludes his work by posing critical questions to the learning sciences, of which we specifically engage theoretically: “How is its [educational intimacy’s] character similar or different when different kinds of social change are the goal?” (p. 71). We embody the prefigurative using this symposium as the current activity that solicits desired ideal futures of ILSSA’s systematized intergenerational partnerships for community building. We mediate this prefiguration and desired future by embracing the current poli tical landscape that seeks to divide us, such as the travel incapabilities of many scholars regarding the 2025 and 2026 ICLS conferences. As border politics and fascism seek to divide us, we embrace this politics as a method of creating imagined futures for our intergenerational relationship and community building. This is our defiance and advocacy toward strengthening our organization and for ILSSA generations to come. Theoretical and practical contributions to LS and ILSSA communities We make important theoretical and practical contributions to both the learning sciences and ILSSA scholarly communities. Our first contribution is the theoretical innovation for learning sciences discourse, specifically advocating for broader applications of educational intimacy to apply to another group and social context. We borrow Uttamchandani's theoretical contribution, generated from a specific queered context, in order to demonstrate how educational intimacy can apply to other contexts concerned with advocacy and transformation. In our specific context, we engage with the notion of educational intimacy for social transformation towards strategic partnerships and community building. 2425 For our practical contributions to the ILSSA community, there are several goals. The first is to draw stronger connections between the board and its members, emphasizing the personhood and intimacy that brings each person to their respective roles as core representatives for the sub -bodies of learning sciences that each chair leads. The second goal is to reach into and connect more deeply and intimately with the communities that we represent, creating the space for us to experience this community, a sense o f safety, and belongingness . Thirdly, we aim to embrace the political as inherent to our work . This provides a framework for more strategic and intentional action in our initiatives, instead of ignoring what dictates and shapes the extent of our power and agency within our respective spaces. And finally, four, we aim to establish continuity of board writing initiatives as a scholarly representation of what brings us together to support this work (Lave & Wenger, 1991). These theoretical and practical implica tions, taken with a systematic approach to this work, provide an avenue for replicability and further applications of educational intimacy for groups and organizations that are concerned with the intersections of advocacy, social transformation, and partnerships for community building. Approach: Intergenerational collaborative duoethnographies As we explore the questions, what does community mean to ILSSA, and how do we support that in ways that are equitable and just, we employ a method of intergenerational collaborative autoethnography, specifically through duoethnographies. Burleigh and Brum (2022) define duoethnography as a juxtaposition of stories among two or more persons who have experienced a similar phenomenon. We tell these stories adopting educational intimacy through an intergenerational lens (Hernandez et al., 2015; Ropes, 2013), pos itioning our individual stories as located through shared experiences based on service in the same/similar roles across generations. We write together and share our stories through each leadership role of ILSSA, as a representation of intergenerational discourses. We each draw on our lived experiences, both personally and professionally, to inform our positionality in our respective roles and, more broadly, the learning sciences community. We then each define what community means to us, making explicit ties to the representative contexts and communities that we represent. We then expound on initiatives – particularly those working toward more just and equitable communal spaces –- through forms of educational intimacy as mediums of partnership among ourselves and within our broader, decentralized communities. Co-chairs: Leadership, advocacy, democracy, solidarity Morgan Vickery, John Louis-Strakes Lopez, Lisa Siciliano Students are the bottom of the academic food chain. We do the grunt labor that keeps the wheels of the academy turning while being paid in poverty- level wages under the mantra that “it will be worth it” eventually. Being an ‘academic-in-training’ in the learning sciences can be exhaustingly lonely at best and exploitatively dehumanizing at worst. Much of this work is reactive to the waves of hardship of those students who get siloed and assume their experiences are t oo niche to be empathized with. As co- chairs, we are not exceptions – our presence has been ignored and our work excluded from the learning sciences canon. Thus, instead of waiting for the gates to be opened, we open them ourselves. Our work as co- chairs designs against this future; we dream of community where these hardships are acknowledged, where insider knowledge is not gatekept from those who it is most consequential for; where institutional oppression can be named and fought against; where we can bask in our imposter syndrome; where we can learn to shamelessly promote the fruits of our labor, and where one can safely validate the ways we are not okay. This form of community requires labor beyond monthly meetings — it requires a politicized trust. ILSSA co -chairs wear many hats; we are performers, volunteers, managers, informants, translators, boundary-crossers, messengers, and advocates. We beg for labor that we have no means of compensating. We awake at 5am to reach members in multiple time zones. We bear witness to more- than-qualified soon- to-be- graduates facing unemployment. We join as a collective voice such that those with power take action beyond words. We formalize our own representation and democratize it. We ensure that student voices are present across the society’s committees. We are blessed -yet-cursed with insider information. We attempt to build mutual trust by yelling into an (often reactionless) digital void. All the while, we struggle to navigate the same system that we seek to educate our constituents around – and we do it anyway – because we know that community is what enables us to persist . It reminds us to care for the human at the heart of the research we dedicate years of our lives to discover. Lisa’s service (2023-2024) was marked by the creation of space that otherwise would not exist for those without representation in the rooms where decisions are made. Morgan’s (2024 -2026) service can be defined by an insistent call for transparency around i nstitutional mechanisms and cultural norms that most impact junior scholars in the spirit of critical hope and ‘remembering the human’ behind every act of knowledge construction. 2426 John's (2025-present) service seeks to dismantle socially-configured walls and siloes toward a culture of being in- relation-with each other, focusing on improving initiatives such as the Mentorship Program, which he co - established with Golnoush (Lia) Haddadian during his time as Membership Chair. Together, we represent, model, and sustain a humane space to safely be in -solidarity in the struggle. We form spaces of shared inquiry such that we create meaningful relationships between people who may otherwise b e socially positioned as diametrically - opposed. We construct a culture of humility, grace, and vulnerability, and hope our members carry on these values as they serve others. We put on our brave faces such that even one siloed student realizes they are not alone. Secretaries: Bridging divides and co-creating community Grace (Yaxin) Xing, Jinho Kim As international graduate students navigating life across continents and disciplines, we have come to understand community not as a static identity or geographic cluster, but as something connecting across divides through relational care, shared vulnerabil ity, and collective imagination. We both arrived at our first ISLS conferences feeling small and uncertain, but some warm moments planted seeds of belonging: a warm welcome at orientation, a kind conversation at an ILSSA social, and, in the years that followed, a growing sense of confidence through meaningful involvement in ILSSA. These were early signs of what educational intimacy can look like in action: care that prefigures the kind of community we want to co-create. Grace described it as “co-creating spaces where people can bring their full selves, both from academic work and lived experience.” Serving within ILSSA has helped us transform those feelings into initiatives. Grace’s work as a local representative, and later as secretary, marked “a turning point in her professional growth,” deepening her sense of belonging and reaffirming her commitment to ensuring that other students could feel the same welcome she once received. Jinho, informed by her interdisciplinary background, sees ILSSA as “a bridge connecting people across diverse career stages, geographies, and disciplinary backgrounds.” Through these experiences, we began to see ourselves not only as participants in the learning sciences but as co- constructors of its future. We see ILSSA not only as a student organization but as a prefigurative space. As Jinho noted, “Having a diverse group of board members is the first step; the way forward is to extend this so that all members of the ILSSA community can feel they are part of this bridge of connection.” Similarly, Grace mentioned, “ILSSA has modeled educational intimacy beautifully through intergenerational mentorship, collaborative labor, and shared care, and I hope to carry that forward.” Together, we believe ILSSA serves as a politically conscious, internationally inclusive, and relationally grounded space. In a time when global border restr ictions, visa limitations, and geopolitical tensions continue to constrain who can fully participate in academic life, ILSSA stands as a counterexample: a student-led space where solidarity is practiced across difference, where care is scaffolded intentionally, and where we co -create the conditions for belonging, advocacy, and transformation. Communications chairs: The whole self, personally and professionally Chaewon Kim, Yisha Zhao While serving as an outreach chair in ILSSA, Chaewon joined the communications committee of ISLS, serving in a role somewhat representative of students, but more importantly, one where she had a chance to step into a space where her contribution was not exactly expertise but rather her attentiveness and willingness to learn. This experience proved invaluable in shaping how she understands herself as a scholar, particularly in an international context. One vivid memory she recalls was an in-person committee meeting in Helsinki, where senior professors discussed how to provide travel support for students from low -income countries. The gravity with which they approached this was striking; they debated not only how much support would be fair and justifiable but also how to communicate their intentions in ways that preserved dignity and avoided unintentionally offending those they sought to help. As a doctoral student, Chaewon confessed that she had rarely thought about such issues; her world still centered on research, coursework, and personal milestones. Yet through ILSSA, she was confronted with the reality that being a scholar in a global society involves far more than advancing individual academic interests. It requires grappling with systemic inequities, questions of justice, and the responsibility of fostering inclusion on an international scale. Yisha shares her experience about the intimate community from a different angle. As a visual artist doing arts-based learning research in a field rooted in STEM education, Yisha often felt isolated. When she first joined the ILSSA Discord server, she was n ot sure what to expect; she assumed it might be a “dead” channel for announcements. Yisha was then encouraged by Morgan Vickery to introduce herself on who she is and what kind of research she is doing. At that point, Yisha reminisces, she felt something different — there were actual people interested in knowing more about her. Then she put a short bio. People reacted to her post. Lisa Siciliano 2427 immediately commented, “OOOHHH!!! ANOTHER ARTS PERSON!!!!!!!” That was the very first moment she thought, “This is my community.” Yisha also remarks that her first month on the ILSSA board as communications chair was one of her busiest personally. Co- chair, John Lopez, checked in with her, and Morgan was incredibly supportive, responding quickly, giving feedback on early posts, and collaborating on newsletters. After the first ILSSA newsletter went out, she received emails from members affirming the effort, which was another moment where she felt she belonged here. Chaewon and Yisha’s notion of community has been reshaped through the service at ILSSA: Now Chaewon defines community not as a bounded group of peers who share academic interests, but as a collective with diverse backgrounds, bound together to serve a virtue they believe in. Her vision of community extends beyond institutional or disciplinary borders, encompassing a global society where members take responsibility for one another’s access and well-being. For Yisha, community is not just a roster; it is the feeling of being seen, answered, and able to bring your whole self, both personally and professionally. Practically, it has also clarified ILSSA’s role for Yisha to cultivate educational intimacy, where members are seen, heard, and invited in. Membership and outreach chair: Creating spaces of support and belonging Chaewon Kim Back in 2021, I was working as an elementary school teacher, deeply curious about how students learned from the games I designed, how I could make those games more engaging, and ultimately, how I could grow into a better educator beyond the role of a class room teacher. That curiosity, paired with a desire to explore broader questions of learning, led me to think about pursuing a PhD in the United States, although at the time I had no clear roadmap for how to make that aspiration possible. I quickly realized that my teaching experience alone would likely not be enough to secure admission into doctoral programs, so I knew I needed to engage in research. At that point, I had no awareness of ISLS, and even if I had, it would have seemed too prestigious and out of reach for someone like me. Instead, I began at the local level, presenting at regional conferences in South Korea, slowly building my confidence and my scholarly identity. One milestone I was so proud of at that point was presenting at a conference hosted at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, where Korean, Chinese, Japanese, and Hawaiian educational researchers came together. That experience was transformative: I felt a sense of success and belonging that I had not yet experienced in academic spaces, and I believe it was instrumental in helping me gain admission to four PhD programs in the United States. These experiences really shaped how I see myself as a scholar because they showed me that academic communities can feel very different depending on how they are built. They can come across as distant and intimidating, or they can feel welcoming and empowering, and when I was serving as an outreach chair at ILSSA in my third year of my PhD program, I wanted ILSSA to be the latter. So when we discussed ILSSA’s mission to connect with scholars from East Asia, Africa, and Latin America, the first thing I thought of was that Hawaiian conference, which had been such a warm entry point for me into the larger learning sciences world. I imagined how meaningful it could be for students in those regions to discover ILSSA as something friendly and approachable, not distant or elite. With that in mind, I reached out to the conference organizers, and John and I put together a poster to share our work and promote ILSSA. Doing that was powerful for me —it felt like I was reaching back to help my past self, the version of me who once did not know where to start. In a way, it was healing because by supporting others, I was also affirming my own journey. To me, that is what educational intimacy looks like: creating spaces where people feel seen, supported, and encouraged to belong. Treasurers: Responsibility and reciprocity Aman Desai, Early Sol Gadong We each came to our roles as ILSSA Treasurers from different contexts, yet our experiences converge on a shared belief: community is built not only through formal structures but through relationships grounded in responsibility, reciprocity, and care. Early saw her role as treasurer as not simply a means to ensure that ILSSA’s limited resources were used in ways that aligned with ILSSA’s mission to nurture an inclusive and supportive global community of learning sciences scholars, but also that her role went beyond bookkeeping. From this view, she saw community as being defined by responsibility and reciprocity and understood that communities are sustained when individuals take care of one another’s needs. Aman’s reflections resonate with this vision. He has observed that most academic departments have communities around formal academic structures like labs and coursework. These spaces are important, but they do not always build the trust and cooperation that come from shared responsibility. Non- academic gatherings help build trust and cooperation by relying on voluntary effort, with people contributing time 2428 and care to create what might be considered a “public good,” which everyone can enjoy even if not everyone contributes equally. Our beliefs inspired initiatives that went beyond ILSSA’s annual activities, such as Friday Scholarly Scribbles, a virtual writing community on Discord for dissertation and paper drafts, and First Cup Connections, an online social gathering during the ISLS Annual Meeting. These were modest efforts to make ILSSA a site of belonging, where members could share both their scholarly goals and personal struggles, and find support through shared presence. Educational intimacy, which we saw as small but powerful acts of care that make learning and collaboration possible, was the thread connecting these commitments. In our collective work as ILSSA Treasurers, we learned that stewardship may go beyond managing resources and into nurturing relationships. Africa and Middle East representatives: From resilience to shared community Blessed Mhungu, Golnoush (Lia) Haddadian, Yetunde Mabadeje Our stories began in different places, but they converge around a shared commitment to community as a space for transformation and belonging. For Lia, growing up where educational opportunities were scarce meant learning to invent new pathways by designing tools and personalized systems that made learning possible despite barriers, thus informing her definition of community not as something defined by proximity or affiliation, but as something that emerges when individuals recognize their own struggles in others and commit to walking forward together. For Yetunde, moving to the United States for graduate study surfaced the deep need for a community that reflects and affirms what she calls shared identity and struggles . For Blessed, the philosophy of Ubuntu (“a person is a person through other persons”) offers a moral compass for what community should be to him, which is a place for empathy, care, mutual respect, and intentional inclusion of marginalized voices. Together, our experiences form a tapestry of persistence and purpose. Each of us has confronted systems that often silence, invisibilize, or homogenize difference, and in response, we have chosen to build rather than withdraw—to create spaces of reflection , visibility, mentorship, and solidarity. Our collective work in ILSSA, particularly in representing Africa and the Middle East, models the kind of scholarly community we want to see— one grounded in interdependence, inspiration, and care. In Lia’s words, she envisioned her mentorship initiative within ILSSA (2024-2025) “as more than functional pairings and transactional exchange; but as a way for students across borders and career stages to see their own struggles reflected in another’s story and feel conti nuity in journeys that might otherwise feel isolated”; thus mentorship, in this light, is not a transaction but a gesture of educational intimacy—a way of knowing and being that holds space for vulnerability and growth. Through our intertwined stories, we prefigure a desired future where this learning community (ILSSA) is not defined by hierarchy or geography, but by connection, visibility, reciprocity, and shared becoming. Central and South America representatives: Data-informed intimacy Adelmo Eloy, Breneil Malcolm We jointly contextualize our intergenerational processes through our lived experiences as scholars from the Global South, Latin America, and the Caribbean: Brazil and Grenada. We define community as a form of intimacy that enables a sense of belonging. Ade lmo explains, “Academic communities can feel highly hierarchical, and a student association seemed like a space to elevate students’ voices. This role felt like a natural call, since there are so few of us in the ISLS community. At the same time, represent ing such a large and diverse region was daunting. To navigate that challenge, I used my time as a representative to map and connect with Latin American colleagues who, at any point in their journeys, had engaged with ISLS or ILSSA. Some of our internal dat abases helped identify people, though I often wished they contained richer information. I had thoughtful conversations with about ten colleagues who shared what drew them to the learning sciences and what challenges they faced in joining — and feeling part of — this community.” Adelmo paints a narrative of drawing on existing generational artifacts in supporting his role to build stronger communities within Latin America. As we continue in the spirit of giving voice to Central and South America, and the Global South, and furthering the prior generational work of information and data -informed approaches, Breneil asserts, “we currently embark on creating a database that captures the vast representation of our graduate students and postdoctoral scholars across the global learning sciences community.” ISLS (2025) has started a version of this database from which we can build upon, but our efforts will be to capture programs across the globe, particularly for representation in the Global South. In so doing, we support the goals of this work through a mode of educational intimacy toward reimagining educational transformation for ILSSA’s future. We advocate for more data -informed approaches to ground the work and initiatives that we pursue, as thes e have been transformative for our lived experiences and in supporting our notions and experiences of intergenerational partnerships and community building. 2429 Asia and Pacific representatives: Advancing equity, connection, and care Nisumba Soodhani, Rani Prasad, Yoojin Bae Our shared responsibility as Asia and Pacific representatives emerges from our distinct life journeys, yet bound by our belief in community as an ever-evolving practice that grows through equity, care, and connection. Across two ILSSA generations, we see o ur work as a process from building infrastructures of equity to deepening association through participation and sustaining that care through mentorship. The ILSSA Odyssey: Exploring Learning Sciences in the Asia -Pacific series, initiated by Nisumba (ILSSA’s Asia-Pacific representative: 2023–2024), laid the foundation for this ongoing work. The series featured speakers from the Philippines, India, and Singapore. The series provided entry into global networks, underscoring the subjectivity of “community,” actively constructed through intentional design and shared practice. The series opened spaces for faculty to exchange ideas and created entry points for doctoral students to access global networks, all while centering Asia-Pacific epistemologies as legitimate and vital. The series also tried to support communities equitably and justly, through scheduling across time zones, wide publicity, and openness to participants at all career stages. This ensured accessibility, reflecting the equity and justice that we wish to uphold. For many, including Rani and Yoojin, these initiatives became a platform into a broader scholarly world. Rani’s journey to ILSSA began as a participant in these spaces ILSSA helped to create. As a research scholar in Mumbai, her first international conference experience (ISLS 2025) was made possible through the travel grant, enabling her to present her work on microplastic pollution in Mumbai’s slums. ILSSA’s warm welcome, including a pizza party invitation on Day 1, helped her share candidly in the student association meeting. This helped her transform the idea of “community” into her lived experience. She now serves as the Asia-Pacific representative, committed to building upon these foundations by fostering global connections and more student participation. Yoojin’s story in mentorship with ILSSA further builds on this. As an international student and first - generation scholar studying abroad, she found in ILSSA a supportive community essential for her to thrive in academia. From her first year in her PhD, she attended the ISLS conference (ISLS 2023), where encouragement from kind audience members during her nervous presentation showed her the power of community. She later joined ILSSA and became a mentor in the mentorship program, grateful for the chance to encourage a junior scholar as she had been. For her, ISLS and ILSSA serve as the catalyst that sustains her scholarly journey and connects her to others through care and educational intimacy. Together, our stories represent an intergenerational journey across ILSSA’s Asia -Pacific leadership. What began as Nisumba’s vision for equitable visibility evolved through Rani’s lived experience of inclusion and continues through Yoojin’s enactment of support and care. This journey of practice demonstrates how educational intimacy continues and how structures of community become relationships, and these relationships become infrastructures for others. Through our work, we continue to reimagine community as a dynamic, intergenerational act of care, connection, and equity. Europe and UK representative: Collaborating spontaneously and passionately Sebastian Simon As a PhD candidate with a computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) focus in a laboratory without CSCL scholars, I particularly cherish the possibility of international conferences. ISLS 2023 was my first bigger conference, and I was overwhelmed by the experience, in all possible ways: the conference was big, and finding the CSCL community I was looking for was not easy for someone who did not know even how conferences worked. But with each encounter I had with ISLS members, I felt like these were the kind of people I wanted to do research with, and so I reached out to ILSSA to get more engaged with this community afterwards. The regional representative role itself had just been created, and so, I did whatever possible to reach out to laboratories acr oss Europe to get their PhD students on board and make them aware of the support they could get from this association (that I had not been aware of before coming to the ISLS conference myself). This activity, and pondering how this community could further grow and prosper, taught me the importance of communication for the community. It was also during the ISLS 2023 conference that I came across Raquel Coelho for the first time, a scholar who, after some conversation, just told me, “Let’s write a paper together." While the importance of community was, at that point, relatively new to me, the importance of activities for community building had not even reached my conscience [ironic, given that my first mandatory literature from my supervisors was Lave & Wenger (1991)]. This co-writing project with a then complete stranger would become the driver of now two active research groups of junior scholars that I have the pleasure of being part of. Inspired by this collaboration, I wanted to engage other people in this transformative experience. In 2024, I published a call for participation on the social platform 2430 LinkedIn to anyone who wanted to join for a cowriting experience about the CSCL topic. Twelve scholars replied, and while I was expecting the group to dissolve shortly after the project, the CONNECT collective is engaged in now three parallel projects and steadily growing, maintaining the idea of open calls for collaborative projects and paper writing. These collaborations remain essential to me, even beyond the still impressive cognitive challenge each of these projects brings for me, not least because they allow me as a scholar to develop my research identity. Choosing people over projects that are oftentimes beyond my CSCL comfort zone (postdigital education and research, AI thematic analysis, mental wellbeing, to name a few) has shaped my vision of what I value and how I want to grow my research profile. Both my previous roles in ILSSA and CONNECT support me in thinking that projects, like this symposium, are what make ILSSA an essential and transformative element for the future of ISLS. By collaborating spontaneously and passionately, I believe, we can transform research as it is today into a welcoming space for researchers, practitioners, and the general population –an endeavour that I see today more pressing than ever. Finally, I believe that the learning sciences community is the perfect ground to experiment and spearhead such transformations. Synthesis and discussion: Communities as intimacy, evolution, and advocacy As we weave together generations of partnerships demonstrative of our notions of community, guided by Uttamchandani’s (2020) educational intimacy, we revisit the questions we began with: what does community mean to ILSSA, and how do we support that in ways that are equitable and just? Toward the first question, three themes stand out across our stories as we describe our varying lived experiences that preempt how we define community: (1) community as a space in which people may experience intimacy, care, and belongingness; (2) community as ever-evolving, and 3) community as a form of advocacy. First, Blessed captures an intimacy and care through the philosophy of Ubuntu (“a person is a person through other persons”) , providing a lens that captures many of the perspectives above: as he asserts, “Ubuntu offers a moral compass for what community should be – a place for empathy, care, mutual respect, and intentional inclusion of marginalized voices.” Second, as Grace and Jinho discuss, we recognize how community is ever - evolving, ever-changing, as our needs and various sociocultural, sociopolitical, and geopolitical contexts shift and interact, reciprocally, with our lived experiences: “community is not a static identity or geographic cluster, but something connecting across divides through relational care, shared vulnerability, and collective imagination.” Third, we recognize the centrality of advocacy in grounding and sustaining community – as intergenerational co- chairs, Morgan, John, and Lisa assert: “…we struggle to navigate the same system that we seek to educate our constituents around – and we do it anyway – because we know that community is what enables us to persist. It reminds us to care for the human at the heart of the research we dedicate years of our lives to discover.” As a highly interdisciplinary, cross-cultural space, our stories reveal how ILSSA provides opportunities to connect others within the learning sciences. Our scholars describe different metaphors for this phenomenon, such as bridging others (Jinho) and breaking barriers (Morgan, John, and Lisa), but they represent how ILSSA serves as a way for global scholars to connect. Scholars such as Adelmo facilitate these connections through mapping and connecting scholars across the Latin American region. Serving on t he board serves as a means of these connections. From these connections, scholars such as Chaewon become “ confronted with the reality that being a scholar in a global society involves far more than advancing individual academic interests, ” growing as scholars who advance equity and justice in the work they do. Yet, growth comes with growing pains. Our stories exemplify hardships experienced by many graduate students and early scholars, including experiences of isolation, overwhelm, labor exploitation, and cross -cultural communication; we notice how many of these hardships are exacerbated by our pursuit of ‘nontraditional’research agendas. Scholars like Yisha, who wish to study STEM education with non- traditional approaches (in her case, the arts), may experience isolation from peers as physical separation and research that may be “too niche to be empathized with,” as articulated by Morgan, John, and Lisa. In these ways, our stories reveal a key insight toward advancing equitable community- building in the learning sciences: a sensitivity to how the unique challenges of research in this specific academic community add additional hardships to more commonly -experienced pains of emerging researchers. ILSSA provides an alternative to normative and bureaucratically-laden academic systems that expect us to tolerate isolation & labor exploitation in silence. It is an academic and professional space that refuses to deny the viscerally personal and human nature of being a junior scholar here and now. Extended, we seek to make these realities visible and undeniable to those who otherwise will make decisions about us, without us (inspired by Charlton’s 2004 disability justice work). As Morgan wrote in ILSSA’s 2024- 2025 Annual Report shared with ISLS leadership: 2431 “...it is becoming increasingly difficult to act as if the issues facing established senior scholars are comparable to our own when, simply put, the stakes are different for us. Those of us ‘on the ground’ are expendable and the first to get cut all while our field continues to graduate more scholars than it could ever hire. For us, it’s a matter of survival. We don't expect our leaders and mentors to have all the answers; rather, we ask that they ‘read the room’ when vocalizing their complaints/concerns. W e ask that student perspectives be invited to meaningfully contribute (and be heard) future conversations where decisions are made that directly impact us. Nothing about us, without us.” Such radical calls to those in power beg the question – how do we operationalize such easy- to-dilute concepts as ‘equity’ and ‘justice’? This question can be extended to concretize what a community sustained by connection, visibility, reciprocity, and shar ed becoming (see Blessed, Lia, and Yetty’s commentaries) means. Each of these requires substantial lines of inquiry in their own right. In attending to this multifaceted notion of equitable and just community- building, we highlight the centrality of ILSSA as a space that creates and fosters the experience of our humanness, our need to connect with each other, and our need to see ourselves within each other. As we step into our elected roles each year, we inherit the legacies left by our predecessors and their embedded knowledge, practices, and desired futures all while actualizing a vision of our own. Our Africa and Middle East intergenerational partners, Blessed, Lia, and Yetunde, frame this: “through our intertwined stories, we prefigure a desired future where this learning community (ILSSA) is not defined by hierarchy or geography, but by connection, visibility, reciprocity, and shared becoming. ” Our Asia and Pacific Region intergenerational partners, Nisumba, Rani, and Yoojin, elaborate: “together, our stories represent an intergenerational journey across ILSSA’s Asia-Pacific leadership. What began as Nisumba’s vision for equitable visib ility evolved through Rani’s lived experience of inclusion and continues through Yoojin’s enactment of support and care.” The persistence of these community tenets across generations, physical spaces, and times is not just a product of community action, but interwoven into the blueprints of the community itself. Here, educational intimacy is a central component to the community infrastructure and thus, a catalyst for the formation of relationships, inheritance of legacy, and actualization of cross-generationally desired futures. Educational intimacy: Theoretical expansions and considerations The other theoretical question we sought to engage in this discourse is Uttamchandani’s (2020) charge: “How is its [educational intimacy’s] character similar or different when different kinds of social change are the goal?” (p. 71). In revisiting the core components of educational intimacy’s presence and operationalization within discourse– prefigurations, feminist and queer politics, and relational activity (Uttamchandani, personal communication, October 3, 2025) – we make two important theoretical contributions for the theory’s innovation and expansion. The first is situating the importance of the intergenerational and historical in defining prefigurative activity; that is, we expand the notion of prefigurative activity to move into histories and generations of a conceptualized present. Present activity, then, refers to a specific moment in current time or in historical time. For example, Lisa notes that one of her major goals as the 2023- 2024 co-chair (see Appendix) was to grow the board in number as well as in geographic diversity. As such, the present activities at that point in historical time served to denote the desired future of this numerical and geographic diversity – in the several years since her term, ILSSA has established a robust database of 512 people representing 250 institutions across 40 countries. This desired future at that point in historical time now represents prefigurative activity in the current time, as the board uses these activities to advocate for other desired futures. Our second contribution expands the political beyond queer politics. Uttamchandani’s (2020) theorization was located within the specific context of youth queer activism. While we maintain this commitment to capturing queer politics, (as multiple contributors to this symposium embody queerness and its consequent politicalities), we expand this political to include the other representations of members across the organization, including geopolitics, transnational politics, racialized politics, neurodivergent politics, and intersectional politics. That stated, our expansion of Uttamchandani’s theorization requires careful navigation; we recognize that appropriating a framework designed for queer youth’s collective political sense -making beyond the intended context may inadvertently perpetuate damaging and queer -erasive rhetoric. Here, we adopt a theorization that maintains an explicit commitment to equitable discourse that is not erasive of queer theorizations – we maintain the aforementioned commitment to captu ring queer politics and do not seek to blur lines between contentions of equality and equity. Rather, we seek to adequately capture the myriad of lived experiences, intersectional representations, and their respective politics embodied by our authors and I LSSA as an organization, including queer politics, geopolitics, transnational politics, racialized politics, gender politics, and neurodivergent politics. 2432 Appendix: Author positionality statements Breneil Malcolm (Central & South America Rep, 2025 -2026): I am a critical intersectional Black trans* scholar and learning scientist who specializes in critical and trans* interdisciplinary approaches. My goal is to theorize and establish conscious methods to study trans* bodies and their complex learning processes. As I spent almost the past decade unlearning pathologizing my Black trans* body, knowledge has been at the forefront of this process and remains at the core of my discourse. I do work on behalf of my younger self and present -day youth whose embodied experiences of neurodivergence, trauma, queerness, body image, and disability are not easily embraced or served in traditional educational contexts. My work in ILSSA is an echo of this; I seek to ensure that the experiences of junior scholars are not erased by the academic institutions and cultures that rely on their silence for output. I do this work loudly-yet-tactfully to ensure the next generation of learning scientists don’t struggle in the same way we did. abstract: This symposium introduces Feminist Embodied Computation (FEC), a framework advancing equity in computing by centering epistemological change, identity, and embodiment. Five papers enact FEC across teaching and learning: reframing code as culturally and politically situated discourse; tracing a CS teacher’s journey where e-textiles and material histories make embodiment epistemic; presenting an Indigenous Hawaiian learner’s “rightful presence” through community -centered data science; modeling physics through dance to broaden what counts as rigorous knowledge; and theorizing subversive computational literacy that challenges dominant values of efficiency and abstraction. Collectively, the session demonstrates concrete practices and theoretical moves that honor lived experience, emotion, and culture as central to computation, offering actionable pathways to transform who participates in computing, how knowledge is made, and what computing can become.

conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Communities of Practice & Situated Learning; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Design-Based Research (DBR); Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: Socio-cultural theory, with its emphasis on identity, culture, critique, and power, offers both an explanatory toolkit given the rise in extremism, authoritarianism, and tribalism, but also faces significant challenges, given the increasingly fractured and dynamically-changing nature of life in online worlds. Traditional metaphors of enculturating students into communities of scientific practice face external threats from a public suspicious toward social institutions. This session asks what socio -cultural theory might have to offer for understanding the current moment, and how this current state of the world may be pushing back on our understanding of socio-cultural theory. This session offers three papers and a robust discussion session by four leading researcher / theorist / practitioners from socio -cultural traditions. Each paper offers a look at how learning is occurring in a networked, digital age, with community partners that include Homeboy Industries, the Network of Academic Esports Federations, and with Indigenous Education Partners. This session is particularly focused on how macro trends across culture, specifically occurring through supercapitalist economic and online cultural structures contribute to cultural logics operating upon us. Socio-cultural theory for a supercapitalist society Vygotsky’s formulation that higher order cognitive functions are learned through social processes, occurring first on an outer plane through social interaction preceding internal ization is a cornerstone of socio-cultural learning theory (Vygotsky, 1978). Learning from this perspective is a process of mediation , whereby people internalize the language, tools, and concepts of a culture (Daniels, Cole, & Wertsch, 2007). Appropriation occurs as people make such tools their own, expanding their application to new situations (Wertsch, 1997). Play, the creation of imagined, liminal contexts in which learners can engage within a zone of proximal development, is crucial for understanding rule systems, appropriating representational systems, and employing imagination toward expanding one’s experiences beyond that which has been directly experienced (Vygotsky, 1967). Schools may be important locations of academic learning, but experiences outside of school largely form the experiential foundation for future understanding, provide social identification and belonging, shape the identities and dispositions we bring toward school, and govern how we mobilize such identities outside of school (Cole, 1999; Gutiérrez & Rogoff, 2003; Wertsch, 1997). Cultural historical learning theorists look beyond individual or familial interactions and focus on how learning occurs in complex settings, including workplaces , classrooms, and after school settings (Cole, 1999 ). Cultural Historical Activity Theorists (CHAT) are particularly interested in studying learning as it occurs in complex activity, stretched across people, their tools, and social institutions (including their formal and informal rules and divisions of labor, (Engeström, 2014; Hutchins, 1995). Such analyses reveal the complex social achievement embodied by such professional performances, and outcomes (learning) is shaped by social context. Values, identity, and culture co -constitute emergent understandings; competent action in the world involves identifying resources, employing tools, navigating social structures and institutions, appropriating formal and informal rules, and coordinating with complex networks of divisions of labor (Gee, 1990; Lave & Wenger, 1991). A defining feature of socio -cultural work is learning through participation as a social achievement, recruiting identities from learners as “certain kinds of people” with dispositions, values, and ways of being in the world (Lave & Wenger, 1991). Nowhere is such identity formation clearer than through language , where such work meaning-making work is coordinated, negotiated, and manifested into action (Gee, 1990; Wertsch, 1997). Learning scientists within the socio-cultural tradition have turned toward informal learning spaces, where complex learning configurations can be designed, according to specific values, which might become habits of mind for those engaged in such programs . The 5 th Dimension project (Cole, 2006) uses a game -based metaphor 2504 to engage kids in game-based learning activities, under the mentorship of college students, who themselves gained learning experiences toward their development as teachers, driven by values of diversity. The Migrant Student Leadership Institute created a collective Third Space in which every day and institutional literacy practices are mobilized for critical social thought, using literacy practices to link historical practices, current situations, and possible futures (Gutiérrez, 2008). FUSE Studio creates paths for engaging youth in STEAM practices in after - school settings by challenges based designed in response to youth interests (Stevens et al., 2016). These are but a few design -based research programs that build on socio- cultural learning theory but propose learning environments based on specific underlying social commitments or values that are orthogonal, if not contradictory to those of school, which are often based on sorting. Underlying such socio- cultural approaches to learning is a commitment to defining and articulating underlying values, although recently, values driving such efforts (diversity, equality of opportunity, social justice) are under assault. Re-examining socio-cultural theory in a super capitalist society This session asks what socio-cultural theory might have to offer for understanding the current state of the world, particularly in the United States, and how this current state of the world may be pushing back on our understanding of socio-cultural theory. On the one hand, socio-cultural theorists offer a toolkit with explanatory power: Identity, belonging, and group membership appear to be driving national discourse more than any sort of traditional rational discourse, with the entire enterprise of science being questioned, history rewritten, and institutions such as universities or medicine under assault (Mann & Hotez, 2025). Socio-cultural theory, with its emphasis on identity, culture, power, and social enterprise as the result of historical actors (rather than depoliticized, ahistorical reasoning processes) offer potential tools for understanding this predicament . On the other hand, socio-cultural approaches have often treated contexts as relatively fixed and knowable entities. Communities of practice center definable practices, whether it be tailoring or massively multiplayer gaming) with relatively definable, observable boundaries . Affinity Spaces (Gee, 2018) are one model for describing the ephemeral, less formal spaces that attract people of like- minded interests. However, some of the more pernicious online spaces (QAnon, Red Pill Internet) are less dedicated locations, and more resentment - driven ideologies mobilized over public channel s and are less well described by a ffinity spaces (Lavin, 2020; Marche, 2016). To a degree, fractured selves and participation in distinct, orthogonal, or self-contradictory spaces are part of post -modern existence. How do we conceptualize the nature of such spaces and participation within them? How do we conceptualize participati on within them? What might learning sciences learn from contemporary efforts to moderate and govern activities in sites such as gaming communities? How might research on and in such communities inform our understanding of socio-cultural theories? If understanding the broader social context outside of school is crucial for understanding learning, knowing and participation, what is the impact of the broader socio- cultural systems in which youth are being enculturated? What values and dispositions are being recruited by these systems from youth? In the United States, the top 1% controls roughly half the nation’s wealth, while the bottom half of the country controls roughly 2.5%, meaning that the middle class has in many ways disappeared (Federal Reserve, 2025). Replacing this middle class is a top 10% of America, which controls 2/3 of the country’s wealth. With wealth concentrated within the hands of the view, it is little wonder that confidence in such institutions is at historic lows (Gallup, 2025). Skepticism runs the gamut of institutions; over 70% of American say higher education is headed in the wrong direction (Parker, 2025). Only 1/3 of Americans trust the United States Health care system (Hopkins, 2023). Robert Reich describes this broad pattern as supercapitalism, which is a system marked by extreme wealth and poverty, corporations that exert substantial power over the marketplace, media outlets controlled by individuals or corporate conglomerates, and systems wherein those entities exert undo influence on government to shape regulations (Reich, 2007). Writ large, this process of increased economic concentration, leading to gross power imbalances, creating a lack of social trust, leading to alienation, and then a “take what you can get” mentality has been referred to as “Gangster capitalism.” Gangster capitalism might be best illustrated by the recent pardoning of former Representative George Santos, who lied about his credentials, pled guilty to identity theft and wire fraud, and was expelled from Congress had his sentence commuted by the Pre sident because he was loyalist. In “America is a Scam” Cory Doctorow (2025) articulates this theory of government and business, concluding, “If you are convinced that being honest will get you taken advantage of, there’s nothing for it but to turn scammer yourself.” In the words of President Donald Trump, “That makes me smart. How does living in such a system remediate our goals, drives, and dispositions? What kinds of dispositions does this recruit, and what are the implications for systems such as schools and the designs of learning environments? Socio -cultural theory has long concerned itself with questions of equity, resistance, interest, identity, and resourcefulness among marginalized people, and often posits formal education as a route toward social and economic advancement. How might tools from socio- cultural research be applied to students from 2505 different socio -cultural backgrounds? What models of resistance are there? Should socio -cultural theorists engaged in design-based research embrace counter value systems more explicitly? Papers This panel format proposes five short papers, paired with four discussants. The objective of the panel is to engage a discussion among socio- cultural theorists to discuss opportunities for leveraging socio -cultural theory to understand the current cultural predicament and opportunities to rethink socio- cultural theory in light of recent developments. Whereas the typical ISLS symposi um is a set of papers with a s ingle discussant, this symposium proposes 5-7minutes for each paper, followed by 5- 7 minutes of prepared remarks by each discussant . Each of these discussants is an accomplished researcher and three of the four discussants are members of the National Academies of Education. The panel will leave 20 minutes for discussion and question and answer. Each of these 4 papers investigates issues related to contemporary issue in socio-cultural learning theory, providing a context for a deeper discussion of contemporary issues facing the field. Homeboy technology: Learning digital arts practices among formerly incarcerated and gang-affiliated youth with trauma-informed pedagogy Richard Martinez, Kurt Squire Emerging technologies such as Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) are posited as potentially transforming learning and work, yet if history is a guide, they might exacerbate digital divides in access to employment, education, healthcare, and social services (Lee, Hui, & Dillahunt, 2025; Vogels, 2021). This ongoing, 3 year creative technology program introduced emerging technologies to an arts education program for formerly incarcerated and gang-impacted youth, using trauma-informed pedagogy techniques. Context Based out of Boyle Heights, Los Angeles, Homeboy Technology is a part of The Homeboy Art Academy (HBAA), a trauma-informed art center which itself is embedded in Homeboy Industries, which founded by Father Greg Boyle is the world’s largest and most successful gang rehabilitation program. HBAA serves justice - impacted, gang-affiliated youth who are considered “in crisis” and beyond “at risk” between the ages of 18 -24. HBAA was created by award -winning artist Fabian Debora, a former member of Homeboy Industries and accomplished artist within the Chicano muralist tradition. Under Debora’s direction, the HBAA itself is part of a larger struggle to reclaim creative agency, assert cultural sovereignty, and build alternative pathways into technological and artistic futures—on their terms. Debora’s art studio is located on site, in the building. The study examines freeform exploring emerging technologies, followed by structured design experiences might help youth leverage such skills for their own social, economic, or political advancement, which might be described as appropriation (see also Van Duersen & Helsper, 2015). Program designers sought to improve community digital capacity, which describes “the extent to which the culture, infrastructure, and digital competence of family and community enable and support digital practices.” (Dillahunt et al., 2022) This communal notion of digital capacities seeks to capture the “village- like” sharing economy that exists within underserved communities and that we have observed in Boyle Heights and East Los Angeles, where this work occurs (Karusala et al., 2021).

abstract: This study compares differences in student engagement across tutor types (human, human-like AI, and nonhuman- like AI) in asynchronous online learning. Data were collected from 20 university students using eye -tracking, electroencephalography, and facial expression analysis. Results show the human-like AI tutor attracted visual attention and elicited the highest emotional responses. The human tutor sustained deeper attention and moderate emotional states. The nonhuman- like AI tutor elicited the fewest emotional reactions. This study highlights a hybrid tutoring design.

title: Frustration, Conflict, and Transformative Learning in a Teacher Makeathon
citation: Roey Kafri, Yuval Segev, Erica Halverson (2026). Frustration, Conflict, and Transformative Learning in a Teacher Makeathon. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Kafri, R., Segev, Y., & Halverson, E.

conceptualisations_list: Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA); Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: This poster investigates the role of social and emotional experiences in fostering transformative learning during a three -day Makeathon for in-service teachers. Using reflective journal data analyzed through Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA), I examine how internal feelings of frustration and external experiences of conflict relate to reported transformative learning. Results suggest that frustration, rather than conflict, is more closely linked to transformative learning, offering implications for designing professional learning in maker - based learning environments. Theory A persistent challenge in educators' professional development is designing learning environments that promote transformative rather than superficial learning (Mezirow, 2000). While prior research often treats frustration and conflict as obstacles (D'Mello, 2012), their nuanced relationship with learning remains underexplored. In this study, frustration is conceptualized as an internal affective response to perceived blockage or unmet expectations, whereas conflict refers to interpersonal tension around incompatible goals or decisions. The two are analytically distinct yet often empirically intertwined in collaborative professional learning contexts. Thus, this study examines how frustration and conflict affect transformative learning using reflective journals from a 3 -day professional educational Makeathon for in -service teacher s. Within adult learning theory, Mezirow (2000) proposes a transformative learning framework characterized by disorienting dilemmas, critical reflection, and perspective transformation. However, the impact of conflict is dual -natured, potentially leading e ither to productive reflection or destructive disengagement (Deutsch, 1973). Critical to this theoretical framework is the interactive nature of frustration and conflict within transformative learning. To investigate this interaction, this study employs Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA), a quantitative ethnographic tool that models structural relationships among constructs (Shaffer, 2017).

title: What Changes with a Bit More Data in Learning Experience Network Analysis

abstract: This study examine s how patterns shift as more data accumulates. Expanding a dataset from 13 to 18 student reflections, learning experience network analysis (LENA) investigated what worked, struggles, and learning theory alignments. The addition of five reflections led to a structural shift from five clusters to three broader, more integrative ecologies. Design implications include more nuanced support for feedback processing, time management, resource navigation, and identity building.

abstract: This study used learning experience network analysis to examine nine student reflections in a graduate advanced instructional design course. The analysis identified four distinct learning ecologies, each with unique patterns of struggles, successes, and al ignments with learning theories. Based on these findings, we propose specific, theory- grounded design moves tailored to each ecology. This work demonstrates a method for developing more humanizing and adaptive learning experiences, offering a data- driven alternative to one -size- fits-all course design.

abstract: Systematic reviews on the application of AI technologies in STEM Education recommend the use of age -appropriate AI/ML tools in primary and secondary school settings, in contexts that appeal to students’ interests. In this pilot we incorporate a new modality (body movement) and tool (BBC micro:bit) into an AI/ML unit for young learners to understand how they engage with machine learning concepts. Students articulated novel uses for ML tools, drew connections to other practices, demonstrated metacognitive awareness, and described their roles as designers. These findings highlight the value of scaffolded, collaborative, embodied learning designs in supporting emerging AI literacy.
