subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Teacher education programs often struggle to connect instructional practice with research-based explanations of how learning works. Teacher candidates frequently focus on mastering classroom routines without developing a clear understanding of how those routines influence student learning. At the same time, research from the science of learning is often presented in abstract forms that teachers find difficult to apply in practice. This paper describes a structured reflective framework, DIGPA (Desc ription, Interpretation, Generalization, Planning Action), developed within English language teacher education and later applied in other instructional contexts. We argue that structured reflection can serve as a practical mechanism for connecting instructional practice to research -based explanations of learning within Practice-Based Teacher Education (PBTE).

title: The Impact of Discourse in Knowledge Building Teacher Communities on Professional Agency in Interdisciplinary Instructional Design
citation: Li-Ting Tseng, Mei-Ju Chen, Huang-Yao Hong, Chao-Yu Guo (2026). The Impact of Discourse in Knowledge Building Teacher Communities on Professional Agency in Interdisciplinary Instructional Design. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Tseng, L., Chen, M., Hong, H., & Guo, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This stu dy examines how discourse within a Knowledge -Building (KB) teacher community shapes professional agency in interdisciplinary instructional design. Sixty- nine teachers participated in collaborative design tasks, and their discourse was categorized i nto sharing-oriented and knowledge -building-oriented groups. Mixed- method analyses revealed a shift from exploratory sharing to knowledge -building discourse, characterized by negotiation and i ntegration of teaching strategies. Teachers’ professional agency im proved across all dimensions, particularly in positive interdependence and collective efficacy. The findings underscore the critical role of knowledge -building discourse in fostering teacher agency and supporting interdisciplinary instructional innovation.

citation: Yenda Prado, Pati Ruiz, Joshua Ddamulira (2026). Co-Designing GenAI Reading Technologies: Scaling Practitioner Expertise Within a National R&D Initiative. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: This case study examines the U -GAIN Reading R&D Center’s national leadership cohort, a practitioner -centered initiative exploring how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-enabled learning technologies can enhance early reading instruction in grades 1-3. The cohort brings together 11 educators from 10 school districts across seven U.S. states to collaboratively co -design resources for integrating GenAI -enabled reading interventions in schools. Using participatory and sociocultural approaches, we studied how educators participated in seven co -design meetings to explore effective uses of GenAI- enabled learning technologies in classrooms. Data sources include practitioner -researcher artifacts, meeting notes, and survey and 1:1 check- in responses. Data were an alyzed using directed content and constant comparative methods. title: Item Calibration in Reading Assessment with LLMs: Human Alignment and the Masking Effect
citation: Lingchen Kong (2026). Item Calibration in Reading Assessment with LLMs: Human Alignment and the Masking Effect. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Kong, L.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study evaluates large language models (LLMs) for calibrating item difficulty in grade 8 reading comprehension using 30 NAEP items. LLM-calibrated difficulty estimates were compared with human benchmarks, and masking was used to manipulate input information. Results show no significant differences across human- derived difficulty levels, indicating misalignment with human performance. Masking systematically reduced accuracy, particularly for harder items as more input text was obscured. These findings ra ise concerns about the validity of LLM-based item calibration.

title: Beyond One-Sided Arguments: Evaluating Perspective-Taking in Middle School Essays with GPT-4o and Human Scoring
citation: Yi Song, Michael Suhan (2026). Beyond One-Sided Arguments: Evaluating Perspective-Taking in Middle School Essays with GPT-4o and Human Scoring. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Song, Y. & Suhan, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this exploratory study, we compared GPT-4o zero-shot scoring with human ratings of middle school students’ essays collected across multiple studies. Results showed that GPT - 4o achieved acceptable reliability with human raters, highlighting the potential of GenAI for assessing perspective-taking. Further, we compared linguistic features of essays with a single perspective versus those with multiple perspectives. Future research should examine the quality of perspective -taking, moving beyond recognition of alternative perspectives to evaluating attempts at rebutting counterarguments.

title: Embodied Cognitive Pathways from Dynamic Geometry Software Access to Deductive Geometric Reasoning
citation: Doy Kim, Kelsey E. Schenck, Candace Walkington, Mitchell J. Nathan (2026). Embodied Cognitive Pathways from Dynamic Geometry Software Access to Deductive Geometric Reasoning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Kim, D., Schenck, K. E., Walkington, C., & Nathan, M. J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study examined whether Dynamic Geometry Software (DGS) access influences deductive geometric reasoning through embodied cognitive pathways. Structural equation modeling of data from a randomized within-subjects experiment (n = 1,239 responses) revealed a modest positive total indirect effect of DGS access on deductive reasoning ( β = .052, p = .006), mediated through task- relevant imagery formation and sensorimotor simulation. Both constructs showed strong associations with reasoning, consistent with embodied cognition predictions.

title: Amplifying the Voices of High School Graduates with Special Education and Neurodiversity Experiences to Shape GenAI Practices in Education
citation: Gina Tesoriero (2026). Amplifying the Voices of High School Graduates with Special Education and Neurodiversity Experiences to Shape GenAI Practices in Education. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Tesoriero, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: This qualitative study explores how GenAI Use Case Scenarios spark critical dialogue about GenAI in education among high school graduates with special education and neurodiverse experiences. Drawing on Cultural -Historical Activity Theory (Engeström & Sannino, 2010), justice -driven inclusive education (Waitoller & Artiles, 2013), and DisCrit (Annamma et al., 2013), this study positions youth as philosophers of technology (Vakil & McKinney de Royston, 2022) and co-designers of AI policy. Findings reveal the critical insights marginalized voices bring to conversations about responsible GenAI use in schools.

title: Developing an Approach for Evaluating Designs of Generative AI-Supported Learning
citation: Jun Song Huang, Min Lee (2026). Developing an Approach for Evaluating Designs of Generative AI-Supported Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Huang, J. S. & Lee, M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: While literature observes a surge in Generative AI (GenAI)-supported learning designs, these designs are often evaluated narrowly based on learning outcomes , offering limited insight into how GenAI contributes to pedagogical designs and supports learning processes. This paper addresses this gap by propos ing a holistic evaluation framework that encompasses three interrelated interactions : (1) interactions between learning designers and GenAI in shaping design embodiment, (2) interactions between GenAI and learners in mediating learning processes, and (3) interactions facilitating Explainable AI, focusing on how learning designers and learners understand, validate and improve the responses of GenAI. Grounded in C onjecture Mapping (Sandoval, 2014), the proposed framework organizes the evaluation of these interactions to inform how learning designs lead to intended learning outcomes. The framework provides a systematic means for evaluating and improving GenAI– supported learning designs beyond learning outcomes alone.

title: The Role of Teacher Feedback in Supporting Cocreative Processes
citation: Maria Sitjà Martín, Manoli Pifarré Turmo (2026). The Role of Teacher Feedback in Supporting Cocreative Processes. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Martín, M. S. & Turmo, M. P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Cocreation is a key 21st-century skill, yet few studies examine how teacher feedback supports it in classrooms. This study examined the role of structured, dialogic feedback in fostering students’ creativity and collaborative knowledge building. Twenty- five twelve-year- olds engaged in a technology -enhanced, project -based learning intervention, creating digital infographics using Viacocrea technology. Feedback, guided by the T-SEDA (2022) framework and aligned with Guilford’s creativity dimensions (1950), fo stered idea generation, reasoning, and collaboration. Findings highlight teacher feedback as essential for cocreative learning.

title: Unpacking Modeling-Based Learning in Kindergarten: A Micro-Level Discourse Analysis
citation: Loucas Louca (2026). Unpacking Modeling-Based Learning in Kindergarten: A Micro-Level Discourse Analysis. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Louca, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Accountable Talk & Dialogic Discourse
abstract: This case study explores how Modeling- based Learning (MbL) unfolds in a kindergarten science classroom through a micro- level analysis of the 24 children's discourse (aged 5-6) during a 35-minute whole-class discussion on water diffusion on a napkin. Findings indicate that participating children c ould engage in complex mechanistic reasoning when supported through structured MbL cycles and close teacher facilitation. The study highlights the importance of teacher monitoring different scalar-level mechanistic reasoning and scaffolding the MbL discourse.

title: What is CT Integration and Why does it Matter?: Educator and Researcher Perspectives
citation: Merijke Coenraad, Sharin Jacob, Wanjoo Ahn, Christina Schwarz (2026). What is CT Integration and Why does it Matter?: Educator and Researcher Perspectives. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Coenraad, M., Jacob, S., Ahn, W., & Schwarz, C.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: What computational thinking (CT) integration is and why it is important are often not defined in research and practice. This poster examines researcher and educator definitions of CT integration and their motivations. We found that educators and researchers described CT based on concepts (e.g., problem decomposition) and solution- oriented capabilities. They focused on CT integration as cross -disciplinary. Respondents grounded their rationale for CT integration in building competencies and literacies and school improvement and reform.

title: Graphs Are Arguments: Modeling Choices, Belonging, and Critical Statistical Literacy in Climate Data Visualizations
citation: Eva Thanheiser (2026). Graphs Are Arguments: Modeling Choices, Belonging, and Critical Statistical Literacy in Climate Data Visualizations. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Thanheiser, E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
conceptualisations_list: Accountable Talk & Dialogic Discourse; Classroom Orchestration; Co-Design & Participatory Design; Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: This paper explores how graphs operate as arguments through modeling choices including time window, scale, framing, aggregation, and audience. Drawing on contrasting climate visualizations built from the same data, it shows how representational choices sha pe interpretation and support different claims. It also argues that students were able to critique these choices because the classroom was organized as a Beloved Community, where belonging functioned as participation infrastructure for critical statistical literacy. Overview Public data visualizations are often treated as neutral displays of information, yet they are constructed through choices that shape what becomes visible, what counts as evidence, and what interpretations appear plausible. This paper argues that modeling choices such as time window, scale, framing, aggregation, and audience are central to how graphs make arguments (D’Ignazio & Klein, 2020; Weiland, 2017). It further argues that students were able to critique those choices because the classroom had been organized as a Beloved Community in which belonging functioned as participation infrastructure (Love, 2019). Using contrasting climate visualizations built from the same data but displayed across different time windows as a central example, this paper examines how representational decisions shape interpretation and how students moved from reading graphs to critiquing them. The analysis draws on classroom activity in which students engaged public data visualizations as objects of interpretation, comparison, and redesign. In particular, students examined contrasting climate graphs built from the same underlying data but displayed with different time windows, and they discussed how design choices shaped the claims each graph appeared to support. The analysis focuses on students’ discourse as they interpreted, questioned, and revised visualizations, with attention to the representational choices they named and the forms of critique they developed (Sfard, 2008). A central modeling contrast in this analysis is time window. When the same climate data are shown across a long historical span, the pattern can appear gradual and may invite familiar responses such as “Earth has changed before.” When the time window narrows to the recent past, the same underlying data can instead foreground the rate of increase and support a different interpretation, such as “Climate change is accelerating.” The point is not that one graph is true and the other false. Rather, representational choices shape salience. They influence what viewers notice, what kinds of arguments seem reasonable, and what conclusions become easier to draw. In this sense, graphs do not simply report reality. They organize attention and render some stories more visible than others (D’Ignazio & Klein, 2020). Time window is especially powerful because it often appears innocuous. Yet it works alongside other modeling choices such as scale, framing, aggregation, and attention to audience. Scale influences whether change looks dramatic or muted. Framing shapes how a graph is introduced, labeled, and interpreted in relation to a broader issue. Aggregation can either highlight patterns across groups or flatten important differences within them. Audience matters because graphs are built for someone, and design decisions anticipate particular readers, questions, and consequences. Taken together, these choices show that data visualization is not merely technical presentation. It is rhetorical and political work carried out through mathematical representation (Gutiérrez, 2013; Weiland, 2017). Within this framing, students’ discourse shifted from reading graphs as visual objects to critiquing graphs as designed arguments. Early responses focused on visible features of the display. Students noticed what a graph looked like, identified lines and labels, and described overall patterns. Over time, however, their talk became more analytic and more critical. They began to ask how the graph had been constructed, why certain choices had been made, and what those choices accomplished rhetorically. This movement from reading graphs to critiquing graphs matters because public visualizations often circulate as if they were transparent windows onto the world (D’Ignazio & Klein, 2020). In fact, they are composed artifacts shaped by inclusion, omission, emphasis, and intended audience. These shifts can also be understood as changes in classroom discourse, where students increasingly participated in forms of accountable and sociomathematical argumentation (O’Connor & Michaels, 1996; Yackel & Cobb, 1996). Early in discussion, students described graphs primarily in terms of visible features such as lines, labels, and overall shape. Later, they began to ask what the selected time span emphasized, why that span had been 2566 chosen, and how different viewers might interpret the same data differently. This shift marked a movement from noticing what a graph showed to interrogating how the graph had been built to make a claim. Two interrelated clusters of practice are especially important in this analysis. The first is argument-with- evidence. Students justified scale choices, explained uncertainty, and documented data provenance. In the climate example, this meant treating time window as part of the mathematical argument rather than as a cosmetic formatting decision. Students increasingly recognized that a graph’s domain, labels, and contextual features shape interpretation. They also came to see that uncertainty bands, source notes, and framing devices do mathematical work because they guide what counts as evidence and what can reasonably be inferred (Philip et al., 2016; Weiland, 2017). In this way, representation became a form of warrant rather than decoration. The second cluster of practice involved audience and ethics reasoning. Students questioned categories, disaggregated groups, and critiqued representation choices in relation to who would read the graph and what consequences might follow from the way it was built. These moves extended beyond technical correctness alone. A graph can be statistically defensible and still be ethically misleading if its categories flatten important differences, if its framing obscures the stakes of the issue, or if its design invites viewers toward a simplistic conclusion. Students therefore learned to ask not only whether a display was mathematically acceptable, but also what story it told, what story it hid, and whose experiences were made visible or invisible. This shift positioned critique as both an intellectual and a civic practice (Philip et al., 2016; Weiland, 2024). These critical practices did not emerge in a vacuum. Belonging functioned as participation infrastructure, organized through connection, norms, and shared purpose. In this framing, belonging is not a soft supplement to rigorous mathematical work. It is part of the classroom architecture that enables students to speak publicly, challenge one another’s interpretations, and revise claims without disproportionate interpersonal risk. When students experience connection to one another, participate in negotiated norms, and share a collective purpose, critique can become a communal responsibility rather than a threat to status or safety. Belonging, in other words, supports the conditions under which critical reasoning becomes possible (Goodenow, 1993; Nasir et al., 2014; Walton & Cohen, 2011). This view is consistent with learning sciences work that treats participation, relationship -building, and social change as co-constitutive dimensions of learning (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016). This claim is especially important in work with public data visualizations. To question framing, audience, omission, or aggregation is to question decisions that are often treated as settled, objective, or authoritative. Students are more likely to engage in that questioning when the classroom makes room for uncertainty, disagreement, and accountability to others. In this sense, belonging does not sit beside critical statistical literacy as a separate concern. It helps constitute the social conditions through which such literacy can develop. If educators want students to engage critically with graphs in civic life, instructional design must address not only technical tasks but also the relational and normative conditions that make critique possible (Goodenow, 1993; Walton & Cohen, 2011). This work contributes to research on critical statistical literacy by showing that critique of data visualization is not only a matter of technical competence, but also of the social and relational conditions that make participation possible (Weiland, 2017) . It also contributes to learning sciences discussions of classroom discourse by arguing that belonging operates as infrastructure for critique. When students experience connection, shared norms, and collective purpose, they are better positioned to question authoritative-looking representations, make interpretive claims in public, and revise those claims in response to others (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; O’Connor & Michaels, 1996; Yackel & Cobb, 1996). A key design principle emerging from this work is to show multiple representations of the same data. Representational contrast makes hidden assumptions visible because students can compare what changes in a graph and what changes in interpretation. In the climate example, holding the data constant while changing the time window exposed how design choices shape the story a graph appears to tell. More broadly, such comparison can support critical statistical literacy by inviting students to ask: What story does this graph tell? What story is hidden? Which modeling choices shaped this interpretation? These questions matter beyond a single classroom or a single climate example. They position students to participate more critically in a world saturated with charts, dashboards, and politically consequential data displays (Gutiérrez, 2013; Weiland, 2017, 2024). Taken together, this paper advances a compact but significant claim. Graphs shape arguments. Students can learn to identify and critique that shaping. Belonging is one of the conditions that makes such critique possible in classroom life. When learners com pare representations, attend to audience and ethics, and work within a classroom organized for belonging, they can move from consuming visualizations to interrogating them. That movement is central to critical statistical literacy and to preparing future educators and students to read, question, and remake the quantitative stories that organize public life (Gutstein, 2006; Weiland, 2017). 2567 References Bang, M., & Vossoughi, S. title: Getting Support and Gaining Clarity: Computational Thinking Pathways Communities of Practice
citation: Kyle Dunbar, Quinn Burke, Merijke Coenraad, Kelly Mills, Alessandra Rangel, Sharin Jacob (2026). Getting Support and Gaining Clarity: Computational Thinking Pathways Communities of Practice. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Dunbar, K., Burke, Q., Coenraad, M., Mills, K., Rangel, A., & Jacob, S.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: In response to increasing demand to integrate computational thinking (CT) into K-12 education systems, districts are developing CT P athways that offer cons istent, cumulative, competency-based exposure to CT. The development of these Pathways can be demanding and isolating work. This study examines how communities of practice (CoPs) may be supportive for districts designing and implementing CT Pathways. We found shared ownership in the CoPs was essential for districts participating in CoPs as it promoted ideation, iteration, and knowledge sharing in support of district CT work.

title: Democratizing Algebra: Advancing Conceptual Understanding Through Purpose -Driven Research-Practice-Industry Partnership
citation: Tarik Buli, Amanda Wortman, Stefani Pautz Stephenson, Rebecca Banks (2026). Democratizing Algebra: Advancing Conceptual Understanding Through Purpose -Driven Research-Practice-Industry Partnership. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Buli, T., Wortman, A., Stephenson, S. P., & Banks, R.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This RPIP study refined From Here to There (FH2T), a game -based algebra application, by positioning educators as pedagogical architects. Through iterative feedback loops, practitioners directly influenced critical features like the Teacher Console, ensuring classroom-readiness and scalability. Results demonstrate that FH2T democratizes math by decoupling conceptual logic from computational barriers. By grounding learning in perceptual engagement, the game transforms students from passive rule -followers into agentic "Doers," dismantling traditional gatekeepers to algebraic success.

title: Coding as Cultural Expression: Understanding How Children Draw on and Transform Cultural Resources
citation: Zhiye Fang, Yuqi Wang, Jianing Hu, Qi Yang, Lianmei Dong, Yubo Kou, Junnan Yu (2026). Coding as Cultural Expression: Understanding How Children Draw on and Transform Cultural Resources. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Fang, Z., Wang, Y., Hu, J., Yang, Q., Dong, L., Kou, Y., & Yu, J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Creative coding can support children in expressing identity and drawing on everyday cultural experience, but less is known about how this happens in practice or how tools shape it. This poster reports early findings from a culture-themed workshop with Chinese children using OctoStudio. Using screen and audio recordings, project artifacts, and field notes, we found that children incorporated cultural resources through storytelling, imagery, and speech, such as festivals, family roles, dialects, and mythic imagination. These findings frame coding as a culturally situated practice and inform the design of culturally responsive creative learning technologies.

title: Middle School Teachers' Pedagogical Reasoning about Biomimetic Engineering Design
citation: Geling Xu, Kristen Wendell (2026). Middle School Teachers' Pedagogical Reasoning about Biomimetic Engineering Design. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Xu, G. & Wendell, K.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: We explored middle school STEM teachers' pedagogical reasoning about middle - schoolers’ biomimetic engineering design. Using case study and grounded theory methods, we interviewed four teachers after they participated in professional development and implemented biomimetic design challenges with their students. Our findings suggest that teachers conceptualize biomimicry as a set of eight sub-skills.

title: Upper-Elementary Students’ Baseline Ideas of Computer Vision
citation: Srijita Chakraburty, Chris Cruz-Gonzalez, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver (2026). Upper-Elementary Students’ Baseline Ideas of Computer Vision. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Chakraburty, S., Cruz-Gonzalez, C., & Hmelo-Silver, C. E.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study examines how 14 upper -elementary students conceptualize computer vision as an entry point into AI literacy. Students completed an open -ended drawing task to elicit baseline ideas. Analysis revealed three patterns: intuitive feature noticing, symbolic image matching, and early mechanistic reasoning. Mapping responses to a Computer Vision LP showed that students with prior AI exposure reached higher levels, while those without were at lower levels, underscoring the need to tailor instruction to students’ prior experiences.

title: Social Presence with AI-Integrated Student Agents in a Teaching Simulator Leads to Higher Immersion but Not Learning
citation: Alex Barrett (2026). Social Presence with AI-Integrated Student Agents in a Teaching Simulator Leads to Higher Immersion but Not Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Barrett, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper reports on an experiment examining perceptions of social presence with AI-integrated student agents in a prototype teacher training simulation. I hypothesized that perceived immersion in the simulation would increase social presence, and that social presence would lead to increased learning gains. A univariate analysis showed that immersion significantly predicted social presence, but perceptions of agent fidelity did not. A regression analysis showed that social presence did not impact learning gains. Design implications and future research directions are discussed.

title: Resonant Learning: Tracing Teacher Growth Through a Longitudinal CS Research- Practice Partnership
citation: Nitasha Mathayas, Chrystalla Mouza, Hilary Mead, Lori Pollock (2026). Resonant Learning: Tracing Teacher Growth Through a Longitudinal CS Research- Practice Partnership. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Mathayas, N., Mouza, C., Mead, H., & Pollock, L.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This longitudinal study examines one elementary teacher’s sustained engagement in a computer science (CS) focused professional development (PD) project to understand how she integrated CS into her lessons over three years. Analysis of interviews and lesson plan materials using TPACK and teacher professional growth frameworks demonstrates that she integrated CS instruction with increased task complexity and relevance to students over time. Implications for PD design and sustained teacher engagement follow.

title: Children’s Augmented Reality Narratives: Exploring Forest Entanglements and More-than-Human Storytelling
citation: Kristiina Kumpulainen, Shima Dadkhahfard (2026). Children’s Augmented Reality Narratives: Exploring Forest Entanglements and More-than-Human Storytelling. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Kumpulainen, K. & Dadkhahfard, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines how children’s augmented stories compose multispecies relationality through narrative, spatial, and material engagements with the forest. Grounded in posthuman and sociomaterial perspectives, we analyzed how children, environments, and digital technologies participate in storytelling. Findings show that nonhuman beings act ed as co-narrators, the forest shaped narrative development, and augmented reality intra-acted in situ composition, enabling children to construct hybrid storyworlds through embodied and collaborative engagement with place.

title: Immersive Storytelling and Embodied Experience in Informal Learning Contexts
citation: Shima Dadkhahfard, Farzan Baradaran Rahimi (2026). Immersive Storytelling and Embodied Experience in Informal Learning Contexts. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Dadkhahfard, S. & Rahimi, F. B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates how immersive technologies and narrative strategy enhance embodied learning and presence in informal education. Grounded in embodied cognition, it analyzes three student-designed AR, VR, and smart glasses experiences at a Western Canadian science center. Using a qualitative case study, findings show that bodily interaction, sensory engagement, and storytelling deepen users’ sense of presence. Integrating narrative with physical interaction transforms passive observation into active pa rticipation, reimagining informal learning as engaging, multisensory, and impactful.

title: The PS-I Squared Model: Integrating Failure-driven and Success-driven Scaffolding
citation: Shota Higuchi (2026). The PS-I Squared Model: Integrating Failure-driven and Success-driven Scaffolding. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Higuchi, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Much research has examined Problem -Solving prior to Instruction (PS -I). Recent studies have reported the effectiveness of failure-driven scaffolding during this problem-solving phase. However, concerns remain that such scaffolding may negatively affect stu dents’ confidence. This study proposes the PS -I Squared Model, which integrates failure -driven and success-driven scaffolding. In a lesson on vector dot products for high school sophomores, we compared the effects of the PS-I Squared Model, PS-I with success-driven scaffolding, and PS- I with failure -driven scaffolding. The results indicated that both the PS -I Squared Model and failure-driven scaffolding were more effective than success -driven scaffolding for promoting conceptual knowledge acquisition. Furthermore, the PS -I Squared Model appears to offer a viable approach to addressing the concerns associated with failure-driven scaffolding.

title: Bridging Confidence and Practice: Effects of Data Literacy Professional Development on Teachers’ Knowledge, Self-Efficacy, and Value Beliefs
citation: Ean Teng Khor, Hera Lim, Tanmay Sinha (2026). Bridging Confidence and Practice: Effects of Data Literacy Professional Development on Teachers’ Knowledge, Self-Efficacy, and Value Beliefs. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Khor, E. T., Lim, H., & Sinha, T.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Teachers are increasingly expected to use data for instructional decision-making, yet many report limited preparation. This study evaluated a professional development (PD) program on teacher data literacy in Singapore using a mixed-methods design. Baseline surveys and tests were completed by N = 144 teachers; matched pre– post data were obtained from 21. Quantitative analyses showed small, non- significant gains in data knowledge, stable self - efficacy, and stable perceived value of data use. Attrition limited statistical power, though post- test completers scored higher than the baseline sample. Qualitative interviews with n = 8 teachers indicated that hands -on analysis of authentic datasets supported confidence, but translation of patterns into pedagogy was hindered by time constraints and limited mentoring. Findings suggest that the PD improved knowledge more readily than beliefs, highlighting the need for explicit scaffolds and organizational support to sustain data use.

title: How Thinking Routines Shape Cultures of Thinking: An Exploratory Cross-Case Study in EFL Higher Education
citation: Jou-Yin Chen (2026). How Thinking Routines Shape Cultures of Thinking: An Exploratory Cross-Case Study in EFL Higher Education. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Chen, J.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This exploratory cross-case study examines how thinking routines cultivate a culture of thinking across two university EFL courses —Critical Reading and Movies discussion. Data included students’ written reflections, classroom observations, and focus -group interviews. Thematic analysis results identified four cultural elements: (1) teacher guidance and emotional support, (2) peer interaction and a supportive ethos , (3) structured routines fostering thinking, and (4) confidence and comfort in expression, which pointed to the need for both cognitive scaffolding and cultural mediation in EFL higher education.

title: “On the Graph They’re Talking If It Went Down or Up for the Speed. It’s Not Talking About a Half Pipe”: Authority and Dialogic Mathematics Peer Learning of Functions in 6th Grade
citation: Fati Alipour, Alison Castro Superfine (2026). “On the Graph They’re Talking If It Went Down or Up for the Speed. It’s Not Talking About a Half Pipe”: Authority and Dialogic Mathematics Peer Learning of Functions in 6th Grade. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Alipour, F. & Superfine, A. C.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: A strong conceptual understanding of functions supports future learning of algebra. However, struggles are persistent with learning functions because it requires a conceptual shift. This study uses the dialogic mathematics peer learning framework ( Ben-Dor & Heyd - Metzuyanim, 202 5) to explore how 6 th grade students learn functions in classrooms. Our findings highlight that students’ perception of authority positioned some peers, despite having the wrong answer, more expert that others and it impacted how the conceptual shift occurred.

title: Cultivating Critical Transformative Teacher Agency through Co-Design with Families toward Climate Justice
citation: Wisam Sedawi, Batoul Y. Abdallah, Rachel Sherwin (2026). Cultivating Critical Transformative Teacher Agency through Co-Design with Families toward Climate Justice. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Sedawi, W., Abdallah, B. Y., & Sherwin, R.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Using participatory critical design ethnography, we investigate how a minoritized teacher developed critical transformative agency by collaborating with Arab American immigrant families to co-design and enact climate justice education. Findings show this agency as a hesitant yet protective stance, growing critical consciousness, and action. It emerged through engagement with community epistemologies, relational and cultural anchors, and home-school alliances. We argue that cultivating such agency is essential for advancing climate justice education and community collective thriving.

title: Understanding Play and Inclusion through Interaction Analysis
citation: Mikaela Zetley, Christine Lee (2026). Understanding Play and Inclusion through Interaction Analysis. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Zetley, M. & Lee, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this poster, we present interaction analysis from video data of a playful learning episode in an inclusive elementary classroom. We found that, as a methodology, interaction analysis revealed the ways that adults’ instructional moves expansively position children’s ideas as valid contributions. We aim to spark conversation in the Learning Science community around intersections of dignity, inclusion, and playful learning.

title: Reflections on Developing a Cooperative Virtual Reality Experience for a Character Education Course
citation: Elliot Hu-Au, Jennifer Brown Urban, Mirka Feinstein, Jesse Ha, Miriam Linver (2026). Reflections on Developing a Cooperative Virtual Reality Experience for a Character Education Course. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Hu-Au, E., Urban, J. B., Feinstein, M., Ha, J., & Linver, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: In creating an undergraduate- level virtue and character development course that implements virtual reality (VR) as a learning tool, multiple and diverse stakeholders must come together to collaborate. This paper outlines the initial project actions that we re taken to build teamwork and understanding both across disciplines as well as with the desired theme of the course. This project involves a multidisciplinary team in education, human development, instructional design, computer science, scriptwriting, and visual arts. It effectively brought experts in these disparate fields together to create a complex and thoughtful VR experience. Set in the design cycle framework, the project demonstrates how each step can be utilized for progress. Reflections on the process and how multidisciplinary teams can function effectively are shared. Purpose At Montclair State University (MSU), a new core curriculum, known as SEEDS, seeks to align courses to a character focused mission statement and set of values. A multidisciplinary team with expertise in character development, instructional design, game deve lopment, screenwriting/directing, animation, virtual reality (VR), computer science, and evaluation is developing a character education course that infuses VR experiences and meets the character-focused learning objectives set forth in the new general education curriculum. To date, there has been minimal research on the use of VR in the context of character education, yet “VR has the potential to contribute positively and significantly to the current character education movement” (Harrison, 2024, p. 235). Relying upon the Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (Makransky & Petersen, 2020) and the efficacy in which gamified interactions can promote learning and motivation (Gee, 2005), the VR experiences we are creating aim to give students meaningful and transformative character -building experiences. The particular VR experience this paper focuses on targets the potential biases young adults may have towards aging and attempts to illuminate the emotional complexities encountered in the latter stages of life. The research question explored in this paper is: what strategies and project actions can be employed to enhance the collaborative work done by a multidisciplinary team? Theoretical framework This paper analyzes the multidisciplinary team and their work within the context of Paletz and Schunn’s (2010) social-cognitive framework of multidisciplinary team innovation. This framework combines an understanding of cognitive processes, such as analogi es, information search, and appropriate evaluation, with social constructs, such as formal roles and content knowledge diversity within the team. By analyzing the project’s process and activities within a social- cognitive framework, one can determine where and why progress was made as well as where difficulties were encountered. Within the project, a Relational Developmental Systems meta -theoretical framework is applied to character development, emphasizing the role of individual agency in the development of character (Lerner, 2006).

title: AI Literacy in CS Education
citation: Yob Ha, Chih-Pu Dai (2026). AI Literacy in CS Education. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Ha, Y. & Dai, C.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study systematically reviews 27 peer -reviewed studies on AI literacy in computer science (CS) education, including five broader STEM studies as comparative cases . Using PRISMA, it synthesizes evidence across conceptual, ethical, and pedagogical dimensions. Results show advances in data competencies but persistent challenges in ethics integration, assessment, and teacher preparation. The study highlights both STEM -wide trends and CS-specific needs, offering actionable guidance for designing coherent and sustainable AI literacy curricula.

title: Designing for Resilience as Preparation for Challenging STEM Tasks
citation: Tanmay Sinha, Naseema Beevi, Ria Gavin Dias (2026). Designing for Resilience as Preparation for Challenging STEM Tasks. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Sinha, T., Beevi, N., & Dias, R. G.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: We designed a novel instructional package targeting distinct facets of mental and emotional resilience for thirty -nine primary school students as preparation for a collaborative design challenge in a Singaporean science classroom. Our mental resilience package nudged sensemaking around growth mindset by having students make predictions on myths, and offered vicarious learning opportunities for everyone to evaluate peer quotations of reframing failure. Our emotional resilience package used contrasting cases complemented with expressive writing to help students discern the usefulness of positive and negative emotions in learning. Several data sources – including students’ reflections, their descriptions of enacted resilience behaviors, and observable measures of science learning – showed evidence that this work may have already begun planting seeds for normalizing failure and persevering emotionally through setbacks.

title: Understanding the Effects of LLM-Generated Conversation Initiations with Learners in Popular Science Video-Based Learning
citation: Jingchao Fang, Qingxiaoyang Zhu, Hao-Chuan Wang (2026). Understanding the Effects of LLM-Generated Conversation Initiations with Learners in Popular Science Video-Based Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Fang, J., Zhu, Q., & Wang, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Recent breakthroughs in large language models (LLMs) make it possible to create learning companion agents that boost the interactivity in video-based learning . This study focuses on learning companion agents’ role as conversation initiators. How do different styles of agents’ conversation initiation influence learners’ learning experiences ? We conducted a controlled experiment (N=65) using a technology probe that sends varying types of conversation initiation messages to learners. We reveal how the personas and message styles of learning companion agents shape learners’ experiences.

title: Bloom’s Waterfall
citation: Jonan Phillip Donaldson (2026). Bloom’s Waterfall. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Donaldson, J. P.
subject: STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_pk_labels: Inquiry-Based & Problem-Solving; Productive Failure; Scaffolded & Guided; Co-Design & Participatory
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Communities of Practice & Situated Learning; Productive Failure & Problem Solving; Conceptual Change & Mental Models; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: This poster, a conceptual contribution, reframes Bloom’s Taxonomy’s pyramid model, proposing a waterfall frame where creation is the generative source. Higher -order thinking cascades downward, naturally engaging lower -order skills. Grounded in constructionist learning theory, this model suggests learning starts with complex creation, not remembering or even understanding. It challenges traditional instructional design sequencing and offers a new perspective for designing rich learning environments that better reflect how humans naturally develop deep, contextualized enactive knowledge and skill. The problem with pyramids Bloom's Taxonomy has been a foundational framework for educational design since its introduction in 1956 (Bloom, 1956) and subsequent revision in 2001 (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001). The traditional pyramid representation creates persistent misconceptions about how learning unfolds in authentic contexts. The pyramid suggests a hierarchical climb from simple recall to complex creation, implying that learners must master lower - order skills before attempting higher -order thinking. This bottom -up interpretation is at odds with established learning sciences principles that view knowledge as enacted and learning as a situated, participatory, and tool - mediated process (Fischer et al., 2018; Nasir et al., 2020; Sawyer, 2022). Several scholars have critiqued this pyramidal structure (Crawford & Smith, 2015; Murtonen et al., 2017; Wineburg & Schneider, 2010), arguing that it misrepresents the dynamic and interconnected nature of cognitive development, yet none have proposed a learning-theory-grounded alternative. When learning designers treat the taxonomy as something to climb, they often design learning experiences that isolate knowledge and skills from meaningful contexts. They assume that learners must spend considerable time memorizing facts and practicing decontextualized procedures before being allowed to engage with complex, authentic problems . This is in tension with what learning sciences research suggests about the nature of learning (Donaldson & Allen-Handy, 2019, 2023; Schank, 2016). A waterfall reframing of Bloom’s Taxonomy This conceptual poster proposes an alternative visualization of Bloom's Taxonomy as a waterfall (see Figure 1), with “Create” positioned not as the pinnacle, but as the generative source of all learning. Figure 1 Bloom’s Waterfall with Domains in the Center, Potential Impacts on the Left, and Practices on the Right In this model, higher- order thinking naturally demands and develops lower -order skills as integrated practices. The waterfall metaphor captures how creation flows through evaluation and analysis, gathering force 2626 as it activates and develops remembering, understanding, and applying along the way. Water flowing down a waterfall gains momentum and power as it descends to the pool at the bottom, just as learners engaged in creative and analytical work naturally develop knowledge and skills. The waterfall model challenges conventional instructional sequencing by suggesting that learners should begin with complex, generative tasks rather than working their way up from basic recall. When students create artifacts, evaluate designs, or analyze systems, they must necessarily remember information, develop understanding, and apply concepts. These lower -order skills emerge organically within meaningful contexts rather than requiring separate instructional time. This reframing is grounded in constructionist learning theory ( Kafai, 2006 ; Papert & Harel, 1991), which argues that deep learning occurs when people construct external artifacts that serve as tools for thinking. Constructionism naturally emphasizes the Create level of the taxonomy, positioning making and building as primary learning activities rather than culminating achievements. The theory suggests that learners develop their most robust and transferable knowledge through the process of designing, constructing, and refining tangible or digital objects. Implications for learning design The waterfall model carries significant implications for how researchers and practitioners design learning environments. Rather than sequencing instruction from simple to complex, designers should create rich problem spaces that invite learners to engage i mmediately with high-level cognitive work. This approach does not mean throwing students into deep water without support. Instead, it means structuring activities so that scaffolding and guidance help learners succeed at complex tasks while developing enactive knowledge (Newen et al., 2018 ) in context. Project-based learning exemplifies this approach. When students tackle authentic problems that matter beyond the classroom, they must create solutions, evaluate alternatives, and analyze complex systems. The project naturally integrates all levels of the taxonomy, with creation serving as the driving force that pulls other cognitive skills into play. This also clarifies the mechanism behind knowledge building communities (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2022), where the collective goal of creating new ideas naturally requires members to remember, apply, and synthesize information in service of that higher-order goal. In these environments, students collectively work in generative modalities to advance community knowledge through sustained inquiry. They create theories, evaluate evidence, analyze explanations, and synthesize ideas. The community's shared epistemic goals situate lower-order cognitive work within the higher-order work of knowledge creation. Students remember information because they need it for their theories, not because remembering was specified as a learning objective. The model also suggests reconsidering how we write learning objectives. Traditional instructional design often generates separate objectives for each taxonomy level, treating them as discrete competencies and often requiring objectives targeting the bottom two levels before addressing higher levels. The waterfall model advises writing learning objectives around high- level outcomes. Achieving these complex outcomes will inherently require the development of supporting skills. An objective might specify that students will design and evaluate a solution to an engineering challenge, with the understanding that this work requires applying concepts, understanding principles, and remembering relevant information. Challenges and considerations Implementing waterfall-based design requires significant shifts in educational practice. Assessment systems built around recall and comprehension must evolve toward complex and holistic enactment or performance-based evaluation at the individual level, or collective evaluation at the activity system level (Engeström, 2022). Learning facilitators need professional learning opportunities to develop facilitation skills for supporting students engaged in open- ended creative work. Institutional structures like pacing guides and standardized curricula may need redesign to allow time for sustained, complex projects. The model also requires careful attention to scaffolding and support structures. Starting with creation does not mean removing guidance or structure. Research on productive failure (Kapur, 2008) demonstrates that struggling with complex problems before receiving instruction can enhance learning, but this requires thoughtful design of the problem space and strategic timing of support. Learners need access to resources, models, and feedback that help them succeed at challenging work while developing expertise. The learning sciences community has long emphasized authentic activity ( Papert & Harel, 1991 ), legitimate peripheral participation (Lave & Wenger, 1991), and learning through designing (Kolodner et al., 2003). The waterfall model of Bloom's Taxonomy offers a way to connect these theoretical commitments to a widely recognized framework. The metaphors we use for learning shape how we design for it ( Donaldson & Allen-Handy, 2023), and repositioning creation as the source rather than the summit of cognitive work can help us design learning environments that better reflect how humans naturally develop deep, contextualized expertise. 2627 References Anderson, L. Phi Delta Kappan, 91(4), 56-61. 2628 How Motivation Relates to Generative AI Use: A Large-Scale Survey of Mexican High School Students Echo Zexuan Pan, Harvard University, echozexuanpan@g.harvard.edu Danny Glick, Oranim College of Education, danny.glick@oranim.ac.il Ying Xu, Harvard University, yingxu@g.harvard.edu Abstract: This study examined how high school students with different motivational profiles use generative AI tools in math and writing. Through K -means clustering analysis of survey data from 6,793 Mexican high school students, we identified three distinct motivational profiles based on self-concept and perceived subject value. Results revealed distinct domain-specific AI usage patterns across students with different motivational profiles. Our findings challenge one- size-fits-all AI integration approaches and advocate for motivationally- informed educational interventions.

title: From Resigned to Resolute: Understanding How an Emergent Writer Repositions Himself in a Flexible Assessment Context
citation: Erica Lee Payne (2026). From Resigned to Resolute: Understanding How an Emergent Writer Repositions Himself in a Flexible Assessment Context. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Payne, E. L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The norms of constrained testing environments often limit student agency. Using interaction analysis, I illustrate a counternarrative of a pre-K student who challenges assessment norms in order to reposition himself as a writer. By studying his decisions on a micro -level, I outline how he negotiates new positioning and how he accepts semiotic mediators as invitations to shift from protocol in order to accurately display his abilities.

title: Superpowers and Fears: International School Teachers' Beliefs about AI in Multilingual Classrooms
citation: Gyeongri Kim, Alina Guha, Shivani Choudhary, Shamya Karumbaiah, Esther Bettney Hedit, Mariana Castro (2026). Superpowers and Fears: International School Teachers' Beliefs about AI in Multilingual Classrooms. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Kim, G., Guha, A., Choudhary, S., Karumbaiah, S., Hedit, E. B., & Castro, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines international school teachers’ beliefs about AI in multilingual classrooms through qualitative analysis of 103 survey responses. Teachers primarily desired AI’s pedagogical support, especially for curriculum and instruction and language support. However, they raised concerns about misinformation, limited cultural understanding, and student overreliance on AI. The findings highlight a tension between AI’s benefits and risks, emphasizing the need for ethical implementation, safeguards, and teacher training to support equitable, linguistically responsive AI-integrated learning environments.

title: Boundary learning in a research-practice partnership
citation: Etan Cohen, Hadar Baharav, Linor Hadar (2026). Boundary learning in a research-practice partnership. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Cohen, E., Baharav, H., & Hadar, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Accountable Talk & Dialogic Discourse; Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs) are collaborations between academics and practitioners that focus on problems of practice while engaging with research. Within RPPs, various forms of learning can be mediated by the social boundaries that separate partners. In this case study, we employed ethnographic and discourse analysis methods to understand the types of boundary learning that were afforded by an RPP. Our findings showed that boundaries emerged within practitioner and academic groups, and not just between them. Boundary learning was characterized by modest forms of coordination and reflection, rather than profound transformation. Our findings suggest that RPPs should be understood as sites of complex, multi- layered boundary work.

title: Expertise in Two Dimensions: Mathematical Problem Solving with ChatGPT
citation: Victoria Delaney, Ryan Aniceto, Katya Hernández Holliday (2026). Expertise in Two Dimensions: Mathematical Problem Solving with ChatGPT. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Delaney, V., Aniceto, R., & Holliday, K. H.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Using tools to solve problems within a subject domain requires both knowledge of the domain and of the tool itself. Drawing from perspectives on building expertise, we analyzed task-based episodes where undergraduates solved a mathematics free response question with ChatGPT-4o. We present four contrasting cases of students’ problem solving and discuss how their knowledge of (a) the underlying mathematics and (b) ChatGPT -4o appeared to influence what they did and did not understand. We situate our findings in broader education debates on the role of intelligent agents in developing human expertise.

title: A Common Language for Infrastucturing Maker Education: Mapping Stakeholder Challenges and Opportunities using a Five-Dimensional Framework
citation: Hila Langer, Yuval Segev, Shiri Kashi, Yotam Hod (2026). A Common Language for Infrastucturing Maker Education: Mapping Stakeholder Challenges and Opportunities using a Five-Dimensional Framework. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Langer, H., Segev, Y., Kashi, S., & Hod, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The promise of maker education is frequently constrained by entrenched educational infrastructures. Efforts to create sustainable change, a process known as infrastructuring, require a deep and shared understanding of systemic challenges and opportunities . However, discourse among stakeholders can be diffuse, hindering collective action. To address this, we propose a five -dimensional analytic framework —epistemological, pedagogical, social, material-technological, and organizational —as a tool for mapping the landscape of maker education. We convened a conference of diverse stakeholders and analyzed their roundtable discussions about the future of maker education. Preliminary findings reveal that stakeholders’ articulations of core problems and potential solutions align with the five dimensions of our framework, even without its explicit introduction. This suggests the framework's potential as a tool to help communities surface, structure, and formalize their grounded knowledge, fostering a common language vital for intentional infrastructuring work.

title: Digital Technologies and Philosophy Teaching: Indications of the Need for an Epistemological Turn
citation: Andrews Jobim, Lucia Giraffa (2026). Digital Technologies and Philosophy Teaching: Indications of the Need for an Epistemological Turn. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Jobim, A. & Giraffa, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines the epistemic role of digital technologies in Philosophy teacher education beyond instrumental integration. Using Design- Based Research, we conducted an exploratory cycle involving interviews, institutional document analysis, and cartog raphic mapping. Findings reveal a dominant textual orientation that constrains digital experimentation and reinforces traditional academic legitimation. The study identifies tensions between philosophizing and teaching practice, informing the design of interventions aimed at fostering non-instrumental uses of digital technologies.

title: Linking Data and Community: Design Data-art Inquiry Programs to Foste Civic Engagement
citation: Yilang Zhao, Dennis “Matt” Stevenson, Lynn L. Hodge (2026). Linking Data and Community: Design Data-art Inquiry Programs to Foste Civic Engagement. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Zhao, Y., Stevenson, D. M., & Hodge, L. L.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: This poster introduces the MVP model, a transdisciplinary approach designed to foster civic engagement among upper middle and high school students by linking data science, art, and social studies, through the artistic visualiz ation of community data. Students will investigate locally relevant topics by designing data collection instruments, conducting analyses, and translating findings into creative, artistic data visualizations. Through situating data work within social and emotional contexts, MVP aligns with the civic mission of social studies education—to prepare reflective, informed, and active citizens.

title: Co-Intelligence Instructional Coaching: A Concept Analysis of Human–AI Collaboration in Teacher Professional Development
citation: Zeinab Mokhtari, Seong Ji Jeong (2026). Co-Intelligence Instructional Coaching: A Concept Analysis of Human–AI Collaboration in Teacher Professional Development. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Mokhtari, Z. & Jeong, S. J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), a major driver of educational transformation, can complement instructional coaching to strengthen teacher professional development. While instructional coaching is effective, its scalability is limited by the shortage of qualified coaches. This study introduces Co- Intelligence Instructional Coaching, a hybrid concept combining AI with human expertise. Through conceptual analysis, it identifies the antecedents, attributes, and consequences of this model, providing a foundation for future inquiry and practice with added relevance for underserved contexts.

title: Addressing Cognitive Load and Mental Schema Development for Graduate Research Methods Knowledge
citation: Jacob Robbins, Shaun Hutchins, Jake Pote, Mahjabin Chowdhury (2026). Addressing Cognitive Load and Mental Schema Development for Graduate Research Methods Knowledge. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Robbins, J., Hutchins, S., Pote, J., & Chowdhury, M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Communities of Practice & Situated Learning; Cognitive Load Theory; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: This design- based study examined a graduate research -methods course for 14 doctoral students, grounded in cognitive constructivism, situated learning, and cognitive load theory. Using backward design and cumulative assignments, the course scaffolded proposal writing in professional contexts. Coded reflections and semantic network analysis showed that students valued structure and iterative feedback but struggled with alignment, template confusion, and workload. Two revisions are proposed: a weekly visual “you-are-here” organizer and consolidated cloud- based templates to reduce extraneous load and strengthen workplace transfer.

title: Augmenting LLMs with Knowledge Seeds for Clinical Question Generation
citation: Lingchen Kong, William Muntean, Joe Betts (2026). Augmenting LLMs with Knowledge Seeds for Clinical Question Generation. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Kong, L., Muntean, W., & Betts, J.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: High-stakes clinical assessments require complex, context-rich items that test applied reasoning but are time -consuming to create. This study presents a learning -centered LLM pipeline that generates multiple -choice clinical items using knowledge seeds from validated item banks. The LLM-generated Multiple Choice (MC) items demonstrated comparable option- level ecological validity and distractor plausibility to expert- created items, with the pipeline facilitating item development and accelerating the refresh cycle to maintain item bank integrity.

title: Catalyzing Professional Identity: The Impact of Authentic Assessment in Teacher Education
citation: Clara Bagwell, Cora Causey, Jonan Phillip Donaldson (2026). Catalyzing Professional Identity: The Impact of Authentic Assessment in Teacher Education. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Bagwell, C., Causey, C., & Donaldson, J. P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Developing professional identity in pre -service teachers is a common challenge in teacher education. Authentic reflective assessment practices serve as powerful catalysts for transformative learning and identity formation. Analysis of reflection papers from eleven early childhood education students revealed shifts in their professional perspectives and evidence of critical self-reflection. Our findings suggest that assessment design fosters professional identity, expanding its pedagogical role in teacher education.

title: The Influences of Alternative Onboarding Approaches in a Puzzle Video Game on Learning, Problem-Solving, and Player Experience
citation: Nasim Eshgarf, Zack Carpenter, Craig G. Anderson (2026). The Influences of Alternative Onboarding Approaches in a Puzzle Video Game on Learning, Problem-Solving, and Player Experience. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Eshgarf, N., Carpenter, Z., & Anderson, C. G.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Onboarding shapes how players learn, yet empirical comparisons of theoretically grounded approaches remain scarce. We tested three onboarding variations in Baba Is You— Tutorialized (direct instruction), Safe Problem -Solving (visually guided), and Increased Impasse (productive failure) —against the original game with 122 participants across three sessions. Despite being perceived as the least difficult, the Safe condition produced significantly lower mechanical understanding. Behavioral and experiential differences converged in subsequent sessions, carrying implications for tutorial design in game-based learning.

title: Consequential Intergenerational Learning through Collaborative Video Game Design
citation: Feifei Shen, Lyndsay Schaeffer, Clifford Lee (2026). Consequential Intergenerational Learning through Collaborative Video Game Design. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: This study examines how collaborative video game design between graduate and elementary school students facilitates intergenerational learning. Through semester-long action research, three graduate game design students and thirteen 4th and 5th graders co-d esigned a video game addressing local ecological issues. Using communities of learners, constructionist, and sociocultural frameworks and qualitative analysis, we identified how player -centered design, structured playtesting, and productive communication differences facilitated reciprocal learning while disrupting traditional power dynamics across age and institutional boundaries.

title: Favorite Places and Relationships with Nature in Children’s Drawings from a Forest Kindergarten
citation: Dongrui Tang, Xin You (2026). Favorite Places and Relationships with Nature in Children’s Drawings from a Forest Kindergarten. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Tang, D. & You, X.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines how 5–to 6-year-old children in a forest kindergarten in Japan represented their favorite places through drawings and follow -up conversations. Most children selected outdoor places as their favorites, with 17 of 18 drawings depicting outdoor spaces and 16 of those 17 placing favorite places in natural settings. The findings suggest that children understood favorite spaces not simply as attractive scenery, but through relationships, preferred activities, and everyday participation in a nature -rich environment. Children’s drawings also included remembered and imagined elements, suggesting that meaningful experience with place extended beyond the immediate moment. Together, these findings suggest that everyday interaction with the natural world may support children’s positive and meaningful relationships with nature in early childhood.

title: Teachers Bridging Technical and Reflective Stances in K–9 AI Education

abstract: As AI tools enter K -9 classrooms, teachers face the challenge of supporting both technical understanding and critical reflection. This study examines how lower secondary teachers integrate technical and reflective stances of AI through participatory lesson design with simplified Large Language Model activities. Analysis of classroom enactments, lesson plans, and interviews shows that : First, technical and reflective stances can be bridged in discrete, well-structured activities. Second, teachers stress technical insights before critical reflection. Third, abstract reflection concepts can cause classroom detachment, and fourth, bridging technical and reflective stances requires more than explanation. Additionally, these findings lead us to suggest implications highlighting awareness of teachers’ assumptions, deliberate activity scaffolding, and pedagogical strategies to support teachers in balancing technical and reflective stances of AI literacy.

abstract: Interdisciplinary education equips students to address complex societal challenges by integrating diverse perspectives. Knowledge Integration was shaped by team structure and educator facilitation, reframing differences as epistemic orientations rather than gaps.

The clusters point to personally meaningful paths toward human flourishing and inform targeted design moves that reduce barriers and support a more humane, project-based learning environment.

title: Rural Primary Students’ Early Conceptions of Artificial Intelligence
citation: Yanqiu Li (2026). Rural Primary Students’ Early Conceptions of Artificial Intelligence. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: Young learners’ initial conceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) shape how they engage with AI and have implications for instructional design. 23 Grade 4–5 students in a rural region of China completed a paper -based survey examining how they defined AI, identified it in everyday technologies, and perceive d their interest and confidence in learning it. Students often described AI in functional or robotic terms, with some associating it with automation or simple responsiveness. Students’ interest was generally high, but confidence varied. These findings suggest that early AI education should support both the development of more refined conceptual understanding and learners’ confidence.

title: Bridging Research and Practice: Expanding Access to Transformative Computer Science Teacher Learning
