abstract: This poster discusses the collaborative efforts of a CS education community to develop an open- access, online educational resource. Throughout our design, revision, and publication processes, we show how our community intentionally sought to bridge gaps between research and practice to sustain CS teachers on their equity learning journeys. Motivation A key challenge in educational research is its inaccessibility for the classroom teachers it is intended to help. This gap between research and practice exists because of multiple structural and systemic barriers. Research is often siloed within — rather than integrated across —fields in ways that support the complexity of classroom teaching. Research findings are presented using academic norms (e.g., abstract theoretical arguments, statistical analyses, technical jargon) that are disconnected from the everyday realities of classroom life. Teacher voices are often excluded from research, sidelining their expertise in addressing education challenges (Penuel, 2019). Access to research is generally restricted behind paywalls, requiring institutional connections not generally available to K- 12 teachers (Cook et al., 2024). It is no wonder that teachers already pressed for time and resources perceive a gap between their work and educational researchers. This research -practice gap has particular relevance for computer science education (CS Ed) as an emerging field. Aware of how patterns of inequity have shaped computing and technology, many CS educators are striving to thoughtfully grow the field to make equity -oriented CS education a reality for all students (e.g., Computer Science Teacher Association, n.d.). We conceptualize equity as access to CS learning opportunities and as transforming the field by centering marginalized people, knowledge systems, and technologies (Grapin et al., 2023; Vogel et al., 2017). Realizing this vision requires CS teachers who engage in equity work as an ongoing effort demanding careful identity work, continued learning, and collective reflection and dreaming (Benjamin, 2022, 2024). This poster discusses the collaborative efforts of a CS Ed community to develop an open- access online book entitled Advancing Educational Equity in Computer Science: A Guide for Educators and Their Allies. We show how we intentionally sought to bridge the gap between research and practice in developing our guide to create a resource that supports CS teachers on their equity learning journeys. Project background Our book was published under the collective authorship of the Computer Science Educational Justice Collective (CS-EJC). The CS-EJC is comprised of three teams with different areas of expertise related to equity in CS Ed: DiversFYI, a consultancy focused on racial literacy; the Creative Technology Research Lab at the University of Florida focused on leveraging Universal Design for Learning to disrupt ableism in CS Ed; and the Participating in Literacies and Computer Science team focused on supporting bi/mult ilingual learners in CS Ed. We collaborated from 2020-2025 to iteratively develop summer workshops and school-year professional development sessions as part of a CS -focused professional development (PD) initiative for New York City Public School teachers. Recognizing the local impact of our holistic, equity-centered PD, we decided to take what we had learned from our collaboration and create a new resource that could be available to CS educators across the United States. We began meeting in 2021 and wrote most of the book between 2022 and 2024. We led multiple rounds of revision, feedback, and beta testing during the 2024 -2025 school year and officially launched the book with our original New York City partner teachers in May 2025. Strategies to bridge research and practice Our primary goal was to create a guide that would be accessible and useful for CS educators with different roles and commitments. To achieve these goals, we were intentional in the design elements we incorporated into the book, how we engaged in our feedback and revision process, and our publishing decisions. 2692 Design elements We designed the book to address barriers that may make research inaccessible for teachers. We intentionally integrated our team’s expertise to create a holistic resource that addresses many challenges that teachers face in classrooms. The first four chapters provide a foundation of diversity, equity, and inequity in CS Ed. The remainder of the book expands on issues related to race, language, and ableism, offering strategies for equity- oriented CS Ed. This connected approach emphasizes the interrelatedness of inequity and the intersectional approach needed for transformative CS Ed. We also implemented rhetorical and design features to support teacher engagement. Although our work was grounded in equit y-oriented CS and Learning Sciences theory, we intentionally adopted a more conversational, less academic tone throughout the book, avoiding extensive use of academic jargon and including a glossary and definitions for key terms. Each chapter also contains reflection questions and implications for practice to directly link theory and research with practice. Chapter 5 offers an example of how we concretely illustrated the discussion of abstract ideas. It introduces the theoretical constructs of intersectionality (Crenshaw, 1989, 1991) and multi -layered societal oppression (ideological, institutional, interpersonal, internalized; Bell, 2013; Chinook Fund, n.d.). These theories help teachers interpret what is happening in their classrooms but are often presented in dense and abstract ways that may feel ina ccessible or irrelevant. To address this, Chapter 5 is framed around myths, or common narratives that teachers may hear in connection with CS Ed. Each myth is then debunked by applying theoretical ideas to current CS Ed scenarios. These elements lower barr iers to accessing the book’s content and provide immediate ways for educators to apply their learning to their classroom contexts. Feedback and revision process In our feedback and revision process, we worked to intentionally center rather than sideline teacher voices and expertise. After the book was drafted, we reached out to the New York City Public Schools teachers we had worked with earlier. 25 of them agreed to provide written feedback and participate in focus groups on the book’s content. Teachers’ insights helped us consider different intended audiences and tailor the book’s structure to meet these anticipated needs. For instance, we broke each original chapter into shorter chapters to make the content easier to reference on a need -to-know basis. One of the teachers’ most significant contributions were the stories they provided from their own classrooms that illustrated concepts discussed in the book. With permission and attribution, we incorporated these examples as anchors in each chapter , weaving in teachers’ own words throughout the book. This key addition showed how real teachers applied research to their own practice, building bridges for readers to follow. After revising the book based on teacher feedback, we beta -tested it in three CS teacher education courses, two at New York University and one at SUNY- Buffalo. The book was assigned as a required course reading, and 12 students provided written feedback on their experience using the book. Our beta- testers consistently identified the teacher stories as their favorite and most impactful element of the book. The beta-testers themselves also helped us further refine the book, offering incisive comments that enabled us to nuance our arguments. For instance, one student provided insights into current sociopolitical dynamics related to named languages like Chinese that helped us clarify our terminology (see Chapters 11 and 12). Publication approach We sought to avoid gatekeeping mechanisms that restrict access to knowledge in academia and in CS. We committed to making the book free and open- access instead of behind an academic paywall largely inaccessible to K-12 educators. To that end, we published the book via the SUNY- Buffalo Pressbooks platform as an Open Educational Resource. Pressbooks offered a number of affordances (e.g., accessibility features, multiple formats to increase availability) that allowed us to maintain our equity focus. A second key decision was our choice to publish the book under a Creative Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0) license. Because equity work is an ongoing process that changes over time, the CC license allows the book to become a communal resource where the field can update details like language and elaborate on other issues relevant to equity in CS Ed (e.g., gender) that we did not address due to our team’s resource constraints. Additionally, we look forward to how readers will remix and adapt the book to tailor it to meet local community contexts and needs. Significance The CS-EJC represents a group of scholars committed to transforming CS Ed to achieve its equitable potential. Through intentional efforts to design, revise, and publish our educational resource in ways that bridge between research and practice, we hope our work will sustain teachers in their CS equity efforts. Similarly, we hope that our design approach offers insights into centering equity issues in content creation and publication that can be generative for the broader Learning Sciences community, contributing to ongoing conversations with researchers and practitioners about creating learning spaces where every student can belong and thrive. 2693 References Bell, J. abstract: This mixed -methods study examines how a week- long residential cybersecurity camp integrating generative AI (GenAI) tools influenced underrepresented minority girls’ cybersecurity knowledge, self -efficacy, and interest. Thirty -three middle -grade participan ts engaged in cybersecurity lessons and created GenAI informational videos for local nonprofits using ChatGPT and HeyGen AI. Pre - and post-tests revealed significant gains in knowledge and self-efficacy. Qualitative analysis showed growing confidence and real -world application. Findings suggest GenAI -integrated informal education builds technical knowledge and confidence among underrepresented youth.

abstract: This pilot study explored the potential of an AI-powered simulation to support learning in nursing transitional care . Two nursing students and two nursing educators engaged with the prototype and evaluated its usability using the System Usability Scale (SUS). Findings indicated a generally positive perception , highlighting the simulation's opportunity to foster clinical reasoning and learner engagement. Participants also identified areas for improvement, such as instructional scaffolding and interface design. Insights are discussed through a lens of situated cognition, emphasizing how AI-powered simulations can advance experiential learning while underscoring the need for iterative design to optimize usability and educational effectiveness.

abstract: This study examines how fourth- grade students engage in mathematical thinking while playing non -digital fraction games, with and without teacher facilitation. Conducted within a four -year Research -Practice Partnership, the Games Time project embeds biweekly 30minute game sessions in 3rd- and 4th-grade classrooms to promote equitable, engaging math learning without pull-out intervention. Using video analysis from a design research framework, we compared student discourse and manipulative use across six game sessions. Findings reveal that students engage in meaningful mathematical reasoning in both conditions, though teacher presence extends structured verbal engagement and mathematical discourse, while unsupervised play encourages exploratory intera ction with manipulatives. This work contributes to growing research on non- digital math games, offering low -cost, inclusive strategies for addressing unfinished learning and fostering student agency in mathematics classrooms.

abstract: Effective feedback is essential for supporting student learning in complex tasks such as scientific modeling, yet teachers often struggle to provide high -quality feedback. Overall, participants regarded the feedback as promising. They valued the feedback’s degree of detail, supportive tone, and potential to deepen teachers’ knowledge and enrich classroom discussions . Participants also raised important concerns about the feedback’s alignment with instructional contexts, length, and readability.

abstract: A semi-formal learning group of four doctoral students and one faculty member in art education met biweekly over two years (2023- 2025) to share artworks, written reflections, and personal narratives. Qualitative analysis produced three initial design conjectures: lightweight routines that stabilize participation without pressure, emotion -centered feedback that foregrounds empath y over correction, and shared documentation that links private reflection to public pedagogy.

title: Playful Learning: Debugging in Secondary STEM

abstract: Research demonstrates that playfulness can support learning. Yet, in secondary settings, play is understudied; instead, playfulness is often discouraged as leading to “off-task” behavior. Here, we propose that playfulness can (a) be generative for STEM learning in ways that are unanticipated by the student, teacher, and curriculum, and (b) encourage persistence in students’ explorations. To illustrate these affordances, we present a case in which a 6th grade student, Hunter, playfully engaged in STEM modeli ng. We argue that his playful stance is a resource for STEM learning. Objectives, purpose, and literature review Research demonstrates that playfulness can support learning. A playful mindset allows an individual to “see situations and activities as containing possibilities for leading, exploring, and enjoying” (Mardell et al., 2023, p. 17). Playfulness encourages exploration by promoting enjoyment while reducing the seriousness of consequences (Bateson, 2014; Bruner, 1983; Pellegrini, 2011). In early childhood, play is recognized as a developmental necessity that supports learning and socialization (Paley, 2007; Piaget, 1945; Vygotsky, 1978). The benefits of playfulness extend to adulthood—in professional science, play enables creativity, innovation, and discovery (Bateson, 2014; Erickson, 1976; Feynman, 2010; Maurois, 1959; Watson, 1968). Yet, in secondary school settings, play is understudied (Dean et al., 2025; Johnston et al., 2023; Parker et al., 2022). In such settings (e.g., middle schools, high schools), playfulness is often discouraged as leading to “off-task” behavior. A significant body of research instead focuses on helping children develop skills and dispositions that enable them to stay “on task” by setting goals toward objectives and evaluating their progress toward their goals (Näykki et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024; Ochs et al., 2024). When secondary STEM education research does consider classroom play, it often focuses on guided play (e.g., structured interventions, such as games; Hirsh-Pasek et al., 2020) that scaffold toward specific learning objectives (e.g., Kanter et al., 2011). Yet designing guided play can be challenging, because aiming toward specific goals can violate principles of play (e.g., that play is enjoyable/voluntary, or that play prioritizes means over ends; Pellegrini, 2011). Rather than focusing on play as an intervention, we instead consider how adopting a playful stance can be a resource for secondary STEM learning. We propose that playfulness can (a) be generative for STEM learning in ways that are unanticipated by the student, teacher, and curriculum, and (b) encourage persistence in students’ explorations. To illustra te these affordances, we present a case in which a 6th grade student, Hunter, playfully engaged in STEM modeling activities. We focus on his interaction with his computational model about guppies (fish) and their environment, and we trace the way that his playful stance supported generative learning about science and computational thinking, despite Hunter’s repeated encounters with potentially frustrating bugs. We argue that his playful stance is a resource for STEM learning and debugging.

title: Child-Adult Interviews as Sites for Relational Transformation
citation: Kathryn Lanouette, Mallika Scott (2026). Child-Adult Interviews as Sites for Relational Transformation. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Lanouette, K. & Scott, M.

abstract: Teaching is inherently relational, yet structures of schooling often create distance between teachers and children, making it difficult to authentically listen and find connection. We explore new configurations of adult -child interviews in math and scienc e with a focus on creating spaces for listening and mutuality. We find that these configurations provide opportunities for prospective teachers to be amazed by children’s brilliance, to reconsider their teaching practice, and to engage in playful, reciprocal exchanges with children.

citation: Kay E. Ramey, Bianca Schamberger, Zahra Baradaran Shoraka, Mandy Dunphy, Amy Crowell, Yetunde A. Mabadeje, Phillip Dixon, Jay Gorsh (2026). Distributed Sensemaking Among Formal and Informal Educators Working Together to Support Nature-based Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: Nature-based learning has many documented benefits, but it is inequitably accessible to learners because of infrastructural barriers , including lack of professional learning for educators. This study brings together 33 informal and formal educators and examines how they learned with and from one another and the more -than-human world during nature -based professional learning. Findings from analysis of videos, focus groups, surveys, and field notes show how educators shared distributed expertise and engaged in distributed sensemaking.

abstract: Coherence supports meaningful teacher professional learning. While micro- credentialing offers flexibility, it may lead to fragmentation. abstract: In this work, we explore how three types of free play toys (blocks, clay, and stuffed animals) can serve as tangible manipulatives for computer science learning. We propose that such toys act as entry points to engagement and can then be scaffolded and guided by teachers to help transition children from free play to guided playful learning. Drawing on three cases, we suggest that allowing natural exploration and play can allow children to develop authentic, personal connections to their learning. Once these connections are established, subsequent scaffolding and support can deepen their understanding of new concepts.

abstract: This study examine d how embodied processes in augmented reality (AR) support geometric reasoning by distinguishing among pragmatic , epistemic, and complementary actions. High school students (N=14) reasoned geometry conjectures using GeoGebra-MR. We developed a video coding framework to classify the cognitive functionality of embodied processes. Findings show ed that AR manipulations provided cognitive offloading, while gestures coordinated mental operations. Deductive reasoning elicited all action types, whereas inductive reasoning relied mainly on pragmatic and epistemic actions.

abstract: This study analyzed learner experiences in a graduate course on universal design. Using network analysis on reflections from 15 students, we identified two distinct engagement patterns. One cluster emphasized transformation and identity development while s truggling with technical tools. The other valued structured learning theory and community. Findings suggest that courses preparing learning designers should intentionally support a complex diversity of learning experiences.

title: Small Scientists, Big Insights: What First Graders Teach Us About Science Assessment Design

abstract: This study applies Evidence -Centered Design (ECD) to develop first-grade science assessments aligned with NGSS and early learners’ needs. Observations of five teachers and student responses revealed key design considerations: scaffolds for interpreting graphics, multimodal response options to account for students’ language and literacy variability, and adjustments accounting for development of fine motor skills. Classroom management also shaped task administration. Findings show ECD supports practical, developmentally appropriate assessments that reduce barriers, encourage peer discourse, and authentically capture young learners’ scientific understanding.

citation: Selena Steinberg, Joshua Danish, Nitasha Mathayas, Mengxi Zhou (2026). Many Ways of “Being” a Beaver: Students’ Perceptions of Technology-Enhanced and Dramatized Embodiment in Science. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: There are many ways of embodying a beaver, including through mixed -reality technology and through acting in theatrical skits. In this study, fifth grade students engaged in both to learn about wetland ecosystems. We conducted a thematic analysis of student interviews to understand their perceptions of each kind of embodied activity. We present four themes from their reflections: perspective taking, agency, learning, and the socioemotional experience , and discuss how these perceptions can inform embodied science education.

title: “A Beautiful Little Thing for You”: Emergent Data Visualizations as Contextually Responsive Invitations to Data Reasoning
citation: Leah F. Rosenbaum, Cody Pritchard (2026). “A Beautiful Little Thing for You”: Emergent Data Visualizations as Contextually Responsive Invitations to Data Reasoning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Rosenbaum, L. F. & Pritchard, C.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Though familiar to experts, the use of exclusively canonical data visualizations may foreclose reasoning opportunities consistent with everyday experience. We share an episode of teachers creating a display with materials from their surroundings. In debating this display’s status as a data visualization, teachers reflected on their criteria for data visualizations and on mediators to their learners’ engagement with data and science. We highlight emergent dat a visualizations as potential resources for contextually responsive reasoning with data. Motivation and background Consistent with sound pedagogical practice, data science education seeks to position data as relevant to learners’ lives (e.g., Weiland & Williams, 2024; Wilkerson & Polman, 2020). But many teacher learning opportunities focus on canonical data visualizati ons—such as bar charts and scatter plots —that may foreclose data reasoning processes that support learning by leveraging everyday experience (Bertling & Hodge, 2025). We share an episode in which teachers in a professional development workshop constructed an emergent data display (Figure 1, top) by gathering objects from their immediate surroundings. In evaluating this display as a potential data visualization, teachers surfaced their criteria for data visualizations and considered mediators of their students’ engagement with data and science. Similar to design perspectives that position environmental configurations as sources of information (Lidwell et al., 2010; Figure 1, bottom), we conjecture that emergent data displays could serve as contextually responsive invitations for learners to reason with and about data. abstract: What happens to student -made artifacts once making ends? We have rich accounts of fabrication, but rarely follow objects out the door. We introduce object trajectories as a lens for tracing the social and epistemic lives of artifacts after creation. Drawing on constructionism, material culture, and critical theories of visibility, we develop three dimensions: perceptual seeding, recognition, and visibility, and argue tha t following objects reveals forms of learning that stopping at the moment of making cannot reach.

abstract: This study examines how PreK–12 teacher leaders facilitate knowledge mobilization (KMb) in computer science (CS), acting as brokers between research and classroom practice. Based on interviews with 20 U.S. teachers, it highlights how professional developme nt (PD) supports teachers in applying research, integrating emerging technologies, and navigating systemic barriers. Findings emphasize the importance of positioning teachers as active agents who use, share, and co-construct knowledge, and recommend participatory, iterative PD models that foster collaboration and shape the broader direction of CS education.

Students progress from collecting and analyzing data towards developing personally-relevant narratives, connecting community priorities through data storytelling.

Our co-design partners span curators, artists, and public program participants.

title: What can Computer Science Education Learn from Mathematics Problem Solving Pedagogy?
citation: Laila El-Hamamsy, Morgane Chevalier, Patrick Wang, Engin Bumbacher (2026). What can Computer Science Education Learn from Mathematics Problem Solving Pedagogy?. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: El-Hamamsy, L., Chevalier, M., Wang, P., & Bumbacher, E.

tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Computer Science (CS) offers a promising context to develop transferable Problem Solving (PS) competencies through Computational PS (CPS), yet its instructional foundations are still emerging. As such, we draw on closely related mathematics PS research to advance a conceptual basis for CPS pedagogy and transfer 3 key elements. First, we adopt the concept of “rich” PS activities to CPS, but adapt it through a decision -making lens that views PS as navigating multiple decision paths, which we define by Computational Thinking dimensions. Second, we propose a 4- layer CPS activity design framework organized around design factors that shape a problem’s decision-making space, and integrating classroom discourse — central in mathematics PS education — as a novel layer. Third, we present teacher moves that help preserve and leverage this richness in the design and implementation of CPS activities. Together, these contributions advance a theoretical foundation for CPS pedagogy.

These preliminary findings offer a new perspective on the field's developing intellectual identity.

title: “I Didn’t Drink Any Water That Day”: Marginalized Children’s Understanding of Climate Change–Induced Water Issues in NOLA
citation: Ayça K. Fackler, Gülçin Kaplan (2026). “I Didn’t Drink Any Water That Day”: Marginalized Children’s Understanding of Climate Change–Induced Water Issues in NOLA. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Fackler, A. K. & Kaplan, G.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: Climate change education in the early years of schooling is often overlooked, even though children already experience its effects in their daily lives. In New Orleans, where histories of marginalization are tied to place, the impacts of climate change– related water pollution are both immediate and lived. This qualitative case study draws on a justice-oriented, critical pedagogy of place to examine how kindergarten, second- grade, and fourth- grade students made sense of water quality issues through an interdisciplinary unit focused on Lake Pontchartrain. Children’s responses ranged from personal accounts to affective reflections and critical commentaries on the challenges facing their communit ies. Findings highlight how justice-oriented, place -based climate education can help marginalized children connect disciplinary understanding with lived experience, fostering early awareness, care, and agency. Major issue addressed For children in and around New Orleans, Louisiana (NOLA), daily life is shaped by close ties to the lakes, estuaries, and wetlands that define the region’s livelihood, culture, and recreation (Colten, 2002). Yet these same connections make them and their families especially vulnerable to climate change impacts such as sea level rise, stronger hurricanes, water contamination, and flooding (Environmental Protection Agency, 2016). C limate change education in the early years has often been overlooked, even though children already encounter its effects in their everyday lives. This study responds to this gap by examining how marginalized children made sense of water quality issues in disciplinary, affective, and ethical terms through Our Water, Our Future—a project that engaged kindergarten, second-grade, and fourth-grade students in an interdisciplinary, placemaking unit centered on Lake Pontchartrain in NOLA, a city where histories of marginalization are inscribed in place and community (Fackler et al., 2026) . W e ask: What types of understanding emerge for marginalized children in an interdisciplinary placemaking unit on water quality? Theoretical approach Justice-centered, critical pedagogy of place Justice-centered science pedagogy, grounded in culturally sustaining pedagogy, positions learners as transformative intellectuals by weaving together equitable learning expectations, antiracist teaching, and agency (Morales-Doyle, 2017). Central to this vision is treating marginalized children as producers of knowledge and culture who develop complexity in their thinking, commitment to their communities, and credibility as scientifically capable individuals, reimagining science education as a catalyst for both academic achievement and social transformation (Adah Miller & Fackler, 2024). This vision aligns with the critical pedagogy of place, which situates learning within local communities and issues (Gruenewald, 2003). Placemaking pedagogies emphasize experiential, multidisciplinary learning that connects disciplinary knowledge to the attributes of a place, fostering ecological literacy and care for the environment (Visintainer, 2023). Meaning making in science as stance We conceptualize meaning making as a layered process through which children interpret events, discourse, feelings, and artifacts in relation to place, knowledge, and experience. Drawing on Goodwin’s (2007) framework, we understand participation in meaning- making as stance, whereby children continually shape their roles as intellectual, moral, and social actors. These multidimensional forms of meaning -making, encompassing instrumental, epistemic, affective, moral, and cooperative stances, reflect how children embody, explore, and negotiate their understandings in interaction with others, places, and experiences.

Using Cultural -Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) to analyze the collaboration between one STEM coach and researcher, data from professional learning sessions, videos, and artifacts were analyzed through thematic analysis. Findings revealed that empowering language functioned as a mediating tool in transforming traditional hierarchies and encouraging collaborative partnerships.

title: Cognitive Flexibility in the Acceptance of AI Tools in Mathematics Education within the Framework of the Technology Acceptance Model: The Mediating Role of Technostress

abstract: This study examines the role of cognitive flexibility in mathematics teachers’ acceptance of AI -based tools and the mediating effect of technostress. Using a correlational design with 127 teachers, findings revealed that cognitive flexibility reduces technostress and increases technology acceptance. Mediation analysis showed that technostress partially mediates this relationship. Results suggest that cognitive flexibility facilitates adaptation to technological innovations, while technostress acts as a barrier, highlighting the importance of supporting teachers’ psychological readiness for AI integration.

title: Learning by Teaching an LLM: A New Approach to Writing Instruction
citation: Sydney Miller, Nigel Bosch (2026). Learning by Teaching an LLM: A New Approach to Writing Instruction. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Miller, S. & Bosch, N.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This preliminary study investigates how different instructional modalities – i.e., video lecture versus learning by teaching (LbT) with a large language model (LLM) – influence students’ understanding and application of rhetorical strategies in argumentative writing. Using a within-subjects design, 46 participants completed both a video condition and a LbT condition wherein they instructed an LLM -powered “student” on rhetorical strategies. Each session covered a distinct set of three strategies, with order and content counterbalanced. Learning was evaluated through pre -tests, immediate post- tests, delayed post -tests, and post -lesson essays. Participants used more rhetorical strategies in essays written after the LbT condition (2.70 vs. 2.43 on average) and made fewer errors on immediate (1 vs. 4) and delayed (7 vs. 15) post-tests. Participants who completed the video condition second showed a greater decline in strategy use (55% vs. 29%). T hese findings introduce a replicable experimental framework for studying LLMs as interactive tools for writing instruction. Purpose Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in educational contexts, raising concerns about how they shape student learning in writing. While some scholars argue that generative AI can support reflection and metacognition when used intentionally (Anders, 2023; De Matas, 2023; Graham, 2023; Luckin et al., 2016), others warn that these tools may encourage product -oriented writing and outsourcing of cognitive effort (Cotton et al., 2024; Vee, 2023) . To date, most empirical work positions LLMs as feedback providers or drafting aids, emphasizing textual output rather than deeper cognitive engagement (Akiba & Garte, 2024; Hansen et al., 2025). Learning by teaching (LbT) offers an alternative framework, as explaining concepts and responding to questions can strengthen understanding and transfer (Duran, 2017; Fiorella & Mayer, 2013; Lachner et al., 2021; Roscoe & Chi, 2008), including in AI-based teachable agent systems such as Betty’s Brain (Okita & Schwartz, 2013; Segedy et al., 2015) . Recent advances in LLMs make it possible to extend LbT to open- ended domains like writing through conversational interaction (Malik et al., 2024; Salewski et al., 2023; White et al., 2023). This preliminary study compares a traditional lecture condition with an LbT condition in which students teach rhetorical strategies to an LLM-powered agent, examining post-test performance, strategy use, and essay outcomes.

abstract: This study begins to examine how co -design has been enacted in different ways across two decades of Learning Sciences research. Network analysis of 136 coded ICLS papers (2004–2025) revealed three modular configurations of practice linked by bridging nodes such as museums. The analysis demonstrates how open data on research and bibliometrics can help the pluralistic field of the Learning Sciences better understand and shape how and why co- design is deployed in research and practice.

title: Work in Progress: Training STEM Graduate Students to Collaborate with Stakeholders to Address Socio- scientific Issues
citation: Christina Silva, Jessica Karch (2026). Work in Progress: Training STEM Graduate Students to Collaborate with Stakeholders to Address Socio- scientific Issues. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Socio-scientific issues (SSIs) are complex, real -world problems that arise at the intersection of science and society . SSIs cannot be solved by one discipline alone and should engage stakeholders as part of the problem -solving process. As STEM graduate students are prepared to be scientists and address SSIs, it is imperative that they are trained to collaborate with stakeholders. This scoping review examines how STEM graduate students are trained to collaborate with stakeholders to address SSIs.

title: Middle School Student Science Practices in a Justice-Oriented Wildfire Science Unit
citation: Spencer Eusden, Li Ke (2026). Middle School Student Science Practices in a Justice-Oriented Wildfire Science Unit. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Eusden, S. & Ke, L.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
abstract: The growing impacts of climate change -driven disasters and environmental issues on communities create a compelling case for using these issues as anchoring phenomena to support both science learning and disaster resilience. This poster shares results from a co - produced middle school wildfire science unit. Results include 1) How self-situation in localized data sets shaped student conclusions and 2) How students incorporated knowledge of their community when analyzing data and constructing evidence -based arg uments about wildfire resilience. Poster proposal Climate change-driven disasters and environmental issues (CCDDEI’s) such as wildfires, hurricanes, and extreme weather are increasingly disrupting the lives of both students and their communities (Benvolenza & DeRignez, 2019; Lambrou et al., 2023). Moreover, the impacts of these issues, especially wildfire, are likely to become more severe and unjust in the coming decades (Davies et al., 2018; Méndez et al, 2020; Qui et al., 2025, Smith et al., 2020). Youth are vulnerable to trauma from increasingly destructive wildfires (Brown et al., 2019) and missed school days from school closures due to hazardous air quality (Santana et al., 2021). However, youth can play needed roles in addressing wildfire-related (Codreanu et al., 2014; Cox et al., 2019) and other environmental justice issues through participatory action learning (Ballard et al., 2017; Morales-Doyle & Frausto, 2019). There is potential for using CCDDEI’s as both anchoring phenomena for science learning and pathways to support youth and community resilience to these issues. However, how instructional materials incorporate such phenomena shapes whether the materials help equitably support student learning (Penuel et al., 2022) and resilience to these disruptive issues (Condreau et al., 2014; Park et al., 2024) or reinforce existing inequities in both education (National Academies, 2025) and disaster resilience (Lambrou et al., 2023). This poster draws on the socio-spatial justice work of Tan et al. (2022) to explore how analysis of the spatial aspects of wildfire risk can be used to support students’ engagement in justice- oriented science learning. Empirical research on how students construct arguments and use da ta science practices in instructional materials that blend science learning and community resilience goals can further discussion on effective student learning in these contexts. This paper shares results from a co-produced curriculum pilot that blends western scientific knowledge of wildfire and justice-oriented data sources that center students' perspectives on the impact of wildfire on their community. Research question: How do middle school students construct evidence-based arguments and use data science practices in a justice-oriented wildfire science unit?

title: Building Bodies, Building Minds: A Hands-On STEM Activity in Biomechanical Engineering for Elementary Students

abstract: This study examines how 10 elementary students engaged in a biomedical engineering activity. Students built spine models, designed prosthetic discs, and tested materials through compression and bending tasks. Reflexive thematic analysis of video and survey data revealed four themes: engineering mindset development, embodied anatomical exploration, material testing through interaction, and social collaboration. The findings suggest that hands - on activities grounded in distributed cognition can support students’ engineering mindsets and understanding of anatomy and material properties.

title: What Does It Mean to Be a “Quantum Kind of Person”? Identity Formation in an Emerging STEM Field
citation: Raquel Coelho, Eliza Callahan, Christian Schunn (2026). What Does It Mean to Be a “Quantum Kind of Person”? Identity Formation in an Emerging STEM Field. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Coelho, R., Callahan, E., & Schunn, C.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Quantum information science is an emerging field largely absent from K-12 settings, creating challenges for identity formation. Through cognitive interviews with six high school students and five undergraduate students, we examine how students evaluate quantum identity. Identity and participation in STEM Researchers have conceptualized ‘science identity’ as comprising multiple dimensions, including a sense of community belonging and recognition (Carlone & Johnson, 2007; Vincent- Ruz & Schunn, 2018). Yet, STEM identity research has mostly focused on established disciplines such as physics and engineering (Liu & Schunn, 2020). Emerging STEM areas such as quantum information science (QIS) present a different context within which to explore questions of STEM identity. As a rapidly developing field at the intersection of physics, computer science, and information science (Nielsen & Chuang, 2010), QIS is largely absent from K -12 curricula (Holincheck et al., 2024). Identity research suggests that perceptions of recognition by others are central to developing one’s identity (Vincent -Ruz & Schunn, 2018), and we suggest that identities linked to emerging disciplinary areas may be particularly fragile or difficult to construct. Given students’ limited exposure to QIS, we are interested in investigating what rationales student s might use to determine whether they are “a quantum kind of person” and/or whether they believe others view them as “a quantum kind of person.” Understanding these rationales matters both theoretically and practically. Theoretically, it is unclear whether students draw on perceived math/science ability (Carlone & Johnson, 2007), stereotypes about “hard” or “cutting-edge” science (Master et al., 2016), media representations (Steinke, 2005), or identification with related fields (Hazari et al., 2010) . Practically, insights into these rationales can inform identity measur es that capture early, tentative identification , and guide the design of experiences that counter exclusionary stereotypes and connect quantum concepts to students’ existing interests. Using cognitive interviews with high school and undergraduate students , we ask: What reasons and justifications do students provide for identifying (or not identifying) as “a quantum kind of person,” and/or for believing that others see them (or don’t see them) this way?

title: Sequencing Immersive Simulations for Cybersecurity: Task Complexity and Efficiency
citation: Taehyun Kim, Hyunju Oh, Mustafa Shaky, Janise McNair, Rui Guo, Wanli Xing, Sandip Ray (2026). Sequencing Immersive Simulations for Cybersecurity: Task Complexity and Efficiency. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: VR is increasingly used for safety training, yet how the order of instruction and VR learning influences outcomes remains unclear. We invited students (N = 44) to complete two short vehicle security lessons using PowerPoint and VR materials presented in different orders. Although the order did not significantly affect test scores, students who studied PowerPoint first tended to perform better with fewer attempts, while those starting with VR often showed confusion by revisiting nonessential panels.

title: Supporting Children’s Systems Thinking about Climate Change
citation: Qingna Jin (2026). Supporting Children’s Systems Thinking about Climate Change. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Jin, Q.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This case study examined two Grade 5 climate- learning scaffolds: teacher -guided causal mapping and water-cycle-based feedback loop instruction. Analysis of classroom video, student artefacts, and interviews showed that causal mapping expanded one- step claims into mechanistic chains but rarely produced loop closure or delays. Feedback loop instruction supported recognition of cyclicity and reinforcing loops, yet students still struggled with balancing loops, time lags, and energy-budget reasoning. Rationale and background Systems thinking equips learners to interpret complex, dynamic phenomena by tracing interdependencies, mechanisms, and feedbacks (Ben‑Zvi Assaraf & Orion, 2005; Hmelo‑Silver et al., 2017). Climate change is a paradigmatic “system problem,” marked by nonlinear causality, delays, and reinforcing loops (Roychoudhury et al., 2017; Sterman & Booth Sweeney, 2002). Yet research shows that elementary students often identify components and simple cause –effect links but struggle with multi‑step causal chains and feedback loops (Evagorou et al., 2009; Mambrey et al., 2020; Tripto et al., 2016). Despite growing emphasis on systems thinking in policy and curriculum, there remains a practical gap: classroom‑tested, developmentally appropriate scaffolds that help younger learners move beyond linear reasoning (Gilissen et al., 2020; Leung et al., 2024). This study responds by co‑designing with teachers two complementary, curriculum‑aligned interventions —causal mapping and feedback‑loop instruction—and examining how each supports students’ systems thinking in the context of climate change. Conceptual framework This study builds on the Components –Mechanisms–Phenomena (CMP) framework (Hmelo -Silver et al., 2017), which guides learners to recognize system components (C), infer mechanisms (M) that connect components, and explain emergent phenomena (P). To deepen causal reasoning, the study integrates insights from Ben-Zvi Assaraf and Orion’s (2005) hierarchical systems thinking model, which progresses from identifying system components and simple relations, to recognizing dynamic feedback loops and predicting future s ystem states. Drawing on prior findings that young learners’ systems thinking develops nonlinearly and contextually (Mambrey et al., 2020; Liu & Hmelo -Silver, 2009), this study designed two distinct instructional pathways: (1) Causal mapping is expected to lengthen and clarify causal chains (e.g., “cutting trees for a mall → fewer sinks for CO₂ → higher atmospheric CO₂ → intensified greenhouse effect → warming”); and (2) Feedback-loop instruction leverages the familiar water cycle to foreground cyclicity and transfer those ideas to climate feedbacks (e.g., ice– albedo feedback). Research purpose and questions The study investigates how two different instructional approaches —causal mapping and feedback -loop-based instruction—support Grade 5 students’ development of systems thinking skills in the context of climate change. • RQ1: How do students’ causal explanations evolve when engaged in teacher -guided causal mapping? • RQ2: How do students demonstrate understanding of cyclic and feedback relationships after instruction anchored in the water cycle? • RQ3: What similarities and differences emerge across the two approaches in strengthening students’ abilities to identify components, articulate mechanisms, and explain phenomena (CMP)? This study Participants and context Two elementary science teachers and their Grade 5 classes (Class A: 17 students; Class B: 16 students; ages 10 – 11) from a public school in Eastern Canada participated. Both teachers had experience with inquiry‑based instruction and co‑designed lesson sequences with the research team. Each intervention ran for six weeks (one 90‑minute session per week). • Class A (Causal Mapping Intervention). Lessons centered on tracing multi‑step chains from concrete, local actions (e.g., driving gas‑powered vehicles; cutting trees to build a shopping mall) to broader 2797 climate outcomes. Students constructed causal maps collaboratively and iteratively revised their diagrams with teacher prompts. • Class B (Feedback‑Loop Intervention). Lessons began with the water cycle (already in the elementary curriculum), emphasizing cyclicity and interdependence. The teacher then introduced climate feedbacks (e.g., glacier melt → reduced albedo → increased absor ption → further warming → more melt), supporting students to identify loop structure and effects over time.

title: Participatory Narratives for AI Learning: Integrating Self-Efficacy, Agency, and Ethical Reflection
citation: Jessica Vandenberg, Bradford Mott, Carlos Penilla, James Lester, Elizabeth Ozer (2026). Participatory Narratives for AI Learning: Integrating Self-Efficacy, Agency, and Ethical Reflection. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Vandenberg, J., Mott, B., Penilla, C., Lester, J., & Ozer, E.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This work presents a theory-driven design framework grounded in Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) and informed by participatory learning perspectives to support middle school students’ AI literacy and career interests. Implemented in a narrative- centered game- based learning environment, the framework connects SCT’s motivational constructs ( self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and goals ) with participatory mechanisms such as role -based engagement, consequential decision-making, and ethical reflection. Findings from a pilot study with middle school students illustrate how narrative participation supports the development of self-efficacy, AI understanding, and emerging career awareness.

title: An Unstructured Way: How Students Learn to Provide Feedback in a Reading Club
citation: Shiyao Wei, Xiang Li, Zhichun Liu (2026). An Unstructured Way: How Students Learn to Provide Feedback in a Reading Club. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Wei, S., Li, X., & Liu, Z.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: While peer feedback is beneficial for students’ learning, students a re not always ready to provide constructive feedback to their peers. Prior studies have used cognitive scaffolding, such as review forms , to support students ’ feedback provision, yet the social context of learning has been overlooked. In the current study, we investigate how students naturally learn to provide feedback within a reading club. Over ten weeks of participation in receiving and giv ing feedback, students’ feedback became more specific and targeted to their peers’ work. By participati ng in community activities, students sha red perspectives and knowledge with their peers and found their own ways to provide constructive feedback.

title: Interdisciplinary Contextualizing in Data Storytelling about Immigration Topics
citation: Joseph Polman, Trang C. Tran, Katherine M. Miller, Chad Dorsey (2026). Interdisciplinary Contextualizing in Data Storytelling about Immigration Topics. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Polman, J., Tran, T. C., Miller, K. M., & Dorsey, C.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Social & Civic Studies

abstract: Case studies illuminate interdisciplinary contextualization in data storytelling, within the context of curriculum modules engaging middle school students in data -infused, PBL drawing from disciplines of social studies, English Language Arts, and data science. We address the questions: How do students tell stories with data, and how can data storytelling contribute to students’ data agency and identity? We discuss the potential of telling empirical stories with data and integrating rigorous data analysis with humanistic learning.

title: Computational Qualitative Analysis of Elementary Students’ Understanding of Data and Data Science
citation: Mengxi Zhou (2026). Computational Qualitative Analysis of Elementary Students’ Understanding of Data and Data Science. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Zhou, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study used a computational qualitative approach to examine how a data unit designed around elementary students’ lived, emotional, and embodied experiences impacted their understanding of data. Pre/post-test responses were analyzed using semantic similarity and qualitative open coding to connect measurable patterns with interpretive nuances. Results showed that students expanded their understanding of data and recognized its role in daily life. The qualitative interoperation also identified specific design features for further video analysis.

title: Construal Level Theory of Psychological Distance: Preservice Teacher Learning in Artificial Intelligence-supported Simulations
citation: Chih-Pu Dai, Fengfeng Ke, Nuodi Zhang, Alex Barrett, Sherry Southerland, Saptarshi Bhowmik, Xin Yuan (2026). Construal Level Theory of Psychological Distance: Preservice Teacher Learning in Artificial Intelligence-supported Simulations. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: This study explores how preservice teachers engage with artificial intelligence (AI)- powered virtual students in VR classrooms, focusing on psychological distance and construal - level theory. Using a mixed- methods approach, we analyzed interaction data from 29 participants. Findings show higher levels of abstract thinking and temporal imme diacy during teaching decisions. These results highlight how cognitive distance influences pedagogical reasoning. Insights inform the design of AI agents in immersive environments, supporting adaptive teacher learning through reflective, experience-oriented simulations.

title: Exploring Strategies and Difficulties in Elementary Students’ Data Visualization Construction
citation: Bung-Woo Jun, Secil Caskurlu (2026). Exploring Strategies and Difficulties in Elementary Students’ Data Visualization Construction. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Jun, B. & Caskurlu, S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study used Epistemic Network Analysis to examine 6th-grade students' (n=39) strategies and difficulties in constructing data visualizations via CODAP. Findings show that students who successfully completed data visualization tasks utilized resourcing strategies , seeking help from teachers or peers, whereas non-completed students relied on deducing and trial-and-error strategy. These results emphasize the importance of verbal activities and social interaction in developing elementary students’ data visualization literacy.

title: Pathways to Hope in a Critical Place-Based Science Camp
citation: Tessaly Jen (2026). Pathways to Hope in a Critical Place-Based Science Camp. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Jen, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Youth’s hope has become a central concern as socioecological precarity and anxiety abound. I examined forms of hope youth developed in a critical place-based science camp, and in particular, what nurtured critical hope. Multiple pathways engendered critica l hope, with different youth emphasizing critique and reckoning with harms, focusing on collective action, and rejecting human-nature hierarchies. Findings have implications for designing for hope.

title: Emotional Equity in Education: Rethinking Social-Emotional Learning Across Cultures
citation: Balkhiya Amirkhanova (2026). Emotional Equity in Education: Rethinking Social-Emotional Learning Across Cultures. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Amirkhanova, B.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Social-emotional learning (SEL) is widely presented as a universal framework for student development. However, emotional learning is shaped by cultural values, social norms, and family practices. This conceptual paper introduces the notion of emotional equity , defined as the recognition of culturally diverse emotional norms in education. Drawing on literature from SEL, cultural psychology, and comparative education, the paper argues that educational equity must include emotional equity and that SEL should be understood as a culturally situated process.

title: From Classrooms to Communities: A Systems Framework for Social-Emotional Learning Policy
citation: Balkhiya Amirkhanova (2026). From Classrooms to Communities: A Systems Framework for Social-Emotional Learning Policy. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Amirkhanova, B.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This paper presents a systems -level framework for Social -Emotional Learning that extends beyond classrooms to encompass families, communities, and policy structures. Drawing on the learning sciences and socio- ecological systems theory, the study argues tha t conventional SEL initiatives often operate in isolation. Using examples from the United States and Kazakhstan, the paper highlights how differences in alignment shape children’s experiences. It introduces emotional equity to emphasize the need for more coherent and culturally responsive approaches to SEL.

title: Rubric-Guided Generative AI for Scalable Creativity Assessment in Educational Games
citation: Seyedahmad Rahimi, Hongming Li, Salah Esmaeiligoujar, Deniz Ercan (2026). Rubric-Guided Generative AI for Scalable Creativity Assessment in Educational Games. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Rahimi, S., Li, H., Esmaeiligoujar, S., & Ercan, D.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Assessing creativity at scale remains challenging in learning sciences. This study examined whether GPT-4o could assess creativity in 421 student-designed levels from Physics Playground. Using a structured rubric, GPT -4o ratings were compared with human raters. Results showed strong correlations (r = .74) with multimodal inputs, and reliability analyses showed consistent performance across runs. Findings suggest that rubric -guided LLMs can approximate human creativity judgments efficiently. This approach offers a promising method for scalable automated creativity assessment.

title: Theory Experience Network Analysis of Primary Source Projects
citation: Ananya Mahesh, Jonan Phillip Donaldson, Latham Girona, Kathleen Michelle Clark (2026). Theory Experience Network Analysis of Primary Source Projects. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Mahesh, A., Donaldson, J. P., Girona, L., & Clark, K. M.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study introduces theory experience network analysis (TENA), a proof -of- concept method for examining how principles from multiple learning theories manifest and interact within student learning experiences. We analyzed reflections from students in a mathematics course. Network analysis revealed four distinct clusters representing social constructivist, transformative learning, constructionist, and cognitive constructivist principles while demonstrating that theoretical principles operate as interconnect ed rather than isolated mechanisms. TENA offers an approach for understanding theory -practice relationships in complex learning environments.

title: A First Grader Making Sense of Graphs: A Knowledge-in-Pieces Account of Functional Thinking
citation: Mathías A. López, Susanne Strachota, Johyeon Chang, Bárbara M. Brizuela, Maria Blanton, Angela (2026). A First Grader Making Sense of Graphs: A Knowledge-in-Pieces Account of Functional Thinking. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We present the case of Lucca (pseudonym), a six -year-old who participated in three interviews before, during, and after a classroom teaching experiment on function graphs. We analyzed his reasoning by identifying the resources he drew on: seeds of algebraic thinking and resources tied to the graph. Lucca’s functional thinking can be understood through the lens of Knowledge in Pieces: recursive and functional reasoning was supported by his coordination of resources. As his functional thinking developed, the seeds he used remained consistent, but the resources tied to the graph he coordinated were different.

title: Metacognition, Epistemic Framing, and Knowledge Coordination: A Longitudinal Case Study of Learning in an Intro Biology Course
citation: Alex Waugh, Aeryn Vanderslik, Safana Ismael, Sheela Vemu, Mary Pat Wenderoth, Janet L. Branchaw, Jennifer H. Doherty (2026). Metacognition, Epistemic Framing, and Knowledge Coordination: A Longitudinal Case Study of Learning in an Intro Biology Course. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Waugh, A., Vanderslik, A., Ismael, S., Vemu, S., Wenderoth, M. P., Branchaw, J. L., & Doherty, J. H.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This longitudinal qualitative study examines learning mechanisms underlying conceptual knowledge development in a semester- long, high-structure undergraduate biology course. Drawing on coordination class, metacognition, and epistemic framing theories, we characterize how students developed knowledge underlying the core concept of gradient-driven flow (flux), a broadly applicable principle of physiological systems. Findings reveal a reciprocal relationship in which metacognitive actions and sensemaking epist emic frames promote knowledge development, while growing conceptual understanding fosters metacognitive regulation and sensemaking.

title: Integrating ChatGPT into Writing for a Doctoral STEM Course
citation: Cesar Delgado, Brayan Díaz, Stephen Trembath-Reichert, Elijah Keyes, Matthew Ferrell, Toluwalase Salako, Jessica Thorpe (2026). Integrating ChatGPT into Writing for a Doctoral STEM Course. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: Empirical research on how generative AI (genAI) is transforming academic writing in doctoral education remains scarce. This participatory study examined a STEM doctoral course where students used ChatGPT -4 at various stages. Students found genAI helpful with mechanics and structure, sensemaking, and literature review. This "hybrid AI -human writing process" enhanced both writing and AI literacy. Pedagogical insights are provided.

title: Beyond Symbols: Highlighting Multilingual Learners’ Mathematical Practices in Integrated STEM Space
citation: Esma N. Kahveci, Shakhnoza Kayumova (2026). Beyond Symbols: Highlighting Multilingual Learners’ Mathematical Practices in Integrated STEM Space. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
