tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: This study investigates how multilingual middle school students engaged in mathematical practice during a collaborative engineering design challenge in an integrated STEAM summer program. While mathematics in school contexts is often reduced to symbolic procedures, our analysis reveals that students engaged in rich mathematical practices through spatial reasoning, inference -in-action, generalization, and collaborative problem- solving. Grounded in sociocultural and embodied theories of learning, the study demonstrates how mathematics emerged as a dynamic, bodily, and socially mediated practice embedded in material interaction. Recognizing these practices expands conventional definitions of mathematics, foregrounds the contributions of students from nondominant communities, and underscores the importance of centering mathematics as a vibrant component of STEM education.

title: Developing and Applying a Framework for Teachers’ Learning Sciences Literacy: Conceptualization, Instrument Development, and Empirical Insights from a Nationwide Survey in China
citation: Peng Zhang, Yu Liu, Junjie Shang (2026). Developing and Applying a Framework for Teachers’ Learning Sciences Literacy: Conceptualization, Instrument Development, and Empirical Insights from a Nationwide Survey in China. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Zhang, P., Liu, Y., & Shang, J.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Understanding how teachers apply insights from the Learning Sciences is central to improving teaching quality. This study conceptualized and validated a framework for Teachers’ Learning Sciences Literacy (TLSL). Based on literature synthesis and a three -round Delphi process, four dimensions were identified: Awareness, Knowledge, Skills, and Self-Application & Development. A 54- item self-assessment instrument was developed and validated through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses with samples of 480 and 486 in -service teachers. The model showed strong reliability (α = .992) and validity. Analyses of data from 486 teachers revealed high overall TLSL, with the highest in Skills and the lowest in Knowledge. Regression results showed that teaching experience, professional title, and Learning Sciences engagement were positively associated with TLSL, whereas demographic factors had limited effects. These findings clarify the construct of TLSL, provide a validated measurement tool, and highlight the importance of sustained professional learning in fostering teachers’ Learning Sciences Literacy.

title: From Data to Meaning: Cognitive Resources for Interpreting CO2 Time-Series Graphs
citation: Amber Armstrong, Alyssa Kasahara, Vijay Marupudi, Rina Miyata Harsch, Tristen Landeros, Diana, Moreno Trinidad, Jeffrey K. Bye (2026). From Data to Meaning: Cognitive Resources for Interpreting CO2 Time-Series Graphs. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Armstrong, A., Kasahara, A., Marupudi, V., Harsch, R. M., Landeros, T., Diana, Trinidad, M., & Bye, J. K.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Investigating how individuals understand climate data is crucial for improving the instruction of climate change. The Knowledge in Pieces framework posits that individuals’ knowledge, including climate knowledge, is separated into pieces, which remain isolated or are connected in productive and unproductive ways. We investigated how an individual connects their knowledge about climate change to graphs representing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) concentrations over various timescales. Our ongoing analyses suggest that individuals connected more recent rises in CO 2 to their cognitive resources about human induced climate change, in mostly productive ways.

title: AI-Scaffolded Summarization in STEM: How do Students Differ in Writing and Revision?
citation: Hyunkyu Han, Seora Kim, Mohamed Shameer Abdeen, Min Kyu Kim (2026). AI-Scaffolded Summarization in STEM: How do Students Differ in Writing and Revision?. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Han, H., Kim, S., Abdeen, M. S., & Kim, M. K.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Summarization is a key learning strategy in undergraduate STEM, yet students often struggle without timely, effective feedback. This study investigates how a n AI-scaffolded feedback system (SMART) relates to students’ revision behaviors and how these patterns vary across diverse student backgrounds. We analyzed 1,081 summary revisions from 49 undergraduates in an introductory physics course using a suite of mixed-effects models. Results show that adding concepts and words while maintaining semantic coherence predicted stronger concept learning, whereas excessive deletion corresponded to weaker outcomes. Revision patterns differed meaningfully by gender, race/ethnicity, and academic level, suggesting that AI-scaffolded feedback needs to be tailored to support diverse learners toward productive revision strategies.

title: Dignity-Affirming Music Pedagogy: Reframing Music as Relational Design in Learning Spaces
citation: Melanie West, Shirin Vossoughi, Michael Horn, Melita Morales, Samual Carrol (2026). Dignity-Affirming Music Pedagogy: Reframing Music as Relational Design in Learning Spaces. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: West, M., Vossoughi, S., Horn, M., Morales, M., & Carrol, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In K -12 education settings, music is often framed as an enrichment activity, overlooking its deeper role in shaping dignity -affirming learning spaces and in organizing interaction among community members. We examine music as interactional infrastructure, asking how it makes dignity observable in learning environments. Using Rhythmic Interaction Analysis (RIA), we analyze a drum circle interaction to examine how participation unfolds through rhythmic turns. We trace how vulnerability, attunement, and agency emerge as participants respond to one another, illustrating how dignity can be made visible through coordinated, embodied interaction. Problem / reframe Within K -12 education settings, music is often invoked to motivate participation, support memorization, or improve testable skills (Bhide, Power, & Goswami, 2013; Governor, Hall, & Jackson, 2013; Ashley & Timmers, 2017; Kumar et al., 2022). Such framings risk eclipsing music’s relational, historical, and identity work (Blacking, 1973; Small, 1998; Robinson, 2020; Hess, 2019). At the same time, dignity- affirming education (DAE) calls for learning environments that center learners’ full humanity—supporting vulnerability, agency, and meaningful participation through relational practice (Espinoza, et al., 2020; Vossoughi, et al., 2018; Keifert, et al., 2021). This perspective shifts attention from outcomes alone to the conditions under which learners are recognized, supported, and able to contribute. We take up this shift by approaching music as an epistemic and affective partner that co-organizes learning. In this view, meaning- making unfolds as a collective process of “rhythmic attunement” —people sensing, responding to, and adapting with one another, much like players in an ensemble. Grounded in DAE, ethnomusicology, and sociocultural theories, we ask: How can music -infused pedagogy—listening, speaking about music, and making music together —cultivate learning environments that affirm students’ dignity and agency while expanding relational forms of participation? Conceptual orientation: Dignity as interaction Rhythm has long been understood as a structuring feature of social interaction, shaping how participants coordinate attention, timing, and response (Erickson, 1982; Bassetti & Bottazzi, 2015). We examine how rhythmic interaction organizes participation itself. As participants coordinate through rhythm, they make space for one another’s contributions —creating conditions where participation can be recognized, supported, and sustained. From this perspective, dignity is not an abstract quality of a learning environment, but something enacted in time, as participants recognize, respond to, and sustain one another’s contributions. We ground this work in dignity-affirming education, which frames learning as a relational practice enacted through everyday interaction. To make this construct analytically tractable, we focus on three observable dimensions: vulnerability—moments where participants take risks (e.g., initiating a contribution); attunement—moments of alignment (e.g., synchronized timing or coordinated response); and agency—moments where participants shape the direction of activity.

title: Investigating How Students Plan, Monitor, and Evaluate Learning When Working in Groups in Undergraduate Biology Labs
citation: Jeremy L. Hsu, Olivia Rivet, Lilliona Bentzinger (2026). Investigating How Students Plan, Monitor, and Evaluate Learning When Working in Groups in Undergraduate Biology Labs. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Hsu, J. L., Rivet, O., & Bentzinger, L.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Social metacognition, or the extent that group members working together are aware of and regulate the thinking of other group members, is associated with greater cognition and learning. However, it remains unclear to what extent undergraduate students engage in planning, monitoring, and evaluating their group’s learning in the context of biology labs. Here, we investigate to what extent groups engage in social metacognition through their peer -to-peer questions and characterize different types of questions during groupwork.

title: Speculating, Questioning, and Interpreting: A Mixed-Methods Study of Informal Learning on a Video-Sharing Social Media Platform
citation: Hakeoung Hannah Lee, Gi Woong Choi (2026). Speculating, Questioning, and Interpreting: A Mixed-Methods Study of Informal Learning on a Video-Sharing Social Media Platform. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Lee, H. H. & Choi, G. W.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines how informal learning unfolds on a video-sharing social media platform, focusing on interpretive discourse surrounding explanation videos of a music video. Introducing a mixed methods approach, we integrate computational techniques, including topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and regex- based categorization , with qualitative thematic analysis. This approach enables the examination of a large corpus of comments that would be impractical to analyze manually, carried out across three distinct analytic phases. Our findings reveal that users collaboratively construct meaning through questioning, interpreting, speculating, and debating, engaging in discourse that reflects critical, situated learning practices. These comment sections emerge as dynamic, participatory spaces where cultural interpretation and symbolic analysis are actively negotiated. In addition to these insights, the study presents a scalable, transferable method for analyzing large- scale user-generated discourse in inf ormal, digitally mediated learning environments.

title: Making Theory Visible: A Visual Model for Resource Theory and Mechanistic Reasoning
citation: Safana Ismael, Janet L. Branchaw, Jennifer H. Doherty, Alex Waugh, Mary Pat Wenderoth, Aeryn Vanderslik, Sheela Vemu (2026). Making Theory Visible: A Visual Model for Resource Theory and Mechanistic Reasoning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Ismael, S., Branchaw, J. L., Doherty, J. H., Waugh, A., Wenderoth, M. P., Vanderslik, A., & Vemu, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Understanding conceptual change requires examining how students activate and coordinate cognitive resources while reasoning about a task. Resource Theory (RT) describes how reasoning emerges from the activation and coordination of fine-grained cognitive resources in context, while Mechanistic Reasoning (MR) characterizes how students construct causal explanations by identifying entities, their properties, and their activities. In this paper, we propose a visual model that brings these frameworks together to illustrate how framing, resource activation, and coordination interact during problem solving. The model serves as an analytic tool for tracing how different configurations of these processes can lead to productive mechanistic explanations or to more superficial reasoning.

title: Living the Impossible: Designing Life Happens, an AI-Supported Budget and Justice Simulation
citation: Devan Walton, Haesol Bae, Jaesung Park, Yingru Zhao, Raymond Weiss, Susan Tashjian (2026). Living the Impossible: Designing Life Happens, an AI-Supported Budget and Justice Simulation. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Walton, D., Bae, H., Park, J., Zhao, Y., Weiss, R., & Tashjian, S.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_tk_labels: Generative AI & LLMs; Simulations & Scientific Modeling; Analytics & Dashboards
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
conceptualisations_list: Communities of Practice & Situated Learning; Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition
abstract: This paper reports on the design of Life Happens, a classroom simulation in which students manage household budgets across twelve months while encountering criminal justice– related financial obligations. Grounded in situated learning theory, the simulatio n develops quantitative reasoning and perspective -taking through authentic financial dilemmas. Initial prototypes relied on large language models, producing inconsistencies and outputs that reinforced harmful stereotypes. Informed by a trauma -aware framework, the team restructured the system into a three -layer architecture: a deterministic core, a curated event layer, and a bounded AI layer limited to brief affective text messages. This paper focuses on design principles that emerged from documented failures during deployments at a Hispanic -Serving community college and a Minority-Serving state university. Context, theoretical framing, and focus Faculty at a Hispanic -Serving community college and a Minority- Serving state university in the northeastern United States identified a need for experiential tools conveying how criminal justice involvement compounds household financial hardship (García et al., 2019). The interdisciplinary partnership brought together computer science pedagogy and criminal justice education to serve predominantly first-generation college students (Penuel et al., 2013). Institutional constraints, including limited class time, variable devices, and diverse student demographics, shaped every design decision. We conceptualize learning through situated learning theory (Lave & Wenger, 1991), which holds that knowledge develops through participation in authentic practices. Life Happens situates students within household financial management under justice- system co nstraints, requiring arithmetic computation, budgeting, and quantitative trade-off reasoning as disciplinary competencies that emerge through meaningful decision- making (Gee, 2007). Simultaneously, students develop perspective -taking as they experience cascading consequences of systemic inequities (Belman & Flanagan, 2010). This paper focuses on the simulation’s design and AI integration, tracing how concrete prototype failures led to the principled architecture presented here. Simulation design and learning affordances Life Happens positions students as household decision- makers managing limited resources across twelve simulated months. Each cycle requires allocating funds across housing, food, transportation, healthcare, and phone services. Justice -related obligations such as probation fees, court -ordered payments, and commissary contributions impose additional mandatory costs (Harper et al., 2020). Five well -being indicators update transparently based on decisions, with visible arithmetic enabling students to anticipate consequences (Chernikova et al., 2020). Quarterly reflection prompts emphasize metacognition and discussion (Squire, 2011). The system employs a three -layer architecture. The deterministic core maintains authored family compositions, income parameters, and cost data from regional economic sources, ensuring reproducibility and enabling instructor customization. The event layer introduces curated disruptions ranging from routine expenses to justice -related challenges, each with specified costs and well -being consequences. The affective AI layer generates brief text messages that translate numerical outcomes into personal narratives, adding emotional context while the core mechanics remain fully deterministic. AI integration: From unconstrained generation to bounded use Initial prototypes relied on large language models to generate family scenarios, event narratives, and financial parameters (Yan et al., 2024), producing three categories of documented failure. Generated family compositions contained logical inconsistencies that confused students and undermined budgeting strategies. AI- produced cost structures varied unpredictably across similar scenarios, making it difficult for students to develop reliable 2865 quantitative intuitions. Generated content also perpetuated harmful stereotypes about poverty and justice involvement, particularly affecting overrepresented communities (Lee et al., 2024). These failures demanded a framework for addressing stereotypes and trauma. Drawing on trauma - informed pedagogy (Carello & Butler, 2015), we committed to ensuring that scenarios allow full participation independent of personal history, that content represents systemic patterns while honoring individual complexity, and that instructors retain the ability to modify or disable any element they judge inappropriate. This framework guided the restructuring of AI’s role. Because educator control over sensitive elements is a pedagogical and ethical requirement, all factual elements became authored content maintained in versioned databases (Gibson, 2023). AI was retained solely for generating 280- character text messages formatted as communications from family members, employers, and service providers (see Figure 1). Prompts incorporate strict constraints on tone, relationship dynamics, and prohibited content, and each message passes validation filters before display. Pre - authored fallback messages activate when outputs fail validation or when instructors operate in non -AI mode (Aldrich, 2005). This bounded application introduces meaningful variation across simulation runs and supports empathy-building, all while the deterministic mechanics remain fully intact. Figure 1 The Phone Message Interface Displays AI-Generated Communications from Family Members and Service Providers. Design principles traced to practice The following principles emerged from the documented failures and institutional constraints above, and we trace each to its originating episode (Wang & Hannafin, 2005). Separation of deterministic and generative components arose because AI -generated cost s tructures produced inconsistencies that undermined learning objectives. Educator authorship of core mechanics resolved this while confining AI to a role where variability adds value and fairness is preserved. Trauma- aware content governance emerged from en counters with AI outputs that stereotyped justice-involved families. Instructor override, scenario review, and explicit content boundaries ensure that every version of the simulation actively interrogates these patterns. Privacy-conscious architecture responded to institutional review board concerns, and the minimal state approach transmits only current meter values and recent decisions (Pardo & Siemens, 2014). Redundancy and fallback systems became essential after pilot-session technical failures disrupted engagement, so pre -authored alternatives for every AI feature ensure continuity. Reflection over scoring prioritizes metacognition because early testing revealed that competitive scoring distracted students from systemic insights (Li et al., 2024). Conclusion Life Happens demonstrates that AI can enhance educational simulations when carefully bounded by pedagogical goals and equity commitments. The most consequential design decisions centered on preserving educator authority over content touching systemic inequality, trauma, and identity. These transferable principles confirm that thoughtful AI integration remains accessible across diverse educational settings when guided by clear learning objectives. 2866 References Aldrich, C. title: Games of Representation: Making the Abstract Tangible through Data Representation with Card- Based Games for Understanding AI Ethics Education
citation: Katherine Moore, Irene Lee, Helen Zhang, Shana White, Paige Prescott (2026). Games of Representation: Making the Abstract Tangible through Data Representation with Card- Based Games for Understanding AI Ethics Education. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Moore, K., Lee, I., Zhang, H., White, S., & Prescott, P.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Critical Digital Literacy & AI Ethics
abstract: Middle school students notice that an image search for "physicist" returns predominantly white male faces, but when asked "Who is represented? Who is left out?" they struggle to respond. This reveals a critical gap in AI literacy education: youth lack understanding of representation and the complex interchange between societal patterns and AI systems. Games of Representation (GR) addresses this gap through card-based games that make abstract concepts of dataset representation tangible. Aligned with the Kap or Foundation's Responsible AI and Tech Justice Guide, the design engages players as stakeholders who curate datasets using SET cards. This paper contributes two design principles: (1) scaffolding from individual to system- level understanding of how bias e merges in data, (2) connecting mathematical representation (statistical distributions) to social representation (who gets included or excluded). These principles offer guidance for developing educational responses to emerging technologies where technical and social dimensions are inseparable.

title: A Preliminary Study of Digital Tool Practices and Knowledge Building in Pre -service Teacher Learning within an Emerging Technology
citation: Yi-An Chen, Mei-Ju Chen, Yi-Ju Lin, Chao-Yu Guo, Huang-Yao Hong (2026). A Preliminary Study of Digital Tool Practices and Knowledge Building in Pre -service Teacher Learning within an Emerging Technology. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Chen, Y., Chen, M., Lin, Y., Guo, C., & Hong, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates how pre-service teachers engage in digital tool practices and develop knowledge -building competencies within an Emerging Technology Applications course at a national university in Taiwan. Guided by the frameworks of Knowledge Buildi ng (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2010), reflective practice (Schön, 1983), and the Teaching Artist perspective (Eisner, 2002), the research examines how emerging technologies such as Padlet can transform teacher education into a creative and collaborative learn ing environment. Seventeen pre-service teachers participated in a three- phase design-based course: (1) personal expression and problem awareness, (2) collaborative feedback and campus inquiry, and (3) Sandbox co-creation of interactive materials integratin g SDGs or SEL. Data sources included the AI -TPACK questionnaire and Padlet discourse analyzed through theory- driven content analysis. Results show a developmental progression from individual tool use to community- oriented knowledge building, with Padlet evolving from a platform for expression to a site of co-construction and epistemic agency. The study contributes a replicable model demonstrating how digital design tasks can foster creativity, reflection, and sustained idea improvement in pre- service teacher education.

title: Complex Science, Simple Tools: A Pocketable, Low-Cost Lab for Sophisticated Experiments in Middle-School Science
citation: Xinge Zhang, Carolina Sotério, Paulo Blikstein (2026). Complex Science, Simple Tools: A Pocketable, Low-Cost Lab for Sophisticated Experiments in Middle-School Science. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Zhang, X., Sotério, C., & Blikstein, P.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Although advanced science tools are central to modern research, K –12 students rarely access them due to cost and complexity. Using microfluidic stickers as a design case, this paper explores how such technologies can be repurposed for constructionist “hands-on” science education. By simplifying fabrication, drawing on cultural forms, and enabling hands -on experiments with liquid flow and diffusion, the stickers illustrate pathways to make advanced science tools accessible through everyday making.

title: Co-designing a Teacher Learning Community to Counter Demoralization for Early Career Elementary Teachers
citation: Mallika Scott, Omar Bello (2026). Co-designing a Teacher Learning Community to Counter Demoralization for Early Career Elementary Teachers. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This paper focuses on a math teacher learning community co -designed to nourish, empower, and sustain early career elementary teachers in their commitments to justice . We investigate the moral dilemmas teachers encountered as they tried to bring their commitments into their everyday math teaching in contexts that did not align with these commitments . We find that the co -designed learning community helped teachers renew their sense of agency in their school contexts and counter forces of demoralization.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study characterizes how intellectual humility relates to students’ engagement from moment to moment in a reasoning task. Undergraduates (N = 212) completed an IH survey, and a subset (N = 20) completed interviews. We coded cognitive, behavioral, and affective engagement across Task Initiation, Strategy, Answer Reveal, and Reflection. Using contrasting cases, we identified different engagement patterns: lower -IH showed confirmation bias and negative affect, while higher -IH showed strategy shifts and positive reflection. These patterns illustrate how IH aligns with engagement and informs affective scaffolding.

title: Speculative Futuring for Understanding River Socio-Ecology

subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study investigates how Speculative Futuring (SF) can create space for high school students to critically engage with environmental challenges and envision alternative futures for their communities. Our findings show that students drew on multiple form s of knowledge such as lived experiences, and scientific information to shape their understanding around addressing socio- environmental challenges such as water quality, and accessibility of the natural resources. Artifacts developed during SF reflected their understanding of current socio-ecological systems while envisioning possibilities for the future.

abstract: This paper examines how analog media such as paper and ink can be designed as meaningful tools for science learning through Lab -on-a-Book, a portable, paper-based science kit with interactive pages. Grounded in constructionism, we argue that low -tech materials can provide accessible, modifiable, and multimodal entry points into scientific inquiry, particularly in contexts with limited access to digital technologies.

abstract: Classroom discussions can deepen science learning, but equitable participation, especially for culturally and linguistically diverse students , remains elusive. I developed Equi- Talk, a prototype AI-enabled coaching chatbot for teachers. It applies the Equitable Classroom Discussion Observation Protocol to help teachers plan, reflect on, and facilitate science classroom discussions that engage diverse students. This paper describes the tool's design objectives, framework, and core functionality, and outlines next steps: UI optimization, beta testing, and iterative improvements.

title: From Mechanics to Meaning: Tracing Systems Thinking in Learners’ Game Design Talk
citation: Amrit Pal Singh, Sahana Murthy (2026). From Mechanics to Meaning: Tracing Systems Thinking in Learners’ Game Design Talk. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Singh, A. P. & Murthy, S.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Game design has emerged as a promising context for fostering systems thinking, yet little is known about how such thinking manifests during the design process itself. This study investigates how learners develop systems thinking while collaboratively designing tabletop games. Drawing on frameworks that treat games as systems, we analysed the discourse of two 9th-grade students participating in a two-day game design workshop. Our analysis revealed that learners exhibited five key systems thinking features through their design talk: interconnectedness through rule dependencies, causality through action-consequence mapping, synthesis through coherence checking, emergence through playability patterns, and system function through design evaluation. These findings suggest that systems thinking emerges as an evolving process embedded in the collaborative act of game -making. The study contributes process-level insights into how game-making activities support systems thinking development.

abstract: Educational technologies with young children are currently a highly contested area . Meanwhile, the need for understanding computing and AI has perhaps never been greater. It is shown that slow pedagogy provided teachers with critical perspectives on technology, enabled children to experience, relate to, and establish boundaries with computing and AI.

abstract: This rapid scoping review examines how personalized learning analytics dashboards (LADs) foster self-regulated learning (SRL) and student agency in higher education. title: Designing Equitable Partnerships for the Future of Play
citation: Cristina Paul, Anna Terrazas, Christine Lee (2026). Designing Equitable Partnerships for the Future of Play. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Paul, C., Terrazas, A., & Lee, C.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Conceptual Change & Mental Models; Design-Based Research (DBR); Co-Design & Participatory Design; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: Educators and a university researcher co -designed play-based learning to support children to gain a deep and enduring understanding of scientific concepts, critical consciousness, and practicing joy. We present how reciprocity emerged through our equitabl e partnerships and how these partnerships make research, theory, praxis, and student learning more robust. Play Play is messy; while we wanted to include play in our classrooms as social justice advocates and practitioners, the structures, schedules, and everyday boundaries of typical classrooms make it a challenge. Play allows us to grasp important ideas from multiple angles with empathy and care, both as educators and students. This is a freedom we are slowly losing with the rise of standardized curricula, testing, and the prevalence of unfeeling screen-based learning. Standardized and for-profit curricula can also strip educators of autonomy. Play is learning. Play advocacy and research aren’t just about joy—they’re about justice too. We present four design components from our equitable partnership that made our participatory design- based research successful. Our poster shares how we practiced reciprocity in our researcher -educator partnership. Understanding how future educator - researcher collaborations can design their partnerships in equitable ways is critical for the future of design -based research. Co-designing play The goal of our partnership was to design an interdisciplinary environmental curriculum that empowered young students to learn through play. Throughout the school year, we designed play lessons to support students in learning about interdependent relationships between people, pollinators, and plants. Cristina and Anna are elementary teachers of mixed -age 1st and 2nd grade students at an elementary school in Los Angeles. Cristina teaches in a dual language bilingual education (DLBE) program with 90% instruction in Spanish and 10% instruction in English. Christine, a university researcher, has been interested in designing a curriculum for environmental education through play and has been collaborating with Cristina and Anna since the Spring of 2022. Throughout the academic school year, our team met weekly to co -plan play-based lessons. Our year -long play-based curriculum had three parts that wove together play and movement: first, we investigated plants and flowers; then, we investigated bees as pollinators; an d finally, we investigated how people impact and rely on plants and pollinators. Designing partnerships: Reciprocity While our participatory design-based research study (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) aimed to integrate play into our curriculum, the goal of our poster is to reflect on the design of our equitable partnership that made it possible. The data in this poster are fro m our collective experiences and reflections on educator -researcher relationships in design-based work. Through reflection, we identify and present four components that made our work reciprocal. Our partnership was built on curiosity, trust, humility, and multiple competencies. Instead of focusing on the distinct tasks of rigid roles, we practiced reciprocity through equitable partnerships –sharing responsibilities and making decisions together about how to implement play. Component one: Play Play is a human need and everyone has the right to play (United Nations, 1989). Throughout our work, play was a goal and a means for children, teachers, and researchers. We intentionally designed our curriculum with embedded play, and to accomplish this, we also played with one another and alongside our students. Of course, we played with our lesson designs, with how to collect data on students’ learning, and even played with the design of our classroom spaces by moving furniture to make room for play. More importantly, we made and played with costumes, created art, and pretended to be creatures and plants alongside our students. Play helped us to reflect on and refine our thinking–not only with our own experiences to anticipate challenges, but to revise our lessons, and to make decisions about lesson sequences. This freed us from restrictive, static, and hierarchical ways of learning, designing, and researching. 2907 Component two: Autonomy for all While traditional research methodologies tend to uphold a sense of control in research settings, our participatory work is grounded in the context of our classrooms. We rejected the notion that we could have complete control over research and what happens in the classroom. Instead of controlling how teaching and learning should occur, we embraced unscripted, yet meaningful interactions, discoveries, questions, and misconceptions. For example, children unexpectedly sang during play lessons. When teachers asked children about word choice and how they mixed Spanish and English, the volume, and/or speed of their singing, the children’s responses demonstrated the intentionality of their decisions and their nuanced understanding of big ideas like pollination. If t eachers had simply asked children not to sing during a dance lesson or to follow the instructions with more fidelity and play quietly like a pollinator, these understandings may have never emerged and developed. Play offers opportunities for children to participate in expansive and joyful ways. It gives students space and agency to explore ideas, negotiate meaning, and co -create rules of engagement as they interact with peers. It is impossible to predict all the ways children may engage in a topic, and that should delight educators and researchers. Component three: Support for all Our classrooms have a diverse student population, which includes neurodiverse students, students with disabilities, and emergent multilingual learners. We wanted to design play for all, not just for the majority of our students. Throughout the school year, we noticed some neurodiverse students struggled with noise, lack of explicit directions, and more freedom in moving in classroom spaces. This led us to modify our lesson designs. Some of the design changes included frontloading ideas for where to play, roles to take on with which students might feel most comfortable, creating boundaries in our indoor and outdoor spaces, using noise -reducing headphones for certain children, and including children in decision- making about classroom set up for play. When desi gning classroom spaces or thinking about how to use available outdoor spaces, we ask ourselves if the physical, emotional, and academic environment we’ve created is autonomy -supportive (Amado et al., 2020). Are the materials, furniture, and structures for participation accessible to all children? Are relationships being tended to with care and curiosity? Are researchers and teachers modeling care and curiosity for students? Sometimes it’s not simply the chairs that must be moved; it’s our hearts and minds. Component four: Data sharing Our partnership was designed to share knowledge and resources, which often led us to teach one another new skills. Taking photos or videos for formal research analysis was new for Cristina and Anna. Video recordings allowed us to see and hear movement, con versation, negotiation, discussion, and problem- solving that led to the creation of each movement during play. We could see and hear students' reasoning and decision- making, which demonstrated a clear understanding of the function of each part of a flower. In a busy classroom of students, it is difficult to observe and gain a deep understanding of how each student is making sense of the information. As teachers, video recordings made it possible to follow children’s understanding; we could see how knowledge cross-pollinated between students so they could make deeper connections to the content and each other. More importantly, analyzing and re -watching the video alongside Christine changed how Anna viewed participation structures when students were playing. It changed how Anna listens, observes, and builds on students’ ideas in new ways. Concluding remarks The future we dream of is one of delight. Yet, education and academia are fraught with constraints and seeming barriers to joy -filled work. Educators are taught behavior management strategies. Administrators and other evaluators that walk through classrooms expect to see a level of control that demonstrates that children's behavior is being effectively "managed." Play is the antidote to control. The future is relational. To be in healthy relationships with each other as researchers, teachers, and students is to relate to each other in mutually respectful ways—ways of being that anticipate the beauty and logic of knowledge created in collaboration rather than in isolation. We cannot do reciprocal work without being in equitable partnerships. The future we hope for is one of reciprocity between students and teachers, teachers and researchers, and researchers and children. The democratization of knowledge and expertise in our classrooms and research wasn't accidental. It was dignity -affirming (Espinoza et al., 2020) and humanizing for children, educators, and researchers. 2908 References Amado, D., Molero, P., Del Villar, F., Tapia -Serrano, M. abstract: This case study explores how learners form and negotiate relational ties with Generative AI (GAI) chatbots and human peers during two reflective writing activities. We found learners formed a hierarchical, task -oriented relationship with GAI chatbots, whil e maintaining an equal relationship, reciprocity, and socio -emotional connections with peers. These findings reveal learners’ strategic negotiation to balance writing agency and socio - emotional needs with human-computer collaborative environments.

citation: Lu Liang, Danielle Espino, Seung B. Lee, Yutong Tan, Julia Gibson, Nastassia Jone, Eric R. Hamilton (2026). Evaluating the Impact of a Virtual Collaborative STEM Project on Adolescents’ Social Awareness and Identity Development. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

Utilizing epistemic network analysis (ENA), findings included a strong connection between challenges and social awareness and global cultural awareness, indicating that participation in the learnin g community increased adolescents’ willingness to engage in discussions on personal challenges and an ongoing process of identity development.

title: Dynamics of Social Interaction in Collaborative Debugging
citation: Burcu Şener, Duygu Umutlu (2026). Dynamics of Social Interaction in Collaborative Debugging. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
authors_list: Şener, B. & Umutlu, D.

abstract: This study investigates how novice programmers maintain social interactions during collaborative debugging . A qualitative case study was conducted with five undergraduate students working in small groups on debugging tasks. Recordings from 12 sessions were analyzed. Findings from our thematic analysis show that social interactions function as both emotional regulation tools and collaborative resources, helping group members manage tension, sustain engagement, and maintain group cohesion. Humor and playfulness particularly supported a positive and productive debugging atmosphere.

title: An Exploratory Factor Analysis of K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence in the Classroom
citation: Elham Tajik, Jaesung Park, Nursultan Japashov, Alae Sherat, Haesol Bae, Jonathan K. Foster (2026). An Exploratory Factor Analysis of K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence in the Classroom. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: This study examines K– 12 teachers’ perceptions of AI in education using Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) on survey data from 139 participants. Four interrelated factors were identified: Barriers & Anxiety, Professional Engagement & Instructional Readiness, Ethical & Responsi ble AI Use, and Resource Support & Conceptual Awareness. These findings contribute to understanding how K-12 teachers perceive AI integration.

title: Choosing “Togetherness” in a Teacher-Researcher Partnership

abstract: Partnerships can support teachers as they work toward rehumanizing classrooms. Togetherness among educators, which Baldinger et al. (2025) propose as involving solidarity, mutually, and human connection, can support humanizing, justice -focused learning for educators. This paper investigates ways in which two teachers and a research partner resisted limiting institutional pressures to choose togetherness in their ongoing work to design humanizing and liberatory learning experiences for young people.

title: When Code Shapes Scientific Language: Speaking Photosynthesis in Code
citation: Tamar Fuhrmann, Brendan Henrique, Paulo Blikstein (2026). When Code Shapes Scientific Language: Speaking Photosynthesis in Code. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: Helping students reason about mechanisms in biology is a persistent challenge in science education. This study examines a sixth-grade curricular unit where students engaged in multiple representational practices: natural language, visual model drawings, a nd block-based coding. Students created drawings and explanations before and after using a computational modeling environment. Analyses of students’ drawings and their descriptions revealed a shift from everyday terms to disciplinary vocabulary, as students incorporated molecular -level entities (CO₂, glucose) and mechanistic processes. These changes suggest that coding created a new commognitive space, blending computational and scientific discourse with code serving as a representational scaffold and a medium for scientific reasoning.

title: Exploring Epistemic Affect in Middle School Students’ Peer Critique
citation: Qiuyu Lin, Ravit Golan Duncan, Clark A. Chinn, Ava Lubin, Jinzhi Zhou, Joshua Danish (2026). Exploring Epistemic Affect in Middle School Students’ Peer Critique. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.

abstract: Peer critique is a social epistemic practice. Productive engagement in critique requires attention to its affective dynamics. We conducted discourse analysis of two focus groups across two rounds of peer critique. The groups showed different understandings and enactments of epistemic ideals for critique. The negative epistemic affect that emerged signaled differences in students’ epistemic ideals . Yet students strategically managed affect and negotiated epistemic ideals, thereby transforming affective tensions into opportunities for shared understanding.

abstract: This study explores the dynamics of a formal classroom and nature-based informal learning environment, focusing on their impact on student subjectification and knowledge authority. This comparative case study, involving 27 fifth-grade students and their teacher, examined shifts in teaching approaches and student autonomy across these settings through analysis of observational data, recordings, interviews, and surveys. A didactic approach centralizes knowledge authority in the classroom, while nature-based programs adopt a more dialogical model that promotes exploration. Findings reveal that the environment supports a shift in teacher and student roles, enhancing student agency and subjectification. This research contributes to the discourse on generative learning environments (GLE) and highlights practices that balance teacher authority with student empowerment. It also underscores the need for further research on the connections between informal learning contexts and student subjectification.

title: Routine Care to Build Trust in Co-Research with Young Children
