abstract: Counter to pejorative representations of children’s competencies, we show young children can lead co-research when they trust adults will follow. Our research team—child, caregiver, university-based members—present interactional, multimodal analysis of video data in a relational learning ecology. We examine the role of talk, gaze, touch, body orientation, and facial expressions in communicating care. We then link patterns of care to the establishment of trust; namely children’s trust that adults will follow. We begin with an opening moment of our seventh visit (roughly 6 months into our partnership) to illustrate trust in action, and then detail a focal child’s showing of a valued artifact as a coordinated display of care and affirmation of the child’s dignity as learner and leader.

title: Critical Action Learning: Empowering Students in An Uncertain World
citation: Slotta, J. D., Carvalho, R., Raman, P., & Mattoo, M. (2025). Critical Action Learning: Empowering Students in an Uncertain World. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1016-1024). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Slotta, J. D., Carvalho, R., Raman, P., & Mattoo, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper presents a recent whole-school study of Critical Action Learning, a form of sustained critical inquiry for K-12 classroom communities. Through partnerships in North America, Europe, and Asia, we pursue a deeper understanding of how Critical Action Learning occurs in classrooms and how it influences students, teachers, schools and communities. This paper presents a study of a school located in Bangalore, India, in which teachers and school leaders worked to adopt Critical Action Learning in numerous classrooms. We report on teacher knowledge and practice, features of curriculum, and the growth of the school community.

title: Students Reasoning About Bias and Ethics When Designing Human Subjects Research Studies
citation: Matuk, C., d’Anjou, B., Mansukhani, P., Rissman, J., Zerwas, F., Porteous, F., Burgas, K., Shevchenko, Y., & Dikker, S. (2025). Students Reasoning About Bias and Ethics When Designing Human Subjects Research Studies. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1025-1033). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Matuk, C., d’Anjou, B., Mansukhani, P., Rissman, J., Zerwas, F., Porteous, F., Burgas, K., Shevchenko, Y., & Dikker, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Understanding bias and ethics in research is critical for both researchers and consumers of research. It facilitates sound decision-making, builds public trust in research, and ensures that research contributes positively to society. Authentic research opportunities can be critical for developing these skills, but are lacking in high school contexts. We designed and implemented MindHive, a curriculum and online platform for students to design and conduct online human behavior studies. Qualitative analysis of 98 student-generated research proposals and 21 individual interviews with students from across 6 high schools, identified various ways that students engaged with bias and ethical issues within their projects. Engaging in research about personally relevant questions and contexts may support students in shuttling between personal experiences and data, and taking on perspectives that help to reveal and address assumptions. Findings contribute to an understanding of how curriculum can meaningfully engage students in reasoning about research bias and ethics.

title: Personal Authentic, Expansively Framed, and Culturally Sustaining Cybersecurity and STEM Education
citation: Hickey, D. T. & Kantor, R. J. (2025). Personal Authentic, Expansively Framed, and Culturally Sustaining Cybersecurity and STEM Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1034-1042). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hickey, D. T. & Kantor, R. J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: A 2021 expert consensus study report from the US National Academies of Sciences highlighted personal authenticity to improve computing education. Forming personal connections with new content is consistent with culturally sustaining pedagogy and other asset-based approaches for teaching marginalized learners. This is also consistent with the situative design principles for expansive framing from Randi Engle (1965-2012). The report contrasted personally authentic learning with the more common professionally authentic learning associated with socio-constructivist approaches such as problem-based learning. Our theoretical integration and example curricula use cybersecurity education to illustrate the synergy between personally authentic learning, expansive framing, and culturally relevant pedagogy. We extend Engle’s five explanations of expansive framing to incorporate personal authenticity and culturally relevant pedagogy, all supporting generative learning that transfers readily and widely.

title: Dynamic Equilibrium in Science Education: Cross-Disciplinary Perspectives and Representations in Israel and United States Standards and Textbooks
citation: Dawud, T., Gok, S., Wilensky, U., & Levy, S. T. (2025). Dynamic Equilibrium in Science Education: Cross-Disciplinary Perspectives and Representations in Israel and United States Standards and Textbooks. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1043-1051). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Dawud, T., Gok, S., Wilensky, U., & Levy, S. T.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: The study examines how Dynamic Equilibrium (DE) is represented in science national standards and textbooks for high-school biology, chemistry, and physics in the US and Israel. DE, a crucial concept in understanding dynamic systems, is inconsistently represented across educational materials and students encounter difficulties learning about DE. Analyzing 17 textbooks and national standards, the research combines quantitative and qualitative content analysis to assess the frequency and nature of presentation of DE-related phenomena. The study identifies 256 DE-related phenomena, comprising 14% of all phenomena that are studied in science. The primary systems approach used is System Dynamics, which focuses on stocks and rates of flow at one description level. The main representational format is verbal, and computational models are scarcely used. Differences across disciplines and between countries were found. These findings emphasize the need for powerful representations of DE to enhance students' understanding of dynamic systems and improve science education.

title: Learning in Productive Failure
citation: Brand, C., Loibl, K., & Rummel, N. (2025). Learning in Productive Failure: How Knowledge Gap Awareness and Intermediate Knowledge Link Prior Knowledge Activation and Conceptual Knowledge. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1052-1060). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Brand, C., Loibl, K., & Rummel, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In Productive Failure (PF), students are prepared for subsequent instruction by activating prior knowledge and becoming aware of own knowledge gaps when generating solution attempts to an unknown problem. Intermediate knowledge after solution generation likely affords the subsequent integration of new knowledge, but has only seldom been assessed in composite instructional designs such as PF. We investigated how the learning processes and (intermediate) knowledge in PF vary when manipulating the PF tasks’ goal formulations (learning vs. problem-solving goals). As hypothesized, learning goals led to higher gap awareness prior to instruction, higher closing of gaps after instruction as well as better learning outcomes compared to the problem-solving goals. Moreover, broad knowledge activation during the first learning phase correlated with the intermediate knowledge state. Contrary to our hypotheses, knowledge activation and gap awareness did not mediate the learning outcomes.

title: Teaching Machine Learning as Adaptive Design Work
citation: Delaney, V. & Selbach-Allen, M. (2025). Teaching Machine Learning as Adaptive Design Work. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1061-1069). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Delaney, V. & Selbach-Allen, M.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: To broaden and improve machine learning (ML) education, researchers must partner with teachers and study the affordances and challenges of ML instruction. Yet, most teachers are not ML experts and may need curricula that align ML concepts with their disciplinary expertise. This study explores three cases of classroom enactments of Mathematics of Facial Recognition (FaceID): five co-designed ML lessons aligned to high school statistics standards. Each teacher was encouraged to adapt FaceID to meet their instructional goals. Drawing from Brown’s Design Capacity for Enactment framework, we examine the frequency and substance of teachers’ adaptations of FaceID, and the design resources that enabled their adaptations. We found that teachers’ prior knowledge of ML, their statistics pedagogical content knowledge, and their knowledge of students supported their adaptations. From these findings, we illustrate triumphs and challenges that teachers who are new to ML may face when enacting ML lessons.

title: FLIP: Tabletop Role-Play Game for AI Ethics Education through Cognitive Dissonance
citation: Wang, Y., Ko, Y., Kim, K., Kim, S., & So, H. (2025). FLIP: Tabletop Role-Play Game for Ai Ethics Education Through Cognitive Dissonance. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1070-1078). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wang, Y., Ko, Y., Kim, K., Kim, S., & So, H.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: This study developed a tabletop role-playing game (TRPG), “FLIP,” for AI ethics education by engaging players in the ethical reasoning surrounding “Killer Robots.” Designed as a dialogic space, the game encourages players to explore diverse moral perspectives through cognitive dissonance. Specific game mechanics, such as ethical dilemmas and role conflicts, were incorporated to provoke cognitive dissonance and deepen ethical reasoning. Fifteen undergraduate students participated in the gameplay, and their in-game discourse was analyzed to unpack ethical reasoning. The analysis of their dialogues showed that the game effectively engaged players in understanding the complexity of AI ethics issues by sharing and challenging ethical judgments and arguments through collective reasoning. Overall, this study highlights the potential of TRPGs as a promising approach to AI ethics education.

title: Leveraging Composite Methodologies for Characterizing How Science Teacher Educators’ Critical Consciousness Shaped Their Designs for Professional Learning
citation: Suárez, E. & Crabtree, D. (2025). Leveraging Composite Methodologies for Characterizing How Science Teacher Educators’ Critical Consciousness Shaped Their Designs for Professional Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1079-1087). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Suárez, E. & Crabtree, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study is situated within EMPOWER, a Research-Practice Partnership focused on designing professional learning for secondary science teachers to make their curricula more justice-oriented. We investigate how EMPOWER researchers draw on their understandings of critical consciousness to design professional learning for science teachers. We employ a composite narratives methodology that amalgamates multiple participants’ statements into fictional personas, each representing unique priorities and stances. We conducted interviews at important milestones of the project to understand how participants’ critical lenses shaped their learning designs for teachers. Our multidimensional analytical framework combines Freire’s conscientizaçao with decomposing justice in educational systems in three levels. Through our analysis, we describe two personas that showcase different alignments and tensions that guided the design of the professional learning workshops. Leveraging a composite methodology can help researchers and teacher educators to characterize heterogeneity in what learning was prioritized for science teachers to make their curricula more equitable.

title: From Questions to Impact: Unveiling Teachers' Power to Support Actionable Learning Analytics Design
citation: Wang, N. & Law, N. (2025). From Questions to Impact: Unveiling Teachers' Power to Support Actionable Learning Analytics Design. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1088-1096). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wang, N. & Law, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: With the widespread adoption of e-learning and advances in educational data mining and AI, research publications in learning analytics (LA) have surged in recent years. However, LA has not significantly impacted learning and teaching in authentic educational contexts. As teachers’ uptake of LA depends on whether their pedagogical concerns are addressed, it is important to understand teachers’ LA needs in relation to their learning design contexts. We report on an investigation of the nature of teachers’ LA questions at different levels of design granularity—a learning task, a task sequence, or a course—identified through a systematic review of published empirical LA studies that engage teachers at some stage of the LA research process. The findings show that teachers seek actionable feedback on learning processes and progress. However, available LA often focus on course-level performance or task-level engagement, yet actionable insights need to consider relationships among a sequence of tasks.

title: “My Body was Trapped by the Wall”: A Longitudinal Studyof Teachers’ Sensemaking of Embodiments of ResponsiveTeaching
citation: Underwood, K., Horn, I., Metts, E., Li, S., & Nolting, K. (2025). “My Body Was Trapped by the Wall”: A Longitudinal Studyof Teachers’ Sensemaking of Embodiments of ResponsiveTeaching. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1097-1105). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Underwood, K., Horn, I., Metts, E., Li, S., & Nolting, K.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
conceptualisations_list: Embodied Cognition & Gestures; Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: Recent attention has focused on the multiple strategies teachers use to create responsive classrooms. However, little is known about the embodiments of responsive teaching. Grounded in situative and embodiment learning theories, this study situates teacher learning within dilemmatic spaces. Using a longitudinal exploratory case study, we explored how Kasey, an experienced mathematics teacher, made sense of the embodiments of responsive teaching over time. This case emerged from a multi-year research-practice partnership in a large urban school district in the United States, employing video-based feedback (VFF) and the Interaction Geographic Slicer (IGS) to support reflective teaching practices. Findings reveal that embodiment is a central element in responding to students’ learning needs. Responsive teaching is filled with embodiment dilemmas, which should be recognized as critical resources for teacher learning and development rather than obstacles. This study offers valuable insights for teachers and teacher educators aimed at fostering responsive teaching practices.

title: Can We Trust Large Language Models for Video Analysis: An Exploration of Hallucination in Multimodal LLMs
citation: Zhou, Y., Kang, J., & Nguyen, H. (2025). Can we Trust Large Language Models for Video Analysis: An Exploration of Hallucination in Multimodal LLMs. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 110-118). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhou, Y., Kang, J., & Nguyen, H.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show promise for facilitating qualitative video analysis, potentially reducing the manual effort required for video selection and coding. However, MLLMs are subject to hallucination, where models generate incorrect or unfounded descriptions and interpretations. Current frameworks for evaluating MLLM hallucinations primarily focus on object-centric tasks, with limited focus on behaviors and social interactions common in education data. Applying MLLMs to analyzing 36 video clips of collaborative learning activities, we identify three distinct types of hallucinations: description hallucination (factual inconsistency), interpretation hallucination (misinterpretation of behaviors), and instruction hallucination (deviation from analytical focus). Despite MLLMs’ ability to process educational videos, they exhibit gender misidentification and inaccurate interpretation of student roles and behaviors. This exploratory work develops a domain-specific framework to understand and evaluate MLLM hallucinations, laying the groundwork for more reliable implementation in educational research and calling for further investigations

title: Emergent Patterns of Dyadic Interaction around an Embodied Simulation
citation: Garg, S., Mathayas, N., & Lindgren, R. (2025). Emergent Patterns of Dyadic Interaction Around an Embodied Simulation. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1106-1114). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Garg, S., Mathayas, N., & Lindgren, R.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Gesture-augmented learning environments offer unique opportunities to facilitate learning by enabling tangible physical actions. While the literature on these learning environments is well documented, there remains a need to explore its facilitations for dyads (pairs of students) working together. This study investigates the role of dyadic interactions in learning a scientific concept through an embodied computer simulation. This simulation prompts the pairs of students to manipulate scientific representations using two representational gestures and discuss their observations. We present two such unique interactions of dyads in this paper and in-depth analysis of these two cases reveals how monitoring a partner’s gestural interactions with the simulation serves as a pivotal trigger for conceptual shifts. The findings highlight how gestures and dyadic interactions foster collaborative sensemaking, providing insights into how embodiment mediates learning processes.

title: Educational Attainment, Diversity, and Trust Dynamics in Nigeria
citation: Raj, A., Kushimo, K., & McIntyre, J. C. (2025). Educational Attainment, Diversity, and Trust Dynamics in Nigeria. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1115-1122). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Raj, A., Kushimo, K., & McIntyre, J. C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Trust is a fundamental pillar of societal cohesion, facilitating collaboration and progress. However, trust dynamics in diverse societies remain underexplored, particularly in non-Western contexts. Using the Afrobarometer 2022 dataset, this study investigates how education influences social and institutional (government) trust in Nigeria, one of the world’s most structurally pluralistic nations. Findings reveal that education was initially negatively associated with trust, but its effect diminished when religion and ethnicity were accounted for in a stepwise multiple regression analysis. Lower-educated groups, such as Hausa, Muslims, and non-English speakers, reported higher trust on average, while their higher-educated counterparts exhibited lower trust, reflecting an intricate balancing act that neutralized education’s net effect. Drawing on theories of structural pluralism, social capital, and human capital, this study highlights the importance of inclusive education policies to bridge divides and build trust in pluralistic societies like Nigeria.

title: Qualitative Research in the Age of LLMs: A Human-in-the-Loop Approach to Hybrid Thematic Analysis
citation: Wiebe, J. P., Khan, R., Burns, S., & Slotta, J. D. (2025). Qualitative Research in the Age of LLMs: A Human-in-the-Loop Approach to Hybrid Thematic Analysis. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1123-1131). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wiebe, J. P., Khan, R., Burns, S., & Slotta, J. D.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: This paper introduces a hybrid (deductive-inductive) human-in-the-loop (HHitL) framework for thematic analysis (TA), leveraging large language models (LLMs) while prioritizing human interpretation and decision-making. Grounded in reflexive TA, our resulting six-stage framework is guided by design principles of interoperability, human-LLM transactivity, scalability, and transparency. This method enables mixed-methods displays (e.g., network graphs, code frequency/diversity/magnitude metrics) supporting productive data triangulation. We demonstrate this HHitL-TA approach by analyzing engineering students’ motivations based on Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), illustrating the framework’s application, principles, and triangulation potential. While acknowledging potential risks, the HHitL design actively mitigates passive researcher roles through transactivity and transparency, promoting humans as generative, active directors of the analysis. This work contributes a structured methodology for rigorous, scalable qualitative inquiry using LLMs.

title: Actual and Vicarious Participation in Deliberative and Disputative Argumentation: Effects on Conceptual Learning
citation: Asterhan, C. S. (2025). Actual and Vicarious Participation in Deliberative and Disputative Argumentation: Effects on Conceptual Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1132-1139). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Asterhan, C. S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Theory and research suggests that deliberative argumentation is more likely to result in domain-specific content learning, compared to disputative argumentation. Yet, direct evidence is scarce. In the present work, we report on two controlled, randomized experiments to test these conjectures. In Study 1, undergraduate learners (N = 58) participated in a computer-mediated discussion with a disagreeing confederate on their understanding of a scientific concept they studied (natural selection). The peer confederate’s verbal behavior was scripted to evoke critical discourse on the explanations, while controlling for content, length and type of dialogue moves, but differing in discourse style (disputative/deliberative). In Study 2, learners (N = 88) read a disputative or deliberative discussion between two disagreeing learners. Results confirmed that deliberative argumentive discussion produced superior conceptual learning, both when learners participated in and when they read the discussion. Data on the learners' interaction perceptions provide some insights into reasons behind these differences.

title: “Gotta Learn to Hide Your Mistakes:” Troubling Failure Through Its Interactional Formation Within Enduring Struggles
citation: Elliott, C. H. & Y., J. (2025). “Gotta Learn to Hide Your Mistakes:” Troubling Failure Through Its Interactional Formation Within Enduring Struggles. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1140-1148). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Elliott, C. H. & Y, J.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: There is a growing interest in how learners experience mistakes and failures as opportunities for learning. We analyze the interactional achievement of one mistake surfacing between two youth and the robot over forty-five minutes on a high school robotics team. We conceptualize mistakes to be the interactional accomplishments of problem formulation (Lave, 1988). We then consider how the accomplishment of the mistake in our case can be viewed as what Holland and Lave (2001) called local contentious practice where struggles are mediated between intimate forms of identity development and competing forms of institutional oppression. For the two youth on the team, these intersecting struggles come to matter when the mistake has the possibility of keeping them from having a complete robot at the competition. We posit that the sociopolitical implications – and historical underpinnings – should inform how we consider youth can and should learn from mistakes and failures.

title: Exploring Preschoolers’ Engagement with Intelligent Agents (IA) Mediated by IA Features and Teacher Scaffolding
citation: Cai, Z., Tu, X., Wang, X. C., Sadeghi, S., & Dantu, K. (2025). Exploring Preschoolers’ Engagement With Intelligent Agents (Ia) Mediated by Ia Features and Teacher Scaffolding. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1149-1157). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cai, Z., Tu, X., Wang, X. C., Sadeghi, S., & Dantu, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: As intelligent agents (IAs) become increasingly integrated into young children's lives, it is crucial to understand how children perceive and interact with these technologies. We designed and implemented an IA-centered curriculum in a PreK classroom featuring three robots (GO1, Spot1, and Astro). We apply interaction analysis to unpack how IAs and teachers’ scaffolding facilitate children's understanding of technology. Our findings reveal that IA features (e.g., appearance, functionality, and intelligence levels), combined with teacher facilitation strategies (e.g., revoicing, explicit explanation, and thoughtful questioning), act as mediators shaping children's conceptual understanding and interactions with IAs. These mediations foster young children's sensory exploration, reasoning, and adaptive behaviors with technology. We recommend that future designers incorporate diverse IA features to enhance young children's learning opportunities about technology and its limitations. We also encourage educators to thoughtfully integrate IAs into teaching practices to support young children’s developmentally appropriate growth in this increasingly digital society.

title: Data Reels: An Analytic Approach to Creating Data Stories in Video Analysis
citation: Stornaiuolo, A. & Garg, R. (2025). Data Reels: An Analytic Approach to Creating Data Stories in Video Analysis. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1158-1165). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Stornaiuolo, A. & Garg, R.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This paper introduces the data reel as an analytic approach to working with video data. Like social media reels in which users curate and layer together multimodal content, data reels are short, annotated texts that stitch together video and other multimodal clips to ‘story’ the data. This paper describes how data reels emerged as an analytic approach in a design-research study about youth writing with generative AI. In illustrating how youth writers developed strategies to ensure their writerly voices were not overpowered by AI, we sought to use the methods of the medium to create data stories with screen capture video and other multimodal data collected at different points in time. We found that data reels served as a form of multimodal analysis that made researchers' interpretive work visible and opened space for sense-making with significant (often overwhelming) amounts of video data.

title: How Learners Detect Revision Occasions in Texts Labeled as Peer-Written or AI-Generated
citation: Radtke, A., Ruan, Q., Gurevych, I., & Rummel, N. (2025). How Learners Detect Revision Occasions in Texts Labeled as Peer-Written or AI-Generated. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1168-1172). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Radtke, A., Ruan, Q., Gurevych, I., & Rummel, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Although the potential of large language models in education has been widely recognized, research on how learners revise AI-generated content remains limited. The aim of this study was to determine whether learners detect different revision occasions when revising texts labeled as written by different authors (peer vs. AI). In a controlled study, learners (N = 152) revised a text that was labeled as either peer-written or AI-generated, while the con-tent of this text was in fact identical in both conditions. We found that learners descrip-tively detected fewer surface-level revision occasions in a text labeled as AI-generated, although this difference was not statistically significant. No notable difference was found for semantic (i.e., meaning-changing) revision occasions.

title: The Creativity Landscape Framework for Learning Design and Analysis
citation: Donaldson, J. P. (2025). The Creativity Landscape Framework for Learning Design and Analysis. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1173-1177). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Donaldson, J. P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper advances the understanding of creativity as a complex system through empirical validation of the Creativity Landscape framework, which conceptualizes creativity as emerging from the dynamic interplay of Creative Mindsets, Creative Environment, Creative Processes, and Creative Cognition. Through thematic network analysis of fifty highly-cited creativity research articles, the study provides empirical support for the framework's organization and its complex systems approach. The analysis revealed clusters that align with the framework's categories, demonstrating strong interconnections between elements. The findings validate the framework's emphasis on emergence, non-linearity, self-organization, adaptability, and feedback loops in creative processes. This work contributes to the learning sciences by offering a theoretically grounded and empirically supported tool for understanding and fostering creativity in learning contexts. The complex systems perspective provides new insights into the mechanisms driving creative emergence.

title: Learning Trajectories and Learning Gains: Students with Learning Disabilities in Game Based Fraction Program
citation: Hunt, J. & Taub, M. (2025). Learning Trajectories and Learning Gains: Students With Learning Disabilities in Game Based Fraction Program. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1178-1182). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hunt, J. & Taub, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics
abstract: A triangulation mixed methods design was employed to investigate the impacts of a whole class mathematics intervention based in a serious fraction game. Three teachers and their students with LD took part in the intervention and administered and completed pre and post assessments of fraction performance. A comparison group of two teachers whose students with LD did not take part in the intervention also administered and completed the pre and post assessments. Normalized learning gains revealed positive, medium gains for students with LD who took part in the intervention. However, students with LD in the comparison group experiences negative gains. Students’ learning trajectories, along with implications for practice, are discussed.

title: Prompts or Protocol: Helping Teacher Candidates See Students’ Strengths
citation: Pierson, A., Johnson, H. J., Henrie, A., Keifert, T., Jeong, S., & Daniel, B. (2025). Prompts or Protocol: Helping Teacher Candidates See Students’ Strengths. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1183-1187). subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Science education has shifted from a focus on canonical correctness toward students and sensemaking. In response, teacher educators have explored video analysis as an activity for helping teacher candidates notice students’ strengths. Framing influences what teacher candidates learn through video analysis. In this paper, we analyze a protocol as a support for teacher candidates’ noticing of students’ strengths. We find the protocol supported strengths-based noticing and positioned the facilitator as a collaborator. These findings offer implications for teacher educators aiming to support equitable science teaching.

title: Playful Programming with Computational Thinking as a Pathway to Culturally Responsive Pedagogy
citation: Dinç, E. & Kim, E. (2025). Playful Programming With Computational Thinking as a Pathway to Culturally Responsive Pedagogy. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1188-1192). abstract: We examined teachers’ learning and design processes of playful coding and computational thinking for language teaching in English as a Second Language (ESL) contexts. Data from two teachers were analyzed and collected via workshop recordings, interviews, and projects developed in Scratch. Examining teachers’ project development showed the potential of playful coding with computational thinking for culturally responsive pedagogy.

title: From Sound to Code: Creative Workflows and Problem-Solving in Music and Coding Tasks
citation: Roberts, C. L., Sherin, B., & Horn, M. S. (2025). From Sound to Code: Creative Workflows and Problem-Solving in Music and Coding Tasks. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 119-127). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Roberts, C. L., Sherin, B., & Horn, M. S.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This paper explores the creative workflows and problem-solving strategies individuals use when composing music with code. By analyzing the experiences of seven participants with varying levels of musical and coding expertise, we identified two primary creative workflows for developing and encoding musical ideas: direct translation, where participants developed musical ideas using non-code representations and iteratively decomposed them into code; and tinkering, where participants developed musical ideas through experimentation with code. Additionally, we describe two methods used to resolve discrepancies between their mental conception of music and the coded output, which we call trial-and-error and analytical sound debugging. Our findings highlight the complementary roles of musical intuition and music theory in shaping participants’ reasoning and problem-solving processes for developing and encoding their musical ideas. We conclude by discussing design implications for these findings, both regarding music+coding platforms and curricula, and extending to broader hybrid STEAM contexts.

title: “Nightshade Grows Well Here”: Exploring Rhizomatic Agency with Immigrant Growers in a Community Food Garden
citation: Dutta, D. & Takeuchi, M. A. (2025). “Nightshade Grows Well Here”: Exploring Rhizomatic Agency With Immigrant Growers in a Community Food Garden. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1193-1197). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Dutta, D. & Takeuchi, M. A.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study explores expansive views on agency and learning, focusing on the coupled assemblages between immigrant growers and more-than-human beings in the context of an urban community food garden. Drawing on the notion of meshwork (Ingold, 2016), we highlight previously displaced people’s evolving agentic capacities to navigate the social and geographic contours as dynamic socio-ecological adaptations emerging from the rhizomatic assemblages of food-growing activities, land, bodies and culture. Using an illustrative example of how a tropical edible plant, Nightshade, is grown in a vastly different cold climate by immigrant growers as they try to “root” themselves in a foreign space, we highlight the dynamic correspondence that simultaneously transforms the land and shapes their perspectives. In drawing attention to the relational and processual growth of Nightshade with respect to its surroundings, the study expands on how embodied, affective multi-species entanglements form critical dimensions of human becoming.

title: The Role of Surprise in Learning: Insights from Facial Expression Analysis
citation: Dubovi, I. & Naor, A. P. (2025). The Role of Surprise in Learning: Insights From Facial Expression Analysis. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1198-1201). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Dubovi, I. & Naor, A. P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
tpack_tk_labels: Immersive VR / AR; Simulations & Scientific Modeling
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: Surprise is a cognitive-emotional phenomenon that triggers attentional and cognitive mechanisms and, as such, can impact learning processes and outcomes. To examine how surprise emerges and affects learning, we captured naturally occurring instances of surprise in 28 students during a VR-based simulation. Using facial expression analysis, our findings challenge prior research by showing that surprise significantly aligns with negative emotions—such as fear, anger, and disgust—and correlates with lower knowledge test scores. These negative emotional states and outcomes may stem from the VR environment's high cognitive demands, which potentially hinder the metacognitive processing required to resolve explanatory difficulties and confusion. Further research should investigate the scaffolding needed to support learners effectively in VR-based contexts to resolve cognitive and emotional disequilibrium.

title: Investigating Melting And Freezing: How Different Scalar Levels Of Mechanistic Reasoning Look In Modeling-Based Learning In Kindergarten Science
citation: Louca, L. & Michaelidou, M. (2025). Investigating Melting and Freezing: How Different Scalar Levels of Mechanistic Reasoning Look in Modeling-Based Learning in Kindergarten Science. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 12-20). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Louca, L. & Michaelidou, M.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Modeling has been recognized as a crucial element of science education. Following research on using Modeling-based Learning (MbL) in kindergarten science education with an emphasis of mechanistic reasoning, this case study provides detailed descriptions of the implementation of MbL with a group of 21 kindergarten children studying (a) ice cube melting and (b) water freezing. Data included transcribed lessons and child-developed models. We coded the discourse data for mechanistic reasoning, and child-constructed models using artifact analysis. Findings suggest that participating kindergarten children (a) can think productively across various scalar levels of mechanistic reasoning, although support to move across these levels is necessary; (b) working in a step-by-step process of progressive MbL is crucial for children before moving to lower scalar levels of reasoning; and (c) multiple ways of analyzing the data from children of these ages provide better insights into the MbL process.

title: The Future Landscape of Education: Constructing an Analytical and Application Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education
citation: Xiao, Z., Wang, C., Lai, Y., Wang, H., & Gu, X. (2025). The Future Landscape of Education: Constructing an Analytical and Application Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1202-1206). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Xiao, Z., Wang, C., Lai, Y., Wang, H., & Gu, X.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has infused new vitality into education, making the regulation of its application in higher education a current research focus. This study conducts a systematic literature review to comprehensively assess the application landscape and challenges of GenAI in higher education, constructing an action framework encompassing four key elements: Formulate policy and regulation, Enhance academic integrity and assessment, Advance preparation and training, and Develop teaching and learning strategies. The framework aims to provide structured pathways for universities to ensure the ethical and compliant application of GenAI, uphold academic standards, foster skill development, and promote instructional innovation. Specifically, by delineating action pathways according to educational entities (governmental bodies, educational institutions, educators and students), this study provides clear execution directions for each role, facilitating collaborative efforts. The framework serves as a bridge between policy and practice, offering guidance for integrating GenAI into higher education systems effectively.

title: Critical Algorithmic Literacy for LLM-assisted Decision-making
citation: Wang, G. & Pea, R. (2025). Critical Algorithmic Literacy for Llm-Assisted Decision-Making. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1207-1211). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wang, G. & Pea, R.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: In today’s information landscape, algorithm-driven technologies mediate nearly all aspects of information and communication, profoundly shaping our decisions and societal participation. This paper explores a rapidly evolving example of algorithmic influence: the role of LLMs in human decision-making. As LLMs become increasingly central to these processes, their influence extends beyond simple assistance, potentially transforming how individuals evaluate options and act on recommendations. We examine this through the lens of critical algorithmic literacy, which encompasses the ability to interpret and critically assess algorithmic systems that influence access to information and decision-making. Based on a scoping review of 45 papers, we highlight the need for autonomy-supportive LLM-assisted decision-making approaches that empower learners to critically engage with the entire process and confidently take control of their choices as transformative agents.

title: Interdisciplinary Teaching and Learning in the Humanities: How it Might Go Wrong
citation: Cohen, E. & Novis-Deutsch, N. (2025). Interdisciplinary Teaching and Learning in the Humanities: How it Might Go Wrong. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1212-1216). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cohen, E. & Novis-Deutsch, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: There are relatively few empirical investigations of interdisciplinary teaching and learning (ITL), mostly focusing on the affordances of ITL for teachers and learners. In contrast, this study identifies and examines two critical challenges within ITL classrooms, focusing on coherence and the need for cross-disciplinary expertise. Ethnographic data we collected from two schools revealed (1) that students struggled with fragmented understandings when subjects were not effectively integrated, and (2) that teachers faced limitations in addressing topics outside their disciplinary training. These findings can serve educators and policymakers interested in implementing ITL, as well as scholars interested in understanding and conceptualizing it.

title: “A space to think, read, and observe the world”: What do RPPs Mean to Practitioners?
citation: Cohen, E., Baharav, H., & Hadar, L. (2025). “A Space to Think, Read, and Observe the World”: What do RPPs Mean to Practitioners?. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1217-1221). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cohen, E., Baharav, H., & Hadar, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Accountable Talk & Dialogic Discourse; Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs) are designed to ensure the consequentiality of educational research by focusing on real-world problems of practice. Most of what we know from research on RPPs is grounded in the assumption that the purpose of RPPs is to provide multiple stakeholders with empirical findings that can inform educational policy and practice. This perspective, however, is largely researcher-focused and may not reflect practitioners’ aims and motivations. In this paper, we ask what RPPs mean to practitioners. Using ethnographic and discourse analysis methods, we show that for practitioners, RPPs can serve objectives such as fostering intellectual engagement and mediating cultural change.

title: Artifactual Knowing in Collaborative Modeling Practices
citation: Fackler, A. K., Zangori, L. A., Botkin, M., Elsner, J. N., & Sadler, T. D. (2025). Artifactual Knowing in Collaborative Modeling Practices. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1222-1226). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Fackler, A. K., Zangori, L. A., Botkin, M., Elsner, J. N., & Sadler, T. D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We use artifactual knowing and positioning theory as a lens to examine the development of a small group model. In this exploratory case study, we analyzed how a group of middle school students positioned themselves, their peers, and the emerging modeling artifact during a collaborative modeling task. We find that as the model emerged, it created a space where youth challenged assumptions, negotiated content, and redefined their positions through the artifact. Study implications suggest that how modeling artifacts emerge significantly shapes how modeling practices support student learning.

title: From Learners to Teachers: Mastering Machine Learning While Creating Engaging Environments for Young Learners
citation: Sharma, M., Shen, J., Perry, A., Rai, P., & Lu, R. (2025). From Learners to Teachers: Mastering Machine Learning While Creating Engaging Environments for Young Learners. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1227-1231). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sharma, M., Shen, J., Perry, A., Rai, P., & Lu, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: There is a need for Artificial Intelligence (AI) curricula that are developmentally appropriate and appeal to students’ interests (Lee and Perret, 2022). Embracing a Community of Learners theoretical perspective (Rogoff, 1994) and employing a Project-based Learning framework (Krajcik and Shin, 2014) we designed a unit on Machine Learning (ML) using Google Teachable Machine for early adolescents that incorporates interest-driven practices with the help of two Learner-Teachers. We implemented this unit in a summer camp with 9-14yo campers and documented the learning progress of our primary participants (high school students that assumed hybrid roles as Learner-Teachers) and the campers. The findings suggest that the curriculum produces quality learning outcomes including improved knowledge about ML, the process of training ML models, and a greater appreciation of the role of student interest in our Learner-Teachers in designing and implementing activities.

title: Narratives of Change: Fostering Agency toward Sustainability
citation: Tasquier, G., Jornet, A., & Knain, E. (2025). Narratives of Change: Fostering Agency Toward Sustainability. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1232-1236). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tasquier, G., Jornet, A., & Knain, E.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study explores the role of narratives in empowering young people to engage with sustainability issues, with a focus on fostering agency through narrative-based learning. Using data collected via the SenseMaker tool, this research examines how micro-narratives reveal students' attitudes, personal agency, and reflections on climate change. Findings suggest that narratives enhance understanding, providing a lens through which students envision their roles in sustainability and address complex, real-world challenges.

title: Assessing Directionally-Motivated Reasoning: Students’ Evaluations of a Digital Post on a Relevant Topic
citation: McGrew, S. (2025). Assessing Directionally-Motivated Reasoning: Students’ Evaluations of a Digital Post on a Relevant Topic. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1237-1241). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: McGrew, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Little attention has focused on the role directionally-motivated reasoning plays in students’ evaluations of online information and how lessons on evaluating digital content might address this. This study analyzed student reasoning expressed via a short, written task designed to assess students’ digital evaluations of an online article about a relevant topic. Students were prompted to explain their opinion on whether students should always be allowed to use phones in school and then judged the reliability of a Verizon article that argued for the positive impacts of phones in classrooms. Evidence of students’ directionally-motivated reasoning emerged: Students whose opinions were aligned with the article more commonly argued it was reliable, and students frequently judged the article by engaging with the argument it made. Such tasks could support lessons on evaluating online information that help students consider the role directionally-motivated reasoning plays in their judgments.

title: Feedback Sources in Argumentative Writing: AI Feedback or Peer Feedback?
citation: Ji, J., Zhao, H., & Wu, Y. (2025). Feedback Sources in Argumentative Writing: Ai Feedback or Peer Feedback?. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1242-1246). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ji, J., Zhao, H., & Wu, Y.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study compared AI feedback with peer feedback, examining both the quantity and qualitative aspects of negative feedback. The results indicated that ChatGPT (the AI tool used in the study) generated a consistent volume of feedback across various dimensions, contrasting with the variable amounts observed in peer feedback. Quantitatively, ChatGPT produced more negative feedback than peers. Qualitatively, it provided more mitigating praises and general suggestions for issues related to both essay content and form, as well as more specific solutions for form-focused issues. However, peer feedback excelled in offering more detailed explanations for content-related issues. The implications of the research findings are discussed.

title: Online Learning Strategy Transition in Blended Courses: Learning Analytics Based on Two Cases in Higher Education
citation: Niu, X. & Zhang, J. (2025). Online Learning Strategy Transition in Blended Courses: Learning Analytics Based on Two Cases in Higher Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1247-1251). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Niu, X. & Zhang, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Effective online learning strategies consistently correlate with improved learning performance across learning science and learning analytics. However, students' learning strategies are not static, they evolve through a dynamic process of development and refinement. Despite this established knowledge, research examining the process of strategic shifts and their impact on learning outcomes remains limited. To address this gap, this study analyzed 298,773 behavior log entries and final grade data from 346 learners across two identically designed blended courses. Using K-Means clustering, we identified six distinct learning strategies and tracked their patterns over time. Results revealed that video interaction, comment engagement, progress management, and reply behaviors were the dominant strategies. Notably, transition from a cramming to a deep learning strategy trajectory correlated with significant improvements in final grades.

title: Teacher Candidates’ Identity Construction as Collective Movement along Zones of Sense
citation: Martínez-Álvarez, P. & Kajamaa, A. (2025). Teacher Candidates’ Identity Construction as Collective Movement Along Zones of Sense. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1252-1254). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Martínez-Álvarez, P. & Kajamaa, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this manuscript, we explore how collective sensemaking takes may take place during teacher preparation programs and how this might influence the development of professional teaching identities. Drawing from a cultural historical view of learning, we situate this conceptual manuscript in identity development processes of teacher candidates during graduate courses while engaged in student teaching experiences. We suggest that teacher candidates construct and develop their professional teacher identities as an active social process through sensemaking. Understanding teacher identity development has implications for their professional development, and for teacher preparation programs.

title: Unveiling Critique: Exploring AI’s Future and Societal Impact through Interdisciplinary Epic Theatre and STEM Learning
citation: Timpilis, D. & Shen, J. (2025). Unveiling Critique: Exploring Ai’s Future and Societal Impact Through Interdisciplinary Epic Theatre and STEM Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1255-1259). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Timpilis, D. & Shen, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores the role of student critique within a high school integrated theatre-STEM curriculum focused on Artificial Intelligence (AI). By conceptualizing student critique as a nested activity within the broader learning activity through the lens of Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT), this design-based research examines how students perceive and engage in critique -including peer critique, self-critique, critique of AI concepts, and critique of the curriculum. Thematic analysis of six selected datasets, including student survey responses and live discussions, revealed three key themes: (1) the significant social and emotional dimensions of student critique; (2) the expansion of critique from theatrical elements to interdisciplinary aspects such as technological accuracy and ethical and societal considerations of AI; and (3) contradictions and tensions within the critique activity acted as catalysts for development and transformation. The findings highlight that a theatre-STEM curriculum encouraging and incorporating student critique can promote student agency and enhance interdisciplinary learning.

title: A Long Cycle of Expansive Learning in a Food Cooperative: A Multi-Lens Analysis
citation: Rantavuori, J. & Engeström, Y. (2025). A Long Cycle of Expansive Learning in a Food Cooperative: A Multi-Lens Analysis. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1260-1264). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rantavuori, J. & Engeström, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study presents a longitudinal, multi-lens analysis of expansive learning within the Herttoniemi Food Cooperative, a social movement focused on sustainable food production located in Helsinki. We employ the theory of expansive learning to analyze a year-long process of collective learning among the cooperative's board members. The aim of this study is to understand the innovative learning process of the board as they faced the challenge of financial viability. The data of this study consist of recordings from 26 board meetings and a planning day. Our findings show that the concept of degrowth acted as a central integrative factor for developing tangible solutions. The starting point of innovations was real-world problems that participants encountered in the board meetings as they were trying to solve the complex object of financial sustainability. An intervention planning day was needed to refine new tools in their mature form to be implemented later successfully.

title: Impact of AI Literacy on Student-AI Interactions on Academic Writing
citation: Kim, J., Detrick, R., Lee, S., & Li, N. (2025). Impact of Ai Literacy on Student-Ai Interactions on Academic Writing. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1265-1269). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kim, J., Detrick, R., Lee, S., & Li, N.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)
abstract: Advancements in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) provide an opportunity to evolve student-AI interactions (SAI). Research studying the nature and effects of SAI on learning with students with differing characteristics, such as AI literacy levels. This study examines how students with varying AI literacy engage with AI and whether these differences impact task performance by analyzing three data sources (think-aloud protocols, screen recordings, and chat histories) produced by 36 Chinese graduate students using a GenAI writing system. Epistemic network analysis (ENA) was applied to uncover SAI patterns across students with differing AI literacy levels. Findings reveal that high AI literacy students employ collaborative approaches when interacting with GenAI, while low literacy students interact with GenAI to a lesser extent. Findings further revealed statistical differences in final task performance between AI literacy levels. This research provides insights for designing and implementing GenAI agents in writing tasks and enhancing GenAI-assisted pedagogy.

title: Discrepancies in College Belonging: How Demographics May Shape the Fulfillment of Belonging Expectations
citation: Rayford, T., Jeng, A., Ruedas-Gracia, N., & Song, D. (2025). Discrepancies in College Belonging: How Demographics May Shape the Fulfillment of Belonging Expectations. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1270-1274). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rayford, T., Jeng, A., Ruedas-Gracia, N., & Song, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this paper, we seek to understand belonging fulfillment, which is the difference between how well a student believes they will belong to their college and their actual feelings of belonging to their college. We examined (a) whether students’ expectations about college belonging are fulfilled during their tenure and (b) how demographic background predicts the degree to which students’ expectations about college belonging are fulfilled during their tenure. Participants consisted of 100 undergraduates enrolled at a private research university. We found that the university may be failing to fulfill students’ expectations of college belonging and that low-income students are more likely to have their college belonging expectations fulfilled and surpassed. These results have important implications for higher education practitioners.

title: From the Dominance of Authorities to Residents’ Inclusion to Decision-Making Processes
citation: Lund, V. (2025). From the Dominance of Authorities to Residents’ Inclusion to Decision-Making Processes. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1275-1279). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lund, V.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study aims to investigate the collaboration of civil society and municipal administration in the systematic change process of a neighborhood. Five community workshops were conducted in the City of Espoo, Finland. The method of community workshop provided a structure for examining a complex urban situation and facilitated collective problem-solving. The methodology of cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) enabled to identify the expansive learning actions and follow the transformation of the object of activity during the workshop process. The study shows that the expansive learning actions helped the residents and civil servants collectively resolve contradictions. This in turn enabled them to see the developmental potential of their activities and take actions to transform them. This study reveals a learning process in the context of urban development by addressing contradictions as valuable resources for learning and development.

title: Learning to Thrive and Be Well in Times of Injustice: Teachers’ Approaches to Histories of Police Violence and Resistance
citation: Marshall, J. M. (2025). Learning to Thrive and Be Well in Times of Injustice: Teachers’ Approaches to Histories of Police Violence and Resistance. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 128-136). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Marshall, J. M. W.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: While debates rage about the proper role of schools in addressing histories of racism and injustice, we have few examples of how teachers across school districts navigate the teaching of such histories during times of ongoing injustice. Using sensemaking theory (Spillane, et al, 2002) and research in the learning sciences on the political dimensions of learning (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Philip, et al. 2018), I explore the enactment narratives of teachers tasked with implementing a mandated curriculum on police violence. I argue that teachers’ experiences of navigating the tensions and contradictions of teaching histories of police violence in the wake of the murder of George Floyd and many others, as well as their understanding of their Black and Brown students as deserving of protection and care, led teachers to develop a specific set of learning goals focused on thriving and well-being. Their implementation approaches that linked relational, affective, and political learning illustrate possibilities to engage in learning histories of harm and resistance while also imagining and enacting just futures in the here and now.

title: Reevaluating the Effectiveness of Inquiry-Based Learning through Decades of Long-term Assessment in Japanese STEM Programs
citation: Saito, M., Iikubo, S., & Shirouzu, H. (2025). Reevaluating the Effectiveness of Inquiry-Based Learning Through Decades of Long-Term Assessment in Japanese STEM Programs. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1280-1284). subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper aims to offer methodological insights that demonstrate the long-term advantages of inquiry-based learning (hereafter IBL) by reviewing case reports using a Hypothesis-Experiment-Instruction (hereafter HEI) along with a small-scale retrospective survey. We prepared two measures: retaining the learning process of inquiry and using model-based reasoning skills. Based on previous research showing evidence for Measure 1 with HEI, we conducted a survey focusing on Measure 2, which revealed a tendency to utilize explanatory models (hereafter EMs). However, it was found that the explanatory models used by participants were not always the same as those employed in their past classes. The results imply necessity for an innovative approach to achieving a more continuous view of long-term learning processes, visualizing interactive processes of enriching domain knowledge and skill development, and devising metrics that capture these complex processes.

title: Supporting Middle School Students to Learn AI Through Creative Machine Learning Projects
citation: Wang, C. (2025). Supporting Middle School Students to Learn Ai Through Creative Machine Learning Projects. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1285-1289). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wang, C.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: To fill in the gap of K – 12 AI education, I designed and implemented a middle-school Machine Learning (ML) curriculum in a free online afterschool program. Students were engaged in hands-on ML projects for solving real-world problems. With the Teachable Machine platform, students took photos of themselves to train their own ML models that can automatically recognize if a person wears a mask or not in the context of COVID pandemic. Primary data sources were class recordings and students’ screen recordings. Interaction analysis of these recordings showed that, (1) students’ constant interactions with the learning tools helped them to test, revise, and improve their ML model; (2) students’ interactions with peers and teachers helped them to understand ML mechanisms; and (3) involving family members in data collection and model testing was helpful for students’ learning. The study sheds light on the learning design of AI/ML education for middle schoolers.

title: Finding Out about Science through the News: How Specialist and Non-Specialist Science Journalists’ Epistemic Aims and Practices Vary
citation: Varda, C. & Iordanou, K. (2025). Finding out About Science Through the News: How Specialist and Non-Specialist Science Journalists’ Epistemic Aims and Practices Vary. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1290-1294). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Varda, C. & Iordanou, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: People resort to the news to find out about science, but the evolving media landscape has transformed how science is reported. Due to media’s infrastructural challenges, specialist journalists and non-specialist science journalists report on science. Given that journalists hold an epistemic function by disseminating knowledge claims, this exploratory study sought to understand how epistemic and non-epistemic aims and epistemic practices compare between specialist and non-specialist journalists reporting on science. We adopted a case study analysis and analyzed two focus group with distinct samples (specialist/non-specialist journalists). Both groups mentioned epistemic aims, but these differed: non-specialist journalists aimed for objectivity and fairness, while specialist journalists aimed at explaining science. Non-specialist journalists also verbalized financial incentives and speed as non-epistemic aims. The epistemic practices between the groups also varied extensively; only making science personally relevant applied to both groups. The study holds implications for journalism instruction and curricula for science reporting.

citation: Zhou, X., Gong, Y., Yu, Y., Zhang, Y., Smith, J., & Bai, Z. (2025). Design Ai for My Community: A Case Study of Collaborative Learning in a Freedom-to-Read Summer Camp. abstract: Fostering AI literacy among youth from diverse communities with unique values and challenges is crucial. This requires critical pedagogy and education inclusion that empower students—especially those from marginalized backgrounds—to engage with technology meaningfully and address societal inequities. We developed a summer camp with the theme “Protect the Freedom to READ”. By inviting students to collaboratively design AI for their community, the camp deepened their AI understanding and empowered them to create applications that honor their community’s values. Collaborative AI design developed higher-order thinking skills. Additionally, critical pedagogy played a key role in enabling children to apply AI skills toward innovative, community-focused applications, positioning them as advocates for ethical and inclusive technology.

title: Kindergarteners’ Strategies and Ideas When Reasoning with Function Tables and Graphs
citation: López, M. A., Strachota, S., Brizuela, B. M., Gardiner, A. M., & Blanton, M. (2025). Kindergarteners’ Strategies and Ideas When Reasoning With Function Tables and Graphs. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1300-1304). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: López, M. A., Strachota, S., Brizuela, B. M., Gardiner, A. M., & Blanton, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigated the seeds of algebraic thinking that Kindergarten students use when engaging with function tables and graphs. Through interviews with three Kindergarteners, we explored how they reasoned about functional relationships. Our results illustrate how the Kindergarteners used seeds of algebraic thinking when using function tables and graphs to represent and reason about functional relationships. Building on the seeds of algebraic thinking and Knowledge in Pieces frameworks, we categorized these seeds as either strategies (classify, pair, and compare) or ideas (seeds of covariation). Strategy seeds were goal-oriented, and seeds of covariation were elicited without any goal and reflected a broader understanding of change between quantities.

subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Communities of Practice & Situated Learning; Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: This study examines the effectiveness of generative role-playing game-based learning in a college-level science fiction course. Twenty-three students participated in a semester-long role-playing game designed to enhance understanding of literary concepts and foster internal motivation to learn. The study incorporated seven theoretical frameworks, including constructionist theory, situated learning theory, and transformative learning theory. Findings reveal that role-playing games provided transformational learning experiences, particularly in identity exploration and critical thinking. The study also suggests that role-playing games can be leveraged as a powerful tool for transformational growth across various disciplines, encouraging educators to consider how identity exploration through role-play can enhance learning outcomes in different educational contexts.

title: Community, Creativity, and Identity in Generative Role-Play Based Learning
citation: Cooper, R. P., Chowdury, M., Donaldson, J. P., & Pawson, A. (2025). Community, Creativity, and Identity in Generative Role-Play Based Learning. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cooper, R. P., Chowdury, M., Donaldson, J. P., & Pawson, A.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Productive Failure & Problem Solving; Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: This study examines learner experiences in generative role-playing game-based learning implemented in a university science fiction literature course. Through complex systems thematic network analysis of student reflections, we investigated how principles from learning theories manifested in the game-based learning experience. Analysis revealed five distinct clusters of principles, with constructionist elements showing the highest network centrality. The findings suggest that game creation and world-building serve as powerful tools for literary education, with students navigating multiple identities—both real and fictional—throughout the course. The study identified an important prerequisite for engagement: students must either leverage existing gamer identities or develop new ones before fully engaging in the creative process. This research contributes to understanding how game-based learning can facilitate transformative learning experiences in literature courses, while highlighting the need for better integration of productive failure and tinkering principles in future design iterations.

title: “Push Forward and We Will Help”: Teacher Autonomy and System Support in the Context of Teaching Displaced Students
citation: Ehrenfeld, N., Marco, N., Gilead, T., Nurick, Y., & Kurzweil, L. (2025). “Push Forward and we Will Help”: Teacher Autonomy and System Support in the Context of Teaching Displaced Students. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
