subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this paper, we address the under-investigated topic of teaching displaced students and at the same time build on this unique teaching context to theorize about teachers’ sense of autonomy and support. While it is generally presumed that respecting teachers’ autonomy is important, there is a need to refine our understanding of how and why a sense of autonomy is not always embraced by teachers or perceived as valuable. The study builds on 14 interviews with teachers in provisional schools for displaced students in Israel. We articulate and illustrate a preliminary framework that elaborates on the notion of teacher autonomy by distinguishing the autonomy that teachers are granted from the support they receive to deal with the challenges that might come with such autonomy.

title: Exploring Convergences and Divergences in Pedagogical Judgment During Teacher Workplace Conversations
citation: Ehrenfeld, N., Zgair-Araidy, R., Elgamal, R., Cooper, J., & Sabbah, S. (2025). Exploring Convergences and Divergences in Pedagogical Judgment During Teacher Workplace Conversations. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1319-1323). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ehrenfeld, N., Zgair-Araidy, R., Elgamal, R., Cooper, J., & Sabbah, S.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: While teacher learning is typically studied in the context of formal professional development (PD) activities, many teacher learning opportunities emerge from teachers’ daily workplace conversations. However, these conversations are spread across time and space, difficult to analyze, and are less prominent in the field as the locus of research. In this paper, we explore challenges and opportunities for teachers to hone their pedagogical judgment, amidst convergences and divergences in their perspectives, while teachers are attending to their daily work. To do so, we integrate two frameworks for the study of teachers as agentic sensemakers. We illustrate the integrated perspective through cases of two secondary mathematics teachers’ team meetings from two schools in Israel. The analysis highlights that even when conflicts between pedagogical perspectives are explicit, some aspects of their convergences and divergences are implicit, which poses a challenge for teachers’ productive pedagogical discourse and for researchers’ analysis of workplace conversations.

abstract: Peer review, as a process of knowledge co-construction, involves reviewers and authors in critical dialogue to enhance manuscript quality. Novice reviewers learn this practice by observing experienced peers and gaining hands-on experience. This study analyzed linguistic features in expert peer reviews within an argumentative knowledge co-construction framework, highlighting distinct author and reviewer roles and participation modes. Findings revealed varied social dynamics and confidence levels across review phases, underscoring the need for further research to prepare novice reviewers across disciplines.

abstract: In this study, we have built on critical and creative pedagogy approaches to invite youth to envision desirable futures by addressing social injustices in data-driven societies through creating Futures Headlines. We developed an analytical framework that distinguishes between moral and normative reasoning. These dimensions are elaborated into further categories that allow examining youth’s perceptions of social injustice, as well as how they envision justice. We claim the framework is a valuable tool for research and practice as it helps understanding youth’s thinking about justice as well as identifying areas for further discussion to foster youth’s critical awareness and reflection. Based on our findings, we advocate for embracing a transdisciplinary approach to justice and data literacy, paying special attention to aspects connected to historicity and systemic thinking.

subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This mixed-methods study examined an AI-supported virtual simulation and explored the role of preservice teachers’ (PSTs) in-the-moment interpretations of virtual students’ resources (both epistemic and emotional) in their responsive teaching practices. Thirty-three preservice science and mathematics teachers participated in the study. Linear regression analysis results revealed that PSTs’ interpretative acts can significantly predict their responsive teaching practices. Qualitative analysis corroborated that purposive interpretation enabled PSTs to estimate students’ learning states and teaching scenarios as a whole. It was also found that PSTs struggled to enact interpretations, pointing to future research directions.

title: Emotion Regulation During Failure-driven Learning
citation: Sinha, T. (2025). Emotion Regulation During Failure-Driven Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: Sinha, T.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Fifty-one ninth-grade students self-reported whether and what forms of emotion regulation they pursued during suboptimal idea generation for a math task targeting a yet-to-be-learned topic. Results showed that the majority of students did not try to actively change or manage their emotions. Among those that did, regulation strategies were predominantly cognitively-focused or involved taking an emotionally detached perspective to focus on problem-solving processes. Strategies where students acknowledged and worked with emotions without discrediting their experience were rarer. Furthermore, the awareness of failure critically impacted emotional reactions. Findings hold implications for increasing awareness of useful emotion regulation strategies in the service of improving emotional resilience in classrooms.

abstract: This study provides an updated overview of the concepts and methods in the Learning Sciences (LS) graduate programs, addressing the question posed by Sommerhoff et al. (2018) about what we teach in the LS. Analyzing 88 programs across institutions, we found a quantitative growth in programs. Most are concentrated in North America, with fewer in Europe and minimal representation in Australia and Asia. Key concepts include digital technology to support learning, learning in formal contexts, and the design of learning environments. Programs employ methods, including both quantitative and qualitative approaches, with design-based research and learning analytics being prevalent. Programs teaching non-parametric statistics, collaborative learning, and computational modeling showed the highest homogeneity. A decade later, we see that some former core concepts of LS have shifted to the periphery, while peripheral concepts, like diversity and equity, and methods are merging with the core, reflecting the LS as an innovative, dynamic community of practice.

International Society of the Learning Sciences.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: At present, there is a research gap on which learner characteristics may lead to high and low learning outcomes supported by generative AI. To this end, this study used Qualitative Comparative Analysis (QCA) to explore the configuration effects of learners' motivation, technological dispositions, and prior experiences on learning outcomes. This study involved 29 college students as participants, who were required to use ChatGPT to assist in the revision of English essays. The research identified 3 configurations leading to high learning outcomes and 2 configurations associated with low learning outcomes, shedding light on the complex effects of learners' characteristics in GAI-supported learning. The findings indicate that learners' perceived usefulness of GAI is a critical factor in determining learning outcomes, and strong learning motivation can mitigate the negative effects of a lack of prior experience.

title: Intelligent Assessment of Online Learning Experience Based on Eye-Tracking Technology
citation: Zhan, C., Yaofeng, X., Yiwei, G., & Yisheng, Q. (2025). Intelligent Assessment of Online Learning Experience Based on Eye-Tracking Technology. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhan, C., Yaofeng, X., Yiwei, G., & Yisheng, Q.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores the potential of eye-tracking for evaluating learning experiences in video-based online courses. Eye movements from 26 students were recorded using a Tobii T120 device, yielding fixation, saccade, and pupil-diameter features. Six machine learning models, including Random Forest (RF) and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), were trained via five-fold cross-validation. RF achieved the highest accuracy, demonstrating robust predictive capabilities. Correlation analyses indicated that focusing on core content regions, maintaining stable visual distances, and exhibiting moderate pupil dilation were positively associated with improved learning experiences, while peripheral distractions and frequent attention shifts negatively impacted engagement. These findings underscore the feasibility of integrating eye-tracking data into online learning platforms to enable personalized feedback and optimize interface design.

title: Fostering Familial Presence in STEM Education through an Identities-in-Practice Perspective
citation: Sedawi, W., Barton, A. C., & Tan, E. (2025). Fostering Familial Presence in STEM Education Through an Identities-in-Practice Perspective. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sedawi, W., Barton, A. C., & Tan, E.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Supporting parental/familial presence in STEM education requires forging new parent-teacher relationships and epistemologies to bridge home and school. Through the FamJam project, using participatory critical design ethnographic methods, we collaborated with an urban public-school teacher, immigrant students, and their mothers to foster familial rightful presence in a STEM unit focused on engineering for sustainable communities. Our study employs the “Identities-in-Practice” framework to investigate how relationships among mothers, teachers, and students cultivate emerging epistemologies and new social learning practices. Findings reveal how teachers and mothers acted as allies, developing new relations that yielded three powerful practices: 1) fostering porous boundaries in STEM; 2) incubating new epistemologies into STEM; and 3) authoring new identities/positions among teachers, mothers, and students, while disrupting normative perspectives in STEM learning. We argue for recognizing, supporting, and leveraging new relationships among identities-in-practice to expand opportunities for parent engagement and advance justice in STEM learning.

In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1364-1368). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Weatherton, M. & Aikens, M.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Introductory STEM courses play a critical role in shaping undergraduate students’ success, yet resource use behaviors and their relationship with academic outcomes in these courses remain underexplored. This study examined latent patterns of resource use among 1,884 students in introductory biology courses at seven research-intensive universities using Latent Class Analysis. We identified four distinct resource use groups characterized by variations in the frequency of social and material resource engagement. Demographic factors, including race, gender, and college generation status, significantly predicted latent group membership. Contrary to prior assumptions, minoritized students, such as Black students, women, and first-generation students, reported frequent engagement with multiple resources, including instructors. These findings highlight the complexity of resource use behaviors and challenge deficit-oriented narratives about minoritized students. Future research will link these patterns to academic outcomes to better understand persistent disparities and inform inclusive strategies to promote equitable success in introductory STEM courses.

abstract: This study examines how an NLP-focused AI curriculum was adapted for 5th and 8th graders with different prior experiences. Classroom video analysis revealed that the 5th-grade teacher used structured, hands-on activities, while the 8th-grade teacher fostered autonomous, peer-supported exploration. Both groups showed significant learning gains. Using activity system analysis, we explored how tools, guidance, and collaboration shaped curriculum enactment within students’ Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD). Findings underscore the need for flexible AI curricula, showing that scaffolding and inquiry-driven methods effectively engage students across grade levels.

abstract: An often overlooked but important component of understanding how to support teachers to enact computer science (CS) instruction is investigating how they plan CS activities. This study investigates how teachers in a research-practice partnership (RPP) report planning to integrate culturally relevant CS into their lessons. Teachers were interviewed about how they planned lessons to implement culturally relevant CS in their classrooms. Researchers analyzed the interviews using a framework of persistent challenges that teachers confront when planning and enacting instruction. Findings include that teachers were capable of anticipating and overcoming challenges of supporting students with basic technology skills. However, results also highlight that teachers planning CS instruction may need additional support to anticipate ways to assess student thinking, strategies for managing student behavior, and to develop and reach their personal goals for implementing culturally relevant CS lessons.

abstract: This research explores how the Funds of Knowledge and Funds of Identity frameworks uncover language instructors’ strategies for connecting students' home practices with higher education, aiming to improve foreign language learning. Specifically, it examines how English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instructors at a Costa Rican public university integrate learners' life experiences, skills, and local contexts into English for Specific Purposes lesson planning. Findings highlight how EFL instructors gather and incorporate students' household contexts and identities into the higher education ESP curricula, identify the challenges in bridging ESP curricula and learners’ household contexts, and demonstrate how a visualization tool helps EFL instructors reflect on and discuss FoK and FoI integration. The study underscores the necessity for higher curricular flexibility in higher education EFL programs to better align with language students' local backgrounds and identities.

abstract: Science teacher education faces significant challenges in linking pedagogy with equity and in overcoming the isolation of teacher preparation programs in the United States. Legislation opposing equity and social justice, combined with the idiosyncratic nature of isolated programs, has led to fragmented and inefficient teacher education. This conceptual paper advocates for collective practices and tool development as a means to better prepare science teachers as well as shape the growth of science teacher educators. Using the framework of Cultural and Critical Ambitious Science Teaching (C2AST) as a model, we propose a new paradigm for cross-institutional collaboration that respects local contexts while establishing a shared language and vision. Our framework for equity-focused science education aims to create common tools and practices that enhance pre-service teachers' critical consciousness and instructional skills. By integrating core instructional practices with culturally responsive pedagogy, we envision a more unified and effective approach to teacher preparation.

title: 도토리묵 (Acorn Jelly) as an Actor to Connect Culture and Science

abstract: In response to research arguing for integrating culture into science education contexts, this analysis looks at how culture was an actor with agency in an elementary teacher professional development (PD) project. Drawing on actor network theory, we asked: How does culture as an actor exercise agency to shape an assemblage within elementary science PD activity? We focused on the Korean language and 도토리묵 (dotori-muk: Korean acorn jelly) as manifestations of Korean culture within our assemblage. Microgenetic analysis revealed three transitions where relationships between actors were re-assembled and translated into new learning trajectories. These transitions involved 1) the Korean language and 2) 도토리묵 exercising agency to influence the PD activity, and 3) Korean language and cultural practices influencing the teachers’ and researchers’ relationship to science. Findings provide insights for future research recognizing the agency and influence of culture on knowledge production.

title: Evaluating Language Models Using Linguistic Variations in Multilingual Learners’ Writing: A Teacher Study
citation: Barron, K., Tseng, N., Karumbaiah, S., & Baeza, C. T. (2025). Evaluating Language Models Using Linguistic Variations in Multilingual Learners’ Writing: A Teacher Study. abstract: This paper investigates teachers’ perceptions on linguistic variations in bi/multilingual learners’ (MLs) writing to evaluate the (in)effectiveness of Multilingual Large Language Models (MLLMs), which are artificial intelligence (AI) models that generate texts in multiple languages. Due to their inherent linguistic biases, these models often struggle to interpret MLs’ linguistic variations. To address this gap, we elicit teacher feedback on prevalent linguistic variations in MLs’ writing and assess how Meta Llama 3.1, a state-of-the-art MLLM, responds to these variations. Using translanguaging as a lens—the fluid use of multiple languages to convey meaning across social contexts—we propose a new approach to evaluate MLLMs in multilingual learning contexts. With the increasing prevalence of AI in K12 classrooms, this paper advocates for the inclusion of bi/multilingual educators to better align the use of AI with progressive pedagogies such as translanguaging.

title: Exploring Emotion-related Individual Differences in Adolescents' Daily Lives: An Analysis Using Large Language Models
citation: Chen, J., Liu, X., Qi, X., & Zhang, Y. (2025). Exploring Emotion-Related Individual Differences in Adolescents' Daily Lives: An Analysis Using Large Language Models. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Diary methods can help us understand how adolescents recognize and manage emotions in their daily lives, which aids in optimizing social-emotional learning practices. This exploratory study invited 30 students to write their daily entries. These unstructured texts were then automatically coded with the help of large language models, which performed comparably to human raters. Importantly, two indicators (semantic similarity and emotional event alignment) were used to assess how an individual's feelings in specific contexts align with the common understanding of those contexts. We found positive associations between diary-derived indicators for positive entries and performance on emotion perception tasks, while students with lower semantic similarity for negative entries showed higher performance on the emotion regulation task, indicating self-regulation in negative contexts. The study highlighted the potential of using large language models to characterize students' daily emotions and preliminarily demonstrated how individual differences manifest in adolescents' emotional lives.

title: Pedagogies for Executing Impactful AI Literacy Programs
citation: Sinha, T. (2025). Pedagogies for Executing Impactful Ai Literacy Programs. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. abstract: Given the recent democratization of artificial intelligence (AI), it is imperative to equip educators with the essential conceptual knowledge and competencies required for success as professionals. We describe design and evaluation of two iterations of a two-day synchronous workshop for N = 62 in-service teachers, which offered a non-technical introduction to AI and its cutting-edge applications in education. Teachers’ readiness to engage and build with AI using pre-post validated surveys showed improvements of up to Cohen’s d = 1.63, reflecting the significant potential of brief well-designed AI literacy programs in upskilling educators.

citation: Wang, H., Xiao, Z., Lai, Y., Bao, C., & Wang, C. (2025). Knowledge Mapping and Trend Analysis of Ai Agents in Education: A Bibliometric Study From 2004-2024. subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence technologies is reshaping the paradigm of educational technology applications. Against this backdrop, the application of AI agents in the field of education has emerged as a cutting-edge topic in academia. However, existing studies lack a systematic theoretical framework. To address this research gap, this study employs bibliometric methods to analyze relevant literature from the Scopus database spanning 2004 to 2024, constructing a comprehensive knowledge map of AI agent research in education. Through multidimensional analytical approaches, including co-occurrence analysis, clustering analysis, and burst analysis, the study systematically examines the developmental trajectory and evolutionary pathways of AI agents in education. Overall, this research presents a clear framework of existing studies on AI agents in education, offering deep insights into the intelligent transformation of educational technology.

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Applications on the Development of Techno-Mathematical Literacy Among Pre-service Mathematics Teachers
citation: Beyazhancer, R. & Demir, B. (2025). The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Applications on the Development of Techno-Mathematical Literacy Among Pre-Service Mathematics Teachers. subject: STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Recent studies have increasingly focused on how techno-mathematical literacy (TmL) develops among teachers. This study examines the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) applications on pre-service mathematics teachers (PMTs’) techno-mathematical literacy (TmL) and AI self-efficacy perceptions. In the study, Solomon four-group experimental design was used to control the effect of pre-test on the results. Eighty PMTs’ selected by simple random sampling method were assigned to two experimental and two control groups. In experimental groups, AI-oriented activities were implemented in addition to the standard content of the technology-assisted mathematics teaching course. Data were collected using the Techno-Mathematical Literacy Scale (TmLS) and Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale (AISES) and analyzed with parametric tests such as independent sample t-test and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). As a result of the 10-week study, it was found that the AI practices had positive effects on PMTs' TmL levels and AI self-efficacy perceptions. The study reveals that the integration of AI into teacher education programs offers an important opportunity to develop PMTs' technological and mathematical competencies.

abstract: Engagement is a multifaceted construct that can influence learning outcomes. In this ex post facto study, we examined the correlations between different engagement constructs, as well as the impact of engagement on preservice teachers’ teaching knowledge and skills. We collected and analyzed video data from fourteen individual sessions with a coding scheme for engagement in VR-based teaching practices using AI-powered virtual students, as well as a teaching knowledge and skills posttest. The preliminary findings suggested that preservice teachers’ VR movement may correlate with disengagement, while emotional engagement, particularly confusion, can support learning opportunities. Engagement observed in the current study significantly predicted teaching knowledge and skills development.

abstract: This study explores the reciprocal relationship between the development of interdisciplinary teaching knowledge and Teachers' Professional Agency (TPA) in an interdisciplinary pedagogical context. Through a case study at an Israeli high school, we examine how teachers expand their knowledge and adapt their teaching practices to navigate uncertainty, foster collaboration, and innovate within interdisciplinary settings. Our findings suggest that the development of interdisciplinary knowledge activates TPA, creating a dynamic cycle where each element reinforces the other. These insights highlight how interdisciplinary contexts can support both teacher agency and knowledge development in education.

title: Taking a Scientist Perspective: Constructing Science Identities through Embodied Modeling

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In embodied science modeling, perspective taking is often used to help students take on the different points of view within a scientific phenomenon to understand how it arises. Perspective taking is also a central practice in identity construction (e.g. imagining and taking on new roles), yet the implications of perspective taking as scientific entities for students’ science identities is under explored. Therefore, we ask how fifth grade students construct science identities when they are taking on the perspective of a scientist in an embodied model versus acting as themselves. We draw on discursive psychology to conceptualize science identity, viewing it as the ways that students position themselves and are positioned by others in relation to science through discursive resources. We found that when students were acting as scientists, they positioned themselves and each other as scientific, but when they talked about their own scientific practices, they positioned themselves as non-scientific.

title: The Making of Competent Outsiders: Using Epistemic Practices of Science to Enhance Student’s Critical Evaluation of Misleading Scientific Explanations in Classrooms
citation: Noushad, N. F., Yoon, S. A., Chinn, C. A., Yang, Z., LeBodvidge, C., Hussain-Abidi, H., & Hunkar, K. (2025). abstract: Eroding public trust in science has become a critical challenge due to the proliferation of misleading scientific explanations in the media. Scholars recommend integrating scientific epistemic practices into classrooms to help students become competent outsiders—citizens who can critically evaluate misleading scientific explanations without being subject matter experts. However, limited empirical evidence exists on how teaching these practices influences students’ evaluation of misleading scientific claims. This study examines the performance of four high school students during a two-week inquiry unit where they used scientific epistemic practices to construct explanations for containing an epidemic similar to COVID-19. Students then evaluated misleading scientific explanations on three newspaper articles. Analysis of their pre- and post-responses revealed that students improved in identifying and critiquing erroneous representation of science in these articles. We discuss the implications of using epistemic practices to develop competent outsiders in classrooms.

abstract: Mechanistic explanations are essential in science education, helping students understand phenomena through exploring entities and their interactions. This study examines how high school biology students construct mechanistic explanations iteratively and how epistemic strategies shape their learning trajectories. Using the AIR theoretical framework, we analyzed students’ strategies within trajectories as they explored the tanning mechanism through an intervention involving “black box cards”. Data from 65 students revealed three distinct learning trajectories: linear, outcome-centered, and non-linear. Each was correlated with different combinations of six strategies, with simpler strategies more common in outcome-centered groups. The findings suggest that cultivating a repertoire of strategies can help students navigate mechanistic explanations with greater flexibility.

This study highlights the value of combining and contrasting physical and digital visualizations of data to help students recognize the unique affordances of each to learn historical concepts and appreciate the benefits of using them in a complementary way.

abstract: In this paper, we examine how people reason about space during virtual neighborhood explorations (NEs): iterative, disciplined, and virtual walking tours of local neighborhoods designed to teach people about issues of spatial justice. We video recorded STEM preservice teachers who participated in three virtual NEs - using maps, readings, and Google Street View - to learn about urban heat islands and their racist legacies. Using interaction and stance analysis, we document how ideologies about place constrained teachers’ efforts to more critically reason about space. To make virtual NEs more fruitful, we believe instructors must recognize and disrupt dominant ideologies about place that hamper critical spatial reasoning.

title: Towards Expansive and Equitable Modeling: Syncretic Modeling through the Lenses of Dance, Science, and computation

abstract: Modeling is a cornerstone of professional scientific practice, however, there aren’t enough opportunities for youth to leverage their own perspectives when engaging in modeling inquiry. This paper describes three design dimensions—interdisciplinarity, intermodality, & intergenerationality--of a 2-week long summer camp that leveraged theories of syncretism to integrate dance, science and computing in order to support youth contributions in modeling practices. The camp engaged 12 middle school youth, 2 scientists and 3 choreographers in adopting a complex systems lens and engaging in collaborative inquiry around the scientists’ research systems using choreographic and digital NetLogo modeling. Using discourse, video stills, and narrative description of a group that modeled spinal cord injuries, we show how these three dimensions disrupted barriers between disciplines (science & dance), modes of sense-making (movement & computation), and inequitable power dynamics (youth and adults). In the discussion, we draw out contributions to the literature particularly on scientific modeling.

abstract: Connected Spaces (C/S) is a collection of technologies that serve as an ecosystem for connecting students traditionally underrepresented in STEM+C to peers and mentors for collective maker identity development. To understand the efficacy of C/S, this study follows Isaiah as he uses C/S tools to seek help with his summer maker camp project. Using an adaptation of Nasir & Cooks (2009) identity resources framework, we document Isaiah’s choices of which C/S technologies to use, and when. This analysis highlights how the affordances of each C/S technology enabled Isaiah to find support from remote mentors in an adaptive manner and how this process contributed to the development of his computational identity, and recognition as a valuable member of a distributed network of makerspaces.

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lu, M. H., Azevedo, R., Kiesow, D., Darici, D., Jiang, W., & Schneider, B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Misinformation susceptibility is often attributed to motivational lapses (failure to engage in analytical reasoning) or information gaps (lack of necessary knowledge). While prior research has explored these factors separately, little is known about their interaction. This study examines how monetary incentives (to increase motivation) and AI-generated credibility analyses (to provide informational support) influence misinformation discernment. In a 2×3 factorial experiment (N=300), we find that high monetary incentives reduce discernment by increasing skepticism and false negatives. However, when paired with AI analyses, this effect is reversed, improving performance beyond baseline. AI access alone had no significant impact. Qualitative findings suggest trust in AI depends on self-reliance, skepticism, and alignment with personal judgment. These results highlight the need for interventions that balance motivation and cognitive support to enhance misinformation discernment and calls for more research to understand the cognitive and metacognitive processes during misinformation discernment.

abstract: This study explores the role of Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) in undergraduates' learning and research, and its growing significance in higher education. Against this backdrop, understanding students' attitudes, behaviors, and intentions towards AIGC can better guide their learning under intelligent technology for high-quality development. Therefore, based on the Theory of Planned Behavior, this paper surveyed 336 Chinese undergraduates. The results revealed that: (1) Students hold a positive attitude toward AIGC, perceive behavioral control, and intend to use it, although some lack peer and institutional support. (2) Among users, attitudes toward AIGC, subjective norms, and perceived control each positively impact the intention to use it, with attitude and subjective norms as the strongest predictors. (3) For non-users, attitudes and subjective norms influence behavioral intentions only through perceived control, which fully mediates their effect on intentions. The study provides valuable insights for enhancing college students' application of AIGC.

abstract: This design-based implementation research project sought to understand and improve science, technology, engineering, arts, and math (STEAM) learning infrastructure for K-12 students and preservice teachers in one local ecosystem in the Midwestern United States. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and infrastructuring, we analyze the process of creating a STEAM workshop series for preservice teachers and an elementary afterschool STEAM club, co-facilitated by these preservice teachers. We identify specific elements of higher education and K-12 infrastructure that supported or impeded implementation.

abstract: This case study explored students’ emotions while learning in an environment that incorporated extended reality and generative AI (GAI). In this study, twelve fourth graders participated in the eight-day technology-supported STEAM instructional program. They were required to create, set up, and arrange a virtual ecology corner in their classrooms using extended reality (XR), which combines immersive virtual reality (IVR) and mixed reality (MR). We evaluated students’ emotions while using different technologies during the learning process. The results showed that students experienced positive emotions, such as enjoyment and hope, throughout the learning activities, regardless of the technologies they used. However, the functional complexity of the technologies increased students’ anxiety levels. Furthermore, girls exhibited marginally higher levels of anxiety compared to boys.

abstract: Computer science education continues to be a factor in the leaky pipeline for students in STEM. To support the development of computational thinking (CT) skills and self-efficacy (SE) in computer science, we introduce BarrelBots, a puzzle-based block coding activity in Minecraft designed for middle school participants. We conducted an initial investigation on the context of a summer camp where participants (n = 15) solved researcher-designed puzzles that incorporated basic coding skills including sequencing, loops, conditionals, and functions. They also had the opportunity to design their own puzzles and share them with a partner and the class. In this paper, we investigate to what extent the BarrelBots activity promoted CT and SE development. In addition, we analyzed log data to examine correlations between in-game behaviors and participant post-test scores. We found that there was a significant improvement in STEM SE and some large significant correlations between the individual problem-solving log data behaviors and the CT post-test scores.
