abstract: The development of scientific inquiry abilities is not only essential for students to thrive but also a fundamental skill that drives innovation and discovery in science. This study proposes a framework grounded in design thinking to optimize problem-driven teaching and develop scientific inquiry abilities. The framework has four key features: project-based, subproblem linkage, multi-context, and practice-focused. A quasi-experimental study in a high school science classroom evaluated its effectiveness. Preliminary findings indicate that it successfully enhances students’ scientific inquiry abilities, particularly in formulating questions, generating hypotheses, designing experiments, and drawing conclusions. Additionally, the framework significantly boosts students’ motivation and interest in learning, further supporting the improvement of their scientific inquiry abilities.

title: Inclusive Space to Amplify Youth Transformative Agency in Educational Policy Design
citation: Mawene, D. & Schrader, E. (2025). Inclusive Space to Amplify Youth Transformative Agency in Educational Policy Design. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1484-1488). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Mawene, D. & Schrader, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper presents the Learning Lab intervention to address systemic injustice in a predominantly White school district in the U.S. Specifically, we focus on how a diverse group of students, parents, educators, and administrators fostered students' transformative agency amidst contradictions and the diverse motives members brought to the Learning Lab to create district level policy named Protocol for Addressing Harassment and Discrimination. The preliminary analysis indicated that students’ transformative agency was a collective process mediated by cultural perceptions about roles, rules, and norms. Lab members amplified students' transformative agency by: 1) challenging the expert/novice and adult/student dichotomies, and 2) cultivating a collaborative culture. We conclude the paper with students’ reflections on their learning and development during the Learning Lab intervention.

title: Assessing the Effectiveness of Automatic Feedback in Self-Assessment for Enhancing Student Learning from Mistakes
citation: Cao, J. (2025). Assessing the Effectiveness of Automatic Feedback in Self-Assessment for Enhancing Student Learning From Mistakes. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1489-1493). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cao, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Learning from mistakes is essential for students' learning, with self-assessment being a key method. Existing self-assessment tools help students reflect on their mistakes but lack automatic feedback. Thus, this study investigates the impact of a newly designed self-assessment tool incorporating automatic feedback, leveraging knowledge graphs to enhance student learning from mistakes. A quasi-experiment was conducted with 51 middle school students to compare the new tool against traditional self-assessment methods lacking automatic feedback. The findings show that the new tool significantly enhanced academic performance, especially for students with lower prior knowledge.

title: Interactivity in Extended Reality: Towards A Hierarchical Model for Defining and Designing Learning Experiences
citation: McGowin, G. & Fiore, S. M. (2025). Interactivity in Extended Reality: Towards a Hierarchical Model for Defining and Designing Learning Experiences. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1494-1499). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: McGowin, G. & Fiore, S. M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Extended realities (XR), encompassing virtual , augmented , and mixed reality (MR), offer transformative learning opportunities through interactive experiences. However, the concept of interactivity within XR remains ambiguously defined. This work reviews interdisciplinary definitions of interactivity and constructs a conceptual definition, operationalized using Schulmeister’s (2003) hierarchical model. From this, the paper presents a taxonomy of interactivity, clarifies its role as a key learning affordance, and offers a framework for analyzing and designing XR experiences. By exploring XR's unique capabilities for learning, this work guides the development of immersive environments and proposes recommendations for advancing the field. These insights set the stage for future empirical studies examining the relationship between interactivity, affordances, and learning outcomes, ultimately helping developers and educators maximize XR's potential for effective learning.

title: Learning Trajectories in Large-Scale Communities
citation: Sherin, B. & Chavey, L. (2025). Learning Trajectories in Large-Scale Communities. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1500-1504). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sherin, B. & Chavey, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Over two decades ago, Lave and Wenger introduced an image of learning that remains popular to this day. In that image, learners are viewed as participating in a community of practice, and learning is conceptualized as a movement from the periphery of that community toward the center. In this paper, we describe attempts to produce plots of learning trajectories for online communities that capture this movement. Our goal in this paper is to show it is possible to produce plots that capture qualitative differences in trajectories.

title: Exploring the Synthesis of Geologic Concepts in a Field Geology Setting
citation: Adams, A. L. & Barth-Cohen, L. (2025). Exploring the Synthesis of Geologic Concepts in a Field Geology Setting. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1505-1509). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Adams, A. L. & Barth-Cohen, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Scientific observation is a complex process involving synthesizing varied information. While research has documented learners’ struggles with scientific observation, less attention has been given to how they successfully navigate multiple concepts when making and interpreting observations in the field. This study uses Coordination Class Theory to examine the concepts learners employ during scientific observation in a field geology setting. Data comes from video recordings of teachers’ participation in a field geology professional development experience. The analysis identified several key concepts teachers used when interpreting observations, composition, weathering, and sedimentary structures, which were crucial for making broader interpretations about sedimentary rock depositional environments. The findings suggest that depositional environment is a coordination cluster involving multiple geologic concepts that learners navigate to make interpretations. Future work can examine how learners form connections between concepts in both formal and informal learning settings.

title: Insights from Expert Maker Teachers' Embodied Learning Designs
citation: Segev, Y., Kashi, S., & Hod, Y. (2025). Insights From Expert Maker Teachers' Embodied Learning Designs. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1510-1514). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Segev, Y., Kashi, S., & Hod, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper addresses the need for knowledge on designing maker education to support its successful integration into formal schooling. We present a case study of a learning design iteratively refined by an expert teacher to support the learning of 6th-grade students in a maker course. In this course, students design and manufacture laser-cut escape room riddles. This case study is part of a larger research project examining the learning designs of four expert maker teachers, using the grammar of conjecture mapping. The aim is to advance principled practical knowledge on how to design maker education that effectively supports students' learning in school contexts. We focus on unveiling and articulating the learning trajectories that expert teachers foster and the embodied learning designs they use.

title: From Discomfort to Growth: Embedding Frustration in Makeathon Design for Teacher Development
citation: Segev, Y., Kafri, R., Hod, Y., Berland, M., & Halverson, E. (2025). From Discomfort to Growth: Embedding Frustration in Makeathon Design for Teacher Development. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1515-1519). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Segev, Y., Kafri, R., Hod, Y., Berland, M., & Halverson, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: This research explores the learning design of a three-day educational makeathon for in-service teachers. The makeathon aimed to provide an exemplary learning experience, challenging participants while incorporating learning scaffolds to support them. We examined the learning trajectories that emerged as teachers navigated teamwork-related challenges and group dynamics in a complex project. This paper specifically investigates how these challenges fostered teacher learning and growth, and identifies the design elements that supported participants throughout the process. Our findings present a range of learning outcomes, including teachers’ increased appreciation of diverse team collaboration and, in some cases, disengagement due to sustained frustrations. This study highlights how immersing teachers in challenging teamwork during an educational makeathon can deepen their understanding of maker learning, offering insights into effective teacher training designs.

title: Using AI-Based Virtual Labs, Log Data, and Reasoning Statements to Assess High School Students’ Understanding of Energy Conservation
citation: Segan, E., Gobert, J., Pedro, M. S., & Adair, A. (2025). Using Ai-Based Virtual Labs, Log Data, and Reasoning Statements to Assess High School Students’ Understanding of Energy Conservation. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1520-1524). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Segan, E., Gobert, J., Pedro, M. S., & Adair, A.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Conservation of energy is a challenging high school science topic, especially when the integration of mathematics is expected, as per the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). To address these challenges, Inq-ITS labs were developed to automatically assess and scaffold students’ mathematical competencies on developing models about energy conservation, both with and without air resistance, the latter of which introduces additional complexity. Using real-time assessment data, we examined whether students’ science and math competencies varied across two labs. Further, we performed a qualitative analysis of students’ log data and reasoning statements to determine potential alternative conceptions about their mathematical models as evidence for their claim(s). By analyzing students at the practice level, including qualitative data about their reasoning, we can (1) provide rich data on students’ science and mathematical investigation competencies, (2) identify common alternative conceptions, and (3) identify difficulties students have when linking their mathematical models to their claims about conservation of energy.

title: The Role of Surprise in Teachers’ Construction of Teaching Successes and Failures
citation: Azevedo, F. S., Sherard, M. K., Novelli, M., & Freed, N. (2025). The Role of Surprise in Teachers’ Construction of Teaching Successes and Failures. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1525-1529). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Azevedo, F. S., Sherard, M. K., Novelli, M., & Freed, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Teacher surprise refers to classroom events or experiences that a teacher interprets as unexpected occurrences in their teaching practice. We investigate preservice teachers’ expression of, and narrative elaboration of surprising events as they publicly made sense of their field-teach successes and failures. Our findings suggest that there is a rich everyday language for capturing and describing classroom occurrences that somehow do not follow the expected or projected course of events—what we term the “language of surprise”—and its use by teachers and teacher educators can be a productive means for inquiring deeply into one’s classroom practice, its challenges and successes.

title: “The Heart of the Matter”: Addressing College Composition Problems of Practice in a Research Practice Partnership
citation: James, C. L., Kaczmarczyk-Smith, W., & Moss, A. P. (2025). “The Heart of the Matter”: Addressing College Composition Problems of Practice in a Research Practice Partnership. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1530-1534). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: James, C. L., Kaczmarczyk-Smith, W., & Moss, A. P.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: A research-practice partnership (RPP) made up of college composition instructors and researchers came together to address a problem of practice facing writing teachers – engaging students in exigent rhetorical situations and real audiences. In this paper we use case study methods to describe the ways that RPP members collaborated in a professional learning community to address this problem in college composition by adopting human-centered design as a pedagogical tool. Through thematic coding, we noted the different moves participants made and how those moves productively guided practitioners in tackling and designing instructional experiences that responded to the problem of practice. We also note the ways in which these moves also aligned with another RPP goal – fostering mutually beneficial relationships. These findings suggest that professional learning communities, especially those within an RPP, provide an effective frame for addressing problems of practice in mutually beneficial ways.

title: Mapping Organizational Infrastructure: Semiotic Cluster Analysis in a School District Change Initiative
citation: Van Doren, S., Lopez, J. L., Salazar, J., Nguyen, J., Gomez, A., Long, K., Woolley, D., & Ahn, J. (2025). Mapping Organizational Infrastructure: Semiotic Cluster Analysis in a School District Change Initiative. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1535-1539). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Doren, S. V., Lopez, J. L., Salazar, J., Nguyen, J., Gomez, A., Long, K., Woolley, D., & Ahn, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Designing for organizational change has become an increasingly important goal in the learning sciences. To do so, we must develop processes that highlight organizational infrastructures that inform both research and design. In this paper, we share our experience conducting semiotic cluster analysis to map organizational infrastructures within a research practice partnership. We describe how semiotic analysis attuned us to relationships that speak to organizational factors influencing the objectives of our RPP. Then, we share our process for generating design conjectures that attend to the organizational infrastructure identified through semiotic analysis. Our work provides an example of tracing surface level observations to core organizational needs.

title: A Case Study of the Barriers to Learning Social-Emotional Learning
citation: Crowell, A. M., Ramey, K. E., & Brown, E. (2025). A Case Study of the Barriers to Learning Social-Emotional Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1540-1544). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Crowell, A. M., Ramey, K. E., & Brown, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This is a qualitative case study of a midwestern United States educator’s journey to learn and implement social-emotional learning (SEL) in an economically disadvantaged, public school district, the infrastructural challenges that she faced, and the design she was able to implement when these infrastructural challenges were removed. This case study unwraps a teacher learning story that highlights her perceptions of systemic pathways for SEL implementation as well as challenges, such as standardized testing, educational bureaucracy, and unmet child welfare needs.

title: High School Teachers’ Approaches for Integrating AI Literacy into Planned Instruction: Uniformity or Heterogeneity?
citation: Adisa, I. O., Mah, C., & Lee, V. R. (2025). High School Teachers’ Approaches for Integrating Ai Literacy Into Planned Instruction: Uniformity or Heterogeneity?. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1545-1549). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Adisa, I. O., Mah, C., & Lee, V. R.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA); Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: While various frameworks exist to promote K-12 AI education, little is known about how teachers bring AI literacy into their classrooms. In this study, we examined how two teachers designed and implemented AI literacy in their individual classes. Using epistemic network analysis (ENA) to analyze co-design records and interviews, we found that both teachers shared a common goal of enhancing student learning with AI but diverged in how they emphasized foundational and technical understanding of AI versus responsible and practical use. These varied approaches highlight the complexity of AI literacy and illustrate that a one-size-fits-all model does not apply. By examining these multiple pathways, we offer insight into how educators can tailor AI literacy instruction to meet diverse student needs and instructional contexts.

title: Factors Influencing Students' Perceptions of Automated Feedback and Their Impact on Revision
citation: Dey, I., Gnesdilow, D., Smith, R., Kim, C., Passonneau, R. J., & Puntambekar, S. (2025). Factors Influencing Students' Perceptions of Automated Feedback and Their Impact on Revision. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 155-163). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Dey, I., Gnesdilow, D., Smith, R., Kim, C., Passonneau, R. J., & Puntambekar, S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Automated feedback can provide students with timely information about their writing, but students' willingness to engage meaningfully with the feedback to revise their writing may be influenced by their perceptions of its usefulness. We explored the factors that may have influenced 339, 8th-grade students’ perceptions of receiving automated feedback on their writing and whether their perceptions impacted their revisions and writing improvement. Using HLM and logistic regression analyses, we found that: 1) students with more positive perceptions of the automated feedback made revisions that resulted in significant improvements in their writing, and 2) students who received feedback indicating they included more important ideas in their essays had significantly higher perceptions of the usefulness of the feedback, but were significantly less likely to engage in substantive revisions. Implications and the importance of helping students evaluate and reflect on the feedback to make substantive revisions, no matter their initial feedback, are discussed.

title: Supporting Justice-Oriented Data Science in a Secondary Science Classroom: Pathways and Tensions
citation: Leung, V., Chen, B., Bartucz, J., DeLiema, D., & Scharber, C. (2025). Supporting Justice-Oriented Data Science in a Secondary Science Classroom: Pathways and Tensions. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1550-1554). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Leung, V., Chen, B., Bartucz, J., DeLiema, D., & Scharber, C.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study explores how a secondary science teacher enacted a justice-oriented data science module in a seventh-grade life science classroom. Co-designed by the teacher and a group of researchers, the module engaged students in investigating quality of life using real-world datasets about their own neighborhoods. Classroom observations and debrief interviews revealed that the teacher effectively connected data science to life science and students’ lived experiences, facilitating discussions that linked data practices with justice issues. However, challenges emerged in addressing justice topics of relevance to students. These findings underscore the need for enhanced support and professional development to help teachers navigate the complexities of facilitating justice-oriented data science in diverse K-12 contexts.

title: Adaptive Scaffolding with Generative AI Chatbot for Solving Ill-Structured Problems
citation: Jang, H. & So, H. (2025). Adaptive Scaffolding With Generative Ai Chatbot for Solving Ill-Structured Problems. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1555-1559). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jang, H. & So, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)
abstract: This study investigates the role of generative AI (GenAI) chatbots in supporting students’ ill-structured problem-solving. A GenAI chatbot, Probot, was developed to offer adaptive scaffolding through question prompts during problem representation, solution generation and selection, justification, and monitoring and evaluation. Sixty-one undergraduate students in Korea were divided into control and experimental groups. The experimental group solved an ill-structured problem with Probot while the control group used a non-adaptive chatbot. Interaction patterns with GenAI chatbots were analyzed using Epistemic Network Analysis. Results showed the experimental group had strong connections with orientation in problem analysis, solution analysis, and solution elaboration, suggesting that Probot supported students’ analytical and elaborative thinking. The control group showed strong connections between problem analysis, solution analysis, and solution suggestions, indicating a focus on information and idea-seeking. The findings highlight Probot’s potential in guiding ill-structured problem-solving and offer design insights for adaptive scaffolding.

title: Building Capacity for K-12 AI Education: A Non-Computer Science Teacher’s Experience
citation: Boulden, D., Uchidiuno, J., Vandenberg, J., Cateté, V., Min, W., & Mott, B. (2025). Building Capacity for K-12 Ai Education: A Non-Computer Science Teacher’s Experience. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1560-1564). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Boulden, D., Uchidiuno, J., Vandenberg, J., Cateté, V., Min, W., & Mott, B.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This case study explores the experiences of a non-computer science educator participating in a professional development program designed to support AI teaching in rural middle schools. Using Cultural-Historical Activity Theory and expansive learning as analytical lenses, the research examines how the educator leveraged supportive elements within her environment to overcome challenges, gradually building confidence while adopting new teaching practices. Findings underscore the need for tailored professional development, ongoing support, and progressive teacher learning for effective AI education. This study contributes to understanding how non-computer science educators can be supported in bringing AI learning experiences to their students, thereby making AI education more accessible.

title: The Components to “Make it Your Own”: A Framework to Study Youth Agency via Modification in Science Center Demonstrations
citation: Chew, P. & LeTourneau, S. (2025). The Components to “Make it Your Own”: A Framework to Study Youth Agency via Modification in Science Center Demonstrations. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1565-1568). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chew, P. & LeTourneau, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Science center demonstrations allow science to come alive on the floor through youth facilitators. However, they replicate presentations of epistemic hegemony in science that perpetuate inequitable access and identification with STEM. This paper centers youth agency, as studied through modification of science demonstrations, as a learning process with possible contribution to transforming epistemic practices in out-of-school science. In a science center where youth work as facilitators of science demonstrations, we present a framework for places of agency in science demonstrations: introduction of ideas, session scaffolding and framing, physical environment and materials, and incorporation of audience. We discuss how differences in these categories across cases led to unique affordances and constraints to modification and present implications for the design of facilitative science sessions and professional development for facilitators.

title: MORF ENA – A Tool for Making MOOC Discussion Forum Data More Accessible for Epistemic Network Analysis
citation: Wei, Z., Liu, X., Barany, A., Vanacore, K., Baker, R. S., Slater, S., Pratt, J., Shah, M., & Mogessie, M. (2025). MORF Ena – A Tool for Making MOOC Discussion Forum Data More Accessible for Epistemic Network Analysis. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1569-1573). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wei, Z., Liu, X., Barany, A., Vanacore, K., Baker, R. S., Slater, S., Pratt, J., Shah, M., & Mogessie, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA); Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: MOOC discussion forum data can help researchers answer questions about learners' engagement, thought processes, and knowledge development. However, this data is often inaccessible due to technical and privacy constraints. We introduce MORF-ENA, an automated tool that enables researchers to conduct Quantitative Ethnographic research using Epistemic Network Analysis on MOOC data without direct access to learner data. Developed through a participatory design approach, MORF-ENA enables researchers to visualize and explore learners' behaviors within discussions. We present the tool's capabilities with an example, examining how learners' engagement with MOOCs changed before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. The results of this design process point toward future directions for the tool's development and use in learning sciences as well as for improving access to learning data.

title: Storiza: A Platform to Support Children’s Oral Reading Fluency Development with Generative AI
citation: Leite, W. L., Hammerschmidt-Snidarich, S., Huggins-Manley, A. C., Karakis, H. K., Lane, H., Rahimi, S., Shen, Q., Tai, X., & Schmidt, M. (2025). Storiza: A Platform to Support Children’s Oral Reading Fluency Development With Generative Ai. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1574-1578). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Leite, W. L., Hammerschmidt-Snidarich, S., Huggins-Manley, A. C., Karakis, H. K., Lane, H., Rahimi, S., Shen, Q., Tai, X., & Schmidt, M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Oral reading fluency (ORF) is critical for reading comprehension and success in academic and professional goals. Children in elementary school frequently struggle to develop ORF, particularly those with specific learning disabilities, such as dyslexia. This study describes the initial development of an app to enable students to improve ORF by practicing reading stories created with generative AI according to the student’s interests and cultural background and aligned with a reading curriculum. The study describes the collection of the teacher, parent and school administrator interviews and qualitative analyses that provided information to create the app’s prototype. The app follows universal design principles and learning experience design, incorporating a range of assistive technologies to ensure the success of students with learning differences. Future directions for development are discussed.

title: Orientations to Material Agency in Science Learning
citation: Goodwin, A. Y., Watkins, J., & Tang, Y. (2025). Orientations to Material Agency in Science Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1579-1583). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Goodwin, A. Y., Watkins, J., & Tang, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In the absence of adequate conceptual and methodological frameworks to notice how materials contribute to ontological shifts in science learning, it becomes difficult to set up conditions for these shifts to occur. We present our framework of orientations to material agency in order to recognize when materials become more than mediational tools of learning and instead gain a social presence as agentic participants that help build scientific knowledge. We illustrate this framework through examples of interactional experiences of secondary school science teachers, showing how orienting to material agency can begin to move them toward shifts in how they view and value the non-human in science. This in turn demonstrates ways in which working with materials has the potential to become central to culturally rich engagements in science learning.

title: (How) Do Children 3–6 Experience and Express Meaning in Life?
citation: Launonen, L. (2025). (How) do Children 3–6 Experience and Express Meaning in Life?. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1584-1588). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Launonen, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper discusses early findings of an ongoing study investigating whether and how children aged 3–6 experience and articulate a sense of meaning in life (MIL). The tripartite model of MIL—comprising significance/mattering, purpose/direction, and coherence/comprehension—was operationalized into three questions guiding a task where children documented what they found important in life using tablet computers. The children created photos, videos, recordings, and drawings, which were used as prompts for qualitative interviews. Preliminary findings suggest that young children have a clear sense of their lives as significant to themselves and, to some extent, as mattering to others. Their sense of purpose and coherence, however, is largely limited to short timeframes. Understanding MIL development in childhood is vital for education aimed at fostering meaningfulness in young lives. Educating for meaningful living also holds promise for promoting a sustainable lifestyle.

title: “It Takes Two to Tango”: Power Dynamics in Researcher-Coach Collaborations
citation: McClain, J., Victor, L., Miller, J., Danish, J., Fusco, J., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Walter, W., Buli, T., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., Glazewski, K., Walker, J. T., & Bae, H. (2025). “It Takes Two to Tango”: Power Dynamics in Researcher-Coach Collaborations. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1589-1593). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: McClain, J., Victor, L., Miller, J., Danish, J., Fusco, J., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Walter, W., Buli, T., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., Glazewski, K., Walker, J. T., & Bae, H.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: Effective researcher-coach relationships need reciprocal learning, which allows practitioners to share valuable contextual knowledge while researchers share evidence-based ideas. Nevertheless, these collaborations encounter obstacles due to power imbalances, which frequently establish researchers as authorities and reduce the role of practitioners as co-creators. Therefore, this study examines power dynamics in researcher-coach partnerships within educational contexts, emphasizing equitable collaboration strategies. Using Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) as a framework, this study analyzes video data from a writing intensive to explore interactions between two participants, Ashley and Russell. Findings reveal that initial tensions foster deeper understanding through negotiated power exchanges. The study underscores that openness, mutual trust, and reflective dialogue are essential for sustainable partnerships, advancing the understanding of power dynamics in researcher-coach collaborations.

title: “Wow, I Can Actually Do This Now”: Girls’ Science Identity Development at Science Summer Camps
citation: Lundgren, L. (2025). “Wow, I Can Actually do This Now”: Girls’ Science Identity Development at Science Summer Camps. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1594-1598). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lundgren, L.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Science identity research has grown exponentially in the past ten years and for good reason: researchers are recognizing how identity/identities affect science interest, career development, and peoples’ worldviews. Science identity comprises four aspects: competence, recognition, performance, and interest. I studied science identity development in girls aged 10-16 at a two-week science summer day camp. Drawing from pre-post camp interviews and observations, I examined three girls’ science identity development as they explored different science aspects (e.g. herpetology, marine biology) and communicated about science. Girls were categorized as having burgeoning, intermediate, and established science identities based on different levels of self-recognition, recognition by others, and performance, and competence. I show how recognition by others who represent the girls’ backgrounds and ideals was an important aspect of girls’ science identity as well as provide additional evidence for the importance of informal science learning contexts for science identity development.

title: Diagnose Academic Emotions from Facial Expressions: Relationship with Science Learning Performance in Web-Based Self-directed Learning
citation: He, J., Jin, B., Xie, K., & Zhang, D. (2025). Diagnose Academic Emotions From Facial Expressions: Relationship With Science Learning Performance in Web-Based Self-Directed Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1599-1603). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: He, J., Jin, B., Xie, K., & Zhang, D.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study delves into elementary school students emotional engagement in web-based, self-directed science inquiry. Through the lens of Facial Action Coding System (FACS) analysis across 96 video recordings of 53 students, we investigate the prevalence and patterns of emotions exhibited during three distinct science experiments. We seek to understand the emotional combinations and how these affective states transition in relation to academic performance. Our methodology includes using z-score of each type of emotion (happiness, surprise, sadness, neutral) as threshold to discern the primary 12 emotion combinations. Using Markov Chain sequential pattern analysis, we found notable differences in emotional transitions between higher and lower-performing students, indicating a potential link between emotional trajectories and learning outcomes. High performers appear to have more positive emotional experiences, as indicated by transitions to 'happiness.' In contrast, low performers might keep staying at negative emotions. These differences may impact the learning effectiveness.

title: Enhancing Learning and Design Processes through Online Collaborative Environments: Integrating the 4C/ID Model in a Learning by Design Approach
citation: Tan, L. & Reimann, P. (2025). Enhancing Learning and Design Processes Through Online Collaborative Environments: Integrating the 4c/id Model in a Learning by Design Approach. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1604-1608). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tan, L. & Reimann, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines the integration of the Four-Component Instructional Design Model (4C/ID) and Peer-Assisted Learning (PAL) within a collaborative e-learning environment to enhance the feasibility of interactive online tutorials development by future learning designers. The 4C/ID model is known for facilitating complex learning challenges by aligning technological tools with pedagogical theories, while PAL provides a framework for the collaborative acquisition of knowledge and skills. Employing a qualitative approach, we explored how these models enhance learning designers' understanding of instructional processes and the development of engaging educational materials. Preliminary findings suggest that the combined use of PAL and 4C/ID improves the quality and engagement of the design process and learning content, highlighting the potential of collaborative strategies in instructional design. This research contributes insights into the learning-by-designing perspective, proposing a model that enhances the professional development of learning designers and could be beneficial for future educational practices.

title: Datafying Spaces and Places: Synergies and Disconnects between Youth-Authored Maps and Data Visualizations
citation: Rosenbaum, L. F., Lanouette, K., & Blikstein, P. (2025). Datafying Spaces and Places: Synergies and Disconnects Between Youth-Authored Maps and Data Visualizations. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1609-1613). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rosenbaum, L. F., Lanouette, K., & Blikstein, P.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Research on informal learning often elevates the knowledge that youth develop in their daily interactions, relationships, and movement across their homes and communities. Youth-authored geographies - whether in drawings, maps, or photographs - offer one rich perspective into this knowledge. We extend analytic techniques developed for youth geographies to another kind of youth-authored representation: data visualizations. Specifically, we use Davis and Barsoum’s (2022) framework to identify ways that the spatial/temporal layers, hierarchies, relationships, and rhythms of phenomena that youth elevate within their communities are reflected or obscured within visualizations they create of sensor data collected in those spaces. We also emphasize annotations as a powerful tool for youth to surface these elements. We propose that awareness of these synergies and disconnects could inform data science education that leverages youth’s everyday knowledge.

title: Improving Math Instruction at Scale: High-Quality Coaching as Socially Mediated Professional Learning
citation: Perlman, H. & Correnti, R. (2025). Improving Math Instruction at Scale: High-Quality Coaching as Socially Mediated Professional Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1614-1618). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Perlman, H. & Correnti, R.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: High-quality instructional coaching can improve teachers’ ambitious instructional practice in mathematics, and in turn, positively impact student achievement. This study provides a quasi-experimental design on prospectively matched mathematics teachers receiving job-embedded one-on-one coaching. Utilizing multiple imputation methods, we present evidence to support a treatment effect in a full representative sample of 250 mathematics teachers in two distinct outcome measures of teaching. We further explore whether any coaching measures were associated with teaching growth and contributed to an explanation of any observed treatment. This paper demonstrates treatment effects from survey-based and observation measures of the effect of this coaching model to improve teachers’ instructional practices. This contributes to research on how the effects of coaching change instruction and contributes methodological insights to potential mechanisms for teaching improvement.

title: Epistemic Agency Across Disciplines: Shared Commitments and Challenges in Science and History Education
citation: Conrad, J., Stroupe, D., & Reisman, A. (2025). Epistemic Agency Across Disciplines: Shared Commitments and Challenges in Science and History Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1619-1623). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Conrad, J., Stroupe, D., & Reisman, A.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Student-driven inquiry has long represented a central goal in both history and science education, and the two subject areas despite substantive differences, conceptualize inquiry in similar ways. Still, classrooms abound with missed opportunities. We argue that missed opportunities for inquiry reflect a deeper challenge for teachers and teacher educators related to how they conceptualize students’ epistemic agency. In this unique conceptual paper, we look across our fields of history and science education research to better understand how each field has considered students’ epistemic agency. We look across fields to identify common features and points of convergence. We conclude with challenges and recommendations for teacher educators and teachers.

title: From Self-Reflection to Action: Supporting Teachers as Agentic Professionals to Improve Digital Competence Capacity
citation: Kyza, E. A. & Georgiou, Y. (2025). From Self-Reflection to Action: Supporting Teachers as Agentic Professionals to Improve Digital Competence Capacity. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1624-1628). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kyza, E. A. & Georgiou, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: In today's rapidly evolving digital landscape, teachers’ digital competence is a critical component of professional development. This study investigated how self-determination processes, such as self-reflection and self-efficacy, can empower teachers to enhance their digital skills. Self-determination theory suggests that individuals can achieve their personal goals if they have autonomy (feeling of control), competence (feeling capable) and are connected to others (feeling of community). When these psychological needs are fulfilled, individuals gain agency to take control of their own learning. Data were collected from three case studies with in-service teachers. Qualitative analyses showed that teachers required substantial scaffolding to progress from awareness to self-regulation and agency. Findings indicate the importance of fostering an environment where teachers can critically assess their digital competence and set meaningful goals for improvement. We conclude our discussion with recommendations for designing professional development programs that encourage self-regulated learning and reflective practices to promote digital competence.

title: Do Teachers Protect Their Students’ Data? A Qualitative Interview Study Probing Teachers’ Knowledge of Data Security
citation: Menebhi, S., Nachtigall, V., Mertineit, A., & Rummel, N. (2025). Do Teachers Protect Their Students’ Data? A Qualitative Interview Study Probing Teachers’ Knowledge of Data Security. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1629-1633). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Menebhi, S., Nachtigall, V., Mertineit, A., & Rummel, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In our digital age, teachers’ responsibility for data protection and the handling of their students’ sensitive data is steadily increasing. However, neither professional development programs nor IT security trainings are specifically designed to educate teachers on IT security or take their existing knowledge into account to create targeted interventions. Therefore, the present study aims to investigate teachers’ knowledge of internet security and, in particular, how they protect their students’ data. A typological content analysis of interview data from 14 teachers revealed that the majority have inadequate knowledge about secure email communication and do not adequately protect their students’ data, highlighting the need for interventions that address these critical gaps in teachers’ knowledge and skills.

title: Learning to Engage in Climate Activism in High School Classrooms towards Collective and Systemic Changes
citation: Tsai, N., Shin, M., & Kang, H. (2025). Learning to Engage in Climate Activism in High School Classrooms Towards Collective and Systemic Changes. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1634-1638). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tsai, N., Shin, M., & Kang, H.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: This qualitative ethnographic case study examines how two school students learn to take collective, informed actions toward systemic change in a year-long climate change course. The data include artifacts produced from students’ climate civic action projects and the course activities, 10 video-taped lessons, and interviews. The analysis is guided by two questions: (1) How did the students respond to deliberately designed curricular activities that support their climate activism throughout the year? (2) How did the two students narrate their experiences? Using the notion of ‘collective care,’ the analysis reveals the processes in which the students connected their personal experiences with the climate issues discussed in the class; turned their anxieties into materialized doings with others to create a more just and sustainable world while navigating politics associated with proposed changes. The implications for supporting students’ climate civic actions through formal education are discussed.

title: Navigating Local versus Colonial Languages of Instruction in Out-of-School Contexts: Insights from a Randomized Controlled Trial in Uganda
citation: Kwon, C., Yao, Y., Che, Y., Stamper, J., & Ogan, A. (2025). Navigating Local Versus Colonial Languages of Instruction in Out-of-School Contexts: Insights From a Randomized Controlled Trial in Uganda. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1639-1643). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kwon, C., Yao, Y., Che, Y., Stamper, J., & Ogan, A.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Colonial and local languages shape the complex linguistic environment in most African countries, creating misalignments between language policy goals, local perceptions, and the realities of learning in rural contexts. To understand these differences, we studied a randomized controlled trial (RCT) in a rural region within Northern Uganda, comparing a local versus colonial language as a medium of instruction in an engineering course for out-of-school learners. Key findings showed that both instructors and students perceived students in the local language condition as having faster comprehension of STEM course content, while students from both language conditions encountered literacy challenges and valued cultural cohesion, balancing the desire to appear knowledgeable in a colonial language with the need to respect and contribute to their community through their local language.

title: Orienting Attention to Natural Co-Participants: How and When Educators Prioritize Material Sensing in a Nature-Based Preschool
citation: Goeke, M. (2025). Orienting Attention to Natural Co-Participants: How and When Educators Prioritize Material Sensing in a Nature-Based Preschool. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 164-172). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Goeke, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In nature-based learning (NBL), the natural material environment is understood to actively shape student learning and foster positive human-nature relationships. However, the process through which the natural environment shapes student learning in NBL environments is under-researched. I contribute to this area by examining the relationship between situational variables and how educators orient learners’ attention to natural material co-participants. By analyzing video collected in a 4-week nature-based preschool day camp, we find that educators vary their approach to orienting the preschoolers’ attention on the basis of whether the children are already engaged with an activity, if there is a need to redirect children’s actions, and how ephemeral the experience of the natural co-participant is. These varying approaches ultimately reinforce particular messages about nature-culture relations, including a hierarchy of importance among natural co-participants and human supremacy.

title: Placemaking Through Artistic Pedagogy: Advancing Anti-Oppression in Public Spaces
citation: Lee, S. & Shulyakovskaya, L. (2025). Placemaking Through Artistic Pedagogy: Advancing Anti-Oppression in Public Spaces. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1644-1648). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lee, S. & Shulyakovskaya, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This duoethnographic study explores how placemaking through the arts can serve as a pedagogical method to advance anti-oppression efforts in public spaces. It draws from two projects: graffiti workshops in Toronto’s Graffiti Alley and the creation of a school-based anti-oppression garden. The authors examine systemic barriers, including exclusionary policies and institutional resistance. Through personal narrative and critical reflection, the study shows how public art can foster equity, amplify marginalized voices, and reimagine public spaces as inclusive platforms for learning. The findings offer insights for educators, researchers, and policymakers on the pedagogical potential of community-driven art to support transformative learning.

title: Designing for “Layered” Sensemaking About Environmental Injustice: The “Guided Tour” Activity
citation: Barton, J. C. & Fitzmaurice, H. L. (2025). Designing for “Layered” Sensemaking About Environmental Injustice: The “Guided Tour” Activity. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1649-1653). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Barton, J. C. & Fitzmaurice, H. L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Issues of spatial and environmental (in)justice are fundamentally “layered,” comprised of heterogeneous sets of experiences, materialities, and histories. To investigate these issues in the classroom, then, teachers and students must develop multidisciplinary strategies for sensemaking across these layers: practices we call “layering”. This paper describes an inquiry activity – the “Guided Tour” – developed for K-12 teacher professional development settings and classrooms using a framework that identifies four such layers, including data from lived experiences, local histories, social sciences, and natural sciences (Barton et al., In Press). We ask: what forms of reasoning across these layers emerged as teacher participants (N=8) crafted their “Tours” focused on local environmental justice issues, and how else did participants engage in “layering” beyond them? We found frequent instances of layering in participants’ work, as well as opportunities for redesign to better support emergent forms.

title: Less Speed, More Thought: Message Pacing in Student-AI Interactions
citation: Walton, D., Bae, H., Park, J., & Zhao, Y. (2025). Less Speed, More Thought: Message Pacing in Student-Ai Interactions. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1654-1658). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Walton, D., Bae, H., Park, J., & Zhao, Y.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study investigates the impact of interaction pacing on student engagement and problem-solving when using an AI chatbot embedded in a programming code editor (Integrated Development Environment, IDE). By comparing two groups—one with unrestricted messaging and one limited to sending a message every 60 seconds—we observe that slowing down AI interactions leads to more thoughtful communication, deeper cognitive processing, and improved problem-solving skills. The goal is to determine whether deliberate pacing of student–AI interactions can enhance learning quality and foster deeper engagement with programming concepts. Findings support slow computing principles, suggesting that deliberate pacing in AI-assisted learning environments enhances educational interactions.

title: Sustainability in Doctoral Education? A Student-Experience Perspective
citation: Taka, M., Aarnio, H., Suviniitty, J., & Varis, O. (2025). Sustainability in Doctoral Education? A Student-Experience Perspective. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1659-1663). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Taka, M., Aarnio, H., Suviniitty, J., & Varis, O.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: The sustainability claim increases the need to integrate more interdisciplinary, collaborative research activities into doctoral education in engineering. This introduces new challenges and opportunities for educators and students. In this paper, we examined 12 doctoral students' experiences during their entire journey of gaining engineering doctorates. Using a novel journey mapping method, we collected the participants’ documentation about their academic paths, reflecting on activities, milestones, and emotions. The individual observations (n=416) were clustered into nine main categories, emphasizing the self-management challenges (30% positive), and non-PhD life factors (53% positive), in addition to the research process (88% positive). Positive experiences were linked to teamwork, social support, and interdisciplinary collaboration, while challenges included self-management and personal well-being. Corpus analysis further highlighted linguistic differences between the groups, reflecting variations in their academic cultures. Our findings emphasize the need for sustainable doctoral practices, balancing autonomy and social support to foster students’ well-being and research breakthroughs.

title: Temporality: Meditations on Time and Learning in the ‘Anthropocene’
citation: Lotz-Sisitka, H. & Kronlid, D. (2025). Temporality: Meditations on Time and Learning in the ‘Anthropocene’. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1664-1668). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lotz-Sisitka, H. & Kronlid, D.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This paper explores the intersection of temporality and learning in the context of transformative education, particularly in response to the Anthropocene and climate change. Recognizing the paradoxes inherent in modern education—where the urgency of transformation conflicts with the time required for deep learning—we engage in two philosophical meditations to critically examine how time constructs shape and constrain educational practices. Drawing from continental philosophy, we interrogate dominant temporal paradigms in modern schooling, particularly the accelerationist pressures of neoliberalism, which prioritize efficiency and assessment over reflective learning. We argue that enriched conceptions of temporality—rooted in expansive, relational, and historically situated understandings—offer pathways for world-making practices that support just and sustainable futures. Through engagement with cultural tools, decolonial perspectives, and alternative knowledge systems, we propose an expanded temporality for education that fosters deep, transgressive learning. Our meditations invite further contemplation on how time can be refigured in the learning sciences to support transformative change.

title: Non-Disruptive Teacher Evaluation: From Case Analysis to Key Implementation Processes
citation: Chen, Y. & Yan, H. (2025). Non-Disruptive Teacher Evaluation: From Case Analysis to Key Implementation Processes. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1669-1673). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chen, Y. & Yan, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Reforming teacher evaluation is essential for promoting educational innovation and advancing sustainable development goals. Non-disruptive assessment offers a promising direction by embedding evaluation into everyday teaching practices with minimal interference. Yet, its implementation remains conceptually and practically underdeveloped. This study investigates the theoretical foundations and design principles of non-disruptive teacher evaluation through six representative cases. It identifies three key challenges: (1) technological tools support seamless data capture, but struggle with diagnostic precision; (2) online representations of teaching are expanding, yet fail to reflect critical offline practices; and (3) indicator frameworks are advancing, but linking evidence to competencies remains difficult. In response, we propose a four-step process—unify concepts, clarify standards, establish mappings, and formulate guidelines—to guide system design and support teacher growth through embedded, adaptive evaluation. The framework aims to support professional growth while contributing to more equitable and sustainable education systems.

title: The Process of Transforming Interdisciplinarity Perception Through Research Activities in an Interdisciplinary Department
citation: Shoji, G. & Ozawa, S. (2025). The Process of Transforming Interdisciplinarity Perception Through Research Activities in an Interdisciplinary Department. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1674-1678). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Shoji, G. & Ozawa, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines how students' perceptions of interdisciplinarity transform through research activities in an interdisciplinary department. Through qualitative analysis of seven master’s degree students using the Trajectory Equifinality Approach (TEA), we identified two patterns of transformation: interdisciplinarity as strategic boundary-crossing while maintaining disciplinary depth, and as a paradoxical process where interdisciplinary engagement enhances disciplinary expertise. The results reveal that these transformations occur as students expand their networks of academic actors, deepening their understanding of disciplinary positioning. The findings suggest the importance of supporting students in repositioning their research questions across multiple disciplinary frameworks, contributing to our understanding of interdisciplinary thinking development.

title: A Design Space for Articulating and Addressing the Risks of Integrating Generative AI in Education
citation: Coelho, R., Logan, C., Agkün, S., & Pea, R. (2025). A Design Space for Articulating and Addressing the Risks of Integrating Generative Ai in Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1679-1683). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Coelho, R., Logan, C., Agkün, S., & Pea, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Generative AI in Education must be approached with caution. While it might offer learning benefits, it also poses risks. Ethics frameworks have proliferated to guide responsible design, but they often lack enforceability and can be vague or overwhelming to implement in practice. We draw inspiration from Human-Computer Interaction to argue for the development of a systematic and community-driven design space to articulate, prioritize, and address the risks associated with Generative AI systems in Education.

title: Exploring AI-Generated Expert Models: Instructor Interaction and Learner Perceptions in a Physics Class
citation: Haddadian, G., Han, H., Kim, J., Abdeen, M. S., & Kim, M. K. (2025). Exploring Ai-Generated Expert Models: Instructor Interaction and Learner Perceptions in a Physics Class. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1684-1688). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Haddadian, G., Han, H., Kim, J., Abdeen, M. S., & Kim, M. K.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) offers opportunities for automatically creating expert model summaries, though creating them is demanding, requiring significant time and effort. Using a case study, we explored three types of expert model summaries, generated by human, AI, and human-AI collaboration. A new, AI-augmented expert modeling tool, which supports summarization activities, was deployed. Human-AI interaction, linguistic differences among the summaries, and learners’ perceptions were explored. Data sources included instructor log data, linguistic measures, and a student evaluation survey. Results showed that students preferred AI-generated summaries for their clarity, depth, and coherence, while human-AI collaboration achieved a balance between fluency and accuracy. Findings signify GenAI’s potential to reduce workload but underscore the need to address its limitations.

title: Exploring Middle School Students’ Agency in an Integrated Social Studies Unit
citation: Bamidele, B., Searle, K., Jiang, M., Harper, M., Bell, K., Ahmad, W., & Griffin, E. (2025). Exploring Middle School Students’ Agency in an Integrated Social Studies Unit. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1689-1693). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bamidele, B., Searle, K., Jiang, M., Harper, M., Bell, K., Ahmad, W., & Griffin, E.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: This study explores how middle school students express agency in an integrated social studies unit designed to foster critical thinking and sociopolitical critique. Centered on why treaties still matter for Indigenous peoples today, the curriculum utilized the lens of food sovereignty to make abstract ideas more concrete and to connect to students’ lives. Findings reveal students performing expert and investigator roles, which empowered them to reflect on the implications of limited food access and to imagine future social change. This research contributes to understanding student agency in social studies education and provides practical implications for designing curricula that support student agency and critical thinking.

title: Exploring Computational Action: Summer Camp Influence on Computing Attitudes among Middle School Students
citation: Tabares, S. O., Tissenbaum, M., & Bawankule, A. (2025). Exploring Computational Action: Summer Camp Influence on Computing Attitudes Among Middle School Students. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1694-1698). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tabares, S. O., Tissenbaum, M., & Bawankule, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Computational action, grounded in culturally responsive computing, emphasizes student reflection on their identities and communities through designing computing solutions for personally relevant social issues. Though some research exists, there is limited work on developing tools to assess its effective implementation. This mixed-methods study uses an existing validated pre/post survey of computing attitudes, observations, and interviews as a first step to effectively assessing computational action’s impact on attitudes. Quantitative results show no significant attitude changes, yet interviews and observations reveal strong interest in computing and students’ sense of computational empowerment. Convergent findings also indicate participants’ enjoyment of project-based learning and a sense of community. Results highlight the value of mixed methods approaches to capture data in complex contexts and the need for tailored instruments and methods to measure computational action’s impact. Findings also suggest computational action's potential to foster positive attitudes and engagement in computing.

title: Nest-building as World-building: Exploring Multispecies Sensemaking and Aesthetic Practices Among Two Youth Participating in a STEAM Summer Program
citation: Fisher, K. S., Kelton, M. L., & Pautzke, K. (2025). Nest-Building as World-Building: Exploring Multispecies Sensemaking and Aesthetic Practices Among Two Youth Participating in a STEAM Summer Program. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1699-1703). abstract: This study explores multispecies sensemaking and aesthetic practices of youth participating in a STEAM summer program. The program focused on ecological concepts and cartographic arts and was implemented in a rural, Latina/o/x agricultural community in the Inland Northwest. We share our early insights by presenting a case of multispecies sensemaking by two youth, Rafa and Arturo, as they build a nest for pet rocks they created. In this activity, designed to engage youth in resource ecology, the participants created pet rocks using paint markers and then used GoPro cameras to document finding food, water, and shelter for their rocks. Our video-based analysis traces Rafa and Arturo constructing a nest, with a focus on the emerging themes of seeking, friendship, and care-taking. The analysis aims to disrupt dominant solutionist narratives around crisis by centering the subtleties, resistances, and resiliencies embedded in youth’s everyday engagement with the more-than-human during times of precarity.

title: A Socio-Cultural Approach to Personalization in Education: Case Studies in Empowering Learners as Knowers with AI
citation: Li, F., Ziegler, H., Gonzales, A., Galloway, E. P., & Wise, A. F. (2025). A Socio-Cultural Approach to Personalization in Education: Case Studies in Empowering Learners as Knowers With Ai. abstract: In this conceptual design paper, we outline a novel socio-cultural approach to personalization that values diverse ways of knowing, learner agency, and co-construction of learning outcomes as an alternative to system-driven adaptation. We present two illustrative cases of AI agents developed to probe the viability of this approach. The TRANSLATE Buddy facilitates collaborative translation activities in multilingual classrooms aimed at empowering students as linguistic knowers and fostering metalinguistic engagement. The Scholar’s Table fosters a dialogue between post-secondary students and academic voices to promote active meaning-making of disciplinary texts. Both agents showed notable strength in supporting emergent learning directions, but variability in honoring multiplicity / relationality of meaning and positioning student-as-knower. Implications and future work are discussed.

title: Exploring Out-of-Tutor Interventions by Teachers in Supporting Student Learning with AI Tutors

abstract: Learning analytics has embraced the complexities of modeling student learning and engagement in ecological settings like K12 classrooms. While analyzing AI tutor interaction logs remains common, there is a growing need to include events that happen outside the AI tutor. Studies indicate teachers play active roles when students use AI tutors, and teacher support tools improve learning outcomes. However, methodological challenges exist in studying how such out-of-tutor interventions in the classroom shape learning (e.g., no counterfactual data, ethical issues in collecting control data). We propose a simple reconceptualization of the problem with which we could use standard statistical approaches to quantify the relationship between out-of-tutor interventions and student learning in the AI tutor. We study how moments of teacher help relate to improvements in students' performance on the skill or concept they were helped with. Our analysis reveals that teacher help has a significantly positive effect.

title: Lessons from Snails: Learning to Care for Nature
citation: Lee, C. (2025). Lessons From Snails: Learning to Care for Nature. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: Lee, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper explores how gardening supports affective experiences that are critical to fostering long-term care and action for the environment. Using thematic analysis, this case study examines the gardening experiences of four girls who initially saw snails as pests but later wrestled with the ethics of removing them from the garden. The study demonstrates that gardening exposed the students to real-life challenges and ethical questions, which in turn nurtured their sense of care for the environment.

title: “This World is a University”: Farmers’ Epistemic Agency in Climate Change Adaptation
citation: Carr, A., Gebre, E., & Shaw, W. (2025). “This World is a University”: Farmers’ Epistemic Agency in Climate Change Adaptation. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1719-1723). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Carr, A., Gebre, E., & Shaw, W.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Climate change poses significant challenges to agriculture, including increased vulnerability to extreme weather, crop disruptions, and reduced productivity. Agricultural extension systems aim to support farmers to adapt and respond to climate change through knowledge transfer and capacity-building. However, research suggests that farmers engage in multiple and distinct ways of knowing and often rely on informal learning to inform their adaptive practices (Berkes 2009; Anh Tran, 2020). Grounded in interviews with farmers in Jamaica this study examines farmers’ epistemic agency and the ways in which they integrate new ideas into their farming practices. Our preliminary analysis indicated that farmers don’t tend to separate learning from living and they seek out new information with the goal of solving problems in their everyday practice. However, we also observed that farmers experience epistemic tensions and attempt to address those tensions in context-specific ways. The study has implications for researching farmers’ ways of knowing and designing relevant learning environments in the context of agricultural extension and climate change discourse

title: What is Data? Youths’ Conceptualizations and Criteria within a Project-Based Data Science Camp
citation: Lanouette, K., Warnke, A., Johnston, A., Russo, R., Rosenbaum, L. F., & Blikstein, P. (2025). What is Data? Youths’ Conceptualizations and Criteria Within a Project-Based Data Science Camp. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lanouette, K., Warnke, A., Johnston, A., Russo, R., Rosenbaum, L. F., & Blikstein, P.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Data is ubiquitous in young people’s daily lives, yet its meaning and purpose are continually changing in relation to context, infrastructure, and intent. In this pilot study, we explore five 11- to 12-year olds’ conceptualizations and criteria for what makes something “data.” Analyzing semi-structured interviews as part of an embedded assessment where young people were presented with five different data visualizations, we find shifts and consistencies in their conceptualizations and criteria for including or excluding something as data, elevating the attributes of the data (numeracy, increasing volume) and the inferred intents of data producers (related to collection practices and purported purpose) in their decision making. These findings point to the complexity of defining data’s properties and functionalities and the need to develop taken-as-shared expectations and definitions of what data is and can be within educational contexts among youth, researchers, and educators.

title: Analyzing Creative Works within a Community of Transformation
