authors_list: Davis, S. C., Svihla, V., Ferris, K., Kellam, N., Lee, E., Palacio, C. R., & Getz, K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: While organizational change in academia is difficult, change efforts that aim at diversity, equity, inclusion, and justice (DEIJ) are particularly challenging. We formed a community of transformation that employs arts-based practices—speculative design, remixing, and futurisms—to support change agents. The current study investigates ways these arts practices can engage members in critiquing systems of oppression, strategically envisioning change mechanisms, and holding tight to DEIJ commitments. We analyzed community members’ creative works and discussion in terms of intention, process, remixing, and change agency. We found evidence that remixing problematic materials supported a merging of activism and aesthetics. Our approach to coding and activities can be adapted by others who support DEIJ change initiatives.

abstract: Centering students’ Funds of Identity (FOI) in the classroom is important for moving towards asset-based frameworks for learning. However, it can be challenging to identify the FOI of an entire class and use those FOI to design instruction. Motivated by this challenge, we explore how network visualizations in which students create a network that displays connections between themselves and classroom content can simultaneously elicit and connect students’ FOI to instruction. We conducted this work with five middle school World History classes taught by a single teacher, who built a collective network visualization about Greek Mythology. Using an iterative process of analytic memoing, coding, and content analysis, we identified three ways in which the network visualization activity connected to students’ identities: 1) they could share about themselves (particularly personality descriptions and practical FOI); 2) they could connect to content from their history class; and 3) they could connect to their peers.

title: Self-Determined Storytelling: Native Youths’ Digital Restorying Practices in an American Indian Education Summer Camp
citation: Litts, B. K., Haws, D., Morgan, C., Quintana, E., Allison, A., & Mills, T. (2025). abstract: Native communities maintain a rich history of community education, despite historical atrocities that have severely damaged the relationship between Native peoples and the U.S. education system. From this historicity, Native educators remain committed to supporting culturally sustaining/revitalizing learning experiences for Native youth. Within an ongoing collaboration between Native educators, university researchers, designers, and cultural technologists, in this paper, we share our exploration of integrating digital restorying practices in a summer camp for Native youth and their families. Findings illustrate three cases that demonstrate three forms of self-determination in Native youths’ digital restorying practices: how, whose, and what stories are told. Insights from findings present technological and rhetorical self-determination as two enactments of restorying as a critical practice of digital storytelling. This work contributes to the ongoing conversation around the cultural learning experiences of Native youth as they connect with their communities.

title: A Case Study on the Impact of Game Design Variations on Students’ Reasoning About Fraction Concepts
citation: Lee, B. (2025). A Case Study on the Impact of Game Design Variations on Students’ Reasoning About Fraction Concepts. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lee, B.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Previous studies have demonstrated the potential of digital video games to support students’ fraction learning, but few have explored how students’ understanding about fractions evolves during gameplay. Grounded in Maturana and Varela’s conceptualization of cognition as effective action and the goal-directed nature of human behavior, this study conceptualizes cognition as emerging through three fundamental actions: identification, association, and retention, and posits that goals direct the three actions to specific elements within a given context. Through an analysis of the elements identified, associated, and retained by a single student across two distinct game designs, this study reveals how different game designs elicit varied mathematical reasoning around targeted concepts. The findings underscore the influence of game design on shaping students’ engagement with targeted mathematical concepts.

citation: Yu, L., Sung, H., Plumley, R. D., Bernacki, M., & Greene, J. A. (2025). Exploring Sequential Patterns in Academic Help-Seeking: Transitions and Performance in a College Science Course. International Society of the Learning Sciences.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Academic help-seeking is a critical self-regulated learning strategy that supports academic performance, particularly in complex learning environments like flipped classrooms. Previous researchers highlight the role of diverse help-seeking sources, yet little is known about how students transition between these sources over time. In this study, we examined academic help-seeking behaviors in an introductory science course throughout a semester. Undergraduates relied heavily on system-embedded help and generally remained within the same help category. Higher-performing students favored system-embedded and personalized support sources, whereas lower-performing students relied more on structured supplemental sessions and information search forums. These findings underscore the importance of understanding dynamic help-seeking patterns and their relationships to academic outcomes. This work advances the study of help-seeking behaviors in real-world educational settings.

abstract: This systematic review explores how ChatGPT has been integrated into digital learning games, focusing on its role as a feedback provider. Analyzing 17 empirical studies, the review found that ChatGPT is mainly used to deliver cognitive and motivational feedback, often leading to improved engagement and learning. While students generally appreciate the immediate support, concerns remain about the accuracy and depth of its responses.

abstract: This paper explores the teaching, learning, and practices of climate change science in an intergenerational setting of an Indigenous Maya Tzotzil Muslim community in Chiapas, Mexico. By focusing on a formal and intergenerational educational setting involving three generations of women from this Maya Muslim community, we show two critical aspects of this climate change paradigm: First, how the community approaches their more-than-human environment as relatives with emotions, intelligence, and agency; Second, how they define care, respect, and responsibility as being central to maintaining sustainable relationships with their more-than-human relatives. We argue that this sensemaking and practices of climate change science are grounded in the ways this community sees themselves in relationship with nature.

title: Cognitive Load and Epistemic Emotions Interact to Determine Students’ Performance in a Technology-Rich Environment

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Researchers have examined the separate roles of cognitive load and epistemic emotions in influencing students’ performance; however, more evidence is needed to explore the interaction of these two constructs and their joint effects on performance. In this study, a total of 107 students solved a clinical problem within a technology-rich environment, during which they reported their perceptions of cognitive load (i.e., intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load), surprise, confusion, curiosity, and enjoyment. Task performance was indicated by diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. Results of path analyses revealed that intrinsic and extraneous load positively predicted surprise and confusion, whereas germane load negatively predicted curiosity and enjoyment. Moreover, this study found four significant mediation effects: intrinsic loadsurpriseaccuracy (negative); extraneous loadconfusionefficiency (negative); germane loadenjoymentaccuracy (positive); and germane loadcuriosityefficiency (positive). Overall, these findings suggested that the predictive effects of cognitive load could be mediated by different epistemic emotions.

abstract: This study investigates how virtual reality (VR) technology can support embodied learning in professional education, focusing on posture training in dental education. We developed a VR-based training system that integrates motion tracking technology with real-time postural feedback based on rapid upper limb assessment (RULA) criteria. In an experimental study with 36 dental students, we examined both system usability and effectiveness in improving ergonomic posture. The results revealed high system usability scores with no significant differences between experimental and control groups, and low perceived workload. For effectiveness, the experimental group showed significant improvement with feedback and maintained this improvement after feedback removal. This study demonstrates the potential of VR environments to support embodied learning through immediate feedback, suggesting implications for how VR technology can bridge the gap between knowledge and physical practice in professional education.

abstract: Proportional reasoning understanding is considered necessary for student success in upper-level mathematics as well as science, technology, and engineering. Research on middle grades mathematics learning shows that students tend to development stronger understandings of mathematical concepts when they learn through constructionist real-world projects that are relevant and meaningful to them. In this work, we conducted an exploratory qualitative study to investigate how middle school students demonstrate their understanding of proportional reasoning through making in a Challenge-Based Learning project. Our findings showed that students accurately represented their understanding of proportionality through their digital artifacts more than any other modality available, contrasting previous findings in the relevant literature. Findings regarding the integration of professional technology and the prevalence of mathematical estimation in digital modeling provide avenues for further research vis-a-vis the role of estimation in spatial reasoning for design. Implications for the practice and the field of STEM learning are discussed.

title: The Overlooked Potential of Gamebooks

abstract: Gamebooks are non-linear narratives where reader choice determines what happens next in the story. While such books are popular with readers, there is limited research on their use as educational resources. This paper presents the initial results of a literature review on research on educational gamebooks, exploring the context in which gamebooks are used, the impact they have on readers and the theory that underpins gamebook design. It is argued that the educational potential of gamebooks has been overlooked and that they are worthy of further research.

title: Mind-Wandering in Education: From Attention Shifting to Inner Engagement
citation: Dario, N. & Lund, K. (2025). Mind-Wandering in Education: From Attention Shifting to Inner Engagement. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We explore the phenomenon of mind-wandering (MW) in the classroom. Challenging its traditional negative view, we reframe MW as an engagement with one’s inner world and as a dynamic and transformative process. We analyze case studies of MW experiences of eight students and three teachers across classroom lectures, testing, and group work. Through two interview techniques, and using classroom video recordings, we examine the relationship between activities and MW, MW episode content and types, emotional states associated with MW, and contextual influences. MW is not just a lapse in attention but coexists with and complements ongoing activities. We invite educators to rethink classroom practices as MW is a potential resource for fostering deeper, student-centered learning.

The findings reveal that students actively participate in interactions, demonstrating both cognitive activities and regulatory activities. Students generally hold positive perceptions of AI agents, particularly regarding their cognitive support and ability to provide personalized learning experiences. However, limitations were identified in the emotional domain, with students noting a lack of emotional resonance in their interactions with the agents. These results highlight the potential of multi-agent systems to enrich educational experiences, while also pointing to areas for improvement in emotional engagement.

citation: Palzer, K., Flottmann, J., & Bodemer, D. (2025). Immersion and Motivation in Educational AR Games: Investigating Narrative Design and Feedback Type. abstract: Game-based learning (GBL) in Augmented Reality (AR) has great potential to make learning experiences interactive, immersive, and motivating. We investigated the impact of narrative and feedback on immersion and motivation while learning about soil science through an AR game using HoloLens 2. An experimental study with N = 123 participants employed a 2×2 between-subjects design with narrative (absence vs. presence) and feedback type (pure outcome information vs. additional process information) as factors. Results indicate that feedback on the process significantly increases immersion, flow, and focus of attention. The effect of the narrative and feedback type on motivation is interdependent: only when the feedback lacks process information the integration of a narrative boosts motivation by increasing their confidence and satisfaction, and emotional attachment. Considering feedback and narrative in research and practice can help fully realize the potential of AR learning games.

title: Co-Constructing (Twisted) Knowledge: Argumentation in Far-Right YouTube Comments on Brazil’s War with X’s Elon Musk
citation: Sotério, C., Russo, R., & Blikstein, P. (2025). Co-Constructing (Twisted) Knowledge: Argumentation in Far-Right YouTube Comments on Brazil’s War With X’s Elon Musk. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1799-1803). subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Social & Civic Studies

abstract: Social media can foster collective knowledge construction alongside communication. However, these platforms can also be hubs for disseminating distorted or “twisted” knowledge, particularly within extremist contexts. This study analyzes argument negotiation in the comments section of a far-right YouTube channel implicated in anti-democratic activities in Brazil. Using an adapted coding scheme from Dubovi and Tabak (2020), we examined 123 comments to identify patterns of argumentation and knowledge construction. Findings reveal three key insights: (1) users engage in logical reasoning that often leads to the construction of misinformation, reinforcing ideological polarization; (2) participants primarily act as consumers interacting with the influencer rather than engaging in peer-to-peer dialogue, limiting the potential for civic discourse; (3) instances of deeper argumentation reveal the potential for fostering critical engagement. These results highlight the interplay between argument negotiation and disinformation on social media, emphasizing the need for strategies to mitigate extremism and foster constructive dialogue online.

title: In Screams, Shouts, and Symbols: Noticing Young Children’s “Knowing” in a STEM + Arts Unit
citation: Wargo, J. M. (2025). In Screams, Shouts, and Symbols: Noticing Young Children’s “Knowing” in a STEM + Arts Unit. abstract: This paper examines how a class of Pre-Kindergarten children exhibited - through play - the physical properties of sound-art production. More specifically, it focuses on how, through language, embodiment, and the material infrastructure of the learning environment, children enacted and recognized one another’s knowledge states to interactionally accomplish varying iterations of ‘sounding out’ their learning to peers. In so doing, it traces the embodied and multimodal resources of exhibiting how sound moved – using couplings of talk, gesture, and visual renderings – to render children’s visible and embodied knowledges across time. Drawing on three larger “tracks” across the integrative STEM+ Arts unit, this paper illustrates how a trajectory of “knowing-in-interaction” came to be rendered public and how, through these more micro-analytic moves of children’s microgenetic learning, brilliance and heterogeneity in early STEM + Arts was showcased.

abstract: We contribute to the field of embodied technology by designing a Multiple External Representation (MER) learning environment that integrates gesture-guided haptic feedback with an interactive computer visualization. A think-aloud protocol was conducted to determine how students use the MER environment to reason about a complex system in biochemistry. We assessed how students interpret MERs and found that haptic feedback supported students’ learning by (1) complementing the visualization, or (2) introducing conceptual confusion. In a few cases, however, the haptic feedback left students’ interpretations unchanged. Our case analysis highlights how the introduction of haptic feedback transformed students' interpretations of the visualization, prompting them to recognize previously overlooked influences.

title: The Influence of Colonial Legacy on Science Teachers’ Perspectives of Real-World Science Issues
citation: Gopal, S. D. & Honwad, S. (2025). The Influence of Colonial Legacy on Science Teachers’ Perspectives of Real-World Science Issues. subject: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Science education has become increasingly linked to social justice, as global challenges like climate change and public health crises reveal underlying societal inequities. Scholars emphasize that science educators must engage with social and political movements to prevent reinforcing harmful ideologies that sustain these inequities. This submission explores the influence of colonial legacy on science teachers’ perspectives of science issues. Using narrative interview data about how secondary school science teachers in Guyana perceive and address socio-political dimensions of science, we explore in what ways the view of land and natural resources as commodities shows up in their perspectives. Findings reveal that, while teachers express concerns about sustainability and environmental health, their views often reflect colonial attitudes toward land and resources, treating them as opportunities for economic gain. This submission raises critical questions about how science education can authentically integrate social justice and challenge colonial ideologies in both curriculum and teaching practices.

title: An Exploration of Family Engagement in STEM Identity Work
citation: Peczuh, M. C. & Varma, K. (2025). An Exploration of Family Engagement in STEM Identity Work. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. abstract: While learning sciences research has identified various processes involved in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) identity work, important gaps in the field remain. This conceptual paper reviews previous work on STEM identity and family engagement in STEM, arguing that the role of families within STEM identity work has not been deeply explored. Families may be uniquely positioned to provide support for STEM identity through facilitating connections across STEM experiences and navigating multiple identities. Future work should explore STEM identity work within family interactions using qualitative methods and within informal STEM learning programs. Through recognizing the funds of knowledge and identity that families contribute to STEM identity work, research can demonstrate more expansive forms of STEM identity.

title: Developing a Counter-Space for Learning, Belonging, and Becoming in and Through Calculus

abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of a counter-space that integrates disciplinary rigor with identity-empowering practices to support historically marginalized STEM students at the University of California, Berkeley. Situated within a social design experiment, the counter-space fostered a collaborative community where students engaged deeply with core calculus ideas while cultivating positive mathematical identities and a stronger sense of belonging. The paper elaborates on the key design principles of the counter-space as well as its structure and curriculum. Analysis of students’ weekly reflection journals revealed significant gains in students’ mathematical understanding, performance, confidence, sense of belonging, and self-perceptions as capable mathematical thinkers. This study offers a model for disciplinary-rigorous and identity-empowering counter-spaces that institutions can adapt to address systemic barriers and promote sustainable STEM pathways for historically marginalized students.

title: Promoting Culturally Responsive Teaching via Educational Game Design –Teachers as Educational Game Designers
citation: Li, T., Fisher, J. A., & Hong, Y. (2025). Promoting Culturally Responsive Teaching via Educational Game Design –Teachers as Educational Game Designers. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Li, T., Fisher, J. A., & Hong, Y.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: As schools become culturally diverse, integrating students' cultural backgrounds into teaching practices is essential. Culturally Responsive Teaching (CRT) has emerged as a critical focus in professional development (PD) for educators. However, many PD programs inadequately train teachers in CRT, resulting in superficial cultural integration. This exploratory study investigates the impact of educational game design workshops on promoting CRT, positioning teachers as serious game designers. Nine elementary mathematics teachers participated in a workshop that involved designing culturally responsive educational games. Through thematic analysis of interview data, findings reveal that game design fosters teachers’ empathy and understanding of students' cultural contexts, enabling the incorporation of diverse cultural elements into their teaching. Challenges identified include cultural gaps and limited design skills. The study highlights the potential of collaborative game design in enhancing CRT, suggesting that hands-on, creative PD approaches can deepen teachers’ cultural awareness and instructional practices.

abstract: This study explored in-service teachers’ perceptions of large language models, focusing on their ability to generate human-like responses. The data were collected from 47 in-service teachers who enrolled in a graduate-level computer science education and technology course. In a weekly module, teachers were asked to compare data-driven machine intelligence to humans based on the characteristic features of responses. Qualitative content analysis revealed that teachers perceived machine intelligence as limited in replicating human qualities. However, they saw utility value, suggesting meaningful interactions could still be established. Implications for the field of teacher education and professional development in AI literacies are discussed.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Science teachers seeking to engage students in collective sensemaking must attend to not only students’ epistemic development, but also to their relationships with each other. This paper examines the intertwined epistemic and relational responsibilities of science teaching through a case study of Ms. Shaw, a fifth-grade teacher. The analysis reveals the responsibilities that Ms. Shaw felt in creating an equitable learning environment where all students felt valued, as well as emerging tensions between her epistemic and relational goals for classroom activity. Ms. Shaw’s reflections highlight the complexity of navigating these dual responsibilities as well as the difficulties in disrupting inequitable patterns of classroom participation.

title: Apt Epistemic Vigilance
citation: Pimentel, D. & Zummo, L. M. (2025). Apt Epistemic Vigilance. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: In an increasingly complex information landscape, students can face challenges when evaluating scientific information due to discrepancies between the nature of classroom information environments and the unregulated nature of online information environments. This paper introduces the concept of apt epistemic vigilance, a framework that integrates epistemic vigilance and apt epistemic performance to address these challenges. Epistemic vigilance involves critically assessing both content and sources, while apt epistemic performance emphasizes achieving epistemic aims through competence, adaptability, and meta-epistemic awareness. By fostering skillful and adaptive engagement with both content-focused and source-focused evaluations, the apt epistemic vigilance framework prepares students to navigate epistemically unfriendly environments effectively. The paper concludes with implications for instructional approaches to enhance and promote apt epistemic vigilance in science classrooms. The goal of this approach is to equip researchers and educators with a framework for promoting informed information evaluation in civic and scientific contexts.

abstract: Today’s youth have extensive experience interacting with artificial intelligence and machine learning applications on popular social media platforms, putting youth in a unique position to examine, evaluate, and even challenge these applications. Algorithm auditing is a promising candidate for connecting youth’s everyday practices in using AI applications with more formal scientific literacies (i.e., syncretic designs). In this paper, we analyze high school youth participants’ everyday algorithm auditing practices when interacting with generative AI filters on TikTok, revealing thorough and extensive examinations, with youth rapidly testing filters with sophisticated camera variations and facial manipulations to identify filter limitations. In the discussion, we address how these findings can provide a foundation for developing designs that bring together everyday and more formal algorithm auditing.

abstract: This paper shares findings from a participatory study with a large urban library system to center staff perspectives in shaping teen services. Through surveys, site visits, and collaborative analysis, staff highlighted disconnects between their relational goals and system-level priorities and shared strategies for design and connection. Findings surfaced opportunities for cross-branch learning and system-level shifts in priorities and support.

abstract: Failure – both conceptually and in practice – is a ripe site for theorizing learning. In the learning sciences, failure is heterogeneous, with many of its semantic offshoots (e.g., uncertainty, misconception) intimating how the experience of “failing” is dependent on broader questions of context (e.g., how and where failing occurred). Drawing on data from a larger qualitative study examining how five players learned to “escape” a series of increasingly difficulty escape rooms, this paper demonstrates that learning to escape - like all multi-part phenomena - requires the conceptual breakdown of a system’s constituent components and the lamination of semiotic substrates that contribute to and advance cooperative action among individuals.

title: Parents as Design Partners in Fostering Curiosity and Connection
citation: Martin, C. K., Barron, B., & Chen, S. (2025). Parents as Design Partners in Fostering Curiosity and Connection. abstract: This study employs a longitudinal diary approach to explore how adult caregivers at home characterized and supported children’s learning with technology during and after the pandemic. By enabling in-the-moment, multimodal storytelling, the approach provides unique insights into how families navigate tensions, foster connections, and adapt digital tools to their needs. Implications include advancing remote, scalable methods for studying family learning practices and sharing stories as inspiration for design. Initial findings suggest caregiver attention to technology opportunities that support authentic inquiry, transparency in joining in collective exploration and learning, and colocated experiences.

title: Towards Consequential Arts: Educators’ Conceptions of the Arts’ Roles in Learning and Change Making
citation: Field, N. & Bang, M. (2025). Towards Consequential Arts: Educators’ Conceptions of the Arts’ Roles in Learning and Change Making. abstract: The arts have great potential to contribute to learning and change making. However, many educational environments have not meaningfully invested in supporting consequential art. In exploring the potential of arts in both disciplinary and transdisciplinary learning, it is essential to consider educators' conceptions of the arts and how these conceptions might be shaped by sociocultural factors. This study analyzed 51 interviews with educators and found that 90.1% articulated views about the arts’ roles in learning and change making, which can be grouped into 20 conceptions, 5 of which were especially prominent.

abstract: This study examines how arts education fosters identity development and strengthens ties between learners and their communities. With arts often marginalized in schools due to budget cuts or an emphasis on standardized assessments, after-school or summer programs funded by nonprofits increasingly supplement arts learning. Focusing on an Out-of-School Arts (OSA) program in Los Angeles, this study investigates how art-making practices support personal growth and community connection. Through life-history interviews with two alumni, both women of color who participated in the program 7–10 years ago, the study highlights how arts practices that honor learners’ cultural backgrounds promote empowering identities and community bonds. Findings emphasize the importance of arts as a medium for learners to connect with their communities and build shared understanding, showing how such programs offer vital opportunities for cultural engagement and identity construction.

abstract: This study investigates how seven achievement motivation constructs derived from Eccles’ EVT relate to self-efficacy and performance among 8th-9th grade female and male students in an AI curriculum. Both groups showed significant, medium-sized gains in self-efficacy and performance. However, gender-specific patterns emerged: female students’ performance was weakly but significantly correlated with EVT constructs, while male students’ self-efficacy showed weak-to-medium correlations. Hierarchical regression revealed that self-efficacy could be predicted for males but not for females, despite known links between self-efficacy, performance, and motivation. These findings call for further investigation, especially given the role of self-efficacy in shaping disciplinary identity, career choice, and the persistent gender gap in AI fields.

title: Future Trends in Digital Learning for Enabling Holistic Student Development: Review of Educational Policy
citation: Dasgupta, C., Dmoshinskaia, N., Xhauflair, M., & van der Linden, S. (2025). Future Trends in Digital Learning for Enabling Holistic Student Development: Review of Educational Policy. International Society of the Learning Sciences.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: There is a push to adopt educational practices fostering holistic student development in K-12 due to current uncertain times. To understand what these new practices entail, we take a global policy perspective and identify trends that will likely shape the future of education focused on holistic student development. We identified eight trends for future-focused education and discuss how these can be mapped to holistic student development. These trends represent three interconnected dimensions of education – Why (goals for education), How (the design and organization of education), and What (the content of education). We identified 20 sub-trends that reflect the multifaceted nature of the trends. Teacher capabilities required to facilitate the implementation of these trends were described as well. These provide a robust base for (re)imagining how to prepare K-12 students (and teachers) as change-agents instead of only a workforce.

title: Towards a Learning Sciences-Informed Framework for Investigating “Twisted” Knowledge Construction on Social Media
citation: Russo, R. & Blikstein, P. (2025). Towards a Learning Sciences-Informed Framework for Investigating “Twisted” Knowledge Construction on Social Media. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 1884-1888). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Russo, R. & Blikstein, P.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This paper proposes a framework to investigate a phenomenon we term twisted knowledge construction on social media from a Learning Sciences perspective. We first analyze and then draw connections between literature from four fields of scholarship, with varying levels of connection to the Learning Sciences: social media from the perspective of Internet and Communication Studies; foundational theories of learning; social media as contexts for learning; and epistemic cognition with an emphasis on emotions. We articulate these connections as a loop-like system supported by the socio-technical affordances of social media. This system is fueled by ideologically motivated content and interactions that shape knowledge construction, whose affective and repertoire-based outcomes loop back into itself, leading to a cycle of distorted knowledge construction. Considerations for future research are proposed from a Learning Sciences perspective.

title: Scaffolding Students’

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Students experience uncertainties while solving open-ended collaborative problems. They can feel overwhelmed and question their abilities to manage these uncertainties and, thus, need to be supported in this process. Scaffolds such as concept-maps and reflection prompts have shown to be useful in supporting students’ collaborative problem-solving. Hence, we investigate the influence of concept-maps and reflection prompts on students’ self-efficacy while managing uncertainty in an open-ended collaborative problem-solving task. Twenty-three master’s students participated in mixed-method classroom research where they collaboratively designed an online learning environment. Findings suggest that the scaffolds can foster productive uncertainty management by initiating productive discussions to manage uncertainties. Maintaining and reducing uncertainties emerged as popular strategies indicating that students became comfortable with uncertainties and were willing to leave them unresolved before reducing them for making final decisions. Furthermore, their self-efficacy increased significantly over time while managing uncertainty.

title: Desiring Learning in a Hospital School Arts Education Program

abstract: This study analyzes desire as a dynamic force driving learning in a children’s hospital school arts education program. Data come from an ongoing, three-year co-design project addressing a challenge for hospital schools in designing learning opportunities that move students to participate through ongoing social and emotional disruption, and that maintain continuity in students’ sense of themselves as learners. Analysis shows how students’ affective revelations while working collaboratively on a map-based art project are inseparable from the ongoing production of desiring learning that is essential to their elective participation. This conceptualization of affective revelations contributes to learning sciences research theorizing how affect relates to learning and learning ecology design. Drawing on critical design-based research in the learning sciences, the project challenges infirming narratives of children undergoing hospitalization, and it illustrates how coming to feel differently is an essential dimension of coming to know differently while learning in the arts.

abstract: Research suggests that scaffolding students’ Computational Thinking before coding can support their learning experience. We examine how a CT App supports students’ learning process and how the MyTurn social robotics curriculum impacts students’ perceptions of Computer Science and sense of belonging in an in-classroom deployment. We find evidence that pre-coding scaffolds benefited students’ CT and coding process and that the open-ended, design-based robotics curriculum influenced many students’ perceptions of CS.

title: What are the Capacities Needed to be a Problem Solver?

abstract: Educators encounter an ongoing challenge in effectively preparing learners to become innovative problem-solvers for the future. Despite continuous advocacy for equipping youth with future-ready skills, significant changes in educational practices remain scarce. One contributing factor appears to be the absence of clear, consistent terminology, definitions, and indicators related to the capacities required for learners to develop inventiveness. To address this issue, we conducted a modified Delphi study with a diverse panel of experts to investigate the research question: What capacities do youth need to become inventive problem-solvers? Through multiple rounds of surveys and analysis, we developed a comprehensive set of 43 capacities and strategies relevant to problem-solving. This presentation will outline our methodology and findings and will encourage discussion on how these insights can inform future research and educational reform.

title: Utilizing Activity Theory to Analyze how Tensions were Negotiated in a Teacher Video Club

abstract: Focusing on a semester-long video club with five high school science teachers, the research describes elements of the video club as an activity system and examines how facilitator decisions and design choices surfaced and resolved tensions. Four levels of contradictions emerged during the professional learning: primary (video clip selection), secondary (changing norms and roles), tertiary (eliciting and working with student ideas), and quaternary (reconciling video club goals with district goals). The findings reveal that activity theory provides a nuanced framework for understanding the impacts of facilitator decision-making and highlights the importance of flexible facilitation, carefully selected artifacts, and responsive design in supporting teachers' professional growth and instructional exploration.

title: Growth Mindset Interventions to Make Failure Desired in Learning
citation: Sinha, T. (2025). Growth Mindset Interventions to Make Failure Desired in Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. abstract: We tested the impact of developing and validating a growth mindset intervention targeting domain-general and domain-specific skillsets that affect learning from failure for sixty six ninth-grade students. Repeated prediction followed by explanation cycles were used to trap myths associated with growth mindset and induce surprise in the learning process. Following mixed methods analyses, results showed a significant pre-post improvement in beliefs about the malleability of mental abilities and expectations for success in future math tasks. Internalizing the growth mindset message also positively impacted persistence in idea generation on a challenging follow-up math task. Qualitative student reflections suggested transformed perceptions about the desirability of failure, with students articulating a contrast between their revised conceptions about the value of failure and past cognitive/affective approaches towards dealing with those failures. Compared to past work, our intervention produced stronger effects.

abstract: Data science education scholars are looking for guidance about how to teach youth to practice making ethical considerations throughout the data science lifecycle (National Academies, 2018). Such guidance should draw from images of data science that are grounded in empirical studies of professionals. In this paper, I present a case study of a data scientist at a 501(c)(3) non-profit who investigated a city policy designed to reduce CO2 emissions. I examine how the data scientist sensed whether a set of values, that he shared with the public, were represented in the policy. I will discuss implications for data science education.

abstract: Data literacy is increasingly becoming an essential ability in our age of information. Core skills to be data literate include reading, writing, and interpreting data. When reading and writing data, the interpretation of data requires considerations of authorship as part of the sensemaking process. In this paper, we interpret data interactions with respect to authorship, which we operationalize as acting, sensing, and writing data. We highlight what that means for reading self-authored data. With data from a summer program, we examine youth’s sensemaking across a four part activity, wherein they use a jump rope sensor, recreate it with a new sensor, and then create their own version of a jump counter. This analysis presents emerging relationships between different configurations of author and reader and how those structures afford different sensemaking opportunities with data.

abstract: Previous engineering education research highlights the role that community resources—language practices and cultural understandings—play in the learning experiences of students. Theoretical and pedagogical approaches in engineering vary widely and rarely incorporate these community resources to understand and support the engineering identity development of historically underrepresented students. In this paper, we document our journey attempting to make visible the experiences of Black-Latinx communities, Latino/a/x/e of Black ancestry, in engineering practices. In a collaborative inquiry following ethnographic methods, we, multilingual women in engineering, reflect about our own identities as we attempt to make sense of community resources in the discipline. We present how our identities influence the ways in which we think about the research design, the opportunities and challenges of integrating cultural and linguistic systems of practices and understandings in engineering courses at a predominantly White institution (PWI) and Hispanic-serving institutions (HSI). By engaging with our own experiences conducting this work, we hope to motivate other researchers and faculty to also reflect on how our intersecting identities shape who we are, how we approach our work, and how others may view our approaches.

abstract: In this paper, and as part of a broader research program on the role of collective care in sustainability transformations, we discuss how nurses working in hospitals in the U.S. co-create and rely on informal forms of collective support to compensate for the lack of sufficient organizational support. By exploring collective care as affective contextures that are part of everyday nursing work, we aim to show how the affective aspects of everyday life are intertwined with organizational, institutional, and economic dimensions and how such intertwining is key for understanding ecosocial transitions to more sustainable ways of living and learning. We draw on a narrative case study based on interviews with nurses in the U.S. context to illustrate how practices of collective care, though often at the expense of nurses’ own health and well-being, also mobilize creative, informal forms of resilience and communal support that prefigure more humane, sustainable practices.

abstract: Scholars who employ humanizing research methodologies are also tasked with the labor of developing infrastructure and resources to support the mutually beneficial and reciprocal partnerships required. In response, we share our process of building a “research interface” that invites participation from community partners and centers community needs. We present our year-long partnership-building process guided by the research question: what are effective practices in conducting community-driven design research among partnerships with researchers, designers, educators, and Tribal Elders? Through a critical ethnographic approach, we identified practices that served as guides in our partnership-building process. Insights from our findings contribute to current understandings for how community-driven design research practices support humanizing and healing approaches to research.

abstract: This study examines how boundary infrastructures in Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs) facilitate learning and collaboration between a rural school district and two universities. Using the Learning at the Boundaries framework, we analyze design team meetings, teacher feedback, and co-designed curricular materials. Our findings highlight the roles of boundary spanners, practices, and objects in bridging gaps among stakeholders and fostering sustainable collaboration. This research contributes to the learning sciences by documenting effective processes for organizational learning, emphasizing the importance of structured co-design in educational improvement.

abstract: This conceptual paper explores the integration of Systems Thinking (ST) into Environmental Education (EE) to address interconnected socio-environmental challenges, drawing on theories of critical pedagogy, Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT), and Situated Learning Theory (SLT). It argues that promoting environmental stewardship necessitates a transdisciplinary and systemic approach beyond fragmented and siloed practices. Using Engeström’s (2009) Activity Theory, the research frames EE programs across public, private, and civil society sectors as activity systems and investigates how their interactions can create new collective activity systems through multi-sector partnerships (MSPs). These partnerships are analyzed through the lens of boundary objects emphasizing collaboration, shared goals, and expansive learning. The paper proposes viewing different sectors that implement EE programs as collective activity systems to facilitate the co-construction of local EE programs that are more systems-thinking oriented approaches.

abstract: Science practices are a critical component of science education. Theory-building practices such as modeling lie at the heart of the scientific enterprise. To develop instructional activities that engage students in theory-building practices and assessments that track their development of expertise, it is necessary to understand the knowledge underlying students’ engagement in theory building. This paper presents a framework for modeling this knowledge, called the epistemic systems framework (ESF). Grounded in the knowledge in pieces (KiP) perspective, the ESF is designed to produce high-precision models of the structure, dynamics, and development of the knowledge students use to construct and refine theoretical artifacts, including models and explanations. The paper outlines the framework’s theoretical foundations and unpacks its major components.

abstract: This study examines high school students’ epistemic cognition about research in connection with their research experiences. We analyzed the metaphors about research generated by a class of 12th graders, who participated in community-based research with professional organizations. Students generated metaphors to reflect on the nature of research using the prompt “research is like... because..." Qualitative analysis of student-generated metaphors revealed their epistemic notions of research as an ever-deepening process with uncertainty. Students’ metaphorical embodiments of research make abstract epistemic notions tangible, shaping their ongoing engagement in research work.

abstract: This paper examines the STEM learning trajectories of two Black male youths, Chicke and Brandon, who participated in a STEM cycling program. A video recording by Chicke on one of the group bicycle rides is examined to understand how the program served as a juncture through which the two boys engaged in spatial literacy practices, application of science knowledge, and active participation in norms and social practices of group bicycle riding for safety and efficiency. Mediated discourse analysis is used to render findings from the video clip in relationship to the larger data corpus of the three-year project. The study has implications for how youth are positioned in and invited to STEM learning opportunities.

abstract: This study addresses the need for responsive teaching in light of current science education reforms. Responsive teaching involves recognizing and building on students' ideas, adapting instruction, and engaging with their thinking (Robertson et al., 2016; Thompson et al., 2016). However, this approach is challenging for pre-service teachers (Haverly et al., 2020). This qualitative study investigates how pre-service secondary science teachers (PSSTs) learn to use students’ ideas in instruction during their teacher preparation science methods (TPSM) course as we adopt the Ambitious Science Teaching (AST) conceptual framework (Windschitl et al., 2018). Interviews with four PSSTs and their instructor identify the perceived course features that support PSSTs in learning to use students’ ideas, including class community, peer teaching, and the problem-based unit plan assignment. We examine the alignment between the instructor’s and PSSTs’ perceived course features and provide recommendations for teacher education programs to support PSSTs in developing responsive teaching practices.

abstract: In a black box theater on a university campus, a duel for control over a contested territory erupts between actors and their stage manager. The territory in question? The dressing room. The key combatants? Rihanna and Olivia Rodrigo. Through micro-analysis of a pre-show rehearsal, this study explores how theatre artists learn the malleability of space and place through negotiating territories, paying particular attention to the interactional entangling of affect, bodies, and sound in defining and mediating which spaces and places are enacted.

abstract: There is consensus that computational modeling can support integration of science with computing for student learning. However, it can be challenging for teachers to gain comfort with this relatively new practice, reconcile how it relates to science, and recognize its pedagogical value. In this paper, we illustrate how teachers working with a (serendipitous) analogy between a familiar process and a topic covered in chemistry class–frogs catching flies and reaction rates–enabled them to take up computational modeling in their science teaching. Drawing on notes from co-design sessions, teacher interviews and student worksheets, we illustrate how a focal teacher shifted from initial reluctance to taking ownership of designing and teaching a computational modeling lesson sequence. We also briefly show how her students took up this work. Finally, we reflect on the importance of leveraging teachers’ existing domain and pedagogical expertise as we bring these new practices into their classrooms.

abstract: K-12 students need to understand technical and ethical knowledge about Artificial Intelligence to utilize ubiquitous AI-powered technologies responsibly. Recent studies have explored ways to teach AI to K-12 students effectively, but little is known about ways to assess their learning. In this study, we describe how five computer science teachers from urban and rural Georgia school districts designed, adapted, and implemented assessments in their classrooms while teaching a middle school elective course aligned with the Five Big Ideas of AI. Analyzing artifacts from 201 students, we explore the efficacy of different assessment instruments co-designed with teachers, measuring students’ understanding of sensors and the societal impacts of autonomous vehicles. We suggest design considerations for AI knowledge assessments to meet the needs and challenges in diverse classroom contexts.

abstract: This paper examines the dynamics of a researcher-teacher partnership in co-designing computational thinking (CT) learning experiences for young children. While CT integration in early childhood education has gained increasing attention, the gap between theoretical frameworks and practical implementation remains a significant challenge. Through the lens of co-design in professional learning, we analyze the synergistic effort between researchers and a teacher during a five-day summer program involving 14 children (ages 4-12) in eastern China. Our findings reveal distinct patterns of engagement among different stakeholders, highlighting the complementary nature of theoretical and practical expertise in the co-design practices. The insights contribute to our understanding of effective professional learning experiences for CT education and offer practical implications for scaling similar initiatives in diverse cultural contexts.

abstract: There is a critical need to incorporate Computational Thinking (CT) into a broad range of STEM courses to promote access to computing education. This study explored whether this could be achieved through engineering design activities embedded in a high school biology course. An interdisciplinary team of researchers and teachers developed a curricular unit where high school students design and program a simplified model of a bionic arm from the sensors up. Quantitative findings revealed significant pre-to-post improvements in some aspects of CT and in engineering design self-efficacy. Qualitative data highlighted students’ initial apprehension with programming and engineering tasks, which evolved into engagement through scaffolded support and the use of a visual programming interface. The real-world context of the unit motivated students by linking CT and engineering to biological concepts. This study illustrates the potential of interdisciplinary approaches to the integration of CT and engineering design in STEM courses.

abstract: Conjecture maps have long been considered instrumental in systematizing and clarifying various design and theoretical conjectures in design-based research. However, beyond enhancing design-based research, there is opportunity to clarify how the conjecture map may be used to design an intervention itself. Following the backward design logic from curricular and instructional planning, we outline here a process followed to design the first iteration of a multi-year anti-racist teacher professional development intervention that articulated the high-level conjecture, outcomes, mediating processes, and embodiments, in that order. We also present our current conjecture map and invite other researchers and practitioners to engage with in the pursuit of more effective designs for anti-racist teacher learning.

abstract: Drawing on a prominent theorization of collaboration, this paper analyzes interaction between a teacher and a researcher engaged in curricular co-design. The episode occurred during a process to develop a new interdisciplinary teaching sequence for secondary students on the sustainable use of electric vehicle batteries. The analysis illustrates the dynamics of collaboration in curricular co-design, highlighting joint work on the problem of what topics to teach. The participants’ work on this problem proceeded by co-elaborating candidate topics; evaluating the suitability of topics for the teaching at hand; and reformulating one topic in light of participants’ knowledge and expertise. This activity involved the teacher and researcher orienting to different knowledge resources, only some of which had been introduced in the task. This empirical illustration demonstrates how collaboration in the domain of curricular co-design may proceed, and contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how teachers and researchers learn in co-design processes.

abstract: As computer science (CS) is integrated in elementary science curricula, it is important to consider teachers’ perceptions in how they access CS and support students to engage in CS skills and standards through NGSS-aligned activities. This single case study utilizes the Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (IMPG) to examine teacher change and explore the perspectives of a teacher, through semi-structured interviews, as he implements an NGSS-aligned, project-based CS unit over the course of four years. Findings indicate that the teacher perceived that changes in his practice helped inform changes in student outcomes and the curriculum and, in turn, these changes in outcomes further informed his teaching practice in the next iteration of the unit. Results highlight the importance of reflection and feedback as a way to impact the teaching practice of integrating CS in elementary science education.

title: Knowledge in New Pieces (KiNP): Intuitive Experiences of Social Media Viral Growth as Building Blocks for Understanding Advanced Mathematics and Network Theory
citation: Blikstein, P., Voorhis, J. K., & Rosenbaum, L. F. (2025). authors_list: Blikstein, P., Voorhis, J. K., & Rosenbaum, L. F.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Youth today navigate complex systems—technological, natural, and social—that profoundly shape their cognitive development. These interconnected environments foster intuitive knowledge, such as understanding exponential growth from everyday interactions with social media and “viral” content. The Knowledge-in-Pieces framework highlights these fragmented but functional knowledge units (p-prims) and their evolution into organized concepts. Through a series of case studies involving youth in semi-clinical, task-based interviews, this paper extends KiP to modern contexts, exploring how youth interactions with technology impact their understanding of exponential mathematics and network theory.

title: Instructional Principles for Inclusive AI in K-12 Education
citation: Lee, H., Kim, H., & Yan, W. (2025). Instructional Principles for Inclusive Ai in K-12 Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2007-2012). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lee, H., Kim, H., & Yan, W.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: As AI becomes prevalent in education, it offers transformative opportunities but also risks widening inequalities, particularly for underserved students. This study explores instructional strategies and design considerations for fostering inclusive participation in AI and technology through a scoping review. After applying screening criteria, 17 articles were analyzed, revealing five main themes and 14 pedagogical principles. These findings provide valuable insights for educators and researchers in developing inclusive and equitable AI curricula.

title: Toward Critical Joy in Learning: Lessons from Trans Youths’ Placemaking in Virtual reality
citation: Paré, D. (2025). Toward Critical Joy in Learning: Lessons From Trans Youths’ Placemaking in Virtual Reality. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2013-2017). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Paré, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this paper, I analyze the film Creative Futures to illustrate how trans youth expressed trans joy, a form of critical joy, in their virtual reality art by challenging societal control and visualizing community belonging. In my analysis, I draw from speculative education, particularly marginalized youths’ practices of envisioning more just futures and research on restorying by marginalized youth to challenge harmful narratives. My analysis focuses on the public artifacts of the two-part documentary film, with particular emphasis on the 3D virtual art created by the three transgender youth and their explanations of their art. The youth show in their art that supporting trans youths’ survival and joy requires life-sustaining practices—celebration, acceptance, collectivity, and togetherness—supported by communities and trans kinship. The film further demonstrates how trans youth can be supported by providing social movement learning spaces with access to creative technologies to envision their futures.

title: Developing Assessment Systems for Engagement, Learning, and Transfer Using GenAI and an LMS
citation: Hickey, D. T. & Luo, Q. M. (2025). Developing Assessment Systems for Engagement, Learning, and Transfer Using GenAI and an Lms. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2018-2021). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hickey, D. T. & Luo, Q. M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Developing effective assessment “systems” is challenging for many educators. Learning management systems streamline administration and scoring, but creating quality items that support engagement, learning, and transfer demands expertise. Meanwhile, Generative AI has introduced new integrity challenges. We present design principles and examples from research on an online graduate course on educational assessment, demonstrating ChatGPT's capacity for creating high-quality formative and summative items. These include proximal items (from specific resources) and distal items (aligned to standards). ChatGPT can generate quality item pools that capture disciplinary nuances, supporting transfer, validity, and credibility. This approach aligns formative and summative assessment functions, reducing construct-irrelevant variance and promoting "generative" learning that transfers widely.

title: Perspective and Context Bids in Middle School Sociotechnical Discussions
citation: Rahman, F., Wendell, K. B., Andrews, C., Mabour, L. C., & Pérez, G. (2025). Perspective and Context Bids in Middle School Sociotechnical Discussions. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2022-2026). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rahman, F., Wendell, K. B., Andrews, C., Mabour, L. C., & Pérez, G.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: We explore how sixth-graders engage in a sociotechnical whole-class discussion about the unequal impacts of technology and engineering on their own communities. In particular, we focus on how a group of students and one teacher try to make sense of the question: why are lower-income areas and more diverse areas more exposed to higher temperatures in their city? Through discourse analysis we identify perspective and context bids that help maintain complexity and build a systems-level understanding of the existing inequity.

title: Scaffolding Third Graders’ Computational Thinking in an Artificial Intelligence Course: Concepts, Practice, and Perspectives
citation: Lin, Y., Yang, Y., Zhang, Y., & Sun, D. (2025). Scaffolding Third Graders’ Computational Thinking in an Artificial Intelligence Course: Concepts, Practice, and Perspectives. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2027-2031). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lin, Y., Yang, Y., Zhang, Y., & Sun, D.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: The effect of scaffolding type and timing on computational thinking (CT) for elementary school students in artificial intelligence (AI) learning is unknown. To address this research gap, a 2×2 factorial experiment was conducted in this study to examine the effect of scaffolding type (conceptual versus problem-solving) and timing (immediate versus delayed) on CT concepts, practices, and perspectives. A total of 136 third graders from four classes were assigned to four experimental conditions. The results, as measured by knowledge tests, showed that problem-solving scaffolding and immediate scaffolding were more effective in developing students’ CT concepts. Lag sequential analysis indicated that students guided by problem-solving scaffolding and delayed scaffolding developed more complete problem-solving paths and achieved higher levels of CT practice. Additionally, an analysis of students’ learning reflections revealed that most students could explain the functions of machine learning techniques. By highlighting effective scaffolding methods, this study advances CT education.

title: Multiple Tiers of Responsiveness in Professional Learning Facilitation: A Call for Praxis in Design-Based Research
citation: Krist, C., Hug, B., Hall, K., Leonardi, N., & Lauren, L. H. (2025). Multiple Tiers of Responsiveness in Professional Learning Facilitation: A Call for Praxis in Design-Based Research. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2032-2036). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Krist, C., Hug, B., Hall, K., Leonardi, N., & Lauren, L. H.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This paper explores the authors’ facilitation of a week-long teacher professional learning (PL) workshop focused on adapting teachers’ curriculum materials to support students’ epistemic agency (EA). Most literature on supporting students’ EA has focused on the shift of epistemic authority from teacher to students. However, little work has captured what this shift requires of teachers beyond “giving up” of their own epistemic authority. We present findings from a workshop in which our PL facilitation required responsiveness to teachers’ ideas, ideologies, and vulnerabilities. In particular, we showcase two moves of facilitator vulnerability that marked transition points from cycles of deficit talk and resistance, towards teacher-initiated expressions of their pedagogical responsibilities and strategies for supporting students’ EA. We discuss implications for integrating studies of facilitator praxis into design-based research.

title: Supporting Coherence from Students’ Perspective in Middle School Science Classrooms Using Students’ Experience Data
citation: Raza, A., Penuel, W. R., Li, J., & Frank, K. A. (2025). Supporting Coherence From Students’ Perspective in Middle School Science Classrooms Using Students’ Experience Data. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2037-2041). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Raza, A., Penuel, W. R., Li, J., & Frank, K. A.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: A key goal of science education is to give students a feeling for what it is to do science. This aim is supported when students perceive instruction to be coherent from their point of view. Teachers can facilitate coherence by building a classroom culture focused on collective knowledge building, supporting student agency in the direction of their own learning, and helping students to see the arc of their own learning. In this study, teachers participated in a virtual cycle of inquiry called the Student Experience Improvement Cycle (SEIC), in which they tested strategies for enhancing students’ perceptions of coherence. Over the course of the experience, students’ sense of coherence increased significantly. However, students’ growth was not the same for students of different backgrounds. The study shows the initial potential of teacher collaborative inquiry for enhancing students’ experience of science learning.

title: Playful Semiotic Assemblages: Agency in Task-Based Interviews With Multilingual College Students in STEM
citation: Jeong, M., Jayathilaka, A., & Ryu, M. (2025). Playful Semiotic Assemblages: Agency in Task-Based Interviews With Multilingual College Students in STEM. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2042-2046). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jeong, M., Jayathilaka, A., & Ryu, M.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Supporting multilingual learners in leveraging diverse semiotic resources is essential to inclusive and effective science education. Hence, we examined how activity is shaped in a novel, STEM task-based interview with multilingual college students, focusing on how agency is enacted and distributed within the space through the lens of semiotic assemblage (Pennycook, 2017, 2024). We detail the shaping of activity by two pairs—Spanish speakers, Dani and Eva, and Cantonese-Mandarin speakers, Emma and Sophia. We discuss the production of agency through their affective responses and performative interaction with the research tools, like the camera and microphone. Additionally, we elaborate on how they expressed their sense of humor, integrated their interests, and established their own standards within the interview setting. These findings hold implications for conducting video-recorded research and designing learning environments that engage multilingual learners in using diverse repertoires in science.

title: Enhancing the Relevance of Science Learning: Exploring the Potential of the Student Experience Improvement Cycle
citation: Raza, A., Penuel, W. R., Li, J., & Frank, K. A. (2025). Enhancing the Relevance of Science Learning: Exploring the Potential of the Student Experience Improvement Cycle. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2047-2051). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Raza, A., Penuel, W. R., Li, J., & Frank, K. A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: To support equitable instruction in science, the Framework envisions implementing science instruction around students’ interests and experiences. In this study, we tested a strategy for using student experience data for data-informed decision-making called the Student Experience Improvement Cycle (SEIC), which engages groups of educators and a coach in adapting evidence-based practices for enhancing the relevance of instruction to students and their communities. This study investigated the effects of the SEIC using a single-group, pretest-posttest design using experience-based exit ticket surveys collected from middle school science students. Analyses from hierarchical linear modeling indicated students’ perceptions of relevance increased significantly over time and that Black/African American students’ perceptions of experience increased more than a reference group of Latinx students.

title: Towards InCoRe - An Interactive Co-Regulation Model for training Teacher Classroom Communication Skills
citation: Bhuvaneshwara, C., Chehayeb, L., Haberl, A., Siedentopf, J., Gebhard, P., & Tsovaltzi, D. (2025). Towards InCoRe - An Interactive Co-Regulation Model for Training Teacher Classroom Communication Skills. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2052-2055). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bhuvaneshwara, C., Chehayeb, L., Haberl, A., Siedentopf, J., Gebhard, P., & Tsovaltzi, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This short paper introduces InCoRe, a conceptual and early-stage implementation of an interactive co-regulation model aimed at supporting teacher training in classroom communication and socio-emotional conflict management. InCoRe is embedded within MITHOS, a hybrid AI training system combining psychodynamic theory and computational affect modeling to interpret teacher emotional experiences during classroom conflicts. Grounded in Operationalized Psychodynamic Diagnostics and conflict resolution theory, the model identifies internal conflicts, lead affects, and behavioral intentions to guide virtual student responses. We present findings from a Wizard-of-Oz study validating the mapping between subjective emotional experiences and conflict regulation styles. Results demonstrate the feasibility of InCoRe for real-time interpretation of co-regulation behavior, setting the stage for more comprehensive system deployment and large-scale validation.

title: Customizing ChatGPT for Second Language Speaking Practice: Genuine Support or Just a Marketing Gimmick?
citation: Meng, F. (2025). Customizing ChatGPT for Second Language Speaking Practice: Genuine Support or Just a Marketing Gimmick?. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2056-2060). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Meng, F.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: ChatGPT, with its customization features and Voice Mode, has the potential for more engaging and personalized ESL (English as a second language) education. This study examines the efficacy of customized ChatGPT conversational features in facilitating ESL speaking practice, comparing the performance of four versions of ChatGPT Voice Mode: uncustomized Standard mode, uncustomized Advanced mode, customized Standard mode, and customized Advanced mode. Customization was guided by prompt engineering principles and grounded in relevant theories, including Motivation Theory, Culturally Responsive Teaching (CRT), Communicative Language Teaching (CLT), and the Affective Filter Hypothesis. Content analysis found that customized versions generally provided more balanced feedback and emotional support, contributing to a positive and motivating learning environment. However, cultural responsiveness did not show significant improvement despite targeted customization efforts. These initial findings suggest that customization could enhance ChatGPT’s capacity as a more effective language tutor, with the standard model already capable of meeting the learning needs. The study underscores the importance of prompt engineering and AI literacy in maximizing AI’s potential in language learning.

title: Critical AI Literacy through Exploring Generative AI Limitations
citation: Solyst, J., Pan, M. Y., Andam, A., Poblete, I. P., Eslami, M., Hammer, J., Ogan, A., & Stewart, A. E. (2025). Critical Ai Literacy Through Exploring Generative Ai Limitations. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2061-2065). abstract: Critical AI literacy enables understanding of the limitations of AI. In this work, we investigated how Black girls (N=11, ages 9-12) critically engaged with generative AI (genAI) through exploring ChatGPT’s limitations. Learners used various approaches and leveraged their funds of knowledge (e.g., knowledge of pop culture) to investigate where genAI did not perform satisfactorily. We discuss how taking an asset-based approach can support critical AI literacy.

title: My Beliefs Matter: Role of Teachers’ Beliefs in their Use of Analytics
citation: Chavan, P. & Mitra, R. (2025). My Beliefs Matter: Role of Teachers’ Beliefs in Their Use of Analytics. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2066-2070). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chavan, P. & Mitra, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The use of analytics to inform pedagogical decision-making is a complex socio-technical process. While research has explored how analytic data is interpreted and applied to guide instructional actions, the influence of teachers’ beliefs - a critical social factor - has received limited attention. This study examines how four instructors engage with analytics and how their beliefs shape pedagogical decision-making. Using Wise and Jung’s (2019) model of instructors’ use of analytics, we perform content analysis of interviews with the teachers to reveal their beliefs about teaching and learning. We found that beliefs shape pedagogical actions quite considerably. Based on these insights, we propose simple modifications to Wise & Jung's (2019) model to account for the critical role of teacher beliefs in analytics-informed pedagogical decision-making.

title: Towards Better Understanding Students’ Choices in Advanced Learning Technology
citation: Nagashima, T. & Su, M. (2025). Towards Better Understanding Students’ Choices in Advanced Learning Technology. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2071-2075). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Nagashima, T. & Su, M.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: One main goal of research in the learning sciences is to promote autonomous, self-regulated learners who can make strategic choices during learning. Yet, prior studies have not systematically conceptualized, measured, and supported students’ various choices in a way that enhances our understanding of how students make choices and how strategic choices can be supported. We present the Metacognitive Choice-Making Model of Learning to better understand and support students’ fine-grained choices in advanced learning technologies. We demonstrate the applicability of the model using an example from an algebra intelligent tutor where students made choices on when to use visual scaffolding to aid their problem solving.

title: Strategies for Self-Regulated Learning with AI in an Undergraduate Research Methods Course
citation: Shao, A. A., Maram, S. S., Matuk, C., Shirshekar, S., Carstendottir, E., Melcer, E., Sutherland, S., El-Nasr, M. S., & Harteveld, C. (2025).
