authors_list: Shao, A. A., Maram, S. S., Matuk, C., Shirshekar, S., Carstendottir, E., Melcer, E., Sutherland, S., El-Nasr, M. S., & Harteveld, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Undergraduate research methods education faces numerous challenges with respect to student affect, interest, and conceptual understanding. We incorporated a set of artificial intelligence chatbots into an introductory psychology research methods course, designed to promote students’ self-regulation while learning to design their own research studies. Analyses of student-AI interactions and student focus group interviews revealed instances in which students used AI to exercise agency over their learning, deepening their understanding of a topic, and engaging in self-regulation. Findings also revealed instances of students’ overreliance on AI. This study has implications for the design of AI chatbots to support research methods education, and self-regulated learning more broadly.

title: Effects of a Co-Regulation Model for MR Teacher Training: HRV and Self-Compassion as Indicators of Emotion Regulation
citation: Chehayeb, L., Olszynska, K., Bhuvaneshwara, C., & Tsovaltzi, D. (2025). authors_list: Chehayeb, L., Olszynska, K., Bhuvaneshwara, C., & Tsovaltzi, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
tpack_tk_labels: Immersive VR / AR; Simulations & Scientific Modeling
abstract: Teachers' effective emotion regulation is essential for supporting students' emotional and cognitive development, and technology-based trainings need objective measures. This study examines the relationship between self-compassion and physiological stress (HRV) in a Mixed Reality (MR) teacher training simulation. HRV was measured during emotionally challenging classroom scenarios. Post-training interviews were analyzed for self-compassion behaviors. Results show that lower physiological stress correlates with higher self-compassion and perspective-taking. MR training and self-compassion may serve as effective tools to enhance teachers’ emotion regulation and well-being.

title: How Do Motivation and Self-Regulation Shape Learners’ Satisfaction with E-Learning?
citation: Farrokhnia, M., Taghizade, A., Ahmadi, R., Papadopoulos, P. M., & Noroozi, O. (2025). How do Motivation and Self-Regulation Shape Learners’ Satisfaction With E-Learning?. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2085-2089). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Farrokhnia, M., Taghizade, A., Ahmadi, R., Papadopoulos, P. M., & Noroozi, O.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Learner satisfaction is a crucial indicator of the overall quality of the e-learning experience. While numerous studies have focused on identifying the “what”—the factors that predict satisfaction—there has been limited investigation into the “how,” or the mechanisms linking these factors to satisfaction. This study addresses this gap by examining the role of two key individual factors: motivation and self-regulation. It posits that while these factors are directly related to learner satisfaction, they also have an indirect effect through their connection with the Community of Inquiry (CoI) presences, namely, social, cognitive, and teaching presences. Data were collected from 247 master's students enrolled in online programs at three state universities in Iran, and path analysis was conducted to explore the interactions between these variables. The findings provide valuable insights into the complex relationships at play, revealing that self-regulation is a more significant predictor of learner satisfaction than motivation. Moreover, while both factors were directly associated with satisfaction, their effects were also mediated by the three CoI presences. Among these, cognitive presence emerged as the most influential mediator, emphasizing its pivotal role in enhancing the e-learning experience. The findings of this study offer new insights into designing effective e-learning environments that not only engage learners but also effectively support their satisfaction.

title: Answerable Research Practice Partnerships: Practicing Aloha ʻĀina, Cultivating Pilina, and Co-Producing Knowledge Accountable to Hawaiʻi
citation: Fukumitsu, K., Kāne, K., & Chang, E. (2025). Answerable Research Practice Partnerships: Practicing Aloha ʻāina, Cultivating Pilina, and Co-Producing Knowledge Accountable to Hawaiʻi. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 209-216). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Fukumitsu, K., Kāne, K., & Chang, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Over the past 15 years, public and private investments in Research Practice Partnerships (RPPs), long-term collaborations that use research to improve education, have soared. But attention to how RPPs answer to Native places and peoples remains limited. In this critical, self-reflexive case study, we ask: How do participants in one RPP author meanings about “research,” “practice,” and “partnership” that answer to Hawaiʻi? Informed by Patel’s ethics of answerability and analytical tools drawn from the critical learning sciences, we analyze three years of fieldnote data generated through our efforts to transform ourselves and education in Hawaiʻi. We argue that daily practices of aloha ʻāina (devotion to caring for the land) forged lifelong pilina (binding, relationships). These reciprocal, land-based relations animated a research focus on (re)designing learning that enhances life and Kanaka ‘Ōiwi (Hawaiian) self-determination.

title: An Exploratory Study of Using Interactive Volumetric Video in VR for Embodied Learning
citation: Jin, Q., Liu, Y., Huang, Y., Han, B., Qian, F., & Yarosh, S. (2025). An Exploratory Study of Using Interactive Volumetric Video in Vr for Embodied Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2090-2094). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jin, Q., Liu, Y., Huang, Y., Han, B., Qian, F., & Yarosh, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Volumetric video (VV) has the potential to revolutionize traditional video-based learning (VBL) by offering immersive, 3D content that enhances student engagement and comprehension. However, the limited interactivity of current pre-recorded VV restricts its educational applications. To address this, we developed and evaluated an interactive VV viewing system that enables learners to engage with spatial interactive areas. These areas trigger multimodal outcomes and support both static and continuous interactions tailored to specific educational objectives. In this work, we utilized the Lego construction learning task as an exploratory caser. Compared to the basic condition (VV without interaction), the interactive VV condition demonstrated higher germane cognitive load and interest in learning but showed no significant differences in short-term memory retention.

title: Visioning Schooling in 2050: Analyzing Pre-Service Teachers’ Futures Consciousness
citation: Hyyppä, I., Södervik, I., Krzywacki, H., & Laherto, A. (2025). Visioning Schooling in 2050: Analyzing Pre-Service Teachers’ Futures Consciousness. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2095-2099). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hyyppä, I., Södervik, I., Krzywacki, H., & Laherto, A.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Amid global ecological and societal crises, the role of education and teachers in driving societies towards more sustainable futures is ever more crucial. To drive desired changes, one must first be able to vision them. This study explores pre-service teachers' futures consciousness by analyzing their visions of a desired school day as a teacher in 2050 through the 5 dimensions of futures consciousness: agency beliefs, systems perceptions, time perspectives, openness to alternatives, and concern for others. 100 pre-service teachers’ short essays, consisting of their desired future visions and backcasting tasks exploring the steps to their desired futures, were analyzed through an abductive thematic analysis. Findings indicate that pre-service teachers manifest all dimensions of futures consciousness. Agency beliefs and systems perceptions are manifested more frequently in the backcasting task. The study aims to develop teacher education to encourage teachers to drive societal change.

title: The Effects of Emotion Regulation and Students’ Perceived Challenges on Emotion Synchrony in Collaborative Learning
citation: Huang, X., Li, S., Wang, T., & Lajoie, S. P. (2025). The Effects of Emotion Regulation and Students’ Perceived Challenges on Emotion Synchrony in Collaborative Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 21-28). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Huang, X., Li, S., Wang, T., & Lajoie, S. P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this study, we explored the relationships among students’ perceived challenges in collaborative learning, emotion regulation strategies (i.e., reappraisal and suppression), and emotion synchrony (i.e., valence synchrony and arousal synchrony) in natural classroom settings. We performed the partial least squares structural equation modeling for data analysis. The results revealed a positive and direct effect of cognitive reappraisal on arousal synchrony, and a negative and direct effect of cognitive reappraisal on valence synchrony. Students’ perceived challenges had a negative effect on their arousal synchrony. Students’ perceived challenges also played a mediating role in the relationship between cognitive reappraisal and arousal synchrony. As a total effect, cognitive reappraisal still positively and significantly predicted arousal synchrony. This study provided insights into students’ emotional responses in collaborative learning and informed the design of collaborative learning environments. This study has also methodological implications regarding the analysis of emotion synchrony.

abstract: This study examines how teens engage in sensemaking processes when encountering news through their social networks and social media feeds. Using a small stories approach and debriefing participant-collected social media artifacts during interviews, we show how an initial information encounter reflects one’s network and algorithms. We then follow that information encounter through subsequent, related small stories to discover how and why teens pursue additional related information, whether on or offline. Findings show the importance of identity, family and other adults, and social interactions in the sensemaking process, and also support the concept of sensemaking as an ongoing process of revisiting an earlier small story and building upon it. The findings have implications for both how parents and teachers support teens as they navigate these sensemaking processes and how future researchers might use small stories to support research with teens in digital environments.

title: Zone of Playful Development: Play for Transformational Equity in Multilingual STEM Classrooms
citation: Raj, A. & Kayumova, S. (2025). Zone of Playful Development: Play for Transformational Equity in Multilingual STEM Classrooms. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2105-2109). authors_list: Raj, A. & Kayumova, S.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies
abstract: Play is a vital yet underutilized tool for advancing equity and engagement in multilingual STEM classrooms. While traditional frameworks like scaffolding emphasize guidance from adults or advanced peers, play offers a dynamic space where students independently or interdependently explore, learn, and create, thus transcending linguistic and systemic barriers. Grounded in Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory, this study introduces the Zone of Playful Development (ZPlayD), positioning play as central to authentic science learning, culturally responsive teaching, and transformational equity. Using qualitative video analysis of emergent multilingual students, our findings reveal how play supported engagement with Science and Engineering Practices, bridged lived experiences with academic content, enabled creative role-playing, and fostered multimodal expressions of competence. We recommend integrating play as an intentional, equity-driven practice in STEM education—one that acknowledges multilingual students’ ways of knowing as scientific, honors the cultural resources they bring, and reimagines what counts as meaningful science learning.

abstract: Understanding intersubjectivity is crucial for advancing theories of learning in social contexts. While existing research has largely focused on verbal interactions, silence is also a significant aspect of classroom dynamics. This study investigates how intersubjectivity between teacher and students is established through silence, and examines the role silence plays in fostering such connections. Interaction analysis of data from a 6th-grade science classroom in Shanghai reveals how silence shifts students’ focus from peers to the teacher and from verbal to nonverbal cues, encouraging deeper reflection and ultimately facilitating the establishment of intersubjectivity. Additionally, the study highlights the cultural dimensions, drawing on Confucian traditions and showing how silence reflects a bidirectional cultural co-construction. Contrary to views of silence as passive, the findings highlight its role in fostering teacher-student connections and cultural understanding. This research illuminates silent intersubjectivity, offering insights for creating reflective, collaborative educational spaces.

abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic presented unprecedented challenges for teachers, demanding adaptability, resilience, and growth. This study explores the experiences of secondary science teachers from a New England state, focusing on how they navigated internal and external challenges during remote instruction. Using the integrated framework of Teacher Resilience and Transformative Learning, we examine how educators relied on personal resources (mindset, optimism, and empathy), contextual supports (relationships with students, colleagues, and school leaders), and pedagogical strategies (streamlining and outsourcing), while critically reflecting to achieve transformative growth. Their narratives, highlight the interplay of resilience and transformation in adapting to crises. This study offers a novel framework to understand teachers’ experiences in challenging contexts—such as socio-political turmoil and natural disasters—while contributing nuanced insights to existing literature on teacher retention, and well-being. Caution is drawn to use this framework for action, not inaction.

abstract: This study explores the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) with peer feedback to leverage their complementary strengths in formative assessment within higher education. Using data from 217 participants across two academic terms, it evaluates the three dimensions of feedback: Quality, Usefulness, and Actionability; and five feedback classifications: Task Constraints, Concepts, Procedure, Mistakes, and Meta-cognition provided by AI and peers. The results reveal complementary strengths of AI and peer feedback: AI excels in structured, precise, and consistent evaluations, while peer feedback fosters critical reflection and human-centered insights. The sequencing of feedback modalities is shown to influence learning outcomes, with AI feedback effectively setting a foundation for deeper engagement with peer feedback. These findings support a hybrid feedback system that balances AI’s consistency with peer feedback’s relational depth, offering pedagogical insights for a scalable, learner-centered approach to enhance educational outcomes in an AI-driven learning landscape.

citation: Park, J., Chen, Y., Jordan, M., & Meza-Torres, C. (2025). Exploring How Dispositions Toward Navigating Scientific Uncertainty (DSUN) Influence Epistemic Curiosity and Learning Achievement. abstract: Students’ Dispositions toward Scientific Uncertainty Navigation (DSUN) can play a pivotal role in impacting student learning achievement. However, understanding of the underlying mechanism of DSUN influencing learning achievement is limited. Drawing from related research, this study investigates the roles of epistemic curiosity and learning engagement in mediating the relationship between DSUN and learning achievement. A survey study design was employed, involving 1,137 middle school students who participated in an uncertainty-driven learning environment when learning solar energy. A sequential mediation model was tested using data collected through validated measures assessing DSUN, epistemic curiosity, learning engagement, and learning achievement. Results revealed that while DSUN positively predicts learning achievement, this relationship is sequentially mediated by epistemic curiosity and learning engagement, with epistemic curiosity not serving as a significant mediator on its own. These findings underscore the importance of fostering both epistemic curiosity and engagement in science classroom activities when students encounter scientific uncertainty.

abstract: While researchers in other fields have begun to more regularly theorize the learning that occurs at academic conferences, the learning sciences have broadly ignored this topic. We use this paper to begin conceptualizing the kinds of learning that occur at the Annual Meeting of the International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS). Taking a theoretical approach, we map the learning landscape of ISLS by applying a participational lens. We propose valuable possibilities of learning that occur both during and beyond the sanctioned events of the conference. We then critically reorient this work towards missing forms of knowledge production as a pathway forward. This paper represents a starting point for a valuable conversation about the kinds of learning that should occur at ISLS in future iterations.

abstract: This paper examines the design of the Youth Activism and Advocacy program within the Clubhouse Network. Young people at ten of the Clubhouse sites around the world used their creativity, lived experiences, and civic imagination to develop and sustain social justice campaigns in their communities. This paper focuses on the design elements that allow young people who have been marginalized to leverage their lived experiences in their research, development, and implementation of their campaigns. Qualitative results indicate that providing participatory design training to the adults supporting the campaigns allowed the youth participants to take relevant civic action that led to positive impacts within their communities.

citation: Park, J., Chen, Y., Deng, Y., Agrawal, G., & Liu, H. (2025). A Latent Growth Modeling for Individual Differences in Dispositions Toward Uncertainty Navigation in Computing Problem-Solving. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In authentic problem-solving, students may exhibit various patterns of uncertainty navigation, reflecting their dispositions toward uncertainty navigation in computing problem-solving (DUNC). This study investigates how DUNC evolves—advancing, maintaining, or retreating— over time across multiple problem-solving learning sessions. A latent growth model was tested to examine inter- and intra-individual differences in DUNC and the impact of achievement goals (mastery and performance) and gender. Data collected from 431 Fall 2023 cloud-computing students was used. Results revealed variability in DUNC trajectories: some students showed increases, decreases, or stability over time. Higher mastery goals were associated with higher initial DUNC and faster changes, while higher performance goals correlated with lower initial DUNC and slower changes. Gender did not significantly predict DUNC changes. The findings highlight that authentic problem-solving sessions can enhance DUNC and that fostering mastery goal orientations may accelerate its development, reinforcing the value of DUNC in preparing future computer scientists.

abstract: This study explores how in-service teachers engage with generative AI tools, Claude 3.0, to enhance critical thinking and design AI-infused lesson plans. Using the dual frameworks of Situated Learning Theory (SLT) and Transformative Learning Theory (TLT), the research investigates how teachers develop expertise in AI integration through legitimate peripheral participation (LPP) and experience cognitive transformation in their instructional practices. Data from 250 teacher-AI interaction episodes, lesson plans, reflection papers and interviews were analyzed to identify engagement patterns, prompting strategies, and critical thinking practices. Findings reveal a progression from intermittent to continuous engagement, reflecting a developmental trajectory of expertise. Critical prompting strategies such as clarification, ethical awareness, and reflective adaptation highlighted the transformative potential of AI tools in fostering teachers’ pedagogical and ethical literacy. This paper concludes with recommendations for professional development programs that scaffold AI literacy through situated and transformative learning experiences.

abstract: This short paper previews ongoing research exploring joyful learning as a construct of well-being-centered learning experience design. It examines industry-based interpretations of joyful learning and how designers embed it into educational technology (EdTech) products. This study uses Likert-scale surveys (Boone & Boone, 2012; Tanujaya et al., 2022) to assess participants’ beliefs about their design practices, and structured interviews to understand how they conceptualize and promote joyful learning through their products. Descriptive statistical and thematic analyses are in progress. This research aims to contribute to the learning sciences by promoting discourse on theories of well-being at the intersection of learning experience design and human-computer interaction. It also aims to develop actionable strategies for scaffolding joyful learning in the design of EdTech.

abstract: One of the key challenges in science education is that students often perceive science lessons as irrelevant to their everyday lives. Biodesign, which leverages the properties of living organisms to design functional or creative artifacts, presents opportunities to bridge this gap by connecting life science education with real-life contexts. Consequently, there is growing interest in integrating biodesign into K-12 settings, especially as an engaging, hands-on approach to explore synthetic biology. Our study investigates how the iGEM competition fosters science learning experiences that are relevant to high school students. iGEM is an international synthetic biology competition where students use biodesign to develop artifacts to address real-world issues. Our findings reveal how the competition facilitates life science learning that is personally, societally, and vocationally relevant to students. We offer insights for designing learning environments that support engagement with biodesign and synthetic biology in ways that better align with students’ needs and interests.

abstract: Although the number of multicultural students is increasing in South Korea, many pre-service teachers are undertrained when it comes to understanding the challenges these students face in the classroom. This study developed a virtual reality (VR) training simulation aimed at fostering empathy among pre-service teachers toward multicultural students. The simulation helps pre-service teachers experience linguistic challenges from multicultural students' perspectives, enhancing empathy through perspective-taking. Twenty-four pre-service teachers participated in this study which included pre- and post-tests, pre- and post-activity, VR simulation, and interviews. This study found a significant enhancement in pre-service teachers' empathy and multicultural attitudes after experiencing the VR simulation. The VR simulation enabled pre-service teachers to establish meaningful connections with multicultural students, enhancing their cultural sensitivity and commitment to inclusive teaching strategies. These findings highlight the substantial benefits of VR in fostering empathy through perspective-taking in pre-service teacher education.

abstract: This praxis-oriented paper draws from a yearlong multispecies ethnography of preschoolers’ encounters in an urban garden through child-led documentation. Thinking-with common worlds pedagogies, I attend to young children’s everyday multispecies encounters with worms, bees, and flowers and describe their embodied, affective, and relational learning-with the more-than-human that was messy, situated, and relational. Important to navigating the environmental precarity of the Anthropocene, I share moments of children’s developing ethics of relational care and environmental vulnerability as hope. Seeking to unsettle disconnected, humancentric, nature-as-resource scientific learning, I mobilized a pedagogy of refiguring more-than-human presences to center human/more-than-human entanglement, interconnectedness, and interdependency. Findings narrate learning encounters and pedagogical moves through vignettes and children’s documentation of photographs, drawings, and writings.

title: Examining Self-Regulated Learning Processes in Design Tasks with Large Language Models

abstract: Focusing on human-AI collaboration process, where humans and AI work together toward shared goals, has implications for designing AI-enabled learning tasks. We explore self-regulated learning (SRL) in two tasks leveraging generative AI (Large Language Models; LLMs): (1) co-write a story with GPT-4 and (2) brainstorm ideas for design sketches with GPT-3.5. We develop a codebook that accounts for SRL phases (forethought, performance, self-reflection) and fine-grained cognitive and socioemotional interactions with LLMs. We conduct Ordered Network Analysis to compare SRL processes between participants scoring higher and lower in design artifacts. The higher-scoring participants more frequently utilized metacognitive strategies like monitoring and self-instruction to maintain focus in performing tasks, in conjunction with cognitive interactions to prompt and evaluate LLMs’ outputs. We discuss the design of learning systems and tasks to promote evaluative strategies in working with LLMs.

The findings suggest that blending natural and digital spaces may enhance collaborative learning, audience engagement, and ecological awareness. These efforts aim to contribute to ongoing discussions on inclusive and interdisciplinary educational approaches within curatorial practices.

abstract: This practice-oriented paper seeks to examine the role of Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs) in promoting educational improvement in the digital era. The RPP co-development project described here aimed to bridge the gap between research and practice by providing school practitioners with research-informed knowledge while simultaneously offering researchers insights into practical development processes. The study focuses on a case school participating in the RPP co-development project to enhance its development initiatives through additional support in the form of knowledge and resources. The university partner played a pivotal role by supplying research-based knowledge, resources for data collection and analysis, and ongoing mentoring throughout the iterative co-development cycle. This two-year collaboration resulted in significant structural and pedagogical advancements within the school, as well as substantial professional growth for participating teachers. Key areas of development included enhancing home-school collaboration, effectively utilizing digital tools for internal communication, and fostering students’ well-being and sense of belonging.

abstract: This practice-oriented paper illustrates the evolution of a knowledge-building (KB) approach in a fast-paced, content-driven educational setting. The practitioner’s 13 years of teaching experience with 9 years of KB practice, highlights a change in knowledge creation. Over four iterations, the practitioner refined a methodology emphasizing student agency through inquiry-based, gamified approach that fosters continuous metacognitive discourse. The latest iteration showcases the efficiency of the differentiated KB cube (KB3) for autonomous team discourse, a catalyst designed to drive inquiry across subjects while accommodating diverse learner profiles. Differentiation ensures meaningful participation for all students, while gamification promotes motivation and inclusivity. This shifts the teacher's role from a knowledge provider to a facilitator, fostering a student-idea-centric environment (Hong & Sullivan, 2009) where learners lead co-constructive discourse. By integrating Bloom’s revised taxonomy into theory-building questions, a shift in pedagogy is evident, whereby knowledge is created and improvised by students than teachers.

abstract: This study describes the development of a design thinking course created through collaboration between researchers and design practitioners in higher education. It addresses challenges to teaching design thinking, such as oversimplification and lack of guidance for diverse student groups, by incorporating real-world contexts and scaffolding. Using design-based research (DBR), the course was refined to teach interdisciplinary undergraduate students, with reflective practice guiding its evolution. The collaboration emphasized integrating professional insights and theoretical frameworks and led to adaptive scaffolding based on team progress and problem complexity. The study underscores the significance of researcher-practitioner collaboration in enhancing design thinking pedagogy in higher education.

abstract: Implementing and sustaining large-scale technology-focused educational programs in public systems requires robust professional development (PD) programs. In this paper, we share our experience of creating shared meanings for teachers during a 17-week PD program as part of introducing a large-scale public policy that implements digital fabrication and maker labs in Brazil’s largest municipal public school network. We illustrate how a well-structured PD program, featuring constructionist hands-on investigative, creative, and reflective workshops, is key to instigating mindset changes and building shared meanings among teachers, which are essential for the implementation and sustainability of a large-scale educational reform centered on systems thinking, investigation, making, and project-based learning.

abstract: This paper examines the implementation of Knowledge Building (KB) in a primary school in Singapore, focusing on practitioner reflections of their classroom practices and ways in which they shifted their practice to include higher level of student’s voice and agency by focusing on translation of KB principles into practice. The group of teachers formed a grounds-up interest-based community in the school to explore KB. They were cognizant of their school strategic thrusts of differentiated instruction and emerging 21st Century Competencies and saw the potential of KB in redesigning and transforming their pedagogical repertoire to achieve the strategic thrust. Through the reflections of these trailblazers in the school, we traced how they translate KB principles into practical knowledge and how they saw knowledge building practice brings about agentic teaching and learning across subjects, and with different learner profiles.

abstract: This practice paper presents the design and implementation of the “I and My Waste” program in Raigarh, India. The program empowers students to develop scientific literacy and socio-scientific reasoning through hands-on engagement with waste management. Using place-based pedagogy, fosters critical thinking, ethical decision-making, and collaboration. Students evolve from passive learners to active changemakers. The paper examines how lived experiences support socio-scientific inquiry and contribute to sustainable practices through action-oriented science education.

abstract: This practice paper shares our insights about the journey we took in co-designing an innovative model of assessment for learning with living heritage as a foundation of learning. Although attempts to integrate learning with heritage in curriculum have been documented, there is paucity of information on assessing these practices. This paper reports the development process for an assessment practice tool which draws from the co-design process carried out with teachers in the two selected case study countries, Namibia and Zimbabwe, and the pilot online course gathering an international reference group of teachers. Teachers made significant contributions in re-structuring and strengthening the assessment model through the implementation of focus group workshops, surveys, and of the toolkit, resulting in the addition of two critical petals to the Education for Sustainable Development assessment for significant learning model, which we originally utilized as an anchor to the work that we were doing.

abstract: This study explores the practical application of a chatbot driven in Chinese and Science classes, focusing on cultivating students' metacognitive thinking and guiding students' subject learning. The chatbot embedded prompts are designed to stimulate students' inquiry skills, guide subjective learning, and metacognitive thinking. At the same time, teachers have designed supplementary prompts to provide scaffolding support for students' interactions. This two-tiered design approach ensures that Fairbot can both serve as an effective learning assistant and align with subject-specific teaching frameworks. The study involved 94 fifth-grade primary school students and two teachers, and the data sources included classroom observations, teacher reflections and student feedback. The findings show that Fairbot demonstrates its potential in supporting reflective thinking, teaching guidance, and text comprehension. This study highlights the potential of AI tools in classroom while pointing out the importance of integrating AI capabilities with instructional strategies through collaborative instructional design.

abstract: The design and implementation of a project-based undergraduate course, Digital Pedagogies and Assistive Technologies, highlights effective approaches to preparing pre-service teachers for contemporary K-12 classrooms. The course combines instructional design theories with a variety of emerging digital tools embedded in Project-Based Learning (PBL) principles to enable learners to engage in weekly mini-projects, fostering critical thinking, collaboration, problem-solving, and technology integration. The mini-projects emphasized the creation of instructional activities and materials applicable to classrooms, bridging theory with practice. A clear outline of the course structure and design selected mini-projects, final project, and scaffolding strategies used to support learning and collaboration are provided. Challenges faced during implementation, reflection, and recommendations provide actionable insights for educators aiming to integrate PBL into their courses.

abstract: The increasing complexity of societal challenges requires interdisciplinary approaches in education to cultivate critical thinking, adaptability, and a holistic understanding of global issues. In response, the Quebec college system’s Social Science program introduced the Thematic Issues course (TI), a single-instructor course designed to engage students in interdisciplinary inquiry through instructor-selected themes and three prescribed social science disciplines. To navigate the challenges of teaching across disciplines in an unstructured framework, instructors formed a Faculty Learning Community (FLC) to collaboratively refine course design and instructional strategies. This paper examines three TI course models: the serial model, offering compartmentalized insights; the spiral model, promoting cumulative, integrated learning; and the jigsaw model emphasizes collaborative synthesis by combining specialized disciplinary perspectives into a cohesive understanding. By analyzing these models, this practice-centered study highlights the pedagogical affordances and constraints of single-teacher interdisciplinary instruction.

abstract: Through university-community partnerships (UCPs), educators and practitioners identify practices that leverage students’ assets to enhance science learning. We study Nuestra Ciencia, a UCP where undergraduates teach microbiology in Spanish to elementary students in bilingual schools in the United States. We describe how the program’s design transformations impacted elementary and undergraduate students’ perceptions of science, scientists, and their heritage language. Design-based framing enabled ongoing programmatic adjustments while identifying best practices for asset-based science learning. From analyzing 200 pre-post questionnaires, we found elementary students learned microbiology content and felt more like scientists after activities. We also analyzed focus groups with 34 Spanish-speaking undergraduates, revealing three themes related to science identity: using Spanish as a tool, reframing science as relevant, and healing their younger self. We describe how participants’ perceptions of science and science education helped us understand the impact of the program and ways to improve it.

abstract: Technology enhanced curriculum, and pedagogical innovations take place in schools, which are sociotechnical systems. Achieving scalable educational innovation necessitates infrastructuring changes as learning outcomes at multiple levels. Thus, research practice partnerships (RPP) need to provide guidance beyond the design and implementation of learning at the classroom level. Scaffolding schools in their organizational level self-directed learning journey is crucial for achieving their educational innovation goals. This is a practitioner-led study that reflects on a school’s 16-month RPP journey in a joint-school STEM innovation network. The RPP network adopted the Multilevel Multiscale (MLMS) framework as a design principle for guiding schools in their infrastructuring efforts. The school’s intentional infrastructuring re-design to support cross-disciplinary collaboration and peer learning led to enhanced student agency, teacher creativity, and leadership agility. The findings also highlight the feedback and feed-forward roles of the MLMS framework in facilitating scaling during the innovation mobilization process.

abstract: This study examines an approach to teacher professional development (PD) that supports the mastery of project-based learning (PBL) in K-12 education. The "Learn PBL through a PBL Approach" PD program, integrated with a custom-designed "PBL Action Kit", facilitated 127 teachers' deep engagement with the essential PBL design elements. Analysis of 18 PBL units developed by the teachers revealed strong incorporation of the core elements, except for the "Reflection" element. The findings underscore the importance of aligning teacher PD with instructional methods and using educative curriculum materials to enhance teachers' pedagogical design capacity, thereby promoting the effective implementation of PBL.

abstract: This practice-oriented paper explores how informal STEM learning (ISL) can address inequities and broaden participation by leveraging nontraditional, culturally relevant spaces. Many ISL activities occur in science centers that fail to engage underserved communities, resulting in the "Lost Einsteins" phenomenon—missed potential innovators due to systemic barriers. Grounded in culturally responsive pedagogy, this pilot project used community-centered methodologies to transform informal spaces into hubs for STEM learning. Through partnerships with local organizations and retailers, ISL experiences were delivered in environments reflecting community values, reducing access barriers and fostering belonging. Early findings from post-activity surveys revealed significant first-time exposure to STEM technologies and increased interest in further learning. By prioritizing cultural relevance, the project reimagines STEM accessibility, presenting a scalable ISL model that builds equitable pathways for historically excluded groups. This initiative demonstrates how rethinking STEM learning spaces can catalyze diversity, inclusion, and innovation within STEM fields.

abstract: This paper explores an approach to mentoring youth researchers for a community-based participatory research project and the impact of that approach on the youth researchers. The paper highlights the importance of providing both training and continued support after training to ensure youth researchers feel empowered as members of the research team and have opportunities to develop transferable skills like communication, critical thinking, and ownership. In examining the impact of the training, findings revealed the youth gained practical research experience, as well as developed a deeper understanding of interview techniques and ethical considerations. The project emphasized the value of youth-led research in amplifying underrepresented voices and offering young people a platform to actively engage in decision-making processes. Ultimately, the study concludes that equipping young people with research skills, alongside ongoing support, profoundly impacts their personal growth and enables meaningful contributions to their communities.

abstract: This practice-oriented paper shares insights from a research-practice partnership for designing learning experiences through curation of open educational resources (OERs). The collaboration aimed to improve classroom interactions, inclusivity, and learning outcomes in secondary schools by maximizing the pedagogical affordances of Interactive Flat Panels (IFP). This paper identifies the curation process as a complex exercise entailing design iterations while negotiating stakeholder expectations and outlines the intricacies and challenges faced during this process. It highlights how the curation team navigated these challenges to co-design learning experiences, emphasizing that pedagogically informed curation is not just about identifying relevant educational resources and mapping to curricular requirements – it is very much a design process. Exploring the practice of curation as design, the paper reveals emergence of negotiated space in a research-practice partnership and shares insights about the considerations involved in OER curation for large-scale implementation in a state education system.

abstract: This study examined the experiences of Indigenous American youth and adults participating in a culturally revitalizing science, technology, engineering, arts, and math (STEAM) learning workshop. Specifically, we examined how this workshop provided space for participants to explore, develop, and express their individual and collective identities through their creation of ribbon skirts and ribbon shirts, incorporating electronics and digital embroidery, and pottery beads painted with locally sourced, earth-based pigments. We analyzed video recordings, interviews, field notes, surveys, and participant-created artifacts, collected as part of a participatory design study. Drawing on situated, sociocultural, and ecological theories of learning, we identified five types of identities expressed and developed through design work during the workshop: individual identities, family identities, tribal identities, Indigenous community identities, and dual or hybrid identities. We also identified aspects of the workshop design, such as intergenerational, community based, and participant-driven learning that supported the exploration and expression of these identities.

abstract: Over the past decade there has been exponential growth in artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) applications moving out of the lab and into the world, impacting everyday lives. To date, most AI/ML and learning research efforts have centered learners as recipients of instruction from, or collaborators with, AI agents. This symposium brings together a group of scholars who will discuss how learners and teachers can engage with AI/ML technologies as creative resources, or CreateAI. CreateAI refers to the use of AI tools and methods for creative expression, that is, involving students not just in using AI for pre-determined productive ends, but also as creators who can design and build projects with AI/ML.

abstract: This symposium critically examines existing educational research methodologies through the intersection of Quantitative Critical Theory (QuantCrit) and Learning Sciences frameworks. Drawing inspiration from Garcia et al.’s (2018) QuantCrit principles—which emphasize the centrality of racism, the non-neutrality of numbers, and the importance of critically examining research categories—the symposium addresses how quantitative data can reinforce deficit-oriented narratives and underscores the necessity of incorporating and centering marginalized voices. Paper 1 explores how young adolescents from historically minoritized backgrounds engage with and resist artificial intelligence technologies within community contexts. Paper 2 presents findings from a Differential Item Functioning (DIF) analysis of an identity survey in a university biology setting, revealing how survey items may exhibit bias despite intentions toward equity. Paper 3 utilizes (post)qualitative inquiry to deconstruct power dynamics, question normative knowledge production, and center diverse voices, highlighting the co-constitutive relationships between researchers, participants, and environments.

abstract: This symposium explores the complex relationship between emotions and epistemic engagement across diverse learning contexts. Emotions, integral to cognitive processes, can enhance epistemic engagement by triggering curiosity, focus, and critical evaluation, especially when knowledge-building is the goal. This session will present studies on the relationships between emotions and epistemic cognition, within different thematic areas, such as social media interactions, bioinformatics education, data-infused interdisciplinary learning, and knowledge-building collaborative online platforms. Each presentation aims to uncover the roles emotions play in fostering or inhibiting epistemic actions. The discussant will synthesize insights from these studies to shed light on the generative potential of emotions in supporting critical and reflective engagement. The outcomes of this symposium can deepen our understanding of the role emotions can play in fostering epistemic engagement in formal and informal settings.

abstract: This symposium brings together leading scholars from four continents to explore the potential of expansive learning in enacting utopias, understood as practical alternatives to the logic of profit and exploitation. By drawing on the theoretical framework of cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT), the symposium highlights the role of expansive learning in addressing societal challenges and fostering social change. The contributions presented in this symposium showcase a diverse range of case studies, including community-based initiatives, formative interventions, and social movements. These studies demonstrate how expansive learning can be used to challenge the status quo, enact alternative futures, and create more just and equitable societies.

abstract: Despite the growing popularity and educational potential of simulation-based learning, a notable research gap exists in understanding the role of theoretical frameworks and research-based analytical models in facilitating learning through simulation in the context of work. This gap is critical as the complexity of organizational systems increases, necessitating a comprehensive understanding of how in situ simulation can drive individual, collective and interdisciplinary learning. To address this gap, this symposium presents studies on in situ simulation in higher education settings, focusing on sociocultural studies that support practice change, collective learning and the development of the simulation participants' transformative agency. Understanding the simulation participants as active transformative agents or world-makers of the future is essential for developing effective in situ simulation interventions that can enhance high-quality education and promote students’ learning.

abstract: Our symposium is a confluence of researchers/pedagogues/designers/practitioners who embrace porousness of these identity categories, toward collectively questioning and challenging knowledge and environmental monoculture (Shiva, 1993). We recognize the resurgence of endangered ways of knowing and ways of living as a necessary intervention to environmental destruction and coloniality. While facing the overwhelming devastation of environmental degradation and repercussions from globalization and colonialism, we refuse to cede with ontological negation (Bang, 2020). Instead, we together seek to ground ourselves in community-rooted praxis and pedagogy of hope (Freire, 1992; Gutiérrez, 2016). We collectively present locally and globally relevant socio-environmental issues that arose from communities beyond academic siloes. Together, we highlight community-based actions of hope representing diverse geographical localities and histories. Collectively, we gesture toward knowledge polyculture that is life affirming and orients us toward plural alternative visions of multi-species flourishing.

abstract: Regional conflicts, nuclear threats, resource depletion, climate change, and societal polarization—these global crises have escalated sharply in recent years. For the first time in history, humanity faces urgent questions about the very survival of present and future generations. As educational researchers, we are compelled to reflect: What is the true purpose of education, and what can we do to make a difference? Over the past few years, a group of researchers in Asia have explored the possibility of establishing a global educational goal—one centered on global harmony and wellbeing. Such a goal could offer a unifying vision and direction for education systems worldwide. This symposium aims to provide a platform for researchers around the world to engage in meaningful dialogue and establish a shared consensus on the future of education and coordinated actions moving forward.

abstract: This symposium, presented as a hybrid structured poster session, brings together work that helps us grow queer-trans perspectives within the learning sciences. Contributors examine a variety of spaces that work either with or against LGBTQ+ youth and adults. We think with prior work in the learning sciences and deploy queer theories, designs, methodologies, and axiologies to better understand learning. These papers are united by their engagement with queer people, places, and perspectives to advance understandings of learning in the current political climate. The papers help us understand how communities position LGBTQ+ people, for good or for ill. The studies here highlight how learning can unfold as oppressive or can unfold as joy, resistance, or resilience in the face of oppression. Together, these papers put queerness and learning into conversation to highlight the affordances of queer-trans perspectives for building actionable, equitable, and rigorous theories of learning.

abstract: Advancing new directions in design research is crucial, especially as our understanding of learning is confronted by novel semi-autonomous and AI technologies, social phenomena, and global environmental crises. This symposium seeks to advance a vision for the future(s) of educational design research and consider questions that rupture core assumptions about design in the learning sciences. These include who and what design agents are, how sustainability can become core to educational design, and how design processes and responsibilities can shift considering new design purposes and partners. The papers present four contributions to design research, allowing us to explore: (1) Commitments and groundings for design, (2) lifecycle approaches made visible when materials are treated as contributors, (3) the importance of new co-analysis approaches, and (4) the unfinished and unexpected nature of educational design.

abstract: Outdoor experiences for K-12 youth are often conceptualized as just fun, with little learning benefit. And when disciplinary learning is incorporated, science is often emphasized, to the detriment of other relevant disciplines, such as social studies. One reason is that teachers lack professional learning opportunities to make use of nature-based resources for (inter) disciplinary engagement. Here, we merge and expand Randi Engle’s frameworks to become expansively framed productive interdisciplinary engagement (PIE) in examining a case study of one teacher and sixth-grade students participating in a week-long, school-based outdoor learning program. We examine moments where sensemaking in science and social studies can create PIE and identify examples of teacher-led productive interdisciplinary inquiry as well as missed opportunities to go deeper or better leverage student sensemaking. These findings have implications for making the pedagogical principles of PIE more explicit in the teacher professional learning program offered for School of the Wild.

abstract: This symposium brings together diverse research exploring the intersections of climate change education, social justice, and community empowerment. As climate change increasingly impacts vulnerable populations, the importance of integrating justice-oriented approaches in K-12 education becomes urgent. Studies featured in this symposium investigate how climate education can leverage community strengths, foster empathy through quantitative reasoning, and critique the racialized nature of data to promote environmental justice. Presentations will examine innovative uses of data in teaching, highlighting its role in addressing inequities and engaging students in climate justice advocacy. Key themes include fostering climate agency through cross-disciplinary approaches, rethinking the "natural disaster" narrative to highlight systemic inequalities, and designing professional learning programs to equip educators with tools to navigate climate-related injustices. Together, these studies underscore the need for inclusive, justice-focused climate education that empowers students to engage meaningfully with the climate crisis and advocate for systemic change.

abstract: In a world increasingly shaped by misinformation and polarization, education should equip individuals to critically engage with sensitive and controversial issues (SCI). This symposium addresses key challenges in navigating these, offering innovative frameworks and strategies to enhance critical thinking, foster resilience against misinformation, and promote constructive dialogue. Contributions explore the role of social identity in shaping openness to diverse perspectives, the productivity of non-convergent discussions in fostering deeper understanding, and the impact of group membership on attitude change and argument evaluation. Additionally, the symposium examines the tension faced by educators in addressing SCIs and provides actionable insights to transform challenges into opportunities for meaningful engagement.

Together the papers serve as an invitation and a provocation to unsettle normative colonial knowledge practices within the Learning Sciences. We ask, ‘how might the Learning Sciences rearticulate theories of learning that serve life rather than capital accumulation, and racialized and gendered hierarchy?’

Neurodiversity calls for a valuing of neurological diversity, critiquing deficit-oriented framings of minoritized neurotypes such as autism and dyslexia. This symposium challenges the learning sciences to reckon with this emerging paradigm’s implications for the core theory, approaches, and aims of the field, focusing on possibilities within STEM education research.

abstract: This symposium explores the potential of co-design in creating inclusive and accessible learning innovations by foregrounding the expertise of neurodivergent and historically minoritized youth. Presenting six federally funded projects, the session showcases how co-design methodologies empower learners to shape tools and interventions that prioritize equity, access, and belonging. These initiatives leverage emerging technologies, including AI, AR, VR, and BCI, as well as museum- and place-based STEM activities, to address barriers to learning while fostering agency and identity development. Each project exemplifies how co-design not only creates more effective and responsive tools but also builds communities and promotes systemic change. Attendees will gain practical insights into recruiting and engaging co-designers, navigating challenges, and sustaining equitable collaborations, with a focus on scaling these practices for broader impact. Through these examples, the symposium illustrates how co-design can reimagine learning systems to better serve all learners and create more equitable educational experiences.

Together, we consider the potential for play in supporting disciplinary learning as well as student autonomy and agency and make a case for why the disappearance of play is about more than a loss of simple fun.

abstract: World-making has not been commonly considered in data science education. We were inspired to explore how a lens of world-making might deepen and expand our relational understandings of data. We are scholars working in diverse contexts united by a broad interpretation of what data is and can be. By entering a collaborative, sustained dialog, grounded within and across our research projects, we recognized that adopting a world-making lens supported us to envision the now and future more pluralistically and agentically by recognizing the multidimensional, multifaceted world(s) present in our research. Exploring world-making prompted explication and clarification of obscured relations, pointed to bridges across worlds, and surfaced assumptions about worlds. We convene this symposium to share how world-making operated in our work and to invite symposium attendees to take up these approaches in positioning data and data science education in service of greater societal and global goals.

abstract: Fifteen years ago, Noah Feinstein introduced the idea of the competent outsider to argue for a comprehensive re-thinking of the purposes of science education. The idea orients competence away from science disciplines, per se, and toward the goals that everyday people might frame for themselves for which science may be useful. Despite its increasing use as a goal, however, answers to the question of what sorts of knowledge and skill renders anyone a competent outsider remain elusive. As the concept of the competent outsider has been taken up in recent arguments for how to organize science education in a post-truth era, it is a good time to reconsider the idea and to interrogate both of its components: what renders one competent with respect to science and what is a competent outsider actually outside of?

abstract: This study explores the navigation of elementary science teacher candidates (TCs) as they seek to humanize their assessments in an educational system that centers neoliberal testing practices. This paper is the first step in addressing the need for more research on supporting TCs who desire to implement humanizing pedagogy in their assessments. With rhizomatic analysis and the use of Deleuze and Guattari’s concepts of territorialization, deterritorialization, and reterritorialization, we examine the lines of flight the TCs took in their science methods course (Dimitriadis & Kamberelis, 2006; St. Pierre, 2019). Findings show deterritorialization moves with the ways that TCs approached humanizing pedagogy in their talk and implementation of assessments. However, the findings demonstrate territorialization and reterritorialization moves as TCs planned these assessments in their 5E lessons. We discuss implications for promoting humanizing pedagogy in science assessments and supporting TCs as they navigate tensions.

abstract: Learning in times of climate change and ongoing inequality, requires ethical-political engagements that are transgressive of unsustainable norms, including those left in coloniality’s wake (Lotz-Sisitka et al., 2017; 2023). However, a question arises as to when such transgressions become developmental (cf. Williams et al., 2018). This symposium addresses this question through analysis of five formative interventions (cf. Engeström et al., 2014). The studies advance a decolonial dialectic of transformation, enacted as a process of expansive, transgressive learning and emancipatory agency from below, grounded and expanding from living heritage and place; reflexively returning to it. Here co-engagement in expansive learning actions strengthen African relationality (Ubuntu relations), and collective (emancipatory) transformative agency (cf. Engeström and Sannino, 2010; 2021; Lotz-Sisitka et al., 2023). Studies emphasise ethical-political expansion of the object of activity in expansive learning struggles to address environmental degradation, gender and racial discrimination, and exclusions of living heritage, youth, and indigenous cultures.

abstract: Learning for complex world-making practices cannot be understood without embracing theoretical perspectives that acknowledge the complexity and dynamics of the interconnected and distributed among people and their environments nature of such practices. This symposium aims to advance the conceptual foundations for studying learning as an ecological phenomenon. It builds upon the recent special issue of Journal of the Learning Sciences, “Beyond disciplinary engagement: Researching the ecologies of interdisciplinary learning” (Markauskaite et al., 2024). The papers in this special issue adopted diverse ecological perspectives to study interdisciplinary learning, offering unique insights into how personal resourcefulness, teamwork dynamics, institutional processes, and disciplinary cultures intertwine in this context. However, the underpinning conceptual issues of theorizing and empirically studying learning as an ecological phenomenon were not specifically examined. In this symposium, we extend this work to unpack different ecological conceptualizations of learning and discuss critical directions for further development.

title: Constructions of Feasibility within Expansive Designs for Justice with Communities
citation: Chang, M. A., Rajala, A., Philip, T. M., Cortez, A., Shaw, M., Lehtinen, J., Taimela, I., Garcia, J. E., Vishwanath, A., Pea, R., & Mirra, N. (2025). authors_list: Chang, M. A., Rajala, A., Philip, T. M., Cortez, A., Shaw, M., Lehtinen, J., Taimela, I., Garcia, J. E., Vishwanath, A., Pea, R., & Mirra, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Design-based research (DBR) has served as an important methodological building block for researchers interested in working with communities to envision equitable possibilities for learning, particularly ones that differ from the status quo. Especially within these expansive design contexts, feasibility is a thorny issue precisely because it has historically been leveraged as a rigid, objective means to delimit what is possible in the world as it is, as opposed to what it could be. At the same time, we cannot ignore issues of feasibility if our goal is to realize expansive designs in real learning environments. This symposium brings together five papers across different phases of DBR and collectively illustrate a conception of feasibility that is dynamic, contextual, and contested. We design this symposium specifically to engage the learning sciences community about how such conceptions of feasibility can open up expansive possibilities for design.

subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: As emerging digital technologies and AI reshape education, Computational Thinking (CT) skills such as abstraction, problem decomposition, and algorithm design are crucial for learners to navigate this landscape. This symposium brings together a set of diverse studies that highlight the relevance of CT and problem-solving skills in the age of AI. The studies demonstrate how CT can be comprehensively addressed in learning sciences research at different educational levels from primary school to teacher education, in different learning designs spanning from individual programming tasks to collaborative activities, and through multimodal multichannel data. The discussion will focus on the relevance of CT as a core concept supporting learning with and about AI while preserving critical pedagogical values such as agency, creativity, and critical thinking with human-centered approaches.

citation: Y., J., Radinsky, J., Gutiérrez, K. D., Castro, A., Daniel, B., Gholson, M., Keifert, D. T., Kothari, V., Philip, T. M., Pierson, A., & Tabak, I. (2025). subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This symposium brings together four research projects that investigate how people construct and contest racialized identities in interaction. We use Goodwin’s (2018) construct of substrate to examine how “kinds of people” (Hacking, 2007) are constructed in relation to racialized identities (Nasir, 2011). First, we introduce a particular methodological approach for racial interactional analysis and attend to the representational, theoretical and ethical complexities entailed. Second, we unpack the role of race-explicit and color-evasive language in constructing “kinds of students” in an elementary science teacher PD. Third, we examine how shared substrates of “social justice” discourses can be unintentionally leveraged to racialize students. Fourth, we examine how pre-service teachers constructed racialized categories by combing demographic data patterns with societal narratives. These analyses are valuable not only for understanding how we construct “races” in discourse, but also for thinking through learning objectives and instructional designs with respect to racialized identity construction.

abstract: Increasingly, calls from within the natural and computational sciences are recognizing the need for more expansive forms of disciplinary theory building and practice to connect social theories in the study of natural systems. Within science education and science teacher education, there is an increasing recognition of the need for expansive forms science teaching that connect sociopolitical contexts of science with both the professional learning of teachers and the science taught in K12 classrooms. In this symposium, we explore designs for expansive STEAM disciplinary engagement across classroom, professional learning, and informal Indigenous STEAM settings to understand the ways in which work at the edges of disciplines can transform STEAM teaching and learning for educators and students.

abstract: There is a pressing need to reimagine education for social and ecological well-being. Persistent inequalities and underimagined forms of education not only prevent these developments, but continue to erode human well-being and creativity. Substantive changes require paradigm shifts in foundational conceptualizations of educational challenges and possibilities, including transformative understandings of students’ sense making and holistic cultural and intellectual lives. This symposium brings together scholarship focused on storywork, relationality or kinship and affect in the design of learning environments. Further the studies in this symposium are specifically focused on these dimensions of learning tied to field based or land and water based learning environments.

abstract: This symposium brings together research aimed at better understanding how teachers and educators take on roles such as curriculum co-designers, reflective practitioners, and collaborators, bridging relationships across classroom walls while being transformational agents of change within and outside their classrooms. Each of the contributions considers teachers’ work in relation to culturally responsive and/or critical pedagogies. We frame this work in the context of rising resistance to equity, diversity, and inclusion work, and continued deprofessionalization of teachers through “teacher-proof” approaches to curriculum and technological tool design. In this symposium, we bring together teams that have explored different roles teachers take on, their voices, and experiences, as world-making agents and as learners themselves.

abstract: Critical data literacy (CDL) is essential in data science education, requiring collaborative approaches that extend beyond quantitative reasoning. While literature on CDL is growing, more exploration is needed on how students apply data science practices to support CDL in a summer program. Using a descriptive case study, we examine differences between classroom learning and real-world applications in social justice projects. Findings indicate that practical engagement enhances students' understanding of data tools and ethical considerations.

abstract: Research indicates that students underutilize self-explanation. Thematic analysis of survey data revealed that students value self-explanation for enhancing active reading, comprehension monitoring, and personal relevance. However, barriers such as time constraints, perceived effort, and fear of misapplication impede its use. Students assess the need for self-explanation based on their existing strategies and goals, underscoring the need for interventions that leverage effective application of self-explanation as a useful and meaningful learning strategy.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The purpose of this study is to describe four faculty learning communities (FLCs) coordinators’ strategies, challenges, and how they perceived their roles. Data include (i) FLC coordinators’ reflective reports; (ii) in-depth interviews; and (iii) videotaped reflective discussions. Findings revealed five themes: the composition of the FLC, the importance of a pre-existing familiarity between the FLC members, the time constraints, prior pedagogical knowledge, and issues relating to reflective processes.

title: Promoting Learning and STEM Interest with Serious Games
citation: Hunt, J. & Taub, M. (2025). Promoting Learning and STEM Interest With Serious Games. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. abstract: Using a robust experimental design, the research explores how game-based interventions can augment traditional fraction instruction and promote STEM interest among a diverse group of elementary school students, including students with disabilities. The curriculum, grounded in Scheme Theory and Learning Trajectories, significantly improved students’ fraction understanding and STEM interest. The findings highlight the potential of integrating game-based learning into mathematics education to address foundational STEM concepts and advocate for further research to explore scalability and broader applicability.

title: Authenticity and Entomology Knowledge in Science Classrooms
citation: Stroupe, D., Walser, M., & White, P. (2025). Authenticity and Entomology Knowledge in Science Classrooms. authors_list: Stroupe, D., Walser, M., & White, P.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: A long-standing goal of science education has been for students to engage in “authentic” science. This goal of authentic science has appeared in many policy documents, and most recently, in the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS, Achieve, 2013) in the United States. Thirteen years after the release of NGSS, we still wonder about how to support students to engage in “authentic” science in classrooms. Our presentation will examine relationships between authenticity, epistemic agency, and uncertainty, and equity. The presentations will approach the topic in two ways: expectations and norms for students, and the role of teachers. Students may be engaging in “authentic” science when they are exercising epistemic agency. We will conclude with questions for the field to consider.

title: Children Watching (and Seeing) Each Other: A Lesson on Black Aliveness
citation: Love, C., Vescio, J., & Lu, S. (2025). Children Watching (And Seeing) Each Other: A Lesson on Black Aliveness. International Society of the Learning Sciences.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In the post-COVID era, many early educational stakeholders have expressed worry over children’s loss of Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) opportunities, with hopes to correct for this through formal instruction. However, in this paper we invited children to interpret a video of their own play and we observed the emotional labor that they engaged in, especially through their ability to take on the perspective of other group members. This emotional labor, which we call relationality, appeared to be especially humanizing for Quentin, a Black boy, and the ways that he played and engaged with others. This work hopes to recognize the SEL resources that children already bring to school, and offer an example of how these resources show their ability to see one another.

title: Computational Thinking in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Charting Directions for Learning Sciences Research and Practice
citation: Kafai, Y. & Grover, S. (2025). Computational Thinking in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Charting Directions for Learning Sciences Research and Practice. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kafai, Y. & Grover, S.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: The introduction of artificial intelligence and machine learning applications to the public has led to heated discussions about its potential impacts and risks for K-12 education. One particular challenge has been to decide what students should learn about these topics, and how this relates to computational thinking, which has served as an umbrella for introducing CS education in schools. We propose CT+, an expanded version of computational thinking,, to include artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies and outline different directions for future research in the learning sciences. We also discuss how these efforts can be informed by lessons learned from the last decade in designing instructional programs, integrating it with other subjects, and addressing issues of algorithmic bias and justice in teaching computing in schools.

title: Fostering Learners’ Environmental Literacy through Augmented Reality and Virtual Reality: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Chen, B. (2025). Fostering Learners’ Environmental Literacy Through Augmented Reality and Virtual Reality: A Meta-Analysis. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chen, B.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This review addresses the dearth of meta-analyses investigating the effects of augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) within the domain of environmental education. The analysis of thirty peer-reviewed journal articles encompassing fifty-two independent studies indicated that the implementation of AR and VR technologies, in comparison to traditional educational methods that do not utilize these tools, resulted in small yet statistically significant improvement in knowledge achievement and student dispositions. Furthermore, the technologies exhibited a large effect on skill acquisition and a minimal effect on environmentally responsible behavior. Additionally, the influence on dispositions was found to be moderated by educational level and learning time.

title: Playful Uncertainty: Parents as STEM Educators in the Home

subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: This study examined playful uncertainties—moments when parents feigned uncertainty—to foster children’s engineering development in their home environment. Grounded in sociocultural theories of guided participation and family culture, we conducted a case study of four families. Findings suggest that playful uncertainties empowered children to take initiative, explore, and refine their understanding through collaborative discovery and problem-solving. This study also positioned parents as transformative agents, using playful uncertainties as creative epistemic support.

title: Food for Thought: An Analogy for Digital Sovereignty in Education

abstract: Digital sovereignty (DS) in education refers to the educational community's capacity to exercise self-governance over technology use, aligning it with educational goals. Many educators, with limited familiarity with critical digital literacy, struggle to represent technological issues using domain principles and values, restricting engagement with its ethical, environmental, and agency-focused principles. This paper proposes using food sovereignty principles as an analogy to foster abstract representations by linking DS to a familiar context.

abstract: This study explores middle-grade girls' understanding of Critical Data Literacy (CDL) after participating in a week-long residential STEM camp. This research examines how informal learning settings can foster CDL among predominantly underrepresented minoritized (URM) girls. Through qualitative interviews, the study reveals how participants engaged with CDL components: formulating questions, gathering relevant data, employing analytical tools, and interpreting findings. The insights aim to inform strategies for enhancing CDL in informal environments, contributing to broader educational goals in data science and supporting the development of critical thinking skills for addressing societal issues.

title: More or Fewer? Effects of Multiple Representation Simulations in Secondary Physics Classrooms
citation: Jia, W., Chen, F., Xin, J., & Chen, G. (2025). More or Fewer? Effects of Multiple Representation Simulations in Secondary Physics Classrooms. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
