subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study examined how simulations with multiple representations affect secondary students’ physics learning. Simulations employed in the experiment group (n = 36) instruction with multiple representations, whereas the control group (n = 42) used single ones, taught by the same teacher. Results revealed that experimental group students outperformed their counterparts in academic achievement, with less positive emotional engagement. These results indicated that multiple representations enhanced learning outcomes, but single representations fostered greater emotional engagement.

title: Developing a Theory of Conceptualizations of Learning
citation: Donaldson, J. P. (2025). Developing a Theory of Conceptualizations of Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: Donaldson, J. P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This conceptual paper presents a theory viewing conceptualizations of learning as complex systems. Synthesizing design experience, analyses (legislation, research, interviews), and theories (metaphor, frame, complex systems), it posits conceptualizations comprise interacting, self-organizing elements (interdependent ideas) generating emergent practices. These systems seek equilibrium but allow transformation through strategic leveraging of core ideas. This framework aims to understand and shift how learning is perceived and enacted.

title: Conceptualizations of Creativity as Complex Systems in Learning
citation: Donaldson, J. P. & Katompa, J. (2025). Conceptualizations of Creativity as Complex Systems in Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2551-2553). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Donaldson, J. P. & Katompa, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Complex systems theory was used to explore creativity conceptualizations in learning. Network/cluster analyses of 200 participants’ definitions identified co-existing attractor states—distinct clusters of interconnected ideas. Assuming learning is inherently creative, findings revealed creativity conceptualizations as emergent systems, advocating for inclusive environments that recognize varied pathways. By transcending reductionist views of creativity as isolated traits, this systems-based perspective supports diverse creative potentials, informing designs for adaptive, culturally responsive learning communities aligned with their dynamic complexity.

title: Enhancing Elementary Teachers’ AI-TPACK through a Professional Development Workshop
citation: Wu, Y., Wang, L., & Shih, T. (2025). Enhancing Elementary Teachers’ Ai-TPACK Through a Professional Development Workshop. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2554-2556). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wu, Y., Wang, L., & Shih, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The rapid advancement of generative AI presents new opportunities for personalized learning and adaptive instruction in elementary education. However, many teachers lack the necessary AI-TPACK competencies to integrate AI effectively. This study examines the impact of a two-day professional development workshop designed to enhance elementary educators' AI knowledge, pedagogical applications, and ethical awareness. Findings from pre- and post-workshop assessments indicate significant improvements in AI proficiency, instructional integration, and ethical considerations. Educators reported increased confidence in using AI for lesson planning and student engagement, yet highlighted the need for ongoing training in ethical AI use, privacy, and fairness. These results underscore the importance of structured, hands-on AI training to support responsible and effective AI integration in classrooms. Future research should explore long-term impacts on teacher engagement and student learning outcomes.

title: Four Causal Problems that Engage Laypeople in Interacting with Science
citation: London, A. & Haskel-Ittah, M. (2025). Four Causal Problems That Engage Laypeople in Interacting With Science. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: London, A. & Haskel-Ittah, M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study explores how laypeople in a clinical context engage with causal scientific information. Using a framework of four causal scientific problems—causal inference, explanation, prediction, and control— We examined the questions posed to medical staff in online cancer-related forums. The findings showed that most of the questions raised were causal in nature, with the most common goal being a desire for control—that is, seeking ways to influence various situations. Framing lay engagement with science through causal problems provides a valuable lens for understanding laypeople’s diverse aims and may be used for enhancing their scientific literacy through tailored educational approaches.

title: Social Studies Teachers’ Goals for Teaching Online Evaluations
citation: McGrew, S. & Reynolds, E. C. (2025). Social Studies Teachers’ Goals for Teaching Online Evaluations. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: McGrew, S. & Reynolds, E. C.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies

abstract: Teachers need professional learning opportunities aligned with their existing goals to help them prepare to teach digital media literacy. Using interview data from 23 high school social studies teachers, we analyzed how teachers described their goals for teaching online evaluations and the alignment they saw between those goals and their overall goals as social studies teachers. Implications for digital media literacy curriculum development and professional learning are explored.

title: Dignity-Affirming Care in the Context of Large-Scale Instructional Systems Change
citation: Ryoo, J. J., Phelps, D., Santo, R., Vogel, S., Patel, A., & Tello, J. V. (2025). Dignity-Affirming Care in the Context of Large-Scale Instructional Systems Change. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2563-2565). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ryoo, J. J., Phelps, D., Santo, R., Vogel, S., Patel, A., & Tello, J. V.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Through a case study of five colleges participating in a city-wide university system’s effort to bring computational and digital literacies into Schools of Education, this poster describes how relationships of dignity-affirming care (Riedy and Penuel, 2024) can support systems change efforts by encouraging: 1) faculty professional learning toward systems change goals, 2) buy-in to larger efforts, and 3) incorporation of new ideas and practices in courses/syllabi. Connections to related research in research-practice partnerships are shared.

citation: Capparozza, M., Eder, T., Wagner, S., & Lachner, A. (2025). Barriers and Facilitators to K-12 Teachers’ Engagement With Open Educational Resources (Oer): A Systematic Review. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2566-2568). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Capparozza, M., Eder, T., Wagner, S., & Lachner, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Despite their learning potential, Open Educational Resources (OER) are rarely used. This poster presents preliminary results from a systematic review of the barriers and facilitators that influence K-12 teachers’ engagement with OER. A thematic analysis of 63 studies identified barriers and facilitators related to five key factors. The findings underscore the need for support to enhance teachers' engagement with OER by providing high-quality, adaptable, and contextually relevant OER, sufficient school support, and professional development.

title: The Adventures of Pauline and Paul: How Game Design Elements Can Influence Cognitive Performance Development
citation: Pickal, A. J., Stadler, M., Bai, S., Koch, M., & Sailer, M. (2025). The Adventures of Pauline and Paul: How Game Design Elements Can Influence Cognitive Performance Development. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Pickal, A. J., Stadler, M., Bai, S., Koch, M., & Sailer, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Gamification, that is, the implementation of game design elements (e.g., stories) within learning tasks, has the potential to foster learners’ cognitive performance. However, results regarding the positive effects of game design elements, such as stories, are often ambiguous. This may be due to their adaptivity and, consequently, differences in feedback learners receive within gamified learning tasks (e.g., with stories, in terms of narrative progress). This study presents preliminary results on how implementing a story with different narrative conditions (without narrative, with progressing narrative, or with stagnating narrative) in a cognitive performance task affects learners’ performance development. The results showed no significant differences between the three conditions in terms of cognitive performance development, which is, to some extent, in line with previous research.

citation: Tchetgen, P. N. (2025). Designing a Culturally Grounded Ecology for Mediating Multimodal Literacy Experiences Through Parent-Child Technology Interactions. authors_list: Tchetgen, P. N.

tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies
abstract: The Urban Griots Playground (UGP) study investigates how culturally grounded, embodied learning environments impact early literacy and socio-emotional development in young children through a family workshop series. Using the researcher-developed Drumball-Alphariddims system—a digital tool integrating rhythmic call-and-response—UGP helped scaffold literacy and social skills in five child-parent dyads over four weeks. Findings suggest that this embodied, rhythmic and multimodal approach stimulated early literacy behaviors and social participation, though younger children struggled with the complexity of the Alphariddim code. The workshops also improved emotional understanding through storytelling and culturally relevant proverbs. While the study highlights the potential of culturally grounded, family-centered music-based interventions (MBI) for at-risk children, limitations such as small sample size and technological constraints call for further refinement and longitudinal research.

title: Navigating AI Ethics: Pre-service Teachers’ Reflexivity of Ethical Knowledge about Artificial Intelligence
citation: Boos, J., Wagner, S., Backfisch, I., Eder, T., & Lachner, A. (2025). Navigating Ai Ethics: Pre-Service Teachers’ Reflexivity of Ethical Knowledge About Artificial Intelligence. authors_list: Boos, J., Wagner, S., Backfisch, I., Eder, T., & Lachner, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General

abstract: This field study within an authentic teacher education lecture explores how pre-service teachers (N = 274) process diverse knowledge, such as technological and ethical knowledge about artificial intelligence. We found that instructional support targeting cognitive processing significantly supports acquiring and applying AI-related knowledge. To deepen our understanding of processing different knowledge domains, we will assess teachers’ navigation behaviors and knowledge acquisition patterns within epistemic network analysis, offering insights into effective instructional design.

title: Undergraduate Formation and Digital Technologies: The Case of the Philosophy Subject
citation: Jobim, A. & Giraffa, L. (2025). Undergraduate Formation and Digital Technologies: The Case of the Philosophy Subject. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2578-2580). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jobim, A. & Giraffa, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines the urgent need and the exciting possibilities of integrating digital technologies into the undergraduate formation of philosophy teachers. Its objective is an integration that does not instrumentalize technology. It proposes using the Design-Based Research in three cycles: developing training solutions that value technologies as mediators of critical thinking, promoting pedagogical innovation, and a critical philosophical practice that impacts teaching and reflection on the role of technologies in society.

title: Understanding How Thinking Routines Mediate Student Thinking and Interaction: Insights from a Design-Based Research
citation: Chen, J. & Jan, M. (2025). Understanding How Thinking Routines Mediate Student Thinking and Interaction: Insights From a Design-Based Research. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2581-2583). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chen, J. & Jan, M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This design-based research explores how to develop curriculum-level instructional design principles integrating thinking routines. Based on our findings from earlier iterations, we revised the conjecture map and implemented the revised instruction in a university English reading class in Taiwan. We examined how thinking routines mediate student thinking and interaction, with the aim of refining the design principles. Research results showed that thinking routines promoted interaction, deeper thinking, and created a thinking classroom ethos.

title: Breaking Out of Mathematical Silos: Exploring Expansive Framing and Value Beliefs in Undergraduate STEM Education
citation: Beck, K. E. (2025). Breaking out of Mathematical Silos: Exploring Expansive Framing and Value Beliefs in Undergraduate STEM Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2584-2586). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Beck, K. E.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This ongoing study investigates how Expansive Framing (EF) might foster transfer of mathematics learning in undergraduate STEM education through a conceptual framework that integrates EF with Expectancy Value (EV) theory. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, we analyzed instructor interviews, and plan to analyze classroom observations and student surveys, to examine how EF principles operate in STEM contexts. Preliminary findings suggest that EF may provide a pathway for breaking traditional disciplinary boundaries while enhancing undergraduate students' value beliefs in STEM courses.

title: Bridging Schools and Industry: Lessons from Victorian Tech Schools in Entrepreneurship Education
citation: Clark, J. C. & Palisse, J. (2025). Bridging Schools and Industry: Lessons From Victorian Tech Schools in Entrepreneurship Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2587-2588). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Clark, J. C. & Palisse, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Entrepreneurship is increasingly viewed as a critical 21st-century capability, yet in secondary schools, programs are limited and fragmented. Design thinking and experiential learning are promising pedagogies for entrepreneurship education, but require time, expertise, and industry links. These are things traditional schools often lack. Tech Schools in Victoria, Australia address this gap through flexible, industry-connected programs.

title: Growing Community: School Gardens in Secondary Schools
citation: Clark, J. C., Wallace, H., & Jenkins, G. (2025). Growing Community: School Gardens in Secondary Schools. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2589-2590). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Clark, J. C., Wallace, H., & Jenkins, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The potential of school gardens to involve students in authentic learning is widely accepted in Australian primary schools and this is spreading to secondary schools. We report on a study on the use of school gardens in regional secondary schools: exploring, in terms of social capital, why they are developed and how they are used. We have found that, while the impetus varies, they offer unique opportunities to provide richer, more authentic experiences to their students and forge closer links to their communities. Unlike primary schools where parents are often invited to assist with a range of educational programs, the building of connections between secondary schools and their communities, needs to be active and targeted, through the building of a shared vision and communication pathways to facilitate breaking barriers and building social capital.

title: Fostering Science Understanding with Imaginative Digital Drawing
citation: Jin, Q. (2025). Fostering Science Understanding With Imaginative Digital Drawing. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: Jin, Q.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Drawing and imagination are integral to scientific thinking and reasoning. This study explored how elementary students learn astronomy through engaging in imaginative drawing with digital tools. Data were collected from multiple sources and analyzed qualitatively. Findings from this study indicated that imaginative drawing with digital tools enabled students to explore topics that were beyond their immediately experienced world and construct refined, plausible knowledge claims.

citation: Celik, I., Zabolotna, K., & Viberg, O. (2025). Enhancing Teacher-Ai Collaboration: The Impact of Prompt Engineering on Generative Ai's Instructional Effectiveness. authors_list: Celik, I., Zabolotna, K., & Viberg, O.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Little is known about the instructional value of generative AI (GenAI) outputs in response to different prompts. This study designed prompts for ChatGPT based on the Knowledge Construction (KC) framework and evaluated outcomes in three subjects using the TPACK framework. Results show that higher KC phases produced more pedagogically meaningful outputs. “Integration of technology” and “student engagement” emerged as key usage aims, highlighting the importance of theory-informed prompt engineering in enhancing teacher-AI collaboration.

title: A Systematic Literature Review of Large Language Model Applications in the Algebra Domain
citation: Song, Y., Zhang, Y., Precup, D., Rabbany, R., & Cutumisu, M. (2025). A Systematic Literature Review of Large Language Model Applications in the Algebra Domain. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Song, Y., Zhang, Y., Precup, D., Rabbany, R., & Cutumisu, M.
subject: STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Algebra is often challenging to teach and learn. While large language models (LLMs) are gaining attention in education, their role in algebra remains unclear. This systematic review, guided by the PRISMA framework, analyzed 21 studies from 532 records. Findings revealed that LLMs were mostly used on secondary data, for assessment, with ChatGPT, using zero-shot prompts but struggled with complex reasoning. This review offers theoretical insights and practical guidance for effectively applying LLMs in algebra education.

title: Integrating Real-World Authenticity into a High School Data Science Curriculum
citation: Israel-Fishelson, R. & Weintrop, D. (2025). Integrating Real-World Authenticity Into a High School Data Science Curriculum. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2599-2601). authors_list: Israel-Fishelson, R. & Weintrop, D.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: In an increasingly data-driven society, it is essential that students understand and critically engage with the data that surrounds them. A key aspect of accomplishing this is helping students understand the importance of data and the impact it can have on their lives. This paper examines the role of real-world authenticity in a high school interest-driven data science curriculum. Through student reflections and project outcomes analysis, the study highlights how real-world data use fosters data practices by allowing students to see data science as relevant and applicable to real-life issues. Findings indicate that students perceived the data exploration activities as authentic and valued the meaningfulness of the data, recognizing its relevance to real-life contexts.

title: Classroom Intervention to Support Secondary School Students’ Motivation and Regulated Learning
citation: Törmänen, T., Turunen, M., Lehtoaho, E., Suoraniemi, J., & Järvenoja, H. (2025). Classroom Intervention to Support Secondary School Students’ Motivation and Regulated Learning. abstract: The study design aims to identify motivational classroom interaction practices that support secondary school students' motivation and regulated learning and examine their effects on students' motivational beliefs in short and long term. During the intervention, teachers apply practices developed as part of the study, while situational and general self-report data are collected from intervention and control schools over four semesters. The results will reveal practices that support motivation both in the moment and over time.

title: Game-based Ambiguity Resolution to Promote Sustainability Ethics Dialog
citation: Gaydos, M., Usui, R., Engelken, S., & Hirasawa, H. (2025). Game-Based Ambiguity Resolution to Promote Sustainability Ethics Dialog. authors_list: Gaydos, M., Usui, R., Engelken, S., & Hirasawa, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: While models of game-based learning have been used for disciplinary understanding and practices, ethics education poses a unique design challenge given its combination of subject matter content and values-informed decision-making. This poster presents a novel design and results from a sustainability ethics game designed to compel player discussion. Results focus on characterizing different ways in which ambiguity arose through play and suggest further work in exploring how ambiguity can support productive ethical deliberation.

title: Game-Based Simulation for Ethics Understanding
citation: Gaydos, M., Lu, J., Gilmutdinova, R., & Nardo, A. (2025). Game-Based Simulation for Ethics Understanding. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2608-2610). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Gaydos, M., Lu, J., Gilmutdinova, R., & Nardo, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Though games have been proposed as potentially useful tools for research ethics education, designs have tended to focus on content-oriented understanding, ethics reasoning, and compliance. We explore a game in which contexts and pressures that tend to complicate typical research ethics decision-making were simulated. Preliminary findings suggest that the simulation was better than a traditional, video-based training in helping students realize the socially situated factors influencing ethical research decisions.

title: Translanguaging Spaces: Exploring Scientific Meaning-Making Through Conceptual Metaphors
citation: Priyadarshini, R., Alekh, V., Dasgupta, C., & Murthy, S. (2025). Translanguaging Spaces: Exploring Scientific Meaning-Making Through Conceptual Metaphors. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 261-269). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Priyadarshini, R., Alekh, V., Dasgupta, C., & Murthy, S.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Translanguaging beyond language allows researchers to examine how learners mobilize their full communicative repertoire, crossing languages, modes, and sensory inputs, to engage with and understand complex everyday phenomena. Using Conceptual Metaphor Theory and distributed social semiotics, this study explores how verbal, gestural, and material interactions in translanguaging spaces facilitate learners’ meaning making of everyday phenomena through conceptual metaphors. Findings reveal that, students’ use of Hindi and English, interwoven with gestures, their conceptual repertoire and physical engagement with materials in the translanguaging space triggers specific metaphors, anchoring scientific reasoning in sensory experiences. Collaborative interactions, mediated by objects like cups and tables, highlight how temperature differences and embodied actions support negotiating abstract concepts. The study restates the importance of multimodal interactions in connecting concrete sensory experiences with abstract scientific meaning making and calls for inclusive, multimodal approaches to scientific discourse.

title: Co-Creation of Visual Stories: Representing Agency for Mathematics Learning with Forcibly Displaced Students
citation: Dadkhahfard, S. & Takeuchi, M. A. (2025). Co-Creation of Visual Stories: Representing Agency for Mathematics Learning With Forcibly Displaced Students. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Dadkhahfard, S. & Takeuchi, M. A.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study examines the impact of visual stories co-created with forcibly displaced children to express their agentic possibilities within the school context, particularly in mathematics classrooms. Using participatory co-design processes, six arts-based workshops were designed and facilitated for families to collaboratively illustrate stories of agency, identity, and belonging. Findings, in the form of co-designed visual stories, demonstrate students' use of visual representations to reclaim agency after experiencing forced displacement. The visual stories also highlight educators' roles in facilitating in-school mathematics learning experiences. This research underscores the potential of arts-based co-creation as a tool for children experiencing intersectional oppression to voice their lived experiences.

title: Exploring Hidden Affordances of Modeling Infrastructures for Epistemic Agency
citation: Pierson, A., Lanouette, K., & Brady, C. (2025). Exploring Hidden Affordances of Modeling Infrastructures for Epistemic Agency. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Pierson, A., Lanouette, K., & Brady, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In science curricula, there are tensions between providing access to disciplinary practices and empowering students’ epistemic agency. To address this tension, we present a case of a student’s work with a computational model. The student’s creative and intuitive work deviated from the trajectory intended by the curriculum. By illustrating how the student’s resistance to classroom activities produced meaningful learning, our analysis will challenge what researchers and educators might consider “on task” or “productive” engagement.

title: Potions: Caring in Showing with an Asynchronous Partner
citation: Keifert, D. T. & Poppins, D. (2025). Potions: Caring in Showing With an Asynchronous Partner. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: Keifert, D. T. & Poppins, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We conceptualize showings as interactions when someone shares and contextualizes their perspectives, experience, practice, and/or interests and provides contextualization. Showings are opportunities for demonstrating care for children and their experience. We analyze how one child demonstrated that she trusted an asynchronous adult interactional partner would care about her and her telling across multiple instances of video-recording her potion making practice. This work contributes to understanding of learning in COVID-competent relations and co-research partnerships.

authors_list: Cruz-Gonzalez, C., Coenraad, M., Steinberg, S., Danish, J., Lau, N. G., & Hmelo-Silver, C. E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study examines the methodological challenges of coding student identity within classroom activities using the Funds of Identity (FoI) framework. Analyzing eighth-grade students’ engagement in a network visualization activity, we explored distinctions between expressions of interest and identity. Results highlight complexities in interpreting student participants’ identity within brief classroom interactions, offering nuances in categorizing student contributions and prompting refinements in coding practices.

title: Cultural Humility Through Dance
citation: Slater, E. & Lundgren, L. (2025). Cultural Humility Through Dance. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: Slater, E. & Lundgren, L.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Students, faculty, and staff at American universities are currently grappling with policies that seek to limit or ban diversity, equity, and inclusion measures. Higher education is a place where people from diverse backgrounds converge, creating opportunities for learning about oneself and others. To explore how people can learn collaboratively about each other's backgrounds and cultures, we created a Cultural Humility Immersion program centered on dance. The four-week program culminated in a workshop where participants created the learning artifact of dances that represented their cultures. We will analyze this workshop through interviews with participants. Additionally, we will interpret observations of the dance workshop using embodied practice as our framework. The novelty of this work, in which dance is combined with the theoretical framework of Cultural Humility, will lead to productive conversations about the design of future workshops as well as ways that this kind of activity can promote increased cultural understanding.

citation: Wan, S. W., Lam, A. P., Yeung, L., Poon, D. K., Ng, W., Li, J., Leung, S. K., Orchard, J., Hui, E., & Cheng, A. (2025). abstract: This study explores how prospective teachers in Hong Kong engage in transformative pedagogy within climate change education through the Global Dialogue for Climate Change Education (pseudonym), a collaborative program involving online dialogues with UK peers. Using positioning theory, we examine how participants articulate their roles and identities in climate education. Key themes include self-awareness, ethical responsibility, admiration for global peers, collaborative engagement, and commitment to action planning, highlighting transformative practices that promote sustainability and equity in educational settings.

title: Evaluating Efficacy of Problematizing Chatbot in Higher Education
citation: Sinha, T. (2025). Evaluating Efficacy of Problematizing Chatbot in Higher Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. abstract: Five graduate students brainstormed with a problematizing chatbot for project work. Reflections showed that despite some discomfort with persistent questioning, the brainstorming experience was rich and productive overall. Grading student chats showed high engagement but inadequate use of prompting strategies and weak critical analyses of AI-generated responses. Results implicate a greater focus on AI literacy training that facilitates knowledge of effective prompting and awareness of the limitations of generative AI to encourage critiquing its output.

abstract: With the rise of social media as a primary source of information on topics like climate change, educators need strong critical information literacy skills to guide students effectively. This study examines how pre-service teachers evaluate the credibility of digital information about climate change. Twenty-one pre-service teachers from a Canadian post-secondary institution participated in this study. Findings show that pre-service teachers prioritize sources they perceive as objective and evidence-based. When assessing social media content, participants considered the content, source, and presentation, showing skepticism toward sensationalized posts and preferring professionally presented information with citations. The study highlights the need for teacher education programs to include training in critical information literacy, especially on complex issues like climate change.

abstract: This study investigates the learning strategies of 98 first-year STEM college students through the lens of information processing theory, self-regulated learning, and Dunlosky’s 10 learning strategies. Through analyzing open-ended survey responses, the study identifies six prevalent strategies for academic learning. The findings suggest that integrating foundational cognitive theories with current student practices can provide valuable instructional insights for supporting STEM learning.

abstract: This study design explores the role of group-level regulation of learning in pre-service teachers’ co-construction of Technological, Pedagogical, and Content Knowledge (TPACK). Teacher education students participate in a university course on technology-enhanced learning and working. Self-report data, learning products and video recorded data are collected to reveal how TPACK develops through social interaction and highlight the importance of regulation in the process. Practical implications for teacher education that support effective training will be discussed.

subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: The study examined the development of coding skills and computational thinking of in-service teachers in the context of an e-learning Master-level course. Analysis of teacher Scratch projects and interviews showed that teachers became able to apply several computer science concepts and processes. The e-learning format of the course did not present additional learning challenges, which has significant practical implications because online programs require fewer resources, are more flexible, and are easier to scale up.

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) approaches to analyzing multimodal data often rely on cognitive learning theories. More research is needed to explore AI’s role in analyzing and identifying learning from a sociocultural perspective (Giannakos & Cukurova, 2023). This poster demonstrates an exploration of integrating computational methods into Interaction Analysis (Jordan & Henderson, 1995) and reports observed promises and challenges.

abstract: This proposal presents the design of a translanguaging learning environment. It integrates multimodal technologies, including a haptic glove and an interactive computer visualization, to deliver a multisensory experience. It contributes to translanguaging pedagogy by leveraging fluid language practices with multimodal learning technology, enabling English Language Learners (ELLs) to utilize their full linguistic and sensory resources to make sense of the science concept.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning; Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies
abstract: In this work, we implement computing tools in athletic spaces where youth leverage their pre-existing interests and expertises in sports to make sense of technology. Through this, we aim to create culturally sustaining computing experiences. We analyze young learners and facilitators making sense of a volleyball themed iPad-based training game through play and embodied interactions. We find participants leveraging a variety of athletic resources to tinker with and make sense of how this technology works. We call this embodied and athletic engagement with technology athletic tinkering. This presents an example of culturally sustaining conceptualizations of STEM and computing learning, and it offers heuristics on how to design for similar activity-linked embodied interaction experiences.

authors_list: Lee, U., Nicolas, O. S., Wu, X., Nguyen, M. H., Ngo, F., Hong, C., Wan, A., Park, A., & Munshi, S.

abstract: Federal Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander Serving Institutions (AANAPISI) funding is intended to serve the racialized needs of Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) students in higher education (HE) in the United States. This requires institutions, and practitioners within them, to learn to move beyond colorblind norms in HE and offer race-conscious programming. We report on how a research-practice partnership (RPP) between an AANAPISI program and a research team organized learning to ensure the AANAPISI program responds to the racialized contexts and needs of AAPI students. We share three core practices in the partnership that organizes learning: building on Asian American and Ethnic Studies, leveraging interdisciplinary expertise, and engaging in multi-level sensemaking.

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lee, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study is about how eSports, a global phenomenon in organized, competitive video gaming, serves as a dynamic learning platform for university students. Through identity exploration, community building, and ethical engagement, students developed critical skills such as teamwork, resilience, and digital citizenship. Over six weeks, 109 students participated in gameplay, written reflections, class discussions, and follow-up interviews that offered deeper insight into their experiences. The analysis is grounded in sociocultural learning theory, affinity spaces, and digital self-representation. Findings position eSports as a valuable educational tool that bridges formal education and digital culture, supporting personal growth and meaningful social connections.

title: Equitable Classrooms through Learning Spaces
citation: Novelli, M. (2025). Equitable Classrooms Through Learning Spaces. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This literature review examines how the spatial organization of learning environments reproduces inequities, particularly in STEM education, by maintaining exclusionary practices that disproportionately affect students from historically marginalized communities. By integrating historical and contemporary research and a DisCrit Classroom Ecologies framework to analyze the physical layout of STEM classrooms, the paper explores how these spatial arrangements are linked to student learning, feelings of belonging, and persistence in STEM fields.

abstract: In this comparative case study, we used activity theory to explain how and why different middle-school STEM teachers from the same professional development community made different curricular adaptation choices for biomimetic design activities. Analysis of teacher interviews, classroom observations, and lesson artifacts revealed that teachers’ choices for biomimicry activities were particularly influenced by confidence with and access to particular tools and by rules related to learning goals and time constraints.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines the implications of the question "What do you see that makes you say that?” compared with “Why do you think so?” in facilitating art appreciation classes in an elementary school. An analysis of teacher-child interactions across four classes revealed that children who were asked “What?” questions by teacher were better able to identify visual clues within the artwork’s content compared to those who were asked “Why” questions. These findings suggest that employing “What?” questions may foster more in-depth discussion among children about artworks.

title: Students’ Enactment of Self-Regulated Learning: How does Prior Knowledge Contribute to Learning Traces?
citation: Lämsä, J. & Järvelä, S. (2025). Students’ Enactment of Self-Regulated Learning: How Does Prior Knowledge Contribute to Learning Traces?. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2668-2670). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lämsä, J. & Järvelä, S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: The use of digital trace data has enhanced the measurement of self-regulated learning (SRL). However, these learning traces without information about students’ internal conditions (e.g., prior domain knowledge) are not sufficient to understand how SRL manifests as a strategic activity. This study investigates how secondary education students’ (N = 75) SRL processes differ depending on their prior knowledge on the given source materials while writing from multiple source texts. We used AI to label a set of cognitive and metacognitive processes (e.g., writing, reading, orientation, monitoring) from the trace data and coupled these insights with students’ prior domain knowledge test items to label whether a student had high or low prior knowledge of the different source materials. When students engaged with source materials they had high prior knowledge of, they more frequently enacted metacognitive processes together with cognitive ones. We discuss how considering students' internal conditions can enhance the understanding and support of SRL as a strategic activity through human-AI collaboration.

subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Pedagogical agents in adaptive learning systems can enhance learning outcomes and support self-regulated learning processes, but their role in fostering strategic choice making remains underexplored. To fill the gap, this project designs an interactive algebra learning system with motivational pedagogical agents to foster learning and choice-making behaviors. To test its effectiveness, we conducted a classroom experiment with 49 students with findings that shed light to the future design of adaptive learning environments.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines the development of secondary science teachers’ expertise in geology as they observe sedimentary rocks in the field. We describe how their knowledge-building was shaped over time by the learning tasks, social and material tools, and physical space. The analysis revealed shifts in the teachers’ complex mechanistic reasoning resulting from affordances in instruction and the physical setting. The results document the development of expertise in field geology as a multifaceted process.

title: Developing an Evaluation Method for Inquiry-Based Courses Using ‘Dialogical Reports'
citation: Kobayashi, A. & Ozawa, S. (2025). Developing an Evaluation Method for Inquiry-Based Courses Using ‘Dialogical Reports'. authors_list: Kobayashi, A. & Ozawa, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores dialogical reports as an assessment method for inquiry-based learning in higher education. These Q&A-style reports, structured as interview articles, enable students to articulate and reflect on their learning experiences. An analysis of 144 reports identified two main question types: factual clarification (35.8%) and interpretative reflection (61.8%), the latter linking class content to personal experiences. The findings highlight the potential of dialogical reports to effectively make learning processes visible and deepen student engagement.

title: Placemaking in Dentistry: Enhancing Patient Engagement through Collaborative Art and Digital Storyboards
citation: Lee, S. & Kim, B. (2025). Placemaking in Dentistry: Enhancing Patient Engagement Through Collaborative Art and Digital Storyboards. abstract: This project explored how placemaking principles and participatory art can transform dental offices into engaging and collaborative environments. Over four months (May - September, 2014), 15 patients and four dental specialists co-created digital storyboards, building connections and reducing anxiety within the space. By integrating art and storytelling, the initiative enhanced patient engagement and learning. The findings demonstrate how creativity and collaboration can redefine a healthcare space as an inclusive place that fosters a sense of community.

title: Beyond School: On Lingering Effects of Mathematical Learning Difficulties in University Students
citation: Staller, L., Moeller, K., Weiss, E. M., & Dresen, V. (2025). Beyond School: On Lingering Effects of Mathematical Learning Difficulties in University Students. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2683-2685). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Staller, L., Moeller, K., Weiss, E. M., & Dresen, V.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Mathematical skills are crucial in our knowledge society. Consequently, poor mathematical skills significantly impact academic, but also life prospects more generally. However, little is known about mathematical learning difficulties (MLD) in university students. Here, we conducted thematic analysis on anamnestic interview data of 16 students presenting at a service facility for students with special needs. Results indicated three major themes. First, all participants reported significant number-related key deficits with basic mathematical skills and arithmetic operations. Based on these, the second theme reflected considerable daily struggles, in particular regarding money usage and time management. A final theme represented severe emotional and behavioral consequences, such as shame, mathematics anxiety, and avoidance behavior. Taken together, our findings underscore the impact of untreated MLD on the academic, but also personal lives of students with considerably daily struggles as well as lasting emotional and behavioral consequences – and call for appropriate MLD intervention for adults.

abstract: This study aims to explore how an equity-focused 5E instruction approach can be aligned with Culturally Responsive Teaching (CRT). We analyzed eight teacher candidates’ interviews, focusing on their experiences of planning inquiry-based 5E lessons. Our findings propose that 5E instruction has potential to help teacher candidates make sense of how to create a learning environment to teach science content using students’ cultural background knowledge.

authors_list: Hernandez, A., Pei, J., Nguyen, H., Ludovise, S., & Santagata, R.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Place-based education facilitates understanding of the links between human activities and ecosystems. We outline the design process to integrate local knowledge into Large Language Models (LLMs) chatbots to promote environmental education. We find that chatbot responses vary with chatbot profiles in discussing climate change’s root causes and economic impacts. Our chatbots ask more questions to connect to students, compared to a default LLM. We discuss how to design LLM-based technology to support learning about place.

title: Do Gamers Learn Better From Games? – Insights From Hierarchical Linear Modelling
citation: Kim, C. & Zhang, Q. (2025). Do Gamers Learn Better From Games? – Insights From Hierarchical Linear Modelling. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kim, C. & Zhang, Q.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines how learner characteristics, including gaming experience, prior knowledge, and gender, influence learning gains in game-based learning. Using hierarchical linear modeling, the study found that gaming experience was the strongest predictor of learning outcomes, though marginally significant, while prior knowledge showed the greatest per-unit increase. Gender did not significantly affect outcomes, contradicting some previous findings. These results highlight the nuanced relationship between individual factors and game-based learning, emphasizing the importance of game type and instructional context.

title: Unveiling Learning Dynamics in Nursing Educational Escape Rooms: Insights from Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) Analysis and Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)

authors_list: Kim, C.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: While educational escape rooms (EER) are quickly integrated as widely accepted learning strategies in nursing education, the need to take a learning science approach into its mechanics emerges. Using linguistic inquiry and word count (LIWC) analysis and epistemic network analysis (ENA), this study highlights the learning dynamics among 31 first-year nursing student teams in an escape room themed around sepsis. The results reveal the temporal and cognitive dimensions of students’ interaction in escape rooms.

title: Climate Emotions in a Pre-service Teacher Course on Climate Change
citation: Olsen, E. K., Grzywacz, A. E., & Plummer, J. D. (2025). Climate Emotions in a Pre-Service Teacher Course on Climate Change. abstract: Emotions and their role in climate change education (CCE) is a small but growing area of research. A case study was conducted with pre-service teachers in a course on climate change and their emotional processing throughout the course. Findings highlight that they had emotional growth over the course related to building a classroom community and a relationship with the more-than-human world, as well as emotional interest increasing due to relevant course content.

title: Attending to Teacher Perspective on the Role of Network Visualizations in the Humanities
citation: Dunbar, K. M., Miller, J., Alanís, J., Coenraad, M., Craig, K., Danish, J., & Zhou, M. (2025). Attending to Teacher Perspective on the Role of Network Visualizations in the Humanities. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 270-278). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Dunbar, K. M., Miller, J., Alanís, J., Coenraad, M., Craig, K., Danish, J., & Zhou, M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: To provide students with opportunities to develop data and network literacy in K-12 learning, we aim to understand how to support teachers in their design and implementation of network visualization lessons. This study examines teacher reflections on the enactment of network visualization lessons in middle school humanities classrooms, a relatively nascent field. Teacher adoption of new practices like network visualization requires changes in knowledge and attitudes that are influenced by and have influence on teachers’ implementation of these new strategies. We used Clarke and Hollingsworth’s Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (2002) to identify shifts in teachers’ knowledge and attitudes when implementing these lessons. We found student social and cognitive engagement salient for teachers, impacting their changes in beliefs about network visualizations in the humanities. Findings indicate professional development for network visualization in the humanities should be designed with a focus on student connections and interests as well as curricular alignment.

title: Towards Possibility Discourse: Teacher-Facilitator Interactions in Professional Development Focused on Ambitious Instruction
citation: Hakak-Koll, T., Lefstein, A., & Kolikant, Y. B. (2025). Towards Possibility Discourse: Teacher-Facilitator Interactions in Professional Development Focused on Ambitious Instruction. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2700-2701). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hakak-Koll, T., Lefstein, A., & Kolikant, Y. B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Teachers' assumptions about learning can limit their openness to ambitious instructional practices. Yet professional development research lacks a focus on how these assumptions are challenged through interaction. This study addresses that gap by examining how teacher-facilitator interactions navigate resistance to support possibility discourse—where assumptions are reexamined. Using micro-ethnographic analysis of sessions on controversial classroom issues, we identify two discursive devices: "manage and solve", which closes examination, and "proactive re-authoring", which opens space for rethinking.

title: Where Do Pre-Service Teachers Look at During the Observation of Classroom Videos? A Matter of Salience
citation: Gabel, S. & Gegenfurtner, A. (2025). Where do Pre-Service Teachers Look at During the Observation of Classroom Videos? A Matter of Salience.. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Gabel, S. & Gegenfurtner, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Understanding where pre-service teachers direct their gaze during classroom video observations offers valuable insights into their visual priorities. Using a mixed-methods approach, we analyzed n=45 pre-service teachers’ gaze distribution through eye-tracking technology and retrospective interviews. They prioritized surface-level cues such as teachers’ tone or students’ sitting posture over deeper content-related elements. This highlights the need for trainings to enhance professional vision, directing their attention beyond salient features for a more comprehensive understanding of classroom interactions.

subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Do the positive learning effects spaced interleaving (i.e., mixing problems that require a different solution strategy within an assignment) remain in authentic middle school mathematics classrooms? Our replication study seeks to expand our understanding of interleaving’s potential impact with a larger sample, more diverse educational settings, more realistic time period, and multimodal intervention delivery. We conducted a cluster randomized trial with our sample representing 10 teachers from 6 schools across 3 districts (n = 239 students). Preliminary results from our first cohort (out of three planned) show effects in the predicted direction, with interleaved students performing higher than control students, but the difference is not statistically significant. Though our early-stage study lacks sufficient power to detect small effects, we describe our process of scaling the intervention for this study and contribute to a growing body of research that seeks to understand how to optimally scale learning principles.

abstract: This study explores how participatory research and mentorship enhance critical information literacy (CIL) regarding climate change information. Grounded in socio-constructivist theory, the research involved a Grade 11 student mentor working with Grade 6 students. Findings indicate that through collaborative activities, students developed their knowledge about climate change-related topics and strategies for critically evaluating digital information, demonstrating increased empowerment and engagement.

abstract: This study develops and tests a Large Language Model-based AI framework for analyzing written responses on assessment tasks, generating scoring reasoning, and identifying response uncertainties to provide feedback that supports learning. Using prompt engineering and aggregation methods, the proposed AI models achieved an overall accuracy of 85% when scoring 834 written responses. These findings demonstrate the framework’s potential to enhance the rationale of classroom assessments by providing timely, feedback to improve teaching and learning.

abstract: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) into daily life underscores the need for comprehensive AI literacy education within computer science (CS curricula. In this systematic review, we revealed insights into educational strategies, tools, and evaluation procedures. Our findings highlighted the necessity for a holistic framework that incorporates ethical issues and age-appropriate tools. This study provided recommendations for cultivating AI literacy into CS education and emphasized the necessity for additional research.

abstract: This study explores how sustainability-oriented problem-based learning (PBL) impacts students’ identity. Through twelve interviews with master’s students from three Nordic universities, we identified changes in students’ personal, disciplinary, and professional identities. Our analysis revealed that these identities were impacted in four ways: reinforcing, deepening, broadening or reorienting. Deepening and broadening were the most common, suggesting PBL’s potential in fostering greater self-awareness and a more profound understanding of students’ roles and engagement with societal challenges.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examined higher education students’ attitudes toward F2F learning vs. online learning using a Self-Determination Theory (SDT) framework. Overall, 113 undergraduates completed a 12-item SDT-based questionnaire twice, once for each learning format. Exploratory factor analysis supported the SDT framework. While students’ sense of competence and relatedness were higher for F2F learning, their sense of autonomy was higher for online learning. Specifically, the ability to focus was a barrier to benefit from learning online.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores pre-service teachers’ perceptions of teaching methods for sustainable development. Using focus group interviews, the research investigates holistic, pluralistic, and action-oriented approaches to Education for Sustainable Development (ESD). Thematic content analysis was used to analyze the data. Challenges include aligning sustainability topics with the curriculum, student fatigue, and generating relevant examples. Findings highlight critical thinking, hope, partnership with external partners, and integrating sustainable practices into everyday life.

title: Principles and Practices of Building Teacher Learning Communities
citation: Soundararaj, G. (2025). Principles and Practices of Building Teacher Learning Communities. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: Soundararaj, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This poster examines the design and structure of teacher learning communities as an alternative to traditional professional development (PD) models. Anchored in socio cultural theory and situated cognition, it draws insights from expert interviews to outline key principles of a teacher learning community: rootedness in practice, integration in school culture with flexibility, reliable support structures and sustainability mechanisms. This study contributes to the discourse on teacher learning highlighting the transformative potential of teacher learning communities.

title: Learning about Artificial Intelligence in (an Imagined) Museum Setting: Investigating the Effects of Critical and Everyday Context

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: To investigate how different ways of presenting information about AI affect learning, we conducted an experiment with 200 adults who were asked to imagine visiting a museum and received information about AI in the mining industry. We tested whether adding an everyday AI example or a critical message had an effect on recall, attitudes towards AI, and situational interest. Everyday context negatively affected participants’ information recall. Neither intervention had significant effects on attitudes or interest.

citation: Babichenko, M., Weingarden, M., & Abu Asaad, I. (2025). Ambitious Teaching for Struggling Students: Exploring Teachers’ Problems of Practice. subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Ambitious teaching is essential for fostering deep mathematical understanding, yet many teachers encounter challenges in implementing such practices, particularly with struggling students. Drawing on data from professional learning community meetings of mathematics teachers in three middle schools, this study investigates teachers' problems of practice as they experience ambitious teaching practices in their classrooms. Findings reveal that teachers raised significant concerns about facilitating whole-class discussions. A detailed analysis identified key teachers’ problems of practice, including maintaining student engagement, eliciting diverse solution strategies, and protecting students from being mocked or labeled by peers when sharing incorrect solutions. These findings are discussed in the context of teacher learning processes, highlighting the importance of facilitators and teacher educators being responsive to teachers and aware of their problems of practice.

title: Equity in the Making: Opportunities and Barriers for Productive Engagement in a Primary School Makerspace
citation: Leskinen, J., Kumpulainen, K., & Kajamaa, A. (2025). Equity in the Making: Opportunities and Barriers for Productive Engagement in a Primary School Makerspace. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Leskinen, J., Kumpulainen, K., & Kajamaa, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: School makerspaces are claimed to represent accessible learning environments. Concurrently, concerns are being raised about whether makerspaces serve all students on equal grounds. This study uses nexus analysis to examine social practices that define productive engagement in a school’s makerspace from an equity perspective. Over a year, video interactions of 94 fourth to sixth graders were documented in a makerspace in a primary school in Finland. Preliminary findings highlight three key social practices that were pivotal for productive engagement in the makerspace, thus affecting students’ equal engagement in making: Students’ agency in making, becoming co-directed, and engaging in active knowledge creation. We illustrate these through two case students with attention to situated examples about the opportunities and challenges for productive engagement in the makerspace. The results advocate for tailored pedagogical design strategies to ensure equity in the making.

subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: We present an interdisciplinary design for civic-environmental education in which 7th graders identified environmental issues in their urban communities and imagined solutions. Our analysis of artifacts and discussions found that how students attuned to social justice and expressed agency depended on the conceptualized scale of the issue (local vs. national) and connections to lived experiences. Our study explores speculative approaches as powerful for learning and youth agency for both civic and environmental education.

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have the potential to deliver individualized formative feedback that supports the writing and revision processes. However, more research is needed to understand how to design prompts that generate effective feedback for young adolescents. To address this gap, this study illustrates an approach to integrating learning theory into prompt design to generate feedback that has the potential to improve young adolescents’ conceptual understanding of effective revision in a specific genre. Future directions for research are discussed.

Results of the study share how coaches: partnered with teachers to set goals for instructional improvement and improved upon those goals through programmatic support.

abstract: This study explored how researcher–coach dyads collaborated to create research-based briefs for classroom use. Data from a two-day workshop and dyads’ final products were analyzed using interaction analysis. The dyad’s work illuminated how products and relationships evolved together, fostering ownership and collaboration. These findings inform future researcher–practitioner partnerships and guide facilitation of effective collaborations by highlighting relationship building, agency, and ownership to shape joint work.

abstract: Cross-cultural collaborations are essential to solving complex global health problems like the COVID-19 pandemic. Virtual academic conferences can enable collaboration and facilitate cross-cultural collaborative learning. This study will explore the success of a virtual global health conference as it pertains to cross-cultural collaborative learning from the perspective of student participants and conference designers, in addition to identifying practical considerations for educators designing and implementing similar cross-cultural collaborative learning experiences for medical trainees.

abstract: This paper presents an empirical study of high school teachers’ perspectives on context-based learning about Artificial Intelligence (AI) and data science. Four teachers were interviewed after they had enacted a curriculum contextualized in healthcare. The data were coded for teachers’ perspectives on what students learned; on the kinds of tasks that engaged students; and on the challenges and needs in teaching and learning about these fields. While context-based learning has the potential to promote students’ career awareness and appreciation of AI and data science, future research needs to examine how best to sequence and structure tasks to help students develop requisite knowledge and how best to curate complex data sets.

abstract: This study examines researcher-practitioner collaborations in educational research, using Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) to analyze interactions between STEM coaches and researchers. It explores a two-day workshop focused on practitioner-identified challenges. The research highlighted the need to shift from researcher-centric approaches to balanced, collaborative methods. This study provides insights for developing bidirectional learning models that center practitioners' perspectives, aiming to bridge the gap between research and educational practice through more equitable and transformative partnerships.

subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Knowledge brokers play an essential role in bridging research and practice and mobilizing knowledge. Yet, literature offers little guidance and few examples for people and organizations engaging with educational systems in this capacity. Drawing on literature and our extensive knowledge brokerage experience, we address this gap and introduce the Learn, Illuminate, Nucleate, and Communicate (LINC) knowledge mobilization framework for knowledge brokers. We explain framework components and give examples from our project.

title: “I was debating and now I’m on board”: Supporting Shifts in Teacher Uptake of Computational Modeling in Science Classrooms
citation: Wagh, A., Mesiner, J. E., & Wendel, D. (2025). “I Was Debating and Now I’m on Board”: Supporting Shifts in Teacher Uptake of Computational Modeling in Science Classrooms. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: There is a need to examine how to support teacher uptake of computational modeling in science classrooms. This poster presents code-the-familiar modeling to foster teacher uptake of computational modeling using code. Drawing on a case study of two high school teachers from a research-practice partnership, we examine data from professional development and interviews to illustrate how teachers shift in their uptake, and share two lessons learned: Supporting bite-sized changes and leaning into teachers’ conceptual expertise.

title: Weaving Knowledges: Digital Technology Pedagogy as Situated Community Practices
citation: Jimenez, E. S. (2025). Weaving Knowledges: Digital Technology Pedagogy as Situated Community Practices. authors_list: Jimenez, E. S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This ethnographic study explores how Indigenous teachers and communities in Oaxaca, Mexico, design digital pedagogies that are grounded in local social, cultural, and linguistic knowledge systems. These approaches challenge dominant educational technology frameworks by reimagining digital pedagogies as situated, relational, and community-centered practices, challenging assumptions that frame Indigeneity as incompatible with technological innovation. This research contributes to conversations on the politics of learning with digital technologies by advancing place-based, community-grounded pedagogical designs.

citation: Lee, V. R. & Nomura, N. (2025). Interpretive Discourse of Data Visualizations: An Exploratory Case Study From a Middle School English Language Arts Classroom. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lee, V. R. & Nomura, N.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: We report findings from an exploratory case study in a middle-school classroom that illustrates the use of a data visualization to support English Language Arts (ELA) learning outcomes. Students used visualizations of sentence length before and after reading a short story. Students not only initially noticed features of the data visualization, but they also immediately proposed explanations for those features without being able to situate those features in the story, advancing possible causal explanations before aligning the story to the visualization. This case illustrates an additional pathway for interpretive discourse that integrates story and data visualization and suggests a larger opportunity space for interpretative data discussion research in the future.

title: The Interrelated Nature of Belonging and Self-Assessments in Computing Students’ Decisions to Persist

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Fasiang, K., Chen, M., & O’Rourke, E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Understanding small moments that influence students’ decisions to leave CS is crucial for supporting diverse participation. Research has found that students’ sense of belonging and perceptions of their ability affect persistence, but how students develop these perceptions in specific moments is less clear. We analyzed how eight introductory CS students discussed their belonging and self-assessments during common programming moments, showing how these factors are intertwined and arise from shared underlying experiences.

title: The Connected Spaces Dashboard: Capturing Productive Resistance Through Design Based Research
citation: Hopping, D. A. & Tissenbaum, M. (2025). The Connected Spaces Dashboard: Capturing Productive Resistance Through Design Based Research. abstract: The Connected Spaces (CxS) project aims to foster communities of practice between disparate makers through a suite of co-constructed technologies. This study focuses on one of those technologies, the CxS Dashboard, as a useful case study in Design Based Research (DBR). Through a systematic process of mapping students’ resistances and researchers’ accommodations, our DBR approach allowed us to make rapid, theoretically-backed adjustments to the technology in order to refine and evaluate it in context.

title: Challenges of Integrating ChatGPT into EFL Writing: An Activity Theory Framework
citation: Jung, J., Joo, S., Park, H., & Han, I. (2025). Challenges of Integrating ChatGPT Into Efl Writing: An Activity Theory Framework. abstract: This study explores EFL students' challenges with ChatGPT in English writing tasks through Activity Theory analysis. Thirteen university students completed two writing tasks and interviews. Findings reveal primary contradictions (need for additional tools, ChatGPT version inconsistencies); secondary contradictions (feedback discrepancies, low proficiency limiting feedback utilization, trust issues, ethical concerns, ChatGPT dependence, culturally insensitive feedback, and limitations compared to human feedback); and a quaternary contradiction regarding structured AI tool education. Implications include balancing AI use with independent practice, establishing educational frameworks for AI tools, and maintaining human instruction alongside AI implementation.

title: ABCDE: An Action-Oriented Framework for Collaborative Activities
citation: Lin, G. C., Stevens, C., Toutziaridi, A. C., Ravi, P., & Anderson, E. (2025). ABCDE: An Action-Oriented Framework for Collaborative Activities. authors_list: Lin, G. C., Stevens, C., Toutziaridi, A. C., Ravi, P., & Anderson, E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Although group work is a common classroom practice, understanding how students collaborate during these activities remain complex. In this paper, we introduce the ABCDE framework, which outlines five essential actions learners can take—and teachers can encourage—to foster an inclusive environment for sharing ideas and deepening understanding. Specifically, A represents agreeing, B represents building on ideas, C represents chatting, D represents differing perspectives, and E represents eliciting responses or actions. We demonstrate the framework’s application in two distinct scenarios: one with high schoolers participating in a data science activity, and the other with adults involved in a team-building survival exercise. The framework successfully revealed distinct interaction patterns in these activities.

title: Articulating Ideologies of Power and Epistemological Assumptions to Construct Deficit Perspectives About Learners

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We contribute to research on STEM teachers’ sensemaking about classroom events by investigating how teachers’ construction of students as bearers of learning deficits relies on the articulation of ideologies of social difference and epistemological assumptions.

title: Seeds of Algebraic Thinking When Programming a Motorized Swing
citation: López, M. A. & Xu, G. (2025). Seeds of Algebraic Thinking When Programming a Motorized Swing. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2786-2788). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: López, M. A. & Xu, G.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This case study examines the seeds of algebraic thinking that a fifth grader used in a programming task. By reviewing video data and interviews, we showcase how the student used two seeds of algebraic thinking to program the movement of a swing: closing-in and more x, more y. Our findings illustrate how programming tasks can elicit early algebraic thinking and provide meaningful contexts for developing foundational mathematical concepts.

title: Exploring the Path to Assessment Reform: Transforming Teachers’ Perspectives Through Insights into Students' Thought Processes
citation: Ikeda, Y., Masukawa, H., Shirouzu, H., Iikubo, S., & Saito, M. (2025). Exploring the Path to Assessment Reform: Transforming Teachers’ Perspectives Through Insights Into Students' Thought Processes. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2789-2791). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ikeda, Y., Masukawa, H., Shirouzu, H., Iikubo, S., & Saito, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores how focusing on students’ cognitive processes can help teachers rethink assessment design. In a professional development workshop, high school teachers examined student thinking using data collected during test-taking. Their reflections provided insights that facilitated the alignment of assessments with instructional goals and deeper learning. The findings highlight the potential of using student cognition to bridge the gap between instruction and testing, ultimately enhancing classroom practices.

title: Pedagogical Responsibility in the Age of AI: Preservice Teachers’ Reasoning About Automated Scoring Technologies
citation: Watkins, J. (2025). Pedagogical Responsibility in the Age of Ai: Preservice Teachers’ Reasoning About Automated Scoring Technologies. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 279-287). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Watkins, J.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: The use of AI for automated scoring of student work has been positioned as both transformative for and damaging to ambitious and equitable teaching. Yet throughout these debates, teachers’ voices have been noticeably absent. This paper considers how preservice teachers reason about the use of AI for assessing students’ science models. Within a teacher education course on science modeling, students discussed current literature on machine learning methods for assessment. Drawing on discourse analysis, I highlight how students made sense of the ideological, axiological, epistemological, and ontological dimensions of their role as future educators alongside their meaning making about the use of AI. The students alternately position AI as a “useful tool” for, “replica” of, or “unproductive barrier” to teachers’ work. With this analysis, I argue that supporting teacher learning about these technologies should involve helping them develop their pedagogical judgment about not just how, but whether these tools should be used.

title: “Biological Controls Will Best Your Beasties!”: Visitor Learning at Outreach Events in Novel Informal Learning Spaces
citation: Lundgren, L., Jahani, Z., Mychajliw, A., Swafford, A., Pask, G., & Santos, G.
