In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2792-2794). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lundgren, L., Jahani, Z., Mychajliw, A., Swafford, A., Pask, G., & Santos, G.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Concepts central to scientific understanding, including evolution, species distribution, and the effects of invasive species, are often misunderstood by or are unappealing to non-practicing scientists. Such limited interest in science can pose challenges in developing a science-literate populace. Connecting peoples’ existing interests to science topics might alleviate scientific illiteracy. We describe three instances of public outreach which occurred at two comic cons and a brewery in which scientists helped people connect their existing interest in pop culture to science topics. We collected responses from audiences following each event, finding that audiences were somewhat able to connect science with their existing interests. Situating science to align with peoples’ existing interests might be a solution for increasing science literacy.

title: Pre-Service Teachers and Co-construction of Pedagogical Terminology
citation: Novelli, M. & Azevedo, F. S. (2025). Pre-Service Teachers and Co-Construction of Pedagogical Terminology. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2795-2797). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Novelli, M. & Azevedo, F. S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We show three examples of terms that create situations of discursive contestation for pre-service teachers using data from a larger project. The ways that the pre-service teachers construct their meanings independently or communally is described. This work has implications for teacher education and the importance of training pre-service teachers to be flexible in their understanding of and approach to the role of teacher.

title:
A Scoping Review of Interdisciplinary Learning Research 
in Higher Education Contexts

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Naganuma, S., Shoji, G., & Oshima, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study conducted a scoping review on 19 interdisciplinary education/learning research articles in higher education contexts. Citation network analysis and qualitative analysis revealed that 1) the articles were categorized into three clusters, 2) only 14 articles were cited more than twice, and 3) each cluster cited different articles with different focuses. These findings suggest that interdisciplinary education/learning research is in the phase of establishing shared vocabularies and engaging with conceptual tools.

title: Design-Based Research for Scenario-Based, Generative AI-Augmented Simulation in Nursing Education
citation: Kim, J., Galindo-Parra, M. F., Kim, S., Bae, Y., Hendry, T. M., Galen, S. S., & Kim, M. K. (2025). subject: Interdisciplinary & General

abstract: Simulation-based learning is vital in nursing education but faces scalability and authenticity challenges. This study explores using generative AI as a role-playing agent in nursing simulations. Using a design-based research approach, we developed an evaluation framework and question set to evaluate AI model performance. Findings highlight accurate role-based dialogue but limitations in common-sense reasoning. Recommendations include clearer evaluation criteria, diverse question sets to comprehensively evaluate ambiguity handling, and refining scenarios iteratively for consistency and clarity.

title: Developing Active Learning Pedagogy in Teacher Candidates: Bridging Theory to Future Practice
citation: Burron, G., Cavalcante, A., & Slotta, J. D. (2025). Developing Active Learning Pedagogy in Teacher Candidates: Bridging Theory to Future Practice. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Burron, G., Cavalcante, A., & Slotta, J. D.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study explores active learning pedagogies in a Secondary-Level Math Pedagogy course at a large teacher’s training faculty in Canada. Using the ICAP Framework, the research presents various active learning activities to develop teacher candidates' (TCs) active learning pedagogy. Observations and interviews reveal that smaller activities, such as problem-solving on whiteboards and mind-mapping, effectively engage TCs. Larger activities, like a Collatz Conjecture Representation activity, create authentic mathematical problems that provide deep, interactive, and domain-specific active learning experiences. The study suggests that simple, adaptable activities can significantly prepare TCs for implementing active learning in their future classrooms.

title: Educator-Learner Interactions in Failure-Based Problem-Solving During STEM Activities: Patterns in Solo and Group Contexts
citation: Ruisi, J., Simpson, A., & Paul, K. (2025). Educator-Learner Interactions in Failure-Based Problem-Solving During STEM Activities: Patterns in Solo and Group Contexts. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ruisi, J., Simpson, A., & Paul, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The purpose of this study was to examine common failure problem-solving patterns within one learner-one educator interactions (i.e., solo) and many learners-one educator interactions (i.e., group) when experiencing failure moments during STEM activities in museum settings. The results of this study indicate that educators engage in the problem-solving process more cyclically than learners, regardless of context. In addition, educators and learner(s) engage in the failure-based problem-solving cycle together with no clear divide between roles.

title: Parents’ Information Seeking for Children’s STEM Learning
citation: Kim, S. H., Choi, G. W., Kang, J. H., & Kasar, M. (2025). Parents’ Information Seeking for Children’s STEM Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2810-2812). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kim, S. H., Choi, G. W., Kang, J. H., & Kasar, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: An understanding of information sources parents find useful and trustworthy can inform the development of supplementary learning materials for at-home STEM kits. This study investigates types of information sources parents seek out to support their children’s STEM learning at home and their perceived level of trust for the information sources. Through participants’ information horizons map, follow-up interviews, and surveys, preliminary findings demonstrate that information sources that were frequently used were not always the sources that were trusted. Implications for supplementary materials for at-home STEM kits that align with parents’ information seeking practices are discussed.

title: Curiosity Portals: Designing Entryways for Tangible Exploration
citation: Kshirsagar, K., Horn, M. S., & Worsley, M. (2025). Curiosity Portals: Designing Entryways for Tangible Exploration. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2813-2815). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kshirsagar, K., Horn, M. S., & Worsley, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Curiosity is a fundamental human drive that propels exploration, discovery, and learning. While extensively studied, a gap remains in understanding how curiosity is sparked in social settings during initial interactions with tangible objects. This research introduces the concept of Curiosity Portals as a framework for designing and understanding these initial moments of curiosity. Through interviews with staff, artists, and attendees at the Metro Independent Comics Expo (MICE), the study identifies configurations of invitational entryways or "portals" that catalyze curiosity. These portals, categorized as sensorial, novel, accessible, social, and aesthetic, are shaped by the distinct curiosities of each participant group. The study reveals how these portals foster curiosity by providing opportunities for hands-on engagement, surprise, social interaction, and exploration. The proposed framework provides a toolkit to understand and leverage these entry points of curiosity to enhance the design of tactile objects and playthings to foster continuous exploration and deeper learning.

title: Toward a Method for Visualizing Interactional Copresence
citation: Chapman, K. C. & Metts, E. (2025). Toward a Method for Visualizing Interactional Copresence. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: Chapman, K. C. & Metts, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This poster presents a provocation for methodological advancements in qualitative inquiry into spatial pedagogy. Using classroom data that includes student talk during groupwork sessions and a dynamic map of teacher location, we offer several visualizations to invite speculation about how we might amend these tools to think more deeply about the joint accomplishment of copresence in classrooms.

title: Co-Constructing Research Questions with Informal Practitioners within a Networked Improvement Community

authors_list: Penney, L., Anderson, A., Simpson, A., Bijur, J., Garcia, D., & Maltese, A. V.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Through a collaboration among six informal learning organizations and a research team across the United States, our goal was to consider how to engage parents, caregivers, and classroom teachers as facilitators of learning with their children when experiencing failure within making activities. In this paper, we describe how we worked together to develop research questions that recognize the complexity of collaborating with organizations that have different ideas, theories of change, and organizational capacity. We further highlight this through sharing the journey of one organization, Creative Reuse Center. We intend for this paper to serve as an example for building partnerships focused on solving problems of practice according to practitioners’ needs rather than researchers’ interests.

title: Designing Supports for Science Teachers to Integrate Mathematics into Storyline Science Units
citation: McElhaney, K. W., Hodkowski, N. M., McMahon, L., Henson, K., Penuel, W. R., Jacobs, J., & Baker, A. (2025). abstract: We examine what professional learning (PL) experiences and resources can support middle school science teachers to integrate mathematics powerfully in storyline science units. We describe the design of PL activities and resources aimed to help teachers integrate mathematics reasoning into storyline science instruction. An analysis of teacher questions and questionnaires from the PL workshop illustrate potential benefits of the resources to teachers.

title: Cultural Context and Participation in Online Learning Communities in Post-Secondary Environments
citation: Davey, R. (2025). Cultural Context and Participation in Online Learning Communities in Post-Secondary Environments. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2825-2827). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Davey, R.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Critical to success in online education is the ability for students to navigate online spaces and to participate in learning communities. If pedagogical characteristics of online learning environments emphasize, and rely upon, interaction and collaboration (Garrison et al., 2000), it is critical to examine digital spaces and resulting online learning communities for cultural inclusivity. This systematic literature review outlines some of the arguments for using critical pedagogy to design online learning communities that are inclusive of diverse learners, creating space for multiple epistemologies and cultural contexts. It will begin with a brief outline of the search strategy used to source fifteen peer-reviewed journal articles, followed by benefits and challenges for students from non-dominant cultural contexts.

title: Fostering Reflective Practice for Addressing Social Justice in Education: Experiences with Preservice Teachers
citation: Bailie, A. L. & Gebre, E. (2025). Fostering Reflective Practice for Addressing Social Justice in Education: Experiences With Preservice Teachers. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bailie, A. L. & Gebre, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In Canada, social justice and reflective practice have been crucial elements of preservice teacher education. However, recent challenges have underscored the need to rethink how teacher education can effectively address inequities and injustices within the education system. The aim of this study was to examine the focus and levels of preservice teachers (PSTs) reflections in a social justice-oriented foundation of education course. Analysis of 13 portfolios indicated that intentionally designing courses allowed PSTs to promote diversity, question privileges, and be aware of injustices, together with articulating a commitment to action.

title: If The Field of Black Digital Humanities (Black DH) Speaks to the Learning Sciences
citation: Bayeck, R. Y. (2025). If the Field of Black Digital Humanities (Black Dh) Speaks to the Learning Sciences. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bayeck, R. Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The field of learning sciences is increasingly concerned about issues of power, equity, and justice. Though researchers can draw on theoretical frameworks such as critical race theory, (CRT), this paper argues that the emerging field of Black Digital Humanities (Black DH) can also provide the field with additional perspectives that can further help the field understand and develop approaches that continue to address issues of race, power, equity, and justice in the learning sciences. I write to seed a meaningful conversation among scholars in these fields as we collectively aim to center the learner in our research,design, and practices.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: : Education research has argued in epistemic terms for the value of debates in science classrooms; here, we consider the social dynamics and how they impact students’ engagement with uncertainty. We draw on 14 interviews of students in an upper-level undergraduate biochemistry course. The results suggest complexity and nuance to the value of debates in science classes.

abstract: Learning is a dynamic and social process involving various relationships that unfold over time. Current analytical network models in Learning Sciences, grounded in classical graph theory, are inherently restricted to modeling pairwise relationships in learning. This study proposes the use of temporal hypergraph approach to Learning Sciences, a framework that enables the dynamic analysis of many-body interactions in learning contexts.

abstract: This pilot study explores how preservice teachers engage with paper-pencil, systems dynamic, and block-based computational models during a two-week science methods course. Despite recognizing the benefits of computational modeling, participants preferred paper-pencil models for future teaching. Data from screencasts and questionnaires revealed challenges in using computational tools to represent scientific concepts and suggested that static paper-pencil models may limit scaffolding for systems modeling. Findings highlight the need for scalable professional development in diverse modeling practices.

title: Learning on the Move: Ljavek’s Indigenous Mobilities and Relationalities in Taiwan’s Urban Spaces
citation: Hou, Y. S. (2025). Learning on the Move: Ljavek’s Indigenous Mobilities and Relationalities in Taiwan’s Urban Spaces. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2843-2845). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hou, Y. S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This project centers the intergenerational teaching and learning practices necessary within Indigenous sovereignties during forced and coerced relocation and displacement, collaborating with Ljavek, a Paiwan Indigenous community in Taiwan. Globally, Indigenous mobilities are shaped by ongoing settler colonialism that perpetuates Indigenous erasure and elimination, but Indigenous mobilities are also informed by Indigenous agency, self-determination, and survivance that re-makes relational structures to ensure the flourishing of communities, lands, and waters. Displaced by urban expansion, Ljavek resisted relocation through legal trials, built a Paiwan community on lands and waters that they were not familiar with, and created kinships that subverted capitalistic pressures and perpetuated Paiwan languages and cultural practices. By working alongside Ljavek and informed by Indigenous Research Methodologies and Participatory Action Research, this qualitative research project expands definitions of where learning takes place and what constitutes learning by focusing on learning in resistance, community building, partnerships, and placemaking.

title: Long and Winding Road to Coconstructing Knowledge in Design-Based Research Practice Partnerships

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Barak, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Boundary Crossing & Brokerage; Design-Based Research (DBR); Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: Design-based research-practice partnerships (RPPs) bridge research and practice through shared design and knowledge co-construction. This paper examines two frameworks – design cycles and boundary crossing – while arguing they often understate inherent conflicts. Analysis of RPP data reveals how conflicts are minimized, sometimes marginalizing perspectives. Two additional frameworks – the narrative fiction act and the crossroad – are introduced as metaphors to understand discord's transformative potential in strengthening collaboration and promoting inclusive knowledge co-construction in design-based RPPs.

title: Balancing Infrastructural Constraints and Learning Goals during the Redesign of Games
citation: Laina, V. & Mayrhofer, J. (2025). Balancing Infrastructural Constraints and Learning Goals During the Redesign of Games. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Laina, V. & Mayrhofer, J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Despite the potential benefits of game-based learning, infrastructural constraints often prevent educators from introducing it in classrooms. We were interested in understanding how student teachers balance learning objectives and infrastructural constraints when redesigning games for secondary mathematics. Preliminary findings suggest that student teachers might sometimes lead their redesign efforts with those constraints, rather than with learning goals. This has implications for how teacher training programs can empower and support student teachers’ capacity for instructional innovation.

title: BlockTalk: GenAI Simulations for Conversational Debugging Practice
citation: Haduong, P., Yu, B., Shen, M., Gerami, B., & Brennan, K. (2025). BlockTalk: GenAI Simulations for Conversational Debugging Practice. abstract: Conversing with students about challenges is central to the work of teaching computing through opportunities to create self-directed and open-ended programming projects. We introduce BlockTalk, a generative AI tool for teachers to practice conversational debugging through simulations. Our exploratory analysis examines teachers’ interactions with the AI and offers insights for debugging pedagogy.

title: How Individual Preparation Before Collaboration Shapes Learners’ Verbal Communication Patterns: An Epistemic Network Analysis​
citation: Chen, W., Zheng, L., Chen, X., & Ho, M. (2025). How Individual Preparation Before Collaboration Shapes Learners’ Verbal Communication Patterns: An Epistemic Network Analysis​. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2855-2857). abstract: This study examines how individual preparation (IP) before collaboration influences learners’ verbal communication during collaborative learning. By comparing immediate collaboration with collaboration following IP, this study employed the Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) to investigate the differences in learners’ verbal discourse patterns. The results indicate that while IP before collaboration fosters more structured communication, marked by enhanced task coordination and responsiveness, it reduces spontaneous negotiation. The findings suggest a trade-off between structured preparedness and flexibility, with implications for optimizing collaborative learning design.

authors_list: Duvall, M., Li, H., Li, Y., Liu, R., Shah, H., & Zhong, Z.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Game-based learning can effectively engage students. However, teachers have difficulty evaluating educational video games (EVGs). Dube and colleagues proposed five benchmarks for the descriptions of learning apps. Independently, we developed the Teacher Lens for Digital Relevance (TLDR) evaluation model for EVG play. We compared the descriptions versus game play of four award-winning EVGs. While the descriptions included all Dube’s benchmarks, game play ratings differed. For EVGs, teachers should consider both the description and the play experience.

title: Discourse and Disability: Understanding Special Education Talk in Science
citation: Conrath, B., McCausland, J., Winters, G., Jacobson, E., & McDonald, S. P. (2025). Discourse and Disability: Understanding Special Education Talk in Science. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Conrath, B., McCausland, J., Winters, G., Jacobson, E., & McDonald, S. P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Engaging in discourse is central to students developing scientific knowledge. However, how students with disabilities engage in productive talk remains understudied. We analyze a case of two middle school special education students as they participate in an online plate tectonics curriculum. Analysis suggests explicit discussion-based instruction sparks more productive science talk and sensemaking than side-by-side and contrary to deficit stereotypes, students with disabilities can engage in meaningful discourse around scientific ideas.

title: Efficacy of Dialogic Teaching for Learning with Multiple Representation Simulations in Secondary Physics Classrooms
citation: Jia, W. & Chen, G. (2025). Efficacy of Dialogic Teaching for Learning With Multiple Representation Simulations in Secondary Physics Classrooms. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jia, W. & Chen, G.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study investigated how dialogic teaching supports physics learning with multiple representation simulations. Three secondary teachers and their 268 students were recruited from China with a two-month intervention. The present results indicated that teachers in the treatment groups employed more various talk moves than comparison groups. Students in the treatment had significantly higher discursive engagement and positive emotional engagement than the comparison group. The findings contributed to the effectiveness of dialogic teaching on multiple representations.

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Xia, Y. & Zheng, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This poster presents a single-case study where teacher praise failed to provide emotional support to the students. We found this failure occurred because the teacher’s recognition of the speaker’s identity misaligned with the students’ perception of her role. This poster shows students are particularly sensitive to peer identities, particularly “representative” ones. If teachers ignore this, it may result in failing to offer praise.

International Society of the Learning Sciences.

subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Electrodermal activity (EDA) is a widely used psychophysiological measure given its sensitivity to cognitive and affective processes via sympathetic arousal. Although interest in this data modality for studying learning processes has been boosted by the advances in biosensors, its research tradition spans over a century. In this work, we systematically review the empirical literature using EDA in the learning sciences from both theoretical (e.g., frameworks and constructs) and methodological (e.g., collection and analysis) perspectives.

title: The Practitioner's Voice in Co-Design: Agentic Boundary Crossing

authors_list: Adams, R. & Charles, E. S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Boundary Crossing & Brokerage; Design-Based Research (DBR); Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: Practitioner knowledge is essential to the success of co-design teams. This case study reports on a teacher’s role within a design-based research team, over four projects spanning a decade. Using a boundary crossing lens, the analysis describes the change from passive to active co-designer involving the use of boundary objects and agentic actions. Findings contribute to the growing literature on teachers as boundary spanners and their roles in making educational change sustainable.

title: Where Do We Start And Where Do We Go? Emerging Findings Informing the Design of Responsive Professional Learning With Secondary Science Teachers
citation: Krist, C., Hall, K., Hoang, N., Hug, B., Ko, M. M., Lauren, L. H., Leonardi, N., Suárez, E., & Wingert, K. (2025). Where do we Start and Where do we Go? abstract: This poster examines secondary science teachers’ curricular adaptation work during summer workshops as part of the EMPOWER project, which supports teachers in adapting their curriculum to foster students’ epistemic and critical science agency. Through a comparative case study, we demonstrate how two teacher teams started with different goals but each navigated tensions between connecting goals for epistemic agency (EA) and cultural relevance and responsiveness (CRR) in both the content and the moment-to-moment interactions of their focal lessons. Their varied trajectories underscore the importance of supporting teachers in toggling between these dimensions when designing justice-oriented science curricula.

title: Building Student Epistemic Practices through Curriculum Design:  Investigating Learning Outcomes and Engagement
citation: Yang, Z., Yoon, S. A., Chinn, C. A., Hunkar, K., Hussain-Abidi, H., & Noushad, N. F. (2025). Building Student Epistemic Practices Through Curriculum Design: Investigating Learning Outcomes and Engagement. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 288-296). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Yang, Z., Yoon, S. A., Chinn, C. A., Hunkar, K., Hussain-Abidi, H., & Noushad, N. F.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: As scientific advancements grow more complex, the public increasingly struggles to critically evaluate scientific claims, partly due to limited understanding of how scientific knowledge is generated, validated, and applied. To address this challenge, science education has sought to embed epistemic practices (EP) into curricula, equipping students with the skills to make informed decisions on real-world scientific issues. However, while empirical studies have examined the impact of such curricula on students’ use of EP, few have utilized open-ended assessments within contextualized scenarios. To address this gap, we developed a contextualized scenario to assess the impact of a science curriculum on students’ epistemic practices. Pre- and post-implementation data from 75 high school students were analyzed to answer two questions: (1) Does the curriculum enhance students’ engagement in EP? and (2) Does it lead to measurable gains in EP skills? Findings provide empirical evidence that the curriculum significantly improved students’ epistemic practices.

citation: Manchester, E. J. & Sheridan, K. M. (2025). How do Libraries, Archives, and Museums Portray Learning? A Discourse Analysis of Mission and Vision Statements. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Manchester, E. J. & Sheridan, K. M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Approaches to learning in library, archive, and museum (LAM) spaces vary and institutional barriers make it challenging to design connected learning experiences involving more than one type of LAM. To support the design of high-quality educational experiences, this discourse analysis investigates learning in LAMs as portrayed by their mission and vision statements. The analysis reveals that libraries, archives, and museums use similar linguistic strategies to construct rhetorical communities along geographic, disciplinary, and interest-driven lines. Libraries and archives differed from museums in that they positioned themselves as conduits to learning resources rather than as direct providers of learning experiences. Shared elements of organizational discourses around learning present promising starting points for conversation and collaboration.

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Im, S., Kim, M. K., & Heo, J.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This review examines digital literacy in physical education (PE), an underexplored area despite increasing technological integration. We address three key questions: (1) What theoretical frameworks are used? (2) How is digital literacy reported in PE? (3) What areas need further development? A systematic review of 12 studies shows digital literacy in PE is mainly framed through digital literacy and digital competence models. While overall levels were moderate to high, disparities emerged by gender, grade level, and experience. Key barriers include inadequate professional development and a lack of standardized assessment tools. This review highlights the need for targeted training and objective evaluation methods to better capture digital literacy in PE.

citation: Tehee, M., Litts, B. K., Parry, D., Baggaley, S., Jenkins, J., Cardona-Rivera, R. E., Quayle, K., & Cawley, J. (2025). abstract: Issues of (mis)representation of cultures across K-12 education remain a challenge, especially for representations of Indigenous communities. As a team of Tribal knowledge holders, K-12 educators, cultural technologists, and university researchers, we created a cultural representation and teaching resources to support respectful stewardship of Indigenous representations in classroom learning. In this poster, we share insights from our design and implementation process of an Indigenous-created digital interactive narrative experience, Pemmican Experience, for K-12 classrooms.

title: Exploring Teachers’ Value Beliefs about AI in K-12 Education

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Park, J., Bae, H., Zhao, Y., & Walton, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) technology advances rapidly, teachers are required to critically assess and incorporate it into their classrooms. However, since teachers have concerns and biases about AI’s role in education, they hesitate to adopt AI. Teachers’ value beliefs are thought to have a positive influence on their technology integration. Exploring in-service teachers’ value beliefs about AI in K-12 education, this study identified how they evaluate AI and how they want to use AI pedagogically.

abstract: Open-source software development is a longstanding form of collaboration in the technology sector. As high school teachers, we explore the open-source model as a pedagogical framework, building on our work in a graduate-level Knowledge Building course at the Ontario Institute for Studies in Education. We suggest that framing computer science education around the open-source model can support pervasive and authentic knowledge building discourses, by producing explicit artifacts made accessible to the local community and beyond to support continual idea improvement.

abstract: This study investigates the challenges programming beginners face when using Generative AI to describe coding intentions. We analyzed data from 120 students where students described problems, and AI generated code. Performance was evaluated across 48 tasks in eight categories using metrics. Our findings indicate that tasks in the “dictionaries” category are the most challenging for beginners. Additionally, we identified recurring interaction issues such as ambiguous instructions, assumptions about AI understanding, and misalignment with code logic.

abstract: This poster reports on a co-design research partnership between a sixth grade English teacher and a learning scientist to create a table-top roleplaying game (TTRPG) for a U.S. classroom. The goals of the codesign were to support critical engagement around power structures in ways that supported “moves to elsewhere” (Davis et al., 2020) for youth players. Findings discuss how game design choices such as word limits and the removal of the teacher as the narrator envisioned making space for youth to engage in processes of collaborative and consequential decision-making.

citation: Zhang, Y. & Chen, G. (2025). Knowing for Using: Tracking Mathematics Preservice Teachers’ Knowledge of Dialogic Teaching in a Semester-Long Pd Program. abstract: Dialogic teaching pedagogy is widely acknowledged for its effectiveness in orchestrating meaningful discussions in mathematics classrooms. However, mathematics preservice teachers (MPSTs) often lack the knowledge to structure mathematical discussions, resulting in teacher-dominated classrooms. This study seeks to monitor the process of acquiring knowledge in dialogic teaching through three knowledge tests conducted during a semester-long professional development (PD) program for MPSTs. The study involved a group of 39 Chinese MPSTs. The findings revealed a positive trend in the acquisition of dialogic teaching knowledge among participants. Those MPSTs who received targeted training and guidance in dialogic teaching demonstrated significant improvement in the knowledge tests compared to their peers. This study represents an initial attempt to examine the changes in teacher knowledge related to dialogic teaching within PD initiatives. It underscores the importance of incorporating knowledge assessments to enhance the development of initial teacher education programs.

authors_list: Dixon, P., Sieprawski, K., Tang, A., & Lira, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We used student-generated drawings to assess students’ understandings of dynamic equilibrium. A pre-/post-design was used to determine how students track physical quantities across time and space. Initial and final subsystem drawings revealed conceptual dynamics depicting entities in dynamic equilibrium. The findings suggest students productively extracted quantitative information from a computational simulation but in a spatially fragmented fashion. These findings underscore the potential of drawing assessments that determine how students understand quantified complex systems.

citation: Mabadeje, Y. A., Dunphy, M., & Ramey, K. E. (2025). “I Didn’t Know I Was Into Birds”: Understanding Students' Perceptions of Nature-Based Learning. authors_list: Mabadeje, Y. A., Dunphy, M., & Ramey, K. E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This qualitative study ventures into the wilds of nature-based learning (NBL). Despite documented health and academic outcomes of NBL, students’ perspectives on its challenges and benefits are underexplored. To bridge this gap, we examined students’ views through qualitative surveys and focus group interviews during a weeklong NBL program. Guided by experiential and situated learning theories, we analyzed survey responses and focus group interviews from 140 fifth and sixth grade students. We identified three major themes for benefits: connectedness with nature, exploration and freedom, and interest and skill development. For challenges, themes included: physical demands, preparation and logistics, and discomfort. The study concludes with recommendations for implementation strategies to support positive student experiences.

abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) presents remarkable prospects for education, but its impact on students' thinking processes remains largely unexplored. This research explores the thinking processes of 20 students when programming supported by GAI. Twenty participants recorded hour-long programming sessions with GAI and submitted reflection reports on key interactions and challenges. We developed an AI-augmented thinking framework based on the screen recordings (including chat history with GAI). In reflection reports, students identified prompt skills, programming knowledge, and debugging skills as key factors influencing AI-augmented thinking in programming. This study contributes to the theoretical and practical understanding of students’ thinking processes when supported by GAI.

abstract: The study describes the design and evaluation of a measurement for analytical thinking to judge news credibility in simulated social media contexts. With responses from 94 university students, we generated Kernel density estimation plots and regression models to evaluate the construct validity of the instrument. We conclude by discussing further instrument revisions and the complexity of analytical thinking in social media contexts.

citation: Tanabashi, S. (2025). Fostering Ethical Thinking for a Peaceful Society Through Dark Heritage and Objects for Cross-Disciplinary Learning in Japan. abstract: To design and establish a sustainable, peaceful society, peace museums which are dark heritage sites, can serve as learning materials to foster ethical thinking in peace education. This study developed an object-based learning approach that utilizes dark heritage sites and nuclear experiments for cross-disciplinary learning. Findings suggested that object-based learning, through the use of dark heritage and related objects, fosters ethical thinking in education for peace.

citation: McElhaney, K. W., Yang, H., Jain, S., & Basu, S. (2025). Adapting the Use-Decode-Modify-Create Framework for Teacher Professional Learning About STEM-Based Computational Activities. abstract: To effectively facilitate integrated STEM and computing instruction, K-12 teachers must support students’ engagement in computational practices. In interviews, teachers indicated that exploring simulations and evaluating code were helpful scaffolds for learning to construct computational models. Teachers also identified the need for additional supports for code interpretation and evaluation.

abstract: We explored how non-STEM majors reason while programming geometric patterns in Scratch. Participants (a) used recursive reasoning to transform patterns into manipulable forms via visual cues and (b) applied nested loops to expand patterns across distant cases. Fraction-based reasoning emerged while adjusting proportions to refine pattern components.

abstract: Acquiring vocabulary is an essential but daunting part of learning a new language, therefore impacting students’ motivation. Words vary in difficulty (e.g., similarity or dissimilarity to known words). This study compares different wordlist strategies for learning easy and difficult words in an experimental design. Participants will study Finnish words (encoding) and their English translations and test their learning (recall). To understand the most effective strategy, participants’ self-efficacy, perceived cognitive load, and sympathetic arousal will be measured.

abstract: Children learn cause-and-effect relations through family conversations and play. Two behaviors key to this development are exploring the environment and constructing explanations about an experience with other people. This research leverages sociomateriality to link principles of exhibit design to patterns in family conversations that may be productive for causal learning. This work characterizes dynamic transitions between parent-child exploring and explaining as oscillations and identifies specific exhibit design principles that facilitate oscillatory patterns of interaction.

abstract: Narratives and feedback are crucial in educational AR games, yet their interplay remains underexplored. A laboratory study (N = 123) investigating narrative and process-oriented feedback (i.e., presence vs. absence) showed no significant relationship between them on cognitive load and learning, but process-oriented feedback improved transfer. Immersion mediated by germane cognitive load, extraneous and germane cognitive load effect recall. Further disentangling the relationship between both factors in AR learning games is essential for deeper understanding.

subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This pilot study investigates the impact of an intervention aimed at demystifying foundational text generation models to enhance AI literacy among ninth-grade English Language Arts students. Pre- and post-surveys revealed significant gains in self-assessed performance, while qualitative analysis showed improved understanding of concepts like predictive modeling. However, students struggled to connect foundational knowledge to advanced AI systems like ChatGPT. The findings highlight the importance of teaching foundational models and developing strategies to bridge this gap, supporting comprehensive AI literacy in K-12 education.

title: Sharing About Risks on Social Media: Learning Environments to Address
citation: Hurtado, S. & Keune, A. (2025). Sharing About Risks on Social Media: Learning Environments to Address Social Media. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2933-2935). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hurtado, S. & Keune, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Youth navigate social media risks daily, yet their strategies to address them are often underrepresented. This study explores how youth identify and address these risks within learning environments. Three workshops were conducted with 32 8th-grade participants in Germany. Findings indicate that sharing facilitated risk identification and addressing. Creating learning environments that encourage sharing experiences can leverage youth cultural practices for online safety and could empower youth to enhance their social media experiences.

citation: Wagh, A., Dickes, A., LaBonte, J., & Thibodeau, T. (2025). authors_list: Wagh, A., Dickes, A., LaBonte, J., & Thibodeau, T.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics

abstract: This paper draws on a Research-Practice Partnership in which we introduced organizational routines (ORs) involving co-design and co-reflection cycles for teachers and coaches to integrate computational thinking (CT) into math and science instruction. Using thematic analysis of educator interviews and class observation notes, we characterize coaches as co-designers and brokers for supporting boundary crossings of integrated CT knowledge and practice within and across schools, and advancing shifts away from techno-centric to learner-centric perspectives on design.

citation: Mehrvarz, M., Abdoli, S., Kahveci, E. N., Rahimi, S., & McLaren, B. M. (2025). The Impact of Hint Modality in Digital Game-Based Learning: A Systematic Literature Review. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Mehrvarz, M., Abdoli, S., Kahveci, E. N., Rahimi, S., & McLaren, B. M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Digital learning games often use hints to support learners, but the effectiveness of different hint types remains underexplored. This systematic review examines 68 empirical studies (2000–2024) on hint modalities—text, graphic, and multi-type—across educational levels. Multi-type hints were the most commonly used and showed generally positive outcomes, especially in elementary and higher education. Text-based hints had mixed results, while graphical hints, though less studied, were mostly effective. Future work should investigate the mechanisms behind hint effectiveness to optimize their design in digital learning environments.

title: Exploring How Rural Teachers’ Place Identity Relates to Place-Based Curriculum Implementation
citation: Akturk, A., Zangori, L. A., Cole, L., Webb, C., & Snyder, R. (2025). Exploring How Rural Teachers’ Place Identity Relates to Place-Based Curriculum Implementation. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Akturk, A., Zangori, L. A., Cole, L., Webb, C., & Snyder, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Implementing place-based education (PBE) requires teachers to access place resources as pedagogical tools. In this qualitative study, we focus on how rural teachers (n = 17) drew upon their place experiences to define their (dis)connections to place to access resources for a PBE unit. Results suggest that how teachers described their teaching place experiences was linked to whether they viewed instructional resources as affordances or constraints to PBE implementation.

citation: Murphy, D., Underwood, T., Alekh, V., & Zhou, J. (2025). Sustainable Interdisciplinary Collaboration Among Early Career Learning Scientists. authors_list: Murphy, D., Underwood, T., Alekh, V., & Zhou, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: : We invite learning scientists to explore ways to foster interdisciplinary collaboration among early career scholars. Drawing on collaborative reflections, we examine our experiences highlighting challenges and potential future research to cultivate sustainable interdisciplinary collaboration among early career scholars in ISLS. We propose creating tangible entry points, committing to shared goals, weaving mentorship with open-ended inquiry, and supporting flow-like states of play as actionable starting points for building a more robust and inclusive infrastructure to support early career scholars.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates how everyday objects can enhance architecture students’ understanding of structural concepts. 186 first-year students designed balancing structures using everyday objects. Data from small group learning diaries and photographs of design outcomes and processes were analyzed to identify recurring concepts (stacking, spanning, cantilevering) used. The findings highlight the use of familiar materials in architectural education for structural learning.

citation: Waight, N., Rish, R. M., Tripp, J., Scheuneman, S. M., Mozaffari, F., Goehrig, F., Jackson, D. W., Robert, S., Wisoff, S., & Marks, D. R. (2025). subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Out-of-school, informal STEM education opportunities have potential to move beyond patterns of didactic, teacher-focused, factual recall that have been a mainstay in traditional STEM teaching and learning contexts. In this study, we present portraitures of two Black youth who participated in a one-week STEMcyclists summer program across two years, designed to circumvent status quo modes of teaching and learning by honoring minoritized youths’ lives, genius, and joy through science and engineering activities related to the bike and community biking. Through the portraiture method and cycles of descriptive and deductive coding informed by Muhammad’s (2023) cultivating genius and joy framework, we uncovered youths’ experiences in the program. Findings from these portraitures surfaced the STEMcyclists program as a context for learning that amplifies youth past experiences, identities, and knowledge while repositioning and cultivating youth as STEM knowledge possessors who engage in re-seeing, rebuilding, and forging new knowledge.

title: Evaluating Student Agency in AI-Generated Lesson Plans

authors_list: Cheng, J., Wang, C., & Chen, B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Generative AI tools are increasingly deployed in education to support practices such as lesson planning, while little attention has been given to the alignment between these tools and core values in education. This poster reports on the extent of student agency reflected in AI-generated lesson plans across four conditions. The findings reveal AI’s underlying assumptions and bias against student agency and demonstrate the possibility of strengthening student agency in lesson plan generation.

title: Interpreting Student Nonparticipation in Teams
citation: Moffat, A. D., Matz, R. L., Fowler, R. R., & Henderson, T. S. (2025). Interpreting Student Nonparticipation in Teams. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Moffat, A. D., Matz, R. L., Fowler, R. R., & Henderson, T. S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We explored nonparticipation in teamwork through an analysis of 42 studies about equitable teamwork, which revealed two prominent perspectives. The dominant view blames individuals, labeling nonparticipation as social loafing—a term we contest. The second perspective views nonparticipation as a result of structural barriers, emphasizing equity but ignoring personal agency. We propose a Domain Theory-based approach that considers nonparticipation to be a complex issue, encouraging balance between individual responsibility and structural factors and reevaluation of how student nonparticipation is perceived.

citation: Voorhis, J. K., Lemée, M., Rosenbaum, L. F., & Blikstein, P. (2025). Taking on “Big Problems”: Spatial Scales in Youth Work at a Data Science Camp. abstract: Data science education (DSE) has recently gained increased attention. We present a framework for analyzing youth-authored community data science investigations and illustrate our framework with case studies demonstrating the benefits of scaffolding learners’ trajectories across spatial scales. Our findings suggest that “sliding” between personal, community, and global scales supports reasoning about complex problems, offering insights for educators to support youth in tackling “big problems” and making sense of their world through data.

abstract: Mentoring is increasingly recognized as an important developmental process in STEM; however, most research and programming has focused on academic research contexts. Here we examine a pilot mentoring program in a geosciences professional society, investigating situated perspectives on mentoring in this distinct setting. Early findings from surveys and participant observations highlight unique affordances of professional society mentorship for identity development and culture change, emphasizing the importance of this context for design and research.

title: Research Practice Partnership Model for Non-Western Education Settings: A Case Study from Rural India

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Theories and methods in the Learning Sciences have pointed out that building research-practice partnerships is an impactful pathway to designing equitable learning environments. However, most of the research on building research-practice partnerships is being conducted in Western contexts. In this paper, we describe a research practice partnership model that is being built in rural India. Researchers from Learning Sciences and educators/practitioners who work with a rural school that serves Tribal and Rural students in western India started to work together three years ago to think about how to teach critical thinking and collaboration skills to students from Tribal and rural parts of India. This paper focuses on the process of how the partnership was built and contributes to the theories of design-based implementation research and participatory design research.

title: Teacher Instructional Adaptations to Support Language Learning in Elementary STEM

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bateman, J. M., Miller, E. A., & Reigh, E. V.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Research supporting adaptations for multilingual learners (MLLs) in elementary science classrooms, particularly within project-based learning (PBL) frameworks, remains limited. This qualitative ethnographic study investigates how a fourth-grade STEM teacher in a dual language immersion (DLI) classroom adapted the Multiple Literacies in Project-Based Learning (ML-PBL) curriculum to support students’ science sensemaking across language. Data were collected through teacher observations, interviews, and video recordings, focusing on instructional adaptations. Findings show that the teacher recognized one adaptation, strategic grouping of students, but did not mention two others that were identified by researchers, supporting translanguaging and using multiple modalities.

citation: Ko, M. M., Wingert, K., Hoang, N., & Campanella, M. (2025). Developing Teachers’ Pedagogical Design Capacity to Amplify Students’ Epistemic Agency Through Curriculum Adaptation. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ko, M. M., Wingert, K., Hoang, N., & Campanella, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this study, we analyze teachers' participation in a professional learning (PL) workshop that aims to deepen teachers’ pedagogical design capacity, with an emphasis on increasing students’ epistemic agency. We describe the design of a four-day workshop, our analytic process, and how three teachers made sense of and deepened their sensemaking of students’ epistemic agency. Although the three teachers began with different conceptions of epistemic agency, each of them shifted their conceptions over the course of the workshop, toward a deeper reflection of how talk, tasks, and teacher moves support or hamper opportunities to let students co-construct ideas. We conclude with a discussion of the implications and future directions for our work.

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Matsumura, L. C., Walsh, M., Li, T., Correnti, R., & Litman, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Our study explores the potential of generative AI (ChatGPT 4) to select segments from classroom text discussion to support a productive professional learning conversation. We compare the quality of segments chosen by GPT 4 to those chosen by an expert coach. Results show that nearly half (43%) of the GPT selected segments are of a similar quality to those chosen by the expert coach. An additional quarter are close to this level of quality.

title: “Like Driving in a Storm at Night”: How Students Use Metaphors to Describe Confusion During Learning
citation: Hur, P., Twidale, M., & Bosch, N. (2025). “Like Driving in a Storm at Night”: How Students Use Metaphors to Describe Confusion During Learning. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hur, P., Twidale, M., & Bosch, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Confusion during learning is complex as it can either deepen understanding or hinder progress, depending on its resolution. This study explored how students personally experience and conceptualize the feeling of confusion through metaphors. Fourteen students participated in a video-based learning task on introductory statistics, self-reported their confusion levels, and were prompted during interviews to use metaphors to describe what it feels like to be confused. Analysis of the collected metaphors revealed descriptions of confusion during learning often involving themes of “Lack of Familiarity”, “Cognitive Overstimulation”, and “Effort Against Impending Failure”. These findings highlight the potential of metaphor analysis to access subjective emotional states in learning and suggest that current measurement tools may not fully capture the complexity of confusion.

title: Youth Designers’ Insights on Information Literacy Learning Tools
citation: Southerton, E., Pimentel, D., & Gallagher, S. (2025). Youth Designers’ Insights on Information Literacy Learning Tools. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Southerton, E., Pimentel, D., & Gallagher, S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study examines youth designers’ insights on the Publication Facts Label (PFL), a tool designed to enhance the evaluation of research articles. Using a Youth Participatory Design Research approach, high school students redesigned the PFL to better meet local needs. Students emphasized features like summative evaluations of trustworthiness (e.g., approval stamps, percentage scores) and simplified access to critical information. We discuss implications for empowering communities to evaluate information while fostering critical literacy skills.

title: Principles for a Balanced Narrative-Paradigmatic Approach for Climate Change Education
citation: D’Orto, E. & Tasquier, G. (2025). Principles for a Balanced Narrative-Paradigmatic Approach for Climate Change Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 2979-2981). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: D’Orto, E. & Tasquier, G.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Narratives are fundamental means through which humans organize experiences, interpret phenomena, and construct meaning by weaving events into coherent structures. This intrinsic role in sensemaking makes them particularly valuable in Climate Change Education. However, within the context of science education, they also present certain limitations and risks. Drawing on Bruner’s theory of the dual modes of thought—narrative and paradigmatic—this study introduces two core design principles aimed at fostering a balanced educational approach. From this perspective, narratives are not merely tools for communication but represent a distinct mode of thinking that is essential to the learning process to be integrated with logico-scientific reasoning.

subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study describes the implementation of two curricular versions (coding-centric and data science-centric) of a two-week physical computing project by one Grade 8 science teacher. In both versions, we conducted students’ pre- and post-surveys, post-implementation semi-structured teacher interviews, and classroom observations. This convergent mixed methods study highlights the role of the physical computing context for implementing either curricular versions, their impact on students, and the affordances and constraints the teacher experienced while implementing them.

citation: Eisenlauer, V., Fink, M. C., Hart, L., & Ertl, B. (2025). Enhancing Educational Engagement: Evaluating the Potential of 360° Virtual Field Trips in Immersive Learning Environments. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Eisenlauer, V., Fink, M. C., Hart, L., & Ertl, B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Virtual Field Trips (VFTs) using 360° technologies represent a transformative approach in education, merging accessibility with immersive learning. This study examines a 360° virtual paleontology exhibition developed as a Web VR experience. It focuses on fostering learner engagement and enhancing educational motivation. A mixed-method evaluation involving 20 undergraduate students revealed that the virtual environment significantly exceeded expectations in terms of learner attention and acceptance. The results indicate that VFTs may offer engaging and motivating learning experiences that share similarities with those reported for physical museum visits, though direct comparisons were not part of this study.

title: Toward a Collective Understanding of Designing STEM Learning for Equity and Justice
citation: Gyles, S., McGowan, V. C., Starks, E., White, B., Bang, M., & Tzou, C. (2025). Toward a Collective Understanding of Designing STEM Learning for Equity and Justice. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Gyles, S., McGowan, V. C., Starks, E., White, B., Bang, M., & Tzou, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Due to assumptions of “cultural neutrality,” STEM education has neglected designing for equity and justice, especially in higher education. This study investigates how a group of learning scientists, STEM faculty, and a computer scientist engaged in collective knowledge building to develop a common understanding of designing for equity and justice in STEM. Findings demonstrate how critical readings and discussions supported building a common foundation of what designing for equity and justice means across STEM disciplines.

title: Pursuing Equity for Youth of Color through Informal Science Programming: A Situative Motivation Study
citation: Adams-Wiggins, K. R., Tierney, G., Cerda-Lezama, S., Ramirez, A. R., Segura, G., & Adanna, T. (2025). authors_list: Adams-Wiggins, K. R., Tierney, G., Cerda-Lezama, S., Ramirez, A. R., Segura, G., & Adanna, T.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Acceptable modes of engagement and knowledge legitimation processes in science classrooms can alienate racially-minoritized students. We employ a situative motivation framework to conduct qualitative analyses of ethnographic interviews from partnership work with a teacher of color and 7 students participating in an informal science program. We discuss connections between teachers’ workplace experiences, teachers’ and students’ equity frames, teachers’ motivation, and students’ science motivation. We illustrate links between participation, racialized identities, and power in science motivation.

title: Exploring Tensions in University Policies and Students Practices on Generative AI
citation: Sun, Z., Møller, A., & Dohn, N. B. (2025). Exploring Tensions in University Policies and Students Practices on Generative Ai. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The integration of Generative AI (GAI) in higher education creates tensions in policy, pedagogy, and ethics. This mixed-methods study analyzes university policies and interviews with master’s students, revealing positive sentiment toward teaching and students but negativity toward GAI, assessment, and ethics. Students report confusion over ethical guidelines and divergent views on GAI’s impact on learning. Findings highlight the need for clearer policies and pedagogical support, addressing contradictions in how GAI affects skill development and education.

abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy education is in bloom and extending its reach to increase accessibility of foundational concepts to younger audiences. However, our prior research has shown that adolescents at the lower secondary school age tend to struggle with some fundamental concepts, one of which is decision trees (DTs). This paper probes into students’ struggles with DTs through a distractor analysis of 3 multiple choice survey items administered to lower secondary students (n=699) before and after a curricular intervention.

authors_list: Liu, S. K., Berger, W., Green, P., & Pinkard, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Opportunity Landscaping's premise is inherently ambitious—to document learning ecosystems at multiple levels of granularity, striving to understand how city-wide trends affect individual actors. We propose approaches for Opportunity Landscaping that provide a combination of the flexibility and structure required to study dynamic learning ecosystems.

title: Teacher Candidates Co-Constructing Anti-Deficit Narratives about Learners in Video Club
citation: Keifert, D. T., Gentry, A., Johnson, H. J., Daniel, B., Henrie, A., Pierson, A., Jeong, S., & Lee, S. J. (2025). Teacher Candidates Co-Constructing Anti-Deficit Narratives About Learners in Video Club. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 3-11). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Keifert, D. T., Gentry, A., Johnson, H. J., Daniel, B., Henrie, A., Pierson, A., Jeong, S., & Lee, S. J.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: We extend prior work to elucidate ideological sensemaking as an interactional process that supports teachers’ anti-deficit noticing in Video Clubs. Our framework positions noticing as a political act, shaped by the frames (Louie et al., 2021) teachers and facilitators use to contextualize learners’ activity. Through understanding framing in relation to ideological sensemaking, we show how individual stances contribute to teachers and facilitators’ co-development of anti-deficit narratives. We demonstrate this by analyzing a Video Club of undergraduate teacher candidates. We highlight patterns (i.e., attending to learners’ gesture, positioning learners to listen and learn with and from each other, recognizing the value of silly contributions) that resisted dominant ideologies and positioned learners’ activity within transformative visions of science teaching and learning. We contextualize these findings within prior professional learning sequences to inform future Video Club designs.

title: Academic Productive Dialogue in Practice: Teacher Insights on Approach Benefits and Application Challenges
citation: Levin, M., Gröschner, A., & Asterhan, C. S. (2025). Academic Productive Dialogue in Practice: Teacher Insights on Approach Benefits and Application Challenges. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 3001-3003). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Levin, M., Gröschner, A., & Asterhan, C. S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Accountable Talk & Dialogic Discourse; Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: Despite the well-documented benefits of academically productive classroom dialogue—and the central role teachers play in facilitating it—dialogic pedagogy remains relatively rare in practice. This study investigates teachers’ perspectives on the perceived benefits and challenges of implementing dialogic teaching. As part of a four-year research-practice partnership aimed at promoting dialogic instruction in 4th–6th-grade language arts classrooms, we conducted thematic analysis of 17 elementary teachers' interviews. Findings indicate that teachers perceive dialogic teaching as offering both academic and social-emotional benefits. However, they also report two key challenges: establishing discourse norms and managing the cognitive demands of facilitating rich classroom dialogue. Notably, the benefits teachers describe suggest that their use of dialogic teaching may differ from how researchers typically define or measure it. The challenges, in turn, underscore the significant demands placed on teachers. Together, these findings offer insights into the gap between research and classroom implementation of dialogic pedagogy.

title: Shifting Toward a Connected Perspective in an Out-of-School STEM Program
citation: Cawelti, L., Dahn, M., Corrigan, S., & Peppler, K. (2025). Shifting Toward a Connected Perspective in an Out-of-School STEM Program. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 3004-3006). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cawelti, L., Dahn, M., Corrigan, S., & Peppler, K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Out-of-school time (OST) programs have a positive effect on fostering youth STEM interests and are important nodes in a STEM learning ecosystem. Despite this, leaders in OST programs often have an insular, org-focused mindset. By tracking two program leaders over a year, this study investigates the process and results of shifting toward a connected mindset. Findings show that brokering stronger connections with partners supported youth and resulted in greater participation in programs. Implications highlight how shifting toward a connected perspective can strengthen the nodes of a STEM learning ecosystem.

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Guan, X., Russo, R., & Blikstein, P.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: We present a pilot study examining three years of conference papers in the proceedings of the International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS) Annual Meetings from 2022 to 2024 to explore the connections and collaborations among authors in three fields of investigation: data science instruction, misinformation/disinformation, and social media. We found initial evidence of a cyclical pattern indicating that at times, sub-communities collaborate, while at other times, they operate more independently in isolation.

title: Unlocking Young Minds: How K-12 Students Define Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
citation: Tatar, C., Zhang, Y., Jung, Y., Chao, J., & Rosé, C. P. (2025). Unlocking Young Minds: How K-12 Students Define Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tatar, C., Zhang, Y., Jung, Y., Chao, J., & Rosé, C. P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This case study explores 437 K-12 students’ ontological descriptions of AI before and after they completed AI curricula in ELA classes. In this study, we explored students’ conceptual understandings through a text-mining approach. Initial findings indicate that before the intervention, students primarily offered examples of AI functions. However, after engaging with the curriculum modules, their descriptions became more comprehensive, including discussions on AI limitations and the significance of datasets for task completion.

title: The Design, Implementation and Evaluation of a Human-Centered Design Professional Learning Community in a High School Setting
citation: Guerrero, B. & Shehab, S. (2025). The Design, Implementation and Evaluation of a Human-Centered Design Professional Learning Community in a High School Setting. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Guerrero, B. & Shehab, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study integrated participatory action research into a Professional Learning Community (PLC) at a high school to explore how teachers from various disciplines could integrate Human-Centered Design (HCD) in their teaching. Teachers valued students' development of empathy, collaboration, and creativity, but faced obstacles including time constraints and student buy-in. While teachers felt knowledgeable about HCD, they preferred incorporating individual tools into existing lesson plans rather than creating multi-day lessons.

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Anderson, E., Wendel, D., Conlin, L., Schoenfeld, I., & Wagh, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Drawing on co-design work with teachers, this poster presents four approaches to developing units that bring domain-general agent-based modeling into high school science classrooms. In each unit, scientific phenomena contextualize and support sense-making of code while students engage with code to make sense of phenomena. Across the approaches, students use domain-general modeling to attend to structural and conceptual similarities and differences across phenomena and models, and extend their model/s to explore key scientific ideas.

title: Establishing Radical Spaces for Dismantling Scientific Objectivity in Learning
citation: Howard, I., Ladhani, S., Turner, K., Schaffer, K., & Adams, J. (2025). Establishing Radical Spaces for Dismantling Scientific Objectivity in Learning. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Howard, I., Ladhani, S., Turner, K., Schaffer, K., & Adams, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: It is necessary to engage in dialogue that deconstructs the normative structures and perspectives of Western Modern Science (WMS) and include the voices of non-white racialized groups and non-cis male genders. Design innovations should engage in speculative and justices-based methodologies to help learners radically reimagine STEMM. This paper proposes an emerging research design innovation that engages learners in reimagining the dominant perspective of WMS using syllabus co-constructions and action research cycles.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We describe contrasting cases in a middle school STEM summer camp to investigate how learners negotiate their agency with different materials to make connections to the land – querencia – using visual content analysis and material agency. We found that students created anatopic buildings with few alterations when using templates but made locally-authentic designs when using less structured materials, shedding light on authentic ways to learn.

title: Mirror Agents: A Dynamic Metacognitive Multi-Agent Framework for Real-Time Metacognitive Development
citation: Liu, J., Liu, R., Wang, C., Wang, P., & Gu, X. (2025). Mirror Agents: A Dynamic Metacognitive Multi-Agent Framework for Real-Time Metacognitive Development. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 3025-3027). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Liu, J., Liu, R., Wang, C., Wang, P., & Gu, X.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: This research introduces a novel multi-agent framework, "Mirror Agents," to support K-12 students' metacognitive development through dynamic, real-time scaffolding. Building on the MAPS model, the system deploys four specialized agents—Guide, Progress, Reflection, and Strategy—that collaboratively monitor and respond to learners' cognitive and metacognitive activities. Unlike traditional systems offering static feedback, Mirror Agents continuously synthesize cognitive mirroring data (learning behaviors and outcomes) with metacognitive mirroring data (strategy use and self-regulation). Through multimodal inputs—including behavioral indicators, interface interactions, and physiological signals—the framework creates a comprehensive mirror of students' learning processes. This study explores patterns of metacognitive monitoring emerging from agent interactions and examines how learners adapt strategies in response to multi-agent feedback. The framework advances current educational technologies by offering a dynamic, interconnected agent model that enhances real-time metacognitive growth and provides design principles for intelligent learning environments.

title: University Instructors' Aesthetic Encounters in Maker-Centered Learning through Posthumanist and New Materialist Perspectives
citation: Lin, Z. & Murai, Y. (2025). University Instructors' Aesthetic Encounters in Maker-Centered Learning Through Posthumanist and New Materialist Perspectives. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lin, Z. & Murai, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines university instructors’ aesthetic encounters in maker-centered learning, drawing on posthumanist and new materialist perspectives. Two key themes emerged—material-sensory entanglement and distributed agency for aesthetic engagement—suggesting how material and sensory engagement foster imagination and emotional resonance while aesthetic encounters are distributed through dynamic interactions with peers and materials. The findings suggest the potential of prioritizing aesthetic encounters in maker-centered learning and provide implications for future studies.

title:

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Adam, K., Joseph, M., & Chowdury, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines the impact of a competency-based education (CBE) grading schema on students' motivation in a higher education pharmacy lab. Grounded in constructivism and self-determination theory, the study utilized a design-based mixed-methods research approach with 200 students over two semesters. Findings indicate that a CBE grading schema fosters intrinsic motivation by prioritizing skill mastery and self-directed learning. The results highlight CBE's potential to transform higher education by shifting from traditional grading to skill-based assessments that enhance engagement and better prepare students for their professional careers.

title: What “Ice” do Ice-Breakers Break or Ice?
citation: Turan, N., Chaparian, S., & Y., J. (2025). What “Ice” do Ice-Breakers Break or Ice?. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: Turan, N., Chaparian, S., & Y, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper reimagines ice-breakers beyond warm-ups, reframing them as integral to learning. While traditionally they are seen as tools to reduce tension and build community, they can reveal group dynamics, roles, and identities. Through figured worlds and participation structures, we argue ice-breakers may serve as interactional spaces where students negotiate identities, use humor, and bring cultural artifacts into learning. Well-designed ice-breakers can strategically support educational goals, fostering critical thinking, engagement, and collaboration across diverse contexts.

authors_list: Cordner, H.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Despite improvements in pre-college engineering education curricula over the past decade, student motivation to continue with engineering as a career path remains low. Queering these curricula is proposed as a method of enabling a wider variety of students to envision themselves as engineers.

title: Integrating the Interdisciplinary Research Process (IRP) into the undergraduate course Theory and Application of Motor Learning
citation: Perinova, R. (2025). Integrating the Interdisciplinary Research Process (Irp) Into the Undergraduate Course Theory and Application of Motor Learning.
