International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Perinova, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of a semester-long motor learning course embedding the Interdisciplinary Research Process (IRP) in undergraduate PE students’ education. Employing a design-based research approach, it examines how structured interdisciplinary collaboration fosters autonomy, critical thinking, and competence. Findings suggest that integrating IRP improves engagement and interdisciplinary understanding, though challenges remain in coordination and task clarity. Students developed deeper insights into selected curriculum areas. Implications for future iterations are discussed.

title: A Humanities Approach to Data Literacy: Contextualizing and Relating Data with Network Visualization
citation: Parker, D. A., Lau, N. G., Coenraad, M., Danish, J., & Craig, K. (2025). A Humanities Approach to Data Literacy: Contextualizing and Relating Data With Network Visualization. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 3043-3045). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Parker, D. A., Lau, N. G., Coenraad, M., Danish, J., & Craig, K.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: In this paper, we propose situating data literacy within a humanities framework as a complementary method in data literacy education, using network visualization as a tool. As data becomes increasingly essential in understanding our world, there is a growing need for a multidisciplinary approach to data literacy. We argue that network visualization techniques can foster deeper engagement with data's complexities in certain contexts. We explore various definitions and frameworks of data literacy, emphasizing context, critical thinking, and holistic understanding, and highlight network visualization as a tool to explore data within a humanistic framework. By using networks, students can develop a critical and contextual understanding of data, preparing them to navigate the complexities of our data-driven society more effectively.

title: Global Approaches to AIED: Common Voices and Silences about the Sustainable Use of Generative AI in Education

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: So, H., Tan, L., & Kim, B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: International organizations (e.g., UNESCO, UNICEF, and OECD) have published recommendations for generative AI (GenAI) in education, addressing pedagogical, ethical, and safety concerns. Our study conducted a thematic analysis through topic modeling to investigate global guidelines for GenAI use and explored critical considerations for educators, policymakers, and researchers. We aim to present common voices, and amplify silences about GenAI in education and discuss the ethical and moral implications of its sustainable uses.

title: Beyond Boundaries: Rethinking Family, Nature, and Learning with More-Than-Human ‘Wild’ Others
citation: Hoogland, E. & Gebre, E. (2025). Beyond Boundaries: Rethinking Family, Nature, and Learning With More-Than-Human ‘Wild’ Others. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hoogland, E. & Gebre, E.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: As society faces large-scale environmental challenges, promoting positive relationships between people and nature is extremely important. To better understand how education can foster lasting relationships between children and nature, we engage with Ecoportraiture, drawing on narratives, go-along interviews, and creative reflections with families whose teenagers have been recognized for their environmental contributions. Preliminary findings from one case highlight the importance of adopting a family assemblage perspective to appreciate and understand how more-than-human wild others mediate practices of care and forge connections to broader ecological systems. The everyday interactions with more-than-human wild others serve as a boundary object, fostering empathy and intergenerational practices of care and respect for life.

title: Investigating the Role of Perceived Intra-Unit Coherence for Science Learning
citation: Kubsch, M., Neumann, K., Nordine, J., & Fortus, D. (2025). Investigating the Role of Perceived Intra-Unit Coherence for Science Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 305-313). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kubsch, M., Neumann, K., Nordine, J., & Fortus, D.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: While instructional coherence is widely regarded as essential for effective science education, little evidence exists on how students’ perceptions of coherence influence their learning and motivation. This study investigates the role of perceived intra-unit coherence—retrospective, prospective, and in-toto coherence—in shaping learning outcomes. Drawing on data from 771 students across seven energy units, results indicate that retrospective and in-toto coherence positively impact immediate and unit-level learning but not broader conceptual understanding. Additionally, situational interest emerged as a key factor influencing coherence perceptions. These findings highlight the importance of designing instruction that aligns with students’ perspectives, enhancing engagement and achievement in science education.

abstract: Here we introduce a “Disciplinary Analytics” approach to helping learning scientists see and understand research communities and themes in the field. We suggest that such analytics could support (inter)disciplinary collaboration, equitable convening practices, and effective knowledge sharing. Using “codesign” as an initial thematic focus, we present example visualizations based on public conference proceedings, and articulate opportunities for developing disciplinary infrastructures and routines that could help researchers, particularly newcomers, navigate the “big tent” of learning sciences.

citation: Ha, J., Su, M., Jeong, S., Yan, L., Yoon, S., Hu-Au, E., & Ghosh, A. (2025). abstract: The Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive (ICAP) framework has gained traction in the learning sciences community as a tool for understanding how students learn. It suggests that deeper learning occurs when students are engaged in generative and collaborative activities. This study evaluated the design of a university-level chemistry course and examined the relationship between ICAP engagement modes and student performance. Regression analysis revealed that collaboration had the strongest positive impact on academic outcomes.

Findings indicate that teachers enrolled in elementary programs emphasized designer bias, while non-elementary program teachers focused more on data bias, critical data literacy, and employed critical inquiry strategies. These differences highlight the need for tailored professional development and further research on integrating critical technology education across grade levels

abstract: This study explores how 5th-grade learners express their identities through creative computing projects using, a platform for coding music with Python. Through case studies, the research highlights the integration of personal interests, societal themes, and advocacy in learners’ coding work. The case studies demonstrate how humanizing the learning environment by centering creative self-expression fosters personally meaningful learner engagement, amplifies learner voice, and supports equity in CS education.

title: Analyzing Teacher-AI Interaction Patterns in Student-Centered Lesson Design

abstract: This study investigates the interaction patterns of elementary school teachers utilizing generative AI for student-centered lesson design. By analyzing teachers with varying levels of teaching experience and AI proficiency, this qualitative study employs CORDTRA diagrams to examine teacher-AI interactions. The findings reveal seven distinct interaction patterns, with distinctive differences based on teachers’ experience and AI proficiency. These results highlight the need for differentiated AI training and tool development that accommodate teachers’ varying levels of expertise and interaction styles.

abstract: Using an interactional ethnography approach, this study traced the two-year co-design process of three teachers to support student-driven authentic research at an innovative high school, collaborating with community partners. Grounded theory analysis of teacher interviews, lesson documents, and teacher meeting observations revealed six learning design areas, including ill-defined goals, supportive materials and student-driven learning processes. These elements initialized and evolved over time through co-design by complex partnerships involving interdisciplinary teachers, researchers, and business partners.

abstract: Educational systems still struggle to institutionalize cross-disciplinary collaboration among educators in post-secondary institutions. Furthermore, there is limited understanding of how exposure to interdisciplinary learning might influence students’ epistemic beliefs. To address this gap, our team developed and piloted the Student Attitude Toward Interdisciplinarity Survey (SATIS). Preliminary findings reveal that while students acknowledge the importance of integrating multiple disciplines to tackle complex problems, it remains uncertain whether they independently apply knowledge from diverse courses to real-world challenges.

This study explores how one teaching artist designed and used representational infrastructure in a youth ensemble theatrical devising process, generating numerous opportunities to develop participant agency, and ultimately resulting in the creation and performance of an original play.

abstract: Within a collaborative map-building experience, the six participants, all women between the ages of 45 and 85, chose a hands-off approach to ArcGIS StoryMap technology, instead insisting the facilitator act as a technology conduit. This choice, which contradicts commonly held ideas about the importance of hands-on technology design, produced no discernable negative impact in participant’s sense of agency or engagement. Rather, participants report that avoiding direct engagement with technology enhanced their design experience.

abstract: School-making is not simply a replication of real-world making; it undergoes recontextualization, shifting tools, practices, and meanings to fit institutional priorities. This paper centers on objects as mediators, shaping student engagement with materials, epistemic practices, and disciplinary knowledge. School-making is not a deficit but a generative space for hybrid-making that sustains exploration, creativity, embodied learning, and relational engagement while embracing institutional constraints and possibilities.

abstract: Engaging with computational models is central to both scientific and computational learning. A promising approach to “lower the floor” and make computational modeling more accessible is the development of domain-specific and block-based environments, which reduce programming complexity while leveraging students’ intuitions about scientific ideas. To balance usability and expressiveness in these environments, we develop the feature of “unpacking” blocks, allowing users to open and modify high-level blocks into the simpler constituent elements that define them. In this study, we analyze high school students’ models, screen recordings, and artifact-based interviews to investigate their motivation for modifying domain-specific blocks for eutrophication in aquatic ecosystems. We found that unpacking and modifying blocks supported students in both exploring scientific ideas and addressing specific goals of computational modeling, providing insights on how unpacking domain-specific blocks can support both computing and science learning.

abstract: The study investigates whether Dynamic Equilibrium (DE) can serve as a “powerful idea” (Papert, 1980) that bridges phenomena across STEM fields. Through semi-structured interviews with five scientists, we identified three themes: DE was rarely used explicitly but appeared across fields; reflection on DE prompted a more generalized framing; and DE spanned scales from molecules to human populations. These findings suggest DE’s potential as a cross-cutting concept that connects otherwise fragmented content in STEM education.

Our participants began noticing racial inequity upon seeing bias in computer vision AI.

abstract: This paper examines how dominant U.S. cultural values, particularly entrepreneurialism, shape success in STEM and Maker education. Through illustrative cases, we analyze how ideas of productivity, individualism, and impact frame who is valued as a learner. Drawing on constructionist and critical traditions, we argue for redefining success to include epistemic diversity, reflective practice, and “non-linear” learning, challenging outcome-driven norms, and expanding what counts as meaningful engagement.

abstract: This study explores how novice and experienced teachers interact with generative AI during learner-centered lesson planning. To ensure that generative AI supports lesson planning regardless of a teacher’s experience, it is essential to understand the differences between novice and experienced teachers. Ordered Network Analysis showed that experienced teachers considered learners and context before evaluating generative AI responses, unlike novice teachers. This finding implies the need for tailored AI guidelines based on experience level.

As part of a design-based implementation research study, we trace two teachers’ Culturally Responsive design journey designing and (re)designing a land-based curricular unit over five years. Findings illustrate an ontological shift as teachers design for disruption and move toward culturally responsive design. Insights expand current understandings of culturally responsive design and teachers’ role in supporting students’ engagement with diverse cultures.

We found multiple design considerations tied to each approach, with critical approaches often deprioritized and related to tensions with the other approaches.

This research underscores the potential of AI tools to bridge academic gaps by delivering tailored learning experiences and influencing students' learning trajectories.

abstract: This study investigated associations among students’ impulsivity, engagement patterns, and learning outcomes during online problem-solving. Using latent profile analysis, we analyzed keystroke data from 788 middle school students during Korean language problem-solving tasks, with impulsivity scores and learning outcomes including correct answer, comprehension, and attitude scores. Results revealed two distinct patterns: Profile 1 showed lower total keystroke count and longer release-press duration than Profile 2. Impulsivity did not correlate with keystroke patterns; however, lower impulsivity and Profile 2 keystroke patterns were associated with better learning outcomes. Findings suggest keystroke patterns provide meaningful insights about student engagement and performance during online problem-solving.

In collaboration with a community organization and public school district, we employed participatory design to transform playgrounds into inclusive computational thinking environments for kindergarteners. We shifted from accommodation-focused design to centering the experiences of learners with disabilities. These vignettes highlight how culturally sustaining design can empower marginalized communities, extend design paradigms, and create equitable educational environments that serve all children through inclusive play.

This study seeks to understand how play and playful learning activities influenced peer collaboration in an Art History course on Museum Marketing.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines the relationship between epistemic curiosity (EC) and perceived uncertainty, which is posited to form an inverted U-shape, in the context of uncertainty-driven science learning (UDSL). Using path analysis, survey data from 181 middle school students collected at multiple timepoints across a three-week photosynthesis unit designed to facilitate UDSL were analyzed. Results show that the inverted U-shaped relationship between EC and uncertainty does not consistently hold over time. Instead, prior uncertainty negatively affects this relationship unless mediated by EC or sustained uncertainty in subsequent activities. At the trait level, the study highlights the mediating role of epistemic orientation toward uncertainty in fostering trait EC in UDSL. The findings underscore the importance of supporting students' productive uncertainty navigation and signify the positive impacts of UDSL in fostering EC.

abstract: Children’s wholeness, particularly for racialized, multilingual refugee learners, is often fragmented in institutionalized educational spaces. This work highlights spirituality as a vital, yet often silenced, dimension of learning. Within a co-designed land-based program, educators and children collaboratively created a multilingual poster that honored diverse spiritual and ecological connections to soil. This pedagogical moment illuminates the transformative potential of centering children’s languages, spiritual knowledges, and relational ties to land in educational spaces.

This study evaluates the ways in which binary oppositions were ruptured in the course, subverting normative practices through an engagement with materials-to-queer-with and uncovering new ways of engaging in the “doing of mathematics.”

The findings demonstrate how micro-moments of justice can be incorporated into informal learning space design principles to create more just learning in STEM and beyond.

Through micro-interaction analysis, we highlight how multimodal participation enabled students to be repositioned as knowers and doers of science, fostering dignity, engagement, and epistemic agency in science classrooms.

abstract: As teens and adolescents are developing personal interests and imagining potential futures, it can be an exciting time for educators and trusted adults to make connections across domains and interests explicit. In this study, teens participated in an out-of-school science-based creative writing workshop. This work is based on the idea that STEAM (science, technology, engineering, arts, and mathematics) approaches can lead to meaningful learning, and that opportunities to create and construct are especially powerful. Findings from the analysis of written artifacts show that participants used science in their creative writing in a variety of ways, and that they imagine multiple roles for science in their current or future lives. Implications of this work suggest some ways educators might consider the relationships between identity and power, STEM/STEAM learning, and Connected Learning when designing opportunities for adolescents.

abstract: First-generation students often experience increased challenges in higher education institutions even though a variety of supports are offered. This case study explored the experiences of family members and first-generation students in a non-matriculated general education program. The students had many positive and challenging experiences, while their family members expressed gratitude for the opportunity and were concerned for the well-being of their student. The principles learned from this program could help other student success programs.

abstract: Persistence is crucial in maker-based learning, where challenges are inherent to the creative process and one of the important behavioral markers of motivation. This study examines how students respond to obstacles during making activities, reflecting persistence, using the socio cognitive theory framework of triadic reciprocal causation. We conducted a multi-level video analysis of two student teams engaged in electronic-making projects as case studies. At the macro level, we visualized 8.9 hours of making activities segmented into 1-minute intervals using making-process rugs. At the intermediate level, we identified ‘trouble and repair’ episodes that required persistence. At the micro level, we analyzed these episodes using interaction analysis, focusing on verbal and embodied actions with peers, facilitators, and the physical environment. By integrating micro-level interaction data into SCT, we provide empirical insights into the interplay of personal beliefs and environmental factors influencing persistence.

title: Examining Knowledge-Sharing Across Digital Modalities: Preliminary Insights from Goodreads and TikTok Book Reviews
citation: Roeroe, C. T. (2025). Examining Knowledge-Sharing Across Digital Modalities: Preliminary Insights From Goodreads and TikTok Book Reviews. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 3147-3149). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Roeroe, C. T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Digital content platforms have become key spaces for informal, self-directed learning. Understanding how knowledge takes form and evolve within these environments is crucial to understanding the nature of learning that unfolds. This study compares 34 book reviews from Goodreads, a text-based platform, and TikTok, a short-form video platform, to explore how distinct modalities influence knowledge-sharing. Preliminary findings suggest that Goodreads emphasizes evaluative reasoning, while TikTok highlights personal learning and growth.

title: Collaborative and Adaptive Learning: Designing AI Educational Systems with and for Educators
citation: Sarkar, S., Liu, A., Shapiro, R. B., & Sun, M. (2025). Collaborative and Adaptive Learning: Designing Ai Educational Systems With and for Educators. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sarkar, S., Liu, A., Shapiro, R. B., & Sun, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The COALESCE framework extends DBIR principles to AI-powered educational technology development, positioning educators as active co-creators. This study evaluates COALESCE through its application in designing an AI-assisted lesson-planning tool. Our findings show how deep educator involvement supports trust, ownership, and domain-specific improvements in AI-generated content. We discuss implications for participatory AI design and offer a replicable model for context-aware, educator-aligned innovation.

title: Rethinking Cognitive Apprenticeship Through Studio Pedagogy
citation: Bouton, E., Lefstein, A., Bekerman, Z., & Michaels, S. (2025). Rethinking Cognitive Apprenticeship Through Studio Pedagogy. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 3153-3155). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bouton, E., Lefstein, A., Bekerman, Z., & Michaels, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This poster critically examines cognitive apprenticeship theory through systematic analysis of studio pedagogy in practice. Both pedagogies are rooted in traditional apprenticeship practices. Drawing on a semester-long observational study of a ceramics design studio in leading arts academy in Israel, we analyze interactional episodes to identify fundamental differences between the cognitive apprenticeship theoretical prescriptions and actual studio practices. We found that studio pedagogy manages to achieve many stated goals of cognitive apprenticeship, within educational and academic settings, while successfully maintaining the challenges that many cognitive apprenticeship implementation efforts face. There are several fundamental misalignments between cognitive apprenticeship theory and studio practices. First, studios shifts the traditional master-apprentice power dynamic, with instructors supporting students' visions rather than imposing their own. Second, modeling in studios occurs reactively and fragmentally within students' work process, contrary to the theory's prescribed proactive, comprehensive, performative demonstrations. Third, studio instructional support intensifies with project complexity, challenging the theory's fading support model. While studio pedagogy and cognitive apprenticeship in k12 settings are inherently different, learning from successful studio settings can enrich our understanding of apprenticeship-based learning in educational and academic settings.

title: Playing at the Crossroads: Exploring Intersections of Research, Education, and Design in a Case of Musical Improvisation

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rubin, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: While research, education, and design involve distinct priorities and practices, they frequently intersect. Scholars and practitioners have called for further study of how to navigate these roles. This study presents a case of playtesting a game that supports musicians developing improvision skills. Through qualitative analysis based in design research and autoethnography, I elaborate the priorities and practices involved in navigating simultaneous roles of researcher, designer, and educator and highlight areas of confluence and tension.

title: Reimagining Community Futures: Supporting Science Teachers and Students as Climate Justice Action Researchers and Change Agents
citation: Visintainer, T., Baidwan, M., & Wright, K. (2025). Reimagining Community Futures: Supporting Science Teachers and Students as Climate Justice Action Researchers and Change Agents. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 3159-3161). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Visintainer, T., Baidwan, M., & Wright, K.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: To explore the interrelated issues of racial and climate justice, this study examines how engaging teachers and students in climate justice action research (CJAR), a novel approach to community-based science at the intersection of history, race, place, and community health, supports learning, identity construction, and opportunities for reimagining sustainable futures. Using teacher/student interviews, surveys, and classroom observations this study examines: 1) How participation in a year-long professional learning experience shaped science teachers’ knowledge and practice as they designed/implemented CJAR units in their classrooms, and 2) How engaging in CJAR practices (e.g., science, mapping, arts-based storytelling) shaped student learning, identity construction, and the futures they imagined for themselves and their communities. Findings show that teachers were empowered as designers of climate justice experiences that fostered a shared sense of humanity, and that engaging in CJAR practices supported student identity construction, critical sense making, and provided opportunities to reimagine just community futures.

citation: Shaikh, R., Sharma, R., Kadam, S., Prasad, R., Singh, A., & Das, M. K. (2025). Facilitating Learning of Socio-Scientific Issues Through an Adaptive Critical Pedagogy Module. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Shaikh, R., Sharma, R., Kadam, S., Prasad, R., Singh, A., & Das, M. K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores Grade 9 students' engagement with microplastic pollution as a socio-scientific issue (SSI) using a critical pedagogy approach in Mumbai, India. Through a two-day workshop involving Foldscope microscopes, students transitioned from limited initial engagement to active, inquiry-driven exploration. Analysis highlights the influence of cultural contexts and the potential of critical pedagogy to enhance understanding and critical thinking about SSI. Recommendations for culturally adaptive, scaffolded, and sustained pedagogical interventions are discussed.

citation: Ha, J. E., Kim, S., Kim, D., Tae, J., & So, H. (2025). Interaction Patterns in Community College Students’ Use of ChatGPT for Computational Problem-Solving Tasks. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ha, J. E., Kim, S., Kim, D., Tae, J., & So, H.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study explores how community college students interact with ChatGPT during computational problem-solving tasks in Excel. A mixed-method approach was employed through thematic coding and Epistemic Network Analysis. Results highlight that instructor guidance enhanced perceived task motivation and task value, fostering the use of ChatGPT as a collaborative partner. Findings underscore the importance of instructor guidance and designing instructional environments that promote the ethical and effective use of generative AI for supporting student agency in computational problem-solving tasks.

citation: Mehto, V. & Valasmo, V. (2025). Centralizing the Multispecies Margins: Learning With Wild Barnacle Geese in a Zoo Day Camp. authors_list: Mehto, V. & Valasmo, V.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: To recognize education as more-than-human, this study examines how wild barnacle geese participated in learning practices at a zoo day camp. We focused on the open-ended assemblages of various materialities and lifeways with multispecies ethnography. Although the geese were not the main educational focus, their presence shaped the camp’s atmosphere and required embodied adaptation. Attentiveness emerged during mundane activities, highlighting the need for pedagogies and research to attend to vibrant multispecies margins of education.

abstract: This paper discuss the recent developments of a Critical Action Learning Exchange with a K-12 school in India. Briefly examining a Participatory Action Research (PAR) project curricula where a pair of local teachers designed a community-engaged learning project about fibre and fabrics. This PAR curriculum was cross-analyzed in relation to the CALE framework, teacher and student reflections, and cultural aspects. Future directions and implications of the project are also discussed.

citation: Ji, J., Feng, J., Ren, P., & Wu, Y. (2025). Student Assessors’ Engagement With Online Peer Feedback. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. abstract: We investigated how two EFL students of different writing proficiency engaged with online PF behaviorally, cognitively, and affectively as assessors by multiple data sources. Key findings include: the HWP (high writing proficiency) student had high behavioral, cognitive and affective engagement; the LWP (low writing proficiency) student displayed high affective engagement but limited behavioral and cognitive engagement. The findings suggest the complex relationships among the three dimensions of EFL student assessors’ engagement with online PF.

citation: Otis, B. M., Vakil, S., Ross, K., Pinkard, N., Dada, A., Moore, S., & Green, P. (2025). Exploring Black Communities’ Futures-Thinking Towards Education and STEM Learning. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores how Black residents in the United States envision liberatory futures for STEM education amid enduring racialized harm. Drawing on Black futurity and a community-practice partnership, we analyze interviews and archival data to examine how local histories and lived experiences shape Black dreams for STEM learning. Findings highlight desires for holistic, affirming, and community-rooted STEM spaces, offering insights for designing culturally sustaining education grounded in Black educational traditions, community expertise, and collective care.

title: Speaking of Engagement: From Student Voice to a Practical Frame for Motivation in Learning

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Samuels, J. L.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This grounded qualitative study analyzes nine interviews from a fourth-grade arts-integrated in-class learning experience to explore what makes learning engaging for students. Using thematic coding, 27 student-identified motivators were synthesized into four categories—Community, Action, Intriguing, and Upliftment. These findings highlight the potential of a student-informed framework to support motivation in K–12 learning and offer practical guidance for pedagogical and instructional action, while pointing to further research with larger, diverse datasets.

citation: Simšič, Ž. & Keune, A. (2025). Delighted to Share: Youth-Centered Design Documentation and Portfolio Practices in Architectural Learning. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Simšič, I. & Keune, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Architectural education often reinforces inequities through high-pressure critiques and subjective evaluations. This study explores how design documentation and portfolio creation, grounded in constructionism, fosters engagement and excitement in architectural learning. During a 4-day summer camp, youth (ages 13-15) created portfolios to document their design work. Findings highlight how integrating youth-centered documentation practices fosters an exciting learning environment, transforming portfolio creation into an engaging process that sustains interest in architecture.

citation: Kim, A. E. & Farris, A. V. (2025). Not Just What to Do, but How to Know: Epistemological Messages in Science Notebook Prompts. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kim, A. E. & Farris, A. V.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study explores the relationships among preservice teachers’ notebook entries and the epistemological messages in instructors’ prompts. We analyzed 24 students’ digital notebooks from an introductory physics class and compared responses to two types of prompts: empirically-focused and design-focused. Empirically-focused prompts elicited resources such as knowledge-as-propagated and accumulation, while design-focused prompts more often elicited knowledge-as-fabricated and knowledge formation. Our findings highlight ways that features of prompts influence students’ sensemaking approaches in science notebooking tasks.

title: Integrating Student Interests into Curriculum Design: A Mixed-Methods Approach to Fostering Creativity and Innovation for Addressing Global Crises
citation: Cho, E. (2025). Integrating Student Interests Into Curriculum Design: A Mixed-Methods Approach to Fostering Creativity and Innovation for Addressing Global Crises. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 3189-3191). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cho, E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Design-Based Research (DBR); Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies
abstract: This study explores the integration of students’ interests into 21st-century curricula to foster creativity and enhance problem-solving skills. Using a mixed-methods approach within a design-based research framework, the research examines how aligning educational practices with students' interests bridges the gap between formal and informal learning, empowering students to address community challenges effectively. Drawing on foundational theories, including Wallas's (1926) four stages of creative activity and Csikszentmihalyi's Flow Theory (1990), the study emphasizes the role of motivation, curiosity, and cultural norms in shaping creativity. It also investigates how Information and Communication Technology (ICT) supports innovation by connecting theoretical knowledge with real-world applications. Preliminary findings from a 12-week enrichment program indicate that while creative problem-solving activities did not directly enhance creativity, they significantly fostered students' interest and community engagement. The study offers actionable insights for educators and policymakers to develop culturally responsive, creativity-driven curricula that support diverse global contexts.

title: Collaborative Authentic Professional Development on AI Uses: Reducing Teacher Workload and Fostering Communities of Practice
citation: Choi, S. & Han, I. (2025). Collaborative Authentic Professional Development on Ai Uses: Reducing Teacher Workload and Fostering Communities of Practice. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Choi, S. & Han, I.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Communities of Practice & Situated Learning; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: This study examines the impact of a collaborative authentic professional development (CAPD) program on reducing teachers' workload, improving self-efficacy, and fostering collaborative learning through Communities of Practice (CoP). The eight-session program led to significant reductions in workload, improved teachers’ self-efficacy, and statistically significant increases in AI usage across eight key areas of professional tasks. Teachers noted the benefits of AI in automating administrative duties, creating innovative lesson ideas, and offering emotional support while also addressing challenges such as reliability, ethical concerns, and adoption barriers.

title: From Deficit Thinking to Reflective Practice: Examining Teacher Sensemaking about Student Participation and its Shift
citation: He, W. (2025). From Deficit Thinking to Reflective Practice: Examining Teacher Sensemaking About Student Participation and Its Shift. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 3195-3196). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: He, W.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines a novice middle school science teacher’s evolving sensemaking about students not participating in science discussions. Drawing on 15 lesson debriefs, this study shows that the teacher initially framed student silence through deficit and hierarchical discourses—attributing silence to students’ cognitive limitations (“cannot think”) or lack of effort (“unwilling to think”). Over time, her sensemaking shifted toward a more reflective stance, focusing on how instructional practices, especially questioning strategies, could foster participation.

title: Held Between Two Fingers: Exploring the Bounds of Storying Land
citation: Ortiz, O. (2025). Held Between Two Fingers: Exploring the Bounds of Storying Land. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: Ortiz, O.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Contributing to scholarship attending to the uprooting of settled threads of coloniality in informal science learning environments, this paper aims to explore the ways youth workers dissuade and/or invite relational practices between and among humans and the more-than-human, and how these moments shape the resources young people take up to story land. Preliminary findings demonstrate that despite physical, programmatic, and institutional constraints, young people, alongside adult allies, still find ways to resist nature-culture divides.

title: Rethinking Differentiated Instruction: Lessons from the Pandemic for Today's Classrooms
citation: Raj, A., Wittmann, M. C., & Kayumova, S. (2025). Rethinking Differentiated Instruction: Lessons From the Pandemic for Today's Classrooms. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Raj, A., Wittmann, M. C., & Kayumova, S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Our study examines teachers’ experiences with Differentiated Instruction (DI) during the pandemic, focusing on teaching modality and student choice. Using interviews with ten teachers, we found that asynchronous formats supported individualized differentiation, while synchronous formats posed challenges. Increased student choice emerged as a key practice, prompting reflection and perspective shifts among teachers. Grounded in student choice literature and Mezirow’s Transformative Learning Theory, findings inform DI research and highlight the importance of reflection in teacher education.

title: Making Processes Visible in Distributed Maker Communities

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Danzig, B., Correa, I., & Holbert, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper explores Make-in-Progress (MIP), a tool for learners to document and share photos of their making processes within a distributed community. We examine the initial set of maker posts to the MIP carousel in two concurrently running maker camp groups, along with video recordings of maker sessions and participant interviews. Through this analysis, we identify the elements of the making process made visible in these artifacts and the documentation styles and communication techniques employed.

title: What Tasks Do Learners Delegate to ChatGPT? Analysis of Student Queries
citation: Piatnitckaia, L., Corneloup, V., & Zenasni, F. (2025). What Tasks do Learners Delegate to ChatGPT? Analysis of Student Queries. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Piatnitckaia, L., Corneloup, V., & Zenasni, F.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigated how students use ChatGPT during their exam preparation period. We explored 3,047 messages from students to ChatGPT to assess what kinds of questions and tasks students are keen to delegate to AI. Using the OpenAI API, we annotated these messages, categorizing question types and mapping them to Bloom's taxonomy levels. The results show that students are using ChatGPT not only to recall information but to deepen their understanding and analytical skills.

title: Imagining Inclusive Makerspaces Through a Creative Process with Tangible Materials and AI-Generative Arts
citation: Keune, A. & Bermúdez, D. V. (2025). Imagining Inclusive Makerspaces Through a Creative Process With Tangible Materials and Ai-Generative Arts. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Keune, A. & Bermúdez, D. V.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Co-Design & Participatory Design; Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: The educational maker movement promotes design with innovative technologies, encouraging community collaboration. However, exclusionary settings can hinder participation. The participatory design offers opportunities for creating inclusive makerspaces, allowing young people and other community members to shape their learning environments and foster socio-emotional learning, such as respect for diversity. This study explores opportunities for co-designing inclusive makerspaces for broadening participation and fostering socio-emotional learning by combining AI-generated art and tangible tools.

title: Patterns of Cognitive Offloading and Extended Mind in Digital Academic Reading with AI-generated Annotations
citation: Shin, B., Kang, M., Eun, S., & Cho, Y. H. (2025). Patterns of Cognitive Offloading and Extended Mind in Digital Academic Reading With Ai-Generated Annotations. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Shin, B., Kang, M., Eun, S., & Cho, Y. H.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study investigates patterns of distributed intelligence in digital academic reading. Data was collected from 47 higher education students in South Korea engaging with two types of AI-generated annotations: Korean translations (cognitive offloading) and deep-reasoning questions (extended mind). Process mining of trace data and interview data showed that translation annotations enabled more linear, purposeful reading processes, whereas question annotations led to more complex integration of information. The findings contribute to our understanding of actions that represent cognitive offloading and extended mind, informing the design of distributed intelligence in digital academic reading.

title: Student Teacher Learning as a Means to Increase the Capacity of a Design-Centric Research-Practice Partnership
citation: Dektor, R. & Severance, S. (2025). Student Teacher Learning as a Means to Increase the Capacity of a Design-Centric Research-Practice Partnership. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Dektor, R. & Severance, S.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Research-practice partnerships (RPPs) can provide effective means to design and implement school materials but can face capacity issues. This study explores efforts to integrate 10 student teachers into an RPP focused on computer science learning to increase capacity of the RPP. These efforts led to (1) increased implementation of CS-integrated lessons, (2) establishment of a pipeline for pre-service teachers to become new hires, and (3) spurred development of professional development tools used across the RPP.

title: Teacher SEL Matters: How Interventions Shape Teachers’ Well-Being and Professional Growth
citation: Chen, Y., Lei, J., & Wu, S. (2025). Teacher Sel Matters: How Interventions Shape Teachers’ Well-Being and Professional Growth. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 3218-3220). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chen, Y., Lei, J., & Wu, S.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This systematic review analyzed 15 empirical studies on Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) interventions for teachers. Results indicate a focus on emotional regulation, stress management, and resilience for in-service teachers, while pre-service programs emphasize emotional intelligence, interpersonal skills, and decision-making. Mindfulness-based programs are most common. In-service teachers benefit from classroom strategies, whereas pre-service teachers gain foundational competencies. Gaps in cultural awareness and theoretical grounding suggest the need for more inclusive and theory informed SEL program design.

title: Emerging Debugging Strategies of Novice Programmers: The Role of Self-Efficacy
citation: Yun, H., Sung, G., Feng, Y., & Schneider, B. (2025). Emerging Debugging Strategies of Novice Programmers: The Role of Self-Efficacy. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Yun, H., Sung, G., Feng, Y., & Schneider, B.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Self-efficacy in novice programming affects problem-solving approaches. Analysis revealed three clusters (underconfident, confident, overconfident) based on debugging self-efficacy versus ability. Misalignment between perceived and actual ability may reduce future programming interest. Sequence analysis showed strategy quality, not quantity, determined debugging success, with confident students showing adaptive behaviors. Findings suggest interventions promoting well-calibrated self-efficacy and metacognitive skills.

title: The Relationship between Learning Sentiments and Cognitive Engagement in MOOC Discussion Forums
citation: Chen, S. (2025). The Relationship Between Learning Sentiments and Cognitive Engagement in MOOC Discussion Forums. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 3224-3226). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chen, S.

abstract: Learning sentiments and cognitive engagement are crucial indicators of learning performance in MOOC discussion forums. While their relationship has not been thoroughly investigated in MOOC contexts, this study examined the impact of learning sentiments on cognitive engagement. Data from 220 participants (college students and K-12 teachers) generated 4,341 discussion posts across three forum types (analysis, reflection and discussion, and creation) based on Bloom’s Taxonomy. Using the Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive (ICAP) framework, findings revealed that creation forums fostered diverse sentiment patterns and higher constructive engagement. While active engagement dominated across forums, positive and negative sentiments correlated with active engagement, insightful sentiments with constructive engagement, and confused sentiments with interactive engagement. These findings inform MOOC discussion design to enhance meaningful learning engagement.

abstract: This study explores two major disconnections in cleanroom learning: limited hands-on engagement due to advanced automation and the disconnect between theoretical learning goals and students' focus on procedural tasks. Implementing a mixed reality (MR)-enhanced training approach shows thematic analysis evidence that it bridges these educational gaps and connects conceptual knowledge with practical procedures, also motivating students.

title: Fostering Inclusive Practices in Educational Policy Reform
citation: Mawene, D. & Schrader, E. (2025). Fostering Inclusive Practices in Educational Policy Reform. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. abstract: In this paper, we examine how a group of diverse stakeholders in a predominantly White school district expanded their practice of inclusion through an intentional co-design process. The Aleph School District (ASD) in New England, U.S., co-designed a protocol for addressing discrimination and harassment, a persistent concern affecting historically marginalized students with and without disabilities. The school district partnered with the local university and employed the Learning Lab intervention (Bal et al., 2016; 2018), an inclusive, process-oriented methodology to enable the local stakeholders most impacted the chance to better understand and address their concerns. Our analysis of data suggests that, in addition to producing a needed and useful protocol, this process expanded authentic inclusion of student voice in the school district. Further, we identify practices that fostered meaningful inclusion within the Learning Lab and tangible and intangible outcomes that extended beyond the Learning Lab space.

title: Equity-Logics for Designing New Activity Systems Toward Rightful Familial Presence in Middle School STEM

abstract: Minoritized parents have historically been sidelined in parent-school engagement opportunities. Research-practice-partnerships (RPP) have been one way to bring together stakeholders across communities in collective sense-making. We explore the design and enactment of a new activity system where minoritized parents, their middle school children and science teacher and researchers, engaged in the FamJam RPP, to co-design and enact engineering curriculum that centers community and seeds rightful familial presence in middle school STEM. Guided by frameworks of rightful presence, RPPs for learning at the boundaries, and cultural historical activity theory, the findings highlight new possibilities for family engagement through considering the underlying logics of equity. These include spatial and temporal equity, solidarity for equitable collaboration, collective responsibility for justice-oriented STEM, and fostering STEM for thriving and democratic citizenry. The study explores how these equity-focused logics can disrupt and transform systemic injustices in educational practices through new modes of relationalities and role/boundary mediation.

abstract: The expectations within the maker mindset of persisting through challenges and risk taking assume that makers are comfortable with failing. However, for marginalized youth who have been traditionally told they do not belong in STEM communities, this is not the case. In response, we seek to reframe the maker mindset through a lens of computational action, suggesting that students are more likely to persist through failure when their making is driven by the identities and communities that are meaningful to them. To illustrate this, we apply a case study approach to two makers in a summer camp, to reveal how they persisted through the evolution of their projects that reflected their identities, consequently demonstrating and developing maker mindsets. We also explore practices in our maker camp that supported their identity driven maker mindsets, namely availability and aesthetics of materials, adequate mentor support, and curriculum scaffolds to integrate identity and computing.

title: Find It First, Don’t Cheat, Make Your Code Useful: Norming “Novelty” in Early Childhood Computer Science
citation: Silvis, D., Ashineh, A., Lee, B., Shumway, J., & Clarke-Midura, J. (2025). Find it First, Don’t Cheat, Make Your Code Useful: Norming “Novelty” in Early Childhood Computer Science. abstract: As young children now regularly learn to code in early childhood learning environments, computer science is becoming a new context for establishing social norms. Not only must children learn new disciplinary concepts (e.g., “code,” “loop,” “debug”), but they also collaboratively define what is proper conduct for creating code, what makes “good” code, and how to act and think like coders. This paper explores how children produce a sociocomputational expectation to create novel code. Through qualitative analysis of interactions in a second-grade classroom, we focus on three small groups who created novel solutions to integrated math-and-coding problems using a tangible programming robot. We found that while they were learning how to use a loop command to repeat units of code, children were conversely trying not to repeat the programs of their peers and other groups. We argue that this is reflective of innovation norms inherent in broader tech culture.

title: Engagement in Computational Thinking: The Role of Mother, Father with Daughters in After-school Learning
citation: Xing, G. (2025). Engagement in Computational Thinking: The Role of Mother, Father With Daughters in After-School Learning. abstract: Parent-child interactions are pivotal for nurturing Computational Thinking (CT) in children, yet existing research often centers on parents with coding or STEM backgrounds interacting with one child, overlooking non-STEM parents, unique parental contributions, and sibling dynamics. This case study bridges these gaps by exploring how a mother and father without STEM backgrounds interact with their two daughters during an after-school CT program. Adopting Family System Theory and micro-analysis of video-recorded interactions, this study identified eleven shared and unique parental roles. The father uniquely acted as active observer and playful companion, while the mother displayed mediator and conflict navigator, maintainer of focus, and negotiator of autonomy. Viewing family as an interconnected system, these parental roles influenced children’s engagement and were shaped by individual and sibling characteristics. The findings affirm the importance of diverse family dynamics in creating supportive environments for CT education, with implications for parents, educators, and program designers.

title: “I Guess It Makes Me Feel Better About Myself”: High-Achievement of Adolescent Girls in Middle School

abstract: This research explores how high-achieving middle school girls see themselves as learners and how academic performance shapes their sense of self. Aiming to provide a nuanced understanding of the stresses, pressures, and coping strategies these girls experience, the study uses the Listening Guide method, a feminist, qualitative, voice-centered approach to discovery through listening. Data include multiple interviews with 19 high-achieving middle school girls from a large city in the northeastern United States, highlighting four key narratives. The findings contribute to the larger academic discourse on the extreme levels of daily stresses these girls experience and adds novel insights to how it affects their sense of self as learners, the coping mechanisms they adopt, and the impact of rigidly adhering to a high-achieving identity.

title: Designing for Discourse: Enacting Responsive Teaching through Code Reflections in a Computational Modeling Unit

authors_list: Wagh, A., Rosenbaum, L. F., Eloy, A., Fuhrmann, T., Henrique, B., Blikstein, P., & Wilkerson, M. H.

abstract: An emerging body of work in the learning sciences has examined how computational models can support teachers in responding to students' prompts, inquiry, and ideas. This work has highlighted how teachers make discursive moves in relation to computational models to support classroom discussion. In this paper, we focus on a complementary phenomenon: teachers' design of code reflections, or curricular modifications that deepen students' engagement with one another's code for scientific and computational sensemaking. We highlight how these code reflections advanced student discourse and how both the code reflections and discourse became more sophisticated over time, shifting towards making connections across code, behaviors, simulation outcomes, data and the scientific process being represented. We reflect on how this progression was driven by shifts in the teachers’ comfort with code and computational modeling and the resources designers can offer to educators to support the development of code reflections.

title: Illustrating Four Synergistic Approaches to Equity Among Preservice Elementary Teachers of Science: “If This is How We Do Science, Then The Future Could Be a Lot Better”
citation: Davis, E. A., Bautista, J., & Nifoussi, V. P. (2025). subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Learning to engage in justice-oriented science teaching as a new elementary teacher is challenging. We explore how six focal preservice elementary teachers demonstrate beginning versions of equity-oriented science teaching. We focus on these teachers’ assets and strengths, using these to highlight what is possible and, at the same time, to identify where teacher educators may need to provide additional support. Drawing on interviews, lesson plans, and videorecordings of lesson enactments, we use these six teachers to provide examples of novice engagement in four approaches to equity: increasing opportunity and access to science, increasing representation and identification in science, expanding what counts as science, and seeing science as a part of justice movements. Our findings show how committed teachers who are supported in learning to engage in justice-oriented teaching are able to provide early versions of equitable experiences in their classrooms. We close with implications for practice and theory.

title: Exploring Students' Interest-Driven Patterns of Scientific Observation in Minecraft

abstract: Students bring different levels of interest to learning experiences, which impacts how they engage with learning materials. This study aims to understand the relationship between student's interest levels and their scientific observation behaviors within a Minecraft-based learning system. Motivated by the growing interest in integrating human-AI collaboration within educational research, we combine the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) with the expertise of human researchers to capture the emerging themes within students’ observations. Using epistemic network analysis, we then visualized and compared the observational patterns of students with high and low situational interest. Our findings indicate that students with higher situational interest tend to make observations across a broader range of topics, with a particular emphasis on scientific content. These results highlight the potential for developing timely interventions to support students with low situational interest.

title: Space and Time as Elements to Design With in Engineering for Sustainability
citation: Sherard, M. K., Zarazaga, J., & Petrosino, A. J. (2025). Space and Time as Elements to Design With in Engineering for Sustainability. abstract: Engineering co-design projects have great potential for developing sustainable solutions to global environmental and social crises. Rooted in sociocultural and sociomaterial theories of learning and activity, we examined a group of engineers, architects, and community members who gathered in rural Tanzania to co-design a sustainable roof tile. Using tools from microethnography and interaction analysis, we demonstrate how the successful co-design of the roof tile required collaboration between individuals (from different disciplinary, linguistic, and cultural backgrounds) and materials. This collaboration illuminated how the spatial and temporal trajectories of one material, rice husks, was critical for the design of the roof tile. This research highlights the central importance of local knowledge, systems thinking, and spatiotemporal reasoning for sustainability-focused engineering co-design.

abstract: This paper explores the mathematical participation of one kindergarten student, Quentin, across two differing settings: whole-group instruction versus small-group play centers. Leveraging Gee’s (2000) definition of identity as an act of recognition, we examine how Quentin’s bids for social interaction were more or less recognized by his peers across these varying contexts. We highlight the potential role of play in facilitating a space for Quentin’s ways of being to be taken up as part of, rather than separate from, mathematics.

abstract: We investigated the barriers experienced by neurodivergent students across multiple universities. Employing a conceptual framework grounded in diversity, equity, inclusion, neurodivergence, and socio-emotional viewpoint, we identified (a) systemic barriers to accommodations, (b) reasons for social isolation, and (c) the need for faculty training as themes. We offered recommendations, including streamlining accommodation processes, implementing faculty development programs, and creating peer support systems. The findings offer a pathway toward more equitable and inclusive environments for neurodivergent students, advancing academic success and well-being.

title: Teachers' Resistance to Implementing Interdisciplinary Education: En Route to Educational Change, Heed the Objections
citation: Novis-Deutsch, N. & Cohen, E. (2025). Teachers' Resistance to Implementing Interdisciplinary Education: En Route to Educational Change, Heed the Objections. subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Educational innovations hinge on teacher support, making it important to understand their attitudes. This study examines dispositional, situational, and innovation-specific aspects of teachers' attitudes toward changing a disciplinary humanities program to an interdisciplinary one. We followed 117 teachers in 10 schools, collecting quantitative and qualitative data to compare Supporters and Resistors. Resistors were significantly lower on dispositional Openness and focused on challenges for teachers and on epistemic issues related to the structure of the disciplines, while Supporters emphasized student benefits. Most Supporters viewed interdisciplinarity as a means to other ends, such as class management, rather than valuing it intrinsically for its epistemic benefits. Based on these findings, we recommend addressing teachers' concerns about disciplinary integrity and professional autonomy, providing clear epistemic justifications for interdisciplinarity, and tailoring implementation strategies to align with teachers' motivations and readiness for change.

title: When Interdisciplinary Groups Succeed: The Role of Direct Critiques

abstract: This study examines the dynamics of dialogic argumentation among physics teachers with different disciplinary backgrounds in a professional development program. The discourse of seventeen teacher triads participating in structured argumentative activities was analyzed using detailed coding schemes for dialogic moves and epistemic practices. We found that heterogeneous groups of teachers were on average more successful in engaging in deliberative and epistemically-rich dialogues compared to homogeneous groups. However, the success of heterogeneous groups varied widely. Further analysis showed that the heterogeneous groups differed in the nature of their interactions: participants in deliberative groups tended to challenge each other directly, whereas in less deliberative groups direct challenges were often avoided. Qualitative analysis reveals how direct challenges act to create space for deliberation in heterogeneous groups. This study challenges the assumption that interdisciplinary collaboration is always beneficial, pointing to the crucial role of direct, cross-disciplinary challenges in stimulating productive dialogue.

title: Empowering Undergraduate Computer Science Majors Through AI Literacy Research

abstract: The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) in post-secondary education has prompted educational researchers to develop definitions of undergraduate AI literacy. However, undergraduate AI literacy in practice is unclear and overly theoretical. This multiple case study analysis centers the perspectives of five undergraduate students as they learned about and defined AI literacy during an intensive 8-week research course. Creating and enacting their own unique AI literacy research projects, the undergraduate students interrogated existing AI literacy literature, analyzed undergraduate AI literacy survey data, and conducted focus groups with undergraduate students to interrogate the relationship between AI and undergraduate education. Through the research process, the undergraduates constantly negotiated their understanding of AI literacy and developed research-based conclusions that merged theory with practice. We describe the implications of these findings on undergraduate computer science education, highlighting the role of social science research in computing education.

abstract: Educators’ self-perception as individuals who could engineer influences their motivation and support they provide during engineering learning. This study examines ways to support engineering identity development of library professionals and position them as educators for children’s engineering learning. Drawing from the theory of identities-in-practice and the concept of boundary crossing, this study conducts a case study to investigate how rural library professionals developed traces of emerging engineering identity. By examining nine library professionals’ engagement over two years in a three-year project to co-design and facilitate an online engineering program for children and their parents, this study contributes to the understanding of how public library professionals perform boundary crossing practices to position themselves as engineering learners and educators. The study further illuminates the potential of public libraries to serve as transformative spaces for engineering engagement and encourages public libraries to redefine library professionals’ roles.

title: Embodied Improvisation: Exploring How Teachers Support Young Children’s Engagement with Intelligent Agents
citation: Xing, G., Wang, X. C., Yamamoto, Y., Cai, Z., Sadeghi, S., & Dantu, K. (2025). Embodied Improvisation: Exploring How Teachers Support Young Children’s Engagement With Intelligent Agents. abstract: Early childhood teachers are increasingly introducing intelligent agents (IAs) into their classrooms but often face challenges in balancing structured lessons with the spontaneity required to address children’s natural curiosity and unexpected exploration with IAs. To address this challenge, we propose an Embodied Improvisation framework to investigate how teachers support young children’s engagement with IAs. The Embodied Improvisation framework adapts embodied responsive teaching and the “Yes, and…” improv principle to highlight the embodied and fluid nature of teachers’ scaffolding. Through interactional video analysis of teacher-child interactions with a robot in a toddler (2-3 years old) classroom, we demonstrate how teachers address children’s cognitive and emotional needs and enhance their engagement and agency through embodied improvisation. Based on the findings, we advocate a flexible approach to integrating IAs into developmentally appropriate classroom practices for young children.

title: Leveraging Symbolic Representations to Understand Young Learners’ Interactions with Computational Thinking Concepts
citation: Fofang, J. B. & Weintrop, D. (2025). Leveraging Symbolic Representations to Understand Young Learners’ Interactions With Computational Thinking Concepts. abstract: Computational thinking (CT) holds significant value in STEM education because it emphasizes cultivating problem-solving skills mediated by computational technologies. This aspect of CT enhances the educational experience for learners and can open promising opportunities for supporting and assessing learning with new technologies. Using a 14-week curriculum designed to integrate CT into fourth-grade mathematics classrooms using a programmable robot, we explore how young learners use symbolic representations to translate across contexts. We investigate the potential of symbolic representations in developing CT skills, including decomposition and abstraction. We present vignettes to show how young learners’ use of symbolic representations in CT tasks can contribute to a deeper understanding of how students conceptualize and engage with computational problem-solving. This work advances our understanding of how integrating CT in early-grade classrooms can significantly enrich STEM education thus highlighting the importance of developing CT skills for early-grade learners.

title: Preservice Teachers’ Computational Thinking Profiles
citation: Chichekian, T., Cutumisu, M., & Savard, A. (2025). Preservice Teachers’ Computational Thinking Profiles. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 47-55). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chichekian, T., Cutumisu, M., & Savard, A.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: In our technology-driven world, developing computational thinking (CT) skills among preservice teachers is essential for fostering digital innovation. This study investigates how metacognitive strategies and prior coding experience impact preservice teachers’ CT skills and behaviors during an online CT challenge. Preservice teachers (n=129) completed a survey and an interactive CT challenge. A latent profile analysis using CT skills identified three distinct profiles (Developing, Novice, and Proficient) and linear discriminant analysis assessed potential predictors of these profiles. Results revealed that higher levels of CT skills correlated positively with better performance on the CT challenge, as well as lower perceptions regarding the difficulty level associated with the CT challenge. Both metacognitive strategies and prior coding experience were effective predictors of CT skills. This study underscores the importance of incorporating practical coding exercises and metacognitive activities into teacher education programs to better prepare future educators for the effective implementation of digital technologies in their teaching.

title: The Effects of Digital Games on Pre-K-12 Students’ Growth Mindset: A Systematic Review
citation: Rahimi, S., Esmaeiligoujar, S., Gao, R., Ercan, D., & Keawphonkrang, S. (2025). The Effects of Digital Games on Pre-K-12 Students’ Growth Mindset: A Systematic Review. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rahimi, S., Esmaeiligoujar, S., Gao, R., Ercan, D., & Keawphonkrang, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The concept of a “growth mindset” refers to the belief that one’s abilities and intelligence can be developed through effort, learning, and persistence. This systematic review examines the impact of digital games on fostering a growth mindset in pre-K-12 educational settings. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, we analyzed 13 studies focused on digital games designed to enhance a growth mindset. Findings indicate that most games positively influence growth mindset along with other competencies (e.g., creativity and persistence), while a minority show mixed or negligible effects, often linked to the game design or context. The review identifies trends across various game genres, targeted skills, and geographical regions, reflecting a growing interest in growth mindset research. It suggests that digital games represent a valuable avenue for educational interventions which emphasize the need for thoughtful design informed by evidence on effective game features.

title: Reinterpreting Lamarckianism as Generative Mechanistic Reasoning about Natural Selection
citation: Svoboda, J., Dabholkar, S., Wang, Y., & Benjamin, S. (2025). Reinterpreting Lamarckianism as Generative Mechanistic Reasoning About Natural Selection. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 484-492). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Svoboda, J., Dabholkar, S., Wang, Y., & Benjamin, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Students often express Lamarckian ideas—that changes acquired during an organism’s lifetime can be inherited—when reasoning about natural selection. Researchers have described this reasoning as arising from incorrect and unproductive misconceptions. Using the theoretical tools of resource theory and data from interviews with college students, we argue that an alternative explanation for students’ apparent Lamarckian reasoning is that they are seeking to provide mechanisms that can account for trait change. Unlike canonical population-level mechanisms, organism-level mechanisms are grounded in plausible changes to organismal forms, physiologies, or behaviors. We found that organism-level mechanistic reasoning arose in interviews when students recognized a need for a mechanistic explanation and shifted into an epistemological framing of in-the-moment knowledge construction. Rather than interpret Lamarckian ideas as misconceptions, we argue that they can be viewed as evidence of students' generative epistemological resources for seeking and providing mechanisms.

title: Unplugged Activities as Opportunities to Enhance Mixed Reality Educational Technology through Personal Connections
citation: Ayalon, E., Lane, A. C., Anton, G., Jen, T., Lee, S. J., & Enyedy, N. (2025). abstract: This paper explores how unplugged activities can enhance learning in mixed-reality (MR) science environments by supporting students in connecting classroom modeling with their lived experiences. Drawing on funds of knowledge (FoK) and embodied modeling learning theories, we analyze a case study of fourth-grade students engaged in a multi-modal ecosystem simulation. Through storytelling and design activities, students integrated personal experiences—such as caring for pets—into the modeling process, shaping how they modified the MR environment and reasoned about ecological systems. We find that unplugged activities can boost engagement by “doubling down” on the immersive, affective strengths of MR or counterbalance its limitations by rooting inquiry in students’ everyday knowledge. However, we also identify tensions when students’ emotional attachments to modeled agents override broader system-level reasoning. This work highlights the importance of designing unplugged activities as intentional mediational tools in socio-technical learning systems.
