abstract: This study explores the experience and perceptions of undergraduate STEM majors in the STEM voices mentorship program grounded in the theoretical framework of communities of practice (CoP). This research investigates how undergraduate STEM mentors perceive their growth and development within the STEM Voices program, designed to engage African American middle school youth in STEM as a tool for social justice. Using a qualitative research design, the study collected data through semi-structured interviews with nine undergraduate STEM majors who participated in the program in 2023-24 school year. Thematic analysis revealed that relationships were central to their experiences, with significant connections to youth engagement, personal growth, community service, and a sense of belonging. Building relationships was viewed as fundamental to participants' experiences and development within the program.

title: The What and How of Becoming “Co-Conspirators of Social Justice” in Computing Education
citation: Jayathirtha, G., Goode, J., Chapman, G., Jones, K., Elmeligui, T., Taylor, M., Ottina, J., & Crocker, T. (2025). The What and How of Becoming “Co-Conspirators of Social Justice” in Computing Education: Perspectives From and for High School Computing Teachers. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 511-519). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jayathirtha, G., Goode, J., Chapman, G., Jones, K., Elmeligui, T., Taylor, M., Ottina, J., & Crocker, T.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Co-Design & Participatory Design; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: Teachers play a crucial role in shaping learning opportunities within classrooms, and yet their voices are often missing from educational design efforts. Our work resists the normative roles ascribed to teachers in world-making efforts and partners with them to (re)design a justice-oriented high school computing program. We present findings from a collaborative video analysis of a co-design session (~40 minutes) where nine high school computing teachers, two researchers, and a senior designer engaged in a design activity uncovering what it means to center justice within computing classrooms and to support new teachers to teach justice-oriented computing. Teachers resisted language divorced from practice and argued for deepening and clarifying the meaning of equitable teaching practices. They emphasized ongoing professional and personal growth, relatable professional learning experiences, and opportunities for reflection as teachers become “co-conspirators” for social justice. We discuss findings in connection to STEM teacher preparation and solidarity.

title: Learners’ Attitudes, Wishes, and Concerns Toward Learning Analytics in Higher Education: Students’ Opinions and Teachers’ Views
citation: Radtke, A., Serova, K., Osinski, M., Scheffel, M., & Rummel, N. (2025). Learners’ Attitudes, Wishes, and Concerns Toward Learning Analytics in Higher Education: Students’ Opinions and Teachers’ Views. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Radtke, A., Serova, K., Osinski, M., Scheffel, M., & Rummel, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: To facilitate the optimal use of Learning Analytics (LA) in educational settings, it is es-sential to ensure that learners’ needs and preferences for LA are aligned with teachers’ as-sumptions about these. This study examined students’ attitudes, wishes, and concerns to-ward LA in higher education and investigated the accuracy of teachers’ assumptions about their students’ opinions. Two surveys were conducted: one with Educational Science stu-dents (N = 19) and another with their lecturers (N = 12). The results revealed a general matching between students’ and lecturers’ assessments. For example, both groups indicat-ed that students favor LA that refer to learners’ individual learning histories against LA that promote social comparison with peers. But we also observed some notable discrepan-cies. Teachers considered their students to be most in need of support on the motivational dimension of self-regulation, while students indicated the least need for support on this dimension.

title: Differences in Novice and Expert Evaluations of Generative AI-Produced Definitions
citation: Williams-Pierce, C. (2025). Differences in Novice and Expert Evaluations of Generative Ai-Produced Definitions. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 529-537). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Williams-Pierce, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Widely available generative AI products such as ChatGPT are transforming the ways in which students and professionals work and learn, but little is known about how novices and experts perceive, evaluate, and judge generative AI-produced materials. Established research from cognitive science suggests that novices and experts will attend differently to surface and deep structures of content-specific materials. This preliminary study focuses on examining the accuracy and confidence judgements and annotations from experts and novices in the field of Information Science, comparing their evaluations across three different conditions: a ChatGPT produced definition of ‘data’; a human crowd-sourced definition of ‘data’; and a ChatGPT produced definition of a nonexistent word, ‘techno-data.’ The paper concludes with next steps in this research study, as well as potential implications for learning, education, and expertise.

title: Generative Inquiry: Creativity Assessments of Youth Epistemic Agency and in a Computational Data Science Workshop
citation: Walker, J. T., Rahimi, S., Barany, A., & Lin-Lipsmeyer, L. (2025). Generative Inquiry: Creativity Assessments of Youth Epistemic Agency and in a Computational Data Science Workshop. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 538-546). subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy

abstract: Computational data science (CDS) is relevant in areas of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for reasons related to field innovation and public literacy. Much is known about pre-college learning with guided CDS in traditional subjects, and comparatively less about how to design and identify generative moments in open inquiry, which are inherent and valued in the field. We examine two illustrative cases of high school-aged youth’s final projects to assess strategies used when enacting a self-directed inquiry project. We report how creativity indicators show up in activities emphasizing learner agency. Our findings represent an initial effort to use creativity to assess process outcomes in the context of open inquiry. We recommend creativity-based assessments of inquiry-driven by generative acts to promote knowledge construction and learning. Insights are discussed in terms of how they extend ideas about assessing constructs such as epistemic agency in open-ended learning.

title: “It Goes Both Ways”: Envisioning Mutually Compassionate Relations between Teachers and Students
citation: Chang, M. A., Penuel, W. R., & Philip, T. M. (2025). “It Goes Both Ways”: Envisioning Mutually Compassionate Relations Between Teachers and Students. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 547-555). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chang, M. A., Penuel, W. R., & Philip, T. M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Cultivating compassion has been shown to support teachers in caring for non-dominant youth in K-12 schools. While students often show compassion for other students, students’ skillful caring for teachers has remained relatively underexplored. Here, within an intergenerational co-design context with students and their teachers, we explore the pedagogical conditions that support students and teachers to surface and develop the conditions for mutual compassionate relations. Our findings demonstrate that, when used in tandem, a User Persona activity and Theater of the Oppressed Activity supported students and their teachers in adopting compassionate stances towards each others’ suffering, thereby creating the relatively unusual opportunity for teacher participants to vulnerably share their suffering incurred while trying to care for the students. We conclude by showing how cultivating mutual compassionate relations as a goal of co-design spaces can open up expansive objects, including systemic changes motivated by the interlinked suffering of intergenerational stakeholders.

title: Amplifying Teacher Voice in Collaborative Research
citation: Luehmann, A., van Es, E. A., Gama-Krummel, A., Munzer, A., & Wilson, E. (2025). Amplifying Teacher Voice in Collaborative Research. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 556-564). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Luehmann, A., Es, E. A. V., Gama-Krummel, A., Munzer, A., & Wilson, E.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Research practice partnerships (RPPs) are a promising approach to transforming educational practice by amplifying the voices of teachers. This approach is especially powerful for disrupting educational inequities by positioning local actors as experts to generate solutions and take action. This cross-case study examines how engaging mathematics and science teachers in collaborative inquiry gave voice to teachers’ experiences as they sought to transform their instruction for equity and justice. Informed by process and practice theory perspectives, we describe how the social arrangement of cowriting supported teacher researchers in generating new concepts and practices for equitable and just instruction. We identify four specific practices - gaining clarity and consensus on equity for STEM instruction, generating representations, thinking through example cases, and cycles of feedback and accountability. Together, these practices enabled teachers to contribute to knowledge generation by advancing theory on instructional practice for justice-oriented practice through experimentation and analysis of teaching practice.

title: Children’s Play With Video Data as a Methodological Invitation
citation: Vescio, J. (2025). Children’s Play With Video Data as a Methodological Invitation. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 56-64). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Vescio, J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This paper investigates young children’s leveraging of play as an analytic tool when interpreting video data of themselves. Employing interaction analysis (Jordan & Henderson, 1995), I explore the epistemic and social frames that differing conversational spaces afforded for young children as they engaged in the playful act of watching their own participation in a kindergarten mathematics classroom. In doing so, I argue for the expansion of playful methodological contexts in order to better facilitate adults’ learning from young children.

title: GenAI as a Peer Review Support: Impact on Feedback Quality, Quantity, and Student Perceptions
citation: Chase, C. & Venook, R. (2025). GenAI as a Peer Review Support: Impact on Feedback Quality, Quantity, and Student Perceptions. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chase, C. & Venook, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Peer feedback is an efficient way to give students feedback while promoting their learning. However, peer feedback often lacks the depth and volume of expert instructor feedback. This study explored whether generative AI (GenAI) could be harnessed to boost the quantity or quality of peer feedback. In a crossover study, 29 college students wrote reviews of a peer team’s scientific paper with and without using ChatGPT to revise their reviews. When students used GenAI, their reviews contained more feedback, more explanations, and more positive and descriptive comments. Evidence suggests that GenAI was most helpful as a peer feedback support for certain topics – those for which students had low prior knowledge. When receiving reviews of their own work, students preferred GenAI-supported peer reviews compared to those written by peers alone, even though they could not accurately distinguish between them. GenAI shows promise as a feedback support tool when used alongside human peers.

title: To Be or Not to Be: A Study on Shakespeare, Incarcerated Youth, and Future-Orientation
citation: Ecford, O. L. & Horn, M. S. (2025). To Be or Not to Be: A Study on Shakespeare, Incarcerated Youth, and Future-Orientation. authors_list: Ecford, O. L. & Horn, M. S.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This ongoing study examines how the Shakespeare Behind Bars (SBB) arts education program impacts future orientation development in five incarcerated youth aged 16-18. SBB engages participants in creating original artistic performances based on Shakespearean works, adapting them into modern contexts through podcasts, songs, plays, and films. Using a mixed-methods approach combining qualitative, quantitative, and ethnographic data, this preliminary analysis focuses specifically on how participants' future orientation emerges and evolves through engagement with the program's creative processes. This initial study begins a larger corpus investigating how interdisciplinary arts education influences incarcerated youths' socio-emotional development across multiple domains. Drawing on practice-driven and design-based research methodology, the analysis examines how personal narrative-based creative projects contribute to participants' ability to envision and plan for their futures in four domains of future orientation we have identified: Professional, Educational, Social Emotional, and Survival-Based Future Orientation.. Early findings suggest that artistic engagement creates unique opportunities for processing past experiences while developing future-oriented thinking.

citation: Fofang, J. B. & Weintrop, D. (2025). Using Embodiment to Reason About Geometry in an Integrated Computational Thinking and Mathematics Activity. abstract: This work uses grounded and embodied cognition (GEC) perspectives to explore how young learners reason through computational thinking (CT) concepts and geometric angles in integrated mathematics and CT-enhanced robotics activities. Findings from video data reveal that different modalities (e.g., Sphero robot, Sphero.edu app, tape, a triangle path) enabled learners to reason through geometry. We highlight the importance of examining the complex contexts in which young learners learn and apply CT and mathematical knowledge. We show that embodied gestures can advance our understanding of young learners’ reasoning about geometry, particularly in robotics activities requiring spatial reasoning abilities for navigation. Analyses support claims that geometry and spatial thinking skills in integrated mathematics, CT and, robotics environments for young learners can be expressed through embodied gestures. These findings have implications for instructional practices and the design of educational technologies and activities to support students' embodiment of concepts in ways that can support learning.

title: Exploring Students’ Perceptions of Contextualized Computing in an Introductory Computing Science Course for Non-majors
citation: Li, Y., Chen, M., Hunt, A., Horn, M. S., & O’Rourke, E. (2025). Exploring Students’ Perceptions of Contextualized Computing in an Introductory Computing Science Course for Non-Majors. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Li, Y., Chen, M., Hunt, A., Horn, M. S., & O’Rourke, E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Introductory computer science courses for non-majors (CS0) aim to increase diversity and highlight the relevance of computing across disciplines. To enhance the accessibility and engagement of CS0, researchers have explored contextualized computing, where computing is integrated with another subject, to teach course content. While research has explored various designs for contextualized courses, we know less about how contextualized computing tasks impact students’ learning experiences. Through the lens of metacognition and affect, we conducted a secondary qualitative analysis on daily diary and retrospective interview data from 20 students in a CS0 course that applied coding to different contexts. Our findings demonstrate that students’ feeling of knowing and their perception of the task are two central themes that shape their affect and interest in the course. We conclude with design suggestions for contextualized computing in CS0 to better support students.

title: Freeze Framing: A Socio-Spatial Approach for Capturing Out-of-School Time Engagement
citation: Green, P. & Pinkard, N. (2025). Freeze Framing: A Socio-Spatial Approach for Capturing Out-of-School Time Engagement. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 601-609). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Green, P. & Pinkard, N.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Out-of-school time (OST) landscapes offer critical opportunities for youth to explore interests, build agency, and develop socio-spatial connections that traditional schooling often overlooks. However, inequities in mobility, resource distribution, and access to OST opportunities persist, limiting youth engagement in these spaces. This study introduces Freeze Framing, an iterative activity system that employs Freeze Frame, its eponymous geocapture app enabling youth to document and reflect on their OST experiences. Grounded in Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) and Expansive Learning, Freeze Framing is designed to reveal socio-spatial patterns of youth engagement and foster agency in navigating OST landscapes. Through spatial mapping, thematic coding, and activity system analysis, findings highlight the tensions and contradictions shaping youth participation, such as mobility constraints and social influence. By addressing these dynamics, Freeze Framing offers a promising model for how designing youth-driven activity systems can reveal socio-spatial inequities and inform the design of more equitable and accessible OST opportunities.

title: Critical Thinking Habits of Mind in Media Arts Learning
citation: Beale, J., Castro, F., Huang, X., Scheirer, C., Lyu, C., Gao, Y., & DesPortes, K. (2025). Critical Thinking Habits of Mind in Media Arts Learning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 610-618). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Beale, J., Castro, F., Huang, X., Scheirer, C., Lyu, C., Gao, Y., & DesPortes, K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Media arts programs offer youth opportunities to develop critical thinking through creative inquiry, yet little is known about how young people practice critical thinking in these learning environments. This research aims to create a framework for understanding the critical thinking habits of mind practiced throughout media arts learning. Using observations, reflective interviews, and creative artifacts from an exploratory case study at a youth filmmaking lab, we examined the production process for six young filmmakers. We used process coding to analyze the filmmakers’ reflections and artistic decisions and identified habits such as perspective-taking, adapting, synthesizing, and assessing. From our iterative analyses of filmmakers' data, we developed a codebook for Critical Thinking Habits of Mind in Media Arts Learning. This codebook is the first step in creating a framework for studying critical thinking in media arts learning and can be used to study this phenomenon across diverse settings.

title: The Role of Teacher Framing in Shaping Student Agency in Human-AI Partnered Science Classrooms
citation: Kim, C., Ha, J. E., Gnesdilow, D., Passonneau, R. J., & Puntambekar, S. (2025). The Role of Teacher Framing in Shaping Student Agency in Human-Ai Partnered Science Classrooms. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 619-627). authors_list: Kim, C., Ha, J. E., Gnesdilow, D., Passonneau, R. J., & Puntambekar, S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study is part of a larger research project aimed at developing and implementing an NLP-enabled AI feedback tool called PyrEval to support middle school students’ science explanation writing. We explored how human-AI integrated classrooms can invite students to harness AI tools while still being agentic learners. Building on theory of new materialism with posthumanist perspectives, we examined teacher framing to see how the nature of PyrEval was communicated, thereby orienting students to partner with or rely on PyrEval. We analyzed one teacher’s talk in multiple classrooms as well as that of students in small groups. We found student agency was fostered through teacher framing of (a) PyrEval as a non-neutral actor and a co-investigator and (b) students’ participation as an author and their understanding of the nature of PyrEval as core task and purpose. Findings and implications are discussed.

abstract: Integrating computer science (CS) concepts and practices into K-12 education mainly emphasizes science, technology, engineering, and mathematics subjects, more than social studies. We examine the transformation of a middle school geography teacher’s perspective as the teacher incorporates CS content into their teaching through a co-design process. Utilizing the Interconnected Model of Teacher Professional Growth, we analyze interviews and classroom observations to describe shifts in the teacher’s practices, beliefs, and understanding of CS integration. Our findings suggest that the teacher redefined CS from a set of technical skills to a human-centered discipline, making geography learning more engaging. Additionally, the co-design allowed the teacher to view students as active creators of digital artifacts and to embrace their own role as a creator able to modify existing technologies to better suit their educational context. Our findings indicate promising ways to engage teachers from non-STEM backgrounds in effectively connecting their subjects with CS.

title: Downshifting: The Nuanced Antecedents of Seeking Easier Content
citation: Vanacore, K., Barany, A., Mehta, S., Ocumpaugh, J., Baker, R. S., Al Nahin, N., Kuvar, V., Mills, C., & Henkel, O. (2025). Downshifting: The Nuanced Antecedents of Seeking Easier Content. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 637-645). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Vanacore, K., Barany, A., Mehta, S., Ocumpaugh, J., Baker, R. S., Nahin, N. A., Kuvar, V., Mills, C., & Henkel, O.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Learning involves challenge, and students respond to challenging content in different ways. This study investigates the antecedents and contexts of downshifting: seeking out easier questions while using a digital learning platform. We study this behavior using student data from Rori – a chatbot-based math intelligent tutoring system that operates over WhatsApp and is widely used in several African countries. Specifically, we use Sequential Pattern Mining to study the behaviors that immediately precede and follow downshifting and Bayesian Knowledge Tracing to evaluate students' mastery of the content prior to downshifting. Results show that the behavior is often preceded by sequences of incorrect answers, suggesting that some students may be adaptively downshifting to avoid failure. However, some students seem to downshift despite being on track to master the current content. We also find that students using Rori in schools as part of their regular curricula are likelier to downshift than those who access Rori independently. We position downshifting within a general taxonomy of behaviors related to persistence in ITSs and suggest further research into the causes of the behavior.

title: Being “Someone Actually Doing This” Work: Consequential Learning by Youth Through the Travel of People, Knowledge, and Practices
citation: Leung, V. & Chen, B. (2025). Being “Someone Actually Doing This” Work: Consequential Learning by Youth Through the Travel of People, Knowledge, and Practices. abstract: This study examines mechanisms of consequential learning by tracing the “travels” of people, knowledge, and practices across contexts. Drawing on sociocultural perspectives, we analyze the experiences of three high school students who engaged in tackling interdisciplinary, data-intensive environmental justice issues. Through qualitative case studies, we explore how travel—both literal and metaphorical—enabled students to connect disciplinary knowledge with real-world problems, navigate tensions between knowledge systems, and develop agency and aspirations. Findings highlight travel as a mechanism that fosters authentic engagement and consequential learning that are transformative for learners. This study advances the consequential learning literature and contributes to equity-oriented educational research by surfacing practical pathways for bridging disciplines, communities, and identities, as well as obstacles to making these learning opportunities even more authentic and meaningful.

title: Towards an Equity-Oriented Theory of Instruction: A Sociopolitical Analysis of Concreteness Fading
citation: Luu, R. L. (2025). Towards an Equity-Oriented Theory of Instruction: A Sociopolitical Analysis of Concreteness Fading. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 65-73). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Luu, R. L.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: In this conceptual paper, I analyze the affordances and limitations of concreteness fading towards advancing equitable student learning in mathematics education. Concreteness fading is an instructional theory that aims to support learning through strategic use of multiple representations. Many studies have focused on how concreteness fading benefits students positioned as less successful in mathematics. However, there is little research that explores concreteness fading in relation to equity. I utilize a sociopolitical lens to analyze the theory’s underlying assumptions about what knowledge is valued, who is valued as knowledgeable, and how contexts are valued as resources for knowing. From this analysis, I conclude that concreteness fading as currently conceived does not support equitable learning, as it reifies narrow forms of mathematical knowing that privilege some learners and ways of thinking over others. I offer suggestions for reorienting concreteness fading theory towards fostering more equitable student learning outcomes in mathematics education.

title: Intertwining Epistemic and Relational Work in Scientific Modeling
citation: Manz, E. & Stoler, A. (2025). Intertwining Epistemic and Relational Work in Scientific Modeling. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 655-663). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Manz, E. & Stoler, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: As youth and teachers engage in modeling conversations, they are simultaneously negotiating how knowledge is generated and how people are accountable to each other in a community. Typically, design and analysis have privileged the epistemic focus, including within a recent emphasis on sensemaking and collective knowledge development. In this paper, we examine epistemic and relational work during science classroom modeling conversations. We share a close analysis of a typical conversation structure, where individuals present models and other students evaluate and build from their ideas. We show how classroom members experienced relational challenges and opportunities in these conversations. We also examine how alternative structures taken up by teachers and students presented different opportunities and constraints. This work contributes to the field’s understanding of science practices and suggests implications for work on evaluation and care in science classrooms.

title: Pluriversal Frameworks for Equitable and Sustainable Learning Designs. Knowledge Co-construction Experiences along Lands, Territories, and AI in Colombia
citation: Sandoval-Llanos, J., Becerra, T., Ojeda-Ramirez, S., Hakim, N., & Turano, G. D. (2025). Pluriversal Frameworks for Equitable and Sustainable Learning Designs. Knowledge Co-Construction Experiences Along Lands, Territories, and Ai in Colombia. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: Sandoval-Llanos, J., Becerra, T., Ojeda-Ramirez, S., Hakim, N., & Turano, G. D.

abstract: This paper explores how Arturo Escobar’s decolonial concepts of the pluriverse and autonomous design can contribute to learning sciences research. We draw from Escobar’s designs for the pluriverse framework, focusing on three principal components: the pluriverse, political ontology, and autonomous design, to guide learning scientists toward more sustainable and inclusive designs. Initially, we discuss these concepts and their current applications in the learning sciences. We then present three vignettes that illustrate the application of this framework in community-based research projects and instructional practices across various urban and rural contexts in Colombia. Through these examples, we examine the potential of Escobar’s proposal to facilitate equity-oriented, culturally sustaining learning designs that foster inclusion and resilience in diverse educational settings. By highlighting how local knowledges can challenge dominant Western ontologies and epistemologies, we advocate for a more pluralistic approach in learning sciences research to address the ecological and social crises we currently face.

title: Teachers’ Dilemmatic Sensemaking as a Source of Knowledge Making: Explaining to Process and Explaining to Explore
citation: Underwood, K., Horn, I., Metts, E., Li, S., & Nolting, K. (2025). Teachers’ Dilemmatic Sensemaking as a Source of Knowledge Making: Explaining to Process and Explaining to Explore. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 673-681). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Underwood, K., Horn, I., Metts, E., Li, S., & Nolting, K.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: In recent years, there have been calls for teachers to engage in responsive instruction. Simultaneously, teacher education has focused on ‘best’ practices and routines to support classroom responsiveness. However, responsive instruction is definitionally non-routine, and existing professional development often fails to attend to the complexities of responsive instruction, often expressed as dilemmas. Our project collaborates with a professional development organization aimed at supporting teachers in equitable and ambitious mathematics teaching by facilitating video-based formative feedback (VFF) cycles, centered on teachers’ inquiry questions and representations of practice. Looking at VFF cycles of two experienced teachers, we found that both teachers grounded their dilemmatic sensemaking in explanations of tensions they experienced, but subsequent discussions differed. This analysis furthers understanding of teachers’ learning through collaborative talk and points to a need to attend to the dilemmatic nature of teaching to support educators developing responsive practice.

title: Montgomery’s Lessons for Desettling Science Learning: Understanding Black Feminist Knowledge-Making in Science
citation: Rae, N. (2025). Montgomery’s Lessons for Desettling Science Learning: Understanding Black Feminist Knowledge-Making in Science. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 682-690). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rae, N.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: In this conceptual paper, I suggest cultivating Black feminist knowledge-making within science education can address the alienation and marginalization experienced by Black women. I begin by identifying features of Black feminist knowledge-making involved with developing critical consciousness among Black women, explaining how Western science perpetuates white masculine norms. To analyze an example of Black feminist knowledge-making in science, I focus on storytelling as a modality of Black women’s oppositional knowledge-making. I highlight how Beronda Montgomery's (2021) storytelling in Lessons from Plants both contributes to and draws on an intellectual genealogy of Black feminist thought in interdisciplinary ways. I conclude with theoretical and methodological implications for designing science educational environments that foster Black feminist knowledge-making, aiming to create more meaningful and liberatory science learning experiences. This work underscores the need to reimagine science education to support diverse ways of knowing and being, ultimately challenging the dominance of Western scientific paradigms.

title: Community-Wide Infrastructuring: Extending Infrastructure Theories Toward Learning Ecosystems
citation: Berger, W. & Hayden, R. (2025). Community-Wide Infrastructuring: Extending Infrastructure Theories Toward Learning Ecosystems. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 691-699). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Berger, W. & Hayden, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper examines community-wide infrastructuring as a framework for fostering equitable learning ecosystems. Motivated by the need to address inequities in access to educational opportunities across learning experiences in a community, we extend prior theories of infrastructuring to community-level contexts. We apply infrastructuring theoretical models to recent work on learning ecosystem mapping and design. This highlights the potential of community-wide infrastructuring to surface invisible infrastructures, identify key social actors, and address systemic barriers. By bridging theoretical concepts with practical considerations, the paper offers a lens for designing learning ecosystems that are locally resonant and collaboratively developed. This work provides an opening for future research on addressing inequities through participatory and sustainable infrastructuring practices.

title: Learning with Latinx Futurisms in Computer Science Education
citation: Ojeda-Ramirez, S. & Perez, M. (2025). Learning With Latinx Futurisms in Computer Science Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Learning environments for Computer Science (CS) education need to contend with the ways technological growth is positioned as an inevitable future. Justice-centered approaches to CS education aim to challenge the values that undergird ‘technological inevitability,’ through paying attention to ethics, political visions, and learners’ politicized identities. In this paper, we offer insights from imagining justice-centered CS education through the lens of Latinx Futurism, which centers imagination and world-building from the perspective of people in and of the U.S., Latin America, and the Caribbean.

title: Teachers of Students with Visual Impairments’ Role in Supporting Nonvisual Spatial and Graphical Literacies for Blind and Low Vision Students
citation: Foley, E. A., Liu, Y., & Wilkerson, M. H. (2025). Teachers of Students With Visual Impairments’ Role in Supporting Nonvisual Spatial and Graphical Literacies for Blind and Low Vision Students. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 709-717). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Foley, E. A., Liu, Y., & Wilkerson, M. H.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Teachers of students with visual impairments (TVIs) are a specialized subset of special education teachers who differentiate instruction and learning media for students who need low vision or nonvisual accommodations. Oftentimes, these strategies involve tactual, auditory, and kinesthetic modalities. Recent US standards and policy documents (e.g., CCSSI, 2010; GAISE, 2020; NGSS, 2013) promote the use of visuals to support comprehension, analysis, and communication of core content in all curricular areas. For blind and low vision (BLV) students, the very modality meant to make information easier to grasp is a barrier to learning. Additionally, the ability to make sense of visuals is not trivial even for sighted children (Roth and McGinn, 1997). In this paper, we report an analysis of seven interviews conducted with three BLV access technology specialists and four TVIs as they discussed the teaching strategies and tools they used to support BLV students’ sensemaking of information typically presented visually.

title: Complexities in Developing Socioecological Care: A Case Study of Engagement in a Critical Place-Based Science Camp
citation: Jen, T. (2025). Complexities in Developing Socioecological Care: A Case Study of Engagement in a Critical Place-Based Science Camp. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 718-726). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jen, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores the complexities of developing and enacting socioecological care in the context of a critical place-based science camp with middle school youth. I draw on Indigenous, feminist, and multispecies understandings of care as an embodied, dynamic, ethical practice of understanding and assuming responsibility within more-than-human entanglements. A case study of one youth’s experiences and sensemaking, through analysis of video records, interviews, and student artifacts, revealed the complexities of disciplinary engagement, touch, and assuming responsibility in relation to socioecological care. I conclude by reflecting on the inherent tensions and messiness involved in care and the importance of explicitly grappling with this messiness with youth.

title: Building Capacity for Educational Innovation: Strategies to Scale Computational Thinking Pathways in K-12 School Districts
citation: Mills, K., Coenraad, M., Dunbar, K. M., Rangel, A., & Burke, Q. (2025). Building Capacity for Educational Innovation: Strategies to Scale Computational Thinking Pathways in K-12 School Districts. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 727-735). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Mills, K., Coenraad, M., Dunbar, K. M., Rangel, A., & Burke, Q.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: There are many examples of innovation within education, but oftentimes innovation happens in a single classroom or school without being able to scale to an entire district or beyond. When scaling innovations, it is difficult to adapt to new contexts and student needs while promoting authenticity and sustainability. In this paper, we examine how three districts within a research-practice partnership scaled computational thinking (CT) pathways to provide CT learning opportunities across their district. We first detail case studies of how the three districts scaled their CT pathway implementation. Then, we present cross-district strategies promoting depth, spread, ownership, and sustainability: Clarity and Awareness, Alignment with Existing Priorities, Standards and Curricula Integration, School Based Leadership, Sustained Professional Learning, and Student Voice. These strategies support educational leaders to strategically design implementations that promote the scale of new initiatives.

title: Speculative Biotechnologies: AI as a Catalyst for Biodesign Education
citation: Ojeda-Ramirez, S., Hakim, N., & Turano, G. D. (2025). Speculative Biotechnologies: Ai as a Catalyst for Biodesign Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 736-744). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ojeda-Ramirez, S., Hakim, N., & Turano, G. D.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study examines how integrating generative AI and speculative design into biodesign education can enhance students’ ability to envision and articulate sustainable and socially just futures. Conducted in a Colombian university with design students, the study employed three speculative scenarios—fatalistic, optimistic, and practical futures—alongside continuous reflection. Findings indicate that generative AI helped students visualize biotechnological solutions, such as hydrogel barriers and biosustainable leather production, enabling them to connect speculative futures with tangible societal and ecological applications. This process encouraged critical engagement, ethical awareness, and strengthened students’ identities as ethical designers. Digital AI-generated artifacts bridged gaps in students’ knowledge of biological systems, making abstract concepts accessible and empowering them to imagine impactful, community-driven solutions. By integrating speculative design and AI into biodesign education, this study demonstrates the potential of such approaches to support interdisciplinary learning, develop critical design agency, and prepare students to address complex global challenges through innovative, localized solutions.

title: Exclusionary and Emancipatory Learning Praxes of Gender Nonconforming Noise Musicians
citation: Woods, P. J. (2025). Exclusionary and Emancipatory Learning Praxes of Gender Nonconforming Noise Musicians. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 74-82). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Woods, P. J.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
conceptualisations_list: Communities of Practice & Situated Learning; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: Building on the recent growth of explicitly queer approaches to learning sciences scholarship, this paper explores the learning praxes of gender nonconforming noise musicians. The community of practice (CoP) surrounding noise music, a caustic subgenre of experimental music, provides a fruitful site of research because of its history of tensions related to marginalized gender identities. Through this study, I address the following research questions: What exclusionary practices do gender nonconforming musicians recognize in noise music scenes? And how do gender nonconforming noise musicians challenge those issues to produce a safer and more just informal learning environment? In analyzing interviews with 36 globally dispersed musicians, I discuss a series of exclusionary and liberatory learning praxes that create tensions and opportunities for marginalized participants. These findings hold implications for other studies of power within CoPs and informal learning contexts more broadly.

title: Utopian Futures, Ends of the World, and Other Stories We Tell Ourselves About the Roles of Race in the Learning Sciences
citation: Jones, S. T. (2025). Utopian Futures, Ends of the World, and Other Stories we Tell Ourselves About the Roles of Race in the Learning Sciences. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jones, S. T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this paper I make plain the need for the Learning Sciences to think more closely with Black Studies due to the ways race and anti-Black racism shape learning. In thinking about utopias, I contribute the theoretical perspective of Plantation Prophecy to illustrate how, utopia can require the subjugation of group(s) of people. In conversation with interviews of Black computing practitioners, I further explicate how this is linked with computing and computing learning through critical discourse analysis.

title: Engineering and Robotics Learning in Haitian-Dominican Communities: An Analysis of Positionalities as Latine and Haitian Researchers in Multilingual Spaces

abstract: Researchers designed learning experiences to engage Haitian-Dominican youths’ curiosities about engineering and robotics through multilingual/multidialectal and multimodal lessons in the Dominican Republic. Researchers and community organizers who identified as Dominican, Haitian, and Latine conducted an analysis of their experiences and positionalities as multilingual/multidialectal researchers by doing a collaborative inquiry. Researchers considered how their identities shaped the design and execution of the program and how their positionalities framed their perceptions of learning. Findings suggest that researchers perceived multilingual/multidialectal learning environments for engineering and robotics as supportive of (1) learners using their linguistic and cultural practices to develop engineering designs, (2) mutual learning relationships between researchers and students, and (3) interactions that sustained researchers' identities. This work exemplifies how multilingual/multidialectal researchers' identities frame how they view the co-construction of STEM learning and relationships with multilingual/multidialectal learners and their communities.

title: Cultivating Socioecological Care through a Speculative Approach to Science Education
citation: Jen, T. (2025). Cultivating Socioecological Care Through a Speculative Approach to Science Education. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 763-771). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jen, T.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Socioecological crises plaguing the world demand that education strives toward otherwise futures. Unfortunately, dominant approaches to education, and science education in particular, continue to perpetuate anthropocentric and technoscientific worldviews that do more to prolong than disrupt these crises. In this conceptual paper, I present an alternative, approach to science education centered around cultivating socioecological care. Drawing on the work of feminist and Indigenous scholars who center entanglement and interconnectedness, I conceptualize the practice of socioecological care as multidirectional flows of care, performed by all entities (human and more-than-human) to sustain collective flourishing. I offer a speculative approach comprised of paying attention, recognizing, and envisioning as a tool for designing and studying science learning toward socioecological care.

title: Making in the Magic Valley: Historical Actors and the Making of Speculative Props
citation: Perez, M. (2025). Making in the Magic Valley: Historical Actors and the Making of Speculative Props. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 772-780). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Perez, M.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: In this paper, I explore how Latinx participants in a making-based activity create speculative props that represent a combination of their histories, experiences, and desired futures. I do this in the context of a making space within a history museum whose focus is on telling stories of a largely Latinx region in the U.S., the Lower Rio Grande Valley. I position participants’ work as materializing a double bind, one of the indicators of becoming a historical actor. Specifically, participants are creating speculative props, which are tools for imagination and enacting futures in the present. I present three examples of speculative props and how they bring together pasts, presents, and futures. From this work, I argue that we can design making-based activities that facilitate reflection towards imagining desired futures.

title: Emotional Dynamics in Asynchronous Math Discussions: Analyzing the Impact of Negative Emotions on Learning Outcomes
citation: Kim, T., Liu, Z., Xing, W., Li, H., & Oh, H. (2025). Emotional Dynamics in Asynchronous Math Discussions: Analyzing the Impact of Negative Emotions on Learning Outcomes. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 781-789). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kim, T., Liu, Z., Xing, W., Li, H., & Oh, H.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study investigates the role of negative emotions in asynchronous online math discussions and their impact on learning. Using data from 402 students and 3,084 discussion posts, the study employs sentiment analysis and machine learning to categorize emotions. Findings reveal that low levels of negative emotions can enhance learning by fostering active engagement, while higher levels correlate with lower performance. Topic modeling and sequential pattern mining show that students with low negative emotions engage more productively, focusing on both 'Help-seeking behaviors' and 'Understanding.' In contrast, high negative emotions lead to shorter interactions and focusing primarily on 'Help-seeking behaviors.' Sequential analysis indicates that low negative emotions often transition to neutral or positive states, supporting continued engagement, while high negative emotions result in repetitive negative sequences and disengagement. These findings underscore the importance of understanding negative emotions and providing appropriate support in asynchronous learning environments to foster engagement and improve outcomes.

title: Fostering Sociopolitical Awareness in Genetic Education: Investigating Racial Health Disparities in Diabetes
citation: Duncan, R. G., Hassan, D., Av-Shalom, N. Y., & Krishnamoorthy, R. (2025). Fostering Sociopolitical Awareness in Genetic Education: Investigating Racial Health Disparities in Diabetes. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 790-798). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Duncan, R. G., Hassan, D., Av-Shalom, N. Y., & Krishnamoorthy, R.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Schools are not neutral sites of learning, and (re)produce white supremacy through seemingly neutral teaching and learning interactions. Heeding the calls to incorporate the sociopolitical into science education, we developed a high school biology unit that critically engages genetics education. The unit highlights environments as not neutral and not benign, and that the inequities plaguing these environments were created through structures and forces of oppression. We analyzed post interviews to understand the extent to which students developed non-deterministic views of genes and sociopolitical awareness of the nature of the environments in gene-environment interactions. Our findings suggest that students understood trait variation as resulting from interactions between genes and the environment and were able to reason about the environment in these interactions as non-neutral and harmful for marginalized communities. However, they struggled to explain how gene-environment interactions work at the biological level and the intentionality of environmental inequities.

title: Towards Decolonizing Agency in Addressing Racialization of Behaviors in Settler Colonial Schools
citation: Mawene, D., Bal, A., Ko, D., Orie, L., Schrader, E., & Yoo, J. (2025). Towards Decolonizing Agency in Addressing Racialization of Behaviors in Settler Colonial Schools. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 799-807). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Mawene, D., Bal, A., Ko, D., Orie, L., Schrader, E., & Yoo, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Co-Design & Participatory Design; Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies
abstract: This paper proposes a decolonizing agency framework, emphasizing how a diverse group of policy actors center Indigenous sovereignty, histories, lived experiences, and expertise to address racial disproportionality within a school community. Decolonizing agency builds upon existing frameworks on agency, in particular relational agency (Edwards, 2005; 2007) and expands the concepts in practice by incorporating decolonizing methodologies (Brayboy, 2005; Lomawaima, 2000; Smith, 2018; 2021) and cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT). We have developed the concept of decolonizing agency through a five-year-long transformative research partnership with an Anishanabee (Ojibwe) Nation to address the overrepresentation of Indigenous students in exclusionary school discipline and special education for “behavioral disturbance” at a rural high school. Six dimensions of decolonizing agency emerged based on our research-practice partnership to address the racialization of behavioral problems in a school serving Indigenous students.

title: Data Literacy Beyond Logic: Entanglements of Logical Reasoning and Emotion in a Data Science Camp
citation: Russo, R. & Blikstein, P. (2025). Data Literacy Beyond Logic: Entanglements of Logical Reasoning and Emotion in a Data Science Camp. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Russo, R. & Blikstein, P.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Both dis- and misinformation based on data exploit the belief that more data inevitably leads to more informed decisions. This study explores how logical reasoning is entangled with emotion and technology in sense-making processes. We present a case study of a middle-school student working with environmental data in a data science camp, a context paralleling “in-the-wild” misinformation. Drawing on current scholarship on embodied and affective dimensions of data work, we argue that emotional entanglements shape how students interpret evidence. Results point to the need for educational approaches that move beyond logical reasoning to include these affective dimensions.

title: Prototyping Possibility: Leveraging Afrofuturism in the Design of Justice-centered Future Educator Learning Environments
citation: McKoy, A. (2025). Prototyping Possibility: Leveraging Afrofuturism in the Design of Justice-Centered Future Educator Learning Environments. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: McKoy, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper explores justice-centered sensemaking and practice among future educators within the context of a redesigned future educator technology course at a Primarily White Institution (PWI) that brings together sociocultural theories of learning with Afrofuturist principles of learning and design. Specifically, this paper highlights justice-centered educator reflection and practice or Afrofuturist pedagogical prototypes within course final projects. These prototypes embody learning around four main Afrofuturist principles: justice-centered, future-oriented, tech-mediated, and collective. Findings from this study point to the importance of tech-mediated co-design with youth for the imagination and enactment of more just learning futures and technologies.

title: Improving Pre-K–12 Students’ Executive Functions Using Digital Games: A Systematic Review
citation: Ercan, D., Esmaeiligoujar, S., & Rahimi, S. (2025). Improving Pre-K–12 Students’ Executive Functions Using Digital Games: A Systematic Review. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 826-834). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ercan, D., Esmaeiligoujar, S., & Rahimi, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Executive functions (EFs) are critical cognitive skills that influence learning, decision-making, and problem-solving. This systematic review examines the impact of digital games on improving EF skills in Pre-K–12 settings by following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Contributions from diverse fields, including psychology, education, and technology, reflect the interdisciplinary interest in this area. Based on the analysis of game design integrations, this systematic review organizes game design elements into two categories: high-impact, where games are purposefully designed to improve EF skills, and low-impact, where games are not intentionally designed to target EFs. The findings reveal trends in game design elements, such as adaptive challenges and feedback systems, that contribute to EFs improvements. This study highlights digital games as promising tools for enhancing EFs. Findings underscore the need for more rigorous designs and future research on higher-order EFs.

title: Finding the Side Doors: Learners’ Uptake and Rejection of Frames in a Museum Exhibit about Climate Change
citation: Zummo, L. M., Janney, B., Kinshella, K., Giron, J., & Whiting, M. (2025). Finding the Side Doors: Learners’ Uptake and Rejection of Frames in a Museum Exhibit About Climate Change. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 83-91). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zummo, L. M., Janney, B., Kinshella, K., Giron, J., & Whiting, M.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Climate change presents major problems to communities globally. While education is seen as a path towards public engagement, educators often encounter challenges, particularly in the United States (US), where climate change remains contentious. Prior research explains this difficulty, showing that climate learning processes are complex, multifaceted, and often influenced by one’s sociopolitical ideologies. Building from such research, this paper positions side doors frames as a means to fostering effective climate education for ideologically diverse audiences. We integrate framing theory with Bakhtinian theory of discourse to conceptualize side door moments and apply this conceptualization to qualitative discourse analysis of empirical data collected at a US natural history museum. Our analysis demonstrates moment-to-moment processes by which learners take up and/or reject framings of climate change. It contributes to learning sciences through a deepened conceptualization of side doors that integrates learning theory towards approaches for effective climate education.

title: Exploring How Teacher Educators Critically Reason with Data
citation: Shah, Z. (2025). Exploring How Teacher Educators Critically Reason With Data. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. authors_list: Shah, Z.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Data literacy is now required for civic participation and engagement in a society embedded in datafication (Gebre, 2022). Teacher educators must integrate statistics and data science across the pre-service curriculum to equip students with the tools to be data literate. This paper reports on how teacher educators in a public university system integrate data investigations into their courses and examines the conceptualization of data literacy across interdisciplinary contexts. We found that these teacher educators 1) framed data as text to bring light to the ideologies at play behind data collection and analysis, 2) negotiated the disconnect between lived experiences and statistical reasoning to claim data authorship, 3) presented data in ways that enable richer understandings of diversity and complexity in systems. Our findings suggest that in classes where data is not a core stated learning goal, it illustrates the complexity and diversity of the content they teach.

title: Designing Curricula for an Uncertain World: A Critical Action Learning Approach
citation: Dasgupta, C., Raman, P., Carvalho, R., Gijlers, H. A., & Slotta, J. D. (2025). Designing Curricula for an Uncertain World: A Critical Action Learning Approach. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 844-852). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Dasgupta, C., Raman, P., Carvalho, R., Gijlers, H. A., & Slotta, J. D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this paper, we focus on engaging student educational designers in critical action learning and design. While ongoing efforts have investigated how to build capacity amongst schoolteachers, we argue for building capacity amongst student educational designers who will be engaged in designing resources for schoolteachers and students. This research builds on theories of critical pedagogy and critical action learning. We follow a design-based research approach to iteratively design a critical action learning toolbox that can be used to foster a generation of designers capable of producing educational technologies that prioritize equity and social responsibility. Findings suggest that adopting a layered approach – CALE researcher/educator (Layer 0), student educational designer (Layer 1), and schoolteacher (Layer 2) – provide the required reflective space to design curricula using critical action learning approach. Scaffolds such as designing a collective problem case and emergent mirrors are important constituents in this reflective space.

title: Collaborative Sensemaking as Social Studies Teachers’ Professional Learning: Adapting to Thematic Instruction
citation: Schamberger, B. (2025). Collaborative Sensemaking as Social Studies Teachers’ Professional Learning: Adapting to Thematic Instruction. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 853-861). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Schamberger, B.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Educators’ ongoing engagement with questions of epistemology and pedagogy is vital in delineating the repertoire of instructional strategies they will apply in their classrooms. For in-service teachers, opportunities to think with epistemology and pedagogy can come through teacher professional learning (TPL) workshops. There, teachers’ thinking is challenged by innovative instructional strategies, new resources, and conversations with educators from different backgrounds. In the TPL analyzed here, teachers were given the opportunity to apply a novel instructional strategy to their own teaching materials. Participants leveraged their distributed expertise to collaboratively interpret and negotiate prerequisites and core principles of student-driven inquiry necessary to implement this pedagogical strategy with integrity. Using interaction analysis, this study illustrates the principled adaptation of a second-year social studies teacher’s world history unit on ancient civilizations. It is an example of distributed expertise and collaborative sensemaking with implications for the instructional design of TPL.

title: The Complexity of Adopting and Sustaining a Listening Stance
citation: Ajilore, O., Appleby, L., Svoboda, J., Hammer, D., & Tobin, R. G. (2025). The Complexity of Adopting and Sustaining a Listening Stance. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 862-870). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ajilore, O., Appleby, L., Svoboda, J., Hammer, D., & Tobin, R. G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Prior research has emphasized the importance of centering students’ thinking in STEM classrooms, particularly the need for STEM instructors to notice, interpret, and engage with the substance of student thinking. Our work builds on this, focusing on supporting postsecondary STEM faculty in cultivating their abilities to listen to student thinking in ways that recognize productivity in their sensemaking. We provide an empirical account of faculty listening to student thinking during a professional development session. We argue that the deep disciplinary expertise of college faculty can sometimes constrain their attempts to listen to student thinking in respectful and constructive ways, as they navigate the tension between being responsive to students’ attempts at productive sensemaking and maintaining fidelity to disciplinary meanings. Including faculty from multiple disciplines in the conversation may be helpful, by raising alternative interpretations that may seem sensible to novices but are difficult for disciplinary experts to consider.

title: Podcasts as Public Pedagogy: Diagnostic and Prognostic Framing as Processes of Ideological Articulation in the Politics of Women’s Sports
citation: Vea, T. & Shea, M. V. (2025). Podcasts as Public Pedagogy: Diagnostic and Prognostic Framing as Processes of Ideological Articulation in the Politics of Women’s Sports. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 871-879). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Vea, T. & Shea, M. V.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Podcasts have taken a prominent role in the construction of sociopolitical reality. In this paper, we use critical discourse analysis with a focus on discourses of victimhood to analyze two podcast episodes about women’s sports, “The Fundamental Rule of the W: No Place for -isms” from the podcast A Touch More and “A Stolen Dream” from The Joyful Warriors Podcast. We combine recent learning sciences theorizations of ideology as interactional sensemaking with conceptualizations of diagnostic and prognostic framing from social movement studies to show how podcast participants construct divergent visions of social problems in women’s sports and their solutions, modeling sociopolitical sensemaking as a form of public pedagogy. Broader social concerns about race and gender both become problems for women’s sports and echo out into a more encompassing sociopolitical landscape, with implications for collective sensemaking that will shape who belongs in society.

title: Culturally Sustaining Computing Education for Tibetan Diaspora Youth: Engaging Heritage Identity Through Computing
citation: Paljor, Y., Proctor, C., Honwad, S., Decker, A., & Hoadley, C. (2025). Culturally Sustaining Computing Education for Tibetan Diaspora Youth: Engaging Heritage Identity Through Computing. abstract: This study integrates sociocultural dimensions into computing education to support identity preservation and engagement among Tibetan diaspora youth in Queens, New York. Conducted during a 5-week summer program in 2024, the research investigated culturally sustaining pedagogies that integrate technical learning and cultural heritage. Students engaged in collaborative, project-based learning incorporating Tibetan sociocultural and political values into computing practices. Findings highlight six key themes, including pride in accomplishments, personal agency, and cultural resilience, showing how computing education can affirm cultural identity while fostering technical skills. Such integration is valuable to meaningful computing education as well as engaging and preserving their heritage identity. The study underscores the transformative potential of culturally aligned computing education to empower marginalized communities, offering a model for designing equitable, identity-affirming STEM programs that address community-specific concerns.

title: Lenses for Characterizing Equitable College STEM Teaching
citation: Phuong, A. E., Nguyen, J., Huang, F., Vo, J., Mejia, F. D., & Hunn, C. T. (2025). Lenses for Characterizing Equitable College STEM Teaching: Aligning Equity and Academic Goals. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 889-897). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Phuong, A. E., Nguyen, J., Huang, F., Vo, J., Mejia, F. D., & Hunn, C. T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines what helps university STEM instructors learn and adopt inclusive teaching practices, such as Adaptive Equity-Oriented Pedagogy (AEP). AEP has been shown to improve student achievement by over a full-letter grade. This study draws on data from a randomized controlled trial of 129 student-instructors who were either in a treatment course that modeled AEP or a control course that taught about AEP. This paper reports qualitative analyses of instructors in the top and bottom 25% of the treatment condition that modeled AEP. High-growth instructors more frequently aligned their academic and equity goals for student learning (e.g., promoting students’ sense of belonging as they developed academic skills). Similarly, high-growth instructors more often defined equity as adapting to students’ needs than low-growth instructors. A few low-growth instructors defined equity as giving everyone the same thing, but this definition was not consistently used when describing their pedagogical practices.

abstract: This convergent mixed-methods study investigates the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) for providing formative feedback in higher education. The study explores the perspectives of eleven experienced instructors regarding GenAI-generated feedback in an online graduate program. Participants reviewed sample feedback and shared their evaluations via a numerical questionnaire, an open-ended survey, and a focus group discussion. Results indicated that instructors generally viewed GenAI feedback positively, noting its relevance, clarity, actionability, usefulness, and comprehensiveness, highlighting its effective alignment with course rubrics and comprehensive guidance. However, challenges were also noted, including redundancy and overly lengthy suggestions that could overwhelm students. The study concludes with recommendations for refining GenAI to enhance its feedback effectiveness and improve the learning experience of higher education students.

title: The Role of Science Proficiency in Students’ Engagement with Computational Modeling Practices
citation: Basu, S., Rachmatullah, A., Jain, S., Lee, K., & McElhaney, K. W. (2025). The Role of Science Proficiency in Students’ Engagement With Computational Modeling Practices. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 908-916).
