subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Computational modeling of scientific systems is a powerful approach for fostering science and computational thinking (CT) proficiencies. However, the role of programming activities for this synergistic learning remains unclear. This paper examines alternative ways to engage with computational models (CM) beyond programming. Students participated in an integrated Science, Engineering, and Computational Modeling unit through one of three distinct instructional versions: Construct a CM, Interpret-and-Evaluate a CM, and Explore-and-Evaluate a simulation. Analyzing 188 student responses to a science+CT embedded assessment task, we investigate how science proficiency and instructional versions related to pseudocode interpretation and debugging performances. We found that students in the Explore-and-Evaluate a simulation outperformed students in the programming-based versions on the CT assessment items. Additionally, science proficiency strongly predicted students’ CT performance, unlike prior programming experience. These results highlight the promise of diverse approaches for fostering CT practices with implications for STEM+C instruction and assessment design.

title: Embodied Transfer of Mathematical Ideas Through Gestural Replay
citation: Xia, F., Kim, C., Beier, J. P., Swart, M. I., Schenck, K. E., & Nathan, M. J. (2025). Embodied Transfer of Mathematical Ideas Through Gestural Replay. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 917-925). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Xia, F., Kim, C., Beier, J. P., Swart, M. I., Schenck, K. E., & Nathan, M. J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study examines how students embodied their ideas about geometric relationships and how those ideas transfer between groups. High school students used The Hidden Village – Online, a motion capture video game that allows them to create new content through movements and perform these movements while evaluating the veracity of geometric conjectures. Each group (1) co-designed directed actions—a sequence of movements representing a body-based interpretation of the structure and transformation of mathematical objects—for other groups and (2) played the game with conjectures and directed actions created by their peers. Qualitative analyses of multiple cases demonstrated that students used gestures to develop directed actions that simulated the generalized geometric properties. When directed actions were spontaneously replayed by other groups, these gestural replays facilitated a form of distributed transfer. This study offers new insights into redesigning mathematics curricula that emphasize embodied interactions to support generalization and transfer.

title: Grounding Mathematics Learning in Culturally Authentic Movement Practices: From Attentional Anchors in Balinese Dancing to Auxiliary Lines in Geometry Reasoning
citation: Apsari, R. A. & Abrahamson, D. (2025). Grounding Mathematics Learning in Culturally Authentic Movement Practices: From Attentional Anchors in Balinese Dancing to Auxiliary Lines in Geometry Reasoning. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 92-100). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Apsari, R. A. & Abrahamson, D.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Solving geometry problems often requires generating auxiliary lines. Yet, learning to generate auxiliary lines is challenging, because it involves envisioning figural elements that by definition are not yet overtly available for students’ visual sensing or teachers’ direct indexing. Espousing an enactivist perspective, this design-based research project explores dance as a culturally authentic grounding context for geometrical reasoning. Learning new dance movements often elicits the spontaneous mental generation of attentional anchors, imaginary perceptual structures enabling dancers to perform complex coordinations. We conjectured that, given appropriate semiotic resources, dancers could objectify their tacit attentional anchors from dance practice as explicit auxiliary lines for geometry practice. We report on a pilot evaluation of GRiD, a low-cost resource for blending dance and geometry. Microgenetic analysis of a young Balinese dancer’s multimodal actions and utterances reveals the emergence of an interdisciplinary nexus of practice imbricating dance and mathematics and benefiting both discourses.

title: How Attending STEM Camps for Multiple Years Impacts Students’ Science Identity
citation: Shah, A., Park, J. H., Beheshti, M., Phatak, J. U., Perret, B., Hira, A., Zhang, H., & Barnett, M. (2025). How Attending STEM Camps for Multiple Years Impacts Students’ Science Identity. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 926-934). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Shah, A., Park, J. H., Beheshti, M., Phatak, J. U., Perret, B., Hira, A., Zhang, H., & Barnett, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Research shows that science identity plays a crucial role in shaping students’ inclination in pursuing advanced STEM degrees and careers. Individuals from historically underserved populations often struggle to see themselves as a ‘science person’ and tend to receive less recognition in such roles from teachers, family members, and peers. This study investigates how persistent participation in out-of-school STEM camps impacts science identity development among high school students. We found that returning participants, progressing from campers to mentors and leaders over the years, exhibited enhanced levels of science identity. Statistical analyses and student experiences from their interviews reveal that long-term engagement, coupled with evolving roles and opportunities to explore novel STEM activities, motivates continued participation and fosters stronger science identities. This persistent participation plays a crucial role in the development and reinforcement of a robust science identity, offering valuable insights for designing programs that can enhance it, particularly for underrepresented groups.

title: Justice-Centered Environmental Learning: A Design Tool
citation: Reigh, E. V., Sayavedra, A., Dunhill, G., Barton, J. C., Slown, C., & Fitzmaurice, H. L. (2025). Justice-Centered Environmental Learning: A Design Tool. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 935-943). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Reigh, E. V., Sayavedra, A., Dunhill, G., Barton, J. C., Slown, C., & Fitzmaurice, H. L.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Climate change and other environmental harms disproportionately impact communities of color and low-income communities, and therefore represent existential social justice issues for science classrooms to address. Although learning scientists and science educators have theorized sociopolitical dimensions of environmental learning, there are few practical tools for justice-centered design. To this end, we developed a design tool that consists of four environmental justice lenses: address positionality, engage multiple ways of knowing, analyze structures of oppression, and engage in justice-focused action. We illustrate these lenses with vignettes from an institute on air quality for in-service teachers. We discuss the potential of this tool to guide environmental learning and inform future research.

title: Competing to See
citation: Metts, E. (2025). Competing to See: Disciplining Perception Across Mathematics and Data Science. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 944-952). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Metts, E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study explores how an experienced mathematics teacher organized and disciplined a student’s perception during a lesson that incorporated data science practices. As data science gains national attention, this research addresses the complexities teachers face in integrating data practices into mathematics curricula. Drawing from a multiyear design-based study, the analysis focuses on classroom interactions during a “Barbie Bungee” lesson, highlighting competing disciplinary goals of mathematics and data science. Using an interactionist perspective and the construct of disciplined perception, this paper illuminates the breakdowns and interactional work involved in aligning student understanding with mathematical concepts like slope while grappling with noisy, real-world data. This case underscores the need to address competing disciplinary practices in classroom contexts, offering insights into fostering interdisciplinary engagement and reshaping data science integration in mathematics education.

title: Neural correlates of cognitive load variation in elementary school students during mental arithmetic tasks
citation: Zeng, J., Yang, H., Tan, S., & Shang, J. (2025). Neural Correlates of Cognitive Load Variation in Elementary School Students During Mental Arithmetic Tasks. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 953-961). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zeng, J., Yang, H., Tan, S., & Shang, J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Cognitive load theory emphasizes the limited capacity of working memory in processing new information, with excessive cognitive load potentially inhibiting learning outcomes. This study investigated the use of electroencephalography (EEG) signals to interpret cognitive load variation in elementary school students during arithmetic operations in an authentic school environment, addressing gaps in existing research that has primarily focused on adults in laboratory settings. We manipulated the task complexity of mental addition to induce a low and a high complexity level of cognitive load amongst a sample of 82 fourth graders. Self-report cognitive load, task performance, and oscillation-band powers were collected. Our results show that increased cognitive load induced by arithmetic task complexity was associated with increased theta power and theta/alpha ratio, as well as decreased alpha power and low beta power. These findings demonstrate the potential of EEG signals to provide non-disruptive, objective insights into the temporal dynamics of cognitive load in educational settings.

title: Physics Students’ Metaphorical Gestures About Energy
citation: Zhu, M., Booth, E. T., Flood, V. J., & Harrer, B. W. (2025). Physics Students’ Metaphorical Gestures About Energy. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 962-970). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhu, M., Booth, E. T., Flood, V. J., & Harrer, B. W.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Energy is a central, cross-cutting concept in science, but its abstract nature poses challenges for learners. Metaphor has been recognized as a productive resource used by students, teachers, and scientists to understand and communicate about energy. While much research has focused on metaphors about energy expressed in learners’ speech, we know less about the range of ways learners use gesture to evoke metaphors about energy. In particular, the metaphor energy as substance has been found to be useful for conceptualizing various features of energy. Using a microethnographic approach, we demonstrate how students in an introductory algebra-based university physics course use gesture in three different ways to evoke substance-like metaphors that offer valuable affordances for sensemaking about energy: These include (1) container metaphor gestures, (2) stimulus metaphor gestures, and (3) accounting metaphor gestures. Implications for learning and teaching about energy are discussed.

title: Teachers Grappling with Representing Historical and Political Contexts in Science Curriculum Materials
citation: Bogdanov, K. P. (2025). Teachers Grappling With Representing Historical and Political Contexts in Science Curriculum Materials. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 971-979). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bogdanov, K. P.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Science learning environments have been primarily shaped by Eurocentric ideologies that center science as a set of culturally neutral and color-blind systems which science teachers are often reluctant to acknowledge. However, current reforms in the U.S. ask science teachers to connect science to real world environmental and societal problems, which create opportunities to teach in more justice-oriented ways. This requires challenging shifts in teachers’ approaches. Co-design environments can be helpful learning spaces for teachers because they support deliberations around dilemmas through which teachers can deepen their content knowledge or practices. Dilemmas during design revolve around curricular values teachers bring into the design process. I use a curricular values framework to examine deliberations between values – specifically the intersections of ones related to historical and political contexts in science – to understand how teachers negotiate and redefine science to be represented in justice-oriented ways.

title: Practical Measures for Teacher Noticing: Developing an Interpretive Practice
citation: Mendez, J. & van Es, E. A. (2025). Practical Measures for Teacher Noticing: Developing an Interpretive Practice. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 980-988). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Mendez, J. & Es, E. A. V.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: This study examines a researcher-practitioner collaboration focused on developing equitable noticing practices through iterative engagement with practical measures. Drawing on an expansive learning framework, we explore how a secondary mathematics teacher, Lorenzo, engages in a four-stage process to adopt an interpretive practice. Our findings reveal that Lorenzo’s involvement in co-designing, administering, and analyzing practical measures validates his interpretations of students’ academic and relational success and fosters a deeper understanding of how equitable noticing can support student learning and belonging. These findings illuminate how practical measures and their iterative use in Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycles create opportunities for teachers to hone their equitable noticing within a collaborative professional learning context. This work contributes to teacher education by identifying interpretive practice as a promising focus for fostering equity-oriented teaching.

title: “Yes, And” or “Yes, Let’s Reflect”: Children and Adult Perceptions of Journaling in Cooperative Inquiry Co-design
citation: Blinder, E., Clegg, T., & Bonsignore, E. (2025). “Yes, And” or “Yes, Let’s Reflect”: Children and Adult Perceptions of Journaling in Cooperative Inquiry Co-Design. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 989-997). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Blinder, E., Clegg, T., & Bonsignore, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Within the learning sciences, reflection is portrayed as an important component of learning. Written reflection, in the form of journaling, has been shown to improve learners’ self-awareness, development, intentionality, and agency; however, it can be difficult to foster in out-of-classroom informal learning contexts. In this paper, we explore how adults and children in one such context—Cooperative Inquiry adult-child co-design teams—conceptualized the goals, opportunities, and challenges associated with reflective journaling. We interviewed six children and eleven adults with Cooperative Inquiry expertise about their perspectives and experiences with journaling in co-design. Our findings indicate tensions between children’s and adults’ perceptions of journaling objectives and practical and ideological challenges that complicated the implementation of journaling routines. Based on these findings, we highlight four opportunities to enhance reflective journaling in co-design and other informal learning contexts.

title: “Is There Anyone in This Room Who Wouldn’t Be Counted?” Pedagogy at the Intersection of History, Data Literacy, and Justice
citation: Lisinker, R., DeLiema, D., Scharber, C., Chen, B., & Voigt, M. In Rajala, A., Cortez, A., Hofmann, R., Jornet, A., Lotz-Sisitka, H., & Markauskaite, L. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2025 (pp. 998-1006). abstract: Data literacy explorations are becoming commonplace across a wide range of school subjects. While disciplinary inquiry with data is relatively new to the history classroom, social justice topics are familiar to the setting. Pedagogical practices at the intersection of history, data literacy, and justice have not been studied in depth. This paper identifies pedagogical practices and reflections that shape justice-oriented, high school U.S. history units that center data literacy. Videos of curriculum design meetings, whole-classroom pedagogy, and post hoc reflections on the curricular units were collected and analyzed. Themes from the units, which center the U.S. Census Act of 1790 and W.E.B. Du Bois’ transformative work in data visualization, highlight historical inquiry with data and the ways in which data can be used for social change toward justice visions.

title: LLM Bazaar: A Service Design for Supporting Collaborative Learning with an LLM-Powered Multi-Party Collaboration Infrastructure
citation: Wu, Z., Shi, J., Murray, R. C., Rosé, C., & San Andres, M. (2025). Llm Bazaar: A Service Design for Supporting Collaborative Learning With an Llm-Powered Multi-Party Collaboration Infrastructure. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: For nearly two decades, conversational agents have played a critical role in structuring interactions in collaborative learning, shaping group dynamics, and supporting student engagement. The recent integration of large language models (LLMs) into these agents offers new possibilities for fostering critical thinking and collaborative problem solving. In this work, we begin with an open source collaboration support architecture called Bazaar and integrate an LLM-agent shell that enables introduction of LLM-empowered, real time, context sensitive collaborative support for group learning. This design and infrastructure paves the way for exploring how tailored LLM-empowered environments can reshape collaborative learning outcomes and interaction patterns.

title: Mental Effort and Task Performance in Collaborative Learning: The Impact of Group Awareness
citation: Chen, W., Peng, T. W., Caryn, N. E., Mavis, H. M., Zheng, L., & Chen, X. (2025). Mental Effort and Task Performance in Collaborative Learning: The Impact of Group Awareness. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 116-123). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chen, W., Peng, T. W., Caryn, N. E. E., Mavis, H. M. Y., Zheng, L., & Chen, X.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigated the role of group awareness in supporting collaborative learning by examining its impact on mental effort (as measured by brain activation levels) and task performance during collaboration activities. 70 individuals from a university were recruited, with mental effort measured from the right temporoparietal junction (rTPJ) region of the brain using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and task performance was assessed under two collaborative learning conditions: with and without group awareness. The results showed that learners performed significantly better on the task with group awareness , but exhibited significantly greater mental effort without group awareness, suggesting that group awareness facilitated improvements in learners’ collaborative learning performance while reducing the learners’ mental effort for task completion. Researchers and educators could consider incorporating group awareness tools to allow learners to view and track each other’s contributions, progress, and engagement levels, to manage students’ mental demands and foster their collaborative learning performance.

title: Quantitative Evaluation of Collaborative Discussions Based on the Abstractness of Words in Utterance
citation: Nishimura, R. & Egi, H. (2025). Quantitative Evaluation of Collaborative Discussions Based on the Abstractness of Words in Utterance. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 12-19). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Nishimura, R. & Egi, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The evaluation of collaborative discussions often relies on qualitative approaches, limiting insights into the speed and degree of knowledge convergence. This study proposes a quantitative method for the evaluation of collaborative discussions by analyzing the abstractness of words in utterances. Six groups engaged in 10-min discussions and their utterances were numerically represented as abstractness sequences, analyzed using a moving average. Results revealed that concretization and abstraction during knowledge convergence promoted the use of concrete and abstract words, leading to variations in the moving average of abstractness. Most groups showed a rise in abstractness toward the end of the discussions, reflecting a gradual shift from concrete examples to abstract conclusions. This method captures iterative shifts between concretization and abstraction, providing deeper insights into communication dynamics in collaborative learning. This innovative method bridges qualitative and quantitative perspectives, enabling precise analysis of knowledge convergence and offering practical applications in the area of CSCL.

title: Reification of Dialogic Practices Through Collaborative Coding: Teacher Learning During Classroom Video Analysis
citation: Wang, P. & Chen, G. (2025). Reification of Dialogic Practices Through Collaborative Coding: Teacher Learning During Classroom Video Analysis. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 124-132). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wang, P. & Chen, G.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Academically productive talk (APT) moves are strategies that teachers use to extend student responses for further elaboration and reasoning, thereby creating a dialogic classroom. In this study, nine teachers collaboratively coded APT moves in lesson video recordings during two workshops using the Classroom Discourse Analyser, alongside their colleagues and a facilitator. Qualitative analysis of the interactions during the workshops showed that this coding process created opportunities to resolve misunderstandings and solidify knowledge of APT through discussions about the videos. The coding process helped teachers develop their noticing skills and professional vision for dialogic teaching. We found that the workshops increased teachers’ awareness of APT, improved their understanding of classroom discourse, and enhanced their ability to apply APT. Overall, these findings indicate that collaborative coding facilitated the process of knowledge reification, during which teachers co-constructed knowledge from ‘raw’ video recordings to ‘structured’ visualised representations.

title: Co-Regulation and Multimodal Synchrony in Pair Programming
citation: Sharma, K. & Nguyen, A. (2025). Co-Regulation and Multimodal Synchrony in Pair Programming. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 133-141). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sharma, K. & Nguyen, A.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA); Accountable Talk & Dialogic Discourse
abstract: Gaze, emotional, and physiological synchronies are predictive of collaborative performance and quality. However, these synchronies are studied mostly in unimodal settings. We present a pair programming study to understand the relationship between multimodal synchrony and co-regulation processes. We collected eye-tracking, heart rate variability, electrodermal activity, facial expressions, dialogues from 40 pairs while they were collaboratively debugging a given program. We then coded their dialogues to examine co-regulation-based differences between the high and low performing pairs. Next, we computed gaze, facial expressions, stress and engagement based synchronies. We then examined the relationships between different synchronies and co-regulation dialogues. Our results show that argumentation and negotiation are negatively related to performance while cooperation, monitoring, goal-setting and co-regulation have a positive relationship with performance. We also find that argumentation and negotiation have lower joint attention and lower joint mental effort with high average mental effort and lower joint stress with high average stress.

title: Meaningful Automated Feedback? Balancing Tensions in Participatory Learning Analytics Design
citation: Harrington, S., Klein, S., Fratoni, A. C., Sellberg, C., & Lindwall, O. (2025). Meaningful Automated Feedback? Balancing Tensions in Participatory Learning Analytics Design. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 142-150). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Harrington, S., Klein, S., Fratoni, A. C., Sellberg, C., & Lindwall, O.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA); Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: Simulators have become central in professional training, in this case maritime education, where they support the development and assessment of skills and competencies required of competent seafarers. This study aims to inform the design of a learning analytics dashboard utilizing multimodal learning analytics to deliver automated, adaptive feedback to maritime students. Feedback is critical in simulator-based training, yet the characteristics of meaningful automated feedback in professional training remain underexplored. Drawing on a participatory design workshop with maritime students, the study examines tensions arising from the conceptualization of automated feedback. Using cultural historical activity theory, we frame tensions as opportunities for innovation, highlighting the dynamic interplay between students, instructors, and technology. In doing so, we offer insights into designing meaningful automated feedback for simulation training, and the need to balance students’ dual roles as learners and future professionals, reconciling collaborative learning with personalized feedback, and prioritizing educational goals over technological innovation.

title: Becoming an Algorithm: Girls Develop Expansive Computing Practices Through Collective-Embodied Computational Thinking
citation: Ayalon, E., Anton, G., Lane, A. C., & Enyedy, N. (2025). Becoming an Algorithm: Girls Develop Expansive Computing Practices Through Collective-Embodied Computational Thinking. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 151-159). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ayalon, E., Anton, G., Lane, A. C., & Enyedy, N.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Stereotypes in computing often deter underrepresented groups, particularly girls, from entering or staying in the field. This study explores how collective-embodied computational thinking (CT) can broaden perceptions of computing. We introduced a four-day curriculum featuring an embodied mixed-reality environment where youth collaboratively play-acted sorting algorithms. Using mixed-methods analysis—including word embedding, a WEAT test, and qualitative analysis of interviews—we examined shifts in students’ perceptions. Findings reveal that girls moved from technical to introspective, creative computing descriptors after the activity, while boys’ views remained largely unchanged. Interviews indicate that girls linked computing to everyday experiences, suggesting that collective embodied CT can highlight cultural assets and disrupt prevailing stereotypes in computing education.

title: Weaving Collaboration: Promoting Effective Interdisciplinary Learning with a Robotic Loom
citation: Ojeda-Ramirez, S., Rich, A., Huang, J., Speer, S., Martinez, M. O., Rosé, C. P., & Peppler, K. (2025). Weaving Collaboration: Promoting Effective Interdisciplinary Learning With a Robotic Loom. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 160-168). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ojeda-Ramirez, S., Rich, A., Huang, J., Speer, S., Martinez, M. O., Rosé, C. P., & Peppler, K.
subject: STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: This study investigates the conditions that foster effective interdisciplinary collaboration—defined as the integration of knowledge, practices, and perspectives from different disciplines—through qualitative analysis of project-based learning in higher education. Grounded in theories from the Learning Sciences and Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, we analyze how knowledge transfer and leadership dynamics mediate interdisciplinary engagement in a course combining robotics, mathematics, and textile arts. Systematic analysis of qualitative data from 23 undergraduate students across six groups reveals three distinct patterns of collaborative engagement. Our findings show that successful collaboration hinges on (1) fluid leadership transitions that leverage diverse expertise and (2) structured opportunities for knowledge exchange. Groups with distributed leadership and consistent knowledge-sharing practices produced higher-quality projects than those with centralized leadership. These findings contribute to theoretical understandings of interdisciplinary learning and offer practical guidelines for designing collaborative learning environments in higher education.

title: Examining Support Moments With a Conversational AI Partner
citation: Dey, I., Doherty, E., Zhang, R., Hoang, N., Bush, J. B., Hirshfield, L., & Puntambekar, S. (2025). Examining Support Moments With a Conversational Ai Partner. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Dey, I., Doherty, E., Zhang, R., Hoang, N., Bush, J. B., Hirshfield, L., & Puntambekar, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: AI systems can facilitate collaborative learning, but few studies examine how conversational AI partners can support collaboration. This study continues our application of the MOSAIC-AI protocol to explore support moments between a collaborative group and an educational expert serving as a Wizard-of-Oz (WoZ) agent. We present our refinement of the protocol, explore the nature of student-AI interactions, and discuss implications for building a dialog policy for informing the design of fully autonomous agents to support collaboration.

title: Cultivate a Research Mindset: How Do High School Students Understand and Approach Authentic Research?
citation: Ding, L., Sherafat, A., Zhang, J., Underwood, T., Guo, D., Muirhead, J., Hower, L., & Kerr, J. (2025). authors_list: Ding, L., Sherafat, A., Zhang, J., Underwood, T., Guo, D., Muirhead, J., Hower, L., & Kerr, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates students’ understanding of good research as related to their own research experiences and future research interests. The participants were 12th-grade students (17-to-18-year-olds) who participated in the Innovative Solutions project supported by three teachers and a cluster of professional partners from community-based organizations. An individual interview was conducted at the end of the project focused on students’ research experiences and outcomes, their understanding of good research, their interests to do research in the future. Grounded theory analysis of the interview data revealed core facets of students’ epistemic understanding of good research including aims, criteria, and process. As a compelling theme, students embrace research as a progressive, ever-deepening process to uncover deeper problems as research progresses. Detailed analysis of two student cases elaborates on how students’ epistemic understandings connect with their research experiences and future research interests. The findings inform educational designs to cultivate authentic research experiences among students.

title: Learning from Failure Through Game Testing Feedback in Virtual Collaborative Design
citation: Yan, S. & Xia, Y. (2025). Learning From Failure Through Game Testing Feedback in Virtual Collaborative Design. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 187-195). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Yan, S. & Xia, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Boundary Crossing & Brokerage; Productive Failure & Problem Solving; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: This study investigates how learning from failure can be supported through game design feedback activities in a virtual collaborative environment. Through analyzing video recordings of three checkpoint sessions in a two-week virtual game design camp with nine youth participants (ages 8-13), we identified six feedback styles and examined how designers responded to feedback. Our findings reveal that game design feedback in virtual environments transcends traditional linear relationships, forming a complex discursive relationship among testers, designers, and game artifacts. Screen sharing emerged as a crucial boundary object, facilitating communication and transforming traditional critique sessions into collaborative learning experiences. Facilitators played vital roles by modeling playfulness, vulnerability, and productive failure responses. The study demonstrates that successful virtual design feedback requires thoughtfully curated environments that balance structured facilitation with playful engagement. These findings have implications for design education in virtual settings and suggest new approaches for supporting learning from failure in collaborative contexts.

title: Toward Teacher-Centered AI Design: Exploring the Role of Pedagogical Values and Contextual Factors in K-12 Teachers' Perceptions of Responsible AI
citation: Yin, Y., Karumbaiah, S., Lim, J., Acquaye, S., & Schwartz, S. (2025). Toward Teacher-Centered Ai Design: Exploring the Role of Pedagogical Values and Contextual Factors in K-12 Teachers' Perceptions of Responsible Ai. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 196-204). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Yin, Y., Karumbaiah, S., Lim, J., Acquaye, S., & Schwartz, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Classroom Orchestration; Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) offer transformative opportunities for education, yet the alignment between Responsible AI principles and K-12 educators' pedagogical values remains unclear, potentially hindering effective teacher-AI collaboration. To address this, we surveyed 98 K-12 teachers to explore their prioritization of five Responsible AI (RAI) principles—autonomy, transparency, safety, fairness, and performance—alongside five pedagogical values—teacher-centered, behaviorism, constructivism, constructionism, and critical pedagogy—across three classroom scenarios: grading, scaffolding science learning, and classroom orchestration. Our findings reveal that educators' pedagogical values significantly influence their RAI priorities, with critical pedagogy aligning with transparency and safety, constructivism with autonomy, and teacher-centered and behaviorism negatively associated with fairness and safety. These results highlight the importance of designing AI systems that accommodate diverse teaching philosophies while addressing potential mismatches, fostering trust, and ensuring equitable integration into K-12 education.

title: The Conditions for Collaborative Groups’ Regulation of Learning: What can Multimodal Data Showcase?
citation: Järvenoja, H., Zabolotna, K., & Törmänen, T. (2025). The Conditions for Collaborative Groups’ Regulation of Learning: What Can Multimodal Data Showcase?. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 20-28). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Järvenoja, H., Zabolotna, K., & Törmänen, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA); Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: It is argued that collaborative learning flourishes when groups effectively regulate their learning processes, but understanding the conditions enabling such regulation remains a challenge. Despite evidence that a positive socio-emotional atmosphere supports learning, little is known about its role in metacognitive monitoring that initiates regulation. Recent advances in process methods and socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) research enable us to expand the focus from regulatory processes to the conditions enabling and supporting them. This paper demonstrates our recent research through multimodal data examples from two different studies with the aim to bridge collaborative groups’ regulatory activities with socio-emotional conditions of collaboration. Multimodal data—including psychophysiological measures, video, and audio—provides insights into how socio-emotional and metacognitive conditions within collaborative learning contexts shape regulation. Our findings highlight how multimodal methods capture detailed, temporally interconnected processes that drive group collaboration.

title: Designing Scientific Practices Through Exploration, Collaboration, Creation, and Reflection: A Multi-Layered Model
citation: Feng, X., Yang, Y., Chan, C. K., & Zhao, J. (2025). Designing Scientific Practices Through Exploration, Collaboration, Creation, and Reflection: A Multi-Layered Model. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 205-213). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Feng, X., Yang, Y., Chan, C. K. K., & Zhao, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examined a knowledge-building environment mediated by Knowledge Forum®, enhanced by a multi-layered scientific practices model designed to foster collective knowledge advancement. Forty-eight Grade 5 students participated in scientific practices centered on Lighting a Small Bulb, engaging in the model comprising four interconnected layers: exploration, collaboration, creation, and reflection. Quantitative analyses revealed significant improvements in students’ contributions to collective knowledge advancement across phases, with notable variations among high-, medium-, and low-contribution groups. Qualitative findings illustrated how students engaged in increasingly sophisticated scientific practices, transitioning from group exploration to scientific communication, extending scientific field knowledge, and incorporating epistemic reflection. This study highlights the role of the multi-layered model in scaffolding young learners to participate in authentic scientific practices, promoting collective epistemic agency and sustained knowledge advancement.

title: Scaffolding Knowledge Building Processes through ONA-Supported Collective Reflective Assessment
citation: Zhang, X., Chan, C., Feng, S., Ouyang, W., Xie, Y., Zhao, J., & Feng, X. (2025). Scaffolding Knowledge Building Processes Through Ona-Supported Collective Reflective Assessment. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 214-222). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhang, X., Chan, C., Feng, S., Ouyang, W., Xie, Y., Zhao, J., & Feng, X.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: This study designed a learning analytics-supported reflective assessment that utilizes ordered-epistemic-network-analysis (ONA) tool to scaffold students’ reflection on their epistemic actions by visualizing their knowledge building (KB) discourse moves. KB, supported by Knowledge Forum, emphasizes students’ collective contributions to community knowledge advancement. Previous research indicated that learning analytics-supported reflective assessment can effectively foster students’ metacognition and regulation; this study extends to ONA-based reflective assessment. Data were obtained from two classes of elementary-school students (n = 86) engaging in collective inquiry into Earth sciences; experimental students experiencing ONA-based reflective assessment. Quantitative analysis indicated that students in a designed KB environment enriched with analytics-supported reflection showed improved domain understanding and social interactions. Qualitative analysis showed how students engaged in the KB journey and how ONA-supported reflective assessment promoted their collective inquiry. This study contributes to knowledge-building pedagogy by demonstrating that reflective assessments on students’ discourse as epistemic engagement can promote collaborative knowledge development.

title: “Jupyter-Notebook-as-Script”: Investigating the Nature and Impact of Implicit Collaboration Scripts in Computational Notebooks
citation: Cai, Z., Davis, R. L., Tormey, R., & Dillenbourg, P. (2025). “Jupyter-Notebook-as-Script”: Investigating the Nature and Impact of Implicit Collaboration Scripts in Computational Notebooks. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 223-231). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cai, Z., Davis, R. L., Tormey, R., & Dillenbourg, P.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: There are a variety of CSCL scripts that offer different levels of flexibility, ranging from high-structured guidance towards low-rigidity support. This study is grounded in the view that scripts should be designed with a certain degree of structuredness, and we aim to examine the presence of implicit scripts based on data collected from collaborative programming activities in authentic classroom settings. By extracting the task dependencies within Jupyter notebooks, we adopted Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) to operationalize the concept of implicit scripts. Next, we analyzed the group interaction data and measured their collaboration strategy alignment with the implicit scripts. Notably, we found that introducing a planning phase significantly improved groups' adherence to the implicit scripts. Qualitative data were reported to triangulate our findings. We discuss pedagogical and technological implications for more general CSCL contexts.

title: The Emotional Dynamics of Collaborative Argumentation: Examining the Role of Framing and Alignment in Discourse Quality
citation: Das, R. & Murthy, S. (2025). The Emotional Dynamics of Collaborative Argumentation: Examining the Role of Framing and Alignment in Discourse Quality. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Das, R. & Murthy, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Accountable Talk & Dialogic Discourse
abstract: This study explores the emotional dynamics of collaborative argumentation, emphasizing the influence of emotional framing and interactional alignment on the quality of group discourse. Situated in a computer-supported environment, the research analyzes how positive and negative emotional cues shape argument complexity and group talk among middle school students engaged in socio-scientific debates. Findings reveal that emotional framing mediates engagement and focus, while alignment strategies determine the depth and coherence of collaborative reasoning. The integration of emotional and cognitive processes offers valuable insights for educational strategies and the design of collaborative learning tools.

title: Education for Sustainable Development: A Cross-Community Knowledge Building Approach
citation: Cao, L., Scardamalia, M., Boluda, P., Haber, J., & Khanlari, A. (2025). Education for Sustainable Development: A Cross-Community Knowledge Building Approach. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 241-249). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cao, L., Scardamalia, M., Boluda, P., Haber, J., & Khanlari, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates Cross-community Knowledge Building (CKBS) as an approach to Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) that empowers diverse communities of learners to take collective responsibility for advancing sustainable development goals (SDGs) through Knowledge Building. A Grade 1 class in Toronto, Canada and a Grade 9 class in Tarragona, Spain engaged in collaboration on sustainability challenges over four months. Using natural language processing, semantic network analysis, and temporal analysis of student contributions on Knowledge Forum, we examined cross-age and cross-community collaboration patterns that emerged during one phase of their sustainability inquiry. We found that Grade 1 students introduced foundational concepts grounded in their lived experiences while Grade 9 students expanded and deepened these ideas with more sophisticated concepts. However, the collaboration also surfaced challenges related to asymmetric participation and technological constraints for the younger learners. This study demonstrates the potential of CKBS as a model for Sustainability Education.

subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
