conceptualisations_list: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: This study designed and examined an approach using ChatGPT for automatic coding of students’ reflection data in a Virtual Reality (VR) collaborative maker activity. We developed a coding scheme focusing on social-collaborative interactions and used few-shot prompting strategies for ChatGPT automatic coding. The results showed strong correspondence between ChatGPT and human coding on all eight codes (Kappa from 0.81 to 0.90), but variations exist on the overall performance of Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) for different codes based on F1 scores. Different explanations are proposed including clear definition of the codes and number of responses in different coding categories. The study contributed to illuminating processes underlying collaborative learning in maker activities, demonstrated the promise of GAI for automatic coding, and suggested implications for research and practice.

title: Using Collaborative Video Annotation to Foster Epistemic Coherence in Teacher Education
citation: Strøm, A. K., Hontvedt, M., & Silseth, K. (2025). Using Collaborative Video Annotation to Foster Epistemic Coherence in Teacher Education. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 261-265). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Strøm, A. K., Hontvedt, M., & Silseth, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In order to achieve epistemic coherence in teacher education, student teachers must connect theoretical and practical forms of knowledge in meaningful ways. This study investigates uses of collaborative video annotation as a method for facilitating epistemic coherence among teacher education students. Through a design-based approach and interaction analysis, we examine how student teachers in co-located groups annotate video clips of teaching from elementary classrooms. The analysis displays student teachers’ knowledge practices and illustrates how they structure their collaboration and connect key concepts from their pedagogy course to observed events in the particular video annotation context. The findings show how concrete video annotations stimulates joint negotiation of meaning when student teachers connect diverse forms of knowledge, thereby fostering professional development and epistemic coherence in teacher education.

title: Deepening our Epistemic Scripts: CSCL at the Intersection of Learning, Collaboration, and Information Sciences
citation: Reimann, P. & Baker, M. (2025). Deepening Our Epistemic Scripts: CSCL at the Intersection of Learning, Collaboration, and Information Sciences. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 266-270). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Reimann, P. & Baker, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The field of Computer Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) research has always needed to refine and deepen its conceptual core in order to regulate the centrifugal and centripetal forces inherent in its multidisciplinarity. Whilst the concept of shared meaning making has been influential as a focus for CSCL, we argue firstly that three main changes over the past decades—collaborative learning becoming mainstream, bespoke systems giving way to platform infrastructures and changes in the scale of collaboration—necessitate rethinking the focus and boundaries of the domain. Secondly, we argue that CSCL needs to be re-situated with respect to adjacent fields, such as learning, information and collaboration sciences. Finally, we propose the utility of focussing on the forms of theorizing within CSCL, drawing on the concept of “epistemic scripts” that give greater precedence to theorizing the role of technology.

title: How do Students Build Community Knowledge for Sustainability through Collaborative Discourse?
citation: Ong, A., Teo, C. L., Lee, A. V., & Yuan, G. (2025). How do Students Build Community Knowledge for Sustainability Through Collaborative Discourse?. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 271-275). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ong, A., Teo, C. L., Lee, A. V. Y., & Yuan, G.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Student questioning is key to fostering critical thinking, yet opportunities for student-directed inquiry are often limited in K-12 classrooms. This paper examines how students engage in collective inquiry on sustainability issues through a collaborative learning program based on Knowledge Building. Held biannually at a tertiary institution, the program brings together students from different schools to advance community knowledge on sustainability. Students identify and explore their own sustainability problems in this interest-based design. Data were collected from two iterations of the program: 35 primary school students (Grade 5) in October 2023 and 25 secondary school students (Grade 9) in June 2024. The primary data source was student discussion notes posted on an online forum, which were analyzed to identify questions that deepened inquiry. Results show that students' questions, especially “wonderment” and “explanation-seeking” questions, played a central role in driving learning and advancing their collective understanding of sustainability.

title: Frequency Transition Network Analysis (FTNA)
citation: Saqr, M., Misiejuk, K., Törmänen, T., Kaliisa, R., Tikka, S., & López-Pernas, S. (2025). Frequency Transition Network Analysis (FTNA). In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 276-280). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Saqr, M., Misiejuk, K., Törmänen, T., Kaliisa, R., Tikka, S., & López-Pernas, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper introduces Frequency-based Transition Network Analysis (FTNA), a novel method to model transitions between learning states. FTNA provides a framework for analyzing the relational dynamics, enabling researchers to uncover dominant events and notable patterns, compare different processes, and gain deeper insights into how events unfold over time. Moreover, FTNA’s capability to use statistical techniques like bootstrapping and permutation tests allows for rigorous validation of the observed interactions to establish the reliability of the identified patterns and transitions. This helps ensure that the findings are not just artifacts of the data but reflect genuine interaction dynamics. This paper presents FTNA’s theoretical grounding, compares it to existing methods with a large-scale simulation study across 10,000 datasets.

title: Teacher Orchestration Load in Collaborative Learning Activities in Robotics
citation: van Mierop, E. S. & Molinari, G. (2025). Teacher Orchestration Load in Collaborative Learning Activities in Robotics. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 281-285). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Mierop, E. S. V. & Molinari, G.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
conceptualisations_list: Cognitive Load Theory; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Classroom Orchestration
abstract: This study investigates teachers’ orchestration tasks during collaborative robotics activities, focusing on the cognitive, physical, and emotional components of orchestration load. Using a mixed-method approach, we compared a self-orchestrated session to one structured by the Pyramid script, a collaborative learning flow pattern. Findings indicate that structured scripts effectively reduce emotional and cognitive load for junior teachers by clearly guiding orchestration, enabling a shift from continuous monitoring to strategic classroom management. In contrast, senior teachers experienced increased emotional and cognitive loads due to conflicts with established routines. By highlighting emotional load as an orchestration component, this study deepens the understanding of teacher orchestration load in CSCL environments. Further research involving diverse teaching contexts is needed to validate these findings.

title: The Evolution of Shared Artifacts in CSCL: A Knowledge Synthesis Intervention for Productive Collaborative Discourse
citation: Zhu, X. & Chen, B. (2025). The Evolution of Shared Artifacts in CSCL: A Knowledge Synthesis Intervention for Productive Collaborative Discourse. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 286-290). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhu, X. & Chen, B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In CSCL, productive collaborative discourse requires continual advancement of student ideas, often through the creation and modification of digital artifacts. To support this process, this study proposes a knowledge synthesis intervention, supported by technological and pedagogical designs, to facilitate the continual development of digital artifacts in a graduate class. To examine the enactment of this intervention, we asked: How did the knowledge synthesis artifacts facilitate the progression of collaborative discourse? How did they facilitate the development of shared group artifacts? Findings revealed diverse ways in which synthesis artifacts facilitated discourse navigation, fostered various knowledge practices, and facilitated the evolution of group artifacts. This study contributes to CSCL and online learning research by facilitating knowledge synthesis and examining its role in deepening collaborative discourse, generating technological and pedagogical designs applicable in broader contexts.

title: Friendly Controversy: Synergistic Scaffolding for Practices of Providing Peer Critique
citation: Zhou, J., Lin, Q., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Danish, J., Duncan, R. G., Chinn, C. A., & Desai, A. (2025). Friendly Controversy: Synergistic Scaffolding for Practices of Providing Peer Critique. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 29-37). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhou, J., Lin, Q., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Danish, J., Duncan, R. G., Chinn, C. A., & Desai, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: Peer critique is essential for collaborative learning of science but presents challenges for students. Drawing on distributed and synergistic scaffolding, we designed multiple supports within a CSCL modeling environment, including integrated evidence and peer-feedback mechanisms, to help 6th-grade students develop peer critique practices. Through analysis of students’ comments and engagement patterns during critique activities, we found that students demonstrated progressive uptake of peer critique practices that the scaffolds were designed to promote, evident in more balanced, specific critiques over time. These findings inform the design of distributed scaffolds for supporting peer critique in science classrooms.

title: Team-Based Dynamics of Diagnosis and Intervention in a VR Simulation: Towards a Reasoning Process Model
citation: Richters, C., Fischer, M. R., Fischer, F., & Popov, V. (2025). Team-Based Dynamics of Diagnosis and Intervention in a Vr Simulation: Towards a Reasoning Process Model. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 291-295). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Richters, C., Fischer, M. R., Fischer, F., & Popov, V.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
tpack_tk_labels: Immersive VR / AR; Simulations & Scientific Modeling
conceptualisations_list: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)
abstract: Accounting neglect of intervention reasoning in CSCL research, we propose a new process model for team-based diagnostic and intervention reasoning in acute care, focusing on interactions among diagnostic activities (DAs), intervention activities (IAs), and collaborative activities (CAs) such as joint information processing, coordination, and communication. Using epistemic network analysis, we analyzed data from a VR-based cardiac arrest simulation to validate this model by comparing expert- and novice-led teams. As expected, expert-led teams demonstrated faster, more cohesive transitions between DAs and IAs, with a streamlined, linear CA pattern, while novice-led teams exhibited slower, fragmented transitions with cyclical CA patterns. These findings support the model’s potential to capture expertise-driven coordination and efficiency in high-stakes settings. Future research may expand this model across diverse team compositions and problem contexts. By refining understanding of acute care team dynamics, this model paves the way for instructional strategies enhancing coordination and performance in collaborative problem solving.

title: Integrating Culture to Ignite STEM Passion in U.S. Students
citation: Akumbu, R., Hamilton, E., & Knox, K. (2025). Integrating Culture to Ignite STEM Passion in U.s. Students. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 296-300). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Akumbu, R., Hamilton, E., & Knox, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The Asset-Based Learning Environment (ABLE) project examines how integration of cultural variables in project design enhances STEM interest and motivation among U.S. students aged 12-18. Using the Interest-Driven Creator (IDC) Theory alongside cultural frameworks like Cultural Integration and Augmentation (CIA), the study indicates significant connections between cultural elements, local STEM practices, and interest/motivation. Findings emphasize the transformative role of culturally tailored STEM education in fostering curiosity, intrinsic motivation, and sustained engagement within diverse learning environments.

title: Using Epistemic Network Analysis and Sequential Pattern Mining to Explore the Impacts of Human Facilitation on Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving
citation: Jiang, Y., Graf, E. A., & Todd, J. A. (2025). Using Epistemic Network Analysis and Sequential Pattern Mining to Explore the Impacts of Human Facilitation on Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 3-11). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jiang, Y., Graf, E. A., & Todd, J. A.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)
abstract: Learning algebra concepts, particularly those involving functions, is crucial yet challenging in mathematics education. Research suggests that collaborative learning, where students work in small teams to solve math problems, can support conceptual learning. However, collaborative problem solving (CPS) is complex and requires students’ social and cognitive skills for success. This study investigates the impacts of guided facilitation on supporting CPS in mathematics tasks during small-team collaboration. Using epistemic network analysis and sequential pattern mining, we analyzed chat logs from student teams and human facilitators and compared the interactions in facilitated and unfacilitated teams. Results indicated that near-peer facilitation effectively promoted constructive behaviors like multiple turns of social negotiation, while reducing inappropriate communications. Different facilitation strategies, such as encouraging students to respond to each other or clarify their statements, elicited targeted CPS behaviors, possibly leading to improved team performance. Findings have practical implications for facilitating CPS in mathematics classrooms.

title: Teachers Learning: Interaction and Discourse in a Virtual Community: A Design Model
citation: Saban, I. & Hadar, L. (2025). Teachers Learning: Interaction and Discourse in a Virtual Community: A Design Model. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 301-305). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Saban, I. & Hadar, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This practice-oriented paper presents a model for a virtual learning community for teachers and examines teacher learning within this framework. The community’s learning primarily occurs through discourse on the WhatsApp messaging platform. The paper begins by describing the community learning model, emphasizing key characteristics of online professional development. Using qualitative content analysis, we analyzed WhatsApp activity from the first month of the 2021 school year, encompassing 137 posts, and identified learning discourse topics, interaction frequency, and interaction types. The WhatsApp-based community addresses a major challenge in online learning: fostering frequent and spontaneous interactions among members. The paper demonstrates the model’s potential to promote an active and engaging approach to professional development.

title: Exploring the Effects of Integrating Online Knowledge Building Activities into Elementary Students’ Collaborative Scientific Inquiry Learning
citation: Wu, Y., Wang, L., Zeng, Y., & Shih, T. (2025). Exploring the Effects of Integrating Online Knowledge Building Activities Into Elementary Students’ Collaborative Scientific Inquiry Learning. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 306-310). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wu, Y., Wang, L., Zeng, Y., & Shih, T.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study explores the integration of online knowledge-building (KB) activities into elementary students’ collaborative scientific inquiry learning through the “Inquiry Together” platform. Grounded in Knowledge Building Theory, the platform offers tools for collaborative idea refinement, progress monitoring, and dynamic scaffolding, addressing persistent challenges in elementary science education. 52 fifth-grade students participated in the study, divided into an experimental group using the platform and a control group engaged in conventional KB-based activities. Pre- and post-test analyses revealed improvements in both groups regarding science learning attitudes, scientific inquiry skills, and perceptions of KB-oriented learning environments. The experimental group showed significantly greater gains in science learning interest, recognition of science's value, scientific inquiry skills, and perceptions of a collaborative and agentive learning environment, attributed to the platform’s targeted scaffolding. These findings highlight the potential of "Inquiry Together" to enhance KB-based pedagogy by promoting engagement, critical thinking, and collaboration in elementary science learning.

title: Supporting Productive Dialogue with Collaborative Conversational Agents: Frequency and Sequence of Learner Behavior
citation: Papadopoulos, P. M., de Araujo, A., & Martens, J. (2025). Supporting Productive Dialogue With Collaborative Conversational Agents: Frequency and Sequence of Learner Behavior. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 311-315). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Papadopoulos, P. M., Araujo, A. D., & Martens, J.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study presents the impact of a collaborative conversational agent on the chat dialogues of 17 dyads. Specifically, participants were asked to study two cases of climate change using the chat tool of a learning platform to communicate. The agent was available only in the second case and was able to monitor the participants’ discussion and intervene using the talk moves of the academically productive talk framework (e.g., prompting for elaboration, examples, etc.). Analysis of the chat logs showed higher levels of elaboration for the second case, while the agent acted as a catalyst increasing the chances for elaboration and transactivity.

title: A Complex Systems Perspective on Educational Makerspaces: Leveraging Mixed Methods for Enhanced System Insights
citation: Litherland, K. T. & Mørch, A. I. (2025). A Complex Systems Perspective on Educational Makerspaces: Leveraging Mixed Methods for Enhanced System Insights. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 316-320). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Litherland, K. T. & Mørch, A. I.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Makerspaces are complex systems composed of various interacting parts and actors, including materials (physical and digital), learners, and educators. Complex systems have properties and qualities that are useful for researchers to study collaborative learning in this environment. Towards that end, we present a mixed methods approach for analyzing group understanding and network-level properties using video data exclusively. Our research design combines two complementary methods: qualitative interaction analysis and quantitative sociotechnical network analysis. The latter is an extension of social network analysis. We combine these methods to identify challenges in educational makerspaces, such as access to resources and curriculum integration. The main challenge identified with our complex systems perspective is rapid build-up of complexity in making activities, which is manifest as nested structures in the network analysis and lack of shared understanding in the interactions analysis.

title: Automatic Analysis of Transactivity in Collaborative Problem Solving Dialogues: The Relationship of Novelty and Reference
citation: Otten, D. M., Papadopoulos, P. M., Haeri, M. A., & Endedijk, M. D. (2025). Automatic Analysis of Transactivity in Collaborative Problem Solving Dialogues: The Relationship of Novelty and Reference. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 321-325). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Otten, D. M., Papadopoulos, P. M., Haeri, M. A., & Endedijk, M. D.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: Recent research has proposed a two-dimensional model for transactivity, encompassing the elements of novelty and reference. In this study, we further operationalize this model by identifying three distinguish levels for each dimension and we examine the relationship of novelty and reference in a case study. Specifically, we employ ChatGPT for the automatic coding of 12 chat dialogues of collaborative problem solving and examine how novelty and reference change over time and when and how the dialogues become transactive. Results indicated that both novelty and reference are volatile, with isolated peaks or short transactive sequences within a dialogue without a gradual build-up. In addition, it was evident that it was easier for students to reach higher levels of reference with novelty levels lagging. The study provides preliminary insights into the nature and dynamics of transactive dialogue and offers a way to instructional designers for supporting transactivity in collaborative learning.

title: Exploring Students’ Interdisciplinary Collaborative Learning Outcomes and Processes with Varying Degrees of Knowledge Heterogeneity
citation: Su, G., Chen, W., Zhu, G., Xu, J. S., & Le, C. (2025). Exploring Students’ Interdisciplinary Collaborative Learning Outcomes and Processes With Varying Degrees of Knowledge Heterogeneity. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 326-329). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Su, G., Chen, W., Zhu, G., Xu, J. S., & Le, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Interdisciplinary collaborative learning (ICL) is key to 21st-century education. Knowledge heterogeneity (KH) plays an important role in interdisciplinary collaborative learning, but few empirical studies investigated how different degrees of knowledge heterogeneity shape the ICL in detail. This quasi-experimental study investigated how various degrees of knowledge heterogeneity affect student groups’ ICL outcomes and processes. A total of 48 undergraduates participated in this study. Group solution reports and verbal discussions were collected and analyzed. The findings showed that groups with a higher degree of KH performed significantly better than those with a lower degree of KH in adopting disciplinary insights. Different behavioural patterns were identified in knowledge integration, problem-solving, and coordination during ICL.

title: Exploring the Design of Pedagogical Agent Roles in Collaborative STEM+C Learning
citation: Cohn, C., Fonteles, J. H., Snyder, C., Srivastava, N., S., A. T., Campbell, D., Montenegro, J., & Biswas, G. (2025). Exploring the Design of Pedagogical Agent Roles in Collaborative STEM+c Learning. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 330-334). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cohn, C., Fonteles, J. H., Snyder, C., Srivastava, N., S, A. T., Campbell, D., Montenegro, J., & Biswas, G.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This paper explores the design of two types of pedagogical agents—teaching and peer—in a collaborative STEM+C learning environment, C2STEM, where high school students learn physics (kinematics) and computing by building computational models that simulate the motion of objects. Through in-depth case study interviews with teachers and students, we identify role-based features for these agents to support collaborative learning in open-ended STEM+C learning environments. We propose twelve design principles—four for teaching agents, four for peer agents, and four shared by both—contributing to foundational guidelines for developing agents that enhance collaborative learning through computational modeling.

title: Supporting Preparation for Peer Tutoring with a Dialogue Planning Tool
citation: Cui, Y. & Reimann, P. (2025). Supporting Preparation for Peer Tutoring With a Dialogue Planning Tool. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 335-339). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cui, Y. & Reimann, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Peer tutoring has been widely recognized as an effective learning strategy, yet the reported modest effect sizes indicate room for improvement. Research indicates that unprepared peer tutors mostly rely on knowledge telling, while few studies have specifically focused on the preparation phase. To address this gap, we developed a dialogue planning tool that provides structured question-answer prompts combined with a network graph to support tutoring preparation. This paper reports an ongoing small-scale empirical study testing the tool in science tutoring by comparing dialogue-based with slide-based tutoring plans. Initial findings reveal that dialogue planning facilitates a higher number of question-answer turns and adaptive guidance and increases the frequency of evaluating-level cognition and metacognitive-level knowledge. Future research will leverage the tutoring plan database, incorporating Large Language Models, to provide feedback on developing tutoring plans, aiming to support peer tutors’ transition from knowledge-telling to knowledge-construction.

title: Generative AI-Supported Collaboration in Interdisciplinary Research Practice
citation: Naganuma, S., Minematsu, T., Matsueda, K., & Oshima, J. (2025). Generative Ai-Supported Collaboration in Interdisciplinary Research Practice. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 340-344). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Naganuma, S., Minematsu, T., Matsueda, K., & Oshima, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We report an empirical study of a three-day workshop on interdisciplinary research practice by 14 doctoral students supported by generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to investigate how they use GenAI for their knowledge-building. They formed five teams and conducted presentations on promising interdisciplinary research proposals. Two high-performing teams’ discourses were analyzed in detail using a mixed-methods approach. We found that 1) students assigned four roles to GenAI (e.g., theme generation), 2) the frequency of students’ GenAI use was considerably limited, and 3) while GenAI use was limited to the initial theme establishment phase, students engaged in idea improvement by effectively integrating GenAI’s ideas. These findings suggest that the most difficult part of interdisciplinary collaboration for doctoral students is setting boundary objects in the initial phase, where GenAI can well-function. This study demonstrated that knowledge creators, such as doctoral students, can effectively collaborate using GenAI to create quality interdisciplinary collaborative research proposals.

title: Using Markov Chains to Understand Clinical Decision-Making Process
citation: Du, H. & Popov, V. (2025). Using Markov Chains to Understand Clinical Decision-Making Process. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 345-349). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Du, H. & Popov, V.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Clinical reasoning is a critical yet complex cognitive process of diagnostic and therapeutic decision-making in medical practice that has long challenged precise understanding and assessment. Sequential analysis can be used to uncover patterns and trends in clinical practices, contributing to improved training and ultimately leading to better patient care outcomes. In this study, 21 board-certified anesthesiologists participated in a simulated-based learning scenario requiring them to promptly recognize patient’s condition and initiate appropriate treatment. They were assigned into either the low-performing or high-performing group based on their performance. We utilized Markov Chain Transition Matrix, a robust statistical model for sequential data, to analyze participants’ practices using team reflection behavioral observation system and identified statistically significant differences between their transition matrices. The high-performing group had a much higher transition probability from evaluating information to implementation and from planning to planning. The implications are then discussed.

title: Doors, Decisions, and Discovery: An Interactive Smart Door Lock System to Promote Children’s Understanding of AI Classification
citation: Dangol, A., Wolfe, R., Landesman, R., Yip, J. C., & Kientz, J. A. (2025). Doors, Decisions, and Discovery: An Interactive Smart Door Lock System to Promote Children’s Understanding of Ai Classification. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 350-354). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Dangol, A., Wolfe, R., Landesman, R., Yip, J. C., & Kientz, J. A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Understanding AI’s decision-making process is essential for children as they navigate a world increasingly influenced by AI-driven technologies. Despite frequently interacting with AI-powered systems, children often have limited knowledge about how these systems make classification decisions. We present AI-Smartlock, an educational platform designed to teach young learners about the various parameters that influence AI classification, including classification rules, confidence scores, and decision thresholds. Through image classification tasks that simulate a smart door lock, children can interactively explore these parameters. This paper describes how we designed the system and our results from a participatory design session with a group of seven children (ages 7-12).

title: How Students Ground Mathematics Through Distributed Gestures: Designing Computer-Supported Collaborative Embodied Learning
citation: Kim, C., Xia, F., Beier, J. P., Swart, M. I., Schenck, K. E., & Nathan, M. J. (2025). How Students Ground Mathematics Through Distributed Gestures: Designing Computer-Supported Collaborative Embodied Learning. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 355-359). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kim, C., Xia, F., Beier, J. P., Swart, M. I., Schenck, K. E., & Nathan, M. J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
conceptualisations_list: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Co-Design & Participatory Design
abstract: We explored how students interact with a computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) system for embodied learning in geometry. With The Hidden Village-Online (THV-O), fifteen high school students (six dyads, one triad) used movements to construct directed actions that depict geometry transformations collaboratively. THV-O is a web-based CSCL video game that uses a motion-capture to detect players’ movements, save movements they create, and play those created by their peers. By observing dyads’ co-design processes and semi-structured reflections, researchers found two important shortcomings in the design of THV-O for embodied learning: (1) players experienced difficulty in conveying geometric transformations through poses, which could hinder their ability to represent generalizable properties of space and shape; and (2) players faced challenges in jointly co-constructing a single mathematical object, limiting their ability to collaborate actively and develop shared mathematical ideas. We offer guidelines for an improved design of embodied collaborative reasoning and learning.

title: Two Spaces, One Goal: Examining a Dyad’s Scientific Inquiry in Game-Based Learning and Beyond
citation: Chen, Y., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Lester, J. C. (2025). Two Spaces, One Goal: Examining a Dyad’s Scientific Inquiry in Game-Based Learning and Beyond. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 360-364). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chen, Y., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Lester, J. C.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Engaging students in scientific inquiry across digital and physical spaces presents both opportunities and challenges in K-12 STEM education. This study explores how a pair of learners collaboratively engage in the inquiry process through a single-player educational game. Using interaction analysis, we examine how the learners construct, refine, and revisit their hypotheses, leveraging both digital and physical tools designed to support inquiry learning. Our findings emphasize how these hybrid scaffolds facilitate collaborative discourse and hypothesis generation, while also identifying gaps in students' evidence evaluation and justification processes. This study provides empirical evidence on the potential of hybrid scaffolds to support collaborative inquiry and highlights the necessity of instructional strategies to help students develop robust criteria for evidence-based reasoning and hypothesis reflection.

title: The Role of Transactivity in Pre-service Teachers‘ Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning
citation: Tews, S., Weinberger, A., & Vogel, F. (2025). The Role of Transactivity in Pre-Service Teachers‘ Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 365-369). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tews, S., Weinberger, A., & Vogel, F.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Diagnostic competences are vital for teachers, enabling them to interpret classroom situations and provide effective feedback. This exploratory study investigates transactivity patterns in collaborative diagnostic reasoning (CDR) among pre-service teachers from same- and multidisciplinary dyads. Transactivity is operationalized through the factors of novelty (introducing new ideas) and reference (connecting to prior contributions). Four dyads diagnosed the instructional quality of a lesson depicted in a short video. Their discourse was recorded and analyzed for sequential changes in novelty and reference. The results reveal that changes in novelty and reference are partly in parallel, partly opposite. While novelty generally decreases over time, the pattern for reference is more inconsistent. Notable differences emerge between same- and multidisciplinary groups, with the latter showing higher reference scores in later phases of the discussion. These findings highlight the dynamics of novelty and reference in collaborative problem-solving over time and inform scaffolding of video-based CDR.

title: Cognitive Equilibrium and Multimodal Synchrony: A Case Study from Pair Programming
citation: Sharma, K. & Azevedo, R. (2025). Cognitive Equilibrium and Multimodal Synchrony: A Case Study From Pair Programming. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 370-374). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sharma, K. & Azevedo, R.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Gaze, emotional, and physiological synchronies are predictive of collaborative performance and quality. However the relationship among these synchronies are not clear. We present a pair programming study to understand the relationship between facial expression synchrony, joint visual attention, joint mental effort, joint stress and joint engagement. We collected eye-tracking, heart rate variability, electrodermal activity, facial expressions from 40 pairs while they were collaboratively debugging a given program. We computed gaze, facial expressions, stress and engagement based synchronies. We also computed the joint facial expression cycles and compared the different cycles with the debugging performance. We then examined the relationships between different synchronies and joint facial expression cycles. Our results show a clear difference between the high and low performing pairs based on their joint facial expression cycles. Moreover, our results also show that there are significant relationships between joint facial expression cycles and the multimodal synchronies.

title: Educational Makerspaces: Embodied Learning for World-Making
citation: Groth, C., Søyland, L., Kolesnyk, L., Høibo, I. H., & Olafsson, B. (2025). Educational Makerspaces: Embodied Learning for World-Making. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 375-379). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Groth, C., Søyland, L., Kolesnyk, L., Høibo, I. H., & Olafsson, B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: How can we educate for worldmaking in makerspaces? In our study on Makerspaces in the Norwegian context we conducted research-practice partnerships in several school-based makers spaces over a period of three years. Through engaging in the teachers and students everyday school life and context, we were able to follow, learn and co-create the events unfolding in them. In this paper we present two learning settings and the understandings that were developed in them. The two settings both pointed at opportunities for worldmaking in relation to personal sense making through material interactions and the role of the environment for equitable engagement and inclusivity. We also saw the importance of having enough time for planning truly meaningful learning experiences that involve open ended embodied exploration of materials and technologies.

title: Supporting STEAM Design Collaboration via Knowledge Building Principles in an Online Teacher Professional Development Course
citation: Chang, C., Seet, C. H., Chang, Y., Chen, M., Chen, B., Chai, C., & Hong, H. (2025). Supporting STEAM Design Collaboration via Knowledge Building Principles in an Online Teacher Professional Development Course. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of a professional development course that integrates Knowledge Building (KB) principles into Design Thinking (DT) activities to empower and engage teachers in collaborative STEAM lesson design activities. The course aimed to equip teachers with the knowledge and skills necessary to develop effective STEAM lessons for fostering student agency. Results indicate that the course significantly improved teachers' design thinking mindset, perceived understanding and perceived importance of KB principles, and their competency to develop effective lesson prototypes aligned with KB principles. The findings suggest that integrating KB principles into DT processes can be a useful approach for teacher professional development, leading to more collaborative, innovative and effective teaching practices.

title: CocoNote: Agents-aided Collaborative Learning Environment Enhances Socially Shared Regulation
citation: Xin, H., Li, S., Huang, L., Yip, V. W., Niu, Q., Chen, X., & Liu, J. (2025). CocoNote: Agents-Aided Collaborative Learning Environment Enhances Socially Shared Regulation. abstract: This study aims to develop CocoNote, an agent-aided collaborative learning platform that enhances students' Socially Shared Regulation (SSRL) in collaborative learning. CocoNote integrates reactive agents to facilitate students' planning, monitoring, and reflection alongside a proactive agent that actively intervenes to provide metacognitive, socio-emotional, and motivational support. A quasi-experimental study involving sixth-grade students examined their SSRL abilities in a STEM course. Quantitative findings indicated that students using CocoNote (n = 38) demonstrated significant improvements in SSRL and exhibited more balanced group interactions compared to the control group (n = 40). Qualitative data analysis illustrated how agents guided discussions, increased participation and improved metacognitive processes. These findings highlight the effectiveness of AI-assisted tools in fostering SSRL abilities and suggest design principles for agent-aided collaborative learning environments.

title: Technology-Mediated Lesson Study to Improve Teacher Outcomes
citation: Hudson, M., Leary, H., Sansom, R., Longhurst, M., Stowers, J., Smith, C., & Moore, A. (2025). Technology-Mediated Lesson Study to Improve Teacher Outcomes. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 385-389). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hudson, M., Leary, H., Sansom, R., Longhurst, M., Stowers, J., Smith, C., & Moore, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Professional development is crucial for teachers to build their skills and adopt three-dimensional science. Effective professional development should be ongoing, collaborative, and spread over time to ensure lasting changes in teaching practices. Rural teachers often face isolation and less training compared to their urban counterparts, limiting their opportunities for collaboration. This research explored how technology-mediated lesson study (TMLS) helped rural teachers improve their teaching abilities and three-dimensional science skills. TMLS adapts lesson study using technology, allowing teachers to collaborate remotely. Based on four years of evidence, this research developed and refined the steps of TMLS with rural science teachers. This work also aimed to improve their three-dimensional science teaching abilities by forming small, collaborative groups that co-design, implement, and evaluate lesson plans together. Overall, TMLS offers rural teachers a valuable platform to enhance their teaching skills, collaborate meaningfully, and overcome the challenges of isolation.

title: A Collaborative Learning Framework for Post-IVR Environments
citation: Johnson, J. & Stephenson, V. (2025). A Collaborative Learning Framework for Post-Ivr Environments. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 390-394). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Johnson, J. & Stephenson, V.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: This paper examines the integration of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) and Knowledge Building Theory (KBT) in post-Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) contexts to propose a conceptual framework for post-IVR collaborative learning. While IVR offers rich interaction data and collaborative opportunities, current post-IVR activities often replicate traditional teacher-led methods, failing to utilize these affordances for deeper knowledge creation and collaborative learning. We reviewed 18 papers focusing on post-IVR processes and supports. Findings highlight underutilized opportunities to integrate during-IVR data—such as behavioral analytics and interaction patterns—into post-IVR tasks to enhance problem-solving, reflection, and collaborative engagement. The proposed framework emphasizes scaffolds, tools, and feedback to bridge IVR experiences with meaningful post-activity learning and future work in this area.

title: Are You Seeing What I Am Talking About? Joint Attention Instruction for Collaborative Learners at A Digital Whiteboard
citation: Pfannenstiel, W., Grajcevci, A., Korbach, A., & Weinberger, A. (2025). Are you Seeing What I Am Talking About? Joint Attention Instruction for Collaborative Learners at a Digital Whiteboard. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 395-398). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Pfannenstiel, W., Grajcevci, A., Korbach, A., & Weinberger, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Joint attention is a crucial element in collaborative learning, often facilitated by group awareness tools highlighting the partner’s visual focus. Little is known, however, to what extent joint attention can also be differentially instructed guiding shared and mutual gaze. To determine if joint attention can be effectively instructed for, we conducted a 2×2 experimental laboratory study with the factors shared gaze instruction (with versus without) and dyadic gaze instruction (with versus without), consisting of 47 dyads (n = 94). Participants discussed the impact of social media use supported with a concept map on a digital whiteboard. We built on a multi-modal learning analytics framework to analyze participants’ behavioral responses via EDA and gaze tracking measurements. The results revealed that instructing for dyadic gaze reduces shared attention. Furthermore, there are differential correlations between shared moments of arousal and joint attention. Overall, joint attention instruction can guide learners’ focus in CSCL settings.

title: Towards Supporting Group Learning through Design-based Research and Multimodal Data-based Tools
citation: Damşa, C., Kaliisa, R., Esterhazy, R., Langford, M., & Lie, R. H. (2025). Towards Supporting Group Learning Through Design-Based Research and Multimodal Data-Based Tools. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 399-403). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Damşa, C., Kaliisa, R., Esterhazy, R., Langford, M., & Lie, R. H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper presents an iterative design-based research study that generated a multimodal analytics dashboard to support feedback and reflection in student groups enrolled in an undergraduate legal education course. Across two iterations, involving eight groups with 28 students and 7 teachers, we explored students’ collaborative project work and teachers’ pedagogical needs for guiding groups. We co-designed a multimodal analytics-based dashboard prototype that visualized meeting activities, project documents and survey reflections, and which was used to support reflection on group work. The findings indicate that students value analytics related to the collaboration progress and quality of collaborative input, while teachers are more interested in accessing data about students’ development of subject matter knowledge and the collaborative process.

title: Reflective AI-Partnerships: How Middle Schoolers Balance Creativity and AI Collaboration
citation: Ojeda-Ramirez, S., Han, A., Rich, A., Han, S., & Peppler, K. (2025). Reflective Ai-Partnerships: How Middle Schoolers Balance Creativity and Ai Collaboration. subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: This study explores how middle school students navigate collaboration with generative AI in storytelling, focusing on their ability to balance AI contributions with their creative agency. Conducted during a workshop with Story AI, an interactive narrative-writing platform, this research involved participants aged 6 to 12 years from a predominantly Latinx community. Data from surveys, interviews, and writing outputs reveal that students engaged in reflective practices and demonstrated an emerging ability to critically modulate AI contributions. These findings engage with recent CSCL studies, including Cress and Kimmerle’s (2023) insights into knowledge transformation and Borge et al.’s (2024) exploration of metacognitive reflection, by situating co-writing as a dynamic context for fostering collaboration and agency. Implications include designing learning environments that explicitly scaffold student reflection on AI collaboration as an essential skill for navigating human-AI partnerships. This research highlights co-writing as a valuable avenue for advancing reflective and creative thinking in educational settings.

title: Number of Players, Zero: Using Multi-Agent Collaboration to Evaluate Unsolvable Collaborative Items
citation: Wang, Y. & Bergner, Y. (2025). Number of Players, Zero: Using Multi-Agent Collaboration to Evaluate Unsolvable Collaborative Items. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 409-414). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wang, Y. & Bergner, Y.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: While the importance of collaborative problem-solving (CPS) is widely acknowledged, developing and evaluating CPS items remains challenging. This study extends to multi-agent systems (MASs) prior work on CPS item templates and the use of large language models for evaluation of collaborative interdependence in math problems designed for two solvers working together. Specifically, we test the hypothesis that MASs more accurately handle evaluation of flawed items that are unsolvable even if both students collaborate with respect to the information and/or answer affordances provided to them.

title: Processes Matter: How ML/GAI Approaches Could Support Open Qualitative Coding of Online Discourse Datasets
citation: Chen, J., Lotsos, A., Wang, G., Zhao, L., Sherin, B., Wilensky, U., & Horn, M. (2025). Processes Matter: How Ml/gai Approaches Could Support Open Qualitative Coding of Online Discourse Datasets. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 415-419). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chen, J., Lotsos, A., Wang, G., Zhao, L., Sherin, B., Wilensky, U., & Horn, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Open coding, a key inductive step in qualitative research, discovers and constructs concepts from human datasets. However, capturing extensive and nuanced aspects or “coding moments” can be challenging, especially with large discourse datasets. While some studies explore machine learning (ML)/Generative AI (GAI)'s potential for open coding, few evaluation studies exist. We compare open coding results by five recently published ML/GAI approaches and four human coders, using a dataset of online chat messages around a mobile learning software. Our systematic analysis reveals ML/GAI approaches' strengths and weaknesses, uncovering the complementary potential between humans and AI. Line-by-line AI approaches effectively identify content-based codes, while humans excel in interpreting conversational dynamics. We discussed how embedded analytical processes could shape the results of ML/GAI approaches. Instead of replacing humans in open coding, researchers should integrate AI with and according to their analytical processes, e.g., as parallel co-coders.

title: Mirroring What’s in the Shared Repertoires of Two Communities of Practice: A Cultural-Historical Perspective Using Generative AI
citation: Laferrière, T. & Charles, E. S. (2025). Mirroring What’s in the Shared Repertoires of Two Communities of Practice: A Cultural-Historical Perspective Using Generative Ai. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Laferrière, T. & Charles, E. S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Communities of Practice & Situated Learning
abstract: This paper explores the development of the shared repertoires (Wenger, 1998) of two web-supported Communities of Practice (CoPs). The co-authors of this paper were the initiators of these CoPs and continue to be involved in them. Using the shared repertoire of each of these communities as a lens, the evolution of their activity was explored. Referring to the CHAT’s change lab process of mirroring to participants their past activity (Engeström, 1987, 2015), two generative AI tools were prompted to focus on the websites of the two CoPs, especially collaborative activities and artefacts, and to ‘report on’ the evolution of their shared repertoires. Accounts underwent human validation. For ethical reasons, no transcript was analysed of the interactions between the participants that may have led, through meaning negotiation, to the production or use of artefacts as well as to problem setting, problem solving or knowledge building. Results show that 1) the generative AI tools were accurate in their ‘reports’; and 2) identified possible limitations in the shared repertoires; such observations providing topics for future negotiation of values among members and between these communities.

title: Interaction Analysis between Generative AI and High School Students in Scientific Projects
citation: Ohsaki, A. & Matsukawa, H. (2025). Interaction Analysis Between Generative Ai and High School Students in Scientific Projects. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. authors_list: Ohsaki, A. & Matsukawa, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates interaction patterns between generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and high school students as they develop science research projects. Specifically, it examines GenAI’s behavior, focusing on interaction patterns and response appropriateness. The analysis indicates that GenAI frequently provides unsolicited advice and generates responses eight times longer than student inputs despite predefined constraints. This study proposes a visualization method for the interaction imbalance between learners and GenAI, providing valuable insight into the relationship between interaction balance and learning in future computer-supported collaborative learning research.

title: The Role of Free Movement in the Physical Space for Productive Disequilibration in Collaborative Simulations

abstract: This paper examined how City Settlers, a simulation that is mapped onto the physical environment, impacts students’ interaction and learning, both within and between groups. In particular, we examined how the open-ended nature of the game and students’ ability to freely move in the space, helped generate productive disequilibrating events. Analysis of group discourse showed that when a member of the group physically leaves and comes back, or a member of another group physically moves to their group, can disequilibrate group discourse towards new productive discourse around the game’s science, civics, and strategic concepts.

citation: Xiao, Y. & Xu, J. (2025). Design and Play in Real Time: A Participatory Design Approach for Autistic Children to Design Online Play With Peers. abstract: This paper presents a participatory design approach for children, designers, and educators to collaboratively create inclusive digital play environments that foster interactions between neurodiverse and neurotypical children. Integrating generative AI (GenAI) empowers children to actively contribute to game design while engaging in the play with their peers without adult mediation, highlighting the potential of such methods to foster inclusive collaboration among children, between children and adults, and between children and technology.

title: Using Markov Chain Analysis to Study the Relations Between Emotions, Cognitive Actions, and Performance in Collaborative Learning
citation: S., A. T., Snyder, C., Prasanna, S. M., Mohammed, N., & Biswas, G. (2025). Using Markov Chain Analysis to Study the Relations Between Emotions, Cognitive Actions, and Performance in Collaborative Learning. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. authors_list: S, A. T., Snyder, C., Prasanna, S. M., Mohammed, N., & Biswas, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Collaborative problem-solving (CPS) in STEM+C education involves cognitive coordination and emotional regulation during joint tasks. Prior research has examined discrete affective states in learning environments but less is known about how these emotions evolve over time and affect CPS behavior. This study investigates the temporal dynamics of five emotions—engagement, confusion, boredom, delight, and frustration—using Markov Chain analysis of data from high school pairs building computational models in the C2STEM environment. Emotional transitions aligned with cognitive processes, seen in interaction patterns like PLAY, ADJUST, and BUILD, to analyze affect during modeling. Results show that emotional trajectories closely relate to cognitive actions, including construction, simulation testing, and debugging. Transitions that maintained engagement linked to productive collaboration and stronger performance, while ongoing frustration and boredom indicated disengagement progress.

title: Stories, Printing Press, Internet, and now ChatGPT: Examined via the SMART Framework
citation: Raj, A., Stroup, W. M., & Kayumova, S. (2025). Stories, Printing Press, Internet, and Now ChatGPT: Examined via the SMART Framework. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 445-449). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Raj, A., Stroup, W. M., & Kayumova, S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) represents a transformative leap in education technology, with profound implications for policy, classrooms, teachers, and students worldwide. This paper explores AI’s impact using the proposed SMART framework (Source, Medium, Agency, Reach, and Transformation), comparing it to three pivotal milestones in educational technology: storytelling, the printing press, and the internet. Building on discussions of existing educational frameworks, AI literacy, and systemic approaches, we highlight how earlier technologies integrated into human-driven systems, while AI functions as an adaptive agent that is capable of generating knowledge, influencing relationships, and shaping learning experiences in real-time. By addressing the philosophical debates surrounding AI’s human-like intelligence and the practical implications of its widespread adoption, this critical-technocentric perspective recognizes both its transformative potential and its risks, including inequities and ethical concerns. Ultimately, we call for proactive regulation and equity-driven strategies to navigate AI’s promises and challenges in education.

title: Generative AI in Project-Based Learning for Sustainable Development
citation: Hernández-Leo, D., Theophilou, E., & Alkhasawneh, S. N. (2025). Generative Ai in Project-Based Learning for Sustainable Development. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 450-454). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hernández-Leo, D., Theophilou, E., & Alkhasawneh, S. N.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Generative AI (genAI) offers potential to enhance learning scenarios. However, research on specific use-cases and roles within educational frameworks is limited. This paper focuses on UNESCO’s Education for Sustainable Development framework and its recommendation to use Project-Based Learning (PBL) to develop key-competences for addressing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The research investigates expert teachers' views on the potential for human-AI collaboration, focusing on the role of genAI in use-cases designed to enhance individual and collaborative learning within PBLxSDG. A workshop involving 33 participants yielded 11 use-cases. Along with 10 use-cases derived from the literature and evaluations from participants, forming the foundation of our analysis. Insights from our analysis saw genAI assuming diverse roles for human-AI collaboration within PBLxSDG. However, concerns were raised about overreliance on AI, learning outcomes, and the need for teacher guidance. This work provides insights for educators and researchers exploring genAI implementation in collaborative, active learning scenarios.

title: Balancing the Imbalance: Enhancing MOOC Discussion Forum Urgency Prediction with LLM-Generated Data Augmentation
citation: Li, H. & Botelho, A. F. (2025). Balancing the Imbalance: Enhancing MOOC Discussion Forum Urgency Prediction With Llm-Generated Data Augmentation. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 455-459). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Li, H. & Botelho, A. F.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General

abstract: Discussion forums in Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) often contain urgent posts requiring timely instructor intervention, but identifying these posts is challenging due to severe class imbalance in urgency levels. This study presents a novel approach combining Large Language Models (LLMs) and traditional machine learning to address this challenge. We develop a two-stage pipeline that first uses LLMs to generate synthetic forum posts, creating a balanced dataset across seven urgency levels, then evaluates five different machine learning models on both original and balanced datasets. Our results demonstrate significant improvements across all models, with the Support Vector Regression achieving the highest performance (R² improvement from 0.298 to 0.857). Through comprehensive evaluation using multiple metrics and cross-validation, we show that our approach not only improves model performance but also enhances prediction stability across different urgency levels. This work contributes to both educational data mining methodology and practical MOOC forum management.

title: Experimental Investigation on Reciprocal Teaching Using Misconception-Based Teachable Agents in Collaborative Learning

International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hayashi, Y., Shimojo, S., & Kawamura, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Conceptual Change & Mental Models; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: This study examines methods to promote mutual explanatory activities in collaborative learning using a teachable virtual peer learner. Its purpose is to determine whether the quality (error level) of knowledge generated by a teachable virtual peer learner can encourage learners to reevaluate their understanding. This study uses the ACT-R cognitive architecture to examine a teachable agent that learns from learners' concept maps and generates feedback maps. Further, a comparative experiment is conducted on a non-agent, an erroneous knowledge agent, and a non-erroneous agent. Results reveal that the use of a teachable agent enhances the learning activities of learners. Specifically, when learners interact with the erroneous knowledge agent, they actively revise their concept maps and, thereby, improve learning outcomes. This revision process was prompted by observing incorrect maps and encouraging learners to review and correct their knowledge.

title: Teachers' Strategies: Collaborative Learning in Second Language Classroom

abstract: The study explores strategies teachers use to design, monitor, manage, and evaluate collaborative group activities in second language learning within higher education. Twenty second language teachers from diverse educational contexts and countries participated in semi-structured interviews. A total of 68 Critical Incidents were obtained. We elaborated a coding schema and analyzed critical incidents focusing on task objectives, teacher actions, student interactions, and evaluation outcomes. Teachers found that culturally relevant tasks content led to greater student engagement, while challenges such as high learning objectives, unclear instructions, and imbalanced group participation affected group work and task success. The study emphasizes the importance of balancing group size, task complexity, and cultural context in collaborative second language learning. The findings attempt to bridge theoretical and methodological foundations of collaborative learning with strategies applied in the classroom.

title: Designing and Promoting Primary Students’ Knowledge-building Trajectories and Authentic Scientific Inquiry
citation: Ma, X., Chan, C. K., & Feng, X. (2025). Designing and Promoting Primary Students’ Knowledge-Building Trajectories and Authentic Scientific Inquiry. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ma, X., Chan, C. K. K., & Feng, X.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study investigated fourth graders’ authentic scientific inquiry within a knowledge-building environment supported by Knowledge Forum. Designed to cultivate students as scientists, the environment facilitated collaborative inquiry through problem formulation, explanation co-construction, and theory building – key practices aligned with authentic scientific practice. Quantitative analyses revealed significant improvements in both domain and epistemic understanding. Qualitative data, including Knowledge Forum discourse and classroom artifacts, demonstrated how the environment fostered students’ sustained scientific engagement and supported the progressive development of their ideas. The study identified shifts in students’ domain understanding and reflective practices, highlighting the value of tracing knowledge building trajectories to support reflective learning and foster authentic scientific inquiry.

abstract: Since the inception of learning analytics, the CSCL community has been applying a range of methods to examine collaborative discourse, such as natural language processing and networked approaches. Despite significant advancements in methods, a critical gap persists in translating these data-driven insights into actionable strategies to inform pedagogical decisions. The proposed hybrid symposium seeks to bridge this gap by engaging learning scientists, CSCL researchers, and educators in discussions that integrate advanced discourse analytics with pedagogical design. Through five diverse presentations, the symposium will explore the integration of advanced discourse analysis techniques, such as networked approaches, multimodal analytics, and clustering analysis, into pedagogically meaningful designs and actionable pedagogical insights for collaborative learning environments. By fostering dialogue on the challenges and opportunities in contextualizing computational insights, this symposium aims to establish actionable approaches for enriching collaborative discourse and advancing the broader CSCL community’s theoretical, methodological, and practical understanding.

The four papers dis-cuss human-AI interactions in various learning tasks and domains, especially from an augmentation perspective. The studies examine how these interactions can support learn-ing processes and how learners perceive AI as an interaction partner (or not). By exploring these augmentation dynamics across tasks and domains, the symposium contributes to the evolving understanding of human-AI collaboration in teaching and learning. The sympo-sium’s discussant will synthesize insights from these studies to shed light on how these studies contribute knowledge and how these approaches need to be further developed to contribute to future hybrid intelligence (HI) systems in education.

abstract: Providing peer feedback is a powerful learning activity. However, its potential is not always realized. To improve feedback provision and uptake, AI can augment peer feedback provision and reception processes. However, little is known about how students use AI in the context of peer feedback, what aspects of AI feedback are associated with higher quality of human peer feedback, and how AI feedback can be implemented as part of the instructional design to best facilitate learning. In addition, research needs to find ways to harness the power of AI while minimizing its high resource requirements. This symposium will answer these questions and provide insights into the latest developments in using AI in peer feedback research.

abstract: Since the release of OpenAI ChatGPT along with other Large Language Models (LLMs), a surge of AI tools has been offered to teachers and students. Beyond LLMs’ common uses as efficiency tools and 1:1 tutors, we contend that AI advancements provide opportunities to support robust student learning in other approaches, specifically in collaborative learning groups. In this symposium, we present the ways in which generative AI can be used to facilitate jigsaw work, promote discussion, identify confusions and conflicts, and create new knowledge with student groups. Interactive demonstration of the tools is built into the symposium so together as a group, we can learn more about how to use Gen AI to facilitate and promote group learning.

abstract: This symposium gathers the results from several different research projects conducted in maker education in Finland and Norway. Educational makerspaces, in connection to school premises, offer multiple possibilities for students to take part in world-making - quite concretely. The enthusiastic and participatory approach inherited from the maker-movement meets the more static frames of our formal education systems, shaking them up in a good way. When given open-ended design tasks related to real-world problems in the form of projects-based learning, students are encouraged to acknowledge their role in the preferred “futuring” of their own worlds, their personal beliefs and wishes, their home environment, their school or their local neighborhoods. Research results will be presented and discussed by educational researchers, who have studied how maker-centered practices can educate for personal growth, creativity, innovation, citizenship, equity and participatory democracy – all skills and abilities in the important work of world-making for a better future.

abstract: Simulation-based learning has become a cornerstone of healthcare education, fostering essential skills like communication, teamwork or decision-making in safe, controlled environments. However, participants’ reflection on simulations often rely on subjective recollections, limiting their effectiveness in promoting learning. This symposium explores how multimodal analytics and AI can enhance simulation-based education by automating teamwork analysis data, providing structured feedback, and supporting reflective practices. The papers examine real-time analytics for closed-loop communication in cardiac arrest simulations, multimodal data use to refine feedback in ICU nursing simulations, generative AI-powered chatbots facilitating nursing students' interpretation of multimodal learning analytics dashboards, and culturally sensitive, AI-based scenarios for Breaking Bad News in an Indian context. Collectively, these contributions highlight the transformative potential of using data and AI-enhanced solutions, emphasizing personalization, cultural sensitivity, and human-centered design, and invite dialogue on the pedagogical, technological and ethical implications of introducing data-based practices and AI-based tools in medical education.

abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools, driven by large language models (LLMs), are increasingly explored for their potential in educational contexts. However, significant concerns remain regarding their efficacy, cognitive impacts, and ethical implications. The Computer Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) community faces critical questions regarding the broader implications of this technology for the field. While GenAI offers advanced opportunities for collaborative learning through conversational interactions and other functions, research in this area is still in its early stages. This symposium presents five contributions that explore the opportunities, challenges, and initial findings of integrating GenAI into educational settings. The goal is to provide evidence-based recommendations for practice and identify key research directions and challenges for the future of CSCL in the context of GenAI.

abstract: This study explores the impact of collaborative discourse in STEAM teacher communities on interdisciplinary perspectives and professional agency. Using a mixed-methods approach, 69 teachers participated in discussions on the Knowledge Forum. Discourse data and quantitative analysis were collected through pre- and post-tests. The results indicated (1) collaborative discourse evolved from sharing to argumentative and innovative modes. (2) Knowledge-Building collaboration enhanced interdisciplinary perspectives, especially in integrated STEAM practices. (3) professional agency improved, particularly in positive interdependence.

abstract: We present the Experiential Game Design Model as a student-centered approach to fostering collaborative learning through game design. Rooted in experiential learning theory and Vygotsky’s emphasis on social interaction, this model addresses common challenges, such as conflict and disengagement, by focusing on four core components: knowledge, identity, culture, and values. Students collaboratively plan, design, and revise games. Teachers guide students through iterative development and reflective practices. Emphasizing culturally responsive pedagogy and shared goal-setting, the model offers a framework where students can express unique perspectives and engage in meaningful and collaborative learning.

abstract: Epistemic emotions are vital in collaborative learning and knowledge building but are challenging to recognize and understand at the group-level. This study introduces EmoSense as an approach and novel prototype that leverages facial recognition and self-reported surveys to recognize students' epistemic emotions during knowledge building activities, demonstrating its feasibility in an authentic knowledge building environment. Through this study, EmoSense provided valuable insights into collaborative learning’s affective dimension, informing better design of learning environments. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of epistemic emotions and the influence on knowledge building processes, while informing development of innovative approaches for advancement towards group-based emotions.

abstract: This study investigated paired students’ sequential actions and their relation to the productivity of collaborative problem solving (CPS). Logfile data from 166 Finnish sixth graders working in pairs to solve a CPS task in a computer-based assessment environment showed that continuous 2- and 3-action of chatting in sequences were likely to be key action sequences for productive CPS. However, continuous 6-action of chats and chats with other mouse clicking actions contributed to unproductive CPS.
