abstract: This study applies CMDA to analyze communication in a game-based CSCL setting. Examining two groups with differing outcomes, we explored participation, speech acts, and topic development. Findings show interaction density and balanced contributions impact performance, while communicative acts like “Inquire” and “Elaborate” shape collaboration. Topic coherence influences group effectiveness. Visualizations illustrate these dynamics. Despite limitations, CMDA provides insights into CSCL processes and informs adaptive support for collaborative learning.

citation: Xu, Q., Lin, Z., Zhou, X., Ge, Z., & Zhu, M. (2025). Process Features in the Initial Phases of Virtual Collaboration That Predict Ultimate Collaborative Problem-Solving Outcomes. abstract: Collaborative problem-solving (CPS) is crucial for virtual team performance, yet the specific behavioral factors influencing team success, especially in the early stages, are under-explored. This study examines which behavioral characteristics in the early phases predict team performance through two representative tasks, the Mondrian Geometric Fantasy task and the Three-Resistor Activity. The research reveals that the skill of real-time monitoring and evaluation is the most important predictor of team performance in the early stages of CPS, followed by exploring collaborative goals. The former provides continuous evaluation through timely feedback and correction, while the latter sets a directional framework for interaction, reducing cognitive load, thereby improving performance. This study offers insights into the behaviors of student teams in the early stages of CPS and their relationship with team performance, especially in virtual settings. These behavioral characteristics can be utilized to identify key assessment and intervention points for developing CPS skills.

abstract: This study examines the collaborative writing strategies and work modes employed by university students during collaborative writing tasks. 32 first-year master’s students in educational sciences completed a nine-week collaborative research paper in dyads without specific writing or collaboration guidance. Data were collected through shared Google Docs, logbooks, and semi-structured interviews. The findings indicate that students predominantly utilized horizontal-division writing involving the division of text sections to individual members, often initiated by group single-author writing (i.e., joint text planning). The asynchronous work mode was most frequently used, but students alternated these with face-to-face interactions, particularly near deadlines. These findings suggest that students balance independent and collaborative work, raising implications for designing interventions and exploring how collaboration impacts learning outcomes and text quality.

These points highlight key moments when collaborative activities such as coordination and negotiation are essential. Based on these identified points, a virtual reality (VR) simulation will be developed with prompts to promote interprofessional collaboration. The simulation will be tested for its effectiveness in promoting collaboration, improving procedural knowledge, and improving communication and decision making across disciplines.

We investigated students’ knowledge creation learning in makerspaces with a particular focus on; collaboration, communication, equal access to resources and opportunities among students of various backgrounds and culture. We found that Makerspaces as educational environments have a good potential to teach for equitable engagement.

abstract: This study conducted interviews using video recordings of the Teaching Assistant (TA) wearing a wearable camera as the stimulus for recall, and analyzed the TA's support process in small group discussions from the interview utterances of the TA. It answered the following the research questions: Does the presence or absence of Web applications affect TA intervention? It was found that using a Web application made it possible to diagnose students’ levels of understanding and provide cognitive support more efficiently.

abstract: This study explores differences in gaze behavior between higher- and lower-performing groups in a university-level CSCL setting. Sixty-eight engineering students completed a collaborative task, with performance judged by design artifacts. Using computer vision, gaze patterns were analyzed. Higher-performing groups focused more on their own screens, while lower-performing groups looked more at peers and off-task areas. Findings reveal distinct visual attention strategies and highlight the potential of multimodal analytics to examine interactions in tech-rich collaborative learning environments.

abstract: Progressive Design Method (PDM) is a method that can be used in higher education to engage students in project development. This case study investigates whether PDM fosters participatory and transformative agency in university students and examines any potential relationship between these two forms of agency. Participatory agency measured using degree centrality each of PDM. Furthermore, thematic analysis of student activity reflections used to assess transformative agency. Results indicated that student participatory agency increased during PDM activities. Additionally, students demonstrated transformative agency by identifying the strengths, weaknesses, and areas for improvement the PDM. A correlation between participatory and transformative agency also found. The implications of the findings for the further development of PDM are discussed.

abstract: The study explores how transactivity in different phases of regulation of learning unfolds in a six-week online collaboration and their association with the socio-emotional climate of the group. Video recordings of two case groups were coded and analyzed using qualitative content analysis and Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA). The findings indicated the role of quick consensus building in regulation of learning, suggesting associations between transactivity and regulation to be meaningful in constructing a group’s emotional climate.

abstract: In the context of computer-supported collaborative learning, primary school students' (N = 21) use of self-regulated learning (SRL) and socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) strategies was supported with group-level digital learning diaries during a fifteen-week-long STEAM learning module. The aim was to explore used SRL and SSRL strategies and their relation to motivation in terms of interest. This study provides detailed information about the regulation processes of primary school students during a collaborative STEAM module.

authors_list: Seet, C. H., Chai, C., Hung, G., Chang, C., & Hong, H.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study examines how 55 Taiwanese teachers understood and applied knowledge-building principles in their lesson design after a teacher training program. Using qualitative and quantitative methods, including theme-based open-coding and paired t-tests, the study found that the teachers' understanding of KBPs improved significantly, enabling them to effectively implement KB theory in their lesson design.

title: Skills and Dispositions for PFL: Promoting Data Literacy for Middle School Students in a Summer Camp
citation: Li, Y., Endert, A., Wise, C. F., Dobar, E. B., Koval, J., Grossman, S., McKlin, T., & Roberts, J. (2025). Skills and Dispositions for Pfl: Promoting Data Literacy for Middle School Students in a Summer Camp. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. authors_list: Li, Y., Endert, A., Wise, C. F., Dobar, E. B., Koval, J., Grossman, S., McKlin, T., & Roberts, J.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: We designed a two-week summer camp to support Preparation for Future Learning (PFL) in data literacy by fostering both skills and dispositions. Middle schoolers create data visualization stories to address community-related issues they identified. Analysis showed growth in data visualization skills, self-efficacy, and recognition of data visualization’s value. We observed frequent student decision-making, suggesting agency as a key factor. This work prompts future studies on activating agency support PFL for data literacy.

title: Behavioral Transition Patterns in Online Collaborative Problem-Solving: A Lag Sequential Analysis of High School Teams
citation: Xu, Q., Luo, C., Ge, Z., & Zhu, M. (2025). Behavioral Transition Patterns in Online Collaborative Problem-Solving: A Lag Sequential Analysis of High School Teams. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 583-584). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Xu, Q., Luo, C., Ge, Z., & Zhu, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Understanding behavioral patterns in collaborative problem-solving (CPS) is crucial for developing effective educational interventions. However, previous studies have not fully explored the most basic behavioral transition patterns. Here, we present a lag sequential analysis of behavioral transitions in online CPS tasks among high school students (229 teams). Using the PISA 2015 CPS framework, we identify 34 significant behavioral transitions, revealing four patterns. Our findings suggest effective CPS interventions should strengthen planning and monitoring behaviors while minimizing task-irrelevant interactions.

title: Visualized Course Design Analytics - a Case Study for Blended Learning
citation: Gedrimiene, E., Korpi, J., Silvola, A., & Muukkonen, H. (2025). Visualized Course Design Analytics - A Case Study for Blended Learning. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. authors_list: Gedrimiene, E., Korpi, J., Silvola, A., & Muukkonen, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This case study examines the use of learning design and analytics in higher education course development. The focus is on a course with pre-defined structure and two teachers separately developing and implementing the course in two consecutive years. The teacher created learning designs, automatically produced analytics visualizations and teacher reflections were analyzed. Preliminary results reflect how visualized learning design analytics function as tangible support for insights into teachers’ design thinking and can support learning design reflection. SWOT analysis reveals helpful as well as hindering factors for teachers’ practices.

title: Students’ Collaborative Roles and Perceived Learning During Making Processes as Part of a Programming and Robotics Tournament
citation: Laakso, N., Hannula, E., Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, P., Hakkarainen, K., & Korhonen, T. (2025). (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 587-589). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Laakso, N., Hannula, E., Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, P., Hakkarainen, K., & Korhonen, T.

abstract: This study examined the experiences of students participating in collaborative making processes as part of preparing for a national programming and robotics tournament in Finland. Data were collected in three tournaments (2021–2023) through student interviews (n=40) and a self-report survey (n=58). Preliminary results suggest that students adapted their roles during making processes. The collaborative roles were coder, fabricator, designer, performer, and team leader. Perceived learning outcomes were classified into technological, social, and thinking skills.

title: Raising Teachers’ Awareness to Embrace Diversity in Knowledge Building
citation: Han, H. W. (2025). Raising Teachers’ Awareness to Embrace Diversity in Knowledge Building. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 590-592). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Han, H. W.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Participating in Knowledge Building discourses for learners with visual impairments means that they can move from the current meritocratic and individual performance-based learning to ‘Currere,’ where they realize their existential meaning as members of society through others. This study compares the perspectives of special education teachers with those of general education teachers to promote inclusive Knowledge Building support through a mixed-methods case study, and analyzes the contradictions and tensions they currently face through Activity Theory.

title: Towards Playful Computational Empowerment - Teenagers Designing Their Learning Environment
citation: Tikkanen, R. & Iivari, N. (2025). Towards Playful Computational Empowerment - Teenagers Designing Their Learning Environment. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 593-595). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tikkanen, R. & Iivari, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores play and computational empowerment, focusing on how design activities support teenagers' computational skills. By integrating play into participatory design workshops, teenagers can ideate, create and test game environments in an age-appropriate and engaging manner. Findings highlight the role of directed and free play, as well as individual and social play. The paper advocates the use of playful computational methods in education to better prepare students for a technology-driven future.

title: Teachers' Experiences of Learning Analytics Support for Learning Design in Higher Education
citation: Takalo-Kastari, H., Gedrimiene, E., Kajamaa, A., Kulmala, P., & Muukkonen, H. (2025). Teachers' Experiences of Learning Analytics Support for Learning Design in Higher Education. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores the role of the Balanced Learning Design Planning tool in supporting higher education teachers' design practices. The tool and concept aim to enhance learning design by focusing on learning outcomes, student workload, and constructive alignment. Using design-based research principles, this study investigates teachers' experiences through stimulated recall interviews and abductive thematic analysis. Findings indicated that the tool could offer support in various aspects of design thinking.

title: Theorizing on the Intersection of Futures Thinking and Sociomaterial Approaches when Designing Learning Environments
citation: Turcotte, N., McCausland, J., McDonald, S. P., Asino, T. I., Rook, M. M., Tissenbaum, M., & Hollett, T. (2025). Theorizing on the Intersection of Futures Thinking and Sociomaterial Approaches When Designing Learning Environments. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. authors_list: Turcotte, N., McCausland, J., McDonald, S. P., Asino, T. I., Rook, M. M., Tissenbaum, M., & Hollett, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: ISLS 2025 calls for Learning Sciences researchers to embrace utopias, agency, imagination, speculation, and futures thinking, as central aspects of education and educational research. This poster investigates how designers of new learning environments can incorporate these central aspects by focusing on five design principles: broadening voices in defining and embracing utopias, analyzing the sociomaterial actors, implementing practices to imagine futures such as improv, using new methods to reflect with others on the utility of environments, and acknowledging and considering marginalized voices in framing “that-which-ought-to-be” (Nørgård & Holflod, 2024, p. 2, emphasis in original).

abstract: This poster examines students' evaluations of the analytics and visualization tool, Software KBAT, designed to facilitate reflective self-assessments within Knowledge Building communities supported by Knowledge Forum. Adopting a design-based research methodology, data were collected through a survey assessing students’ perceptions of the tool's value. The study involved 42 students from an educational research course at the University of Granada. This poster highlights students’ view on KBAT and identifies opportunities for improvement.

title: Generative AI in Norwegian Classrooms: Differences in Teaching About, With and Through GAI
citation: Tjønn, H., Ludvigsen, S., & Mørch, A. I. (2025). Generative Ai in Norwegian Classrooms: Differences in Teaching About, With and Through Gai. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 605-607). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tjønn, H., Ludvigsen, S., & Mørch, A. I.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The use of chatbots in classroom teaching presents both challenges and opportunities for students' learning. From a CSCL standpoint, our analysis reveals that many students encounter difficulties in their communication with adapted chatbots, even though the chatbots were designed to support students' work with domain knowledge, in their learning activities. This indicates that teachers need to devote more time and effort to support students' learning processes by balancing the tensions between learning about generative AI and learning with generative AI in various domains. Teachers must carefully consider, select, and remind students about specific lesson aims and relevant content.

title: Taking the Lead: Exploring Collaborative Initiative in CSCL Contexts
citation: Rajarathinam, R. J. & Kang, J. (2025). Taking the Lead: Exploring Collaborative Initiative in CSCL Contexts. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 608-610). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rajarathinam, R. J. & Kang, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
tpack_tk_labels: Immersive VR / AR; Simulations & Scientific Modeling
abstract: In computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) environments, students' ability to engage proactively is crucial for effective collaboration and problem-solving. This study reexamines the concept of initiative in CSCL contexts, redefining it as collaborative initiative, which refers to students' spontaneous and voluntary contributions that are intended to enhance peer interaction and learning experiences. Building upon existing frameworks, we propose a refined model that emphasizes unprompted, proactive student actions categorized into task-related and dialogue-based initiatives. Using the HoloOrbits simulation, designed for augmented reality headsets to support student learning about planetary motion, we analyzed interactions among 12 university students. Our findings delineate six sub-facets of collaborative initiative, highlighting how students propose strategies, share divergent ideas, and invite peer contributions without external prompting. The study highlights the potential of fostering collaborative initiative to advance collaborative problem-solving and enhance the effectiveness of CSCL environments.

title: Crafting Computational Thinking with Rope Weaving
citation: Huang, J., Han, S., Speer, S., Ojeda-Ramirez, S., Rosé, C. P., Martinez, M. O., & Peppler, K. (2025). Crafting Computational Thinking With Rope Weaving. abstract: This study explores how integrating computational thinking (CT) with weaving can make CT more accessible and engaging. Nineteen undergraduates participated in a rope weaving activity to recreate patterns, test structures, and connect math to tangible materials. Analysis of reflections and video data revealed students applying CT practices like pattern recognition and algorithmic thinking. Findings highlight the value of tactile, craft-based activities in supporting CT learning and bridging abstract concepts with real-world, embodied experiences.

title: Curriculum Routines and a Community Builder AI Agent: Synergy to Mediate the Convergent Tendencies of AI
citation: Bush, J. B., Biddy, Q., Chang, M. A., Grab, G. B., Breideband, T., Sumner, T., Penuel, W. R., Weatherley, J., Singh, T., D’Mello, S., & Chang, M. A. (2025). Curriculum Routines and a Community Builder Ai Agent: Synergy to Mediate the Convergent Tendencies of Ai. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 614-616). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bush, J. B., Biddy, Q., Chang, M. A., Grab, G. B., Breideband, T., Sumner, T., Penuel, W. R., Weatherley, J., Singh, T., & D’Mello, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: AI technologies, while powerful and the subject of much innovation, have inherent bias towards convergent thinking: reproducing and mimicking patterns already seen in its training data. Learning sciences and CSCL research focus on studying tools, including AI, in authentic spaces where diversity of thought and contributions are highly valued. Focusing on an AI agent designed for supporting socio-collaborative learning in classroom spaces, we explore how these design tensions can be mediated through boundary-spanning curriculum routines. This analysis provides a roadmap from theory to practice for AI powered tools in classroom spaces that aim to leverage diversity in collaborative learning while mitigating the harms of over-attending to convergent thinking.

title: A Multi-Agent System (MAS)-Based Tool to Support Novice Teachers in Knowledge Building Pedagogy
citation: Xin, H., Lan, L., Niu, Q., Hu, Z., & Zhang, Y. (2025). A Multi-Agent System (Mas)-Based Tool to Support Novice Teachers in Knowledge Building Pedagogy. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 617-618). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Xin, H., Lan, L., Niu, Q., Hu, Z., & Zhang, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study introduces a Multi-Agent System (MAS)-based tool to support novice teachers in Knowledge Building (KB) pedagogy. By addressing challenges in lesson planning and student-driven learning, the tool enhances teaching confidence and KB alignment. Empirical findings confirm its effectiveness while identifying areas for improvement, such as interface design and resource integration.

title: Appropriate Reliance in Human-AI Collaborative Problem-Solving: The Role of Critical Thinking
citation: Hou, C., Zhu, G., & Sudarshan, V. (2025). Appropriate Reliance in Human-Ai Collaborative Problem-Solving: The Role of Critical Thinking. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 619-621). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hou, C., Zhu, G., & Sudarshan, V.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Reliance behaviors describe the frequencies and ways that people use AI tools for tasks such as problem-solving. There is a rising concern that students are over-reliant on Generative AI so that their critical thinking are being compromised. The notion of strategy-graded reliance argues that reliance behaviors are affected by a cognitive process in which an individual evaluates AI’s performance against human performance. We use critical thinking to capture this cognitive process. By analyzing 808 survey responses, including students’ critical thinking disposition, critical thinking skills, and reliance behaviors during a collaborative problem-solving task among undergraduate students, we find that collaborative, reflective, and cautious use of Generative AI is positively related to critical thinking. Therefore, we further conclude that desirable reliance on human-AI collaborative problem-solving is characterized by collaborative, reflective, and cautious use of Generative AI.

title: Measuring the Effect of GenAI Chatbots in CSCL environments: A Study with PyramidApp
citation: Sánchez-Reina, J. R., Gutiérrez-Ferré, A., & Hernández-Leo, D. (2025). Measuring the Effect of GenAI Chatbots in CSCL Environments: A Study With PyramidApp. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. authors_list: Sánchez-Reina, J. R., Gutiérrez-Ferré, A., & Hernández-Leo, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The present study explored the impact of a Generative AI (GenAI) chatbot in the PyramidApp (CSCL) tool), using a within-subjects design. Results showed the chatbot improved student answer accuracy and positively influenced both individual and group interactions. Also suggest that GenAI chatbots are valued in the educational sphere by enhancing learning outcomes and collaboration in digital education environments.

title: Generative Failure: Learning Design in Programming with Generative AI
citation: Kondo, H., Tohyama, S., Iseri, S., & Ishii, M. (2025). Generative Failure: Learning Design in Programming With Generative Ai. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. authors_list: Kondo, H., Tohyama, S., Iseri, S., & Ishii, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study proposes the Generative Failure Method (GFM) to address challenges in applying Productive Failure to novice programming. Beginners often struggle with syntax errors, rarely compare diverse solutions, and lack tasks aligned with interests. Leveraging large language models (LLMs), GFM helps novices overcome initial barriers, adapt project goals, and incrementally cultivate open-ended exploration. Rather than imposing open-ended tasks, GFM expands problem contexts as learners progress. A pilot study found that LLM support enabled learners to produce functional applications, engage in iterative trial-and-error, and reframe “failure” as a constructive resource for learning.

title: Building Ladder: Leveraging Knowledge Building Principles to Foster Interaction Between Human and Generative AI
citation: Liao, S., Hong, H., Guo, C., & Chen, M. (2025). Building Ladder: Leveraging Knowledge Building Principles to Foster Interaction Between Human and Generative Ai. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 628-630). International Society of the Learning Sciences.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This DBR study (n=33) explored human-AI collaborative patterns and how teacher-GAI collaboration can be optimized for knowledge building in STEAM teaching designs. The results indicated (1) four categories of human-AI collaboration: Operator-Supplier, Apprentice-Mentor, Ally-Ally and Agent-Producer. (2) Constructive use of GAI with community-based principle facilitated teachers’ knowledge building on prompting strategies and intention, making collaboration between teachers a conducive design principle to prove more productive interaction between teachers and GAI in the teaching design. (3) Implications for human-AI interactions are discussed.

title: Shared Conceptual Ground in CSCL: Evidence from a Global Survey
citation: Simon, S., Borchers, C., Ataş, A. H., Tajik, E., Çelik, B., Čarapina, M., Liu, Y., Shahrokhian, B., Sankaranarayanan, S., Balzan, F., Molinari, G., Jagušt, T., & Liang, L. (2025). Shared Conceptual Ground in CSCL: Evidence From a Global Survey. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. authors_list: Simon, S., Borchers, C., Ataş, A. H., Tajik, E., Çelik, B., Čarapina, M., Liu, Y., Shahrokhian, B., Sankaranarayanan, S., Balzan, F., Molinari, G., Jagušt, T., & Liang, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The maturity of scientific communities can be measured by their degree of alignment on a common conceptual vision to guide research efforts. Recently, scholars in the CSCL community have called for increased efforts to establish shared theoretical frameworks to accelerate progress in the field of CSCL. We investigate if the CSCL community aligns with key concepts, such as CSCL and collaborative learning. We conducted a survey with a sample of 50 CSCL scholars across 18 countries, prompting them to respond to open-ended questions related to key concepts in the field and future directions for the community. Findings revealed that while broad agreement exists on the importance of collaborative processes, interpretations of these key concepts diverge substantially, highlighting conceptual fragmentation. This study offers insights into the current state of a CSCL paradigm by identifying the extent of conceptual alignment among its members.

title: Traced Dialogic Assessment in Teacher Education
citation: Hontvedt, M., Steier, R., Beal, C., Solem, M. S., & Oddvik, M. (2025). Traced Dialogic Assessment in Teacher Education. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. authors_list: Hontvedt, M., Steier, R., Beal, C., Solem, M. S., & Oddvik, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This poster introduces traced dialogic assessment, a computer-supported summative assessment format. Combining oral assessment with digital tracing, the approach uses AI-driven video transcription to capture, visualize, and aid assessors and students in analyzing oral exam interactions. Grounded in design-based research, we explore how theoretical insights from CSCL can inform the assessment design. This work addresses challenges in assessing talk-based interaction and in balancing relational dynamics with objective assessment criteria.

title: Understanding the Impact of Physical, Online, and Hybrid Modalities on Self and Co-Regulation during Collaborative Problem Solving
citation: Kaliisa, R., Damşa, C., Misiejuk, K., & Eagan, B. (2025). Understanding the Impact of Physical, Online, and Hybrid Modalities on Self and Co-Regulation During Collaborative Problem Solving. International Society of the Learning Sciences.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)
abstract: Despite substantial research on self-regulated learning (SRL) and co-regulated learning, the interplay of these behaviors across different modes of presence is understudied. Using data from six groups with meetings across three modalities (physical, online, and hybrid), we used Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) to model regulation behaviors and how they vary based on modalities. Preliminary findings reveal significant differences in self and co-regulation patterns across the modalities, emphasizing the need for modality-specific support strategies and tools in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) environments to address the unique challenges of each modality.

title: Improving “Classi in rete” Model through Teachers’ Reflections: A Design Based Research Case Analysis
citation: Cacciamani, S., Mangione, G. R., & Pieri, M. (2025). Improving “Classi in Rete” Model Through Teachers’ Reflections: A Design Based Research Case Analysis. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cacciamani, S., Mangione, G. R. J., & Pieri, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: “Classi in rete” is an innovative organizational model designed to overcome the social and cultural isolation of small schools. By using a Design-Based Research methodological approach, the study aims to identify the strengths, critical points and proposals for improvement related to the first iteration of this model and to define the changes to be introduced for its second iteration. The reflections of 20 teachers produced at the end of the three periods of activity in an online environment in the first iteration of the model has been analyzed through a coding scheme created with reference to the Conjecture Mapping technique and applied by two independents . The results of this analysis allowed us to identify the changes in the “Classi in rete” model to be introduced for the second iteration. Implications for the model refinement are discussed.

title: On Black Sheep and Harmonic Groups: A Case Study about Group Rules and Social Norms During Collaborative Learning
citation: Eberle, J., Strauß, S., & Zumbach, J. (2025). On Black Sheep and Harmonic Groups: A Case Study About Group Rules and Social Norms During Collaborative Learning. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 640-642). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Eberle, J., Strauß, S., & Zumbach, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Long-term collaborative learning is often used in higher education, but its potential for enhancing students' collaboration skills is rarely fully realized. In this qualitative study, we investigated groups in a multi-week project-based learning course that were prompted to create group rules and reflect weekly on their collaboration process. The analysis of their data reveals that the groups devised rules addressing relevant aspects of collaborative learning, but these rules did not prevent problematic interaction patterns. A detailed analysis of three cases reveals the struggles of two groups, and the success of the third group. Addressing violations of group rules is very challenging when members perceive these violations as personal failures rather than as issues stemming from inefficient collaboration structures

abstract: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) focuses on designing tools and strategies to enhance collaborative learning. However, design knowledge within CSCL is often embedded in empirical studies without explicit emphasis, limiting its systematic documentation and dissemination. We analyzed literature from the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (ijCSCL) and identified five design patterns for online collaborative learning in higher education, highlighting components such as learning outcomes, task structures, technology affordances, and collaborative processes. This work seeks to elevate design knowledge in CSCL, encouraging the community to refine and share effective designs.

Preparing AI-literate students requires teachers to have some AI background, which is often a challenge to teachers. This work-in-progress study explores using LLMs to provide teachers with reports on how AI literacy is addressed in existing materials to inform their AI literacy integration. Our findings aim to offer interdisciplinary solutions to technology design that supports teachers’ AI literacy for achieving AI literacy integration in K-12.

This model enhances epistemic agency providing personalized learning paths, with content curation by authoritative domain experts, and real-time interactive learning with analytics incorporated to optimize collective learning experiences over time.

This review (2019–2024) explores how AI can enhance equity and access while addressing ethical challenges like bias and the digital divide.

abstract: This study presents how novice teachers approach knowledge building (KB) principles and how they perceived their first KB teaching in the classroom, and a CSCL environment called Knowledge Forum (KF) to facilitate collaborative learning. Four novice teachers in northern Taiwan were recruited to share how they perceived and reflected through in-depth interviews. Qualitative analysis showed novice teachers begin to develop KB strategies to value collaborative learning in KB principles and identify ideas evaluation in KF environments.

abstract: The study explores adolescent identity development across psychological, social, and environmental factors in the USA, Ghana, and Kenya. It analyzes pre-assessment data from a virtual STEM program, focusing on how adolescents navigate self-understanding, resilience, and emotional growth (psychological factors), peer relationships and leadership (social factors), and the role of school and STEM exposure (environmental factors). The findings reveal both universal and culturally specific influences, showing that while the developmental processes are similar, each region's unique context shapes how identity is formed.

abstract: This study investigates the influence of adolescent social media interactions on academic self-identity in China. It explores the relationship between peer relationships, online social capital, and academic self-identity, considering demographic factors. Through retrospective analysis and questionnaires, significant correlations were found between peer relationships and academic self-identity, and between online social capital and peer relationships. Peer relationships mediate the impact of online social capital on academic self-identity, with variations by gender, major, and region. The study contributes to understanding the role of virtual peer relationships in academic identity formation within an East Asian context.

abstract: Collaboration is a multidimensional process. Our case study explores ways to visualize these multiple dimensions within a collaborating group, incorporating both verbal and nonverbal interactions while considering the individual and group, as well as temporality. We discuss the affordances and limitations of these visualizations on the insights they provide.

abstract: Generative AI tools like ChatGPT have shown great potential in enhancing the effectiveness of L2 writing instruction. We compared the feedback generated by ChatGPT and teachers regarding feedback quantity and features. Key findings include: ChatGPT produced more negative feedback than teachers and more mitigating praises, general suggestions and specific solutions concerning both content and form. Teachers feedback delivered more explanations on the essay content. The findings suggested the positive impact of AI in generating feedback on student writing and promoting students’ writing ability.

We present education students’ reflections on their learning experience after a collaborative activity discussing with three AI characters representing different perspectives to climate change. Based on our findings, we present some redesign directions for integrating the activity into a multidisciplinary teacher education course.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Higher education is experiencing an increase in the use of Active Learning Classrooms (ALCs), which present educators with the challenge of utilizing the spatial and technological resources of these spaces effectively to foster dynamic, student-centered learning. Traditional tools often fail to provide practical and flexible strategies to optimize the use of ALC spaces. To fill this gap, this paper presents the Intelligent Design Environment for Active Learning (IDEAL) project, an AI-assisted design environment leveraging two architectural visualization approaches. IDEAL enables educators to rethink and redesign curriculum tailored for ALCs by managing hands-on spatial understanding through physical models or interactive scenario planning using a 3D virtual environment. The project not only inspires innovative curriculum design but also deepens educators’ engagement with ALC resources, fostering collaborative communities for future curriculum development.

abstract: This study analyzed system logs and written reflections from 111 secondary school students engaged in collaborative Virtual Reality (VR) content creation. Twenty-six student groups of 4–5 members were classified into 13 low-performing and 13 high-performing groups based on their final VR artifacts scores. Results showed that high-performing groups exhibited superior collaboration quality and more proactive problem-solving approaches, than low-performing groups.

abstract: “Equal” participation has been considered appropriate in transactive discourse, rather than imbalanced participation. This study investigates the interrelation between the leadership of transactivity and the equality of participation. Eight groups of three undergraduates participated in 45-minute collaborative problem-solving. Results suggested that not only equal participation but also a collaborative division of labor was crucial for collective and rotating leadership of transactivity. In contrast, cooperative division of labor was interrelated with dominant and fixed leadership of transactivity.

The approach encourages the creation of new phrases and sentences as design products in design and belief modes. The strength of this approach lies in its promotion of higher-order thinking about meaningful language-content patterns and connections, emphasizing the role of language as a dynamic driver of thought and knowledge advancement.

This study explores how generative AI (GenAI) can enhance this process via interactive and co-constructive collaboration. A hybrid teacher-GenAI co-design model was developed and tested on an online platform. Results indicate high user satisfaction and improved lesson planning competency. Teachers with stronger AI skills reported greater psychological need fulfillment, though this did not extend to co-design engagement or perceived competency.

abstract: This study examines the impact of support provided by generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on the quality of pre-service teachers’ instructional design (ID) outcomes – lesson blueprints. An experiment was conducted with one control and two experimental conditions: 1) producing ID outcomes with a generic GenAI bot (ChatGPT), and 2) producing ID outcomes with a Co-instructional designer bot customized with a single ID model (Systems approach). Participants included 78 pre-service teachers from diverse fields such as behavioral sciences, physics, and architecture. ID outcomes were blindly analyzed by experts in ID and evaluated using a pairwise comparison technique, where two ID outcomes are holistically compared to determine which one is better. The findings reveal a significant improvement in the Co-instructional designer condition compared to the control, suggesting that a GenAI bot can support pre-service teachers in ID when customized with an ID theory.

This study contributes to the research area of computer-supported collaborative learning and gives practical information about human-AI-human interaction possibilities in higher education contexts.

It highlights a paradigm shift away from human-centric approaches in learning design toward frameworks that acknowledge the entangled agency of both human and non-human actors—such as conversational agents—with the aim of fostering authentic collaboration, characterized by shared objectives, processes, and outcomes for both actors involved.

citation: Schultze, L., Bürger, N., Koßmann, R., & Wecker, C. (2025). When Collaborative Viewing of Instructional Videos Fails. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. abstract: This study examines to what extent the collaborative viewing of instructional videos supported by a collaboration script affects the acquisition of grammar knowledge and collaborative and digitalization-related skills. A pretest-posttest control group design with viewing mode (collaborative vs. individual) as the independent variable was implemented. No statistically significant effects of collaborative viewing on learning outcomes were found. Several correlations of learning activities and learning outcomes contradicted expectations. The results emphasize the need for further research.

abstract: Underpinned by identity-based motivation, this study examines identity development among adolescents after one year of participation in a global, virtual, STEM-focused project-based learning community. Pre- and post-assessment interviews with 29 students from the US, Brazil, Ghana, Kenya, and Mexico reveal shifts in constructs such as encountering challenges, deficiency awareness, and collaborative openness. Visualizations using epistemic network analysis (ENA) highlight differences between students in the US and outside the US. Findings indicate that US students became more open to sharing their deficiencies with math and science, and both students in and outside of the US were able to address challenges in their experiences by demonstrating more consideration in interacting with others.

title: Capturing Collaborative Competency with GPT-4o and ENA
citation: Lee, Y., Kwon, C., Seoh, S., Gweon, G., Stamper, J., & Rosé, C. P. (2025). Capturing Collaborative Competency With Gpt-4o and Ena. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. authors_list: Lee, Y., Kwon, C., Seoh, S., Gweon, G., Stamper, J., & Rosé, C. P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Collaboration is a critical learning skill employed across many educational domains. Since moments of collaborative competencies frequently occur in student discourse, there has been a growing body of work in automatic collaborative process analysis. With recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs), it became feasible to automate the collaborative process analysis through simple prompting methods. In this study, we develop CoComTag, an LLM-powered approach using GPT-4o that captures students' collaborative competency using four prompting techniques. Our findings demonstrate that CoComTag shows substantial agreement with humans (kappa of 0.67). Such a result shows that LLM yields comparable performance with prior studies using only prompting strategies without additional fine-tuning. Next, using qualitative error analysis and epistemic network analysis (ENA), we examine how CoComTag differs from humans in detecting collaborative competency. Our analysis shows that ENA provides visual cues on where collaborative competencies co-occur, revealing the differences between LLM and human annotation patterns.

abstract: The paper proposes a collaborative problem solving (CPS) clustering approach using a set of CPS indicators derived from process and discourse data to capture students' CPS practices within a CSCL context. We utilized a dataset generated from 68 middle schoolers in 17 groups interacting with a game-based CSCL environment as the clustering model input. We identify four patterns of CPS engagement and examine whether the model effectively conveys information regarding students’ CPS engagement in relation to their learning performance. Lastly, we discuss the implications of the approach and its potential for further development.

title: "Memorize the Source!" — Does Focusing on Learning Partners Improve Source Memory Without Impairing Content Learning?
citation: Ülker, O. & Bodemer, D. (2025). "memorize the Source!" — Does Focusing on Learning Partners Improve Source Memory Without Impairing Content Learning?. In Oshima, J., Chen, B., Vogel, F., & Järvelä, J. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2025 (pp. 90-98). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ülker, O. & Bodemer, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Remembering which learning partner shared certain information (source memory) helps learners to identify whom to approach for more information (academic help-seeking). Research suggests that while explicit tasks to remember sources can improve source memory, they may also impair learning the content. Our experimental pseudo-collaborative study (112 participants) applied a 2×2 between-subjects design (with vs. without source-related and content-related tasks), testing beneficial or detrimental effects of tasks on source memory and learning. Participants received information from three learning partners with different knowledge levels (high vs. medium vs. low). Source memory and learning correlated positively but were not influenced overall by tasks. However, content-related tasks improved source memory for high-knowledge partners. Supplementary analyses of two real collaborating groups revealed that source-related tasks promote self-regulative strategies (taking notes who said what). Our complementary results indicate that learners might need tasks with more guidance targeting group-level processes to support source memory in collaborative learning.

subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Mathematics

abstract: Collaborative learning, a proven method for supporting differentiated learning, is often underutilized in schools, particularly when there are staffing challenges to facilitate and monitor group interactions. OKO is an intelligent platform for small-group collaborative learning in elementary and middle school classrooms, with an initial focus on math games and puzzles. It leverages an Artificial Intelligence-based agent to interact with small groups of students, facilitating social and collaborative activities. This paper introduces the OKO collaborative learning platform and examines how using OKO in small groups over a two-week period in classrooms affected student math learning, attitudes towards math, and collaboration skills. Despite a short implementation period, findings suggest that OKO shows promise in improving math learning and reducing math anxiety. The paper also discusses how teacher training can better support implementation of the program in classrooms.

abstract: In collaborative problem-solving (CPS), students work together to solve problems using their collective knowledge and social interactions to understand the problem and progress towards a solution. This study focuses on how students engage in CPS while working in pairs in a STEM+C (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics, and Computing) environment that involves open-ended computational modeling tasks. Specifically, we study how groups with different prior knowledge in physics and computing concepts differ in their information pooling and consensus building behaviors. In addition, we examine how these differences impact the development of their shared understanding and learning. Our study consisted of a high school kinematics curriculum with 1D and 2D modeling tasks. Using an exploratory approach, we performed in-depth case studies to analyze the behaviors of groups with different prior knowledge distributions across these tasks. We identify effective information pooling and consensus building behaviors in addition to difficulties students faced when developing a shared understanding of physics and computing concepts.

abstract: This study investigated effective methods for using conversational agents for learner-learner support in a collaborative explanation task using concept maps. Scripted facilitation methods that use conversational agents were compared with the proposed method that integrates the reciprocal teaching strategy. This method uses an ACT-R cognitive architecture-based virtual peer learner agent to identify, reason, and construct a concept map from dyads in real time. An experiment was conducted under two conditions: 1) a tutor as a mediating agent that prescribes metacognitive scripts, and 2) an adaptive virtual peer agent that prescribes concept maps. The results demonstrated that both methods improved the learning performance compared with the control condition. Notably, learners working with the peer learner agent made better use of procedural knowledge during tasks. This study suggests that a “horizontal” learning approach with the agent as a peer is as effective as the methods with facilitated instruction using scripts.

authors_list: Farrokhnia, M., Noroozi, O., Biemans, H., & Baggen, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Previous research has shown that hybrid brainstorming, which combines individual and group methods, generates more ideas than either approach alone. However, the quality of these ideas remains similar across different methods. This study, guided by the dual-pathway to creativity model, tested two computer-supported scaffolds – scripting and group awareness support – for enhancing idea quality in hybrid brainstorming. 94 higher education students, grouped into triads, were tasked with generating ideas in three conditions. The Control condition used standard hybrid brainstorming without extra support. In Experimental 1 condition, students received scripting support during individual brainstorming, and students in the Experimental 2 condition were provided with group awareness support during the group phase in addition. While the quantity of ideas was similar across all conditions, the Experimental 2 condition produced ideas of higher quality, and the Experimental 1 condition also showed improved idea quality in the individual phase compared to the Control condition.

title: Towards a Framework to Link Them All: A Provocation in the Ongoing Debate on Collaborative Learning
citation: Simon, S., Marfisi-Schottman, I., & George, S. (2024). Towards a Framework to Link Them All: A Provocation in the Ongoing Debate on Collaborative Learning. In Clarke-Midura, J., Kollar, I., Gu, X., & D'Angelo, C. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2024 (pp. 123-130). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Simon, S., Marfisi-Schottman, I., & George, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Common ground is a well-studied concept in the CSCL (Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning) community. Interestingly, while well-studied, its discovery did not seem to lead to common conceptual ground within the CSCL community. Since its beginnings 30 years ago, the community has produced a variety of frameworks, studies and theories around the concept of collaboration, collaborative learning and, in particular, collaborative learning tools. Missing common ground is a problem for analyzing collaboration itself and comparability across studies, which researchers such as Rummel, Wise and Schwarz highlight in a recent exchange on the subject. In this paper, we analyze existing frameworks and whether contradictions between different frameworks exist. We further propose an attempt to a joint definition and framework as a starting point and provocation for discussion in the community.

title: A Meta-Space for “Super Notes”: How Two Teachers Supported Cross-Classroom Collaboration for Knowledge Building
citation: Sun, Y. & Zhang, J. (2024). A Meta-Space for “Super Notes”: How Two Teachers Supported Cross-Classroom Collaboration for Knowledge Building. In Clarke-Midura, J., Kollar, I., Gu, X., & D'Angelo, C. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2024 (pp. 131-138). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sun, Y. & Zhang, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Existing research on teacher support for collaborative learning has focused on small groups in individual classrooms. The current study investigates how two teachers supported cross-classroom interaction between two Grade 5/6 classrooms. Students in the two classrooms studied human body systems for 10 weeks with the support of Knowledge Forum. While students in each classroom advanced their thinking in the discourse space of their home class, they had access to a shared meta-space for sharing knowledge advances across classrooms, presented in the format of “super notes.” Qualitative analyses of teacher interviews and classroom observations provided a detailed account of the teachers’ pedagogical approach to the meta-space and classroom support to guide students’ cross-classroom interaction.

title: Shall We Play a Game? Distributed Games with a Generative AI Player
citation: Matthews, J., Nguyen, H., & Swanson, H. (2024). Shall We Play a Game? Distributed Games with a Generative AI Player. In Clarke-Midura, J., Kollar, I., Gu, X., & D'Angelo, C. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2024 (pp. 139-146). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Matthews, J., Nguyen, H., & Swanson, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The prevalence of generative AI tools – especially large language models that enable human-like conversation – provides an opportunity to study how human learners interact with AI as collaborative ideators in the learning process. We expand the framework of distributed games (which initially focused on epistemic games of discovery as distributed processes) to investigate learner interaction with generative AI in design tasks. Through a comparative case study of two undergraduates using a generative AI tool in design tasks, we illustrate different ways in which learners orient themselves to the elements of the game (task, form, other players, etc.) and the corresponding complexity of the game played. We discuss implications for the design of learning environments that facilitate interaction with AI tools in distributed creative tasks.

title: Developing Participation Equity Criteria: A Fresh Perspective via Turn-Taking Simulation
citation: Hu, L. & Wu, J. (2024). Developing Participation Equity Criteria: A Fresh Perspective via Turn-Taking Simulation. In Clarke-Midura, J., Kollar, I., Gu, X., & D'Angelo, C. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2024 (pp. 147-154). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hu, L. & Wu, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Participation equity plays a crucial role in shaping students’ cognitive and social benefits derived from collaborative efforts. Nevertheless, a lack of quantitative benchmarks for assessing the fairness of group participation persists. This study addresses this gap by employing a simulation-based approach to establish measurable criteria, leveraging empirical data to estimate model parameters. Our research introduces evaluation metrics for gauging participation and opportunity inequalities across varying numbers of turns, derived from the simulation outcomes. The practical significance of our findings lies in providing specific guidelines for evaluating participation equity in collaborative learning and problem-solving contexts. Additionally, from a theoretical standpoint, our study highlights the sensitivity of evaluating participation equity to the number of turns and offers insights into the dynamics of human dialogue. We also discuss limitations and avenues for future research in this area.

title: A Knowledge Building-Modeling Approach to Scientific Inquiry
citation: Soliman, D. & Feng, X. (2024). A Knowledge Building-Modeling Approach to Scientific Inquiry. In Clarke-Midura, J., Kollar, I., Gu, X., & D'Angelo, C. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2024 (pp. 155-162). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Soliman, D. & Feng, X.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study explores how a Knowledge Building - Modeling approach (KBM) was used to enhance grade 5 students’ understanding of dynamic mechanisms related to natural hazards. Forty-three students collectively engaged in an iterative KBM process involving idea-driven discourse on Knowledge Forum. Additionally, students created models in response to emerging theories and questions. Iterations were driven by students’ discourse and supported by learning analytics to advance idea and model building. Results show that students engaged in deeper discourse practices over time. Their models increasingly reflected complex causal reasoning and their knowledge of natural hazards improved. Analysis revealed that knowledge building discourse was a good predictor of both scientific understanding and modeling practices. We discuss the work that informed our intervention and highlight the KBM approach. Implications of designing knowledge building environments enriched with modeling to promote complex reasoning and modeling practices are discussed.

title: Exploring Teacher Orchestration Load in Scripted CSCL: The Role of Heart Rate Variability
citation: Hakami, L., Sayis, B., Amarasinghe, I., & Hernández-Leo, D. (2024). Exploring Teacher Orchestration Load in Scripted CSCL: The Role of Heart Rate Variability. In Clarke-Midura, J., Kollar, I., Gu, X., & D'Angelo, C. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2024 (pp. 163-170). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hakami, L., Sayis, B., Amarasinghe, I., & Hernández-Leo, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA); Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL); Classroom Orchestration
abstract: Integrating Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) tools in the educational environment is considered to enhance collaborative learning experiences. However, previous research findings have indicated that classroom orchestration adds to the workload of the teachers, therefore potentially introducing their perceived stress levels. This study investigates the extent to which teachers experience stress when orchestrating CSCL activities using multimodal data. Physiological data such as heart rate variability (HRV) was used in this study in addition to subjective data such as self-reported questionnaires and observation notes. A combination of multimodal data and single-subject research design (SSRD) allowed us to investigate the influence of the CSCL orchestration tool on teachers' stress levels. Based on the collected multimodal data, the findings show that the studied tool does not increase the stress levels of the teachers.

title: Enhancing Argumentative Essay Structure and Quality through a Collaborative Argumentation Environment in University EFL Students
citation: Wang, L., Wu, Y., & Cheng, T. (2024). Enhancing Argumentative Essay Structure and Quality through a Collaborative Argumentation Environment in University EFL Students. In Clarke-Midura, J., Kollar, I., Gu, X., & D'Angelo, C. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2024 (pp. 173-176). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wang, L., Wu, Y., & Cheng, T.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Previous research has highlighted significant challenges faced by university-level English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students in their argumentative essay writing. In this study, a collaborative argumentation environment was adopted where students could collectively generate and refine writing ideas before composing their argumentative essays. A quasi-experimental study was conducted to examine the impact of this environment on the EFL university students’ argumentative writing performance in terms of structure and quality. Two groups of students participated: A control group (n=30) exposed to a face-to-face discussion environment, and an experimental group (n=25) using the collaborative argumentation environment. Both groups underwent pre- and post-study evaluations of their argumentative essays. The results showed that there were no statistically significant differences between the two learning environments when it came to improving argumentative essay structure and claims for both groups. In terms of grounds and rebuttals, the experimental group outperformed the control group (P< 0.05).

title: Using Pose Data to Explore Changes in Students’ Self-Efficacy and Community Belonging in Makerspaces
citation: Schneider, B. & Chng, E. (2024). Using Pose Data to Explore Changes in Students’ Self-Efficacy and Community Belonging in Makerspaces. In Clarke-Midura, J., Kollar, I., Gu, X., & D'Angelo, C. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2024 (pp. 177-180). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Schneider, B. & Chng, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA); Constructionism & Maker-Centered Learning
abstract: Constructionist learning (Papert, 1980) can be a powerful way of fostering students’ self-efficacy and their connection to a community. Makerspaces and digital fabrication labs epitomize this philosophy, by encouraging community-based, project-oriented learning through the creation of both physical and digital products. Because makerspaces are open-ended, messy learning environments, understanding why some students have transformative experiences, while others do not, remains a challenge. In this paper, we explore how multimodal learning analytics can provide a complementary lens to quantify and visualize students’ learning trajectories. We collected students’ 3D poses from video data collected during a semester-long course and used unsupervised machine learning approaches to identify behavioral states. We present preliminary correlational results with students’ reports of self-efficacy and community belonging. We discuss these findings and how they could be used to support constructionist learning and teaching.

title: Toward an Assessment of Students’ (Social) Computational Literacy
citation: Foster, M., Dunham, M., Cammarota, C., Verostek, M., Zwickl, B., & Wong, T. E. (2024). Toward an Assessment of Students’ (Social) Computational Literacy. In Clarke-Midura, J., Kollar, I., Gu, X., & D'Angelo, C. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2024 (pp. 181-184). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Foster, M., Dunham, M., Cammarota, C., Verostek, M., Zwickl, B., & Wong, T. E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Computational tools, particularly computer programming and statistical software, have enabled new forms of computational course assignments using tools such as Jupyter Notebooks and Minitab. With computation becoming ubiquitous within STEM, and society writ large, computational literacy – or the skills, knowledge, and beliefs students need in order to use computation – is an important construct to assess. Indeed, there is a need for an assessment rubric that can be used across multiple computational tools to better understand students’ performances with these tools. In this study, we focused on the development of an assessment rubric for students’ social computational literacy. Building off Odden et al.’s (2019) framework, we analyzed three students’ artifacts and interviews for social practices, knowledge, and beliefs. We present the beginning phase of an assessment rubric identifying social computational literacy through students’ social knowledge and beliefs.

title: Examine Student Resource Uses in a Game-based CSCL
citation: Zou, X., Hong, D., Chen, F., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Glazewski, K., Wang, T., Mott, B., & Lester, J. (2024). Examine Student Resource Uses in a Game-based CSCL. In Clarke-Midura, J., Kollar, I., Gu, X., & D'Angelo, C. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning - CSCL 2024 (pp. 185-188). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zou, X., Hong, D., Chen, F., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Glazewski, K., Wang, T., Mott, B., & Lester, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
