authors_list: Clark, H. F.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: The Connective and Productive Disciplinary Engagement framework provides design and analysis tools to explore the affordances of foregrounding power dynamics as students learn about climate change. In this study of Black and Latinx high school chemistry students, I focus on the principle of resources to show how youths’ critical awareness of social issues is a sensemaking resource for learning about climate change in their community. Through analysis of interactions, I show how the teacher routinely invited students to use their personal, out-of-school experiences in classroom activities and how students responded by drawing on their critical awareness of racial, socioeconomic, and local inequities to explain and model climate change’s causes and solutions. These data contribute to uplifting the generative sensemaking resources and practices of marginalized youth. I suggest these youths’ critical awareness be foregrounded in science education to support critical and equitable learning opportunities.

title: Making Listening Visible: An Exploratory Case of Mathematics Teacher Listening
citation:

authors_list: Metts, E. & Shapiro, B. R.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Situative studies of teaching have long examined classroom discourse to characterize pedagogy and student learning as an interactional accomplishment between teachers, students, and the institutional settings in which they work. Despite this focus, less work has explored teachers’ listening practices and how these practices are enacted spatially across classroom lessons as a component of responsive pedagogies. In this paper, we present an exploratory case of one mathematics teacher’s listening practice, drawing from a multi-year research-practice partnership in a large urban school district in the United States studying teacher learning around collaborative groupwork. Our analysis and findings integrate qualitative and spatial visualization methods to offer an initial framework to characterize teachers’ listening across spatial, embodied, and mobile dimensions. We also offer methodological insights about how to employ different qualitative, visual, and spatial methods to characterize teacher listening.

title: Embodied and Digital Network Visualization of Data Design for Elementary Students

abstract: This paper explores how transitioning from embodied to digital representations of network-data supports elementary students in understanding and interpreting network visualizations. We analyzed students’ post-interviews and classroom videos to understand their perceptions of the embodied activity design and how moving between representations enhances their understanding. We used thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2012) to generate four themes from students’ interviews on the use of embodied and digital representations. We used interaction analysis (Jordan & Henderson, 1995) to reveal nuances of the instructional sequence.

title: Preparing Graduate Students to Enact Equity-Oriented Pedagogies for Science Outreach Programs
citation: Light, E., Suárez, E., & Adler, L. (2024). Preparing Graduate Students to Enact Equity-Oriented Pedagogies for Science Outreach Programs. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Informal Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math (STEM) outreach programs have been promoted as a mechanism to redress under-representation of minoritized students in STEM fields. However, few studies have investigated how to support program leaders and implementers, who are often graduate students, to teach science for equity and justice. In this design-based research study, we explore how professional development (PD), grounded in situated teacher learning theories, facilitated life science graduate students’ development of a multilevel, equity-oriented pedagogy for a science outreach program with minoritized youth. Through qualitatively analyzing PD video recordings, interviews, and artifacts for evidence of graduate students’ attention to micro, meso, and macro levels of equitable science education, we found that situated PD challenged their baseline conceptions of equity work and aligned their multilevel pedagogical praxis. Our study contributes to scholarship on how to support informal science educators’ learning towards equity-oriented pedagogies.

title: “I’m one of the Kids who is Perceived as Smart”: Exploring Student Experiences in a Fifth-Grade Science Classroom
citation: Stoler, A. (2024). “I’m one of the Kids who is Perceived as Smart”: Exploring Student Experiences in a Fifth-Grade Science Classroom. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. authors_list: Stoler, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study seeks to understand children’s experiences in a fifth-grade science classroom designed to incorporate the principles of collective activity, heterogeneity, and epistemic agency. Using a semi-structured interview approach, children were asked to describe their experiences within their class community. The findings reveal that the inequitable distribution of status in the classroom affected students’ engagement with science practice as well as the risks they perceived in participating in collective learning. This study provides student perspectives on what it means to engage in the practices of science and has implications for how educators and researchers attend to student experience when designing and analyzing learning environments.

title: “There Will Always be a Yes and No Side”: Facilitating Ethical Sensemaking Around Technology with Teens
citation: Landesman, R., Salac, J., Lim, J. O., & Ko, A. J.(2024). “There Will Always be a Yes and No Side”: Facilitating Ethical Sensemaking Around Technology with Teens. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Landesman, R., Salac, J., Lim, J. O., & Ko, A. J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: As awareness of computing’s impact on teens’ lives grows, efforts to educate about the ethical complexities of technology are increasing. We present a pedagogical intervention that blends techniques from Philosophy for Children, which teaches reasoning and argumentative skills, with Youth as Philosophers of Technology, which foregrounds decoding technology’s relationship with power through moral, and humanistic inquiry. We evaluated this intervention in a summer elective class with 12 students aged 14-18 in the US. Our preliminary analyses identified: (1) launchpads for ethical sensemaking, instances where students leveraged their lived experiences, community discussion, and ethical scaffolding to begin reasoning about moral dilemmas, and (2) expressions of ethical sensemaking, signals within students’ reasoning processes that indicated critical sensemaking was taking place. We hope to catalyze discussions for researchers on characterizations and trajectories of ethical sensemaking around technology, as well as practitioners on implementations of these concepts in their classrooms.

title: Evaluating Learning Progression-Based Mathematics Rubrics for Validity and Reliability
citation: Graf, E. A., Lizano, C. L., Agyapong, F., & van Rijn, P. W. (2024). Evaluating Learning Progression-Based Mathematics Rubrics for Validity and Reliability. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Graf, E. A., Lizano, C. L., Agyapong, F., & Rijn, P. W. V.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: We describe a validity and reliability examination of learning progression-based mathematics rubrics. Although rubric agreements were generally high, this does not guarantee a valid rubric. Nevertheless, lower agreements are indicative of possible validity and reliability issues, and we trace through a rubric with relatively lower agreement. We concluded that the rubric should provide more example responses. While agreements are useful indicators it is only through the process of reflection and discussion that validity issues with rubrics are uncovered.

title: From Abstract to Tangible: Leveraging Virtual Reality and GeoGebra for Playful Math Education
citation: Daughrity, L. A., Walkington, C., Sherard, M., Pande, P., Beauchamp, T., & Cuevas, A. (2024). From Abstract to Tangible: Leveraging Virtual Reality and GeoGebra for Playful Math Education. abstract: This study investigates the use of GeoGebra, a Dynamic Geometry Software for math learning in Virtual Reality using Head-Mounted Displays. Investigators provided a rich environment for learner engagement through a novel application of these tools, including hand manipulation of mathematical objects within VR and play-based learning strategies. This paper focuses on distinguishing between mathematical and non-mathematical play in this VR environment and understanding the role each takes in the learning process. Key findings highlight how mathematical play in an immersive VR environment using DGS allows mathematical misconceptions to surface, allows students to explore mathematical ideas, and allows for new kinds of opportunities to build off of play experiences.

title: Characterization of Students’ Learning and Reasoning about Mental Folding in a Spatial Educational Game
citation: Zeng, J., Zhang, Y., & Shang, J. (2024). Characterization of Students’ Learning and Reasoning about Mental Folding in a Spatial Educational Game. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zeng, J., Zhang, Y., & Shang, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explores the characteristics of elementary school students’ learning and reasoning patterns of mental folding training in a spatial educational game, where students imagine folding a cube net and finding its opposing sides. A total of 402 fourth graders used the educational game for three weeks, with one lesson per week. Behavioral log data and interview data were collected. The results show that students developed the exclusion strategy, identifying easier pairs of opposing sides first and leaving the harder ones for last. They also employed a sequential strategy when the three pairs of sides had similar difficulty levels.

title: STEM Curricular Adaptations as Ideological Stances
citation: Pierson, A. (2024). STEM Curricular Adaptations as Ideological Stances. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1135-1138). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Pierson, A.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: As Edelson et al. (2021) explain, “well-designed instructional materials can support shifts in teacher and student practices” (p. 782). Yet, these resources are not one-size-fits-all—teachers adapt instructional materials for use in their classrooms (Taylor, 2013). The ways that teachers modify curricula likely depend on ideologies about students, interactions, and STEM. In this paper, I propose that teachers’ curricular adaptations are a form of ideological stance-taking (Louie, 2020; Philip, 2011) through which teachers express commonsense understandings about STEM education. I analyze 31 5th grade teachers’ adaptations of a 4-week STEM robotics curriculum to illustrate the ways that ideological assumptions influence their implementation of a district-designed curriculum. These findings contribute to our understanding of the role of ideologies in teaching, which can help researchers, administrators, and teacher educators contextualize and support the use of generic instructional materials.

citation: Chan, J. Y., Chong, C. W., & Tsang, S. Y. (2024). Participatory Design of Early Math Learning: A Culturally Situated Playful Approach in Hong Kong. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. abstract: In this work, we aim to address Hong Kong caregivers’ needs in early childhood math learning by taking a participatory design approach. Through an online questionnaire, we found that parents supported math learning less frequently compared to language learning, with particularly low frequencies in promoting spatial reasoning through drawing maps and patterning through digital tools. Based on these findings, we conducted a workshop with caregivers to generate playful ideas that promote children’s math learning. The workshop resulted in two culturally situated activities: shopping and dessert making. This work has implications for future research in designing resources that meet stakeholders’ needs and collaborating with stakeholders to support early math learning grounded in the local context.

title: Negotiating Mathematics Teachers’ Professional Vision: Noticing and Naming Strengths in Video Records of Practice
citation: Hoffmann, A. & Munson, J. (2024). Negotiating Mathematics Teachers’ Professional Vision: Noticing and Naming Strengths in Video Records of Practice. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. authors_list: Hoffmann, A. & Munson, J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: While much of the literature on supporting teacher noticing in video records of practice advocates for a neutral, non-evaluative approach, recent research has pointed to the value of intentionally applying a strength-based lens, introducing a potential tension in the design of teacher professional development. Aiming to study the affordances of strengths-based noticing in mathematics teacher development, we asked what teachers identify as strengths in video records of mathematics teaching and to whom they attribute these strengths. Analysis of memos of small group discussions that included mathematics teachers naming strengths of videotaped lessons, identified five main themes: (1) Designing and engaging in the mathematical space, (2) Designing and engaging in the discursive and collaborative space, (3) Establishing norms, (4) Growth, and (5) Engagement. This study suggests affordances for designing protocols for teacher noticing of video records of practice with a particular attention to strengths.

title: Students Self-Regulate Learning in Hidden Ways
citation: Dario, N. & Lund, K. (2024). Students Self-Regulate Learning in Hidden Ways. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. authors_list: Dario, N. & Lund, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Visual Marginalia (VM) are visual, collateral, personal productions elaborated in secret during classroom lessons by students. Data collected in our third study on this topic give additional evidence to support the Visual Marginalia elaboration Model (VMeM), based on two orthogonal axes: intentionality and marginalization. VM are more or less deliberate and marginalized production, shifting along the axes. The model shows how VMs are useful for students’ self-regulation and learning processes. Results reveal how they impact emotion, attention, motivation, memory, knowledge integration and reorganization. We exemplify a new phenomenon, named Dynamic Visual Marginalia, where one VM evolves into another, showing how self-regulation interacts temporally with local context.

abstract: This paper presents a study that explores students’ learning of electric circuits in physics through constructing computational models of complex systems using the Much.Matter.in.Motion (MMM) platform. The study employed a quasi-experimental, pretest-intervention-posttest-control comparison-group design with 33 eighth-grade students using MMM compared to 23 students who followed a traditional curriculum using textbooks. Both groups had six 1.5-hour sessions and answered identical pre- and posttest questionnaires. Log files while using MMM were collected. Results show: Learning by constructing models with MMM better supports science concepts and systems-level understanding than those who followed the traditional teaching approach; In more advanced construction activities, students tend to construct fewer models but make more comprehensive changes within each model compared to earlier activities. This is the first study that analyzed the development of model construction practices through MMM log files.

abstract: Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) frequently overlook learning design aspects and pedagogical theories in feedback provision. The current paper presents an exploratory study aiming to understand how different learning design elements (e.g., course difficulty and resource types) influence instructor-led feedback in MOOCs. We conducted six design sessions with MOOC instructors who used a feedback design tool, e-FeeD4Mi, to outline their course components, anticipate potential student problems and create feedback interventions with different timing and focus. The results showed the type of problem, the task difficulty and the instructor’s educational philosophy influence the timing of feedback.

subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: In this qualitative case study of policymaking in one school district, I found that leaders’ sensemaking about equity interacted with meanings about school mathematics, constraining policy solutions for equity in mathematics to access and achievement gaps while also rendering issues of identity peripheral to mathematics. Findings highlight a need for policy designers to attend to and address the learning demands posed by the subject.

title: Exploring Interest-Driven Data Science Through Participatory Design
citation: Israel-Fishelson, R., Moon, P. F., Pauw, D., & Weintrop, D. (2024). Exploring Interest-Driven Data Science Through Participatory Design. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science

abstract: Interest is a powerful catalyst for learning. Cultivating student interest is critical in data science education, where complex concepts and practical skills intersect. This paper explores the use of participatory design as a methodology for applying interest development theory to inform the design of an innovative data science curriculum for high school students. This study presents an analysis of participatory design activities using the Integrated Interest Development for Computing Education Framework (Michalis & Weintrop, 2022), highlighting various operationalizations of interest in data science contexts. By examining the multifaceted dimensions of interest, this work demonstrates how diverse activities provide a context for students to voice their interests. The paper’s findings contribute to the discourse on innovative educational approaches that engage students in data science by aligning with their interests.

title: Clusters of Math Anxiety and Performance in a Digital Learning Game: Differences in Hint Usage and Pause Time
citation: Egorova, A., Lee, J., Shaw, S. T., & Ottmar, E. (2024). Clusters of Math Anxiety and Performance in a Digital Learning Game: Differences in Hint Usage and Pause Time. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1163-1166). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Egorova, A., Lee, J., Shaw, S. T., & Ottmar, E.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Math learning research shows that math performance (MP) and math anxiety (MA) are correlated; however, some studies demonstrate less straightforward relationships between them. We explored how students could be clustered based on their MP and MA levels and whether students from different clusters differed in their behaviors in a digital math learning game. Our analysis revealed that students were divided into four clusters of similar sizes. While the profiles of the two groups showed similar patterns that were found in previous research – high MP low MA and low MP high MA, – the other two groups showed a different pattern. Specifically, about one-fourth of the participants showed high MP and high MA, and the rest of the students demonstrated low MP and low MA. Moreover, when solving math problems in a digital learning game, students from most groups differed in how often they asked for hints, and some clusters showed distinct patterns of pause time.

title: Escape Rooms in Nursing Education: How GPA, Collaborative Problem Solving, and Gameful Experience are related
citation: Kim, C., Gray, J., Brewer, V., Rahman, M. S., & Panday, S. (2024). Escape Rooms in Nursing Education: How GPA, Collaborative Problem Solving, and Gameful Experience are related. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kim, C., Gray, J., Brewer, V., Rahman, M. S., & Panday, S.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study investigates students’ experience in escape rooms in nursing education, focusing on the difference between the gameful experience and collaborative problem solving (CPS) score based on students’ GPA. 68 first-year nursing students participated in four different types of escape rooms in teams of two or three. Utilizing natural language processing data analysis, their conversations were processed to calculate CPS scores. The results revealed that the students generally found the escape rooms to be entertaining and educational. Students in the low GPA group found the experience more challenging and felt less guided, performing worse in rooms where they had to thoroughly collect available information and reflect on what they knew to reach a conclusion. The research addresses a critical gap in existing literature by employing NLP to delve into students’ conversations and provides practitioners with insights for designing a meaningful and engaging learning experience.

title: An Exploration of how Adults Guide Play in Ways that Foster Mutual Intellectual Respect: The Cases of a Kelp Forest and a Guess My Pattern

authors_list: Lee, C. & Jasien, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: As a non-binary pedagogical model, guided play involves a delicate dance between child-centered play and adult guidance. Using interaction analysis, we examine two contrasting cases of learning through guided-play activities. Our analysis expands the theory of guided play by articulating how adults can foster and maintain mutual intellectual respect during play across contexts, conceptualizing particular versions of guided play as joint inquiry with children.

title: Healing Metabolic Rifts Through Bridges of Conviviality: An Exploration of Urban Gardening Practices in Indian Cities
citation: Dutta, D. (2024). Healing Metabolic Rifts Through Bridges of Conviviality: An Exploration of Urban Gardening Practices in Indian Cities. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. authors_list: Dutta, D.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Diverse, interconnected socio-ecological issues beset societies with an increasing urgency to respond in meaningful, substantive ways. However, the abstract, temporally stretched, and geographically diffused and distributed nature of the issues presents a significant cognitive challenge, thereby diluting the moral imagination necessary to nurture transformative changes directed at collective wellbeing. Using the context of urban spaces in Indian cities, this study describes the ‘metabolic rift’ created in food systems through opaque, efficiency-driven systems of industrial agriculture and modern supply chains while exploring alternate practices that lay the ground for civic participation. Drawing on Illich’s idea of ‘tools for conviviality’, the paper describes a qualitative study with urban farming practitioners to argue that food gardens can scaffold affect-based, collaborative spaces based on social, emotional, and physical feedback offered through plant-care practices. Such initiatives can provide crucial grounding to challenge dominant narratives and build a praxis of relational wellbeing based on pluralistic epistemologies.

abstract: In this paper we look at an informal science learning environment, the Choreographing Science Camp, where middle school youth, scientists, and choreographers engaged in scientific inquiry together. We attend to how timid, quiet idea proposals by youth were taken up by the group in dignity affirming ways that led to collective wonderings, creating space for the group to grow into their half-baked ideas and questions together.

title: One-on-One Coaching to Support Connection Making: Moving Professional Learning to Practice

abstract: In this paper, we explore how one-on-one coaching supported one teacher in implementing ideas about computational thinking in her classroom. We draw from existing literature on coaching strategies but recognize those tend to have been developed in large-group or small-group settings rather than one-on-one. Our findings consider two kinds of questions that seemed to support the teacher in engaging with discourse practices that have been shown effective for coaching (Lefstein et al, 2020). Our findings suggest that coaching made the instruction and activity from PL workshops more relevant and tangible for the teacher.

title: Integrating Socio-scientific Reasoning into STEM Project-based Learning
citation: Zheng, J., Liu, S., Zhu, G., Li, S., Jiang, R., & Xie, C. (2024). Integrating Socio-scientific Reasoning into STEM Project-based Learning. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study utilized a computer-simulated learning environment (i.e., Aladdin) to implement collaborative socio-scientific reasoning activities into a project-based learning (PBL) curriculum. Twenty-one students from a suburban middle school in the Midwestern United States participated in the study. Assigned different social roles (e.g., planning board members, residents, and a solar company), students worked together to design a profitable solar farm while addressing the controversial local issue of granting a permit for its construction. The research findings indicate that students were engaged in socio-scientific reasoning activities despite their different social roles. This study provides implications for both research and practice in STEM education, particularly for efforts to enhance students’ PBL experiences.

title: Pre-Service Teacher Identity Crucibles and “Good” Teaching
citation: Novelli, M., Freed, N., Sherard, M., & Azevedo, F. (2024). Pre-Service Teacher Identity Crucibles and “Good” Teaching. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1191-1194). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Novelli, M., Freed, N., Sherard, M., & Azevedo, F.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this research, we draw connections between Tyack and Tobin’s grammars of schooling and contextualized pre-service teachers conceptualizations of their teacher identities to make sense of the ways that deficit oriented binary thinking patterns prevail in classrooms even in the face of coursework designed to challenge the status quo. Video data was collected during final reflections of pre-service STEM teachers during a Project Based Instruction course that included a field-teach element. Through vignette analysis, we bring to light the ways in which binary perspectives in PST reflective practices exhibit how grammars of schooling are integrated into teacher identity. Two binaries are discussed: “learning and reinforcing time” and “fast and slow students”. Each binary is analyzed to reveal perceptions of knowledge and learning held by the pre-service teachers as well as how PST are actively engaging in negotiation of what it means to “be a teacher”.

title: Teaching in the Wild: Dilemmas Experienced by K-12 Teachers Learning to Facilitate Outdoor Education
citation: Ramey, K., Dunphy, M., Schamberger, B., Shoraka, Z. B., Mabadeje, Y., & Tu, L. (2024). Teaching in the Wild: Dilemmas Experienced by K-12 Teachers Learning to Facilitate Outdoor Education. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1195-1198). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ramey, K., Dunphy, M., Schamberger, B., Shoraka, Z. B., Mabadeje, Y., & Tu, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Benefits of learning in nature are well documented. However, there are many challenges and open questions in preparing educators, particularly K-12 teachers, to facilitate engaging and impactful outdoor learning experiences. Here, we take a cultural historical activity-theoretical approach to analyzing the dilemmas faced by 14 fifth- and sixth-grade teachers and one principal as they prepared for and facilitated a week-long outdoor learning experience for students. Drawing on surveys and video data, we identified four dilemmas negotiated by teachers and illustrate how they represent systemic contradictions between the activity systems of classroom learning and learning in the wild. We discuss implications for understanding and designing for learning in nature and teacher professional development.

title: Kindergarteners’ Understandings and Representations of the Additive Inverse
citation: López, M. A., Strachota, S., Brizuela, B. M., del Carmen Pérez-Martos, M., Gardiner, A. M., & Blanton, M. (2024). authors_list: López, M. A., Strachota, S., Brizuela, B. M., Pérez-Martos, M. D. C., Gardiner, A. M., & Blanton, M.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study involved a 7-lesson generalized arithmetic classroom teaching experiment (CTE) with kindergarten students. We interviewed four students individually before and after the seven weeks to explore their understandings and representations of arithmetic properties. Here, we report on students' responses to questions on the additive inverse property. Using Skemp’s framework of relational and instrumental understandings (2006), our analysis revealed that most of the interviewed kindergarteners could understand the additive inverse relationally by the end of the CTE. Our interviews revealed that tables and number lines enabled students to articulate more sophisticated understandings of the additive inverse.

title: More Than a Feeling: Using Portraiture to Explore Undergraduate Students’ Emotional Responses to Feedback
citation: Lundquist, H., Steadman, C., Weisen, S., & Van Boekel, M. (2024). More Than a Feeling: Using Portraiture to Explore Undergraduate Students’ Emotional Responses to Feedback. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1203-1206). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lundquist, H., Steadman, C., Weisen, S., & Boekel, M. V.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The purpose of this study was to examine students’ emotional responses to feedback as it is being processed. We used the think-aloud method, allowing students to express what they are thinking and feeling as they read through their feedback provided by the instructor on an authentic classroom assignment. Feedback type, feedback valence, and emotional responses were coded. Six students verbalized emotional responses to their feedback. The emotional responses for these students were examined using the portraiture method -a critical, narrative story-telling analysis. The results suggest that the type of feedback (process-focused) was more often met with future-focused thinking compared to task-focused feedback. This was despite the study finding positive task-focused feedback was more likely to elicit positive reactions. The think-aloud method, combined with portraiture analysis allowed for a holistic view of the feedback process. A thorough write-up of the student portraitures are described, and the implications of this are discussed.

title: Causal Pattern Diagrams in Science Texts Support Explanation
citation: Subramonyam, H., Adar, E., Shah, P., & Seifert, C. M. (2024). Causal Pattern Diagrams in Science Texts Support Explanation. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1207-1210). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Subramonyam, H., Adar, E., Shah, P., & Seifert, C. M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Conceptual Change & Mental Models; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: Understanding causal models in science texts requires learners to construct a mental model of complex causal relationships despite unfamiliar vocabulary and limited knowledge. Prior studies show presenting diagrams helps learners improve, but little is known about how learning improves with causal diagrams. In an online study, we tested adults’ explanations of five science phenomena after reading text with or without a schematic causal diagram. The quantitative and qualitative results show causal pattern diagrams promote holistic quality in learners' explanations. Providing visualizations of complex causal relationships within science texts can scaffold learning by highlighting the need to understand causal patterns in science.

title: Reimagining Learning Contexts and Learner Agency in K-12 Science Education: A Critical Review
citation: Hoogland, E., Gebre, E., & Bailie, A. L. (2024). Reimagining Learning Contexts and Learner Agency in K-12 Science Education: A Critical Review. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1211-1214). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hoogland, E., Gebre, E., & Bailie, A. L.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: In the last few decades, the purpose of science education has been called into question mainly for not being impactful enough for students’ everyday lives. In part, this has to do with the framing and use of learning contexts; what educators consider as influential contexts are external to the students thereby providing learners with limited agency to modify and work with them. In this paper, we examined how contexts were articulated in K-12 science education research. Based on our preliminary results, we created a four-category continuum ranging from contexts as indexical factors to contexts as constitutive elements. The study has relevance for educators in terms of reconceptualizing our understanding and use of learning contexts in research and learning design.

title: The Beauty in Science: Understanding the Role of Art in Youth STEAM Identity Development
citation: Hill, K., Allen, C. D., & Keifert, D. T. (2024). The Beauty in Science: Understanding the Role of Art in Youth STEAM Identity Development. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hill, K., Allen, C. D., & Keifert, D. T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this paper we expand on discussions of STEM identity to make space for including discourse on creativity, art, and making within science spaces and further normalize the use of STEAM (STEM plus Art) in academic discourse, and within science practice. ArtScience provides a space for youth and adults in a STEM project setting to honor the appreciation of aesthetics within science practice and further our understanding of STEAM identity development. We present findings from a participatory design research project involving high school youth and educators working alongside scientists to further their interests in STEM areas.

title: Culturally Sustaining Game Redesign: Developing Criticality through Redesign of the Tabletop Game Forbidden Island
citation: Poppendorf, A., Kim, B., Bastani, R., Gierus, B., & Clyde, J. (2024). Culturally Sustaining Game Redesign: Developing Criticality through Redesign of the Tabletop Game Forbidden Island. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Poppendorf, A., Kim, B., Bastani, R., Gierus, B., & Clyde, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Gaming allows for play, creativity, and expression. This study draws from ethnographic data collected over a six-month period when students at a culturally and linguistically diverse Canadian junior high school redesigned the analog tabletop game Forbidden Island. Tabletop games are more accessible and adaptable to complex school contexts than digital games. This study shows students engaged in critical, culturally sustaining processes through their engagement with this project. This paper explores the criticality expressed by one group and the importance of the tactile experience of tabletop game redesign to these student conversations and experiences.

title: Identify Negotiations of Reluctant Makers in STEM-rich Makerspaces
citation: Parekh, P. (2024). Identify Negotiations of Reluctant Makers in STEM-rich Makerspaces. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1223-1226). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Parekh, P.
subject: STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Makerspaces are technology-rich environments that foster Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) -rich practices. Making is a cultural learning model founded upon constructionism and beliefs of STEM-mediated social mobility. Acknowledging the complex ways of participation and learning in makerspaces, this paper examines the identity work of four girls aged eleven to fourteen in a tinkering workshop. Using intersectionality (Crenshaw, 1989), this paper describes how the girls negotiated identities in relation to coparticipants, others’ expectations, and their self-understanding. Despite the commonality of the girls’ unwillingness to engage meaningfully in workshop activities and intense negotiations, only some girls negotiated positive identities. Analysis reveals that several factors affected their identity work, including others’ participation and perceptions, while robust identities in other domains presented opportunities and challenges. The paper underscores considering social and individual factors influencing engagement in makerspaces to accommodate diverse identities and encourages understanding the implications of seemingly inclusive technology-rich learning environments.

title: Predicting Short Response Ratings with Non-Content Related Features: A Hierarchical Modeling Approach
citation: Condor, A. (2024). Predicting Short Response Ratings with Non-Content Related Features: A Hierarchical Modeling Approach. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1227-1230). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Condor, A.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: We explore whether the human ratings of open-ended responses can be explained with non-content related features, and if such effects vary across different mathematics-related items. When scoring is rigorously defined and rooted in a measurement framework, educators intend that the features of a response which are indicative of the respondent’s level of ability are contributing to scores. However, we find that features such as response length, a grammar score of the response, and a metric relating to key phrase frequency are significant predictors for response ratings. Although our findings are not causally conclusive, they may propel us to be more critical of the way in which we assess open-ended responses, especially in high-stakes scenarios. Educators take great care to provide unbiased, consistent ratings, but it may be that extraneous features unrelated to those which were intended to be rated are being evaluated.

title: How Pedagogical Hints Impact Embodied Geometric Reasoning
citation: Xia, F., Schenck, K. E., Swart, M. I., Grondin, M., Kim, D., Kwon, O. H., Walkington, C., & Nathan, M. J. (2024). How Pedagogical Hints Impact Embodied Geometric Reasoning. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 123-130). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Xia, F., Schenck, K. E., Swart, M. I., Grondin, M., Kim, D., Kwon, O. H., Walkington, C., & Nathan, M. J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Actions relevant to mathematical ideas can benefit thinking and learning. However, actions alone are insufficient to generate generalizable mathematical reasoning. Pedagogical language that connects actions to mathematical ideas may promote generalizable mathematical reasoning. This study investigated the role of pedagogical language on geometric reasoning and gesture production. College students (N=94) were assigned to either receive “social” hints that linked actions to social norms or “math” hints that linked actions to geometry conjectures. Results indicated that students’ mathematical insights and proofs did not differ between conditions, but the speech and gestures of their explanations did. Students with valid proofs were more likely to use transformational speech that described cohesive situational models and showed a perspectival shift from egocentric to allocentric. Moreover, between conditions, students receiving math hints were more likely to produce dynamic depictive gestures as part of their justifications, which have been shown to contribute to superior generalizable geometric proofs.

title: The Role of Epistemic Vexations in Elementary Preservice Teachers’ Sense-Making about Responsive Science Teaching
citation: Kaya, R. A. & Southerland, S. A. (2024). The Role of Epistemic Vexations in Elementary Preservice Teachers’ Sense-Making about Responsive Science Teaching. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1231-1234). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kaya, R. A. & Southerland, S. A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Preservice science teachers (PSTs) often experience vexation when ideas and practices do not fit with their current ways of thinking, as this lack of fit is accompanied by emotions such as confusion or frustration. This study focuses on PSTs’ vexations that emerged as PSTs were positioned as sense-makers during scientific explorations in the science method class. This cross-case study revealed that PSTs experienced epistemic and pedagogical vexations as they engaged in scientific explorations supported by responsive teaching strategies. The PSTs’ experience of epistemic vexations was a precursor for resolving pedagogical vexations and was necessary for their learning and feeling of accomplishment in resolving vexations. This discovery of their resources and science capabilities motivated them to embrace responsive pedagogies for future teaching. This study also speaks to PSTs’ perception of power dynamics in the schooling system, and these perceptions shaped their embrace of responsive pedagogies for their future teaching.

citation: Gordon, V. (2024). Youth Navigating Educational and Social Contexts Through Micro, Meso, and Macro Positioning: A Study of Memoir. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study focuses on how women who have endured difficult childhoods are positioned within micro, meso, and macro level scales in educational and social contexts. Findings suggest that although the women experienced unwanted positioning within the three levels, they used improvisation to seek persons or contexts in which they experienced desired positioning to promote their agency.

authors_list: Gordon, V.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study focuses on the identity transformation of women who come from a traumatic childhood to later become a college educated through improvisation. Using the lens of Holland et al.’s figured worlds, I explore the identity negotiation in of two women who have recounted their experiences in memoir. Results indicate improvisations in early educational experiences and role models helped to transform the identity of the women in the shifting figured worlds of childhood survival to being college educated.

title: Recognizing Cherry-Picked Data in Scientific Information: Epistemic Challenge toward Understanding Comprehensive Evidence
citation: Mochizuki, T., Chinn, C. A., Oura, H., & Yamaguchi, E. (2024). Recognizing Cherry-Picked Data in Scientific Information: Epistemic Challenge toward Understanding Comprehensive Evidence. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1243-1246). subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: An abundance of everyday scientific information circulates with insufficient scrutiny and often contains inaccuracies. This can be challenging for laypeople since sources frequently lack systematic integration of evidence, opting instead to cherry pick specific data in a study to bolster their claims. To address this challenge, we conducted an experimental study to investigate how undergraduates perceive and respond to cherry-picked data and when they become attuned to the potential omission of some data by sources. The analysis revealed that laypeople had difficulty recognizing cherry-picked or hidden data, even when provided with cues. When students are made aware of the potential presence of concealed data with an explicit warning and a vivid example, their reasoning aligns more closely with people exposed to all comprehensive data. We discussed the pressing need to develop an educational program to foster students’ awareness of cherry-picking data for their scientific information literacy in a post-truth era.

International Society of the Learning Sciences.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: To support scientific observation, we conducted a research study using a place-based, mobile augmented reality (AR) app to assist families in learning about healthy habitats for pollinators. By analyzing videos and transcripts from 17 families, we found the significant effects of seven learning activities on families’ scientific observation along four dimensions. The study contributes findings related to how engaging with various features of an AR app can influence aspects of families’ scientific observation.

title: Creating Our Makerspace: Designing Social and Material Conditions for Community Engagement in the Makerspace
citation: Feng, X. (2024). Creating Our Makerspace: Designing Social and Material Conditions for Community Engagement in the Makerspace. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study presents a case for designing social and material conditions to privilege community knowledge in the makerspace with members from non-dominant communities. I conduct a design-based research where young people and community members worked together to design a new makerspace. I explore how re-mediating the social and material aspects of the learning environment can shift maker education from dominant narratives to relevant and consequential communal learning. I find that intergenerational interactions in story and artifact sharing enabled participants to reconsider the value of community assets in the makerspace.

title: Supporting Multidimensional Data Analysis for High-School Students in the Era of Machine Learning
citation: Zhou, X., Tang, J., Xiao, Q., Zhou, Y., & Bai, Z. (2024). Supporting Multidimensional Data Analysis for High-School Students in the Era of Machine Learning. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1255-1258). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhou, X., Tang, J., Xiao, Q., Zhou, Y., & Bai, Z.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Machine Learning (ML) opens exciting scientific opportunities in K-12 STEM classrooms. However, students struggle with interpreting ML patterns due to limited data literacy. Face glyphs offer unique benefits by leveraging our brain’s facial feature processing. Yet, they have limitations like lacking contextual information and data biases. To address this, we created three enhanced face glyph visualizations: feature-independent and feature-aligned range views, and the sequential feature inspector. In a study with 25 high school students, feature-aligned range visualization helped contextual analysis, and the sequential feature inspector reduced missing data risks. Face glyphs also benefit the global interpretation of data.

title: Qualitative Eliciting of Tacit Knowledge in Machinists
citation: Ojeda-Ramirez, S., Yong, Z., Zhang, Y., Liu, R., Rantanen, E., Peng, C., & Peppler, K. (2024). Qualitative Eliciting of Tacit Knowledge in Machinists. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1259-1262). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ojeda-Ramirez, S., Yong, Z., Zhang, Y., Liu, R., Rantanen, E., Peng, C., & Peppler, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Machining, plays a pivotal role in aerospace, medical, and automotive sectors. However, the industry faces labor shortages, exacerbated by the extensive training required for machinists. The learning sciences can elucidate ways to improve such training, addressing labor shortages by optimizing learning pathways for aspiring machinists. Central to this training is the transfer of tacit knowledge—or knowledge with meaning that is rooted in unspeakable tacit dimensions, which is deeply personal, context-specific, and challenging to formalize. With the imminent retirement of experienced machinists, there is an urgent need to capture and transfer this tacit expertise. In this study, part of a broader research to optimize tacit knowledge transmission, we employ qualitative methodologies to understand machinists' tacit knowledge. Leveraging Generative Knowledge Interviewing and Video Stimulating Interviewing, we trace key constructs into tacit knowledge acquisition in machining such as: socialization, reflective practice, formal learning of machining, sensory tacit knowledge and barriers.

title: The Role of Instruction in Shaping Reasoning about Bodies of Evidence: An Experimental Comparison
citation: Oura, H., Mochizuki, T., Chinn, C. A., Yamaguchi, E., & Lin, Q. (2024). The Role of Instruction in Shaping Reasoning about Bodies of Evidence: An Experimental Comparison. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Oura, H., Mochizuki, T., Chinn, C. A., Yamaguchi, E., & Lin, Q.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The public often falls prey to skewed narratives on social media, such as when these narratives are built on cherry-picked evidence, overlooking larger bodies of evidence. We compared three instructional conditions (control with complementary information only, invention task and cued questions, and invention task and text-based instruction in evidence evaluation) to develop Japanese undergraduate students’ epistemic reasoning to discern and lean towards claims backed by a larger body of research as well as detailed descriptions of its evidence sources. Results showed that students with an invention task and text-based instruction more critically evaluated the strength of evidence and trustworthiness who presented cherry-picked evidence than those in the other conditions, which indicates the effect of instruction.

title: The Relationship between Teachers’ Dialogic Questioning Strategies and Students’ Creative Thinking in Elementary School Language Classrooms
citation: Tao, Y. & Chen, G. (2024). The Relationship between Teachers’ Dialogic Questioning Strategies and Students’ Creative Thinking in Elementary School Language Classrooms. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tao, Y. & Chen, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigates the utilization of dialogic questioning strategies by elementary school teachers to foster students’ creative thinking during Chinese language lessons. The sample comprised five teachers and their 224 students. Employing a mixed-method analysis, we found substantial variation in the efficacy of different dialogic strategies in provoking creative thinking. Notably, the dialogic strategy of inviting students to build on ideas exhibited the strongest association with creative thinking, while persistently questioning the same student proved less effective. The analysis contributes to a deeper understanding of how teachers implement discursive moves to facilitate creative thinking in the language classroom.

title: Epistemic Agency in Teacher Education: A Design-Based Research Study of Students’ Video Reflections on Course Readings
citation: Hontvedt, M., Oddvik, M., & Næss, R. R. (2024). Epistemic Agency in Teacher Education: A Design-Based Research Study of Students’ Video Reflections on Course Readings. authors_list: Hontvedt, M., Oddvik, M., & Næss, R. R.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: In higher education, reading research-based literature is a key practice for students and their educators. However, students are newcomers to this practice, and to support them, educators need to find ways to monitor the “silent” processes of student reading. Thus, we employed a sociocultural perspective to design the concept of “video reflections,” allowing insight into students’ reading processes. The analysis revealed that students used video clips to reflect upon their course readings and that, as part of the material, the students oriented toward relations between texts. Such link-making is a possible focus of attention for identifying and supporting epistemic agency among students in future practice.

title: Mapping a School-based Ecology of Learning In and Through Music
citation: Woods, P. J. (2024). Mapping a School-based Ecology of Learning In and Through Music. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1275-1278). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Woods, P. J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Within the small amount of existing music-centric learning sciences research, the majority of these studies overtly center the outcomes of singular pedagogical interventions. However, extant (and foundational) research also shows that music learning occurs across multiple, distinct experiences and environments. Music-centric learning sciences research therefore needs to expand to consider how individuals learn in and through music beyond individual educative experiences. In response, I consider the following research question: how do early childhood educators and musicians conceptualize the process of learning in and through music within schools? Drawing on interviews with teachers and musicians from a multi-school embedded music program, I provide an emergent framework for categorizing music-centered learning that incorporates four themes: music as skill set, cultural artifact, pedagogy, and context. This framework presents an opportunity to structure future learning sciences research into learning in and through music across multiple encounters with the art form.

title: Convincing Novices: The Effect of Notifications on Student Motivation in a Blended Learning Support Environment
citation: Hamzah, A. & Sosnovsky, S. (2024). Convincing Novices: The Effect of Notifications on Student Motivation in a Blended Learning Support Environment. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. abstract: Notifications have become a common tool enhancing the interaction between users and different online systems. Their main goal is to inform users about a particular fact, event, or upcoming activity that needs to be taken care of. This paper explores the use of notifications in a learning support system developed for blended courses with the aim of encouraging students to practice at home. The system has been evaluated in an undergraduate university course. The results show several positive effects of notification. In particular, they indicate that notifications enhance the engagement among novice students in learning activities; that is, students engage in a greater number of exercises throughout the course consistently. The findings provide valuable insights on several aspects of the design of notifications for blended learning support.

title: Hypermedia Philosophy Teaching: An Approach
citation: Jobim, A. & Giraffa, L. (2024). Hypermedia Philosophy Teaching: An Approach. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. abstract: This paper proposes an educational framework for integrating digital technologies and teaching philosophy. It starts from the necessary identification to think of another type of theoretical contribution considering cyberculture. For this, it proposes the triangulation between the work of Deleuze & Guattari, Piérre Lévy, and Silvio Gallo, giving an account of thinking about a concept of philosophy, digital technology, and its consequences and teaching philosophy, giving theoretical support to teachers of his /her it. This proposal rigidly comes through the application of the Design-Based Research methodology, which, by applying two cycles with two philosophy professors, produced an activity capable of integrating digital technologies and philosophical contents efficiently and meaningfully.

citation: Ashiq, M. H., Shah, M., Davis, A. J., Wang, Y., Eagan, B., Jimenez, F. A., Wilson, C. L., & Shaffer, D. W. (2024). abstract: In this study, we used Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) to illustrate how nursing students’ behavioral patterns related to their practice of clinical judgment, person-centered care, and professionalism competencies in a virtual patient simulation, Elsevier’s Shadow Health Digital Clinical Experiences™ (DCE). We obtained transcripts (dialog and click data) from two undergraduate nursing students who completed one Contact Tracing assignment and two Focused Exam assignments using the DCE. We coded each learning event based on three behavioral interaction types and six cognitive and psychosocial competencies recommended by nursing regulatory bodies. Findings revealed that the two students made strong connections to clinical competencies through questioning the patient in the Contact Tracing assignment versus answering system prompts for patient assessment and care planning in the Focused Exam assignments. This study unpacks how simulation-based learning facilitates competency-based education for nursing students’ practice readiness, offering valuable insights for future analytics and design.

authors_list: Chernikova, O., Heitzmann, N., Holzberger, D., Neuhaus, B., Kron, S., Ufer, S., & Fischer, F.

abstract: This research synthesis aggregates the evidence on effects of simulation-based learning on fostering diagnostic skills in higher education. It includes evidence from 237 primary studies aggregated using meta-analytic procedures as well as qualitative analysis. Findings show that (1) improvements in learning processes and outcomes occurring during simulation-based learning do not happen automatically just as a learner is confronted with a diagnostic task, but because learners engage in diagnostic activities during the diagnostic process; (2) facilitating this engagement can be facilitated through providing authentic and engaging tasks in different contexts, as well as personalized scaffolding.

title: Emergent Interests to Well-developed Interests in STEM
citation: Lee, H. H., Celedón-Pattichis, S., LópezLeiva, C., Pattichis, M., & Song, Y. (2024). Emergent Interests to Well-developed Interests in STEM. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. abstract: This study uncovers the intricate dynamics of interest development among three focal students from marginalized backgrounds as they engage in the Advancing Out-of-school Learning in Mathematics and Engineering (AOLME) program. It delves into how their emergent interests in STEM evolve (or does not take hold) into well-developed interests. We approach learning from the perspective that an individual's learning is intricately linked to the broader sociocultural environment they engage with and, in this context, interest plays a central role. The selected cases exhibited both similarities and differences in their paths before, during, and after the program, demonstrating how multiple facets contribute to the emergence and sustainability of interests. Observing how discontinuities and continuities, intertwined with affect and the cultivation of multiple identities, weave into one's lines of practice, provides insights into the interconnectedness that extends into subsequent activities, highlighting the role of learning in this ongoing process.

title: Empowering Teachers’ Competencies: A Task-Centered Teacher Development to Integrating Robotics in STEM Education
citation: Saad, D., Verner, I., & Rosenberg-Kima, R. B. (2024). Empowering Teachers’ Competencies: A Task-Centered Teacher Development to Integrating Robotics in STEM Education. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1299-1302). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Saad, D., Verner, I., & Rosenberg-Kima, R. B.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Robotics can promote Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics education as well as 21st-century skills such as creativity and computational thinking. Nevertheless, robotics is not a mandatory part of the curriculum in many countries. One possible solution could be to integrate robotics into existing subjects such as science. Integrating robotics may be challenging because teachers lack relevant pedagogical and technological competencies, and their self-efficacy is correspondingly low. In this study, we examined how a task-centered teacher development program for integrating robotics in science education can be used to foster competencies science teachers need to integrate robotics activities into their teaching. We found that the task-centered instructional strategy is an approach that can potentially foster teachers’ competencies to integrate robotics activities into science education.

title: Physics Faculty and Empathy in Academic Spaces
citation: Merrill, R., Hamdan, A., Bista, A., & Franklin, S. (2024). Physics Faculty and Empathy in Academic Spaces. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1303-1306). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Merrill, R., Hamdan, A., Bista, A., & Franklin, S.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: The ability to emotionally or intellectually understand another person’s thoughts and feelings — empathy — can foster critical connections that facilitate learning and collaboration. We present a case study of physics faculty that examines their experiences empathizing with students, both in and outside of the classroom. We expand on frameworks for understanding the empathy process by identifying key mediating factors, and note various barriers that faculty express as preventing them from taking empathetic action. Our analysis unpacks the mechanisms of communication and contextual information, which play key roles in the empathetic process, with implications for programs that rely on empathy to develop more inclusive STEM academic spaces.

title: Theorizing Mathematics Teacher Noticing for Equity Through Collaborative Design
citation: Rubin, E. & van Es, E. A. (2024). Theorizing Mathematics Teacher Noticing for Equity Through Collaborative Design. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D.
