authors_list: Rubin, E. & Es, E. A. V.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Research on equity in teacher noticing indicates the multi-dimensionality of teacher noticing and the sociopolitical awareness teachers employ to disrupt longstanding practices that persistently marginalize students from culturally, racially, and linguistically diverse communities. We draw on participatory design research to emphasize the value of theorizing with teachers, as methodologies that center practitioner expertise provide insight into the unique character of noticing and how it unfolds in local contexts. Informed by this perspective, we collaborated with mathematics teachers to jointly develop a model of noticing for equity rooted in their perspectives and experience. In doing so, we shed light on how noticing for equity is enacted in practice, bridging between theories of noticing and firsthand experiences of noticing and decision making that teachers engage in during instruction.

title: Exploring an Interactive Technology for Supporting Embodied Geometric Reasoning
citation: Schenck, K. E., Kim, D., Xia, F., Swart, M. I., Walkington, C., & Nathan, M. J. (2024). Exploring an Interactive Technology for Supporting Embodied Geometric Reasoning. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 131-138). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Schenck, K. E., Kim, D., Xia, F., Swart, M. I., Walkington, C., & Nathan, M. J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Access to body-based resources has been shown to augment cognitive processes, but not all movements equally aid reasoning. Interactive technologies, like dynamic geometry systems (DGS), potentially amplify the link between movement and geometric representation, thereby deepening students' understanding of geometric properties. This study investigated the influence of access to a DGS on students' geometric reasoning and gesture production compared to the impact of only spontaneous gestures. Access to simulations did not significantly increase the likelihood of students producing correct mathematical insights compared to spontaneous gestures. However, when controlling gesture production, DGS access became a significant predictor for transformational proof production. We also found that access to DGS influenced the type of gestures students produced during geometric reasoning tasks. This study underlines the vital role of gestures in geometric reasoning and suggests that while DGS offers benefits, spontaneous gestures remain a crucial embodied resource for exploring geometric concepts.

title: How AI Evaluates Learner Comprehension: A Comparison of Knowledge-Based and Large Language Model (LLM)-Based AI Approaches
citation: Kim, M. K., Kim, J., Bae, Y., Morris, W., Holmes, L., & Crossley, S. (2024). How AI Evaluates Learner Comprehension: A Comparison of Knowledge-Based and Large Language Model (LLM)-Based AI Approaches. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1311-1314). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kim, M. K., Kim, J., Bae, Y., Morris, W., Holmes, L., & Crossley, S.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study investigated two AI techniques for evaluating learners’ summaries and explored the relationship between them: the SMART knowledge-based AI tool, which generated multidimensional measures representing knowledge models derived from learner summaries, and a Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuned for summary scoring. The LLM model incorporated both the summary and source texts in the input sequence to calculate two component scores related to text content and wording. Summary revisions from 172 undergraduates in English and Biology classes were analyzed. The results of linear mixed-effects models revealed that both AI techniques detected changes during revisions. Several SMART measures were positively associated with an increase in the LLM’s Content scores. These findings support the notion that the LLM model excels at broad and comprehensive assessment, while SMART measures are more effective in providing fine-grained feedback on specific dimensions of knowledge structures.

title: Students’ Strategies for Understanding Visualizations about Space and Time
citation: Pagano, L. C., Miller, K. M., Kolvoord, R. A., Uttal, D. H., & Dorsey, C. (2024). Students’ Strategies for Understanding Visualizations about Space and Time. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1315-1318). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Pagano, L. C., Miller, K. M., Kolvoord, R. A., Uttal, D. H., & Dorsey, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Spatiotemporal (ST) data are used to illustrate information across a wide range of disciplines, so it is crucial that students learn to interpret the ST data. Twenty-three undergraduate students were presented with different ST data visualizations (both with and without context) and asked which were most/least useful, what they noticed, what strategies they used, and what they wondered about the data. Students found thematic U.S. maps easiest to interpret, whereas raster maps were most challenging. Video representations were reported to be the most interesting. We identified fifteen unique strategies that students employed when interpreting different types of ST data representations, including color grouping, comparing images, using prior knowledge, and horizontal/vertical scanning. Color grouping was the most common strategy used, but strategies varied across ST data types and level of context.

title: Making Space for Expansive Thinking in Socio-Technical Small-Group Undergraduate Discussions
citation: Rahman, F., Wendell, K., & Andrews, C. (2024). Making Space for Expansive Thinking in Socio-Technical Small-Group Undergraduate Discussions. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1319-1322). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rahman, F., Wendell, K., & Andrews, C.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Engineering & Robotics; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: In this qualitative case study, we explore how first- and second year undergraduate students make space for expansive thinking in their engineering modeling work. We focus on the ways in which one group of five women negotiated the inclusion of different social, political, and economic factors in their design model, particularly energy distribution and transboundary equity. Drawing on discourse analysis methods, we analyzed a small-group in-class discussion and identified five expansive moves that helped the students to make space for rethinking what they could include in their model. These included being explicit about their assumptions and uncertainties and acknowledging task difficulties.

title: Culturally and linguistically “Blind” or Biased? Challenges for AI Assessment of Models with Multiple Language Students
citation: Li, T., Miller, E. A., & He, P. (2024). Culturally and linguistically “Blind” or Biased? Challenges for AI Assessment of Models with Multiple Language Students. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1323-1326). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Li, T., Miller, E. A., & He, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Investigating AI's role in educational assessments, this study compares AI- provided and teacher scores of hand-drawn scientific models by Multilingual Language Learners (MLLs) in elementary classrooms. Using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for scoring, we aligned AI assessments with those of experienced teachers. The results show moderate agreement (Kappa = 0.326), with AI favoring mid-range scores, while teachers provided a broader score spectrum. This suggests AI's consistency may miss the interpretive nuances teachers offer. The study emphasizes careful AI integration to support the diverse assessments of MLLs, though it notes the limitations of a small sample size and the opaque AI scoring rationale. Our findings advocate for combining AI's analytical strengths with teacher expertise to enhance equitable, effective educational assessments.

title: Cartographic Syntonicity as a Tool for Equitable Computer Science Education
citation: Uttamchandani, S., Curinga, M. X., & Drew, J. (2024). Cartographic Syntonicity as a Tool for Equitable Computer Science Education. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1327-1330). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Uttamchandani, S., Curinga, M. X., & Drew, J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
abstract: We discuss the notion of cartographic syntonicity, which we define as compatibility of computer science (and specifically computational thinking and computational practices) with learner’s knowledge of place and space. We first overview Papert’s notions of syntonicity and how they relate to computing education. Then, we explore the role of place in learning. We link these together alongside theories of equitable computer science education to justify why cartographic syntonicity might be uniquely effective in supporting equitable computer science learning. We close with an outline of future research.

title: Professors Exploring Large Language Models
citation: Coelho, R. & Pea, R. (2024). Professors Exploring Large Language Models. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1331-1334). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Coelho, R. & Pea, R.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study explores specific insights of university professors using large language models (LLMs) across their different roles. Using think-aloud protocols, we interviewed ten Norwegian professors from mathematics and natural sciences actively engaged in a project integrating these tools in teaching. The study surfaces emergent applications of LLMs in higher education with professors’ reflections on using LLMs in teaching & research practices.

title: Representing Students: Teachers’ Conversational Stories in Workgroups
citation: Topham, T. (2024). Representing Students: Teachers’ Conversational Stories in Workgroups. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1335-1338). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Topham, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Programs to support teachers’ learning often rely heavily on representations of classroom practice to afford opportunities for teachers to learn. Among the various forms of representation, teachers’ stories about their classroom practice have received little attention relative to their ubiquity in teacher workgroup conversations. This study focuses on teachers’ stories of their classroom practice and analyzes at what degree of generality those stories represented students as actors. It finds that students were most represented at the aggregate level of the class. These findings suggest that studying teachers’ stories as representations of practice can help us understand what aspects of practice are made visible in these stories.

title: Elementary Students’ Emergent and Divergent Goals in Collective Embodied Modeling Activities
citation: Zhou, M., Mathayas, N., & Danish, J. (2024). Elementary Students’ Emergent and Divergent Goals in Collective Embodied Modeling Activities. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1339-1342). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhou, M., Mathayas, N., & Danish, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper aims to understand how elementary students construct and pursue individual goals in a loosely structured collective embodied modeling activity. We explore how engaging in negotiating diverse goals impacts students’ sensemaking about an ecosystem they are modeling. We used Interaction Analysis (Jordan & Henderson, 1995) to discern students’ individual goals in their embodiment and communication and compared them to the collective goals stated by the facilitator and/or group strategies. Our findings lead to recommendations for educators and designers, emphasizing the importance of supporting students’ diverse goals to enhance their agency and foster a more inclusive learning environment.

title: How Gesture Protects Against Failures in Spatial Problem-Solving
citation: Clingan-Siverly, S., Demir‐Lira, Ö. E., Stieff, M., & Lira, M. (2024). How Gesture Protects Against Failures in Spatial Problem-Solving. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1343-1346). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Clingan-Siverly, S., Demir‐Lira, E., Stieff, M., & Lira, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Embodied Cognition & Gestures; Spatial Reasoning & Manipulation
abstract: Student-generated gestures improve their spatial problem solving. Embodiment perspectives theorize that the mechanisms that underpin gesture’s role in spatial reasoning lie in the motor system. Some embodiment theorists, however, jettison working memory models while many information processing theorists assimilate embodiment into their working memory models. We therefore leveraged innovations in neuroimaging technologies to begin addressing this case of underdetermination of theory by data. Using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) we determined that students who learned to solve spatial problems successfully recruit brain regions associated with cognitive effort more so than students who learned to solve problems with non-gesture-based strategies. We discuss the theoretical implications for future educational research on gesture-based learning strategies.

title: Using Student Experience Reports as a Window for Teacher Reflections on Inquiry Science Instructional Practices
citation: Nixon, J. & Recker, M. (2024). Using Student Experience Reports as a Window for Teacher Reflections on Inquiry Science Instructional Practices. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1347-1350). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Nixon, J. & Recker, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper examines how student experience reports, collected as exit tickets, can be leveraged during professional learning to support science teachers’ understanding of their students and inform future classroom practices. Our analysis frames exit ticket data as a boundary object, which bridges across researchers’, teachers’, and students’ perspectives of the learning environment. During two successive professional learning activities, teachers examined and reflected upon their students’ exit ticket data. A thematic analysis of teachers’ discourse during these activities distilled two themes. The first theme surfaced how exit data helped teachers form new views about their students’ emerging science identities; the second revealed how teachers gained new insights into their students’ perceptions of contributions to classroom discourse, which both challenged and validated their own intuitions.

title: Where Material Impact Matters: Fostering Equitable Teaching Practices through Working Differences in Elementary Science Methods Course
citation: Jeong, S., Pierson, A., Keifert, D. T., Henrie, A., Johnson, H., Daniel, B., & Lee, S. (2024). Where Material Impact Matters: Fostering Equitable Teaching Practices through Working Differences in Elementary Science Methods Course. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1351-1353). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jeong, S., Pierson, A., Keifert, D. T., Henrie, A., Johnson, H., Daniel, B., & Lee, S.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This conceptual paper empirically illustrates the journey of preservice science teachers' becoming, presenting narratives of working differences. It involves juxtaposing differences to disrupt the sameness ontology prevalent in science education and broader societal contexts. We map preservice teachers' paths of becoming in an elementary science methods course, sharing key juncture points where transformative science teaching practices emerge. This is achieved by noticing ways to reconfigure their classroom environment that significantly impact their teaching and their students’ learning experiences.

title: Cultivating Feedback Loops: Factors and Contradictions Impacting Groups Developing Emerging Technologies
citation: Coenraad, M., Fusco, J., & Ruiz, P. (2024). Cultivating Feedback Loops: Factors and Contradictions Impacting Groups Developing Emerging Technologies. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1354-1357). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Coenraad, M., Fusco, J., & Ruiz, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Feedback loops bring together participants from multiple contributing groups in purposeful, multi-directional, iterative, and transformative interactions to design or develop an innovation. We present the idea of three-way feedback loops between researchers, educators, and product teams. Using cultural-historical activity theory, we examine the cultural, historical, and contextual factors impacting each group’s participation in a feedback loop and the contradictions that arise within and between the systems. As research increasingly aims to center the voices of individuals who are most impacted by its outcomes and ensure innovations best serve the communities for whom they are created, feedback loops are a promising collaboration strategy. However, cultivating a productive feedback loop requires careful navigation of the different contexts and the contradictions between the groups.

title: Characterizing Maker-Material Encounters in Collaborative Creative Making
citation: V, A. & Dasgupta, C. (2024). Characterizing Maker-Material Encounters in Collaborative Creative Making. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1358-1361). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: V, A. & Dasgupta, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The article aims to contribute to the understanding of relational dynamics of maker-material assemblages in collaborative making. In this study, we examine the encounters between makers and material entities in design problem solving scenarios. We specifically look at data from two collaborative making contexts: 1) a medical device innovation camp, 2) a maker activity-centered workshop, to characterize maker-material encounters and argue the emergent nature of creative making. Our analysis suggests that makers and materials engage in various forms of conversations where maker-material audits occur, maker-material synchrony shapes up, material configure collaboration, and materials exhibit epistemic characteristics.

title: Immersive Virtual Field Trips to Enhance Inquiry-Based Learning on Climate Change
citation: Paksoy, I. & Oner, D. (2024). Immersive Virtual Field Trips to Enhance Inquiry-Based Learning on Climate Change. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1362-1365). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Paksoy, I. & Oner, D.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study investigates the use of immersive virtual reality in climate change education as part of an inquiry-based learning environment designed for middle school students. A pre-existing 360-degree documentary about melting glaciers and a newly designed interactive sea level rise experience were used as field trips in the exploration phase of the 5E inquiry model. We employed a learning progression based on sea level rise to identify learning outcomes and assessment strategies. Students' test scores significantly improved after the learning experience. This finding was further supported by students’ responses written in a formative assessment tool. The results demonstrate the successful integration of immersive technologies into learning environments related to climate change education and highlight its effectiveness.

title: Black Prompts not Included: AI Bias Impeding Real-Time Co-Creative Ideation in Black Students' Conceptual Design
citation: Edouard, K. (2024). Black Prompts not Included: AI Bias Impeding Real-Time Co-Creative Ideation in Black Students' Conceptual Design. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1366-1369). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Edouard, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This research paper investigates using artificial intelligence (AI) and image generators to foster rapid ideation among Black design students. It centers on Devonte, a Black undergraduate game design student, and his experiences using image generators as a co-creative tool for designing game characters. Pilot study finds racial and cultural biases in image generators, hindering culturally relevant designs. These biases not only challenge Devonte's creative process but also underscore the broader issue of inclusivity in technological tools. The paper advocates for further discussion and research on addressing these biases, emphasizing the need for image generators that support the diverse cultural backgrounds of users. This is crucial for unlocking the full creative potential of Black students in STEM spaces and ensuring equitable access to technological advancements.

title: Addressing Misconceptions in Science through Minecraft
citation: Gadbury, M. (2024). Addressing Misconceptions in Science through Minecraft. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1370-1373). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Gadbury, M.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Misconceptions in science are common among young learners, and addressing misconceptions is an important step in guiding learners towards deeper understanding of concepts in various science domains. One suggested strategy for addressing misconceptions in science is to use scenarios requiring counterfactual reasoning, such as asking “What if the earth had two moons?”. Early to middle-adolescent learners were asked to explore custom designed “What if?” scenarios in Minecraft as part of an informal summer camp experience. Learners completed an assessment of astronomy misconceptions before and after the summer camp. Results showed an overall significant increase in scores on the post-test. Counterfactual scenarios in Minecraft stand as an adequate learning environment to address misconceptions.

title: Teacher and Student Perceptions of Co-Learning
citation: Apedoe, X., Phillips, M., & Nielsen, K. (2024). Teacher and Student Perceptions of Co-Learning. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1374-1377). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Apedoe, X., Phillips, M., & Nielsen, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Co-learning is a novel hybridization of teacher professional learning and student out-of-school learning, wherein students and teachers collaborate and learn together. Because of its novelty, both questions and skepticism exist about co-learning as a useful professional learning model for teachers and an out-of-school learning model for students. We believe it offers great promise, and thus, this study is a first step at exploring teachers’ and students’ experiences with co-learning to define its strengths and limitations. In this paper, we share insights gained from teachers and students about their experiences co-learning during the Cellular Construction Workshop.

title: Developing Learning Science Competencies and Curriculum for Teacher Education
citation: Moussavi, R., Castle, C., & Dudek, J. (2024). Developing Learning Science Competencies and Curriculum for Teacher Education. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1378-1381). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Moussavi, R., Castle, C., & Dudek, J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This design-based case study follows the design and implementation of Science of Learning and Development (SoLD) competencies across two successive Competency-Based Education (CBE) programs, the first a STEM focused licensure program and the second a program focusing on design, equity, and justice for in-service teachers. The goal of positioning the Science of Learning and Development as a core competency and integrating it within the two programs was to support educators in becoming well-equipped to support their students’ learning and development through the whole child approach. We offer insights on the conceptualization of an overarching framework and competencies, development of assessments and curricular designs, and strategic supports/learner interactions as a possible model for SoLD–focused teacher preparation/education. Furthermore, this approach reinforces the importance of SoLD and communicates that SoLD is not distinct from pedagogy which marks a shift from how SoLD is often presented to pre and in service teachers.

title: Build Resilience in Knowledge Building Communities: Teacher’s Growth Mindset Oriented Feedback to Support Grade 5 Students’ Yearlong Science Inquiry
citation: Zhou, H. & Zhang, J. (2024). Build Resilience in Knowledge Building Communities: Teacher’s Growth Mindset Oriented Feedback to Support Grade 5 Students’ Yearlong Science Inquiry. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1382-1385). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhou, H. & Zhang, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study examines students’ social-emotional experience with knowledge building pedagogy. The goal of this study is to understand how student interest, persistence and growth mindset oriented feedback sustain students’ inquiry and discourse. The data source includes video-recordings and transcripts of nine classroom meetings. Deductive and inductive approaches to data analysis were applied to analyze the class recording data. The findings suggest that teacher’s growth mindset oriented feedback in the knowledge building community engage students social emotionally to face and overcome inquiry challenges to achieve community knowledge advancement.

title: I’m a STEM Person, But do I Belong?
citation: Apedoe, X. & Nielsen, K. (2024). I’m a STEM Person, But do I Belong?. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1386-1389). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Apedoe, X. & Nielsen, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: While individuals may have a positive STEM identity, they may not feel they belong to a STEM community. STEM identity is a related but distinct concept from STEM sense of belonging. Yet, there is much to be learned about the similarities and differences between STEM identity and STEM sense of belonging and how they might separately or jointly affect students’ interest and persistence in STEM. This mixed-method case study explores the unique perspectives, reflections, and insights about STEM identity and feelings of belonging in STEM of STEM-inclined high school students who identify with communities historically marginalized in STEM. Drawing on survey and interview data, we share insights from these eight students and offer suggestions for future research directions.

title: Students’ Representational and Relational Caring in STEM
citation: Pierson, A., Brady, C., Lee, S., Shuler, D., Clark, D. B., & Sengupta, P. (2024). Students’ Representational and Relational Caring in STEM. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 139-146). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Pierson, A., Brady, C., Lee, S., Shuler, D., Clark, D. B., & Sengupta, P.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Studies of both professional science practice and children’s science learning show that emotions, including care, are not simply ancillary to disciplinary work but a generative part of science practice. In science education research, however, students’ care is often overlooked. In this paper, we describe the nature and expression of care across two classrooms studying biology and ecology and participating in a pen pal exchange. We analyze artifacts from the pen pal exchange, as well as students’ retrospective interviews and written reflections. Two dimensions of care surfaced in students’ letters: representational care and relational care. We discuss practical implications for learning environment design and methodological implications for recognizing and analyzing how students’ caring manifests in the classroom.

title: Data Visualization Renarrated: Probing the Role of Renarrating in Data Visualization Reimagining
citation: Zhao, Y. & Dyer, E. B. (2024). Data Visualization Renarrated: Probing the Role of Renarrating in Data Visualization Reimagining. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1390-1393). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhao, Y. & Dyer, E. B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Data visualization reimagining can be an effective way for students to develop a deep understanding of a given data visualization. It encompasses three different dimensions: reformatting, reframing, and renarrating. In this study, we explored the role of renarrating in a data reimagining activity. With semi-structured interviews, we found that renarrating can support reformatting and reframing by providing a concrete context and renarrating established personally meaningful connections between students and the data visualization. Our study suggested a data visualization reimagining practice should initiate with renarrating and utilize renarrating to support personally meaningful learning.

title: Transitioning an Active Learning Physics Course Between Professors was More Successful with a Third Person Acting as a Bridging Agent
citation: Burron, G., Sealfon, C., & Sinervo, P. (2024). Transitioning an Active Learning Physics Course Between Professors was More Successful with a Third Person Acting as a Bridging Agent. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Burron, G., Sealfon, C., & Sinervo, P.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: In this study, we discuss how the presence of a self-study critical friend acted as a bridging agent to aid the transition of a Physical Science in Contemporary Society active learning course design between physics professors at a major Central Canadian research university. We also examine the roles the participants took, how the background of the participants may have aided the transition, and how these characteristics may assist transitions of active learning course designs in the future. Given the propensity of active learning courses to lose their active learning characteristic during the transition between instructors, techniques to retain the design of these courses are critically important.

title: Middle School Students’ Engagement with Quantitative Data Representations of Fictional Texts
citation: Coelho, R., Levine, S., Abdi, D., Phalen, L., Harris, L., Demszky, D., & Lee, V. R. (2024). Middle School Students’ Engagement with Quantitative Data Representations of Fictional Texts. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1398-1401). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Coelho, R., Levine, S., Abdi, D., Phalen, L., Harris, L., Demszky, D., & Lee, V. R.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Advances in computing and digital data are changing approaches to literacy not just in STEM fields, but humanities. For instance, at the university level, students use digital humanities to enrich their literary literacy, such as understandings of authorial craft and the power of language. We hypothesized that applying digital humanities tools--especially text analytics-based visualizations, such as word clouds and line graphs--could enrich both language arts literacy of younger students, who tend to focus on surface features of literary texts. We report findings from think-aloud interviews with U.S. middle school students engaging with text analytics-based visualizations of familiar stories like Cinderella. Students engaged in aspects of literary literacy, including analysis of authorial craft, as well as data literacy, including analysis of frequency and change over time in relation to the stories. Integrating text analytics-based visualizations into middle school literacy instruction may support both language arts and data literacy learning goals.

title: Everyday Entry Points to Visual-spatial Thinking: Implications from a Thai Farmer’s Reservoir Planning
citation: Rosenbaum, L. F., Fields, D. A., Sipitakiat, A., & Blikstein, P. (2024). Everyday Entry Points to Visual-spatial Thinking: Implications from a Thai Farmer’s Reservoir Planning. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1402-1405). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rosenbaum, L. F., Fields, D. A., Sipitakiat, A., & Blikstein, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Visual-spatial skills underlay reasoning in a range of domains, making their development of continued interest. While a range of computer-based spatial reasoning platforms have been created recently, they remain inaccessible to many learners in the Global South and may supplant the real-world problem-solving work through which spatial reasoning was historically developed. We present a narrative vignette of a Thai farmer who developed paper-and-pencil representations to solve a spatial reasoning task in her village. Drawing on theories of how representation guides cognition, we document how this farmer’s representations enabled her consequential work and shaped it in interesting ways. This example could inform educational design and facilitation efforts to offer life-relevant activities to develop visual-spatial skills.

title: Electrodermal Activities During Self-Regulated Learning Relate to Learning Performance Within a Technology-Rich Environment
citation: Wang, T., Liu, S., Zheng, J., Ruiz-Segura, A., & Lajoie, S. (2024). Electrodermal Activities During Self-Regulated Learning Relate to Learning Performance Within a Technology-Rich Environment. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1406-1409). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wang, T., Liu, S., Zheng, J., Ruiz-Segura, A., & Lajoie, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study employed computer trace data and electrodermal activities (EDA) to examine students’ temporal dynamics of self-regulated learning (SRL). Specifically, 106 students accomplished a diagnostic task in an intelligent tutoring system. During the task, we recorded students’ interactive activities within BioWorld and EDA signals. Then we coded the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phase of SRL from computer trace data and extracted four EDA features for further analysis. The results of Friedman tests revealed that students’ had higher skin conductance levels (SCL) and more skin conductance response (SCR) peaks in the forethought phase. However, the average amplitude and duration of SCR peaks were significantly higher in the performance phase than forethought and self-reflection phases. Furthermore, Graphic Gaussian Model indicated that students’ SCR features during the self-reflection phase were more associated with learning performance. These findings provide evidence regarding using EDA to identify temporal dynamics of SRL processes.

title: What Youth Know: “Knowledge in New Pieces” and the Uncovering Nuanced Intuitive Thinking about Everyday Complex Systems
citation: Blikstein, P., Rosenbaum, L. F., & Voorhis, J. K. (2024). What Youth Know: “Knowledge in New Pieces” and the Uncovering Nuanced Intuitive Thinking about Everyday Complex Systems. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1410-1413). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Blikstein, P., Rosenbaum, L. F., & Voorhis, J. K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Youth today learn, play, and live in inextricably digital and analog worlds that are becoming ever bigger and more connected. Accordingly, the intuitive knowledge youth generate in navigating and authoring those worlds might evolve similarly, perhaps in ways that could inform their formal education. Building on foundational theories in conceptual change, we present pilot findings of a broader research program that studies what and how youth know about complex systems based on their everyday lived experiences. We document intuitive knowledge about topics such as supply and resource chains, globalization, and industrial agriculture. Beyond simply documenting youth’s modern intuitive knowledge pieces, this line of research could inform the design of educational activities and curricula that leverage youth’s intuitive knowledge in preparing them for 21st-century life.

title: Intricate but Often Overlooked Challenges of Elementary Students’ Programming with Educational Robotics: A Case Study
citation: Jung, Y., Xie, Y., Tscholl, M., & Tun, M. M. (2024). Intricate but Often Overlooked Challenges of Elementary Students’ Programming with Educational Robotics: A Case Study. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1414-1417). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jung, Y., Xie, Y., Tscholl, M., & Tun, M. M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: The integration of educational robotics (ER) in K-12 classrooms has grown substantially recently, with research indicating a positive impact on academic achievement and learning. These educational robotics have been particularly beneficial in advancing students’ Computer Science and Computational Thinking (CT). While prior research has predominantly studied the effect of educational robotics on overall cognitive computational thinking skills, limited research has examined students’ robotic programming processes in detail. In this paper, we analyzed the findings of a case study, shedding light on the beyond CT frameworks faced by upper elementary students as they engaged with educational robotics. By offering a close-up examination, we found difficulties in understanding the robot’s serial program processing, that students adopt an egocentric perspective, and are unable to think in terms of the notion of ‘flow of control.’ These findings will be beneficial for teachers and curriculum designers in developing proper activities for upper elementary students.

title: Collectively Becoming Racially Literate Through Organizing for Educational Justice
citation: Leibovitz, T. (2024). Collectively Becoming Racially Literate Through Organizing for Educational Justice. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1418-1421). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Leibovitz, T.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: This study reveals how a group of white and/or socio-economically privileged parents organizing for educational justice collectively became racially literate. I illustrate how participants collectively utilize and develop tools, epistemologies, and practices to identify, address, and organize against racism in the socio-political context of their organizing. In demonstrating how becoming racially literate can be a collective action, I reveal how learning resides within the organization rather than within the individuals of the organization. I also illustrate how collective literacy resides within the organizational strategies. This has important implications for how we understand organizing apparatus’ including the organization itself and how collective learning about racial justice occurs.

title: Customization of Curriculum Materials as a Site for Identifying and Taking Action on Shared Problems of Practice
citation: McNeill, K. L., Lee, S., Zhang, Y., Moore, A., Buell, J., Reiser, B. J., Affolter, R., Fine, C., & Vera, M. M. (2024). Customization of Curriculum Materials as a Site for Identifying and Taking Action on Shared Problems of Practice. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1422-1425). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: McNeill, K. L., Lee, S., Zhang, Y., Moore, A., Buell, J., Reiser, B. J., Affolter, R., Fine, C., & Vera, M. M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Science learning reforms require shifting epistemic and power structures so students and teachers build knowledge together within the context of meaningful questions and problems. Curricular customization allows teachers to preserve these reform-oriented goals while adapting for their specific contexts and students. This paper presents three cases from professional learning communities (PLCs) who followed the same curriculum customization model, but with different equity goals: supporting bi/multilingual learners’ ownership of learning, increasing the relevance of curriculum for students, and encouraging more student voices and multiple perspectives. Together, these cases highlight how the collaborative customization model facilitated productive tensions that lead to teacher learning.

title: Third Space Extensions of Sociopolitical Development: Unlearning through Sensory, Discursive, and Collective Spaces
citation: Chew, P. (2024). Third Space Extensions of Sociopolitical Development: Unlearning through Sensory, Discursive, and Collective Spaces. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1426-1429). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chew, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper answers calls toward critical and decolonial shifts in learning through conceptualizing sociopolitical development as an unlearning process within the learning sciences. By distinguishing the unlearning process as continuous, recursive, endeavors rooted in reflexivity, I distinguish unlearning as a dynamic process towards resisting the many ever-changing reifications of oppression. Through excerpts from life histories from alumni of community arts programs, I demonstrate the process through which participants unlearn dominant ways of being and relating through means of deciphering the encoded fabric of macro sociopolitical realities within passing, quotidian moments. I present and instantiate three metaphysical expansions of Third Spaces in which participants’ unlearning occurred: sensory spaces, discursive spaces, and collective spaces.

title: What Social Representations Tell Us About Teacher Well-Being: The Crucial Role of Time
citation: Vassaux, C., Felder, J., & Molinari, G. (2024). What Social Representations Tell Us About Teacher Well-Being: The Crucial Role of Time. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1430-1433). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Vassaux, C., Felder, J., & Molinari, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Recently, the concept of teacher well-being has received growing interest. However, how teachers perceive their well-being is still unknown. This study aims to understand teacher well-being as a subject of social representation. To grasp its content and structure, a sample of 70 teachers had to complete a hierarchical evocation test and evaluate the valence of each cited term. To analyse the data, the ranked importance method was employed. Results indicate a prevalence of terms connoted positively and a limited number of words with negative valence. Findings suggest the social representation of teacher well-being is constituted of different representational areas such as time management, hedonism, human values, students’ relationships, or teachers’ social interactions. Teachers attached particular importance to time management, which was the most cited term for the social representation of their well-being. By employing the social representation approach to the study of teacher well-being, this contribution provides new research perspectives.

title: Immersive Learning in Professional Wildlife Training: The Role of VR in Supporting Novice and Expert Interaction
citation: Bowles, S. & Sharma, P. (2024). Immersive Learning in Professional Wildlife Training: The Role of VR in Supporting Novice and Expert Interaction. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1434-1437). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bowles, S. & Sharma, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This research delves into the role of Virtual Reality (VR) in wildlife training, specifically examining its influence on novice and expert interactions in animal husbandry. Rooted in sociocultural theories, the research unfolds within an ongoing co-design initiative at an Environmental Center, capturing real-time work practices through 360-degree videos later showcased in VR. Two episodes illustrate the strategic integration of VR within an informal workplace setting, showcasing its adaptability and impact on knowledge construction. The findings suggest that VR offers nuanced and responsive affordances for joint attention on artifacts by novices and experts, leading to more personalized opportunities for learning and practice.

title: A Core Set of Practices for Justice-Centered Ambitious Science
citation: Luehmann, A., Merliss, G., Campbell, T., Zhang, Y., Cooke, H., & Scipio, D. (2024). A Core Set of Practices for Justice-Centered Ambitious Science. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1438-1441). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Luehmann, A., Merliss, G., Campbell, T., Zhang, Y., Cooke, H., & Scipio, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: Core teaching practices, consisting of strategies, routines, and tools, are effective supports for teachers in developing competence with pedagogical practice that centers collaborative student sensemaking with disciplinary ideas and practices. Though these practices can nurture diverse students’ access, achievement, and identities in science, they stop short of meeting more critical demands of equity, namely that of challenging and expanding what counts as science and using science as part of social justice movements. The Justice-Centered Ambitious Science Teaching framework presented below was empirically developed yet theoretically aligned with the current priorities related to justice-centered teaching. This framework offers teachers core practices as scaffolds for centering justice in planning and instruction for science learning.

title: Co-design and Co-Creation of Knowledge in Collaborative Teacher Teams
citation: Damşa, C., Gudmundsdottir, G. B., & Vasbø, K. B. (2024). Co-design and Co-Creation of Knowledge in Collaborative Teacher Teams. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1442-1445). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Damşa, C., Gudmundsdottir, G. B., & Vasbø, K. B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper examines collaborative knowledge creation in teams, through analyzing the ways a team of academic teachers worked collaboratively on curricular innovation over the period of an academic year. The focus is on the creation of shared knowledge artifacts (syllabus, assignments, assessment, etc.), which serve both as focus of their collaborative co-design process and as mediating tools for innovating their teaching practices. The paper proposes a conceptual framework entailing epistemic, interactional and objectual dimensions, and spans interactions, resources, and outcomes being created or being instrumental in the process. The qualitative analyses of the team’s dialogues, products, and reflections show that knowledge creation in teams is constituted through a combination of processes, dimensions and mechanisms, which materialize into new knowledge or novel practices for individual and collective benefits.

title: A Comparison of Deep Learning and Supervised Machine Learning Methods in RF tracking for Neurodivergent Learners
citation: Sokolikj, Z., Ke, F., Chakraborty, S., & Moon, J. (2024). A Comparison of Deep Learning and Supervised Machine Learning Methods in RF tracking for Neurodivergent Learners. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1446-1449). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sokolikj, Z., Ke, F., Chakraborty, S., & Moon, J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
tpack_tk_labels: Immersive VR / AR; Simulations & Scientific Modeling
abstract: Representational Flexibility (RF) is an individual's cognitive ability to select, coordinate and create alternative representations during information processing. Students with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) typically lack representational flexibility and therefore are underrepresented in the fields of STEM. Research has used virtual reality-based (VR) 3D simulations to promote RF development of ASD adolescent learners. However, to promote RF development, the need to be able to track RF throughout the intervention is critical. In this paper we report RF tracking in a VR-based learning program intended for RF development. We studied the performance of state-of-the-art deep neural network models to track RF subsets throughout the intervention. We trained these models, along with multiple classical machine-learning classifiers, using multimodal data collected from 209 sessions with ten ASD adolescents. Our empirical analysis shows promising evidence that deep learning can be used to track the cognitive-affective states of learners with ASD in real time.

title: A Study on AI-Augmented Concept Learning: Impact on Learner Perceptions and Outcomes in STEM Education
citation: Bae, Y., Kim, J., Davis, A., & Kim, M. K. (2024). A Study on AI-Augmented Concept Learning: Impact on Learner Perceptions and Outcomes in STEM Education. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1450-1453). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bae, Y., Kim, J., Davis, A., & Kim, M. K.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Conceptual Change & Mental Models
abstract: This study explores the efficacy of AI-enhanced concept learning among adult learners, aiming to bolster their comprehension and facilitate the transition to embracing technology, refining metacognitive reading strategies, and improving subsequent knowledge test scores. Leveraging an AI-driven formative assessment feedback system, named SMART, AI integration was implemented in pre-class activities within a Biology course. Learners demonstrated enhanced mental models of STEM readings, and while the levels of technology acceptance were not statistically significant, we observed numerical increases in perceived AI usefulness. However, no significant relations were found with perceived ease of use and metacognitive awareness. The impact of concept learning through SMART on knowledge test scores demonstrated partial visibility. This research underscores the holistic integration of AI tools, highlighting the importance of educators to align instructional methods such as AI with learning objectives, content, assessment tests, and learners’ AI literacy levels, particularly within the domain of online STEM education.

title: Unraveling Learner Self-Efficacy in the Electronic Making: Insights from Interaction Analysis, Self-Reports and Interview
citation: K, N. S., V, A., Saxena, A., & Rajendran, R. (2024). Unraveling Learner Self-Efficacy in the Electronic Making: Insights from Interaction Analysis, Self-Reports and Interview. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1454-1457). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: K, N. S., V, A., Saxena, A., & Rajendran, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Makerspaces serve as collaborative environments nurturing creativity and hands-on learning. Despite their potential to cultivate twenty-first-century skills, concerns persist regarding diverse participation and sustained engagement, particularly in STEM fields. Motivation, notably self-efficacy, emerges as a crucial determinant of participation and persistence. While existing studies employ surveys and longitudinal analyses, they fail to capture nuanced changes during task engagement. This research proposes the integration of interaction analysis alongside interviews and surveys to provide a comprehensive understanding of self-efficacy dynamics within makerspaces. By addressing the "why" and "what" behind self-efficacy changes, we aim to shed light on the intricate interplay between motivation and makerspace engagement. The study endeavors to answer the research question: How does interaction analysis enhance our understanding of self-efficacy dynamics in makerspaces?

title: Measuring the Effects of Combining Field Trips with Classroom Instruction on Two Different Types of Knowledge
citation: Saavedra, A., Blair, K. P., & Schwartz, D. L. (2024). Measuring the Effects of Combining Field Trips with Classroom Instruction on Two Different Types of Knowledge. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1458-1461). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Saavedra, A., Blair, K. P., & Schwartz, D. L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Field trips can represent discovery learning at its best and their outcomes are well documented. However, more research is needed to understand how FTs can be used to support student learning in combination with other instructional models. We conducted an experiment with a group of second-grade Colombian students (N=51) to investigate the effects of field trips when used in combination with classroom instruction at two different time points (before and after). We addressed two kinds of knowledge: acquisition of landscape vocabulary and orientation skills, which were covered both in the classroom instruction and as part of the field trip. For landscape vocabulary, those who received the classroom instruction before the field trip scored higher than those who attended the field trip first and then received the classroom instruction. For orientation, the pattern was reversed. Students who attended the field trip first scored higher. These findings provide initial evidence that the timing of FTs to enhance learning may be knowledge- and skill-dependent.

title: Co-Creating Space in Virtual Culinary Afterschool: Insights from Materials and Practices
citation: Chew, P., Cawelti, L., Adesida, T., & Peppler, K. (2024). Co-Creating Space in Virtual Culinary Afterschool: Insights from Materials and Practices. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1462-1465). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chew, P., Cawelti, L., Adesida, T., & Peppler, K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Scholarship in the learning sciences around space-making point to the potential of co-constructed spaces to bifurcate power within arts learning spaces. Within the realm of the culinary arts—a domain that extends learning across spatio-temporal, and sociocultural bounds through its inherent nature, we highlight the potential for leveraging the materiality and practices in food towards the co-creation of more equitable arts learning spaces. Through analyses of interviews with teachers leading a remote after school culinary arts program, we analyze how teachers and students co-constructed a culinary space through shared culinary practices and materials during the pandemic. We highlight co-creating culinary space as a culturally-sustaining practice and emphasize the role of materials and practices in space-making towards disrupting power dynamics in arts learning spaces.

title: Using AI-Based Assessment and Scaffolds to Identify Student Difficulties with Plotting Data and Modeling in Virtual Science Labs
citation: Segan, E., Gobert, J., Pedro, M. S., Adair, A., & Owens, J. A. (2024). Using AI-Based Assessment and Scaffolds to Identify Student Difficulties with Plotting Data and Modeling in Virtual Science Labs. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1466-1469). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Segan, E., Gobert, J., Pedro, M. S., Adair, A., & Owens, J. A.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Developing proficiency in science practices, including using mathematics, outlined in the Next Generation Science Standards is essential for success in STEM courses and future careers. However, students often struggle with developing mathematical models, which limits their ability to understand scientific phenomena. To improve students' learning and teachers' assessment, we extended Inq-ITS to automatically assess and scaffold students' competencies in developing mathematical models of scientific phenomena. We analyzed student data from six virtual science labs in Inq-ITS at both the practice level and the sub-practice level to determine if they maintained their mathematical competencies with scaffolding. By operationalizing and analyzing data at the sub-practice level, the results provide valuable formative data regarding the challenges students face when developing mathematical models about scientific phenomena, which in turn, can inform future scaffolds across science domains.

title: Neural Correlates of Short-Video Application Addiction and Adolescents’ Executive Functions
citation: Xu, Z., Liu, X., Chen, J., & Zhang, Y. (2024). Neural Correlates of Short-Video Application Addiction and Adolescents’ Executive Functions. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 147-153). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Xu, Z., Liu, X., Chen, J., & Zhang, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Considering the widespread influence of short-video applications (SVAs) on adolescent learners, this study aimed to examine whether and how problematic SVA use predicts their executive functions from behavioral and neural perspectives. With a sample of Chinese adolescents (Mage=12.30, N=84), behavioral results show that SVA addiction predicted lower working memory but not cognitive control performance. Their brain activation pattern during SVA use was also collected and linear regression analysis generated a neural indicator of SVA addiction on delta band. This component is proved to be a significant negative predictor of adolescents’ working memory and cognitive control performance. Both behavioral and neural evidence provide complementary perspectives on the relationship between SVA addiction and adolescents’ executive functions. The findings suggest that though SVAs have played increasingly important role in adolescents’ informal learning experiences, the negative association between SVA overuse and their cognitive functioning urges caution.

title: Leveraging Large-Language Models to Understand Self-Regulated Learning Processes in STEM Education
citation: Zhu, J., Zheng, J., Pan, Z., Biegley, L., Liu, S., Wang, T., Xie, C., & Li, M. (2024). Leveraging Large-Language Models to Understand Self-Regulated Learning Processes in STEM Education. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1470-1473). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhu, J., Zheng, J., Pan, Z., Biegley, L., Liu, S., Wang, T., Xie, C., & Li, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The study employed Large-Language Models (LLMs) to analyze students’ sequential patterns in self-regulated learning (SRL). A pre-trained LLM was fine-tuned on 106 high students’ computer trace data to learn the relationship between students’ SRL sequence and their final learning outcome. The LLM was validated against a linear baseline to demonstrate that LLM can model the SRL sequence. Furthermore, an integrated gradient method was employed to compute the sequence attribution to reveal how different sub-sequences contribute to the final learning outcome. The study found that the “evaluation-analysis” sequence had the highest attribution to a positive learning outcome. This finding demonstrated the importance of self-reflection in SRL. The proposed LLM-based analysis is possible to help educators design real-time interventions for different students to enhance their learning process.

title: Impact of Spatial Positioning on Collaborative Small Group Equity
citation: Orman, B. & Hutchison, P. (2024). Impact of Spatial Positioning on Collaborative Small Group Equity. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1474-1477). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Orman, B. & Hutchison, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Using video of collaborative small group work, we focus on three low-participating students in relatively inequitable small groups to develop a better understanding of what contextual features afford and constrain their participation. Several potential features emerged. In this paper, we focus on how students’ spatial positioning impacts in/equitable group dynamics. We propose the concept of a group’s “center of attention” to better understand why certain positioning affords or constrains students’ opportunities to learn. We find these low-participating students’ participation is afforded when their spatial positioning is improved and constrained otherwise. This finding may support more equitable small groups by suggesting strategies to increase the participation of the students who suffer the most from inequity.

title: High Achievement in Middle School: Is it a Blessing or a Curse for Adolescent Girls and Their Relationship with Themselves as Learners?
citation: d’Anjou, B., Matuk, C., & Gilligan, C. (2024). High Achievement in Middle School: Is it a Blessing or a Curse for Adolescent Girls and Their Relationship with Themselves as Learners?. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1478-1481). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: d’Anjou, B., Matuk, C., & Gilligan, C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This research in progress addresses how high-achieving middle school girls’ see themselves as learners in the face of the psychological paradox of high achievements and low self-belief. The purpose of this research is to provide a nuanced understanding of the tensions, pressures, and resistances at play (e.g. internal and external rewards, pressures, gender norms, racialized and ethnic cultural tensions) that shape girls’ sense of self. It employs the Listening Guide method, a feminist qualitative research methodology of psychological inquiry, specialized in discovery research through listening. Preliminary research described in this paper includes multiple interviews with two high-achieving middle school girls in a large city in the northeast of the United States. The contribution of this research in progress includes specific cultural, psychological, and relational patterns across the lived experiences of high-achieving girls that show the psychological logic of how they see themselves as learners.

title: Issues-Based Systems Thinking: Understandings of Complex Systems in Service of Civic Engagement
citation: Kirk, E. A. (2024). Issues-Based Systems Thinking: Understandings of Complex Systems in Service of Civic Engagement. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1482-1485). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kirk, E. A.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Understanding complex systems is vital for navigating the complexities of a globalized society. Although there is an extensive body of research aimed at supporting learners in understanding complex systems, much of this work is geared towards developing scientific knowledge, rather than explicitly preparing learners to address real-world challenges. This paper begins with an introduction to issues-based science education as an instructional context for preparing learners to make sense of complex systems in ways that support civic engagement. Next, trends in existing literature on how people learn about complex systems are reviewed, identifying a need for better alignment between how complex systems are taught in these contexts, and the overarching goal for developing knowledge that empowers learners beyond the classroom. This paper concludes by naming three principles which can be used to guide instructional design in service of these aims.

title: Evaluating Evidence in Epistemically Unfriendly Environments: Strategies and Exemplary Practices for Science Instruction
citation: Kalu-Mamji, H., Boyle, B., Chinn, C. A., & Duncan, R. G. (2024). Evaluating Evidence in Epistemically Unfriendly Environments: Strategies and Exemplary Practices for Science Instruction. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kalu-Mamji, H., Boyle, B., Chinn, C. A., & Duncan, R. G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The digital world is filled with an abundance of unfriendly and complex information. To prepare students to make sense of this information, they must learn how to engage with good and bad qualities of evidence. In this paper, we focus on the evidence evaluation dimension of the Grasp of Evidence framework to operationalize design guidelines with specific strategies that foster students’ evaluation of methodologies that generate evidence (Duncan et al., 2018). These strategies can shape learning environments to problematize good and bad evidence and the methodological processes involved in generating evidence.

title: Exploring the Features and Implications of a Project-Based Professional Development Program
citation: Castle, C., Moussavi, R., Pittack, C., Chow, C., Kang, I., & Karamcheti, M. (2024). Exploring the Features and Implications of a Project-Based Professional Development Program. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1490-1493). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Castle, C., Moussavi, R., Pittack, C., Chow, C., Kang, I., & Karamcheti, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This paper presents a pilot program for educators that focuses on designing for equity, justice, and innovation. The program leverages Project-based Learning (PBL) as an approach for effective teacher professional development. This study analyzes the presence of the core features of effective educator professional development—collaboration, inquiry and active learning, and supportive instructional practices—within the pilot program as well as what program attributes support participants’ experience of these features. The findings have implications for designing and developing teacher professional development programs.

title: Comparing In-person Vs. Online Professional Development for Brazilian Science and Technology Teacher Trainers
citation: Ricci, P. S., Laganá, T. F., Peria, C. G., Fernandez, C., Blikstein, P., & Bevilacqua, M. (2024). Comparing In-person Vs. Online Professional Development for Brazilian Science and Technology Teacher Trainers. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E.
