authors_list: Ricci, P. S., Laganá, T. F., Peria, C. G., Fernandez, C., Blikstein, P., & Bevilacqua, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Pre-service and in-service teacher education in Brazil has increasingly moved online, with 6 out of 10 teachers graduating from exclusively online programs (Todos pela Educação, 2022). While there could be benefits to online learning in terms of access, evidence from the learning sciences and teacher accounts call for limitations of such approach, and more in-person learning experiences in the context of school systems in developing countries. Based on evidence from the design and implementation of a hybrid professional development constructionist learning program, we aim to shed light on the challenges and affordances of synchronous, asynchronous, and in-person modalities for professional development.

title: The Undervalued Disciplinary and Emotional Support Provided By Teaching Assistants in Introductory Computer Science Courses
citation: Li, Y., Zhang, H., & O'Rourke, E. (2024). The Undervalued Disciplinary and Emotional Support Provided By Teaching Assistants in Introductory Computer Science Courses. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1498-1501). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Li, Y., Zhang, H., & O'Rourke, E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: In computer science (CS) higher education, many students in introductory courses (CS1) struggle to learn programming due to both the complexity of the discipline and negative affective experiences while learning. Large class sizes hinder the opportunity to receive support that addresses both disciplinary knowledge and affective experiences, both of which have been shown to influence self-efficacy. Our work utilized a combination of structured daily diaries and retrospective interviews to surface participants’ programming experiences, affective responses, and self-perceptions. Through two case studies, we highlight the intertwined nature of disciplinary knowledge and affective experiences in the learning process of students in CS1, and advocate for increased attention to student interactions with TAs as an opportunity to provide affective support along with disciplinary learning.

title: The Effects of Prompt Scaffolding on Learning to Write Arguments with ChatGPT
citation: Jang, J., Eun, S., Lee, H., Choi, J., & Cho, Y. H. (2024). The Effects of Prompt Scaffolding on Learning to Write Arguments with ChatGPT. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1502-1505). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jang, J., Eun, S., Lee, H., Choi, J., & Cho, Y. H.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Although ChatGPT can be useful for writing, it is not certain whether ChatGPT is beneficial for learning to write particularly when ChatGPT carries out the task instead of learners. To enhance the positive effect of ChatGPT in learning to write, teachers should provide students appropriate scaffoldings on creating prompts, which are crucial in interacting with ChatGPT. This study aims to investigate the effects of prompt scaffoldings on learning to write arguments with ChatGPT. In this study, 179 Korean high school students participated, and they were assigned into experiment and control groups. This study found that the experiment group that received prompt scaffoldings outperformed the control group in regards to self-efficacy, interest, knowledge, and performance in argumentative writing. This study implies that ChatGPT can be beneficial for learning only when learners effectively interact with it.

title: Racial Equity Frames in Creative Learning Organizations
citation: Salvage, A. & Anderson, E. (2024). Racial Equity Frames in Creative Learning Organizations. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1506-1509). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Salvage, A. & Anderson, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Creative learning organizations (CLOs) play an increasingly important role in educational ecosystems—and the pursuit of racial equity. Despite recent efforts, many such organizations serve disproportionately White and affluent visitors, particularly among museums. Utilizing public-facing website text, we used CLO’s "about us,” mission, and DEIA statements, to capture the degree to which racial equity is or is not central to each organization’s overall organizational identity. We identified five overlapping organizational fields in which CLOs hold membership, and found that, despite modest differences across fields, most CLOs make use of exclusively race- and equity- evasive frames, apart from ethnic/cultural organizations. CLOs that do mention race or equity tend to de-center these concepts through location or lack of depth. Implications include insights for both practitioners and researchers, as to what field-level pressures exist for CLOs, and how these pressures may be contested for greater racial equity.

title: Elementary School Students’ Mental Models of Human-AI Relationships: Tool, Servant, and Companion
citation: Cho, S. & Cho, Y. H. (2024). Elementary School Students’ Mental Models of Human-AI Relationships: Tool, Servant, and Companion. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1510-1513). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cho, S. & Cho, Y. H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study explored the mental models of elementary school students on human-AI relationships, which might influence how they interacted with AI in education and everyday lifes. For this purpose, this study provided students a task of drawing the life with AI at home in 10 years, which was followed by interviews. In this study, a total of 51 students from 4th to 6th grades in an elementary school participated in the drawing task, and 27 of the students participated in the interviews. Elementary school students' mental models for the relationship between humans and AI were categorized based on the relationship metaphor, relational distance, and the possibility of conflict. As a result of the study, three mental models were found: User-Tool (UT), Master-Servants (MS), and Companion-Companion (CC).

title: Tracking Sensory Regulation During Embodied Learning with Electrodermal Activity: A Comparative Case Study
citation: Sar-Israel, M., Zhang, F. E., Liu, Y., & Tancredi, S. (2024). Tracking Sensory Regulation During Embodied Learning with Electrodermal Activity: A Comparative Case Study. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1514-1517). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sar-Israel, M., Zhang, F. E., Liu, Y., & Tancredi, S.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Sensory stimulation from motor activity has been found to play a role in regulating learners' arousal levels. Although research on movement and learning is on the rise in the learning sciences, the impact of instructional designs’ incorporation of movement on arousal regulation has not been examined. In this comparative case study, we explore whether and how sensory regulation of arousal unfolds in the context of a highly sensorimotor instruction. Within a larger design-based research project on balance-based math learning, we used electrodermal activity data to explore how the arousal levels of two participants with opposite sensory profiles varied in response to different types of sensory-stimulating movement, finding distinct arousal profiles for each child. Based on our findings, we outline hypotheses and possible next steps towards research integrating sensory regulation into conceptualizing embodied learning.

title: Investigating Cultural Signatures in Game Designs of Middle School Students from Argentina, India, and the United States
citation: Gattupalli, S., Castro, F. E., & Arroyo, I. (2024). Investigating Cultural Signatures in Game Designs of Middle School Students from Argentina, India, and the United States. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1518-1521). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Gattupalli, S., Castro, F. E. V. G., & Arroyo, I.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Cultural signatures can offer insights into the ways that learners draw on their cultural backgrounds and experiences as they engage within learning environments. Our work aims to understand how learners within game design learning contexts use cultural signatures to express their cultural identities within game elements. We analyzed game designs from students in Argentina, India, and the United States and described how cultural signatures reflect specific cultural contexts and connect to game elements and mechanics. Our work highlights the value of creating computing learning experiences that support and engage learners’ rich cultural identities, particularly within game design-based learning environments.

title: “Dirty Waters”: Science Teachers’ Perceptions of Discussing Politics in Science Learning Spaces
citation: Gopal, S. D. & Honwad, S. (2024). “Dirty Waters”: Science Teachers’ Perceptions of Discussing Politics in Science Learning Spaces. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1522-1525). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Gopal, S. D. & Honwad, S.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Science education has historically tended to call itself apolitical or neutral and consequently been unwelcoming to conversations about how science is and has always been politically charged. More recently, scholars underline that science learning spaces must begin to intentionally integrate the way political actors shape how societies respond to present day science issues (e.g., climate change, health) so that students are better prepared to be civic leaders as scientists or other relevant stakeholders. Using narrative interview data from a study exploring influencing factors for what and how science teachers in Guyana teach about socio-political dimensions of science issues, this submission explores the why for the way teachers conceive of the relationship between politics and science learning. We use this to consider what would be required of teachers, of students, and of society to effectively use political discourse as an avenue for developing criticality towards historical healing, resilience, and community.

title: Which Collaborative Behavior can Enhance Inter-Brain Synchronization and Group Performance During STEM Collaboration? A fNIRS Hypersanning Study
citation: Wang, F. Y., Zhang, Y., Zhang, M., Teo, W., & Dong, Y. (2024). Which Collaborative Behavior can Enhance Inter-Brain Synchronization and Group Performance During STEM Collaboration? A fNIRS Hypersanning Study. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1526-1529). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wang, F. Y., Zhang, Y., Zhang, M., Teo, W., & Dong, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Collaboration plays a crucial role in STEM education. This study aimed to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying the benefits of collaborative behaviors using fNIRS hyperscanning. The prefrontal cortex (PFC) and right temporoparietal junction (r-TPJ) were targeted as regions of interest. Three key findings emerged from the analysis. First, IBS in the r-TPJ increased during the initial phases of collaboration, while IBS in the PFC increased during the later phases. Second, the frequency of scaffolding and questioning behaviors exhibited a significant positive correlation with the enhancement of IBS in the r-TPJ. Furthermore, the frequency of scaffolding behavior during the initial phases significantly correlated with task outcomes' fluency, integration, and technology scores. Overall, this study sheds light on the impact of different collaborative behaviors on IBS in different brain regions and task performance and proposes a new perspective on learning science using the brain-scanning method of fNIRS hyperscanning.

title: Personal and Group Identity Processes of Americans and Israelis in a Cross-Continental Educational Journey
citation: Firer, E. & Nikritin, D. (2024). Personal and Group Identity Processes of Americans and Israelis in a Cross-Continental Educational Journey. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1530-1533). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Firer, E. & Nikritin, D.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: In this research, we explore the processes of identity change that occurred among nine Israeli adolescents during a unique educational program. A group comprised of both Israeli and American adolescents embarked on a journey across continents aiming to strengthen both their personal and Jewish identities. We investigated the processes of change experienced by the participants and the factors they reported that led to these changes. Participants indicated that the processes of change were influenced by the places they visited but, more significantly, by their interpersonal and group interactions. They reported changes in perceptions of personal and familial identity, as well as in perceptions of religious and national identity. The findings provide insights into how encounters with others impact identity formation processes, facilitate self-exploration, and foster changes in both personal and broader dimensions of identity.

title: Narrative Interviews for Studying Teacher Sense-making of Equity
citation: Neihaus, A. (2024). Narrative Interviews for Studying Teacher Sense-making of Equity. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1534-1537). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Neihaus, A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: While equity has been an emphasis of teacher education research for several decades, there remains a need for studies that investigate how teachers make sense of equity. In this study, I employed a narrative framework to investigate what educative experiences prospective teachers draw upon when making sense of equity. This short paper describes the methods and underlying theory of that work, as well as initially findings.

title: Youth Identity Enactments through Storytelling during Co-design of an Educational Virtual Game World
citation: Radke, S. C., Hardy, L., & Kahn, J. B. (2024). Youth Identity Enactments through Storytelling during Co-design of an Educational Virtual Game World. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1538-1541). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Radke, S. C., Hardy, L., & Kahn, J. B.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This paper examines youth storytelling during co-design of an identity-expressive educational game for learning data science. Using interaction analysis of co-design interviews with middle school students, we explore how storytelling allows participants to (a) use existing game elements to position themselves and (b) express their interests and identities through imagined game futures. We argue that analyzing youth's interactive storytelling and identity enactments during co-design can inform the development of game narratives that represent diverse youth. Our findings contribute to the design of inclusive virtual worlds for STEM learning that celebrate youth identities and experiences. We discuss implications for engaging youth voices in the co-design process and creating educational games that resonate with diverse learners.

title: Exploring the Potential of Design in Early Childhood Education for Sustainability
citation: Du, Y. & Zhang, W. (2024). Exploring the Potential of Design in Early Childhood Education for Sustainability. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 154-161). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Du, Y. & Zhang, W.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Kindergarteners play a crucial role in driving sustainable changes, and there is a growing interest in combining design approaches with sustainable education. This paper presents empirical research on Early Childhood Education for Sustainability (ECEfS) conducted in China. It aims to examine the current situation of ECEfS implementation in Chinese kindergartens and investigate the role of design in promoting its objectives. Qualitative research techniques were adopted in this study, and data collected from a kindergarten were analyzed. Our findings reveal the integration of relevant practices into their nature-based learning curricula. In summary, their ECEfS-related practices fall into three design-oriented categories: a) project-based activities to foster sustainable awareness, b) environmental design to create sustainable learning spaces, and c) co-design approaches for exploring sustainable materials.

title: Using Adapted Conjecture Maps to Foster Interdisciplinary Collaboration Between Learning Scientists and Novice AI-Ed Researchers
citation: Chang, M. A., Roschelle, J., Dickler-Mann, R., & Bush, J. B. (2024). Using Adapted Conjecture Maps to Foster Interdisciplinary Collaboration Between Learning Scientists and Novice AI-Ed Researchers. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1542-1545). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chang, M. A., Roschelle, J., Dickler-Mann, R., & Bush, J. B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: As the rate of progress in artificial intelligence (AI) research accelerates, learning scientists increasingly engage in deep collaboration with AI researchers to design learning tools. In entering into these interdisciplinary collaborations for the first time, AI researchers bring with them epistemic and practical commitments to design and research that differ significantly from the learning sciences. In this paper, we demonstrate a case study where learning scientists and AI researchers use an adapted form of a conjecture map as a boundary object to improve outcomes of design-based research. We highlight two moves, “zooming in” and “looking across”, that support boundary crossing moments that weave connections between technical decisions and learning processes. We then show how these moves lead to conversations around mitigating unintended consequences of designs based in artificial intelligence.

title: “I See It Less as the Icing on the Cake and More of the Cake Itself”: Educators’ Understandings of Culturally Responsive Pedagogy
citation: Tissenbaum, C. D. & Lane, M. L. (2024). “I See It Less as the Icing on the Cake and More of the Cake Itself”: Educators’ Understandings of Culturally Responsive Pedagogy. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1546-1549). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tissenbaum, C. D. & Lane, M. L.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Culturally responsive pedagogy (CRP) directly embeds learners’ cultural, racial, linguistic, gendered, and classed identities into curricula, materials, and teaching practices. While CRP is increasingly recognized for its capacity to support learners’ academic and emotional growth, educators need information and training to sustainably embed CRP into everyday praxis. In response, we developed an eight-session professional development program that connected PreK-12 teachers and instructional coaches with informal learning educators to deepen their understanding of CRP and collaboratively design lessons and programs. This paper presents a preliminary qualitative analysis of participants’ descriptions of CRP principles and practices, along with barriers to implementing CRP, as evidenced in semi-structured pre-post interviews. Our findings contribute to research about culturally responsive teacher preparation by highlighting strengths and gaps in how professional training about CRP is delivered.

title: A Preliminary Model for Responsive Co-Design
citation: Swanson, H. & Lawrence, L. (2024). A Preliminary Model for Responsive Co-Design. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1550-1553). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Swanson, H. & Lawrence, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Education reform is pushing teachers to teach in ways that are unfamiliar and which present challenges. One approach to helping teachers build comfort and capacity for implementing new and innovative teaching strategies is co-design. In this paper, we build on prior research to concretely articulate how researchers can partner with teachers to foster mutual learning, build capacity, and cultivate comfort through responsive practices. Towards this, we present a theoretical model of a vision of co-design, which we call responsive co-design. Our model borrows concepts from responsive teaching, which is a family of pedagogical approaches that seek to elicit and build on student ideas. Our vision of responsive co-design expands how co-design has been theorized to include the generative, asset-based, and inclusive practices of responsive teaching.

title: The Practice of Mathematical Restorying to Foster Healing for Prospective Elementary Teachers
citation: Scott, M. & Zuniga-Ruiz, S. (2024). The Practice of Mathematical Restorying to Foster Healing for Prospective Elementary Teachers. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1554-1557). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Scott, M. & Zuniga-Ruiz, S.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Research has documented the prevalence of math anxiety and negative emotions related to school mathematics both in the wider population and specifically for elementary teachers. While scholarship has often treated math anxiety as an individual problem, we consider mathematical experiences to be socially and culturally constructed and intertwined with dominant storylines about mathematical competence. In this paper, we explore storytelling and restorying as a way to investigate and support the developing mathematical identities of elementary teachers. We analyze the stories a prospective elementary teacher tells about herself with respect to mathematics, how her stories shift over time as a result of her math methods course and the impacts of the practice of restorying on her views of themselves and of children. We find the process of rewriting their own mathematical stories can support prospective teachers to begin to imagine new mathematical possibilities for themselves and for children.

title: Toward Liberatory Praxis: Facilitative Moves and Tensions in Youth Organizing
citation: Lee, S. P. & Worsley, M. (2024). Toward Liberatory Praxis: Facilitative Moves and Tensions in Youth Organizing. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1558-1561). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lee, S. P. & Worsley, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Building on pedagogies of liberation through youth participatory action research (YPAR), this work explicates the role of adult facilitators as they navigate tensions and make sense of their roles and responsibilities within an emerging youth council. The cases highlight the complexity of intergenerational relationships within youth-centered research, specifically in the context of organizing. This work demonstrates a need for further work that examines the interactional micro-moments between youth and adults that embody a praxis of liberatory education.

title: Exploring STEM Identity and Belonging in Minoritized Girls at a Summer Camp
citation: Milton, S., Sager, M. T., & Walkington, C. (2024). Exploring STEM Identity and Belonging in Minoritized Girls at a Summer Camp. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1562-1565). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Milton, S., Sager, M. T., & Walkington, C.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study explores STEM identity among Underrepresented and Underserved Racially and Ethnically Minoritized (UUREM) middle school girls within informal learning settings. Focusing on micro-level interactions, we explored a single-gendered STEM summer camp where UUREM middle school girls comprised 81% of the participants (N=59). Guided by ecological systems theory as a methodological approach to developing well-designed informal STEM activities, we sought to positively shape UUREM middle school girls’ STEM identity. STEM identity is complex, multi-layered, and inseparable from the intersectionality of their racial and gender identities. This approach is particularly salient in affective factors such as self-efficacy, ability-belief, and a sense of belonging during their pivotal middle school years. Critical implications include (a) single-gender spaces, like STEM camps, provide affirming, safe environments for authentic discussion and belonging in STEM, and (b) role models of similar racial and gender backgrounds support positive STEM identity formation for UUREM middle school girls.

title: How does Gender Influence Math Classes?: A case of a Storytelling Activity about Learning Vector

subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: In this study, the teacher specifically uses storytelling as a tool for drama-based learning, which offers a space for students to co-construct meaning together. The teacher embeds the storytelling teaching method into a math class for a new educational lens. By collecting classroom data and trying to focus on the students’ understanding and engagement, we explore students’ different perspectives on learning the concept of vectors. Through classroom dialogues and students’ storytelling performances, we aim to figure out the relationships between students’ genders and storytelling activities. This study incorporates learning observation and interviews with three 8th graders.

subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Social & Civic Studies

abstract: Developing history education that considers learners' contexts and interests has been a long-standing challenge. To address this issue, this study designed an AI application based on an existing algorithm that can present multiple contemporary news sites with similar causal structures when learners input the causal relationships of interest into what they have learned in history. Formative evaluations with high school students confirmed the effectiveness of the application in providing contemporary news sites that learners find relevant according to their interests, as well as in increasing the significance of history learning in various ways. For example, the effects of new discoveries regarding the relationship between history and recent news increased interest in both were confirmed. The design of this AI application therefore has practical significance for the advancement of education methods.

citation: Park, W., Waight, N., St. Vil., C., Miles, M., & Mozaffari, F. (2024). Reimagining Justice-Oriented Science Education through Disaster Memories: Evidence from the Buffalo Blizzard of 2022. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1574-1577). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Park, W., Waight, N., Vil, C. S., Miles, M., & Mozaffari, F.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Abstract:In line with the increasing emphasis on the role of science education in challenging injustices and promoting social justice, this paper presents an ongoing project that seeks to address disaster justice issues in the context of the Buffalo Blizzard of 2022. The project uses the theoretical lens of disaster justice to document the experiences of families, science teachers and community leaders in Buffalo to identify the injustices during the blizzard that left 31 people dead. The social justice issues revealed from the interviews—those of distribution, representation and recognition—lead to co-constructing principles and priorities for science and climate education in Buffalo, NY. In this paper, we present the study background, theoretical framework, and early findings that emerged from interviews with community members. The findings suggest ways in which science education can help redress the needs and goals of marginalized and vulnerable communities in the context of climate disasters.

title: Towards an Intelligent Augmented Reality Tutoring System for Precision Manufacturing
citation: Torshizi, P. G., Tarashiyoun, H., Moghaddam, M., & Marsella, S. (2024). Towards an Intelligent Augmented Reality Tutoring System for Precision Manufacturing. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1578-1581). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Torshizi, P. G., Tarashiyoun, H., Moghaddam, M., & Marsella, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: With an aging workforce, the manufacturing sector faces an increasing demand for skilled workers. To address this challenge, we introduce an innovative training approach that seeks to couple Augmented Reality (AR) and Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS). Focused on complex psychomotor skills required in precision inspection tasks common to aerospace, medical, and defense industries, our prototype AR tutoring system delivers adaptive and real-time instructions and feedback. Through a Wizard of Oz (WOZ) study, we investigate transitioning from conventional AR systems to an intelligent AR tutoring system that adapts to individual learner needs. This study addresses the benefits and challenges posed by this transition and proposes solutions and recommendations. The study contributes to our understanding of how AR and ITS can jointly tailor instruction to learner needs in complex psychomotor tasks. Results from the WOZ study argue adaptive scaffolding improves training outcomes and helps identify technical challenges in automating the scaffolding.

title: Mapping Disinformation: Agent-Based Modelling Instruction for Cognitive and Systemic Dimensions of Media Ecosystems
citation: Russo, R., Hong, E., Wei, Z., Lei, Y., & Blikstein, P. (2024). Mapping Disinformation: Agent-Based Modelling Instruction for Cognitive and Systemic Dimensions of Media Ecosystems. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1582-1585). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Russo, R., Hong, E., Wei, Z., Lei, Y., & Blikstein, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: As disinformation ecosystems expand, they present numerous threats to society and challenges to educators and researchers, who employ diverse approaches to prepare learners for the increasingly challenging task of assessing the reliability of information. We developed a curriculum unit based on agent-based computational modeling (ABM) and studied how that unit improved learners’ understanding of individual and systems-level factors of disinformation ecosystems. We used concept maps as approximations of learners’ knowledge structures. We identified changes in those concept maps that are associated with concepts addressed by our ABM unit. More markedly, participants included visual features in the concept maps that correlated with both individual and systems-level aspects of disinformation (such as cognitive biases and echo chambers) and represented concepts that we conjecture go beyond recall of variables present in the models. Evidence points to opportunities for employing ABM for the exploration of the multiple dimensions of disinformation.

abstract: This study examines the impact of a two-week long automated greenhouse project on middle school students' interest and competency belief in coding. This intervention involved aspects of physical computing, block-based programming, use of data, and understanding of plant science, which aligns with ideas of transdisciplinary, situated, and project-based learning. By analyzing pre- and post-surveys and interviews, we found an overall increase in students' interest. However, competency belief showed a varied pattern: it increased among students in the lower quartile but decreased among those in the higher quartile. Insights from the interviews highlighted potential improvements to the design of the project, aiming to maximize its benefits for all participants.

citation: Booth, E. T., Flood, V. J., & Harrer, B. W. (2024). The Enactment of an Instant: A Study of Gesture in Introductory Physics. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Gesture has been shown to play an important role in how learners conceptualize phenomena in physics. However, we know little about how gesture is used to conceptualize instantaneity. Drawing on multimodal microanalysis of interaction, we examine how undergraduate physics students use representational gesture to make sense of instants while modeling energy dynamics. Our analysis describes four different forms of representational gesture used to capture instantaneity: These include (1) Replay loop of scenario, (2) Subinterval on timeline, (3) Freeze frame of scenario, and (4) Indexical location on timeline.

abstract: Assessing scientific thinking and inquiry skills can be challenging because of the complexity and divergence in student behaviors. Scholars have advocated the use of more open-ended problems and choice for the assessment of scientific inquiry. In this paper, we interrogate an experimentation mechanic in an educational science game to examine challenges that choice introduces to game-based assessment of science inquiry practices. Descriptive analysis of gameplay elucidates the difference between choices to explore and iterating on choices as a sign of struggling to progress.

title:
ISEA: Instructor-in-the-loop Student Engagement Analytics
via FAccT AI

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: AI has become increasingly popular in analyzing student engagement in online environments over the last decade; however, it is still not widely adopted in practice by instructors, partly due to AI’s black box problem. Engagement analytics may fail to analyze the complexity of the engagement construct in theory, and instructors may lack trust and control in techniques. To tackle these issues, we designed and developed the ISEA toolkit. We then conducted interviews with six instructors to understand their concerns with applying AI in engagement analytics and their experience in using ISEA. Participants showed diverse ways to analyze student engagement via ISEA and expressed how it improved their trust in engagement analytics. The results showcased an effective way to integrate instructors’ opinions, learning theories, and techniques together toward acceptance of AI when analytics are more transparent.

subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study investigated the effect of gamification on university students’ immersion, motivation, and cultural heritage learning in the context of a Virtual Reality (VR) learning environment. An experimental research design was adopted to analyze the experience of forty-six (n=46) undergraduate students who were randomly assigned to two conditions (Gamified / Non-gamified VR environment). Data were collected using pre- and post-learning assessments, immersion and motivation questionnaires. Analyses showed that students in the gamified VR learning environment experienced higher levels of attention and flow, reported greater perceived competence, and exhibited increased learning gains, in comparison to their counterparts who used the non-gamified VR environment. Moreover, higher and more positive correlations were identified between students’ immersion, motivation and learning in the gamified condition. The findings of this study can contribute to the principled design of VR environments to optimize students’ knowledge acquisition and learning experience.

title: Undergraduates’ Prototyping Process in a Design Class about Engineering Education Games and Community-Based Learning
citation: Marvez, G. R. & Pérez, G. (2024). Undergraduates’ Prototyping Process in a Design Class about Engineering Education Games and Community-Based Learning. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. authors_list: Marvez, G. R. & Pérez, G.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: STEM learning games can engage students across subjects at higher levels than lectures and provide avenues for students to “try on” STEM careers. However, many STEM learning games are not positioned around specific STEM concepts within a real-world community, a drawback for teaching highly contextualized topics in STEM. In this study, we investigate learning experiences of undergraduates who co-created game prototypes focused on a local engineering challenge in partnership with young students in local culturally and linguistically diverse communities. Preliminary findings indicate undergraduates understood and were critical towards the iterative co-design process while refining their games in collaboration with younger community members. This research suggests involving undergraduates in designing engineering learning games with and for local communities fosters an understanding of engineering practices and establishes a connection between undergraduate students and the communities they may eventually serve, offering a valuable educational approach for first-year undergraduates majoring in engineering.

subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Prisms VR, a secondary math learning application, allows for users to see, manipulate, and engage with mathematical concepts in an embodied way in Virtual Reality (VR) environment. We examine cases in which mathematics teachers and middle school students worked through Prisms and reflected upon their experiences. Findings indicate that VR environments can help teachers find alternative ways of presenting algebraic concepts in a hands-on, interactive, and embodied manner; and these findings were confirmed based on the student experience. VR allows teachers to make connections through scaffolding and personalized experiences, while also aiding students in the exploration and meaning-making.

title: Constraints and Boundaries for Collective Agency in Co-Design
citation: Tierney, G. & Stamatis, K. (2024). Constraints and Boundaries for Collective Agency in Co-Design. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. authors_list: Tierney, G. & Stamatis, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Co-design in education has emerged as an avenue for including broader perspectives into the creation of curriculum and learning environments, while also positively impacting learning and identity development. This kind of co-design requires designers’ collective agentic participation. In this paper, we look across several sets of data to build understandings of the ways collective agency emerges and is constrained within co-design. While research has pointed to the ways that participation in co-design has potential to increase feelings of agency in practitioners and youth, there is still a need to understand the ways communities of designers build and use collective agency. Without theories that describe the ways that co-design teams leverage their collective identities toward common outcomes, we fear that the power of this kind of work can fall short of its potential.

title: “I'm with Peppa”: University STEM Faculty Listening to Student Reasoning
citation: Ajilore, O., Appleby, L., Gouvea, J., Tobin, R., & Hammer, D. (2024). “I'm with Peppa”: University STEM Faculty Listening to Student Reasoning. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Prior research in K-¬12 STEM education has focused on cultivating teachers’ abilities to notice, interpret, and engage with the substance of student thinking. There has not, however, been similar attention in higher education professional development (PD). We present data from a session of The Listening Project (LP), designed to support university STEM faculty attention to student thinking, based significantly on prior work in K-12 with a key difference: LP faculty work across disciplines. Participants examine and discuss student thinking both within and outside their own disciplines. We argue that interdisciplinary community plays an important role in faculty developing “epistemic empathy”.

title: Toward Onto-epistemic Heterogeneity through Culinary Making: Insights from a Learning Narrative
citation: Chew, P. & Bisht, A. (2024). Toward Onto-epistemic Heterogeneity through Culinary Making: Insights from a Learning Narrative. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. authors_list: Chew, P. & Bisht, A.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Recent discourse within the learning sciences toward onto-epistemic heterogeneity challenges static, hegemonic notions of disciplinarity in learning and their resulting inequities for historically marginalized learners. We present an exploratory autoethnographic learning narrative and reflect on how three sensibilities of onto-epistemic heterogeneity—multiplicity, horizontality, and dialogicality—present in an account of cooking situated in a relational history between the co-authors. This paper operationalizes onto-epistemic heterogeneity as a framework within the understudied domain of culinary learning to surface the following insights on learning: 1) how analogy enables complex, culturally situated, cross-disciplinary maneuvers, and 2) the ways that relational histories sustain and are sustained by learning that centers on them. We emphasize the implications and potential of future work around such learning processes in the quotidian context of culinary learning towards proliferating ontological, epistemic, and axiological shifts in what constitutes disciplinarity and learning.

title: The Relationship between Teacher-Student Interaction and Student Well-Being in South Korea
citation: Choo, Y., Eun, S., & Cho, Y. H. (2024). The Relationship between Teacher-Student Interaction and Student Well-Being in South Korea. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. authors_list: Choo, Y., Eun, S., & Cho, Y. H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Interactions between a teacher and students are vital not only for acquiring knowledge but also for student well-being. Although student well-being is an important goal of K-12 schools, teachers are less likely to focus on it when compared to academic achievements particularly in an exam-oriented society. This study investigates how elementary school students interact with their teacher and how teacher-student interactions are related to student well-being in South Korea. Nine video recordings of a class were collected to analyze teacher-student interaction frequencies, durations, and types. This study found that student well-being was significantly correlated with the frequency and duration of teacher-student interactions. The autonomy-supportive interactions were not significantly correlated with student well-being, which might be influenced by the school culture in South Korea. This study underscores the role of teachers in supporting student well-being.

title: Diving into Joyful Disciplinary Investigation as a Practice of Resistance and Healing
citation: Baldinger, E. M. & Scott, M. (2024). Diving into Joyful Disciplinary Investigation as a Practice of Resistance and Healing. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. authors_list: Baldinger, E. M. & Scott, M.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Experiences of joy can foster learning, connection, and a sense of hope in unjust and dehumanizing environments. Schooling is increasingly organized toward different ends, prioritizing “accountability” and standardization over choice, creativity, and joy. This paper shares our emerging analysis, examining the work of two justice-focused teachers in an alternative school environment, where trends toward checklists and pressure to “earn” credits are particularly pervasive. Drawing from a spiritual and political articulation of joy as involving not only fun but also empathy, empowerment, and engagement with the world, we investigate how these teachers’ repeated choice to dive into disciplinary engagement functioned to bring these multiple dimensions of joy into their work, thus becoming a practice of healing and resistance.

abstract: As part of a larger design-based research study, we developed middle school social studies and computer science units with a focus on food sovereignty to help students understand treaties and their ongoing impact on Indigenous people today. This paper reports on the iterative process of developing and implementing culturally responsive-sustaining computing curricula, particularly focusing on feedback from a master teacher panel. Teachers were excited about engaging students in computer science by linking it to their everyday lives, but also concerned about the difficulty of making complex concepts like food sovereignty accessible to students.

abstract: To centralize disciplinary relationships, we use a critical posthumanist approach towards material agency to conceptualize a conversation as an iterative cycle of attention and responsive action. By characterizing disciplinary conversations as those conversations that are shaped by the discipline and contribute to shaping the discipline, we focus on how conversations both shape relationships and are shaped by relationships.

citation: Ćosić, L. (2024). “Listen to Each Other Through the Whole Self”: Silence, Stillness, and Collective Tuning in Theatre Learning. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. abstract: In a black box theater on a university campus, ten actors stand in a line, shoulder to shoulder. Together, they learn how to do something in perfect unison– without ever visibly communicating. This article centers the methodological tensions that arose in using dominant forms of analysis to understand this ensemble event and investigates the possibility of alternate, relational interpretations that may make the actors’ collective learning visible.

title: Epistemological Framing of Chemistry Assessment Items
citation: Kim, A. E., Farris, A. V., & Lee, E. (2024). Epistemological Framing of Chemistry Assessment Items. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. authors_list: Kim, A. E., Farris, A. V., & Lee, E.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This study explores undergraduate chemistry students’ epistemic frames for stoichiometry assessment items. We interviewed 40 introductory chemistry students to understand their experiences of a selection of items which were presented as pairs containing one traditional format item, typical of what is used in their undergraduate course, and a revised form, modified following principles of the Equitable Framework for Classroom Assessment (Siegel, 2007). Our analysis suggests that how the item is presented (i.e., as an exam or homework item) is very important to students’ epistemic frame and goals. We found that students perceive efficiency (of time) as one key affordance of conceptual problems. Finally, students are cognizant of differences in problems that elicit understanding of concepts rather than mere mathematical manipulation and place substantial value on the former. Our study is a step towards forms of items that support learning aims and assessment aims as joint goals.

title: One Teacher’s Journey toward Inquiry Methods
citation: Zhang, X., Chen, J., Huang, Z., Tian, H., Huang, S., Su, X., Carvalho, R., & Slotta, J. D. (2024). One Teacher’s Journey toward Inquiry Methods. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In response to the increasingly complex social identity development of students, China's education reform focuses on developing students' core competence. The South China PLC is a professional learning community participated by Chinese teachers, which aims to provide support for teachers' professional development, help teachers design and implement inquiry projects, so as to cultivate students' core competence and implement the requirements of education reform. This paper reports on the trajectory of one teacher, Mr. Z, who gradually developed a student-centered teaching philosophy and understanding of inquiry methods with the help of researchers and other participants. Over the course of 2 years, Mr. Z designed and implemented an inquiry curriculum, enacted it in his classroom, then revised the curriculum based on his experience.

title: Between Dead-ends and Meatballs: Mathematical Practice as Embodied and Interactionally Accomplished
citation: Velamur, A. (2024). Between Dead-ends and Meatballs: Mathematical Practice as Embodied and Interactionally Accomplished. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. authors_list: Velamur, A.
subject: STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This paper explores the social collaborative nature of mathematical work through a critical examination of the interactions between two professional mathematicians engaged in an afternoon of reading, writing, and mathematical problem solving. Drawing on Goodwin’s (2003) conceptualization of the semiotic body in its environment, I offer an account of mathematics as an embodied practice that is accomplished through social interaction, the recruitment of tools, the creation of artifacts, and a coordinated assemblage of these tools, artifacts, and actors. Focusing on excerpts of interactions and events from an afternoon spent with mathematicians Natalie and Usman, the analysis presented here seeks to unsettle normative understandings of mathematics as a non-material, abstract practice, instead making a third-world feminist case for the embodied, concrete, social-relational nature of mathematical knowledge production.

title: Play and Design: Faculty Perceptions on Playful Interventions for Collaborative Learning in the Design Studio
citation: John, P. M. & Sharma, P. (2024). Play and Design: Faculty Perceptions on Playful Interventions for Collaborative Learning in the Design Studio. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The design studio is the cornerstone of art and design education where students learn the creative process through working on open ended design problems. These spaces have been critiqued for not reflecting the collaborative nature of the profession where designers work in interdisciplinary teams. Play and playful interventions are known to support creative exploration and collaborative learning. However, play in the context of the design studio has largely been unexplored. In this exploratory study, we interview instructors from different disciplinary backgrounds to understand how play innately manifests in their teaching practice. We synthesize the findings to present considerations for future works that incorporate the notion of play into the design studio model to support collaborative learning.

title: Ambient Identity Cues for Minoritized Students in Elementary STEM Classrooms
citation: Kim, C., Lee, E., Dinç, E., Chatters, S. J., & Belland, B. R. (2024). Ambient Identity Cues for Minoritized Students in Elementary STEM Classrooms. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kim, C., Lee, E., Dinç, E., Chatters, S. J., & Belland, B. R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Children build identity as early as elementary school as they receive messages about who belongs in which disciplines, often through ambient identity cues. We studied how and why elementary STEM teachers create classroom designs and use teaching materials that serve as material, relational, and ideational identity resources with which children build their disciplinary identities. Two elementary STEM teachers, and three minoritized elementary students participated in this study. Data were collected from classroom design, teaching materials, journaling, and artifact-based interviews. Findings include that teachers’ sensemaking of ambient identity cues varied between objects for classroom design and those for content teaching.

abstract: This paper examined how four Latinx women interested in pursuing STEM-Health pathways made meaning of possible futures over three years while they participated in a summer STEM-Health program (HSTEP) and while taking science and math AP and Honors courses in an urban STEM magnet high school. I developed a conceptual framework about how young people make links to the future in connection to STEM learning by drawing on social psychological and sociocultural perspectives from the learning sciences. I found that the types of relational and pedagogical supports each context made available shaped conditions for learning about STEM and, in turn, shaped how participants linked learning experiences to the future. This analysis helps us consider why it is important to design learning environments to experience and envision futures in STEM connected to the goals of STEM education.

title: Paper or Virtual Reality First? The Impact of Material Sequence on Science Learning Outcomes
citation: Kim, T. (2024). Paper or Virtual Reality First? The Impact of Material Sequence on Science Learning Outcomes. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. authors_list: Kim, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
tpack_tk_labels: Immersive VR / AR; Simulations & Scientific Modeling
abstract: Although past research has examined the efficacy of sequencing learning materials, most studies on the use of virtual reality (VR) in educational settings have focused on comparing its effectiveness with traditional learning media. However, insufficient investigation exists exploring how utilizing VR sequencing alongside existing learning materials affects learning outcomes. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by examining learning outcomes when student subjects engaged with scientific concepts via VR simulation and paper-based materials, assessing how the sequence of exposure—VR or paper first—influenced their learning. Results show that students who studied paper materials before learning through VR performed significantly better than those who did the reverse. Furthermore, we found students who first learned the material using VR showed a slight decrease in their ability to verbally explain the concepts they had learned after studying with paper materials.

title: Examining Design Features of a Research Experience for Teachers in Mechanobiology towards Promoting K-12 STEM Integration

abstract: Learning in real-world contexts and problem-solving using interdisciplinary perspectives is essential in education. In this case study, we engaged ten local teachers in a summer research experience with sustained school year professional development, and investigated how specific design features could support teachers in STEM integration. We found the teachers gained essential skills needed for success (e.g., obtaining disciplinary knowledge needed to make explicit connections across STEM fields) but some challenges remained (e.g., in designing relevant and authentic lesson plans based on their experience). This study provides an in-depth analysis of how specific design features can promote the goals of STEM integration, which in turn can increase student interest in STEM pursuits.

subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy

abstract: Situated in an urban teacher residency program at the University of California, Los Angeles, that aims to prepare high school teachers for integrating computational thinking (CT) into equity-focused STEM teaching, this paper investigates the impact of the STEM+C3 program on preservice teachers' conceptualizations and integration of CT in classrooms. Our analysis of 10 interviews suggests that the STEM+C3 program had an overall positive impact on teaching residents’ (TRs) understandings of equity-centered practices in CT pedagogy with a few teachers demonstrating shallower understandings. Most TRs were able to characterize identity and positionality while only a few were able to characterize diversity, inclusion, and social justice in their lesson plans. The findings also contribute to a growing body of literature on how programs may support CT integration in STEM equity pedagogy.

title: Co-Designing an Adaptable Curriculum with Teachers: Affordances and Tensions in Flexible Partnership and Collaboration

abstract: Together with a team of middle school teachers, we have been co-designing flexible, interdisciplinary curriculum focused on the interwoven concepts of personal, community, and ecological resilience. In this paper, we look at teachers’ perspectives on their experiences participating in a series of professional learning workshops and implementing co-designed curriculum in their classrooms. We focus empirical analysis on identifying affordances of this projects’ approach to co-design. We look at the role that flexibility in the co-design process and curricular enactment played in shaping these affordances. We also discuss the emergent tensions tied to this adaptable approach in regard to research and designing high quality curriculum.

title: Transformation of Habits through the Aesthetics of Agency
citation: Beatty, T. (2024). Transformation of Habits through the Aesthetics of Agency. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 1682-1685). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Beatty, T.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This paper explores the affective relationships between learning and games, leveraging Thi Nguyen’s insights on the aesthetic capacity of games and Michalinos Zembylas’ pedagogical framework for habits of social transformation. Focusing on a close reading of the game This War of Mine, the analysis reveals how game-designed agency can provide valuable lessons for educational practices. Employing a material semiotics approach, the study emphasizes the interconnectedness of human and non-human elements in shaping habits. Three actionable recommendations for education researchers emerge: prioritize striving over achievement tasks, focus on the inner agency in learners, and the acceptance that habits are not designed. This paper describes and reiterates that only through thoughtfully designed environments can new agency emerge and potentially transformative habits along with it.

title: Designing for Collaborative Teacher Learning Through Mixed-Reality Teaching Simulations

subject: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: How do novice teachers learn to lead controversial issue discussions in justice-oriented ways that simultaneously attend to today’s contentious political climate and the pedagogical complexity of the task? This paper analyzes teacher learning using mixed-reality simulation technology to approximate a controversial discussion about Dobbs v. Jackson (2022) and abortion jurisprudence. This paper explores the design, affordances, and limitations of teacher learning via collective pedagogical reasoning when novice teachers grapple with a polarized, emotionally-laden, and fraught topic: abortion. We frame our work as engaging with and challenging practice-based teacher education models to focus on the power of culturally situated and collaborative pedagogical reasoning within the shared experience of the mixed-reality simulation to shape teacher learning.

title: Designing for Climate Justice in a Social Studies Methods Course
citation: Washington, S., Shea, M. V., & Miller, F. (2024). Designing for Climate Justice in a Social Studies Methods Course. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. abstract: This paper reports on a community-based design research partnership involving community- and university-based educators and researchers who came together to design for environmental justice in a Social Studies Methods course for preservice teachers in an Elementary Teacher Education Program. The goal of the design work was to develop a process that centers Black and Indigenous voices and sense making in understanding and connecting climate justice to elementary social studies. Through design circles, relationality emerged as integral to the ways the group thought about their relationships and responsibilities to each other and the environment. Further, the design work led to a relational, as opposed to a scientific, approach to climate justice and held racial justice as central to understanding one’s responsibility to care for the natural world and those most impacted by the climate crisis.

abstract: This research focuses on recent studies of AI-Enhanced Personalized Learning, organized into three main sections: understanding key aspects, investigating practical methodologies, and elucidating motivations for AI integration into personalized learning to provide insights for future research in learning science. The methodology involves a rapid literature review, emphasizing eligibility criteria and a precise study selection process. The conclusion underscores the importance of seamlessly integrating AI analytics with human-centric approaches in personalized learning, enriching data, and training algorithms for efficiency, alongside emphasizing the role of human oversight.

title: Gesture in Synthesizing Student Contributions in Whole-Class Discussion of Graphical Representations of Energy
citation: Lee, S., Scheuneman, S. M., Flood, V. J., & Harrer, B. W. (2024). Gesture in Synthesizing Student Contributions in Whole-Class Discussion of Graphical Representations of Energy. International Society of the Learning Sciences.

subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Gesture’s role as a powerful and versatile tool for instruction, especially in STEM domains, is well-established. However, many specific teaching moves accomplished through gesture remain understudied. Using interaction analysis, we examine how an introductory university physics instructor uses gesture during whole-class discussion of graphical representations of energy conservation to synthesize multiple student groups’ solutions. This embodied, whole-class discussion orchestration move distills and summarizes the key points of the lesson while highlighting student contributions and addressing misunderstandings.

title: A Meta-analysis of Integrating 3D Virtual Learning Environment in Language Teaching
citation: Yuanyuan, L., Wenyan, M., Pin, W., & Xiaoqing, G. (2024). A Meta-analysis of Integrating 3D Virtual Learning Environment in Language Teaching. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: 3D virtual learning environments (3DVLEs) have become increasingly popular in language teaching, yet there are few meta-analytical studies examining their effectiveness from the teacher-in-the-loop perspective. This study explored the overall impact of 3DVLEs on language skills and affective achievements while investigating potential moderators. Examining 32 articles published between 2013 and 2023, and sourced from the Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar, our study compared 3DVLE approaches to traditional approaches and indicated that 3DVLEs had a large impact on language skills and a low-medium impact on affective achievements. Although none moderators were identified, this study offered valuable insights due to variations in effect sizes. This study provided a detailed discussion of these findings and their implications for language teachers to integrate 3DVLEs into language teaching.

title: "How Are Acorns Equitable?": Teacher Candidate Perceptions of Immersive Multilingual Experiences
citation: Lee, S., Daniel, B., Keifert, D. T., Pierson, A., Jeong, S., Johnson, H., Henrie, A., O’Beollain, S., & Syifa, M. (2024). "How Are Acorns Equitable?": Teacher Candidate Perceptions of Immersive Multilingual Experiences. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. authors_list: Lee, S., Daniel, B., Keifert, D. T., Pierson, A., Jeong, S., Johnson, H., Henrie, A., O’Beollain, S., & Syifa, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Multilingual learners are often marginalized in science learning environments due to deficit-oriented assumptions about their language and sense-making abilities. This paper explores how an immersive multilingual experience in undergraduate science methods courses supported anti-deficit noticing for teacher candidates. Teacher candidates participated in immersive French and Korean science lessons where multilingualism and multiculturalism were centered as resources for learning. Analyzing post-course interviews with participants who referenced the experiences showed how the immersive experiences supported teacher candidates to recognize multilingual learners’ assets that support scientific sense-making. What participants recognized differed based on the language of instruction, facilitation style, and content of the activity, suggesting implications for equity-oriented research and course design.

title: College Multilingual Students’ Use of Translanguaging in Science Problem Solving Contexts
citation: Jayathilaka, A., Jeong, M., & Ryu, M. (2024). College Multilingual Students’ Use of Translanguaging in Science Problem Solving Contexts. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C.
