abstract: In the context of a design-based (DBR) study in two teacher training colleges in northern Argentina focused on the promotion of biliteracy practices in the Indigenous and dominant languages, two iterations of language teaching materials were developed for one year and four design principles to develop Indigenous languages teaching materials were abstracted.

title: Applying the Understanding by Design (UbD) Model to Support Critical Thinking and Multidisciplinary Inquiry in the Chinese High School Biology Curriculum
citation: Zhang, X., Su, X., Huang, S., Tian, H., Chen, J., Carvalho, R., & Slotta, J. D. (2024). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhang, X., Su, X., Huang, S., Tian, H., Chen, J., Carvalho, R., & Slotta, J. D.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This paper presents a method of guiding teachers to develop “critical action inquiry” curriculum lessons, using a UbD (Understanding by Design) approach. This method is being developed at South China Normal University, as part of an ongoing collaboration with researchers in the Critical Action Learning Exchange (CALE) project, at the University of Toronto. In this design-based research involving 12 faculty and 92 students, the research team and the pedagogical team accompanied teachers in their development of pedagogical scenarios and use UbD as a framework. We present our application of UbD to the design of a Critical Action Inquiry project called the Dongguan Coastal Flooding project. We show how the design of CALE activities can be guided by UbD, and discuss our next steps for applications with teachers in southern China.

title: Active Learning as Joint Achievement in Postsecondary Science Classrooms
citation: Zhang, C. & Breuleux, A. (2024). Active Learning as Joint Achievement in Postsecondary Science Classrooms. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. authors_list: Zhang, C. & Breuleux, A.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: This paper illustrates with a single case drawn from a sample of postsecondary science instructors, how the sociohistorical framework of mediational tools can help further understand the range of instructional moves that instructors can deploy when attempting to engage their class in Active Learning (AL) on a specific physics topic. The findings of this study contribute insights into an understanding of how instructors plan and implement AL lessons. This understanding also has implications to professional development that aims to support instructors’ AL practices.

title: Youth Collaborative Inquiry for Sports-based Computer Science Learning
citation: Quiterio, A. & Worsley, M. A. (2024). Youth Collaborative Inquiry for Sports-based Computer Science Learning. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 2467-2468). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Quiterio, A. & Worsley, M. A. B.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Efforts in computer science (CS) education extend technology across diverse collaborative and interest-based learning environments. This study delves into the intersection of CS and sports. Particularly, we ask how youth collaboratively engage with an AI-embedded sports app to better understand the technology. Pulling from video recordings of youth in-game engagement, this poster explores youth’s collaborative inquiry processes of CS in a sports context. We analyze the interactions between youth and the AI embedded app, so that we can understand youth's sense making about how the technology works through tinkering and the subsequent claims. We discuss how new technologies enter sports related contexts and inspire collaborative youth inquiries about how the technology works. The mix of verbal and embodied experimentation with the technology is increasingly relevant for designing learning environments for learning CS in context.

title: “Pencils Down!” A Critical History of Timed Mathematics Exams
citation: Root, V. & Gutiérrez, J. F. (2024). “Pencils Down!” A Critical History of Timed Mathematics Exams. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. authors_list: Root, V. & Gutiérrez, J. F.
subject: STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Timed mathematics exams have been prevalent throughout the history of public schooling in the United States as measurements of achievement and accountability. However, investigations into the origins and use of timed mathematics exams are still missing from the history of school mathematics. We present an in-process historical literature review that seeks to uncover the origins of timed mathematics exams, analyze the ways their use has changed over time, and discuss their implications for educational equity.

citation: Conlin, L. D., Mesiner, J. E., & Wagh, A. (2024). Exploring the Affective Dimension of Integrating Computational Modeling with Science Learning. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Conlin, L. D., Mesiner, J. E., & Wagh, A.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: There is a movement in science education towards engaging students in authentic disciplinary practices, including computational modeling. This paper reports on a pilot study from a larger project in which we designed computational modeling curricula for public high school STEM classrooms. In this poster, we analyze video data of a pair of students’ computational modeling to illustrate the role that epistemic emotions of surprise and uncertainty played in them conducting their own investigations.

title: Prospective Mathematics Teachers' Perceptions of Mathematics as a Disconnected and Dehumanizing Subject
citation: Turan, N. (2024). Prospective Mathematics Teachers' Perceptions of Mathematics as a Disconnected and Dehumanizing Subject. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 2473-2474). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Turan, N.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study explores prospective mathematics teachers’ perceptions of mathematics based on their experiences of learning and teaching mathematics in relation to prevailing social norms. It seeks to uncover whether they view mathematics as a human endeavor or exhibit (de)humanizing characteristic. Findings suggest participants perceive mathematics as disconnected, with collegiate experiences being dehumanizing, lacking a strong mathematics identity. Future research should investigate the link between these encounters and the development of prospective teachers’ mathematical identities.

title: Exploring Gender Differences on the Impact of Initial Early Coding Motivation and Prior Knowledge of Computational Thinking
citation: Garcia, L. Y. & Warschauer, M. (2024). Exploring Gender Differences on the Impact of Initial Early Coding Motivation and Prior Knowledge of Computational Thinking. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Garcia, L. Y. & Warschauer, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: The relationship between motivation and computational thinking (CT) performance yields mixed findings in existing research on elementary-aged students. This study explored potential relationships among Latinx, upper elementary learners to consider opportunities for broadening participation. Findings revealed that motivation neither influences their CT performance nor does CT skills affect motivation reciprocally. Similarly having higher initial motivation does not influence changes in performance, but having above-average prior CT knowledge influences changes in motivation among Latino students.

subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This ethnographic study examines Kosova youth participation and learning experiences in a community-based empowerment program through a sociocultural learning and critical youth study lens. The initial findings demonstrate how adolescent participants resist deficit discourses of Kosova youth that position them as “functionally illiterate,” how youth club leaders both reify and expand notions adolescence/ts, and how ideas of adolescence/ts simultaneously constrain and enable opportunities for participation and learning.

citation: Peters, V., Pressler, E., Neisler, J., & Means, B. (2024). What Conversational AI Can (and Can’t) Tell Us About Peer Interaction in Higher Education. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. authors_list: Peters, V., Pressler, E., Neisler, J., & Means, B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this paper, we describe a study that explored the use of AI as a method for collecting data on the instructional practices used in undergraduate introductory statistics courses. Six instructors were asked to use an AI app to track classroom discussions over a 12-week term. Comparison with classroom observation data confirmed that classes were lecture-centric with only nominal amounts of student interaction. The findings point to the use of AI as a viable method for learning about postsecondary instructional practices at scale.

title: Student Perceptions of Learning Supports in an Educational Game
citation: Butcher, K. R. & Hampton, J. (2024). Student Perceptions of Learning Supports in an Educational Game. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. authors_list: Butcher, K. R. & Hampton, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This research examined middle school student feedback about the design components that helped them learn from an educational game centered on science learning about predator-prey relationships. Students frequently cited interspersed instructional content (delivered as comics), authentic visual media, and interactive game play as driving their learning. Results suggest that students perceive value in engaging instructional content that serves to reinforce game learning and respond positively to authentic content integrated into gamified experiences.

title: “I Thought the Heart Was at the Center”: The Entwined/Entwining Threads of Care
citation: Barrales, W., Ortiz, O., Vela, L. V., Chaparian, S., Y., J., & Wright, L. (2024). “I Thought the Heart Was at the Center”: The Entwined/Entwining Threads of Care. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 2483-2484). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Barrales, W., Ortiz, O., Vela, L. V., Chaparian, S., Y, J., & Wright, L.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Challenging the hegemonic practices in STEM that privilege quantitative epistemologies, this paper advocates for a care-centered, relational approach within STEM education. We conceptualize care from a feminist lens and explore care practices in informal STEM learning environments/afterschool programs, aiming to highlight care as a set of relational practices that support positive science experiences. Through a partnership with Daphnia, a non-profit focused on student-centered science education for underserved youth, the study follows ethnographic methods to observe care integration in educational settings. The preliminary findings reveal the co-facilitation between Community Scientists and community center educators, prioritizing relationship-building and fostering students’ autonomy where relationality is valued. We argue that valuing care in STEM education disrupts the traditional power dynamics and contributes to a more equitable and inclusive learning environment.

title: Speculative Role of AI in Addressing Inequity
citation: Kim, C., Gnesdilow, D., Passonneau, R., & Puntambekar, S. (2024). Speculative Role of AI in Addressing Inequity. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. authors_list: Kim, C., Gnesdilow, D., Passonneau, R., & Puntambekar, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The present study examined teachers’ conceptualization of the role of AI in addressing inequity. Grounded in speculative design and education, we examined eight secondary public teachers’ thinking about AI in teaching and learning that may go beyond present horizons. Data were collected from individual interviews. Findings suggest that not only equity consciousness but also present engagement in a context of inequities were crucial to future dreaming of AI that does not harm but improve equity.

title: The Process of Constructing Interdisciplinary Thinking Through Graduation Research in an Interdisciplinary Department
citation: Shoji, G. & Ozawa, S. (2024). The Process of Constructing Interdisciplinary Thinking Through Graduation Research in an Interdisciplinary Department. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Shoji, G. & Ozawa, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study aims to investigate how students in an interdisciplinary department construct interdisciplinary thinking through their graduation research. Using Trajectory Equifinality Modeling (TEM), grounded in social constructivism, we conducted a qualitative analysis from the perspective of interdisciplinary thinking. The analysis revealed two types of processes in the construction of interdisciplinary thinking through graduation research. The first involves integrating a secondary field through external resources provided by supervisor, while the second entails developing interest in a secondary field due to the interdisciplinarity of seminars or supervisors. Students expanded their research themes by maintaining their primary field and incorporating insights from secondary fields. This study provides valuable insights for the development of interdisciplinary education designed to foster interdisciplinary thinking.

title: Developing a Collaborative Program for Underrepresented Minoritized Students to Thrive
citation: Leary, H. & Measom, E. (2024). Developing a Collaborative Program for Underrepresented Minoritized Students to Thrive. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. authors_list: Leary, H. & Measom, E.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: It is important in education for students to build skills. Underrepresented students often feel less welcomed and accepted and often fail to thrive in higher education. Mentoring in higher education can mitigate some of the challenges underrepresented students face, in turn helping them succeed. This poster describes a program designed and implemented to support student knowledge, confidence, community, emotional well-being, and career readiness.

title: Teach or not teach? Impacts of Objective Explanation in Game-based Learning: Insights from Gaussian Hidden Markov Analysis
citation: Zhang, P., Su, H., Zeng, J., Zhang, Y., & Shang, J. (2024). Teach or not teach? Impacts of Objective Explanation in Game-based Learning: Insights from Gaussian Hidden Markov Analysis. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 2491-2492). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhang, P., Su, H., Zeng, J., Zhang, Y., & Shang, J.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: We investigated the impact of teachers' explanations of objectives in game-based learning on students’ learning outcomes and processes. The research involved 206 participants, divided into a control group (n=114), which learned objectives through reading, and an experimental group (n=92) receiving teacher explanations. The study incorporated Gaussian Hidden Markov Models to analyze learner states during game-based learning. Findings revealed that teacher explanations direct their learning states towards efficiency, helping learners quickly enter and maintain an efficient learning state. This work provided instructional insights for implementing technology-enhanced learning methods in authentic educational settings.

title: Capturing Futures: Mapping Youth Perspectives through Landscape Biographies
citation: Green, P. E. & Pinkard, N. (2024). Capturing Futures: Mapping Youth Perspectives through Landscape Biographies. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 2493-2494). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Green, P. E. & Pinkard, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Utilizing ArcGIS's QuickCapture app, we enlisted 16 high schoolers from Chicago's South Side to map their daily lives, creating landscape biographies intertwining spatial-physical environments with memories. This poster outlines our phased asset-mapping approach, embracing system-oriented and youth-centric perspectives. As we explore how landscape biographies influence youth engagement, our findings highlight the importance of amplifying young voices, paving the way for future exploration of the interplay between a community’s affordances and opportunities for learning within it.

title: Evaluative Framework for AI Application in College Counseling
citation: Nhu, D. & Zhong, Z. (2024). Evaluative Framework for AI Application in College Counseling. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. authors_list: Nhu, D. & Zhong, Z.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: The shortage of school counselors in the United States necessitates the survey of new tools to assist high school students with accessing information regarding financial aid for college application. The generative AI chatbot ChatGPT may be better than human-written FAQs section in responding to common questions from students about financial aid and the FAFSA applications. Counselors and counseling framework could factor AI into their curriculum, which leads to the need for more comprehensive AI literacy.

citation: Hayden, R. & Roque, R. (2024). Disrupting a Cycle of Disciplinary Harm: Confronting Ghosts in Creative Computing Endeavors with Out of School Educators. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. authors_list: Hayden, R. & Roque, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In designing equity-oriented learning environments around computing, it is important to consider how educators are structurally set up to reinscribe injustice. This poster presents a study of six pre-service teachers that were supported to confront “disciplinary ghosts,” experiences of harm related to computing in order to heal and re-envision alternative possibilities. We use the hauntological processes from Yoon and Chen (2022) as the starting point of a design framework towards healing.

citation: Vallero, A., Markauskaite, L., & Spence, N. (2024). What’s the Problem Worth Solving Together: How Interdisciplinary Student Teams Construct Shared Problems. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. authors_list: Vallero, A., Markauskaite, L., & Spence, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study aims to enhance the design of interdisciplinary collaborative tasks in higher education by examining how university students from diverse disciplinary backgrounds collaborate to define a shared problem. Drawing on mini ethnographic case studies, it compares two student teams. Using a multimodal blending perspective, the analysis explores the resources students utilise in the problem-construction process. Preliminary findings reveal variations in how the teams interpret and approach a task, offering insights to inform the design of interdisciplinary collaborative tasks.

title: The Impact of Middle School Students’ Writing Quality on the Accuracy of the Automated Assessment of Science Content
citation: Gnesdilow, D., Dey, I., Gengler, D., Malkin, L., Puntambekar, S., Passonneau, R., & Kim, C. (2024). The Impact of Middle School Students’ Writing Quality on the Accuracy of the Automated Assessment of Science Content. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 250-257). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Gnesdilow, D., Dey, I., Gengler, D., Malkin, L., Puntambekar, S., Passonneau, R., & Kim, C.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Helping students learn how to write is essential. However, students have few opportunities to develop this skill, since giving timely feedback is difficult for teachers. AI applications can provide quick feedback on students’ writing. But, ensuring accurate assessment can be challenging, since students’ writing quality can vary. We examined the impact of students’ writing quality on the error rate of our natural language processing (NLP) system when assessing scientific content in initial and revised design essays. We also explored whether aspects of writing quality were linked to the number of NLP errors. Despite finding that students’ revised essays were significantly different from their initial essays in a few ways, our NLP systems’ accuracy was similar. Further, our multiple regression analyses showed, overall, that students’ writing quality did not impact our NLP systems’ accuracy. This is promising in terms of ensuring students with different writing skills get similarly accurate feedback.

subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: In this study, we investigated teachers’ flexibility when they attend identifying referent units on their understanding of fractions and fraction operations. We conducted five pilot interviews with middle school math teachers and analyzed the data to identify different levels of mastery in identifying referent units. The results showed that teachers attended to referent units differently, and their level of mastery was related to how they viewed the whole through their thinking.

This paper reports on emergent findings from an ongoing study that examines how different stakeholders think about representations of and simulations of racial and ethnic identity in materials designed for teacher learning. We focus on one sub-question: How do actors playing students in an immersive teaching simulation think about tensions related to acting as a person of a different race?

abstract: Science identities and competencies are influenced by teacher recognition and student self-perception. Drawing on social positioning theory, this study examines which factors can contribute to science identity development among multilingual students. 46 multilingual middle school students in Northeastern U.S., took the Social Positioning of English Language Learners (SPELL) survey and quantitative correlation analysis revealed a connection between teacher recognition and student perceived competence. Furthermore, self-identified ‘science persons’ informed their competence and science career interests.

abstract: This study advances an innovative approach using a dystopian game in a classroom setting to empower youth to be critically involved with complex societal issues within a dystopian fictional world. This design-based research endeavors to develop a critical action game that challenges students to adopt the role of 'troublemakers' (i.e., proactive change agents) in critically addressing divergent social values and beliefs. Engaging in the game provides personal reflection and a secure environment for vulnerable groups to co-create new narratives and restore the public sphere for open discussions and collective decision-making.

citation: Kshirsagar, K. & Kumar, V. (2024). Tangible Mathematical Tinkering Toolkits as a Platform for Understanding Drivers and Trajectories of Curiosity based Exploration. abstract: This poster examines how a paper-based tangible tool, the Zine Machine, facilitates curiosity-driven explorations in math and engineering design. By enabling learners to create mechanical linkages, the Zine Machine promotes open-ended self-expression and fosters deeper conceptual and disciplinary learning. Through observations, we identify the critical roles of manipulatory, conceptual, and goal-based curiosity in driving mathematical and engineering-related engagement. These findings provide initial insights into analyzing learners and designing environments conducive to creative, multidisciplinary learning.

abstract: This study investigates the concept of Math Parenting Identity (MPI) and its influence on the Home Math Environment (HME), particularly examining the differing identities of mothers and fathers using the RESET Framework. With 847 parents surveyed, findings suggest a need for tailored family engagement programs that challenge traditional gender-based parenting paradigms and promote equitable math learning opportunities for young children.

title: Representational Politics in the Learning Sciences: Foundations, Limits, and Alternatives
citation: Uttamchandani, S., Vea, T., Curnow, J., & Scipio, D. (2024). Representational Politics in the Learning Sciences: Foundations, Limits, and Alternatives. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 266-273). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Uttamchandani, S., Vea, T., Curnow, J., & Scipio, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this conceptual paper we interrogate the use and misuse of representational politics within the learning sciences community, including our research, our professional society, and our departments. We argue that representational politics are a necessary but insufficient strategy for advancing equity and justice, and that in many cases they act as a detour that moves us away from more impactful strategies to address harm. To do this, we outline the philosophical underpinnings of representational politics and work through the limitations of these strategies when implemented in our field. We argue that the learning sciences should focus equity and justice strategies around collective liberation approaches rooted in historicized analysis of power and a commitment to solidarity.

title: A Multilevel Analysis of Factors Associated with Secondary School Teachers’ Perceived Digital Competence
citation: Avci, H. (2024). A Multilevel Analysis of Factors Associated with Secondary School Teachers’ Perceived Digital Competence. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. authors_list: Avci, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study aims to examine the relationship between perceived digital competence and potential influencing factors among secondary school teachers. Data were drawn from the OECD’s Teaching and Learning International Survey 2018 U.S. national teacher survey of 165 schools and 2,414 secondary teachers. A two-level multilevel linear modeling was conducted to investigate the impact of (a) teachers' pre- and in-service ICT training, job satisfaction, and collegial collaboration in the teacher level and (b) collective teacher innovativeness, school innovativeness, and digital infrastructure in the school level. Results revealed several factors, including ICT training, collegial collaboration, and digital infrastructure, significantly predicted secondary teachers' perceived digital competence within and across schools. These findings are essential for understanding the multi-level aspects of digital competence and the potential for implementing interventions to fortify teacher training programs and promote collaborative efforts that can help cultivate a resilient and interconnected educational community.

title: ‘Scientists don’t know the truth
citation: Noushad, N. F., Yoon, S. A., Chinn, C. A., Yang, Z., Hussain-Abidi, H., & Hunkar, K. (2024). ‘Scientists don’t know the truth; they tell you what they know to be true!’: Shaping High School Students Understanding of How Scientists Establish Trustworthy Claims Using Epistemic Practices. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 274-281). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Noushad, N. F., Yoon, S. A., Chinn, C. A., Yang, Z., Hussain-Abidi, H., & Hunkar, K.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Science skepticism challenges the trustworthiness of scientific knowledge. Researchers suggest that school science curricula should emphasize the epistemic practices real-world scientists use to generate claims, such as actively seeking contradictory evidence for explanatory models and comparing findings with peers. However, empirical evidence supporting the use of epistemic practices, and its potential impact on students’ trustworthiness of science remains limited. This study examines four ninth-grade biology students who designed experiments to understand a fictional viral outbreak using agent-based simulation data. They iteratively refined their designs and discussed with peers. Analysis of student worksheets and discussions reveals that students used three epistemic practices: considering multiple explanations, systematically evaluating evidence, and comparing findings with similar experiments. However, they struggled to revise their initial models when presented with conflicting evidence by their peers. These findings offer insights into how students engage with epistemic practices and their perceptions of science's trustworthiness.

title: Integrating Local Spaces into Mathematics Learning: An Investigation of Place-Based Mathematics Education
citation: Farid, A., Fenech, M., Anderson, E., & Lin, G. (2024). Integrating Local Spaces into Mathematics Learning: An Investigation of Place-Based Mathematics Education. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 282-289). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Farid, A., Fenech, M., Anderson, E., & Lin, G.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: To address the persistent and well-documented gap between schools and local communities – a gap that looms particularly large for the supposedly abstract discipline of mathematics – there is a growing need to understand the possibilities and challenges posed by approaches that integrate local spaces into learning. Yet few studies have investigated place-based approaches to mathematics learning. This qualitative case study examines the classroom implementation of two high school geometry place-based learning modules. We find that the messiness of doing mathematics in the real world prompted genuine mathematical problem solving. Findings indicate that students’ sense of place (encompassing both knowledge of place as well as the meanings and attachments that places hold) is a valuable resource for, and is itself altered by, mathematics learning. When sense of place is drawn on and displayed in the classroom, teachers come to see the student as a whole person.

title: Exam Implementation of Scientific Epistemic Practices Curricula Through an Adaptive Expertise Lens: A Case Study
citation: Yang, Z., Yoon, S. A., Chinn, C. A., Cottone, A., Richman, T., Noushad, N. F., Hussain-Abidi, H., & Hunkar, K. (2024). Exam Implementation of Scientific Epistemic Practices Curricula Through an Adaptive Expertise Lens: A Case Study. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 290-297). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Yang, Z., Yoon, S. A., Chinn, C. A., Cottone, A., Richman, T., Noushad, N. F., Hussain-Abidi, H., & Hunkar, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Scholars have suggested that one way to promote informed decision making about pressing socioscientific issues is to incorporate epistemic practices in science curricula. However, a key factor in teaching with such curricula is whether and how teachers can adapt instruction from their routine teaching approaches. Through an adaptive expertise lens, in this study, we examine how two teachers, teaching with agent-based computational complex systems models, varied in their implementations of epistemic practices and how consequently students' performance on epistemic practices was impacted. Through qualitative analyses of two teachers’ implementation recordings, this study examines teachers’ adaptive expertise in curricular implementations that aim at promoting student epistemic practices and provides examples of high and low levels of adaptive expertise that result in distinct student classroom experiences. This study carries implications for future teacher professional development geared towards improving students' epistemic practices.

title: Building Digital Competence: Personal and Contextual Factors in Teachers' Professional Learning
citation: Economou, A., Kapsalis, G., Kyza, E. A., Georgiou, Y., Gallagher, S., Galvin, C., Gonida, E., Leo, D. H., Ilomäki, L., Lakkala, M., Moustakas, D., Papadopoulos, P. M., & Garcia, A. R. authors_list: Economou, A., Kapsalis, G., Kyza, E. A., Georgiou, Y., Gallagher, S., Galvin, C., Gonida, E., Leo, D. H., Ilomäki, L., Lakkala, M., Moustakas, D., Papadopoulos, P. M., & Garcia, A. R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Teachers are working within an ever-changing environment where digital transformation requires continuous updating of their digital competence. To support them in developing their digital competence, SELFIEforTEACHERS (SfT) proposes a self-reflection process guiding them to self-assess their digital competence and engage in professional learning practices. The present study comprised 13 case studies from six European countries and explored various use cases of SfT through qualitative analysis. This paper discusses findings in relation to the conditions that can support or hinder teachers in engaging in a self-reflection process using SfT for identifying their learning needs, based on which they design their professional learning paths to further develop their digital competence. These findings can contribute to a better understanding of the opportunities and limitations of the SfT self-reflection process, as a meaningful professional learning process for teachers that can support their agency to further develop their digital competence.

title: Mapping the Complexity of Learning: A Learning Experience Network Analysis Approach for Iterative Design Moves
citation: Donaldson, J. P., Han, A., Yan, S., Lee, S., & Kao, S. (2024). Mapping the Complexity of Learning: A Learning Experience Network Analysis Approach for Iterative Design Moves. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 3-10). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Donaldson, J. P., Han, A., Yan, S., Lee, S., & Kao, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This methodological paper interrogates the potential of network analysis within the design-based research (DBR) framework for improving the design of learning experiences. We present the learning experience network analysis (LENA) approach for analyzing learner-generated data about their experiences in learning activities. Utilizing a complex systems perspective, this study reveals how network analysis elucidates intricate patterns of interdependencies between experiences of struggles, aspects that worked well, and alignment of their experiences with principles from learning theories. Those patterns can be used to construct new design moves for the subsequent DBR iteration. Our findings underscore the capacity of this method to capture the dynamism and complexity inherent in learning environments, thereby informing more adaptive and responsive design strategies. This work extends the methodological toolkit available for DBR, advocating for a more complex, situated understanding of the ways in which the data-informed design can shape the learning experience from the learner’s perspective.

title: “We were doing science, not just talking about science”: Embodied Learning and Science Identity Development
citation: Steinberg, S. & Danish, J. (2024). “We were doing science, not just talking about science”: Embodied Learning and Science Identity Development. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 306-313). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Steinberg, S. & Danish, J.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: In this paper, we explore the affordances of embodied activities for supporting elementary school students to participate in and develop positive relationships with science. We draw on sociocultural perspectives on identity: viewing identity as dynamic and emerging in interaction between students and their environment. We analyze post interviews in which students reflected on their experiences with and feelings about a ten-day series of embodied science activities, and then focus on three focal students in classroom video to understand how these views may have developed. We found that students both enjoyed and felt competent at the embodied science activities; positive views of science seemed to emerge through: a climate where all students could contribute ideas, expert positionings of students, positive socio-emotional experiences during embodiment, and validating challenges. We argue that foregrounding embodiment can be a valuable way to foster positive science identities.

title: Can Speech Ground Mechanical Reasoning During Engineering Discourse?
citation: Grondin, M., Swart, M. I., Fu, K., Nathan, M. J., & Kim, D. (2024). Can Speech Ground Mechanical Reasoning During Engineering Discourse?. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Grondin, M., Swart, M. I., Fu, K., Nathan, M. J., & Kim, D.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Mechanical reasoning is crucial for many engineering fields, yet undergraduate engineering students struggle to understand discipline-specific formalisms from their courses that model mechanical concepts. The current investigation observed undergraduate engineering students’ speech during mechanical reasoning and the benefits of attending to students' speech for assessing their mechanical reasoning and learning. Results from discourse analysis of two undergraduate engineering student dyads enrolled in a Mechanics of Materials course revealed students’ mechanical reasoning through both course-specific and non-course-specific speech. Students generated speech that described functional or dynamic behaviors, as well as structure that described the static features. Students with highly developed formal knowledge of mathematics and physics often reason about mechanical systems in ways not captured traditional formalisms has implications for instruction and assessment.

title: Friendship as a Transformative Process: Cultivating Interest-Driven Connections, Community, and Perspective in the Arts
citation: Dahn, M., Peppler, K., Corrigan, S., Chew, P., DiGiacomo, D., Mejias, S., Nelligan, P., & Sefton-Green, J. (2024). Friendship as a Transformative Process: Cultivating Interest-Driven Connections, Community, and Perspective in the Arts. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. authors_list: Dahn, M., Peppler, K., Corrigan, S., Chew, P., DiGiacomo, D., Mejias, S., Nelligan, P., & Sefton-Green, J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This study takes a retrospective lens on learning to trace how arts participation, learning, and friendship are interconnected over time. Drawing from a dataset of 261 surveys and 102 in-depth interviews with alumni from 32 community arts organizations reflecting on experiences from five or more years ago, this study offers insights into long term impacts and outcomes associated with friendships developed through arts program participation. Survey findings show that the likelihood of reporting that the programs shaped their lives and prepared them for life events were higher for those who reported persistent friendships from their programs. Analysis of purposefully selected interviews suggest that friendships supported the development of networks, cultivated a sense of community, and shifted participants’ perspectives and self-identification both during participation in the program and over time. Implications for research and practice center friendship as a central construct worthy of further exploration in the learning sciences.

title: Young Students’ Understandings of Function Graphs
citation: Strachota, S., López, M. A., Brizuela, B. M., del Carmen Pérez-Martos, M., Gardiner, A. M., & Blanton, M. (2024). Young Students’ Understandings of Function Graphs. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 330-337). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Strachota, S., López, M. A., Brizuela, B. M., Pérez-Martos, M. D. C., Gardiner, A. M., & Blanton, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study involved 14-lesson classroom teaching experiments (CTE) with first and second grade students. We interviewed students at the beginning, middle, and end of the CTEs to assess their understandings of graphs of functional relationships. Here we report the levels of thinking that emerged from our analysis and the progress we observed with the second grade students. In summary, all students began the CTEs with at least an understanding of graphs in which they could coordinate quantities. By the end of the CTEs, one student reached a level of understanding in which she was able to extend beyond the representation at hand. Practical implications include guidance for developing instruction around learning to graph. Theoretical implications include contributing to answering open questions about students’ developing understandings of mathematical representations.

title: Exploring Impacts of Arts Education through Inductive Application of Rhetorical Structure Theory
citation: Corrigan, S., Dahn, M., Chew, P., Trapp, S., DiGiacomo, D., Mejias, S., Sefton-Green, J., & Peppler, K. (2024). Exploring Impacts of Arts Education through Inductive Application of Rhetorical Structure Theory. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 338-345). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Corrigan, S., Dahn, M., Chew, P., Trapp, S., DiGiacomo, D., Mejias, S., Sefton-Green, J., & Peppler, K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Research into the outcomes of youth arts programs and arts participation in general has tended to focus on particular dimensions such as mental health, job readiness, and community development. This article describes development and deployment of a codebook for flexible, inductive coding that aids identification of outcomes interviewees attributed to their participation in out-of-school arts programs, regardless of the dimension. The corpus used to develop the codebook is derived from semi-structured retrospective interviews with 102 international participants discussing their past experiences in the arts. The resulting codebook specifies criteria for recognizing outcome statements, and heavily relies on the rhetorical structure and lexical content of speech. By specifying properties of speech that are characteristic of outcome descriptions in general, the codebook supports inductive exploration of outcomes that were described by participants but may be overlooked or unavailable in public discourse about out–of-school or community based youth arts programming

title: Exploring Impacts of Arts Participation through Automated Inductive Annotation
citation: Corrigan, S., Ojeda-Ramirez, S., Dahn, M., DiGiacomo, D., Sefton-Green, J., & Peppler, K. (2024). Exploring Impacts of Arts Participation through Automated Inductive Annotation. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 346-353). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Corrigan, S., Ojeda-Ramirez, S., Dahn, M., DiGiacomo, D., Sefton-Green, J., & Peppler, K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Researchers have worked to identify the varied outcomes associated with participation in the arts. Historically, those efforts have tended to take a ‘top down’ approach in that they focus on specific types of outcomes, or existing theoretical orientations. In this paper, we demonstrate an approach to annotating transcribed interviews that blends inductive human coding with machine learning in order to support ‘bottom-up’ discovery of previously unrecognized outcomes. We utilize a recent collection of retrospective semi-structured interviews with 102 international participants in the arts. The annotation approach yields a system for clustering and cataloging the interviews according to a set of modeled topics that facilitates corpus-based research, and may promote identification of new categories of outcomes. The work is one part of a project to create a community-driven taxonomy of outcomes of arts participation that encompass a universe of reported outcomes not delimited by domain, type, or theoretical orientations of stakeholders.

title: Replicating the Effectiveness of Sensemaking-focused Pedagogies
citation: Sinha, T. & Kapur, M. (2024). Replicating the Effectiveness of Sensemaking-focused Pedagogies. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 35-42). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sinha, T. & Kapur, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Two hundred and twenty three tenth grade students engaged in one of four preparatory activities – problem solving, worked examples, sensemaking, and contrasting cases—before receiving instruction on the targeted concept of standard deviation. Students in the problem solving condition performed the best on items targeting understanding of the critical features of the concept, whereas those in the worked example condition performed the worst. Consistent with our hypotheses, there was a significant difference between preparatory problem-solving and worked examples on conceptual understanding and transfer assessments, but not on procedural knowledge. Notably, sensemaking (making sense of a correct solution without any explanation) triggered students’ knowledge gap awareness and curiosity significantly greater than all the other conditions, even though outcome performance was not different from the worked examples condition. Finally, studying contrasting cases as preparation led to superior performance on transfer assessments compared to worked examples. Against the backdrop of implementing resource-efficient learning designs in the classroom, our work provides solid empirical evidence to guide educators in their teaching efforts.

title: Switch mode: How Prior Experiences Shapes How Learners Program in a Hybrid Programming Environments
citation: Lin, Y., Weintrop, D., & McKenna, J. (2024). Switch mode: How Prior Experiences Shapes How Learners Program in a Hybrid Programming Environments. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Lin, Y., Weintrop, D., & McKenna, J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: This paper presents a case study on the differing experiences of two students learning to program with a hybrid programming environment designed to support learners transitioning from block-based programming to text-based programming. Despite different levels of prior experience and confidence, both students found their level of comfort with programming by developing their own methods for authoring commands based on the supports available in the environment. This work explores how the same environment supported learners in developing distinct programming approaches suited to their confidence, preference, and previous experiences.

title: Learning About and Against Generative AI Through Mapping Generative AI’s Ecologies and Developing a Luddite Praxis
citation: Logan, C. (2024). Learning About and Against Generative AI Through Mapping Generative AI’s Ecologies and Developing a Luddite Praxis. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 362-369). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Logan, C.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: In this paper, I respond to recent conversations in the learning sciences about how the field might develop research with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Rather than a narrow focus on what we might do with GenAI, I argue that learning scientists should expand our approaches to consider ways to research and learn about and against GenAI. While AI literacy is a common framework for helping people learn with and about artificial intelligence, a literacy framework can struggle to contend with AI’s opaque systems and is vulnerable to hegemonic influences. I suggest an alternative: mapping ecologies of GenAI and its social, technical, and political-economic relations. Finally, I argue that learning scientists can draw inspiration from the Luddites, 19th-century English clothworkers who destroyed machines to defend their craft and dignity, to develop a Luddite praxis that combines mapping ecologies of GenAI with collective interventions against unjust AI systems.

title: “Driving the Ship” or Laying Buoys: Teachers’ Use of Metaphor for Meaning-Making with Storylines
citation: Wingert, K. & Ko, M. M. (2024). “Driving the Ship” or Laying Buoys: Teachers’ Use of Metaphor for Meaning-Making with Storylines. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 370-377). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wingert, K. & Ko, M. M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Science curricula require new conceptualizations of how teachers relate to their materials. In this study of teacher learning, we analyze an experienced group of practicing Storylines teachers’ use of metaphor to describe the roles and responsibilities of students and teachers in curriculum enactment. We found that every metaphor that teachers used to describe the uses of Storylines curriculum entailed a sort of wayfinding: a destination, a timeframe, a place, a journey, or the students’ or teachers’ respective position in that pursuit. These findings continue to indicate the usefulness of metaphor in foregrounding the central role that students play in NGSS-aligned instruction/materials, as well as the institutional forces that shape how curriculum materials get enacted inside the classroom. This study builds and contributes to current scholarship that aims to support teachers in reconceptualizing their role, relationship to students, and the institution of schooling, in the context of constructivist curricula.

title: Expansive Framing as an Asset-based Approach for Transfer: A Theoretical Integration
citation: Harris, T. (2024). Expansive Framing as an Asset-based Approach for Transfer: A Theoretical Integration. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 378-385). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Harris, T.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Expansive framing is a situative model for promoting learning transfer. The model shares several foundational assumptions with asset-based approaches for teaching and learning, including the Funds of Knowledge and Funds of Identity frameworks. Both expansive framing and the Funds of Knowledge and Funds of Identity frameworks recognize students as inherently knowledgeable, experienced social actors who bring valuable breadths of competence to classroom settings, and moreover, hold that students should be empowered to leverage their out-of-school knowledge and experiences to frame disciplinary learning opportunities in the classroom. This paper presents a theoretical integration to surface key synergies between expansive framing and the Funds of Knowledge and Funds of Identity frameworks. Drawing on scholarship focused on each of these frameworks, this theoretical integration aims to open pathways for applying these frameworks together in practice and ultimately to contribute to foundations for advancing equity-centered research and practice for supporting learning transfer.

title: Democratic Interventions on Walls
citation: Ho, W., Lee, S., & Kim, B. (2024). Democratic Interventions on Walls: Embracing Plurality and Differences Through Street Arts. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 386-393). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ho, W., Lee, S., & Kim, B.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Graffiti and street art are unsanctioned urban artifacts outside art institutions. Nevertheless, graffiti and street art are seen as self-expression by their practitioners and these art forms have pedagogical values as they raise questions on political, social, and creative issues within the society. The myriad of voices that echo on these walls resembles a democratic space that accommodates plurality and differences. In this paper, we examine how six graffiti and street artists implicitly or explicitly practice public pedagogy as described in Biesta’s work. Our analysis shows that their urban interventions exhibited “activist”, “experimental” and “demonstrative” qualities of public pedagogy while also being engaged in active learning about their contexts and art practices.

title: Using an Evidence-Centered Design Approach to Examine the Alignment of Computer Science Curricula with Standards
citation: Rutstein, D., Basu, S., Yang, H., Rachmatullah, A., Tate, C., & McGee, S. (2024). Using an Evidence-Centered Design Approach to Examine the Alignment of Computer Science Curricula with Standards. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 394-401). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rutstein, D., Basu, S., Yang, H., Rachmatullah, A., Tate, C., & McGee, S.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: In the early stages of K-12 Computer Science (CS) curriculum development, standards were not yet established, and the primary objective, especially in younger grades, was to spark students' interest in CS. While this remains a vital goal, the development of the CS standards underscores the importance of standards-aligned curriculum, ensuring equitable, content rich CS education for all students. We show that standards alignment is most useful when it includes details about which aspects of the standards a curriculum aligns with. This paper describes our process of decomposing five middle school CS standards into granular learning targets using an evidence-centered design approach and mapping the learning targets onto individual lessons from one widely popular middle school CS curriculum. We discuss the potential implications of this work on curriculum design, curriculum selection, and teacher professional learning.

title: Oral Exams as Social Practice: Questions, Joint Remembering, and Co-construction
citation: Hontvedt, M., Solem, M. S., & Prøitz, T. S. (2024). Oral Exams as Social Practice: Questions, Joint Remembering, and Co-construction. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 402-409). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hontvedt, M., Solem, M. S., & Prøitz, T. S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We adopt a sociocultural perspective to explore a case of oral assessment in a Norwegian secondary school. Our analysis, drawing from video data of a classroom session and subsequent oral examinations in a Norwegian school, underscores that oral assessments serve as more than just tools for measuring content knowledge: they enable epistemological practices specific to talk-based interaction. We argue that oral assessments allow students to dynamically enact and negotiate their subject-specific knowledge with support from an examiner. Indeed, this is an assessment format that is inherently relational, as the examiner and students co-construct meaning and draw on shared background knowledge to display competence. As such, the potential of oral assessment is not an inherent trait but needs to be realized in situ. This research thereby contributes an empirical investigation of oral assessment practices, highlighting their potential benefits and implications for educational contexts.

title: Multilevel Engagement in Learning Architectures for Integrated STEM Education Innovation
citation: Ko, P. & Law, N. (2024). Multilevel Engagement in Learning Architectures for Integrated STEM Education Innovation. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 410-417). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ko, P. & Law, N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Integrated STEM education innovation cherishes the goal of preparing students for a rapidly changing world by developing their ability to generate knowledge and solve complex real-life problems. To achieve this, it is necessary to support teachers in curriculum innovation that aligns with the goals of the innovation. However, school-level constraints often hinder teachers’ innovation and learning. Fostering a conducive environment for innovation might necessitate school leaders’ learning. To investigate how teacher learning for STEM education innovation relates to school leaders’ learning, we used the MultiLevel MultiScale Model as a framework to examine the interdependency of learning at various levels for scalable innovation. This study was conducted within a design-based implementation research context and involved a multiple case study with four schools. The results showed that the engagement of school leaders can facilitate the establishment of school-level infrastructures that support teacher learning for curriculum innovation, leading to positive innovation outcomes.

title: Triggering Social-Emotional and Ethical Learning: A Case Study in a PBL Course
citation: Philip, A. S., Kaur, N., Murthy, S., & Iyer, S. (2024). Triggering Social-Emotional and Ethical Learning: A Case Study in a PBL Course. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 418-425). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Philip, A. S., Kaur, N., Murthy, S., & Iyer, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Social-emotional learning (SEL) plays a significant role in enhancing student wellbeing, interpersonal relationships and academic achievement. While numerous SEL frameworks aim to cultivate social and emotional skills across various contexts, their practical implementation in real educational settings, especially at higher-education levels, remains largely unrealized. This paper presents a case study of a graduate level project-based course on instructional design wherein students created a website aimed at sensitizing a university community to the challenges faced by persons with disabilities. Employing the Social, Emotional, and Ethical (SEE) framework as the analytical lens, this study examines how specific course elements guided students through three distinct levels of SEE learning components. The paper contributes towards advancing discussions on integrating social, emotional and ethical learning into classroom experiences, and offers practical implications for designing for SEE learning, particularly within the PBL model.

title: Pedagogical Issues in Virtual Reality Mathematics Education
citation: Sherard, M., Walkington, C., Daughrity, L. A., Pande, P., Beauchamp, T., Petrosino, A., & Cuevas, A. (2024). Pedagogical Issues in Virtual Reality Mathematics Education. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 426-433). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sherard, M., Walkington, C., Daughrity, L. A., Pande, P., Beauchamp, T., Petrosino, A., & Cuevas, A.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: We discuss pedagogical challenges that arise when head mounted displays (HMDs), are used for mathematics tutoring. 16 middle school students used HMDs to participate in seven VR mathematics tutoring sessions. Sessions were video recorded and analyzed using Social Infrastructural Framework. We identified three pedagogical issues: managing student discipline; enacting social identities; and managing virtual bodies. We describe each issue, illustrate its occurrence, and discuss possible remedies.

title: Turn Charts for Interaction Analysis: Visually Mapping the Conversation Floor
citation: Shapiro, B. R., Hall, R., Mathur, A., & Zhao, E. (2024). Turn Charts for Interaction Analysis: Visually Mapping the Conversation Floor. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 43-50). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Shapiro, B. R., Hall, R., Mathur, A., & Zhao, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In the Learning Sciences and CSCL communities, interaction analysis (IA) is an important methodological approach to studying teaching and learning. IA relies on transcripts to selectively encode, represent, and experience video. However, researchers using IA continue to highlight the need for more dynamic and interactive transcription techniques to interpret, experience, and even speculate about data in context. In this paper, we use a comparative case study to introduce a transcription technique we call turn charts. Turn charts integrate ideas in IA with interactive and alternative visualization to visually map conversation over time, while also providing dynamic ways to select and experience audio and video data. Findings highlight how turn charts extend current transcription techniques to (1) answer common questions in IA, (2) advance exploratory modeling in the early stages of IA, and (3) bridge IA and visualization research to expand how people, things, and context are represented.

abstract: Science communication is shifting towards inclusion, where science communicators’ identities, culture, and backgrounds are valued, not quashed. However, there is a dearth of research that explores how this shift affects science communicators' experiences in everyday spaces. We observed three women, cosplaying scientists who were communicating science at a comic con then interviewed them about their experiences. Using the conceptual framework of figured worlds, we explored how they relate to cultural artifacts, build scientific practices, and re-imagine science identities. We found that women scientists used cosplay characters and costumes to drive conversations with visitors. While experiencing being objectified and sexualized in their scientific practice, they are trying to resist these interactions and share their own experiences to others to construct new narratives on possible identities of scientists. Our findings add to understanding of science identity, how it is constructed, reified, and countered within public spaces.

abstract: Scientific modeling is supported by epistemic criteria to evaluate the “goodness” of scientific products. A central epistemic criterion is causal mechanism which means identifying the underlying causes which generate changes within a system. During a five-week model-based inquiry unit students identified causes of the phenomenon, eutrophication, but it was unclear whether student understood the causes hierarchically, i.e., whether some causes led to others, and whether some were more critical to include in a model than others. In a model evaluation task, students prioritized a model that was complete and had all the causes, deprioritized the model missing the direct causal mechanism, and placed models missing the initial causes in the middle. The results indicate that students thought about mechanisms in terms of chaining which means students thought about how causes led to outcomes within a system.

abstract: Augmented Reality (AR) offers unique opportunities to contextualize learning in authentic environments, connecting learning and its context as emphasized by situated and apprenticeship learning. We explored the impact of differently situated narratives and physical artifacts on AR-context perception, immersion, learning outcome, intrinsic motivation, and workload when learning a medical topic using HoloLens2. An experimental study with N = 40 participants was conducted in a 2´2 between-subjects design with narrative (education context vs. application context) and physical contextualization (presence vs. absence of a physical artifact) as factors. It revealed that the presence of a physical artifact significantly increased the perceived virtual-physical consistency within the AR experience. Application context narratives enhanced enjoyment and knowledge. However, the latter effect decreased when physical artifacts were introduced, potentially contributing to increased frustration. The contextualization of AR material thus influenced factors relevant for learners’ experience and learning processes. Future research should explore this connection more detailed.

abstract: In elementary schools, Computational Thinking is often taught within problem-based learning pedagogies, and learners leverage their generic problem-solving competencies to complete CT tasks. How grade 4 children solve a CT problem is explored in this paper. We conducted time-series analyses to examine which problem-solving steps and CT processes are used as the task progresses, and how problem-solving steps and CT processes interrelate. Findings indicate that while some steps are given appropriate emphasis, others, including problem formulation, are not given enough prominence, overall stymying successful task execution. We also find that abstractions are made only after testing, and that when solutions fail, students tend to fall back on trial-and-error strategies. The findings suggest that students should be taught more explicitly CT problem-solving to prevent use of ineffectual strategies. More broadly, our analyses provide a dynamic view of learning CT enabling the development of operational frameworks for CT teaching.

abstract: This study explored equitable participation and collaborative dynamics in a co-design workshop where students were introduced to an established research-practice partnership that focused on designing and refining a STEM-integrated bioinformatics high-school curriculum. We define equitable participation as partners’ equal say in the decisions and balanced contributions to the co-design processes and outcomes. Accordingly, interviews with two teachers and three students who collaborated with researchers to revise the curriculum were analyzed to explore their perceived participation behaviors. The analysis revealed two primary themes: inclusive contributions through mediation and student-influenced teacher autonomy. Results showed that separate groups for students and teachers and mediation strategies facilitated inclusive contributions and influences on the design outcomes. In addition, strategies promoting psychological safety and balancing knowledge asymmetries were identified. The study contributes insights into achieving democratic and inclusive co-design practices, emphasizing the complexity of establishing equity in co-design partnerships.

abstract: In this paper, I coordinate the salient literature at the intersection of two fields: learning sciences and history/social studies education. Specifically, I take up the notion of dispositions from a sociocognitive perspective to offer greater clarity for the term, which is used widely but imprecisely when referring to the purpose and aims of history education for the public good. I then draw on conceptions of dispositions as the interplay between ability, sensitivity, and inclination in situated context. I describe an overarching Historical Disposition that views history as both useable and useful in informing present-day decisions in pursuit of re-imagined possible futures. I further frame this work within designerly citizenship, which reimagines citizenship as participating in collective designerly agency. I conclude by discussing the implications of this work for how history and social studies education might be reimagined in concert with the learning sciences.

abstract: We investigate how design elements can support sensory engagement and sense-making through discussion and place-based activities offered via a QR code triggered, web-based mobile learning experience. 31 families (116 individuals; 54 adults, 62 youths) were recruited at a nature center to participate in learning activities related to pollinators and native plants. From the learning-on-the-move and science education literatures, two design conjectures guide our work a) sensory engagement via tactile and visual observation of objects and specimens on-site support scientific noticing and b) discussion prompts and place-based activities support sense-making and knowledge integration via focusing conversation on scientific phenomena and big ideas. Families were observed seamlessly engaging in discussions beyond intended geographic boundaries as they observed and engaged in discussions of phenomena across space. This analysis contributes to literature on informal learning environments and the role that QR-triggered web-based science content can provide in outdoor learning settings.

abstract: Young learners today are constantly influenced by AI recommendations, from media choices to social connections. The resulting "filter bubble" can limit their exposure to diverse perspectives, which is especially problematic when they are not aware this manipulation is happening or why. To address the need to support youth AI literacy, we developed "BeeTrap", a mobile Augmented Reality (AR) learning game designed to enlighten young learners about the mechanisms and the ethical issue of recommendation systems. Transformative Experience model was integrated into learning activities design, focusing on making AI concepts relevant to students’ daily experiences, facilitating a new understanding of their digital world, and modeling real-life applications. Our pilot study with middle schoolers in a community-based program primarily investigated how transformative structured AI learning activities affected students’ understanding of recommendation systems and their overall conceptual, emotional, and behavioral changes toward AI.

abstract: We designed and implemented a data visualization project in a seventh-grade classroom focusing on the loss of tribal lands in Montana, United States of America. We aim to understand how students engaged with various scaffolds and how those scaffolds supported them in critically engaging with historical data through making hands-on projects. We analyzed data from multiple sources, including classroom implementation transcripts, student-created artifacts, and pre- and post-surveys. We observed that while students enjoyed creating data visualizations, they struggled to interpret them within their historical context despite the provision of multiple forms of scaffolds. We believe it is important to design a system of scaffolds to further support students in critically engaging with historical data and in developing critical data literacy.

abstract: Our research explored an in-service professional development (PD) program that was iteratively co-designed with educators at a rural school on the Big Island of Hawaii. Many Hawaiian schools are highly ruralized and demonstrate a dire need for meaningful PD in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Due to geographic and community considerations, in-service PD is an essential tool for improving education in low-income, rural communities. This confluence of considerations demands focus on supportive and effective training for rural and highly ruralized teachers. We situate this work in Ginsberg and Wlodkowski’s (2012) motivational framework for culturally responsive teaching which considers the conditions of attitude, meaning, competence, and inclusion. This paper examines the experiences of an Indigenous teacher with over 30 years of experience as she engages in PD that centers her Hawaiian community.

abstract: Children develop repertoires of practice through engagement across communities. Dominant conceptualizations of classrooms-as-containers do not make space for practices developed outside of school. I examine how a metaphor of learning as entanglements supports understanding how practices can and should be entangled with (not transformed by) classroom learning. I ask, how can entanglements as a metaphor support identifying how cultural histories shape present learning and emergent futures? I argue this approach allows for interaction analysis of the impact of historicity and power in interactions. I also claim that the metaphor of learning as entanglements supports recognizing interactional moments through which onto-epistemic heterogeneity can be affirmed and drawn upon as a resource for teacher and student learning, contributing the emergence of hybrid/third-spaces.

abstract: Data bias in AI (artificial intelligence) and ML (machine learning) remains a prominent challenge, with implications ranging from healthcare to criminal justice. As we lean more on these technologies, it becomes vital to educate the youth about the nuances of data bias and its implications. In this paper, we present the SourceML approach, teaching data bias by engaging students in building ML models with primary sources as text data in high school history classrooms. We have developed a web-based tool, StoryQ, designed to allow K-12 students to create ML models. Our results demonstrated that this approach enhances students’ understanding of data bias, helping them recognize diverse bias origins, societal implications, and comprehensive strategies for bias mitigation. The SourceML approach underscores the importance of fostering historical thinking in teaching data bias, highlighting the intricacies of data origin, generation context, and subtle influences shaping data.

abstract: We seek to understand the influence of our positionalities during an equity audit of a reform-oriented secondary mathematics curriculum. In the equity audit, we empirically explored how to support humanizing and just teaching, particularly for Black girls. Drawing on intersectionality theory, we report on how our positionalities—namely as a Black woman, white man, and white woman—influenced our coding with the Black Feminist Mathematics Pedagogies framework (Joseph, 2021). Our data include our coding experiences and a transcript of an hour-long reflective dialogue on how our gendered and racialized experiences as students and teachers influenced our coding in the equity audit. We report on two themes that emerged in reflective dialogue, the savior complex and interest convergence, and connect these to our attempts to design against white supremacy culture in our curriculum equity audit. We conclude with insights about tensions between a truly reimagined mathematics education and making a difference for students now.

abstract: This article reports findings of implementing a novel learning technology called WearableLearning to teach geometry transformations in a math classroom. The paper aims to answer RQ1) To what extent do students learn math with embodied games facilitated by WearableLearning? and RQ2) How do students learn math differently with embodied games enabled by WearableLearning, compared to traditional learning technology? Quantitative results indicate a trend of improvement from pre-test to post-test (t = 1.5, p < 0.1). Qualitative results indicate that games through WearableLearning increase the opportunities for mathematical thinking between students, physical objects, and the learning environment. Qualitative results also indicate that students benefit from additional affordances of support when utilizing WearableLearning compared to traditional learning technologies.
