abstract: Teacher learning in asynchronous online professional development (PD) is often assessed through self-reported instruments, despite uncertainties regarding teachers’ ability to accurately self-assess their learning gains in such settings. This study compared middle school mathematics teachers’ self-perceived and observed learning gains in content knowledge (CK) and pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) after participating in an asynchronous online PD program. By analyzing data collected from 57 teachers, we found a weak and nonsignificant correlation between teachers’ perceived learning gains and observed learning gains. Teachers who frequently monitored their understanding of the learning content tended to underestimate their improvement of CK from the PD program while those using cognitive learning strategies (i.e., organize and elaborate) often overestimated it, controlling for their baseline knowledge level. These findings highlight methodological concerns in using self-reports to evaluate online learning outcomes and the potential distortion in identifying effective learning strategies.

abstract: Researchers collaborated with a social justice organization to co-design a curriculum for elementary and middle school youth to create an interactive map highlighting community assets as an exploration towards how they might combat gun violence. The curriculum was designed around Asset-Based Community Development (ABCD) to engage students in asset mapping for social action. However, the researchers noted a lack of guidance for addressing the systemic underpinnings of gun-violence. In response, the researchers applied a womanist lens—which reflects Black women and women of color’s everyday strategies for ending all forms of oppression—to examine how it might shape reflection and iteration on the curriculum. Analyzing curricular resources and codesign notes, the findings highlight the importance of fostering relationships to redistribute power, center dialogue for engaging in tensions, defining a collective communitarian approach with learners, supporting learners in storying their communities, and engaging in care and wellness as resistance.

abstract: Building from literature connected to mobile learning and sense of place, this study explores the influence of place on families’ experiences while using a mobile augmented reality app about pollinators that was designed to be used in outdoor spaces. From the second data collection of a design-based research study with nine families, we investigated the difference between two families’ experiences completing the app at home or at a local park. This analysis demonstrates how families’ sense of place interacts with the design of mobile augmented reality applications to influence the connections they make with their local outdoor settings and communities. Further attention to the sociocultural and political elements of sense of place within the design of a mobile augmented reality app could potentially help foster ecological stewardship actions and behaviors.

abstract: To support learners in developing career-related identities, we must attend to both their imagined selves in the field and their evolving knowledge of prospective careers. In this study, we designed an educational tool that leverages large language models (LLMs) called Careergram, a career identity reflection tool that prompts students to reflect on their evolving occupational identities and seek out support from their mentors. We piloted the tool in an undergraduate educational data science research fellowship program. Using a lens of identity development, we analyze how this tool was taken up and used by three learners, who represented different profiles of occupational identity development. Through rich descriptions of each participant, we identify different ways that learners utilize Careergram to facilitate conversations with their mentors, and shed light on learning processes that can support learners' development of career-related identities.

abstract: Racialization of school discipline is an enduring systemic problem in the United States. This formative intervention study is based on a collaboration with 14 school stakeholders: American Indian students, parents, community members, and educators at a rural high school in a community-driven problem-solving process called Indigenous Learning Lab (ILL). Members analyzed the root causes of the racialized school discipline and created a new behavioral support system. Utilizing critical geography and decolonizing methodology, this formative intervention study aimed to unpack how ILL members formed Thirdspace—a space of resistance, possibilities, and hopes—to address enduring racial disproportionality in school discipline. Members challenged race-neutral representations of space, mapped out dystopia, revitalized American Indian epistemology, and mapped out a real utopian vision of schooling.

abstract: In Vicarious Failure, students prepare for learning from subsequent instruction by studying other students’ erroneous solution attempts. This preparation activates prior knowledge, which is assumed to help students process the instruction, but it is unclear how it affects students’ learning from activating to building conceptual knowledge during instruction. We analyzed students’ learning by assessing their knowledge based on the number of conceptual features of a targeted concept at three points in time: during the preparation phase, in an intermediate test before instruction, and in a post-test after instruction. We hypothesized that the effect of students’ prior knowledge activation on their learning from instruction would be mediated by their intermediate knowledge, and expected that students’ knowledge of conceptual features would remain consistent from one phase to the next. While no mediation effect emerged, students’ knowledge mostly remained consistent from one point in time to the next.

abstract: Research on improving reasoning practices in classrooms assumes that students will internalize the reasoning practices in which their teachers prompt them to participate. Drawing on recent advances in cognitive psychology which portray reasoning as a distributed phenomenon in which group members build new understanding out of the individual perspectives contributed by members, we present a case study of growth in student reasoning ability in a teacher’s classroom in order to shed light on how such internalization occurs. We find preliminary evidence that students internalize a teacher’s pattern of attention to the metacognitive opportunities afforded by individual discussion contributions.

title: Modeling-Based Learning in Kindergarten Science: Investigating Heat Transfer in a Metal Rod
citation: Louca, L. T. & Xeni, M. (2024). Modeling-Based Learning in Kindergarten Science: Investigating Heat Transfer in a Metal Rod. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 59-66). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Louca, L. T. & Xeni, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Following research on using Modeling-based Learning (MbL) in kindergarten, in this interpretive case study we seek to provide detailed descriptions of the implementation of MbL with a group of 24 kindergarten children studying heat transfer in a metal rod. Focusing on children mechanistic reasoning and their constructed models, findings suggest that participating children successfully engaged in authentic MbL activities and developed several different types of models, utilizing a variety of features of mechanistic reasoning. We use this evidence to argue that (a) different modeling tools may afford different learning opportunities; (b) kindergarten children have modeling resources that can use in order to utilize different MbL tools; and (c) different MbL tools may prevent or support children moving into a lower scalar lever of a more advanced mechanistic account of the phenomenon.

title: Examining Participation and Outcomes Among Middle School Students in a Virtual Camp on Coding with Music
citation: Zhang, Y., Tabares, S. O., Patt, R., Krug, D. L., Mead, H., Mouza, C., Shepherd, D., & Pollock, L. (2024). Examining Participation and Outcomes Among Middle School Students in a Virtual Camp on Coding with Music. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 594-601). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhang, Y., Tabares, S. O., Patt, R., Krug, D. L., Mead, H., Mouza, C., Shepherd, D., & Pollock, L.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Attracting students to computing is crucial for advancing the development of new skills and fostering positive attitudes toward the field, especially among females and minoritized populations. One promising approach involves integrating computing with artistic activities, such as music. This study examines how learner’s prior experiences influence their participation in a virtual summer camp on coding with music. The study also examines how participation in the camp influences participants' attitudes about computing, with an eye toward gender differences. Data were collected through participant surveys (N=73) and focus groups (N=48). Findings suggest that parents’ and guardians' involvement is crucial for participation and integrating coding with artistic work holds promise for attracting students to the field. Findings can inform possible paths to engaging students in computing.

title: Teaching with Representations: How Teachers’ Perception Shift Their Science Teaching
citation: Tu, X., Danish, J., Ryan, Z., Vickery, M., Rogers, M. P., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Philips, A. (2024). Teaching with Representations: How Teachers’ Perception Shift Their Science Teaching. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 602-609). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tu, X., Danish, J., Ryan, Z., Vickery, M., Rogers, M. P., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Philips, A.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Representations are essential to science education. However, few studies explore teacher understanding of their implementation of representations. In particular, there is little attention to how teacher perception influences their in-classroom teaching with representations. To support teachers in using representations in the elementary science classroom, we designed the longitudinal Project, Representation: Teachers as Learners (RepTaL), which includes various professional development activities. This paper explores teachers’ perceptions of science representations that influence the way they incorporate representations in their science teaching. We analyzed six participants’ interviews and classroom recordings across the 2021-2023 academic years. The results revealed after engaging with the (RepTaL), teachers started to try various representations in their science classrooms. Another major change is the teachers would like to have students be the “owners” of the representation rather than the audience. Their in-classroom teaching also showed that they integrated what they learned from PD in their teaching without coaching in the last year.

title: “We are all Learning Here!”: Negotiations of Power within an Intergenerational Participatory Design Research Project
citation: Allen, C. D. & Hill, K. (2024). “We are all Learning Here!”: Negotiations of Power within an Intergenerational Participatory Design Research Project. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 610-617). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Allen, C. D. & Hill, K.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
conceptualisations_list: Co-Design & Participatory Design; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: In this paper, we examine the ways power and privilege were negotiated within the context of a participatory design research project focused on data science as a means to pursuing environmental and social justice through community-engaged projects. Using critical ethnography and interaction analysis methodologies, we explore relational dynamics among the project team – which included high school youth, science educators, graduate students, and university faculty – as they negotiated meanings and action related to local research projects. We draw conceptually on Holland and Lave (2009) and Gutiérrez et al (2019) to understand participants as historical actors and their negotiations of self and possible futures in the context of our program. We consider social positioning and authoring of who has knowledge, who has authority, and who is learning in interactional dynamics among the project team over a two-day kickoff meeting. We highlight the ways youth engage productive resistance to youth-adult hierarchies.

title: Investigating Youths’ Everyday Understanding of Machine Learning Applications: a Knowledge-in-Pieces Perspective
citation: Morales-Navarro, L. & Kafai, Y. B. (2024). Investigating Youths’ Everyday Understanding of Machine Learning Applications: a Knowledge-in-Pieces Perspective. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 618-625). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Morales-Navarro, L. & Kafai, Y. B.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Despite recent calls for including artificial intelligence (AI) literacy in K-12 education, not enough attention has been paid to studying youths’ everyday knowledge about machine learning (ML). Most research has examined how youths attribute intelligence to AI/ML systems. Other studies have centered on youths' theories and hypotheses about ML highlighting their misconceptions and how these may hinder learning. However, research on conceptual change shows that youths may not have coherent theories about scientific phenomena and instead have knowledge pieces that can be productive for formal learning. We investigate teens’ everyday understanding of ML through a knowledge-in-pieces perspective. Our analyses reveal that youths showed some understanding that ML applications learn from training data and that applications recognize patterns in input data and depending on these provide different outputs. We discuss how these findings expand our knowledge base and implications for the design of tools and activities to introduce youths to ML.

title: Engaging Stakeholders in Deliberation for Organizational Design
citation: Wu, M., Easterday, M., & Sherin, B. (2024). Engaging Stakeholders in Deliberation for Organizational Design. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 634-641). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wu, M., Easterday, M., & Sherin, B.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Deliberation involves applying knowledge, synthesizing ideas, weighing different options and reflection by stakeholders who negotiate a decision that leads to implementation. While we know about many of the cognitive processes involved in deliberation, we know little about how stakeholders become involved in deliberation in real-world, non-binding contexts. This study investigates the processes of building up a Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) certificate program for undergraduate students at a private university. We analyzed 334 messages from 57 stakeholders’ email exchanges, meetings, and interview transcripts to reveal the stakeholder-seeking process and outreach strategies. Results showed that deliberation started from a small group of active stakeholders who accounted for most of the work and outreach. Our findings reveal that an effective stakeholder involvement strategy is the key for the outcome of deliberation to factor in implementation in the observed case. We also consider the types of learning required by individuals and the group in deliberation.

title: Four Days to Independent Work: Studying how Professional Coffee Roasters Learn through Proximal Apprenticeship
citation: Davey, B. & Stevens, R. (2024). Four Days to Independent Work: Studying how Professional Coffee Roasters Learn through Proximal Apprenticeship. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Davey, B. & Stevens, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This case study examines the first four days of a proximal apprenticeship among coffee roasters. The intense and effective period of learning presented here challenges studies of apprenticeship, where delegations of responsibility occur over many months and years. To understand this transience, we track a changing web of coordinations over four days: who coordinated what? We discuss implications for apprenticeship-like learning and school science.

title: Pandemic-Related Perseverance During Math Problem-Solving in MathSpring, an Educational Technology Platform that Responds to Student Affect
citation: Brezack, N., Chan, W., & Feng, M. (2024). Pandemic-Related Perseverance During Math Problem-Solving in MathSpring, an Educational Technology Platform that Responds to Student Affect. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 650-657). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Brezack, N., Chan, W., & Feng, M.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Perseverance is critical for students’ achievement and may be particularly important after COVID-19. We analyzed teacher and principal interviews and student educational technology usage data to examine students’ perseverance during math problem-solving across three cohorts of students during and after COVID-19. Data were collected as part of a randomized control trial examining the efficacy of an educational technology platform, MathSpring, in supporting students’ math achievement. The results indicated that teachers and principals were concerned with their students’ perseverance, and students’ usage data similarly demonstrated that students may have reduced perseverance when solving math problems after COVID-19. Teachers and students may benefit from using tools that help foster perseverance in math class. MathSpring and other educational technology tools that support perseverance could be useful for encouraging students to put forth effort when solving math problems, which could in turn support students’ math learning outcomes.

title: Teaching Socio-Scientific Argumentation in two Chinese Science Classrooms: A Case Study
citation: Fan, N., Zhu, M., & Xiao, S. (2024). Teaching Socio-Scientific Argumentation in two Chinese Science Classrooms: A Case Study. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 658-665). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Fan, N., Zhu, M., & Xiao, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Engaging students in socio-scientific argumentation is proven effective for resolving everyday issues, yet its integration and implementation in Chinese science classrooms face challenges due to limited curriculum resources and traditional didactic Confucian pedagogy. To investigate these integration efforts, we collaborated with a Chinese science teacher, analyzing four episodes of her SSI argumentation teaching. We found that the teacher consistently framed SSI argumentation activities as addressing everyday problems and tended to engage students in a more authentic version of science practice along with restricted shared epistemic agency. Our fine-grained analysis on teacher’s discourse moves that facilitated whole-class argumentation revealed four frequently employed categories: setting norms, revoicing, pressing, and summarizing, all contributing to either sustaining or advancing the whole-class argumentation process. Despite challenges, this study provides insights into effective SSI argumentation integration in Chinese science classrooms.

title: Whole Scientist Education in an Authentic-Inquiry Laboratory
citation: Light, E. (2024). Whole Scientist Education in an Authentic-Inquiry Laboratory. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 666-673). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Light, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This report argues for broader implementation of authentic-inquiry courses defined by Buck’s rubric of inquiry as those in which undergraduates pursue their own research goals and process. Addressing this gap in implementation may prepare students for careers as self-directed and transformative researchers by facilitating multidimensional learning outcomes. This study assesses student outcomes from authentic inquiry using a Whole Scientist framework encompassing autonomy, belonging, competence, and purpose. Seven consenting students released the recordings from 15-minute semi-structured qualitative interviews conducted during the final week of the semester. I de-identified and deductively analyzed transcripts for evidence of Whole Scientist learning outcomes and found participants consistently reported outcomes across all domains. The potential of authentic inquiry to facilitate transformative intellectualism is discussed. Broader implementation and assessment of authentic inquiry is recommended.

title: Learners' Presence in VR Field Trips Depends on Design of the Media, Not Novelty
citation: McGivney, E. (2024). Learners' Presence in VR Field Trips Depends on Design of the Media, Not Novelty. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 67-74). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: McGivney, E.
subject: STEM - Mathematics; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Situating science, technology, engineering and math (STEM) education in authentic environments and practices has typically been achieved by taking learning outside of the classroom, but virtual reality (VR) is a promising tool to bring such experiences into classrooms. Using VR to situate learning relies on its ability to engender the feeling of “being there,” or presence, in a virtual place. This study investigated features of VR field trips in STEM education that impact learners’ sense of presence and how it changed over time as students participated in four VR-enabled lessons with immersive videos and videogame-like environments. The results indicate the type of VR media predicts learners’ presence but the novelty of the technology does not, as there were not changes over time. These results contribute a better understanding of presence in educational VR by looking beyond just the devices and studying its impact over time in classroom instruction.

title: Of Barrios and Favelas: Blending Criticality and Imagination Through Freire-Inspired Utopian Workshops
citation: Campos, F. C. (2024). Of Barrios and Favelas: Blending Criticality and Imagination Through Freire-Inspired Utopian Workshops. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 674-681). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Campos, F. C.
subject: Social & Civic Studies
conceptualisations_list: Design-Based Research (DBR); Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: How might we design learning environments that are imaginative enough to go beyond the constraints of reality while sufficiently grounded on the challenges of one's lived experience? This study explores speculative and utopian pedagogies, encouraging students to envision alternative scenarios to current oppressive situations while ensuring a solid understanding of the complexities of inequality and oppression. Central to this research is how educators can integrate criticality and imagination under a speculative civics education paradigm. Drawing inspiration from Brazilian educator Paulo Freire, this study employs a Design-Based Research approach to create a civic imagination workshop, refining it through successive iterations with adolescents in a barrio in California and a favela in Rio de Janeiro. The findings offer robust design principles to guide educators in crafting interventions that blend critical and visionary thinking for marginalized youth.

title: A Case Study of Activity Structures and Resources that Support Teacher Agency and Leadership in an RPP
citation: Billings, K. & Linn, M. C. (2024). A Case Study of Activity Structures and Resources that Support Teacher Agency and Leadership in an RPP. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 682-689). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Billings, K. & Linn, M. C.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This case study reveals how one teacher’s agency and leadership in a Research Practice Partnership (RPP) impacted the design of a justice-centered science unit. We analyze RPP documents and data, from design meetings, workshop transcripts, observations, and informal co-design conversations, to reveal the ways RPP activity structures helped to support the teachers’ leadership. We report our findings in three illustrative episodes. Episode 1 reveals how the teachers’ longstanding involvement with the RPP empowered him to bring a new unit topic to the collaboration. Episode 2 documents the teachers’ leadership during workshops. Episode 3 reveals how conversations between the teacher and the learning scientist during unit implementation supported the refinement of the unit and reflection on teaching practice.

title: Cultivate Research Literacy: High School Students Work with Community Partners to Investigate Real-World Challenges
citation: Zhang, J., Song, G., Underwood, T., Guo, D., Espinosa, K., Hower, L., Muirhead, J., & Kerr, J. (2024). Cultivate Research Literacy: High School Students Work with Community Partners to Investigate Real-World Challenges. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 690-697). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhang, J., Song, G., Underwood, T., Guo, D., Espinosa, K., Hower, L., Muirhead, J., & Kerr, J.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This research explores educational designs for engaging high school students in authentic research in collaboration with a network of professional communities. The design framework features an interdisciplinary community-based approach to research experiences. Students' research activities were supported by a collaborative community, which included a team of teachers, classmates who worked on diverse topics and challenges, and professional community partners. The data collection included students’ research journals, records of student meetings and presentations, interviews with the teachers and students, and an online survey of the community partners. The findings revealed how students navigated the unfolding research processes to address real-world challenges with the support of their teachers and community partners. Based on the findings, we discuss designs for cultivating students’ research literacy.

title: Yalla KIBO: A Research-Practice Partnership for Binational, Youth-Led Kindergarten Robotics in Jerusalem
citation: Levinson, T., Qubti, L., Bekerman, Z., & Bers, M. (2024). Yalla KIBO: A Research-Practice Partnership for Binational, Youth-Led Kindergarten Robotics in Jerusalem. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 698-705). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Levinson, T., Qubti, L., Bekerman, Z., & Bers, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Educational programs working for a shared society are one peacemaking approach for intractable conflicts, such as that between Jewish Israelis and Palestinian Arabs, including Palestinian citizens and residents of Israel. This paper discusses a pilot program where Israeli and Palestinian teenagers, alumni of a binational computer science (CS) and entrepreneurship program, designed, taught, and researched a robotics program at an integrated Arab-Jewish kindergarten, using an iterative design process to construct the program based on their experiences. We found features in both the learning environment and student outcomes relating to the shared society model. Our findings suggest that by incorporating features of education for a shared society into the design of the educational environment, a CS educational leadership program can become not only a coding playground but a coding bridge, leading to outcomes of a shared society as well.

title: Toward an Understanding of “Math Parenting Identity”: Parent Perceptions of the Home Math Environments of Young Children
citation: Betts, A. & Son, J. (2024). Toward an Understanding of “Math Parenting Identity”: Parent Perceptions of the Home Math Environments of Young Children. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 706-713). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Betts, A. & Son, J.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Unveiling a pioneering concept, this research introduces “Math Parenting Identity” (MPI) as an important determinant in the foundational math experiences that take place in the home math environments of young learners prior to the onset of formal schooling in kindergarten. Engaging a national sample of 847 parents of 4 to 5-year-olds, the study employs the RESET framework to explore the existence and complexity of MPI. It articulates important implications for parent decision-making and motivations in fostering the early math learning of their children and provides a new survey instrument to deepen our understanding of how parental beliefs and behaviors not only shape parents’ own MPI, but also children's earliest encounters with mathematics.

title: Fused Representations: Linking Choreographic and Digital NetLogo Modeling through Intermodal Inquiry
citation: Wagh, A., Vogelstein, L., & Champion, D. (2024). Fused Representations: Linking Choreographic and Digital NetLogo Modeling through Intermodal Inquiry. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 714-721). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wagh, A., Vogelstein, L., & Champion, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This paper reports from a summer camp, Dance to Explore Science, in which middle school youth, professional scientists and choreographers collaboratively engaged in intermodal inquiry using choreographic and digital NetLogo modeling to investigate a topic within the scientists’ research areas. Drawing on analysis of youth interviews, one group’s work towards preparing their final share-out, and their final share-out itself, we propose the construct of a fused representation—a distributed model developed by participants in which their physical choreography and NetLogo models expressed a scientific idea in interlinked ways. We present evidence of why we see their share-out as a fused representation, and illuminate how attuning to the relationships between their choreographic and NetLogo models led the group to construct a fused representation. In the discussion, we reflect on the importance of supporting the development of fused representations to leverage multiple modalities for scientific modeling and sense-making.

title: Developing Relational Agency for Addressing Racialization of School Discipline in the U.S
citation: Mawene, D., Ko, D., Bal, A., Orie, L., Schrader, E., Yoo, J., & Mayer-Jochimsen, M. (2024). Developing Relational Agency for Addressing Racialization of School Discipline in the U.S. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 722-729). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Mawene, D., Ko, D., Bal, A., Orie, L., Schrader, E., Yoo, J., & Mayer-Jochimsen, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this paper, we adapt Edwards's (2005; 2007) concept of relational agency, situating it within the context of racialized schooling in the U.S. We posit that the ability to recognize and leverage others' support in addressing a complex problem necessitates the ability to acknowledge the historical legacies of systemic racial violence ingrained in everyday school practices. To support our theoretical argument, we present a case from Indigenous Learning Lab (ILL), an inclusive task force established to design a culturally responsive behavioral support system addressing racial disproportionality in school discipline in a predominantly white high school serving American Indian students. Specifically, we emphasize the relational agency of Mr. Archer, the school principal, as he worked together with ILL members, particularly American Indian members.

title: Teachers Learning to Make Space for Student Agency and Authority in Literature and Math Classroom Discourse
citation: Hall, A. H., Pitvorec, K., & Goldman, S. R. (2024). Teachers Learning to Make Space for Student Agency and Authority in Literature and Math Classroom Discourse. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 730-737). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hall, A. H., Pitvorec, K., & Goldman, S. R.
subject: STEM - Mathematics; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This paper presents case studies of one high school ELA teacher and one middle school math teacher who, through reflecting on their practice with researchers, learned to support students in taking up agency and authority for building disciplinary knowledge. This learning reflected a shift in their understanding of their discipline, of their role as teachers, and of students’ capabilities to do the intellectual work of the discipline. How teachers made these shifts was different in the two cases but in both cases, collaborative reflection on the design and implementation of instruction was the critical mechanism of change.

title: Decomposing Students’ Design Moves when Programming Agent-Based Models
citation: Eloy, A., Fuhrmann, T., Wagh, A., de Deus Lopes, R., Wilkerson, M., & Blikstein, P. (2024). Decomposing Students’ Design Moves when Programming Agent-Based Models. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 738-745). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Eloy, A., Fuhrmann, T., Wagh, A., Lopes, R. D. D., Wilkerson, M., & Blikstein, P.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
tpack_tk_labels: Simulations & Scientific Modeling; Block-based Coding & Authoring
abstract: Constructing computational models is a central practice for K-12 students to refine and validate their understanding of scientific phenomena and develop computational practices. Our work decomposes that practice by investigating the design moves students take while constructing models through programming. Using log data and video recordings from three pairs of students to find patterns in programming actions while interacting with an agent- and block-based modeling environment, we identify six design moves students used. In addition, we situate the occurrence of those moves over time and provide vignettes that illustrate them in context. Finally, we reflect on how our findings support the argument that computational modeling, particularly programming models, provides a fertile ground for promoting modeling and computational practices.

title: “In the lived experience of the lesson”: A Case Study of Novice Teacher Improvisation
citation: Rubin, E. (2024). “In the lived experience of the lesson”: A Case Study of Novice Teacher Improvisation. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 746-753). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rubin, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Improvisation is an essential aspect of teaching, but has not typically been prioritized in teacher education. The prevalence of procedural approaches to teacher education reflects a prevailing notion that novice teachers should master predetermined moves and apply them automatically before beginning to improvise. An emerging line of research counters this view, arguing that novice teachers can and should improvise. This case study of a novice teacher’s practice contributes to that research by drawing on jazz improvisation to highlight improvisational teaching. Starting from the premise that novices can be responsive and improvisational, this study asks: how do novice teachers engage in improvisation in their initial teaching experiences? Analysis shows that this novice teacher improvises purposefully to further instructional goals and support student learning, and that he employs reasoning that is typically associated with experienced teachers. These findings have important implications for theorizing teacher improvisation and for supporting novice teacher learning.

title: Using Learning Analytics in Understanding College Students’ Behavior in ChatGPT-Facilitated Programming Learning
citation: Xu, J., Sun, D., & Li, Y. (2024). Using Learning Analytics in Understanding College Students’ Behavior in ChatGPT-Facilitated Programming Learning. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 75-82). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Xu, J., Sun, D., & Li, Y.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: As a typical generative artificial intelligence tool, ChatGPT has gained wide attention in its application to programming. However, few researchers have conducted empirical studies to explore how learners use ChatGPT for programming learning. This study analyzes learners' programming learning behaviors to explore the characteristics of different performance learners using ChatGPT-assisted programming learning. The study analyzes the programming process of 15 learners adopting the fine-grained programming behavior method. The results indicate that: (1) Learners regard ChatGPT as a useful programming learning resource and rely on it to guide their learning process. (2) Learners tend to copy debug error messages to ChatGPT and copy its feedback, which may potentially weaken their deep understanding of the code. (3) High-performing group learners use ChatGPT more frequently for programming assistance while low-performing group learners use ChatGPT the least. Based on the findings, this study proposes suggestions for using ChatGPT to assist college students in programming learning.

title: Looking Back to See Myself: Analepsis as Tool to Deepen Proleptic Notions of Identity Development
citation: Stamatis, K., Polman, J. L., Tran, T. C., & Hernandez, J. R. (2024). Looking Back to See Myself: Analepsis as Tool to Deepen Proleptic Notions of Identity Development. abstract: Studies of identity development have a long history in educational research; yet there remains a need to deepen understandings of ways communities who have been historically marginalized build identities across cultural contexts. Following scholars who have used the notion of prolepsis to explore youth identity development, we examine the potential for additional tools, such as analepsis, to understand the ways youth draw from family histories to inscribe themselves into the world. This study took place in a local history museum with Latine youth who co-designed a museum exhibit to represent their familial and cultural stories. Findings illustrate the potential for theoretical tools that expand upon studies of identity to unpack the ways youth draw upon the experiences of their ancestors, family members, and cultural figures to make sense of themselves in relation to their experiences as youth with cultural histories both within and outside of the U.S.

title: Narrative inquiry in design-based research
citation: Gouvea, E. & Gravel, B. (2024). Narrative inquiry in design-based research. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. abstract: Material agency is steadily being explored in the Learning Sciences. Most commonly, either Indigenous knowledges or new materialist philosophy (or both) provide theoretical grounding for this work. However, the ontological commitments shared by these relational approaches are incompatible with some of the research assumptions and methodologies commonly found in the Learning Sciences. In this paper, we operationalize a form of postqualitative inquiry in design-based research that can accommodate the critique of representationalism found in Indigenous and new materialist methodologies. We contribute a perspective and a motivation for incorporating the emergent agency of methodology into design-based research in the Learning Sciences.

title: The Paradigm Pivot: The Role of Community Cultural Wealth in Shifting Pedagogical Practices
citation: Menzies, C. M. & Schunn, C. D. (2024). The Paradigm Pivot: The Role of Community Cultural Wealth in Shifting Pedagogical Practices. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. authors_list: Menzies, C. M. & Schunn, C. D.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
conceptualisations_list: Funds of Knowledge & Cultural Wealth; Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL)
abstract: This paper explores the adaptation of a Community Cultural Wealth (CCW) pedagogical framework from mathematics to English Language Arts (ELA) education, focusing on secondary schools in the U.S. Utilizing a qualitative case study, four high school ELA teachers participated in workshops to integrate CCW principles into their teaching. The study probes teacher self-reports to investigate the translation of mathematics-derived CCW pedagogical practices into ELA contexts and their impact on teachers' perceptions and methods. Findings indicate a pedagogical shift from teacher-centered to student and community-directed approaches, emphasizing collaborative learning and leveraging students' cultural capital. This shift suggests CCW's potential in fostering asset-rich learning environments across diverse academic disciplines. Opportunities for further empirical research on CCW pedagogies in K-12 are discussed.

title: River Crossings of our Childhood: Nezuko and Yasmine Dis/orient Computing Education
citation: Sanyal, M., Sengupta, P., Banerjee, P., Dutta, S., & Ozacar, B. H. (2024). River Crossings of our Childhood: Nezuko and Yasmine Dis/orient Computing Education. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. abstract: We present a case of two youth who are sisters and newcomer immigrants of color in Canada as they work towards re-designing and re-imagining computational models entrenched in white, colonial, and masculine ideologies. Through their representational and epistemic work, we show how centering their desires, personal and sensory-affective histories can dis/orient colonial and techno-centric approaches to computational modeling. We also advance a varied range of scholarship that critiques the deficit positioning of newcomer immigrant and refugee youth of color by centring the youths’ proleptic world-making.

abstract: In today’s technology-driven society, mastering Computational Thinking (CT) skills is crucial for students. To develop these skills, leveraging collaborative technology-rich environments (TREs) can be an effective approach. Examples of those TREs include block-based programming learning environments, immersive digital games, and robotic toolkits. In this systematic review, following PRISMA, we identified 56 studies from the literature. We investigated how collaboration within TREs influences the development of CT skills among K-12 students. The findings underscore the value of collaborative learning environments within TREs for effectively fostering students’ CT skills, emphasizing the importance of creating impactful learning environments that prioritize collaboration in CT skill development.

title: Mathematics Teachers Framing of Relational Interactions
citation: Mendez, J. & van Es, E. (2024). Mathematics Teachers Framing of Relational Interactions. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 793-800). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Mendez, J. & Es, E. V.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Research on teacher noticing has theorized how teachers attend to student thinking, but less on how teachers attend to relational interactions. This article draws on frameworks from equitable mathematics instruction (Battey & Neal, 2018) and teacher noticing (Louie et al., 2021) to infer teachers’ framing of relational classroom interactions and its connection to teachers’ attention to, interpretations of, and responses to students. We analyze noticing interview data from 11 secondary mathematics teachers who participated in a research collaborative aimed at theorizing noticing for equity. We infer teachers’ framing by capturing how they interpret and make connections to broader principles of teaching and learning when attending to various relational interactions. Findings suggest that teachers can attend to similar relational events, but interpret and characterize their responses in ways that suggest different types of framing.

title: Activism or Bureaucracy: What Are We Teaching Students Through Local Climate Action Projects?
citation: Fitzmaurice, H. L. & Wilkerson, M. H. (2024). Activism or Bureaucracy: What Are We Teaching Students Through Local Climate Action Projects?. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science

abstract: Advancing student empowerment through climate action projects in K-12 classrooms is an often-cited goal in the climate change education community, specifically to ameliorate the mental health challenges experienced by K-12 students in association with climate change. Less discussed, however, are the orientations-of-action (1) that manifest in classroom activity in the context of such projects: the extent to which classroom activity is oriented more towards critically questioning and reimagining systems (activism) or more towards working within the context of existing systems (bureaucracy). Here, we discuss orientations-of-action within classroom projects in the context of a professional development program around justice-centered climate change pedagogy in an urban school setting. In the context of teacher accounts of classroom activity, we define an orientations-of-action rubric and observe a progression towards bureaucratic orientations-of-action through different elements of classroom projects. Through two focal projects we explore this progression, as well as teacher intentionality with respect to orientations-of-action.

title: Playful Frameworks of Research: Play And Its Potential in Researching Learning Alongside Youth
citation: Ryan, Z. (2024). Playful Frameworks of Research: Play And Its Potential in Researching Learning Alongside Youth. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. authors_list: Ryan, Z.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Recent efforts to envision expansive frameworks of participatory research alongside communities, including youth, have produced particularly rich work in the learning sciences. In this paper, I frame the concept of play as a boundary practice while working alongside youth and unpack its potential role in the research process. I make a call for scholars to begin thinking deeply about how play can be integrated throughout the research process to better center the contributions of youth participants we research alongside. In doing so, I offer three primary dimensions of research that play is best suited for: 1) In the selection of methods, including research sites, topic of study, and methods of data collection; 2) In the capacity of participatory design research projects aimed at fostering material change in communities, and; 3) In the co-analysis of qualitative video data alongside youth to deepen our understanding of meaningful learning situated within playful interaction.

title: Making is not Just About Making: Female Collectivity and Agentic Non-Humans in Clay Pottery and Oven-Making in Brazilian Quilombola Communities

abstract: This paper explores the cultural nuances of clay pottery and oven-making in two quilombola communities in Brazil, offering a critical perspective on the prevailing narratives around maker education. Our research in the Brazilian Amazon reveals a profound connection between the community and the Mãe do Barro, a revered non-human entity involved in the making process, significantly contributing to its technical rigor and effectiveness. In another site in the Southeast of Brazil, the oven-making process facilitates and strengthens conviviality and solidarity among female oven makers. These findings challenge the dominant, often US-centric paradigms (and critiques) in maker education by highlighting diverse, culturally rich making practices. We argue for a more inclusive and globally aware making education curriculum, emphasizing the need to recognize and value the making traditions of historically marginalized communities outside of the US.

abstract: As novice learners advance past the introductory stage, they must coordinate their prior and intuitive knowledge with increasingly abstract information. This assimilation process is especially important in physics as unobservable and counterintuitive topics enter the curriculum. We share three case studies of upper-division physics students working with Lagrangian mechanics to showcase their reliance on and confidence in procedural and mathematical knowledge while navigating this conceptually challenging topic. We introduce an ontological innovation – the operational route – to describe this pattern of behavior and discuss its implications for educational research focusing on intermediate learners.

abstract: This study explored 7th-grade students’ help-seeking behaviors in a digital mathematics learning game. In particular, we applied response time decomposition to examine the relationships among the amount of time a student spent reading a hint (i.e., hint reading time), hint type, and in-game performance. The results showed significant differences in hint reading time by the following action and hint type. Overall, hint reading time was positively related to problem solving efficiency scores. However, this association varied by hint type. The use of an indirect hint was negatively correlated with efficiency on the problem in which the hint was accessed but positively correlated with efficiency on the next problem. These findings suggest that prompting students to pause and think about the hint presented may support efficient problem solving. Although indirect hints may cause students to struggle through the problem, they show the benefits of that struggle in subsequent performance.

title: Teaching Future-Makers: Outcomes of an International Design Workshop for Critical Action Educators

abstract: This paper reports on recent developments of the Critical Action Learning Exchange (Carvalho et al., 2021), an international community of educators who seek to respond to social and environmental issues that affect their students. We report on an international design workshop that engaged a cohort of teachers in designing Critical Action Learning activities for their students in the Summer of 2023. Participants (n=39) completed 16 curriculum designs for grade levels from kindergarten to university, addressing a broad range of socio-environmental issues and adopting diverse approaches, such as Arts-Based Critical Action, Community Engagement, Critical Making, Games for Critical Action, and Storytelling. This paper examines our Professional Development model, together with an analysis of teacher participants' ideas and their design products. We investigate what forms of scaffolding can facilitate the changes of practice needed for teachers to become critical action educators and support their Critical Action Learning designs.

title: Newcomer Youths’ Ethical Stances in Representing War And Forced Migration
citation: Dutta, S., Sengupta, P., & Banerjee, P. (2024). Newcomer Youths’ Ethical Stances in Representing War And Forced Migration. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 841-848). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Dutta, S., Sengupta, P., & Banerjee, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We illustrate how a group of newcomer (refugee) young women of color engaged in filmmaking using stop-motion animation to represent a story of a family becoming refugees in the face of war. We ask the following research question: How did the youth adopt, negotiate, and represent their ethical stances in telling stories of forced migration using stop-motion animation? Our analysis shows that through designing their narratives, and figural and gestural representations of marginal lives, bodies, and interactions, the youth centered axiological dimensions of representing violence, and amplified the ethical complexities experienced by families facing war and violent displacement. The youths’ work offers a necessary counter-imaginary for public education in which representational work through creating animations can become a context for making visible and centering ethical and affective dimensions of their experiences of forced migration that are otherwise silenced and invisibilized by the procedurality of refugee resettlement, and in their schools in Canada.

title: Individual and Group Contributions and Authorship of Objects in Collaborative Knowledge Creation
citation: Spence, N. & Markauskaite, L. (2024). Individual and Group Contributions and Authorship of Objects in Collaborative Knowledge Creation. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 849-856). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Spence, N. & Markauskaite, L.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In the study of object-centered knowledge creation, epistemic objects, technical objects, and boundary objects have been explored in terms of their mutability and role in knowledge creation and collaboration. This paper offers a new taxonomy that enables exploration of conceptual development and authorship of the objects by distinguishing between four types of objects—individual, group, synthesizing and cooperative. Beyond simply individually- versus group-created objects, synthesizing and cooperative objects enable insight into how individuals participate in joint knowledge creation. The synthesizing object, for example, is produced by an individual based on group conceptual development within a collaborative project. The new object types are useful for educational design and in research on collaborative learning and related forms of generative collaborative work, including in professional and interdisciplinary research spheres. Attention to the complexities of authorship in the stages of development augments analysis of epistemic and boundary objects.

title: Generative AI as a Mirror: Educators Exploring and Challenging Dominant Discourses about the Future of AI in Education
citation: Aleman, E., Dilek, M., & Baran, E. (2024). Generative AI as a Mirror: Educators Exploring and Challenging Dominant Discourses about the Future of AI in Education. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. International Society of the Learning Sciences.

subject: Social & Civic Studies
abstract: This study explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in teacher education and the challenges educators face in gaining agency and understanding of AI implementation. Focusing on the concept of discursive closure, it investigates how educators envision the future of AI in education (AIed) and the implications of dominant discourses in their perceptions about the future, but also about its integration today. The study reveals educators' perceptions and the limitations of current narratives about AIed. It uncovers deterministic, trajectoristic, and simplistic binary views that tend to overshadow educators' roles and diminish their sense of agency in classrooms today. Additionally, through a speculative exercise employing a generative AI tool, the study showcases how educators interpret and make sense of these dominant discourses while envisioning educational futures, thereby exposing the normative assumptions ingrained in AIed today. The study emphasizes the need for educators' critical engagement with AI technologies to envision alternative discourses and shape more democratic educational futures for themselves and their communities.

subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) can help students learn successfully, yet little work has explored the role of caregivers in shaping that success. Past interventions to support caregivers in supporting their child’s homework have been largely disjunct from educational technology. The paper presents prototyping design research with nine middle school caregivers. We ask: (1) what are caregivers’ preferences for different prototypes incorporating data-driven recommendations into their math homework support? Integrating caregivers' preferences, we then ask: (2) what are caregivers’ perceptions when interacting with a prototype of an intelligent chatbot tool to support students’ homework? We found caregivers reported feeling comfortable integrating AI into their practices and appreciated chat-based support for understanding content and effective ITS use. Our results highlight the affordances of ITS data and AI to assist caregivers who would otherwise not be able to support their child’s homework, paving the way for more effective and equitable mathematics learning.

title: The Interplay of Affective States and Cognitive Processes in an Open-Ended Learning Environment: A Case Study
citation: Akpanoko, C. E., S, A. T., & Biswas, G. (2024). The Interplay of Affective States and Cognitive Processes in an Open-Ended Learning Environment: A Case Study. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Akpanoko, C. E., S, A. T., & Biswas, G.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Affective states play a pivotal role in learning processes, yet little research has addressed the relations between cognitive processes and affective states, particularly when middle school students work in Open-Ended Learning Environments (OELE). This study seeks to understand these relations and link them to learning outcomes over time using continuous data streams. Leveraging a mixed-method approach, we conducted a case study with six students, analyzing approximately 80 minutes of data per student. Affective states are derived using a comprehensive analysis employing validated valence-arousal scales and a quadrant-based interpretation of educational emotion associated with the affective state. Utilizing D'Mello and Graesser's Affective Dynamics in Complex Learning, the study compares the relations between affective state patterns and cognitive processes of students who completed and could not complete the map-building task. Additionally, we analyze affective state shifts as students progress through the tasks across two different days, shedding light on the potential links between affective states and success in map building.

title: Lines of Infrastructuring: Revealing and Tracing Educators’ Infrastructuring Practices Across Design Implementations
citation: Hayden, R. & Roque, R. (2024). Lines of Infrastructuring: Revealing and Tracing Educators’ Infrastructuring Practices Across Design Implementations. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hayden, R. & Roque, R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Facilitators in informal spaces play an integral role in creating equitable and engaging STEM rich learning environments for youth. However, the complexity of facilitator’s practices is often undertheorized. Infrastructuring, or the process of dynamically designing with infrastructures (Karasti, 2014) gives us one lens to start to understand this complexity. Building on Azevedo’s lines of practice theory (2011), we aim to show the value in tracing infrastructuring work overtime in order to understand how facilitators’ preferences and constraints are shaping their practice. In this paper we present two traces, called lines of infrastructuring, that make visible the dynamic infrastructuring work of facilitators as they engage in a research practice partnership developing and implementing computing activities in their spaces. We argue that this analysis provides a new lens for understanding the practices of facilitators, and the realities of embedded infrastructures that can restrain the potential for equitable transformation in this work.

title: “We were learning from each other:” Nuancing Learner-AI Relationships in Assessing Rhetorical Features of Disinformation
citation: Russo, R., Schechter, B., & Blikstein, P. (2024). “We were learning from each other:” Nuancing Learner-AI Relationships in Assessing Rhetorical Features of Disinformation. International Society of the Learning Sciences.

abstract: Assessing the reliability of information is one among several potential uses of Large Language Models (LLM). However, little research documents its application for educational purposes. We developed an educational conversational agent (Aide) that aims to help learners identify rhetorical aspects of textual disinformation. In this paper, we document different traits that users attribute to Aide through verbs that they use to describe its actions (such as analyze, teach, and explain). We also describe what attributes users in our sample identify as markers of reliability in Aide’s analysis of text (such as reference to data and technical vocabulary). Finally, we present a concise case study to highlight discrepancies between users’ perception of learning outcomes derived from using Aide (perceived as effective) vis-à-vis their approach to evaluate news stories pre- and post-interaction with Aide (unaltered) We conclude with a reflection on implications for the design of technologies that employ conversational agents for instruction aimed at enhancing learners' ability to assess information.

title: Tracking Agency in Open-Ended Making with Young Children
citation: Sheridan, K. M., Zhang, X., & Manchester, E. J. (2024). Tracking Agency in Open-Ended Making with Young Children. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. abstract: Creative open-ended making highlights agency. We use a temporal lens (Emirbayer & Mische, 1998) to understand how agency is expressed, distributed and supported in family making workshops for young children. We found that children expressed their agency across temporal modes, shifting over the design and making process. Parents and educators dynamically supported agency, often supporting shifts across temporal modes. Children showed frequent linguistic markers of agency in their discussions of their projects, and parents often narrated their children’s agency. We argue that open-ended making with adult support that centers children’s agency, supports children’s engagement in the design processes of ideation, problem-solving and iteration, and their sense of agency in their design and making work.

authors_list: Solyst, J., Yang, E., Xie, S., Hammer, J., Ogan, A., & Eslami, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The capabilities of generative AI (genAI) have dramatically increased in recent times, and there are opportunities for children to leverage new features for personal and school-related endeavors. However, while the future of genAI is taking form, there remain potentially harmful limitations, such as generation of outputs with misinformation and bias. We ran a workshop study focused on ChatGPT to explore middle school girls’ (N = 26) attitudes and reasoning about how genAI works. We focused on girls who are often disproportionately impacted by algorithmic bias. We found that: (1) middle school girls were initially overtrusting of genAI, (2) deliberate exposure to the limitations and mistakes of generative AI shifted this overtrust to disillusionment about genAI capabilities, though they were still optimistic for future possibilities of genAI, and (3) their ideas about school policy were nuanced. This work informs how children think about genAI like ChatGPT and its integration in learning settings.

title: Analyzing and Designing for Sustained Organizational Change
citation: Zeller, L., Anderson, E. R., Salvage, A., & Hofman, D. (2024). Analyzing and Designing for Sustained Organizational Change. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 91-98). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zeller, L., Anderson, E. R., Salvage, A., & Hofman, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: When designing, implementing, and studying changes in education, learning scientists and our partners are frequently aiming for sustained impact. However, achieving this is notoriously difficult. Research on organizational change and institutionalization most commonly looks to the past, retrospectively explaining why practices have—or have not—been sustained over time. However, the field is in need of an approach that can give clues about future sustainability in real time and aid in collaborative strategizing and design for long-term change. We argue that the MoRe Institutional framework can complement current design and improvement approaches to serve this purpose, by focusing attention on specific structures likely to aid or hinder durability. We illustrate with two examples of empirical projects drawing on this framework, demonstrating its potential to structure partnered and participatory change efforts, and integrate attention to long-term processes of institutionalization and de-institutionalization into the timescales of iterative design.

title: Math in the Messy: Breaking Down Norms “Queer”-ly
citation: Yankova, N. (2024). Math in the Messy: Breaking Down Norms “Queer”-ly. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 913-920). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Yankova, N.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Falling in line with existing visibility studies centering the queer experience in STEM, this paper zooms in on the lived experiences and perceptions of queer students in mathematics. This qualitative study is grounded in queer theory as aligned with constructionism. Drawing on interview data and through an iterative thematic analysis, this qualitative study highlights four themes, characterizing present curricular practices as inequitable: reinforcing the binary, reinforcing neutrality, math as fixed, math as gendered. Implications point to design principles for a queering of mathematics, aimed at the construction of more equitable learning spaces for queer, and ultimately, all youth.

title: Epistemic Trajectories: Classroom Communities’ Development of Socio-epistemic Disciplinary Norms
citation: Av-Shalom, N. Y. (2024). Epistemic Trajectories: Classroom Communities’ Development of Socio-epistemic Disciplinary Norms. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 921-928). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Av-Shalom, N. Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Science is a social practice involving epistemic engagement with scientific norms, which are established by the scientific through epistemic discourse. Similarly, classroom communities can engage in discourse towards developing socio-epistemic disciplinary (SED) norms: shared norms around what constitute appropriate contributions to science classroom discussions. Using the AIR model of Epistemic Cognition and the Apt-AIR framework, this research presents an analysis of the discourse in a middle school science inquiry intervention to explore how SED norms were negotiated by class communities—i.e., the epistemic trajectories of the norms. The findings highlight two different epistemic trajectories: in one, an SED norm was used and renegotiated throughout the intervention. In the other, the class community was faced with its limited utility and phased it out. This paper furthers our understanding of how science class communities develop norms that inform and are informed by their engagement with authentic scientific practices.

title: It’s Not Working!: Critical Problems in Emergent Infrastructures of Classroom Physical Computing
citation: Elliott, C. H., Nixon, J., Chakarov, A. G., Schneider, M., & Bhaduri, S. (2024). It’s Not Working!: Critical Problems in Emergent Infrastructures of Classroom Physical Computing. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 929-936). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Elliott, C. H., Nixon, J., Chakarov, A. G., Schneider, M., & Bhaduri, S.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Moments of breakdown in any infrastructure make the often-invisible components visible (Star, 1999). In this paper, we explore how the breakdown of one physical computing system used in middle and high school classrooms (the DaSH) made determinant the sociotechnical infrastructure undergirding it. Using ethnography and situational analysis mapping, we make meaning of two major sources of the issue that became barriers to the system operating in teachers’ classrooms: shifting organizational goals & the cloud-based component of the programming environment. Uncovering these sunk components of the computing technologies infrastructure offers insight into what to consider when researching and implementing work with physical computing in K-12 and out of school environments including what large-scale relationships it relies on and how they shape students’ relations to computing.

title: ‘A Black Woman in Geoscience, is Like a Unicorn’: Black Women’s Educational Experiences in The Geosciences
citation: Mitchell, N. D. (2024). ‘A Black Woman in Geoscience, is Like a Unicorn’: Black Women’s Educational Experiences in The Geosciences. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 937-944). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Mitchell, N. D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Empirical research concerning social identity in geoscience education has primarily examined single categories of social difference, centering analysis of either race or gender (Mattheis et al., 2019). To expand the current scope of geoscience education research, I use Black Feminist Epistemology (Hill-Collins, 2022) to center and explore Black women’s educational experiences. Using autobiographies and semi-structured individual interviews with Black woman geoscientists, I explored educational practices and relationships that played a critical role in shaping their experiences in geoscience. Black women participants described their position in and navigation geosciences education as in/hypervisible, non-human, mythical objects using the metaphor of the Lone Black Unicorn. In this paper, I center the narratives of Lone Black Unicorns as a disruption of the persistent underrepresentation of Black women’s voices in academic sensemaking.

title: Enlightenment and Counter-Enlightenment in the Learning Sciences
citation: Cohen, E. (2024). Enlightenment and Counter-Enlightenment in the Learning Sciences. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 947-950). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cohen, E.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Consequential research in the learning sciences aims to tackle real-world educational problems. Two pressing problems that currently face learning scientists are post-truthism and institutional racism. In this short paper, I argue that efforts to address each of these problems rely on conflicting philosophical underpinnings rooted in the enlightenment and counter-enlightenment movements, respectively. Although there is no immediate solution to this problem in sight, I believe that unpacking its roots and implications is worthwhile, nonetheless, because it can help explicate the intellectual foundations underlying a large swath of learning sciences literature.

title: Data Fusion in Classroom-Based Multimodal Learning Analytics: A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Wang, Y. & Gu, X. (2024). Data Fusion in Classroom-Based Multimodal Learning Analytics: A Systematic Literature Review. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 951-954). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wang, Y. & Gu, X.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: In classroom environments, this paper presents a systematic review of Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA) following PRISMA guidelines. It explores the relationship between learning indicators, multimodal data types, and data fusion strategies to improve MMLA's decision-making efficacy. The main findings include: 1) Complex mappings exist between learning indicators and multimodal data, including within learning indicator layers; 2) Engagement stands out as the foremost learning indicator; 3) Video data predominates in MMLA applications; 4) Feature-level fusion is the leading strategy for data integration. The study also highlights both theoretical and technological challenges, emphasizing the vital influence of learning theories.

title: A Systematic Review of Approaches for Building Adolescents’ Geometrical Understanding
citation: Sharma, R. & Dubé, A. K. (2024). A Systematic Review of Approaches for Building Adolescents’ Geometrical Understanding.. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E. A., Looi, C. K., Keifert, D. T., & Suárez, E. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 18th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2024 (pp. 955-958). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sharma, R. & Dubé, A. K.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This systematic review aimed to identify prevalent approaches and tools for building geometrical understanding of adolescents. 54 articles from two educational psychology databases were reviewed. Guiding learning theories and pedagogical approaches are mapped to targeted geometry topics and types of interventions. Overall, the learning theories being applied to the design of geometry instruction are scattered. The results show an inclination towards the use of Dynamic Geometry Software (DGS) for a range of geometry topics, due to the many affordances they offer that support geometrical understanding. The Van Hiele Model (VHM) of geometric thinking is found to be the most prevalent framework for building geometrical understanding due to its geometry-specific structure. However, the VHM is not often used to design digital learning environments for geometry. Future research should focus on studying the design and effectiveness of VHM-based learning environments for building geometrical understanding of adolescents.

title: Refining the Recipe: Ingredients Driving Completion and Satisfaction in Online Hands-On Learning Activities
citation: Urban, A. D. & Sun, X. (2024). Refining the Recipe: Ingredients Driving Completion and Satisfaction in Online Hands-On Learning Activities. In Lindgren, R., Asino, T. I., Kyza, E.
