International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sung, G., Hassan, J., & Schneider, B.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The affective states of students while studying outside of class hold rich information about how students are doing in a course and how instruction could be improved. In this paper, we test the co-occurrence of webcam-based nonverbal metrics with self-reported student affective states during an instructional video. Preliminary results suggest that low-level, selfreported affect can be a promising ground truth data for research, and that nonverbal metrics created from webcam streams can be associated with this self-reported affect.

title: Developing a Boundary Practice for Collaborative Task Design in a Design-Centric Research–practice Partnership
citation: Ehrlich, G. S., Rajarathinam, R. J., & Mercier, E. (2022). Developing a boundary practice for collaborative task design in a design-centric research–practice partnership. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2082-2083). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ehrlich, G. S., Rajarathinam, R. J., & Mercier, E.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Collaborative learning needs tasks suitable for collaboration. As part of a project to study the design of collaborative environments, we describe how a partnership with an undergraduate mathematics professor led to the development of a boundary practice for collaborative task design. Initially there was a tension between the researchers’ preference for ill-structured tasks and the professor’s priority of conceptual over computational problems. We discuss how focus on a single task resolved the tension and gave both researchers and the professor useful design tools for meeting their respective goals in subsequent task revisions.

title: Designing to Support Teacher Mediated Strategies for Student Learning in a Remote Kindergarten Music Class
citation: Cawelti, L. (2022). Designing to support teacher mediated strategies for student learning in a remote kindergarten music class. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2084-2085). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Cawelti, L.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Using a single-setting, iterative DBR approach to program design, along with the multimodal affordances of music learning, I consider resource design to support teacher mediated student learning in remote contexts. Throughout the KinderMus program, teachers adapted their teaching in remote spaces, finding ways to mediate learning through language, social interaction, and active learning, and considering limitations around access to externally oriented artifacts. Findings have implications for design in both remote and in-person settings.

title: The Effects of Affective Feedback on Learners’ Emotions in Asynchronous Video-Based Learning
citation: Ha, S. & So, H. (2022). The effects of affective feedback on learners’ emotions in asynchronous video-based learning. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2088-2089). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ha, S. & So, H.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study examined the effects of affective feedback on learners’ boredom, confusion, and frustration in asynchronous video-based learning. Affective feedback messages and writing activity were used to deliver the utility value of learning topics. Facial expression data from 30 adult learners were collected and analyzed to identify changes in affective states. The findings suggested that the utility value message had a significant on reducing learners’ boredom.

title: Othering: Overcoming a Sociocultural Obstacle to English Proficiency Among ESL Learners in Malaysia
citation: Kapong, J. M. (2022). Othering: Overcoming a sociocultural obstacle to english proficiency among ESL learners in malaysia. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2090-2091). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Kapong, J. M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study aimed to see how othering affects Malaysian students' English language learning. This article presents insights from data acquired during an interview and examined thematically. It explores three themes that emerged from the interview with Malaysian ESL learners regarding their experiences with othering and how personal growth has helped them overcome the effects of othering.

title: Computational Thinking Into K-12 Classrooms: Experiences and Challenges From Professional Learning Experiences
citation: Liu, Z., Gearty, Z., Richard, E., Orrill, C., Kayumova, S., & Balasubramanian, R. (2022). Computational thinking into k-12 classrooms: Experiences and challenges from professional learning experiences. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2100-2101). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Liu, Z., Gearty, Z., Richard, E., Orrill, C., Kayumova, S., & Balasubramanian, R.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Teachers often find it challenging to learn computational thinking (CT) and integrate it with classroom learning. In this systematic review, we focus on how professional learning experiences have supported K-12 teachers to integrate CT into their classrooms. The findings suggest some effective strategies for building professional learning experiences but highlight the need for more agreement about the nature of CT.

title: Rotating Bodies Bulge Outward: A Novel Intuitive Resource for Rotational Motion
citation: Arnell, J., Swanson, H., & Edwards, B. (2022). Rotating bodies bulge outward: A novel intuitive resource for rotational motion. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2102-2103). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Arnell, J., Swanson, H., & Edwards, B.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Physics students routinely struggle to understand the Coriolis force and the centrifugal force. While investigating students’ prior knowledge resources in these domains, we observed the use of an intuitive element regarding the “bulging” demonstrated by rotating bodies. This element exhibits similar characteristics to a previously described class of intuitive knowledge resources for making sense of physics phenomena: phenomenological primitives (pprims). We document the attributes of the “bulging” resource and compare them to the expected traits of p-prims.

title: Discussion-Oriented Teaching in the Digital Classroom: Teachers’ Collaborative Adaptation in the Face of Disruption
citation: Mastrup, K. L., Aiello, L., Athanases, S. Z., Blair, K. P., Higgs, J., Martin, L., Martinez, D. C., Williams, A. D., & Welsh, M. (2022). Discussion-oriented teaching in the digital classroom: Teachers’ collaborative adaptation in the face of disruption. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2104-2105). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Mastrup, K. L., Aiello, L., Athanases, S. Z., Blair, K. P., Higgs, J., Martin, L., Martinez, D. C., Williams, A. D. P., & Welsh, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We examine how a researcher-practitioner research group collaborated to adapt noticing practices in the face of disruptions brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic. We used a progress monitoring tool and cognitive field notes to support teacher partners’ systematic reflection and to gauge teacher learning. Initial findings suggest these tools helped identify tensions around implementing online class discussions. We highlight the process the teacher partners engaged in as they re-conceptualized engagement, participation, and interaction.

title: Examining Learning Opportunities for Integrating AI Education in English Language Art Classrooms
citation: Tatar, C., Jiang, S., Chao, J., Wiedemann, K., Fiacco, J., Finzer, W., & Rosé, C. P. (2022). Examining learning opportunities for integrating AI education in english language art classrooms. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2106-2107). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tatar, C., Jiang, S., Chao, J., Wiedemann, K., Fiacco, J., Finzer, W., & Rosé, C. P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We conducted a co-design study with high school ELA teachers to investigate their perspectives in the integration of a technology-enhanced AI curriculum. The teachers explored the AI and text mining activities and reflected on them from teaching and learning perspectives. The findings of this study suggest that building models with texts positioned ELA teachers as experts in AI teaching and they were empowered to identify existing learning resources and opportunities in ELA classrooms that could be leveraged in integrating AI learning in their classrooms.

title: Attenuation and Amplification of Agency Through Goal Announcements in a Makerspace
citation: Goeke, M. & DeLiema, D. (2022). Attenuation and amplification of agency through goal announcements in a makerspace. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 211-218). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Goeke, M. & DeLiema, D.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Agency in makerspaces is frequently in flux, amplified or attenuated through interactions between the maker and individuals around them. Looking at goal announcements in a makerspace designed to provide no predetermined goals, we see that these moments tend to follow triadic dialog patterns and that makers orient to the potential evaluation through hedging and multimodal demonstration. We argue that maker educators need to carefully attend to how interaction shapes maker agency without assuming that open-endedness alone will suffice.

title: Fake News Literacy: Intuitive vs. Analytic Processing
citation: Scheibenzuber, C., Isik, D., Krasniqi, N., & Nistor, N. (2022). Fake news literacy: intuitive vs. analytic processing. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2110-2111). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Scheibenzuber, C., Isik, D., Krasniqi, N., & Nistor, N.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: Humanities, Language & Literacy; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Understanding the cognitive processing of fake news is essential when planning to counteract fake news effects, such as through media literacy training. In this study, we aim to provide an insight into how news recipients assess dubious information and how accurate their appraisal of exemplary news is. We conducted interviews with N = 51 participants and found evidence for the role of emotions as well as the importance of design and layout when trying to discern true from fake news. Additionally, two particular cases illustrate the different ways of assessing news credibility: through intuition or analytically. In consequence, we suggest a model of online news processing including individual traits such as social influence, attitudes (e.g., political beliefs), and media literacy.

title: Coalescing Knowledge Within Networks of Research Practice Partnerships: The Case of a School-Based Citizen Science Network
citation: Aridor, K., Shaham, R. D., Lavie-Alon, N., Valin, G., Sagy, O., & Kali, Y. (2022). Coalescing knowledge within networks of research practice partnerships: The case of a school-based citizen science network. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2114-2115). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Aridor, K., Shaham, R. D., Lavie-Alon, N., Valin, G., Sagy, O., & Kali, Y.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Synthesizing valuable insights developed within diverse partnerships that are part of a network is challenging. This study explores implementation stories of school participation in Citizen Science and insights shared by participants as part of two workshops, intended to increase cross-fertilization among participants. Six new abstract design principles were identified as corresponding with learning through Citizen Science. This study illustrates how these principles’ identification can support cross-fertilization between partnerships and amalgamation of the dispersed knowledge.

title: “It’s So Frustrating!” Understanding Design Dilemmas in Co-Design Through Curricular Values
citation: Bogdanov, K. P. (2022). “It’s so frustrating!” Understanding design dilemmas in co-design through curricular values. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2116-2117). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bogdanov, K. P.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Co-design is an increasingly common process for curriculum development in science education, where teachers and researchers work together to create curricula, drawing on mutual knowledge and expertise. In efforts to understand this process, I looked at design dilemmas that occurred during design meetings and categorized the ideas that emerged in terms of underlying curricular values. I characterize these emerging curricular values and identify ways in which participants work to achieve and balance them.

title: Science Learning Through Drawing
citation: Jin, Q. (2022). Science learning through drawing. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2118-2119). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jin, Q.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Engaging students in visualization, especially constructing visual representations has been suggested as fruitful to support science learning. This study explored how elementary students learn astronomy, which is a challenging topic for both teaching and learning, through drawing and communicating with others about their drawings. Data were collected from multiple sources and analyzed qualitatively. Findings indicated that drawing as cognitive and epistemic resource facilitated students’ reasoning in both individual and social domains.

title: Empirically-Driven Multiple Choice Response Options
citation: Condor, A. (2022). Empirically-driven multiple choice response options. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2122-2123). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Condor, A.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: We introduce an empirical method for generating multiple choice (MC) response options for educational assessment. Developing quality response options for MC questions is labor intensive, especially when parallel items are necessary for repeated assessments or multiple test forms. We propose a data-driven, iterative approach for creating an item bank of MC questions by first collecting a sample of open-ended student responses that are subsequently rated by subject-matter experts. Contextual sentence embeddings of the observed student responses as well as the expert ratings are used in conjunction with hierarchical clustering to create MC options that span the desired ground truth rating levels specified by the item creator. We evaluate the quality of the automatically generated response options qualitatively, based on existing research relating to best practices for item writing.

title: Predicting Learning Gains in an Educational Game Using Feature Engineering and Machine Learning
citation: Rahimi, S., Fulwider, C., Jiang, S., & Shute, V. J. (2022). Predicting learning gains in an educational game using feature engineering and machine learning. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2124-2125). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rahimi, S., Fulwider, C., Jiang, S., & Shute, V. J.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: In this study, we use feature engineering and machine learning (ML) to develop a regression model to predict students’ learning gain while playing an educational game. Specifically, this study used the log data from 199 students’ gameplay to build a logistic regression model. The model we created includes 14 features with an accuracy of .61.

title: Mentors’ Learning Support Roles and Their Impact on Girls’ Identity Imaginations
citation: Thompson, N., Ju, B., Nacu, D., Erete, S., & Pinkard, N. (2022). Mentors’ learning support roles and their impact on girls’ identity imaginations. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2126-2127). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Thompson, N., Ju, B., Nacu, D., Erete, S., & Pinkard, N.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Mentoring programs have been intentionally designed to support Black and Latina girls in pursuing STEAM. Here, we examine how the support roles mentors play in an OST STEAM program relate to younger girls’ imaginings of their own identities. Findings from surveys taken by middle-school girls and mentors indicate that by the end of the program year, girls showed more willingness to imagine themselves in various identities, relating to the support roles mentors most often played.

title: Stories of Impact: Scientific Narratives and Climate Justice
citation: Schindel, A., Rish, R., Honwad, S., Waight, N., & Miles, M. (2022). Stories of impact: Scientific narratives and climate justice. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2128-2129). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Schindel, A., Rish, R., Honwad, S., Waight, N., & Miles, M.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Social & Civic Studies
abstract: Climate justice involves recognizing the deeply intertwined relationships between people and their environment, along with the recognition and validation of the fact that climate change has a disproportionate effect on the most vulnerable populations on the planet. This poster session shares the design and findings of a Climate Justice Map-mediated Scientific storytelling project designed to support students’ learning and action of climate justice by deepening and personalizing their involvement in locally situated climate issues.

title: Eliciting Multimodal Strategies: Early CT Assessment by Design
citation: Welch, L., Silvis, D., Clarke-Midura, J., Shumway, J., & Lee, V. R. (2022). Eliciting multimodal strategies: Early CT assessment by design. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2132-2133). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Welch, L., Silvis, D., Clarke-Midura, J., Shumway, J., & Lee, V. R.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Performance assessments can provide meaningful insights into young children's knowledge; however, documenting assessment responses as incorrect or correct limits our understanding of students’ abilities. One method of improving our ability to measure student understanding is by documenting the strategies students use to engage with assessment tasks. In this study, we describe how purposeful assessment design can provide insight into students’ thinking by qualitatively examining how students solve performance assessment items using multimodal strategies.

title: Strategies Towards Designing for Sustained Engagement in Computational Modeling in Science Classrooms
citation: Wagh, A., Fuhrmann, T., Eloy, A., Wolf, J., Bumbacher, E., Blikstein, P., & Wilkerson, M. (2022). Strategies towards designing for sustained engagement in computational modeling in science classrooms. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2134-2135). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wagh, A., Fuhrmann, T., Eloy, A., Wolf, J., Bumbacher, E., Blikstein, P., & Wilkerson, M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This poster presents emerging strategies for engaging students in extended investigations with computational modeling. Drawing on the literature on modeling and codesign with teachers over a year, we present 3 strategies and describe how they support student sense making and learning: 1. Curricular coherence and consistency; 2. Integrating multiple forms of data and modeling while foregrounding uncertainty; and, 3. Enabling unpacking blocks as a way to balance between ease of use and expressivity in modeling.

title: Promoting Authentic Research Experiences in the High School Classroom: Opportunities and Challenges
citation: Naipaul, J. C., Davidesco, I., & Glaser, N. (2022). Promoting authentic research experiences in the high school classroom: Opportunities and challenges. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2140-2141). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Naipaul, J. C., Davidesco, I., & Glaser, N.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study examines the nature of student experiences conducting open-ended scientific investigations as part of a new high school neuroscience curriculum. Semi-structured interviews with program participants (37 students and 25 teachers) revealed both challenges, mainly reading primary research articles and making sense of data, as well as opportunities for increasing students’ self-efficacy and college readiness. These findings can inform future efforts to promote authentic research experiences in K-12 classrooms.

title: Positioning Self and Others Through Sympathizing, Empathizing, Anthropomorphizing, and Zoomorphizing: A Case Study
citation: Papendieck, A. & Azevedo, F. S. (2022). Positioning self and others through sympathizing, empathizing, anthropomorphizing, and zoomorphizing: A case study. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2142-2143). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Papendieck, A. & Azevedo, F. S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We investigate the relationship between learning and identity by analyzing students’ positionings and attendant reasoning in the context of a university seminar designed to engage STEM undergraduate and graduate students in examining the broader impacts of their STEM fields and practices. Specifically, we highlight students’ discursive use of sympathizing, empathizing, anthropomorphizing, and zoomorphizing as ways of projecting self onto humans and nonhumans, reasoning “as if the other.”

title: Enabling Self-Regulated Learning in MOOCs Using Community of Practice
citation: Jiang, M. (2022). Enabling self-regulated learning in MOOCs using community of practice. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2144-2145). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jiang, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT); Communities of Practice & Situated Learning; Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition
abstract: One of the main reasons for learners to drop out from Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) is the lack of self-regulated learning (SRL) skills necessary to learn effectively in online environments with low levels of support and guidance. Although there is an agreement on the importance of SRL for MOOC learners, little research has examined which SRL strategies learners need help the most, or how to help them practice those strategies to further develop their SRL skills. This study identifies key SRL strategies that are crucial for MOOC learners to develop in order to improve their learning outcomes and increase course completion. Based on results from interviews and a questionnaire, recommendations were presented on using a chat feature embedded on MOOC platforms to enable the community of practice and help learners practice SRL strategies effectively.

title: Establishing a Teacher Community for Innovation in Chinese Classrooms
citation: Zhang, X., Chen, X., Liu, X., Xu, T., Dong, C., Wang, T., & Slotta, J. D. (2022). Establishing a teacher community for innovation in chinese classrooms. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2150-2151). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Zhang, X., Chen, X., Liu, X., Xu, T., Dong, C., Wang, T., & Slotta, J. D.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: To help Chinese teachers understand and implement competency-based curriculum design, we established a teacher innovation community in China. During the summers of 2020 and 2021, K-12 teachers and researchers jointly designed STEM courses on climate change during 6-week workshops. Researchers use social platforms to share teaching experience to help teachers better understand and implement innovative courses.

title: Emotion as a Condition and Target of Learning Design During Emergency Remote Teaching
citation: Fortman, J. & Quintana, R. M. (2022). Emotion as a condition and target of learning design during emergency remote teaching. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2152-2153). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Fortman, J. & Quintana, R. M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: In this study we seek to understand the recursive relationships between feeling, sense-making, and rapid online course design at the onset of COVID-19. To elucidate how emotion was implicated in learning design decisions, we offer a qualitative analysis of nine instructor interviews from diverse academic disciplines. Originally developed for an open online course, these interviews exemplify how instructors at a large midwestern university moved their residential courses online at the onset of the pandemic.

title: Digital Literacies in Algorithmic Cultures: Critical Literacy as ‘Working the Algorithm’
citation: Ehret, C. & Hagh, A. (2022). Digital literacies in algorithmic cultures: Critical literacy as ‘working the algorithm’. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2154-2155). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ehret, C. & Hagh, A.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Research on literacy learning and algorithms has been limited to how youth understand their operations as computational systems. Through a case study of one young adult’s practice of ‘working algorithms’ across social media platforms, this poster presents new pathways for researching critical, digital literacy learning in algorithmic cultures. It provides evidence of how youth use their literacies in the critical production of algorithmic cultures, and toward more just and diverse communities.

title: Designing for an Emerging Paradigm in Computer Programming - Towards Hybrid Human-Computer Creation of Artifacts
citation: Worsley, M. (2022). Designing for an emerging paradigm in computer programming - towards hybrid human-computer creation of artifacts. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2156-2157). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Worsley, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; STEM - Natural Science
abstract: Computer science education has experienced many noticeable changes since its inception. Today, students encounter considerably more user-friendly and intelligent IDEs, far less confusing error messages, and much simpler program compilation processes. Learners are also likely to encounter programming environments that can combine human created artifacts with programmatically created content. Even so, much of computer science education assumes a paradigm where only the computer directly manipulates the final artifact. This paper describes an emerging human-computer hybrid paradigm as seen through Scratch, Minecraft Education Edition, and the Dash and Dot. By thinking about these three platforms, the paper motivates more intentionality in how we design for learning in this hybrid paradigm.

title: An Exploratory Study of How Informal Educators Engage With Formal Educators in a Community of Practice
citation: Aleman, E. (2022). An exploratory study of how informal educators engage with formal educators in a community of practice. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2160-2161). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Aleman, E.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Expanding graduate programs for educators in the Learning Sciences beyond a traditional focus on classroom instruction requires widening learning contexts to engage outof-school educators. In this preliminary study, a cohort of 24 in-school and out-of-school educators formed a community of practice. Their engagement in discussion forums was analyzed. Preliminary results suggest that reflections through storytelling resulted in higher levels of interaction between formal and informal educators.

title: Measuring Belonging for Neurodiverse Computer Science Students
citation: Bonnette, R. & Abramovich, S. (2022). Measuring belonging for neurodiverse computer science students. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2162-2163). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bonnette, R. & Abramovich, S.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Neurodivergent students can thrive in undergraduate Computer Science programs with support, but research on effective learning and teaching practices is limited. The neurodiversity movement advocates an approach to research and design that examines social (i.e., external) barriers to student success and seeks to remove or mitigate them. We suggest that this research must begin with productive measures of student success. This poster presents a survey instrument to measure neurodivergent CS students’ sense of belonging. Keywords: belonging, computer science, neurodiversity, research, intersectionality

title: Turning Ourselves Inside Out: Reading and Creating Graphic Medicine in Community
citation: Evans, S., Molina, L., & Davis-McElligatt, J. (2022). Turning ourselves inside out: Reading and creating graphic medicine in community. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2164-2165). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Evans, S., Molina, L., & Davis-McElligatt, J.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: An interdisciplinary team designed a graphic medicine project to address health inequalities, implementing it in public libraries with underserved populations. Participants read graphic novels about experiences with illness, then create a 4-8 panel comic about a healthrelated experience of their own. Research questions are 1) what personal insights about health arise when reading and discussing graphic narratives? and 2) what community insights about health arise when creating and sharing stories in the comics format?

title: Can Schools Fix the Gender Gap in STEM? A Comparative Study in the Global South About Gender Participation in Maker Education
citation: Russo, R., Fuhrmann, T., Goya, A., & Blikstein, P. (2022). Can schools fix the gender gap in STEM? A comparative study in the global south about gender participation in maker education. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2168-2169). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Russo, R., Fuhrmann, T., Goya, A., & Blikstein, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Research established that most learners perceive STEM learning environments as settings that exclude diverse ways of thinking. We investigate factors behind this trend in two sites that recently implemented fully-equipped makerspaces, but have deeply different socioeconomic contexts. We identify factors associated with increased self-efficacy and attitudes toward STEM among male and female students.

title: Studying the Development of Marginality in Collaboration: Methods for Examining the Interplay of Peer & Teacher Interactions
citation: Adams-Wiggins, K., Haluska, C. M., Ramirez, A. R., Garcia, G. H., & Romolor, L. S. (2022). Studying the development of marginality in collaboration: Methods for examining the interplay of peer & teacher interactions. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2170-2171). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Adams-Wiggins, K., Haluska, C. M., Ramirez, A. R., Garcia, G. H., & Romolor, L. S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Inquiry-based science learning environments emphasize learners’ engagement in scientific practices, yet we need to better understand how to promote equitable interactions to ensure all students benefit. Using Wenger’s (1998) concept of marginal non-participation, the present study examined patterns of interaction across teacher- and student-led phases of instruction for a focal group in which marginality was previously observed. Findings indicated reliance on ignoring off-task commentary across both phases of instruction, facilitating marginality for two group members.

title: Becoming a STEM Teacher: Examining Teachers’ Practice-Linked Identities Through Practice-Based Autobiographies
citation: Stamatis, K., Friend, M., & Jakopovic, P. (2022). Becoming a STEM teacher: Examining teachers’ practice-linked identities through practice-based autobiographies. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2172-2173). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Stamatis, K., Friend, M., & Jakopovic, P.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: To provide equitable high-quality STEM education, teachers must be prepared to engage with the tools and practices and to adopt STEM identities. This project investigates the ways teachers’ self-described histories and conceptions of materials and relationships embedded in their STEM experiences fostered or inhibited practice-linked STEM identities. Preliminary findings explore how practicing and pre-service educators conceptualize STEM and how their understanding of STEM both supports and challenges their teaching practice.

title: Emergent Social and Emotional Learning Outcomes Through Collaborative Reasoning Discussions
citation: Friedman, G., Kusumaningsih, S., & Sun, J. (2022). Emergent social and emotional learning outcomes through collaborative reasoning discussions. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2178-2179). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Friedman, G., Kusumaningsih, S., & Sun, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Social emotional learning (SEL) has been identified as critical to meet students’ needs. This study examined the potential of a small group discussion approach, Collaborative Reasoning (CR), on supporting students’ SEL. Transcripts of debriefings after CR discussions and students’ post-study interviews were analyzed for indicators of interpersonal competencies. Findings suggested students benefited in social awareness and relationship building skills after taking part in a series of CR discussions.

title: Designing a Method for Turmoilization of Understandings Through Multi-Voiced and Multi-Contextual Reflection
citation: Suzuki, H., Funaoi, H., Kubota, Y., & Kato, H. (2022). Designing a method for turmoilization of understandings through multi-voiced and multi-contextual reflection. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2180-2181). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Suzuki, H., Funaoi, H., Kubota, Y., & Kato, H.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: This study first points out the importance of "Turmoilization of understanding,” that is, reconstructing a coherent understanding once established through multi-voiced and multicontextual reexaminations into a form that incorporates indeterminacy. Then, we propose a method to support the turmoilization of understanding. The pilot study suggests some aspects of the effectiveness of this method. In future work, we will establish a method through a detailed effect examination.

title: Does Where You Start Matter? The Interaction Between Prior Knowledge and Effectiveness of Game-Based Interventions
citation: Liu, A. S., Chan, J. Y., Lee, J., Decker-Woodrow, L. E., Tu, S., Sales, A., & Mason, C. A. (2022). Does where you start matter? The interaction between prior knowledge and effectiveness of game-based interventions. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2182-2183). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Liu, A. S., Chan, J. Y., Lee, J., Decker-Woodrow, L. E., Tu, S., Sales, A., & Mason, C. A.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: The current study investigated how prior knowledge moderated the effects of three educational technologies (From Here to There, DragonBox 12+, and problem sets in ASSISTments) on seventh-grade students’ later algebraic knowledge. Pretest scores only moderated effects of From Here to There, with larger effects among students with higher pretest performance. Our findings have implications for understanding how prior knowledge interacts with design features within game-based applications to impact algebraic understanding.

title: “Bringing New Things to Light”: Examining a Process of Insight-Driven Teacher Learning
citation: Rubin, E. & van Es, E. (2022). “Bringing new things to light”: Examining a process of insight-driven teacher learning. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 219-226). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Rubin, E. & Es, E. V.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: Effective teaching relies on practices of reflection and inquiry that must be cultivated throughout teachers’ careers. Professional development (PD) can support those practices by positioning participants to develop and build on insights. Using data from a PD program focused on teacher noticing for equity, we draw on practice theory to identify the process and associated practices that emerged through participation in collaborative inquiry. Analysis reveals three phases of activity, consisting of interrelated practices that drove insight-based learning: building awareness, collaborative exploration, and learning through design. Through engaging in this process, participants made unconscious aspects of teaching visible that allowed participants to deepen and expand their insights, and through design, articulated new insights and situated their learning back in the context of their teaching. These findings have implications for designing PD that prioritizes participants’ agency to cultivate practices of reflection and inquiry.

title: Developing Dynamic Dashboards for Classroom Orchestration
citation: Goss, W., Dey, I., Dickler, R., Hirshfield, L., Tissenbaum, M., & Puntambekar, S. (2022). Developing dynamic dashboards for classroom orchestration. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2190-2191). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Goss, W., Dey, I., Dickler, R., Hirshfield, L., Tissenbaum, M., & Puntambekar, S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Classroom orchestration is a multifaceted pedagogical challenge, requiring teachers to simultaneously manage activities across multiple social levels and under various constraints. Teacher dashboards are commonly developed tools to aid orchestration; however, many fall short in real-time classrooms. To address this impediment, we used participatory design sessions with teachers to better understand their needs, based on which, we plan to build a dynamic dashboard with real-time actionable metrics.

title: Exploring Epistemic Network Analysis Diagrams as a Tool for Developing Teacher Noticing of Classroom Dialogic Features
citation: Sushil, S. & Clarke, S. N. (2022). Exploring epistemic network analysis diagrams as a tool for developing teacher noticing of classroom dialogic features. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2192-2193). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sushil, S. & Clarke, S. N.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Our designs for teacher learning focus on generating representations that help teachers attend to how they structure opportunities to learn for students of color. This paper explores the affordances of Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) for generating representations of epistemic networks in science class discussions for teacher reflection on their facilitation. We examine representations of data of two secondary science teachers and discuss the possibilities of ENA for mapping the intellective nature of science discussions.

title: Using Participatory Software Design to Reconfigure Traditional Power Asymmetries Between Dominant School Systems and Nondominant Families
citation: Sierschynski, J., Kelly, E., Spaulding, S., & McManus, M. S. (2022). Using participatory software design to reconfigure traditional power asymmetries between dominant school systems and nondominant families. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2196-2197). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sierschynski, J., Kelly, E., Spaulding, S., & McManus, M. S.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: We describe an iterative participatory development of a software application based on Ishimaru’s (2019) model of equitable collaboration between nondominant families and dominant school systems. We share (1) findings from our qualitative analysis and collaborative software design with two family focus groups, (2) the design process that led us to the development of a family notebook to balance traditional power asymmetries, and (3) the current version of the software design.

title: How Do Middle School Students Think About Climate Change?
citation: Bichler, S., Bradford, A., Riordan, B., & Linn, M. C. (2022). How do middle school students think about climate change?. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2198-2199). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bichler, S., Bradford, A., Riordan, B., & Linn, M. C.
subject: STEM - Natural Science
abstract: We use natural language processing (NLP) to train an automated scoring model to assess students’ reasoning on how to slow climate change. We use the insights from scoring over 1000 explanations to design a knowledge integration intervention and test it in three classrooms. The intervention supported students to distinguish relevant evidence, improving connections between ideas in a revised explanation. We discuss next steps for using the NLP model to support teachers and students in classrooms.

title: Writing to Rewrite Dominant Discourse(s): Some Design Dilemmas From Global South
citation: Bisht, G., Avenido, N., & Rosales, K. (2022). Writing to rewrite dominant discourse(s): Some design dilemmas from global south. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2202-2203). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bisht, G., Avenido, N., & Rosales, K.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Culturally Sustaining & Decolonial Pedagogies; Racial Equity, Power & Social Justice
abstract: This poster considers some design elements that can potentially work through the double bind of English education for culturally marginalized students in post-colonial contexts. English writing in such contexts often plays out as an overwriting on native consciousness. Using the framework of counter stories, I look at the Facebook compositions of Sangita, a young indigenous girl from India. Her composition illustrates the potential to rewrite dominant notions around indigenous food systems and offer some possibilities for design.

title: Static and Changing Roles in Transdisciplinary Co-Design
citation: Johnson, M. J., Piantella, B., Lowy, R., Leonard, E., Ryan, N., DiSalvo, B., & DesPortes, K. (2022). Static and changing roles in transdisciplinary co-design. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2204-2205). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Johnson, M. J., Piantella, B., Lowy, R., Leonard, E., Ryan, N., DiSalvo, B., & DesPortes, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Transdisciplinary computing arts experiences provide potential to merge practices and cultures from across disciplines to create an inclusive learning environment. However, this can be hard to do, especially when instructors within these spaces feel their expertise lies mainly within either computing or the arts. In our work, we analyzed facilitator reflections on the codesign and implementation of a 14-week online computing-arts experience designed to integrate computing, poetry, and visual arts. We found that focusing on the static and changing roles assumed by the co-designers provided a lens to understand how to build knowledge across one another’s disciplines in the pursuit of creating new practices within transdisciplinary education.

title: Examining Gender Differences in Identity Development Within an Online, Global, Collaborative, Informal STEM-learning Community
citation: Espino, D. P., Hokama, M., Lowe, T., & Hamilton, E. R. (2022). Examining gender differences in identity development within an online, global, collaborative, informal STEM-learning community. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2206-2207). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Espino, D. P., Hokama, M., Lowe, T., & Hamilton, E. R.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: This study examines how a learning environment that incorporates aspects of intergroup contact might impact identity development and expression. Adolescent students collaborate on creating STEM-related media projects in this global, virtual environment during weekly video conference calls, which were coded for social and self-identity constructs and analyzed using epistemic network analysis (ENA) to compare differences by gender. Literature anticipated that female students would reflect social identity constructs and male students reflect self-identity constructs, but the opposite was found indicating intergroup contact might defy expected outcomes and complement student identity development among adolescents.

title: Chin Youths’ Epistemic Agency in an Afterschool STEM Learning Environment
citation: Jeong, M. & Ryu, M. (2022). Chin youths’ epiSTEMic agency in an afterschool STEM learning environment. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2208-2209). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Jeong, M. & Ryu, M.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Computer Science & Coding; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: We implemented an afterschool STEM program for Chin youth to engage them in critical science literacy while using their full linguistic repertoires. For the present study, we conducted a grounded theory analysis of 24 interviews from this project to reveal how translanguaging supported epistemic agency in this space. Our findings from four youths’ narratives suggest that the youth integrated translanguaging as an extension of their everyday discursive practices to foster shared epistemic agency among their peers. In addition, we identified structures from their school science classrooms that inhibited translanguaging and stunted their epistemic agency.

title: Examining Learning-by-Teaching Effect in a Secondary Math Course
citation: Pan, C. & Chang, B. (2022). Examining learning-by-teaching effect in a secondary math course. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 2212-2213). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Pan, C. & Chang, B.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: The present study aims to identify which phases during learning by teaching play the critical roles and to investigate how student ability and pairing types mutually influence students’ performance in each phase and the overall achievement. To this end, learning-by-teaching was applied with the form of reciprocal peer tutoring in a seventh-grade math course. Students’ achievement scores, preparing-to-teach worksheets and verbal records during tutoring were collected for future conversational and quantitative analysis.

title: Introducing Authentic Datasets Into the Biology Classroom: Teachers’ Considerations When Designing Digital Instruction Units
citation: Bar, C., Dorfman, B., & Yarden, A. (2022). Introducing authentic datasets into the biology classroom: Teachers’ considerations when designing digital instruction units. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 227-234). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Bar, C., Dorfman, B., & Yarden, A.
subject: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
tpack_ck_labels: STEM - Natural Science; Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Introducing datasets into the science classroom may facilitate developing scientific practices and epistemic thinking. However, authentic datasets are rarely used in high school, and little is known about biology teachers’ knowledge considerations regarding dataset-driven instruction. Here we investigated these knowledge considerations in high-school biology teachers. Forty teachers designed dataset-driven instruction units and completed open-ended questionnaires during a professional development workshop. Our analysis, based on the PISA framework of scientific literacy, indicated that although epistemic considerations were the most prominent of teachers' perceived benefits of dataset-driven instruction, they were less pronounced than content and procedural considerations in the instruction units that they designed. This suggests that although teachers recognize the value of epistemic thinking and see authentic datasets as a means to facilitate scientific literacy, further effort is needed to assist teachers in designing instruction units which better reflect these goals.

title: Learning in Practice Space Games
citation: Gaydos, M., Kim, Y., Wardrip, P. S., & Colombino, J. (2022). Learning in practice space games. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 235-242). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Gaydos, M., Kim, Y., Wardrip, P. S., & Colombino, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Classroom-based assessment is essential to good teaching and learning. Nevertheless, pre-service and in-service teacher’s assessment professional development (PD) has been slow to change and the research supporting good assessment PD is still nascent. In this paper, we report the investigation of a relatively new approach to assessment PD, a game-based intervention, MetaRubric, a game designed to provide teachers with a playful experience that supports critical examination of rubrics, including their design and use. Games - and in particular practice space games - have been suggested to be potentially useful for teacher professional development, however little has been written about their design, practical application to teacher professional development, especially in the context of assessment, or mechanisms of action. The data presented here provide preliminary empirical support for and detail the design of one such intervention.

title: How the Shape of the Earth is Argued into Being
citation: Vain, S. R., Dubovi, I., & Tabak, I. (2022). How the shape of the earth is argued into being. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 243-249). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Vain, S. R., Dubovi, I., & Tabak, I.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Claims that depart from Western scientific consensus, such as the relationship between vaccines and autism or the flat shape of the earth are often disparaged. We aim to cultivate greater convergence with scientific consensus, from a stance that rejects attributing alternative explanations to heedless partisanship or emotional susceptibility. We focus on the ‘flat earth’ explanation, and examine argumentative moves, attention to evidence and knowledge co-construction in YouTube discussions between supporters and critics of ‘flat earth.’ We found that Flat Earth supporters engage in argumentation and meta-talk about evidence, even at least as frequently as the critics. These findings suggest that cultivating greater convergence on scientific consensus requires deep and nuanced approaches, because alternative explanations can be couched in scientific, deliberative, and argumentative structures.

title: Mapping Visual Marginalia in Educational Contexts: A Model for New Types of Self-Regulation of Learning
citation: Dario, N., Tateo, L., & Lund, K. (2022). Mapping visual marginalia in educational contexts: A model for new types of self-regulation of learning. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 250-257). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Dario, N., Tateo, L., & Lund, K.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Visual Marginalia (VM) are a common phenomenon in school, but they hold untapped potentials. We aim to understand their nature and role in learning and thinking. Marginalia are described as making annotations in book margins. In this paper, we extend this concept to include visual self-expressions such as para-writings and para-drawings, creative drawings and writings at the margin of books or notebooks, modification of book pictures, titles or texts, squiggling and doodling. VM are part of students’ self-regulatory processes but are frowned upon by teachers. Thus, VM are marginal but also marginalized. We present a theoretical discussion of the topic, a new semiotic methodology that maps visual marginalia in a real classroom, and a model that reveals unstudied ways that students self-regulate.

title: Actor-Network Theory as a New Direction in Research on Educational Dialogues
citation: Tsemach, E. & Schwarz, B. (2022). Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 258-265). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tsemach, E. & Schwarz, B.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: The analysis of educational dialogues has been traditionally undertaken according to pre-given coding schemes, which are often teacher-centered, and in which multiple time scales are not considered. In this paper, we consider the use of Actor-Network Theory (ANT) methodology. While ANT has already been used in education, its application for analyzing the deployment of educational dialogues over time is novel. We analyze some educational dialogues in a program dedicated to dialogic pedagogy. We show that ANT enables us to consider the observation of educational dialogues as the formation and dissolution of networks between humans and non-humans, where roles are not pre-determined but translated in interactions, and the educational design of instructions is black-boxed.

title: Solidarity in Shifting Lines of Practice: Learning in the Weave of Social Movements
citation: Vea, T. & Curnow, J. (2022). Solidarity in shifting lines of practice: Learning in the weave of social movements. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 266-273). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Vea, T. & Curnow, J.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: While learning sciences researchers have explored forms of solidarity underpinning learning and relations across powered forms of social difference, they have largely not integrated insights from social movements literature. Building with lines of practice theory (Azevedo, 2011, 2013), we analyze ethnographic interviews with animal rights activists to understand how power relations and the felt obligations of privilege shape how individual lines of practice develop within the collective pursuit of justice. We find that individual learners feel the implications of their place in the “weave,” as one thread among many, shaping their practice in ways that are neither internal nor external, but fundamentally relational.

title: Why Feedback Literacy Matters for Learning Analytics
citation: Tsai, Y. (2022). Why feedback literacy matters for learning analytics. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 27-34). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Tsai, Y.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
conceptualisations_list: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) & Metacognition; Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry
abstract: Learning analytics (LA) provides data-driven feedback that aims to improve learning and inform action. For learners, LA-based feedback may scaffold self-regulated learning skills, which are crucial to learning success. For teachers, LA-based feedback may help the evaluation of teaching effects and the need for interventions. However, the current development of LA has presented problems related to the cognitive, social-affective, and structural dimensions of feedback. In light of this, this position paper argues that attention needs to shift from the design of LA as a feedback product to one that facilitates a process in which both teachers and students play active roles in meaning-making. To this end, implications for feedback literacy in the context of LA are discussed.

title: Using Epistemic Network Analysis to Explore Discourse Patterns Across Design Iterations of a Teacher Dashboard
citation: Adair, A., Owens, J., & Gobert, J. (2022). Using epistemic network analysis to explore discourse patterns across design iterations of a teacher dashboard. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 297-304). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Adair, A., Owens, J., & Gobert, J.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
conceptualisations_list: Scaffolding & Guided Inquiry; Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA)
abstract: Providing high-level support to students on NGSS inquiry practices can be challenging; however, teacher dashboards can help teachers provide just-in-time instruction to students, both in-person and online. Prior work has shown some success with a dashboard that alerts teachers in real time on students’ science inquiry difficulties, but teachers differed in their use of the alerts. To further support teachers, we designed a second iteration, in which the alerts included actionable, evidence-based Teacher Inquiry Practice Supports (TIPS), a series of suggested scaffolds that teachers can use to support students on the practices with which they are struggling. In this study, we investigate how the discursive support patterns from one teacher differed when using the dashboard alerts without TIPS followed by with TIPS. Findings suggest that TIPS influenced how the teacher incorporated different types of support for her students, and further, that the support given varied across different virtual lab stages.

title: “Everything That’s Hard Got Harder”: Preservice Teachers’ Attempts at Rigorous and Responsive Instruction During Online Pedagogical Rehearsals in the Covid Pandemic
citation: Stroupe, D. & Christensen, J. (2022). “Everything that’s hard got harder”: Preservice teachers’ attempts at rigorous and responsive instruction during online pedagogical rehearsals in the covid pandemic. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 3-10). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Stroupe, D. & Christensen, J.
subject: STEM - Computer Science & Coding
abstract: At the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, our teacher preparation program shifted to an online setting, disrupting a key feature of practice-based teacher preparation: Preservice science teachers’ (PSTs) approximation of rigorous and responsive instruction during extended pedagogical rehearsals called macroteaching. Given this unplanned shock to their preparation, we examined how PSTs viewed macroteaching and their evolving participation in the teaching rehearsal. Using a situative perspective, we collected multiple forms of data. We found that while PSTs wanted to enact rigorous and responsive instruction, their participation was deeply impacted by the sudden shift to an online setting. Our analysis of video-recorded lessons confirmed PSTs’ observations that their instruction became less rigorous and responsive over time. We conclude with questions about teacher preparation during the pandemic.

title: Dancing With Data: Embodying the Numerical and Humanistic Sides of Data
citation: Desportes, K., Vacca, R., Tes, M., Woods, P., Matuk, C., Amato, A., & Silander, M. (2022). Dancing with data: Embodying the numerical and humanistic sides of data. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 305-312). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Desportes, K., Vacca, R., Tes, M., Woods, P., Matuk, C., Amato, A., & Silander, M.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Data literacy is important for supporting individuals to incorporate information from research studies into their own perspectives and decision-making processes. However, it can be challenging for students to read, understand, and relate to data. Students have to be able to traverse the representational forms that data takes on (i.e., numerical, graphical, etc.) and connect it to their understanding of a topic. We explore the implementation of a co-designed data-dance unit in which middle school students created their own embodied metaphors to represent and communicate about graphs through dance. In analyzing dance artifacts and poststudy interviews with the learners and teachers, we demonstrate how the creation of embodied metaphors in dance led to new ways of exploring the data as learners reflected on different perspectives on topics across numerical values, contexts, and implications.

title: ReviewAid: A Scaffolded Approach to Supporting Readers’ Evaluation of Health News
citation: Ko, E., Kim, Y., & Kim, J. (2022). ReviewAid: A scaffolded approach to supporting readers’ evaluation of health news. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 313-320). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Ko, E., Kim, Y., & Kim, J.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: As health news stories affect the audiences’ decision and behavior, readers need to understand and evaluate the information. However, assessing the quality of health news stories is challenging for non-expert readers, as it requires both media and scientific literacy. In this paper, we design a web interface, ReviewAid, that guides online readers’ evaluation of health news stories with the evaluation criteria designed for non-experts. ReviewAid scaffolds readers’ evaluation process by providing 1) explicit guidance that asks readers to distinguish the quality of media and scientific findings and 2) example comments for each criterion. Results from our study with 44 participants show that ReviewAid helps readers better connect the evaluation criteria to the specific news story. ReviewAid also enabled participants to conduct a more grounded and accurate evaluation of the content of scientific research.

title: Supporting Teachers’ Concept Development Through Aggregation
citation: Chen, G. A., Metts, E., Horn, I., & McGugan, K. S. (2022). Supporting teachers’ concept development through aggregation. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 329-336). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Chen, G. A., Metts, E., Horn, I., & McGugan, K. S.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: This study analyzes transcripts of conversations in which mathematics teachers and researchers debrief videotaped lessons by, in part, examining aggregated classroom data from the videotaped lesson. We conclude that aggregating data in debrief conversations can support teachers’ concept development when the aggregation a) demonstrates internal contrasts and b) is underscored by participants’ discursive moves. Consequently, we recommend that facilitators seeking to prompt teacher learning use lesson-level aggregations to identify and press on comparisons and distinctions in teaching practice. This study can inform research on teacher learning by unpacking how a common practice—aggregating data—contributes to teachers’ concept development and has implications both for practitioners and for the emerging field of classroom data visualization.

title: Constructing an “Us” in Teacher Work Groups: Affordances and Limitations for Learning
citation: Louie, N. L. & Scott, M. (2022). Constructing an “us” in teacher work groups: Affordances and limitations for learning. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 337-344). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Louie, N. L. & Scott, M.
subject: STEM - Mathematics
abstract: Research on teacher collaboration suggests that shared values and a sense of solidarity are important resources for generative discourse and robust teacher learning. Drawing on data from two groups of elementary mathematics teachers, this paper examines how teachers construct identities as “us” and the effects of these processes on teachers’ opportunities to engage in equity- and justice-oriented sensemaking and learning. The analysis demonstrates that constructions of “them” sometimes accompany constructions of “us” and shows how this inhibits teachers’ opportunities to learn. Strategies for building solidarity without sparking us/them dynamics, grounded in data, are discussed.

title: “Keep It in the Village”: A 25-Year Journey of Collective Concept Formation Transforming Financial Practices in a Rural Thai Village
citation: Morales-Navarro, L., Fields, D. A., & Blikstein, P. (2022). “Keep it in the village”: A 25-year journey of collective concept formation transforming financial practices in a rural thai village. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 377-384). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Morales-Navarro, L., Fields, D. A., & Blikstein, P.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: Community-generated concepts, namely “germ cells,” can be productive to address problem situations. Yet most literature on germ cells accounts for the initial development of concepts and how these create opportunities for learning and concrete application. This taps into only a small part of the potential power of a germ cell to be generative. In this paper we consider the ongoing development and application of a germ cell in a rural Thai village over 24 years, showing how through a series of learning intraventions, each involving self-analysis and reflection alongside concrete community actions, a germ cell slowly evolved, continuing to orient the village’s transformative work. In this process, the villagers’ family and community financial practices underwent dramatic, productive change. The ongoing unfolding and expanding concrete manifestations of the germ cell shed light on their generative capacity in community learning and transformation. Keywords: germ cell, formative intervention, intravention, activity theory, concept formation

title: Conceptualizing Three Approaches for Integrating Criticality in K-12 Computing Education
citation: Morales-Navarro, L. & Kafai, Y. (2022). Conceptualizing three approaches for integrating criticality in k-12 computing education. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 385-392). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Morales-Navarro, L. & Kafai, Y.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: As several critical issues in computing such as algorithmic bias, discriminatory practices, techno-solutionism have become more visible, numerous approaches are being proposed to integrate criticality in K-12 computing education. Yet, how exactly these approaches address criticality and translate it into classroom practice is not clear. In this conceptual paper, we first historicize how current approaches in critical computing education draw on previous work which has promoted learner empowerment through critical analysis and production. We then identify three emergent framings: (1) inquiry, (2) design and (3) reimagination that build on and expand these critical traditions in todays’ K-12 computing education. Finally, we discuss how these framings highlight issues to be addressed and provide directions for further learning sciences research and design. Keywords: critical computing, computing education, literacies, empowerment, criticality

title: A Lighter Shade of Black Boxes: Students’ Interpretations of the
citation: Alcasid, G. A. & Haskel-Ittah, M. (2022). A lighter shade of black boxes: Students’ interpretations of the distinction between black box explanations and unpacked mechanistic explanations. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 43-50). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Alcasid, G. A. L. & Haskel-Ittah, M.
subject: Interdisciplinary & General
abstract: Scientific explanations rarely include all interactions and entities in a mechanism. Instead, some information is hidden in black boxes, keeping the focus on the explanation’s essence. Studies show that navigating between black-box explanations and detailed mechanistic explanations perplexes students as they misunderstand the reasons for including or omitting mechanistic information. Therefore, we examined students' preference towards information allowing for the formation of either a black-box explanation or a detailed mechanistic explanation. Fifty-two 9th grade students read three scientific problems in three contexts. Students stated and justified their preference of information. Analysis revealed students based choices on problems' context and explanation's productivity. Students preferred black-box information when recognizing the need to make a prediction and detailed information when recognizing a need to control phenomena. Results suggest clear explanatory goals assist students’ navigation between detailed and black-box explanations. This calls for a more explicit discussion around black boxes in the science classroom.

title: Applying Sequence Mining to Explore Students’ Problem-Solving Practices Using an Interactive Simulation-Based Task
citation: Wang, K. D. & Wieman, C. (2022). Applying sequence mining to explore students’ problem-solving practices using an interactive simulation-based task. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 433-439). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Wang, K. D. & Wieman, C.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
abstract: Extensive research has been done to capture and understand human problem solving across different research methods and traditions. This study examines how interaction data generated in an open-ended, interactive task could be used to identify patterns of effective and ineffective practices for solving problems in science and engineering domains. We collected data from 80 undergraduate students on their solutions and problem-solving processes as interaction data logged in the task environment. The log data was parsed to reveal the sequence of test trials conducted by individual participants when solving the problem as well as the pauses in-between test trials. Results of the clustering analysis showed that distinct trial sequence patterns were associated with different levels of performance and provided evidence for specific problem-solving practices. These results have implications for how to assess a complex construct like problem solving and how real-time feedback could be provided to improve students’ problem-solving practices.

title: Summary Writing Support by Structural Organization With Kit-Build Concept Map for EFL Readers
citation: Hayashi, Y., Wu, B., & Hirashima, T. (2022). Summary writing support by structural organization with kit-build concept map for EFL readers. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 440-447). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Hayashi, Y., Wu, B., & Hirashima, T.
subject: Humanities, Language & Literacy
abstract: The activities learners do in making summaries facilitate them to think more carefully than only reading. Although summary writing can be helpful both for fostering and assessing performance in reading, it remains a challenge for most learners, especially in languages learners are not familiar with. Moreover, summary writing can be a problem for students to master because some learners have diﬀiculties identifying the main ideas from detailed information in the text. This study focuses on the issue of improving the performance of English as a foreign language (EFL) learners’ summary writing skills by utilizing the kit-build concept map tool and text structure strategy. A web-based system has been developed, and an online cross-experiment has been conducted, with 75 Indonesian students at the intermediate level of language proficiency involved. Students’ written summaries were collected and evaluated based on two indicators. The result indicates the effect of system use on improving the quality of summary is positive. It supports learners by helping them clarify important ideas and write summaries with organized information.

title: The Learning Must Go On: Experience of Keeping Participants Engaged in Online Robotics Competition During COVID-19 Lockdown
citation: Sabanwar, V., Trimukhe, P., Gudla, A., Kamone, I., & Arya, K. (2022). The learning must go on: Experience of keeping participants engaged in online robotics competition during COVID-19 lockdown. In Chinn, C., Tan, E., Chan, C., & Kali, Y. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences - ICLS 2022 (pp. 448-455). International Society of the Learning Sciences.
authors_list: Sabanwar, V., Trimukhe, P., Gudla, A., Kamone, I., & Arya, K.
subject: STEM - Engineering & Robotics
